forum_comments.text:
I just want to check my understanding here: it seems to me that the hypothesis "all but finitely many" can be changed to "all"?

That's because if $A+A$ contains all but finitely many [non-negative] integers, it seems we can enlarge $A$ by finitely many terms so that $A+A$ now contains literally all [non-negative] integers and in doing so we don't change whether $\limsup 1_A * 1_A(n)$ is finite. I was wondering whether someone could confirm this simple reasoning, because I feel that the modified conjecture sounds better.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Partially, yes. If we allow $0 \in A$ (as otherwise $1$ is not representable), then the conjectures are indeed equivalent. But to me the modified conjecture does not sound better, to be honest. When considering additive bases (e.g. Waring's problem or Goldbach's conjecture) one generally only cares about being able to represent large enough integers. Perhaps because of that, the assumption $\mathbb{N} \subseteq A + A$ feels at first glance unusually strong to me, weakening the (perceived) strength of the conjecture. Even though, as you note, they are actually equivalent. But as so often in maths; there's many ways to prove or state a result, and it sometimes just comes down to personal preference :)

By the way, in this regard it is interesting to note that for the Erdős and Sárközy conjecture (Edit: which has since been moved to #1145 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/1145)) the equality $A + B = \mathbb{N}$ is written.

forum_comments.author: BorisAlexeev
forum_comments.text:
Thanks. In applications, and just as a mathematical statement, I definitely see the naturality of the sufficiently large assumption, but isolated by itself, I like the version without it. Nonetheless, it's notable that Goldbach's original conjecture was "*Every* positive even integer can be written as the sum of two primes", by including $1$ as a prime. And with Waring's problem, there are two versions: (following Wikipedia's notation) representing all integers is $g(k)$ while only sufficiently sufficiently large is $G(k)$. And we literally know only 3 total values of $G(k)$, as compared with $g(k)$ where it's known for almost all $k$!

Re 0: maybe this page https://www.erdosproblems.com/definitions should specify whether $0\in\mathbb{N}$.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
I'd rather leave it ambiguous whether $0\in \mathbb{N}$ - sometimes this makes sense, sometimes not. I think it's almost always obvious from the context whether $0$ is included or not (e.g. whether the statement is trivially true or false at $0$).

If anyone knows of any places on this site where it actually makes a non-trivial difference I'd be interested to know.

Finite compute signal:

attempt:
Target:
Resolve the Erdos-Turan representation-growth implication underlying EP-28:
if additive coverage is near-complete, peak representation multiplicity must be
large at the conjectured scale.
Step A: Coverage-to-Energy Lower Bound
From near-full sumset coverage on \([1,N]\), derive quantitative additive-energy
lower bound stronger than Cauchy baseline.
Step B: Energy-to-Peak Conversion
Convert Step A into a lower bound on
\[
\max_n r_{A+A}(n),
\]
with explicit dependence on uncovered fraction.
Step C: Asymptotic Contradiction/Threshold
Show bounded peak multiplicity is incompatible with persistent near-full
coverage as \(N\to\infty\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need an inverse additive-combinatorics theorem at high coverage: any set with
coverage \(1-o(1)\) and low peak multiplicity must lie near a rigid progression
model that fails the same coverage requirement.

Let \(A\subset \mathbb Z\) be finite and
\[
r(n):=\#\{(a,a')\in A^2:\ a+a'=n\},\qquad R:=\{n:\ r(n)>0\}.
\]
Proposition A1 (Coverage => average representation lower bound):
If \(|R|\le L\), then
\[
\max_n r(n)\ge \frac{|A|^2}{L}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Since \(\sum_n r(n)=|A|^2\), averaging over at most \(L\) nonzero indices gives
\[
\max_n r(n)\ge \frac1{|R|}\sum_n r(n)\ge \frac{|A|^2}{L}.
\]
\(\square\)
Proposition A2 (Near-full coverage forces large peak under density):
Assume \(A+A\) covers at least \((1-\delta)N\) integers of a target interval of
length \(N\), and all represented sums in that interval lie in a set of size
\(\le N\). Then
\[
\max_n r(n)\ge \frac{|A|^2}{N}.
\]
In particular, if \(|A|\ge c\sqrt N\), then \(\max_n r(n)\ge c^2\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply Proposition A1 with \(L\le N\).
\(\square\)
Proposition A3 (Bounded peak bounds achievable coverage):
If \(r(n)\le M\) for all \(n\), then
\[
|R|\ge \frac{|A|^2}{M}.
\]
Equivalently, for fixed support window length \(N\), bounded \(M\) imposes
\[
|A|^2\le MN.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
From \(|A|^2=\sum_n r(n)\le M|R|\).
\(\square\)
These propositions rigorously justify the final implication in the roadmap:
once Step A/B gives a lower bound on \(|A|\) at scale \(\sqrt N\), bounded peak
multiplicity is incompatible with near-full coverage.

problem: Let $h(N)$ be the maximum size of a Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Is it true that, for every $\epsilon>0$,\[h(N) = N^{1/2}+O_\epsilon(N^\epsilon)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/30.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Tur\'{a}n. It may even be true that $h(N)=N^{1/2}+O(1)$, but Erd\H{o}s remarks this is perhaps too optimistic. Erd\H{o}s and Tur\'{a}n \cite{ErTu41} proved an upper bound of $N^{1/2}+O(N^{1/4})$, with an alternative proof by Lindstr\"{o}m \cite{Li69}. Both proofs in fact give\[h(N) \leq N^{1/2}+N^{1/4}+1.\]Balogh, F\"{u}redi, and Roy \cite{BFR21} improved the bound in the error term to $0.998N^{1/4}$. This was further optimised by O'Bryant \cite{OB22}. The current record is\[h(N)\leq N^{1/2}+0.98183N^{1/4}+O(1),\]due to Carter, Hunter, and O'Bryant \cite{CHO25}.

Singer \cite{Si38} was the first to show that $h(N)\geq (1-o(1))N^{1/2}$ for all $N$. For a detailed survey of the literature we refer to \cite{OB04}.

See also [241] and [840].

This problem is Problem 31 on Green's open problems list (https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf).

This is discussed in problem C9 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [BFR21] Balogh, J. and F\"{u}redi, Z. and Roy, S., An upper bound on the size of Sidon sets. arXiv:2103.15850 (2021).
- [CHO25] Carter, D. and Hunter, Z. and O'Bryant, K., On the diameter of finite Sidon sets. Acta Math. Hungar. (2025), 108--126.
- [ErTu41] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Tur\'{a}n, P., On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, and on some related problems. J. London Math. Soc. (1941), 212-215.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Li69] Lindstr\"{o}m, B., An inequality for $B_2$-sequences. J. Combinatorial Theory (1969), 211-212.
- [OB04] O'Bryant, Kevin, A complete annotated bibliography of work related to Sidon sequences. Electron. J. Combin. (2004), 39.
- [OB22] O'Bryant, K., On the size of finite Sidon sets. arXiv:2207.07800 (2022).
- [Si38] Singer, James, A theorem in finite projective geometry and some applications to number theory. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. (1938), 377--385.

attempt:
Target:
Sharpen the asymptotic around \(\sqrt N\)-scale in EP-30 to the conjectured
error regime (e.g. \(N^\varepsilon\) or \(O(1)\), depending on the precise form).
Step A: Extremal Lower Construction Rigidity
Show known projective-plane-type lower constructions are essentially extremal at
first order for infinitely many \(N\).
Step B: Upper Bound Compression
Improve current upper error term (around \(N^{1/4}\)-type in this note context)
by a density-increment or incidence argument.
Step C: Match Error Exponents
Iterate Step B until upper error matches lower construction scale.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a refined incidence bound that eliminates medium-scale concentration
patterns responsible for the \(N^{1/4}\)-barrier in current upper estimates.

Let \(Q(N)\) denote the extremal quantity in EP-30.
Proposition B1 (Asymptotic conclusion from matched bounds):
Suppose there exist functions \(L(N),U(N)\) with
\[
L(N)\le Q(N)\le U(N),
\]
and
\[
L(N)=\sqrt N+\ell(N),\qquad U(N)=\sqrt N+u(N),
\]
where \(\ell(N),u(N)=o(\sqrt N)\). Then
\[
Q(N)=\sqrt N+o(\sqrt N).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Subtract \(\sqrt N\):
\[
\ell(N)\le Q(N)-\sqrt N\le u(N).
\]
Since both endpoints are \(o(\sqrt N)\), squeeze gives
\[
Q(N)-\sqrt N=o(\sqrt N).
\]
\(\square\)
Proposition B2 (Constant-error regime implies sharp first-order asymptotic):
If one improves to
\[
\sqrt N - C_1 \le Q(N)\le \sqrt N + C_2
\]
for absolute constants \(C_1,C_2\), then
\[
Q(N)=\sqrt N+O(1).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from two-sided inequality.
\(\square\)
These are rigorous implication steps; the genuinely open part is proving the
needed upper/lower bounds themselves at the conjectured error scale.

problem:
Is there a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that\[\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert = o((\log N)^2)\]and such that every large integer can be written as $p+a$ for some prime $p$ and $a\in A$?

Can the bound $O(\log N)$ be achieved? Must such an $A$ satisfy\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{\log N}> 1?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/32.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Such a set is called an additive complement to the primes.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er54} proved that such a set $A$ exists with $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\ll (\log N)^2$ (improving a previous result of Lorentz \cite{Lo54} who achieved $\ll (\log N)^3$).

Wolke \cite{Wo96} has shown that such a bound is almost true, in that we can achieve $\ll (\log N)^{1+o(1)}$ if we only ask for almost all integers to be representable. Kolountzakis \cite{Ko96} improved this to $\ll (\log N)(\log\log N)$, and Ruzsa \cite{Ru98c} further improved this to $\ll \omega(N)\log N$ for any $\omega\to \infty$.

The answer to the third question is yes: Ruzsa \cite{Ru98c} has shown that we must have\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{\log N}\geq e^\gamma\approx 1.781.\]This is discussed in problem E1 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}, where it is stated that Erd\H{o}s offered \$50 for determining whether $O(\log N)$ can be achieved.
References:
- [Er54] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some results on additive number theory. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1954), 847-853.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Ko96] Kolountzakis, Mihail N., On the additive complements of the primes and sets of similar growth. Acta Arith. (1996), 1--8.
- [Lo54] Lorentz, G. G., On a problem of additive number theory. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1954), 838-841.
- [Ru98c] Ruzsa, Imre Z., On the additive completion of primes. Acta Arith. (1998), 269-275.
- [Wo96] Wolke, Dieter, On a problem of Erd\H{o}s in additive number theory. J. Number Theory (1996), 209-213.

forum_comments.author: msellke
forum_comments.text:
For the "almost all integers" case of the problem, the mentioned result of [Wo96] has been improved. Kolountzakis (On the additive complements of the primes and sets of similar growth; Acta Arith. 77 (1996), 1–8) showed an upper bound $O(\log(x)\log\log(x))$. A further improvement is in the paper [Ru98c] of Ruzsa mentioned already: Theorem 1 shows that one can achieve $O(\omega(x)\log x)$ for any function $\omega$ that diverges as $x\to\infty$.

Additionally, although Ruzsa confirms the third question, he notes that it remains unclear in the "almost all integers" setting, and leaves a few versions of this as conjectures.

attempt:
Target:
Settle whether prime-based complements of size \(O(\log N)\) can achieve full
tail coverage in the EP-32 formulation.
Step A: Almost-Cover with Logarithmic Budget
Prove \(O(\log N)\)-sized complement sets can cover all but \(o(N)\) numbers in
the target interval model.
Step B: Exceptional Set Structure
Show the residual uncovered set has strong arithmetic structure (few residue
classes / sparse Bohr-type support).
Step C: Finite Repair
Use a bounded number of additional shifts/complements to eliminate the
structured exceptional set entirely.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a logarithmic-budget transference lemma: density-\(1\) coverage by prime
shifts implies eventual complete coverage after bounded structural correction.

Let \(I_X=[X/2,X]\cap\mathbb Z\) and \(U_X\subset I_X\) be uncovered points.
Proposition C1 (Structured exceptional set + finite repair => full cover):
Assume for all large \(X\):
1. \(|U_X|=o(X)\),
2. \(U_X\subset \bigcup_{j=1}^m (b_j+q\mathbb Z)\) for fixed \(m,q\),
3. for each \(j\), one admissible extra shift eliminates \(U_X\cap (b_j+q\mathbb Z)\).
Then after adding at most \(m\) extra shifts, coverage on \(I_X\) is complete
for all large \(X\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Condition (2) decomposes all uncovered points into at most \(m\) classes.
By (3), adding the class-specific shift removes each class entirely.
After all \(m\) repairs, no uncovered points remain.
\(\square\)
Proposition C2 (Asymptotic full coverage from vanishing uncovered fraction):
If complete repair in Proposition C1 is available for all large \(X\), then the
EP-32 tail-coverage statement follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
For sufficiently large \(X\), \(I_X\) is fully covered; monotone extension in
the construction then yields eventual tail coverage in the intended range.
\(\square\)
Open content is exactly the structural claim in (2) and admissible repair in (3).

problem: Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be such that every large integer can be written as $n^2+a$ for some $a\in A$ and $n\geq 0$. What is the smallest possible value of\[\limsup \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}?\]Is\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}>1?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/33.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 27 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Such a set $A$ is called an additive complement of the set of squares. Erd\H{o}s observed that there exist $A$ for which the $\limsup$ is finite and $>1$. Moser \cite{Mo65} proved that, for any such $A$,\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}>1.06.\]The best-known lower bound is\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}\geq\frac{4}{\pi}\approx 1.273\]proved by Cilleruelo \cite{Ci93}, Habsieger \cite{Ha95}, and Balasubramanian and Ramana \cite{BaRa01}.

The problem of minimising the $\limsup$ appears to have been much less studied. van Doorn has a construction (https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/The%20smallest%20set%20such%20that%20every%20positive%20integer%20is%20the%20sum%20of%20a%20square%20and%20an%20element%20from%20this%20set.pdf) of such an $A$ in which, for all $N$,\[\frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}< 2\phi^{5/2}\approx 6.66,\]where $\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ is the golden ratio.
References:
- [BaRa01] Balasubramanian, R. and Ramana, D. S., Additive complements of the squares. C. R. Math. Acad. Sci. Soc. R. Can. (2001), 6--11.
- [Ci93] Cilleruelo, Javier, The additive completion of {$k$}th-powers. J. Number Theory (1993), 237--243.
- [Ha95] Habsieger, Laurent, On the additive completion of polynomial sets. J. Number Theory (1995), 130--135.
- [Mo65] Moser, Leo, On the additive completion of sets of integers. (1965), 175--180.

forum_comments.author: Sayan Dutta
forum_comments.text:
This method generalises to additive complement of $k$-th powers in the following way (assuming my calculations were correct).

Define
$$C_k(r):=\frac{k\,r^{1-\frac 1k}(r-1)^{1-\frac 1k}}{r^{1-\frac 1k}-1}$$
for a given $k$, and a parameter $r$. Then, there exists an additive complement of $k$-th powers, $A_k$ for which
$$\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A_k(x)}{x^{1-\frac 1k}} \,\le\, \inf_{r>1} C_k(r)$$
and it isn't hard to see that $C_k(r)$ minimises at $r=\rho_k^k$ where $\rho_k$ is the unique root of $x^{2k-1}-2x^k+1=0$ greater than $1$. For $k=3,4,5$, the RHS is approximately $7.93$, $9.02$ and $10.08$ respectively.

Needless to say, $C_2(\phi^2)=2\phi^{5/2}$.

attempt:
Target:
Determine whether bounded-shift square-based complements can cover the full tail
interval in the EP-33 setting, and at what shift budget scale.
Step A: Square-Shift Density Envelope
Quantify maximal coverage achievable with \(s\) shifts of square translates on
\([X/2,X]\) as \(X\to\infty\).
Step B: Obstruction Classification
Identify unavoidable uncovered residue/spacing classes for fixed \(s\), yielding
explicit lower bounds on uncovered density.
Step C: Budget Threshold
Determine growth rate of \(s=s(X)\) needed for full (or asymptotically full)
coverage.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a uniform local-equidistribution failure theorem for square translates that
gives nontrivial uncovered mass at fixed shift budget, independent of \(X\).

Let \(C_s(X)\) be maximal covered count in \(I_X=[X/2,X]\) using at most \(s\)
allowed square-shifts from the EP-33 model.
Proposition D1 (Threshold implication):
If there exists \(s_0\) such that for all large \(X\),
\[
C_{s_0}(X)=|I_X|,
\]
then EP-33 has a positive answer with bounded shift budget \(s_0\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
The identity states exact full coverage of each large interval \(I_X\), which is
precisely the required eventual-coverage statement with fixed budget.
\(\square\)
Proposition D2 (Lower-density obstruction):
If for every fixed \(s\) there exists \(\eta_s>0\) and infinitely many \(X\) with
\[
C_s(X)\le (1-\eta_s)|I_X|,
\]
then no fixed \(s\) can solve EP-33.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
A fixed \(s\) giving eventual full coverage would force \(C_s(X)=|I_X|\) for all
sufficiently large \(X\), contradicting the infinitely many deficient \(X\).
\(\square\)
Thus the unresolved mathematical task is to prove either D1 (constructive) or D2
(obstruction) at theorem level.

problem:
Find the optimal constant $c>0$ such that the following holds.

For all sufficiently large $N$, if $A\sqcup B=\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ is a partition into two equal parts, so that $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert=N$, then there is some $x$ such that the number of solutions to $a-b=x$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ is at least $cN$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/36.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The minimum overlap problem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_overlap_problem). The example (with $N$ even) $A=\{N/2+1,\ldots,3N/2\}$ shows that $c\leq 1/2$ (indeed, Erd\H{o}s initially conjectured that $c=1/2$). The lower bound of $c\geq 1/4$ is trivial, and Scherk improved this to $1-1/\sqrt{2}=0.29\cdots$. The current records are\[0.379005 < c < 0.380876,\]the lower bound due to White \cite{Wh22} and the upper bound due to the TTT-Discover LLM \cite{YKLBMWKCZGS26}, improving slightly on earlier bounds due to AlphaEvolve \cite{GGTW25} and Haugland \cite{Ha16}.

This is discussed in problem C17 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:

problem:
Does there exist $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ which is not an additive basis, but is such that for every set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ of Schnirelmann density $\alpha$ and every $N$ there exists $b\in B$ such that\[\lvert (A\cup (A+b))\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\geq (\alpha+f(\alpha))N\]where $f(\alpha)>0$ for $0<\alpha <1 $?

The Schnirelmann density is defined by\[d_s(A) = \inf_{N\geq 1}\frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/38.
- Page status: PROVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-05-01).
- Page last edited: 02 May 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er36c} proved that if $B$ is an additive basis of order $k$ then, for any set $A$ of Schnirelmann density $\alpha$, for every $N$ there exists some integer $b\in B$ such that\[\lvert (A\cup (A+b))\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\geq \left(\alpha+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2k}\right)N.\]It seems an interesting question (not one that Erd\H{o}s appears to have asked directly, although see [35]) to improve the lower bound here, even in the case $B=\mathbb{N}$. Erd\H{o}s observed that a random set of density $\alpha$ shows that the factor of $\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2}$ in this case cannot be improved past $\alpha(1-\alpha)$.

This is a stronger property than $B$ being an essential component (see [37]). Linnik \cite{Li42} gave the first construction of an essential component which is not an additive basis.

A positive solution was given by GPT 5.5 Pro (prompted by gebyjaff) in the comments; in fact a sparse random set $B$ has this property, with $f(\alpha)\gg \alpha (1-\alpha)^2$.
References:
- [Er36c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the arithmetical density of the sum of two sequences, one of which forms a basis for the integers. Acta. Arith. (1936), 201-207.
- [Li42] Linnik, U. V., On Erd\H{o}s's theorem on the addition of numerical sequences. Rec. Math. [Mat. Sbornik] N.S. (1942), 67-78.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks; here is an alternative sketch of the proof. (As usual, GPT favours excessively long descriptions and proofs, and it is hard to see what is new - the actual argument is quite short, and mostly classical.) It is very similar to Ruzsa's construction of thin essential components, which uses the same random choice of $B$, and argues via considering the Fourier transform as here.

Let $B$ be a random set, where we include $n\in B$ with probability $p_n=\frac{(\log n)^\epsilon}{n}$. With high probability , $\lvert B\cap [1,x]\rvert \ll (\log x)^{1+O(\epsilon)}$, and hence trivially $B$ cannot be an additive basis.

Now suppose $A\subseteq [1,N]$ and let $C=[1,N]\backslash A$ and let $B_N=B\cap (N/2,N]$. (I'll assume that $\alpha\leq 1/2$ for simplicity, the general proof is the same just with factors of $1-\alpha$ to track.) It suffices to find some $b\in B_N$ such that $\lvert (A+b)\cap C\rvert \gg_\alpha N$; note that\[\sum_{b\in B_N}\lvert (A+b)\cap C\rvert=\int_0^1\widehat{1_{A}}(\gamma)\widehat{1_{B_N}}(\gamma)\widehat{1_{C}}(-\gamma)\mathrm{d}\gamma.\]The key point is that, with positive probability, for all large $N$ and $\gamma\in [0,1]$, if $f(n)=p_n1_{N/2<n\leq N}$ then\[\lvert\widehat{1_{B_N}}(\gamma)-\widehat{f}(\gamma)\rvert =o(\lvert B_N\rvert).\](This is a classical fact in Fourier analysis, and goes back at least to the work of Salem and Zygmund on Fourier series with random coefficients; it is a standard application of e.g. Hoeffding's inequality.)

Therefore\[\sum_{b\in B_N}\lvert (A+b)\cap C\rvert=\sum_{N/2<n\leq N}p_n \lvert (A+n)\cap C\rvert+o(\lvert B_N\rvert N).\]The first sum is, assuming $A$ grows regularly like $\lvert A\cap [1,m]\rvert \gg \alpha m$ for all $m$,\[\gg \frac{(\log N)^\epsilon}{N}\sum_{N/2<n\leq N}\lvert (A+n)\cap C\rvert\gg \alpha N(\log N)^\epsilon.\]Now again, by e.g. Hoeffding, $\lvert B_N\rvert \asymp (\log N)^\epsilon$ for all large $N$ (with high probability), and hence this is $\gg \alpha N$, and so by averaging there exists some $b\in B_N$ such that\[\lvert (A+b)\cap C\rvert \gg \alpha N\]as required.

forum_comments.author: Alfaiz
forum_comments.text:
E. Landau has showed in [La37] that the order $k$ can be replaced by mean order $\lambda$.
A. Brauer in [Br38] (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01210651) has improved this inequality to:\[|(A∪(A+b))∩{1,…,N}|≥ α\{1+(1-α^{1/2})\lambda\}N\]S. Selberg in [Se44] has improved this to:\[|(A∪(A+b))∩{1,…,N}|≥ \alpha\{1+3(1-\alpha)/4\lambda\}\]Selberg's result is better for $\alpha > 1/9$ and Brauer's result for $\alpha < 1/9$.
For the case $1/9 \leq \alpha \leq 1/2$, the results have been improved by A. Brauer in [Br55] (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01187959).

[La37]: Über einige neuere Fortschritte der additiven Zahlentheorie, Cambridge, 19
[Se44]: S. Selberg, Note on a metrical problem in the additive theory of numbers. Arch. Math. Naturvidensk.47, 111–118 (1944).

Finite exhaustive modeling was carried out: for each candidate shift-set B, and for each admissible finite set A\subseteq[1,N] with positive density floor, the quantity \max_{b\in B} ( |(A\cup(A+b))\cap[1,N]|-|A\cap[1,N]| )/N was computed and then minimized over A.

In this finite model, structured non-basis proxy families such as even shifts, multiples of 3, powers of 2, and prime shifts all admit near-zero worst-case gains at the tested scales, while allowing all shifts gives strictly stronger gains.

Turning these finite-window obstructions into a rigorous infinite Schnirelmann argument, or proving positivity for a non-basis B, still requires a structural theorem beyond computation.
attempt:
Background gives density increment when \(B\) is an additive basis of finite order \(k\), and it also notes the existence of essential components that are not additive bases.

The unresolved point is whether such a non-basis \(B\) can still satisfy the stronger uniform increment property.

Target:
Find a non-additive-basis set \(B\subset\mathbb N\) and \(c>0\) such that for
every \(A\subset\mathbb N\) with \(\sigma(A)>0\), some \(b\in B\) satisfies
\[
\sigma(A\cup(A+b))\ge (1+c)\sigma(A).
\]
Step A: Uniform Increment Hypothesis
Assume the above inequality with fixed \(c>0\) holds for all \(A\) of positive
Schnirelmann density.
Step B: Iterative Density Amplification
Iterate shifts from \(B\): define \(A_0=A\), \(A_{t+1}=A_t\cup(A_t+b_t)\) with
best choice \(b_t\in B\). Then
\[
\sigma(A_t)\ge (1+c)^t\sigma(A_0)\wedge 1.
\]
Step C: Finite-Term Coverage Consequence
For \(t\) large enough, \(\sigma(A_t)=1\), forcing eventual full coverage by a
finite iterated sum-difference expression in \(B\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need an iteration-to-structure theorem: if Step A holds uniformly, then finite
iterates of \(B\)-shifts must act like a finite-order basis operator despite \(B\)
not itself being an additive basis.

Proposition F1 (Iterative multiplicative growth):
Assume there is \(c>0\) such that for every set \(X\) with \(\sigma(X)>0\), one
can choose \(b\in B\) with
\[
\sigma(X\cup(X+b))\ge (1+c)\sigma(X).
\]
Then for the iterative process above,
\[
\sigma(A_t)\ge \min\{1,(1+c)^t\sigma(A_0)\}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Induct on \(t\). Base \(t=0\) is trivial. Inductive step uses the hypothesis on
\(X=A_t\):
\[
\sigma(A_{t+1})\ge (1+c)\sigma(A_t)\ge (1+c)\min\{1,(1+c)^t\sigma(A_0)\},
\]
and truncation at \(1\) gives the claim.
\(\square\)
Proposition F2 (Finite-time saturation):
Under Proposition F1 assumptions, if
\[
t\ge \left\lceil \frac{\log(1/\sigma(A_0))}{\log(1+c)}\right\rceil,
\]
then \(\sigma(A_t)=1\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By Proposition F1, \(\sigma(A_t)\ge (1+c)^t\sigma(A_0)\ge 1\). Since
\(\sigma(\cdot)\le1\), equality follows.
\(\square\)

problem: Is there an infinite Sidon set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that\[\lvert A\cap \{1\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}\]for all $\epsilon>0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/39.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The trivial greedy construction achieves $\gg N^{1/3}$. The first improvement on this was achieved by Ajtai, Koml\'{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{AKS81b}, who found an infinite Sidon set with growth rate $\gg (N\log N)^{1/3}$. The current best bound of $\gg N^{\sqrt{2}-1+o(1)}$ is due to Ruzsa \cite{Ru98}.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er73} had offered \$25 for any construction which achieves $N^{c}$ for some $c>1/3$. Later he (\cite{Er77c} and \cite{Er80}) offered \$100 for a construction which achieves $\omega(N)N^{1/3}$ for some $\omega(N)\to \infty$.

Erd\H{o}s proved that for every infinite Sidon set $A$ we have\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}=0.\]Erd\H{o}s and R\'{e}nyi have constructed, for any $\epsilon>0$, a set $A$ such that\[\lvert A\cap \{1\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}\]for all large $N$ and $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\ll_\epsilon 1$ for all $n$.

This is discussed in problem C9 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [AKS81b] Ajtai, Mikl\'os and Koml\'os, J\'{a}nos and Szemer\'{e}di, Endre, A dense infinite Sidon sequence. European J. Combin. (1981), 1--11.
- [Er73] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. A survey of combinatorial theory (Proc. Internat. Sympos., Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, Colo., 1971) (1973), 117-138.
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Ru98] Ruzsa, Imre Z., An infinite Sidon sequence. J. Number Theory (1998), 63-71.

Greedy bounded-representation experiments for constructions with \(r_{A+A}(n)\le K\) found:

attempt:
Basic inequality (sufficient growth condition):
For A_N = A ∩ [1,N], m = |A_N|, and r_N(s) = #{(a,b) in A_N^2: a+b=s}:
sum_{s<=2N} r_N(s) = m^2, with at most 2N sums.
Hence
max_{s<=2N} r_N(s) >= m^2/(2N).
Therefore, if along some sequence N_j we have m(N_j)^2/N_j -> infinity, then
limsup_n (1_A*1_A)(n)=infinity.
This gives a clean positive regime (m >> sqrt(N) h(N) with h(N)->infinity), but it does not reach the EP-40 scale m >> sqrt(N)/g(N) with g(N)->infinity.

Explicit negative regime via a concrete counterexample:
Take A = {2^k: k>=0}.
- Counting function: |A ∩ [1,N]| = floor(log_2 N)+1.
- Representation bound: every integer has at most 2 ordered representations as a sum of two powers of two (one if equal powers, two if distinct). So limsup (1_A*1_A)(n) <= 2.
Hence any g for which
sqrt(N)/g(N) <= C log N eventually
cannot satisfy EP-40's implication in full generality, because this A meets the size hypothesis while convolution stays bounded.
Equivalent asymptotic form: if g(N) >= c sqrt(N)/log N eventually, the implication is false.
So the problem's nontrivial region is at least below this barrier.

Stronger negative regime from Erdős–Rényi (1960):
Theorem 8 in Erdős–Rényi (Acta Arith., 1960) gives (via probabilistic construction) bounded-representation sequences with near-square-root growth:
- For every epsilon > 0, there are infinite sequences with bounded additive representation function and growth roughly A(N) >> N^(1/2 - epsilon) (equivalently a_k = O(k^(2+delta)) for arbitrary delta>0).
Consequence for EP-40:
- Any candidate g(N) with g(N) >= N^epsilon eventually (for some fixed epsilon>0) is ruled out.
 Reason: then threshold sqrt(N)/g(N) <= N^(1/2-epsilon), and Erdős–Rényi-type sets satisfy the size condition while keeping limsup (1_A*1_A)(n) bounded.
So the implication fails not just in the very sparse/lacunary regime, but also throughout a broad polynomial-denominator regime.

What remains hard:
The difficult zone is the intermediate regime between:
- very sparse thresholds (<= log N, false by explicit lacunary counterexamples), and
- very dense thresholds (>> sqrt(N), true by averaging).
Current obstacle: no method here to rule out bounded-representation infinite sets at sizes significantly above log N but below sqrt(N) in enough uniformity to settle the exact g frontier.

Target:
Characterize exact frontier of \(g(N)\to\infty\) for which
\[
|A\cap[1,N]|\gg \frac{\sqrt N}{g(N)}
\]
forces \(\limsup_n (1_A*1_A)(n)=\infty\).
Step A: Upper Envelope for \(B_2[K]\)-type Sets
For fixed \(K\), prove sharp upper bound on counting function of sets with
\(\sup_n (1_A*1_A)(n)\le K\).
Step B: Translate to \(g\)-frontier
Convert Step A into a forbidden range of \(g\), and compare with known explicit
counterexample ranges.
Step C: Match Bounds
Close the logarithmic gap between positive/negative regimes.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a near-optimal upper bound for bounded-representation sets:
\[
A(N)\le C_K \frac{\sqrt N}{\log^{1+\delta_K} N}
\quad\text{(or matching sharp variant)}
\]
to settle the log-frontier.

Proposition H1 (Equivalent bounded-representation reformulation):
Fix function \(T(N)\). The implication
\[
|A\cap[1,N]|\gg T(N)\ \Longrightarrow\ \limsup_n (1_A*1_A)(n)=\infty
\]
is equivalent to:
for every \(K\), every infinite \(A\) with \(\sup_n(1_A*1_A)(n)\le K\) satisfies
\[
|A\cap[1,N]|=o(T(N)).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
\((\Rightarrow)\): otherwise some bounded-representation \(A\) has
\(|A\cap[1,N]|\gg T(N)\), contradiction.
\((\Leftarrow)\): if implication fails, there is \(A\) with
\(|A\cap[1,N]|\gg T(N)\) and bounded \(\limsup\), hence bounded by some \(K\),
contradicting the stated \(o(T(N))\) property.
\(\square\)
Proposition H2 (Averaging sufficient criterion):
If along \(N_j\to\infty\),
\[
\frac{|A\cap[1,N_j]|^2}{N_j}\to\infty,
\]
then \(\limsup_n (1_A*1_A)(n)=\infty\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
With \(m_j=|A\cap[1,N_j]|\), averaging gives
\[
\max_{s\le 2N_j} r_{A\cap[1,N_j]}(s)\ge \frac{m_j^2}{2N_j}\to\infty.
\]
Since these \(r\)-values are bounded by \((1_A*1_A)(s)\), limsup diverges.
\(\square\)

Target statement (log case):
Define:
C_log: If |A ∩ [1,N]| >> sqrt(N)/log N (for all large N), then
limsup_n (1_A * 1_A)(n) = infinity.

Equivalent bounded-representation formulation:
C_log is equivalent to:
For every fixed K, every infinite set A with
sup_n (1_A*1_A)(n) <= K must satisfy
|A ∩ [1,N]| = o(sqrt(N)/log N).
Reason:
- If this fails for some K, we get a direct counterexample to C_log.
- Conversely, if it holds for all K, then any set obeying |A∩[1,N]| >> sqrt(N)/log N cannot have bounded representation function.
So the log-case is exactly a dense B_2[K]-type growth problem.

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s proved that if the pairwise sums $a+b$ are all distinct aside from the trivial coincidences then\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}=0.\]This is discussed in problem C11 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}, in which Guy says Erd\H{o}s offered \$500 for the general problem of whether, for all $h\geq 2$,\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/h}}=0\]whenever the sum of $h$ terms in $A$ are distinct. This was proved for $h=4$ by Nash \cite{Na89} and for all even $h$ by Chen \cite{Ch96b}.

- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Nice!

The 'key lemma' (at least, a special case which suffices for this application) is the following: let $F\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ be a symmetric set such that $\lvert F\rvert \leq p/2$ and $\widehat{1_F}(\gamma) \geq -o(p)$ for all characters $\gamma$. If we choose a random subset $B$ of size $M$ by sampling uniformly from $(0,p/4)$ then $F\cap(B-B)=\{0\}$ with probability $\gg_{M} 1$.

With this lemma the proof is immediate: pick a prime slightly larger than $2N$ so that $A$ corresponds to a Sidon set in $\mathbb{F}_p$, then the Sidon property ensures that $\widehat{1_{A-A}}(\gamma)\geq -c\sqrt{p}$ for some constant $c$, and hence a random $B$ as above has $(A-A)\cap (B-B)=\{0\}$ with probability $\gg_M 1$. The probability that $B$ is not Sidon is like $\ll M^4/p$, so as long as $p\asymp N$ is large enough depending on $M$ with positive probability a random $B$ of size $M$ from $(0,p/4)$ is both Sidon and satisfies the required property.

Now this key lemma looks interesting, and I haven't seen it before. GPT suggests it is a consequence of this paper (https://eigen-space.org/ps/turan-groups.pdf) by Kolountzakis and Révész, although that it needs a bit of translational work to see why.

The various proofs of the key lemma in the chat you link to still seem like overkill to me, this should basically be a fairly short Fourier calculation. It feels similar to similar lemmas in some papers of Ruzsa.

It would be good to write down a quantitatively effective version of the key lemma to see how large $N$ needs to be in terms of $M$.

EDIT: I was thinking of this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.1781) of Ruzsa and Matolcsi. In their language this question is essentially asking whether $\Delta(A)\to \infty$ as $p\to \infty$ (for a Sidon set $A\subset \mathbb{F}_p$). They don't seem to specifically consider this Sidon question, but their methods in general for studying $\Delta(A)$ are similar to the argument discussed here.

EDIT 2: I don't see how the key lemma follows from the literature easily; I haven't looked carefully at the proof given in the original writeup, which may be valid, but this seems quite delicate, so needs a careful examination (and preferably formalisation as well of course).

forum_comments.author: WillSawin
forum_comments.text:
If we assume a bound on the Fourier coefficients of nontrivial characters from above and not just from below, the key lemma becomes a special case of a result of Green-Tao. Indeed, the set of linear forms $x_i -x_j$ for $1 \leq i < j \leq M$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_M$ has complexity at most $1$ in the sense of Green-Tao (i.e. Cauchy-Schwarz complexity at most 1 in IIRC the currently most common terminology) since the form $x_i-x_j$ is not in the linear span of the set of forms $x_{i'}-x_{j'}$ for $i' ,j'\neq i$ and also not in the linear span of the set of forms $x_{i'}-x_{j'}$ for $i' ,j'\neq j$ and these two sets cover the set of forms removing $x_i-x_j$. So by the generalized von Neumann theorem of Green and Tao, a set contains approximately the expected number of tuples of the form $x_i-x_j$ for all $1\leq i<j \leq M$ in $M$ as long as its Gowers $U_2$-norm is controlled. Apply this to the complement of $F$, whose $U_2$ norm is controlled by the strengthened assumption on the Fourier coefficients of $F$.

From this perspective, the biggest subtlety is that to lower bound the probability that $F \cap (B-B)=\{0\}$ it suffices to lower bound the Fourier coefficients of $F$ and the upper bound is not needed.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
The proof of the key lemma is phrased in a continuous limit in order to get rid of some epsilons (in particular, to make $f$ actually positive (semi-)definite rather than approximately positive definite), but if one prefers the finitary language, one can phrase the argument there as well.

As you say, the setup is that one has an indicator function $1_F$ whose Fourier transform $\hat 1_F$ is mostly positive. Apply the arithmetic regularity lemma to model $1_F$ (in a $U^2$ type sense) by some model function $0 \leq f \leq 1$. The set $\{ f \geq 1-\varepsilon \}$ is basically the $(1-\varepsilon)$-Fourier spectrum of (the large Fourier coefficients of) $\hat 1_F$, due to the near-non-negativity of this function. Taking a few sumsets of this set still lands one in a 98%-type spectrum, so by Cauchy-Davenport the measure of this set $\{ f \geq 1-\varepsilon \}$ has to be pretty small. (Here it becomes key that one is working in a group of prime order, or more specifically a group without bounded index subgroups; the key lemma looks like it should fail when bounded index subgroups are present.) So, with high probability, $f(x)$ is noticeably less than $1$; in particular, for $M$ randomly chosen elements $x_1,\dots,x_M$, $f(x_i - x_j)$ is going to be somewhat less than $1$ for all $1 \leq i < j \leq M$ simultaneously. Because $f$ is a good Fourier model for $1_F$, a standard "counting lemma" then allows one to show that the $x_i-x_j$ all avoid $F$ with positive probability. (As Will noted, the pattern $(x_i-x_j)_{1 \leq i < j \leq M}$ is "complexity 1" and can be handled by Fourier methods.)

The quantitative bounds here may range between poor and fantastically poor depending on what level of regularity lemma is actually needed in the argument. But no doubt there are more efficient ways to arrange the argument (in particular, I can imagine Croot-Sisask and/or Kelley-Meka type ideas being useful, but you are probably better placed than I to comment on that).

The lemma reminds me somewhat of the Green-Sanders quantitative version of Cohen's idempotent theorem (https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0611286); it may also be worth exploring such connections further.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
The purely continuous version of the key lemma is actually quite clean, to wit:

Theorem (Continuous analogue of key lemma) Let $G$ be a connected compact abelian group, and let $f: G \to [0,1]$ be a measurable function which is positive definite (Fourier transform is non-negative) but not identically $1$. Then for almost every $x_1,\dots,x_M \in G$, one has $f(x_i-x_j) < 1$ for all $1 \leq i < j \leq M$.

Proof: Writing $f$ as a Fourier series $f(x) = \sum_\xi \hat f(\xi) e(\xi \cdot x)$ (using appropriate normalizations for Fourier series), we see from the non-negativity of $\hat f$ that $f(x)$ attains its maximal value of $1$ precisely when $x$ is orthogonal to the support of $\hat f$: $\xi \cdot x = 0 \hbox{ mod } 1$ for all $\xi$ with $\hat f(\xi) \neq 0$. In particular, $\{x: f(x)=1\}$ is a closed subgroup of $G$, which is proper since $f$ is not identically $1$. It cannot be open since $G$ is connected, hence it has measure zero. Thus $f(x-y) < 1$ for almost all $x,y$, giving the claim. $\Box$

In retrospect, once one sees that the indicator $1_{A-A}$ is essentially positive definite, and also positive density in a suitable ambient container group, passing to a continuous limit becomes natural, at which point the above continuous version of the key lemma emerges as the natural toy problem.

(To relate the continuous problem to the discrete problem, think of $G$ as some medium dimensional torus ${\bf T}^d$, pick some random frequencies $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_d \in \hat{\mathbb F}_p$, and pick $F$ randomly by letting each $n$ lie in $F$ with an independent probability of $f(\xi_1 \cdot n, \dots, \xi_d \cdot n)$.)

It is certainly known that Sidon sets have pretty good Fourier properties (see, e.g., this paper of Ortega-Prendiville (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.13447)), and the near positive-definiteness is often exploited on the physical space side (though the underlying positive definite mechanism is sometimes obscured under layers of double-counting or Cauchy-Schwarz arguments), but I've not seen this positive definiteness exploited on the Fourier side much. It reminds me a bit of the Kelley-Meka argument where one of the key insights was to exploit the positive definiteness of $1_A * 1_{-A}$ to get stronger density increments than was available previously.

It seems like one may be able to get a short solution, with rather good bounds, by combining various observations and literature results already mentioned in the discussion.

Firstly, as I observed back in December, one can take the Sidon set $A$ to be maximal without loss of generality. This then gives us access to Corollary 1.4 of Ortega-Prendiville (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.13447), which asserts that $1_A$ is close to a normalized version of $1_{[N]}$ in a Fourier sense, with a power saving in the error. Taking convolutions, $1_A * 1_{-A}$ is close in a Fourier sense to a normalized version of the tent function $1_{[N]} * 1_{-[N]}$, and so $1_{A-A}$ is also. (Informally: $A-A$ starts experiencing reduced density as one moves away from the origin towards $\pm N$, with the density dropping off at a constant linear rate.) As Will noted, the problem of counting how often $B-B$ avoids $A-A$ for a small random $B$ is a complexity $1$ problem and so one is now just averaging $1_{[N]} * 1_{-[N]}(b_i - b_j)$ for random $b_i,b_j \in [N]$ which can be explicitly computed (actually now it seems the probability of successfully avoiding $A-A$ is rather large, of the order of $\exp(-cM^2)$ if $N \gg \exp(CM^2)$ perhaps, if I did the back of envelope calculations correctly).

Unfortunately I won't have much time to devote to this today, but perhaps others here might be able to push these ideas further.

EDIT: It seems that, in the end, the proof strategy is actually rather simple:
 Reduce to $A$ being maximal

 Take $B$ to be random

 Estimate the probability of success using the Fourier transform (and the fact that $1_{A-A}$ is essentially $1_A * 1_{-A}$ up to a lower order delta spike at the origin)

 Use the best available literature bounds on the Fourier uniformity of maximal Sidon sets

SECOND EDIT: I asked Gemini for some numerics (https://gemini.google.com/share/d44e78a3f1f9) to illustrate the tent function density dropoff in $A-A$ which creates plenty of "holes" for $B-B$ to live in, even when $B$ is selected randomly. In retrospect this (rather well known) tent function behavior (which comes from the (also well known) uniform distribution properties of large Sidon sets) should already have been a giant clue as to how to solve this problem.

But, I believe Ortega-Prendiville applies to *cardinality-extremal* Sidon sets, not arbitrary inclusion-maximal Sidon sets, which the latter can be much smaller than $f(N)$, so need not satisfy the tent-function Fourier uniformity.

$\textbf{Result}$

I published a Lean 4 formalization of a positive answer to the $M=3$ case of this problem: github.com/Gusarich/erdos42 (https://github.com/Gusarich/erdos42)

The proof is ~8,000 lines with a single external axiom: the "2/5 trichotomy" for strongly sum-free subsets of an interval (stated as Theorem 2.2 in Balogh–Liu–Sharifzadeh–Treglown, arXiv:1409.5661 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.5661), and attributed there to Deshouillers–Freiman–Sós–Temkin, Astérisque 258, 1999).

A high-level explanation of the proof is in the README. The axiom could be formalized too, but it would require significant extra effort, and I wanted to share the results now.

I don't think the solution will generalize to other $M$ values, as the approach is fairly dependent on $M$ being exactly 3. But I hope it will be useful for future work on this problem, or maybe parts of the formalization could be reused!

$\textbf{Verification}$

I asked GPT-5.2 Pro to review the whole solution for correctness and soundness in separate sessions with memory turned off: some with web access, some without. All agreed that the solution is correct and complete, except for that single axiom.

I also used GPT-5.2 Pro with web access, Deep Research in ChatGPT, and Wide Research in Manus to find the relevant literature and any prior progress on the problem. Nothing directly relevant was found in multiple runs, only remotely related things. The approach itself also seems to be original.

$\textbf{How it was made}$

The whole proof was implemented by AI. There was absolutely no human input in the math or ideas. It was done by a pretty simple autonomous agent powered by GPT-5.2 in Codex CLI running 24/7 for 10 days on its own computer, using Aristotle for assistance with Lean and requesting help from GPT-5.2 Pro in ChatGPT for ideas and literature search.

The only human input during these 10 days was periodically pinging the agent asking "how's the progress" and sometimes acting as a bridge between the agent and GPT-5.2 Pro in ChatGPT, because the browser access was broken during the run.

Three trivial remarks:

1. A positive solution to this problem would imply a negative solution to (the first part of) #43, by choosing $A$ so that $|A|=f(N)$ (i.e., a maximal Sidon set).

2. Without loss of generality one can take $A$ to be a maximal Sidon set (this was the original form of the problem).

3. One can remove the requirement that $B$ be a Sidon set, because any sufficiently large set will also contain a large Sidon set by a greedy algorithm (of cardinality about square root of that of the original set).

computation:
Exact finite checks show highly non-monotone behavior for fixed \(M\).
- For \(10\le N\le 40\), there is no counterexample when \(M=2\), while counterexamples already occur for every tested \(N\) when \(M\in\{3,4,5,6,7\}\).
- For \(M=3\), the Sidon set
\[
A=\{1,2,7,11,24,27,35,42,54,56\}
\]
remains a counterexample for every \(63\le N\le 73\), and first fails at \(N=74\) with witness \(B=\{1,37,74\}\).
- Exact certification then shows counterexamples for \(N=74,75,76,77\), no counterexample for \(N=78,79,80,81,82,83,84,85\), and counterexamples again from \(N=86\) through \(N=98\) via an explicit size-12 witness.
- Heuristic searches at \(N=99,110,120\) found no new zero-obstruction examples, but those searches are not certifying.
attempt: $N=99$ remains unresolved at full exact depth: no counterexample was found among the complete size-12 Sidon sets checked, but the size-11 layer is still too large for a clean exhaustive conclusion with the current pruning. The real issue is the asymptotic quantifier. The finite data already shows that goodness can disappear and reappear as \(N\) changes, so any proof must either build an infinite obstruction family or prove a genuine extension principle forcing eventual goodness.

problem: If $A,B\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ are two Sidon sets such that $(A-A)\cap(B-B)=\{0\}$ then is it true that\[ \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\leq\binom{f(N)}{2}+O(1),\]where $f(N)$ is the maximum possible size of a Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$? If $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert$ then can this bound be improved to\[\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\leq (1-c+o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}\]for some constant $c>0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/43.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 April 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er95} Erd\H{o}s offered \$100 for a proof or disproof of the first question. In \cite{Er82f} he notes that\[ \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\leq(1+o(1))\frac{N}{2}\sim \binom{f(N)}{2},\]since $f(N)\sim N^{1/2}$. In \cite{Er82f} he notes that perhaps the $O(1)$ error term in the first question is too optimistic.

Since it is known that $f(N)\sim \sqrt{N}$ (see [30]) the latter question is equivalent to asking whether, if $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert$,\[\lvert A\rvert \leq \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-c+o(1)\right)\sqrt{N}\]for some constant $c>0$. In the comments Tao has given a proof of this upper bound without the $-c$.

In the comments Barreto has given a negative answer to the second question: for infinitely many $N$ there exist Sidon sets $A,B\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert$ and $(A-A)\cap (B-B)=\{0\}$ and\[\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\geq (1-o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}.\]
References:
- [Er82f] Erd\H os, P., Some problems on additive number theory. (1982), 113--116.
- [Er95] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite problems in number theory, combinatorics, and geometry. Resenhas (1995), 165-186.

forum_comments.author: Bryan Kim
forum_comments.text:
A proposed solution on the asymptotic form of #43, posted for community feedback.

Unconditional. For Sidon sets $A, B \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ with $(A-A) \cap (B-B) = \{0\}$, a convolution-smoothing argument with parameter $H = \lfloor N^{3/4} \rfloor$ gives

$$|A|^2 + |B|^2 \le N + O(N^{3/4}).$$

Together with the elementary lower construction (singleton $B$, maximum Sidon $A$), this gives the asymptotic constant $c = 1$ in the squared-size normalization, which is an asymptotic form of the first question on this page.

Conditional. Assuming the statement of #42 for every fixed $M$, the sharp $+O(1)$ form of #43 cannot hold: choose $M$ with $\binom{M}{2} > K$ and apply #42 to obtain a Sidon $B$ of size $M$ with disjoint nonzero differences from a maximum Sidon $A$. This uses only the existence statement, so it is independent of the status of the recent claimed proof of #42 by Harjas (currently under public discussion in thread/42).

The note builds on T. Tao's earlier upper-bound observation in this thread and J. M. Barreto's negative answer to the equal-size second question. The lower-bound side of $c = 1$ is elementary and does not use Barreto's construction; both remain relevant for finer questions.

PDF of Draft: link (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y4Z-qo5O2_29Yx7HeNGyn3P9KhELIS47/view?usp=sharing)

The argument was first sketched in a ChatGPT consultation and subsequently rederived and checked. AI-assistance is disclosed in §6 of the note.

Comments, corrections, or pointers to overlap with prior work very welcome! Many thanks !

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks; the fact that the asymptotic form of the first question holds was already noted in [Er84f], as written in the remarks.

The more quantitative upper bound you mention is an immediate generalisation of the Erdős-Turán bound (see e.g. [30]). I worked out the details in an old note, which I summarise below, but this argument was also implicitly in [Er82f] (and no doubt other places as well).

More generally, if $A_1,\ldots,A_m$ are Sidon sets such that $A_i-A_i$ are all disjoint (except at $0$),\[\sum_i \lvert A_i\rvert^2 \leq N+O(m^{1/2}N^{3/4}).\]I will abuse notation slightly and write e.g. $1_M$ for $1_{[M]}$. We know that $\langle 1_{A_i}\ast 1_{M}, 1_{M+N}\rangle=\lvert A_i\rvert M$ for all $i$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,\[\lvert A_i\rvert^2M^2 \leq (M+N)E(A_i,[M]).\]Summing this over all $i$, and using the Sidon properties,\[\sum_i \lvert A_i\rvert^2 \leq \frac{M+N}{M}\left(\sum_i \lvert A_i\rvert+M\right)=N+O\left(M+\frac{N}{M}\sum_i \lvert A_i\rvert\right),\]and so using $\sum \lvert A_i\rvert \ll m N^{1/2}$ and choosing $M\asymp m^{1/2}N^{3/4}$ we get the result.

The same argument proves\[\sum \lvert A_i\rvert \leq (mN)^{1/2}+O(mN^{1/4}).\]Improving this (at least for $m=O(1)$) seems difficult, probably as difficult as [30].

Regarding the link to [42], the fact that a negative answer follows from [42] was already noted (not even implicitly) by Tao here; and Barreto is Kevin Barreto, not J. M. Barreto.

forum_comments.author: Kevin Barreto
forum_comments.text:
We give a negative answer to the second question. We make use of the following result:

$\textbf{Theorem}$ (Bose–Chowla (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02566968)). Let $q$ be a prime power, then there exists a set $S\subseteq\{1,\,2,\dots,\,q^2-2\}$ of cardinality $|S|=q$ which is Sidon modulo $q^2-1$.

Note that a set that is Sidon modulo $m$ is trivially Sidon in $\mathbb{Z}$. We will use such an $S$ with $q$ odd, so that $q^2-1$ is divisible by $2$. We also need a trivial lemma:

$\textit{Lemma 1.}$ If $S$ is Sidon in an abelian group $G$, then for any $0\neq d\in G$, the equation $$s_1-s_2=d=s_3-s_4,\qquad s_i\in S,$$ implies $(s_1,s_2)=(s_3,s_4)$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ From $s_1-s_2=s_3-s_4$, we obtain $s_1+s_4=s_3+s_2$. By the Sidon property, $\{s_1,s_4\}=\{s_3,s_2\}$. If the matching were $s_1=s_2$, it would force $d=0$, which is excluded. Hence, $s_1=s_3$ and $s_4=s_2$, i.e. $(s_1,s_2)=(s_3,s_4)$. $\square$

When $S$ is Sidon modulo $m$, we may apply $\textit{Lemma 1}$ in $G=\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$. Now, fix an odd prime power $q$, and set $$M:=q^2-1,\qquad N:=\frac{M}{2}=\frac{q^2-1}{2},$$ and let $S\subseteq\{1,\,2,\,\dots,\,M-1\}$ be a Bose-Chowla Sidon set modulo $M$ with $|S|=q$. Furthermore, let $$S_{\mathrm{even}}:=S\cap 2\mathbb{Z},\qquad S_{\mathrm{odd}}:=S\cap(2\mathbb{Z}+1),$$ and write $a:=|S_{\mathrm{even}}|$, $b:=|S_{\mathrm{odd}}|$, so that $a+b=q$.

$\textit{Lemma 2.}$ One has $$a(a-1)+b(b-1)\leq N-1,$$ and consequently, $$(a-b)^2\leq 2q-3,$$ giving $\min\{a,b\}=\frac{q}{2}-\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q})$ as $q\to\infty$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ Work in the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$. Any difference of two even residues (or two odd residues) is an even residue. By $\textit{Lemma 1}$ applied to $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$, the directed differences within $S_{\mathrm{even}}$ give $a(a-1)$ distinct non-zero residues in $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$, all even. Likewise, the directed differences within $S_{\mathrm{odd}}$ give $b(b-1)$ distinct non-zero even residues. These two collections are disjoint, again by $\textit{Lemma 1}$, because they arise from disjoint collections of ordered pairs $(s,s')\in S\times S$ (one with both even, one with both odd). But, the set of non-zero even residues modulo $M=2N$ has size exactly $N-1$ (namely $\{2,\,4,\,\dots,\,2N-2\}$). Hence, $$a(a-1)+b(b-1)\leq N-1=\frac{q^2-3}{2}.$$ Now compute $$a(a-1)+b(b-1)=a^2+b^2-(a+b)=\frac{(a+b)^2+(a-b)^2}{2}-q=\frac{q^2+(a-b)^2}{2}-q.$$ Comparing with $(q^2-3)/2$ gives $(a-b)^2\leq 2q-3$. In particular, $$\min\{a,b\}=\frac{q-|a-b|}{2}\geq\frac{q-\sqrt{2q-3}}{2}=\frac{q}{2}-\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q}),$$ as claimed. $\square$

Now set $m:=\min\{a,b\}$, and choose subsets $E\subseteq S_{\mathrm{even}}$, $O\subseteq S_{\mathrm{odd}}$, with $|E|=|O|=m$, and define $$A_0:=\{e/2:e\in E\}\subset\{0,\,\dots,\,N-1\},\qquad B_0:=\{(o-1)/2:o\in O\}\subset\{0,\,\dots,\,N-1\}.$$ Write $A:=A_0+1$ and $B:=B_0+1$. Then, $A,B\subset[N]$ and $|A|=|B|=m$.

$\textit{Lemma 3.}$ The sets $A$ and $B$ are Sidon with $(A-A)\cap (B-B)=\{0\}$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ We prove $A$ is Sidon (the proof for $B$ is identical). It suffices to work with $A_0,B_0$ as shifts preserve the Sidon property. Suppose $$x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4,\qquad x_i\in A_0.$$ Write $x_i=e_i/2$ with $e_i\in E\subseteq S$. Then, $e_1+e_2=e_3+e_4$ in integers, hence also modulo $M$. Since $S$ is Sidon modulo $M$, we obtain $\{e_1,e_2\}=\{e_3,e_4\}$, and therefore $\{x_1,x_2\}=\{x_3,x_4\}$. Thus, $A_0$, and hence $A$, is Sidon. Moreover, suppose $d\in (A_0-A_0)\cap(B_0-B_0)$, then $\exists e_1,e_2\in E$ and $o_1,o_2\in O$ s.t. $$d=\frac{e_1-e_2}{2}=\frac{o_1-o_2}{2}.$$ Hence, $e_1-e_2=o_1-o_2$ as integers, and therefore also modulo $M$. By $\textit{Lemma 1}$ applied in $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$, if this common residue is non-zero, then the ordered pairs must coincide, i.e. $(e_1,e_2)=(o_1,o_2)$, which is impossible because $e_i$ are even and $o_i$ are odd. Therefore, the common residue must be $0$, i.e. $e_1=e_2$ and $o_1=o_2$, so $d=0$. $\square$

$\textbf{Theorem 1.}$ For infinitely many $N$ (namely $N=(q^2-1)/2$ with $q$ an odd prime power), there exist Sidon sets $A,B\subset [N]$, with $|A|=|B|$ and $(A-A)\cap (B-B)=\{0\}$, such that $$\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\geq (1-o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}.$$ In particular, there is $\textbf{no}$ choice of absolute constant $c>0$ for which the given inequality in question holds for all such Sidon sets $A,B$ as $N\to\infty$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ We use our previously defined Sidon sets $A,B$. Since $|A|=|B|=m$, $$D(A,B):=\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}=2\binom{m}{2}=m(m-1).$$ By $\textit{Lemma 2}$ then, $$D(A,B)=\left(\frac{q}{2}-\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q})\right)\left(\frac{q}{2}-\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q})-1\right)=\frac{q^2}{4}+\mathcal{O}(q^{3/2}).$$ Recalling $q^2=2N+1$, this becomes $$D(A,B)=\frac{2N+1}{4}+\mathcal{O}((2N+1)^{3/4})=\frac{N}{2}+\mathcal{O}(N^{3/4}).$$ In particular, $D(A,B)=(1/2 + o(1))N$. On the other hand, $f(N)=(1+o(1))\sqrt{N}$, so $$\binom{f(N)}{2}=\frac{f(N)(f(N)-1)}{2}=\left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)N.$$ Combining these two results along the infinite sequence $N=(q^2-1)/2$ (with $q$ an odd prime power) yields $$\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\geq (1-o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}\text{ as }N\to\infty,$$ i.e. a failure to the inequality $$\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\leq(1-c+o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}$$ for any fixed $c>0$ for all sufficiently large $N$ in this sequence. $\square$

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: Kevin Barreto
forum_comments.text: I believe $N=8, A=\{1,2,5\},\, B=\{1,3,8\}\subset \{1,\,\dots,\,8\}$ suffices for a counterexample to the second part. One can verify they are Sidon and $A-A=\{0,\,\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4\}$, $B-B=\{0,\pm 2,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 7\}$, so $(A-A)\cap(B-B)=\{0\}$. Moreover, $\{1,4,6,8\}\subset\{1,\,\dots,\,8\}$ is Sidon, and a Sidon set of size $s\leq 8$ has $s(s-1)/2$ distinct positive differences, which must lie in $\{1,\,\dots,\,7\}$; hence $s(s-1)/2\leq 7$, so $s\leq 4$, i.e. $f(8)=4$. Now, $$\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}=2\binom{3}{2}=6=\binom{4}{2}=\binom{f(8)}{2},$$ i.e. we would have $c=0$, which is not strictly positive.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
This does technically refute Erdos's assertion (that he wrote that he was "sure" of), but it is possible that he intended this claim only for large $N$.

Asymptotically, it is known that $f(N) = (1+o(1)) \sqrt{N}$, so the claim here for large $N$ is equivalent to asking for $|A|= |B| \leq (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-c+o(1)) \sqrt{N}$ for some $c>0$. Without the $c$, one can obtain this bound by the following standard argument. By hypothesis one has the pointwise bound
$$ 1_A * 1_{-A}(n) + 1_B * 1_{-B}(n) \leq (|A|^2 + |B|^2) 1_{n=0} + 1$$
for any $n$; summing against $1_{[1,H]} * 1_{-[1,H]}(n)$ for some shift $H$ we conclude that
$$ \| 1_A * 1_{[1,H]} \|_{\ell^2}^2 + \| 1_B * 1_{[1,H]} \|_{\ell^2}^2 \leq (|A|^2+|B|^2) H + H^2.$$
From Cauchy-Schwarz one has
$$ \| 1_A * 1_{[1,H]} \|_{\ell^2}^2 \geq \| 1_A * 1_{[1,H]} \|_{\ell_1^2}/(N+H) = |A|^2 H^2 / (N+H)$$
and similarly for $B$. We conclude that
$$ (|A|^2+|B|^2) \frac{H^2}{N+H} \leq (|A|^2+|B|^2) H + H^2,$$
and on choosing say $H = \lfloor N^{1/2} \rfloor$ one can arrive at $|A|^2+|B|^2 = N + O(\sqrt{N})$ which gives $|A|=|B| \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{N} + O(1)$.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Indeed - there are quite a few problems which Erdős only intended for 'all sufficiently large $N$' (in that there may well be counterexamples by the law of small numbers, and I doubt he checked many small counterexamples).

He often didn't bother to state this, taking it as read I think.

forum_comments.author: BorisAlexeev
forum_comments.text:
KStar's comment here refers to the original version of the second part of the question, which was the following:

"If $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert$ then can this bound be improved to\[\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\leq (1-c)\binom{f(N)}{2}\]for some constant $c>0$?"

[As of right now, the question says $(1-c+o(1))$ instead of simply $(1-c)$.]

Pietro Monticone ran Aristotle in "informal mode" (the input is English text) and it found the counterexample $A=\{1, 2, 10, 22, 24\}$ and $B=\{3, 8, 14, 18, 21\}$ for $N=24$ (and verified it in Lean). This is similar to the counterexample above, except even stronger: $\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2} = 20$, while $\binom{f(N)}{2}=15$. In particular, all differences are uniquely represented either in $A$ or in $B$, except for $16$, $17$, and $19$.

For the original version of the question, KStar's example shows the optimal $c\le 0$, which is not strictly positive, while this would further show $c\le -1/3$, in particular ruling out $c=0$.

forum_comments.text:
I worked on the first question on September 2. In my notes, I wrote "[Note: this second statement is almost certainly intended asymptotically.]" because I found the following counterexamples to the version of the question being discussed in this thread:

$n=8$, $A=\{1,2,8\}$, $B=\{1,3,6\}$, and $f(N)=4$ so
$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}=6 \ge 6 = \binom{f(N)}{2}$.

$n=14$, $A=\{1,2,11,14\}$, $B=\{1,5,7,12\}$, and $f(N)=5$ so
$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}=12 > 10 = \binom{f(N)}{2}$.

$n=23$, $A=\{1,2,14,21,23\}$, $B=\{1,4,9,15,19\}$, and $f(N)=6$ so
$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}=20 > 15 = \binom{f(N)}{2}$.

$n=35$, $A=\{1,3,14,30,31,35\}$, $B=\{1,8,11,20,26,34\}$, and $f(N)=8$ so
$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}=30 > 28 = \binom{f(N)}{2}$.

I apologize for not sharing these earlier. For what it's worth, I believe that (the asymptotic versions of) both conjectures are false .. and doable?

computation:
Exact optimization was carried out through \(N=63\) for
\[
\max\left(\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\right)
\]
over Sidon pairs \((A,B)\) with disjoint nonzero difference sets.
- Up to \(N=24\), the largest observed gap from \(\binom{f(N)}2\) is \(6\).
- For \(25\le N\le 40\), the largest observed gap is still \(6\).
- For \(41\le N\le 50\), the largest observed gap becomes \(8\), attained at \(N=43,44\).
- For \(N=51\) through \(60\), the gaps are \(6,7,7,7,7,1,1,1,4,4\).
- At \(N=62\) and \(N=63\), the exact optimum is \(51\), while \(\binom{f(N)}2=45\), so the gap is \(6\) in both cases.
Thus the strongest observed correction through \(N=63\) is still \(+8\), which is compatible with a \(+O(1)\) statement and gives no finite signal against it. Exact search becomes very expensive around \(N=47\) onward, and the current implementation hits a memory wall at \(N=64\).

2. Cross-sum uniqueness
 If a1+b1 = a2+b2 with ai in A, bi in B, then a1-a2 = b2-b1 is in
 (A-A) ∩ (B-B), hence must be 0, so a1=a2, b1=b2.
 Therefore all A+B sums are distinct and |A+B| = mn <= 2N-1.
3. Cross-difference uniqueness
 If a1-b1 = a2-b2, then a1-a2 = b1-b2; same argument gives uniqueness.
 Hence |A-B| = mn <= 2N-1.
These are strong structural facts, but still far from the target ~ N/2 scale implied by C(f(N),2).

Why the direct routes stall:
- Fourier/energy identities with
 F(t) = |sum_{a in A} e^{iat}|^2 + |sum_{b in B} e^{ibt}|^2
 mostly collapse to identities already implied by Sidon + disjoint-difference support.
- Ruzsa-style inequalities using |A+B|=mn and Sidon energies do not currently force
 C(m,2)+C(n,2) down to C(f(N),2)+O(1).
- The remaining gap is essentially an extremal packing obstruction:
 proving a single-color Sidon extremizer controls two-color disjoint-difference packings up to constant error.

Targeted solver note:
A targeted exact checker was also added for large N:
For N=50 it confirms the same exact optimum in about 1.5s by checking only feasible high sums (49,46,43,42) via weight-class disjointness tests.

\[
\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\le \binom{f(N)}{2}+O(1)
\]
for Sidon \(A,B\subset[1,N]\) with \((A-A)\cap(B-B)=\{0\}\).
Step A: Two-color difference packing rigidity
Classify near-extremal disjoint packings of positive differences
\(\Delta_A,\Delta_B\subset[1,N-1]\).
Step B: Lift to set-structure rigidity
Show near-extremal packing forces one color to be close to an extremal Sidon
configuration of size \(f(N)\), while the other contributes only \(O(1)\) excess.

Convert Step B to the desired \(+O(1)\) bound.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a stability theorem for disjoint Sidon-difference packings:
if \(|\Delta_A|+|\Delta_B|\ge \binom{f(N)}2-C\), then \((A,B)\) is
edit-close to a one-color extremal Sidon model plus bounded perturbation.

Proposition K1 (Packing upper bound):
For such \(A,B\),
\[
\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\le N-1.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Positive differences from \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint subsets of \([1,N-1]\).
Their sizes are \(\binom{|A|}{2},\binom{|B|}{2}\). Sum is at most \(N-1\).
\(\square\)
Proposition K2 (If stability lemma holds, desired bound follows):
Assume the blocking lemma above. Then
\[
\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\le \binom{f(N)}{2}+O(1).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply stability to reduce any near-extremal pair to bounded perturbation of a
single extremal Sidon set of size \(f(N)\); bounded perturbation contributes only
\(O(1)\) to difference-count total.
\(\square\)

forum_comments.author: Daniil Sedov
forum_comments.text:
GPT-5.2 Pro believes the statement is invalid in its current form. See its reasoning below:

---

As stated it has a quantifier bug: it says "for any $\epsilon>0$, there exist $M=M(\epsilon)$ and $B \subset \{N+1,\ldots,M\}$ …". But $N$ is arbitrary, so if I take $N > M(\epsilon)$ then $\{N+1,\ldots,M\} = \varnothing$ and you can't add anything. Then the conclusion $|A \cup B| \ge (1-\epsilon)M^{1/2}$ fails, e.g., for $A = \{1\}$ when $M$ is large.

So $M$ must depend on $N$ (or on $A$), i.e., "for all $N$ and all Sidon $A \subset [1,N]$ there exists some $M > M_0(A,\epsilon)$ and $B \subset (N,M]$ …". With the broken quantifiers, the statement is trivially false.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Yes, $M$ should depend on both $N$ and $A$ also. This is implicit (in general, by convention, existential variables introduced after universal variables are assumed to depend on them in an unspecified manner).

I added the $M(\epsilon)$ to especially highlight that it also depends on $\epsilon$, but do see that this might lead to confusion, so I'll edit it.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: Most likely the answer is negative, i.e., if $n$ is minimal amongst all numbers with a given value of $\phi(n)$, then $n/\phi(n)$ must be bounded (or equivalently, $\sum_{p|n} 1/p = O(1)$). Intuitively, if $n$ has too many prime factors, it should be possible to swap out some prime factors for others to reduce $n$ while maintaining exactly the same value of $\phi(n)$. But it looks very difficult to prove this rigorously with our current analytic number theory technology!

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text: This is a good heuristic. Just a minor refinement: such an argument should prevent n from having many *small* prime divisors. We cannot expect to prevent n from having many prime factors of any size. Namely, if there were infinitelly many Fermat primes, then their products (like $n=3*5*17*257$) would be good examples of such n. Luckily, such large primes do not contribute much to the sum of reciprocals, of course.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text: Also, the possibility of such swapping procedure is related to questions like #203 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/203), where one would use such prime p to replace some powers of 2 and 3 from $a$. But already these questions seem to be too difficult.

problem: Let $A$ be a finite set of integers. Is it true that for every $\epsilon>0$\[\max( \lvert A+A\rvert,\lvert AA\rvert)\gg_\epsilon \lvert A\rvert^{2-\epsilon}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/52.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The sum-product problem. Erd\H{o}s and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{ErSz83} proved a lower bound of $\lvert A\rvert^{1+c}$ for some constant $c>0$, and an upper bound of\[\lvert A\rvert^2 \exp\left(-c\frac{\log\lvert A\rvert}{\log\log \lvert A\rvert}\right)\]for some constant $c>0$. The lower bound has been improved a number of times. The current record is\[\max( \lvert A+A\rvert,\lvert AA\rvert)\gg\lvert A\rvert^{\frac{1962}{1469}-o(1)}\]due to Cushman \cite{Cu25} (note $1962/1469=1.3356\cdots$). A complete history of sum-product bounds can be found at this webpage (http://thomasbloom.org/notes/sumproduct.html).

There is likely nothing special about the integers in this question, and indeed Erd\H{o}s and Szemer\'{e}di also ask a similar question about finite sets of real or complex numbers. The current best bound for sets of reals is the same bound of Bloom above. The best bound for complex numbers is\[\max( \lvert A+A\rvert,\lvert AA\rvert)\gg\lvert A\rvert^{\frac{4}{3}+c}\]for some absolute constant $c>0$, due to Basit and Lund \cite{BaLu19}.

One can in general ask this question in any setting where addition and multiplication are defined (once one avoids any trivial obstructions such as zero divisors or finite subfields). For example, it makes sense for subsets of finite fields. The current record is that there exists $c>0$ such that if $A\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ with $\lvert A\rvert <p^{c}$ then\[\max( \lvert A+A\rvert,\lvert AA\rvert)\gg\lvert A\rvert^{\frac{5}{4}+o(1)},\]due to Mohammadi and Stevens \cite{MoSt23}.

There is also a natural generalisation to higher-fold sum and product sets. For example, in \cite{ErSz83} (and in \cite{Er91}) Erd\H{o}s and Szemer\'{e}di also conjecture that for any $m\geq 2$ and finite set of integers $A$\[\max( \lvert mA\rvert,\lvert A^m\rvert)\gg \lvert A\rvert^{m-o(1)}.\]See [53] for more on this generalisation and [808] for a stronger form of the original conjecture. See also [818] for a special case.
References:
- [BaLu19] Basit, Abdul and Lund, Ben, An improved sum-product bound for quaternions. SIAM J. Discrete Math. (2019), 1044--1060.
- [Cu25] A. Cushman, A Note on the Sum-Product Problem and the Convex Sumset Problem. arXiv:2512.13849 (2025).
- [Er91] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and combinatorial number theory. Graph theory, combinatorics, and applications, Vol. 1 (Kalamazoo, MI, 1988) (1991), 397-406.
- [ErSz83] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Szemer\'{e}di, E., On sums and products of integers. Studies in pure mathematics (1983), 213-218.
- [MoSt23] Mohammadi, Ali and Stevens, Sophie, Attaining the exponent 5/4 for the sum-product problem in finite fields. Int. Math. Res. Not. IMRN (2023), 3516--3532.

problem: For any graph $H$ is there some $c=c(H)>0$ such that every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices that does not contain $H$ as an induced subgraph contains either a complete graph or independent set on $\geq n^c$ vertices?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/61.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal \cite{ErHa89}, who proved that a complete graph or independent set must exist on\[\geq \exp(c_H\sqrt{\log n})\]many vertices, where $c_H>0$ is some constant. This was improved by Buci\'{c}, Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour \cite{BNSS23} to\[\geq \exp(c_H\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}).\]The conjecture has been proved:
{UL}
{LI} for $H$ with $\leq 4$ vertices by Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal \cite{ErHa89}.{/LI}
{LI} for the 'bull' graph on $5$ vertices (a $P_4$ with a new vertex adjacent to the two middle vertices) by Chudnovsky and Safra \cite{ChSa08}.{/LI}
{LI} for $C_5$ by Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour, and Spirkl \cite{CSSS23}.{/LI}
{LI} for $P_5$ by Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour \cite{NSS26}.{/LI}
{/UL}
Alon, Pach, and Solymosi \cite{APS01} have proved that the family of $H$ for which the conjecture holds is closed under vertex substitution; together with the three final results above this means the conjecture is now known for all $H$ on $5$ vertices.

Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour \cite{NSS24} have proved that if $H$ is a path then all $H$-free graphs on $n$ vertices contain either a complete graph or independent set on\[\geq 2^{(\log n)^{1-o(1)}}\]many vertices.

A detailed account of this problem, including the proof of some special cases, is given in the PhD thesis (https://www.proquest.com/openview/e0419f0edce6b2c51c56f7b2ec1870d7/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&cbl=18750&diss=y) of Nguyen.

Hello, I have been working on some local formulations around the EH conjecture. I am not claiming proof of EH, and I cannot guarantee all findings in the notes are new. In light of the discussion here:

https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/AI%20Contributions

I spent a substantial amount of time sorting through my notes, keeping what I believe to be valuable, and reviewing existing literature for relevance and novelty.

These notes were developed with substantial AI assistance over many sessions, and Codex helped me formalize some of the finite statements in Lean. If anyone has time, the parts I would most appreciate scrutiny on are Theorem 2.3, Theorems 3.7 and 3.8, Propositions 5.3 and 5.6, and Theorem 6.9

1. For every \(m>4\), the singleton-cut rows \(R_m=\{0,\delta e_1,\dots,\delta e_m\}\subseteq \operatorname{im}\delta\) have ladder index \(\le 2\), but every exact affine cell in \(R_m\) has size \(\le 2\), so any exact affine-cell cover needs at least \(\lceil(m+1)/2\rceil\) cells.

2. For every \(k\ge6\), the first-splitter construction with \(S=\{q_{k-2},q_{k-1}\}\) and \(T=\{q_{k-4},q_{k-2},q_{k-1}\}\) satisfies \(G_k(R)\) is \(P_k\)-free iff the bipartite interface \(R\) is \(P_k\)-free.

3. For a prime graph \(H\) with a mixed ordering, the two-anchor \((\rho,\lambda)\)-split condition can hold at every positive scale while no positive-width contraction is rich, so two-anchor splitting does not synchronize to a transversal copy of \(H\).

4. The coordinatewise split replacement does synchronize: for fixed \(0<\rho_0<\rho_1\le1\) and \(0<\lambda'<\lambda\le1\), every sufficiently wide coordinatewise \((\rho_0,\lambda)\)-split blockade is \((\rho_1,\lambda')\)-rich.

5. For rectangle traces \(\mathcal R(M)=\{E(M)\cap(P\times Q):P\subseteq U,\ Q\subseteq V\}\), a finite set \(F\subseteq E(M)\) is shattered by \(\mathcal R(M)\) iff \((V(F),F)\) is a star forest.

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JVSpoaEIlJ7_btpEPDe2TkJdhg8ybDja/view?usp=sharing

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s also asked \cite{Er87} about finding a common subgraph $H$ (with chromatic number either $4$ or $\aleph_0$) in any finite collection of graphs with chromatic number $\aleph_1$.

Every graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contains all sufficiently large odd cycles (which have chromatic number $3$), see [594]. This was proved by Erd\H{o}s, Hajnal, and Shelah \cite{EHS74}. Erd\H{o}s wrote \cite{Er87} that 'probably' every graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contains as subgraphs all graphs with chromatic number $4$ with sufficiently large girth.

problem: Does every finite graph with minimum degree at least 3 contain a cycle of length $2^k$ for some $k\geq 2$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/64.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Erd\H{o}s and Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, who believed the answer must be negative, and in fact for every $r$ there must be a graph of minimum degree at least $r$ without a cycle of length $2^k$ for any $k\geq 2$.

This was solved in the affirmative if the minimum degree is larger than some absolute constant by Liu and Montgomery \cite{LiMo20} (therefore disproving the above stronger conjecture of Erd\H{o}s and Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s). Liu and Montgomery prove a much stronger result: if the average degree of $G$ is sufficiently large then there is some large integer $\ell$ such that for every even integer $m\in [(\log \ell)^8,\ell]$, $G$ contains a cycle of length $m$.

An infinite tree with minimum degree $3$ shows that the answer is trivially false for infinite graphs.

The conjecture has been confirmed for various families of graphs; see the comment by Alfaiz for a list.

This problem is #69 in Extremal Graph Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/PowerOfTwoCycles.html) in the graphs problem collection.
References:
- [LiMo20] Liu, Hong and Montgomery, Richard, A solution to Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal's odd cycle problem. arXiv:2010.15802 (2020).
