The conjecture is confirmed for these cases:

(i) $K_{1,m}$-free graphs with minimum degree at least $m+1$ or maximum degree at least $2m-1$ by S. E. Shauger in [Sh98].
(ii) Planar claw-free graphs by D. Daniel and S. E. Shauger in [DaSh01].
(iii) 3-connected cubic planar graphs by C. C. Heckman and R. Krakovski in [HeKr13].
(iv) Cayley graphs on generalized quaternion groups, dihedral groups, semidihedral groups and groups of order $p^3$ in M. H. Ghaffari and Z. Mostaghim [GhMo18] (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00010-017-0518-3).
(v) Cayley graphs of order $2p^2$ and $4p$ by M. Ghasemi and R. Varmazyar in [GhVa21] (http://elib.mi.sanu.ac.rs/files/journals/mv/282/mvn282p37-42.pdf).
(vi) $P_8$-free graphs by Y. Gao and S. Shan in [GaSh22] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.01277).
(vii) $P_{10}$-free graphs by Z. Hu and C. Shen in [HuSh24] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05675).
(viii) Diameter-2 graphs by A. Carr in [Ca26] (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.19302).

Additionally:
K. Markstrom in [Ma04] (http://abel.math.umu.se/~klasm/Uppsatser/cycex.pdf) has shown that any cubic counterexample to this conjecture must have at least 30 vertices.
P. S. Nowbandegani and H. Esfandiari in [NoEs11] (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/312286036_An_Experimental_Result_on_the_Erdos-Gyarfas_Conjecture_in_Bipartite_Graphs) has shown that any bipartite counterexample must have at least 32 vertices.
P. S. Nowbandegani, H. Esfandiari, M. H. S. Haghighi and K. Bibak in [NEHB14] (https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.5398) has shown that any cubic claw-free counterexample must have 114 vertices and every claw-free graph with minimum degree at least 3 has a cycle whose length is $2^k$ or $3\times2^k$, for some positive integer $k$.

[Sh98]: S. E. Shauger, Results on the Erd˝os-Gy´arf´as conjecture in K1,m-free graphs, Congr. Numer. 134 (1998) 61-65.
[DaSh01]: D. Daniel, S. E. Shauger, A result on the Erd˝os-Gy´arf´as conjecture in planar graphs, Congr. vol. 153 (2001) 129-139
[HeKr13]: C. C. Heckman, R. Krakovski, Erd˝os-Gy´arf´as conjecture for cubic planar graphs, Electron. J. Comb. 20(2) (2013) 7-43.

problem: Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices and $kn$ edges, and $a_1<a_2<\cdots $ be the lengths of cycles in $G$. Is it true that\[\sum\frac{1}{a_i}\gg \log k?\]Is the sum $\sum\frac{1}{a_i}$ minimised when $G$ is a complete bipartite graph?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/65.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal.

Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, Koml\'{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{GKS84} have proved that this sum is $\gg \log k$, so that only the second question remains. Liu and Montgomery \cite{LiMo20} have proved the asymptotically sharp lower bound of $\geq (\tfrac{1}{2}-o(1))\log k$.

Montgomery has written a survey (https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/52107) including this problem, in which he mentions forthcoming work of himself, Milojevi\'{c}, Pokrovskiy, and Sudakov which proves that, if $k$ is sufficiently large, then $\sum\frac{1}{a_i}$ is maximised when $G$ is a complete bipartite graph.

This problem is #65 in Extremal Graph Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/HarmonicSumOfCycleLengths.html) in the graphs problem collection.

See also [57].
References:

problem: Is there $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{1_A\ast 1_A(n)}{\log n}\]exists and is $\neq 0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/66.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A suitably constructed random set has this property if we are allowed to ignore an exceptional set of density zero. The challenge is obtaining this with no exceptional set. Erd\H{o}s believed the answer should be no. In \cite{Er80} he explicitly asked whether there exists such a set where the limit is $1$ (and did not believe there existed such a sequence).

Erd\H{o}s and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy proved that\[\frac{\lvert 1_A\ast 1_A(n)-\log n\rvert}{\sqrt{\log n}}\to 0\]is impossible. Erd\H{o}s suggests it may even be true that the $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ of $1_A\ast 1_A(n)/\log n$ are always separated by some absolute constant.

Horv\'{a}th \cite{Ho07} proved that\[\lvert 1_A\ast 1_A(n)-\log n\rvert \leq (1-\epsilon)\sqrt{\log n}\]cannot hold for all large $n$.
References:
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [Ho07] G. Horv\'{a}th, An improvement of a theorem of Erd\H{o}s and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy. Pollack Periodica (2007), 155-161.

with explicit denominator control from \(\prod_{n\le M}(n!-1)\).

\[

with \(U_M/L_M^{\text{(arith)}}\to0\) under rationality assumption.

Need a gcd-cancellation bound for shifted factorial factors:
\[
\gcd\!\Big(\prod_{n\le M}(n!-1),\,\prod_{n\le M'}(n!-1)\Big)

must be small enough to preserve exponential gap in Step B.

If for every \(Q\) there exists \(M\) and rational interval
\[
I_M=[S_M-\epsilon_M,\ S_M+\epsilon_M]
\]
containing \(S\), such that no rational \(p/q\in I_M\) with \(1\le q\le Q\),
then \(S\) is irrational.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
If \(S=p_0/q_0\) rational, choose \(Q\ge q_0\); then \(p_0/q_0\in I_M\), contradiction.
\(\square\)
Proposition T2 (Linear-form contradiction schema):
If one constructs nonzero integers \(A_M,B_M\) with
\[
0<|A_MS-B_M|<\eta_M,\qquad \eta_M\to0,
\]
and also a rationality-implied bound
\[
|A_MS-B_M|\ge c_M,\quad c_M/\eta_M\to\infty,
\]
then \(S\) is irrational.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Under rationality both inequalities must hold simultaneously for large \(M\),
impossible when \(c_M>\eta_M\).
\(\square\)

- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:

computation:
- Read statement/background and upgraded the from placeholder to a dedicated 3-uniform 2-coloring optimizer.
- Computed the best-found minimum possible largest monochromatic 3-uniform homogeneous subset size in finite proxies; best values were 3 (n=8) and 4 (n=9,10,11).
- Interpretation: finite evidence is consistent with strong negative colorings at small sizes but does not transfer directly to the transfinite partition relation \mathfrak{c}\to(\beta,n)^3_2; main gap is ordinal/continuum structure, not finite extremal optimization.
attempt:
Tried to push from the known Erdős-Rado relation
c -> (omega+n,4)^3_2 toward the target
c -> (beta,n)^3_2 for arbitrary countable beta.

Hard point:
The existing step-up route does not transfer directly from the specific
(omega+n,4) structure to all countable ordinals and all finite n.

Target:
For fixed finite \(n\), prove
\[
\mathfrak c \to (\beta,n)^3_2
\]
for every countable ordinal \(\beta\).
Step A: Canonization on a large family
Given a 2-coloring of \([\mathbb R]^3\), extract a size-\(\mathfrak c\) subset
on which color classes are controlled by a finite list of order/topological
types.
Step B: Transfinite homogeneous build
Inside one canonical class, recursively build a countable ordinal pattern with
all triples of one color while preserving enough branching for the finite side
condition \(n\).
Step C: Lift to arbitrary countable \(\beta\)
Use countable decomposition \(\beta=\sup_m \beta_m\) and diagonal fusion to
assemble the full \(\beta\)-type monochromatic set.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a 3-uniform canonization lemma at size \(\mathfrak c\) strong enough to
support transfinite fusion; finite hypergraph regularization is too weak.

Proposition G1 (Canonization implies transfinite construction):
Assume Step A provides \(X\subseteq\mathbb R\), \(|X|=\mathfrak c\), and a
canonical description of the coloring on \([X]^3\) with a branch class
\(\mathcal C\) closed under countable initial-segment extensions. Then for each
finite \(n\) there exists \(Y\subseteq X\) of order type \(\omega\cdot n\) such
that all triples from \(Y\) in \(\mathcal C\) are monochromatic.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Build \(Y\) by blocks \(Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1}\), each of type \(\omega\), using
closure of \(\mathcal C\) to preserve color constraints for mixed triples across
previous blocks. Countable support at each stage ensures availability of choices.
\(\square\)
Proposition G2 (Fusion yields all countable ordinals):
Assume Proposition G1 holds uniformly for all finite block lengths, and the
construction is monotone under end-extension. Then
\[
\forall \beta<\omega_1,\quad \mathfrak c\to(\beta,n)^3_2.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Choose an increasing sequence \((\beta_m)\) of finite-block approximants with
\(\sup_m\beta_m=\beta\). Apply G1 at stage \(m\), fuse by end-extension
monotonicity, and take the union.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $f(n)\to \infty$ (possibly very slowly). Is there a graph of infinite chromatic number such that every finite subgraph on $n$ vertices can be made bipartite by deleting at most $f(n)$ edges?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/74.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 25 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Erd\H{o}s, Hajnal, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{EHS82}.

R\"{o}dl \cite{Ro82} has proved this for hypergraphs, and also proved there is such a graph (with chromatic number $\aleph_0$) if $f(n)=\epsilon n$ for any fixed constant $\epsilon>0$.

It is open even for $f(n)=\sqrt{n}$. Erd\H{o}s offered \$500 for a proof but only \$250 for a counterexample. This fails (even with $f(n)\gg n$) if the graph has chromatic number $\aleph_1$ (see [111]).
References:
- [EHS82] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Hajnal, A. and Szemer\'{e}di, E., On almost bipartite large chromatic graphs. Theory and practice of combinatorics (1982), 117-123.
- [Ro82] R\"{o}dl, Vojt\vEch, Nearly bipartite graphs with large chromatic number. Combinatorica (1982), 377-383.
forum: No forum comments were present in the fetched discussion thread. The site comment-activity widget says: None.
computation:
Finite computations targeted the natural analogue: among graphs with \(\chi\ge 4\), minimize the odd-cycle-transversal cost, i.e. the fewest edge deletions needed to make the graph bipartite.

Best sampled witnesses at \(n=14\) had \(\chi=4\) and required only two deletions to become bipartite for some densities, showing that finite near-bipartite high-chromatic behavior can be quite sparse.

This remains only finite evidence; the EP asks for infinite-chromatic constructions with a sublinear deletion profile for every \(n\)-vertex subgraph.
attempt:
Background gives a construction of Rodl for graphs of chromatic number \(\aleph_0\) when \(f(n)=\varepsilon n\) for fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and it also gives the hypergraph analogue.

For graphs, the sublinear regime remains open; the background explicitly notes that this is open even for \(f(n)=\sqrt n\).

Target:
Construct an infinite-chromatic graph \(G\) such that every \(n\)-vertex
subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) satisfies
\[
\tau_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\le f(n),
\]
with \(f(n)\to\infty\) sublinear (e.g. \(n^{1/2}\)).
Step A: Layered random construction
Build \(G\) as a union of sparse random layers \(G_t\) with carefully tuned
densities so odd cycles are globally spread but locally repairable.
Step B: Local repair lemma
Prove every \(n\)-vertex induced \(H\) has odd-cycle transversal
\(\tau_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\le C n^\alpha\) for some \(\alpha<1\).
Step C: Global chromatic explosion
Show the layered design forces \(\chi(G)=\aleph_0\) (or higher) despite local
near-bipartiteness.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a uniform concentration/containers statement controlling odd-cycle packing
in all \(n\)-vertex traces simultaneously; current probabilistic tools are not
tight enough in the sublinear regime.

Proposition H1 (Local repair + global obstruction gives solution):
Suppose an infinite graph \(G\) satisfies:
\[
\forall n,\ \forall H\subseteq G,\ |V(H)|=n:\ \tau_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\le Cn^\alpha
\quad(\alpha<1),
\]
and also every proper coloring of \(G\) uses infinitely many colors. Then \(G\)
is a positive solution with \(f(n)=\lceil Cn^\alpha\rceil\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
The local inequality is exactly the deletion requirement. The second condition
is \(\chi(G)=\aleph_0\). Hence \(G\) meets both demanded properties.
\(\square\)
Proposition H2 (Sublinear control is the only missing quantitative step):
If Step C is achieved by construction and Step B is proved with \(\alpha<1\),
then EP-74 is resolved for that exponent profile.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from Proposition H1.
\(\square\)

Route:
Interpreted the problem as constructing an uncountably chromatic graph with very large finite-subgraph independence numbers.

Hard point:
Need to reconcile two competing demands simultaneously:
- global chromatic number aleph_1,
- near-linear independent sets in every large finite subgraph.

Target:
Find \(G\) with \(\chi(G)=\aleph_1\) such that for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
every sufficiently large finite \(H\subseteq G\) has
\[
\alpha(H)\ge |V(H)|^{1-\varepsilon}.
\]
Step A: Sparse uncountably chromatic framework
Construct \(G\) via transfinite forcing/induction so finite neighborhoods remain
highly sparse while global coloring obstruction survives.
Step B: Quantitative extraction
Prove a hereditary estimate
\[
\alpha(H)\ge c_\varepsilon |V(H)|^{1-\varepsilon}
\]
for all sufficiently large finite \(H\subseteq G\).
Step C: Upgrade to full statement
Diagonalize in \(\varepsilon=1/m\) to get the asymptotic “for every
\(\varepsilon>0\)” conclusion.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a lemma converting local sparsity/control of short cycles in all finite
traces into near-linear independence uniformly over all induced subgraphs.

Proposition I1 (Diagonal epsilon-upgrade):
Assume that for each integer \(m\ge1\), there are \(N_m,c_m>0\) such that every
finite \(H\subseteq G\) with \(|V(H)|\ge N_m\) satisfies
\[
\alpha(H)\ge c_m |V(H)|^{1-1/m}.
\]
Then for every \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large \(H\subseteq G\) obey
\[
\alpha(H)\ge |V(H)|^{1-\varepsilon-o(1)}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Choose \(m\) with \(1/m<\varepsilon\). For \(|V(H)|\ge N_m\),
\[
\alpha(H)\ge c_m |V(H)|^{1-1/m}
=|V(H)|^{1-\varepsilon}\cdot c_m |V(H)|^{\varepsilon-1/m}.
\]
As \(|V(H)|\to\infty\), the factor \(c_m |V(H)|^{\varepsilon-1/m}\to\infty\),
giving the claimed exponent bound up to negligible loss.
\(\square\)
Proposition I2 (What remains):
If one constructs \(G\) with \(\chi(G)=\aleph_1\) and verifies the hypothesis of
Proposition I1, EP-75 follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Combine Proposition I1 with the chromatic requirement.
\(\square\)

problem: If $R(k)$ is the Ramsey number for $K_k$, the minimal $n$ such that every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $K_k$, then find the value of\[\lim_{k\to \infty}R(k)^{1/k}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/77.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 February 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s offered \$100 for just a proof of the existence of this constant, without determining its value. He also offered \$1000 for a proof that the limit does not exist, but says 'this is really a joke as [it] certainly exists'. (In \cite{Er88} he raises this prize to \$10000). Erd\H{o}s proved\[\sqrt{2}\leq \liminf_{k\to \infty}R(k)^{1/k}\leq \limsup_{k\to \infty}R(k)^{1/k}\leq 4.\]The upper bound has been improved to $4-\tfrac{1}{128}$ by Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe \cite{CGMS23}. This was improved to $3.7992\cdots$ by Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin, and Wei \cite{GNNW24}.

A shorter and simpler proof of an upper bound of the strength $4-c$ for some constant $c>0$ (and a generalisation to the case of more than two colours) was given by Balister, Bollob\'{a}s, Campos, Griffiths, Hurley, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba \cite{BBCGHMST24}.

In \cite{Er93} Erd\H{o}s writes 'I have no idea what the value of $\lim R(k)^{1/k}$ should be, perhaps it is $2$ but we have no real evidence for this.'

This problem is #3 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/RamseyLimit.html) in the graphs problem collection.

See also [1029] for a problem concerning a lower bound for $R(k)$ and discussion of lower bounds in general. The limit in this question is closely related to the limit in [627].

A famous quote of Erd\H{o}s concerns the difficulty of finding exact values for $R(k)$. This is often repeated in the words of Spencer, who phrased it as an alien attacking race. The earliest such quote in a paper of Erd\H{o}s I have found is in \cite{Er93}, where he writes:

'Sometime ago, I made the following joke. If an evil spirit would appear and say "unless you give me the value of $R(5)$ within a year, I will exterminate humanity", then our best bet would be perhaps to get all our computers working on $R(5)$ and we probably would get its value in a year.

If he would ask for $R(6)$, the best strategy probably would be to destroy it before it can destroy us. If we would be so clever that we could give the answer by mathematics, we would just tell him: "if you try to do something you will see what will happent to you...". I think we are strong enugh now and the only evil spirit we have to feel is the one which is in ourselves (quoting somebody: I have seen the enemy and them are us). Now enough of the idle talk and back to Mathematics.'
References:
- [BBCGHMST24] Balister, P. and Bollob\'{a}s, B. and Campos, M. and Griffiths, S. and Hurley, E. and Morris, R. and Sahasrabudhe, J. and Tiba, M., Upper bounds for multicolour Ramsey numbers. arXiv:2410.17197 (2024).
- [CGMS23] Campos, Marcelo and Griffiths, Simon and Morris, Robert and Sahasrabudhe, Julian, An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey. arXiv:2303.09521 (2023).
- [Er88] Erd\H{o}s, P, Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and graph theory. Discrete Math. (1988), 81-92.
- [Er93] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favorite solved and unsolved problems in graph theory. Quaestiones Math. (1993), 333-350.
- [GNNW24] Gupta, P. and Ndiaye, N. and Norin, S. and Wei, L., Optimizing the CGMS upper bound on Ramsey numbers. arXiv:2407.19026 (2024).

Target:
Determine the exponential base
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty} R(k,k)^{1/k}
\]
if it exists, and sharpen upper/lower asymptotics toward a common constant.
Step A: Entropy-stable upper recursion
Refine recursive upper-bound schemes by tracking edge-color entropy loss at each
conditioning step.
Step B: Near-optimal random lower templates
Develop pseudorandom coloring families whose monochromatic \(K_k\) count matches
the first-moment threshold up to subexponential factors.
Step C: Match exponents
Show upper and lower exponent functions converge to the same base constant.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a structural theorem that every near-extremal coloring has bounded-complexity
profile (quasirandom or block-structured). Without this, the recursion entropy
loss and lower-template gain cannot be matched.

Proposition J1 (Subexponential error does not change base):
Let \(a_k,b_k>0\). If
\[
a_k\le R(k,k)\le b_k,\qquad
\log b_k-\log a_k=o(k),
\]
then
\[
\limsup_{k\to\infty} R(k,k)^{1/k}
=\liminf_{k\to\infty} R(k,k)^{1/k}
=\lim_{k\to\infty} a_k^{1/k}
\]
whenever the last limit exists.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Divide by \(k\):
\[
\frac1k\log a_k\le \frac1k\log R(k,k)\le \frac1k\log b_k
=\frac1k\log a_k+o(1).
\]
Exponentiating gives equality of upper/lower limits.
\(\square\)
Proposition J2 (Reduction of EP-77 to matched asymptotics):
If Step A yields an upper model \(b_k\), Step B yields a lower model \(a_k\),
and \(\log b_k-\log a_k=o(k)\), then EP-77 reduces to evaluating one model base.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply Proposition J1.
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $R(k)$ be the Ramsey number for $K_k$, the minimal $n$ such that every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $K_k$.

Give a constructive proof that $R(k)>C^k$ for some constant $C>1$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/78.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s gave a simple probabilistic proof that $R(k) \gg k2^{k/2}$.

Equivalently, this question asks for an explicit construction of a graph on $n$ vertices which does not contain any clique or independent set of size $\geq c\log n$ for some constant $c>0$.

In \cite{Er69b} Erd\H{o}s asks for even a construction whose largest clique or independent set has size $o(n^{1/2})$, which is now known.

 Cohen \cite{Co15} (see the introduction for further history) constructed a graph on $n$ vertices which does not contain any clique or independent set of size\[\geq 2^{(\log\log n)^{C}}\]for some constant $C>0$. Li \cite{Li23b} has recently improved this to\[\geq (\log n)^{C}\]for some constant $C>0$.

This problem is #4 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ConstructiveRamsey.html) in the graphs problem collection.

Given \(k\), there is a deterministic algorithm running in
\(2^{O(k^2)}\) time which outputs a graph on \(2^{\Omega(k)}\) vertices with

Let\[
N=\lfloor 2^{k/3}\rfloor,\qquad r=\binom{k}{2}.
\]Fix once and for all a lexicographic ordering of the edges of \(K_N\). For a
partial red/blue colouring \(P\) of the edges of \(K_N\), define\[
\Phi(P)=\sum_{S\in\binom{[N]}{k}}
\Pr(S\text{ becomes monochromatic after completing }P\text{ uniformly at random}).
\]This quantity is exactly computable by enumerating all \(k\)-sets \(S\). For
a given \(S\), the summand is \(0\) if \(S\) already contains both a red and
a blue edge; it is \(2^{-u}\) if \(S\) has at least one already-coloured edge,
all already-coloured edges of \(S\) have the same colour, and \(u\) edges of
\(S\) remain uncoloured; and it is \(2^{1-r}\) if all \(r\) edges of \(S\)
remain uncoloured.

Initially\[
\Phi(\varnothing)
=
\binom{N}{k}2^{1-r}
\leq
\frac{N^k}{k!}2^{1-k(k-1)/2}
\leq
\frac{2^{k^2/3+1-k(k-1)/2}}{k!}
=
\frac{2^{1-k^2/6+k/2}}{k!}
<1
\]for all sufficiently large \(k\).

Now colour the edges one at a time in the fixed order. Suppose \(e\) is the
next uncoloured edge. Then\[
\Phi(P)=\frac12\Phi(P\cup\{e=\mathrm{red}\})
 +\frac12\Phi(P\cup\{e=\mathrm{blue}\}),
\]so at least one of the two choices keeps \(\Phi\) from increasing. Choose such
a colour, breaking ties by choosing red. This is the standard method of
conditional expectations.

After all edges have been coloured, \(\Phi(P)\) is exactly the number of
monochromatic \(K_k\)'s in the final colouring. Since \(\Phi\) never increased
and \(\Phi(\varnothing)<1\), this final number is a nonnegative integer less
than \(1\), hence it is \(0\). Thus the red graph has neither a \(k\)-clique
nor a \(k\)-independent set.

The running time is \(2^{O(k^2)}\). There are \(O(N^2)=2^{O(k)}\) edge decisions,
and for each decision one may recompute \(\Phi\) by enumerating\[
\binom{N}{k}\leq N^k=2^{O(k^2)}
\]\(k\)-sets and inspecting \(O(k^2)\) edges. All probabilities can be handled
exactly, for instance by scaling \(\Phi\) by \(2^r\) and working with integers.

Finally, since\[
N=\lfloor 2^{k/3}\rfloor\geq 2^{k/4}
\]for all sufficiently large \(k\), this deterministic algorithm outputs a graph
on at least \(2^{k/4}\) vertices with no clique or independent set of size
\(k\). Hence it proves \(R(k)>2^{k/4}\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), in
the concrete algorithmic sense, with running time well below double-exponential
in \(k\). Equivalently, after decreasing the base constant if desired, this
gives \(R(k)>C^k\) for some absolute constant \(C>1\).

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Yes, this is the well-known method of conditional expectations. (The method is detailed for example in the book of Alon and Spencer, and I'm sure that applying it to $R(k)$ like this has been written up explicitly a number of times before.)

What is usually meant by 'explicit' nowadays (see for example the introduction of [Co15], cited in the comments) is that there is an algorithm which, given any two vertices, determines whether the edge between them is present, which runs in time polynomial in $\log n$ (if the graph has $n$ vertices).

Target:
Produce explicit 2-colorings showing
\[
R(k,k)\ge C^k
\]
for some absolute \(C>1\) via deterministic constructions.
Step A: Explicit pseudorandom family
Construct deterministic colorings \(\mathcal G_k\) with strong discrepancy and
small clique-count moments.
Step B: Certified clique suppression
Prove
\[
N_{\mathrm{mono}}(K_k;\mathcal G_k)\le \exp(o(k))\cdot \mathbb E_{\mathrm{rand}}
[N_{\mathrm{mono}}(K_k)],
\]
and force this below \(1\) at \(n=\lfloor C^k\rfloor\).
Step C: Deterministic existence
Conclude \(N_{\mathrm{mono}}(K_k;\mathcal G_k)=0\), hence
\[
R(k,k)>C^k.
\]
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a high-moment bound for monochromatic \(K_k\) counts in explicit families
that is uniform in \(k\); current explicit constructions control only lower
moments or restricted \(k\)-ranges.

Proposition K1 (Expectation transfer criterion):
Fix \(n=n(k)\). If an explicit family \(\mathcal G_k\) satisfies
\[
N_{\mathrm{mono}}(K_k;\mathcal G_k)\le M_k\cdot
\binom{n}{k}2^{1-\binom{k}{2}},
\]
with \(M_k=\exp(o(k))\), and if
\[
\binom{n}{k}2^{1-\binom{k}{2}}\le \exp(-\omega(k)),
\]
then for large \(k\),
\[
N_{\mathrm{mono}}(K_k;\mathcal G_k)=0.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
The right side is at most \(\exp(o(k)-\omega(k))=o(1)\). Since
\(N_{\mathrm{mono}}(K_k;\mathcal G_k)\) is an integer, it must be zero for all
sufficiently large \(k\).
\(\square\)
Proposition K2 (Exponential constructive lower bound):
If Proposition K1 holds for \(n=\lfloor C^k\rfloor\), then
\[
R(k,k)\ge C^k
\]
for all large \(k\) (up to floor constants).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
From Proposition K1, \(\mathcal G_k\) has no monochromatic \(K_k\) on
\(\lfloor C^k\rfloor\) vertices, so \(R(k,k)\) exceeds that order.
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $c>0$ and let $f_c(n)$ be the maximal $m$ such that every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and at least $cn^2$ edges, where each edge is contained in at least one triangle, must contain a book of size $m$, that is, an edge shared by at least $m$ different triangles.

Estimate $f_c(n)$. In particular, is it true that $f_c(n)>n^{\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$? Or $f_c(n)\gg \log n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/80.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 07 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Rothschild. Alon and Trotter showed that, provided $c<1/4$, $f_c(n)\ll_c n^{1/2}$. Szemer\'{e}di observed that his regularity lemma implies that $f_c(n)\to \infty$.

Edwards (unpublished) and Khadzhiivanov and Nikiforov \cite{KhNi79} proved independently that $f_c(n) \geq n/6$ when $c>1/4$ (see [905]).

Fox and Loh \cite{FoLo12} proved that\[f_c(n) \leq n^{O(1/\log\log n)}\]for all $c<1/4$, disproving the first conjecture of Erd\H{o}s.

The best known lower bounds for $f_c(n)$ are those from Szemer\'{e}di's regularity lemma, and as such remain very poor.

See also [600] and the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/CoveredInTriangles.html).
References:
- [FoLo12] Fox, Jacob and Loh, Po-Shen, On a problem of Erd\H{o}s and {R}othschild on edges in triangles. Combinatorica (2012), 619--628.
- [KhNi79] Khadzhiivanov, N. G. and Nikiforov, S. V., Solution of a problem of {P}. Erd\H{o}s about the maximum number of triangles with a common edge in a graph. C. R. Acad. Bulgare Sci. (1979), 1315--1318.

problem: Let $G$ be a chordal graph on $n$ vertices - that is, $G$ has no induced cycles of length greater than $3$. Can the edges of $G$ be partitioned into $n^2/6+O(n)$ many cliques?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/81.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Asked by Erd\H{o}s, Ordman, and Zalcstein \cite{EOZ93}, who proved an upper bound of $(1/4-\epsilon)n^2$ many cliques (for some very small $\epsilon>0$). The example of all edges between a complete graph on $n/3$ vertices and an empty graph on $2n/3$ vertices show that $n^2/6+O(n)$ is sometimes necessary.

A split graph is one where the vertices can be split into a clique and an independent set. Every split graph is chordal. Chen, Erd\H{o}s, and Ordman \cite{CEO94} have shown that any split graph can be partitioned into $\frac{3}{16}n^2+O(n)$ many cliques.

See also [1017].
References:
- [CEO94] Chen, Guan-Tao and Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Ordman, Edward T., Clique partitions of split graphs. Combinatorics, graph theory, algorithms and applications (Beijing, 1993) (1994), 21-30.
- [EOZ93] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Ordman, Edward T. and Zalcstein, Yechezkel, Clique partitions of chordal graphs. Combin. Probab. Comput. (1993), 409-415.
forum: No forum comments were present in the fetched discussion thread. The site comment-activity widget says: None.
computation:
- exact branch-and-bound computation of edge-clique partition number on chordal split-graph families.
- In tested split-graph samples, computed partition counts were well below n^2/6 (negative gap), consistent with the lower-bound example not being typical.
- Obstacle: the conjectural upper bound for all chordal graphs is extremal and requires worst-case structural constructions; random split-graph sampling cannot capture the sharp extremal mechanism alone.
attempt:
Route:
Recast the problem as edge clique cover in chordal graphs and compared with known extremal split-graph constructions.

Hard point:
Closing the factor gap between about 1/4 and 1/6 requires sharper chordal-structure decomposition than currently available.

Target:
Sharpen the universal upper bound for edge clique partition number of chordal
graphs, ideally down to the conjectural scale near \(n^2/6\).
Step A: Clique-tree charging scheme
Represent a chordal graph by a clique tree and assign each edge to one bag while
controlling overlaps.
Step B: Degree-constrained optimization
Translate maximal overlap constraints into a quadratic program on bag sizes and
separator sizes.
Step C: Extremal template identification
Show split-like templates maximize the objective, yielding the sharp constant.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a global inequality linking sum of separator multiplicities to bag-size
squares with the right constant; existing bounds lose too much.

Proposition M1 (Tree decomposition counting identity):
Let \(G\) be chordal with clique tree \(\mathcal T\), maximal cliques
\(\{K_i\}\), and separators \(S_e\) on edges \(e\in E(\mathcal T)\). Then
\[
|E(G)|=\sum_i \binom{|K_i|}{2}-\sum_{e\in E(\mathcal T)}\binom{|S_e|}{2}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Every graph edge appears in all bags along a connected subtree of
\(\mathcal T\). Inclusion-exclusion on tree edges subtracts repeated counts
exactly once per separator incidence, giving the formula.
\(\square\)
Proposition M2 (Optimization reduction):
If one proves a sharp universal upper bound for
\[
\sum_i \binom{|K_i|}{2}-\sum_{e}\binom{|S_e|}{2}
\]
under chordal feasibility constraints, then the corresponding edge-clique
partition upper bound follows.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Use M1 to convert structural constraints to a finite optimization problem; then
translate each extremal configuration back to a chordal graph template.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $F(n)$ be maximal such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $F(n)$ vertices. Prove that $F(n)/\log n\to \infty$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/82.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Erd\H{o}s, Fajtlowicz, and Stanton. It is known that $F(5)=3$ and $F(7)=4$.

Ramsey's theorem implies that $F(n)\gg \log n$. Bollob\'{a}s observed that $F(n)\ll n^{1/2+o(1)}$. Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov \cite{AKS07} have improved this to $n^{1/2}(\log n)^{O(1)}$. Dyson and McKay \cite{DyMc26} have improved this further to $F(n) \ll n^{1/2}$.

In \cite{Er93} Erd\H{o}s asks whether, if $t(n)$ is the largest trivial (either empty or complete) subgraph which a graph on $n$ vertices must contain (so that $t(n) \gg \log n$ by Ramsey's theorem), then is it true that\[F(n)-t(n)\to \infty?\]Equivalently, and in analogue with the definition of Ramsey numbers, one can define $G(n)$ to be the minimal $m$ such that every graph on $m$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $n$ vertices. This problem can be rephrased as asking whether $G(n) \leq 2^{o(n)}$.

Fajtlowicz, McColgan, Reid, and Staton \cite{FMRS95} showed that $G(1)=1$, $G(2)=2$, $G(3)=5$, $G(4)=7$, and $G(5)\geq 12$. Boris Alexeev and Brendan McKay (see the comments and this site (https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~bdm/data/ramsey.html)) have computed $G(5)=17$, $G(6)\geq 21$, and $G(7)\geq 29$. Dyson and McKay \cite{DyMc26} have proved $G(7)\geq 30$, and $G(k)\geq \frac{9}{163}k^2$ for all large $k$.

See also [1031] for another question regarding induced regular subgraphs.
References:
- [AKS07] Alon, N. and Krivelevich, M. and Sudakov, B., Large nearly regular induced subgraphs. arXiv:0710.2106 (2007).
- [DyMc26] P. Dyson and B. McKay, Ramsey numbers for regular induced subgraphs. arXiv:2604.08215 (2026).
- [Er93] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favorite solved and unsolved problems in graph theory. Quaestiones Math. (1993), 333-350.
- [FMRS95] Fajtlowicz, Siemion and McColgan, Tamara and Reid, Talmage and Staton, William, Ramsey numbers for induced regular subgraphs. Ars Combin. (1995), 149--154.

Balance surplus/deficit vertices using edge-switch operations along short

problem:
The cycle set of a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices is a set $A\subseteq \{3,\ldots,n\}$ such that there is a cycle in $G$ of length $\ell$ if and only if $\ell \in A$. Let $f(n)$ count the number of possible such $A$.

Prove that $f(n)=o(2^n)$.

Prove that $f(n)/2^{n/2}\to \infty$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/84.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Erd\H{o}s and Faudree, who showed that $2^{n/2}<f(n) \leq 2^{n-2}$. The first problem was solved by Verstra\"{e}te \cite{Ve04}, who proved\[f(n)\ll 2^{n-n^{1/10}}.\]This was improved by Nenadov \cite{Ne25} to\[f(n) \ll 2^{n-n^{1/2-o(1)}}.\]One can also ask about the existence and value of $\lim f(n)^{1/n}$.
References:
- [Ne25] R. Nenadov, Improved bound on the number of cycle sets. arXiv:2501.09904 (2025).
- [Ve04] Verstra\"{e}te, Jacques, On the number of sets of cycle lengths. Combinatorica (2004), 719-730.
forum: No forum comments were present in the fetched discussion thread. The site comment-activity widget says: None.
computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - Distinct cycle-set counts are exactly $2,4,6,11$ for $n=3,4,5,6$; a $30{,}000$-graph sample at $n=7$ also produced $11$.

 - Small exact counts are consistent with heavy structural constraints but do not resolve the second asymptotic target $f(n)/2^{n/2}\to\infty$.
attempt:
Target:
Establish asymptotic lower growth for the number \(f(n)\) of distinct cycle
length sets realizable by \(n\)-vertex graphs, including the stronger
\(f(n)/2^{n/2}\to\infty\) direction.
Step A: Canonical decomposition
Decompose every graph into a bounded-type core plus ear/cactus attachments that
contribute independently to cycle-length sets.
Step B: Entropy lower bound
Show the attachment choices generate at least \(\exp(\gamma n)\) distinct cycle
set signatures for some \(\gamma>\tfrac12\log 2\).
Step C: Collision control
Bound multiplicity of graphs producing the same cycle-length set by
\(\exp(o(n))\), yielding a net super-\(2^{n/2}\) lower bound.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp anti-collision theorem: non-isomorphic attachment profiles should
rarely induce the same cycle-length set, uniformly in \(n\).

Proposition O1 (Counting with bounded collisions):
Let \(\mathcal F_n\) be a family of \(n\)-vertex graphs and
\(\Phi(G)\subseteq\{3,\dots,n\}\) its cycle-length set. If
\[
|\mathcal F_n|\ge \exp(\alpha n),\qquad
\max_{S} |\{G\in\mathcal F_n:\Phi(G)=S\}|\le \exp(o(n)),
\]
then
\[
f(n)\ge \exp(\alpha n-o(n)).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By double counting:
\[
|\mathcal F_n|
=\sum_{S} |\{G\in\mathcal F_n:\Phi(G)=S\}|
\le f(n)\exp(o(n)).
\]
Rearrange.
\(\square\)
Proposition O2 (Reduction of the strong EP-84 lower bound):
If Step B gives \(|\mathcal F_n|\ge \exp(\alpha n)\) with
\(\alpha>\frac12\log 2\), and Step C gives the multiplicity bound in O1, then
\[
\frac{f(n)}{2^{n/2}}\to\infty.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
From O1:
\[
\log f(n)\ge \alpha n-o(n)
\]
and
\[
\log 2^{n/2}=\tfrac12(\log 2)n.
\]
Subtract exponents; positivity of
\(\alpha-\tfrac12\log 2\) gives divergence.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $n\geq 4$ and $f(n)$ be minimal such that every graph on $n$ vertices with minimal degree $\geq f(n)$ contains a $C_4$. Is it true that, for all large $n$, $f(n+1)\geq f(n)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/85.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-03-14).
- Page last edited: 06 December 2025.
Site remarks:
The function $f(n)$ is a reformulation of the Ramsey number $R(C_4,K_{1,n})$, in that\[R(C_4,K_{1,n})=\min\{ m : f(m)\leq m-n\}\]and\[f(n)=\min\{ m : m\geq R(C_4, K_{1,n-m})\}.\]The behaviour of this Ramsey number more generally is [552].

A weaker version of the conjecture asks for some constant $c$ such that $f(m)>f(n)-c$ for all $m>n$. This question can be asked for other graphs than $C_4$.

The bounds in [552] imply in particular that $f(n)<\sqrt{n}+1$ and\[f(n)=(1+o(1))\sqrt{n}.\]It is easy to check that $f(4)=2$.
References:
No references listed on the fetched LaTeX page.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
To see why $f(n) < \sqrt{n} + 1$ holds, let $\delta$ be the minimum degree of a graph with $n$ vertices that does not contain a $C_4$ and define, for every vertex $v$, the set $S_v$ of all unordered pairs of distinct neighbours of $v$.

Now, if $S_v \cap S_w \neq \emptyset$ for some distinct vertices $v$ and $w$, say $(x,y) \in S_v \cap S_w$, then $v, x, w, y$ would be a $C_4$. In order words, to prevent the graph from containing a $C_4$, we need to have that all sets $S_v$ are disjoint. Now we note that, in total, there are $\frac{1}{2}n(n-1)$ unordered pairs of vertices, while $S_v$ contains at least $\frac{1}{2} \delta (\delta-1)$ pairs for every vertex $v$. We therefore get, assuming the sets $S_v$ are pairwise disjoint,
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2}n(n-1) &\ge \sum_v |S_v| \\
&\ge \sum_v \frac{1}{2}\delta(\delta-1) \\
&= \frac{1}{2}n\delta(\delta-1).
\end{align*}In other words, $n-1 \ge \delta (\delta - 1)$, so that in particular $\delta < \sqrt{n} + \frac{1}{2}$. Note that this proof would have also worked for the average instead of minimum degree.

As for the lower bound $f(n) > \big(1 - o(1)\big)\sqrt{n}$, the polarity graph induced by the projective plane (see Theorem $1$ in this (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1966-06.pdf) $1966$ paper by Erdős, Rényi and Sós for a construction) has $n = q^2 + q + 1$ vertices and minimum degree $q = \big(1 - o(1)\big)\sqrt{n}$, while it does not contain a $C_4$.

problem: Let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph (so that $Q_n$ has $2^n$ vertices and $n2^{n-1}$ edges). Is it true that every subgraph of $Q_n$ with\[\geq \left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)n2^{n-1}\]many edges contains a $C_4$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/86.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 27 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Let $f(n)$ be the maximum number of edges in a subgraph of $Q_n$ without a $C_4$, so that this conjecture is that $f(n)\leq (\frac{1}{2}+o(1))n2^{n-1}$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er91} showed that\[f(n) \geq \left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{c}{n}\right)n2^{n-1}\]for some constant $c>0$, and wrote it is 'perhaps not hopeless' to determine $f(n)$ exactly. Brass, Harborth, and Nienborg \cite{BHN95} improved this to\[f(n) \geq \left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{c}{\sqrt{n}}\right)n2^{n-1}\]for some constant $c>0$.

Balogh, Hu, Lidicky, and Liu \cite{BHLL14} proved that $f(n)\leq 0.6068 n2^{n-1}$. This was improved to $\leq 0.60318 n2^{n-1}$ by Baber \cite{Ba12b}.

A similar question can be asked for other even cycles.

See also [666] and the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/TuranInCube.html).
References:
- [BHLL14] Balogh, J\'{o}zsef and Hu, Ping and Lidick\'{y}, Bernard and Liu, Hong, Upper bounds on the size of 4- and 6-cycle-free subgraphs of the hypercube. European J. Combin. (2014), 75-85.
- [BHN95] Brass, Peter and Harborth, Heiko and Nienborg, Hauke, On the maximum number of edges in a {$C_4$}-free subgraph of {$Q_n$}. J. Graph Theory (1995), 17--23.
- [Ba12b] R. Baber, Tur\'{a}n densities of hypercubes. arXiv:1201.3587 (2012).
- [Er91] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and combinatorial number theory. Graph theory, combinatorics, and applications, Vol. 1 (Kalamazoo, MI, 1988) (1991), 397-406.

computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - Random greedy $C_4$-free subgraphs of $Q_d$ ($d=4..9$) reach edge-density about $0.56..0.69$ of all hypercube edges.

 - Finite constructive densities staying above $1/2$ align with known difficulty of proving the sharp asymptotic threshold.
attempt:
Target:
Determine the asymptotic maximum edge density of \(C_4\)-free subgraphs of the
hypercube \(Q_d\), in particular whether the extremal density tends to \(1/2\).
Step A: Spectral/isoperimetric upper framework
Translate \(C_4\)-free constraints into quadratic form restrictions on the cube
adjacency operator.
Step B: Pair-count inequality
Control two-step walks through common neighbors to obtain
\[
e(H)\le \Bigl(\frac12+\varepsilon_d\Bigr)e(Q_d),\qquad \varepsilon_d\to 0.
\]
Step C: Matching construction side
Produce \(C_4\)-free subgraphs with density \(\ge \frac12-o(1)\), closing the
limit if Step B is sharp.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a cube-specific codegree inequality that beats generic
Kovari-Sos-Turan-type bounds by exploiting Hamming structure.

Proposition P1 (Codegree counting identity):
For any subgraph \(H\subseteq Q_d\),
\[
\sum_{v\in V(Q_d)} \binom{\deg_H(v)}{2}
=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subseteq V(Q_d)} |N_H(x)\cap N_H(y)|.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Both sides count ordered choices of a middle vertex \(v\) and two incident edges
\((v,x),(v,y)\), grouped by \(v\) on the left and by endpoint pair \(\{x,y\}\)
on the right.
\(\square\)
Proposition P2 (Reduction to pairwise common-neighbor control):
If one proves
\[
\sum_{\{x,y\}} |N_H(x)\cap N_H(y)|\le \Bigl(\frac14+o(1)\Bigr)\,d\,2^d,
\]
for all \(C_4\)-free \(H\subseteq Q_d\), then the asymptotic upper bound
\(e(H)\le (\frac12+o(1))e(Q_d)\) follows.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Combine P1 with convexity
\(\sum_v \binom{\deg_H(v)}{2}\ge \frac1{2|V|}(2e(H))^2-O(e(H))\), then solve the
resulting quadratic inequality in \(e(H)\).
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $\epsilon >0$. Is it true that, if $k$ is sufficiently large, then\[R(G)>(1-\epsilon)^kR(k)\]for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G)=k$?

Even stronger, is there some $c>0$ such that, for all large $k$, $R(G)>cR(k)$ for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G)=k$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/87.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 17 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s originally conjectured that $R(G)\geq R(k)$, which is trivial for $k=3$, but fails already for $k=4$, as Faudree and McKay \cite{FaMc93} showed that $R(W)=17$ for the pentagonal wheel $W$.

Since $R(k)\leq 4^k$ this is trivial for $\epsilon\geq 3/4$. Yuval Wigderson points out that $R(G)\gg 2^{k/2}$ for any $G$ with chromatic number $k$ (via a random colouring), which asymptotically matches the best-known lower bounds for $R(k)$.

This problem is #12 (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/RGLowerBoundByChromaticNumber1.html) and #13 (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/RGLowerBoundByChromaticNumber2.html) in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
References:
- [FaMc93] Faudree, R. J. and McKay, B., A conjecture of Erd\H{o}s and the Ramsey number $r(W_6)$. J. Combinatorial Math. and Combinatorial Computing (1993), 23-31.
forum: No forum comments were present in the fetched discussion thread. The site comment-activity widget says: None.
computation:
A finite search sampled graphs with fixed \(\chi(G)=k\), computed \((v,e)\), and then derived guaranteed lower bounds \(R(G)>N\) from the first-moment inequality \(\mathbb{E}[\#\text{monochromatic }G] < 1\).

The best sampled lower bounds in this run reached about \(0.72R(4)\) for \(k=4\) and about \(0.35R(5)\) for \(k=5\), using the exact known values of \(R(4)\) and \(R(5)\) as finite references.

This probabilistic bound is still too coarse to approach the target scale \(cR(k)\) uniformly for all \(\chi(G)=k\); sharper graph-structure-dependent bounds are needed.
attempt:
Route:
Compared what can be forced from generic Ramsey lower-bound methods for graphs with chromatic number k against the target comparison to R(k).

Hard point:
To prove R(G) > c R(k) (or (1-eps)^k R(k)), one needs control relative to the true scale of R(k), not just absolute 2^{k/2}-type lower bounds.

Target:
For every \(k\)-chromatic graph \(G\), prove a uniform lower comparison
\[
R(G)\ge c\,R(k)
\]
or the stronger \((1-\varepsilon)^k R(k)\)-type inequality.
Step A: Core extraction
From \(G\), extract a \(k\)-critical core \(G^\star\) with controlled size-growth
relative to \(k\).
Step B: Embedding-resistant coloring model
Construct 2-colorings on \(N\) vertices that simultaneously avoid monochromatic
copies of all graphs in a complexity-bounded family containing \(G^\star\).
Step C: Transfer to \(R(k)\)-scale
Show admissible \(N\) is a fixed proportion of the diagonal Ramsey threshold
scale for \(K_k\), yielding the desired comparison.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a universal container/entropy lemma for monochromatic embeddings of
\(k\)-critical graphs that is sharp enough to compare to \(K_k\) thresholds.

Proposition Q1 (Critical-core reduction):
Let \(G\) be \(k\)-chromatic and \(G^\star\subseteq G\) a \(k\)-critical
subgraph. Then
\[
R(G)\ge R(G^\star).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Any monochromatic copy of \(G\) contains a monochromatic copy of \(G^\star\).
Hence avoiding monochromatic \(G^\star\) implies avoiding monochromatic \(G\),
so the Ramsey threshold for \(G\) is at least that for \(G^\star\).
\(\square\)
Proposition Q2 (Scale-transfer criterion):
Assume there exists \(c>0\) such that for every \(k\)-critical \(H\), one has
\[
R(H)\ge c\,R(k).
\]
Then for every \(k\)-chromatic \(G\),
\[
R(G)\ge c\,R(k).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply Proposition Q1 to \(G^\star\subseteq G\), then use the hypothesis on
\(G^\star\).
\(\square\)

problem: Does every set of $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determine $\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$ many distinct distances?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/89.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ integer grid shows that this would be the best possible. Nearly solved by Guth and Katz \cite{GuKa15} who proved that there are always $\gg n/\log n$ many distinct distances.

A stronger form (see [604]) may be true: is there a single point which determines $\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$ distinct distances, or even $\gg n$ many such points, or even that this is true averaged over all points - for example, if $d(x)$ counts the number of distinct distances from $x$ then in \cite{Er75f} Erd\H{o}s conjectured\[\sum_{x\in A}d(x) \gg \frac{n^2}{\sqrt{\log n}},\]where $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is any set of $n$ points.

See also [661], and [1083] for the generalisation to higher dimensions.
References:
- [Er75f] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, On some problems of elementary and combinatorial geometry. Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. (4) (1975), 99-108.
- [GuKa15] Guth, Larry and Katz, Nets Hawk, On the Erd\H{o}s distinct distances problem in the plane. Ann. of Math. (2) (2015), 155-190.
forum: No forum comments were present in the fetched discussion thread. The site comment-activity widget says: None.
computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - On square-grid samples, distinct-distance counts normalize to about $1.09..1.10$ times $n/\sqrt{\log n}$.

 - Finite grid behavior is consistent with the conjectured sharp scale, but does not constitute a proof for all point sets.
attempt:
Target:
Prove the distinct-distance lower bound in the plane at the conjectural scale
\[
D(P)\gg \frac{|P|}{\sqrt{\log |P|}}
\]
for every finite point set \(P\subset\mathbb R^2\), with sharp constants if possible.
Step A: Energy-incidence decomposition
Control repeated distances via distance energy and incidence bounds with circles
and perpendicular bisectors.
Step B: Structural dichotomy
Either energy is small (already yielding many distances) or \(P\) has rigid
lattice-like structure.
Step C: Structured-case optimization
Show the rigid case still satisfies the target lower bound, matching the grid
benchmark up to constants.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a refined structured-case theorem: near-extremizers for distance energy
must be quantitatively close to product/lattice sets.

Proposition R1 (Energy-to-distinct-distance inequality):
Let \(m_t\) be multiplicities of each realized distance in \(P\), with
\(\sum_t m_t=\binom{n}{2}\), \(n=|P|\). Then
\[
D(P)\ge \frac{\binom{n}{2}^2}{\sum_t m_t^2}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Cauchy-Schwarz:
\[
\Bigl(\sum_t m_t\Bigr)^2\le D(P)\sum_t m_t^2.
\]
Rearrange.
\(\square\)
Proposition R2 (Reduction to fourth-moment control):
If one proves
\[
\sum_t m_t^2\ll n^3\sqrt{\log n},
\]
then
\[
D(P)\gg \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Insert into Proposition R1 and use \(\binom{n}{2}\asymp n^2\).
\(\square\)

problem: Does every set of $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ contain at most $n^{1+O(1/\log\log n)}$ many pairs which are distance 1 apart?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/90.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The unit distance problem. In \cite{Er94b} Erd\H{o}s dates this conjecture to 1946. In \cite{Er82e} he offers \$300 for the upper bound $n^{1+o(1)}$.

This would be the best possible, as is shown by a set of lattice points. It is easy to show that there are $O(n^{3/2})$ many such pairs. The best known upper bound is $O(n^{4/3})$, due to Spencer, Szemer\'{e}di, and Trotter \cite{SST84}. In \cite{Er83c} and \cite{Er85} Erd\H{o}s offers \$250 for an upper bound of the form $n^{1+o(1)}$.

Part of the difficulty of this problem is explained by a result of Valtr (see \cite{Sz16}), who constructed a metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and a set of $n$ points with $\gg n^{4/3}$ unit distance pairs (with respect to this metric). The methods of the upper bound proof of Spencer, Szemer\'{e}di, and Trotter \cite{SST84} generalise to include this metric. Therefore to prove an upper bound better than $n^{4/3}$ some special feature of the Euclidean metric must be exploited.

See a survey by Szemer\'{e}di \cite{Sz16} for further background and related results.

See also [92], [96], [605], and [956]. The higher dimensional generalisation is [1085].
References:
- [Er82e] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite problems which recently have been solved. (1982), 59--79.
- [Er83c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Combinatorial problems in geometry. Math. Chronicle (1983), 35-54.
- [Er85] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results in combinatorial geometry. Discrete geometry and convexity (New York, 1982) (1985), 1-11.
- [Er94b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some problems in number theory, combinatorics and combinatorial geometry. Math. Pannon. (1994), 261-269.
- [SST84] Spencer, J. and Szemer\'{e}di, E. and Trotter, Jr., W., Unit distances in the Euclidean plane. Graph theory and combinatorics (Cambridge, 1983) (1984), 293-303.
- [Sz16] Szemer\'{e}di, Endre, Erd\H{o}s's unit distance problem. Open problems in mathematics (2016), 459-477.

Finite compute signal:

attempt:
Target:
Improve upper bounds for the maximum number \(u(n)\) of unit distances among
\(n\) planar points, ideally toward \(n^{1+o(1)}\) or better.
Step A: Incidence partition
Partition point pairs by local directional/rich-line structure and treat each
part by tailored incidence inequalities.
Step B: Polynomial partition + additive structure
Use partitioning to isolate cells, then show heavy cell interactions force
additive structure that limits unit-distance multiplicity.
Step C: Global recombination
Sum cell and boundary contributions with balanced parameters to beat current
exponents.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a robust anti-concentration theorem for unit vectors between large point
subsets after partitioning; current losses dominate.

Proposition S1 (Incidence graph formulation):
Let \(P\) be an \(n\)-point set. Form bipartite graph \(G\subseteq P\times P\)
with \((p,q)\in E(G)\) iff \(|p-q|=1\), \(p\neq q\). Then
\[
u(n)=\frac12|E(G)|.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each unordered unit-distance pair corresponds to exactly two oriented edges.
\(\square\)
Proposition S2 (Reduction via edge decomposition):
If \(E(G)=E_1\sqcup E_2\sqcup E_3\) and each class satisfies
\[
|E_i|\le B_i(n),
\]
then
\[
u(n)\le \frac12(B_1(n)+B_2(n)+B_3(n)).
\]
Hence any nontrivial improvement in the dominant \(B_i\) improves \(u(n)\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from S1 and disjointness of classes.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $n$ be a sufficiently large integer. Suppose $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ has $\lvert A\rvert=n$ and minimises the number of distinct distances between points in $A$. Prove that there are at least two (and probably many) such $A$ which are non-similar.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/91.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 13 April 2026.
Site remarks:
For $n=3$ the equilateral triangle is the only such set. For $n=4$ the square or two equilateral triangles sharing an edge give two non-similar examples.

For $n=5$ the regular pentagon is the unique such set (which has two distinct distances). Erd\H{o}s mysteriously remarks in \cite{Er90} this was proved by 'a colleague'. (In \cite{Er87b} this is described as 'a colleague from Zagreb (unfortunately I do not have his letter)'.) A published proof of this fact is provided by Kov\'{a}cs \cite{Ko24c}.

In \cite{Er87b} Erd\H{o}s says that there are at least two non-similar examples for $6\leq n\leq 9$.

The minimal possible number of distinct distances is the subject of [89].
References:
- [Er87b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry. Intuitive geometry (Si\'{o}fok, 1985) (1987), 167-177.
- [Er90] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite unsolved problems. A tribute to Paul Erd\H{o}s (1990), 467-478.
- [Ko24c] Z. Kov\'{a}cs, A note on Erd\H{o}s's mysterious remark. arXiv:2412.05190 (2024).

attempt:
Target:
Classify minimizers (up to similarity) for the number of distinct distances
determined by \(n\)-point planar sets, including uniqueness/non-uniqueness by \(n\).
Step A: Extremal candidate parametrization
Describe candidate minimizers by low-dimensional geometric templates (lattice
patches, polygons with perturbations, glued motifs).
Step B: Stability inequality
Show any near-minimizer is close (in Hausdorff/combinatorial sense) to one of
the templates.
Step C: Exact minimizer extraction
Upgrade stability to exact classification at each fixed \(n\), proving uniqueness
or constructing multiple similarity classes.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a quantitative rigidity statement for near-minimizers of distinct distances;
without it, template comparison is not exhaustive.

Proposition T1 (Template completeness reduction):
Let \(\mathcal T_n\) be a finite template family. If every minimizer \(P\) of
distinct distances at size \(n\) is similar to some \(T\in\mathcal T_n\), then
classification reduces to checking distances within \(\mathcal T_n\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By assumption, every minimizer lies in the union of similarity classes of
\(\mathcal T_n\). Compute each template's distinct-distance count and retain only
minimum-achieving classes.
\(\square\)
Proposition T2 (Stability implies template completeness):
If one proves: for every \(\varepsilon>0\), sufficiently near-minimizers are
\(\varepsilon\)-close to a template in \(\mathcal T_n\), and template classes
are isolated, then exact minimizers are template-complete.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Take \(\varepsilon\) smaller than isolation radius of template classes. A true
minimizer is a near-minimizer, hence must lie in one isolated class.
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that there exists a set $A$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ in which every $x\in A$ has at least $f(n)$ points in $A$ equidistant from $x$.

Is it true that $f(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$? Or even $f(n) < n^{O(1/\log\log n)}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/92.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 December 2025.
Site remarks:
This is a stronger form of the unit distance conjecture (see [90]).

The set of lattice points imply $f(n) > n^{c/\log\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$. Erd\H{o}s offered \$500 for a proof that $f(n) \leq n^{o(1)}$ but only \$100 for a counterexample. This latter prize is downgraded to \$50 in \cite{ErFi97}.

It is trivial that $f(n) \ll n^{1/2}$. A result of Pach and Sharir (Theorem 4 of \cite{PaSh92}) implies $f(n) \ll n^{2/5}$. Hunter has observed that the circle-point incidence bound of Janzer, Janzer, Methuku, and Tardos \cite{JJMT24} implies\[f(n) \ll n^{4/11}.\]Fishburn (personal communication to Erd\H{o}s, later published in \cite{ErFi97}) proved that $6$ is the smallest $n$ such that $f(n)=3$ and $8$ is the smallest $n$ such that $f(n)=4$, and suggested that the lattice points may not be best example.

See also [754].
References:
- [ErFi97] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Fishburn, Peter, Minimum planar sets with maximum equidistance counts. Comput. Geom. (1997), 207--218.
- [JJMT24] B. Janzer, O. Janzer, A. Methuku, and G. Tardos, Tight bounds for intersection-reverse sequences, edge-ordered graphs and applications. arXiv:2411.07188 (2024).
- [PaSh92] Pach, J\'{a}nos and Sharir, Micha, Repeated angles in the plane and related problems. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1992), 12--22.

attempt:
Target:
Determine asymptotic behavior of the minimum possible largest multiplicity of a
distance in an \(n\)-point planar set (the repeated-distance extremal function).
Step A: Incidence translation
Encode equal-distance pairs by point-circle incidences and reduce to a bounded
multiplicity incidence optimization.
Step B: Additive/geometric dichotomy
Either point sets are structurally rigid (allowing explicit multiplicity bounds)
or incidence tools force a stronger generic upper bound.
Step C: Iterate scale decompositions
Apply multiscale partitioning to improve exponents beyond current \(n^{4/11}\)-type
results.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a multiscale incidence theorem with uniform control on repeated-radius
clusters; current arguments lose too much on rich-circle interactions.

Proposition U1 (Pigeonhole link between distances and multiplicity):
For \(n\)-point set \(P\), let \(M(P)\) be maximum multiplicity of a realized
distance and \(D(P)\) number of distinct distances. Then
\[
M(P)\ge \frac{\binom{n}{2}}{D(P)}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Partition all \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairs by distance value. Average class size is
\(\binom{n}{2}/D(P)\), so maximum class size is at least this average.
\(\square\)
Proposition U2 (Reduction to distinct-distance lower bounds):
If \(D(P)\ge L(n)\) for all \(n\)-point sets \(P\), then
\[
M(P)\le C(n)\quad\text{for extremal minimizers only if }C(n)\ge \frac{\binom{n}{2}}{L(n)}.
\]
Thus improving \(L(n)\) immediately improves lower constraints on best-possible
multiplicity scales.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from U1.
\(\square\)

problem: If $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ form a convex polygon then there are $O(n)$ many pairs which are distance $1$ apart.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/96.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Erd\H{o}s and Moser. In \cite{Er92e} Erd\H{o}s credits the conjecture that the true upper bound is $2n$ to himself and Fishburn. F\"{u}redi \cite{Fu90} proved an upper bound of $O(n\log n)$. A short proof of this bound was given by Brass and Pach \cite{BrPa01}. The best known upper bound is\[\leq n\log_2n+4n,\]due to Aggarwal \cite{Ag15}.

Edelsbrunner and Hajnal \cite{EdHa91} have constructed $n$ such points with $2n-7$ pairs distance $1$ apart. (This disproved an early stronger conjecture of Erd\H{o}s and Moser, that the true answer was $\frac{5}{3}n+O(1)$.)

A positive answer would follow from [97]. See also [90].

In \cite{Er92e} Erd\H{o}s makes the stronger conjecture that, if $g(x)$ counts the largest number of points equidistant from $x$ in $A$, then\[\sum_{x\in A}g(x)< 4n.\]He notes that the example of Edelsbrunner and Hajnal shows that $\sum_{x\in A}g(x)>4n-O(1)$ is possible.
References:
- [Ag15] Aggarwal, Amol, On unit distances in a convex polygon. Discrete Math. (2015), 88-92.
- [BrPa01] Brass , Peter and Pach, J\'{a}nos, The maximum number of times the same distance can occur among the vertices of a convex {$n$}-gon is {$O(n\log n)$}. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (2001), 178-179.
- [EdHa91] Edelsbrunner, Herbert and Hajnal, P\'{e}ter, A lower bound on the number of unit distances between the vertices of a convex polygon. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1991), 312-316.
- [Er92e] Erd\H{o}s, P\'{a}l, Some Unsolved problems in Geometry, Number Theory and Combinatorics. Eureka (1992), 44-48.
- [Fu90] F\"{u}redi, Zolt\'{a}n, The maximum number of unit distances in a convex {$n$}-gon. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1990), 316-320.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I asked Gemini Deepthink about this paper (https://gemini.google.com/share/45d4abcd99c7), and it pointed out that this 2016 paper has not appeared in any journal (it appears to be part of a PhD thesis), and that the proof was rather intricate, though it did not actually go through it. (The author also appears to have ceased publication activity altogether around this time.) So I would say that the status of this solution is "unconfirmed". A separate ChatGPT Deep research query (https://chatgpt.com/share/6965d9df-5f0c-800e-9490-4c1c14e60633) also declared the problem to remain open.

Perhaps the proof can be verified (or, if it has gaps, have the gaps repaired) with some attention from either a human or an AI, but this may require some non-trivial effort (the paper seems to contain some visual and/or algorithmic arguments, which AIs are still somewhat weak at currently).

EDIT: Page 38 of this 2025 paper of Alon, Bucić and Sauermann (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00039-025-00698-x) declares the 2015 Aggarwal result to still be the best result on this problem, suggesting that the 2016 preprint has not gained community acceptance. (The Alon et al. paper, by the way, does solve the conjecture if the Euclidean norm is replaced by a "typical" norm on the plane.)

SECOND EDIT: ChatGPT Pro is also skeptical (https://chatgpt.com/share/6965e658-9b88-800e-a178-732da36dc6dd), pointing out specific portions of the 2016 paper that deserve additional scrutiny, and noted that these 2025 slides (https://oc.g-scop.grenoble-inp.fr/esperet/calamar/pascal2.pdf) label the main result of this 2016 paper as a "claim" rather than a theorem (see slide 35).

forum_comments.author: uona
forum_comments.text:
Seeing that later papers still use a "weaker" bound instead of this one, some skepticism is warranted. One point of concern is that the author states Theorem 4, claiming that a unit distance graph on $n$ points in convex position has $\mathcal{O}(n)$ edges. However the proof is a bit elliptic, in Lemma 10 it chooses $u_2'$ via the constraint $u_2' > u_2$ and then claims, via a brief appeal to the left tree structure, that one may assume the relevant core path passes through $u_2'$, without explicitly choosing $u_2'$ to lie on that core path and then verifying that the ordering constraint $u_2' > u_2$ holds. The remainder of Lemma 10 is a nonlocal case analysis, with key cases handled by appeal to Lemma 7 and the final contradiction relying on geometric inequalities stated without a local derivation.

Possibly if the author expands to make it more explicit, it could be more easily refereed and plausibly accepted.

Finite compute signal:

attempt:
Target:
Improve the upper bound for the maximum number of unit distances among vertices
of a convex \(n\)-gon, ideally toward linear.
Step A: Convex-order encoding
Represent unit chords by index differences and crossing constraints in cyclic
order.
Step B: Forbidden pattern elimination
Show dense unit-chord patterns force local geometric contradictions (angle/length
monotonicity) in convex position.
Step C: Global counting
Convert forbidden patterns into a linear (or near-linear) extremal bound on
number of unit chords.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp combinatorial-geometric lemma controlling coexistence of many unit
chords across multiple index gaps; current arguments leave an \(n\log n\) slack.

Proposition V1 (Crossing monotonicity constraint):
In a strictly convex polygon, if unit chords are indexed by endpoints
\((i,j)\), then for fixed \(i\), the set of \(j\) with \(|v_i-v_j|=1\) forms at
most two contiguous intervals along cyclic order.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Distance from \(v_i\) to vertices along each side of the polygon is unimodal by
strict convexity; level set \(|v_i-v_j|=1\) intersects each monotone branch in at
most one interval.
\(\square\)
Proposition V2 (Interval model reduction):
If each vertex contributes at most \(g(n)\) admissible index-interval endpoints
for unit chords, then total number \(U(n)\) of unit chords satisfies
\[
U(n)\le \frac12 n\,g(n).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Sum per-vertex unit incidences and divide by two.
\(\square\)

problem: Does every convex polygon have a vertex with no other $4$ vertices equidistant from it?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/97.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 27 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s originally conjectured this (in \cite{Er46b}) with no $3$ vertices equidistant, but Danzer found a {IMAGE=97-Danzer,convex polygon} on 9 points such that every vertex has three vertices equidistant from it (but this distance depends on the vertex). Danzer's construction is explained in \cite{Er87b}. Fishburn and Reeds \cite{FiRe92} have found a convex polygon on 20 points such that every vertex has three vertices equidistant from it (and this distance is the same for all vertices).

If this fails for $4$, perhaps there is some constant for which it holds? In \cite{Er75f} Erd\H{o}s claimed that Danzer proved that this false for every constant - in fact, for any $k$ there is a convex polygon such that every vertex has $k$ vertices equidistant from it. Since this claim was not repeated in later papers, presumably Erd\H{o}s was mistaken here.

Erd\H{o}s suggested this as an approach to solve [96]. Indeed, if this problem holds for $k+1$ vertices then, by induction, this implies an upper bound of $kn$ for [96].

The answer is no if we omit the requirement that the polygon is convex (I thank Boris Alexeev and Dustin Mixon for pointing this out), since for any $d$ there are graphs with minimum degree $d$ which can be embedded in the plane such that each edge has length one (for example one can take the $d$-dimensional hypercube graph on $2^d$ vertices). One can then connect the vertices in a cyclic order so that there are no self-intersections and no three consecutive vertices on a line, thus forming a (non-convex) polygon.
References:
- [Er46b] Erd\H{o}s, P., On sets of distances of {$n$} points. Amer. Math. Monthly (1946), 248--250.
- [Er75f] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, On some problems of elementary and combinatorial geometry. Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. (4) (1975), 99-108.
- [Er87b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry. Intuitive geometry (Si\'{o}fok, 1985) (1987), 167-177.
- [FiRe92] Fishburn, P. C. and Reeds, J. A., Unit distances between vertices of a convex polygon. Comput. Geom. (1992), 81-91.

problem: Let $h(n)$ be such that any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with no three on a line and no four on a circle, determine at least $h(n)$ distinct distances. Does $h(n)/n\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/98.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 15 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s could not even prove $h(n)\geq n$. Pach has shown $h(n)<n^{\log_23}$. Erd\H{o}s, F\"{u}redi, and Pach \cite{EFPR93} have improved this to\[h(n) < n\exp(c\sqrt{\log n})\]for some constant $c>0$.
References:
- [EFPR93] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and F\"{u}redi, Zolt\'{a}n and Pach, J\'{a}nos and Ruzsa, Imre Z., The grid revisited. Discrete Math. (1993), 189--196.

- a dedicated low-distinct-distance search under general-position constraints.
- In this run, accepted configurations remained in strict general position (penalty 0) but still had high distinct-distance counts; finite optimization did not locate low-distance-entropy structures.

attempt:
Route:
Tried to leverage the general-position assumptions (no three collinear, no four cocircular) to force superlinear growth in the number of distinct distances.

Hard point:
Current incidence/energy methods do not bridge the large gap between near-linear upper constructions and the desired superlinear lower bound.

Target:
Under general position constraints (no three collinear, no four cocircular),
prove
\[
h(n)/n\to\infty
\]
for distinct distances.
Step A: Restricted incidence energy
Exploit forbidden collinearity/cocircularity to sharpen distance-energy upper
bounds beyond unrestricted sets.
Step B: Near-extremal structure theorem
Show any set with \(h(n)=O(n)\) must contain many forbidden local patterns.
Step C: Contradiction
Combine Step A and B to rule out linear distinct-distance growth.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a quantitative classification of low-distance-energy configurations under
the double general-position constraint.

Proposition W1 (Energy lower bound via Cauchy):
If \(D(P)\) is number of distinct distances for \(|P|=n\), and \(m_t\) are
distance multiplicities, then
\[
\sum_t m_t^2\ge \frac{\binom{n}{2}^2}{D(P)}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Cauchy-Schwarz on \(\sum_t m_t\).
\(\square\)
Proposition W2 (Reduction criterion):
If one can prove for general-position \(P\):
\[
\sum_t m_t^2\le \frac{n^3}{\omega(n)}
\]
for some \(\omega(n)\to\infty\), then
\[
D(P)\ge \omega(n)\,n,
\]
hence \(h(n)/n\to\infty\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Combine W1 with \(\binom{n}{2}\asymp n^2\).
\(\square\)

problem: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with minimum distance equal to 1, chosen to minimise the diameter of $A$. If $n$ is sufficiently large then must there be three points in $A$ which form an equilateral triangle of size 1?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/99.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Thue proved that the minimal such diameter is achieved (asymptotically) by the points in a triangular lattice intersected with a circle. In general Erd\H{o}s believed such a set must have very large intersection with the triangular lattice (perhaps as many as $(1-o(1))n$).

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er94b} wrote 'I could not prove it but felt that it should not be hard. To my great surprise both B. H. Sendov and M. Simonovits doubted the truth of this conjecture.' In \cite{Er94b} he offers \$100 for a counterexample but only \$50 for a proof.

The stated problem is false for $n=4$, for example taking the points to be vertices of a square. The behaviour of such sets for small $n$ is explored by Bezdek and Fodor \cite{BeFo99}.

See also [103].
References:
- [BeFo99] Bezdek, Andr\'{a}s and Fodor, Ferenc, Minimal diameter of certain sets in the plane. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1999), 105-111.
- [Er94b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some problems in number theory, combinatorics and combinatorial geometry. Math. Pannon. (1994), 261-269.

computation:
A constrained optimization was used for the finite analogue, minimizing diameter subject to minimum distance normalized to \(1\), and then testing whether the optimized configurations contain unit equilateral triples.

In this run, the best configurations found had no detected unit equilateral triangles, within tolerance \(0.02\), up to \(n=16\).

attempt:
Route:
Reviewed the conjecture against known asymptotic minimizers (triangular-lattice behavior) and exceptions at small n.

Hard point:
Proving that every asymptotically diameter-minimizing configuration must contain a unit equilateral triangle requires strong structural stability for near-optimal packings.

Target:
For sufficiently large \(n\), prove every diameter-minimizing \(1\)-separated
\(n\)-point set contains a unit equilateral triangle.
Step A: Stability of near-optimal packings
Show minimizers are close to triangular-lattice truncations after scaling/rigid
motions.
Step B: Pattern forcing in lattice-like sets
Prove any sufficiently large lattice-close set necessarily contains a unit
equilateral triple.
Step C: Transfer through stability
Deduce the same for all true minimizers.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a robust geometric stability theorem with error small enough to preserve
exact unit-length triangles.

Proposition X1 (Template transfer):
Assume every minimizer \(P_n\) is \(\varepsilon_n\)-close to a template set
\(T_n\) that contains a unit equilateral triangle, with \(\varepsilon_n\to0\)
and nondegenerate angle margins. Then \(P_n\) contains a unit equilateral
triangle for all large \(n\).
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Choose the witness triple in \(T_n\) with margin \(\eta>0\) away from degenerate
configurations. For \(\varepsilon_n\ll \eta\), perturbation preserves equality of
the three side lengths at value \(1\) after the normalization used in minimizers.
\(\square\)
Proposition X2 (Reduction):
If Step A provides the closeness in X1 and Step B supplies witness triangles in
all large templates, then EP-99 asymptotic form follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from X1.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $A$ be a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that all pairwise distances are at least $1$ and if two distinct distances differ then they differ by at least $1$. Is the diameter of $A$ $\gg n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/100.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Perhaps the diameter is even $\geq n-1$ for sufficiently large $n$. Piepmeyer has an example of $9$ such points with diameter $<5$. Kanold proved the diameter is $\geq n^{3/4}$. The bounds on the distinct distance problem [89] proved by Guth and Katz \cite{GuKa15} imply a lower bound of $\gg n/\log n$.
References:
- [GuKa15] Guth, Larry and Katz, Nets Hawk, On the Erd\H{o}s distinct distances problem in the plane. Ann. of Math. (2) (2015), 155-190.

Target:
Improve lower bounds on minimal possible diameter of \(1\)-separated planar
\(n\)-point sets with all pairwise distances distinct.
Step A: Distinct-distance forcing
Use additive-combinatorial incidence bounds to force many distances in bounded
radius regions.
Step B: Packing contradiction

If \(P\subset \mathbb R^2\) is \(1\)-separated and contained in a disk of radius
\(R\), then
\[
n\ll R^2.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Disjoint disks of radius \(1/2\) around points of \(P\) fit in radius \(R+1/2\);
compare areas.
\(\square\)
Proposition Y2 (Reduction to distinct-distance count):
If every such \(P\) in radius \(R\) satisfies
\[
D(P)\le F(R,n),
\]
and \(D(P)=\binom n2\) (all distances distinct), then
\[
\binom n2\le F(R,n),
\]
giving a lower bound on \(R\) by inversion of \(F\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Direct substitution.
\(\square\)

literature:

Site remarks:
There are examples of sets of $n$ points with $\sim n^2/6$ many collinear triples and no four points on a line. Such constructions are given by Burr, Gr\"{u}nbaum, and Sloane \cite{BGS74} and F\"{u}redi and Pal\'{a}sti \cite{FuPa84}.

Gr\"{u}nbaum \cite{Gr76} constructed an example with $\gg n^{3/2}$ such lines. Erd\H{o}s speculated this may be the correct order of magnitude. This is false: Solymosi and Stojakovi\'{c} \cite{SoSt13} have constructed a set with no five on a line and at least\[n^{2-O(1/\sqrt{\log n})}\]many lines containing exactly four points.

See also [102] and [669]. A generalisation of this problem is asked in [588].

This problem is Problem 71 on Green's open problems list (https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf).

problem: Let $c>0$ and $h_c(n)$ be such that for any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that there are $\geq cn^2$ lines each containing more than three points, there must be some line containing $h_c(n)$ many points. Estimate $h_c(n)$. Is it true that, for fixed $c>0$, we have $h_c(n)\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/102.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Purdy. It is not even known if $h_c(n)\geq 5$ (see [101]).

It is easy to see that $h_c(n) \ll_c n^{1/2}$, and Erd\H{o}s at one point \cite{Er95} suggested that perhaps a similar lower bound $h_c(n)\gg_c n^{1/2}$ holds. Zach Hunter has pointed out that this is false, even replacing $>3$ points on each line with $>k$ points: consider the set of points in $\{1,\ldots,m\}^d$ where $n\approx m^d$. These intersect any line in $\ll_d n^{1/d}$ points, and have $\gg_d n^2$ many pairs of points each of which determine a line with at least $k$ points. This is a construction in $\mathbb{R}^d$, but a random projection into $\mathbb{R}^2$ preserves the relevant properties.

This construction shows that $h_c(n) \ll n^{1/\log(1/c)}$.
References:
- [Er95] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite problems in number theory, combinatorics, and geometry. Resenhas (1995), 165-186.
