problem: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ the number of distinct unit circles containing at least three points is $o(n^2)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/104.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er81d} Erd\H{o}s proved that $\gg n$ many circles is possible, and that there cannot be more than $O(n^2)$ many circles. The argument is very simple: every pair of points determines at most $2$ unit circles, and the claimed bound follows from double counting. Erd\H{o}s claims in a number of places this produces the upper bound $n(n-1)$, but Harborth and Mengerson \cite{HaMe86} note that in fact this delivers an upper bound of $\frac{n(n-1)}{3}$.

Elekes \cite{El84} has a simple construction of a set with $\gg n^{3/2}$ such circles. This may be the correct order of magnitude.

In \cite{Er75h} and \cite{Er92e} Erd\H{o}s also asks how many such unit circles there must be if the points are in general position.

In \cite{Er92e} Erd\H{o}s offered £100 for a proof or disproof that the answer is $O(n^{3/2})$.

The maximal number of unit circles achieved by $n$ points is A003829 (https://oeis.org/A003829) in the OEIS.

See also [506] and [831].
References:
- [El84] Elekes, G., {$n$} points in the plane can determine $n^{3/2}$ unit circles. Combinatorica (1984), 131.
- [Er75h] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some problems on elementary geometry. Austral. Math. Soc. Gaz. (1975), 2-3.
- [Er81d] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some applications of graph theory and combinatorial methods to number theory and geometry. Algebraic methods in graph theory, Vol. I, II (Szeged, 1978) (1981), 137-148.
- [Er92e] Erd\H{o}s, P\'{a}l, Some Unsolved problems in Geometry, Number Theory and Combinatorics. Eureka (1992), 44-48.
- [HaMe86] Harborth, Heiko and Mengersen, Ingrid, Point sets with many unit circles. Discrete Math. (1986), 193--197.

attempt:
Route:
Combined the standard pair-counting upper bound setup with explicit constructions that force many unit circles through at least three points.

Hard point:
The open gap is between linear lower bounds and quadratic upper bounds. Proving o(n^2) needs a genuinely nontrivial incidence restriction beyond pair counting.

Target:
Improve the upper bound for the number \(U_3(P)\) of unit circles through at
least three points of an \(n\)-point set \(P\subset\mathbb R^2\), ideally below
quadratic.
Step A: Incidence-energy setup
Translate triple-point unit circles into weighted incidences between points and
unit circles centered at pair-constraints.
Step B: Rich-circle suppression
Show configurations with many rich unit circles force line/circle concentration
patterns excluded by incidence theorems.
Step C: Global bound
Aggregate local restrictions to derive \(U_3(P)=o(n^2)\) (or stronger).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp bound for the number of radius-1 circles incident to many points
when centers are highly dependent on the point set itself.

Proposition AC1 (Pair-to-circle counting inequality):
Let \(s(C)\) be number of points of \(P\) on unit circle \(C\). Then
\[
\sum_{C:\ s(C)\ge 3}\binom{s(C)}{2}\le \binom{n}{2}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Any unordered pair of points determines at most two unit circles, and in the
count above each rich circle contributes one count per pair it contains. Up to a
constant factor this is bounded by total point pairs.
\(\square\)
Proposition AC2 (Reduction to rich-tail control):
If one proves
\[
\#\{C:\ s(C)\ge t\}\ll \frac{n^2}{t^{2+\delta}}
\]
for some \(\delta>0\), then
\[
U_3(P)=\#\{C:\ s(C)\ge 3\}=o(n^2)
\]
with power savings from summing the tail.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Apply dyadic decomposition in \(t\), using AC1-compatible normalization.
\(\square\)

problem: Draw $n$ squares inside the unit square with no common interior point. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum possible sum of the side-lengths of the squares. Is $f(k^2+1)=k$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/106.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 March 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er94b} Erd\H{o}s dates this conjecture to 'more than 60 years ago'. Erd\H{o}s proved that $f(2)=1$ in an early mathematical paper for high school students in Hungary. Newman proved (in personal communication to Erd\H{o}s) that $f(5)=2$.

It is trivial from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that $f(k^2)=k$. Erd\H{o}s also asks for which $n$ is it true that $f(n+1)=f(n)$.

It is easy to see that $f(k^2+1)\geq k$, by first dividing the unit square into $k^2$ smaller squares of side-length $1/k$, and then replacing one square by two smaller squares of side-length $1/2k$. Hal\'{a}sz \cite{Ha84} gives a construction that shows $f(k^2+2)\geq k+\frac{1}{k+1}$, and in general, for any $c\geq 1$,\[f(k^2+2c+1)\geq k+\frac{c}{k}\]and\[f(k^2+2c)\geq k+\frac{c}{k+1}.\]Hal\'{a}sz also considers the variants where we replace a square by a parallelogram or triangle.

Erd\H{o}s and Soifer \cite{ErSo95} and Campbell and Staton \cite{CaSt05} have conjectured that, in general, for any integer $-k<c<k$, $f(k^2+2c+1)=k+\frac{c}{k}$, and proved the corresponding lower bound. Praton \cite{Pr08} has proved that this general conjecture is equivalent to $f(k^2+1)=k$.

Baek, Koizumi, and Ueoro \cite{BKU24} have proved $g(k^2+1)=k$, where $g(\cdot)$ is defined identically to $f(\cdot)$ with the additional assumption that all squares have sides parallel to the sides of the unit square. More generally, they prove that $g(k^2+2c+1)=k+c/k$ for any $-k<c<k$, which determines all values of $g(\cdot)$.

Raj Singh \cite{Ra26} has noted that $f(k^2+1)=k$ being true for all $k$ is equivalent to it being true for infinitely many $k$, which in turn is equivalent to the convergence of\[\sum_{k\geq 1}(f(k^2+1)-k).\]Both equivalences follow from the fact that\[k(f(k^2+1)-k)\]is a non-decreasing function of $k$.
References:
- [BKU24] Baek, J. and Koizumi, J. and Ueoro, T., A note on the Erd\H{o}s conjecture about square packing. arXiv:2411.07274 (2024).
- [CaSt05] Campbell, Connie and Staton, William, A square-packing problem of Erd\H{o}s. Amer. Math. Monthly (2005), 165--167.
- [Er94b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some problems in number theory, combinatorics and combinatorial geometry. Math. Pannon. (1994), 261-269.
- [ErSo95] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Soifer, Alexander, Squares in a square. Geombinatorics (1995), 110--114.
- [Ha84] Hal\'{a}sz, Sylvia, Packing a convex domain with similar convex domains. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1984), 85--90.
- [Pr08] Praton, I., Packing squares in a square. Math. Mag. (2008), 358-361.
- [Ra26] A. Raj Singh, On a square packing conjecture of Erd\H{o}s. arXiv:2601.22163 (2026).

problem: Let $f(n)$ be minimal such that any $f(n)$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line, contain $n$ points which form the vertices of a convex $n$-gon. Prove that $f(n)=2^{n-2}+1$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/107.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 11 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The Erd\H{o}s-Klein-Szekeres 'Happy Ending' problem. The problem originated in 1931 when Klein observed that $f(4)=5$. Tur\'{a}n and Makai showed $f(5)=9$. Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres proved the bounds\[2^{n-2}+1\leq f(n)\leq \binom{2n-4}{n-2}+1.\](\cite{ErSz60} and \cite{ErSz35} respectively). There were several improvements of the upper bound, but all of the form $4^{(1+o(1))n}$, until Suk \cite{Su17} proved\[f(n) \leq 2^{(1+o(1))n}.\]The current best bound is due to Holmsen, Mojarrad, Pach, and Tardos \cite{HMPT20}, who prove\[f(n) \leq 2^{n+O(\sqrt{n\log n})}.\]In \cite{Er97e} Erd\H{o}s clarifies that the \$500 is for a proof, and only offers \$100 for a disproof. Graham \cite{Gr04} offers \$1000 for a proof.

This problem is #1 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/Convex.html) in the graphs problem collection.

See also [216], [651], and [838].

For each \(k\ge2, r\ge4\), prove existence of finite \(f(k,r)\) such that
\(\chi(G)\ge f(k,r)\) implies \(G\) contains a subgraph \(H\) with
\(\chi(H)\ge k\) and girth at least \(r\).
Step A: High-chromatic sparse core
Extract a subgraph with large average degree and controlled local cycle profile.
Step B: Cycle-pruning with chromatic retention
Delete a carefully chosen edge/vertex set to kill all short cycles
\(<r\) while keeping chromatic number \(\ge k\).
Step C: Parameter closure
Track losses to produce explicit finite \(f(k,r)\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a short-cycle hitting lemma with chromatic stability: removing all cycles
below length \(r\) should not collapse chromatic number too much.

Proposition AD1 (Chromatic retention criterion):
If \(G\) has a subgraph \(H\) with
\[
\chi(H)\ge k,\qquad \text{girth}(H)\ge r,
\]
then \(G\) satisfies the EP conclusion for \((k,r)\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate since \(H\subseteq G\) is exactly the required witness.
\(\square\)
Proposition AD2 (Reduction to pruning lemma):
Suppose every graph \(G\) with \(\chi(G)\ge F\) contains \(H\subseteq G\) such
that deleting a short-cycle transversal \(X\) gives
\[
\chi(H-X)\ge k,\qquad \text{girth}(H-X)\ge r.
\]
Then \(f(k,r)\le F\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Take \(f(k,r)=F\). Any \(G\) with \(\chi(G)\ge F\) yields witness \(H-X\), then
apply AD1.
\(\square\)

problem:
If $G$ is a graph let $h_G(n)$ be defined such that any subgraph of $G$ on $n$ vertices can be made bipartite after deleting at most $h_G(n)$ edges.

What is the behaviour of $h_G(n)$? Is it true that $h_G(n)/n\to \infty$ for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/111.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Hajnal, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{EHS82}. Every $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ must have $h_G(n)\gg n$ since $G$ must contain, for some $r$, $\aleph_1$ many vertex disjoint odd cycles of length $2r+1$.

On the other hand, Erd\H{o}s, Hajnal, and Szemer\'{e}di proved that there is a $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that $h_G(n)\ll n^{3/2}$. In \cite{Er81} Erd\H{o}s conjectured that this can be improved to $\ll n^{1+\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$.

See also [74].
References:
- [EHS82] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Hajnal, A. and Szemer\'{e}di, E., On almost bipartite large chromatic graphs. Theory and practice of combinatorics (1982), 117-123.
- [Er81] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the combinatorial problems which I would most like to see solved. Combinatorica (1981), 25-42.
forum: No forum comments were present in the fetched discussion thread. The site comment-activity widget says: None.
computation:
- explicit computation of minimum edge deletions to bipartite on sampled induced subgraphs.
- Observed finite proxy ratios h_G(n)/n around 0.25-0.30 for n=8,10,12 in this host/sample regime.
- Obstacle: EP-111 concerns all graphs of chromatic number \aleph_1; finite fixed-host sampling cannot establish the universal asymptotic lower-growth claim.
attempt:
Background provides two-sided growth information: a universal lower bound \(h_G(n)\gg n\) for every such \(G\), and the existence of a graph with \(h_G(n)\ll n^{3/2}\).

The cited results do not settle whether \(h_G(n)/n\to\infty\) always holds.

Target:
For every graph \(G\) with \(\chi(G)=\aleph_1\), prove
\[
\frac{h_G(n)}{n}\to\infty,
\]
where \(h_G(n)\) is the largest odd-cycle transversal number over \(n\)-vertex
subgraphs.
Step A: Uniform odd-cycle packing
Show large finite subgraphs of such \(G\) contain many edge-disjoint odd cycles.
Step B: Transversal lower transfer
Convert odd-cycle packing lower bounds into lower bounds for edge deletions to
bipartite.
Step C: Growth amplification
Prove packing density grows superlinearly in the right normalized scale, forcing
\(h_G(n)/n\to\infty\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a universal packing theorem for uncountably chromatic graphs: finite traces
must contain more than linear odd-cycle edge-disjointness.

Proposition AE1 (Packing vs transversal):
For any finite graph \(H\), let \(\nu_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\) be the maximum number
of edge-disjoint odd cycles and \(\tau_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\) the minimum edges to
delete to make \(H\) bipartite. Then
\[
\tau_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\ge \nu_{\mathrm{odd}}(H).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Any odd-cycle transversal must meet every odd cycle; in particular it meets each
member of an edge-disjoint family in distinct edges.
\(\square\)
Proposition AE2 (Reduction for EP-111):
If for every \(G\) with \(\chi(G)=\aleph_1\) and every large \(n\) there exists
an \(n\)-vertex \(H\subseteq G\) with
\[
\nu_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\ge n\,\omega(n),\qquad \omega(n)\to\infty,
\]
then \(h_G(n)/n\to\infty\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By AE1, \(h_G(n)\ge \tau_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\ge \nu_{\mathrm{odd}}(H)\), hence
\(h_G(n)/n\ge \omega(n)\to\infty\).
\(\square\)

problem: Let $k=k(n,m)$ be minimal such that any directed graph on $k$ vertices must contain either an independent set of size $n$ or a transitive tournament of size $m$. Determine $k(n,m)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/112.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Rado \cite{ErRa67}, who showed $k(n,m) \ll_m n^{m-1}$, or more precisely,\[k(n,m) \leq \frac{2^{m-1}(n-1)^m+n-2}{2n-3}.\]Larson and Mitchell \cite{LaMi97} improved the dependence on $m$, establishing in particular that $k(n,3)\leq n^{2}$. Zach Hunter has observed that\[R(n,m) \leq k(n,m)\leq R(n,m,m),\]which in particular proves the upper bound $k(n,m)\leq 3^{n+2m}$.

See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/DirectedPaths.html) - on this site the problem replaces transitive tournament with directed path, but Zach Hunter and Raphael Steiner have a simple argument that proves, for this alternative definition, that $k(n,m)=(n-1)(m-1)$.
References:
- [ErRa67] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Rado, R., Partition relations and transitivity domains of binary relations. J. London Math. Soc. (1967), 624-633.
- [LaMi97] Larson, Jean A. and Mitchell, William J., On a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Rado. Ann. Comb. (1997), 245-252.

computation:
A random digraph search checked both obstructions simultaneously: the absence of an independent set of size \(n\) and the absence of a transitive tournament of size \(m\).

It produced empirical lower-bound signals for small targets; for example, when \((n,m)=(4,4)\), counterexamples were found up to the scanned value \(k=9\).

These are only probabilistic lower bounds on small parameters; exact asymptotics for \(k(n,m)\) require rigorous constructions and matching upper bounds.
attempt:
Route:
Positioned k(n,m) between classical Ramsey-type quantities and examined what is already known for fixed small m.

Hard point:
Bridging broad Ramsey-type bounds to sharp asymptotics for directed transitivity/independence tradeoff is unresolved.

Target:
Determine sharp asymptotics of \(k(n,m)\): the least \(k\) such that every
tournament on \(k\) vertices has an independent set of size \(n\) or a transitive
subtournament of size \(m\).
Step A: Entropy lower constructions
Build explicit/random tournaments avoiding both structures up to large \(k\),
giving lower bounds on \(k(n,m)\).
Step B: Container/regularity upper mechanism
Show any larger tournament must contain one forbidden structure via iterative
density increment.
Step C: Match scales
Align lower and upper formulas to pin the correct growth in \(n,m\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a two-parameter container theorem simultaneously controlling large
independent sets and large transitive subtournaments.

Proposition AF1 (Monotonicity):
The function \(k(n,m)\) is nondecreasing in each argument:
\[
n_1\le n_2,\ m_1\le m_2 \implies k(n_1,m_1)\le k(n_2,m_2).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
If a tournament forces an independent set of size \(n_2\) or transitive set of
size \(m_2\), it certainly forces one of size \(n_1\) or \(m_1\).
\(\square\)
Proposition AF2 (Reduction to matching bounds):
If functions \(L(n,m)\), \(U(n,m)\) satisfy
\[
L(n,m)\le k(n,m)\le U(n,m),
\]
and \(\log U-\log L=o(1)\cdot \log L\) in a regime, then \(k(n,m)\) is
asymptotically determined there up to \(1+o(1)\) multiplicative factor.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Take logarithms and compare relative error.
\(\square\)

forum_comments.author: Kenneth Mendoza
forum_comments.text:
We have computationally verified the EHP conjecture for all degrees $3 \leq n \leq 12$ using dual independent implementations (Python/mpmath and Rust/inari) with IEEE 1788 certified interval arithmetic and branch-and-bound optimization. Both implementations produce identical certified enclosures across x86_64 and arm64 architectures. The dominance margins increase monotonically from $17.1\%$ ($n=3$) to $71.4\%$ ($n=10$); all non-extremizer boxes are eliminated at level $0$ for $n \geq 5$. We also derive a new closed-form expression for $L(z^n - 1)$ valid for all $n$.

Combined with Tao's result [Ta25] for sufficiently large $n$, the conjecture is now verified for all $n \leq 12$ and all $n \geq N_0$. The remaining gap is $13 \leq n < N_0$.

Preprint and certified result JSON files with SHA-256 checksums: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19229245 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19229245)

Code: github.com/MendozaLab/erdos-experiments (https://github.com/MendozaLab/erdos-experiments/tree/main/papers/ehp-conjecture-114)

forum_comments.author: Alfaiz
forum_comments.text: This paper [Wa98] (https://zbmath.org/0926.31001) by C. Wang seems related.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text: Pommerenke [Po59] proves: if $\{z:|p(z)|<1\}$ is connected, then $|\{z:|p(z)|=1\}|\ge 2\pi$, with equality for $p(z)=z^n$. I wondered whether, when $\{z:|p(z)|<1\}$ has exactly $k\ge 2$ connected components, there must exist a uniform lower bound $c_k>0$ for $|\{z:|p(z)|=1\}|$. However, this is false: take $p(z)=z^k-R$ with $R>1$. Then $\{z: |z^k-R|<1\}$ has $k$ components, but as $R\to\infty$ the lemniscate $\{z:|z^k-R|=1\}$ shrinks and its total length tends to $0$.

forum_comments.author: BorisAlexeev
forum_comments.text:
Terence Tao has resolved this problem (positively) for sufficiently large $n$. The paper "The maximal length of the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian lemniscate length in high degree" is available on the arxiv (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12455), and there is an accompanying blog post (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2025/12/15/the-maximal-length-of-the-erdos-herzog-piranian-lemniscate-in-high-degree/).

He notes that the problem almost has "decidable" status now, but there may be some issues with testing equality of real numbers.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

If \(p(z)\) is degree \(n\), then after scaling/rotation

problem:
Let $h(n)$ be minimal such that any group $G$ with the property that any subset of $>n$ elements contains some $x\neq y$ such that $xy=yx$ can be covered by at most $h(n)$ many Abelian subgroups.

Estimate $h(n)$ as well as possible.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/117.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Pyber \cite{Py87} has proved there exist constants $c_2>c_1>1$ such that $c_1^n<h(n)<c_2^n$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er97f} writes that the lower bound was already known to Isaacs.
References:
- [Er97f] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some unsolved problems. Combinatorics, geometry and probability (Cambridge, 1993) (1997), 1-10.
- [Py87] Pyber, L., The number of pairwise noncommuting elements and the index of the centre in a finite group. J. London Math. Soc. (2) (1987), 287-295.

computation:
- exact algebraic computations in a concrete group family tied to the EP condition.
- In tested dihedral cases, the computed minimum abelian-subgroup cover matched the maximal pairwise noncommuting subset size, giving a clean finite profile.
- Obstacle: EP-117 asks for worst-case asymptotic behavior across all groups under a global commutativity-threshold condition; small-family exact data gives structure but not the universal exponential-rate constant.
attempt:
Background cites Pyber and earlier lower-bound work proving constants \(c_2>c_1>1\) with \(c_1^n<h(n)<c_2^n\), so the growth type is already known to be exponential in \(n\).

The exact asymptotic rate, such as the sharp exponential base or finer secondary terms, is not determined by the cited references.

Target:
Determine sharp asymptotics of \(h(n)\), the minimal number of abelian subgroups
needed in the covering problem under bounded noncommuting-set size.
Step A: Structural reduction
Reduce to almost-simple / nilpotent-by-abelian decomposition classes with
uniform control on clique number of noncommuting graph.
Step B: Matching upper/lower entropy bounds
Prove exponential upper covers and exponential lower obstructions with matching
base.
Step C: Extremal family identification
Characterize families achieving the asymptotic base.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a universal inequality linking abelian-cover number to noncommuting-clique
number with asymptotically sharp constant factor.

Proposition AH1 (Graph-theoretic reformulation):
Let \(\Gamma_G\) be the noncommuting graph of a finite group \(G\). Then an
abelian-subgroup cover of \(G\) corresponds to a clique cover of the complement
\(\overline{\Gamma_G}\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Vertices commute exactly when adjacent in \(\overline{\Gamma_G}\). Any abelian
subgroup induces a clique in \(\overline{\Gamma_G}\), and covering elements by
abelian subgroups is equivalent to covering vertices by such cliques.
\(\square\)
Proposition AH2 (Reduction to extremal graph parameter):
If one proves, for all admissible \(G\),
\[
c_1^n \le \theta(\overline{\Gamma_G}) \le c_2^n
\]
with matching base \(c_1=c_2\), then \(h(n)\) has a sharp exponential rate.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By AH1, \(h(n)\) is exactly the extremal clique-cover number over the class.
Matching exponentials determine the base.
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $z_i$ be an infinite sequence of complex numbers such that $\lvert z_i\rvert=1$ for all $i\geq 1$, and for $n\geq 1$ let\[p_n(z)=\prod_{i\leq n} (z-z_i).\]Let $M_n=\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert p_n(z)\rvert$.

Is it true that $\limsup M_n=\infty$?

Is it true that there exists $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ we have $M_n > n^c$?

Is it true that there exists $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$,\[\sum_{k\leq n}M_k > n^{1+c}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/119.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
This is Problem 4.1 in \cite{Ha74} where it is attributed to Erd\H{o}s.

The weaker conjecture that $\limsup M_n=\infty$ was proved by Wagner \cite{Wa80}, who show that there is some $c>0$ with $M_n>(\log n)^c$ infinitely often.

The second question was answered by Beck \cite{Be91}, who proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that\[\max_{n\leq N} M_n > N^c.\]Erd\H{o}s (e.g. see \cite{Ha74}) gave a construction of a sequence with $M_n\leq n+1$ for all $n$. Linden \cite{Li77} improved this to give a sequence with $M_n\ll n^{1-c}$ for some $c>0$.

The third question seems to remain open.
References:
- [Be91] Beck, J., The modulus of polynomials with zeros on the unit circle: A problem of Erd\H{o}s. Annals of Math. (1991), 609-651.
- [Ha74] Hayman, W. K., Research problems in function theory: new problems. (1974), 155--180.
- [Li77] Linden, C. N., The modulus of polynomials with zeros on the unit circle. Bull. London Math. Soc. (1977), 65--69.
- [Wa80] Wagner, Gerold, On a problem of {E}rd\H{o}s in {D}iophantine approximation. Bull. London Math. Soc. (1980), 81--88.

computation:
Direct numerical evaluation of \(M_n=\max_{|z|=1}|\prod_{i\le n}(z-z_i)|\) was carried out on dense angle grids.

The finite profiles show strong strategy sensitivity: some constructions produce large spikes, while others keep moderate values for a substantial range before blow-up.

This numerical evidence does not settle the third EP question, namely whether \(\sum_{k\le n}M_k>n^{1+c}\) for all large \(n\), since that requires robust analytic lower bounds.

Split the problem into its three subquestions and tried to push from known pointwise lower bounds on M_n toward cumulative-growth bounds for \sum_{k \le n} M_k.

Hard point:
The remaining open part asks for a persistent lower bound on partial sums (\sum_{k \le n} M_k > n^{1+c} for all large n), which is much stronger than sporadic large spikes.

From the cited literature:
- Wagner proves \(\limsup M_n=\infty\).
- Beck proves a polynomial spike bound
 \[
 \max_{n\le N} M_n > N^c
 \]

So the first two subquestions are theorem-level resolved.
Remaining Open Subquestion:
Need eventual lower bound
\[
\sum_{k\le n} M_k > n^{1+c}
\]

Prove for some \(c>0\) and all large \(n\):
\[
\sum_{k\le n} M_k > n^{1+c}.

Upgrade \(\max_{k\le N}M_k>N^c\) to a counting statement:
there are at least \(N^\theta\) indices \(k\le N\) with \(M_k\ge N^\gamma\).
Step B: Scale-Consistent Lower Envelope
Show such indices occur across nested dyadic scales with controlled losses.
Step C: Summation Upgrade
Sum contributions from Step B to force superlinear power growth of partial sums.

Need a quantitative lower-density theorem for large \(M_n\)-events:
\[
|\{k\le N: M_k\ge N^\gamma\}|\ge N^\theta
\]
for fixed \(\gamma,\theta>0\) with \(\gamma+\theta>1\).

problem: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be an infinite set. Must there be a set $E\subset \mathbb{R}$ of positive measure which does not contain any set of the shape $aA+b$ for some $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $a\neq 0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/120.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The Erd\H{o}s similarity problem.

This is true if $A$ is unbounded or dense in some interval. It therefore suffices to prove this when $A=\{a_1>a_2>\cdots\}$ is a countable strictly monotone sequence which converges to $0$.

Steinhaus \cite{St20} has proved this is false whenever $A$ is a finite set.

This conjecture is known in many special cases (but, for example, it is open when $A=\{1,1/2,1/4,\ldots\}$, which is Problem 94 on Green's open problems list (https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf)). For an overview of progress we recommend a nice survey by Svetic \cite{Sv00} on this problem. A survey of more recent progress was written by Jung, Lai, and Mooroogen \cite{JLM24}.
References:
- [JLM24] Y. Jung and C.-K. Lai and Y. Mooroogen, Some recent progress on the Erd\H{o}s similarity conjecture. arXiv:2412.11062 (2024).
- [St20] Steinhaus, Hugo, Sur les distances des points dans les ensembles de measure positive. Fund. Math. (1920), 93-104.
- [Sv00] Svetic, R. E., The Erd\H{o}s similarity problem: a survey. Real Anal. Exchange (2000/01), 525-539.

forum_comments.author: Moritz Firsching
forum_comments.text:
We had formalised this statement and also Problem 94 from Green’s open problem set (and also Erdős problem 120) and accidentally forgot to require the set to be measurable, while still requiring a positive volume. A Google DeepMind prover agent found a Lean proof demonstrating that omitting the strict 'MeasurableSet' assumption (i.e. only asking for a set of positive outer Measure) in the specific problem that is also Green’s open problem 94, allows for an explicit counterexample. By treating $\mathbb{R}$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$, the formalization verified that the $\mathbb{Z}$-span of a Hamel basis entirely avoids affine copies of the sequence $\{1, \frac12, \frac14, \dots\}$. Because coordinates over this basis are unique, repeatedly halving them forces any sequence $a \cdot 2^{-n} + b$ with $a \neq 0$ to eventually leave the set. This pathological set possesses strictly positive outer measure, but it is not a measurable set. Details can be found in the formal proof here:
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/153d79d6c82c76fe1bee860742af800840c974d9/FormalConjectures/GreensOpenProblems/94.lean#L174
See also https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3526
This variant is not explicitly mentioned here, but it might be interesting nonetheless. Perhaps this is a one of the special cases previously known, pointers to the literature would be welcome!

However, de Reyna's proof is different, using transfinite induction. This is found (https://chatgpt.com/share/69b57974-7e9c-8010-b08f-0ce85df1647f) by GPT-5.4 Thinking.

Let \(A\subset\mathbb R\) measurable with upper density \(\delta>0\). Then for a
sequence of intervals \(I_N\), the discretizations \(A_N=A\cap I_N\) satisfy

|A_N|\ge (\delta-o(1))|I_N|.

\textit{Proof.}

problem: For which number theoretic functions $f$ is it true that, for any $F(n)$ such that $F(n)/f(n)\to 0$ for almost all $n$, there are infinitely many $x$ such that\[\frac{\#\{ n\in \mathbb{N} : n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}\to \infty?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/122.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er97} Erd\H{o}s is only considering number theoretic functions which grow 'slowly' (i.e. slower than $(\log n)^{1-c}$ for some $c>0$).

This is considered by Erd\H{o}s, Pomerance, and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy \cite{EPS97}, who prove in particular that if $\omega(n)$ counts the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$, then for all large $x$ there are intervals $I,J\subset [1,x]$ of width\[\lvert I\rvert\asymp \left(\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}\right)^{1/2}\]and\[\lvert J\rvert \asymp (\log\log x)^{1/2}\]such that if $n\in I$ then $n+\omega(n)\in J$. (Note the normal order of $\omega$ is $\log\log x$, and hence $(\log\log n)^{1/2}/\omega(n)\to 0$ for almost all $n$.)

In \cite{Er97} and \cite{Er97e} Erd\H{o}s reports that he, Pomerance, and S\'{a}rkz\"{o}zy can prove the more general claim above for $f$ being $\tau(n)$, the divisor function, or $\omega(n)$, and states it 'probably fails' for $\phi(n)$ or $\sigma(n)$.
References:
- [EPS97] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Pomerance, Carl and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy, Andr\'{a}s, On locally repeated values of certain arithmetic functions. IV. Ramanujan J. (1997), 227-241.
- [Er97] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems in number theory. New Zealand J. Math. (1997), 155-160.
- [Er97e] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite unsolved problems. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.

forum_comments.author: SkyYang
forum_comments.text:
I think I made a counterexample to this.

A short counterexample to the current online formulation of Problem #122.

Let\[
R(x):=\frac{\#\{n\in \mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}.
\]I am only addressing the current online version of problem#122 as written above. I am not claiming to have resolved the historical original problem behind Problem #122.

Assume throughout that\[
f:\mathbb{N}\to [0,\infty).
\]I claim that for every such nonnegative function \(f\), there exists an integer-valued function \(F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\) such that\[
\frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\to 0 \qquad (n\to\infty),
\]but at the same time\[
R(x)<2 \qquad \text{for every }x\in\mathbb{N}.
\]This shows that the current online formulation is false under any natural interpretation in which the displayed ratio is supposed to become arbitrarily large as \(x\) varies.

Indeed, define\[
F(n):=1+\left\lceil n^2+f(n)^2\right\rceil \qquad (n\in\mathbb{N}).
\]Then \(F(n)\in\mathbb{N}\) and\[
F(n)\ge 1+n^2+f(n)^2.
\]Hence\[
0\le \frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\le \frac{f(n)}{n^2+f(n)^2}.
\]By the elementary inequality\[
n^2+f(n)^2\ge 2nf(n),
\]we get\[
\frac{f(n)}{n^2+f(n)^2}\le \frac{1}{2n}.
\]Therefore\[
0\le \frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\le \frac{1}{2n}\to 0.
\]Now fix \(x\in\mathbb{N}\), and let\[
A_x:=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}.
\]If \(n\in A_x\), then\[
n+f(n)<x+F(x).
\]Since \(f(n)\ge 0\), it follows that\[
n\le n+f(n)<x+F(x).
\]Thus every element of \(A_x\) is a natural number strictly smaller than \(x+F(x)\). Consequently,\[
\#A_x\le x+F(x).
\]Dividing by \(F(x)\), we obtain\[
R(x)=\frac{\#A_x}{F(x)}\le 1+\frac{x}{F(x)}.
\]But\[
F(x)\ge 1+x^2+f(x)^2\ge 1+x^2,
\]so\[
R(x)\le 1+\frac{x}{x^2+1}<2.
\]Hence\[
\frac{\#\{n\in \mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}<2
\qquad \text{for all }x\in\mathbb{N}.
\]

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Yes, I think this is the correct interpretation: in [Er97] and [Er97e] there was just a typo (reproduced here) writing $f/F$ where they meant $F/f$. (Although this is more than just a typo in [Er97], since he explicitly states that the width of the interval (here denoted $F(x)$) 'tends to infinity faster than does [the normal order of $f$]'.

Further evidence is looking at what [EPS97] actually prove - they don't state it as a main result, but their methods prove (implicitly) that there is an interval $I\subset [1,O(x)]$ of width\[\asymp \left(\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}\right)^{1/2}\]such that if $n\in I$ then $n+\omega(n)$ is in $J$, where $J$ is an interval of width $O((\log\log x)^{1/2})$ (and the normal order of $\omega$ is $\log\log x$).

The motivation for this sort of problem is to generalise results like 'there are infinitely many $m$ such that $n+\omega(n)=m$ has many solutions'. In this formulation we replace $m$ with a short interval instead, and want many values of $n+\omega(n)$ in this interval.

As is the case with many of the problems stated in [Er97] and [Er97e] there are definitely some errors here; also in the description of the results obtained (which don't really appear in [EPS97]). I'll email Pomerance to see if he can clarify and/or provide other references.

Route:
Recast the statement as a local-overcrowding criterion for shifted arithmetic-function values under very weak almost-everywhere size assumptions.

The criterion is highly function-dependent and difficult to unify into a clean necessary-and-sufficient condition.

Let \(M_x(y)\) count \(n\) with \(x<n+f(n)\le x+F(x)\) and value \(y\). Then

\textit{Proof.}

problem:
For any $d\geq 1$ and $k\geq 0$ let $P(d,k)$ be the set of integers which are the sum of distinct powers $d^i$ with $i\geq k$. Let $3\leq d_1<d_2<\cdots <d_r$ be integers such that\[\sum_{1\leq i\leq r}\frac{1}{d_r-1}\geq 1.\]Can all sufficiently large integers be written as a sum of the shape $\sum_i c_ia_i$ where $c_i\in \{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,0)$?

If we further have $\mathrm{gcd}(d_1,\ldots,d_r)=1$ then, for any $k\geq 1$, can all sufficiently large integers be written as a sum of the shape $\sum_i c_ia_i$ where $c_i\in \{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,k)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/124.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 December 2025.
Site remarks:
The second question was conjectured by Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Graham, and Li \cite{BEGL96}, who proved it for $\{3,4,7\}$.

The first question was asked separately by Erd\H{o}s in \cite{Er97} and \cite{Er97e} (although there is some ambiguity over whether he intended $P(d,0)$ or $P(d,1)$ - certainly he mentions no gcd condition). A simple positive proof of the first question was provided (and formalised in Lean) by Aristotle (https://aristotle.harmonic.fun/) thanks to Alexeev; see the comments for details.

In \cite{BEGL96} they record that Pomerance observed that the condition $\sum 1/(d_i-1)\geq 1$ is necessary (for both questions), but give no details. Tao has sketched an explanation in the comments. It is trivial that $\mathrm{gcd}(d_1,\ldots,d_r)=1$ is a necessary condition in the second question.

Melfi \cite{Me04} gives a construction, for any $\epsilon>0$, of an infinite set of $d_i$ for which every sufficiently large integer can be written as a finite sum of the shape $\sum_i c_ia_i$ where $c_i\in \{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,0)$ and yet $\sum_{i}\frac{1}{d_i-1}<\epsilon$.

See also [125].
References:
- [BEGL96] Burr, S. A. and Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R. L. and Li, W. Wen-Ching, Complete sequences of sets of integer powers. Acta Arith. (1996), 133-138.
- [Er97] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems in number theory. New Zealand J. Math. (1997), 155-160.
- [Er97e] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite unsolved problems. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [Me04] Melfi, Giuseppe, On certain positive integer sequences. Riv. Mat. Univ. Parma (7) (2004), 253--260.

theorem erdos_124 : ∀ k, ∀ d : Fin k → ℕ,

 n = ∑ i, a i

G. Melfi in this paper (https://www.rivmat.unipr.it/fulltext/2004-3s/pdf/16.pdf) has given the following related result:

A sequence $S = \{s_1, s_2,...\}$ of positive integers is a complete sequence, if $\Sigma (S) := \Sigma^\infty_{i=1} \epsilon_i s_i$, for $\epsilon_i \in \{0,1\}, \Sigma_{i=1}^\infty \epsilon_i < \infty$ contains all sufficiently large integers. forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Just to clarify, Pomerance's observation that Diophantine approximation shows the necessity of $\sum_{a \in A} 1/(a-1) \geq 1$ only applies in the case of finite $A$, whereas Melfi's example is for infinite $A$. (In particular, the description of Pomerance's result in [p. 133, BEGL96] is not quite correct.)

Interestingly, (my reconstruction of) Pomerance's argument is almost identical to Gemini's failed heuristic argument: if $A$ is finite with $\sum_{a \in A} 1/(a-1) < 1$, then there will be infinitely many numbers $n$ that are larger than the sum of all the powers of $a$ preceding it (for this to hold, $n$ has to be slightly less than a power of $a$ for each $a$, which can be accomplished by the Kronecker approximation theorem). Hence $A$ cannot be complete.

This argument shows that the $\sum_{a \in A} 1/(a-1)=1$ case is quite delicate; at a bare minimum, it needs something like Baker's theorem to prevent powers of different $a$ from clustering too close together, which can create potential counterexamples. (And indeed, [p. 137, BEGL96] discusses this issue for specific sets such as {3,4,7}.)

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: As a further experiment, I gave this problem (in the weaker, solved formulation) to Gemini Deepthink with a hint to use Brown's criterion. Interestingly, it declared that it was unlikely that Brown's criterion was strong enough to solve this problem (https://gemini.google.com/share/55370d0a277d). Superficially this is of course a failure on the part of the AI, but an inspection of the reasoning showed that it was a fairly "honorable" mistake. It noted that if one took $d_1=3$ then infinitely often there should be no powers of any of the $d_i$ between $d_1^k$ and $d_1^{k+1}$, so that the ratio between consecutive elements could be as large as $3$. Typically, one needs the ratio of consecutive elements to be $2$ or less on the average for Brown's criterion to apply, so Gemini concluded that heuristically this approach was unlikely to work. This is not a bad analysis actually - it just so happens that the cumulative sum of all the other powers less than $d_1^k$ is (barely) enough to overcome this gap of $3$ and reach $d_1^{k+1}$ after all. I would classify this type of error as one which a human expert could plausibly also make on this problem. Also, I think this analysis also hints at why the stronger version of this problem is more difficult, and unlikely to be resolved by off-the-shelf tests such as Brown's criterion.

forum_comments.text:
Aristotle's solution is as follows. It is surprisingly easy.

Let $(a_n)$ be the sequence of powers of $d_i$ (sorted, with multiplicity). For example, if $d_1=2$ and $d_2=3$, then the sequences is: $1,1,2,3,4,8,9,16,27,\ldots$.

We want to show that every positive integer is a subsequence sum. This is equivalent to $a_{n+1} -1 \leq (a_1+\dots +a_n)$. The RHS is $\sum_{i=1}^k (d_i^{e_{i,n}}-1)/(d_i-1)$, where $e_{i,n}$ is the first power of $d_i$ that has not ocurred in the first $n$ terms. This is bounded below by $\min_i (d_i^{e_{i,n}}-1)$. However, $a_{n+1}=\min_i d_i^{e_{i,n}}$. Done.

Note, there is some ambiguity in the definition of $e_{i,n}$. In the example $d_1=2, d_2=3$, we can decide arbitrarily that $a_1$ is a power of $2$ and $a_2$ is a power of $3$, so $e_{2,1}=0$ but $e_{2,2}=1$.

Thank you tsaf for deciphering the proof! Interestingly, Theorem 2.3 from this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17593) could be thought of as a continuous-parameter loose variant of this problem and the basic proof outline (appearing on pages 13-14 in that paper) is the same: aiming to prove that the representations fill in an interval, sorting the sequence, verifying the continuous-parameter variant of condition $a_{n+1}\leq a_1+\cdots+a_n+1$, doing so by considering the first appearing term associated with each $d_i$, etc.

I am not mentioning this to diminish Aristotle's / BorisAlexeev's proof, on the contrary, it is quite beautiful! My point is that basic ideas reappear at many places; humans often fail to realize that they apply in a different setting, while a machine doesn't have this problem! I remember seeing this problem before and thinking about it briefly. I admit that I haven't noticed this connection, which is only now quite obvious to me!

problem:
Let $A = \{ \sum\epsilon_k3^k : \epsilon_k\in \{0,1\}\}$ be the set of integers which have only the digits $0,1$ when written base $3$, and $B=\{ \sum\epsilon_k4^k : \epsilon_k\in \{0,1\}\}$ be the set of integers which have only the digits $0,1$ when written base $4$.

Does $A+B$ have positive lower density?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/125.
- Page status: DISPROVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-03-30).
- Page last edited: 30 March 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Graham, and Li \cite{BEGL96}. In \cite{BEGL96} they ask whether this set has 'positive density? positive upper density?'. The formulation in \cite{Er97} is equivalent to asking about positive lower density only. It seems likely, and in keeping with the spirit of other similar questions and references, that Erd\H{o}s intended to ask about positive lower density: in other words, does there exist a constant $c>0$ such that $\lvert (A+B)\cap[1,x]\rvert\geq cx$ for all sufficiently large $x$?

More generally, if $n_1<\cdots<n_k$ have\[\sum_{i=1}^k\log_{n_k}(2)>1\]and $A_i$ is the set of integers with only the digits $0,1$ in base $n_i$ then does $A_1+\cdots+A_k$ have positive density? Melfi \cite{Me01} noted this is false as written, with a counterexample given by $\{3,9,81\}$, but suggests it is true if we further insist that the $n_k$ are pairwise coprime.

If $C=A+B$ then Melfi \cite{Me01} showed $\lvert C\cap[1,x]\rvert \gg x^{0.965}$ and Hasler and Melfi \cite{HaMe24} improved this to $\lvert C\cap [1,x]\rvert \gg x^{0.9777}$. Hasler and Melfi also show that the lower density of $C$ is at most\[\frac{1015}{1458}\approx 0.69616.\]An argument found by DeepMind (see the comment section) shows that the upper density is at least $6/5$ times the lower density; in particular $A+B$ cannot have positive density. DeepMind later improved this argument (https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/c27415379b5dbe34105d1fdd707994540c4c6fc7/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/125.lean#L468) to prove that the lower density has to be $0$: for any $\epsilon>0$ there are infinitely many $x$ such that $\lvert (A+B)\cap [1,x]\rvert <\epsilon x$.

See also [124].
References:
- [BEGL96] Burr, S. A. and Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R. L. and Li, W. Wen-Ching, Complete sequences of sets of integer powers. Acta Arith. (1996), 133-138.
- [Er97] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems in number theory. New Zealand J. Math. (1997), 155-160.
- [HaMe24] M. Hasler and G. Melfi, On sums of distinct powers of $3$ and $4$. Combinatorics and Number Theory (2024).
- [Me01] Melfi, Giuseppe, An additive problem about powers of fixed integers. Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo (2) (2001), 239--246.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Here is my understanding of the Lean argument, simplified somewhat using the Kronecker approximation theorem:

The set $A$ contains large gaps of the form $[3^k/2, 3^k)$; and $B$ similarly contains large gaps of the form $[4^m/3, 4^m)$.

Because of this, $A+B$ contains gaps of the form $[4^m/3+3^k/2, \min(3^k,4^m))$.

By the irrationality of $\log 4 / \log 3$ and the Kronecker approximation theorem, there will be infinitely many such gaps of length comparable to their scale; in fact one gets intervals of the form $[(\frac{5}{6}+o(1)) N, N)$ for arbitrarily large $N$. This forces the upper density to be at least $\frac{6}{5}$ times the lower density, which is incompatible with having a positive density. (It also gives an upper bound of $\frac{5}{6} = 0.833\dots$ for the lower density, which is weaker than the current record of $0.696\dots$ of Hasler and Melfi.)

So this does resolve the first formulation of the Erdos problem, but not the second.

EDIT: to put it another way, a priori there are four possibilities regarding the set $A+B$:

1. $A+B$ has zero upper and lower density (and hence also zero density).
2. $A+B$ has zero lower density, but positive upper density (and hence no density)
3. $A+B$ has positive upper and lower density that are equal (and hence positive density).
4. $A+B$ has positive upper and lower density that are unequal (and hence no density).

This argument eliminates Scenario 3, but makes no progress on determining which of the remaining Scenarios 1, 2, 4 is the truth.

forum_comments.text:
The DeepMind prover agent has now autonomously identified a proof in Lean that the lower density of A + B is zero, which rules out Scenario 4 as discussed here, and, if we understand correctly, fully solves the problem under Erdos’s intended interpretation. It uses a similar construction in the proof that eliminated Scenario 3 (A + B does not have positive density), as classified in this discussion here. We provide the proof at this link (https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/c27415379b5dbe34105d1fdd707994540c4c6fc7/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/125.lean#L468). Here is a summary of the new argument:

Our previous proof showed that since there are numbers of the form $3^k \approx 4^m \approx M$ where there is a big gap, $A+B$ cannot have a positive limit density. What this proof does is then look at the density of $A+B$ up to $M \cdot N_0$ for some number $N_0$. It aims to show that the density of $A+B$ up to $M \cdot N_0$ is at most 99% of the density of the set up to $N_0$. By repeating this step many times, it finds a sequence of scales where the density drops exponentially, implying that the lower density has to be zero. This 99% bound comes from a counting argument: any number below $M \cdot N_0$ can be split into its "top" digits and "bottom" digits, so one can map the elements of $A+B$ below $M \cdot N_0$ into a grid of $(y,c)$ coordinates. The number of choices for $y$ is given by the number of elements in $A+B$ below $N_0$, and the number of choices for $c$ is bounded by $5M/6$ because of the gap argument from our first proof.

Note that in the Lean proof (and in the agent’s work) there are references to results due to Pach and Pintz. We weren’t able to identify the literature the agent referenced, so we are unsure whether it exists or is a “hallucination”.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Very nice, congratulations! I was a little confused at first by your summary, so for those curious here is an alternative explanation. We want to go from density $<\delta$ at scale $N$ to density $<c\delta$ at some bigger scale $MN$, where $c<1$ is some fixed constant. Suppose we actually had $3^k=4^m=M$. If $n=a+b\leq MN$ then let $a_0$ be the $k$ 'bottom' bits of $a$ and $a_1$ the top bits, so $Ma_1=a-a_0$, and similarly for $b$, so that\[n=a+b\approx M(a_1+b_1)+a_0+b_0.\](The key point is that e.g. both $a_0$ and $a_1$ are also in $A$, since truncating to either the top or bottom digits preserves the property of being in $A$). Now there are $<\delta N$ choices for $a_1+b_1$ by assumption. But also\[a_0\leq 1+\cdots+3^{k-1}=\frac{3^k-1}{2}\approx M/2\]and similarly $b_0\leq M/3$, so $a_0+b_0$ is an integer at most $\frac{5}{6}M$, and so the number of choices is $\delta N\frac{5}{6}M$ as required.

(And the rest of the argument is some Diophantine technical fiddling about to get around the fact that we can't literally have $3^k=4^m$).

EDIT: This is quite similar to the arguments for [124] in the comment section that discuss whether all large integers can be written as the distinct sum of integers with only $0,1$ digits in base $d_i$, and in particular Tao's reconstruction of Pomerance's argument that $\sum \frac{1}{d_i-1}<1$ is a necessary condition. I believe this argument can be generalised to prove the stronger fact that if $\sum \frac{1}{d_i-1}<1$ then not only is not the case that all large integers are expressible in this way, but the lower density of such sums is actually $0$.

Yes, the argument does generalize to show that for bases $d_1,\dots,d_r$, $r \ge 2$, with $\sigma := \sum 1/(d_i-1) < 1$, the lower density of $S := A_1 + \dots + A_r$, where $A_i := \{ \sum \varepsilon_j d^j: \varepsilon_j \in \{0, 1\} \}$, is $\underline{d}(S) = 0$.

Note that there is no further restriction on the $d_i$ (repetition is even allowed).

By the simultaneous version of Dirichlet's approximation theorem, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there are $m_1,\dots,m_r$ and arbitrarily large $L$ such that $L \le d_i^{m_i} \le (1+\varepsilon)L$.

The rest of the argument goes through the same way as in my previous comment with appropriate but straightforward modifications.

Credit to GPT-5.4 Thinking for discussion (https://chatgpt.com/share/69cad1f3-29f8-839f-868f-a587a1312d33).

forum_comments.author: natso26
forum_comments.text:
Congrats!

Here's my version of the argument as I understand it. Credit to GPT-5.4 Thinking for the explanation (https://chatgpt.com/share/69caa68a-d52c-839d-82ba-0b4962e09633).

Let $D(N) = |(A+B)\cap [0,N)|/N$. We need to make $D(N)$ arbitrarily small.

Let $3^k$ and $4^m$ be close to each other. By Dirichlet’s approximation theorem, given $\varepsilon > 0$, with $L = \min(3^k, 4^m)$ we can make $3^k , 4^m < (1+\varepsilon)L$.

Fix $N$. Consider $D(LN)$. For $x < LN$, take $x = a+b$, $a \in A$, $b \in B$. Then
$$ x = Ly + c, $$
where
$$ \begin{align*}
y &= \lfloor a/3^k \rfloor + \lfloor b/4^m \rfloor, \\
c &= |3^k - 4^m| (\lfloor a/3^k \rfloor \text{ or } \lfloor b/4^m \rfloor) + a \bmod 3^k + b \bmod 4^m.
\end{align*} $$
Note $y < N$ and $y \in A+B$. Note $a \bmod 3^k \le 3^k/2$ and $b \bmod 4^m \le 4^k/3$ due to $a \in A$ and $b \in B$. And
$$ c \le (\varepsilon L)y + 3^k/2 + 4^m/3 \le ((5/6) (1+\varepsilon) +\varepsilon N)L. $$

Let $\delta > 0$. For fixed $N$, we can choose $\varepsilon > 0$ and hence $L := L(N)$, so that $c \le (5/6+\delta)L$. The injection $x \mapsto (y, c)$ then shows $D(LN) \le (5/6+\delta) D(N)$. By iterating, we can make $D(N)$ arbitrarily small.

In 1995, Paul Erdős wrote a letter including this problem to Kannan Soundararajan. He was kind enough to allow me to share a photo of this letter (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plby/lean-proofs/refs/heads/main/other/Erdos125.jpg) in this forum. Here is a transcription attempt:

"1995 II 14

[The University of Georgia Department of Mathematics]

Dear Mr Soundararajan.

Granville told me many good things about you, I hope to see you at the Halberstam meeting. I enclose a few papers with problems which might interest you. You can write here in care of Granville or Pomerance they will forward my mail or you can write Univ of Memphis Math Dept Memphis Tennessee.

Is it true that the integer of the form\[ \sum \varepsilon_i 3^i + \sum \delta_j 4^j,\qquad \varepsilon_i=0\text{ or }1,\quad \delta_j = 0\text{ or }1 \]is positive. We proved that if you add $\sum m_r 7^r$, $m_r = 0\text{ or }1$ then all large integers can be represented. I will try to send you a preprint.

Kind regards
E. P."

This letter does not shed light on the meaning of "positive density", as the specific sentence is even more confusingly-stated here. However, I thought the community might appreciate a small personal touch on this problem that saw some activity this week. (The description of [587] similarly includes a letter from Erdős to a young Terence Tao.) At the time of this letter, I was a child and would occasionally visit The University of Georgia Department of Mathematics, but sadly I do not recall meeting Paul.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
This seems to be corroborated by how subsequent authors interpreted the question. For instance, [Me01 (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02844979)] writes on page 240, "In [BEGL96] the following question is raised: what can we say about lower and upper asymptotic density of $\Sigma(\mathrm{Pow}(A;s))$ [a generalization of $A+B$] ... Erdos [personal communication] asked for a proof that $A+B$ has positive lower asymptotic density. In [BEGL96] the same question is raised."

Admittedly, the later paper [HaMe24 (https://libra.unine.ch/entities/publication/895211f4-d9da-4472-a058-c0bfd2b29e7c)] reverts back to the original wording of "positive asymptotic density" and "positive upper asymptotic density", but the only result in the paper concerning density (Proposition 5) involves lower asymptotic density only, and the proof of that result also relies on large gaps in $A+B$ which immediately contradict the existence of a positive density. Given that there was already one previous demonstration that the literal statement of the more general form of the problem was false on a technicality, re-interpreting the problem to involve lower and upper density instead of density and upper density also seems reasonable to me.

It might be helpful to look at how the problem is formulated in [Er97], though I have had difficulty locating this manuscript online.

problem: Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that if $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ has $\lvert A\rvert=n$ then $\prod_{a\neq b\in A}(a+b)$ has at least $f(n)$ distinct prime factors. Is it true that $f(n)/\log n\to\infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/126.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Investigated by Erd\H{o}s and Tur\'{a}n \cite{ErTu34} (prompted by a question of L\'{a}z\'{a}r and Gr\"{u}nwald) in their first joint paper, where they proved that\[\log n \ll f(n) \ll n/\log n\](the upper bound is trivial, taking $A=\{1,\ldots,n\}$). Erd\H{o}s says that $f(n)=o(n/\log n)$ has never been proved, but perhaps never seriously attacked.

This problem has been formalised in Lean (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/126.lean) as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/).
References:
- [ErTu34] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Turan, Paul, On a Problem in the Elementary Theory of Numbers. Amer. Math. Monthly (1934), 608-611.

The background gives the classical bounds \(\log n\ll f(n)\ll n/\log n\).

Target:
Show
\[
\frac{f(n)}{\log n}\to\infty,
\]
where \(f(n)\) is the guaranteed number of distinct prime divisors of
\(\prod_{a\ne b\in A}(a+b)\), \(|A|=n\).
Step A: Prime-support expansion
Prove many distinct residue classes mod \(p\) must appear among pair sums as
\(A\) varies.
Step B: Multiplicative large-sieve transfer
Convert residue-spread into lower bounds for number of contributing primes.
Step C: Uniform minimax extraction
Upgrade average prime-divisor growth to worst-case guaranteed growth over all
\(A\) of size \(n\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a minimax large-sieve inequality tailored to the pair-sum multiset
\(\{a+b:a\ne b\in A\}\).

Proposition AN1 (Prime divisor counting identity):
Let
\[
P_A=\prod_{a\ne b\in A}(a+b),\qquad \omega(P_A)=\#\{p:\ p\mid P_A\}.
\]
Then
\[
\omega(P_A)=\sum_{p} \mathbf 1_{\exists a\ne b,\ p\mid (a+b)}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By definition, \(p\mid P_A\) iff \(p\) divides at least one factor \(a+b\).
\(\square\)
Proposition AN2 (Reduction to prime-hit lower bounds):
If one proves that for every \(|A|=n\),
\[
\#\{p\le X:\exists a\ne b,\ p\mid(a+b)\}\ge \log n\cdot \omega_1(n),
\quad \omega_1(n)\to\infty,
\]
for some \(X=X(n)\), then \(f(n)/\log n\to\infty\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By AN1, \(f(n)\ge \omega(P_A)\) for worst-case \(A\), and the displayed bound
forces super-logarithmic growth.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices such that every induced subgraph on $\geq \lfloor n/2\rfloor$ vertices has more than $n^2/50$ edges. Must $G$ contain a triangle?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/128.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-10-31).
- Page last edited: 31 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Rousseau. The constant $50$ would be best possible as witnessed by a blow-up of $C_5$ or the Petersen graph.

Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp \cite{EFRS94} proved that this is true with $50$ replaced by $16$. More generally, they prove that, for any $0<\alpha<1$, if every set of $\geq \alpha n$ vertices contains $>\alpha^3n^2/2$ edges then $G$ contains a triangle.

Krivelevich \cite{Kr95} has proved this with $n/2$ replaced by $3n/5$ (and $50$ replaced by $25$).

Keevash and Sudakov \cite{KeSu06} have proved this under the additional assumption that either $G$ has at most $n^2/12$ edges, or that $G$ has at least $n^2/5$ edges. Norin and Yepremyan \cite{NoYe15} proved that this is true if $G$ has at least $(1/5-c)n^2$ edges, for some constant $c>0$.

Razborov \cite{Ra22} proved this is true if $\frac{1}{50}$ is replaced by $\frac{27}{1024}$.

See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/LocalEdgeDensities.html).
References:
- [EFRS94] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Faudree, R. J. and Rousseau, C. C. and Schelp, R. H., A local density condition for triangles. Discrete Math. (1994), 153--161.
- [KeSu06] Keevash, Peter and Sudakov, Benny, Sparse halves in triangle-free graphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2006), 614-620.
- [Kr95] Krivelevich, Michael, On the edge distribution in triangle-free graphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1995), 245-260.
- [NoYe15] Norin, Sergey and Yepremyan, Liana, Sparse halves in dense triangle-free graphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2015), 1--25.
- [Ra22] Razborov, A. A., More about sparse halves in triangle-free graphs. Mat. Sb. (2022), 119--140.

problem: Let $R(n;k,r)$ be the smallest $N$ such that if the edges of $K_N$ are $r$-coloured then there is a set of $n$ vertices which does not contain a copy of $K_k$ in at least one of the $r$ colours. Prove that there is a constant $C=C(r)>1$ such that\[R(n;3,r) < C^{\sqrt{n}}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/129.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Erd\H{o}s and Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, who proved the existence of some $C>1$ such that $R(n;3,r)>C^{\sqrt{n}}$. Note that when $r=k=2$ we recover the classic Ramsey numbers. Erd\H{o}s thought it likely that for all $r,k\geq 2$ there exists some $C_1,C_2>1$ (depending only on $r$) such that\[ C_1^{n^{1/k-1}}< R(n;k,r) < C_2^{n^{1/k-1}}.\]Antonio Girao has pointed out that this problem as written is easily disproved, and indeed $R(n;3,2) \geq C^{n}$:

The obvious probabilistic construction (randomly colour the edges red/blue independently uniformly at random) yields a 2-colouring of the edges of $K_N$ such every set on $n$ vertices contains a red triangle and a blue triangle (using that every set of $n$ vertices contains $\gg n^2$ edge-disjoint triangles), provided $N \leq C^n$ for some absolute constant $C>1$. This implies $R(n;3,2) \geq C^{n}$, contradicting the conjecture.

Perhaps Erd\H{o}s had a different problem in mind, but it is not clear what that might be. It would presumably be one where the natural probabilistic argument would deliver a bound like $C^{\sqrt{n}}$ as Erd\H{o}s and Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s claim to have achieved via the probabilistic method.

No references listed on the fetched LaTeX page.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Does anyone have a guess at a correct statement? The problem seems false for any $n, r$. Here's a GPT-5.2 construction:

Fix an integer $r\ge 2$. For infinitely many $n$ (namely $n\equiv 1$ or $3 \pmod 6$) there exists a Steiner triple system on $n$ points, equivalently a decomposition of the edges of $K_n$ into edge-disjoint triangles. Fix such an $n$, and write\[
t=\frac{\binom{n}{2}}{3}=\frac{n(n-1)}6
\]for the number of triangles in this decomposition. Let $N$ be a parameter and consider the complete graph $K_N$ on vertex set $[N]:=\{1,\dots,N\}$. Colour each edge of $K_N$ independently and uniformly at random with one of the colours $1,\dots,r$.

Fix an $n$-subset $S\subseteq [N]$ and a colour $c\in[r]$. Let $A_{S,c}$ be the event that $S$ contains no copy of $K_3$ in colour $c$ (i.e. the colour-$c$ subgraph induced by $S$ is triangle-free). Identifying $S$ with $\{1,\dots,n\}$, let $T_1,\dots,T_t$ be the $t$ edge-disjoint triangles given by the Steiner triple system. If $A_{S,c}$ holds then, in particular, none of the triangles $T_i$ is monochromatic of colour $c$. Since the $T_i$ are edge-disjoint and edge colours are independent, the events “$T_i$ is monochromatic of colour $c$” are independent, and for each $i$,\[
\mathbb P(T_i\text{ is monochromatic of colour }c)=r^{-3}.
\]Hence\[
\mathbb P(A_{S,c})
\le \mathbb P(\forall i,\ T_i \text{ is not monochromatic of colour }c)
=(1-r^{-3})^{\,t}.
\]Call $S$ bad if $A_{S,c}$ holds for at least one colour $c\in[r]$; this is exactly the kind of $n$-set whose existence the definition of $R(n;3,r)$ would force. By a union bound over $c$,\[
\mathbb P(S\text{ is bad})\le \sum_{c=1}^r \mathbb P(A_{S,c})\le r(1-r^{-3})^{\,t}.
\]Let $B$ be the number of bad $n$-subsets of $[N]$. By linearity of expectation and $\binom{N}{n}\le (eN/n)^n$,\[
\mathbb E[B]\le \binom{N}{n}\, r(1-r^{-3})^{\,t}\le \Bigl(\frac{eN}{n}\Bigr)^n\, r(1-r^{-3})^{\,t}.
\]Choose $N=\lfloor e^{\gamma n}\rfloor$ with $\gamma<\frac16\log\!\bigl(\frac1{1-r^{-3}}\bigr)$. Then\[
\log \mathbb E[B]\le n\log\Bigl(\frac{eN}{n}\Bigr)+\log r+t\log(1-r^{-3})
=\Bigl(\gamma-\frac16\log\!\Bigl(\frac1{1-r^{-3}}\Bigr)\Bigr)n^2+o(n^2),
\]so $\mathbb E[B]<1$ for all sufficiently large admissible $n$. Therefore there exists an $r$-colouring of $E(K_N)$ with $B=0$, i.e. every $n$-subset $S$ contains a monochromatic triangle in every colour.

For these $n$ we have $R(n;3,r)>N\ge e^{c_r n}$ for some constant $c_r>0$ (e.g. any $c_r<\frac16\log(\frac1{1-r^{-3}})$). This contradicts any asserted upper bound $R(n;3,r)<C(r)^{\sqrt n}$, since $\exp(c_r n)$ eventually dominates $\exp((\log C(r))\sqrt n)$ as $n\to\infty$. Thus, under the stated definition of $R(n;3,r)$, the inequality $R(n;3,r)<C(r)^{\sqrt n}$ is false as written.

attempt:
Counterexample route:
Fix any integer r >= 2.
For infinitely many n (n ≡ 1 or 3 mod 6), K_n decomposes into edge-disjoint triangles
(Steiner triple system), with
t = n(n-1)/6.
Fix such an n, and color edges of K_N independently and uniformly with r colors.
For a fixed n-subset S of vertices:
- The induced graph is K_n.
- Using the t edge-disjoint triangles of K_n, the events
 "triangle i is monochromatic in color c" are independent (for each fixed color c).
- Therefore
 P(S has no triangle of color c) <= (1 - r^{-3})^t.
- So
 P(S is bad) <= r(1-r^{-3})^t
 by union bound over colors c=1,...,r.
Let B be the number of bad n-subsets. Then
E[B] <= C(N,n) * r(1-r^{-3})^t.
Using C(N,n) <= (eN/n)^n, choose
N = floor(exp(gamma n)), with
gamma < (1/6) log(1/(1-r^{-3})).
Then
log E[B] <= n log(eN/n) + log r - t log(1/(1-r^{-3}))
has leading term
(gamma - (1/6)log(1/(1-r^{-3}))) n^2 < 0,
so E[B] < 1 for all sufficiently large admissible n.
Hence there exists an r-coloring of K_N with no bad n-subset, i.e.
every n-subset contains a monochromatic triangle in every color.
Therefore
R(n;3,r) > N >= exp(c_r n) (for some c_r>0, infinitely many admissible n).

Contradiction to the claimed upper bound:
If R(n;3,r) < C(r)^{sqrt(n)} held (for all large n, or all n), then for large admissible n we would have
exp(c_r n) <= R(n;3,r) < C(r)^{sqrt(n)},
impossible since c_r n >> sqrt(n).
So the EP-129 statement is false as written.

counterexample mechanism.

Step C: Growth classification
Determine whether \(R^\star\) is polynomial, \(e^{\Theta(\sqrt n)}\), or

Need a theorem identifying exactly which edge-disjoint-triangle decompositions
or quasirandom witnesses survive under the corrected definition.

Proposition AO1 (Original contradiction mechanism):
For fixed \(r\ge2\), if \(K_n\) admits a Steiner triple system and

Any claimed bound \(R(n;3,r)\le C^{\sqrt n}\) contradicts AO1 for admissible

AO1 gives \(R(n;3,r)\ge e^{c_r n}\) infinitely often, which dominates

problem: Let $F(N)$ be the maximal size of $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that no $a\in A$ divides the sum of any distinct elements of $A\backslash\{a\}$. Estimate $F(N)$. In particular, is it true that\[F(N) > N^{1/2-o(1)}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/131.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 September 2025.
Site remarks:
This was studied by Erd\H{o}s, Lev, Rauzy, S\'{a}ndor, and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy \cite{ELRSS99}, where they call such a property 'non-dividing', and prove the explicit bound\[F(N)<3N^{1/2}+1.\]In \cite{Er97b} Erd\H{o}s credits Csaba with a construction that proves $F(N) \gg N^{1/5}$. Such a construction was also given in \cite{ELRSS99}, where it is linked to the problem of non-averaging sets (see [186]).

Indeed, every such set is non-averaging, and hence the result of Pham and Zakharov \cite{PhZa24} implies\[F(N) \leq N^{1/4+o(1)}.\]This shows the answer to the original question is no, but the general question of the correct growth of $F(N)$ remains open.

In \cite{Er75b} Erd\H{o}s writes that he originally thought $F(N) <(\log N)^{O(1)}$, but that Straus proved that\[F(N) > \exp((\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\log 2}}+o(1))\sqrt{\log N}).\]See also [13].

This is discussed in problem C16 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.

problem: Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points. Must there be two distances which occur at least once but between at most $n$ pairs of points? Must the number of such distances $\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/132.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Asked by Erd\H{o}s and Pach. Hopf and Pannowitz \cite{HoPa34} proved that the largest distance between points of $A$ can occur at most $n$ times, but it is unknown whether a second such distance must occur.

It may be true that there are at least $n^{1-o(1)}$ many such distances. In \cite{Er97e} Erd\H{o}s offers \$100 for 'any nontrivial result'.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er84c} believed that for $n\geq 5$ there must always exist at least two such distances. This is false for $n=4$, as witnessed by two equilateral triangles of the same side-length glued together. Erd\H{o}s and Fishburn \cite{ErFi95} proved this is true for $n=5$ and $n=6$.

Clemen, Dumitrescu, and Liu \cite{CDL25} have proved that there always at least two such distances if $A$ is in convex position (that is, no point lies inside the convex hull of the others). They also prove it is true if the set $A$ is 'not too convex', in a specific technical sense.

See also [223], [756], and [957].

- [Er84c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some old and new problems in combinatorial geometry. Convexity and graph theory (Jerusalem, 1981) (1984), 129-136.

- [HoPa34] Hopf, H. and Pannwitz, E., Aufgabe 167. Jber. Deutsch. Math. Verein. (1934), 114.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
Hi all — I wanted to share a short update related to Erdős problem 132 (the “two distances with multiplicity in $[1,n]$” question).

In a brief note I verify the conjectured Erdős–Pach statement for $n=7$, and I also give a structural reduction for $n=8$.

For $n=7$: Let $A$ be a $7$-point set in the plane and let $m_A(d)$ be the multiplicity of distance $d$. If $|D(A)| \ge 4$, then it is impossible that at most one distance has multiplicity $\le 7$: indeed, if all but possibly one distance satisfy $m_A(d) \ge 8$, then
$21 = \sum_{d \in D(A)} m_A(d) \ge 1 + 3\cdot 8 = 25$,
a contradiction. Hence in this case there are at least two distances with multiplicity $\le 7$.

So we may assume $|D(A)| \le 3$. Also $|D(A)| \ne 2$ since planar $2$-distance sets have size at most $5$. Therefore $|D(A)| = 3$ and $A$ is a $7$-point $3$-distance set. Using the known classification of maximum planar $3$-distance sets of size $7$ (regular heptagon $R_7$ or the “regular hexagon + center” configuration $R_6^+$), one checks directly that in each configuration at least two distances have multiplicity $\le 7$. This completes the verification for $n=7$.

For $n=8$: A simple counting reduction shows that any counterexample must be extremely rigid. If $|D(A)| \ge 5$ and at most one distance has multiplicity $\le 8$, then
$28 = \sum_{d \in D(A)} m_A(d) \ge 1 + 4\cdot 9 = 37$,
contradiction, so any counterexample must satisfy $|D(A)| \le 4$. On the other hand $|D(A)|$ cannot be $3$ because $g(3)=7$ (no planar $3$-distance set has $8$ points). Hence a counterexample would have exactly $|D(A)| = 4$. Combining this with the diameter bound (there exists a distance with multiplicity $\le 8$; in particular the diameter has multiplicity $\le 8$), the only possible multiplicity profile is $\{1,9,9,9\}$, where the distance of multiplicity $1$ is the unique diameter and the other three distances occur exactly $9$ times each. In other words: an $n=8$ counterexample would have a unique diametral pair and the remaining $27$ pairs split into three distance classes of size $9$ each.

The note (with references and a small numerical appendix) is available here:
https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.26754.95684 (https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.26754.95684)

Any feedback or ideas for ruling out the $n=8$ profile $\{1,9,9,9\}$ would be very welcome — it seems like a promising “bottleneck” structure for a full solution.

forum_comments.text:
Looks like GPT-5.2 can do n=8 in a pretty straightforward way: Let $A\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a set of $8$ points. For $d>0$ define the multiplicity\[
m_A(d):=\bigl|\{\{x,y\}\subset A:\ |x-y|=d\}\bigr|
\]and let $D(A)$ be the set of distances determined by $A$.
We claim that there exist two distinct distances $d_1\neq d_2$ with
$1\le m_A(d_i)\le 8$ for $i=1,2$.

Assume for contradiction that at most one distance has multiplicity $\le 8$.
Since $\sum_{d\in D(A)} m_A(d)=\binom82=28$, if $|D(A)|\ge 5$ then\[
28=\sum_{d\in D(A)} m_A(d)\ge 1+4\cdot 9=37,
\]a contradiction. Hence a counterexample must satisfy $|D(A)|\le 4$.

It is known that there is no planar $3$-distance set of size $8$ (equivalently, $g_2(3)=7$),
so $|D(A)|\neq 3$. Therefore any counterexample must have $|D(A)|=4$.

Let $\Delta$ be the diameter of $A$. A classical diameter-graph lemma (Hopf--Pannwitz)
implies that in an $n$-point planar set the diameter occurs at most $n$ times; hence here
$m_A(\Delta)\le 8$. Under our counterexample assumption, $\Delta$ must be the unique
distance with multiplicity $\le 8$, so the remaining three distances have multiplicity
$\ge 9$. Since the total sum is $28$, this forces the multiplicity profile\[
\{m_A(d): d\in D(A)\}=\{1,9,9,9\},
\]in particular $m_A(\Delta)=1$ and $A$ has a unique diametral pair.

Now invoke the classification of planar $8$-point $4$-distance sets: up to similarity,
every such set is one of the following types:
(1) the regular octagon $R_8$;
(2) the regular heptagon together with its center $R_7^+$;
(3) the exceptional configuration shown in the classification (often drawn as a square
with four equilateral ''bumps'');
(4) an $8$-point subset of one of the classified $9$-point $4$-distance sets.

For each type one checks the distance multiplicities and finds at least two distinct
distances of multiplicity $\le 8$:
for $R_8$ the four distance classes have multiplicities $(8,8,8,4)$;
for $R_7^+$ all four distances have multiplicity $7$;
for the exceptional configuration two of the distances occur only twice;
and in the remaining finitely many $8$-subsets arising from the $9$-point parents,
the multiplicity tables show that no configuration has profile $\{1,9,9,9\}$.
This contradicts the forced profile above. Hence no counterexample exists, and every
$8$-point planar set determines at least two distances that occur in at most $8$ pairs.

forum_comments.author: Adam Zsolt Wagner
forum_comments.text:
The DeepMind prover agent has found a Lean proof for the difference variant (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos138.erdos_138.variants.difference) as formalised in Formal Conjectures. Formal proof here (https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/2f7fa0ebb45d77f02122a2d18059ecb72cc5a8a5/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/138.lean#L844).

An informal description of the proof is as follows. The argument is rather simple, once one knows what the right thing to prove is.

$\textbf{Claim}$: $W(k+1) \geq W(k) + k$

$\textbf{Proof}$: Given a 2-coloring of the first $W(k)-1$ integers without a monochromatic $k$-AP, we can extend it by $k$ further elements without creating a monochromatic $(k+1)$-AP by proceeding greedily. Adding new elements one by one, suppose we have validly colored up to $M$ (where $M < W(k)-1+k$); we simply color $M+1$ red if doing so doesn't create a red $(k+1)$-AP, and blue otherwise. The only way this algorithm could result in an invalid coloring is if both choices are blocked, meaning there is already a red $k$-AP with some step size $d_R$ and a blue $k$-AP with some step size $d_B$ such that the $(k+1)$-th element for both progressions lands exactly on $M+1$. But this is impossible. Because our original interval up to $W(k)-1$ has no monochromatic $k$-APs, these progressions must contain at least one newly added element, which bounds their step sizes to $d_R, d_B \le k-1$. Hence, if we step backward $d_B$ times along the red progression and $d_R$ times along the blue progression, both calculations land exactly on the positive integer $M + 1 - d_R d_B$, meaning this single point would have to be simultaneously colored red and blue, which is a contradiction.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Nice, thanks! This is quite a fun argument; it's interesting to compare this to the difference of consecutive Ramsey numbers (see [1030]).

Here you're taking advantage of the fact (which has no graph theoretic analogue as far as I can see) that any two arithmetic progressions of length $k$ and step size $<k$ with the same start/end point must have at least one other point in common. I don't recall seeing this nice fact used before, but I'm sure I'm wrong, and would be interested to see other applications.

EDIT: The obvious generalisation proves that\[W(k+1,l+1) \geq W(k,l)+\min(k,l).\]It's interesting to explore what this kind of argument can prove for the $r$-colour variant $W_r(k)$ (in which we want to $r$-colour the integers without any monochromatic $k$-AP). A naive first attempt proves\[W_r(k+1)-W_r(k)\geq k+r-1.\]

forum_comments.author: Abel
forum_comments.text:
It is well known that the existence of arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions of consecutive primes (CPAPs) is open unconditionally. The purpose of this post is to record a clean and explicit argument showing that the conjecture follows conditionally from Schinzel’s Hypothesis H (equivalently, Dickson’s conjecture for linear forms), using a Chinese Remainder Theorem construction to force all intermediate terms to be composite.

This implication is generally regarded as folklore; variants appear implicitly or explicitly in several places (see references below). I am posting this mainly as a self contained exposition.

Conditional theorem (Hypothesis H).

Assume Schinzel’s Hypothesis H (prime values of admissible systems of linear forms).
Then for every $k \ge 3$, there exist infinitely many $k$-term arithmetic progressions of consecutive primes.

Construction.

Fix $k \ge 3$, and let\[
d = k^\# = \prod_{p \le k} p
\]be the primorial.

Define the set of “between-term offsets”
$B := { r : 1 \le r \le (k-1)d - 1,\ d \nmid r }$.

For each $r \in B$, choose a distinct prime
$q_r > (k-1)d$,
and set
$M := \prod_{r \in B} q_r$.

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, choose an integer $b$ such that
$b + r \equiv 0 \pmod{q_r}$ for all $r \in B$,
and
$b \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ for every prime $p \le k$.

Define linear forms
$L_j(n) := Mn + b + jd$ for $j = 0,1,\dots,k-1$.

Properties.

Forced compositeness between terms.
For any $r \in B$,
$Mn + b + r \equiv 0 \pmod{q_r}$,
so every integer strictly between consecutive terms of the progression is composite.

Admissibility.
The system ${L_0,\dots,L_{k-1}}$ has no fixed prime divisor:

– If $p \le k$, then $p \mid d$ and $L_j(n) \equiv b \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$.

– If $p \mid M$, then $p = q_r$ for some $r \in B$, and
$L_j(n) \equiv b + jd \equiv -r + jd \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$,
since $q_r > (k-1)d$.

– If $p > k$ and $p \nmid M$, there are at most $k < p$ forbidden residue classes of $n \pmod p$.

Prime values.
By Schinzel’s Hypothesis H, there exist infinitely many $n$ such that all $L_j(n)$ are prime.

Conclusion.
For such $n$, the primes
$L_0(n), L_1(n), \dots, L_{k-1}(n)$
form an arithmetic progression of length $k$ with common difference $d$, and every integer between consecutive terms is composite. Hence they are $k$ consecutive primes.
Thus, conditional on Hypothesis H, CPAPs of arbitrary length exist.

References / attribution.

Schinzel–Sierpiński (1958), Sur certaines hypothèses concernant les nombres premiers, Acta Arith.

Dubner–Forbes–Lygeros–Mizony–Nelson–Zimmermann (2001), Consecutive primes in arithmetic progression, Math. Comp.

MathOverflow discussion noting the conditional implication as folklore:
https://mathoverflow.net/questions/187096/

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
forum_comments.text:
It's worth noting that if the Hardy-Littlewood prime $k$-tuples conjecture is true, then if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is admissible, then there are infinitely many translations of $A$ into sets of consecutive primes. To see this, let $n_1$ be an element that is in between elements of $A$ but not in $A$ itself, and let $k_1$ be larger than $|A|$. Then we can construct a set $B_1$ by adding elements larger than those in $A$ in a way that preserves admissibility and occupies every residue class of $k_1$ except for the residue class of $n_1$. Then, let $n_2$ be another element in between elements of $A$ that's not in $A$ itself, let $k_2 > |A \cup B_1|$, create $B_2$ similarly, and repeat until each $n_i$ is taken care of.

Let $B$ be the union of all $B_i$. Then the elements of $B$ are all greater than the elements in $A$, $A \cup B$ is admissible, and (with at most finitely many exceptions) any translation of $A \cup B$ into the primes cannot have any primes in between elements of $A$ except for the elements of $A$ themselves. If the prime $k$-tuples conjecture is true, then $A \cup B$ has infinitely many translations into the primes, which completes the proof.

(Side note: I wouldn't be surprised if this argument already appears in the literature somewhere; please do let me know if that's the case. EDIT: Dogmachine has found a reference - thanks!)
