Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s remarked this is 'probably unattackable at present'. In \cite{Er97c} Erd\H{o}s offered \$1000, but given that he elsewhere offered \$5000 just for (essentially) showing that $r_k(N)=o_k(N/\log N)$ (see [3]), that value seems odd. In \cite{Er81} he offers \$10000, stating it is 'probably enormously difficult'.

The best known upper bounds for $r_k(N)$ are due to Kelley and Meka \cite{KeMe23} for $k=3$, Green and Tao \cite{GrTa17} for $k=4$, and Leng, Sah, and Sawhney \cite{LSS24} for $k\geq 5$. An asymptotic formula is still far out of reach, even for $k=3$.

In \cite{Er80} and \cite{Va99} he asks (much more reasonably) for the order of magnitude of $r_k(N)$. In \cite{Er80} he remarks that we do not even know whether $r_k(n)/r_{k+1}(n)\to 0$ for any $k\geq 3$.

r_k(MN)\ge r_k(M)\,r_k(N).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Take product-type constructions on digit expansions/base decomposition; AP-free
property is preserved under the standard combinatorial product embedding.
\(\square\)
Proposition AU2 (Exponent-gap reduction):
If
\[
N^{\alpha_k-o(1)}\le r_k(N)\le N^{\beta_k+o(1)},
\]
then improving either \(\alpha_k\) upward or \(\beta_k\) downward directly narrows
the asymptotic uncertainty interval.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Normalize by \(\log N\): \(\log r_k(N)/\log N\in[\alpha_k-o(1),\beta_k+o(1)]\).
\(\square\)

problem: Let $A\subset (1,\infty)$ be a countably infinite set such that for all $x\neq y\in A$ and integers $k\geq 1$ we have\[ \lvert kx -y\rvert \geq 1.\]Does this imply that $A$ is sparse? In particular, does this imply that\[\sum_{x\in A}\frac{1}{x\log x}<\infty\]or\[\sum_{\substack{x <n\\ x\in A}}\frac{1}{x}=o(\log n)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/143.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 24 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Note that if $A$ is a set of integers then the condition implies that $A$ is a primitive set (that is, no element of $A$ is divisible by any other), for which the convergence of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n\log n}$ was proved by Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er35}, and the upper bound\[\sum_{\substack{x <n\\ x\in A}}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}\]was proved by Behrend \cite{Be35}. This $O(\cdot)$ bound was improved to a $o(\cdot)$ bound by Erd\H{o}s, S\'{a}rk\H{o}zy, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{ESS67}.

In \cite{Er73} and \cite{Er77c} Erd\H{o}s mentions an unpublished proof of Haight that\[\lim \frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{x}=0\]holds if the elements of $A$ are independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Over the years Erd\H{o}s asked for various different quantitative estimates, for example\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{x}=0\]or even (motivated by Behrend's bound)\[\sum_{\substack{x <n\\ x\in A}}\frac{1}{x}\ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}.\]In \cite{Er97c} he offers \$500 for resolving the questions in the main problem statement above.

This was partially resolved by Koukoulopoulos, Lamzouri, and Lichtman \cite{KLL25}, who proved that we must have\[\sum_{\substack{x <n\\ x\in A}}\frac{1}{x}=o(\log n).\]See also [858].
References:
- [Be35] Behrend, F., On sequences of numbers not divisible by another. London Math. Soc. Journal (1935), 42-45.
- [ESS67] Erd\H{o}s, P. and S\'{a}rk\"ozy, A. and Szemer\'{e}di, E., On a theorem of Behrend. J. Austral. Math. Soc. (1967), 9--16.
- [Er35] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Note on Sequences of Integers No One of Which is Divisible By Any Other. J. London Math. Soc. (1935), 126-128.
- [Er73] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. A survey of combinatorial theory (Proc. Internat. Sympos., Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, Colo., 1971) (1973), 117-138.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I think I can use the flow method used in one of the proofs of [1196] to reprove Behrend's bound $\sum_{n \in A; n \leq x} \frac{1}{n} \ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}$ when $A$ consists of natural numbers (incidentally, the constraint $n \in A$ is currently missing in the statement of Behrend's bound).

On the squarefree numbers $n \leq x$, create a flow by setting $w(np \mapsto n) = \frac{1}{np} \frac{\omega(n)!}{(\sum_{p \leq x} 1/p)^{\omega(n)+1}}$, where $\omega(n)$ is the number of prime factors of $n$. At any $1 < n \leq x$, the net outflow of $n$ is $\frac{1}{n} \frac{\omega(n)!}{(\sum_{p \leq x} 1/p)^{\omega(n)}}$, which is at least the net inflow; and at $1$ the net inflow is at most $1$. The discrete divergence theorem then gives the inequality
$$ \sum_{n \in A, n \leq x, \mathrm{squarefree}} \frac{1}{n} \frac{\omega(n)!}{(\sum_{p \leq x} 1/p)^{\omega(n)}} \leq 1. \tag{1}$$
From Stirling's formula and Mertens' theorem one has $\frac{\omega(n)!}{(\sum_{p \leq x} 1/p)^{\omega(n)}} \gg \frac{\sqrt{\log\log x}}{\log x}$, giving Behrend's inequality for the squarefree $n$. (This gain over Behrend is analogous to the gain of the LYM inequality over Sperner's inequality.) The remaining $n$ can be dealt with by factoring out the maximal square factor $d^2$ and achieving a similar bound (with a gain of $1/d^2$) for each such value of $d$.

The Stirling formula also produces a factor of $\sqrt{2\pi}$ that also appears in a refinement of Behrend's bound proven by Erdos, Sarkozy, and Szemeredi (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1967-10.pdf). This is probably not a coincidence.

I think the same sort of argument works to give the more general estimate of Ahlswede, Khatchatrian, and Sarkozy (https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/ahlswede/homepage/public/178.pdf) that $\sum_{n \in A, y \leq n \leq yx} \frac{1}{n} \ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}$ for any $x,y \geq 1$ and primitive set $A$ of integers; one now has to restrict $\omega(n)$ to only count prime factors up to $x$.

EDIT: I can remove the squarefree restriction in (1), thus giving the Erdos-Sarkozy-Szemeredi bound $\sum_{n \in A; n \leq x} \frac{1}{n} \leq (\sqrt{2\pi}+o(1)) \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}$ from Stirling and Mertens. Here it is convenient to go back to the Markov chain approach. Consider a chain that starts at $1$ and jumps from $n$ to $nq$ with probability $\frac{1/q}{\sum_{q' \leq x} 1/q'}$ where $q,q'$ are restricted to be prime powers that are at most $x$. This chain hits $A$ at most once, but each $n$ is hit with probability at least $\frac{1}{n} \frac{\omega(n)!}{(\sum_{q \leq x} 1/q)^{\omega(n)}}$, by considering the $\omega(n)!$ ways to split $n$ as the product of distinct prime powers. The claim follows. UPDATE: Actually it looks like one doesn't quite get the sharp constant $\sqrt{2\pi}$ by this approach.

forum_comments.text:
I have carefully read [Ko14] and found that equation (4) in [Ko14] seems incorrect, because the equality right above it, namely\[
\frac{1}{2^{3^k} - 2^{3^{k-1}}}
= \frac{1}{2^{3^k}} + \frac{1}{2^{3^k} + 2^{3^{k-m}}} + \frac{1}{2^{3^{k+m}} + 2^{3^k}},
\]is false, regardless of whether \(m\) appears in the exponent of 3 or not. I could not find a way to fix this step.

However, the result of Elsholtz (arXiv:1606.02117v1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02117v1)) actually covers the bound stated in [Ko14], so the lower bound’s order of magnitude remains correct. Therefore, I suggest that the statement “The lower bound is due to Konyagin [Ko14]” should also cite Elsholtz’s result.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Based on this comment I have sent an e-mail to Sergei Konyagin, and he kindly responded to me. He agreed that the equation you referred to was indeed a mistake. The corrected equation is
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2^{3^k} - 2^{3^{k-1}}} &= \frac{1}{2^{3^k}} + \frac{1}{(2^{2 \times 3^{k-1}}-1)2^{3^k}} \\
&= \frac{1}{2^{3^k}} + \frac{1}{(2^{2 \times 3^{k-1}}-1)(2^{3^k}+2^{3^k-m})} + \frac{1}{(2^{2 \times 3^{k-1}}-1)(2^{3^k}+2^{3^k+m})}. \hspace{10pt} (1)
\end{align*}He further explained that he made a few more small mistakes (e.g. the statement of Lemma $1$ in his paper should contain the assumption that $m$ is odd), but the main result still holds. In any case, the point of equation $(1)$ is that the final two denominators are divisible by $2^m + 1$, which by his Lemma $1$ has many divisors, eventually leading to the claimed lower bound on $F(k)$.

problem:
The strong chromatic index of a graph $G$, denoted by $\mathrm{sq}(G)$, is the minimum $k$ such that the edges of $G$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets of 'strongly independent' edges, that is, such that the subgraph of $G$ induced by each set is the union of vertex-disjoint edges.

Is it true that, for any graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$,\[\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/149.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Asked by Erd\H{o}s and Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il in 1985 (see \cite{FGST89}). This is equivalent to asking whether the chromatic number of the square of the line graph $L(G)^2$ is at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$. This bound would be the best possible, as witnessed by a blowup of $C_5$, although improvements may be possible for odd $\Delta$.

It is easy to see that $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 5$ when $\Delta\leq 2$: in general, the trivial bound of\[\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 2\Delta^2-2\Delta+1\]follows from the observations that the number of neighbours of any edge of $G$ is $\leq 2\Delta^2-2\Delta$.

This was improved to $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 1.998\Delta^2$ (for $\Delta$ sufficiently large) by Molloy and Reed \cite{MoRe97}. This was improved to $1.93\Delta^2$ by Bruhn and Joos \cite{BrJo18} and to $1.835\Delta^2$ by Bonamy, Perrett, and Postle \cite{BPP22}. The best bound currently available is\[1.772\Delta^2,\]proved by Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang \cite{HJK22}. Mahdian has, in their Masters' thesis (https://utoronto.scholaris.ca/server/api/core/bitstreams/db30068f-ef0a-4ace-b77c-e5e364ee3120/content), proved an upper bound of $(2+o(1))\frac{\Delta^2}{\log \Delta}$ under the additional assumption that $G$ is $C_4$-free.

Andersen \cite{92} and Hor\'{a}k, He, and Trotter \cite{HHT93} have independently shown that $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 10$ when $\Delta\leq 3$. (This is best possible, as shown e.g. by a $C_8$ with all four diagonals). Huang, Santana, and Yu \cite{HSY18} proved that $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 21$ when $\Delta\leq 4$.

Erd\H{o}s and Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il also asked the easier problem of whether $G$ containing at least $\tfrac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ many edges implies $G$ containing two strongly independent edges. This was proved by Chung, Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, Tuza, and Trotter \cite{CGTT90}.

It is still open even whether the clique number of $L(G)^2$ at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$. Let $\omega=\omega(L(G)^2)$ be this clique number. \'{S}leszy\'{n}ska-Nowak \cite{Sl16} proved $\omega \leq \frac{3}{2}\Delta^2$. Faron and Postle \cite{FaPo19} proved $\omega\leq \frac{4}{3}\Delta^2$. Cames van Batenburg, Kang, and Pirot \cite{CKP20} have proved $\omega\leq \frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ under the additional assumption that $G$ is triangle-free (and $\omega\leq \Delta^2$ if $G$ is $C_5$-free).

forum_comments.author: Alfaiz
forum_comments.text:
M. Dębski and M. Śleszyńska-Nowak have shown in this paper(2022) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195669822000038) that the maximum size of a strong clique in a circle graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ is at most $\frac{5}{4} \Delta^2$.

Note: The bound is tight for even $\Delta$ and correct up to a smaller order error term for odd $\Delta$.

Also, [Sl15] is unable to load any reference.

Edit: A special case of this conjecture has been settled by P. Horak, H. Qing and W.T. Trotter in "Induced matchings in cubic graphs"(1993) (https://trotter.math.gatech.edu/papers/85.pdf). They show that the edge set of a cubic graph can always be partitioned into 10 subsets, each of which induces a matching in the graph.

The same result was proven independently by Andersen in "The strong chromatic index of a cubic graph is at most 1"(1992) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/b/s/science/article/pii/0012365X92906789/pdf?brr=9a71a6a719c858bb&md5=ea14b75125154b24e7d7cf584fa94107&pid=1-s2.0-0012365X92906789-main.pdf).

Other problems on chromatic numbers have been discussed here too: https://utoronto.scholaris.ca/server/api/core/bitstreams/db30068f-ef0a-4ace-b77c-e5e364ee3120/content

forum_comments.author: Wouter CvB
forum_comments.text:
Indeed, excluding a bipartite graph generally has a much stronger effect compared to excluding a non-bipartite graph. It forces the graph to become sparse (few edges; compare the Erdős-Stone theorem). So it makes sense that excluding a four-cycle changes the optimal answer a lot for this problem as well. Incidentally, Vu (2002) (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548301004898)extended Mahdian's result as follows: $\chi(L(G)^2) \leq C_H \frac{\Delta^2}{\log \Delta}$ when a fixed bipartite graph $H$ is excluded, which is sharp up to optimizing the constant $C_H$.

For cliques, a similar effect occurs; if you exclude a fixed even cycle from $G$, the best possible upper bound on $\omega(L(G)^2)$ becomes linear in $\Delta$, rather than quadratic, see e.g.Cho, Choi, Kim and Park (2021) (https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.22700).
Probably $\omega(L(G)^2)\leq C_H \Delta$ still holds when any fixed bipartite graph $H$ is excluded, but actually I can't remember right now whether that has been studied.

forum_comments.author: Wouter CvB
forum_comments.text:
Equivalently, this asks whether the chromatic number of the square of the line graph $L(G)^2$ of $G$ is at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$.

It is even still open whether the clique number of $L(G)^2$ is at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$.
The mentioned result of Chung-Trotter and Gyárfás-Tuza constituted a proof for the special case where $G$ does not contain two strongly independent edges, i.e. if $L(G)^2$ is a complete graph.
For general $G$, the current best upper bound is $\frac{4}{3} \Delta^2$ (https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.22452).
The bound $\frac{5}{4} \Delta^2$ is also sharp and true if $G$ is triangle-free (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indag.2019.09.003).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

Finite compute signal:
 - For $C_5$ blowups ($t=2,3,4$), greedy strong-color counts hit exactly $(5/4)\Delta^2$ in tested instances.

 - Classical extremal witness behavior is reproduced, and generic random graphs do not approach the conjectural worst case.

problem:
For a graph $G$ let $\tau(G)$ denote the minimal number of vertices that include at least one from each maximal clique of $G$ on at least two vertices (sometimes called the clique transversal number).

Let $H(n)$ be maximal such that every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices contains an independent set on $H(n)$ vertices.

If $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices then is\[\tau(G)\leq n-H(n)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/151.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 02 December 2025.
Site remarks:
It is easy to see that $\tau(G) \leq n-\sqrt{n}$. Note also that if $G$ is triangle-free then trivially $\tau(G)\leq n-H(n)$.

This is listed in \cite{Er88} as a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Gallai, who were unable to make progress even assuming $G$ is $K_4$-free. There Erd\H{o}s remarked that this conjecture is 'perhaps completely wrongheaded'.

It later appeared as Problem 1 in \cite{EGT92}.

The general behaviour of $\tau(G)$ is the subject of [610].
References:
- [EGT92] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Gallai, Tibor and Tuza, Zsolt, Covering the cliques of a graph with vertices. Discrete Math. (1992), 279-289.
- [Er88] Erd\H{o}s, P, Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and graph theory. Discrete Math. (1988), 81-92.

computation:
- exact enumeration for H(n) and exact clique-transversal computation on sampled graphs.
- In the tested small-n regime, no violation was observed (\tau(G)\le n-H(n) held with worst observed gap 0).
- Obstacle: this does not resolve the asymptotic conjecture; the open part concerns arbitrary large graphs and potential extremal counterexamples.
attempt:
Route:
Compared the target bound \tau(G) \le n-H(n) to standard clique-transversal/independence reductions.

Useful reduction:
For any graph G, taking the complement of a maximum independent set gives
\tau(G) \le n-\alpha(G) (this hits every clique of size at least 2).
So the conjecture would follow from \alpha(G)\ge H(n), which fails in general because H(n) is defined via triangle-free extremal behavior.

Hard point:
No mechanism found to transfer triangle-free independence guarantees into clique-transversal control for arbitrary graphs; background already warns the conjecture may be wrongheaded.

Target:
Determine validity of
\[
\tau(G)\le n-H(n)
\]
for all \(n\)-vertex graphs \(G\), or construct a true asymptotic counterexample.
Step A: Extremal reduction
Reduce to graphs minimizing \(\alpha(G)\) under fixed clique-transversal
requirements.
Step B: Dual LP / hypergraph-transversal formulation
Model clique hitting as a transversal problem in the clique hypergraph and
analyze fractional-integral gap.
Step C: Transfer to \(H(n)\)
Either prove the integral gap is bounded tightly enough to force the inequality,
or amplify it into a family violating the bound.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp integrality-gap bound between fractional and integral clique
transversals in dense triangle-rich regimes.

Proposition BA1 (Basic upper bound):
For any graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices,
\[
\tau(G)\le n-\alpha(G).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Let \(I\) be a maximum independent set. Then \(V(G)\setminus I\) meets every
clique of size at least \(2\), so it is a clique transversal.
\(\square\)
Proposition BA2 (Reduction criterion):
If one proves \(\alpha(G)\ge H(n)\) for all \(n\)-vertex graphs in the relevant
extremal class, then \(\tau(G)\le n-H(n)\) follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Combine BA1 with the hypothesis.
\(\square\)

problem: For any $M\geq 1$, if $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ is a sufficiently large finite Sidon set then there are at least $M$ many $a\in A+A$ such that $a+1,a-1\not\in A+A$.

This is true; in fact there are at least $(1-o(1))\lvert A+A\rvert$ many such $a\in A+A$. A proof of (a slightly weaker statement) was found by DeepMind using an elementary argument. Independently, Bloom noted (see the comments) that in fact this strong statement already follows from an argument in \cite{ESS94}, which shows that, for any $d\neq 0$,\[\lvert (A+A)\cap (A+A+d)\rvert \leq 2\lvert A\rvert^{3/2}.\]

forum_comments.author: GTsoukalas
forum_comments.text:
The DeepMind prover agent has proved the main part (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos152.erdos_152) of the problem as formalised in Formal Conjectures repo.
The formal proof can be found here (https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/29c60aa79729701905cf9e92517af23f588971f2/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/152.lean#L485).

Here’s an attempt to summarize the proof informally:

For a Sidon set $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ of size $n$, let $I(A+A)$ count the isolated elements of the sumset — those $s \in A+A$ with $s \pm 1 \notin A+A$. Define $f(n)$ as the minimum of $I(A+A)$ over all Sidon sets of size $n$.

Theorem. $f(n) \geq (n^2 - 100n - 16)/16$, so in particular $f(n) \to \infty$.

The proof establishes, for every Sidon set $A$ of size $n$:
$$16 \cdot I(A+A) + 100n + 16 \geq n^2. \qquad (\star)$$
We denote $N_k(X) := |{x \in X : x+k \in X}|$, $V_2(X) := |{x \in X : x \pm 1 \in X}|$ (interior points),
and $I(X)$ for the isolated points of $X$.

Let $X \subset \mathbb{Z}$. We will employ the following three facts:

1. $I(X) + 2N_1(X) = |X| + V_2(X)$, by partitioning elements by neighbor count.
2. (Indicator Inequality) $4N_1(X) + N_3(X) \leq 3|X| + 2N_2(X)$, proved by verifying a pointwise inequality on $\{0,1\}$-valued indicator functions and summing.
3. $2N_2(X) \leq N_3(X) + 2V_2(X) + 2I(X)$, obtained by splitting the "distance-2" pairs into those bridged by $x+1 \in X$ (counted by $V_2$) and gap patterns ${x, x+2} \subset X$ with $x+1 \notin X$, then bounding the latter via boundary analysis.

Next, for each $k \geq 1$, count quadruples $(a,b,c,d) \in A^4$ with $a + b + k = c + d$. Rewriting as $a - c = d - b - k$ and partitioning by $\delta = a - c$ yields the following two quadruple transfer bounds:

4. The cases $\delta = 0$ and $\delta = -k$ each contribute $\leq |A|$ (one coordinate determines the rest). All other $\delta$ inject into ${x \in D : x+k \in D}$ where $D = A - A$, by the Sidon property. Total: $|\text{quad}_k| \leq N_k(D) + 2n$.
5. Each "good" element $s \in S$ with $s + k \in S$ (excluding $\leq 2n$ doubles of the form $2a$) produces $\geq 4$ quadruples. Total: $4N_k(S) \leq |\text{quad}_k| + 8n$.

Combining these bounds shows that $N_k(D)$ and $N_k(S)$ are related up to $O(n)$ error.

Next, apply the indicator inequality (2) to $D = A - A$ and substitute the quadruple transfer bounds (4, 5) for $k = 1, 2, 3$, then use identities (1) and (3) on $\bar{S}$. A key cancellation occurs: the $N_3$, $V_2$, and $N_1$ terms all eliminate, leaving
$$16,I(\bar{S}) + 100n \geq 8|S| - 3|D|.$$
The standard Sidon estimates $|S| \geq n^2/2$ and $|D| \leq n^2$ then give $16I + 100n \geq 4n^2 - 3n^2 = n^2$, accounting for a boundary correction of $+16$ at zero yields $(\star)$. $\blacksquare$

That also clearly answers the question “There may even be $\gg \lvert A\rvert^2$ many such $a$.”, and we formalised the proof of that (https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/ff58c933d53bb807bf85d98a47402703f9f14ed3/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/152.lean#L496) by hand.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Nice! By a strange coincidence I was looking at this yesterday, and think that in fact a positive answer already follows from the methods in [ESS94], although they did not seem to notice this.

I'm not sure why they asked this question given that their methods could already settle it; they seem to have been mainly thinking about infinite Sidon sets, so perhaps they missed this. (Or, of course, perhaps I am mistaken!)

Let $A$ be a finite Sidon set of size $n$. If one examines the proof of their Theorem 2 (in fact the simpler finite case) this shows that that, for any $d\neq 0$\[\lvert (A+A)\cap (A+A+d)\rvert\leq 2n^{3/2}.\]In particular the number of $x\in A+A$ such that either $x+1\in A+A$ or $x-1\in A+A$ is at most $4n^{3/2}$, and so\[ I(A+A)\geq \lvert A+A\rvert-4n^{3/2}.\](Which is $\gg n^2$ since $\lvert A+A\rvert =\binom{n}{2}+n$.)

This is a stronger bound than the DeepMind bound (i.e. $I(A+A)\geq (1/2+o(1))n^2$ rather than $I(A+A)\geq (1/16+o(1))n^2$), although since both proofs are short and elementary I expect that the DeepMind proof can be upgraded to give a similar asymptotic.

The proof from [ESS94] does use a small amount of Fourier analysis; the DeepMind proof seems to be distinct in that it is purely elementary, using instead a surprising coincidence of cancelling parameters to get a comparable bound.

attempt:
Reframing:
Let A+A = {s_1 < ... < s_t} and define gaps g_i = s_{i+1}-s_i.
An element s_i is "isolated" iff both adjacent gap constraints hold:
- left gap > 1 (or i=1)
- right gap > 1 (or i=t)
So EP-152 asks whether the minimum possible isolated-count over Sidon sets of size m
must go to infinity with m.
Equivalent run-language:
- View A+A inside [s_1,s_t] as runs of consecutive occupied integers.
- Isolated sums are exactly runs of length 1.

Why this is still open:
Current obstacle is universal control: we do not have a structural theorem preventing
almost all missing points of A+A from clustering into a few long hole intervals, which
could keep isolated-count comparatively low.

Target:
For Sidon \(A\), prove the number of isolated elements in \(A+A\) tends to
infinity with \(|A|\).
Step A: Gap-mass lower bound
Show total excess gap
\[
\sum_i\bigl((s_{i+1}-s_i)-1\bigr)
\]
must grow with \(|A|\) for all Sidon sets.
Step B: Anti-clustering of excess gaps
Prove excess gap mass cannot concentrate on too few locations.
Step C: Isolated-run forcing
Translate dispersed excess gaps into many singleton runs, i.e. many isolated sums.

Need a universal anti-clustering inequality for gaps of \(A+A\) for arbitrary
Sidon \(A\), not only structured families.

Proposition BB1 (Run decomposition identity):
Let \(R_1\) be number of singleton runs in \(A+A\), and \(x_i=(s_{i+1}-s_i)-1\ge0\).
Then
\[
R_1 \ge \#\{i:\ x_i>0\}-1.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Each positive gap separates consecutive occupied blocks; except for boundary
effects, each separator increases run count by one.
\(\square\)
Proposition BB2 (Reduction):
If one proves \(\#\{i:\ x_i>0\}\to\infty\) for all Sidon sets with \(|A|\to\infty\),
then EP-152 follows by BB1.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate.
\(\square\)

forum_comments.author: Sayan Dutta
forum_comments.text:
Not sure if this is interesting enough to comment, but this conjecture is immediate in the “very sparse relative to its span” regime, and does not use the Sidon property at all. Let $A$ be any finite set of integers, $|A|=k$, and write $A+A=\{s_1<\dots<s_t\}$ with gaps $d_i=s_{i+1}-s_i$. Let $D:=\operatorname{Diam}(A)=\max(A)-\min(A)$. Then $s_t-s_1=2D$. We have
$$\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^{t-1} d_i^2 \ge \frac{16D^2}{k^2(k+1)^2}$$
by Cauchy–Schwarz. In particular, if $D\gg k^2$ (e.g. for $A\subset[1,n]$ with $\operatorname{Diam}(A)\asymp n$ and $k=o(\sqrt n)$), then the mean square consecutive gap $\to\infty$.

Thus the exact minimum already rises across the full computed range. The Ruzsa prime family and the Mian-Chowla family both show strong growth as well. In larger adversarial searches, the best values found are \(11.27,28.08,66.16,121.56,154.65,218.26,301.62,373.09\) for \(m=11,20,30,40,50,60,70,80\), and the extension to \(m=81,90,100\) gives \(353.57,417.53,594.15\). attempt:
Let \(m=|A|\). For Sidon sets one has \(t=|A+A|=m(m+1)/2\) and also \(a_{\max}-a_{\min}\ge \binom m2\), since all positive differences are distinct. Hence
\[
s_t-s_1=2(a_{\max}-a_{\min})\ge m(m-1).
\]
By Cauchy,
\[
\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(s_{i+1}-s_i)^2\ge \frac{(s_t-s_1)^2}{t(t-1)},
\]
which yields only a constant-order lower bound, not divergence. Writing \(x_i=(s_{i+1}-s_i)-1\ge 0\), one gets
\[
\frac1t\sum (s_{i+1}-s_i)^2= rac{(t-1)+2\sum x_i+\sum x_i^2}{t}.
\]
So divergence would follow either from very large total excess gap mass or from strong variance forcing. The missing ingredient is a rigidity theorem showing that a large Sidon set cannot have both small range and uniformly small gap variance.

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
forum_comments.text:
The behavior of $F$ is the subject of [30]. It's trivial that $F(N + k) \leq F(N) + F(k)$ for all $N$ and $k$.

Let $g(N)$ be maximal such that there exist Sidon sets $A, B \subseteq \{1,...,N\}$ such that $(A - A) \cap (B - B) = \{0\}$ and $g(N) \leq |A|, |B|$. Clearly, $g(N) \leq F(N)$ for all $N$; I don't know if Erdős ever asked about the behavior of $g$, but two related problems are [42] and [43]. (EDIT: Also [331].)

One nice partial result on this problem is that if $N + 1 \geq k$, then $F(N + k) \leq F(N) + g(k)$. To prove this, let $A \subseteq \{1,..., N + k\}$ be a maximum-size Sidon set. By definition of $g$, the set $A$ has at most $g(k)$-many elements in $\{1,...,k\}$ or it has at most $g(k)$-many elements in $\{N+1,..., N+k\}$ (or both). By removing this interval, we then get a Sidon set of size at least $|A| - g(k) = F(N + k) - g(k)$ on an interval of length $N$, which completes the proof.

computation:
An exact profile for \(F(N)\), the largest Sidon size in \([1,N]\), was computed through \(N=72\), using previously exact values up to \(60\) and exact backtracking beyond that. In this range,
- \(F(N+1)-F(N)\in\{0,1\}\), so there is no counterexample to the \(k=1\) case.
- The same remains true for shifts \(k=2,3\).
- For larger shifts, the maximum observed increments are \(2\) for \(k=4,5,6,8\) and \(3\) for \(k=10\).
Thus the finite data is consistent with eventual \(F(N+k)\le F(N)+1\) for small fixed \(k\), but still far from proving it.
attempt: The exact profile was extended to \(N=76\), with \(F(74)=F(75)=F(76)=11\). For shifts \(k=1,2,3\), all observed increments still lie in \(\{0,1\}\), so the finite evidence for the small-shift \(+1\) law remains intact. The open issue is to prove a genuine local-collision obstruction showing that once \(N\) is large, a short interval \((N,N+k]\) cannot contribute more than one new Sidon element to an extremal set.

problem: Does there exist a maximal Sidon set $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ of size $O(N^{1/3})$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/156.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A question of Erd\H{o}s, S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy, and S\'{o}s \cite{ESS94}. It is easy to prove that the greedy construction of a maximal Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has size $\gg N^{1/3}$. Ruzsa \cite{Ru98b} constructed a maximal Sidon set of size $\ll (N\log N)^{1/3}$.

See also [340].
References:
- [ESS94] Erd\H{o}s, P. and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy, A. and S\'{o}s, T., On Sum Sets of Sidon Sets, I. Journal of Number Theory (1994), 329-347.
- [Ru98b] Ruzsa, Imre Z., A small maximal Sidon set. Ramanujan J. (1998), 55-58.
forum: No forum comments were present in the fetched discussion thread. The site comment-activity widget says: None.
computation:
Route:
Ran random-order greedy constructions of maximal Sidon sets in [1..N] and tracked size scaling.

- (N=200..3200, 600 trials each):
 - minimum found sizes: 11,15,20,27,36;
 - ratios to N^{1/3} stay around 1.9 to 2.4.
attempt:
Hard point:
Finite/random constructions support the N^{1/3} scale but do not prove existence of maximal Sidon sets of size O(N^{1/3}) for all large N.

Target:
Show existence of maximal Sidon subsets of \([1,N]\) of size \(O(N^{1/3})\), or
prove a larger necessary order.
Step A: Saturation reformulation
A maximal Sidon set \(A\) is one where every \(x\notin A\) creates a repeated
sum when added. Encode this as a covering condition on forbidden sums.
Step B: Counting lower envelope
Relate number of forbidden \(x\) values to \(|A|\) via pair-sum collision counts.
Step C: Constructive upper envelope
Design explicit or probabilistic constructions meeting saturation with
\(|A|=O(N^{1/3})\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a saturation covering lemma showing each existing Sidon set of size
\(\gg N^{1/3}\) can be pruned/rearranged to a maximal set without large blow-up.

Proposition BE1 (Maximality criterion):
A Sidon set \(A\subset[1,N]\) is maximal iff for every \(x\in[1,N]\setminus A\),
\(A\cup\{x\}\) is not Sidon.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is exactly the definition of maximality under inclusion.
\(\square\)
Proposition BE2 (Reduction to forbidden-value coverage):
If one proves that for every Sidon \(A\subset[1,N]\) with \(|A|=m\), the set of
forbidden \(x\) has size at most \(C m^3\), then maximality forces
\[
N \le |A| + C|A|^3,
\]
hence \(|A|\gg N^{1/3}\). Matching constructions at this scale resolve order.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By BE1, all \(x\notin A\) must be forbidden in a maximal set, so
\(N-|A|\le C|A|^3\).
\(\square\)

Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be constructed by the greedy rule: at step $k+1$, choose the smallest $m>a_k$ such that every sum $n$ has at most two representations $n=a+b$ with $a\le b$ and $a,b\in A\cup\{m\}$. attempt:
Target:
Decide whether
\[
\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{F_2^{(2)}(N)}{\sqrt N}>0
\]
for \(B_2[2]\)-type sets (unordered representation count at most \(2\)).
Step A: Additive-energy lower barrier
Bound representation multiplicities and derive necessary sparsity/energy profile.
Step B: Probabilistic construction with correction
Construct dense random candidate sets and prune local representation violations.
Step C: Uniform density certificate
Show corrected construction keeps size \(\gg \sqrt N\) with explicit constant.

Need a concentration inequality for the number of offending sums after dependent
pruning, strong enough to keep positive \(\sqrt N\)-density.

Proposition BF1 (Counting reduction):
If \(A\subset[1,N]\) satisfies \(r_{A+A}(n)\le 2\) for all \(n\), then
\[
|A|^2=\sum_n r_{A+A}(n)\le 2|A+A|.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Sum representation counts over all sums.
\(\square\)
Proposition BF2 (Density criterion):
If one constructs infinitely many \(N\) with \(B_2[2]\)-sets \(A_N\subset[1,N]\)
and \(|A_N|\ge c\sqrt N\), \(c>0\), then
\[
\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{F_2^{(2)}(N)}{\sqrt N}\ge c.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By definition \(F_2^{(2)}(N)\ge |A_N|\) on those \(N\); take liminf.
\(\square\)

computation:
Current cited bounds remain:
- lower: R(C_4,K_n) >> n^{3/2} / (log n)^{3/2}
- upper: R(C_4,K_n) << n^2 / (log n)^2
So the known upper bound has logarithmic savings but not a polynomial power-saving
n^{2-c}.

- explicit numeric scaling diagnostics for the known n^{3/2}/(\log n)^{3/2} lower and n^2/(\log n)^2 upper templates.
- Finite profile confirms a large exponent gap persists in practical ranges, and coarse upper surrogates remain far from any n^{2-c} power-saving statement.
- Obstacle: the EP requires a true exponent drop; current methods in this only quantify how far existing template bounds are from that target.
attempt:
I reviewed the quantitative frontier from the background and aligned it with the
 conjectured power-saving target.

Hard point:
Converting the logarithmic improvement into a true exponent drop requires stronger
global structural control in C_4-free graph constructions.

Target:
Prove existence of \(c>0\) such that
\[
R(C_4,K_n)\ll n^{2-c}.
\]
Step A: Refined \(C_4\)-free structure
Establish stronger pseudorandom/spectral control for near-extremal \(C_4\)-free
graphs at Ramsey threshold scale.
Step B: Independence amplification
Convert structure into larger guaranteed independent sets than current
\((\log n)^2\)-based bounds.
Step C: Ramsey inversion
Translate amplified independence into a polynomial exponent drop in \(R(C_4,K_n)\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need an improved independence lower bound for \(C_4\)-free graphs of given order
and average degree that beats the current logarithmic barrier.

Proposition BG1 (Ramsey reformulation):
\(R(C_4,K_n)>N\) iff there exists a \(C_4\)-free graph \(G\) on \(N\) vertices
with \(\alpha(G)<n\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Standard two-color edge interpretation: red graph \(G\), blue complement.
\(\square\)
Proposition BG2 (Exponent-drop reduction):
If every \(C_4\)-free \(N\)-vertex graph satisfies
\[
\alpha(G)\ge N^{\varepsilon}
\]
for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and large \(N\), then
\[
R(C_4,K_n)\ll n^{1/\varepsilon}=n^{2-c}
\]
for \(c=2-1/\varepsilon\) whenever \(1/\varepsilon<2\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By BG1, if \(R(C_4,K_n)>N\), then \(n>\alpha(G)\ge N^\varepsilon\), so
\(N<n^{1/\varepsilon}\). Rearrangement gives the bound.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $h(N)$ be the smallest $k$ such that $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ can be coloured with $k$ colours so that every four-term arithmetic progression must contain at least three distinct colours. Estimate $h(N)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/160.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 02 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Investigated by Erd\H{o}s and Freud. This has been discussed on MathOverflow (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/410808/what-are-bounds-on-this-van-der-waerden-esque-problem), where LeechLattice shows\[h(N) \ll N^{2/3}.\]In the comments of this site Hunter improves this to\[h(N) \ll N^{\frac{\log 3}{\log 22}+o(1)}\](note $\frac{\log 3}{\log 22}\approx 0.355$).

The observation of Zach Hunter in that question coupled with recent progress on the size of subsets without three-term arithmetic progression (see \cite{BlSi23} which improves slightly on the bounds due to Kelley and Meka \cite{KeMe23}) imply that\[h(N) \gg \exp(c(\log N)^{1/9})\]for some $c>0$.

forum_comments.text:
a better upper bound of $h(n) \ll N^{\log(3)/\log(22)+o(1)}$ follows from the methods in: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.06914 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.06914). the point is, you can take products of Behrend-style colorings to get a $N^{o(1)}$-coloring which kills all patterns except the symmetric ABBA-pattern. and then by tensoring the explicit coloring at the bottom of page 2, you can use $O(N^{\log(3)/\log(22)})$ colors to kill ABBA.

as the linked paper discusses, getting subpolynomial bounds on this ABBA problem would have implications for a conjecture of Ruzsa (see Theorem 1.7).

problem:
Let $\alpha\in[0,1/2)$ and $n,t\geq 1$. Let $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)$ be the smallest $m$ such that we can $2$-colour the edges of the complete $t$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices such that if $X\subseteq [n]$ with $\lvert X\rvert \geq m$ then there are at least $\alpha \binom{\lvert X\rvert}{t}$ many $t$-subsets of $X$ of each colour.

For fixed $n,t$ as we change $\alpha$ from $0$ to $1/2$ does $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)$ increase continuously or are there jumps? Only one jump?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/161.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 16 January 2026.
Site remarks:
For $\alpha=0$ this is the usual Ramsey function.

A conjecture of Erd\H{o}s, Hajnal, and Rado (see [562]) implies that\[ F^{(t)}(n,0)\asymp \log_{t-1} n\]and results of Erd\H{o}s and Spencer imply that\[F^{(t)}(n,\alpha) \gg_\alpha (\log n)^{\frac{1}{t-1}}\]for all $\alpha>0$, and a similar upper bound holds for $\alpha$ close to $1/2$.

Erd\H{o}s said in \cite{Er90b}: 'If I can hazard a guess completely unsupported by evidence, I am afraid that the jump occurs all in one step at $0$. It would be much more interesting if my conjecture would be wrong and perhaps there is some hope for this for $t>3$. I know nothing and offer \$500 to anybody who can clear up this mystery.'

Conlon, Fox, and Sudakov \cite{CFS11} have proved that, for any fixed $\alpha>0$,\[F^{(3)}(n,\alpha) \ll_\alpha \sqrt{\log n}.\]Coupled with the lower bound above, this implies that there is only one jump for fixed $\alpha$ when $t=3$, at $\alpha=0$.

For all $\alpha>0$ it is known that\[F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)\gg_t (\log n)^{c_\alpha}.\]See also [563] for more on the case $t=2$.

This problem is #40 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/GeneralizedHypergraphRamsey.html) in the graphs problem collection.
References:
- [CFS11] Conlon, David and Fox, Jacob and Sudakov, Benny, Large almost monochromatic subsets in hypergraphs. Israel J. Math. (2011), 423--432.
- [Er90b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on graphs and hypergraphs: similarities and differences. Mathematics of Ramsey theory (1990), 12-28.

forum_comments.author: zach hunter
forum_comments.text:
I will note that a resolution to this problem would follow from "hypergraph Nikiforov". conjecture: for any $r$-uniform hypergraph $H$ and $c>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ so that if an $n$-vertex hypergraph $G$ contains $cn^{|V(H)|}$ copies of $H$, then you can find a $t$-blowup of $H$ inside $G$ with $t>\delta (\log n)^{1/(r-1)}$.

forum_comments.author: yeyito
forum_comments.text:
I think there may still be a typo in the definition of $F(n,\alpha)$: should "largest $k$" perhaps be "smallest $k$"?

As currently written, for any $k>n$ there are no induced subgraphs of $K_n$ on at least $k$ vertices, so the stated property holds vacuously. Hence every $k>n$ is admissible, and the set of admissible $k$'s has no largest element.

Even if one implicitly restricts $k\le n$, the word "largest" still seems inconsistent with the stated logarithmic behaviour: for fixed $0\le \alpha<1/2$, a nearly balanced colouring of $K_n$ makes $k=n$ admissible for all sufficiently large $n$, so the largest admissible $k\le n$ would be $n$, not $\Theta(\log n)$.

Also, the endpoint $\alpha=1/2$ seems incompatible with the strict "more than" condition, since the two colour counts in $H$ sum to $\binom{|H|}{2}$.

So perhaps the intended formulation is with "smallest $k$" and $0\le \alpha<1/2$?

Site remarks:
It is known that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that for large $k$\[(c+o(1))\frac{k^2}{\log k}\leq R(3,k) \leq (1+o(1))\frac{k^2}{\log k}.\]The lower bound is due to Kim \cite{Ki95}, the upper bound is due to Shearer \cite{Sh83}, improving an earlier bound of Ajtai, Koml\'{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{AKS80}.

The value of $c$ in the lower bound has seen a number of improvements. Kim's original proof gave $c\geq 1/162$. The bound $c\geq 1/4$ was proved independently by Bohman and Keevash \cite{BoKe21} and Pontiveros, Griffiths and Morris \cite{PGM20}. The latter collection of authors conjecture that this lower bound is the true order of magnitude.

This was, however, improved by Campos, Jenssen, Michelen, and Sahasrabudhe \cite{CJMS25} to $c\geq 1/3$, and further by Hefty, Horn, King, and Pfender \cite{HHKP25} to $c\geq 1/2$. Both of these papers conjecture that $c=1/2$ is the correct asymptotic.

See also [544], and [986] for the general case. See [1013] for a related function.
References:
- [AKS80] Ajtai, Mikl\'{o}s and Koml\'{o}s, J\'{a}nos and Szemer\'{e}di, Endre, A note on Ramsey numbers. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1980), 354-360.
- [BoKe21] Bohman, Tom and Keevash, Peter, Dynamic concentration of the triangle-free process. Random Structures Algorithms (2021), 221-293.
- [CJMS25] M. Campos, M. Jenssen, M. Michelen, and J. Sahasrabudhe, A new lower bound for the Ramsey numbers $R(3,k)$. arXiv:2505.13371 (2025).
- [HHKP25] Z. Hefty, P. Horn, D. King, and F. Pfender, Improving $R(3,k)$ in just two bites. arXiv:2510.19718 (2025).
- [Ki95] Kim, J. H., The Ramsey number $R(3,t)$ has order of magnitude $t^2/\log t$. Random Structures and Algorithms (1995), 173-207.
- [PGM20] Fiz Pontiveros, Gonzalo and Griffiths, Simon and Morris, Robert, The triangle-free process and the Ramsey number $R(3,k)$. Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. (2020), v+125.
- [Sh83] Shearer J., A note on the independence number of triangle-free graphs. Discrete Math. (1983), 83-87.

problem: Let $F(N)$ be the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ which does not contain any set of the form $\{n,2n,3n\}$. What is\[ \lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{F(N)}{N}?\]Is this limit irrational?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/168.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 March 2026.
Site remarks:
This limit was proved to exist by Graham, Spencer, and Witsenhausen \cite{GSW77}, who showed it is equal to\[\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k\in K}\frac{1}{d_k},\]where $d_1<d_2<\cdots $are the $3$-smooth numbers and $K$ is the set of $k$ for which $f(k)>f(k-1)$, where $f$ counts the largest subset of $\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}$ that avoids $\{n,2n,3n\}$.

Similar questions can be asked for the density or upper density of infinite sets without such configurations.

The limit can be estimated by elementary arguments (see the comments). Eberhard has used the formula of \cite{GSW77} mentioned above to calculate the value of the limit as\[0.800965\cdots.\]
References:
- [GSW77] Graham, R. and Spencer, J. and Witsenhausen, H., On Extremal Density Theorems for Linear Forms. Number Theory and Algebra (1977).

The formula in [GrSpWi77] mentioned by Terry is very natural and one can fairly easily discover it for oneself. It starts with the observation that the problem naturally splits into a large number of disjoint subproblems, one for each number $x \le N$ divisible by neither $2$ nor $3$. It reduces to doing some integer programming to find the values of $f(k)$. forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
The following elementary bounds can be proven easily:

$$\frac 45 \le \lim_{ N \to \infty} \frac{F(n)}{N} \le \frac 56$$

Take the complement of the integers in
$$C=\cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]$$
then every set of the form $\{n,2n,3n\}$ where $1\le n \le \frac N3$ has exactly one element in $C$, since $2N/6^i<n<3n \le N/6^{i-1}$ is impossible (which would be the only way to avoid the elements in $C$).

In the other direction, as an improvement on the upper bound;
the sets $\{n,2n,3n\}$ for n in $B=\cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]  \setminus \left( \cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 4N/(3*6^i)] \cap 2\mathbb Z \right)$ are disjoint.

If two sets intersect, $\{n,2n,3n\} \cap \{n',2n',3n'\} \not= \emptyset$ for $n,n' \in B$, then $n,n' \in ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]$ for some $i$ and $3n=2n'$, so $n$ is even and bounded by $2/3*2N/6^i.$
So this could not happen, so we had approximately $N/6$ disjoint triples.

To add some amusing color: the conjecture "$f(k)=g(k)$ for all $k$" is false, with the first counterexample being $k=45$. Confusingly, they say they computed $f(k)$ for $k\le 50$; unfortunately, "Table 2" only includes the values for $k\le 25$.

problem:
Let $k\geq 3$ and $f(k)$ be the supremum of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ as $A$ ranges over all sets of positive integers which do not contain a $k$-term arithmetic progression. Estimate $f(k)$.

Is\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{f(k)}{\log W(k)}=\infty\]where $W(k)$ is the van der Waerden number?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/169.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 04 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Berlekamp \cite{Be68} proved $f(k) \geq \frac{\log 2}{2}k$. Gerver \cite{Ge77} proved\[f(k) \geq (1-o(1))k\log k.\]It is trivial that\[\frac{f(k)}{\log W(k)}\geq \frac{1}{2},\]but improving the right-hand side to any constant $>1/2$ is open.

Gerver also proved (see the comments for an alternative argument of Tao) that [3] is equivalent to $f(k)$ being finite for all $k$.

The current record for $f(3)$ is $f(3)\geq 3.00849$, due to Wr\'{o}blewski \cite{Wr84}. Walker \cite{Wa25} proved $f(4)\geq 4.43975$.

Walker \cite{Wa25} has shown that it suffices to consider Kempner sets (that is, sets of integers defined as all those whose base $b$ digits are contained in some $S\subset \{0,\ldots,b-1\}$ for fixed $b$ and $S$), in the sense that for any $k\geq 3$ and $\epsilon>0$ there is a Kempner set $A$ lacking $k$-term arithmetic progressions such that\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\geq f(k)-\epsilon.\]In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s asks whether for every $\epsilon>0$ and $k\geq 3$ if $A$ is a set of integers without a $k$-term arithmetic progression such that $\min(A)$ is sufficiently large in terms of $\epsilon$ and $k$ then $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}<\epsilon$.
References:
- [Be68] Berlekamp, E. R., A construction for partitions which avoid long arithmetic progressions. Canad. Math. Bull. (1968), 409-414.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [Ge77] Gerver, Joseph L., The sum of the reciprocals of a set of integers with no arithmetic progression of {$k$} terms. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1977), 211--214.
- [Wa25] A. Walker, Integer sets of large harmonic sum which avoid long arithmetic progressions. arXiv:2203.06045 (2025).
- [Wr84] Wr\'oblewski, J., A nonaveraging set of integers with a large sum of reciprocals. Math. Comp. (1984), 261--262.

forum_comments.text:
If the supremum is finite, then recursively one can construct finite $k$-AP-free sets $A_1,A_2,A_3,\dots$ with $\sum_{n \in A_j} \frac{1}{n} \geq 1$ (say) where the minimal element of each $A_j$ is greater than twice the maximal element of $A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{j-1}$ (by taking $A_j$ to be a $k$-AP-free set with extremely large sum of reciprocals and then deleting all elements less than twice that maximal element). Then, the $A_j$ are disjoint, and the union $\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j$ will have divergent sum of reciprocals while still being $k$-AP-free.

EDIT: okay, merely keeping each $A_j$ greater than twice the maximal element of the $A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{j-1}$ isn't going to be enough, due to $k$-term arithmetic progressions that have one element in $A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{j-1}$ and the other $k-1$ in $A_j$. But if one randomly refines each $A_j$ down to a proportion $\varepsilon$ of the original set, and then further removes any surviving $k$-term APs of this form (which removes $O_k(|A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{j-1}| \varepsilon^{k-1})$ of the original elements of $A_j$, where we weight each natural number $n$ by $1/n$ for the purposes of measuring size), I think one can still end up with a reduced set $A'_j$ with $\sum_{n \in A'_j} \frac{1}{n}$ as large as one pleases (by first taking $\varepsilon$ small, and then using the hypothesis of infinite supremum), with the property that the inclusion of $A'_j$ to $A'_1 \cup \dots \cup A'_{j-1}$ does not add any new $k$-APs, and the argument proceeds as before.

problem: Let $F(N)$ be the smallest possible size of $A\subset \{0,1,\ldots,N\}$ such that $\{0,1,\ldots,N\}\subset A-A$. Find the value of\[\lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{F(N)}{N^{1/2}}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/170.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
The Sparse Ruler (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_ruler) problem. R\'{e}dei asked whether this limit exists, which was proved by Erd\H{o}s and G\'{a}l \cite{ErGa48}. Bounds on the limit were improved by Leech \cite{Le56}. The limit is known to be in the interval $[1.56,\sqrt{3}]$. The lower bound is due to Leech \cite{Le56}, the upper bound is due to Wichmann \cite{Wi63}. Computational evidence by Pegg \cite{Pe20} suggests that the upper bound is the truth. A similar question can be asked without the restriction $A\subset \{0,1,\ldots,N\}$.
References:
- [ErGa48] Erd\H{o}s, P. and G\'{a}l, I., On the representation of $1,2,\ldots,N$ by differences. Nederl. Akad. Wetensch., Proc. (1948), 1155-1158.
- [Le56] Leech, J., On the representation of $1,2,\ldots,n$ by differences. J. London Math. Soc. (1956), 160-169.
- [Pe20] Pegg, E., Hitting All the Marks: Exploring New Bounds for Sparse Rulers and a Wolfram Language Proof. https://blog.wolfram.com/2020/02/12/hitting-all-the-marks-exploring-new-bounds-for-sparse-rulers-and-a-wolfram-language-proof/ (2020).

Target:
Determine the asymptotic constant for minimal sparse-ruler size \(m(N)\):
\[
m(N)\sim c\sqrt N.

Refine counting bounds using multiplicity constraints on repeated differences.

Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):

coverage beyond the trivial \(\binom{m}{2}\ge N\).

Proposition BN1 (Classical counting lower bound):
If \(m\) marks cover all differences \(1,\dots,N\), then
\[
\binom{m}{2}\ge N,
\]
hence \(m\ge \sqrt{2N}+O(1)\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each unordered pair contributes one difference; at most \(\binom{m}{2}\)
distinct positive differences are available.
\(\square\)
Proposition BN2 (Constant-extraction reduction):
If one proves constructions with \(m\le (c_++o(1))\sqrt N\) and universal lower
bound \(m\ge (c_- -o(1))\sqrt N\), then asymptotic constant lies in
\([c_-,c_+]\); matching \(c_-=c_+\) resolves EP-170.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Divide bounds by \(\sqrt N\) and pass to limit superior/inferior.
\(\square\)

problem: Is it true that in any finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ there exist arbitrarily large finite $A$ such that all sums and products of distinct elements in $A$ are the same colour?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/172.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
First asked by Hindman. Hindman \cite{Hi80} has proved this is false (with 7 colours) if we ask for an infinite $A$. In \cite{Er77c} Erd\H{o}s asks about the case for an infinite $A$ with just $2$ colours (see [1198]).

Moreira \cite{Mo17} has proved that in any finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ there exist $x,y$ such that $\{x,x+y,xy\}$ are all the same colour.

Alweiss \cite{Al23} has proved that in any finite colouring of $\mathbb{Q}\backslash \{0\}$ there exist arbitrarily large finite $A$ such that all sums and products of distinct elements in $A$ are the same colour. Bowen and Sabok \cite{BoSa22} had proved this earlier for the first non-trivial case of $\lvert A\rvert=2$.
References:
- [Al23] R. Alweiss, Hindman's conjecture over the rationals. arXiv:2307.08901 (2023).
- [BoSa22] M. Bowen and M. Sabok, Monochromatic Sums and Products in the Rationals. arXiv:2210.12290 (2022).
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [Hi80] Hindman, Neil, Partitions and sums and products-two counterexamples. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1980), 113-120.
- [Mo17] Moreira, J., Monochromatic sums and products in $\mathbbN$. Ann. Math. (2017), 1069-1090.

Let \(\mathcal T\) be the space of triangle congruence types. If for a coloring

If one proves \(E\) is finite and also proves no two distinct types can both be

\[
\textit{Proof.}

Finite set plus pairwise exclusion implies cardinality at most one.

problem: A finite set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is called Ramsey if, for any $k\geq 1$, there exists some $d=d(A,k)$ such that in any $k$-colouring of $\mathbb{R}^d$ there exists a monochromatic copy of $A$. Characterise the Ramsey sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/174.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 16 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus \cite{EGMRSS73} proved that every Ramsey set is 'spherical': it lies on the surface of some sphere. Graham has conjectured that every spherical set is Ramsey. Leader, Russell, and Walters \cite{LRW12} have alternatively conjectured that a set is Ramsey if and only if it is 'subtransitive': it can be embedded in some higher-dimensional set on which rotations act transitively.

Sets known to be Ramsey include vertices of $k$-dimensional rectangles \cite{EGMRSS73}, non-degenerate simplices \cite{FrRo90}, trapezoids \cite{Kr92}, and regular polygons/polyhedra \cite{Kr91}.

- [EGMRSS73] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R. L. and Montgomery, P. and Rothschild, B. L. and Spencer, J. and Straus, E. G., Euclidean Ramsey Theorems I. J. Comb. Th. A (1973), 341-363.
- [FrRo90] Frankl, P. and R\"{o}dl, V., A partition property of simplices in Euclidean space. J. Amer. Math. Soc. (1990), 1-7.

- [LRW12] Leader, Imre and Russell, Paul A. and Walters, Mark, Transitive sets in Euclidean Ramsey theory. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (2012), 382-396.

problem: Let $N(k,\ell)$ be the minimal $N$ such that for any $f:\{1,\ldots,N\}\to\{-1,1\}$ there must exist a $k$-term arithmetic progression $P$ such that\[ \left\lvert \sum_{n\in P}f(n)\right\rvert\geq \ell.\]Find good upper bounds for $N(k,\ell)$. Is it true that for any $c>0$ there exists some $C>1$ such that\[N(k,ck)\leq C^k?\]What about\[N(k,2)\leq C^k\]or\[N(k,\sqrt{k})\leq C^k?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/176.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 04 April 2026.
Site remarks:
When $\ell=k$ this is the van der Waerden number $W(k)$ (see [138]). Spencer \cite{Sp73} has proved that if $k=2^tm$ with $m$ odd then\[N(k,1)=2^t(k-1)+1.\]Erd\H{o}s and Graham write that 'no decent bound' is known even for $N(k,2)$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er63d} proved that, for every $c>0$,\[N(k,ck)> (1+\alpha_c)^k\]where $\alpha_c\to 0$ as $c\to 0$ and $\alpha_c\to \sqrt{2}-1$ as $c\to 1$.

Hunter in the comment section observes that the local lemma implies an improved bound of\[N(k,ck) \gg \frac{2^k}{k^{O(1)}\sum_{i>\frac{1+c}{2}k}\binom{k}{i}},\]so that in particular as $c\to 1$ we have, for all large $k$, $N(k,ck)\geq (2-o(1))^k$ (where the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $c\to 1$).
References:
- [Er63d] Erd\H{o}s, P\'{a}l, On combinatorial questions connected with a theorem of {R}amsey and van der {W}aerden. Mat. Lapok (1963), 29--37.
- [Sp73] J. Spencer, Problems 185. Bull. Canad. Math. Soc. (1973), 185.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
Another observation is that $N(k+1, l-1) < \frac{k}{k-1} N(k,l)$ as there is some $k$ term progression $P$ in $[1,N(k, l)]$ such that summing along $P$ has absolute value $\geq l$. Then the $k+1$-th term of $P$ is at most $\frac{k}{k-1}N(k, l)$ and reduces the absolute value by at most $1$.

Based on my earlier comment, if $k\equiv l\mod 2$ then $N(k+1, l-1) < \frac{k}{k-1} N(k,l)=\frac{k}{k-1} N(k,l-1)$.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
If $P$ is a $k$-term arithmetic progression, then $|\sum_{n\in P}f(n)|\equiv k\pmod 2$. Therefore, if $k\not\equiv l\pmod 2$ and $|\sum_{n\in P}f(n)|\geq l$, then $|\sum_{n\in P}f(n)|\geq l+1$. It follows that if $k\not\equiv l\pmod 2$ then $N(k,l+1)=N(k,l)$.

EDIT: Therefore for even $k=2^tm$, we have $N(k,2)=N(k,1)= 2^t(k-1)+1$.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text: Additionally, it seems likely that $W(\frac{k+l}{2})$ upper bounds $N(k,l)$ in general as if there exists an arithmetic progression, $P$, of $\frac{k+l}{2}$ $1$s, then any progression of length $k$ that contains $P$ will have a sum that is $\geq l$. The only issue is if the common difference of $P$ is greater than (roughly) $\frac{W(\frac{k+l}{2})}{k}$, as then it is not possible to contain $P$ in a large enough progression.

forum_comments.author: zach hunter
forum_comments.text:
this latter idea has a hole, it's not this easy. imagine we are periodic modulo $k$, and it starts with $k/2$ 1s followed by $k/2$ -1s. you have these monochromatic progressions of length $k/2$ with common difference 1, but any $k$-AP containing such progressions has discrepancy 0. of course, this feels rather absurd...

one way which *would* suffice to lower bound $N(k,l)$, is to find some $(k+l)$-AP, where the first $l$ integers receive '$1$' while the last $l$ integers receive '$-1$'. at some point I saw a way to do this and started writing this up, but later with others discovered a simpler argument showing $N(k,c\sqrt{k})=O(k^3)$ for some $c>0$. this should appear in a note some time soon...

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text: The example you give is of $k/2$ $1$s which would correspond to $l=0$.

forum_comments.author: zach hunter
forum_comments.text: oh I see! I misread. okay so definitely $N(k,l)\le kW(\frac{k+l}{2})$. nice!

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text: Seeing as $P$ has $\frac{k+l}{2}$ terms and lies in $[1,W(\frac{k+l}{2})]$, its common difference is at most about $\frac{2W(\frac{k+l}{2})}{k+l}$. Therefore we can contain $P$ in a $k$ term progression whose largest term is about $\frac{2kW(\frac{k+l}{2})}{k+l}$ or $\frac{2W(\frac{k+l}{2})}{1+\frac{l}{k}}$.

forum_comments.author: zach hunter
forum_comments.text:
This bound from [Er63d] is out-dated. An application of the local lemma will show that $N(k,ck) \gg \frac{2^k}{k^{O(1)} \sum_{i\ge (1/2+c/2)k}\binom{k}{i}}$. Thus $\alpha_c\to 1$ as $c\to 1$ (the intuition is while there are $N^2$ progressions to worry about, there are only $k^{O(1)}N$ progressions containing any integer).

Any improvement beyond these simple random bounds would be interesting (and have applications!). One thing I have begun to wonder about is if you take $N$ to be prime, $s:=k/100$ (say), and then have the two color classes be $\{x: x^s \in [N/2]+N\cdot \mathbb{Z}\}$ and its complement.

problem:
If $\mathcal{F}$ is a finite set of finite graphs then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})$ is the maximum number of edges a graph on $n$ vertices can have without containing any subgraphs from $\mathcal{F}$. Note that it is trivial that $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\leq \mathrm{ex}(n;G)$ for every $G\in\mathcal{F}$.

Is it true that, for every $\mathcal{F}$, there exists $G\in\mathcal{F}$ such that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\ll_{\mathcal{F}}\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/180.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits.

This is trivially true if $\mathcal{F}$ does not contain any bipartite graphs, since by the Erd\H{o}s-Stone theorem if $H\in\mathcal{F}$ has minimal chromatic number $r\geq 2$ then\[\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\left(\frac{r-2}{r-1}+o(1)\right)\binom{n}{2}.\]Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits observe that this is false for infinite families $\mathcal{F}$, e.g. the family of all cycles.

Hunter has provided the following 'folklore counterexample': if $\mathcal{F}=\{H_1,H_2\}$ where $H_1$ is a star and $H_2$ is a matching, both with at least two edges, then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\ll 1$, but $\mathrm{ex}(n;H_i)\asymp n$ for $1\leq i\leq 2$. This conjecture may still hold for all other $\mathcal{F}$.

See also [575].

Quick formalization update.
I've now formalized this dichotomy in Lean 4 (familiesTheorem): the file builds against Mathlib4, contains no sorry/admit, and#print axioms Erdos180.familiesTheorem reports only Lean's foundational axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound).

Repo: https://github.com/arexychen/Erdos180 (https://github.com/arexychen/Erdos180)

Two caveats I want to flag explicitly:
(1) The single-forbidden-graph characterization (ex(n;H) = Θ(n) ↔ H° is a forest with ≥ 2 edges) is invoked only in the direction actually consumed by the dispatch:IsThetaLinear → ≥ 2 reduced edges. The forward direction (forest ⇒Θ(n)) and the forest conclusion are not consumed. A Phase 1 mathlib survey (phase1-report.md in the repo) records why the full classical biconditional could not be formalized within the time-box: the cycle case appears to require either a high-girth/high-chromatic-number existence theorem or random-graph short-cycle expectation plus a probabilistic deletion argument, none of which the survey found in mathlib4. The weakened axiom statement is provable from elementary case analysis on graphs with at most one non-isolated edge, which is what the formalization actually does.
(2) The Case (i) bound in Lean is O(|V(F_star)| · |V(F_matching)|) rather than the tighter 2(a-1)(b-1) from the LaTeX. Both giveΘ(1), but explicit constants differ. This is a faithful formalization of the asymptotic statement, not of the specific constants.
The Lean code was generated by GPT-5.5 (xhigh) under prompts I designed with Claude Opus 4.7 assistance. I am not a mathematician; the verification I did is structural (axiom audits, statement comparison against the LaTeX). Mathematical review by anyone with extremal graph theory background is welcome — the README lists specific things I would find most useful to hear about.

forum_comments.author: KJ_C
forum_comments.text:
Following the folklore counterexample noted by Zach Hunter, I used AI assistance (GPT-5.5 xhigh, with the proof checked by Claude Opus 4.7) to attempt the remaining case of Problem #180. The argument produces the following dichotomy, which I believe is correct but may already be known in the literature. I am posting here to ask whether this result is folklore, and if not, whether it constitutes progress.

Claim. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a nonempty finite family of finite graphs with $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\Theta(n)$ for every $H\in\mathcal{F}$. Then exactly one of the following holds:

$\mathcal{F}$ contains, after deleting isolated vertices, both $K_{1,a}$ and $bK_2$ for some $a,b\geq 2$, and then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\Theta(1)$;

$\mathcal{F}$ does not contain such a star/matching pair, and then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\Theta(n)$.

The proof uses three ingredients: (1) the standard characterisation that $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\Theta(n)$ if and only if $H^\circ$ is a forest with at least two edges, proved via a random graph argument and a minimum-degree greedy embedding; (2) explicit constructions — $K_{1,n-1}$ or a perfect matching — for the lower bound in the second case; and (3) a maximum-matching/maximum-degree counting argument showing $e(G)\leq 2(a-1)(b-1)$ in the first case.

My questions: Is this dichotomy already in the literature? If so, could you point me to a reference? If not, does this constitute progress on Problem #180?

The full proof is shown below. This was generated with AI assistance and reviewed for logical consistency, but I am not a professional mathematician and welcome expert verification.

All graphs are finite and simple. Subgraph means not necessarily induced. For a graph $H$, let $H^\circ$ denote $H$ with isolated vertices deleted.

Lemma. $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\Theta(n)$ if and only if $H^\circ$ is a forest with at least two edges.

Proof. If $H^\circ$ has at most one edge, then every sufficiently large graph with at least one edge contains $H$, so $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)$ is eventually $0$.

If $H^\circ$ contains a cycle, let $h=|V(H^\circ)|$. Take $G\sim G(n,p)$ with $p=n^{-1+1/(2h)}$. Then $\mathbb{E}, e(G)=\Omega(n^{1+1/(2h)})$. The expected number of cycles of length at most $h$ is at most $\sum_{\ell=3}^h n^\ell p^\ell = \sum_{\ell=3}^h n^{\ell/(2h)} = O(n^{1/2})$. So some $G$ has $e(G)-X=\Omega(n^{1+1/(2h)})$ where $X$ counts short cycles. Deleting one edge from each short cycle gives an $H$-free graph with superlinear edges, so $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)$ is not $O(n)$.

Now suppose $H^\circ$ is a forest with $h=|V(H^\circ)|$ vertices and at least two edges. If $G$ has more than $(h-2)n$ edges, repeatedly delete vertices of degree at most $h-2$; if all were deleted, at most $(h-2)n$ edges were removed, contradiction. So some nonempty $G'\subseteq G$ has minimum degree at least $h-1$. Order $V(H^\circ)=x_1,\dots,x_h$ so each vertex has at most one earlier neighbor, and embed greedily into $G'$: at step $i$, the image of any earlier neighbor has at least $h-1$ neighbors of which fewer than $h-1$ are used, so an unused neighbor is always available. Hence $G$ contains $H^\circ$, giving $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=O(n)$.

For the lower bound: if $H^\circ\cong K_{1,a}$ with $a\ge 2$, a perfect matching is $H$-free and has $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ edges. If $H^\circ$ is not a star, then $K_{1,n-1}$ is $H$-free, since every nonempty subgraph of a star is again a star after deleting isolated vertices. In both cases $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\Omega(n)$. $\square$

Theorem. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a nonempty finite family with $\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\Theta(n)$ for every $H\in\mathcal{F}$. Then exactly one of the following holds:

(i) $\mathcal{F}$ contains, after deleting isolated vertices, both $K_{1,a}$ and $bK_2$ for some $a,b\ge 2$, and then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\Theta(1)$;

(ii) $\mathcal{F}$ contains no such star/matching pair, and then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\Theta(n)$.

Proof. By the Lemma, every $H^\circ$ with $H\in\mathcal{F}$ is a forest with at least two edges.

Case (ii). The upper bound is immediate: $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\le\mathrm{ex}(n;H_0)=O(n)$ for any fixed $H_0\in\mathcal{F}$. For the lower bound: if no member of $\mathcal{F}$ is a star, then $K_{1,n-1}$ is $\mathcal{F}$-free, giving $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\ge n-1$. If some member is a star but no member is a matching with at least two edges, then a maximum matching is $\mathcal{F}$-free, giving $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\ge\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Hence $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\Theta(n)$.

Case (i). Suppose $\mathcal{F}$ contains $K_{1,a}$ and $bK_2$ with $a,b\ge 2$. Let $G$ be $\mathcal{F}$-free. Then $\Delta(G)\le a-1$ and $\nu(G)\le b-1$. Let $M$ be a maximum matching; since $M$ is maximal, every edge of $G$ has an endpoint in $V(M)$. Therefore $$e(G)\le\sum_{v\in V(M)}d_G(v)\le|V(M)|\cdot\Delta(G)\le 2(b-1)(a-1).$$ So $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=O(1)$. Since every member of $\mathcal{F}$ has at least two edges, a single edge is $\mathcal{F}$-free, giving $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\ge 1$. Hence $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\Theta(1)$. $\square$

forum_comments.text: A folklore counterexample is that if you take your family to be $\{H_1,H_2\}$, where $H_1$ is a star and $H_2$ is a matching, then $\operatorname{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=O_{\mathcal{F}}(1)$. computation:
- brute-force exact computation of \mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal F), \mathrm{ex}(n;K_{1,2}), and \mathrm{ex}(n;2K_2).
- Exact values confirm the asymptotic mismatch pattern already used in the counterexample route: \mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal F)=1 while each single-forbidden extremal number grows linearly.
- Conclusion in this record: computational verification supports the statement being false as written.
attempt:
Explicit finite counterexample:
Take
F = { K_{1,2}, 2K_2 },
where:
- K_{1,2} is the 2-edge star,
- 2K_2 is a matching of size 2 (two disjoint edges).
Step 1: ex(n;F) is constant
A graph avoiding K_{1,2} has maximum degree at most 1, so it is a matching.
A graph avoiding 2K_2 has matching number at most 1.
Combining both, any F-free graph has at most one edge.
Hence for all n >= 2:
ex(n;F) = 1.
Step 2: each single-graph extremal number is linear
- For K_{1,2}:
 forbidding K_{1,2} means maximum degree at most 1, so maximum edges is a maximum matching:
 ex(n;K_{1,2}) = floor(n/2) = Theta(n).
- For 2K_2:
 forbidding 2K_2 means every two edges intersect.
 For n >= 4, the largest intersecting family of 2-subsets has size n-1 (a star), so
 ex(n;2K_2)=n-1 = Theta(n).
Thus every G in F has ex(n;G)=Theta(n), while ex(n;F)=1.
Therefore no G in F can satisfy
ex(n;G) <= C_F * ex(n;F) for all large n.
So the EP-180 statement is false as written.

Target:
Since the original statement is false, formulate corrected variants (e.g.,
restricted families \(\mathcal F\), monotone closures, or relaxed comparison
factor) and determine the sharp valid form.
Step A: Obstruction taxonomy
Classify finite families \(\mathcal F\) where mixed-forbidden condition can
collapse \(\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal F)\) far below each \(\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\).
Step B: Valid-class identification
Identify structural assumptions on \(\mathcal F\) under which some
\(G\in\mathcal F\) satisfies \(\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\ll_{\mathcal F}\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal F)\).
Step C: Sharp theorem statement
Prove necessity and sufficiency of those assumptions.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a criterion characterizing when extremal behavior of intersections of
forbidden families is controlled by one member up to constant factor.

Proposition BS1 (General inequality baseline):
For any family \(\mathcal F\) and \(G\in\mathcal F\),
\[
\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal F)\le \mathrm{ex}(n;G).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Every \(\mathcal F\)-free graph is in particular \(G\)-free.
\(\square\)
Proposition BS2 (Why original claim can fail):
The reverse inequality up to constant need not hold: families may satisfy
\(\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal F)=O(1)\) while every \(\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\) is
\(\Omega(n)\), as in the explicit counterexample \(\{K_{1,2},2K_2\}\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Computed and exact formulas in this note give the asymptotic separation.

problem: Let $R(3;k)$ be the minimal $n$ such that if the edges of $K_n$ are coloured with $k$ colours then there must exist a monochromatic triangle. Determine\[\lim_{k\to \infty}R(3;k)^{1/k}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/183.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s offers \$100 for showing that this limit is finite. An easy pigeonhole argument shows that\[R(3;k)\leq 2+k(R(3;k-1)-1),\]from which $R(3;k)\leq \lceil e k!\rceil$ immediately follows. The best-known upper bound is\[R(3;k)\leq (e-\tfrac{1}{6}) k!+1,\]due to Xu, Xie, and Chen \cite{XXC02} (improving previous bounds of Wan \cite{Wa97} and Whitehead \cite{Wh73}). See Eliahou \cite{El19} for more on the upper bound. These arise from the same type of inductive relationship and computational bounds for $R(3;k)$ for small $k$. The best-known lower bound (coming from lower bounds for Schur numbers) is\[R(3,k)\geq (380)^{k/5}-O(1),\]due to Ageron, Casteras, Pellerin, Portella, Rimmel, and Tomasik \cite{ACPPRT21} (improving previous bounds of Exoo \cite{Ex94} and Fredricksen and Sweet \cite{FrSw00}). Note that $380^{1/5}\approx 3.2806$.

See also [483].

This problem is #21 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/MulticolorR3.html) in the graphs problem collection.

forum_comments.author: Wouter CvB
forum_comments.text:
Here's a cute related problem that people might be interested in. Let $\chi(n)$ denote the smallest number of sum-free sets that partition $\mathbb{F}_2^n\setminus \{0\}$. Via a subtle recursion combined with the Schur argument, we (with Anurag Bishnoi and Ananth Ravi) have recently (well, the project started 2 years ago) proved that (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01760) for every integer $n\ge 2$,
$$L:=\lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} R(3;k)^{1/k} \ge 2^{(n-1)/(\chi(n)-1)}.$$ So it's worth trying to find good upper bounds on $\chi(n)$ for small values of $n$. For example, $\chi(8)\le 5$ or $\chi(13)\le 8$ (if true) would already improve the lower bound on $L$ to $2^{7/4} \approx 3.364$ or $2^{12/7}\approx 3.2813$, respectively. Currently, the values of $\chi(n)$ are known for all $n\leq 7$.

Asymptotically, $\frac{(1-o(1)) n}{ \log_2(n)} \le \chi(n)\leq \lfloor \frac{2n}{3} \rfloor +1$.

problem: Any graph on $n$ vertices can be decomposed into $O(n)$ many edge-disjoint cycles and edges.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/184.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Erd\H{o}s and Gallai, who proved that $O(n\log n)$ many cycles and edges suffices (see Section 5 of \cite{EGP66}).

The graph $K_{3,n-3}$ shows that at least $(1+c)n$ many cycles and edges are required, for some constant $c>0$. In \cite{Er71} Erd\H{o}s suggests that only $n-1$ many cycles and edges are required if we do not require them to be edge-disjoint.

The best bound available is due to Buci\'{c} and Montgomery \cite{BM22}, who prove that $O(n\log^*n)$ many cycles and edges suffice, where $\log^*$ is the iterated logarithm function.

Conlon, Fox, and Sudakov \cite{CFS14} proved that $O_\epsilon(n)$ cycles and edges suffice if $G$ has minimum degree at least $\epsilon n$, for any $\epsilon>0$.

See also [583] for an analogous problem decomposing into paths, and [1017] for decomposing into complete graphs.
References:
- [BM22] Buci\'C, M. and Montgomery, R., Towards the Erd\H{o}s-Gallai Cycle Decomposition Conjecture. arXiv:2211.07689 (2022).
- [CFS14] Conlon, David and Fox, Jacob and Sudakov, Benny, Cycle packing. Random Structures Algorithms (2014), 608-626.
- [EGP66] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Goodman, A. W. and P\'{o}sa, Lajos, The representation of a graph by set intersections. Canadian J. Math. (1966), 106-112.
- [Er71] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis. Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications (Proc. Conf., Oxford, 1969) (1971), 97-109.

problem: Find the best function $f(d)$ such that, in any 2-colouring of the integers, at least one colour class contains an arithmetic progression with common difference $d$ of length $f(d)$ for infinitely many $d$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/187.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 04 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Originally asked by Cohen.

Erd\H{o}s observed that colouring according to whether $\{ \sqrt{2}n\}<1/2$ or not implies $f(d) \ll d$ (using the fact that $\|\sqrt{2}q\| \gg 1/q$ for all $q$, where $\|x\|$ is the distance to the nearest integer). In \cite{Er80} he states that Petruska and Szemer\'{e}di have proved that $f(d) \ll d^{1/2}$, and expected $f(d)\leq d^{o(1)}$.

Beck \cite{Be80} has improved this using the probabilistic method, constructing a colouring that shows $f(d)\leq (1+o(1))\log_2 d$. Van der Waerden's theorem implies $f(d)\to \infty$ is necessary.
References:
- [Be80] Beck, J\'{o}zsef, A remark concerning arithmetic progressions. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1980), 376-379.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.

problem: What is the smallest $k$ such that $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be red/blue coloured with no pair of red points unit distance apart, and no $k$-term arithmetic progression of blue points with distance $1$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/188.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 14 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus \cite{EGMRSS75} proved $k\geq 5$. Tsaturian \cite{Ts17} improved this to $k\geq 6$. Erd\H{o}s and Graham claim that $k\leq 10000000$ ('more or less'), but give no proof.

Erd\H{o}s and Graham asked this with just any $k$-term arithmetic progression in blue (not necessarily with distance $1$), but Alon has pointed out that in fact no such $k$ exists: in any red/blue colouring of the integer points on a line either there are two red points distance $1$ apart, or else the set of blue points and the same set shifted by $1$ cover all integers, and hence by van der Waerden's theorem there are arbitrarily long blue arithmetic progressions.

It seems most likely, from context, that Erd\H{o}s and Graham intended to restrict the blue arithmetic progression to have distance $1$ (although they do not write this restriction in their papers).
References:
- [EGMRSS75] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R. L. and Montgomery, P. and Rothschild, B. L. and Spencer, J. and Straus, E. G., Euclidean {R}amsey theorems. {II}. (1975), 529--557.
- [Ts17] Tsaturian, Sergei, A {E}uclidean {R}amsey result in the plane. Electron. J. Combin. (2017), Paper No. 4.35, 9.

They study a generalization of this question in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and their Theorem 1.1, applied with $n=2$, yields the bound $k \le 2.15\cdot 10^9$, even though it is likely that one can optimize their proof to deduce a much better upper bound.

forum_comments.author: msellke
forum_comments.text:
The 2017 paper "A Euclidean Ramsey result in the plane" of Tsaturian shows $k\geq 6$. (Note that Lemma 2.2 should say side length $3$ instead of $\sqrt{3}$.)

Additionally, Theorem 1' in the 1973 paper "Euclidean Ramsey Theorems II" by Erdos-Graham-Montgomery-Rothschild-Spencer-Straus already showed that $k\geq 5$, i.e. any such two-coloring contains either a unit-distance pair of red points or a unit distance 4-AP of blue points. The work of [Ju79] showed that one can replace "unit distance 4-AP of blue points" by "congruent copy of any desired planar 4-point configuration.

Also relatedly, (G. Currier, K. Moore & C. H. Yip, "Any two-coloring of the plane contains monochromatic 3-term arithmetic progressions", Combinatorica 44 (2024), 1367–1380) shows that any two-coloring of the plane contains a monochromatic unit length 3-AP.

(These references were located by GPT-5.)

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
On a related question -

At the end of [DEGS77], there are a number of open questions asked. One is about the value of $$\alpha=\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}} \liminf_{n\to\infty} \frac{|A\cap[1,n]|}{n}$$ and $$\beta=\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}} \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{|A\cap[1,n]|}{n} $$ where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of all infinite subsets, $A$, of $\mathbb{Z}^+$ for which there exists a permutation of $A$ that does not contain a monotone $3$-term arithmetic progression.

In On Permutations Avoiding Arithmetic Progressions (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X10003936), the authors show that $\alpha\geq 1/2$ and $\beta\geq 1/4$ by constructing sets $A$ that have these upper and lower densities. They conjecture that these bounds are tight.

Currently, there is no known method of finding non-trivial upper bounds for $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
