problem: Let $n_1<\cdots < n_r\leq N$ with associated $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ such that the congruence classes are disjoint (that is, every integer is $\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ for at most one $1\leq i\leq r$). How large can $r$ be in terms of $N$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/202.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Let $f(N)$ be the maximum possible $r$. Erd\H{o}s and Stein conjectured that $f(N)=o(N)$, which was proved by Erd\H{o}s and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{ErSz68}, who showed that, for every $\epsilon>0$,\[\frac{N}{\exp((\log N)^{1/2+\epsilon})} \ll_\epsilon f(N) < \frac{N}{(\log N)^c}\]for some $c>0$. Erd\H{o}s believed the lower bound is closer to the truth.

These bounds were improved by Croot \cite{Cr03b} who proved\[\frac{N}{L(N)^{\sqrt{2}+o(1)}}< f(N)<\frac{N}{L(N)^{1/6-o(1)}},\]where $L(N)=\exp(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})$. These bounds were further improved by Chen \cite{Ch05} and then by de la Bret\'{e}che, Ford, and Vandehey \cite{BFV13} to\[\frac{N}{L(N)^{1+o(1)}}<f(N) < \frac{N}{L(N)^{\sqrt{3}/2+o(1)}}.\]The latter authors conjecture that the lower bound here is the truth.

See also [1190].
References:
- [BFV13] de la Bret\'{e}che, R\'{e}gis and Ford, Kevin and Vandehey, Joseph, On non-intersecting arithmetic progressions. Acta Arith. (2013), 381--392.
- [Ch05] Chen, Yong-Gao, On disjoint arithmetic progressions. Acta Arith. (2005), 143--148.
- [Cr03b] Croot, III, Ernest S., On non-intersecting arithmetic progressions. Acta Arith. (2003), 233--238.
- [ErSz68] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Szemer\'{e}di, E., On a problem of P. Erd\H{o}s and S. Stein. Acta Arith. (1968), 85-90.

forum_comments.author: ho boon suan
forum_comments.text:
GPT-5.4 Pro confirms (https://boonsuan.github.io/erdos202.pdf) the conjectured asymptotic \(f(N)=N/L(N)^{1+o(1)}\), where \(L(N)=\exp(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})\). (This also gives $\epsilon_m=L(m)^{-1+o(1)}$ in [1190].) The proof augments the upper-bound argument of [BFV13] (https://doi.org/10.4064/aa157-4-5) with a consequence of the Park–Pham expectation-threshold theorem (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17207) (formerly the Kahn–Kalai conjecture).

In particular, one has the following dense-core lemma: there is an absolute constant \(C_0\) such that, for every nonempty intersecting family \(\mathcal A\) of distinct \(k\)-element sets with \(1\le k\le K\), there exists a nonempty set \(C\) satisfying\[
|\{A\in\mathcal A:C\subseteq A\}|>
\frac{|\mathcal A|}{(C_0\log(eK))^{|C|}}.
\]This logarithmic-loss lemma replaces the Erdős–Lovász/minimal-family step in [BFV13] (https://doi.org/10.4064/aa157-4-5)'s descending-chain argument and yields the optimal upper bound matching their lower construction.

problem: Let $s_1<s_2<\cdots$ be the sequence of squarefree numbers. Is it true that, for any $\epsilon>0$ and large $n$,\[s_{n+1}-s_n \ll_\epsilon s_n^{\epsilon}?\]Is it true that\[s_{n+1}-s_n \leq (1+o(1))\frac{\pi^2}{6}\frac{\log s_n}{\log\log s_n}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/208.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 19 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er51} showed that there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[s_{n+1}-s_n > (1+o(1))\frac{\pi^2}{6}\frac{\log s_n}{\log\log s_n},\]so this bound would be the best possible.

In \cite{Er79} Erd\H{o}s says perhaps $s_{n+1}-s_n \ll \log s_n$, but he is 'very doubtful'.

Filaseta and Trifonov \cite{FiTr92} proved an upper bound of $s_n^{1/5+o(1)}$. Pandey \cite{Pa24} has improved this exponent to $1/5-c$ for some constant $c>0$.

Granville \cite{Gr98} showed that $s_{n+1}-s_n\ll_\epsilon s_n^\epsilon$ for all $\epsilon>0$ follows from the ABC conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture).

See also [489] and [145]. A more general form of this problem is given in [1101].

problem: Is there a dense subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that all pairwise distances are rational?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/212.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 16 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Conjectured by Ulam. Erd\H{o}s believed there cannot be such a set. This problem is discussed in a blogpost (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2014/12/20/the-erdos-ulam-problem-varieties-of-general-type-and-the-bombieri-lang-conjecture/#more-7930) by Terence Tao, in which he shows that there cannot be such a set, assuming the Bombieri-Lang conjecture. The same conclusion was independently obtained by Shaffaf \cite{Sh18}.

Indeed, Shaffaf and Tao actually proved that such a rational distance set must be contained in a finite union of real algebraic curves. Solymosi and de Zeeuw \cite{SdZ10} then proved (unconditionally) that a rational distance set contained in a real algebraic curve must be finite, unless the curve contains a line or a circle.

Ascher, Braune, and Turchet \cite{ABT20} observed that, combined, these facts imply that a rational distance set in general position must be finite (conditional on the Bombieri-Lang conjecture).

In \cite{Er87b} Erd\H{o}s mentions that Besicovitch conjectured that the limit points of a rational distance set cannot contain arbitrarily large convex sets.
References:
- [ABT20] Ascher, K. and Braune, L. and Turchet, A., The Erd\H{o}s-Ulam problem, Lang's conjecture, and uniformity. arXiv:1901.02616 (2020).

- [SdZ10] Solymosi, Jozsef and de Zeeuw, Frank, On a question of Erd\H{o}s and Ulam. Discrete Comput. Geom. (2010), 393-401.
- [Sh18] Shaffaf, Jafar, A solution of the Erd\H{o}s-Ulam problem on rational distance sets assuming the Bombieri-Lang conjecture. Discrete Comput. Geom. (2018), 283-293.

problem: Let $n\geq 4$. Are there $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line and no four on a circle, such that all pairwise distances are integers?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/213.

- Page last edited: 16 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Anning and Erd\H{o}s \cite{AnEr45} proved there cannot exist an infinite such set. Harborth constructed such a set when $n=5$. The best construction to date, due to Kreisel and Kurz \cite{KK08}, has $n=7$.

Ascher, Braune, and Turchet \cite{ABT20} have shown that there is a uniform upper bound on the size of such a set, conditional on the Bombieri-Lang conjecture. problem: For which $n$ are there $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line and no four on a circle, which determine $n-1$ distinct distances and so that (in some ordering of the distances) the $i$th distance occurs $i$ times?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/217.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 13 April 2026.
Site remarks:
An example with $n=4$ is an isosceles triangle with the point in the centre. Erd\H{o}s originally believed this was impossible for $n\geq 5$, but Pomerance constructed a set with $n=5$ (see \cite{Er83c} for a description).

Pal\'{a}sti \cite{Pa87} constructed such a set with $n=7$. According to \cite{Pa89} when Erd\H{o}s saw this he asked whether there exists such a set of $5$ points with no equilateral triangles; Pal\'{a}sti \cite{Pa89} {IMAGE=217a,constructed a set} of $n=6$ points, satisfying these restrictions, with no equilateral triangles.

Pal\'{a}sti \cite{Pa89b} has {IMAGE=217b,constructed a set} with $n=8$.

Erd\H{o}s believed this is impossible for all sufficiently large $n$. This would follow from $h(n)\geq n$ for sufficiently large $n$, where $h(n)$ is as in [98].

forum_comments.author: John N. Dvorak
forum_comments.text:
So are there any rules to accepting conditional solutions for problems reduced to well-known conjectures? I followed my (GPT assisted) work above with a uniform Hardy--Littlewood prime $k$-tuple conjecture obtain the solution. Obviously no one is solving that any time soon, so where would this go?

Uniform Hardy--Littlewood correlations (conjectural).
Fix $k \ge 1$ and $\lambda > 0$. Uniformly for distinct integers\[
0 \le h_1 < h_2 < \cdots < h_k \le \lambda \log x,
\]one has\[
\sum_{n \le x} \prod_{j=1}^k \Lambda(n+h_j)
=
\bigl(\mathfrak{S}(\{h_1,\dots,h_k\}) + o_{k,\lambda}(1)\bigr)\,x,
\]where $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt function and
$\mathfrak{S}(\{h_1,\dots,h_k\})$ is the Hardy--Littlewood singular series.

Assume this conjecture holds for all $k \ge 1$.
Fix $\lambda > 0$. For $x$ large, form the scaled point set\[
\mathcal{P}_x
=
\left\{
\frac{p-x}{\log x} \in [0,\lambda]
:\ p \text{ prime},\ x < p \le x + \lambda \log x
\right\}.
\]Then $\mathcal{P}_x$ converges in finite-dimensional distributions
to a rate-$1$ Poisson point process on $[0,\lambda]$.

Let\[
0 \le a_1 < b_1 \le \cdots \le a_m < b_m \le \lambda,
\]and let $N_i(x)$ count primes in the interval\[
(x + a_i \log x,\ x + b_i \log x].
\]Joint convergence to independent Poisson random variables with means
$(b_i - a_i)$ follows by computing mixed factorial moments\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_i (N_i)_{r_i}\right]
\]averaged over $x$.
Expanding these moments reduces to sums of the above type with
$k = \sum r_i$, where the shifts $h_j$ range over a set of size
$O(\log x)$.
The conjectural asymptotic supplies the main term, and the remaining
singular-series averages match those of a Poisson process.

Let $(T_0 < T_1 < T_2 < \cdots)$ be the points of a rate-$1$ Poisson point
process on $\mathbb{R}$, conditioned to have a point at $0$.
Then the successive gaps\[
G_i = T_{i+1} - T_i
\]are independent $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ random variables.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ random variables.
For each $c > 0$,\[
\mathbb{P}(Y \ge cX) = \frac{1}{1+c}.
\]In particular,\[
\mathbb{P}(Y > X) = \mathbb{P}(Y < X) = \tfrac12,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(Y = X) = 0.
\]Indeed,\[
\mathbb{P}(Y \ge cX)
=
\int_0^\infty \mathbb{P}(Y \ge cx)\,e^{-x}\,dx
=
\int_0^\infty e^{-cx}e^{-x}\,dx
=
\frac{1}{1+c}.
\]Assume the uniform Hardy--Littlewood conjecture above.
Choose a prime $p_n$ uniformly at random among primes $\le x$ and consider
the local prime configuration in the interval\[
[p_n,\ p_n + \lambda \log p_n].
\]After rescaling by $\log p_n$, the consecutive gaps\[
\left(
\frac{d_n}{\log p_n},
\frac{d_{n+1}}{\log p_n}
\right)
\]converge in distribution to independent $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ random variables
$(X,Y)$.
Therefore, for each fixed $c > 0$, the limiting density exists and equals\[
\delta(\{n : d_{n+1} \ge c\,d_n\})
=
\mathbb{P}(Y \ge cX)
=
\frac{1}{1+c}.
\]Taking $c = 1$ gives density $1/2$.
Since ties have density zero, the same limit holds with $\ge$ replaced by
$>$, and similarly for $<$.

forum_comments.text:
So to review the bidding of a conditional resolution:

1) We show that ($d_n = d_{n+1} \le y$) and ($d_n = d_{n+1} > y$) have density zero:

The argument partitions at $y = (\log x)^{4/3}$.
Small equal gaps ($d_n = d_{n+1} \le y$) are bounded by uniform Brun sieve estimates for $3$-tuples.
Large equal gaps ($d_n = d_{n+1} > y$) are bounded using the telescoping sum
$$\sum_{m \le \pi(x)} d_m = p_{\pi(x)+1} - 2 \ll x,$$
which implies that the number of gaps exceeding $y$ is $\ll x/y$.
With the choice $y = (\log x)^{4/3}$, both contributions are $o(\pi(x))$, so
$$T(x)/\pi(x) \to 0.$$

2) We follow Banks [Ba23] who gives a heuristic argument, assuming a quantitative form of the prime tuples conjecture, that the first statement is true, and in fact for any $c\geq 0$ and $\epsilon>0$ the number of $n$ such that $p_n\leq x$ and $d_{n+1}\geq cd_n$ is\[\frac{\pi(x)}{c+1}+O\left(\frac{x}{(\log x)^{3/2+\epsilon}}\right).\]

forum_comments.author: John N. Dvorak
forum_comments.text:
Followed Terry Tao's suggestion above to use sieve theory methods.

After several iterations (and outstanding help from Kimi K2, Grok, and Gemini) on the optimal splitting threshold, the proof is now complete: equal consecutive prime gaps have asymptotic density zero, thereby reducing Erdős Problem #218 to showing that each strict inequality $d_{n+1} > d_n$ and $d_{n+1} < d_n$ has density $1/2$.

The argument partitions at $y = (\log x)^{4/3}$.
Small equal gaps ($d_n = d_{n+1} \le y$) are bounded by uniform Brun sieve estimates for $3$-tuples.
Large equal gaps ($d_n = d_{n+1} > y$) are bounded using the telescoping sum
$$\sum_{m \le \pi(x)} d_m = p_{\pi(x)+1} - 2 \ll x,$$
which implies that the number of gaps exceeding $y$ is $\ll x/y$.
With the choice $y = (\log x)^{4/3}$, both contributions are $o(\pi(x))$, so
$$T(x)/\pi(x) \to 0.$$

Cramer \cite{Cr36} proved an upper bound of $O(N(\log N)^4)$ conditional on the Riemann hypothesis. forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Note that a positive solution to this problem would automatically imply the prime gap bound $d_n \ll n^{1/2} \log n$, which was established by Cramer under the Riemann hypothesis but is not known in general; even the strongest forms of the prime tuples conjecture are not known to imply this bound. So it is extremely unlikely that one will be able to establish this result even assuming the prime tuples conjecture, if RH is not also assumed. (*Possibly* one might be able to make some progress assuming *both* RH and the prime tuples conjecture, but it is not clear how these rather different inputs could be combined.)

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Indeed, looks like the following argument would work:

Let $c_1,c_2>0$ and put $c=\lfloor c_2\rfloor$. We seek a block of $>c_1\log x$ consecutive primes $\le x$ whose adjacent gaps all exceed $c$. A natural conditional route is to assume a short-interval, uniformly averaged Hardy--Littlewood $k$-tuple conjecture at the scale $T\asymp(\log x)^2$: for each fixed $m\ge1$, uniformly over intervals $I=[u,u+T]\subset[x/2,x]$ and distinct shifts $H=\{h_1,\dots,h_m\}\subset[0,T+c]$,\[
\#\{n\in I:\ n+h_i\ \text{prime for all }i\}
=
(1+o(1))\,\mathfrak S(H)\,\frac{T}{(\log x)^m},\]as $x\to \infty$, with $o(1)$ uniform in $I,H$. (One can weaken “uniform in $I$” to “for all but $o(1)$ of such intervals”, consistent with Maier-type irregularities.) This hypothesis implies both concentration of the prime count $N(I)$ around $T/\log x$ and Poisson-type statistics for rare local patterns such as prime pairs at separations $\le c$ inside a typical interval of length $T$.

Take $T=A(\log x)^2$ with fixed $A>c_1$ and partition $[x/2,x]$ into disjoint intervals $I_j$ of length $T$. By the $m=1,2$ cases, $N(I_j)$ has mean $\sim A\log x$ and variance $O(\log x)$, so $N(I_j)\ge c_1\log x$ for all but $o(1)$ of the $I_j$ (Chebyshev). Let $B(I_j)$ be the number of prime pairs $(p,q)\subset I_j$ with $0<q-p\le c$. Using the fixed-$m$ cases of the conjecture and inclusion--exclusion/moment methods (à la Gallagher), one gets that $B(I_j)$ converges in distribution to $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ with $\lambda=A\sum_{h=1}^c \mathfrak S(\{0,h\})$, hence $\mathbb P(B(I_j)=0)\to e^{-\lambda}>0$ for a positive proportion of intervals. Therefore some $I_j$ simultaneously satisfies $N(I_j)\ge c_1\log x$ and $B(I_j)=0$; the primes in that interval are automatically consecutive in the global sequence and, since there is no pair within distance $\le c$, every adjacent prime gap inside the block exceeds $c$, yielding $>c_1\log x$ consecutive primes $\le x$ with all pairwise differences $>c_2$.

What is not settled here is the uniform claim for arbitrary prescribed positive \(c_1,c_2\).

Target:
For fixed \(c_1,c_2>0\), decide when long runs of consecutive prime gaps
exceeding \(c_2\) force run length \(>c_1\log x\) for all large \(x\).
Step A: Long-gap Bernoulli model with correction
Model events \((p_{n+1}-p_n)>c_2\) and quantify dependencies.
Step B: Run-length large deviations
Prove lower and upper bounds for maximum run length among primes up to \(x\).
Step C: Parameter map
Identify the admissible \((c_1,c_2)\)-region for guaranteed inequalities.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need uniform estimates for dependence between nearby long-gap events to justify
run-length asymptotics beyond independent heuristics.

Proposition CQ1 (Run-threshold equivalence):
Let \(R_x(c_2)\) be maximum length of consecutive prime gaps \(>c_2\) among
primes \(\le x\). Then the EP statement is equivalent to
\[
R_x(c_2)>c_1\log x
\]
for all large \(x\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is exactly the definition of the counted run condition.
\(\square\)
Proposition CQ2 (Reduction):
If one proves
\[
R_x(c_2)\sim \kappa(c_2)\log x
\]
with explicit \(\kappa(c_2)\), then the inequality in CQ1 holds iff
\(c_1<\kappa(c_2)\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Compare asymptotic coefficients.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $f(N)$ be the maximum size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that the sums $a+b+c$ with $a,b,c\in A$ are all distinct (aside from the trivial coincidences). Is it true that\[ f(N)\sim N^{1/3}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/241.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Originally asked to Erd\H{o}s by Bose. Bose and Chowla \cite{BoCh62} provided a construction proving one half of this, namely\[(1+o(1))N^{1/3}\leq f(N).\]The best upper bound known to date is due to Green \cite{Gr01},\[f(N) \leq ((7/2)^{1/3}+o(1))N^{1/3}\](note that $(7/2)^{1/3}\approx 1.519$).

More generally, Bose and Chowla conjectured that the maximum size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with all $r$-fold sums distinct (aside from the trivial coincidences) then\[\lvert A\rvert \sim N^{1/r}.\]This is known only for $r=2$ (see [30]).

This is discussed in problem C11 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [BoCh62] Bose, R. C. and Chowla, S., Theorems in the additive theory of numbers. Comment. Math. Helv. (1962/63), 141-147.
- [Gr01] Green, Ben, The number of squares and {$B_h[g]$} sets. Acta Arith. (2001), 365-390.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

Proposition CR1 (Scaling sandwich template):
If constants \(c_1,c_2>0\) satisfy
\[
c_1 N^{1/3}\le F(N)\le c_2 N^{1/3}
\]
for large \(N\), then \(F(N)=\Theta(N^{1/3})\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Direct definition of \(\Theta(\cdot)\).

Proposition CR2 (Constant extraction reduction):
If one proves
\[
\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{F(N)}{N^{1/3}}
\ge c
\quad\text{and}\quad
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{F(N)}{N^{1/3}}
\le c,
\]
then \(F(N)\sim cN^{1/3}\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Matching liminf/limsup imply existence of the limit equal to \(c\).
\(\square\)

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
See the remarks for some well-known parametric solutions (which I assume your formalisation is using). In particular it's not too hard to prove via elementary methods that this conjecture follows from (and is in fact equivalent to) the statement that for any prime $p$, there exist integers $a,c,d\geq 1$ such that either $p\equiv -a/c\pmod{4acd-1}$ or $p\equiv -\frac{4c^2d+1}{k}\pmod{4cd}$ for some $k\mid 4c^2d+1$. This might be nice, and not too hard, to formalise, see Theorem 1 of [BlEl22] for a proof of the equivalence.

Using this you can prove the conjecture for many congruence classes, and can efficiently check it's true for all small primes $p$. One can certainly refine Mordell's modulo $840$ conditions for example - this was already done by Terzi in 1971 to a modulo $120120$ condition. I'm sure that by continuing computations one can forever narrow down the congruential conditions, but I don't think this is a viable path to the full conjecture.

problem: Let $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be a sequence of integers such that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}^2}=1\]and $\sum\frac{1}{a_n}\in \mathbb{Q}$. Then, for all sufficiently large $n\geq 1$,\[ a_n = a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/243.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 21 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Straus \cite{ErSt64} proved that if $\lim a_n/a_{n-1}^2=1$ and $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is rational, and $a_n$ does not satisfy the recurrence, then\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} \frac{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]}{a_{n+1}}\left(\frac{a_n^2}{a_{n+1}}-1\right)>0.\]A sequence satisfying the reucrrence $a_n = a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1$ is known as Sylvester's sequence (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester%27s_sequence).

Duverney \cite{Du01} proved a weaker version of this problem: if\[\sum_{n\geq 0}\left(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^2}-1\right)\]converges then $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is rational if and only if\[a_{n}=a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1\]for all large $n$.
References:
- [Du01] Duverney, Daniel, Irrationality of fast converging series of rational numbers. J. Math. Sci. Univ. Tokyo (2001), 275--316.
- [ErSt64] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Straus, E. G., On the irrationality of certain {A}hmes series. J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1964), 129--133.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Such sequences can be described (after discarding a finite segment) via a deterministic recurrence applied to an initial pair $b,c$ of natural numbers; in particular, there are only countably many such sequences.

Indeed, if $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is rational, write $\frac{b_n}{c_n} = \sum_{n' \geq n} \frac{1}{a_n}$, then $\frac{b_n}{c_n} = \frac{1}{a_n} + \frac{b_{n+1}}{c_{n+1}}$. Writing $b_n a_n = c_n + h_n$, we have $b_n | c_n + h_n$, $b_{n+1} = h_n$, and $c_{n+1} = c_n \frac{c_n+h_n}{b_n}$. The condition $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}^2}=1$ means that $a_{n+1} = (1+o(1)) a_n^2$, that $\frac{b_n}{c_n} = (1+o(1)) \frac{1}{a_n}$, and thus $\frac{b_{n+1}}{c_{n+1}} = (1+o(1)) \frac{b_n^2}{c_n^2}$, which after some more algebra leads to $h_n = (1+o(1)) b_n$. Because of this, for $n$ sufficiently large one can solve for $\frac{c_n+h_n}{b_n}$ exactly as the nearest integer $\lfloor \frac{c_n}{b_n}+1 \rceil$ to $\frac{c_n}{b_n}+1$, and so the pair $(b_n,c_n)$ iterates via the recurrence

$$ (b_{n+1}, c_{n+1}) = (b_n \lfloor \frac{c_n}{b_n}+1 \rceil - c_n, c_n \lfloor \frac{c_n}{b_n}+1 \rceil).$$
This iteration yields a sequence of the desired form if and only if $\mathrm{dist}(c_n/b_n, {\mathbf Z}) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ (or equivalently $b_{n+1} = (1+o(1)) b_n$). If the $b_n$ stayed bounded, then this would force the $b_n$ to eventually become constant, at which point the $c_n$ must be multiples of $b_n$ and one can check that one becomes a Sylvester sequence at that point. So the question comes down to whether there is a solution to the above recurrence in which the $b_{n+1}/b_n$ tend to $1$ but never actually equal $1$ (if $b_{n+1}=b_n$ one can check that $b_m = b_n$ for all $m > n$).

Heuristically, any such sequence should have a zero probability of $b_{n+1}/b_n$ converging to 1 (it requires $c_n/b_n$ to be inexplicably close to an integer for all sufficiently large $n$), which indicates that the answer to this question is "no" [EDIT: I meant "yes"]; but the recurrence looks quite difficult to analyze (especially as the $c_n$ grow doubly exponentially fast) and I see no plausible way to rigorously prove the claim.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
Very similar observations were made by Junnosuke Koizumi in this recent preprint (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05933). He formulated them as a conditional result: that the claim holds if and only if (what he calls) a "pseudo-greedy expansion" of a rational number (a variant of a greedy Egyptian fraction algorithm) always terminates. He gives some numerical evidence for the opposite heuristics than you, checking his Conjecture 6 for rationals $p/q$ such that $p,q\leq100000$ and also reasoning probabilistically "on average" (Remark 17). Thus, the question might in fact likely have positive answer, but it is hard to say what really is a good heuristics here.

Slightly off-topic: I suggested exploiting a bit more the connection between (ir)rationality questions and greedy algorithms for (restricted) Egyptian fractions, under somewhat open-ended [282].

Target:
Prove rigidity/uniqueness of the Sylvester-type recurrence under the original
EP-243 hypotheses.
Step A: Telescoping identity extraction
Rewrite the key reciprocal sum as a near-telescoping expression determined by

Proposition CS1 (First-perturbation residual):
Assume sequence \((a_n)\) agrees with Sylvester recursion up to index \(j-1\), but
fails at \(j\). Then the telescoping defect after \(j\) is nonzero.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Compute symbolic difference between exact Sylvester telescoping identity and the
perturbed term; defect is rational with nonzero numerator.
\(\square\)
Proposition CS2 (Rigidity reduction):
If one proves defects from CS1 cannot be canceled by tail terms, uniqueness
follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Any non-Sylvester sequence has a first perturbation index \(j\); by CS1 and
non-cancellation, it violates the target identity.
\(\square\)

forum_comments.text: This type of problem is one step above other arithmetical problems, like, say, Erdos Straus conjecture, in terms of difficulty. Because the latter at least can have at most countably many counterexampĺes, but here uncountably many exceptions could exist, making the prospect of eliminating every single one of them very ambitious.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: Progress here may be linked to progress on Mahler's 3/2 problem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_3/2_problem). A key difficulty is that theoretically the integer parts $\lfloor C^k \rfloor$ could be almost all concentrated in a single residue class $b \hbox{ mod } W$, which would (morally at least) place an upper limit of $\phi(W)/W$ on the density. If this type of concentration happened for a lot of $W$, then one could conceivably end up with zero density overall. Excluding this type of scenario seems related to making more progress on the 3/2 problem.

attempt:
Target:
Establish positive lower density of numbers representable as
\[
n=p+\lfloor C^k\rfloor
\]
for fixed \(C>1\), ideally for all \(C\) outside a thin exceptional set.
Step A: Exponential-sequence distribution
Control distribution of \(\lfloor C^k\rfloor\) modulo \(q\) and in intervals.
Step B: Romanoff-type convolution
Combine prime distribution and exponential-sequence distribution via additive
energy/sieve convolution.
Step C: Density positivity
Derive positive lower density from main term dominance over error terms.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need uniform discrepancy bounds for \(\lfloor C^k\rfloor\) in residue classes
that are strong enough for lower-bound sieve across almost all \(C\).

Proposition CT1 (Representation count decomposition):
Let
\[
R_C(n)=\#\{(p,k): n=p+\lfloor C^k\rfloor\}.
\]
Then for \(N\),
\[
\sum_{n\le N} R_C(n)
= \sum_{k:\,\lfloor C^k\rfloor\le N}\pi(N-\lfloor C^k\rfloor).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Count representations by fixing \(k\), then summing allowable primes.
\(\square\)
Proposition CT2 (Density reduction):
If one proves
\[
\sum_{n\le N}\mathbf 1_{R_C(n)\ge1}\ge \delta N
\]
for some \(\delta>0\) and large \(N\), then representable numbers have positive
lower density.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is exactly the definition of positive lower density.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be a sequence of integers such that\[\limsup \frac{a_n}{n}=\infty.\]Is\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^{a_n}}\]transcendental?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/247.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 20 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er75c} proved the answer is yes under the stronger condition that $\limsup n_k/k^t=\infty$ for all $t\geq 1$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er88c} says 'many of these problems seem hopeless at present, but perhaps one can prove that if $a_n>cn^2$ then $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^{a_n}}$ is not the root of any quadratic polynomial'.

This problem has been formalised in Lean (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/247.lean) as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/).
References:
- [Er75c] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some problems and results on the irrationality of the sum of infinite series. J. Math. Sci. (1975), 1-7 (1976).
- [Er88c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 102-109.

computation:
Finite tests were carried out against eventual periodicity in the binary tail, a necessary signature of rationality, with periods checked up to \(600\).

All tested sparse-growth models showed persistent mismatch rates above zero, with no strong periodic-tail fit.

This remains heuristic evidence only: failure of finite periodicity tests does not prove transcendence, which requires genuinely arithmetic input.
attempt:
The background proves transcendence under a much stronger sparsity condition, namely \(\limsup n_k/k^t=\infty\) for every \(t\ge 1\).

The condition asked here, \(\limsup a_n/n=\infty\), is much weaker and allows denser subsequences than the known transcendence criteria currently handle.

Target:
Under the weak condition \(\limsup a_n/n=\infty\), prove transcendence, or at least irrationality, of the associated sparse binary series.
Step A: Growth-window extraction
From the limsup condition, extract infinitely many long gaps or rapid-growth windows.
Step B: Rational-approximation obstruction
Use those windows to rule out eventual periodicity and derive strong irrationality bounds.
Step C: Transcendence upgrade
Apply Mahler-type or Subspace Theorem machinery to pass from approximation bounds to transcendence.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a theorem translating sparse but irregular exponent growth into non-automaticity or non-periodicity strong enough for transcendence criteria.

Proposition CU1 (Periodic-tail criterion):
If a binary expansion is eventually periodic, the represented real number is rational.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Eventually periodic base-\(2\) expansions correspond to rational geometric tail sums.
\(\square\)
Proposition CU2 (Reduction to approximation bounds):
If one proves that for infinitely many \(m\), every rational \(p/q\) with \(q\le Q_m\) has
\[
\left|x-\frac pq\right|\ge Q_m^{-2-\eta},
\]
and this contradicts any algebraic-degree-\(D\) approximation bound pattern, then transcendence follows.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Combine the lower approximation barrier with Roth or Subspace-type upper restrictions for algebraic numbers.
\(\square\)

problem: Is\[\sum \frac{p_n}{2^n}\]irrational? (Here $p_n$ is the $n$th prime.)
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/251.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 September 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er58b} proved that $\sum \frac{p_n^k}{n!}$ is irrational for every $k\geq 1$.

In \cite{Er88c} he further conjectures that $\sum \frac{p_n^k}{2^n}$ is irrational for every $k$, and that if $g_n\geq 2$ and $g_n=o(p_n)$ then\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{p_n}{g_1\cdots g_n}\]is irrational. (The example $g_n=p_n+1$ shows that some condition on the growth of the $g_n$ is necessary here.)

The decimal expansion of this sum is A098990 (https://oeis.org/A098990) on the OEIS.
References:
- [Er58b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Sur certaines s\'{e}ries \`a{} valeur irrationnelle. Enseign. Math. (2) (1958), 93--100.
- [Er88c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 102-109.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
The last conjecture below the main problem statement has an (overly simple) negative answer. The idea is elementary, just make the series telescope by choosing positive integers $(c_n)$ such that\[ \frac{p_n}{g_1\cdots g_n} = \frac{c_n}{g_1\cdots g_{n-1}} - \frac{c_{n+1}}{g_1\cdots g_n}, \]i.e. $c_{n+1}=c_n g_n - p_n$. Thus, one can define $(c_n)$ recursively, by only making sure that\[ c_{n+1} \equiv -p_n \ (\text{mod} \ c_n) \]and that it is bounded from below by something that grows slowly but steadily. Afterwards one just sets\[ g_n := \frac{c_{n+1}+p_n}{c_n}. \]I got ChatGPT 5.4 Pro figure out the proof (https://chatgpt.com/share/69df7105-03cc-838a-a4a5-cbb6301e199d) and write up the details (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/files/Erdos_problem_251.pdf) with only minimal orchestration from my side.

It is possible that Erdős also wanted $(g_n)$ to be increasing, but then it would be weird to emphasize $g_n\geq2$ and switch the notation from $a_n$ to $g_n$ for this particular problem in [Er88c].

forum_comments.text:
Thanks! I ran standard check (https://chatgpt.com/share/69dfc4df-87f0-83a1-986e-59aa310c9c25) which found no issues.

It seems this proof is a bit stronger than $g_n = o(p_n)$. It may be of interest to see what the best provable statement is.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: By summation by parts, this is equivalent to the irrationality of $\sum_n \frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{2^n}$. It is possible that a sufficiently quantitative and uniform version of the prime tuples conjecture can resolve this problem, if it gives sufficient statistical control on the binary expansion of about $\log \log n$ consecutive prime gaps $p_{n+1}-p_n$ (which is usually of size $\asymp \log n$) to show that the binary expansion of $\sum_n \frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{2^n}$ cannot be periodic. The theory of Shannon entropy may be helpful in this regard.

Route:
Related the problem to known irrationality results for prime-weighted series with factorial denominators.

Hard point:
Methods exploiting factorial denominators do not directly transfer to geometric denominators.

Target:
Prove irrationality (or stronger) of
\[
\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{p_n}{2^n},
\]
where \(p_n\) is the \(n\)-th prime.
Step A: Prime-growth decomposition
Split into smooth main approximation using \(p_n\sim n\log n\) and fluctuation
error.
Step B: Binary-expansion irregularity
Show prime fluctuations induce non-periodic binary tail behavior incompatible with
rationality.
Step C: Diophantine conclusion
Convert tail irregularity into irrationality/transcendence criterion.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a quantitative lower bound on binary-tail complexity generated by the prime
sequence that cannot occur for rational numbers.

Proposition CW1 (Tail estimate):
For \(T_N=\sum_{n>N} p_n/2^n\),
\[
T_N\ll \frac{N\log N}{2^N}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Use \(p_n\ll n\log n\) and compare to weighted geometric tail.
\(\square\)
Proposition CW2 (Rationality obstruction reduction):
If one proves infinitely many \(N\) such that the first \(m(N)\) bits after
position \(N\) of partial sums cannot match any eventually periodic pattern with
period \(<P(N)\), where \(m(N)\gg \log P(N)\), then the full sum is irrational.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Rational numbers have eventually periodic binary expansions with fixed period; a
violating infinite sequence of windows contradicts this.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $k\geq 1$ and $\sigma_k(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^k$. Is\[\sum \frac{\sigma_k(n)}{n!}\]irrational?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/252.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 22 January 2026.
Site remarks:
This is known now for $1\leq k\leq 4$. The cases $k=1,2$ are reasonably straightforward, as observed by Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er52}. The case $k=3$ was proved independently by Schlage-Puchta \cite{ScPu06} and Friedlander, Luca, and Stoiciu \cite{FLC07}. The case $k=4$ was proved by Pratt \cite{Pr22}.

It is known that this sum is irrational for all $k\geq 1$ conditional on either Schinzel's conjecture (Schlage-Puchta \cite{ScPu06}) or Dickson's conjecture (Friedlander, Luca, and Stoiciu \cite{FLC07}).

This is discussed in problem B14 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [Er52] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problem 4493. Amer. Math. Monthly (1952), 557-558.
- [FLC07] Friedlander, J. B. and Luca, F. and Stoiciu, M., On the irrationality of a divisor function series. Integers (2007).
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Pr22] Pratt, K., The irrationality of a divisor function series of Erd\H{o}s and Kac. arXiv:2209.11124 (2022).
- [ScPu06] Schlage-Puchta, J. C., The irrationality of a number theoretical series. Ramanujan J. (2006), 455-460.

problem: Let $n\geq 1$ and $f(n)$ be maximal such that for any integers $1\leq a_1\leq \cdots \leq a_n$ we have\[\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\left\lvert \prod_{i}(1-z^{a_i})\right\rvert\geq f(n).\]Estimate $f(n)$ - in particular, is it true that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that\[\log f(n) \gg n^c?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/256.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 20 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres \cite{ErSz59} proved that $\lim f(n)^{1/n}=1$ and $f(n)>\sqrt{2n}$. Erd\H{o}s proved an upper bound of $\log f(n) \ll n^{1-c}$ for some constant $c>0$ with probabilistic methods. Atkinson \cite{At61} showed that $\log f(n) \ll n^{1/2}\log n$.

This was improved to\[\log f(n) \ll n^{1/3}(\log n)^{4/3}\]by Odlyzko \cite{Od82}.

If we denote by $f^*(n)$ the analogous quantity with the assumption that $a_1<\cdots<a_n$ then Bourgain and Chang \cite{BoCh18} prove that\[\log f^*(n)\ll (n\log n)^{1/2}\log\log n.\]Atkinson \cite{At61} noted this is related to the Chowla cosine problem [510], in that if for any set of $n$ integers $A$ there exists $\theta$ such that $\sum_{n\in A}\cos(n\theta) < -M_n$ then\[\log f^*(n) \ll M_n \log n.\]The answer to the specific question asked is no - Belov and Konyagin \cite{BeKo96} proved that\[\log f(n) \ll (\log n)^4.\]
References:
- [At61] Atkinson, F. V., On a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres. Canad. Math. Bull. (1961), 7-12.
- [BeKo96] Belov, A. S. and Konyagin, S. V., An estimate for the free term of a nonnegative trigonometric polynomial with integer coefficients. Mat. Zametki (1996), 627--629.
- [BoCh18] Bourgain, J. and Chang, Mei-Chu, On a paper of Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres. J. Anal. Math. (2018), 253-271.
- [ErSz59] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Szekeres, G., On the product $\Pi^n_{k=1}(1-z^ak)$. Acad. Serbe Sci. Publ. Inst. Math. (1959), 29-34.

I would like to add a follow-up to my earlier comment at 08:55 on 16 Sep 2025.
At that time I posed the following conjecture: For every choice of positive integers $s_1,\dots,s_n$, if $P_n(z) = \prod_{j=1}^n \bigl(1 - z^{s_j}\bigr) = \sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^k$, then $\sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \ge 2n$. I have now proved this conjecture, details can be found in my next comment.

forum_comments.author: bkbedert
forum_comments.text: Looking at the original paper of Erdös-Szekeres, it seems that this is essentially a more detailed write-up of their argument proving the lower bound $f(n)\geqslant\sqrt{2n}$. Though the observation from your previous post this bound $\sum_k|a_k|^2\geqslant 2n$ can be used to give $f(n)\geqslant 2\sqrt{n}$ by using the result of O’Hara--Rodriguez as a black box is new.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text: Thanks for your comment! Indeed the argument is close in spirit to Erdős–Szekeres, but the inequality $\sum_k |a_k|^2 \ge 2n$ is new, and combining it with O’Hara–Rodriguez gives $f(n)\ge 2\sqrt{n}$, which to my knowledge is the first general improvement since 1959.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
I have just written up my result proving that\[ f(n) \ge 2\sqrt{n}, \]and it is now available on arXiv: arXiv:2509.14182 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14182). Although this is not a very major improvement (since Erdős even conjectured that for sufficiently large $n$, $f(n)$ grows faster than any power of $n$), I believe it is still worthwhile to record.

In fact, this can be viewed as a fix of the original 1959 proof of Erdős–Szekeres (See also Section 2 of my paper.) The original Erdős–Szekeres idea considered the identity\[\sum_{j=1}^r z^{a_j} - \sum_{j=1}^r z^{b_j} \;=\; \prod_{j=1}^n (1-z^{s_j}),\]where $\{a_j\}$ and $\{b_j\}$ are disjoint sets of integers. In this formulation all nonzero coefficients on the left-hand side are $\pm 1$. Since $z=1$ is a zero of multiplicity $n$, together with the classical Prouhet–Tarry–Escott problem, one would conclude that $P_n(z)$ has at least $2n$ nonzero coefficients $a_k$, hence\[\sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \;\ge\; 2n.\]Applying Parseval’s identity gives\[\| P_n \|_{L^\infty(|z|=1)}^2 \geq \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |P_n(e^{it})|^2 dt = \sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \ge 2n,\]which in turn implies $f(n) \ge \sqrt{2n}$.

However, the gap is that the coefficients of $P_n(z)$ are not necessarily all $\pm 1$, so this argument fails.

In the paper of Billsborough–Freedman–Hart–Kowalsky–Lubinsky–Pomeranz–Sammel (Proc. AMS 149 (2021), 4233–4246, link (https://math.gatech.edu/sites/default/files/images/erdosszekeresproductsnovember30.pdf)), the authors gave a corrected proof showing that $P_n(z)$ has at least $n$ nonzero coefficients, and by using a result of O’Hara and Rodriguez they again obtained $f(n) \ge \sqrt{2n}$. Moreover, they remarked:
"If the original Erdős--Szekeres proof could be fixed, the O’Hara--Rodriguez bound would give $f(n)\ge 2\sqrt{n}$."

My result may thus be regarded as precisely providing such a fix, thereby confirming their expectation.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
In my previous comment at 07:32 on 16 Sep 2025, I noted that the classical bound $f(n)\ge \sqrt{2n}$ can be slightly sharpened to $f(n)\ \ge\ \sqrt{2n+2}$.

Here I would like to suggest a stronger conjecture based on further experiments.

**Conjecture**. For every choice of positive integers $s_1,\dots,s_n$, if $P_n(z)=\prod_{j=1}^n(1-z^{s_j})=\sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^k$, then $$ \sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2\ \ge\ 2n.$$

If this conjecture is true, then by Corollary 1 of O’Hara--Rodriguez "Some properties of self-inversive polynomials", we have\[
\|P_n\|_{L^\infty(|z|=1)}^2 \ \ge\ 2\sum_k |a_k|^2 \ \ge\ 4 n,
\]and thus\[
\|P_n\|_{L^\infty(|z|=1)}\ \ge\ 2\sqrt{n},
\]which is stronger than the classical $\sqrt{2n}$ (and also the $\sqrt{2n+2}$ refinement).

Numerical evidence (global searches for small $n$).
For each $n$ I searched over many sequences $s=(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ (with repetitions allowed) and minimized $\sum_k|a_k|^2$; a representative minimizer is shown.
In all cases below the nonzero coefficients of $P_n$ are $\pm1$.\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
n & \min\sum |a_k|^2 & \text{one minimizing }(s_1,\dots,s_n)\\\hline
1 & 2 & (1)\\
2 & 4 & (1,2)\\
3 & 6 & (1,2,3)\\
4 & 8 & (1,2,3,5)\\
5 & 10 & (1,2,3,5,7)\\
6 & 12 & (1,2,3,4,5,7)\\
7 & 16 & (1,2,3,4,5,7,11)\\
8 & 16 & (1,2,3,5,7,8,11,13)\\
9 & 20 & (1,2,3,5,7,8,9,11,13)
\end{array}
\]Thus for $n=1,2,3,4,5,6,8$ we observe $\min\sum|a_k|^2=2n$, while for $n=7$ and $n=9$ the minimum is even larger ($16>2n$ and $20>2n$, respectively).

I would be very interested in proofs, counterexamples, or further data for larger $n$.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
According to Lubinsky’s "A Survey of Erdős–Szekeres Products" (Springer link (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-87057-6_12), p.300), “Nor has there been an improvement on the lower bound $f(n) \ge \sqrt{2n}$ in general.”
I would like to point out a slight sharpening: in fact\[
f(n) \;\ge\; \sqrt{2n+2}.
\]Proof. Write\[
P_n(z) = \prod_{j=1}^n (1 - z^{s_j}) = \sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^k.
\]Since $z=1$ is a zero of multiplicity $n$, we have\[
\sum_{k=0}^N a_k (k)_j = 0, \qquad j=0,1,\dots,n-1,
\]where $(k)_j = k(k-1)\cdots(k-j+1)$.

Let $\operatorname{supp}(P_n)=\{t_1<\cdots<t_m\}$ be the exponents with $a_{t_i}\neq 0$. Restricting to $j=0,\dots,m-1$ gives a square system with coefficient matrix\[
F = \big[(t_i)_j\big]_{\;0\le j\le m-1}^{\;1\le i\le m}.
\]Using $(t)_j = j!\binom{t}{j}$, a standard change-of-basis argument gives\[
\det F = \prod_{1\le i<\ell\le m}(t_\ell - t_i) \;\neq\; 0.
\]Thus $m \ge n+1$, so $P_n$ has at least $n+1$ nonzero coefficients. (This bound is sharp, attained by $(1-z)^n$.)

Therefore\[
\sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \;\ge\; n+1.
\]By Corollary 1 of O’Hara--Rodriguez "Some properties of self-inversive polynomials" (JSTOR link (https://www.jstor.org/stable/2040432?seq=3)), if all zeros lie on the unit circle then\[
\|P_n\|_{L^\infty (|z|=1)}^2 \;\ge\; 2\sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \;\ge\; 2(n+1),
\]which yields\[
\|P_n\|_{L^\infty (|z|=1)} \;\ge\; \sqrt{2n+2}.
\]So the classical universal lower bound $\sqrt{2n}$ can be sharpened slightly to $\sqrt{2n+2}$.
This slight sharpening is clearly more useful than the original bound, and it is tight when $n=1$, since $f(1)=2>\sqrt{2}$.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
As a related remark, let $\{s_j\}_{j=1}^n$ be positive integers. In 1959, Erdős and Szekeres posed a number of problems about the size of polynomials of the form $$
\prod_{j=1}^n (1 - z^{s_j}),
$$ where $\{s_j\}_{j=1}^n$ are positive integers. A recent survey of these problems and related questions can be found in Lubinsky’s "A Survey of Erdős–Szekeres Products", available at (link) (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-87057-6_12).

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
It seems that the second question in the problem statement has already been resolved in the negative. In fact, Belov and Konyagin proved in Corollary 0.3 of the paper "An estimate of the free term of a non-negative trigonometric polynomial with integer coefficients"(link (https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=im&paperid=95&option_lang=eng)) that $$
\log f(n) = O\!\big((\log n)^4\big),
$$ so $f(n) \le \exp\!\big(C (\log n)^4\big)$. This shows in particular that no exponential lower bound of the form $\exp(n^c)$ can hold. Clearly, there is a lot of scope for work on both upper and lower bounds. The first question is still far from solved.

problem: Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set. Is\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-1}\]irrational?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/257.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 15 April 2026.
Site remarks:
If $A=\mathbb{N}$ then this series is $\sum_{n}\frac{\tau(n)}{2^n}$, where $\tau(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$, which Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er48} proved is irrational. In general, if $f_A(n)$ counts the number of divisors of $n$ which are elements of $A$ then\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-1}=\sum_n \frac{f_A(n)}{2^n}.\]The case when $A$ is the set of primes is [69]. This case (and when $A$ is the set of prime powers) was settled in the affirmative by Tao and Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen \cite{TaTe25}.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er68d} proved this sum is irrational whenever $(a,b)=1$ for all $a\neq b\in A$ and $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}<\infty$ (and thought that the condition $(a,b)=1$ could be dropped by complicating his proof).

There is nothing special about $2$ here, and this sum is likely irrational with $2$ replaced by any integer $t\geq 2$.

In \cite{Er88c} Erd\H{o}s goes further and speculates that $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-t_n}$ is irrational for every infinite set $A$ and bounded sequence $t_n$ (presumably of integers, and presumably excluding the case when $t_n=0$ for all $n$). This was disproved by Kova\v{c} and Tao \cite{KoTa24}, and in the comments Kova\v{c} has sketched a proof that there exists some choice of $t_n$ with $1\leq t_n\leq 6$ such that this sum is rational.
References:
- [Er48] Erd\H{o}s, P., On arithmetical properties of Lambert series. J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1948), 63-66.
- [Er68d] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series. Math. Student (1968), 222--226.
- [Er88c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 102-109.
- [KoTa24] Kova\vC, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series. arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).
- [TaTe25] T. Tao and J. Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen, Quantitative correlations and some problems on prime factors of consecutive integers. arXiv:2512.01739 (2025).

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
The last claim in the comments, on $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-t_n}$ being irrational for integers $(t_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ such that $0<|t_n|<C$, is easily seen to be false, even when $A=\mathbb{N}$. This has already been disproved under [264], in this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17593) - see the more general Theorem 2.5, but a very short argument for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n+b_n}$ is also sketched in a paragraph on p.17.

However, the question was written quite ambiguously in [Er88c] (as Erdős forgot to say that $t_n\neq0$), so one might also interpret it by requiring $0<t_n<C$. In that case the negative answer also easily follows from the ideas of the same paper, but this is not explicitly written there. Thus, I sketch the same very simple argument here, without taking any extra credit. :-)

Consider the set of all sums $\sum_{n=100}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n-t_n}$, where each $t_n$ ranges over $1,2,3,4,5,6$. They form a non-degenerate interval (and thus can be equal to some rational numbers), which can be seen by choosing $t_n$ inductively, so that the series sums to a desired target value. Namely, in each step, choosing $t_n$ achieves an approximation precision dictated by the largest gap:\[ \frac{1}{2^n-t_n-1} -\frac{1}{2^n-t_n} = \frac{1}{(2^n-t_n-1)(2^n-t_n)} \leq \frac{1}{(2^n-6)^2}, \]while the values of the series' tail can fully cover an interval of length\[ \sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty} \Big( \frac{1}{2^k-6} -\frac{1}{2^k-1} \Big) > \frac{1}{2^{n+1}-6} -\frac{1}{2^{n+1}-1} = \frac{5}{(2^{n+1}-6)(2^{n+1}-1)} > \frac{1}{(2^n-6)^2} \]for $n\geq100$.

If one doesn't feel like working out the details, then rather just apply Lemma 4 (a) from this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18712) to the above collection of sums.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
Let \(q ≥ 2\) be an integer. We can use the following reference to settle some special cases:
Yohei Tachiya, “Irrationality of Certain Lambert Series,” Tokyo J. Math. 27 (2004), 73–85.
PDF: https://projecteuclid.org/journals/tokyo-journal-of-mathematics/volume-27/issue-1/Irrationality-of-Certain-Lambert-Series/10.3836/tjm/1244208475.pdf

Tachiya’s Theorem 1 states that for any period-2 sequence \({a_n}\) (not identically zero),\[
\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{1-q^n}\notin\mathbb{Q}.
\]Taking \(a_n=\mathbf{1}_{\{n\text{ is even}\}}\) (or \(a_n=\mathbf{1}_{\{n\text{ is odd}\}}\)), which are period-2 and not identically zero, we get\[
\sum_{n\in 2\mathbb{N}}\frac{1}{q^n-1}
= -\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{1-q^n}\notin\mathbb{Q},
\qquad
\sum_{n\in (2\mathbb{N}-1)}\frac{1}{q^n-1}
= -\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{1-q^n}\notin\mathbb{Q}.
\]Thus, for \(A = 2\mathbb{N}\) (positive even integers) or \(A = 2\mathbb{N} - 1\) (positive odd integers), the subseries\[
\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{q^n-1}
\]is irrational (in particular for \(q=2\) posed in the problem).

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text: Well, ok, but the case of even positive integers is a consequence of a much older paper by Erdős (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1948-04.pdf), by writing\[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{q^{2n}-1} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(q^{2})^{n}-1}. \]Similarly, the case of odd positive integers is a consequence of an older paper by Borwein (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-314X(05)80041-1), by writing\[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{q^{2n-1}-1} = q \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(q^{2})^{n}-q}. \]

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
Thanks for pointing this out — you are right that the even- and odd-positive-integer cases follow from the much earlier results of Erdős and Borwein, respectively.
What Tachiya’s Theorem 1 offers here is a uniform way to handle any nontrivial period-2 coefficient sequence, not just the pure even or pure odd subsets.
Beyond these two special cases in this problem, I am not sure if it yields further consequences here, though.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text: The question about subseries of $\sum 1/(t^n-1)$ has been asked for every integer $t\geq2$, but I believe that the case $t=2$ is quite special. In the case $t=2$ the corresponding subsums form a fat (i.e., positive-measure) Cantor set, and it is very likely that it contains many rationals. If its gaps were even smaller (as for, say, $\sum 1/(2^n-2^{-2^n})$), then one could easily prove that it does not even miss many rationals within range. In the cases $t\geq3$ the subsums form a zero-measure Cantor set, which is quite possibly irrational.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
Erdős asked about variants of this problem even earlier, see for instance this paper from 1965 (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1969-09.pdf).

A simpler variant of this problem, where one has a bit more freedom and can choose, say, infinitely many terms of the form $\frac{1}{2^n-1}$ or $\frac{1}{11^m-1}$ has an easy negative answer, simply because the corresponding infinite subsums fill out a union of non-degenerate intervals (from which one simply picks a rational number); see Theorem 2.3 in this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17593).

The set\[ S = \Big\{ \sum_{n\in A} \frac{1}{2^n-1} : A\subseteq\mathbb{N} \Big\} \]appearing in [257] now has empty interior, so the same trick no longer applies. However, the answer is very likely negative again. Namely, the above set $S$ still has positive Lebesgue measure, i.e., it is a fat Cantor set. Thus, $S$ "almost surely" contains, say, at least one of the dyadic rationals $1/2,1/4,1/8,\ldots$. However, this argument alone cannot be turned into a rigorous proof, since there exist fat Cantor sets containing no rational numbers; a nonconstructive proof was given by Boes, Darst, and Erdős (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1981-05.pdf).

problem: Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots$ be a sequence of positive integers with $a_n\to \infty$. Is\[\sum_{n} \frac{\tau(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}\]irrational, where $\tau(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/258.
- Page status: PROVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-04-21).
- Page last edited: 15 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Straus \cite{ErSt71} proved this is true if $a_n$ is monotone, i.e. $a_{n-1}\leq a_n$ for all $n$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er48} proved that $\sum_n \frac{\tau(n)}{t^n}$ is irrational for any integer $t\geq 2$.

Chojeckl and GPT-5.4 Pro have answered this question (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos258.pdf) in the affirmative, using the work of Tao and Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen \cite{TaTe25} (see [69] and [248]).

Erd\H{o}s and Straus further conjectured that if $a_{n-1}\leq a_n$ for all $n$ then\[\sum_{n} \frac{\phi(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}\]and\[\sum_{n} \frac{\sigma(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}\]are both irrational.
References:
- [Er48] Erd\H{o}s, P., On arithmetical properties of Lambert series. J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1948), 63-66.
- [ErSt71] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Straus, E. G., Some number theoretic results. Pacific J. Math. (1971), 635-646.
- [TaTe25] T. Tao and J. Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen, Quantitative correlations and some problems on prime factors of consecutive integers. arXiv:2512.01739 (2025).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Thanks for doing this! I am using the standard from the Erdos problem repository: " formalizations conditional on past results will be accepted, as long as these past results are either (a) widely accepted, published results that do not simply contain the solution to the problem as a quick corollary, or (b) themselves formalized (or in the process of being formalized) by similar standards."

I guess as my result with Joni is not yet published (it is still being refereed), this does not yet qualify as a formalization for the purposes of the repository, but I would say it would become so after that paper is published (assuming that nothing suspicious is found in that paper in the meantime).

Incidentally, this result nicely bridges two disparate parts of our paper. Our first result from that paper solved [248 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/248)], which Erdos and Graham had hoped to be useful in solving the irrationality problem [69 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/69)], but we could not figure out how to do so, and ended up solving that problem by a different method. But now we see that the solution to 248 (adapted for the divisor function rather than the prime divisor function) does quickly solve this irrationality problem instead!

computation:
- rational-approximation scans of finite truncations of \sum \tau(n)/(a_1\cdots a_n).
- Across tested models, no exceptionally strong rational approximations emerged in the scanned denominator range.
- Obstacle: finite approximation scans are heuristic and cannot settle irrationality for the full infinite series in the general non-monotone case.
attempt:
The background says that Erdos and Straus proved irrationality when \((a_n)\) is monotone nondecreasing.

A natural extension attempt is to pass from monotone sequences to broader non-monotone classes by block or effective-monotone decompositions of the denominator products. The main obstruction is that after truncation or shifting, the resulting tails involve \(\tau(n+\text{offset})\) in the numerator, so the monotone theorem does not transfer in a black-box way.

Target:
Extend irrationality from monotone \(a_n\) to all positive integer sequences
\(a_n\to\infty\) in
\[
\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\tau(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}.
\]
Step A: Product-growth normalization
Analyze denominator products \(Q_n=a_1\cdots a_n\) and extract subsequences with
controlled growth ratios.
Step B: Shifted-divisor handling
Control the effect of non-monotone blocks that introduce \(\tau(n+\Delta)\)-type
tails in reduction attempts.
Step C: Irrationality criterion
Prove no eventual periodic or rational-tail structure can persist under
\(a_n\to\infty\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a robust irrationality criterion that depends only on \(Q_{n+1}/Q_n\to\infty\)
along subsequences, without monotonicity of \(a_n\).

Proposition DE1 (Tail control):
Let \(S=\sum_{n\ge1}\tau(n)/Q_n\), \(Q_n=a_1\cdots a_n\). Then
\[
0<S-S_N\le \sum_{n>N}\frac{n^\varepsilon}{Q_n}
\]
for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and large \(n\), using \(\tau(n)\ll_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply the standard divisor-function bound termwise.
\(\square\)
Proposition DE2 (Reduction):
If one proves infinitely many \(N\) with denominator-growth windows where no
rational with denominator \(\le Q_N^\theta\) approximates \(S\) within the DE1
tail scale, then \(S\) is irrational.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
A rational \(S=p/q\) would force compatible approximations from partial sums at
all large \(N\), contradicting the windowed exclusion.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be an increasing sequence such that $a_n/n\to \infty$. Is the sum\[\sum_n \frac{a_n}{2^{a_n}}\]irrational?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/260.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er81l} proved this is true under either of the stronger assumptions that
{UL}
{LI} $a_{n+1}-a_n\to \infty$ or {/LI}
{LI} $a_n \gg n\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}$.{/LI}
{/UL}
Erd\H{o}s and Graham speculate that the condition $\limsup a_{n+1}-a_n=\infty$ is not sufficient, but know of no example.

In \cite{Va99} this is asked with $a_n/n\to \infty$ replaced by $a_{n+1}-a_n\to \infty$, which as above was proved by Erd\H{o}s in \cite{Er81l}.
References:
- [Er81l] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Sur l'irrationalit\'{e}{} d'une certaine s\'{e}rie. C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris S\'{e}r. I Math. (1981), 765--768.
- [Va99] Various, Some of Paul's favorite problems. Booklet produced for the conference "Paul Erd\H{o}s and his mathematics", Budapest, July 1999 (1999).

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text: For people interested in this problem and other irrationality problems about the subseries $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{n}{2^n}$, an old reference is a paper by Borwein and Loring (https://www.jstor.org/stable/2008700?origin=crossref) from 1990, who called these $\ast$-binary representations. However, the actual problem is still open (both questions), as far as I know.

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg

computation:
- exact dyadic partial-sum arithmetic and deep rational-approximation scans.
- The tested families did not exhibit anomalously tiny rational-approximation errors in scanned ranges.
- Obstacle: this remains computational evidence only; proving irrationality under the full a_n/n\to\infty hypothesis requires theoretical arguments beyond finite scans.
attempt:
The background gives two stronger hypotheses under which irrationality is already proved:
1. \(a_{n+1}-a_n\to\infty\).
2. \(a_n\gg n\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}\).

What remains open is whether the weaker condition \(a_n/n\to\infty\) alone suffices.

Target:
Under only
\[
a_n\uparrow\infty,\qquad \frac{a_n}{n}\to\infty,
\]
prove irrationality of
\[
S=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{2^{a_n}}.
\]
Step A: Binary-block rigidity reduction
Translate irrationality into non-eventual-periodicity of the binary expansion of
\(S\). Show each summand contributes a localized binary block around bit-scale
\(a_n\), with carry interaction controlled by tails.
Step B: Sparse-carry separation
Prove infinitely many indices \(n\) where tail mass
\(\sum_{m>n}a_m2^{-a_m}\) is too small to alter a prescribed finite window of bits
created by the \(n\)-th summand.
Step C: Periodicity contradiction
If the expansion were eventually periodic, hence rational, sufficiently far windows
would repeat with fixed period; Step B yields infinitely many non-repeating
witness windows, a contradiction.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a uniform isolated-window lemma: existence of infinitely many \(n\) such
that
\[
\sum_{m>n}\frac{a_m}{2^{a_m}}<2^{-a_n-\Delta_n}
\]
with \(\Delta_n\to\infty\), and simultaneously the \(n\)-th summand produces a
nontrivial bit pattern within \([a_n,a_n+\Delta_n]\). This is automatic under
\(a_{n+1}-a_n\to\infty\), but open under only \(a_n/n\to\infty\).

Proposition DF1 (Rational implies eventual periodicity):
If \(S\in\mathbb Q\), its base-2 expansion is eventually periodic.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Standard characterization of rational numbers in integer bases.
\(\square\)
Proposition DF2 (Tail localization bound):
For \(S_n=\sum_{m\le n}a_m2^{-a_m}\),
\[
0<S-S_n\le \sum_{m>n}\frac{a_m}{2^{a_m}}.
\]
Hence if the right-hand side is \(<2^{-T}\), then the binary digits of \(S\) and \(S_n\) agree up to position \(T-1\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from absolute convergence and binary place-value stability.
\(\square\)
Proposition DF3 (Reduction to isolated windows):
If infinitely many \(n\) satisfy the blocking lemma above, then \(S\notin\mathbb Q\).
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Using DF2, each such \(n\) certifies a bit window determined by one summand and
immune to tail carries. Eventual periodicity would force eventual repetition of
all long windows, contradicting infinitely many isolated non-repeating windows.
\(\square\)

problem: Are there infinitely many $n$ such that there exists some $t\geq 2$ and distinct integers $a_1,\ldots,a_t\geq 1$ such that\[\frac{n}{2^n}=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}\frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}?\]Is this true for all $n$? Is there a rational $x$ such that\[x = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}\]has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ solutions?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/261.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Related to [260].

In \cite{Er88c} Erd\H{o}s notes that Cusick had a simple proof that there do exist infinitely many such $n$. Erd\H{o}s does not record what this was, but a later paper by Borwein and Loring \cite{BoLo90} provides the following proof: for every positive integer $m$ and $n=2^{m+1}-m-2$ we have\[\frac{n}{2^n}=\sum_{n<k\leq n+m}\frac{k}{2^k}.\]Tengely, Ulas, and Zygadlo \cite{TUZ20} have verified that all $n\leq 10000$ have the required property.

In \cite{Er88c} Erd\H{o}s weakens the second question to asking for the existence of a rational $x$ which has two solutions.
References:
- [BoLo90] Borwein, Peter and Loring, Terry A., Some questions of {E}rd\H{o}s and {G}raham on numbers of the form {$\sum g_n/2^{g_n}$}. Math. Comp. (1990), 377--394.
- [Er88c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 102-109.
- [TUZ20] Tengely, Szabolcs and Ulas, Maciej and Zygad\l o, Jakub, On a {D}iophantine equation of {E}rd\H{o}s and {G}raham. J. Number Theory (2020), 445--459.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
I would like to point out a small observation about the weakened question
mentioned in [Er88c], namely the existence of a rational number \(x\)
which has two representations.

Interpreting a representation as a choice of a set \(A\subseteq \mathbb N\)
of distinct positive integers, so that\[
x=\sum_{a\in A}\frac{a}{2^a},
\]one gets such an example from the finite identity\[
\frac{4}{2^4}=\frac{5}{2^5}+\frac{6}{2^6}.
\]Both sides are equal to \(1/4\).

Now use the classical identity\[
\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{m}{2^m}=2.
\]Let\[
A=\mathbb N\setminus\{5,6\},
\qquad
B=\mathbb N\setminus\{4\}.
\]Then\[
\sum_{a\in A}\frac{a}{2^a}
=
2-\frac{5}{2^5}-\frac{6}{2^6}
=
2-\frac14
=
\frac74,
\]whereas\[
\sum_{b\in B}\frac{b}{2^b}
=
2-\frac{4}{2^4}
=
2-\frac14
=
\frac74.
\]Therefore the rational number\[
x=\frac74
\]has two different representations:\[
\frac74
=
\sum_{a\in \mathbb N\setminus\{5,6\}}\frac{a}{2^a}
=
\sum_{b\in \mathbb N\setminus\{4\}}\frac{b}{2^b}.
\]Thus, under this literal interpretation, the weakened question has a positive
answer. Of course, this uses two representations with a large common tail;
if the intended question requires some stronger non-cancellation or
non-degeneracy condition, then that would be a different version.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
1) One should add the requirement that $a_1,\ldots,a_t$ are all mutually distinct integers. This is understood in all papers and it is needed to make the problem nontrivial.

2) The remark on the identity stated below the problem (giving representations for infinitely many $n$) is erroneously attributed to me. Later, when I searched the literature, I found exactly the same identity in the paper by Borwein and Loring (https://www.jstor.org/stable/2008700?origin=crossref) from 1990. But I think that Cusick should still be credited too.

3) It is still open whether the equation has a solution for all positive integers $n$, but Tengely, Ulas, and Zygadło (https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.01501) verified this for $n\leq10000$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

Finite compute signal:

attempt:
Target:
Promote known infinite-family constructions plus finite verification to a full
all-\(n\) theorem for the EP-261 representation property.
Step A: Congruence-complete backbone
Extract an explicit parametric identity family covering infinitely many \(n\) in
each relevant congruence class.
Step B: Finite-gap bridge
Show every sufficiently large interval between consecutive backbone values is
fillable by local transformation moves preserving the representation property.
Step C: Global completion
Combine Step A and B to deduce all large \(n\) are representable.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a bounded-diameter transition lemma on the representation state graph:
there exists \(L\) such that from any representable \(n\), one can reach every
\(n+t\) for \(1\le t\le L\) by a controlled modification of a witness.

Proposition DG1 (Backbone suffices with bounded gaps):
Let \(B\subset\mathbb N\) be representable integers with
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb N}\min\{b\in B: b\ge x\}-x \le L.
\]
If every representable \(n\) implies representability of \(n+1,\dots,n+L\), then
all sufficiently large integers are representable.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Given large \(x\), choose \(b\in B\) with \(x\le b\le x+L\). Backward/forward
closure across a length-\(L\) interval fills the gap.
\(\square\)
Proposition DG2 (Finite verification reduction):
If Step A gives representability on an infinite backbone and Step B provides
uniform transition length \(L\), then proving all \(n\le N_0\) directly finishes
the theorem.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply DG1 above \(N_0\); finite check covers the rest.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $a_n$ be an increasing sequence of positive integers such that for every sequence of positive integers $b_n$ with $b_n/a_n\to 1$ the sum\[\sum\frac{1}{b_n}\]is irrational. Is $a_n=2^{2^n}$ such a sequence? Must such a sequence satisfy $a_n^{1/n}\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/263.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 02 April 2026.
Site remarks:
One possible definition of an 'irrationality sequence' (see also [262] and [264]). A folklore result states that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is irrational whenever $\lim a_n^{1/2^n}=\infty$.

Kova\v{c} and Tao \cite{KoTa24} have proved that any strictly increasing sequence such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and $\lim a_{n+1}/a_n^2=0$ is not such an irrationality sequence. On the other hand, if\[\liminf \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^{2+\epsilon}}>0\]for some $\epsilon>0$ then the above folklore result implies that $a_n$ is such an irrationality sequence.

This problem was originally wrongly stated without the assumption that the sequence be increasing; DeepMind has given a counterexample without this assumption (see the comments).

Koizumi \cite{Ko25c} has proved that $a_n=\lfloor \alpha^{2^n}\rfloor$ is an irrationality sequence of this type for all but countably many $\alpha>1$.
References:
- [Ko25c] J. Koizumi, Irrationality of the reciprocal sum of doubly exponential sequences. arXiv:2504.05933 (2025).
- [KoTa24] Kova\vC, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series. arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).

forum_comments.author: SwaratChaudhuri
forum_comments.text:
Our DeepMind prover agent has falsified the second question in Lean. The proof was found fully autonomously; the only problem-specific human input was the formal problem statement, drawn from Formal Conjectures (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/263.lean). The proof (compilable with Lean 4.22) is available here (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/c8cf651906abe91051cf835d4232ad5648412113/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/263.lean) (theorem erdos_263.parts.ii).

Here's an informal summary of the proof (due to Adam Zsolt Wagner):

Let $a_n = 2^{3^n}$, except on a very sparse subset of indices where we set $a_n = 2^n$. For this sequence, the limit of $a_n ^ {1/n}$ does not exist, but standard arguments show that for every sequence $(b_n)$ as above, $\sum 1/b_n$ is irrational.

Looking at the proof and the problem more closely, we realized that Erdos’s original problem statement (https://renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1988-22.pdf (https://renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1988-22.pdf); p.105) required $a_n$ to be increasing. Assuming you agree, it would be good to correct the statement. That said, the counterexample still seems somewhat interesting, so we thought we would share it with the community.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problem: Let $a_n$ be a sequence of positive integers such that for every bounded sequence of integers $b_n$ (with $a_n+b_n\neq 0$ and $b_n\neq 0$ for all $n$) the sum\[\sum \frac{1}{a_n+b_n}\]is irrational. Are $a_n=2^n$ or $a_n=n!$ examples of such a sequence?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/264.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 20 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A possible definition of an 'irrationality sequence' (see also [262] and [263]). One example is $a_n=2^{2^n}$. In \cite{ErGr80} they also ask whether such a sequence can have polynomial growth, but Erd\H{o}s later retracted this in \cite{Er88c}, claiming 'It is not hard to show that it cannot increase slower than exponentially'.

Kova\v{c} and Tao \cite{KoTa24} have proved that $2^n$ is not such an irrationality sequence. More generally, they prove that any strictly increasing sequence of positive integers such that $\sum\frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and\[\liminf \left(a_n^2\sum_{k>n}\frac{1}{a_k^2}\right) >0 \]is not such an irrationality sequence. In particular, any strictly increasing sequence with $\limsup a_{n+1}/a_n <\infty$ is not such an irrationality sequence.

On the other hand, Kova\v{c} and Tao do prove that for any function $F$ with $\lim F(n+1)/F(n)=\infty$ there exists such an irrationality sequence with $a_n\sim F(n)$.
References:
- [Er88c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 102-109.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [KoTa24] Kova\vC, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series. arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
This is very nice and quite impressive!

Regarding $a_n=2^n$: You and Aristotle are right. It is sufficient to range $b_n$ over $\{1,2,3,4\}$; I haven't observed this before. The range $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ was simply more convenient, since one only needs a single term from the tail to dominate the "gap" from the preceding term.

Regarding $a_n=2^{2^n}$: Correct, this was not discussed in the paper [KoTa24]; it is a more classical result. Namely, Erdős and Straus in this paper (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1964-19.pdf) from 1964 (Theorem 1) proved the following:
If a sequence of positive integers $(c_n)$ satisfies\[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{c_n^2}{c_{n+1}}\leq1,\quad
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{LCM(c_1,\ldots,c_n)}{c_{n+1}}<\infty,\quad
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{c_n}\in\mathbb{Q}, \]then it has to satisfy the recurrence relation $c_{n+1}=c_n^2-c_n+1$ for sufficiently large indices $n$.
Now just apply this to $c_n=2^{2^n}+b_n$ for a bounded sequence $(b_n)$, also estimating trivially $LCM(c_1,\ldots,c_n)\leq c_1\cdots c_n$. If the sequence $(c_n)$ satisfied the recurrence relation for large $n$, we would have that $(2b_n-1)2^{2^n}$ is bounded, but $|2b_n-1|\geq1$, so it is not.
However, it is still impressive that Aristotle figured it all out just by itself!

By the way, yesterday I ran Aristotle for several hours with the same irrationality question but for $a_n=n!$ (entered manually as text), but there was no luck. I believe that this part of the problem is still open.

A centralized place where you can ask these questions is the Lean Zulip (https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/), many of them specifically on the topic "Discussion thread for Aristotle API (https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/Discussion.20thread.20for.20Aristotle.20API/with/564270157)". But in this case, it's relatively easy to manually strip down the Lean file to something like this:

import Mathlib
def IsIrrationalitySequence (a : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop := ∀ b : ℕ → ℕ, BddAbove (Set.range b) →
 0 ∉ Set.range (a + b) → 0 ∉ Set.range b → Irrational (∑' n, (1 : ℝ) / (a n + b n))
theorem erdos_264.parts.i : ¬IsIrrationalitySequence (2 ^ ·) := by sorry

Regarding using an LLM to translate back from Lean to English ("de-formalize"): in my experience looking at a bunch of misformalized statements, ChatGPT Pro was able to identify approximately half of the misformalizations. So perhaps there is still noticeable risk in that regard.

However, if you present an LLM with a misformalized statement AND a proof that "cheats" by taking advantage of the misformalization, I have found a very high success rate with the LLM catching that.

The remaining case would be a misformalized statement but with a "proper" proof (for the "real" statement). I'd guess that the LLM would be more likely to miss the misformalization there, because it's accompanied by a proof that doesn't "cheat", but I haven't actually tried this configuration because it hasn't come up.

problem: Let $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be an increasing sequence of integers. How fast can $a_n\to \infty$ grow if\[\sum\frac{1}{a_n}\quad\textrm{and}\quad\sum\frac{1}{a_n-1}\]are both rational?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/265.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 21 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Cantor observed that $a_n=\binom{n}{2}$ is such a sequence. If we replace $-1$ by a different constant then higher degree polynomials can be used - for example if we consider $\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac{1}{a_n}$ and $\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac{1}{a_n-12}$ then $a_n=n^3+6n^2+5n$ is an example of both series being rational.

Erd\H{o}s believed that $a_n^{1/n}\to \infty$ is possible, but $a_n^{1/2^n}\to 1$ is necessary.

This has been almost completely solved by Kova\v{c} and Tao \cite{KoTa24}, who prove that such a sequence can grow doubly exponentially. More precisely, there exists such a sequence such that $a_n^{1/\beta^n}\to \infty$ for some $\beta >1$.

It remains open whether one can achieve\[\limsup a_n^{1/2^n}>1.\]A folklore result states that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is irrational whenever $\lim a_n^{1/2^n}=\infty$, and hence such a sequence cannot grow faster than doubly exponentially - the remaining question is the precise exponent possible.
References:
- [KoTa24] Kova\vC, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series. arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).

This problem should have an extra condition that $(a_n)$ is strictly increasing. I find it implicitly understood in [ErGr80,p.64] that this condition carries over from the previous page. In a later paper (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1985-10.pdf) dedicated to his late colleague (p. 334) Erdős begins the paragraph with $n_1\leqq\cdots$, suggesting that the sequence was assumed to be at least non-decreasing. In [KoTa24] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17593) we assumed that $a_1<a_2<a_3<\cdots$ was understood in all questions of this type.

Another argument supporting the monotonicity condition: without it the remaining problem on whether it is possible to achieve $\limsup a_n^{1/2^n}>1$ would be entirely trivial. Just take any sequence making both $\sum_{n}1/a_n$ and $\sum_{n}1/(a_n-1)$ rational and rearrange it to have an extremely rapidly growing subsequence.

This whole remark might be obvious and redundant. I agree that it only makes sense to take $a_n$ in the increasing order, but it wouldn't hurt to be precise, to avoid trivial "solutions" to the problem or its subproblems.

problem: Let $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_{n+1}=F_n+F_{n-1}$ be the Fibonacci sequence. Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots $ be an infinite sequence with $n_{k+1}/n_k \geq c>1$. Must\[\sum_k\frac{1}{F_{n_k}}\]be irrational?
