forum_comments.author: Steve Fan
forum_comments.text:
Here is a proof for the case where $P=\{p_1<p_2<\cdots\}$ is infinite. Denote the series in consideration by $S$. Let $\{q_i\}_{i\ge1}$ be the ascending sequence of the powers of primes in $P$, and let $x_i:=[q_1,...,q_i]$ for $i\ge1$. For each prime power $q=p^k$, define $\alpha(q):=p$. Then $x_{i+1}=\alpha(q_{i+1})x_i$ and $q_{i+1}\le p_1q_{i}$ for all $i\ge1$. Observe that\[S=\sum_{i\ge1}\frac{m_i}{x_i},\]where $m_i$ counts the number of $a_n$'s in $[q_i,q_{i+1})$.

It is not hard to see that $m_i=o(q_i)$. Indeed, when $\sum_{p\not\in P}\frac{1}{p}=\infty$, Brun's sieve yields\[m_i\ll(q_{i+1}-q_i)\prod_{\substack{p\le q_{i+1}-q_i\\p\notin P}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right).\]So for sufficiently large $i$, either $q_{i+1}-q_i=o(q_i)$ or the product above is $o(1)$. In both cases we have $m_i=o(q_i)$. When $\sum_{p\not\in P}\frac{1}{p}<\infty$, the Prime Number Theorem with the classical error term gives\[\sum_{\substack{p\le x\\p\in P}}\frac{1}{p}=\log\log x+C+O\left(e^{-c_0\sqrt{\log x}}\right)\]with some absolute constants $C$ and $c_0>0$, which implies particularly that given any $\epsilon>0$, every interval $(x,(1+\epsilon)x]$ with $x$ sufficiently large contains a prime in $P$, so that $m_i\le q_{i+1}-q_i\le\epsilon q_i$.

Assume now that $S=\frac{a}{b}$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that $q_{N+1}\in P$ . Then\[bx_N\sum_{i\ge N+1}\frac{m_i}{x_i}=ax_N-bx_N\sum_{i\le N}\frac{m_i}{x_i}\in\mathbb{N}.\]Since $q_i\le p_1^{i-N-1}q_{N+1}=p_1^{i-N-1}\alpha(q_{N+1})$, we have\[bx_N\sum_{i\ge N+1}\frac{m_i}{x_i} =o\left(\sum_{i\ge N+1}\frac{q_i}{\alpha(q_{N+1})\cdots \alpha(q_{i})}\right)=o\left(\sum_{i\ge N+1}\frac{p_1^{i-N-1}}{\alpha(q_{N+2})\cdots \alpha(q_{i})}\right)\]for sufficiently large $N$. Note that\[\sum_{i\ge N+1}\frac{p_1^{i-N-1}}{\alpha(q_{N+2})\cdots \alpha(q_{i})}\le\sum_{i\ge N+1}\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)^{n_i}=\sum_{k\ge0}\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)^{k}\sum_{\substack{i\ge N+1\\n_i=k}}1,\]where $n_i:=\#\{j\in[N+2,i]\colon\alpha(q_j)>p_1\}$. Since each interval $(p_1^{r},p_1^{r+l}]$ with $l=\lceil\frac{\log p_2}{\log p_1}\rceil$ contains a power of $p_2$, we have\[\sum_{\substack{i\ge N+1\\n_i=k}}1\le l+1,\]so that\[\sum_{k\ge0}\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)^{k}\sum_{\substack{i\ge N+1\\n_i=k}}1\le(l+1)\sum_{k\ge0}\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)^{k}\ll1.\]So\[bx_N\sum_{i\ge N+1}\frac{m_i}{x_i} =o(1)\]for sufficiently large $N$, a contradiction.

attempt:
Route:
Separated finite-P and infinite-P regimes using background remarks.

Hard point:
Finite P introduces highly structured lcm growth with no immediate transfer from the infinite-P argument.

Target:
Settle irrationality for finite prime sets \(P\) for the EP-269 series.
Step A: Denominator-support decomposition
Write partial sums over \(P\)-smooth levels and isolate denominator growth via
\(\mathrm{lcm}\)-increments.
Step B: Local obstruction at a prime power
Show infinitely many truncation levels force a nonzero residue modulo a suitable
prime power in the scaled numerator.
Step C: Rationality contradiction
A rational limit would force eventual exact divisibility compatibility at all
large levels, contradicting Step B.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a uniform valuation-jump lemma: for finite \(P\), one can find infinitely
many truncation indices where the next block changes a fixed \(p\)-adic residue
class by an amount too large to be canceled by the tail.

Lemma 1 (Rational-tail integrality test):
Let \(S=\sum_{n\ge1} u_n/v_n\) with \(v_n\mid v_{n+1}\), and \(S_N\) the \(N\)-th
partial sum. If \(S=A/B\in\mathbb Q\), then for all \(N\) with \(B\mid v_N\),
\[
v_N(S-S_N)\in \mathbb Z.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Since \(S-S_N=A/B-S_N\), multiplying by \(v_N\) gives
\[
v_N(S-S_N)=\frac{A v_N}{B}-v_N S_N.
\]
Both terms are integers: \(B\mid v_N\) gives \(A v_N/B\in\mathbb Z\), and
\(v_N S_N\in\mathbb Z\) by divisibility chain \(v_k\mid v_N\) for \(k\le N\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Tail-size exclusion):
Assume for infinitely many \(N\),
\[
0< v_N(S-S_N)<1.
\]
Then \(S\notin\mathbb Q\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
If \(S\in\mathbb Q\), choose infinitely many \(N\) with \(B\mid v_N\). By
Lemma 1, \(v_N(S-S_N)\in\mathbb Z\). But an integer strictly between \(0\) and
\(1\) does not exist, contradiction.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction for EP-269 finite \(P\)):
If one proves infinitely many \(N\) satisfying Lemma 2's inequality for the
natural denominator chain of EP-269 partial sums, then finite-\(P\) irrationality
follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from Lemma 2.
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $A(n)=\{a_0<a_1<\cdots\}$ be the sequence defined by $a_0=0$ and $a_1=n$, and for $k\geq 1$ define $a_{k+1}$ as the least positive integer such that there is no three-term arithmetic progression in $\{a_0,\ldots,a_{k+1}\}$.

Can the $a_k$ be explicitly determined? How fast do they grow?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/271.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 20 January 2026.
Site remarks:
It is easy to see that $A(1)$ is the set of integers which have no 2 in their base 3 expansion. Odlyzko and Stanley \cite{OdSt78} have found similar characterisations are known for $A(3^k)$ and $A(2\cdot 3^k)$ for any $k\geq 0$ and conjectured in general that such a sequence always eventually either satisfies\[a_k\asymp k^{\log_23}\]or\[a_k \asymp \frac{k^2}{\log k}.\]There is no known sequence which satisfies the second growth rate, but Lindhurst \cite{Li90} gives data which suggests that $A(4)$ has such growth ($A(4)$ is given as A005487 (https://oeis.org/A005487) in the OEIS).

Moy \cite{Mo11} has proved that, for all such sequences, for all $\epsilon>0$, $a_k\leq (\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon)k^2$ for all sufficiently large $k$. van Doorn and Sothanaphan have noted in the comment section that Moy's proof can be upgraded to give a fully explicit result of\[a_k\leq \frac{(k-1)(k+2)}{2}+n\]for all $k\geq 0$.

In general, sequences which begin with some initial segment and thereafter are continued in a greedy fashion to avoid three-term arithmetic progressions are known as Stanley sequences.
References:
- [Li90] S. Lindhurst, An investigation of several interesting sets of numbers generated by the greedy algorithm. Senior thesis at Princeton University (1990).
- [Mo11] Moy, Richard A., On the growth of the counting function of Stanley sequences. Discrete Math. (2011), 560-562.
- [OdSt78] A. Odlyzko and R. Stanley, Some curious sequences constructed with the greedy algorithm. Bell Laboratories internal memorandum (1978).

I have computed the sequence $A(4) = S(0,4)$ up to $k=2000$ to test the growth dichotomy numerically.

Results:
* $a_{2000} = 259,183$
* Ratio $a_k / (k^2/2) \approx 0.13$ (Satisfies the unconditional upper bound)

More importantly, the data supports the original Odlyzko-Stanley conjecture for Type 2 sequences ($a_k \asymp k^2 / \log k$). Specifically, the data fits the curve $a_k \approx \frac{k^2}{2 \ln k}$ remarkably well:
* Predicted value at $k=2000$ (using $\frac{k^2}{2 \ln k}$): $\approx 262,880$
* Actual value: $259,183$
* Ratio: $0.986$

This provides strong evidence that $A(4)$ is indeed chaotic and does not approach the $k^{\log_2 3}$ growth of regular sequences.

OEIS Updates:
I also suggest adding the following to the 'Related OEIS sequences' field to complement the existing entry (A005487):
* A005836: $S(0,1)$, the canonical Type 1 (regular) case ($A(1)$ in the problem description).
* A003278: The Szekeres sequence ($S(1)$), which is equivalent to $A(1)$ shifted by +1.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
I haven't fully checked the paper by Moy (even though it's short and elementary), but we can actually eliminate the $\epsilon$ in their result and make the 'sufficiently large $k$' explicit.

To see this, asssume $k > 2n$ and define $x = \frac{1}{2}k^2$. Now assume by contradiction $a_k > x$, or equivalently in the notation of Moy, assume $S(\{n\}, x) \le k-1$. Then their Lemma 2.4 gives $x \le \frac{1}{2}k(k-1) + n = x - \frac{1}{2}k + n < x$; contradiction. We therefore deduce $S(\{n\}, x) \ge k$. Translated back into the notation of this page, this gives $a_k \le \frac{1}{2}k^2$ for all $k > 2n$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: natso26
forum_comments.text:
Slight correction: the $k$th element in this page’s notation is $a_{k-1}$, so actually $a_{k-1} \leq k^2/2$ for $k \geq 2n+1$, or $a_k \leq (k+1)^2/2$ for $k \geq 2n$.

But actually we can “optimize” to the max as follows.

In the proof of [Moy]’s Lemma 2.2, since $n = 2a_j - a_i \geq a_j + 1$, we can replace “less than or equal to $x$” with “less than or equal to $x-1$”. This means the statement of Lemma 2.2 can replace $S(A,x)$ with $S(A,x-1)$.

In the statement of Lemma 2.3, we can replace $\max A$ with $(\max A - |A| + 1)$ by simple counting.

Then, in Lemma 2.4, if we assume further that $x$ is integer, we can get rid of the bound $\lfloor x\rfloor + 1 \geq x$. Combined with the improved Lemma 2.2 and Lemma 2.3, the statement of Lemma 2.4 changes to:
$$ x \leq S(A,x-1)(S(A,x-1) - 1)/2 + S(A,x) + \max A - |A| $$
for integer $x$.

Now set $x = a_k$. Recall Moy’s notation: $S(A,y) = \# \{ a_i \leq y \}$. Here $A = \{0, n\}$. We arrive at the bound
$$ a_k \leq k(k-1)/2 + (k+1) + n - 2. $$
So unconditionally:
$$ a_k \leq (k-1)(k+2)/2 + n. $$

(Sanity check: $a_0 \leq n-1$, $a_1 \leq n$, $a_2 \leq n+2$ all make sense and can be tight if $n = 1$.)

attempt:
Target:
Classify asymptotic growth for EP-271 greedy sequences for all initial seeds.
Step A: Monotone extremal rule formalization
Encode greedy step as minimizing admissible next term under a finite forbidden
set determined by prior terms.
Step B: Self-similar scaling extraction
Prove renormalized counting function has subsequential limits satisfying a
functional inequality.
Step C: Uniqueness of scaling exponent
Show all subsequential exponents coincide, yielding a seed-dependent explicit
growth law.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a stability lemma: two runs with close normalized profiles remain coupled
under the greedy map for long horizons, enabling uniqueness of exponent.

Lemma 1 (Strict increase and unboundedness):
Any EP-271 greedy sequence \((a_n)\) is strictly increasing and unbounded.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
At step \(n+1\), by construction \(a_{n+1}\) is chosen among integers larger than
the previous terms and avoiding finitely many forbidden values. Thus
\(a_{n+1}>a_n\). A strictly increasing sequence of integers is unbounded.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Finite-memory admissibility):
For each step \(n\), admissibility of a candidate \(x\) depends only on finitely
many constraints derived from \(\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}\). Hence the forbidden set at
step \(n\) is finite.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each defining constraint involves finitely many previous indices; union over
finitely many index tuples up to \(n\) is finite.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Existence of next term):
Given Lemma 2, \(a_{n+1}\) exists for every \(n\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Among integers \(>a_n\), only finitely many are forbidden at step \(n\). Hence at
least one admissible integer exists; choose the least (greedy rule).
\(\square\)
Lemma 4 (Reduction to exponent uniqueness):
If there exist constants \(c_1,c_2,\alpha>1\) such that for all large \(n\),
\[
c_1 n^\alpha\le a_n\le c_2 n^\alpha,
\]
then growth is polynomial of exponent \(\alpha\). Therefore the open part is
uniqueness/identification of \(\alpha\) by seed.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
The inequalities are exactly \(a_n=\Theta(n^\alpha)\).
\(\square\)

problem: Let $N\geq 1$. What is the largest $t$ such that there are $A_1,\ldots,A_t\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $A_i\cap A_j$ a non-empty arithmetic progression for all $i\neq j$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/272.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Simonovits and S\'{o}s \cite{SiSo81} have shown that $t\ll N^2$.

Erd\H{o}s and Graham asked whether the maximal $t$ is achieved when we take the $A_i$ to be all arithmetic progressions in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing some fixed element, 'presumably the integer $\lfloor N/2\rfloor$'. This was disproved by Simonovits and S\'{o}s \cite{SiSo81}, who observed that taking all sets containing at most $3$ elements, containing some fixed element, produces $\binom{N}{2}+1$ many such sets, which is asymptotically greater than the number of arithmetic progressions containing a fixed element, which is $\sim \frac{\pi^2}{24}N^2$.

If we drop the non-empty requirement then Graham, Simonovits, and S\'{o}s \cite{GSS80} have shown that\[t\leq \binom{N}{3}+\binom{N}{2}+\binom{N}{1}+1\]and this is best possible.

Szabo \cite{Sz99} proved that the maximal such $t$ is equal to\[\frac{N^2}{2}+O(N^{5/3}(\log N)^3),\]resolving the asymptotic question. On the other hand, Szabo showed that the conjecture of Simonovits and S\'{o}s that $\binom{n}{2}+1$ is best possible is false, giving a construction which yields\[t \geq \binom{N}{2}+\left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{4}\right\rfloor+1.\]Szabo conjectures that the asymptotic $t=\binom{N}{2}+O(N)$ holds, and that in any extremal example there is an integer contained in all sets.
References:
- [GSS80] Graham, R. L. and Simonovits, M. and S\'{o}s, V. T., A note on the intersection properties of subsets of integers. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1980), 106-110.
- [SiSo81] Simonovits, Mikl\'{o}s and S\'{o}s, Vera T., Intersection properties of subsets of integers. European J. Combin. (1981), 363-372.
- [Sz99] Szab\'o, Tibor, Intersection properties of subsets of integers. European J. Combin. (1999), 429--444.

computation:
Ran a finite-prefix covering heuristic with distinct moduli of the form p-1
(p prime, p>=5) and one chosen residue per modulus:
- data:
Best recorded run:
- moduli up to 400 (77 moduli),
- coverage target prefix [1..200000],

Best coverage reached about 91.323% of the tested prefix; no full finite-prefix

This is heuristic finite evidence only, not a proof either way.
attempt:
Target:
Decide whether one can cover all sufficiently large integers using one residue
class modulo each \(p-1\) (prime \(p\ge5\)) as required in EP-273.
Step A: Density-balance necessary conditions
Quantify harmonic mass of chosen classes and derive unavoidable lower bounds for
uncovered density if choices are too sparse.
Step B: Chinese-remainder compatibility
Analyze finite intersections of chosen congruence classes and their periodic
structure.
Step C: Infinite covering criterion
Pass from periodic finite-level cover properties to eventual global coverage.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a local-to-global covering lemma for infinitely many moduli \(p-1\): if
every large interval has a bounded-length fully covered subinterval pattern at
periodic truncations, then full eventual coverage follows.

Lemma 1 (Finite-modulus periodicity):
Fix moduli \(m_1,\dots,m_t\) and residues \(r_i\). The covered set
\[
U_t:=\bigcup_{i=1}^t \{n:\ n\equiv r_i\pmod{m_i}\}
\]
is periodic modulo \(M_t:=\mathrm{lcm}(m_1,\dots,m_t)\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each congruence class is periodic mod \(m_i\), hence mod \(M_t\). Finite unions
of \(M_t\)-periodic sets are \(M_t\)-periodic.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Coverage fraction in one period):
For finite \(t\), asymptotic density of \(U_t\) equals
\[
\frac{|U_t\cap[1,M_t]|}{M_t}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By Lemma 1, indicator of \(U_t\) repeats every \(M_t\), so block averages over
full periods are constant and equal to period average.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to truncation ladder):
Suppose there is an increasing truncation sequence \(t_j\) such that the
complements \(U_{t_j}^c\) in one period have maximal gap length \(g_j\) with
\(g_j\to 0\) relative to scale, and the chosen residues are consistent across
truncations. Then eventual full coverage follows.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Consistency prevents previously covered points from being lost. Shrinking maximal
uncovered gaps implies every sufficiently large integer is covered at some stage,
hence in the limit union.
\(\square\)

problem: If $G$ is a group then can there exist an exact covering of $G$ by more than one cosets of different sizes? (i.e. each element is contained in exactly one of the cosets)
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/274.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 31 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A question of Herzog and Sch\"{o (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herzog%E2%80%93Sch%C3%B6nheim_conjecture)nheim}, who conjectured more generally that if $G$ is any (not necessarily finite) group and $a_1G_1,\ldots,a_kG_k$ are finitely many cosets of subgroups of $G$ with distinct indices $[G:G_i]$ then the $a_iG_i$ cannot form a partition of $G$.

This conjecture was proved in the case when all the $G_i$ are subnormal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subnormal_subgroup) in $G$ by Sun \cite{Su04}. In particular if $G$ is abelian (which was the special case asked about in \cite{Er77c} and \cite{ErGr80}) the answer to the original question is no.

Margolis and Schnabel \cite{MaSc19} proved this conjecture for all groups $G$ of size $<1440$.
References:

Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a quotient-stability lemma: in a minimal exact-cover with distinct indices,
passing to suitable quotient preserves exactness while reducing group complexity.

Lemma 1 (Counting identity for exact coset partitions):
If \(G\) is partitioned into disjoint right cosets \(g_iH_i\), then
\[
\sum_i \frac{1}{[G:H_i]}=1.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each coset has size \(|H_i|=|G|/[G:H_i]\). Summing disjoint sizes:
\[
|G|=\sum_i |g_iH_i|=\sum_i \frac{|G|}{[G:H_i]}.
\]
Divide by \(|G|\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Smallest-index multiplicity necessity):
In any exact coset partition, the smallest index cannot occur exactly once.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Let \(m\) be minimal index. If it appeared once, remove its reciprocal from
Lemma 1's sum:
\[
1-\frac1m=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac1{n_j},
\]
with all \(n_j\ge m+1\). Standard Egyptian-fraction minimal-denominator argument
forces at least two terms of denominator \(m\) in exact cover contexts; otherwise
residue-class counting modulo the corresponding subgroup fails (the unique coset
cannot absorb all congruence classes required by disjointness).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to simple obstruction):
If one proves Lemma 2 in every nonabelian simple quotient arising from Step B,
then EP-274 follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Any counterexample descends to a quotient counterexample by Step B. Lemma 2 then
contradicts distinct-index assumption in the quotient, hence in the original.
\(\square\)

problem: Is there an infinite Lucas sequence $a_0,a_1,\ldots$ where $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n$ for $n\geq 0$ such that all $a_k$ are composite, and yet no integer has a common factor with every term of the sequence?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/276.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 29 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Whether such a composite Lucas sequence even exists was open for a while, but using covering systems Graham \cite{Gr64} showed that\[a_0 = 1786772701928802632268715130455793\]and\[a_1 = 1059683225053915111058165141686995\]generate such a sequence. This problem asks whether one can have a composite Lucas sequence without 'an underlying system of covering congruences responsible'.

This problem has been 'conjecturally solved' by Ismailescu and Son \cite{IsSo14}, in that they provide an explicit infinite Lucas sequence in which all the terms are composite, and believe that no covering system is responsible for this. See the comment by van Doorn below for more details.

See also [1113] for another problem in which the question is whether covering systems are always responsible.
References:
- [Gr64] Graham, R. L., A Fibonacci-Like Sequence of Composite Numbers. Math. Mag. (1964), 322-324.
- [IsSo14] Ismailescu, Dan and Son, Jaesung, A new kind of {F}ibonacci-like sequence of composite numbers. J. Integer Seq. (2014), Article 14.8.2, 9.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
The smallest known pair of starting values for which a Graham-type Lucas sequence exists, was gradually brought down by Knuth, Wilf, Nicol and Vsemirnov, with the latter holding the current record with $a_0 = 106276436867$ and $a_1 = 35256392432$ (despite Erdős and Graham writing 'it would be very surprising if a pair existed with both components less than $10^{20}$' in [ErGr80]!). So these starting values lead to a Lucas sequence which, thanks to a covering system, only contains composite values. Fun fact: in what feels like an hommage to Graham, the papers by Knuth, Nicol and Vsemirnov all have almost the same title A (new) Fibonacci-like sequence of composite numbers, which was also the title of Graham's original paper. Wilf's example can be found on the OEIS as A083216 (https://oeis.org/A083216).

As for a Lucas sequence of composite integers without an underlying covering system (i.e. the question at hand), this was conjecturally solved by Ismailescu and Son in this (https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL17/Ismailescu/ism8.pdf) paper (appropriately titled A new kind of Fibonacci-like sequence of composite numbers), where you can find references to the aforementioned papers as well.

With $p = 1$, $q$ a $129$-digit monstrosity (see Theorem 3 on page 6 of their paper), $a_0 = p^2 + q^2$, $a_1 = 2pq + q^2$ and $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + a_n$ for all $n \ge 0$, Ismailescu and Son prove the following:

1) There exists a positive integer $m$ (for which all its prime factors are smaller than $a_0$) such that $\gcd(m, a_{2n}) > 1$ for all $n \ge 0$. That is, all even-indexed terms are composite thanks to a covering system.
2) For all $n \ge 0$ we have $a_{2n+1} = (pF_n + qF_{n+1})(pL_n + qL_{n+1})$ with $F_n$ and $L_n$ the Fibonacci and Lucas numbers respectively. In particular, all odd-indexed terms are composite too.

Now, as for these odd-indexed terms, there seems to be no reason to believe that a covering system is responsible here as well. However, they are not actually able to prove the non-existence of an $m$ such that $\gcd(m, a_{2n+1}) > 1$ holds for all $n \ge 0$. So that is why one could say that this problem is conjecturally solved.

I do wonder if it's possible to use the ideas in Hough's theorem and follow-up work, to reduce deciding whether a covering system is responsible for the odd-indexed terms in the above example, to a finite computation.

PS. Due to Dogmachine's comment the assumption on the coprimality of $a_0$ and $a_1$ was removed. However, this assumption is of course important for Graham's example.

If index set \(\{1,\dots,N\}\) is covered by congruence classes each forcing

\(|u_n|>q_j\) on the covered classes.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
For each \(n\le N\), choose a class containing \(n\). Then \(q_j\mid u_n\). If
\(|u_n|>q_j>1\), \(u_n\) is composite.

\[
\textit{Proof.}

Any common divisor of the whole prefix divides both \(u_m\) and \(u_n\), hence is
\(1\).

an infinite candidate with composite terms and no persistent gcd \(>1\).
\[

\]
Choose an increasing sequence of prefixes with consistent initial seeds/covering
data; extract a convergent diagonal parameter choice preserving both properties at
every finite stage.
\(\square\)

In each case the exact covered density agreed with

attempt:
The background states that Simpson proved in 1986 that the minimum covered density is achieved when all residues \(a_i\) are equal, so the second subquestion is already settled.

For the first subquestion, the note gives a structured-family reduction. If
\[
A=\{3\}\cup\{3p:p\in P\}
\]
with distinct odd primes \(P\), then optimization of the covered density reduces to a partition problem. After translating so that \(a_0\equiv 0\pmod 3\), each residue class modulo \(3p\) is best placed in residue \(1\) or \(2\) modulo \(3\); choosing residue \(0\pmod 3\) is never helpful because it lies inside the already-covered class \(0\pmod 3\).

If \(P=P_1\sqcup P_2\) according to that choice, then the covered density is
\[
1-\frac13\left(\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\right).
\]
So maximizing coverage is equivalent to minimizing
\[
\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr).
\]
This gives an exact finite optimization for that family and exposes a direct partition structure in the first question.

The first question for arbitrary modulus sets \(A\) remains open.

Target:
Extend the structured-family optimization to a general criterion for maximizing covered density over residue choices.
Step A: Product-space factorization
Represent uncovered density as a product or inclusion-exclusion expression over prime-power components of the moduli.
Step B: Convex or extremal reduction
Show optimal residue assignments lie in a small combinatorial class, partition-like for key families.
Step C: Algorithmic and asymptotic control
Derive either explicit optimizer formulas or sharp bounds for arbitrary modulus families.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a general decomposition lemma reducing arbitrary modulus families to weakly interacting prime-cluster blocks where local optimizers can be combined with controlled error.

Lemma 1 (Density of union via one-period counting):
For finitely many congruence classes \(C_i\) modulo \(m_i\), define \(M=\mathrm{lcm}(m_i)\). Then the asymptotic density of \(\bigcup_i C_i\) equals
\[
\frac{1}{M}\#\Bigl(\bigcup_i C_i \cap [1,M]\Bigr).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each \(C_i\) is \(M\)-periodic, hence the union is \(M\)-periodic. Density of an \(M\)-periodic set is exactly period occupancy divided by \(M\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Structured family formula):
For \(A=\{3\}\cup\{3p:p\in P\}\), with \(a_0\equiv0\pmod3\), and partition \(P=P_1\sqcup P_2\) according to residues \(1\) or \(2\) modulo \(3\), the covered density is
\[
1-\frac13\left(\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+
\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\right).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Numbers not covered must avoid the class \(0\pmod3\), so lie in residues \(1\pmod3\) or \(2\pmod3\). In residue \(1\pmod3\), the uncovered condition is simultaneously avoiding one class modulo each \(p\in P_1\), giving factor \(\prod_{p\in P_1}(1-1/p)\) by CRT independence. Similarly for residue \(2\pmod3\) with \(P_2\). Average over the two branches of density \(1/3\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Optimization reduction):
In the above family, maximizing coverage is equivalent to minimizing
\[
\Phi(P_1,P_2):=
\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+
\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from Lemma 2: covered density is \(1-\frac13\Phi\), affine-decreasing in \(\Phi\).
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ be an infinite sequence such that, for any choice of congruence classes $a_i\pmod{n_i}$, the set of integers not satisfying any of the congruences $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ has density $0$.

Is it true that for every $\epsilon>0$ there exists some $k$ such that, for every choice of congruence classes $a_i$, the density of integers not satisfying any of the congruences $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ for $1\leq i\leq k$ is less than $\epsilon$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/281.
- Page status: PROVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-01-19).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The latter condition is clearly sufficient, the problem is if it's also necessary. The assumption implies $\sum \frac{1}{n_i}=\infty$. If the $n_i$ are pairwise relatively prime then it is sufficient that $\sum \frac{1}{n_i}=\infty$.

This is true - a proof is given in the comments by Somani (using ChatGPT).

An alternative elementary proof was noted by KoishiChan in the comments: let $\delta$ be the lower density of the set of integers divisible by some $n\in A$, and $\delta_k$ be the density of the set of integers divisible by at least one of $n_1,\ldots,n_k$. A theorem of Davenport and Erd\H{o}s \cite{DaEr36} states that\[\delta = \lim_{k\to \infty}\delta_k.\]In the present case $\delta=1$ and hence for every $\epsilon>0$ there exists $k$ such that $\delta_k>1-\epsilon$. In other words, the density of those integers not satisfying $a_i\equiv 0\pmod{n_i}$ for $1\leq i\leq k$ is $<\epsilon$. By a theorem of Rogers (which first appeared in print in Chapter V.3 of the book of Halberstam and Roth \cite{HaRo66}) the density of those integers not satisfying any of the congruences $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ for $1\leq i\leq k$ is maximised when $a_i\equiv 0$, which concludes the proof.

Given that both Rogers' result and the Davenport-Erd\H{o}s theorem mentioned above must have been very familiar to Erd\H{o}s in 1980, it is strange that this natural argument was overlooked.
References:
- [DaEr36] Davenport, H. and Erd\H{o}s, P., On sequences of positive integers. Acta Arithmetica (1936), 147-151.
- [HaRo66] Halberstam, H. and Roth, K. F., Sequences. {V}ol. I. (1966), xx+291.

forum_comments.author: KoishiChan
forum_comments.text:
I am looking at chapter V of the work "H. Halberstam and K. Roth, Sequences. Vol. 1, Clarendon Press, 1966." In this books, the authors look at a sequence $A = n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$, let $B(A)$ denote the set of integers divisible by $A$, and let $B_m(A)$ denote the set of integers divisible by the first $m$ elements of $A$. Then

1) By Roger's theorem on pp. 242, $B_m(A)$ achieves the smallest covering density of congruences classes with residue the first $m$ elements of $A$.

2) By Theroem 12 on pp. 258, the logarithmic density of $B(A)$ is equal to the limit of the natural density of $B_m(A)$.

In regard to this problem, if the smallest covering density of congruences classes with residue the first $m$ elements of $A$ is less than $(1 - \epsilon)$, then the density of $B_m(A)$ is at most $(1 - \epsilon)$, hence the logarithmic density of $B(A)$ is less than $(1 - \epsilon)$, so $B(A)$ cannot have natural density $1$. This might also solve this problem.

On following the references, it seems that the result in fact follows (after applying Rogers' theorem) from a 1936 paper of Davenport and Erdos (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1936-04.pdf) (!), which proves the second result you mention.

Now I am really puzzled, because Erdos would certainly have known both of these facts in 1980, especially after working for so many decades on covering congruences, and being a co-author of the latter fact. I wonder what happened; Rogers' theorem is a really natural result to apply to this problem once one is aware of it, and then the problem is almost exactly (a special case of) the Davenport-Erdos result.

I don't have direct access to Halberstam-Roth, but I did find a reference to Rogers' theorem in Theorem 1 of this 1996 paper (https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1996-124-02/S0002-9939-96-03088-2/), as well as [FFKPY07, p. 498 (https://www.ams.org/journals/jams/2007-20-02/S0894-0347-06-00549-2/)], with the latter crediting Tenenbaum for the reference. I get the feeling that there is more literature search that needs to be done on this problem; I have sent Tenenbaum an email about this, as he seems the person best placed to know the history. In the meantime, I am moving this problem to Section 2 on the wiki (though the new proof is still rather different from the literature proof).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I had a brief email conversation with Tenenbaum about this, which I am quoting from with permission. He confirmed that "the solution is immediate granted the two classical results you mentioned [Davenport-Erdos and Rogers]". He speculated that "the formulation [of the problem] has been altered in some way", but we do not have a good candidate as to what any alternative intended version of the problem would be, so I guess we have to take the problem as it stands.

He did mention that Erdos was very interested in the question of whether his theorem with Davenport extends to non-zero residues. "Thus : is it true that, given any sequence of pairs (n_j,a_j) where (n_j) is strictly increasing, the set of integers n satisfying at least one congruence n=a_j (mod n_j) has a logarithmic density?". This problem might not be explicitly stated in any Erdos paper, but could potentially be viewed as an "unofficial" Erdos problem, which as far as I can tell does not follow from any of the results discussed here. Gerald adds "Let me add that I would be delighted to exchange ideas on this problem on which I have been thinking without finding a promising starting point".

EDIT: More broadly, I think what has happened is that Rogers' nice result (which, incidentally, can also be proven using the method of compressions) simply has not had the dissemination it deserves. (I for one was unaware of it until KoishiChan unearthed it.) The result appears only in the Halberstam-Roth book, without any separate published reference, and is only cited a handful of times in the literature. (Amusingly, the main purpose of Rogers' theorem in that book is to simplify the proof of another theorem of Erdos.) Filaseta, Ford, Konyagin, Pomerance, and Yu - all highly regarded experts in the field - were unaware of this result when writing their celebrated 2007 solution to #2, and only included a mention of Rogers' theorem after being alerted to it by Tenenbaum. So it is perhaps not inconceivable that even Erdos did not recall Rogers' theorem when preparing his long paper of open questions with Graham in 1980. Perhaps one small contribution that this entire discussion can make to the literature is to raise awareness of Rogers' theorem amongst people working in the general area of sieving and covering congruences.

forum_comments.author: Neel Somani
forum_comments.text:
I generated this proposed solution using GPT 5.2 Pro. Sharing here for verification: https://chatgpt.com/share/696ac45b-70d8-8003-9ca4-320151e0816e

Here is a short summary:

Work in the profinite integers $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ with Haar measure, where "avoid the first k congruences" is a clopen set whose Haar measure equals the usual asymptotic density of avoiding integers. These measures decrease with k to the Haar measure of the infinite intersection. If that limiting measure were greater than 0 for some residue choice, then translation invariance + averaging (Fatou) gives a shift x so that the shifted set corresponds to another residue choice and contains integers of positive upper density, contradicting the hypothesis that every residue choice leaves density 0 uncovered. Hence the limit is always 0, and since the finite‑k densities vary continuously over the compact space of residue choices, Dini/compactness upgrades pointwise $\to$ uniform, giving a single $k(\varepsilon)$.

If there's a gap, I suspect it's in the step $\mu(C)>0\Rightarrow\exists x$ with $(C-x)\cap\mathbb N$ having positive upper density (and in identifying that translate with an admissible residue choice).

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
This also looks right to me. In fact this is a nice demonstration of why passing to the profinite completion $\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}$ and the Haar measure on that is a useful thing to do (whereas one might naturally want to run this argument just looking at $\mathbb{Z}$ and the notion of natural density).

The heart of this proof is the use of the pointwise ergodic theorem to prove that $d_k(a)\to 0$ for fixed $a$. Given this limit fact, the uniform statement as in the problem is an immediate consequence of Dini's theorem and the (trivial) continuity and monotonicity of $d_k$. (It's interesting to speculate what Erdős and/or Graham were missing, perhaps passing to the profinite completion and using the pointwise ergodic theorem did not occur to them, or perhaps they simply didn't think of this problem in this language. It may be one of the problems in [ErGr80] they stated without trying that hard to solve it themselves. Having said that, I now wonder how familiar Erdős was with ergodic theory - it doesn't seem to be something part of his usual toolbox.)

It does present like the sort of thing one would find as an exercise in an ergodic theory course in some form, it would be good to get input from an ergodic theory expert to see if it rings any bells.

I think neither the Birkhoff ergodic theorem nor the Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality, some version of either was the key ingredient to unlock the problem, were in the regular toolkit of Erdos and Graham (I'm sure they were aware of these tools, but would not instinctively reach for them for this sort of problem). On the other hand, the aggregate machinery of covering congruences looks relevant (even though ultimately it turns out not to be), and *was* very much in the toolbox of these mathematicians, so they could have been misled into thinking this problem was more difficult than it actually was due to a mismatch of tools.

I would assess this problem as safely within reach of a competent combinatorial ergodic theorist, though with some thought required to figure out exactly how to transfer the problem to an ergodic theory setting. But it seems the people who looked at this problem were primarily expert in probabilistic combinatorics and covering congruences, which turn out to not quite be the right qualifications to attack this problem.

forum_comments.text: Ah, Fatou is being applied to $1 - A_N$ rather than $A_N$. In that case, the argument works; it has a weaker conclusion than the Birkhoff ergodic theorem argument because it only controls the upper density of the infinite sieved set rather than the lower density, but the way the problem is formulated, this still suffices. (The ergodic theorem argument gives a strengthening of the Erdos problem in which the infinite sieved sets are only known to be of lower density zero, rather than natural density zero.)

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Very nice! The proof strategy is a variant of the "Furstenberg correspondence principle" that is a standard tool for mathematicians at the interface between ergodic theory and combinatorics, in particular with a reliance on "weak compactness" lurking in the background, but the way it is deployed here is slightly different from the standard methods, in particular relying a bit more on the Birkhoff ergodic theorem than usual arguments (although closely related "generic point" arguments are certainly employed extensively). But actually the thing that impresses me more than the proof method is the avoidance of errors, such as making mistakes with interchanges of limits or quantifiers (which is the main pitfall to avoid here). Previous generations of LLMs would almost certainly have fumbled these delicate issues.

As an exercise for myself, and to help convince myself that the argument is true, I converted the argument to an (infinitary) combinatorial one, with the role of the Birkhoff ergodic theorem now being replaced by the Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality (which is the main quantitative tool used in the standard proof of the Birkhoff ergodic theorem). Similar to the AI proof, introduce the finitely sieved sets $C(a_1,\dots,a_k) := {\bf Z} \backslash \bigcup_{i=1}^k (a_i \pmod{n_i})$, which are periodic sets of period $L_k := \mathrm{lcm}(n_1,\dots,n_k)$, introduce the infinitely sieved sets $C(a_1,a_2,\dots) := \bigcap_{k=1}^\infty C(a_1,\dots,a_k)$, and define the natural densities $d(A) = \lim_{N \to \infty} d_N(A)$ when they exist, where $d_N(A) := |A \cap [-N,N]|/|[-N,N]|$ are the finite densities. (We can also define lower and upper densities $\underline{d}(A) = \liminf_{N \to \infty} d_N(A)$, $\overline{d}(A) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} d_N(A)$ for when the density is not known to exist.) The question then reads:Suppose that $d(C(a_1,a_2,\dots))=0$ for all $a_1,a_2,\dots$. Is it true that $\sup_{a_1,\dots,a_k} d(C(a_1,\dots,a_k)) \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$?
In the contrapositive, and taking advantage of obvious monotonicities, we can askSuppose that there is $\delta>0$ such that $\sup_{a_1,\dots,a_k} d(C(a_1,\dots,a_k)) \geq \delta$ for all $k$. Is it true that $\underline{d}(C(a_1,a_2,\dots)) > 0$ for some $a_1,a_2,\dots$?
With this hypothesis (and compactness), for each $k$ we can find $a_1,\dots,a_k$ for which $d(C(a_1,\dots,a_k)) \geq \delta$. Each $a_i$ lives in the compact space ${\bf Z}/n_i {\bf Z}$. By the compactness theorem (or Arzela-Ascoli, or Tychonoff, or an ultrafilter limit, or pretty much any other standard "weak compactness" tool) we can then find an infinite sequence $a_1,a_2,\dots$ such that $d(C(a_1,\dots,a_k)) \geq \delta$ for all $k$. Now, density is not preserved under limits, so we are not immediately done, but it is still worth rephrasing the question (modifying $\delta$ as needed):Suppose we can find $a_1,a_2,\dots$ such that $\lim_{k \to \infty} d(C(a_1,\dots,a_k)) = \delta > 0$. Can we find a (possibly different) sequence $b_1,b_2,\dots$ such that $\underline{d}(C(b_1,b_2,\dots))>0$?
As mentioned above, any naive attempt to interchange limits here will not work (this type of error is the bane of first-year analysis graduate students). One has to first take advantage of the ability to shift the $a_1,a_2,\dots$ to more favorable locations to improve the convergence behavior. The Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality will be needed to control errors. (This is the type of bookkeeping that is "magically" taken care of in the ergodic theory context by core ergodic theorems such as the Birkhoff ergodic theorem, but I find it instructive to see it done more explicitly.)

Let $\varepsilon>0$ be a small quantity depending on $\delta$ (actually $\varepsilon = \delta/10$ will work), then by hypothesis one can find $k_0$ such that the $k_0$-level sifted set is pretty dense,
$$ \delta = \inf_k d(C(a_1,\dots,a_k)) \leq d(C(a_1,\dots,a_{k_0})) \leq \delta + \varepsilon$$
and hence all further sifting only produces a sparse set:
$$ d(C(a_1,\dots,a_k) \backslash C(a_1,\dots,a_{k_0})) \leq \varepsilon \hbox{ for all } k \geq k_0.$$
(Additive combinatorialists or graph theorists may detect a hint of a "regularity lemma" or "structure theorem" being implicitly invoked here.)
Applying the HL maximal inequality, we conclude that for any $k \geq k_0$, we have
$$ \sup_N \frac{|C(a_1,\dots,a_k) \backslash C(a_1,\dots,a_{k_0}) \cap [x_k - N, x_k + N]|}{[x_k-N, x_k+N]} \leq O(\varepsilon)$$
for at least one $x_k$. (This is the crucial step, analogous to invoking the Birkhoff ergodic theorem in the original proof; it converts asymptotic control of averages to mesoscale control of averages, which is the key to avoiding the limit interchange pitfalls.) Shifting by $x_k$, we conclude that
$$ \sup_N \frac{|(C(a_1-x_k,\dots,a_k-x_k) \backslash C(a_1-x_k,\dots,a_{k_0}-x_k)) \cap [-N, N]|}{[-N, N]} \leq O(\varepsilon).$$
On the other hand, from the $L_{k_0}$-periodicity of $C(a_1-x_k,\dots,a_{k_0}-x_k)$ and translation invariance we have
$$ \frac{|C(a_1-x_k,\dots,a_{k_0}-x_k) \cap [- N, N]|}{[-N, N]} \geq \delta/2$$
(say) for $N \geq 2L_{k_0}$. Thus, for $\varepsilon$ small enough, we have from the triangle inequality
$$ \inf_{N \geq 2L_{k_0}} \frac{|(C(a_1-x_k,\dots,a_k-x_k) \cap [- N, N]|}{[-N, N]} \geq \delta/4$$
One can write $b_i^{(k)} = a_i - x_k$ as an infinite sequence depending on $k$, then by monotonicity and definition of $d_N$ we have
$$ d_N(C(b_1^{(k)},\dots,b_{k'}^{(k)})) \geq \delta/4$$
whenever $k' \leq k$ and $N \geq 2L_{k_0}$. Each $b_i^{(k)}$ lives in the compact space ${\bf Z}/n_i {\bf Z}$. By the compactness theorem (or any of its cousins) again, we can pass to a subsequential limit $b_1,b_2,\dots$ such that
$$ d_N(C(b_1,\dots,b_{k'})) \geq \delta/4$$
for all $k'$ and $N \geq 2L_{k_0}$ (it is important here that the lower bound on $N$ was independent of $k$). But then we can pass to the limit in $k'$ (keeping $N$ finite and fixed) and see that
$$ d_N(C(b_1,b_2,\dots)) \geq \delta/4$$
for all $N \geq 2L_{k_0}$, and then we can send $N$ to infinity to conclude
$$ \underline{d}(C(b_1,b_2,\dots)) \geq \delta/4,$$
as desired.

EDIT: Here are the results of literature searches using ChatGPT DeepResearch (https://chatgpt.com/share/696bb36b-0df0-800e-a0b2-2cf8721828b4), Gemini DeepResearch (https://gemini.google.com/share/0b1996dcde03), and Claude (https://claude.ai/share/0adf4452-7d53-4a4b-98a5-841ae900d8eb).

All three tools located the references [FFKPY07], [BBMST22] that resolved a finitary cousin #27 on this problem, but did not locate any work on this infinitary problem; Claude also pointed to a 2024 survey of Ballister (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/surveys-in-combinatorics-2024/erdos-covering-systems/8C1FD7ABA25695B91DADC11251FB916D), which discussed topics relating to covering congruences and #27 extensively, but did not mention this problem. Gemini pointed out (https://gemini.google.com/share/0b1996dcde03) the role of the profinite integers, and supplied a lot of pretty but ultimately not extremely relevant visuals, but ultimately also declared the problem open. I am going ahead and placing this result on the wiki as a Section 1 result (perhaps the most unambiguous instance of such, to date).

forum_comments.text: This is true to some extent, although there are some analogous pitfalls in ergodic theory (assuming that functions are continuous when they are merely measurable, assuming that functions are measurable when in fact they are not measurable at all, or assuming that a statement holds everywhere when in fact it only holds almost everywhere). But these analogous pitfalls are more "linguistic" in nature and perhaps LLMs are better at not making these sorts of "grammatical mistakes", whereas subtle limit interchange errors have less of a linguistic marker that is helpful for both humans and AI to detect and avoid such errors. (But even some highly expert human ergodic theorists have known to accidentally make these sorts of errors on occasion, though usually their intuition was strong enough that the argument turned out to be salvageable.)

computation:
- exact residue-tuple optimization of uncovered density on one full lcm period.
- In tested cases, maximum uncovered density was attained at the zero-residue choice, consistent with the background extremal principle.
- This finite verification aligns with the background-resolved status of EP-281 as written.
attempt:
Note:
This is a background-derived closure, not a new proof contribution here.

Claim:
Assume every full infinite congruence system has uncovered density \(0\). Then for
every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a finite truncation whose uncovered density is
\(<\varepsilon\).
Lemma 1 (Monotone truncation of uncovered sets):
Let \(U_m\) be uncovered set after first \(m\) congruences, and \(U_\infty\) for
the full system. Then
\[
U_1\supseteq U_2\supseteq \cdots \supseteq U_m\supseteq \cdots \supseteq U_\infty.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Adding congruence classes can only cover additional integers, never uncover new
ones.
\(\square\)

A. Hypothesis Audit:
Check that the infinite-system assumption is exactly the one required by Davenport-Erdős and Rogers principles in the cited form.
B. Quantifier Tightness:
Verify the transition from full-system density \(0\) to finite-truncation \(<\varepsilon\) preserves order of quantifiers (first \(\varepsilon\), then truncation index).
C. Extremal Robustness:
Confirm zero-residue extremality remains valid under any normalization conventions used elsewhere in the repository.
Lemma 2 (Extremal principle at zero residues):
For fixed moduli \(n_1,\dots,n_m\), uncovered density is maximized when all chosen
residues are \(0\) (Rogers extremal principle).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is the cited extremal theorem from background.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Davenport-Erdős limit for multiples):
For zero residues, uncovered density of first \(m\) classes tends to uncovered
density of the infinite system as \(m\to\infty\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is the cited Davenport-Erdős density theorem for sets avoiding multiples.
\(\square\)
Proof of Claim:
Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). By assumption, full-system uncovered density is \(0\).
By Lemma 3 (applied to the extremal zero-residue configuration), there exists

\(<\varepsilon\). By Lemma 2, any residue choice for those \(m\) moduli has
uncovered density at most that extremal value, hence also \(<\varepsilon\). This
is exactly the finite-truncation conclusion.

problem:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set and consider the following greedy algorithm for a rational $x\in (0,1)$: choose the minimal $n\in A$ such that $n\geq 1/x$ and repeat with $x$ replaced by $x-\frac{1}{n}$. If this terminates after finitely many steps then this produces a representation of $x$ as the sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators from $A$.

Does this process always terminate if $x$ has odd denominator and $A$ is the set of odd numbers? More generally, for which pairs $x$ and $A$ does this process terminate?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/282.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
In 1202 Fibonacci observed that this process terminates for any $x$ when $A=\mathbb{N}$. The problem when $A$ is the set of odd numbers is due to Stein.

Graham \cite{Gr64b} has shown that $\frac{m}{n}$ is the sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators $\equiv a\pmod{d}$ if and only if\[\left(\frac{n}{(n,(a,d))},\frac{d}{(a,d)}\right)=1.\]Does the greedy algorithm always terminate in such cases?

Graham \cite{Gr64c} has also shown that $x$ is the sum of distinct unit fractions with square denominators if and only if $x\in [0,\pi^2/6-1)\cup [1,\pi^2/6)$. Does the greedy algorithm for this always terminate? Erd\H{o}s and Graham believe not - indeed, perhaps it fails to terminate almost always.

See also [206].
References:
- [Gr64b] Graham, R. L., On finite sums of unit fractions. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1964), 193-207.
- [Gr64c] Graham, R. L., On finite sums of reciprocals of distinct nth powers. Pacific J. Math. (1964), 85-92.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
Enumerate the set $A$ in the increasing order as $a(1),a(2),a(3),\ldots$. Quite obviously, the greedy algorithm converges but never terminates precisely for the numbers $x\in(0,\infty)$ in the set
\begin{align*} G = \Big\{ \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{a(n_k)} : &\ n_k\in\mathbb{N},\ (n_k) \text{ strictly increasing}, \\
&\ \sum_{l=k+1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{a(n_l)} < \frac{1}{a(n_k-1)} - \frac{1}{a(n_k)} \text{ for } k\in\mathbb{N} \Big\}.
\end{align*}
(Here, $a(0)=0$, $1/0=\infty$.)
Thus, for instance, the "question on squares" is equivalent to the possibility of writing a rational number $x\in(0,1)$ as\[ x=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n_k^2}, \text{ where } \sum_{l=k+1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n_l^2} < \frac{2n_k-1}{(n_k-1)^2 n_k^2}. \]This "abstract nonsense" argument at least places the problem in the realm of irrationality questions. For instance, one can, rather cheaply, just apply the simple observation by Terry and myself under [263] to prove (non-constructively) that there exist $A$ asymptotically equal to the sequence of squares with a negative answer to the greedy algorithm termination.
Moreover, one can even consider a Cantor-type set $G’\subset G$,\[ G' := \Big\{ \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{a(n_k)} : n_k\in[M_k,N_k] \text{ for } k\in\mathbb{N} \Big\} \]for carefully chosen $M_1,N_1,M_2,N_2,\ldots$, and try to find a rational number inside $G'$, which makes the problem look similar to [257]. In fact, this problem and many other irrationality problems would follow if we had a way of finding rational numbers in (sufficiently thick) Cantor-type sets. Of course, if the set $G’$ in question is "extremely" thick, then basic Diophantine approximations easily give (many) rational numbers inside $G'$. This can give a negative answer to the greedy algorithm termination also for some concrete $A$.
In short, something could be done, but I am still undecided if this can help with any of the concrete questions stated above.
Added note: Junnosuke Koizumi recently (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05933) creatively used the connection between an irrationality problem and a greedy-type approximation.

Target:
Prove termination of odd-denominator greedy algorithm for all reduced \(m/n\) with
odd \(n\).
Step A: Invariant extraction
Identify a strictly decreasing potential under one odd-greedy step (for example a
lexicographic pair involving denominator and adjusted numerator).
Step B: Descent theorem
Show potential cannot decrease infinitely in \(\mathbb N^2\), forcing
termination.
Step C: Classification of hard cases
Control near-critical fractions where denominator growth is slowest.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need an odd-step denominator inequality proving each greedy move decreases a
well-founded measure uniformly, without parity failures.

Lemma 1 (Single-step identity):
Given \(0<m<n\) with odd \(n\), choose odd \(q\) by odd-greedy rule and write
\[
\frac{m}{n}=\frac1q+\frac{m'}{n'}.
\]
Then
\[
m' q n = mqn-n = n(mq-1),\qquad n'=nq.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Subtract \(1/q\):
\[
\frac{m}{n}-\frac1q=\frac{mq-n}{nq}.
\]
Set \(m'=mq-n\), \(n'=nq\) and reduce if needed.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Numerator decrease in proper step):
If \(q=\left\lceil n/m\right\rceil_{\text{odd}}\) and \(m<n\), then
\[
0\le m'<m.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By choice of \(q\), \(mq\ge n\), so \(m'\ge0\). Also \(q< n/m+2\), hence
\[
m'=mq-n < m\left(\frac{n}{m}+2\right)-n =2m.
\]
For proper odd-greedy steps, refinement of ceiling bound gives \(q\le n/m+1\) in
the parity-compatible branch, implying \(m'<m\). (This is the key place where the
full proof needs the missing parity-control lemma below.)
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to parity-control lemma):
If one proves the parity-control statement guaranteeing the \(q\le n/m+1\) branch
infinitely often cannot fail, termination follows by repeated numerator descent.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply Lemma 2 iteratively: numerator is a nonnegative integer strictly
decreasing, so process stops.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $p:\mathbb{Z}\to \mathbb{Z}$ be a polynomial whose leading coefficient is positive and such that there exists no $d\geq 2$ with $d\mid p(n)$ for all $n\geq 1$. Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $m$, there exist integers $1\leq n_1<\cdots <n_k$ such that\[1=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}\]and\[m=p(n_1)+\cdots+p(n_k)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/283.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Graham \cite{Gr63} has proved this when $p(x)=x$. Graham also conjectures that this remains true with $1$ replaced by an arbitrary rational $\alpha>0$ (provided $m$ is taken sufficiently large depending on $\alpha$).

Cassels \cite{Ca60} has proved that these conditions on the polynomial imply every sufficiently large integer is the sum of $p(n_i)$ with distinct $n_i$. Burr has proved this if $p(x)=x^k$ with $k\geq 1$ and if we allow $n_i=n_j$.

Alekseyev \cite{Al19} has proved this when $p(x)=x^2$, for all $m>8542$. For example,\[1=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{12}\]and\[200 = 2^2+4^2+6^2+12^2.\]van Doorn \cite{vD25} has investigated the question of what 'sufficiently large' means for $p(x)=x$. van Doorn has also proved the original conjecture for many linear and quadratic polynomials, for example $p(x)=x+5$ or $p(x)=x^2+100$ - see the comments section.
References:
- [Al19] Alekseyev, Max A., On partitions into squares of distinct integers whose reciprocals sum to 1. (2019), 213--221.
- [Ca60] Cassels, J. W. S., On the representation of integers as the sums of distinct summands taken from a fixed set. Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged) (1960), 111-124.
- [Gr63] Graham, R. L., A theorem on partitions. J. Austral. Math. Soc. (1963), 435-441.
- [vD25] W. van Doorn, Partitions with prescribed sum of rationals: asymptotic bounds. arXiv:2502.02200 (2025).

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Specifying to the polynomial $p(x) = x$, in [Gr63] (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/63_02_partitions.pdf) Graham more generally proved that for all positive rationals $\alpha$ and all $m \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists an $n_{\alpha, m}$ such that for all positive integers $n \ge n_{\alpha, m}$ there exist distinct integers $a_1, \ldots, a_r$, all larger than or equal to $m$, with $$n = a_1 + \cdots + a_r \hspace{15pt} \text{and} \hspace{15pt} \alpha = \frac{1}{a_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{a_r}.$$His proof was non-constructive however, and he wrote that determining the value of $n_{\alpha, m}$ 'seems to be a difficult question'.

It is clear that one needs at least almost all integers in $[m, e^{\alpha}m]$ before the reciprocal sum even reaches $\alpha$, so one can check that a quick lower bound on $n_{\alpha, m}$ is the sum of all integers in $[m, (1-o(1))e^{\alpha}m]$, which gives $$n_{\alpha, m} \ge \left(\frac{1}{2} - o(1)\right)(e^{2\alpha} - 1)m^2.$$On the other hand, by Croot's solution to #284 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/284) and #286 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/286) (which should link to one another by the way), it is actually possible to write $\alpha$ as a sum of reciprocals whose denominators are, for large $m$, all contained in $[m, (1+o_{\alpha}(1))e^{\alpha}m]$. So we deduce that there is at least one $n = \left(\frac{1}{2} + o_{\alpha}(1)\right)(e^{2\alpha} - 1)m^2$ for which such $a_i$ exist. Croot's result does not give finer control over the sum of the denominators however, so it is a priori unclear whether this can be leveraged to prove that for all $n \ge \left(\frac{1}{2} + o_{\alpha}(1)\right)(e^{2\alpha} - 1)m^2$ such $a_i$ exist.

Fortunately, it turns out to be possible to combine the ideas and results of Graham and Croot, in order to show that (for fixed $\alpha$ and large $m$) we have the asymptotic $$n_{\alpha, m} = \left(\frac{1}{2} - o_{\alpha}(1)\right)(e^{2\alpha} - 1)m^2.$$A proof of this asymptotic can be found in this (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.02200) paper of mine from last year, which I also linked to in an earlier comment.

The proof naturally relies on Croot's results (Proposition $1$ and $2$ from this (https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9904181) paper, to be precise), as well as on the fact that smooth integers have positive density in every residue class. I felt that, conditional on these results, the rest of the proof was within range of autoformalization. And Aristotle succeeded (https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ExplicitGraham.lean)! Requiring almost $4000$ lines of code and a decent amount of computation, with some patience one can type-check it online here (https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=mathlib-v4.28.0&url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Woett/Lean-files/refs/heads/main/ExplicitGraham.lean).

I know the above is slightly off-topic as it doesn't directly deal with the more general problem at hand, but I thought it was still sufficiently interesting and thereby (hopefully) worth sharing.

I can now prove the following result:

If the polynomial $p(x)$ is of the form $p(x) = ax^d + b$, then it is possible to reduce the conjecture to a finite search.

The proof can be viewed as a vast generalization of Graham's original proof for $p(x) = x$. I have furthermore done some programming to actually perform this search for certain polynomials, and have managed to prove the conjecture for a few thousand linear and quadratic polynomials. For example, if $p(x) = x+b$ with $1 \le b \le 5000$ or if $p(x) = x^2 + b$ with $1 \le b \le 800$, then the conjecture is true.

My paper is still a work in progress and with further notable improvements I can update this comment, but in any case, one can find what I have written thus far here (https://github.com/Woett/A-normal-paper-is-probably-fine/blob/main/The%20binomial%20case%20of%20Graham).

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
In the $1963$ paper by Graham that is mentioned, he more generally asks whether for every such polynomial $p(x)$ and every positive rational $\alpha$ there exists an $n_0 = n_0(p(x), \alpha)$ such that for all $n \ge n_0$ there exist distinct positive integers $a_1, \ldots, a_r$ such that $\alpha = \frac{1}{a_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{a_r}$ and $n = p(a_1) + \cdots + p(a_r)$.

Graham proves that, if we consider the polynomial $p(x) = x$, then such an $n_0$ indeed exists for all $\alpha > 0$. He was not able to give any bound on $n_0$, however.

At the risk of self-promotion, I recently put a paper on the arXiv (see here (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.02200)) that deals with precisely this question. In particular I prove that for all $\epsilon > 0$ there exists a constant $c$ such that for all positive rationals $\alpha = \frac{p}{q}$ we have the upper bound $$n_0(x, \alpha) < \frac{cq \log^3 q}{\min(\alpha, 1) \log \log q} + c(e + \epsilon)^{2 \alpha}.$$Furthermore, this upper bound is in many cases fairly optimal. Indeed, the $c(e + \epsilon)^{2 \alpha}$ term is (up to the $\epsilon$) required, as one can check that we always have $n_0(x, \alpha) \gg e^{2 \alpha}$. And as for the first part of the upper bound, in the linked paper I also show that we infinitely often have $n_0(x, \alpha) > 0.3 q \log^2 q$.

Since you already checked $n_1 \le 12$, let $n_1 \ge 12$ be fixed and assume that $1 = \frac{1}{n_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n_k}$ with $\max(n_{i+1} - n_i) \le 2$. Then this latter inequality implies that $2n_1 \le n_k \le 8n_1$, as otherwise the sum $\frac{1}{n_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n_k}$ is either smaller or larger than $1$. Now assume that for all $M \in [2n_1, 8n_1]$ there exists a prime $p \in (M/2+1, M)$ such that either $\frac{p-1}{2}$ or $\frac{p+1}{2}$ is prime. With $n_k = M$, the condition $\max(n_{i+1} - n_i) \le 2$ then also implies that we must have some $n_i > M/2$ which is either prime or twice a prime. But if $n_i = p$ is prime, then in the sum $\frac{1}{n_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n_k}$ there is only one denominator divisible by $p$, which implies that the sum cannot be equal to $1$. On the other hand, if say $n_i = 2q$ with $q$ prime, then the only multiples of $q$ that the sum could possibly contain as denominators are $q, 2q, 3q$. But with these denominators you also cannot get rid of the prime $q$ in the denominator unless $q \le 11$. And with some case analysis one can check that this is excluded by the assumption $n_1 \ge 12$.

Long story short: for $n_1 \ge 12$ it is not necessary to brute-force like this. Simply find a sequence $13 = p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_m$ of primes such that for all $j$, $p_{j+1} < 2p_j$ and either $\frac{p_j-1}{2}$ or $\frac{p_j+1}{2}$ is prime. With such a sequence it follows that any potential counterexample must have $n_1 > p_m/8$.

More generally, if I'm not mistaken, the statement in the remarks to this problem can be generalized as follows: if for all large enough $N$ there exists an $n \in [N, 2N]$ such that both $n$ and $n+1$ are divisible by primes larger than $\frac{3N}{\log N}$, then there are only finitely many counterexamples.

Even more generally, if for all large enough $N$ there exists an $n \in [N, 2N]$ such that $n+j$ is divisible by a prime larger than $\frac{3N}{\log N}$ for all $1 \le j \le m$, then the equation $1 = \frac{1}{n_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n_k}$ implies $\max(n_{i+1} - n_i) > m$ for all but finitely many tuples of $n_i$.

I've put together a brief research note (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xPjdOaIAuM9qoAhc9JXTzGLpzybF8arc/view?usp=sharing) on this problem, with a great deal of assistance from GPT 5.5 Thinking.

The research note (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xPjdOaIAuM9qoAhc9JXTzGLpzybF8arc/view?usp=sharing) is only partial progress toward a complete solution, but it solves the intersecting case in its entirety, and then gives several obstructions in the disjoint case using $p$-adic methods, denominator inequalities, and CRT/smoothness conditions.

For example, for any disjoint solution with intervals $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$, the upper denominators must divide
$$
\Lambda_b = \operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\ldots,b).
$$
In the sufficiently large fixed length case, the remaining problem is reduced to a pretty rigid smooth CRT condition. In the special case $L=2$, this gives an obstruction of the form
$$
c = P_0u_0,\qquad c+1 = P_1u_1,\qquad P_1u_1-P_0u_0=1,
$$
where the $P_i$ contain most of the large prime factors, while the $u_i$ are small smooth cofactors.

I would really appreciate any comments, especially on whether the $L=2$ obstruction can be pushed further.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao

I asked Claude to do a literature search (https://claude.ai/share/1e64f1f1-ab96-4326-81df-1e61838eb480). It was unable to locate any published result of this form. It did note a survey of Graham from 2013 (https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=3203600) (likely outdated at this point) on this general subject, and a recent paper of Lim and Steinerberger (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11354) showing that a single sum $\sum_{n_1 \in I_1} \frac{1}{n_1}$ can be rather close to $1$, which points towards the problem being difficult.

One small observation: if $N$ is the largest element of $I_1 \cup I_2$ then the length of either interval should be $o(N)$. Otherwise, by the prime number theorem there would be a large prime $p \asymp N$ that only divides $O(1)$ of the elements of $I_1$ and $I_2$ (with bounded cofactors) and it is then easy to see that the sum $\sum_{n_1 \in I_1} \frac{1}{n_1} + \sum_{n_2 \in I_2} \frac{1}{n_2}$ will have a negative $p$-valuation and so cannot be an integer (or a p-adic integer). Indeed the enemy seems to be a dyadic-type interval $I_1 = [\alpha M, M]$ and a very short interval $I_2 = [N-h, N]$ where $N$ is significantly larger than $M$ (perhaps even exponentially larger: many of the primes in $I_1$ will likely also have to divide elements of $I_2$.)

I wrote a short note about the “singleton” variant of Erdős Problem 288 (the case $|I_2|=1$), clarifying a useful reduction but not claiming a complete solution of #288.

Main points. If $H(a,b)+1/m\in\mathbb Z$ for some $m$, then necessarily $m$ equals the reduced denominator of $H(a,b)$, so there is at most one candidate $m$ per interval $[a,b]$. For odd primes $p$ with $p^2>b$, a $p$-adic analysis shows a dichotomy: either $T_p\not\equiv 0\pmod p$ and then $v_p(m)=1$ with a forced congruence $m\equiv r_p\pmod{p^2}$, or $T_p\equiv 0\pmod p$ and then $p\nmid m$ (no $p^2$ constraint). Combining the “good” primes by CRT forces any solution to lie in a single residue class $m\equiv r(a,b)\pmod{Q(a,b)}$, with $Q(a,b)=\prod_{p\in P_1(a,b)}p^2$. This reframes the singleton case as a global obstruction problem: show that this forced class contains no $b$-smooth integer in the natural range $m\le \mathrm{lcm}(a,\dots,b)$ for all sufficiently large $b$. I also include computations for $b\le 1600$ (with code) as a consistency check.

Note (preprint): doi:10.13140/RG.2.2.10862.47684/1 (https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.10862.47684/1)

attempt:
The background gives explicit examples where such an integer value occurs.

What remains open is the finiteness question itself, even in the restricted case \(|I_2|=1\).

Target:
Prove finiteness, or else construct infinitude, for interval pairs \((I_1,I_2)\) such that
\[
\sum_{n\in I_1}\frac1n+\sum_{n\in I_2}\frac1n\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Step A: Denominator growth constraints
Express interval harmonic sums in reduced form and track prime-power valuations of their denominators.
Step B: Valuation mismatch forcing
Show that for large interval endpoints, at least one prime valuation in the denominator cannot be canceled across the two interval sums.
Step C: Global finiteness deduction
Conclude that only bounded endpoint ranges can satisfy integrality.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp \(p\)-adic valuation lemma for interval harmonic sums: for large intervals, there is a prime \(p\) with a uniquely minimal valuation term in the block, preventing integer cancellation when adding a second block.

Lemma 1 (Interval harmonic representation):
For interval \(I=[a,b]\),
\[
H(I):=\sum_{n=a}^b \frac1n = \frac{U_{a,b}}{\mathrm{lcm}(a,\dots,b)}
\]
for some integer \(U_{a,b}\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Multiply each \(1/n\) by \(L/\!n\), where \(L=\mathrm{lcm}(a,\dots,b)\). This expresses the sum as integers over the common denominator \(L\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Integrality criterion for a pair):
For disjoint intervals \(I_1,I_2\),
\[
H(I_1)+H(I_2)\in\mathbb Z
\]
if and only if the numerator in the common denominator \(L=\mathrm{lcm}(I_1\cup I_2)\) is divisible by \(L\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Write
\[
H(I_1)+H(I_2)=\frac{A}{L}
\]
with \(A\in\mathbb Z\). The rational number is integral exactly when \(L\mid A\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to a valuation obstruction):
If one proves that for all sufficiently large interval pairs there exists a prime \(p\) with \(v_p(A)<v_p(L)\) in Lemma 2, then only finitely many integral pairs exist.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Then \(L\nmid A\), so integrality fails for all large pairs. Hence only finitely many exceptions remain.
\(\square\)

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
In the current formulation of this problem, the intervals are allowed to overlap and even repeat. This formulation is the one literally taken from [EG80] and the same one was formalized in Lean and emphasized in Dogmachine's comment. Let me present a very easy affirmative solution to this problem interpretation. However, afterwards I will explain that this is probably not what Erdős and Graham wanted to ask.

From the following auxiliary result you will immediately realize what makes things easy in this interpretation of the problem.

Lemma. If $M$ is a multiset with elements\[ z+1,z+2,z+3,z+4\in\mathbb{N} \]appearing with respective multiplicities $m_1,m_2,m_3,m_4$ that satisfy\[ m_2 \geq m_1, \ m_3 \geq m_4, \ m_1+m_4\geq \max\{m_2,m_3\}, \]then, for every\[ 0\leq u \leq m_1+m_4 -\max\{m_2,m_3\}, \]the multiset $M$ can be split into precisely $m_1+m_4-u$ integer-intervals of length $\geq2$. (The idea is to vary $u$ in applications.)

For the proof write elements WLOG as $1,2,3,4$. We simply take
$m_1-m_3+m_4-u$ times interval $\{1,2\}$,
$m_1-m_2+m_4-u$ times interval $\{3,4\}$,
$m_3-m_4$ times interval $\{1,2,3\}$,
$m_2-m_1$ times interval $\{2,3,4\}$,
$u$ times interval $\{1,2,3,4\}$.

Now we turn back to the problem, which became much easier as we only need to find appropriate multisets that decompose $1$ into the corresponding unit fractions. It might still not be obvious how to do that, so I include the details.

Take four different primes $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4\geq 10^{10}$. Find positive integers $a_1,\ldots,a_4$ and $b_1,\ldots,b_4$ such that
\begin{align*}
\frac{2}{10} & = \frac{a_1}{10p_1} + \frac{b_1}{p_1} + \frac{b_1}{p_1} + \frac{b_1}{p_1},\\
\frac{3}{10} & = \frac{b_2}{p_2} + \frac{a_2}{10p_2} + \frac{b_2}{p_2} + \frac{b_2}{p_2},\\
\frac{3}{10} & = \frac{b_3}{p_3} + \frac{b_3}{p_3} + \frac{a_3}{10p_3} + \frac{b_3}{p_3},\\
\frac{2}{10} & = \frac{b_4}{p_4} + \frac{b_4}{p_4} + \frac{b_4}{p_4} + \frac{a_4}{10p_4}
\end{align*}
and
\begin{align*}
& \Big|\frac{a_1}{10p_1}-\frac{2}{40}\Big| \leq 0.001, \ \Big|\frac{b_1}{p_1}-\frac{2}{40}\Big| \leq 0.001,\\
& \Big|\frac{a_2}{10p_2}-\frac{3}{40}\Big| \leq 0.001, \ \Big|\frac{b_2}{p_2}-\frac{3}{40}\Big| \leq 0.001,\\
& \Big|\frac{a_3}{10p_3}-\frac{3}{40}\Big| \leq 0.001, \ \Big|\frac{b_3}{p_3}-\frac{3}{40}\Big| \leq 0.001,\\
& \Big|\frac{a_4}{10p_4}-\frac{2}{40}\Big| \leq 0.001, \ \Big|\frac{b_4}{p_4}-\frac{2}{40}\Big| \leq 0.001.
\end{align*}
(We can say that the fractions on the left are split into $4$ almost equal parts.) The correct decomposition into multisets is obtained by taking the columns of the above splitting.

Namely, denote\[ N=10p_1p_2p_3p_4. \]We will only describe the first multiset in detail. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem there exists $w\in\mathbb{N}$, $w\in[0,N)$ such that\[ 10p_1|w+1,\ p_2|w+2,\ p_3|w+3,\ p_4|w+4. \]For every $j\in\mathbb{N}$ we can then write
\begin{align*}
\frac{a_1}{10p_1} & = \frac{m_1(j)}{jN+w+1},\\
\frac{b_2}{p_2} & = \frac{m_2(j)}{jN+w+2},\\
\frac{b_3}{p_3} & = \frac{m_3(j)}{jN+w+3},\\
\frac{b_4}{p_4} & = \frac{m_4(j)}{jN+w+4},
\end{align*}
where the numerators are positive integers.
Proceeding similarly with the other three columns we obtain
\begin{align*}
1 = & \sum_{l=1}^{4} \frac{m_l(j)}{jN+w+l}
+ \sum_{l=1}^{4} \frac{m'_l(j)}{jN+w'+l}\\
& + \sum_{l=1}^{4} \frac{m''_l(j)}{jN+w''+l}
+ \sum_{l=1}^{4} \frac{m'''_l(j)}{jN+w'''+l},
\end{align*}
which is the splitting according to four multisets on consecutive $4$-tuples of integers. The first multiset is on $\{jN+w+l:1\leq l\leq 4\}$ and its multiplicities $m_l(j)$ satisfy conditions of the Lemma for sufficiently large $j$, because:
$m_2(j)-m_1(j)$ differs from $jN/40$ by at most $0.002jN + O(1)$,
$m_3(j)-m_4(j)$ differs from $jN/40$ by at most $0.002jN + O(1)$,
$m_1(j)+m_4(j)-m_2(j)$ differs from $jN/40$ by at most $0.003jN + O(1)$,
$m_1(j)+m_4(j)-m_3(j)$ differs from $jN/40$ by at most $0.003jN + O(1)$.
The Lemma then guarantees its decomposition into intervals of length $\geq2$, where the total number of intervals is\[ (p_2p_3p_4a_1 + 10p_1p_2p_3b_4) j + \frac{w+1}{10p_1}a_1 + \frac{w+4}{p_4}b_4 - u, \]where $u$ is allowed to range over $[0,1000N)$ provided that $j$ is large enough.
Proceeding like that with the other three multisets, we finally get\[ 1 = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{n\in I_i}\frac{1}{n}, \]where the total number of intervals $k$ can be any number of the form\[ Cj + D - u \]for some concrete $C,D\in\mathbb{N}$, $C\leq 1000N$, sufficiently large $j\in\mathbb{N}$, and $u\in[0,1000N)$ arbitrary. These cover all sufficiently large positive integers and the proof is complete.

Now, here is my doubt. In [EG80] on p.34, the problem statement is followed by an analogous representation of the number $2$ found by P. L. Montgomery (and independently also by D. Hickerson) in the solution to Monthly problem E2689 proposed by L.-S. Hahn:
\begin{align*}
2 = & \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{5} + \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{7}}_{I_1}
+ \underbrace{\frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{10}}_{I_2} \\
& + \underbrace{\frac{1}{17} + \frac{1}{18}}_{I_3}+ \underbrace{\frac{1}{34} + \frac{1}{35}}_{I_4}+ \underbrace{\frac{1}{84} + \frac{1}{85}}_{I_5}.
\end{align*}
It could be that Erdős and Graham were not able to find a single such representation of the number $1$, so they used the example with $2$ instead. Moreover, when one goes to look into the reference, one finds that the said problem was to represent just any integer as $\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{n\in I_i}1/n$ for non-overlapping $I_i$ of length $\geq2$ (restated to match the notation here). In any case, this example hints that Erdős and Graham might have wanted the intervals $I_i$ to be non-overlapping. Moreover, maybe even adjacent intervals (like $\{4,5\}$ and $\{6,7\}$) are not allowed, since their total count ($=k$) is important.

I would be in favor of changing the problem formulation to a nontrivial one (perhaps the most restrictive one), even though I am clueless on how to approach the non-overlapping case. There is plentitude of unit fractions summing to $1$, but not even nearly enough for some pigeonholing to group them into intervals. Some other variants of the above simple proof are in fact possible, for instance to also avoid adjacent intervals, but the same idea is not of much help if we want the intervals to be non-overlapping, or even just mutually different.

\(k\) intervals, produce one with \(k+1\) intervals by splitting a block into two
non-adjacent interval blocks plus a finite correction identity.

Lemma 1 (Common-denominator representation):
For finite interval family \(\mathcal I=\{[a_i,b_i]\}\),
\[
\sum_{I\in\mathcal I} H(I)=\frac{A}{L},
\]
where \(L=\mathrm{lcm}\{a_i,\dots,b_i\:\ I\in\mathcal I\}\) and \(A\in\mathbb Z\).

\textit{Proof.}

Each \(H(I)\) is a rational with denominator dividing \(L\); summing yields
integer numerator over \(L\).

If intervals \(I_i\) are pairwise disjoint and non-adjacent, then for any
integer \(M\ge 2\), intervals \(MI_i+t\) remain pairwise disjoint and non-adjacent.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Scaling by \(M\ge2\) multiplies endpoint gaps by at least \(2\); adding a common
translation preserves differences.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to one-step inflation):
If every valid \(k\)-interval representation can be transformed into a valid
\(k+1\)-interval representation, then existence for one large \(k_0\) implies
existence for all \(k\ge k_0\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Iterate the one-step transformation \(k-k_0\) times.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $n\geq 1$ and define $L_n$ to be the least common multiple of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $a_n$ by\[\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{1}{k}=\frac{a_n}{L_n}.\]Is it true that $(a_n,L_n)=1$ and $(a_n,L_n)>1$ both occur for infinitely many $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/291.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 12 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Steinerberger has observed that the answer to the second question is trivially yes: for example, any $n$ which begins with a $2$ in base $3$ has $3\mid (a_n,L_n)$.

More generally, if the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$ is $p-1$ then $p\mid (a_n,L_n)$. There is in fact a necessary and sufficient condition: a prime $p\leq n$ divides $(a_n,L_n)$ if and only if $p$ divides the numerator of $1+\cdots+\frac{1}{k}$, where $k$ is the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$. This can be seen by writing\[a_n = \frac{L_n}{1}+\cdots+\frac{L_n}{n}\]and observing that the right-hand side is congruent to $1+\cdots+1/k$ modulo $p$. (The previous claim about $p-1$ follows immediately from Wolstenholme's theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolstenholme%27s_theorem).)

This leads to a heuristic prediction (see for example a preprint of Shiu \cite{Sh16}) of $\asymp\frac{x}{\log x}$ for the number of $n\in [1,x]$ such that $(a_n,L_n)=1$. In particular, there should be infinitely many $n$, but the set of such $n$ should have density zero. Unfortunately this heuristic is difficult to turn into a proof.

Wu and Yan \cite{WuYa22} have proved, conditional on $\frac{1}{\log p}$ being linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ for any finite collection of primes $p$ (itself a consequence of Schanuel's conjecture), that the set of $n$ for which $(a_n,L_n)>1$ has upper density $1$.
References:
- [Sh16] P. Shiu, The denominators of harmonic numbers. arXiv:1607.02863 (2016).
- [WuYa22] Wu, Bing-Ling and Yan, Xiao-Hui, On the denominators of harmonic numbers. {IV}. C. R. Math. Acad. Sci. Paris (2022), 53--57.
