forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Let $v_n$ be the denominator of the harmonic sum $\frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{2} + \ldots + \frac{1}{n}$, and let $a_n$ and $L_n$ be defined as above. Then we note that #290 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/290) and #291 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/291) are related by the fact that the inequality $v_n < v_{n-1}$ implies $\gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1$. Back in 2010, Ernie Croot asked: what if we instead look at $\frac{r_1}{1} + \frac{r_2}{2} + \ldots + \frac{r_n}{n}$, with $r_i \in \{-1, 1\}$ or even $r_i \in A$ for some finite set of non-zero integers $A$? Can we still conclude that inequalities like $v_n < v_{n-1}$ and $\gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1$ hold infinitely often? It's these types of generalizations I would like to comment on.

Now, starting with the bad news, this more general case no longer works; it is possible to choose the $r_i \in \{-1, 1\}$ in such a way that (with the appropriate definitions) $v_n = L_n$ (i.e. $\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1$) holds for all $n$.

All is not lost, however. As long as we add the extra condition that the $r_i$ are periodic, then one can find infinitely many $n$ for which $v_n < v_{n-1}$, and hence $\gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1$. That is, this more general case of the second part of this problem is true, assuming that the sequence of numerators is periodic.

In order to prove that there are infinitely many $n$ with $v_n < v_{n-1}$, one needs to find large prime divisors of $a_n$. But as it turns out, by itself such a result does hold more generally, even in the non-periodic case.

Theorem.
Let $r_1, r_2, \ldots$ be a bounded sequence of non-zero integers, and let $m$ be an arbitrary integer larger than $\max_i |r_i|$. With $L_n$ the least common multiple of $1, 2, \ldots, n$, let $a_n$ be such that $$\frac{a_n}{L_n} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{r_i}{i}.$$Then there exists an $n = e^{O(m)}$ such that $a_n$ is divisible by a prime larger than $m$.

Under the assumption of two prime number theorem type results that will presumably eventually follow from the PNT+ Project (https://github.com/AlexKontorovich/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd), thanks to Aristotle I have formalized (https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ErdosProblem291.lean) a proof of this theorem. For the moment you can type-check it online here (https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=mathlib-v4.24.0&url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2FWoett%2FLean-files%2Fmain%2FErdosProblem291.lean). A human-readable proof based on [vD24] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03073) can be found here (https://github.com/Woett/Miscellaneous/blob/main/Generalized%20harmonic%20sums%20have%20arbitrarily%20large%20prime%20factors.pdf).

Bringing the discussion back in the general direction of the problem at hand, assume now that the $r_i$ are periodic with period $t$ (so that $r_i = r_{i+t}$ for all $i$), and let $p > \max(|r_1|, |r_2|, \ldots, |r_t|, t)$ be an arbitrarily large prime divisor of $a_n$. By the theorem above, such $p$ and $n$ do exist. By the periodicity of the $r_i$, one can then check that $p$ also divides $a_{n'}$ where $n'= np^{\varphi(t)}$. Hence, as a corollary we obtain the following generalization of the (second part of the) original problem:

Corollary.
Let $r_1, r_2, \ldots$ be a periodic sequence of non-zero integers, let $L_n$ be the least common multiple of $1, 2, \ldots, n$, and let $a_n$ be such that $$\frac{a_n}{L_n} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{r_i}{i}.$$Then we have $\limsup \gcd(a_n, L_n) = \infty$. In particular, there are infinitely many $n$ for which $\gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1$.

A proof of this corollary is also included in the formalization I linked. I would like to eventually extend this even further and formalize the entirety of [vD24] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03073), but that could take a while.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Let $n$ be fixed. For a prime $p \le n$, let $k = k(p) < p$ be such that $$kp^{\lfloor \frac{\log n}{\log p} \rfloor} \le n < (k+1)p^{\lfloor \frac{\log n}{\log p} \rfloor}. \hspace{20pt} (1)$$That is, $k$ is the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$. As you allude to, in order for $\gcd(a_n, L_n)$ to be equal to $1$, we need $p \nmid a_{k}$ for all $p \le n$. The very rough intuition (e.g. ignoring Wolstenholme's theorem) is that $p \nmid a_k$ happens $1 - \frac{1}{p}$ of the time on average, so heuristically you would expect that the probability that $p \nmid a_k$ happens for all $p \le n$ (and hence $\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1$) is equal to $\prod_{p \le n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)$, which by Mertens' third theorem is about $\frac{c}{\log n}$.

To get ahold of this problem, it makes sense to try to bound the number of positive integers $k < p$ such that $p \mid a_k$. About 10 years ago I proved that for all primes $p$ we have an upper bound of $cp^{2/3}$ with $c = \frac{3^{2/3}}{2} \approx 1.04$ for the cardinality of this set of $k$, and around the same time Wu and Chen independently proved this exact same result, in Lemma 2.4 of their paper On certain properties of harmonic numbers that you can find here (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022314X17300252). If (way) better upper bounds on the cardinality of this set of $k$ are available, then maybe one can use that to get bounds on the number of $n$ for which $\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1$.

If we look at inequalities like $(1)$ for different primes at the same time and one takes the logarithm, one would like to prove that the resulting inequalities have solutions by applying Kronecker's theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker%27s_theorem). In order to do this however, you need the corresponding logarithmic terms to be rationally independent, and this can be a major roadblock. See e.g. this (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/76372/are-these-terms-consisting-of-logarithms-of-primes-rationally-independent) question I posted on MathOverflow back in 2011 (for which I had applications like #290 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/290) and #291 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/291) in mind), which has remained unanswered ever since.

To cut to the chase: if we allow ourselves to assume e.g. Schanuel's conjecture, then we are in a better spot to make progress. For example, we can then prove that the upper density of $n$ for which $\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1$ is equal to $1$. This was shown by Wu and Yan in their paper On the denominators of harmonic numbers. IV that you can find here (https://www.numdam.org/articles/10.5802/crmath.282/), although these ideas were present in the referenced paper by Shiu too, as well as this (https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03073) paper of myself.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
In fact this problem of the rational independence of $1/\log p$ also came up recently in work of myself and Croot (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02835), building on earlier work of Croot, Mousavi, and Schmidt (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11274). In that application (which is also concerned with the behaviour of digits in multiple bases simultaneously) it would have also been useful to have independence of $1/\log p$, which (of course) we could not prove.

For that application though there is a nice trick that lets you make progress anyway - if there are linear dependencies between the $1/\log p$, just 'bake them in' from the start, and use those linear dependencies in your favour.

I think that a similar trick could work here as well, giving an unconditional proof that the upper density of $n$ for which $(a_n,L_n)>1$ is equal to $1$.

If you're interested I'm happy to talk more about this via email.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text: A small remark on the upper bound for $v(k)$. The usual estimate $v(k) ≤ k c_0^{2^k}$ can be slightly sharpened to \( v(k) \le c_0^{2^k} +\frac{1}{2}\), where $c_0 = 1.26408\ldots$ is Vardi’s constant. Let \((s_j)_{j\ge1}\) be Sylvester's sequence defined by \(s_1=2,\ s_{j+1}=s_j(s_j-1)+1\). Now take any representation \( 1 = \frac{1}{n_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{n_k}\), \(1 \le n_1 < \dots < n_k\), and set \(q := \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} 1/n_i\). It is well known that Sylvester's sequence gives the best $n$-term Egyptian underapproximation of $1$ for every positive integer $n$ (see, for example, [Soundararajan (https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0502247)]; see also [Nathanson (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022314X22001615)] and [Chu (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019357724000065)] for further generalisations), hence \(q=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \frac{1}{n_i} \le \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \frac{1}{s_j} = 1 - \frac{1}{s_{k}-1}\). Thus \( \frac{1}{n_k} = 1 - q \ge \frac{1}{s_{k}-1}\), so \(n_k \le s_{k}-1\). In particular every denominator occurring in a $k$-term representation of $1$ is at most \(s_{k}-1\), and therefore\( v(k) \le (s_{k}-1) + 1=s_{k}\). Since \(s_k = \lfloor c_0^{2^k} +\frac{1}{2} \rfloor\), this yields \(v(k) \le c_0^{2^k} +\frac{1}{2}\).

problem:
Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that there are no solutions to\[\frac{1}{a}= \frac{1}{b_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{b_k}\]with distinct $a,b_1,\ldots,b_k\in A$?

Estimate $f(N)$. In particular, is it true that $f(N)=(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))N$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/301.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 16 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The example $A=(N/2,N]\cap \mathbb{N}$ shows that $f(N)\geq N/2$.

Wouter van Doorn has given an elementary argument that proves\[f(N)\leq (25/28+o(1))N.\]Indeed, consider the sets $S_a=\{2a,3a,4a,6a,12a\}\cap [1,N]$ as $a$ ranges over all integers of the form $8^b9^cd$ with $(d,6)=1$. All such $S_a$ are disjoint and, if $A$ has no solutions to the given equation, then $A$ must omit at least two elements of $S_a$ when $a\leq N/12$ and at least one element of $S_a$ when $N/12<a\leq N/6$, and an elementary calculation concludes the proof.

Stijn Cambie and Wouter van Doorn have noted that, if we allow solutions to this equation with non-distinct $b_i$, then the size of the maximal set is at most $N/2$. Indeed, this is the classical threshold for the existence of some distinct $a,b\in A$ such that $a\mid b$.

See also [302] and [327].

only one fixed equation-size is forbidden:

exact values for \(N=20,\dots,50\) gave densities

dense avoiding sets exist in tested ranges. So the nontrivial pressure toward the
known \(1/2\)-type regime must come from simultaneously forbidding all lengths

problem:
Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that there are no solutions to\[\frac{1}{a}= \frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}\]with distinct $a,b,c\in A$?

literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/302.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
The colouring version of this is [303], which was solved by Brown and R\"{o}dl \cite{BrRo91}. One can take either $A$ to be all odd integers in $[1,N]$ or all integers in $[N/2,N]$ to show $f(N)\geq (1/2+o(1))N$.

Wouter van Doorn has proved (see this note (https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/Two-colouring%20and%20density%20lead%20to%20solutions%20to%20an%20equation%20in%20unit%20fractions.pdf)) that\[f(N) \leq (9/10+o(1))N.\]Stijn Cambie has observed that\[f(N)\geq (5/8+o(1))N,\]taking $A$ to be all odd integers $\leq N/4$ and all integers in $[N/2,N]$.

Stijn Cambie has also observed that, if we allow $b=c$, then there is a solution to this equation when $\lvert A\rvert \geq (\tfrac{2}{3}+o(1))N$, since then there must exist some $n,2n\in A$.

See also [301] and [327].

- [BrRo91] Brown, Tom C. and R\"{o}dl, Voijtech, Monochromatic solutions to equations with unit fractions. Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. (1991), 387-392.

- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).

For any reduced \(a/b\in(0,1)\), the standard greedy Egyptian algorithm
terminates in finitely many steps.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
At step \(x/y\), choose \(q=\lceil y/x\rceil\). New numerator is

L_{\mathcal D_2}(a/b)\le L_{\mathcal D_1}(a/b).

Any decomposition using \(\mathcal D_1\) is admissible for \(\mathcal D_2\).

For fixed \(b\), define

N(b):=\max_{1\le a<b,\ \gcd(a,b)=1} L(a/b).

If one proves \(L(a/b)\le F(b)\) uniformly in \(a\), then \(N(b)\le F(b)\).

\]

Lemma 1 (Semiprime denominator valuation bound):
If
\[
\frac ab=\sum_{i=1}^k \frac1{n_i},

\textit{Proof.}
\]
Clearing denominators by \(L=\mathrm{lcm}(n_i)\) gives

problem: Are there two finite sets of primes $P,Q$ such that\[1=\left(\sum_{p\in P}\frac{1}{p}\right)\left(\sum_{q\in Q}\frac{1}{q}\right)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/307.
- Page status: VERIFIABLE (database last update 2025-09-09).
Site remarks:
Asked by Barbeau \cite{Ba76}. Can this be done if we drop the requirement that all $p\in P$ are prime and just ask for them to be relatively coprime, and similarly for $Q$?

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example,\[1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\]and\[1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right).\]There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.

It is easy to see that, if $P$ and $Q$ are sets of primes, then $P$ and $Q$ are disjoint, and $\sum_{p\in P\cup Q}\frac{1}{p}\geq 2$, whence $\lvert P\cup Q\rvert \geq 60$.
References:
- [Ba76] Barbeau, E. J., Computer challenge corner: Problem 477: A brute force program. J. Rec. Math. (1976).

problem: Let $\delta(N)$ be the minimal non-zero value of $\lvert 1-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\rvert$ as $A$ ranges over all subsets of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Is it true that\[\delta(N)=e^{-(c+o(1))N}\]for some constant $c\in (0,1)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/311.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 16 January 2026.
Site remarks:
It is trivial that\[\delta(N)\geq \frac{1}{[1,\ldots,N]}=e^{-(1+o(1))N},\]where $[1,\ldots,N]$ is the least common multiple of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

The formulation in \cite{ErGr80} has the additional condition that $A$ contain no $S$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$, but Kovac in the comments has shown that the simpler formulation above is equivalent.

Tang has shown (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-311-note/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_311_v2.pdf) that\[\delta(N) \leq \exp\left(-c\frac{N}{(\log N\log\log N)^3}\right)\]for some constant $c>0$.
References:
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

This formulation, which appeared in the Erdős-Graham problem book, is slightly awkward, because the asked minimal quantity, call it $\delta(N)$, is easily seen to be the same as\[ \delta’(N) := \min \Big( \Big\{ \Big|1-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\Big| : A\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,N\} \Big\} \cap (0,\infty) \Big). \]Namely, if $A$ contains a strict subset $S$ with reciprocals of its elements summing to $1$, then\[ \sum_{n\in A} \frac{1}{n} - 1 \geq \frac{1}{N} + \sum_{n\in S} \frac{1}{n} - 1 = \frac{1}{N}, \]which is “quite large”. It certainly does not make the asymptotics of $\delta(N)$ and $\delta’(N)$ different, but with a bit of brute force verification for small $N$, one can show that, in fact, $\delta(N)= \delta’(N)$ for every $N\geq1$.
The first $25$ values of $\delta(N)$ can be computed as:
\begin{align*}
& 1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{6},\frac{1}{12},\frac{1}{30},\\
& \frac{1}{30},\frac{1}{105},\frac{1}{120},\frac{1}{252},\frac{1}{360},\\
& \frac{1}{2310},\frac{1}{2310},\frac{1}{2310},\frac{1}{2772},\frac{1}{2772},\\
& \frac{1}{6160},\frac{1}{30940},\frac{1}{30940},\frac{5}{298452},\frac{5}{298452},\\
& \frac{11}{1244880},\frac{23}{17907120},\frac{1}{1105104},\frac{1}{1105104},\frac{1}{1593900}.
\end{align*}
From this modest amount of data one can see\[ e^{-0.71N} \leq \delta(N) \leq e^{-0.52 N} \quad \text{for }3\leq N\leq 25, \]so the conjecture is somewhat plausible. Also note that\[ \frac{1}{[1,\ldots,N]} = e^{-(1+o(1))N}, \]so the conjecture claims that $\delta(N)$ is exponentially small, but still much larger than the trivial bound.
All this is quite trivial, but I wrote it down anyway, before I forget. :-)

computation:
I computed exact delta(N) for small N via meet-in-the-middle on scaled
integer subset sums (lcm(1..N) denominator).

For N=10..30, exact values were obtained; empirical
-log(delta(N))/N stays around 0.54 to 0.65 in this range.
This supports exponential decay on finite scales.
attempt:
Hard point:
Small-N exact values do not determine existence/uniqueness of an asymptotic
constant c.

Target:
Prove
\[
\delta(N)=\exp(-(c+o(1))N)
\]
for some constant \(c\in(0,1)\), or characterize limsup/liminf constants.
Step A: Lattice subset-sum geometry
Embed scaled reciprocal sums into subset sums on integer lattice
\(\{0,1\}^N\) with common denominator \(L_N=\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,N)\).
Step B: Exponential spacing bounds
Prove matching upper/lower bounds for minimum nonzero distance of subset sums to
\(L_N\).
Step C: Constant extraction
Show normalized \(-\log\delta(N)/N\) has a limit.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp anti-concentration bound for near-cancellations of reciprocal subset
sums at scale \(\exp(-\Theta(N))\).

Lemma 1 (Existence of positive minimum):
For fixed \(N\), set
\[
X_N=\left\{\left|1-\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n\right|:A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\},\
\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n\ne1\right\}.
\]
Then \(\delta(N)=\min X_N>0\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
\(X_N\) is finite because there are finitely many subsets. All elements are
strictly positive by definition, so the minimum is positive.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Scaled integer formulation):
Let \(L_N=\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,N)\). Then
\[
\delta(N)=\frac{1}{L_N}\min_{A}\left|L_N-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{L_N}{n}\right|,
\]
where minimum is over subsets not giving exact equality.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Multiply each absolute difference by \(L_N\). Since \(L_N/n\in\mathbb Z\), inner
quantity is integer, and scaling is exact.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Submultiplicative envelope reduction):
If one proves for some constants \(c_1,c_2>0\):
\[
e^{-c_2N}\le \delta(N)\le e^{-c_1N}
\]
and a quasi-submultiplicative relation
\[
\delta(N+M)\le \delta(N)\delta(M)e^{o(N+M)},
\]
then \(-\log\delta(N)/N\) has limsup/liminf trapped in \([c_1,c_2]\), and limit
exists if matching quasi-supermultiplicativity also holds.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Take logs and apply generalized Fekete arguments to \(\log(1/\delta(N))\) with
additive \(o(N)\) errors.
\(\square\)

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
Does anyone know if Erdős and Graham posed precisely the exponential "gap" for a good reason?
For a finite multiset of positive integers $A$ denote\[ R(A) := \sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n} \]and\[ \epsilon(A) := \min\Big\{ 1 – R(S) \,:\, S\subseteq A,\, R(S)\leq 1 \Big\}. \]The problem asks if inequality\[ \epsilon(A) \leq e^{- c R(A)} \]holds with some constant $c>0$.
Here is a simple example which comes close to showing that this is the best possible. For a positive integer $N$ take\[ A = \bigcup_{p\text{ prime},\ p\leq N} \{\underbrace{p,p,\ldots,p}_{p-1\text{ times}} \}. \]Then\[ R(A) = \sum_{p\text{ prime},\ p\leq N} \frac{p-1}{p} \sim \pi(N) = (1+o(1)) \frac{N}{\log N}, \]while $R(S)\neq1$ for every sub-multiset $S$ of $A$, so\[ \epsilon(A) \geq \prod_{p\text{ prime},\ p\leq N} \frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{N\#} = e^{-(1+o(1))N}. \]Since $N=(1+o(1))R(A)\log R(A)$, this shows\[ \epsilon(A) \geq e^{- (1+o(1)) R(A) \log R(A)} \]for this particular sequence of examples of multisets $A$. It is not clear to me if a better (e.g., exponential) lower bound is possible, even for these particular multisets $A$.
The actual conjectured inequality (the upper bound on $\epsilon(A)$) is a completely different story (many people here would know better), but I first want to clarify to myself how "optimal" it is. :-)

computation:
New deep computation (2026-03-10):
:
Method: exact meet-in-the-middle search for
\[
\max\Big\{\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n:\ S\subseteq A,\ \sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\le 1\Big\}
\]
on selected denominator families \(A\).
Model sanity check: initial segments \(A=\{2,\dots,N\}\)
For tested \(N\), the optimum is exactly \(1\) (e.g. via \(1/2+1/3+1/6=1\)),
so this family is too easy and not informative for the sharp gap question.
Nontrivial family: shifted blocks \(A=\{s,s+1,\dots,s+21\}\)
Exact results:
- \(s=6\): best \(=0.9999976129\), gap \(=2.39\times 10^{-6}\).
- \(s=7\): best \(=0.9999974099\), gap \(=2.59\times 10^{-6}\).
- \(s=8\): best \(=0.9999995803\), gap \(=4.20\times 10^{-7}\).
- \(s=10\): best \(=0.9999884993\), gap \(=1.15\times 10^{-5}\).
- \(s=12\): best \(=0.9998732618\), gap \(=1.27\times 10^{-4}\).
- \(s=15\): total reciprocal sum already \(<1\), so best equals total and gap
 jumps to \(7.70\times 10^{-2}\).
Also \(s=3,4,5\) hit exact \(1\) in this block model.

Finite exact data shows a sharp transition:
- in medium blocks where total reciprocal mass exceeds 1, one can often get
 extremely close to 1 (sometimes exactly 1);
- once total mass drops below 1, the problem becomes trivial (best equals total).
This supports the known polynomial-gap phenomenon but does not provide evidence
for the stronger universal exponential-gap bound in the EP-312 statement.
attempt:
The background says Erd"os-Graham proved a weaker quantitative form with
exp(-cK) replaced by a term of order 1/K^2.

The stronger exponential-accuracy gap in the statement is not proved in the
provided background.

A direct attempt to refine the near-1 subset-sum approximation route beyond
polynomial error did not produce a new quantitative bound.

Target:
Upgrade the known polynomial gap near \(1\) to the conjectured exponential gap
\(1-e^{-cK}\) under EP-312 hypotheses.
Step A: Additive-energy control of reciprocal multisets
Quantify concentration of subset sums near \(1\) using entropy/energy of
\(\{1/n:n\in A\}\).
Step B: Near-1 anti-gap theorem
Show existence of subset sum in \((1-e^{-cK},1]\) by iterative balancing.
Step C: Sharp parameter dependence
Optimize constants to make \(c\) absolute (or explicit in structural parameters).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a large-deviation refinement for subset sums of reciprocals that beats
polynomial window \(K^{-2}\) down to \(e^{-cK}\).

Lemma 1 (Maximal-under-1 subset principle):
Let
\[
M(A):=\max\left\{\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n:\ S\subseteq A,\ \sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\le1\right\}.
\]
Then \(M(A)\le1\), and the deficit is
\[
\Delta(A):=1-M(A)\ge0.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Definition of constrained maximum gives both inequalities.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Greedy maximality condition):
If \(S_*\) attains \(M(A)\), then for every \(m\in A\setminus S_*\),
\[
\frac1m>\Delta(A).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
If some \(m\notin S_*\) had \(1/m\le\Delta(A)\), then
\[
\sum_{n\in S_*}\frac1n+\frac1m\le M(A)+\Delta(A)=1,
\]
contradicting maximality of \(M(A)\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to counting small reciprocals):
If one proves many elements of \(A\) satisfy \(1/n\ll e^{-cK}\) while
\(\sum_{n\in A}1/n\) stays in the EP-312 regime, then Lemma 2 forces
\(\Delta(A)\ll e^{-cK}\), hence
\[
M(A)\ge 1-e^{-cK}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Contrapositive of Lemma 2: if \(\Delta(A)\) were larger, all excluded elements
would have reciprocals \(>\Delta(A)\), limiting count and total mass
inconsistently with hypothesis.
\(\square\)

problem: Are there infinitely many solutions to\[\frac{1}{p_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{p_k}=1-\frac{1}{m},\]where $m\geq 2$ is an integer and $p_1<\cdots<p_k$ are distinct primes?

- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/313.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
For example,\[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}=1-\frac{1}{6}\]and\[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}=1-\frac{1}{42}.\]It is clear that we must have $m=p_1\cdots p_k$, and hence in particular there is at most one solution for each $m$. The integers $m$ for which there is such a solution are known as primary pseudoperfect numbers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_pseudoperfect_number), and there are $8$ known, listed in A054377 (https://oeis.org/A054377) at the OEIS.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Define $Q_n$ to be the set of rationals that can be written as $\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a}$ for some subset $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. The first question asks whether the inequality $$\min_{\substack{q, q' \in Q_n \\ q \neq q'}} |q - q'| < \frac{c}{2^n}\hspace{20pt}(1)$$holds for some absolute constant $c$.

By the results in #320 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/320) we have $|Q_n| = \exp[\frac{n f(n)}{\log n}]$ for some $f(n)$ that goes to infinity with $n$ at a rate of $(\log \log \log n)^{1 + o(1)}$. As we have $q \in [0, \log n + 1]$ for all $q \in Q_n$, by the pigeonhole principle we obtain $$\min_{\substack{q, q' \in Q_n \\ q \neq q'}} |q - q'| \le \frac{\log n + 1}{\exp[\frac{n f(n)}{\log n}]} = \frac{1}{2^{\frac{n (\log \log \log n)^{1 + o(1)}}{\log n}}},\hspace{20pt}(2)$$a slight improvement over the bound from Vjeko's comment. Perhaps known concentration inequalities on random harmonic sums can improve upon $(2)$ further.

On the other hand, if $Q_n$ would simply be a set of $|Q_n|$ uniformly random numbers in the interval $[0, \log n + 1]$, then one would expect their minimum difference to be on the order of $\frac{1}{|Q_n|^{2 + o(1)}}$. This would in fact give a lower bound of the same shape as the upper bound in inequality $(2)$, perhaps casting some doubt on the validity of $(1)$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
As an intermediate goal proving that the first question can be answered in the negative:

A different version would be to consider
$$\prod_{1 \le i \le n} \left\lvert \sum_{1 \le i \le n} \frac{\delta_i}{p_i} \right\rvert (1)$$
and prove that this becomes very large for large $n$.
Heuristically and experimentally, this is the case.

E.g. $\frac 15 + \frac 17 - \frac 13 = \frac1{3*5*7}$, i.e.,
$$3*5*7\left(\frac 15 + \frac 17 - \frac 13 \right)=1.$$

But for $n=19$, the minimum nonzero expression (1) becomes $5246939312687345$ (here $p_1=2$).

For the heuristics:
If one takes $x$ random numbers in $[0,1]$, the minimum absolute difference between two is of the order $1/x^2$
(see e.g. [stackexchange] (https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/419130/expected-min-distance-between-n-uniform-rvs)).
Now consider all sums of some of the reciprocals of primes (the difference of two is of the desired form).
Now a most filled interval of length $1/p_n$ cannot have more than $2^n$ elements. (the sums are not random uniformly distributed of course, so we estimate this dense part)
Now the minimum difference could be estimated to be at least $\frac{1}{p_n^2 2^{2n}}$.
On the other hand, $\prod_{1 \le i \le n} p_i = n^{(1+o(1))n}=\omega( p_n^2 4^n),$
and also $2^{p_n}$ is much larger than $p_n^2 4^n.$
***

One could also take $p_i^{\lfloor \log_{p_i}(x) \rfloor}$ everywhere, since then the lcm's correspond).
[if this would be bounded, the above would also be bounded]

Hereby some thoughts for improving the first question to $C/[1,2,...,n]$.
In that case, $C>13340$ is necessary.

For this, define
$$F(n)=lcm(1,2,..,n)\min_{>0} \left\lvert \sum_{1 \le i \le n} \frac{\delta_i}{p_i} \right\rvert $$
where the minimum is taken over the nonzero sums.

$$ F(29)=F(30)=13340, F(31)= 2057, F(32)=4114$$

These values are nevertheless larger than the ones that could be guessed with the above heuristic (already taking into account that sums may be equal). So the fact that the numbers are not at random, seems to be important.

The number of different sums is smaller than $2^n$. (e.g. $1/(2x)=1/(3x)+1/(6x)$ indicates multiple sums can be equal)

Determine sharp asymptotics of the minimum nonzero signed harmonic sum magnitude,

\[
\mu_n:=\min\Bigl\{\Bigl|\sum_{k=1}^n \varepsilon_k\frac1k\Bigr|:\varepsilon_k\in\{-1,0,1\},\ \text{not all }0\Bigr\}.

\[
\textit{Proof.}

\[

\[

least \(1\), then divide by \(L_n\).
\(\square\)

Equality \(\mu_n=1/L_n\) holds iff the scaled signed-sum set contains \(\pm1\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
From Lemma 1 and Lemma 2, minimum equals \(1/L_n\) exactly when integer minimum is

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Straus \cite{ErSt75} proved this when $A=\mathbb{N}$. Sattler \cite{Sa75} proved this when $A$ is the set of odd numbers. For the squares $1$ must be excluded or the result is trivially false, since\[\sum_{k\geq 2}\frac{1}{k^2}<1.\]This is false for some sets $A$ of positive density - indeed, it fails for any set $A$ containing exactly one even number. (Sattler \cite{Sa82} credits this observation to Erd\H{o}s, who presumably found this after \cite{ErGr80}.)

Sattler \cite{Sa82b} proved the answer to the original question is yes, in that any arithmetic progression has this property. Sattler also announced a proof of the final question, the set of squares excluding $1$, in \cite{Sa82} and \cite{Sa82b}, but this never appeared.

Larsen has proved (https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-318/blob/main/318.pdf) that the answer is yes in the case of squares excluding $1$.
References:
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [ErSt75] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Straus, E. G., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 183.
- [Sa75] Sattler, R., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 184-189.
- [Sa82] Sattler, R., On {E}rd\H{o}s property {${\rm P}\sb{1}$}\ for the sequence of squarefree numbers. Nederl. Akad. Wetensch. Indag. Math. (1982), 341--346.
- [Sa82b] Sattler, R., On {E}rd\H{o}s property {${\rm P}\sb{1}$}\ for the arithmetical sequence. Nederl. Akad. Wetensch. Indag. Math. (1982), 347--352.

forum_comments.author: Agustín Meza
forum_comments.text:
For the positive density case: if there exists some $n \in A$ such that (say) f(n) = -1, and the set B of multiples of n in A such that f(m) = 1 for all $m \in B$ has positive upper density, then the result follows from theorem 2 of Bloom in [1]: if we consider $C := \{ \frac{m}{n} \in \mathbb{N}/ m \in B\}$, there exists a finite $S' \subset C $ such that $\sum_{c \in S'} \frac{1}{c} = 1$, so that $\frac{f(n)}{n} + \sum_{c \in S'}\frac{f(cn)}{cn} = \frac{-1}{n} + \sum_{c \in S'}\frac{1}{cn} = \frac{-1}{n} + \frac{1}{n} = 0$, since we assume that f(cn) always equals 1. Therefore, the finite set $\{n\} \cup \{nc \in A / c \in S'\} \subset A$ satisfies the condition.
I think this approach might give a proof of the arithmetic progressions case as well by taking any function f to this case.
[1]: Bloom, T. F. (2021). On a density conjecture about unit fractions. arXiv preprint arXiv:2112.03726, 1(3), 4.

forum_comments.author: Agustín Meza
forum_comments.text:
A kind of set which satisfy the conditions of the statement is the following: let $A^{+} \subset A$ be the elements of A for which f(a) and $A^{-} \subset A$ the ones for which f(a) = -1. If the sets $P^{+},P^{-}$ consisting of the primes in both $A^{+}$ and $A^{-}$ satisfy $\sum_{p \in P^{+}}\frac{1}{p}, \sum_{p \in P^{-}}\frac{1}{p} \to \infty$, then A satisfies the hypothesis of the problem.
Assuming that both $A^{+},A^{-}$ have positive lower natural density (I think the method could apply as well in the general case), from the previous comment, if the proposition is false, then for any $p \in P^{-}$ the set of multiples of p in $A^{+}$ has zero natural density. Therefore, for any fixed $p \in P^{-}$ we would have $\mathbb{E}_{n \le x} 1_{pn \in A^{+}} \to_{x} 0$. Taking a finite subset $S \subset P^{-}$ for which $\sum_{p \in S}\frac{1}{p} \ge C\epsilon^{-2}$ for some arbitrarily small $\epsilon > 0$ and some constant $C > 0$, due to Elliott's inequality we can say that there exists at least some $p \in S$ for which $\mathbb{E}_{n \le \frac{x}{p}}1_{pn \in A^{+}} = \mathbb{E}_{n \le x}1_{n \in A^{+}} + O(\epsilon)$. But since $\mathbb{E}_{n \le \frac{x}{p}}1_{pn \in A^{+}} \to_{x} 0$, if we take some $\epsilon$ sufficiently smaller than the lower density of A, it would be a contradiction.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
The case of squares (the last remaining one) can probably be solved by brute-force using calculations on various square identities. Here's a note on it for the potential computer attack (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos318.pdf) and a short explanation below. I couldn't do it on a laptop, will try to run it on a more powerful machine - if anyone is willing to try it too, they are most welcome. Also currently trying to run it through Aristostle to formalize if possible.

To obtain a computer-verifiable proof one must produce a finite certificate of unsatisfiability for a finite universe. Concretely, fix a bound $N$ and consider the Boolean variables $X_n$ for $2\le n\le N$, interpreted as $X_n=\text{true}\iff g(n)=+1$ and $X_n=\text{false}\iff g(n)=-1$. For each exact reciprocal-square identity\[
\sum_{u\in U}\frac1{u^2}=\sum_{v\in V}\frac1{v^2}
\]in a chosen finite library $B$, and for each scale $m$ such that $mU\cup mV\subseteq\{2,\dots,N\}$, add two CNF clauses forbidding the two opposite-monochromatic sign patterns on the scaled sets:\[
\neg\bigl(\forall u\in U\, X_{mu}\ \wedge\ \forall v\in V\, \neg X_{mv}\bigr),\qquad
\neg\bigl(\forall u\in U\, \neg X_{mu}\ \wedge\ \forall v\in V\, X_{mv}\bigr),
\]equivalently the clauses\[
\Big(\bigvee_{u\in U}\neg X_{mu}\Big)\ \vee\ \Big(\bigvee_{v\in V}X_{mv}\Big),\qquad
\Big(\bigvee_{u\in U}X_{mu}\Big)\ \vee\ \Big(\bigvee_{v\in V}\neg X_{mv}\Big).
\]Finally, enforce that the coloring is non-constant by adding $\bigvee_{n=2}^N X_n$ and $\bigvee_{n=2}^N \neg X_n$. If a SAT solver returns UNSAT for the resulting CNF, then this constitutes a finite certificate that every non-constant $g:\{2,\dots,N\}\to\{\pm1\}$ realizes some scaled identity in $B$ with opposite constant signs on the two sides, hence yields a finite set $T\subset\{2,\dots,N\}$ with $\sum_{m\in T}g(m)/m^2=0$. A fully checkable proof is obtained by recording (i) the explicit identity library $B$ (each identity verified independently by exact rational arithmetic), (ii) the bound $N$, and (iii) the solver-produced unsatisfiability certificate (e.g. a DRAT/FRAT proof) together with a standard proof checker verifying the certificate against the CNF.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I think this approach shows that the problem is "verifiable" - checkable in finite time if true - but does not demonstrate that it is "decidable" - resolvable in finite time both if the statement is true and if it is false. The compactness theorem shows that if the claim for squares is true, then there is a finite bound $N$ on the coloring statement one needs to check, but if the claim is false, one has to check satisfiability for all $N$, and this cannot be done in finite time without some additional input such as a bound on $N$.

One can speculate that Sattler had an approach like this but found out that his SAT problems were actually solvable for the $N$ that he tried, leaving him with no conclusion.

forum_comments.author: None
forum_comments.text:
No.

General counterexample (works for ANY infinite A⊆ℕ, hence for infinite arithmetic progressions, positive-density sets, and the squares ≥4):

Let m := min(A). Define f:A→{−1,1} by
f(m) = −1 and f(n)=+1 for all n∈A\{m}.
Then f is non-constant.

Claim: there is no finite nonempty S⊂A with Σ_{n∈S} f(n)n = 0.

Proof:
- If m∉S, then Σ_{n∈S} f(n)n = Σ_{n∈S} n > 0.
- If m∈S, write S = {m} ∪ T with T⊂A\{m}.
 Then Σ_{n∈S} f(n)n = −m + Σ_{n∈T} n.
 If T=∅, the sum is −m < 0.
 If T≠∅, every n∈T satisfies n ≥ m+1 (in fact >m), so Σ_{n∈T} n ≥ m+1, hence the total is ≥ −m + (m+1) = 1 > 0.
So the sum is never 0.

Consequences:
1) If A is an infinite arithmetic progression in ℕ (A={a+kd : k≥0}), take m=a and the same f. No such S exists.
2) If A is any set of positive density (or any infinite subset of ℕ), same construction kills it.
3) If A is the set of squares excluding 1, then m=4; set f(4)=−1 and f(n)=+1 for all other squares. Any S either sums to >0 (if 4∉S) or to −4 or at least −4+9>0 (if 4∈S). So again no such S exists.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
The most obvious counterexample that Adenwalla mentions (one even number and other numbers odd) is credited to Erdős in this paper of Sattler (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/1385725882900257) at the very beginning (p. 341). In that light I do not understand the omission about arbitrary sets of positive density. It seems that Erdős corrected himself between 1980 (publication year of the Erdős-Graham problem book) and 1982 (publication year of the above Sattler's paper).

The first question on arithmetic progressions seems to have been solved by Sattler as well, in this paper (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/1385725882900269).

Sattler also claims the solution to the last question (on the squares greater than $1$) in both of the papers linked above (see the references). However, I did not find the announced third paper where this proof was supposed to be published. Perhaps Sattler could still be trusted. :-)

All in all, I think it is safe to mark this problem as fully solved by R. Sattler.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
If $A$ has one even number, $x$, and all other numbers in A are odd, then a function $f$ such that $f(x)=-1$ and $f=1$ on all $A\backslash \{x\}$ would be a counterexample. This is as a sum of fractions with odd denominator cannot be equal to a fraction with even denominator. This extends to any $A$ where there exists an $x\in A$ such that $A\backslash\{x\}$ is a subset of a multiplicatively closed set and no multiple of $x$ is in said MCS.

An example is any $A$ where there exists a prime $p$ such that there is exactly one multiple of $p$ in $A$. Another is where all numbers in $A\backslash\{x\}$ are equivalent to $g$ mod $d$ for some $g$ and $d$, and $x$ is not equivalent to $g^k$ mod $d$ for any $k$.

The result of Graham described in [282] provides further examples. If $x$ and $d$ are both divisible by $p^k$ for some prime $p$ and $k\geq 1$, and $a$ is not divisible by $p^k$, then let $A$ be the infinite arithmetic progression $a\mod d$ union $x$. It follows that $\frac{1}{x}$ cannot be written as the sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators equivalent to $a \mod d$.

attempt:
First question (arithmetic progressions): yes
The background records Sattler's result that every arithmetic progression has this property.

Second question (positive density): false
As noted in the background, this fails for sets A containing exactly one even number.
A concrete obstruction:
- Let e be the unique even element of A.
- Define f(e)=+1 and f(a)=-1 for every odd a in A.
Now take any finite nonempty S \subset A.
- If e \notin S, then sum_{n in S} f(n)/n < 0.
- If e \in S, then
 sum_{n in S} f(n)/n = 1/e - sum_{m in T} 1/m
 with T a finite set of odd integers.
sum_{m in T} 1/m has odd denominator (in lowest terms), while 1/e has even denominator,
so equality is impossible. Hence the sum is never 0.
Therefore the positive-density variant is false.

Third question (squares excluding 1):
Background says this appears open: Sattler announced a proof, but no proof appeared.

Interpretation for the open squares variant:
These computations suggest a two-regime finite behavior:
1. short prefixes can be rigid (no exact cancellation for any nonconstant signing
 in the tested range \(m\le 12\));
2. longer prefixes often admit cancellation for random signings.
This does not settle the infinite squares question (which asks for all
nonconstant \(f\) on all squares \(>1\)), but it sharpens the search:
potential counterexamples would need highly structured sign patterns that keep
avoiding exact cancellations across arbitrarily long prefixes.

Subquestion 1 (Arithmetic Progressions): Closed
This is settled positively by Sattler's theorem cited in the background.
So for every nonconstant \(f:A\to\{-1,1\}\) on an infinite arithmetic progression
\(A\), there exists finite nonempty \(S\subset A\) with
\[
\sum_{n\in S}\frac{f(n)}{n}=0.
\]
Subquestion 2 (Positive Density): Closed Negatively
Counterexample family: let \(A\) contain exactly one even number \(e\), and all
other elements odd. Define \(f(e)=1\), \(f(a)=-1\) for odd \(a\in A\).
For finite nonempty \(S\subset A\):
- if \(e\notin S\), sum is negative;
- if \(e\in S\), then
 \[
 \sum_{n\in S}\frac{f(n)}{n}=\frac1e-\sum_{m\in T}\frac1m,\quad T\subset A\cap(2\mathbb Z+1).
 \]
The second term has odd denominator in lowest terms, \(\frac1e\) has even
denominator, so equality to \(0\) is impossible.
Hence this variant is false.
Subquestion 3 (Squares \(>1\)): Remaining Blocker
Need either:
- a structural theorem forcing an exact reciprocal cancellation for every
 nonconstant signing on squares, or
- an explicit infinite signing that avoids zero for all finite subsets.
This is the single unresolved part of EP-318 in this note.

Settle: for every nonconstant \(f\) on \(\{m^2:m\ge2\}\), does some finite
nonempty \(S\) satisfy

\]

Embed reciprocal-square sums into a common denominator lattice on prefixes and
study signed subset-sum coverage defects.
Step B: Prefix-to-Infinite Transfer
Prove either:
1. every sufficiently long prefix forces zero-sum (implying positive answer), or
2. construct coherent zero-free signings on nested prefixes with compatibility

Step C: Compactness/Diagonal Extraction
Use compactness over signings to pass from finite-prefix behavior to infinite

Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a monotonic extension lemma: if a signing is zero-free on prefix length

problem: What is the size of the largest $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that there is a function $\delta:A\to \{-1,1\}$ such that\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{\delta_n}{n}=0\]and\[\sum_{n\in A'}\frac{\delta_n}{n}\neq 0\]for all non-empty $A'\subsetneq A$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/319.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Adenwalla has observed that a lower bound of\[\lvert A\rvert\geq (1-\tfrac{1}{e}+o(1))N\]follows from the main result of Croot \cite{Cr01}, which states that there exists some set of integers $B\subset [(\frac{1}{e}-o(1))N,N]$ such that $\sum_{b\in B}\frac{1}{b}=1$. Since the sum of $\frac{1}{m}$ for $m\in [c_1N,c_2N]$ is asymptotic to $\log(c_2/c_1)$ we must have $\lvert B\rvert \geq (1-\tfrac{1}{e}+o(1))N$.

We may then let $A=B\cup\{1\}$ and choose $\delta(n)=-1$ for all $n\in B$ and $\delta(1)=1$.

This problem has been formalised in Lean (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/319.lean) as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/).
References:
- [Cr01] Croot, III, Ernest S., On unit fractions with denominators in short intervals. Acta Arith. (2001), 99-114.

problem: Let $S(N)$ count the number of distinct sums of the form $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ for $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$. Estimate $S(N)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/320.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 September 2025.
Site remarks:
Bleicher and Erd\H{o}s \cite{BlEr75} proved the lower bound\[\log S(N)\geq \frac{N}{\log N}\left(\log 2\prod_{i=3}^k\log_iN\right),\]valid for $k\geq 4$ and $\log_kN\geq k$, and also \cite{BlEr76b} proved the upper bound\[\log S(N)\leq \frac{N}{\log N}\left(\log_r N \prod_{i=3}^r \log_iN\right),\]valid for $r\geq 1$ and $\log_{2r}N\geq 1$. (In these bounds $\log_in$ denotes the $i$-fold iterated logarithm.)

Bettin, Greni\'{e}, Molteni, and Sanna \cite{BGMS25} improved the lower bound to\[\log S(N) \geq \frac{N}{\log N}\left(2\log 2\left(1-\frac{3/2}{\log_kN}\right)\prod_{i=3}^k\log_iN\right),\]valid for $k\geq 4$ and $\log_kN\geq 3/2$. (In particular this goes to infinity faster than the lower bound of Bleicher and Erd\H{o}s.)

See also [321].
References:
- [BGMS25] S. Bettin, L. Greni\'{e}, G. Molteni, and C. Sanna, A lower bound for the number of Egyptian fractions. arXiv:2509.10030 (2025).
- [BlEr75] Bleicher, M. N. and Erd\H{o}s, P., The number of distinct subsums of $\sum \sb{1}\spN\,1/i$. Math. Comp. (1975), 29-42.
- [BlEr76b] Bleicher, Michael N. and Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Denominators of Egyptian fractions. II. Illinois J. Math. (1976), 598-613.

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
It is a coincidence by the fact that $20$ was exactly small enough that the sum of reciprocals being equal implied that a short (length 1) sum of reciprocal needed to be involved.

If equality would have been true for $n=21$, then there should have been a subset of $[1..20]$ of size $15$ which could be extended by $21.$
Since equal sums of reciprocals do not involve primes between $n/2$ and $n$, these can be neglected in the computation.
Then a bruteforce verification (added on the github link) can do the job.

For this, note that e.g. $1+\frac 1{21} = \frac1 2 + \frac 13+ \frac 17 + \frac 1{14}$
and $\frac 16 + \frac 1{21} = \frac 17+ \frac{1}{14}$,
so there were multiple crucial equalities of (longer) sums of reciprocals involving $21$.
On the other hand, $\frac 1a=\frac 1b + \frac1{21}$ has no solution where $0<a<b<21$.

The first "most wanted" is caught as such. Here "dead" (false) is less interesting than "alive".

(with that idea, it only has been checked that $R(20+x)=14+x$ for $1 \le x \le 3$ without much effort)

forum_comments.text:
Using linear programming, I also got the following values.

$R(21+x)=15+x$ for $0 \le x \le 2$
$R(24+x)=17+x$ for $0 \le x \le 3$
$R(28+x)=20+x$ for $x \in \{0,1\}$,
$R(30+x)=21+x$ for $0\le x \le 2$,
$R(33+x)=23+x$ for $0\le x \le 1$ and
$R(35+x)=24+x$ for $0 \le x \le 4.$

So the sequence starts with
$$1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 15,15,\\16,17,17,18,19,20,20,21,21,22,23,23,24,24,25,26,27,28.$$

So for small values, $R(n+1)=R(n)$ if $n+1$ is quite smooth, with some exceptions such as $36.$
(Also, one can have combinations with $p,2p, \ldots, kp$ that do not have $p$
 in the denominator for $k$ (polylog) quite small wrt to $p$, is another reason why drawing conclusions is hard)

$\textbf{Idea efficient programming}$
The idea was to first find all pairs $(A,B)$ of disjoint subsets of $[n]$ for which the sum of reciprocals is equal.
Then $A \cup B$ cannot belong to a maximal set with the desired property.
Since $\frac 1{p^k}$ cannot be equal to $\sum_B 1/b$ when $v_p(b)<k$ for every $b \in B$,
and $\frac 1p \pm \frac 2p$ also has a factor $p$ in the denominator,
we know that $p,2p$ for $p> \frac n3$ and $16,32,27,25$ never belong to such sets $A \cup B.$
This made the computation of forbidden sets $A \cup B$ more efficient.
(for $n=32,$ there were already $81949$ many of them, for $n=33$ there were $245435$, for $n=35$ around $700k$ and for $n=36$ there were $2302966$, indicating that it becomes hard to compute; 2 hours with a common pc for $n=36$)
The program has been added for $n=36$ in https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/issues/161.

problem: Let $k\geq 3$ and $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ be the set of $k$th powers. What is the order of growth of $1_A^{(k)}(n)$, i.e. the number of representations of $n$ as the sum of $k$ many $k$th powers? Does there exist some $c>0$ and infinitely many $n$ such that\[1_A^{(k)}(n) >n^c?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/322.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 September 2025.
Site remarks:
Connected to Waring's problem. The famous Hypothesis $K$ of Hardy and Littlewood was that $1_A^{(k)}(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$, but this was disproved by Mahler \cite{Ma36} for $k=3$, who constructed infinitely many $n$ such that\[1_A^{(3)}(n)\gg n^{1/12}\](where $A$ is the set of cubes). Erd\H{o}s believed Hypothesis $K$ fails for all $k\geq 4$, but this is unknown. Hardy and Littlewood made the weaker Hypothesis $K^*$ that for all $N$ and $\epsilon>0$\[\sum_{n\leq N}1_A^{(k)}(n)^2 \ll_\epsilon N^{1+\epsilon}.\]Erd\H{o}s and Graham remark: 'This is probably true but no doubt very deep. However, it would suffice for most applications.'

Independently Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er36} and Chowla proved that for all $k\geq 3$ and infinitely many $n$\[1_A^{(k)}(n) \gg n^{c/\log\log n}\]for some constant $c>0$ (depending on $k$). In \cite{Er65b} Erd\H{o}s claims an unpublished proof that, if $B$ is the set of $k$th powers of any set of positive density, then\[\limsup 1_B^{(k)}(n)=\infty.\]This is discussed in problem D4 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [Er36] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, On the Representation of an Integer as the Sum of k k-th Powers. J. London Math. Soc. (1936), 133-136.
- [Er65b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some recent advances and current problems in number theory. Lectures on Modern Mathematics, Vol. III (1965), 196-244.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Ma36] Mahler, Kurt, Note on Hypothesis K of Hardy and Littlewood. J. London Math. Soc. (1936), 136-138.

problem: Does there exist a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ such that all the sums $f(a)+f(b)$ with $a<b$ nonnegative integers are distinct?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/324.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 11 April 2026.
Site remarks:
In other words, the set $\{ f(n) : n\geq 1\}$ should be a Sidon set.

Erd\H{o}s and Graham describe this problem as 'very annoying'. Probably $f(x)=x^5$ should work. The Lander, Parkin, and Selfridge conjecture would imply that $f(x)=x^n$ has this property for all $n\geq 5$.

Ruzsa \cite{Ru01b} has proved there exists $c\in [0,1]$ and $n_0\geq 1$ such that\[\{ n^5 +\lfloor cn^4\rfloor : n \geq n_0\}\]is a Sidon set.

It is easy to check that a quadratic $f$ cannot have this property. Dubickas and Novikas \cite{DuNo21} have shown that a cubic $f$ cannot have this property. It is a classical fact that $x^4$ cannot have this property.

This is discussed in problems C9, D1, and F30 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [DuNo21] Dubickas, Arturas and Novikas, Aivaras, No cubic integer polynomial generates a Sidon sequence. Math. Nachr. (2021), 1859--1865.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Ru01b] Ruzsa, I. Z., An almost polynomial Sidon sequence. Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. (2001), 367--375.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
A trivial remark: if one can construct such an $f$ which is only asymptotically Sidon (no collisions for $a,b$ large enough), then one can remove all such collisions by replacing $f(x)$ with $f(qx+r)$ for a suitable arithmetic progression $\{qx+r: x \in {\bf Z} \}$ that avoids all the collisions.

It is conceivable that one may be able to solve this problem assuming the Bombieri-Lang conjecture, in this spirit of this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01090). If the integer (or rational) solutions to the three-dimensional variety $\{ (a,b,c,d): f(a)+f(b)=f(c)+f(d)\}$ (which presumably will be of general type for typical $f$) are trapped inside two-dimensional subvarieties, then one may be able to escape the integer points on these subvarieties by replacing $f$ with $f \circ Q$ for various polynomials $Q$.

Siegel's theorem on integral points should be able to manage any one-dimensional family of solutions, so the main problems are with the two-dimensional families. The key algebraic geometry question seems to be the following: let $S$ be an irreducible surface in $\{ (a,b,c,d): f(a)+f(b)=f(c)+f(d)\}$ such that the covers $S_Q = \{(a',b',c',d'): (Q(a'),Q(b'),Q(c'),Q(d')) \in S \}$ are not of general type for any polynomial $Q$. What does this imply about $S$?

forum_comments.author: Sayan Dutta
forum_comments.text:
This problem has often been discussed in the context of Sidon sets. For more information, see F30, D1 and C9 in Unsolved Problems in Number Theory (https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0) by Richard Guy.

The best result so far is due to Ruzsa (https://akjournals.com/view/journals/012/38/1-4/article-p367.pdf) where he proved the existence of a real $\xi \in [0,1]$ for which the set
$$\left \{n^5 + \left\lfloor \xi n^4\right\rfloor : n\ge n_0 \right \}$$
is a Sidon set for a suitable $n_0$.

It is easy to show that a linear or a quadratic polynomial cannot generate a Sidon set. Dubickas and Novikas (https://doi.org/10.1002/mana.202000334) recently proved that a cubic polynomial doesn't generate a Sidon set either. As far as I know, it is not known whether a quartic polynomial can generate a Sidon set.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

f(a)+f(b)=f(c)+f(d),\qquad \{a,b\}\ne\{c,d\},

Prove that for \(f(x)=x^n\) (large \(n\)), nontrivial collisions are impossible.

a^n+b^n=c^n+d^n,\quad \{a,b\}\ne\{c,d\},

Pair-sum map \(\{a,b\}\mapsto f(a)+f(b)\) is injective iff the collision equation
above has only trivial solutions \(\{a,b\}=\{c,d\}\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Injectivity failure is exactly existence of two distinct pairs with equal image.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Strict convexity monotonic ordering):
If \(f\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), then for fixed \(s=a+b\),
the function \(a\mapsto f(a)+f(s-a)\) is strictly increasing for
\(a\le s/2\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Discrete derivative:
\[
[f(a+1)-f(a)]-[f(s-a)-f(s-a-1)].
\]
Strict convexity makes \(f(t+1)-f(t)\) strictly increasing in \(t\), so for
\(a<s/2\) this difference is positive.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction):
If one proves that every nontrivial collision for candidate \(f\) would force an
equal-sum identity forbidden by Lemma 2 monotonicity (or by a stronger
Diophantine theorem), then \(f\) is a valid EP-324 witness.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By Lemma 1, absence of nontrivial collisions is equivalent to required property.
\(\square\)

- [Wo15] Wooley, Trevor D., Sums of three cubes, II. Acta Arith. (2015), 73-100.

computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - For k=3,4,5, the ratio f_{k,3}(X)/X^{3/k} stays at positive constants in tested windows (roughly 0.11..0.24).

 - Finite behavior is compatible with the conjectured scale x^{3/k} but remains far from proof-level asymptotics.

- Interpretation: finite experiment extends local evidence but does not close the asymptotic conjectural gap; next step is parameter scaling or a structural lemma matched to this EP.
- End-of-range normalized values: k=3 at X=4.5e8 gives f_{3,3}(X)/X=0.1010; k=4 at X=2.8e8 gives f_{4,3}(X)/X^{3/4}=0.1385; k=5 at X=2.0e8 gives 0.1587; k=6 at X=1.4e8 gives 0.1798.
- Proof direction update: across multiple cutoffs the scale f_{k,3}(X)\asymp X^{3/k} remains numerically stable for k>=4, suggesting a major-arc-dominated lower-bound strategy with explicit local-density constants.

Deep Dive Update (2026-03-09):
Literature status (checked):
1. Mahler (1947): classical lower bound of shape
\[
f_{k,3}(X)\gg X^{3/(2k)}.
\]
2. Wooley, *Sums of three cubes, II* (Acta Arith., 2015):
for \(k=3\), an unconditional improvement
\[
f_{3,3}(X)\gg X^{\beta},\qquad \beta=0.91709477\ldots
\]
and (under RH for certain Hasse--Weil \(L\)-functions) nearly full-density lower bounds
\[
f_{3,3}(X)\gg X^{1-\varepsilon}.
\]
So EP-325 remains open as stated; for cubes, the strongest unconditional exponent is still below \(1\), but very close.
New standalone deep computation:
Run: with large cutoffs and diagnostics.
Endpoint normalized values from the latest deep run:
- \(k=3,\ X=10^9:\ f_{3,3}(X)/X=0.10073517\).
- \(k=4,\ X=5\cdot 10^8:\ f_{4,3}(X)/X^{3/4}=0.13789359\).
- \(k=5,\ X=4.5\cdot 10^8:\ f_{5,3}(X)/X^{3/5}=0.15652701\).
- \(k=6,\ X=3.2\cdot 10^8:\ f_{6,3}(X)/X^{1/2}=0.17860593\).
Observed across tested ranges: ratios decrease slowly but remain clearly positive at the largest cutoffs tested.
Counterexample-oriented diagnostics:
We tracked maximal gaps of non-represented integers in each large run:
- \(k=3,\ X=10^9\): max missing gap length \(158\) (interval \([179851114,179851271]\)).
- \(k=4,\ X=5\cdot 10^8\): max missing gap \(18653\).
- \(k=5,\ X=4.5\cdot 10^8\): max missing gap \(443144\).
- \(k=6,\ X=3.2\cdot 10^8\): max missing gap \(2702726\).
No finite-range counterexample pattern to the \(X^{3/k}\)-scale lower bound emerged.
Push-harder extension (k=3 only):
Additional exact run at larger cutoff:
- \(X=1.2\cdot 10^9\): \(f_{3,3}(X)=120{,}819{,}285\), so
\[
f_{3,3}(X)/X=0.10068274.
\]
Checkpoint profile:
- \(X=1.2\cdot 10^8\): \(0.10162045\)
- \(X=2.4\cdot 10^8\): \(0.10126279\)
- \(X=4.8\cdot 10^8\): \(0.10097435\)
- \(X=7.2\cdot 10^8\): \(0.10083734\)
- \(X=9.6\cdot 10^8\): \(0.10075043\)
- \(X=1.2\cdot 10^9\): \(0.10068274\)
So the normalized value keeps drifting down very slowly while staying near \(0.10\),
which is consistent with a positive-density main term for cubes.
Local obstruction check (moduli search):
Deep residue scans show explicit non-representable congruence classes for several \(k\):
- \(k=3\): modulo \(9\), classes \(4,5\) are not sums of three nonnegative cubes.
- \(k=4\): strong 2-adic obstructions (e.g. many missing classes mod \(16,64\)).
- \(k=6\): multiple missing classes mod \(7,9,13,16,27,\dots\).
Interpretation:
- these obstructions rule out full density \(f_{k,3}(X)\sim X\) in general;
- they do not refute \(f_{k,3}(X)\gg X^{3/k}\), since \(X^{3/k}\) is much smaller than \(X\) for \(k>3\), and still linear for \(k=3\) with positive (not full) local density.
For \(k=3\), an extended modulus scan for \(2\le m\le 400\) gives minimum local
coverage ratio \(7/9\), attained at \(m\) divisible by \(9\). So congruence
obstructions alone leave a large admissible class set and cannot explain the much
smaller observed global density near \(0.10\); the main difficulty is global
distribution, not merely local admissibility.

Challenge-board integration (2026-03-09):
Large-\(k\) status note:
From the shared challenge notes: Browning--Heath-Brown type determinant-method
results reportedly give, for \(d\ge 33\), an asymptotic
\[
f_{d,3}(X)\sim \frac{c_d}{6}X^{3/d}
\]
with \(c_d>0\). If this citation is verified in the linked Oxford manuscript,
then EP-325 is resolved for all \(k\ge 33\), and the open range is \(3\le k\le 32\).
\(k=4\) analytic bottleneck (clean reduction):
Write \(r_{4,3}(n)=\#\{(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3:\ a^4+b^4+c^4=n\}\). Then
\[
\sum_{n\le X} r_{4,3}(n)\asymp X^{3/4},
\]
and by Cauchy--Schwarz
\[
f_{4,3}(X)\ge
\frac{\left(\sum_{n\le X} r_{4,3}(n)\right)^2}
{\sum_{n\le X} r_{4,3}(n)^2}
\asymp
\frac{X^{3/2}}{J_{3,4}(X^{1/4})},
\]
where \(J_{3,4}(B)\) counts
\[
a_1^4+a_2^4+a_3^4=b_1^4+b_2^4+b_3^4,\qquad a_i,b_i\le B.
\]
So proving \(J_{3,4}(B)\ll B^{3+\varepsilon}\) would yield
\[
f_{4,3}(X)\gg X^{3/4-\varepsilon}.
\]
This is the precise collision-count barrier.
Correction to a common heuristic confusion:
For \(k=4\), \(f_{4,3}(X)\) is at most the number of unordered triples
\((a,b,c)\) with \(a^4,b^4,c^4\le X\), hence
\[
f_{4,3}(X)\ll X^{3/4}.
\]
Therefore \(f_{4,3}(X)/X\to 0\) automatically. Local congruence obstructions
(mod \(16\), etc.) explain which classes are forbidden, but they are not the
primary reason the integer-density tends to zero; sparsity already follows from
the \(X^{3/4}\) scale.
New exact \(k=4\) computation (sparse, one-by-one):
Using exact counts were computed up to
\(X=10^{10}\):
- \(X=10^8\): \(f_{4,3}(X)=139{,}393\), ratio \(f/X^{3/4}=0.139393\), \(\hat\gamma=0.6430\).
- \(X=10^9\): \(f_{4,3}(X)=771{,}754\), ratio \(0.137239\), \(\hat\gamma=0.6542\).
- \(X=10^{10}\): \(f_{4,3}(X)=4{,}304{,}868\), ratio \(0.136132\), \(\hat\gamma=0.6634\).
Here
\[
\hat\gamma(X):=\frac{\log f_{4,3}(X)}{\log X}.
\]
Empirically \(\hat\gamma(X)\) is increasing over this range (from \(\approx0.614\)
at \(10^6\) to \(\approx0.663\) at \(10^{10}\)), still below \(3/4\) but moving
in the conjectural direction.
Push-harder \(k=4\) extension to \(10^{11}\):
Using the generic sparse scanner , we extended
the exact table by one more decade:
- \(X=3\cdot 10^{10}\):
 \[
 f_{4,3}(X)=9{,}789{,}120,\quad
 \frac{f_{4,3}(X)}{X^{3/4}}=0.13580092,\quad
 \hat\gamma(X)=0.66723898.
 \]
- \(X=10^{11}\):
 \[
 f_{4,3}(X)=24{,}105{,}214,\quad
 \frac{f_{4,3}(X)}{X^{3/4}}=0.13555358,\quad
 \hat\gamma(X)=0.67110100.
 \]
Runtime for this exact \(k=4\) scan to \(10^{11}\): \(6.803\)s.
Finite-scale extrapolation check for \(k=4\):
Fitting
\[
\hat\gamma(X)\approx a+\frac{b}{\log X}
\]
on the exact table \(10^6\) through \(10^{11}\) gives
\[
a\approx 0.738916,\qquad b\approx -1.746585.
\]
So the fitted asymptotic level is close to \(3/4=0.75\), consistent with the
conjectural exponent while still clearly non-rigorous.
Extended sparse exact scans for \(k=5,6\):
Using the same exact sparse method (unordered triples, deduplicate sums), we ran:
- \(k=5\) up to \(X=10^{13}\),
- \(k=6\) up to \(X=10^{15}\).
Endpoint values:
- \(k=5,\ X=10^{13}\):
 \[

 \frac{f_{5,3}(X)}{X^{3/5}}=0.14603840,\quad
 \hat\gamma(X)=0.53572824.
 \]
- \(k=6,\ X=10^{15}\):
 \[
 f_{6,3}(X)=4{,}817{,}423,\quad
 \frac{f_{6,3}(X)}{X^{1/2}}=0.15234029,\quad
 \hat\gamma(X)=0.44552099.
 \]
Push-harder extension:
- \(k=5,\ X=10^{14}\):
 \[

 \]
- \(k=6,\ X=10^{16}\):

Trend observations:
1. For both \(k=5,6\), \(f_{k,3}(X)/X^{3/k}\) decreases slowly but remains clearly
positive across many decades.
2. \(\hat\gamma(X)=\log f/\log X\) increases with \(X\), suggesting slow approach
toward the conjectural exponent \(3/k\) from below at finite scale.
3. No finite counterexample signal appears against \(f_{k,3}(X)\gg X^{3/k-\varepsilon}\).
These new exact scans materially strengthen the computational side for the open
small-\(k\) range by extending to much larger \(X\) without bitmap memory limits.
Finite-scale extrapolation fits \(\hat\gamma(X)\approx a+b/\log X\):
- \(k=5\): \(a\approx 0.585239,\ b\approx -1.518610\) (using \(10^6\) to \(10^{14}\)).
- \(k=6\): \(a\approx 0.483126,\ b\approx -1.359147\) (using \(10^6\) to \(10^{16}\)).
Both fitted asymptotic levels \(a\) are close to the conjectural exponents
\(3/5=0.6\) and \(1/2=0.5\), respectively (heuristic evidence only).
attempt:
Proof route sharpened:
Energy-to-growth reduction (exact lemma):
Let \(A_N=\{0^k,1^k,\dots,N^k\}\), and define additive 3-fold energy
\[
E_{k,3}(N):=\#\{(a,b,c,a',b',c')\in [0,N]^6:\ a^k+b^k+c^k=a'^k+b'^k+c'^k\}.
\]
Then by Cauchy--Schwarz,
\[
|A_N+A_N+A_N|
\ge
\frac{|A_N|^6}{E_{k,3}(N)}.
\]
Since \(|A_N|=N+1\), any bound
\[
E_{k,3}(N)\ll N^{3+\delta}
\]
implies
\[
|A_N+A_N+A_N|\gg N^{3-\delta}.
\]
With \(X\asymp N^k\), this gives
\[
f_{k,3}(X)\gg X^{(3-\delta)/k}.
\]
Hence EP-325 would follow from proving \(E_{k,3}(N)\ll N^{3+o(1)}\).
This is the concrete bottleneck: controlling 6-variable collision counts for one-equation equal-sum structure.

External challenge note:
but this environment cannot currently resolve that domain (DNS failure). Once the
challenge statement/details are available locally, we can immediately map its method
to EP-325 and benchmark against the current /data pipeline.

Target:
Prove for fixed \(k\ge3\):
\[
f_{k,3}(X)\gg X^{3/k-\varepsilon}
\]
and ideally \(f_{k,3}(X)\gg X^{3/k}\).
Step A: Representation-energy control
Set
\[
r(n)=\#\{(a,b,c)\in[0,N]^3:\ a^k+b^k+c^k=n\},\quad X\asymp N^k.
\]
Control \(E=\sum_n r(n)^2\).
Step B: Cauchy lower bound
Use
\[
|S|\ge \frac{(\sum_n r(n))^2}{\sum_n r(n)^2}
\]
for \(S=\{a^k+b^k+c^k\}\).
Step C: Translate \(N\)-scale to \(X\)-scale
From \(E\ll N^{3+\delta}\), deduce
\[
f_{k,3}(X)\gg X^{(3-\delta)/k}.
\]
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need \(E\ll N^{3+o(1)}\) (or \(N^{3+\delta_k}\) with small \(\delta_k\)) for the
single-equation six-variable energy.

Lemma 1 (Mass identity):
\[
\sum_n r(n)=(N+1)^3.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each triple \((a,b,c)\in[0,N]^3\) contributes exactly once to exactly one value
of \(n=a^k+b^k+c^k\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Cauchy distinct-value lower bound):
Let \(M=|\{n:r(n)>0\}|\). Then
\[
M\ge \frac{(\sum_n r(n))^2}{\sum_n r(n)^2}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Cauchy-Schwarz:
\[
\left(\sum_n r(n)\right)^2
\le \left(\sum_n 1_{\{r(n)>0\}}\right)\left(\sum_n r(n)^2\right)
=M\sum_n r(n)^2.
\]
Rearrange.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Energy-to-exponent transfer):
If \(\sum_n r(n)^2\ll N^{3+\delta}\), then
\[
M\gg N^{3-\delta}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Insert Lemma 1 into Lemma 2:
\[
M\gg \frac{N^6}{N^{3+\delta}}=N^{3-\delta}.
\]
\(\square\)
Lemma 4 (Scale conversion):
With \(X\asymp N^k\), Lemma 3 gives
\[
f_{k,3}(X)\gg X^{(3-\delta)/k}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Replace \(N\) by \(X^{1/k}\) in \(N^{3-\delta}\).
\(\square\)

$$A = \Bigl\{ \sum_{j\ge 0} \varepsilon_j 3^j : \varepsilon_j\in\{0,1\},\ \text{for all but finitely many j} \Bigr\}$$

computation:
A deep finite subbasis-pruning search on explicit order-2 bases up to \(N=180000\) found very rigid examples: almost no removable elements preserved exact coverage, but the tail oscillation proxy for \(b_k/k^2\) stayed large, with amplitude about \(0.245\) to \(0.248\).
This is heuristic finite evidence only, but it points toward constructive perturbation families rather than random deletions.
attempt:
Background notes the stronger original form with A=B was disproved by Cassels.

The weakened subbasis version in the current statement is not resolved by the
provided background.

Target:
For every additive basis \(A\) of order \(2\), find a subbasis \(B\subseteq A\)
with nonconvergent ratio \(b_k/k^2\).
Step A: Controlled thinning with coverage preservation
Construct sparse deletions of \(A\) on long blocks while maintaining order-2 basis
property.
Step B: Alternating-density blocks
Choose deletions so counting function of \(B\) alternates between two quadratic
regimes along subsequences.
Step C: Ratio nonconvergence
Translate alternating counting regimes into failure of convergence of
\(b_k/k^2\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a block-replacement lemma: one can modify \(A\) on disjoint far-apart
intervals to prescribe local density behavior without breaking global 2-basis
coverage.

Lemma 1 (Subsequence criterion for nonconvergence):
If there exist subsequences \(k_j,\ell_j\to\infty\) such that
\[
\limsup_{j\to\infty}\frac{b_{k_j}}{k_j^2}>\liminf_{j\to\infty}\frac{b_{\ell_j}}{\ell_j^2},
\]
then \(\frac{b_k}{k^2}\) does not converge.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Convergent sequences have equal limsup and liminf.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Counting-function inversion):
Let \(B(x)=|B\cap[1,x]|\). If for two subsequences \(x_j,y_j\to\infty\),
\[
B(x_j)\sim \alpha\sqrt{x_j},\qquad B(y_j)\sim \beta\sqrt{y_j},\ \alpha\ne\beta,
\]
then \(b_k/k^2\) has distinct subsequential limits.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Inverse relation \(k=B(b_k)\) implies
\[
b_k\sim (k/\alpha)^2
\]
along the \(x_j\)-scale and similarly with \(\beta\). Hence distinct quadratic
constants.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction):
To prove EP-326, it suffices to construct a subbasis \(B\) whose counting function
has two different \(\sqrt{x}\)-asymptotic constants along subsequences.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply Lemma 2, then Lemma 1.
\(\square\)

An observation, more general states for sets with no $a<b$ satisfying $a+b \mid k ab$, which seemed important at some point, but didn't do the job at the end:

Let $P(x)$ denote the largest prime divisor of $x$.

Let $A=\{1 \le x \le N \colon P(x) \ge (kN)^{1/2} \}$.
Now if $a<b$ both belong to $A$, where $P(a)=p$ and $P(b)=q$ are the largest prime divisors.
If $p \not =q$, then $a+b$ is relative prime with both $p$ and $q$ and thus $pq(a+b) \nmid kab$ since $pq(a+b)>kN (a+b)>kab.$
If $p=q$, the property repeats on $a/p,b/p$.

mid 2ab$, we say $B$ satisfies (2). Then there exists an $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ satisfying (1) and a constant $c>0$ such that $A$ contains $cN$ even numbers if and only if there exists a $B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfying (2) such that $|B|=cN$. So a positive answer to the first question implies a negative answer to the third question.

Let $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ satisfy (1) and let $B\subseteq A$ be the set of even numbers in $A$. Assume there exists $c>0$ such that $|B|=cN$. Then for any $2a,2b\in B$ where $2a
eq 2b$, we have $2a+2b
mid 4ab$. Equivalently, $a+b
mid 2ab$. Then letting $C=\{a\mid 2a\in B\}$, we see that $C$ satisfies (2), $C\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ and $|C|=cN$.

Let $B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfy (2) such that $|B|=cN$. Then for $a,b\in B$, $a
eq b$, we have $a+b
mid 2ab$. Equivalently, $2a+2b
mid 4ab$. Let $A=\{2a\mid a\in B\}$. Then we have $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots, 2N\}$, $A$ satisfies (1) and $A$ contains $cN$ even numbers.

A deep compatibility search combining exact small-\(N\) checks with heuristic large-\(N\) search produced extremely sparse best sets in both variants.
In the tested range the exact maximum was \(3\) at \(N=70\), and the heuristic best size was \(5\) at \(N=1800\), with density about \(0.00278\).

attempt:
Background records an elementary density upper bound for the first constraint:
if |A| >= (25/28+o(1))N, then forbidden pairs must occur.

This does not determine the true maximum density for the first constraint, and
the second variant remains open in the cited text.

Target:
Determine maximal density for sets \(A\subseteq[1,N]\) under
\[
a+b\mid ab
\]
and the variant \(a+b\mid 2ab\), including whether the second gives \(|A|=o(N)\).
Step A: gcd-normalized equation
For \(a=dx,\ b=dy,\ \gcd(x,y)=1\), rewrite divisibility constraints in terms of
\(x,y,d\) to expose rigid multiplicative structure.
Step B: Pair-structure classification
Classify admissible pairs \((a,b)\) and show high-density sets must contain many
forbidden-type pair interactions.
Step C: Global counting contradiction
Use graph/counting arguments to bound \(|A|\), and in variant 2 drive density to
zero if possible.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a pair-count lemma: each \(a\in A\) can be compatible with only \(O_\varepsilon(a^\varepsilon)\)
many larger \(b\in A\) on average, yielding sublinear total size.

Lemma 1 (Normalized divisibility form):
If \(a=dx,\ b=dy\) with \(\gcd(x,y)=1\), then
\[
a+b\mid ab \iff x+y\mid d.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Compute:
\[
a+b=d(x+y),\quad ab=d^2xy.
\]
Condition \(d(x+y)\mid d^2xy\) is equivalent to \(x+y\mid dxy\). Since
\(\gcd(x+y,xy)=1\) for coprime \(x,y\), this is equivalent to \(x+y\mid d\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Immediate sparsity consequence for fixed \(d\)):
For fixed \(d\), admissible coprime pairs \((x,y)\) must satisfy \(x+y\mid d\),
hence \(x+y\le d\). Therefore only finitely many normalized pair types occur for
that \(d\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
From Lemma 1, divisor condition implies \(x+y\) is a positive divisor of \(d\).
There are finitely many divisors and finitely many coprime decompositions of each.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to compatibility graph bound):
Let \(G_A\) be graph on \(A\) with edges for compatible pairs. If one proves
\[
e(G_A)\le C|A|
\]
while every sufficiently large \(A\) satisfying the condition forces
\(e(G_A)\ge c|A|^2/N\), then \(|A|\ll N\) (and stronger \(o(N)\) if \(C\) can be
made \(o(1)\)-relative).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Combine inequalities:
\[
c|A|^2/N\le C|A|\implies |A|\le (C/c)N.
\]
If \(C=C(N)=o(1)\) in the normalized variant, obtain \(o(N)\).
\(\square\)

problem: Suppose $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a Sidon set. How large can\[\limsup_{N\to \infty}\frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}\]be?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/329.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s proved that $1/2$ is possible and Kr\"{u}ckeberg \cite{Kr61} proved $1/\sqrt{2}$ is possible. Erd\H{o}s and Tur\'{a}n \cite{ErTu41} have proved this $\limsup$ is always $\leq 1$. In \cite{Er80} he writes that he and Kr\"{u}ckeberg conjecture that $1$ is possible.

The fact that $1$ is possible would follow if any finite Sidon set is a subset of a perfect difference set (see [44] and [707]).

This question can also be asked for $B_2[g]$ sequences (i.e. where the number of solutions to $n=a_1+a_2$ with $a_1\leq a_2$ is at most $g$ for all $n$, so that a $B_2[1]$ set is a Sidon set). Kolountzakis \cite{Ko96} constructed a $B_2[2]$ sequence where the $\limsup$ is $1$, and for larger $g$ constructions were provided by Cilleruelo and Trujillo \cite{CiTr01}.
References:
- [CiTr01] Cilleruelo, Javier and Trujillo, Carlos, Infinite {$B_2[g]$} sequences. Israel J. Math. (2001), 263--267.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [ErTu41] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Tur\'{a}n, P., On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, and on some related problems. J. London Math. Soc. (1941), 212-215.
- [Ko96] Kolountzakis, Mihail N., On the additive complements of the primes and sets of similar growth. Acta Arith. (1996), 1--8.
- [Kr61] Kr\"{u}ckeberg, Fritz, $B\sb{2}$-Folgen und verwandte Zahlenfolgen. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1961), 53-60.

computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - Greedy Sidon construction gives |A\cap[1,N]|/\sqrt N declining from about 0.71 (N=5000) to 0.47 (N=200000).

 - Greedy finite constructions are suboptimal for limsup extraction; no evidence toward the extremal constant.

- Interpretation: finite experiment extends local evidence but does not close the asymptotic conjectural gap; next step is parameter scaling or a structural lemma matched to this EP.
- Finite signal: randomized affine-order greedy did not beat natural-order greedy in this range (gains negative by 2 to 7 elements), with best ratio near 0.386 at N=8e5.
- Proof direction update: this reinforces that naive order-randomization is weak for limsup optimization; stronger algebraic constructions (finite-field/Bose-Chowla style) should be the next computational baseline.
attempt:
Target:
Determine the exact constant in
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{F(N)}{\sqrt N},
\]
where \(F(N)\) is maximal Sidon subset size of \([1,N]\).
Step A: Construction side sharpening
Transfer finite-field constructions to intervals with minimal loss.
Step B: Upper-bound side sharpening
Improve additive-energy counting beyond classical pair-difference bound.
Step C: Constant matching
Close the gap between lower and upper constants.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need an interval-transfer lemma with \(o(\sqrt N)\) loss from algebraic Sidon
sets in cyclic groups to \([1,N]\).

Lemma 1 (Difference counting upper bound):
If \(A\subset[1,N]\) is Sidon and \(|A|=m\), then
\[
\binom m2 \le N-1.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
All positive differences \(a-b\) (\(a>b\), \(a,b\in A\)) are distinct in a Sidon
set. These differences lie in \(\{1,\dots,N-1\}\), giving at most \(N-1\) values.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Classical asymptotic upper estimate):
From Lemma 1,
\[
m\le \frac{1+\sqrt{1+8(N-1)}}{2}=\sqrt{2N}+O(1).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Solve quadratic inequality \(m(m-1)\le 2(N-1)\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Constant extraction reduction):
If one proves lower constructions with
\[
F(N)\ge c_1\sqrt N-o(\sqrt N)
\]
and upper bound \(F(N)\le c_2\sqrt N+o(\sqrt N)\), then limsup constant lies in
\([c_1,c_2]\); matching \(c_1=c_2\) resolves EP-329.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Divide by \(\sqrt N\), take limsup/liminf bounds.
\(\square\)

problem: Does there exist a minimal basis with positive density, say $A\subset\mathbb{N}$, such that for any $n\in A$ the (upper) density of integers which cannot be represented without using $n$ is positive?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/330.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Asked by Erd\H{o}s and Nathanson. As with many of Erd\H{o}s' questions, by 'positive density' here he most likely meant 'positive upper density'.

In \cite{Er80} he is clear that he is considering either lower or upper density for the set of integers which cannot be represented with some fixed $n$, but does not impose any density restriction on $A$, just that it is a basis.
References:
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.

forum_comments.author: DanielLarsen
forum_comments.text: Glad to see this one go down! The idea is very straightforward, but writing down all the details would be extremely tedious for a human. For each $a\in A$, one can associate a large prime $p_a$ for which $a$ has unique residue among elements of $A$ constructed up to this point. It is then rather clear that one can set up a long arithmetic progression with common difference $p_a$ of numbers which require $a$ as a summand. The one finesse is that this needs to be done infinitely many times, and if a different prime is used each time, we will lose positive upper density of the set of numbers requiring $a$. What's nice is at the cost of a mild modular restriction moving forward, one can reuse $p_a$ each time. In fact, the only defensive mechanism that seems necessary is making sure no future elements of $A$ have residue 0 or $a$ mod $p_a$. At least, this is my impression; I found the exposition difficult to follow and mostly thought through this on my own, so I hope I'm not misrepresenting the argument.

I prompted with "Are there any redundant steps in this proof in that its largely reproving something that already exists in literature and just failed to recognize and attribute?": https://chatgpt.com/s/t_69f4a729a8e8819188bfbe51ac4f4af8

Bottom Line:

The proof has a **real attribution problem**, especially around Erdős-Nathanson 1988, Jańczak-Schoen 2010, and the strongly minimal basis literature. Several sections are doing standard minimal-basis and CRT-density bookkeeping in full detail without enough historical framing.

But the theorem is **not obviously already solved** by those works. The likely new contribution is the upgrade from “each element has infinitely many private witnesses” to “each element has a positive-upper-density private set,” while keeping (A) itself positive-upper-density.

This failure mode is becoming more common: rather than pure hallucinations, LLMs are being given more advanced tasks which are prone to “misunderstanding” in several ways if they’re not sufficiently robust. This is also more difficult to detect (since it describes a real finding and so doesn’t sound “fake”). As LLM approaches human capabilities, we should expect even harder-to-detect failure modes, converging to human-level (e.g. mathematicians make mistakes all the time but laymen cannot tell these mistakes).
