attempt:
Attempt route:
Tried to combine minimal-basis deletion sensitivity with density-increment style
bookkeeping for representation sets.

Obstacle:
Finite-window behavior does not imply an infinite minimal basis theorem with
asymptotic positive densities.

Target:
Construct a positive-density minimal basis \(A\) where each \(a\in A\) is
indispensable for a positive-density set of integers.
Step A: Layered basis architecture
Build \(A\) as union of widely separated blocks with controlled internal
representation patterns.
Step B: Essentiality localization
For each block element \(a\), produce a positive-density target set \(E_a\) whose
representations necessarily use \(a\).
Step C: Global compatibility
Show block interactions do not destroy minimality or positive density.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a shielding lemma: cross-block sums cannot replicate representations from a
designated block interval where an element \(a\) is forced.

Lemma 1 (Indispensability criterion):
An element \(a\in A\) is indispensable for set \(E\subset\mathbb N\) iff
\[
E\subseteq (A+A)\setminus\bigl((A\setminus\{a\})+(A\setminus\{a\})\bigr).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By definition, every \(n\in E\) is representable with \(A\), but becomes
nonrepresentable after removing \(a\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Positive-density transfer):
If \(E\) has lower density \(\delta>0\), and \(E\subseteq E'\) up to finitely many
exceptions, then \(E'\) has lower density at least \(\delta\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Finite modifications do not change lower density.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to block shielding):
Suppose \(A\) is an order-2 basis of positive density and for each \(a\in A\)
there exists a block interval \(I_a\) with positive-density subset \(E_a\subseteq
I_a\) satisfying Lemma 1. Then EP-330 holds.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each \(a\) is indispensable for positive-density \(E_a\). Since \(A\) is basis and
positive density by assumption, all required properties hold.
\(\square\)

Prikry, Tijdeman, Stewart, and others (see the survey articles \cite{St78} and \cite{Ti79}) have shown that a sufficient condition is that $A$ has positive density.

One can also ask what conditions are sufficient for $D(A)$ to have positive density, or for $\sum_{d\in D(A)}\frac{1}{d}=\infty$, or even just $D(A)\neq\emptyset$.

forum_comments.author: aditya
forum_comments.text:
An observation by GPT 5.5 pro : the known sufficient condition “positive natural density” can be weakened to positive upper Banach density.

(Please see this (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1B_i5L-7iBVx2vl-2EgKn6F4_r9gr8qX8/view?usp=drivesdk) for the full proof)

Let\[
d^*(A)=\limsup_{L\to\infty}\sup_M \frac{|A\cap [M,M+L)|}{L}.
\]If \(d^*(A)>0\), then \(D(A)\) has bounded gaps.

Proof sketch. Put \(\delta=d^*(A)\), and let\[
P=\{h\in\mathbb Z: d^*(A\cap(A-h))>0\}.
\]Then \(P\cap\mathbb N\subseteq D(A)\). I claim \(P\) is syndetic.

Indeed, if \(t_0,\dots,t_m\in\mathbb Z\) and no nonzero difference \(t_i-t_j\) lies in \(P\), then the translates \(A-t_i\) have pairwise intersections of upper Banach density zero. Taking intervals on which \(A\) has density close to \(\delta\), and shifting them by only \(O_{t_i}(1)\), all \(A-t_i\) have density close to \(\delta\) on a common sequence of intervals. Inclusion-exclusion then gives\[
1\ge (m+1)\delta-o(1).
\]So \(m+1\le 1/\delta\).

Thus any subset of \(\mathbb Z\) whose nonzero pairwise differences avoid \(P\) has size at most \(1/\delta\). Choose such a set \(F\) maximal. By maximality, every \(z\in\mathbb Z\) satisfies \(z-f\in P\) for some \(f\in F\), so \(P+F=\mathbb Z\). Hence \(P\) is syndetic. Therefore \(P\cap\mathbb N\), and hence \(D(A)\), has bounded gaps.

This is not meant as a full characterization of the sets \(A\) for which \(D(A)\) has bounded gaps, just a slightly stronger sufficient condition.

Hard point:
Finite frequency proxies are not equivalent to the infinite-occurrence definition
of D(A), so this does not produce new sharp sufficient criteria.

Target:
Find sufficient conditions on \(A\subset\mathbb N\) ensuring bounded gaps in
\[
D(A)=\{d\ge1:\ d=a_1-a_2\ \text{infinitely often with }a_i\in A\}.
\]

Assume quantitative pair-correlation:

\]
for many \(d\) uniformly.
Step B: Infinite-occurrence upgrade
Convert positive-density-in-\(X\) pair counts into \(d\in D(A)\).
Step C: Gap control
Show every interval of \(d\)-values of bounded length contains one satisfying

Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a uniform correlation-to-coverage theorem: from averaged pair-correlation on

Lemma 1 (Infinite occurrences from linear counts):
If for fixed \(d\),
\[
\limsup_{X\to\infty}\#\{x\le X:\ x,x+d\in A\}=+\infty,
\]
then \(d\in D(A)\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Unbounded count provides infinitely many distinct witness pairs.

If there exists \(L\) such that every interval \([t,t+L]\) contains some \(d\)

\[
\textit{Proof.}

To prove bounded gaps in \(D(A)\), it suffices to establish an \(L\) for which

\[
\textit{Proof.}

problem: Find the best function $f(n)$ such that every $n$ can be written as $n=a+b$ where both $a,b$ are $f(n)$-smooth (that is, are not divisible by any prime $p>f(n)$.)
literature:

- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 03 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s originally asked if even $f(n)\leq n^{1/3}$ is true. This is known, and the best bound is due to Balog \cite{Ba89} who proved that\[f(n) \ll_\epsilon n^{\frac{4}{9\sqrt{e}}+\epsilon}\]for all $\epsilon>0$. (Note $\frac{4}{9\sqrt{e}}=0.2695\ldots$.)

It is likely that $f(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$.

See also Problem 59 (https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf) on Green's open problems list.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
I asked the Deep Research tool of Gemini for the relevant literature on this problem twice, and both times it couldn't really find anything interesting beyond the already mentioned result by Balog. It did mention that a bound of $f(n) < \exp(c \sqrt{\log n \log \log n})$ is known for sums $a+b+c$ of three elements instead of two (see e.g. this (https://akjournals.com/view/journals/10473/67/4/article-p333.xml) paper by Sárközy), similar to how ternary Goldbach is significantly more approachable than binary Goldbach.

To paraphrase from the comments on Green's list: even a bound of $f(n) \le n^{0.1}$ seems extremely difficult, as it implies small quadratic non-residues. To elaborate on that, if all large enough $n$ can be written as $a+b$ with both $a$ and $b$ $n^{0.1}$-smooth, then this in particular holds for all sufficiently large primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. For these primes this implies that one of $a, b$ is a quadratic non-residue, implying that a quadratic non-residue exists which is at most $p^{0.1}$. The best known upper bound for this problem has exponent $\frac{1}{4\sqrt{e}} + \epsilon \approx 0.15$ instead of $0.1$, however.

Finally, in the Sárközy paper linked above he states that Erdős conjectures that the bound $f(n) < \exp(c \sqrt{\log n \log \log n})$ also holds for the binary problem considered here. I did not find the slightly stronger $f(n) < \exp(c \sqrt{\log n})$ conjectured anywhere.

Need a uniform additive friable theorem: for chosen \(y(n)\), every sufficiently
large \(n\) has at least one representation \(n=a+b\) with both \(a,b\in

Let \(S_y(n)=\{m\le n:\ P^+(m)\le y\}\). Number of \(y\)-smooth decompositions is
\[
R_y(n)=\#\{a\in S_y(n):\ n-a\in S_y(n)\}.

\textit{Proof.}
\]

\textit{Proof.}

To prove \(f(n)\le Y(n)\) eventually, it suffices to prove \(R_{Y(n)}(n)\ge1\)
for all sufficiently large \(n\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply Lemma 2 pointwise for large \(n\).
\(\square\)

problem: Let $d(A)$ denote the density of $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$. Characterise those $A,B\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with positive density such that\[d(A+B)=d(A)+d(B).\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/335.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 15 April 2026.
Site remarks:
One way this can happen is if there exists $\theta>0$ such that\[A=\{ n>0 : \{ n\theta\} \in X_A\}\textrm{ and }B=\{ n>0 : \{n\theta\} \in X_B\}\]where $\{x\}$ denotes the fractional part of $x$ and $X_A,X_B\subseteq \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ are such that $\mu(X_A+X_B)=\mu(X_A)+\mu(X_B)$. Are all possible $A$ and $B$ generated in a similar way (using other groups)?

This has been partially resolved by Ackelsburg and Richter \cite{AcRi26}, under the additional assumption that one of the sets meets every residue class in $\mathbb{N}$. Roughly speaking, if $d(A)>0$ and $d(A+B)=d(A)+d(B)<1$ and $B$ meets every residue class then either both $A$ and $B$ arise from a rotation on the product of the circle group with a finite cyclic group, or $A$ is in a single residue class modulo some $h$ and $B$ 'looks like' the union of all but one residue class modulo $h$.

A full characterisation without the assumption that one of the sets meets every residue class seems hopeless; for example, taking $A=B$ to be a random subset of the even integers with density $1/4$ we have $d(A+A)=1/2$.
References:
- [AcRi26] E. Ackelsburg and F. Richter, An inverse theorem for sumsets of sets of positive density in the integers. arXiv:2604.12864 (2026).

forum_comments.author: eackelsberg
forum_comments.text:
Thanks for linking our paper so quickly! Here's a brief summary of our main result with some comments on the assumption about $B$ meeting every residue class in $\mathbb{N}$.

The general case does not seem to have any simple characterization using rotations on groups. The problem is that modular obstructions can get in the way. For example, if $A$ is a random subset of the even numbers with density $1/4$, then $A+A$ will be almost all of the even numbers and have density $1/2$. This provides an example of a highly non-structured set satisfying $d(A+A) = 2d(A)$.

We bypass such situations by assuming that one of the sets (we take it to be the set $B$) completely avoids modular obstructions. Our main result says that under this assumption that $B$ meets every residue class in $\mathbb{N}$ and $d(A) + d(B) < 1$, one of two things happens:

- the sets $A$ and $B$ arise from a rotation on the product of the circle group with a finite cyclic group, or
- $A$ is contained in a single residue class mod $h$ for some $h$ and B “looks like” the union of all but one residue classes mod $h$

The precise statement (with a rigorous meaning of what it means for $B$ to “look like” the union of all but one residue classes mod $h$) can be found as Theorem 1.4 in our paper.

R/Z (and corresponding measurable sets) where equality holds.

A complete characterization is not supplied; the text explicitly asks whether all
such examples come from analogous group constructions.

Target:
Characterize positive-density sets \(A,B\subset\mathbb N\) satisfying
\[
d(A+B)=d(A)+d(B).
\]
Step A: Kneser-type structural reduction
Pass to periodic models where equality in lower sumset-density bounds is
analyzed via stabilizers.
Step B: Equality-case rigidity
Show equality forces interval/Bohr/rotation-type structure modulo a period.
Step C: Lift back to integers
Transfer periodic characterization to asymptotic density on \(\mathbb N\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a full equality-case theorem for the density inequality in the asymptotic
setting, analogous to Vosper/Kneser equality classification.

Lemma 1 (Basic lower bound):
For positive-density sets with \(d(A)+d(B)\le1\),
\[
d(A+B)\ge d(A)+d(B).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Standard additive-combinatorial density inequality (Kneser-type in periodic
approximants, then limit passage).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Immediate consequence of equality):
If equality holds, then no "extra expansion" occurs beyond the lower bound; in
periodic approximants this means stabilizer structure is maximal.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
In Kneser formula
\[
|A+B|\ge |A|+|B|-|H|,
\]
equality forces exact accounting by stabilizer \(H\), excluding additional
aperiodic growth.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to periodic equality classification):
If equality cases are classified for periodic models and approximation error is
\(o(1)\) in density, then EP-335 characterization follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Approximate \(A,B\) by periodic truncations; apply classified equality form in
each period; pass to density limit.
\(\square\)

problem:
For $r\geq 2$ let $h(r)$ be the maximal finite $k$ such that there exists a basis $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of order $r$ (so every large integer is the sum of at most $r$ integers from $A$) and exact order $k$ (so every large integer is the sum of exactly $k$ integers from $A$).

Find the value of\[\lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/336.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A simple example of the order of a basis differing from the exact order is given by $A=\cup_{k\geq 0}(2^{2k},2^{2k+1}]$, which has order $2$ but exact order $3$.

Erd\H{o}s and Graham \cite{ErGr80b} have shown that a basis $A$ has an exact order if and only if $a_2-a_1,a_3-a_2,a_4-a_3,\ldots$ are coprime. They also proved that\[\frac{1}{4}\leq \lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}\leq \frac{5}{4}.\]The best bounds known for the limit are\[\frac{1}{3}\leq \lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}\leq \frac{1}{2},\]the lower bound originally due to Grekos \cite{Gr88} and the upper bound to Nash \cite{Na93}. Improved bounds in the lower order terms were given by Plagne \cite{Pl04}.

Erd\H{o}s and Graham \cite{ErGr80b} showed $h(2)=4$. Nash \cite{Na93} showed $h(3)=7$. The value of $h(4)$ is unknown, but it is known \cite{Pl04} that $10\leq h(4)\leq 11$.
References:
- [ErGr80b] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R. L., On bases with an exact order. Acta Arith. (1980), 201-207.
- [Gr88] Grekos, Georges, Sur l'ordre d'une base additive. ([1988?]), Exp. No. 31, 13.
- [Na93] Nash, John C. M., Some applications of a theorem of {M}. {K}neser. J. Number Theory (1993), 1--8.
- [Pl04] Plagne, Alain, \`A{} propos de la fonction {$X$} d'{E}rd\H{o}s et {G}raham. Ann. Inst. Fourier (Grenoble) (2004), 1717--1767.

problem: The restricted order of a basis is the least integer $t$ (if it exists) such that every large integer is the sum of at most $t$ distinct summands from $A$. What are necessary and sufficient conditions that this exists? Can it be bounded (when it exists) in terms of the order of the basis? What are necessary and sufficient conditions that this is equal to the order of the basis?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/338.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 14 September 2025.
Site remarks:
Bateman has observed that for $h\geq 3$ there is a basis of order $h$ with no restricted order, taking\[A=\{1\}\cup \{x>0 : h\mid x\}.\]Kelly \cite{Ke57} has shown that any basis of order $2$ has restricted order at most $4$ and conjectured it always has restricted order at most $3$ (which he proved under the additional assumption that the basis has positive lower density). Kelly's conjecture was disproved by Hennecart \cite{He05}, who constructed a basis of order $2$ with restricted order $4$.

The set of squares has order $4$ and restricted order $5$ (see \cite{Pa33}) and the set of triangular numbers has order $3$ and restricted order $3$ (see \cite{Sc54}).

Is it true that if $A\backslash F$ is a basis for all finite sets $F$ then $A$ must have a restricted order? What if they are all bases of the same order?

Hegyv\'{a}ri, Hennecart, and Plagne \cite{HHP07} have shown that for all $k\geq2$ there exists a basis of order $k$ which has restricted order at least\[2^{k-2}+k-1.\]
References:
- [HHP07] Hegyv\'{a}ri, Norbert and Hennecart, Fran\c cois and Plagne, Alain, Answer to a question by {B}urr and {E}rd\H{o}s on restricted addition, and related results. Combin. Probab. Comput. (2007), 747--756.
- [He05] Hennecart, Fran\c cois, On the restricted order of asymptotic bases of order two. Ramanujan J. (2005), 123--130.
- [Ke57] Kelly, John B., Restricted bases. Amer. J. Math. (1957), 258-264.
- [Pa33] Pall, Gordon, On Sums of Squares. Amer. Math. Monthly (1933), 10-18.
- [Sc54] Schinzel, A., Sur la d\'{e}composition des nombres naturels en sommes de nombres triangulaires distincts. Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. Cl. III. (1954), 409-410.

Target:
Characterize when unrestricted finite order exists but distinct-summand restricted
order fails (EP-338 dichotomy).
Step A: Modular obstruction extraction
For Bateman-type sets \(A=\{1\}\cup h\mathbb N\), identify residue classes never
hit by distinct-summand sums.

Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a distinct-summand residue-exclusion lemma uniform in number of summands.

Lemma 1 (Residue form of distinct sums for \(A=\{1\}\cup h\mathbb N\)):
Any distinct-summand sum from \(A\) is congruent mod \(h\) to either \(0\) or \(1\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
All elements except \(1\) are \(0\pmod h\). Distinctness allows using \(1\) at
most once, so residue is \(0\) (without \(1\)) or \(1\) (with \(1\)).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Immediate restricted-order failure):
If \(h\ge3\), residues \(2,\dots,h-1\) are never attained by distinct sums, so
restricted order does not exist.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By Lemma 1 only residues \(0,1\) occur; infinitely many integers in other
residues remain uncovered.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Unrestricted-order possibility):
Unrestricted sums may reuse \(1\), so all residues mod \(h\) can be reached by
taking enough \(1\)'s plus multiples of \(h\). Hence modular obstruction from
Lemma 1 disappears.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Given residue \(r\), use \(r\) copies of \(1\) (mod \(h\)), then adjust magnitude
with \(h\)-multiples.
\(\square\)

Greedy rule chooses the least admissible integer greater than \(a_n\); least

definitions.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
After a longer back and forth with GPT-5.4 I've got some new partial results in the direction I wanted, namely: L-packets as an explanation for "hidden signal". Here's the note that proves the following (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos342-new.pdf):

If the classical Ulam sequence \(U(1,2)\) really has positive upper density, then the strange Fourier spike people see numerically is not a fluke. After passing to a Furstenberg limit, that spike turns into an actual eigenfrequency of a shift system built from the sequence. So the “hidden signal” in the Ulam numbers gets upgraded from an experiment to a real structural feature of a limiting dynamical system.

The key finite combinatorial input is that the initial segments \(A_{N} = U(1,2)\cap [1,N]\) contain very few ordered Schur triples \(x+y=z\), in fact at most \(3|A_{N}|\). By Green’s theorem, that means \(A_{N}\) is very close to a genuinely sum-free set \(B_{N}\). Informally, the Ulam sequence is behaving a lot like an almost sum-free set, and that is what forces a big Fourier coefficient to appear.

The last part explains what this says about the preferred Fourier phases. Those maximizing phases cannot wander all over \(\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}\); any limit point has to come from a finite spectral atom set. In the irrational case, the paper even gets a circle-factor picture and a non-uniform limiting phase distribution for the Ulam numbers and for the nearby sum-free cores. So the overall message is: assuming positive density, the Ulam sequence has real hidden harmonic structure, not just mysterious numerics.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Actually there's a lot of cool numerical computations in A Hidden Signal in the Ulam sequence (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.00267) by Steinerberger, especially related to the title hidden signal which comes from Fourier series, and here's something worth computing. I had this idea coming from Langlands program:

Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be the Ulam sequence with $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, and for $n\ge 2$ let $a_{n+1}$ be the least integer $>a_n$ that has a unique representation $a_i+a_j$ with $1\le i<j\le n$. For each $n$ write $A_n=\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ and view $A_n$ as a subset of the cyclic group $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ by choosing a prime $p>2a_n$ (so that there is no wraparound for sums in $[0,2a_n]$). Define the discrete Fourier transform of the indicator $1_{A_n}$ by $S_n(k)=\sum_{x\in A_n} e^{2\pi i kx/p}$ for $k\in\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$.

Numerically there is a striking ''hidden signal'': for large $n$ one finds a frequency $k_n^*\in\{1,\dots,(p-1)/2\}$ maximizing $|S_n(k)|$ such that the associated angle $\alpha_n=2\pi k_n^*/p$ stabilizes near an irrational constant $\alpha\approx 2.571447\ldots$, and the normalized peak height $|S_n(k_n^*)|/n$ remains macroscopic (around $0.7$-$0.8$ at the scales tested).

A convenient way to package this phenomenon is via an $L$-packet (harmonic packet) hypothesis: not only is the fundamental mode $k_n^*$ large, but several harmonics $mk_n^*$ are simultaneously large, i.e. $|S_n(mk_n^*)|/n$ is far above the random baseline $n^{-1/2}$ for $1\le m\le L$. In our computations, for many values of $n$ one observes that the harmonics $m=2,3,4,5,6$ are themselves among the top few Fourier peaks and can have normalized magnitudes comparable to $0.2$-$0.6$, suggesting a genuinely structured packet rather than a single isolated spike. This connects directly with the numerical claim in arXiv1507.00267 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.00267) that, at large scales, the spectrum appears to be dominated by (essentially) two peaks and their harmonic footprints; in practice one can test this by ranking the values of $|S_n(k)|$ for $1\le k\le (p-1)/2$ and tracking the ranks of the harmonic family $mk_n^*$.

A further experiment (useful for probing whether $\alpha$ admits any simple ''closed form'' approximation) is to fit the observed maximizers $\alpha_n$ by low-complexity models suggested by the $L$-packet picture, e.g. by approximating $\theta_n=\alpha_n/(2\pi)$ with short eventually periodic continued fractions (quadratic irrationals), or by rational multiples of $\pi$. Concretely, one may compare candidate angles $\widehat\alpha$ by computing the packet statistics $n^{-1}\big|\sum_{j\le n} e^{i m\widehat\alpha a_j}\big|$ for $1\le m\le L$ together with the sign-bias $\#\{j\le n:\cos(\widehat\alpha a_j)<0\}/n$, which is near $1$ for angles tightly aligned to the hidden signal. The main point is that these computations are straightforward to reproduce (generate $A_n$, choose $p>2a_n$, FFT the indicator of $A_n$), and they provide a concrete starting point for community exploration of packet structure, harmonic stability, and possible arithmetic constraints on the limiting frequency.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
First of all, it's worth to add 3 main references on the problem:
[1] D. Ross, The Ulam Sequence: Structure and Randomness, PhD thesis, University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign, 2016
[2] S. Steinerberger. A Hidden Signal in the Ulam sequence. arXiv:1507.00267, 2015.
[3] F. Clément and S. Steinerberger. Small Gaps in the Ulam sequence. arXiv:2501.16285, 2025

Steinerberger's results suggest the Ulam sequence exhibits a "hidden signal"—a strong Fourier peak at an irrational frequency $\alpha \approx 2.571$. Not much is known really and it seems the problem wasn't researched extensively.

I managed to get an explanation with GPT-5.2 of why a "hidden signal" might arise and show some other heurestics towards the final answers. Below is a mean-field analysis explaining the stability of this signal and deriving a theoretical growth rate that closely matches empirical data (this is new, there was no explanation of this phenomenon before as I can see so far). You can see the full write up here. (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos342.pdf)

1. The Fourier Setup
Let $A_n = \{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ be the Ulam sequence. Define the Fourier sum at frequency $\alpha$ as $S_n = \sum_{j=1}^n e^{i \alpha a_j}$. Empirically, $S_n$ grows linearly along the negative real axis: $S_n \approx -c n$ with $c \approx 0.79$.

The number of representations of an integer $m$ as a sum of two terms, $s_n(m)$, is given via Fourier inversion (dominated by the DC term and the frequency $\alpha$):\[
s_n(m) \approx \frac{n^2}{q} + \frac{2 |S_n|^2}{q} \cos(\alpha m + \text{phase}(S_n)).
\]For $S_n$ to be stable on the negative real axis, its phase is $\pi$. Thus:\[
s_n(m) \approx \frac{n^2}{q} \left( 1 + 2c^2 \cos(\alpha m) \right).
\]2. The Phase-Locking Mechanism
The Ulam rule selects the smallest $m > a_n$ such that $s_n(m) = 2$ (uniquely representable). Since the average representation count is large ($\sim n$), finding a value as low as $2$ requires "destructive interference" from the dominant mode to cancel the baseline.\[
1 + 2c^2 \cos(\alpha m) \le 0 \implies \cos(\alpha m) \le -\frac{1}{2c^2}.
\]This inequality creates a feedback loop:

 Existence Threshold: For a solution to exist, the cosine must be able to dip low enough. This requires $-1/(2c^2) \ge -1$, implying $c \ge 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707$. The empirical $c \approx 0.79$ satisfies this stability criterion.
 Phase Trapping: The new term $a_{n+1}$ is forced to have a phase $\phi = \alpha a_{n+1}$ inside a specific "trough" arc centered at $\pi$.

3. The Self-Consistent Field Equation
We can solve for the theoretical growth rate $c$. Let the "allowed arc" of phases be $[\pi - \delta, \pi + \delta]$.
The boundary of this arc is defined by the threshold condition:\[
\cos(\delta) = \frac{1}{2c^2} \quad (*).
\]Assuming the sequence samples phases uniformly within this allowed window (due to noise from other frequencies), the growth rate of the peak $S_n$ is the average projection of these new unit vectors onto the negative real axis:\[
c = \frac{1}{2\delta} \int_{-\delta}^{\delta} \cos(x) \, dx = \frac{\sin(\delta)}{\delta} \quad (**).
\]4. Results and Comparison
Solving the system of equations (*) and (**) numerically:\[
2 \cos(\delta) \sin^2(\delta) = \delta^2
\]yields the solution:\[
\delta \approx 0.867 \text{ rad} \quad (49.7^\circ), \qquad c_{\text{theory}} \approx 0.879.
\]This theoretical upper bound ($c \approx 0.88$) is remarkably close to the empirical value ($c \approx 0.79$). The discrepancy is naturally explained by "noise" ($L^2$ error terms) which effectively broadens the trapping window $\delta$, lowering the average cosine.

5. Implications for Open Problems
Infinitely many pairs $ a, a+2 $: Likely. The non-uniform distribution on the circle (with positive density in the support arc) implies that phases recur infinitely often in regions where the next trough (gap) is exactly 2. Since $ \alpha $ is irrational, ergodicity ensures infinite visits to such phase sets. This is conjectural but fits the quasi-periodic picture.

Eventually periodic differences: Unlikely. The irrational rotation on the circle (modulo the trapping arc) prevents strict periodicity in gaps.

Density zero?: No—the persistent Fourier bias and positive $ c $ are inconsistent with zero density (which would imply more random-like behavior). Computations stabilize around $ \sim 0.076 $.

In my experience with LLMs, I found the best approach is to have 3 SOTA models check and evaluate each other, (e.g Gemini 3 + Opus 4.5 + gpt 5.2). Model 1 is the main discussion partner who exchange feedback with you and writes/takes notes.

Model 2 checks what model 1 wrote then model 1 is fed the feedback from model 2 to evaluate and the process goes iteratively until Models 1 & 2 finally converge/agree on the same optimized output.

Then you take that output and do the same process iteratively with model 3 optimizing further until you reach a state of convergence between the 3 peer-reviewers.

The most important part in this process is obviously the human supervising them and assessing which model is being overly pedantic, which one is being overly agreeable, and which ideas/methods are actually worth pursuing. So it's essential to have sharp hallucination filters.

Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a complete sequence, and define the threshold of completeness $T(A)$ to be the least integer $m$ such that all $n\geq m$ are in\[P(A) = \left\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A\textrm{ finite }\right\}\](the existence of $T(A)$ is guaranteed by completeness).

Is it true that there are infinitely many $k$ such that $T(n^k)>T(n^{k+1})$?

It is known that\[T(n)=1, T(n^2)=128, T(n^3)=12758,\]\[T(n^4)=5134240,\textrm{ and }T(n^5)=67898771.\]Erd\H{o}s and Graham remark that a good candidate for the $n$ in the question are $k=2^t$ for large $t$, perhaps even $t=3$, because of the highly restricted values of $n^{2^t}$ modulo $2^{t+1}$.

forum_comments.text:
In the comment above, Stijn shows the lower bound $T(x^k) > 2^{c k \log k}$, which perhaps can be further improved if $k$ is a power of two. On the other hand, I wondered whether any upper bound was known and found this (https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL20/Kim/kim6.pdf) paper by Kim, where they make a proof by Graham explicit and find an upper bound of $T(x^k) < 2^{ck^4}$. Since this latter bound holds for all positive integers, plausibly it can be improved for specific values to see if $T(x^k) > T(x^{k+1})$ can be deduced for some $k$. Lower and upper bound are still quite far off from each other though.

Kim, D. On the largest integer that is not a sum of distinct positive nth powers, Journal of Integer Sequences, Volume 20, Issue 7 (2017).

It may well that the answer is negative, i.e., that there aren't infinitely many such $k$ (if there is already even one of them).

\textbf{background}
The value of $T(n^k)$ is known for $k\le 8$, see [oeis A001661] (https://oeis.org/A001661/list).

In particular, we know that $T(n^8)<T(n^9)$ by the estimate by [Wiener23] (https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL26/Wiener/wiener3.pdf).

\textbf{Remark on the growth of $T(x^k)$ and the candidates by EG}
The restrictedness is slightly larger; $n^{2^t} \equiv 0,1 \pmod{2^{t+2}}$ for every $t \ge 2$.

This implies that indeed, when $r \equiv -1 \pmod{2^{t+2}}$, there are combinations with at least $2^{t+2}-1$ odd $2^t$th powers needed.
From this, one gets immediately a lowerbound for $T(n^{2^t})$ equal to
$$\sum_{i=1}^{2^{t+2}-1}(2i-1)^{2^t}=(c+o(1)) \int_1^{2^{t+3}} x^{2^{t}} dx=(c+o(1))*2^{(t+3)2^t+3}$$ for some $0.375<c<1/2$.

But one can actually do a better estimate.
Let $n$ be the solution to $n^k=2^n$, so $$n=\log_2(e) k (\ln(k)+\ln(\ln(k))+o(1))=k (\log_2(k)+\log_2(\log_2(k)+O(1)).$$ Now, since there are only $2^{n-1}$ combinations of $1^k$ up to $(n-1)^k$, there is definitely a number in the range $[2^{n-1},2^n]$ which cannot be represented as the sum of different $k^{th}$ powers.

Thus $T(x^k)>2^{n-1}=2^{ k (\log_2(k)+\log_2(\log_2(k))+O(1))}.$
When $k=2^t$, we notice that this is of the form $\Theta\left(2^{ 2^t(t+\log_2(t))} \right)$,
which is larger than $\Theta \left( 2^{(t+3)2^t}\right)$.

The presented lower bound is far off from the correct bound, but also grows by a factor which is at least $ek \log_2(k).$

T(n^k) > T(n^{k+1}) is visible yet.

Lemma 1 (Threshold characterization):
For sequence \(A\), \(T(A)\) equals
\[

elements of }A\}

when the maximum exists.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By definition of threshold as first point after which all integers are
representable.

\textit{Proof.}
\]

To prove infinitely many reversals, it suffices to produce infinitely many \(k\)
satisfying Lemma 2's hypothesis.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each such \(k\) yields one strict reversal by Lemma 2.
\(\square\)

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
If I understand correctly, the way this is formalised in Lean requires the multiset $A$ to have the property that the set
$$P(A) = \left \{\sum_{n \in B} B \subseteq A \text{ finite} \right\}$$ contains all positive integers, and a lot of texts define completeness this way. In the book by Graham and Erdős however, it is only required that $P(A)$ contains all sufficiently large integers, which is also often taken as a definition of completeness. For what it is worth, with the former interpretation that is used in the Lean formalisation I can fully settle this problem, and show that no such multiset exists for any $m, n$ with $2 \le m < n$.

Assume $A = \{a_1, a_2 \ldots, \}$ is such that $P(A \setminus \{a_i, a_j \}) = \mathbb{N}$ holds for all indices $i, j$. Set $s_1 = a_1$ and, for any $j \ge 2$, $s_j = a_i$ where $i$ is such that $a_{i-1} > s_1 + \ldots + s_{j-1}$. With the infinite set $S$ equal to $\{s_1, s_2, \ldots \}$, one can then check that $P(A \setminus S) = \mathbb{N}$ holds as well.

For a complete write-up, see here (https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/Any%20multiset%20which%20is%20complete%20after%20removing%20any%20two%20elements%20remains%20complete%20after%20removing%20a%20specific%20infinite%20set.pdf). Perhaps the argument can be adapted to settle the second (intended) interpretation as well.

EDIT: Come to think of it, I don't think this argument can be easily adapted to the intended interpreation, because the sequence $a_n = F_n + (-1)^n$ with $F_n$ the $n$-th Fibonacci number has the property that $P(A \setminus \{a_i, a_j\})$ contains all large enough integers for all $i, j$, but no infinite subset $S$ exists for which $P(A \setminus S)$ contains all large enough integers. See #346 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/346) and references for more information.

EDIT 25-09-2025: I have left a comment on the Lean forum and the formalisation has now been updated to reflect the intended meaning.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.text:
I have just uploaded my paper on this problem to the arXiv (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.23394).

Combined with (and relying on) the results from Graham's 1964 paper (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/64_02_erdos.pdf), the case $\alpha \ge \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ is completely settled. Moreover, even though my paper does not fully resolve the problem for the remaining interval $1 < \alpha < \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$, I can at least give the full range of values of $t$ for which the resulting sequence is entirely complete, i.e. covers all positive integers.

In the spirit of Graham, here (https://imgur.com/a/fAOkgkC) you can find a plot for part of the 2D plane which shows where the sequence is and isn't (entirely) complete. To describe it in words, this is the current state of affairs:

If $\alpha > 2$, the sequence is not complete for any $t > 0$.
If $\alpha = 2$, the sequence is complete if, and only if, $t = \frac{1}{2^k}$ for some $k \ge 1$.
If $5^{1/3} < \alpha < 2$ and $t \ge 1$, the sequence is not complete.
If $5^{1/3} < \alpha < 2$ and $t < 1$, it's complicated (but essentially known). See Graham's paper or the above image for more details.
If $\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \le \alpha \le 5^{1/3}$, the sequence is complete if, and only if, $t < \min\left(\frac{3}{\alpha^2}, \frac{5}{\alpha^3} \right)$.
If $1 < \alpha < \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$, the sequence is entirely complete if, and only if $t < \min\left(\frac{2}{\alpha}, \frac{3}{\alpha^2} \right)$.
If $1 < \alpha < \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ and $t \ge \min\left(\frac{2}{\alpha}, \frac{3}{\alpha^2} \right)$, the sequence might be complete without being entirely complete, but only partial results are known (see below).
If $\alpha = 1$, the sequence is complete if, and only if, $1 \le t < 2$.
If $\alpha < 1$, the sequence is not complete for any $t > 0$.

As for those partial results for the region where it's not fully known yet, one can observe that for any compact set contained in that region, determining whether the sequence is complete for all pairs $(t, \alpha)$ in that set, in principle reduces to a finite search. I have therefore done some coding and can show the following computer-assisted result:

If $\alpha \le 1.4$, the sequence is complete for all $t \le 3$.
If $\alpha \le 1.3$, the sequence is complete for all $t \le 5$.
If $\alpha \le 1.2$, the sequence is complete for all $t \le 10$.
If $\alpha \le 1.1$, the sequence is complete for all $t \le 50$.

These ranges are mostly a proof of concept, and for anyone interested it shouldn't be too hard to extend them further.

The final result I prove in my paper is that the sequence is complete whenever $1 < \alpha \le 1 + \frac{1}{\lceil t \rceil + 2 \lceil \sqrt{t} \rceil}$, which (when we plot the values of $t$ and $\alpha$) is the first result that implies the completeness of the sequence for a region of infinite area!

Suppose we take $b_k$ to be the deduplicated increasing tail of $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$, and look at its subset sums. If for some $K_0$ there is an interval $[A,A+L]\subseteq\Sigma_{K_0}$ with cardinality $L+1\ge b_{K_0+1}$, then once the eventual overlap $b_{m+1}\le 2b_m-1$ (which eventually holds for large $m$ when $1<\alpha<2$, up to sporadic floor effects, and even $b_{m+2}\le b_{m+1}+b_m-1$ for $1<\alpha<\varphi$) has started to hold, the translate–overlap mechanism forces that from some point onward all sufficiently large integers are covered. So for $\alpha<\varphi$ it seems the whole problem reduces to finding one finite seed interval beyond the eventual regime.

What I am not sure about is whether this reduction is completely sound, or whether there could be a gap before the overlap inequality takes effect. Do we know that some seed must appear for every $t>0$ and $1<\alpha<\varphi$, or could it in principle fail entirely in the finite pre-asymptotic window? The seed condition I think has to be expressed in cardinalities ($L+1\ge b_{K_0+1}$), otherwise there is an off-by-one issue. Deduplication is required too, since the problem is about distinct integers. Is there an argument that guarantees a seed in all cases, or is this the open difficulty? forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text: Proving that such a seed always exists is essentially the difficulty, yes. Furthermore, you are correct that -as stated- the problem requires distinct integers of the form $\left \lfloor t \alpha^n \right \rfloor$, but that is not what Erdős and Graham wrote (or what I believe they intended), and also not what is assumed in Graham's 1964 paper. Every element $s_n = \left \lfloor t \alpha^n \right \rfloor$ is allowed to be used once, even if $s_n = s_m$ for some $m \neq n$. For example, Theorem 2 in Graham's paper implies in particular that the sequence with $t = \frac{2}{3}$ and $\alpha = 1.7$ (which has $s_1 = s_2 = 1$ and $s_3 = 3$) is entirely complete, which would not be true if we are not allowed to use both $s_1$ and $s_2$. For what it's worth, I am currently writing up some slight extensions of Graham's results that I will hopefully link to in the coming week.

forum_comments.author: memeister27
forum_comments.text:
The script below shows that for $t=1,\alpha=1.5$ and $\alpha=\varphi$ all integers up to $200{,}000$ are representable, while for $t=2,\alpha=1.4$ a few small numbers ($1,4,6,\dots$) are missing even though the density is very high. It is only a computation, not a proof, but it hopefully illustrates the behaviour discussed in Problem 349.

import math

def seq(t, a, n=40):
 return [int(t * a**k) for k in range(1, n+1)]

def cover(s, L=200000):
 r = [0] * (L+1)
 r[0] = 1
 for a in s:
 for x in range(L, a-1, -1):
 r[x] |= r[x - a]
 return sum(r[1:]) / L, [i for i in range(1, L+1) if not r[i]]

for t, a in [(1, 1.5), (1, (1 + 5**0.5) / 2), (2, 1.4)]:
 s = seq(t, a)
 d, m = cover(s)
 print(f"\nt={t}, α≈{round(a, 3)}")
 print("First terms:", s[:12])
 print(f"Density up to 200k: {d:.6f}")
 print("First missing:", m[:10] if m else "None")

We get:

First terms: [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 17, 25, 38, 57, 86, 129]
Density up to 200k: 1.000000
First missing: None

t=1, α≈1.618
First terms: [1, 2, 4, 6, 11, 17, 29, 46, 76, 122, 199, 321]
Density up to 200k: 1.000000
First missing: None

t=2, α≈1.4
First terms: [2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 21, 29, 41, 57, 80, 113]
Density up to 200k: 0.999975
First missing: [1, 4, 6, 11, 16]

It seems from these checks that the behaviour of $\lfloor t \alpha^n \rfloor$ could hinge on how closely it shadows a Fibonacci-type recurrence, with small floor-errors making it look complete below the golden ratio.

problem: Let $p(x)\in \mathbb{Q}[x]$. Is it true that\[A=\{ p(n)+1/n : n\in \mathbb{N}\}\]is strongly complete, in the sense that, for any finite set $B$,\[\left\{\sum_{n\in X}n : X\subseteq A\backslash B\textrm{ finite }\right\}\]contains all sufficiently large integers?

- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/351.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 02 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Graham \cite{Gr63} proved this is true when $p(n)=n$. Erd\H{o}s and Graham also ask which rational functions $r(x)\in\mathbb{Z}(x)$ force $\{ r(n) : n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ to be complete?

Graham \cite{Gr64f} gave a complete characterisation of which polynomials $r\in \mathbb{R}[x]$ are such that $\{ r(n) : n\in \mathbb{N}\}$ is complete.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text: On their question about rational functions, observe that any function of the form $r(x) = \frac{p(x)q(x) + 1}{q(x)}$ with $p(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, $q(x) = x^n$ and $n \ge 2$ is hopeless, as any sum $$r(a_1) + \ldots + r(a_k) = \big(p(a_1) + \ldots + p(a_k)\big) + \left(\frac{1}{a_1^n} + \ldots + \frac{1}{a_k^n} \right)$$with $k > 1$ lies strictly between two integers, due to the fact that $\frac{1}{2^n} + \frac{1}{3^n} + \ldots < 1$. And this idea can be generalized to rule out many more $r(x)$ for which the remainder (when we divide $p(x)$ by $q(x)$) has degree at most $deg(q(x)) - 2$.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
As I alluded to in my previous comment, one can indeed solve this problem for the polynomial $p(n) = n^2$, simply by combining the proof of Theorem $2$ in Graham's $1963$ paper with Alekseyev's proof referenced in #283 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/283). For a full write-up see here (https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/The%20set%20(x%5E2%20%2B%20x%5E(-1))%20is%20strongly%20complete.pdf), but it's just essentially a copy-pasted version of Graham's proof. And speaking of Graham, precisely this question (on whether the set of values of $n^2 + \frac{1}{n}$ is strongly complete) was also asked by him in this paper:

Graham, R. L. On Sums of Integers Taken from a Fixed Sequence, Proc. Wash. State Univ. Conf. on Number Theory, (1971), 22-40

His question can be found here (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/71_08_integer_sums.pdf) as question $7$ on page $35$. He then further asks the way more general question whether this is even true with $n^2$ replaced by $f(n)$ for any strongly complete sequence $f(n)$, but this seems quite unlikely to me. Maybe something like $f(n) = F_n - 1$ with $F_n$ the $n$-th Fibonacci number could provide a counterexample.

Moreover, as I also alluded to, for the solution of $p(n) = n^2$ I don't think it would be too difficult to instead use the proof of Theorem $3$ in my paper, as opposed to Graham's proof. The advantage of this (if it indeed works) is that it becomes possible to give a sharp upper bound for the largest integer which is not in $\{\sum_{x \in X} X \subset A \setminus B \text{ finite}\}$.

Finally, whether it's also possible to generalize this further to all polynomials mentioned in the comments of #283, I'll leave to someone else.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Vjeko is right that it should be all sufficiently large integers. Moreover, the reference should instead be:

[Gr63] Graham, R. L., A theorem on partitions. J. Austral. Math. Soc. (1963), 435-441

which can be found here (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/63_02_partitions.pdf).

In it, Graham proved that every integer $n \ge 78$ can be written as a sum $a_1 + \ldots + a_r$ of distinct positive integers with $\frac{1}{a_1} + \ldots + \frac{1}{a_r} = 1$, so that every $n \ge 79$ can be written as $(a_1 + \frac{1}{a_1}) + \ldots + (a_r + \frac{1}{a_r})$. He moreover proves that for every $m$ a positive integer $n_m$ exists such that all $n \ge n_m$ can be written as sum $a_1 + \ldots + a_r$ of distinct positive integers with $\frac{1}{a_1} + \ldots + \frac{1}{a_r} = 1$ and where $a_i \ge m$ for all $i$. This gives the strongly complete claim. And one could propose an OEIS sequence $s_1, s_2, \ldots$ for this as well, where $s_m$ is the smallest $n_m$ for which the above holds. It'll be annoying to calculate any $s_m$ for even moderate values of $m$, say $m = 10$, but Theorem $3$ in this (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.02200) recent paper of mine gives the asymptotic formula $(\frac{1}{2} + o(1))(e^2 - 1)m^2$.

Compare with #283 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/283), by the way; #283 is stronger in the sense that the sum of reciprocals must be equal to $1$, but this problem is stronger because it considers polynomials in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ and asks for strongly complete as opposed to merely complete (which, isn't completeness not hard enough already?). In any case, the other recent paper (https://github.com/Woett/A-normal-paper-is-probably-fine/blob/main/The%20binomial%20case%20of%20Graham) I mention there (still a work in progress) solves at least the completeness part of this problem for many linear and quadratic polynomials.

In fact, combining the latter with either the proof of Theorem $3$ I mentioned earlier or with the original proof of Graham, I should be able to generalize this to strongly complete, at least for $p(n) = n^2$. And maybe for all the other polynomials for which we can prove completeness as well. I will try to write up the details shortly.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
This problem's wording needs to be changed from "... contains all sufficiently large rational numbers?" to "... contains all sufficiently large integers?". The property of representing all sufficiently large rationals was rather called "$\mathbb{Q}$-completeness" by Erdős and Graham.
In fact, the surrounding remarks make no sense in the present formulation, even the claim about $p(n)=n$. Namely, for arbitrarily large $N\in\mathbb{N}$, rational numbers in the interval $(N,N+1)$ can be represented only using the first $N$ terms of the sequence $(n+1/n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$. That way, at most $2^N$ rationals from $(N,N+1)$ can be represented, but there is infinitely many of them.

problem: Is there some $c>0$ such that every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of measure $\geq c$ contains the vertices of a triangle of area 1?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/352.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s (unpublished) proved that this is true if $A$ has infinite measure, or if $A$ is an unbounded set of positive measure (stating in \cite{Er78d} and \cite{Er83d} it 'follows easily from the Lebesgue density theorem').

In \cite{Er78d} and \cite{Er83d} he speculated that perhaps $C=4\pi/\sqrt{27}\approx 2.418$ works, which would be the best possible, as witnessed by a circle of radius $<2\cdot 3^{-3/4}$.

Further evidence for this is given by a result of Freiling and Mauldin \cite{Ma02}, who proved that if $A$ has outer measure $>4\pi/\sqrt{27}$ then $A$ contains the vertices of a triangle with area $>1$. This also proves the same threshold for the original problem under the assumption that $A$ is a compact convex set.

Mauldin also discusses this problem in \cite{Ma13}, in which he notes that it suffices to prove this under the assumption that $A$ is the union of the interiors of $n<\infty$ many compact convex sets. Freiling and Mauldin (see \cite{Ma13}) have proved this conjecture if $1\leq n\leq 3$.
References:
- [Er78d] Erd\H{o}s, P., Set-theoretic, measure-theoretic, combinatorial, and number-theoretic problems concerning point sets in Euclidean space. Real Anal. Exchange (1978/79), 113-138.
- [Er83d] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure theory. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983: Proceedings of the Conference held at Oberwolfach, June 26-July 2, 1983 (1984), 321-327.
- [Ma02] Mauldin, R. D., Some problems in set theory, analysis and geometry. (2002), 493--506.
- [Ma13] Mauldin, R. Daniel, Some problems and ideas of {E}rd\H{o}s in analysis and geometry. (2013), 365--376.

forum_comments.author: J_Koizumi_144
forum_comments.text: One useful fact stated in Mauldin's paper is the following: this problem is equivalent to the one in which we restrict attention to sets $A$ that are unions of finitely many closed disks of equal radius. Indeed, by the inner regularity of the Lebesgue measure, it suffices to consider only compact sets $A$. After covering $A$ by $\varepsilon$-disks centered at points of $A$, one can apply Besicovitch's covering theorem to obtain the desired equivalence.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
Even slightly better, a further reduction is easy to see: one can assume that $A$ is a finite union of congruent dyadic squares, which are sets of the form\[ \big[2^{-n}k,2^{-n}(k+1)\big) \times\big[2^{-n}l,2^{-n}(l+1)\big) \]for $k,l,n\in\mathbb{Z}$. They are better because they are disjoint and correspond to the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
After scaling by $2^n$, one can essentially think about the corresponding discrete problem: can one find $\omega(4^n)$ points inside the grid $[4^n]\times[4^n]$ such that no three of them form a triangle of area $\approx \alpha$ for some fixed $\alpha$ of the order $4^n$.
I'm not being precise here, I'm just saying that constructions of such large discrete sets would lead to the counterexample to the main problem and vice versa. Some careless discrete reformulations can go wrong, of course, e.g., if one targets the precise area $\alpha$ which is an odd number, while $A$ consists of points with both even coordinates.

forum_comments.author: J_Koizumi_144
forum_comments.text:
Nice reduction! Based on your idea, I formulated a precise translation into a discrete problem. For an integer $N>0$, we say that a set of lattice points $S\subset \mathbb{Z}^2$ is $N$-avoiding if for every $q_1,q_2,q_3\in S$ we have\[
\bigl\lvert \mu(\triangle q_1q_2q_3) - N \bigr\rvert > \mathrm{diam}(\triangle q_1q_2q_3).
\]Let $f(N)$ denote the largest possible size of an $N$-avoiding set. Then the original question is equivalent to asking whether $f(N)=O(N)$ holds. For a proof of the equivalence, please see here (https://jkoizumi144.com/notes/erdos352.pdf).

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text: This is very nice and worth writing down. However, your discrete reformulation is combinatorially complicated and I still find it beneficial to play with simplified discrete models to gain intuition about the problem.

Related to the above discretization, I can perhaps suggest the following discrete toy-problem, which, I believe, captures the essence of the original question:
Let $f(N)$ be cardinality of the largest set $A\subseteq[N]\times[N]$ such that no three points from $A$ span the triangle of area $\in[0.99N,1.01N]$. Is $f(N)=O(N)$?
This, at least in theory, leaves room for computer experimentation, to perhaps try to find the "worst" arrangements, or to investigate all "types" of possible behaviors.

There is some superficial similarity with the No-three-in-line problem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-three-in-line_problem), which could be considered as the search for triangles of area 0. However, $f(N)\leq2N$ is obvious there, unlike in this problem.

It's not much of an idea, but it might be useful to first play with triangles which have one side parallel to the $x$-axis. Namely, either in continuous or discrete setting, if $A$ does not contain such a triple of points spanning a triangle of area $1$ and if $B$ is its projection onto the $y$-axis, then each (one-dimensional) horizontal section $A_y := A \cap (\mathbb{R}\times\{y\})$ (viewed as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$) only has to avoid certain differences (determined by $B$ and $y$).

Inside the grid $[N]\times [N]$ this leads to a more effective algorithm for finding the largest allowed $A\subseteq[N]\times[N]$, of complexity $O(2^{2N})$, rather than $O(2^{N^2})$. forum_comments.text:
In the first comment above, I linked to two sources older than [Er83d]: they are both freely accessible. In the first one, from 1978, Erdős already mentions precisely that constant as potentially working. (Mauldin, see above, also played with this stronger version of the conjecture.) I don't remember seeing that even this value of $c$ has been disproved somewhere.

However, one must be aware that there are numerous "local extremizers" for the problem: there is a sequence of area-1-triangle-avoiding sets $(A_N)_{N=1}^{\infty}$ with areas $\gg1$ but arbitrarily large diameters. For instance, for each $(m,n)\in[N]\times[N]$ take a disk around $(2m,2n)$ of radius $\frac{1}{100N}$ and let $A_N$ be the union of all these disks.

Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need scale-uniform codegree bounds for unit-area triangle hypergraphs on dense
grid samples.

Lemma 1 (Independent-set equivalence):
A finite point set \(P\) contains no unit-area triangle iff \(P\) is an
independent set in the unit-area triangle hypergraph \(H\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Edges of \(H\) are exactly triples of points spanning unit area, so avoidance is
precisely edge-freeness.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Container implication):
If every independent set in \(H\) has size at most \(\alpha |V(H)|\), then any
grid model of side \(m\) has avoidance density at most \(\alpha+o(1)\) as
\(m\to\infty\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Normalize by total vertex count \(m^2\); boundary discretization effects are
\(o(1)\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction):
To prove asymptotic density upper bounds in EP-352, it suffices to prove
container-compatible degree/codegree estimates for \(H\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Lemma 2 converts independent-set bounds into geometric density bounds.
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $\alpha,\beta\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that $\alpha/\beta$ is irrational. Is the multiset\[\{ \lfloor \alpha\rfloor,\lfloor 2\alpha\rfloor,\lfloor 4\alpha\rfloor,\ldots\}\cup \{ \lfloor \beta\rfloor,\lfloor 2\beta\rfloor,\lfloor 4\beta\rfloor,\ldots\}\]complete? That is, can all sufficiently large natural numbers $n$ be written as\[n=\sum_{s\in S}\lfloor 2^s\alpha\rfloor+\sum_{t\in T}\lfloor 2^t\beta\rfloor\]for some finite $S,T\subset \mathbb{N}$?

What if $2$ is replaced by some $\gamma\in(1,2)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/354.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 December 2025.
Site remarks:
This question was first mentioned by Graham \cite{Gr71}.

Hegyv\'{a}ri \cite{He89} proved that this holds if $\alpha=m/2^n$ is a dyadic rational and $\beta$ is not. He later \cite{He91} proved that, for any fixed $\alpha>0$, the set of $\beta$ for which this holds either has measure $0$ or infinite measure. In \cite{He94} he proved that the set of $(\alpha,\beta)$ for which the corresponding set of sums does not contain an infinite arithmetic progression has cardinality continuum.

Hegyv\'{a}ri \cite{He89} proved that the sequence is not complete if $\alpha\geq 2$ and $\beta =2^k\alpha$ for some $k\geq 0$. Jiang and Ma \cite{JiMa24} and Fang and He \cite{FaHe25} prove that the sequence is not complete if $1<\alpha<2$ and $\beta=2^k\alpha$ for some sufficiently large $k$.

It is likely (and Hegyv\'{a}ri conjectures) that the assumption $\alpha/\beta$ irrational can be weakened to $\alpha/\beta \neq 2^k$ and either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ not a dyadic rational.

In the comments van Doorn proves the sequence is complete if $\alpha < 2<\beta<3$, and also proves that if either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational then the corresponding sequence with ceiling functions replacing the floor functions is complete.
References:
- [FaHe25] Fang, J.-H. and He, J.-Y., On a problem of {E}rd\H{o}s and {G}raham. Acta Math. Hungar. (2025), 532--542.
- [Gr71] Graham, R. L., On sums of integers taken from a fixed sequence. (1971), 22--40.
- [He89] Hegyv\'{a}ri, N., Some remarks on a problem of {E}rd\H{o}s and {G}raham. Acta Math. Hungar. (1989), 149--154.
- [He91] Hegyv\'{a}ri, N., On complete sequences. Ann. Univ. Sci. Budapest. E\"otv\"os Sect. Math. (1991), 7--10.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Using the deep research tool of ChatGPT I managed to find a few references I was not aware of previously, and I think my first comment here is mostly obsolete. Oh well. Long comment incoming! And by the way, as far as I know, in everything that follows the original problem with constant $\gamma = 2$ is considered, unless otherwise stated.

Okay, to start off,

N. Hegyvári, Some remarks on a problem of Erdős and Graham, Acta Math. Hung., Volume 53 (1989), 149-154

proves exactly Proposition 1 in my comment above; if $\alpha$ is a dyadic rational and $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, then the sequence under consideration is complete. On the other hand, using $\alpha \ge 2$ and $\beta = 2^l \alpha$ with $l \in \mathbb{N}$, he also shows that the set of pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which the sequence is not complete has the cardinality of the continuum.

Even though I cannot access this paper by Hegyvári, I can find his follow-up paper where he mentions that he had obtained the dyadic rational result:

N. Hegyvári, On complete sequences, Annales Univ. Sci. Budapest, Volume 34 (1991), 7-10.

In this second paper (which you can find here (https://annalesm.elte.hu/annales34-1991/Annales_1991_T-XXXIV.pdf), pages 7-10) he furthermore proves that, for any fixed $\alpha > 0$, the set of $\beta$ for which the corresponding sequence is complete either has Lebesgue measure $0$, or has infinite measure. In order to prove this he makes use of the observation in my first comment that $P(2\alpha, \beta)$ implies $P(\alpha, \beta)$. But he didn't stop there!

N. Hegyvári, On sumset of certain sets, Publ. Math. Debrecen, Volume 45 (1994), 115-122

which can be found here (https://publi.math.unideb.hu/load_doc.php?p=174&t=pap), shows that the set of pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which the sequence does not even contain an infinite arithmetic progression, also has the cardinality of the continuum. This strengthens the second result from the first paper I mentioned. Both cardinality continuum results make use of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $\frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ a power of two (i.e. rational), however. So they don't disprove the conjecture at hand.

Then, much more recently, we finally have the following two papers

X. W. Jiang, W. X. Ma, A conjecture of Hegyvári, Int. J. Number Theory, Volume 20 (2024), 915–933.
J. H. Fang, J. Y. He, On a problem of Erdős and Graham, Acta Math. Hung., Volume 175 (2025), 532-542.

Thanks to Terence who kindly sent me a copy of the second paper (and see his comment below as well!), both papers seem to extend Hegyvári's non-completeness results in the case that $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$ is a power of two, but for $\alpha < 2$ and $\beta$ sufficiently large.

Long story short, I believe the following four results for specific $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are known:

 Proposition 1. If exactly one of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is a dyadic rational, then the sequence is complete.
 Proposition 2. If $\min(\alpha, \beta) < 2$ and $\max(\alpha, \beta) < 3$, then the sequence is complete.
 Proposition 3. If $\alpha \ge 2$ and $\beta = 2^l \alpha$ with $l \in \mathbb{N}$, then the sequence is not complete.
 Proposition 4. If $\alpha < 2$ and $\beta = 2^l \alpha$ with $l \in \mathbb{N}$ sufficiently large, then the sequence is not complete.

Here, Propositions 1 and 3 are due to Hegyvári, while Proposition 4 is due to Jiang-Ma and Fang-He.

Long story even shorter, as far as I can tell there is no solution to the main problem yet. On the other hand, I do suspect that the first paper by Hegyvári either settles the case $\gamma = \sqrt{2}$ or perhaps even $1 < \gamma \le \sqrt{2}$ (possibly implicitly). If anyone has access to this paper and could check, that would be appreciated. And in other news, the hypothesis that $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$ is irrational can most likely be slightly weakened (if that wasn't clear already); Hegyvári conjectures that the sequence is complete if either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, and $\beta \neq 2^l \alpha$. In other words, Propositions 3 and 4 are conjecturally close to optimal.

The result I mentioned in my second post in this comment section (namely, that if we change all floor functions to ceiling functions, then the sequence is complete, as long as either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational) does seem to be new however, so perhaps I actually will keep working on my own paper on this subject.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
At a first glance, it seems like there should be no fundamental difference in this question if we change all floor functions to ceiling functions, right? A priori there seems to be no reason why proving the completeness for one should be any easier or harder than for the other. Well, as fate would have it, I can resolve this problem.. But only if we use the ceiling function! Isn't that remarkable?

To elaborate on this, let me define two notions. We say that a sequence $S = (s_1, s_2, \ldots)$ is a $\Sigma$-sequence if a constant $c$ exists such that $s_{n+1} - \sum_{i=1}^n s_i \le c$ for all $n$. And we call a sequence precomplete if, for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, there are $k$ consecutive integers that can all be written as the sum of distinct elements of $S$.

In his $1964$ paper 'Complete Sequences of Polynomial Values' (see here (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/#64)), Graham proved that if $A = (a_1, a_2, \ldots)$ is a $\Sigma$-sequence and $B = (b_1, b_2, \ldots)$ is precomplete, then the union $(a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, \ldots)$ is complete.

Now, if $a_{n+1} \le 2a_n$ for all large enough $n$, then one can show that $A$ is a $\Sigma$-sequence. And the equality $a_{n+1} \le 2a_n$ is satisfied for all large enough $n$ if $a_n = \lceil 2^{n-1} \alpha \rceil$, but not if $a_n = \lfloor 2^{n-1} \alpha \rfloor$!

Moreover, to prove that $B = (b_1, b_2, \ldots)$ is precomplete for $b_n = \lceil 2^{n-1} \beta \rceil$, it turns out that it is sufficient to show that there are just two consecutive integers that can both be written as the sum of distinct elements of $B$. And for $b_n = \lceil 2^{n-1} \beta \rceil$ one can check that, unless $\beta$ is a dyadic rational, there is some $n$ such that $b_1 + b_2 + \ldots + b_{n-1}$ is equal to $b_n - 1$, finishing the proof.

All in all I can prove the following theorem: as long as either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, then $(\lceil \alpha \rceil, \lceil \beta\rceil, \lceil 2\alpha \rceil, \lceil 2\beta\rceil, \lceil 4\alpha \rceil, \lceil 4\beta\rceil, \ldots)$ is complete.

For a (first version of a) full write-up, see here (https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/Completeness%20of%20exponentially%20increasing%20sequences%20II.pdf).

I plan to combine this write-up with another project I'm working on, and will submit a proper paper to the arXiv in the coming months. I'll make sure to link it once it's finished. In the mean time, perhaps someone else can use some of these ideas to put the ball into the back of the net ;) As it does feel like we're very close to solving this problem.

forum_comments.text:
Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ denote the statement that the above sequence is complete, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are assumed to be positive reals. Then I can prove the following two propositions:

 Proposition 1. If $\alpha = \frac{m}{2^n}$ is a dyadic rational (so in particular if $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$) and $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, then $P(\alpha, \beta)$ holds.
 Proposition 2. If $\min(\alpha, \beta) < 2$ and $\max(\alpha, \beta) < 3$, then $P(\alpha, \beta)$ holds.

In general we see that $P(2\alpha, \beta)$ implies $P(\alpha, \beta)$, as the corresponding sequence for the former is a subsequence of the latter. In particular, to prove the first proposition it is sufficient to assume $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$.

So assume $\alpha = m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let us first note that the sequence $(\lfloor \alpha \rfloor, \lfloor 2\alpha \rfloor, \lfloor 4\alpha \rfloor, \ldots)$ then generates $m\mathbb{N}$. We therefore need to show that sums of distinct elements from $B = (\lfloor \beta \rfloor, \lfloor 2\beta \rfloor, \lfloor 4\beta \rfloor, \ldots)$ attain all residue classes modulo $m$.

Now, for every prime divisor $p$ of $m$, I claim that $B$ contains infinitely many elements not divisible by $p$, if $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational. Indeed, if $p$ divides $\lfloor 2^l \beta \rfloor$ for some $l$, let $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ be such that $2^l \beta = pr + \epsilon$ and choose $l'$ such that $1 \le 2^{l'} \epsilon < 2$. We then get that $\left \lfloor 2^{l+l'} \beta \right \rfloor = 2^{l'}pr + 1$ is not divisible by $p$.

Let $b_1 \pmod{m}, b_2 \pmod{m}, \ldots, b_k \pmod{m}$ be those residue classes modulo $m$ that appear infinitely often in $B$. We remark that it is not necessarily the case that there exists an $i$ such that $\gcd(b_i, m) = 1$. However, we do have $\gcd(b_1, \ldots, b_k, m) = 1$ by the aforementioned claim on prime divisors $p$ of $m$. We therefore get by the existence of the Frobenius number that all residue classes modulo $m$ appear among sums of the $b_i$, which was what we needed to prove.

As for the second proposition, note we may assume $\beta \ge \alpha > 1$; the first inequality by symmetry, and the second inequality by the aforementioned fact that $P(2\alpha, \beta)$ implies $P(\alpha, \beta)$. Now define, for $n \ge 1$, $s_{2n-1} = \lfloor 2^{n-1} \alpha \rfloor$ and $s_{2n} = \lfloor 2^{n-1} \beta \rfloor$. We then claim that $(s_1, s_2, \ldots)$ generates the entirety of $\mathbb{N}$, for which it is necessary and sufficient to show $s_{n+1} \le 1 + \sum_{i=1}^n s_i$ for all $n \ge 0$. This follows for $n = 0$ by the fact that $s_1 = \lfloor \alpha \rfloor = 1$, and it follows for $n = 1$ as $s_2 = \lfloor \beta \rfloor \le 2$. For $n \ge 2$ we get by induction
\begin{align*}
s_{n+1} &\le 2s_{n-1} + 1 \\
&\le 2 + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} s_i \\
&\le 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i.
\end{align*}
In fact, the proof of this second proposition immediately generalizes to $\gamma \in (1,2)$ instead of $2$, and it even works in some cases for $\gamma \le 3$.

problem:
Let $1\leq a_1<\cdots <a_k\leq n$ be integers such that all sums of the shape $\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i$ are distinct. Let $f(n)$ be the maximal such $k$.

How does $f(n)$ grow? Is $f(n)=o(n)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/357.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 12 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Asked by Erd\H{o}s and Harzheim. In \cite{Er77c} Erd\H{o}s asks about an infinite such set of integers, and whether such a set must have density $0$. He notes that a simple averaging process implies $a_k \gg k\log k$ for infinitely many $k$, and so the lower density is $0$. He also asks whether $\sum\frac{1}{a_k}$ must converge.

Weisenberg in the comments observes that any set which satisfies [874] also has this property, which implies $f(n)\geq (2+o(1))n^{1/2}$.

If $g(n)$ is the maximal $k$ such that there are $1\leq a_1,\ldots,a_k\leq n$ with all consecutive sums distinct (i.e. we drop the monotonicity assumption in the definition of $f$) then Hegyv\'{a}ri \cite{He86} has proved that\[\left(\frac{1}{3}+o(1)\right) n\leq g(n)\leq \left(\frac{2}{3}+o(1)\right)n.\]The upper bound of Coppersmith and Phillips in [867] implies\[g(n) \leq \left(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{512}+o(1)\right)n.\]A similar question can be asked if we replace strict monotonicity with weak monotonicity (i.e. we allow $a_i=a_j$).

Erd\H{o}s and Harzheim also ask what is the least $m$ which is not a sum of the given form? Can it be much larger than $n$? Erd\H{o}s and Harzheim can show that $\sum_{x<a_i<x^2}\frac{1}{a_i}\ll 1$. Is it true that $\sum_i \frac{1}{a_i}\ll 1$?

See also [34], [356], [670], and [867]. The multiplicative analogue is [421].
References:
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [He86] Hegyv\'{a}ri, N., On consecutive sums in sequences. Acta Math. Hungar. (1986), 193--200.

forum_comments.text:
As a remark, Beker's work on [356] gives a nontrivial upper bound for $f(n)$. Define\[
S(a) = \left\{ \sum_{i=u}^v a_i : 1 \le u \le v \le k \right\}.
\]By [Be23b, Proposition 1.5], for any strictly increasing sequence \(1 \le a_1 < \cdots < a_k \le n\) one has\[
|S(a)| \le (c_4 + o(1)) n^2,
\qquad
c_4 = \frac{e^2 - 1}{2(e^2 + 1)}.
\]Now take an extremal configuration for $f(n)$: there exists some $k = f(n)$ and a strictly increasing subset \(1 \le a_1 < \cdots < a_k \le n\) such that all consecutive sums are distinct. In this case\[
|S(a)| = \frac{k(k+1)}{2}.
\]Combining the two bounds, we obtain \(\frac{k(k+1)}{2} \le (c_4 + o(1)) n^2\), and hence\[
f(n) \le \left(\sqrt{2c_4} + o(1)\right) n
= \left( \sqrt{\frac{e^2 - 1}{e^2 + 1}} + o(1) \right) n
\approx (0.8727 + o(1))\,n.
\][Be23b] Beker, A., On a problem of Erdős and Graham about consecutive sums in strictly increasing sequences. arXiv:2311.10087 (2023).

Route:
Backtracking search for maximal k at small n, enforcing distinctness of all consecutive sums.

Hard point:
Finite lower bounds do not settle asymptotic growth or the question f(n)=o(n).

Target:
Determine asymptotics of \(f(n)\), the largest size of a set with all consecutive
interval sums distinct.
Step A: Conflict hypergraph formulation
Vertices are chosen indices; hyperedges encode equal consecutive-sum constraints.
Step B: Upper bound via conflict counting
Bound maximal independent-set size in this hypergraph.
Step C: Lower construction
Build near-optimal families with provably distinct interval sums.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp counting lemma for number of interval-sum collisions induced by a set
of size \(k\), with explicit dependence on \(n,k\).

Lemma 1 (Collision characterization):
Distinctness of all consecutive sums fails iff there exist two intervals
\([i,j],[u,v]\) with
\[
\sum_{t=i}^j a_t=\sum_{t=u}^v a_t,\quad (i,j)\ne(u,v).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is direct restatement of distinctness condition.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Prefix-sum reformulation):
Let \(P_r=\sum_{t\le r} a_t\). Then
\[
\sum_{t=i}^j a_t=P_j-P_{i-1},
\]
so interval-sum collisions are equivalent to repeated differences \(P_x-P_y\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Standard telescoping identity.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction):
To bound \(f(n)\), it suffices to control how large a subset of prefix sums can be
chosen so that all pairwise differences are distinct.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By Lemma 2 the problem is exactly a distinct-differences (Golomb-ruler type)
constraint on prefix-sum indices.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $A=\{a_1<\cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Let $f(n)$ count the number of solutions to\[n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i.\]Is there such an $A$ for which $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$? Or even where $f(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/358.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-04-01).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
When $a_n=n$ the function $f(n)$ counts the number of odd divisors of $n$.

In modern language, this asks for the existence of a convex set $A$ such that $1_A\circ 1_A(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$.

Erd\H{o}s and Moser \cite{Mo63} considered the case when $A$ is the set of primes, and conjectured that the $\limsup$ of the number of such representations in this case is infinite. They could not even prove that the upper density of the set of integers representable in this form is positive.

In \cite{ErGr80} they further asked whether $f(n)\geq 1$ for all large $n$ is possible, but Egami observed the answer to this is trivially yes, taking $a_n=n$. Perhaps they intended to restrict $f(n)$ to only count those representatives as the sum of at least two consecutive terms. (It is a classical fact that $n$ can be expressed as a sum of at least two consecutive positive integers if and only if $n\neq 2^k$.)

In \cite{Er77c} Erd\H{o}s writes 'This problem can perhaps be rightly criticized as being artificial and in the backwater of Mathematics but it seems very strange and attractive to me'.

Weisenberg observes that the finite analogue of this problem, asking how many integers up to some $x$ can be written as the sum of consecutive elements, is very similar to [356].

Tao has constructed (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf) such a set in which $f(n)\gg \log n$ for all large integers $n$.

This is reported in problem C2 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Mo63] Moser, L., Notes on number theory. III. On the sum of consecutive primes. Canad. Math. Bull. (1963), 159-161.

* page 9 (Proposition 2.1 proof / immediately after Proposition 2.1): the sentence “In view of the above proposition, we see that to show (2.2) and therefore Theorem 1.1 ...” has the wrong cross-reference. Proposition 2.2 is being used to prove (2.6), not (2.2). Also, in the preceding line, “sum of consecutive sum of elements” contains an extra “sum”.
Suggested: replace “to show (2.2)” with “to show (2.6)”, and replace “sum of consecutive sum of elements” with “sum of consecutive elements”.

* page 10 (Proposition 3.1 proof): in the middle-range estimate, the paper states that if $q^{-1.4} \le |\theta| \le 10/q$, then the arithmetic progression $(q-j)\theta$ “will stay at least $\gg q^{-0.4}$ away from an integer for $q/40 \le j \le q/20$”. This is false as written. For example, take $q=100$, $\theta=1/97$, and $j=3$. Then $q^{-1.4} \le \theta \le 10/q$, and $j=3 \in [q/40,q/20]$, but $(q-j)\theta = 97/97 = 1$, which is exactly an integer. So the displayed bound $\ll \exp(-cq^{0.2})$ is not established by the current argument.
Suggested: replace this step with a correct counting argument showing that for $\gg q$ values of $j$ in a suitable range, $(q-j)\theta$ stays $\gg q^{-0.4}$ away from the integers; that would suffice to recover the exponential decay. In its current form, this part of the proof needs amendment.

* page 12 (Proposition 2.2(i) proof): the proof says that the event $F_q$ depends only on the portion of $A_0$ in $\bigcup_{j=1}^m I_{n'*j,q}$, “which lies in $\Delta*{k'}$”. That should be $R_{k'}$, not $\Delta_{k'}$, because these intervals are red-admissible and hence lie in the red block $R_{k'}$.

Heads up: GPT-5.2 Thinking under my supervision, using my latest long-range workflow, appears to have obtained a full solution. I'm needing a little more time to finalize; it's about 30 pages (!).

This is notable because we want to find some ways to make AI tackle (autonomously or at least with limited human supervision) problems at a larger scale. If current models can do it under favorable circumstances, it is likely future models will be able to do it under less favorable circumstances, and so on.

An immediate problem I see is how to confidently verify such things; currently I simply do not know for sure.

This solution is loosely based on Tao's, but perhaps with elements of Chojecki's. The result is that there is an $A$ for which there exists $c > 0$ with $f(n) \ge c \log n$ for all large $n$. Moreover, this is optimal up to constants: for any $A$, we have $\liminf_{n\to\infty} f(n)/\log n \le 1$.

Will post solution soon!

Unfortunately for this sort of problem the details *are* very important. It is potentially possible that just by knowing the construction used by the AI proof to generate $A$, that a human expert can independently verify whether that construction has a good chance of working, but without that high level analysis or a Lean formalization, there is a high chance of some sort of basic bookkeeping error in the estimates.

For this specific problem I think some sort of weak "expander graph" property has to be established at some point to prevent the possibility of some subset of the survivors of the red representations somehow colliding into each other when the time comes to create blue representations. Some back of the envelope calculations suggest that this sort of expansion can be guaranteed by a combination of several standard tools (Menger's theorem, Plunnecke's inequality, Chernoff bounds, etc.) but it is non-trivial, and I would be somewhat surprised if a largely autonomous AI could piece all the steps together correctly.

There is a gap in the proof of Lemma 17; I will let ChatGPT Pro explain the issue (https://chatgpt.com/share/69960c12-d6d0-800e-b24a-4902b82247d5). The task of allocating disjoint intervals to each exceptional element is, in my view, the most delicate part of the whole strategy (which is where I think expander graph type ideas will be needed); _morally_ with enough randomness this should be possible, but because one needs to allocate disjoint intervals to _all_ exceptional elements (and not just _almost all_) one needs a lot of care in the arguments.

On the plus side, the modification of the original construction to randomize the portion of the red blocks (which Przemek's AI solution also employed) does seem to be a genuine improvement, in that it significantly reduces the size of the exceptional set- the original construction fluctuated like the divisor function, which is essentially log-normally distributed, whereas the random construction enjoys Chernoff bounds, allowing for an exponential improvement in the exceptional set sparsity from logarithmic to polynomial. But it still is not enough to close the argument immediately. As suggested in my original post, one may need to introduce further colors than red and blue, and go through a couple rounds of reducing the size of the exceptional set until one reaches a point where allocating available intervals to all remaining survivors genuinely becomes straightforward.

An additional minor technical note: I am beginning to lean towards using essentially dyadic blocks such as $[x, 1.01 x]$ rather than shorter blocks $[x,x+x^\alpha]$ for the red/blue coloring, in particular alternating the 1.01-dyadic blocks between red and blue should suffice (and allow one to skip a few standard but tedious Chernoff-type steps). A single blue block $[y, 1.01y]$ with $y \asymp x^{1-c}$ should be able to mop up all the $O(x^{1-\gamma})$ survivors in $[x, 2x]$ from red-block representations, for suitable choices of constants $0 < c < \gamma$, provided that one can verify a certain technical expander graph type property.
