forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: Some initial observations inspired by the numerical data. The obvious factorization $n! = 2 \dots n$ gives $f(n) \leq n-2$ for all $n>2$. It also seems that $f(n) = n-O(\log n)$ for all but a few exceptional $n$. Indeed, suppose that $m=f(n) < n - C \log n$ for a large $C$. By Kummer's theorem, $2$ divides $n!$ $n-O(\log n)$ times, and if $2^k$ is the largest power of $2$ that divides one of the $a_i$, then the number of powers of $2$ dividing $a_1 \dots a_t$ is at most $\sum_{j=1}^k \min( \frac{m}{2^j}+1, t)$, which one can bound by $m+k$ by ignoring the $t$ factor; thus $k > 10 \log n$ (say) by hypothesis, which makes at least one of the $a_i$ of size at least $2^k \geq n^{10}$ hence all of them are at least this size since $m \leq n$. By Stirling's formula this gives the bound $t k \ll n \log n$, so $t$ is less than a small multiple of $n$. The inequality $n - O(\log n) \leq \sum_{j=1}^k \min( \frac{m}{2^j}+1, t) \ll k + t \log \frac{m}{t}$ then forces $k \gg n$, and hence $t = O(\log n)$. Thus $n!$ has somehow been factored into only $O(\log n)$ factors that are distance $O(n)$ apart and size at least $n^{10}$, which seems like quite a rare occurrence. These factors would need to be divisible by a lot of small primes, and perhaps one could rule a lot of scenarios out using the abc conjecture or similar tools.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
To continue the previous analysis: suppose that one has $t = O(\log n)$ for some large $n$ as above. For any prime $p \leq n^{0.99}$, $p$ divides $n! = a_1 \dots a_t$ about $n/p$ times, but if $l > 10 \log n$ (say) then at most one of the $a_1,\dots,a_t$ can be divisible by $p^l$. From this and the assumption $t = O(\log n)$ one can conclude that one of the $a_i$ is divisible by $p$ at least $0.99 n/p$ times (say). The product $\prod_{p \leq n^{0.99}} p^{0.99 n/p}$ is something like $(n!)^{0.98}$, so by the pigeonhole principle one should be able to find two $a_i,a_j$ each of which is divisible by a product of prime powers $p^{0.99 n/p}$ of size $\gg a_i^{0.95}, a_j^{0.95}$ say, which makes the radical of $a_i$ or $a_j$ of size $O(a_i^{0.1})$ or $O(a_j^{0.1})$. But as $a_i = a_j + O(n)$ and $a_i, a_j \geq n^{10}$, this would violate the abc conjecture. So I think one can get a bound of the form $f(n) = n - O(\log n)$ assuming the abc conjecture.

Another observation: if one can find some small $j,l$ such that $(j+1) \dots (j+l) | \binom{n+j}{j} = \frac{(j+1) \dots (j+n)}{n!}$, then this almost certainly leads to the bound $f(n) \leq n-l-1$, because $(j+l+1) \dots (j+n)$ is now a moderately large multiple of $n!$ and one should be able to remove some terms from this product to recover $n!$ exactly. Thus for instance the trivial $1 | \binom{n+0}{0}$ gives the trivial bound $f(n) \leq n-2$, $2 \times 3 | \binom{n+1}{1}$ or $3 \times 4 | \binom{n+2}{2}$ should lead to $f(n) \leq n-3$, and so forth.

problem:
Let $t_k(n)$ denote the least $m$ such that\[n\mid m(m+1)(m+2)\cdots (m+k-1).\]Is it true that\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{x^2}{(\log x)^c}\]for some $c>0$?

Is it true that, for $k\geq 2$,\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_{k+1}(n) =o\left(\sum_{n\leq x}t_k(n)\right)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/394.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-10-28).
- Page last edited: 28 October 2025.
Site remarks:
In \cite{ErGr80} they mention a conjecture of Erd\H{o}s that the sum is $o(x^2)$. This was proved by Erd\H{o}s and Hall \cite{ErHa78}, who proved that in fact\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}x^2.\]Erd\H{o}s and Hall conjecture that the sum is $o(x^2/(\log x)^c)$ for any $c<\log 2$.

Since $t_2(p)=p-1$ for prime $p$ it is trivial that\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\gg \frac{x^2}{\log x}.\]Erd\H{o}s and Hall \cite{ErHa78} also note that $t_{n-1}(n!)=2$ and $t_{n-2}(n!)\ll n$, which $n=2^r$ shows is the best possible. They ask about the behaviour of $t_{n-3}(n!)$ and also ask ask whether, for infinitely many $n$,\[t_k(n!)< t_{k-1}(n!)-1\]for all $1\leq k<n$. They proved (with Selfridge) that this holds for $n=10$.
References:
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [ErHa78] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Hall, R. R., On some unconventional problems on the divisors of integers. J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A (1978), 479--485.

A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Establish uniform distribution control of solution residues for
\[
n\mid m(m+1)\cdots(m+k-1),
\]
showing average minimal \(m\) contracts by a fixed factor when \(k\mapsto k+1\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (definition monotonicity in \(k\)):
\[
t_{k+1}(n)\le t_k(n).
\]
Proof.
Any \(m\) satisfying divisibility by a \(k\)-block also satisfies it for \((k+1)\)-block by multiplying one extra factor. Minimum cannot increase. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (sum comparison consequence):
From B1,
\[
\sum_{n\le x} t_{k+1}(n)\le \sum_{n\le x} t_k(n).
\]
Proof.
Summing termwise inequality over \(n\le x\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies strict asymptotic separation):
If A yields average contraction \(t_{k+1}(n)\le (1-\delta_k)t_k(n)\) on density-1 set, then
\[
\sum_{n\le x} t_{k+1}(n)=o\!\left(\sum_{n\le x} t_k(n)\right).
\]
Proof.
Split by good density-1 set and negligible exceptional set; good set gives fixed-factor gain repeatedly, forcing ratio to \(0\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving quantitative average contraction beyond monotonicity, uniformly in large \(n\).

problem: Is it true that for every $k$ there exists $n$ such that\[\prod_{0\leq i\leq k}(n-i) \mid \binom{2n}{n}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/396.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Graham write that $n+1$ always divides $\binom{2n}{n}$ (indeed $\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ is the $n$th Catalan number (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_number)), but it is quite rare that $n$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$.

Pomerance \cite{Po14} has shown that for any $k\geq 0$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that $n-k\mid\binom{2n}{n}$, although the set of such $n$ has upper density $<1/3$. Pomerance also shows that the set of $n$ such that\[\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)\mid \binom{2n}{n}\]has density $1$.

The smallest $n$ for each $k$ are listed as A375077 (https://oeis.org/A375077) on the OEIS.
References:
- [Po14] Pomerance, C., Divisors of the middle binomial coefficient. American Mathematical Monthly (2014).

forum_comments.text:
I looked at (https://chatgpt.com/share/69d282af-aa94-839e-b49f-fadc93864d72) the theoretical side a little bit with GPT-5.4 Thinking.

Let $E_k := \{ n : n(n-1)\dots(n-k) \mid \binom{2n}{n} \}$. Let $d$ denote density and $\overline{d}$ denote upper density.

Pomerance proved $\overline{d}(E_0) < 1/3$. In fact his argument gave $\overline{d}(E_0) \le 1-\log 2 = 0.306\dots$. Nevertheless, Ford and Konyagin (2021) (https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.03903) has completely settled this as $d(E_0) = c_1 := 0.114\dots$; in particular the density of the set exists.

It follows trivially that $\overline{d}(E_k) \le c_1$. But we were not able to even prove $\overline{d}(E_k) < c_1$ for $k > 0$. However, heuristically we do expect $\overline{d}(E_k) \approx c_1^{k+1}$. This is confirmed to line up well with the available computational evidence. In particular, the smallest $n$ for each $k$ should increase by about $1/c_1 \approx 8.75$ each time.

forum_comments.author: Justin Dehorty
forum_comments.text:
Very interesting chat w/ GPT 5.4...thanks for sharing that link. I went through the entire chat you had, but was a bit surprised your LLM bailed out after 9 mins when you asked for the ordinary upper density proof for $d(E_k) < c_1$ for $k>0$.

I pushed it to think a bit harder (https://chatgpt.com/share/69d4ce8a-a8cc-832a-bf2a-6e74d7d1c357) on your last question using the Pro setting, and it ended up thinking for roughly an order of magnitude more compute than your earlier pass (~93 mins total). It seems it was able to at least get a genuine strict gap below $c_1$, but for logarithmic density rather than ordinary upper density.

Let

$$E_k := \left\{ n > k : \prod_{j=0}^k (n-j) \mid \binom{2n}{n} \right\},$$

and let $\overline{\delta}$ denote upper logarithmic density.

For any fixed $k \ge 1$, if $n \in E_k$, then in particular both $n \mid \binom{2n}{n}$ and $n-1 \mid \binom{2n}{n}$. Apply the same no-carry argument used by Pomerance: if $p \mid (n-j)$ with $p > \sqrt{2n}$, then $p \nmid \binom{2n}{n}$. Hence every $n \in E_k$ must satisfy

$$P^+(n) \le \sqrt{2n} \qquad \text{and} \qquad P^+(n-1) \le \sqrt{2n},$$

where $P^+$ is the largest prime factor.

So $E_k$ is contained in the set of consecutive $\sqrt{2x}$-smooth pairs up to $x$. Recent work of Tao-Teräväinen on consecutive smooth numbers then gives, on a set of $x$'s of logarithmic density $1$,

$$\#\left\{ m \le x : P^+(m) \le x^{1/u},\; P^+(m-1) \le x^{1/u} \right\} = (\rho(u)^2 + o(1))\,x.$$

Taking $u \to 2$ gives

$$\overline{\delta}(E_k) \le \rho(2)^2 = (1-\log 2)^2 \approx 0.09416.$$

Since Ford–Konyagin proved

$$d(E_0) = c_1 \approx 0.11424,$$

this yields the strict inequality

$$\overline{\delta}(E_k) \le (1-\log 2)^2 < c_1 \qquad (k \ge 1).$$

So while this may not prove $\overline{d}(E_k) < c_1$ in the ordinary sense, it does show that once you ask for even one backward step, the set is already strictly sparser than the governor set at the logarithmic-density level. In particular, if the ordinary density $d(E_k)$ happens to exist, then automatically

$$d(E_k) < c_1.$$

At least to me, that seems significant: it says the $k > 0$ problem is not just "the $k = 0$ problem with a bounded shift" but a genuinely more correlated/rarer pattern problem.

$\large\textbf{Extending OEIS A375077 through } k=13$

$\textbf{Exhaustive search, validation, and a formally verified barrier theorem}$

Over the past several months I have been running an exhaustive computational search for [396] witnesses, extending OEIS A375077 with 6 new terms at the initial time of discovery (2 new terms at the time of this post). The full codebase, validation certificates, and a machine-checked proof are publicly available at github.com/jdehorty/erdos396 (https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396).

New values:

$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
k & a(k) & \text{Search range} & \text{Date found*} \\ \hline
8 & 339{,}949{,}252 & 0\text{–}340\text{M} & \text{2025-01-17} \\
9 & 1{,}019{,}547{,}844 & 0\text{–}17.6\text{B} & \text{2026-03-16 (corrected)} \\
10 & 17{,}609{,}764{,}994 & 0\text{–}17.6\text{B} & \text{2025-01-20} \\
11 & 1{,}070{,}858{,}041{,}585 & 0\text{–}2\text{T} & \text{2026-02-09} \\
12 & 5{,}048{,}891{,}644{,}646 & 0\text{–}6.15\text{T} & \text{2026-02-11} \\
13 & 18{,}253{,}129{,}921{,}842 & 0\text{–}25\text{T} & \text{2026-02-16}
\end{array}$

*Note: Dates reflect my own personal records of when each value was first found, not when results were submitted or published. The jumps in pace (particularly from k=11 onward) correspond to successive sieve improvements: the v1 prefilter (7x), the fused sieve pass (15x), and finally Kummer-based valuation for all primes (31x single-threaded throughput).

Each value has a computational certificate of minimality: every integer below the claimed witness has been checked and ruled out.

Note on $k=9$: the original governor-run search found a witness at $17{,}609{,}764{,}993$. A subsequent full validation pass (checking every integer, not just governor-run candidates) found the true minimum at $1{,}019{,}547{,}844$.

$\textbf{Method.}$ The search is built around the Governor Set $G = \{n : n \mid \binom{2n}{n}\}$ (OEIS A014847, density $\approx 12.3\%$ by Ford-Konyagin). All known witnesses have every block term $n, n-1, \ldots, n-k$ in $G$. A fused segmented sieve strips small prime factors and checks the Kummer carry condition $\nu_p(n) \leq \nu_p\!\binom{2n}{n}$ inline, rejecting ${\sim}87\%$ of integers in a single pass. The $\sqrt{2n}$ large-prime-factor barrier provides additional fast rejection. Runs of $k+1$ consecutive governors are candidate witnesses, each verified by the full inequality $\sum_{i=0}^{k} \nu_p(n-i) \leq \nu_p\!\binom{2n}{n}$ at every prime $p$.

$\textbf{The Small Prime Barrier Theorem.}$ The governor-run search cannot detect witnesses where some block term fails to be a governor. I proved that any such non-governor failure must occur at a prime $p < 2k+1$. For $k=13$ this is just 9 primes: $\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\}$. The proof uses Kummer's theorem and a carry invariance lemma for base-$p$ self-addition; the bound $2k+1$ is tight (via Bertrand's postulate). The Small Prime Barrier Theorem and its tightness are formally verified in Lean 4 + Mathlib (no sorry/admit); the formal proof covers the carry invariance lemma, the barrier theorem itself, and the tightness result via Bertrand's postulate - not the computational search.

This yields a provably complete validation method: screen every integer at the barrier primes, then fully verify survivors. The validate binary implements this for $k=8$ through $k=13$, producing minimality certificates independent of the Governor Set Completeness Conjecture.

$\textbf{Verification.}$ The repository includes: (1) a Rust verifier and a stdlib-only Python verifier for witness validity; (2) the Lean 4 formal proof of the Small Prime Barrier Theorem (justifying the completeness of the validation algorithm); (3) published validation certificates with coverage invariants and build metadata tied to specific source revisions; (4) an independent report checker that recomputes invariants from the JSON reports. Full details at github.com/jdehorty/erdos396 (https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396).

Note: AI usage comprised GPT-5.4 Pro (extended thinking) and Google Gemini 3.1 DeepThink for proof exploration and adversarial review, and Claude Opus 4.6 for coding the Rust-based search pipeline and Lean 4 formalization. The Lean 4 formal proof is machine-checked (no sorry/admit), and all computational claims are backed by deterministic validation certificates; see docs/trust.md in the repository.

forum_comments.author: Justin Dehorty
forum_comments.text:
Thanks for the review! I've created GitHub issues for each finding and will address them there, but to provide a brief summary and clarify a few points:

1) ValidateBatch residual misclassification (issue (https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396/issues/1))

This is an interesting point by GPT-5.4. The batch path is indeed missing a guard that the naive reference implementation has, which means a small barrier prime can technically be misclassified as a large-prime failure when the sieve limit falls below the barrier threshold. Technically speaking, this is a real soundness gap in the validator's general contract and I'll fix it.

That said, this does not affect the quality of any published results. The bug requires the batch's maximum $n$ to be below $2k^2$, which for $k=11$ means $n < 242$. With the default batch size of $10^6$, the very first batch is already six orders of magnitude above this threshold. No validation run I've produced has come anywhere near triggering this. The certified minima stand.

2) Search misses cross-worker runs (issue (https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396/issues/2))

This is also an interesting point. The search binary is the fast discovery pass. In the original planning phase, it was very important to me to have a separate validation pass, since the possibility of a false negative could exist in theory. For example, in exceedingly rare circumstances, there could exist a valid Erdős 396 witness where some term $m=n-j$ in the falling factorial divides the ambient binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$, even though m itself does not divide $\binom{2m}{m}$. Part of the reason I held off so long in posting my results is that I don't consider the integers technically "discovered" unless both false positives AND false negatives are ruled out. And since the initial forward pass does not protect against these extremely rare scenarios where n = m+j creates an extra prime that m does not have on its own, it is necessary to have that backwards certifier as a backstop. So the architecture is intentional: the search discovers candidates quickly, and the "validate" pass provides the provably complete certificate.

However, I do appreciate the observation that varying the worker count can silently change search output. From a correctness standpoint, this is a good suggestion. I'm open to hardening this by overlapping worker ranges or stitching boundary state in the aggregation pass, and I'll think about the best way to do that. To be clear, this does not affect the certified minima, since the validate binary checks every integer independently and its results are not impacted by the search tool's parallelism.

3) Corollary 6 documentation (issue (https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396/issues/3))

Fair note. Technically, if you look at the source code, the inline comments at the call site clearly describe stage 1 as the contrapositive of the barrier theorem applied as a pre-filter. The detailed docs also describe the two-stage structure accurately. But I agree the top-of-file header comment compresses the story by branding the whole algorithm as "Corollary 6," and that could be more precise. I'll tighten the wording there. Of course, since this is purely a documentation issue, it does not affect any of the results.

forum_comments.author: Sharvil Kesarwani
forum_comments.text: I thought I'd return the favour with an optimisation suggestion of my own - division is slow. You can instead precompute magic numbers and shifts (which are accurate for all int64 values) and reduce the total number of clock cycles it takes to do the division by using multiplication. There's a C/C++ library which does this called 'libdivide', but I've just done a bespoke version of it in my program. I believe there's a Rust crate for it here: https://docs.rs/libdivide/latest/libdivide/. I got an extremely solid speedup to 400M candidates/s with it (about 33%).

forum_comments.author: Justin Dehorty
forum_comments.text:
Great suggestion! The runtime $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{div}}$ is definitely brutal...takes ~30–40 cycles on x86-64 vs ~3–4 for multiply+shift.

I actually already do this for part of the pipeline: the Kummer computation uses Rust const generics for $v_p\binom{2n}{n}$, so the 15 primes from 2 through 47 get monomorphised into the same multiply+shift codegen that libdivide would produce. For $p = 2$, it's actually even faster since $v_2\binom{2n}{n} = \mathrm{popcount}(n)$ reduces to a single instruction.

But interestingly, it does seem like there's another spot this could be implemented...the fused sieve inner loop in $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{FusedBatchResult::compute }}$ (https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396/blob/main/src/prefilter.rs#L104-L131) does $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{remaining[idx]}}$ % $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{p}}$ and $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{remaining[idx] /= p}}$ where $p$ comes from a &$\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{[u64]}}$ slice, so the compiler emits a hardware $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{div}}$ every time - even for $p = 3$, which is the highest-traffic prime. That loop runs $O(\texttt{batch\_size}/p)$ times per prime, so the small primes dominate and this is likely one of my remaining bottlenecks.

The difference in compiled code is quite pronounced in Compiler Explorer...
- Current code (runtime $p$ hardware $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{div}}$): godbolt.org/z/bcTn1seEs (https://godbolt.org/z/bcTn1seEs)
- With const generic (compile-time $P$ multiply+shift, no $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{div}}$): godbolt.org/z/andf51Wv5 (https://godbolt.org/z/andf51Wv5)

The runtime version is dominated by $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{div rsi}}$ / $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{div esi}}$ instructions - there are 6 of them in the loop body, each a ~30–40 cycle stall. The const-generic version for $p = 3$ replaces all of them with a single $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{mul}}$ + $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{shr}}$ for the quotient and an $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{imul}}$ + $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{cmp}}$ for the divisibility test (using the magic constant).

No $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{div}}$ anywhere in the output. The $p = 7$ instantiation is the same pattern with a different magic constant...$\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{mul}}$ + $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{sub}}$ + $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{shr}}$ + $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{add}}$ + $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{shr}}$, still no $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{div}}$.

One thought on taking it further: inside the $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{while remaining}}$ % $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{p == 0}}$ body I already know $p$ divides the value, so I could use the modular inverse of $p \bmod 2^{64}$ for exact division - a single $\bbox[#f6f8fa,2px,border:1px solid #d0d7de]{\texttt{imul}}$, no shift. The divisibility test itself becomes $n \cdot p_{\mathrm{inv}} \leq \lfloor 2^{64} / p \rfloor$ iff $p \mid n$. That reduces the whole strip-factor loop to two multiplies and a compare. Might squeeze a few more percent beyond what libdivide gives.

In any case, definitely worth integrating precomputed magic constants or modular inverses into the sieve pass.

forum_comments.author: Sharvil Kesarwani
forum_comments.text:
Some surprising updates - turns out sometimes there's some simple things that can achieve radical speedups. I've crossed the $2$ billion candidates/s barrier (at $k\in\{7,8,9\}$), with a gradual slowdown for $k \geq 11$.

Some major speedups you might be interested in:
1. Like you said, you can compute the multiplicative inverse $\pmod{2^{64}}$, which you can use Newton-Raphson iteration to do very quickly.
2. In the final array you check for smoothness, you can use Boyer-Moore string-search algorithm to reduce the search *significantly*.
3. You don't need to check every prime. Small primes you can let the compiler optimise for you, medium size primes you can do the same thing we always do, but for large primes, often the interval you're checking on doesn't have any such elements so you can skip them.
4. If you're using multi-threading, do some profiling to see if your threads are being starved etc, there's some ways to shuffle around how they compute to minimise. Also be careful of threads stalling cuz they're trying to write out to a file. I found that I had a bunch of data getting streamed from L3 to L2, and I realised that my chunks I processed were just too big to fit in the L2 cache.
5. Make sure you're not running other programs in parallel (my previous numbers were with me running VSCode and FireFox at the same time)
In general, get a proper profiler to look at the code - I have been using Intel VTune Profiler, which is free but can't give me everything since I have an AMD Ryzen 7 processor - I tried using AMD uProf, but it would just crash whenever I ran a program.

I've run it overnight now, and it was able to solve for all $k \leq 13$ in under $8$ hours, also confirming the values you've found. There are probably still some improvements to be made but its getting harder and harder not to regress.

The ratios remain wildly irregular.

### A necessary large-prime-factor bound

Claim. If $\prod_{i=0}^{n}(K - i)$ divides $\binom{2K}{K}$ and $K > n$, then every prime $p > 2n$ dividing some $K - j$ satisfies $p \leq \sqrt{2K}$.

Proof. Suppose $p > 2n$, $p > \sqrt{2K}$, and $p \mid (K - j)$ for some $0 \leq j \leq n$. Write $K = ap + j$. Since $p^2 > 2K$, we have $a < K/p < p/2$, so $K$ has at most two base-$p$ digits with leading digit $a < p/2$ and units digit $j \leq n < p/2$. Adding $K + K$ in base $p$: the units digit gives $2j < p$ (no carry), the leading digit gives $2a < p$ (no carry). By Kummer's theorem, $\nu_p(\binom{2K}{K}) = 0$. But $\nu_p(\prod(K - i)) \geq \nu_p(K - j) \geq 1$, so the divisibility fails. $\square$

In other words:

$$P^{+}\!\left(\prod_{i=0}^{n}(K - i)\right) \leq \max(2n, \lfloor\sqrt{2K}\rfloor).$$

So any solution must have all prime factors of the descending block below the natural threshold $\sqrt{2K}$ (aside from the trivial small-prime range $p \leq 2n$).

### Empirical confirmation

For $a(8) = 339{,}949{,}252$, the bound gives $\lfloor\sqrt{2 \cdot 339{,}949{,}252}\rfloor = 26{,}075$. The actual largest prime factor across the block $k, k-1, \ldots, k-8$ is $25{,}643$ (from $k - 1 = 3^3 \cdot 491 \cdot 25{,}643$). The margin is only $432$.

More strikingly, the factorization of the full block is:

term | factorization | largest PF
$k$ | $2^2 \cdot 29 \cdot 541 \cdot 5417$ | 5417
$k-1$ | $3^3 \cdot 491 \cdot 25643$ | 25643
$k-2$ | $2 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 859 \cdot 1583$ | 1583
$k-3$ | $191 \cdot 701 \cdot 2539$ | 2539
$k-4$ | $2^6 \cdot 3 \cdot 743 \cdot 2383$ | 2383
$k-5$ | $11 \cdot 73 \cdot 331 \cdot 1279$ | 1279
$k-6$ | $2 \cdot 7 \cdot 13^2 \cdot 23 \cdot 6247$ | 6247
$k-7$ | $3 \cdot 5 \cdot 41 \cdot 79 \cdot 6997$ | 6997
$k-8$ | $2^2 \cdot 4127 \cdot 20593$ | 20593

For all known values checked so far, every large prime factor $p > 31$ is exactly saturated on the Kummer side: $\kappa_p(k) = 1 = \nu_p(k - j)$. In other words, the large-prime constraints are met with zero slack.

### Connection to #728

Problem #728 (arXiv:2601.07421) proved the existence of "carry-rich but spike-free" integers for ascending windows $m+1, \ldots, m+k$ using the fact that when $p > 2k$ and $p^r \mid (m+i)$, the low base-$p$ digits of $m$ are forced to be large, automatically producing carries (Lemma 5). For descending blocks $K, K-1, \ldots, K-n$, this mechanism reverses: $p \mid (K - j)$ forces low digits of $K$ to be small, so no carries are automatic. This is why the #728 argument does not directly prove $a(n) < \infty$.

The large-prime-factor bound above makes this precise. The new obstruction appears to lie not in the small-prime Kummer analysis addressed in #728, but in controlling the large prime factors of the descending block. This aligns with Tao's observation (Sep 2025) that the initial difficulty is "securing a string of consecutive smooth numbers."

This suggests a two-part structure:
A small/medium-prime digit-pattern problem: this may be approachable by adapting the carry-rich ideas of #728.

A large-prime-factor problem: any solution must satisfy $P^{+}(\prod_{i=0}^n (K-i)) \leq \max(2n, \lfloor\sqrt{2K}\rfloor)$, and #728 provides no mechanism for forcing this in descending blocks.

For primes $p > 2n$ in the intermediate range $\sqrt{K} < p \leq \sqrt{2K}$, any divisor $p \mid (K - j)$ can contribute at most one carry on the Kummer side. For all known values checked so far, these primes are satisfied with exactly one carry and zero slack. So the "one-carry regime" appears to be the binding large-prime constraint in practice.

Love the work you guys have done on this. I've been independently working on Problem #396 as well (in Rust) and it's fun to see someone else exploring the same space.

Our approaches converge on a lot of the same ideas: fused block sieve with inline Kummer checks, and large-prime factor rejection as a natural fallout of the sieve pass. A few things I've found that might be useful to you:

Since $\nu_2\binom{2n}{n} = \operatorname{popcount}(n)$ (Kummer's theorem for $p=2$), you can replace the carry loop entirely with a single hardware instruction for the most common prime. This gave me a noticeable bump in performance. Similarly, compile-time constant divisors with branchless carry let you avoid the general loop for $p=3$ and $p=5$. And no odd prime can be a Governor ($\nu_p\binom{2p}{p} = 0$), so you can skip the Kummer check entirely for odd-prime candidates, catching about 4.3% of numbers for free before any heavier work.

For reference, I'm seeing about 31M candidates/sec single-threaded at $n = 10^{10}$, which works out to roughly 3.6x your per-core throughput if I'm reading the 59M / 7-thread figure correctly. Happy to share more implementation details if any of that is interesting.

I've also been running with checkpointing (JSON save/resume), which has been a lifesaver for long searches on shared compute. It might be worth adding if you're planning longer runs for $k \geq 12$.

Following up on my earlier computational post (a(8), a(9), smoothness bound; thanks to natso26 for the corrections on the floor value and one-carry scope).

## A specific open subproblem

After more work on the structure of the divisibility condition, one route I’ve been exploring leads to a medium-prime subproblem that now seems to be a main obstacle. I’m not claiming a full reduction here; I just want to state the subproblem in case it connects to something known.

**Setup.** By Kummer,\[
\prod_{j=0}^n (K-j)\mid \binom{2K}{K}
\]iff at every prime \(p\), the carry count \(\kappa_p(K)\) satisfies\[
\kappa_p(K)\ge \sum_{j=0}^n \nu_p(K-j).
\]For large primes \((p > \sqrt{2K})\), the smoothness bound from my earlier post handles these.

For small primes \((p \le Y\), with \(Y\) a fixed parameter depending on \(n)\), I have a plausible truncation/low-digit approach, but I do not yet regard that part as complete.

The range where I am currently stuck is the **medium-prime range \(Y < p \le \sqrt K\)**.

## The medium-prime question

After restricting to \(K\) with \(p^2 \nmid (K-j)\) for all \(p > Y\) and all \(j \le n\), one loses at most\[
O_n\!\left(\sum_{p>Y}\frac{1}{p^2}\right)
\]in density, so this loss can be made arbitrarily small by taking \(Y\) large. On this restricted set, any medium prime \(p > Y\) dividing some \(K-j\) has \(\nu_p(K-j)=1\). Since \(p > Y \ge n\), at most one \(j\) has \(p \mid (K-j)\). So the condition at such a prime is simply \(\kappa_p(K)\ge 1\): at least one carry when doubling \(K\) in base \(p\).

Here is the key structural observation: if \(p > 2n\) and \(p \mid (K-j)\) for some \(0 \le j \le n\), then \(K \equiv j \pmod p\), so the base-\(p\) units digit of \(K\) is \(j \le n < p/2\). Doubling gives \(2j < p\), so there is no carry at the units position. Any carry must come from a higher-order digit.

For primes near \(\sqrt K\) with only \(2\)–\(3\) base-\(p\) digits total, this is genuinely restrictive — the carry condition fails for a positive fraction of \(K\) in each residue class.

Define\[
f(K)=\#\{\,\text{primes } Y < p \le \sqrt K : \exists j \le n \text{ with } p \mid (K-j)\text{ and }\kappa_p(K)=0\,\}.
\]A first-moment calculation suggests \(E[f(K)] = O_n(1)\); heuristically the dominant contribution comes from primes with \(3\) base-\(p\) digits.

If the small-prime piece can be completed, then along this route it would remain to show \(P(f=0)>0\). A natural way to try to do this is via Poisson approximation methods (e.g. Stein–Chen), which would require adequate control on the pairwise covariances \(\operatorname{Cov}(1_{B_p},1_{B_q})\).

For “easy” prime pairs with \(p^{L_p} q^{L_q} \ll X\), approximate independence should follow from CRT (the base-\(p\) and base-\(q\) digit constraints live on coprime moduli that fit inside the interval). But for primes \(p, q\) both in \((X^{1/3}, \sqrt X]\) — each with only \(3\) base-digits — the product \(p^3 q^3\) exceeds \(X\), so the interval contains fewer than one full CRT period, and I don’t see how to decouple the events.

This hard-pair regime contributes a bounded but nonzero amount to the mean, so it cannot simply be discarded.

**The concrete question.** For primes \(p, q \asymp X^{1/3}\) and a fixed integer \(\Delta\), let\[
T_p = \{\,m \le X/p : \text{every base-}p\text{ digit of }m\text{ is }< \lceil p/2\rceil \,\}.
\]What can be said about\[
\#\{(a,b)\in T_p\times T_q : pa-qb=\Delta\}\,?
\]This is a lattice point count on a product of digit-restricted sets under a linear constraint. Has this type of intersection problem appeared in the digital restrictions or additive combinatorics literature? Any pointers would be appreciated.

## Computational update

\(a(9)=1{,}019{,}547{,}844\) (previously reported). Max prime factor of the block: \(42{,}979\) vs bound \(\lfloor \sqrt{2k}\rfloor = 45{,}156\).

Partial progress on Problem 396: small n and a reduction for general n

I've been working on this problem and have some partial results plus a precise formulation of what seems to be the remaining obstacle for general n. AI tools (Claude, GPT) were used throughout. The computations were checked directly, and the mathematical reductions below are the parts I currently trust most.

Setup

By Kummer's theorem, the divisibility condition reduces to: for every prime p, the sum of p-adic valuations of K, K−1, …, K−n must not exceed the number of carries when doubling K in base p.

After a standard squarefree sieve (restricting to K with p² ∤ (K−j) for large primes), this simplifies for primes p > Y to: whenever p divides some K−j, we need at least one carry in the base-p addition K+K.

Small primes

For primes p ≤ Y, the carry count κ_p(K) grows with the number of base-p digits via a 2-state Markov chain with spectral gap (p−1)/p. The required valuation sum is bounded above by ν_p((n+1)!) (Legendre). I believe the right route is to combine this factorial bound with a carry-concentration argument in a fixed CRT progression, but I have not yet written this up as a formal standalone proof.

 Medium primes: the key structural observation

For a medium prime p > Y dividing K−j, write K = j + pa and decompose the "bad" event B_p (all base-p digits of a are < ⌈p/2⌉, giving zero carries) as B_p = C_p ∩ M_p, where:

- C_p restricts the higher digits of a (a "top-digit" condition)
- M_p restricts the lowest digit: d₁ = a mod p < ⌈p/2⌉ (a "middle-digit" condition)

Since B_p ⊆ M_p, avoiding all M_p events is sufficient for the medium-prime range.

The event M_p is equivalent to K belonging to (n+1)⌈p/2⌉ forbidden residue classes modulo p² (these are distinct for p > n, by a short congruence argument). The local forbidden density is g(p) = (n+1)/(2p) + O(1/p²).

 CRT independence in the product space

Since the moduli p² are pairwise coprime, the M_p events are exactly independent in the abstract CRT product space ∏ ℤ/p²ℤ. The density of the "good" set there is ∏(1 − g(p)), which by a Mertens-type evaluation is of order C_n/(log X)^{(n+1)/2} — positive but shrinking. The unresolved step is transferring that product-space density back to the interval [1, X].

What works for small n

For the medium-prime layer with L ≥ 3 base-p digits, the expected number of bad primes is E[g] = Σ_p P(B_p) ≈ 0.16(n+1). For n ≤ 5 this is less than 1, so Markov's inequality gives P(g = 0) > 0 directly — no sieve or independence argument needed for that layer. A complete proof integrating the small-prime and squarefree constraints with this would need a more careful writeup, but I believe no fundamental obstacle remains for small n.

My more recent computations also show that bad-prime events in the L = 3 layer are positively correlated (pairwise ratio ≈ 2) rather than Poisson-independent, which is why I am not claiming a probabilistic closure for general n.

What I'm stuck on for general n

I need to show the "good" set in the CRT product space actually intersects [1, X]. The CRT product-space heuristic predicts a count of order X/(log X)^{(n+1)/2}, and direct computation confirms this for all tested n. But proving it requires one of:

1. A sieve lower bound for {K ≤ X : K mod p² ∉ A_p for all medium p}. The Brun–Selberg sieve runs into trouble because ω(p) = (n+1)⌈p/2⌉ grows with p (remainder control fails for moduli p²), or because the sieve dimension κ = n+1 exceeds the sieving limit at s = 2 (for moduli p). I checked this against Friedlander–Iwaniec and the DHR higher-dimensional sieve; neither framework gives a positive lower bound in this parameter regime.

2. A Fourier discrepancy estimate showing the CRT product forbidden set doesn't cluster in [1, X]. The per-prime Fourier transform of 1_{A_p} factors as S₁(k)·S₂(k) with explicit geometric-sum bounds, and CRT gives multiplicative factorization of hat(1_{A_d}). But controlling the low-frequency sum when d = ∏ p² ≫ X requires cancellation beyond what absolute-value bounds can provide; a CRT-profile analysis shows "enemy families" of low-frequency k where no per-prime Fourier saving is available.

Computational evidence concerns only the L >= 3 medium-prime layer not the full sieve problem.

P(g = 0) is stable and positive for all tested parameters:

| n | Observed P(g=0), X = 100,000 | CRT product-space prediction (2/3)^{(n+1)/2} |
|---|-------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| 1 | 0.668 | 0.667 |
| 3 | 0.446 | 0.444 |
| 5 | 0.298 | 0.296 |
| 10 | 0.108 | 0.108 |

### Question

Has anyone encountered the problem of proving a lower bound for |{K ≤ X : K mod p² ∉ A_p for all primes Y < p ≤ √X}| where A_p has ~(n+1)p/2 forbidden classes mod p²? The CRT product space gives exact independence and a positive-density good set, but transferring this to [1,X] when ∏ p² ≫ X is the obstacle. Any pointers to relevant tools — perhaps from the sieve theory of "dense" forbidden sets, or from discrepancy theory for structured CRT products; would be very welcome.

Work was checked by Me. If anyone can help me advance the problem it would be greatly appreciated. Thanks.

problem: Are the only solutions to\[n!=x^2-1\]when $n=4,5,7$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/398.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The Brocard-Ramanujan conjecture. Erd\H{o}s and Graham describe this as an old conjecture, and write it 'is almost certainly true but it is intractable at present'.

Overholt \cite{Ov93} has shown that this has only finitely many solutions assuming a weak form of the ABC conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture).

There are no other solutions below $10^9$ (see the OEIS page (https://oeis.org/A146968)).

Naciri \cite{Na25} has proved that there are only finitely many solutions if $x\pm 1$ is either $k$-free (for some $k\geq 2$) or a prime power (and Cambie explains both facts in the comments), and that if $x\pm 1$ is $7$-free then $n=4,5,7$ give the only solutions.
References:
- [Na25] A. M. Naciri, On the Brocard-Ramanujan equation with $7$-free integers and prime powers. Integers (2025), A71.
- [Ov93] Overholt, Marius, The Diophantine equation $n!+1=m^2$. Bull. London Math. Soc. (1993), 104.

Target:
Prove asymptotics
\[
\sum_{n\le x} g_k(n)\sim c_k x\log x
\]
and almost-all law \(g_k(n)\sim c_k\log n\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show a local limit theorem for valuation-feasibility vectors of factorial factors, yielding concentration of \(g_k(n)\) around \(c_k\log n\) with integrable error.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (known logarithmic upper scale):
\[
g_k(n)\ll_k \log n.
\]
Proof.
This is the cited known bound from background. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (summatory-from-pointwise transfer):
If \(g_k(n)=c_k\log n+o(\log n)\) for density-1 \(n\), then
\[
\sum_{n\le x} g_k(n)=c_k x\log x+o(x\log x).
\]
Proof.
Average the pointwise relation; exceptional set contributes lower-order term by density-1 assumption and B1 bound. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies both targets):
If A yields almost-all concentration with explicit \(c_k\), then B2 gives summatory asymptotic, and the almost-all statement is immediate.
Proof.
Direct application of B2 and definition of concentration. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is deriving a precise probabilistic model for interacting prime valuations in factorial-divisibility constraints with enough uniformity to identify constants \(c_k\).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
It seems to me that $f(1,5)$ is already extremely large, and possibly even infinite; for each $m$, it appears that there are lots of ways to recursively find a set of factorials up to $(5m-1)!$ and starting at $1!$ that sum to something that divides at least as many powers of $5$ as $5!$. For instance
$$ 1! + 4! = 100_5$$
$$1!+4!+10!+11! = 42121430000_5$$
$$1! + 4! + 10! + 11! + 20! + 21! + 23! = 102401442411110300413412001000000_5$$
Things get a little tricky every time one reaches $5m$ is a multiple of $5^2$ or higher powers, but there is a combinatorial explosion of possible cases and it seems very likely that one could continue this sort of process for quite a while.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao

forum_comments.text:
I do not understand the first two questions. The first one makes no sense: the uniform bound on $f(a,p)$ is not possible, since we can find $k$ as large as we want if we allow $a$ to be sufficiently large. Taking a look into the Graham-Erdos problem book (p. 79), I also see that it is not what they wanted: the power of $p$ in $p^k$ and the number of summands in $a_1!+\cdots+a_k!$ were not supposed to be the same.
To make changes minimal I suggest to replace the first half of the problem (i.e., the first two questions) with:

For which positive integers $a$ and which primes $p$ there exists a finite least upper bound $f(a,p)$ on the exponents $m$ such that\[ p^m | (a_1!+\cdots+a_k!) \]for some $k\geq1$ and some integers $a=a_1<\cdots< a_k$?

The comment on Lin's result should then be $f(2,2)=254$. The third question seems to be ok.

problem: Is it true that there are only finitely many powers of $2$ which have only the digits $0$ and $1$ when written in base $3$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/406.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 13 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The only examples seem to be $1$, $4=1+3$, and $256=1+3+3^2+3^5$. If we only allow the digits $1$ and $2$ then $2^{15}$ seems to be the largest such power of $2$.

This would imply via Kummer's theorem that\[3\mid \binom{2^{k+1}}{2^k}\]for all large $k$.

Saye \cite{Sa22} has computed that $2^n$ contains every possible ternary digit for $16\leq n \leq 5.9\times 10^{21}$.

Let $N(x)$ count the number of $n\leq x$ such that $2^n$ has only the digits $0$ and $1$ in base $3$. Narkiewicz \cite{Na80} proved\[N(x)\leq 1.62 x^{\log_32}\]This is mentioned in problem B33 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}. There are many generalisations possible - see, for example, \cite{AbLa14} and \cite{La09}.
References:
- [AbLa14] Abram, William C. and Lagarias, Jeffrey C., Intersections of multiplicative translates of 3-adic {C}antor sets. J. Fractal Geom. (2014), 349--390.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [La09] Lagarias, Jeffrey C., Ternary expansions of powers of 2. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2) (2009), 562--588.
- [Na80] Narkiewicz, W., A note on a paper of {H}. {G}upta concerning powers of two and three: ``{P}owers of {$2$}\ and sums of distinct powers of {$3$}''\ [{U}niv. {B}eograd. {P}ubl. {E}lektrotehn. {F}ak. Ser. {M}at. {F}iz. {N}o. 602-633 (1978), 151--158 (1979);\ {MR} 81g:10016]. Univ. Beograd. Publ. Elektrotehn. Fak. Ser. Mat. Fiz. (1980), 173--174.
- [Sa22] Saye, Robert I., On two conjectures concerning the ternary digits of powers of two. J. Integer Seq. (2022), Art. 22.3.4, 9.

As mentioned, the non-averaged version of the main result of "Bits of $3^n$ in binary, Wieferich primes and a conjecture of Erdos(2016)" (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022314X15002139) by T. Dupuy and D. E. Weirich would imply this conjecture.

Moreover, they mention that the progress on this conjecture has been done on this one by improving the bounds on the function $N(X)$, where $N(X) =$ {$\# n \leq X : (2^n)_3$ omits a $2$}
(For a prime $q$ and a number $N$ we will let $(N)q$ denote the base $q$ expansion of $N$. We view a base $q$ expansion as a string of numbers from the set $\{0, 1, ..., q − 1\}$).

The best known bound is due to Narkiewicz in [Na80]: $N(X) \leq 1.62X^{\alpha_0}$, where $\alpha_0= \log_3(2) \approx 0.630$.

[Na80]: W. Narkiewicz, A note on a paper of H. Gupta concerning powers of 2 and 3, Publ. Elektroteh. Fak. Univ. Beogr., Ser. Mat. Fiz. 678–715 (1980) 173–174.

Prove finiteness of exponents \(n\) such that base-3 expansion of \(2^n\) uses only digits \(\{0,1\}\).

Establish an \(S\)-unit gap lemma: if

\(2\) is invertible modulo \(3^M\), so powers are periodic with period dividing \(\varphi(3^M)\). \(\square\)

If A gives explicit bound on \(n\), only finitely many exponents remain to check.
Proof.
Finite search on bounded \(n\)-range completes proof. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is sharpening transcendence bounds enough to beat combinatorial growth of admissible digit patterns.

problem: Let $\phi(n)$ be the Euler totient function and $\phi_k(n)$ be the iterated $\phi$ function, so that $\phi_1(n)=\phi(n)$ and $\phi_k(n)=\phi(\phi_{k-1}(n))$. Let\[f(n) = \min \{ k : \phi_k(n)=1\}.\]Does $f(n)/\log n$ have a distribution function? Is $f(n)/\log n$ almost always constant? What can be said about the largest prime factor of $\phi_k(n)$ when, say, $k=\log\log n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/408.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 September 2025.
Site remarks:
Pillai \cite{Pi29} was the first to investigate this function, and proved\[\log_3 n < f(n) < \log_2 n\]for all large $n$. Shapiro \cite{Sh50} proved that $f(n)$ is essentially multiplicative.

Erd\H{o}s, Granville, Pomerance, and Spiro \cite{EGPS90} have proved that the answer to the first two questions is yes, conditional on a form of the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture.

It is likely true that, if $k\to \infty$ however slowly with $n$, then for almost all $n$ the largest prime factor of $\phi_k(n)$ is $\leq n^{o(1)}$.

This is discussed in problem B41 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [EGPS90] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Granville, A. and Pomerance, C. and Spiro, C., On the normal behavior of the iterates of some arithmetic functions. Analytic number theory (Allerton Park, IL, 1989) (1990), 165-204.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Pi29] Pillai, S. Sivasankaranarayana, On some functions connected with {$\phi(n)$}. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (1929), 832-836.
- [Sh50] Shapiro, Harold N., On the iterates of a certain class of arithmetic functions. Comm. Pure Appl. Math. (1950), 259-272.

Establish unconditional distribution/normal-order behavior for \(f(n)\) (totient depth) and largest-prime-factor decay after \(k\approx\log\log n\) iterations.

Repeated exponentiation contraction reduces \(\log m\) geometrically; solve iteration count to reach \(O(1)\). \(\square\)

Iterating A for \(k\sim \log\log n\) forces largest prime factors of \(\phi_k(n)\) below \(n^\eta\) for small \(\eta\).

problem: How many iterations of $n\mapsto \phi(n)+1$ are needed before a prime is reached? Can infinitely many $n$ reach the same prime? What is the density of $n$ which reach any fixed prime?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/409.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 20 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Finucane. One can also ask similar questions about $n\mapsto \sigma(n)-1$: do iterates of this always reach a prime? If so, how soon? (It is easily seen that iterates of this cannot reach the same prime infinitely often, since they are non-decreasing.)

This problem is somewhat ambiguously phrased. Let $F(n)$ count the number of iterations of $n\mapsto \phi(n)+1$ before reaching a prime. The number of iterations required is A039651 (https://oeis.org/A039651) in the OEIS.

Cambie notes in the comments that $F(n)=o(n)$ is trivial, and $F(n)=1$ infinitely often. Presumably the intended question is to find 'good' upper bounds for $F(n)$.

This is discussed in problem B41 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.

problem: Let $g_1=g(n)=n+\phi(n)$ and $g_k(n)=g(g_{k-1}(n))$. For which $n$ and $r$ is it true that $g_{k+r}(n)=2g_k(n)$ for all large $k$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/411.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 October 2025.
Site remarks:
The known solutions to $g_{k+2}(n)=2g_k(n)$ are $n=10$ and $n=94$. Selfridge and Weintraub found solutions to $g_{k+9}(n)=9g_k(n)$ and Weintraub found\[g_{k+25}(3114)=729g_k(3114)\]for all $k\geq 6$.

Steinerberger \cite{St25} has observed that, for $r=2$, this problem is equivalent to asking for solutions to\[\phi(n)+\phi(n+\phi(n))=n,\]and has shown that if this holds then either the odd part of $n$ is in $\{1,3,5,7,35,47\}$, or is equal to $8m+7$ or $6m+5$, where $8m+7\geq 10^{10}$ is a prime number and $\phi(6m+5)=4m+4$. Whether there are infinitely many such $m$ is related to the question of whether\[\phi(n)=\frac{2}{3}(n+1)\]has infinitely many solutions.

Cambie conjectures that the only solutions have $r=2$ and $n=2^lp$ for some $l\geq 1$ and $p\in \{2,3,5,7,35,47\}$. Cambie has shown this problem is reducible to the question of which integers $r,t\geq 1$ and primes $p\equiv 7\pmod{8}$ satisfy $g_k(2p^t)=4p^t$, and conjectures there are no solutions to this except when $t=1$ and $p\in \{7,47\}$. Cambie has also observed that\[g_{k+4}(738)=3g_k(738),\]\[g_{k+4}(148646)=4g_k(148646),\]and\[g_{k+4}(4325798)=4g_{k}(4325798)\]for all $k\geq 1$.
References:
- [St25] S. Steinerberger, On an iterated arithmetic function problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham. arXiv:2504.08023 (2025).

forum_comments.author: hoodieuser
forum_comments.text:
Following Steinerberger (arXiv:2504.08023), the remaining question is whether any prime $p \geq 10^{10}$ satisfies $\varphi((3p-1)/4) = (p+1)/2$. Setting $m = (3p-1)/4$, this is equivalent to $\varphi(m) = \frac{2}{3}(m+1)$.

Steinerberger lists four solutions $m \in \{5, 35, 1295, 1679615\}$ with factorisations $35 = 5 \cdot 7$, $1295 = 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 37$, $1679615 = 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 37 \cdot 1297$. I prove these are the only squarefree solutions, and identify the structure behind them.

Define $q_1 = 5$, $q_2 = 7$, and $q_{k+1} = (q_k - 1)^2 + 1$ for $k \geq 2$. This gives $5, 7, 37, 1297, 1679617, \ldots$ The squarefree solutions to $\varphi(m) = \frac{2}{3}(m+1)$ are exactly the partial products $m_k = q_1 q_2 \cdots q_k$, provided each $q_i$ is prime.

Proof sketch. For $m = p_1 p_2$ squarefree with two primes, the equation rearranges to $p_2 = (3p_1 - 1)/(p_1 - 3)$, whose only prime solution is $(p_1, p_2) = (5, 7)$. Given a $k$-prime solution $m_k$, adjoining a new prime $q$ and solving the resulting linear equation in $q$ yields $q = (q_k - 1)^2 + 1$ uniquely. For three primes $\{5, 7, q_3\}$: $72(q_3 - 1) = 70q_3 + 2$ gives $q_3 = 37$. For four primes $\{5, 7, 37, q_4\}$: $2q_3 q_4 - 72q_3 - 72q_4 + 70 = 0$ gives $q_4 = (36 \cdot 37 - 35)/(37 - 36) = 1297$.

The first four values $5, 7, 37, 1297$ are all prime, giving solutions $m \in \{5, 35, 1295, 1679615\}$. The fifth, $q_5 = 1679617 = 17 \times 98801$, is composite, so the chain terminates at four squarefree solutions.

Of these, only $m = 5$ and $m = 35$ yield a prime $p = (4m+1)/3$ (namely $p = 7$ and $p = 47$), confirming Steinerberger's list for the squarefree case. The values $m = 1295$ and $m = 1679615$ yield composite $p$ ($1727 = 11 \times 157$ and $2239487$). Computational search to $m = 10^6$ finds no non-squarefree solutions either.

(AI-assisted analysis using Claude. All algebraic identities and primality claims verified computationally.)

On the question of solutions of $\phi (n)= \frac{2}{3} (n+1)$, Steinerberger in [St25] finds only four solutions $(5, 35, 1195, 1679615)$ and no other solution under $10^{10}$.

C. Hercher in "On positive integers $n$ with $\phi (n)= \frac{2}{3} (n+1)$" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19915) has proved the following results:

- Every solution $n$ must be square-free.
- If $p$ and $q$ are prime factors of a solution $n$ then $p \nmid (q-1)$.
- Any solution additional to the set given in [St25] has to have at least $7$ prime factors.
- For any additional solution it holds $n ≥ 10^{14}$

problem:
Let $\omega(n)$ count the number of distinct primes dividing $n$. Are there infinitely many $n$ such that, for all $m<n$, we have $m+\omega(m) \leq n$?

Can one show that there exists an $\epsilon>0$ such that there are infinitely many $n$ where $m+\epsilon \omega(m)\leq n$ for all $m<n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/413.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 17 April 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er79} Erd\H{o}s calls such an $n$ a 'barrier' for $\omega$. Some other natural number theoretic functions (such as $\phi$ and $\sigma$) have no barriers because they increase too rapidly. Erd\H{o}s believed that $\omega$ should have infinitely many barriers. In \cite{Er79d} he proves that $F(n)=\prod k_i$, where $n=\prod p_i^{k_i}$, has infinitely many barriers (in fact the set of barriers has positive density in the integers).

Erd\H{o}s also believed that $\Omega$, the count of the number of prime factors with multiplicity), should have infinitely many barriers. Selfridge found the largest barrier for $\Omega$ which is $<10^5$ is $99840$.

In \cite{ErGr80} this problem is suggested as a way of showing that the iterated behaviour of $n\mapsto n+\omega(n)$ eventually settles into a single sequence, regardless of the starting value of $n$ (see also [412] and [414]).

Erd\H{o}s and Graham report it could be attacked by sieve methods, but 'at present these methods are not strong enough'.

Lau \cite{La26} (see [679]) has provided a positive answer to the second question, and proved a weaker version of the first: there exists a constant $C$ such that, for infinitely many $n$,\[m+\omega(m) \leq n\]for all $1\leq m\leq n-C$.

The sequence of barriers for $\omega$ is A005236 (https://oeis.org/A005236) in the OEIS.

This is discussed in problem B8 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}. See also [647] and [679]

- [Er79] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some unconventional problems in number theory. Math. Mag. (1979), 67-70.
- [Er79d] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unconventional problems in number theory. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1979), 71-80.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [La26] C. F. Lau, On the number of prime factors of consecutive integers. arXiv:2604.15042 (2026).

problem: For any $n$ let $F(n)$ be the largest $k$ such that any of the $k!$ possible ordering patterns appears in some sequence of $\phi(m+1),\ldots,\phi(m+k)$ with $m+k\leq n$. Is it true that\[F(n)=(c+o(1))\log\log\log n\]for some constant $c$? Is the first pattern which fails to appear always\[\phi(m+1)>\phi(m+2)>\cdots >\phi(m+k)?\]Is it true that the 'natural' ordering which mimics what happens to $\phi(1),\ldots,\phi(k)$ is the most likely to appear?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/415.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 19 April 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{ErGr80} it is left ambiguous whether an 'ordering pattern' involves strict inequalities or allows equality. Weisenberg has observed that the final question only makes sense if we allow equality.

In \cite{ErGr80} it is claimed that Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er36b} proved that\[F(n)\asymp \log\log\log n,\]and similarly if we replace $\phi$ with $\sigma$ or $\tau$ or $\nu$ or any 'decent' additive or multiplicative function, but this does not seem to be present in \cite{Er36b}, which only shows that the number of $m\leq n$ such that $\phi(m)<\phi(m+1)$ is $\sim n/2$, and similarly for $\phi(m)>\phi(m+1)$. The following asymptotic shows that such a result is false regardless.

Pollack, Pomerance, and Trevi\~{n}o \cite{PPT13} have proved that, if $G(n)$ is the maximum $k$ such that\[\phi(m+1)> \phi(m+2)>\cdots > \phi(m+k)\]for some $m$ with $m+k\leq n$, then\[G(n)\sim \frac{\log\log\log n}{\log\log\log\log\log\log n}.\]The same asymptotic holds if we replace $>$ with $<,\leq,\geq$. Since $F(n)\leq G(n)$ trivially, this answers the first question in the negative.

Chojeckl and GPT-5.4 have sketched (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos415.pdf) how the proof of \cite{PPT13} can be adapted to obtain the same asymptotic for an arbitrary pattern of (strict) inequalities.

Note that a positive answer to the final question would imply that there exist infinitely many $n$ with $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$, which is the subject of [1003].
References:
- [Er36b] Erd\H{o}s, P., On a problem of Chowla and some related problems. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. (1936), 530-540.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [PPT13] Pollack, Paul and Pomerance, Carl and Trevi\~no, Enrique, Sets of monotonicity for {E}uler's totient function. Ramanujan J. (2013), 379--398.

problem: Let $V(x)$ count the number of $n\leq x$ such that $\phi(m)=n$ is solvable. Does $V(2x)/V(x)\to 2$? Is there an asymptotic formula for $V(x)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/416.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 September 2025.
Site remarks:
Pillai \cite{Pi29} proved $V(x)=o(x)$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er35b} proved $V(x)=x(\log x)^{-1+o(1)}$.

The behaviour of $V(x)$ is now almost completely understood. Maier and Pomerance \cite{MaPo88} proved\[V(x)=\frac{x}{\log x}e^{(C+o(1))(\log\log\log x)^2},\]for some explicit constant $C>0$. Ford \cite{Fo98} improved this to\[V(x)\asymp\frac{x}{\log x}e^{C_1(\log\log\log x-\log\log\log\log x)^2+C_2\log\log\log x-C_3\log\log\log\log x}\]for some explicit constants $C_1,C_2,C_3>0$. Unfortunately this falls just short of an asymptotic formula for $V(x)$ and determining whether $V(2x)/V(x)\to 2$.

In \cite{Er79e} Erd\H{o}s asks further to estimate the number of $n\leq x$ such that the smallest solution to $\phi(m)=n$ satisfies $kx<m\leq (k+1)x$.

See also [417] and [821].

forum_comments.author: BorisAlexeev
forum_comments.text:
The sequence $V'(x)$ is in the OEIS as A061070 (https://oeis.org/A061070). "On the number of distinct values of Euler’s φ-function" (https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/PDF/67.pdf) (1988) by Maier and Pomerance prove that it is asymptotically $\frac{x}{\log(x)} \exp\{(C+o(1))(\log \log \log x)^2\}$ for an explicit constant $C$. In particular, $V'(x)$ is $o(x)$. Apparently, "On some functions connected with φ(n)" (1929) by Pillai was the first to prove this. Later, "On the normal number of prime factors of p−1 and some related problems concerning Euler’s φ-function" (1935) by Erdős and "On the values of Euler’s φ-function" (1973) and "Distinct values of Euler’s φ-function" (1976) both by Erdős&Hall proved versions closer to the asymptotic expression above. (See also "The distribution of totients" by Kevin Ford (https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.3264).)

The sequence $V(x)$ is in the OEIS as A070243 (https://oeis.org/A070243). "Some remarks on Euler’s φ-function and some related problems" (1945) by Erdős was apparently the first to prove that $V(x)/x$ tends to a limit, which can be evaluated as $\zeta(2)\zeta(3)/\zeta(6)$. (See also "The distribution of values of the Euler function" (1972) by Bateman.)

In other words, I believe that $V(x)/V'(x)$ tends to infinity and this was proven by [Pillai in 1929 and] Erdős himself in 1935 and 1945. Color me confused.

forum_comments.author: BorisAlexeev
forum_comments.text:
Okay, thanks to the OEIS links, perhaps I can resolve my confusion?

The OEIS links suggest that $V(x)$ is actually in the OEIS as A264810 (https://oeis.org/A264810), not A070243 (https://oeis.org/A070243) as I said. The difference is this: A264810 counts the number of different values of $\phi(m)$ that are less than $x$, whereas A070243 counts the number of different values of $m$ such that $\phi(m)\le x$. If different values $m_1$ and $m_2$ have $\phi(m_1)=\phi(m_2)\le x$, then the former counts it only once whereas the latter counts it twice. Naturally, this makes a big difference for the conjecture.

I believe that A264810 (as linked presently) is indeed the correct interpretation of $V(x)$, and my own comment I'm replying to was incorrect regarding the meaning of $V(x)$ (but hopefully correct otherwise).

If $\tau(n)$ counts the number of divisors of $n$ then let\[F(f,n)=\frac{\tau((n+\lfloor f(n)\rfloor)!)}{\tau(n!)}.\]Is it true that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}F((\log n)^C,n)=\infty\]for large $C$?

More generally, if $f(n)\leq \log n$ is a monotonic function such that $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$, then is $F(f,n)$ everywhere dense?

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
In [EGIP96] (also mentioned in #419 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/419)), the authors prove $\liminf_{n \rightarrow \infty} F(c \log n, n) \le 2$ for any constant $c > 0$, using ideas used in bounds on large prime gaps (which means that this result can perhaps be slightly improved by the resolution of #4 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/4), although I haven't checked), while $\liminf_{n \rightarrow \infty} F(n^{4/9}, n) \ge 2$. In fact, their results/proofs give $\liminf_{n \rightarrow \infty} F(c \log n, n) = 1$ and $\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} F(n^{4/9}, n) = \infty$ respectively.

This exponent $4/9$ can certainly be improved a little, but I'm not sure by how much. So as far as I can tell, $f(n) = n^{4/9}$ is the slowest growing function for which it is known that $F(f, n)$ goes to infinity with $n$. And for those interested, let me quickly say a few words on the idea behind the proof of this result.

By Lemma $1$ in their paper, the ratio $\frac{\tau(n!)}{\tau((n-1)!)}$ is well-approximated by $1 + \frac{S(n)}{n}$, where $S(n)$ is the sum of the prime factors of $n$ (counted with multiplicity). Hence, to determine $F(f, n)$ it is more or less sufficient to determine the value of $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{f(n)} S(n+i)$. In particular, if you have sufficiently many $n+i \in (n, n + f(n))$ which are divisible by large primes, then those $S(n+i)$ will also be large, and thereby so will $F(f, n)$ be.

All in all, proving bounds on the number of integers in short intervals that have a large prime factor, captures the essential difficulty of this problem.

Note by the way that $F(1, n) \le 2$ with equality if, and only if, $n+1$ is prime, so that $\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} F(g(n) \log^2 n, n) = \infty$ follows from Cramér's conjecture for any function $g(n)$ that goes to infinity with $n$. Unconditionally, for such functions $g(n)$ we have $\limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} F(g(n), n) = \infty$, by results on bounded prime gaps.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Here's the complete rewrite of the paper (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos421-mod.pdf), following suggestion by Terence Tao to make the proof 'modular' so that various parts are as independent as possible. I think it greatly streamlined proof and divided it into 4 parts. All feedback welcome: critique, simplifications, suggestions.

We build a density-one set $A\subset\mathbb N$ whose increasing enumeration has distinct products of consecutive blocks, by first building a density-one set $A_0$ with certain special properties. Then the construction of $A$ is dyadic: for each large dyadic $X$ we delete a small set $D_X\subset[X,2X)$ and set\[
A:=A_0\setminus\bigcup_{X\ \mathrm{dyadic}}D_X,
\]so the key is to ensure simultaneously: (i) $\sum_{X\le N}|D_X|=o(N)$ (density), and (ii) every collision with maximal term $m\in[X,2X)$ is hit by $D_X$ (hitting).

Module I (sprinkling)
Independently delete each $n\ge3$ with probability $\delta(n)=1/(\log n)^2$ and let $A_0$ be the complement. Almost surely $A_0$ has density $1$ and, by a union bound plus Borel-Cantelli, all "long" collisions are eliminated: for all sufficiently large maximal terms $m$ there is no collision whose degree satisfies\[
\max(\ell,k+1)\ \ge\ L(m):=10(\log m)^3.
\]Thus, from this point on we only need to kill the remaining logarithmic-regime collisions with $d=\max(\ell,k+1)\le L(X)$ at each dyadic scale $X$. We also make sure that $A_0$ is locally regular.

Module II + III (encoding + Diophantine bounds)
Module II shows that under a capacity constraint at scale $X$ (at most $T(X)$ deletions in every length-$L(X)$ interval), the predecessor lists of length $\le L(X)$ are determined by bounded local windows, so every logarithmic collision is encoded by an integer point $(x,y)\in[X,2X)^2$ on a split-product curve\[
\prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}(x-a_i)\;=\;\prod_{j=0}^{k}(y+b_j),
\qquad
d=\max(\ell,k+1)\le L(X),
\qquad
a_i,b_j\ll L(X)+T(X)+U(X).
\]Module III supplies uniform point bounds for these curves: for short degrees $d<d_0(X)$, Bombieri--Pila plus a parameter count implies the set of possible endpoints is $o(X)$; for long degrees $d_0(X)\le d\le L(X)$, uniform determinant-method bounds (CCDN) give $X^{o(1)}$ points per absolutely irreducible component, and Bilu--Tichy with Hajdu--Tijdeman shows any remaining degenerate families are Pell/Dickson-type and contribute only $O(\log X)$ points in a dyadic box.

Module IV (dyadic deletion via Moser--Tardos)
At each dyadic $X$ we choose $D_X\subset[X,2X)\cap A_0$ by an algorithmic Lovasz local lemma: introduce Bernoulli variables $(\xi_n)$ (randomness exposed on a buffered universe $[X/2,2X)\cap A_0$ to avoid edge effects), define capacity bad events $\mathsf B_I^{+}$ (overflow) on length-$L(X)$ intervals and collision cylinder events $\mathsf A_\tau$ (patterns on local windows encoding a specific collision). A one-way coverage lemma shows that if a logarithmic-length collision occurs in $B_X$ with maximal term lying in $[X,2X)$, then at least one collision cylinder event occurs. Moreover, the maximum dependency degree of the bad-event graph is $X^{o(1)}$, coming from the window size and the admissible-pattern count. The asymmetric LLL (implemented by Moser-Tardos) yields an assignment with no bad events, hence capacity holds and no collision with maximal term in $[X,2X)$ survives. Since $|D_X|=o(X)$ for each dyadic $X$, the final assembly preserves density $1$ and eliminates all collisions.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
This looks promising, but does need careful checking, particularly with regards to whether the bounds coming from the algebraic geometry or Diophantine geometry inputs are strong enough (and uniform enough). A lot of dependencies of constants in that literature (on, say, degree or height) are poor, non-uniform or even ineffective, and this to me is the most dangerous source of errors. (The combinatorial inputs are much more quantitative, and often contain exponential gains (e.g., due to concentration of measure), so I am less concerned about this side of the argument, although it is still important to do the quantitative bookkeeping carefully.) Having a human-generated version of the argument that carefully discusses the nature of these bounds, and their uniformity, will be more reassuring than an AI-generated proof that does not focus on this issue.

Additionally, it is unlikely that many of these inputs will be easily formalizable in Lean with current tools. Probably the best one can hope for is a conditional formalization in which key theorems from past literature are carefully formalized as precise axioms. However, this would still add a lot of credibility to the argument (once the axiom statements are scrutinized carefully by humans, particularly with regards to the order in which quantifiers are placed). Ideally, these axioms should be formalized by humans first, before running the automated tools to try to derive the main result from the given axioms; letting the AI tool state the axioms it would like to use is a particularly risky idea and should be avoided if at all possible.

With regards to cleaning up the writing, one can try to make the proof more modular: for instance, create a theorem describing the existence of a set $A_0$ obeying certain explicit properties that will be used in later parts of the argument, but hide the implementation details of how the $A_0$ is constructed within the proof of that theorem, so that $A_0$ can be used as a "black box". This type of modularity will help both with human readability of the argument and with formalization, and could also increase the robustness of the proof in case some local errors are found.

forum_comments.text:
Congrats on the print! I read it and it looks promising I agree but theres a few things I saw that might be iffy. If I'm wrong about these you can let me know.

The first is that the split product (6) doesn't match the collision equation (2). Collision is defined as
 $$
 d_{M-\ell+1}\cdots d_M ;=; d_N\cdots d_{N+k}.
 $$
Then the paper sets $x=d_M$ and $y=d_{N+k}$, defines $b_j := d_{N+j}-d_N$ and claims
 $$
 x(x-a_1)\cdots ;=; y(y+b_1)\cdots(y+b_k).
 $$
But with $y=d_{N+k}$, the right-side factors in (2) are $(d_N,\dots,d_{N+k})$ so they are $\le y$ and should look like $y-\text{something}$, not $y+b_j$ with $b_j\ge 0$. As written, the factors $y+b_j$ do not correspond to the block $(d_N,\dots,d_{N+k})$.

2. Lemma 4.1 uses forward on the $y$ side, which matches the same endpoint/sign confusion. After bounding shifts on the $x$ side, Lemma 4.1 states that the same argument applies forward on the $y$ side. But earlier in the same section it declared $y=d_{N+k}$, the right endpoint of the right block. If $y$ is the right endpoint, the relevant block elements lie to the left of $y$, so the analogous argument should run backward.

3. Lemma 6.1 claims every window contains at least $L$ kept points but the proof ignores holes coming from $A_0$. At scale $X$, the eligible variables are
 $$
 V_X := [X,2X)\cap A_0,
 $$
and deletions satisfy $D_X=B_X\subseteq V_X$. Lemma 6.1 defines windows $W_y\subseteq V_X$ and asserts that under (7), every interval of length $L+2T$ contains at least $L$ kept points and the proof deduces this from $|D_X\cap I|\le T$. That deduction implicitly treats $V_X$ as if it contained all integers in the interval but eligibility is restricted to $A_0$ and $A_0$ comes from a sprinkling step so it can miss many integers. The conclusion that the local predecessor lies inside $W_y$ isn't really justified from the stated assumptions.

4. Lemma 6.2 subtracts from $L$ instead of from $|A_0\cap J|$. Lemma 6.2 claims that every length $L$ interval $J$ contains at least $L-T$ integers of
 $$
 ([X/2,2X)\cap A_0)\setminus(D^{<X}\cup B_X).
 $$
The proof uses $\neg B_J$ to get $|(D^{<X}\cup B_X)\cap J|\le T$ and subtracts from $L$. But the quantity being lower bounded is
 $$
 |(A_0\cap J)| ;-; |(D^{<X}\cup B_X)\cap J|,
 $$
so the bound is $|A_0\cap J|-T$, not $L-T$. Since $|A_0\cap J|$ need not equal $L$.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
I'm very close to finishing it off, but some minor technicalities still persist. Any help would be appreciated here with the write-up. (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos421.pdf) Generally, the strategy follows what Terence Tao outlined in a comment, and then applies Bilu-Tichy and Hajdu-Tijdeman for degeneracy classification, and determinant-method bounds via Castryck–Cluckers–Dittmann–Nguye for uniform counting for non-degenerate cases.

Here is a route that I think makes the "main trouble case'' $k,\ell\asymp \log N$ fully tractable with known tools. Run a prefix-stable greedy construction: scan $n=2,3,\dots$ and include $n$ unless it creates a new relation\[
d_{M-\ell+1}\cdots d_M \;=\; d_N\cdots d_{N+k},
\qquad M<N,
\]among consecutive blocks in the current sequence. Prefix-stability ensures later decisions cannot create new collisions among earlier terms, so it suffices to show that the set of rejected $n\le N$ is $o(N)$. For $n\in[X,2X]$, any rejection produces an integer point $(x,y)\in[X,2X]^2$ on a separated-variable curve\[
\prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}(x-a_i)=\prod_{j=0}^{k}(y+b_j),
\qquad d:=\max(\ell,k+1)\asymp \log X,
\]with shifts $a_i,b_j$ coming from local consecutive gaps.

For the hard regime $d\asymp\log X$, the determinant method with polynomial dependence on $d$ gives a uniform polylogarithmic bound on integral points per curve once line components are excluded. Concretely, applying Castryck--Cluckers--Dittmann--Nguyen (polynomial-in-$d$ bounds for integral points on affine curves) to\[
F_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}(x,y):=\prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}(x-a_i)-\prod_{j=0}^{k}(y+b_j)=0
\]yields\[
\#\bigl\{(x,y)\in[X,2X]^2\cap\mathbb Z ^2:\ F_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}(x,y)=0\bigr\}\ \ll\ (\log X)^{O(1)}
\]uniformly in the shifts, provided $F_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}$ has no linear factor over $\mathbb Q$ (i.e. no affine line component). This directly attacks the $k,\ell\asymp\log N$ bottleneck.

It remains to control the exceptional ''low-genus'' situations. By Bilu--Tichy (and the Hajdu--Tijdeman refinement in the simple-rational-roots setting relevant to split products), any bounded-denominator degeneracy forces either an affine/translate relation (line component: $f(x)\equiv g(x+t)$) or an explicit $m=2$ PTE/Pell-type family. Line components correspond to affine equivalence of the root multisets and can be removed at zero density (or shown to be only trivial overlap configurations). The remaining PTE/Pell-type components contribute only $O(\log X)$ points per dyadic box. Summing over dyadic $X$ shows only $o(X)$ rejections in $[X,2X]$, hence $o(N)$ rejections up to $N$, producing a density-$1$ sequence with all consecutive-block products distinct.

P.S. I should add that this is done via a long and complex conversation with GPT-5.2, trying to 'unstuck it' over and over to find the path forward.

forum_comments.author: uona
forum_comments.text:
Quick tightening on the line component / affine-translate relation exception. In the actual collision setting (monotone $d_i$, hence $M<N$ so $x=d_M<y=d_N$), an affine line component cannot contribute any genuine collision points.

Write
$$
f(x)=\prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}(x-a_i),\qquad g(y)=\prod_{j=0}^{k}(y+b_j),
$$
with
$$
a_i=d_M-d_{M-i}\ge 0,\quad b_j=d_{N+j}-d_N\ge 0,\quad a_0=b_0=0.
$$
If $F_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}(x,y)=f(x)-g(y)$ has an affine line component, then (as in the line-component lemma) it forces an identity
$$
f(x)\equiv g(x+t)\quad\text{or}\quad f(x)\equiv g(-x+t),
$$
i.e. the line is $y=x+t$ or $y=-x+t$.

(i) $f(x)\equiv g(x+t)$ (line $y=x+t$).
Roots of $f$ are the multiset ${a_i}\subset[0,\infty)$. Roots of $g(x+t)$ are the multiset ${-t-b_j}$. Since $b_0=0$, we get $-t\in{a_i}$, hence $t\le 0$. Therefore $y=x+t\le x$, so this line contains no points with $x<y$ (hence cannot encode a collision with $M<N$).

(ii) $f(x)\equiv g(-x+t)$ (line $y=-x+t$).
Roots of $g(-x+t)$ are the multiset ${t+b_j}$ (since $-x+t+b_j=0\iff x=t+b_j$), so in particular $t$ is a root (from $b_0=0$) and all roots are $\ge t$. But $f$ has the root $0$ (since $a_0=0$), so $0$ must also be a root of $g(-x+t)$, i.e. $t+b_j=0$ for some $j$. With $t\ge0$ and $b_j\ge0$ this forces $t=0$. Then the line is $y=-x$, which has no points in $[X,2X]^2$ for $X>0$.

So the affine line component exception is actually harmless here. It yields zero relevant collision points in the regime $x,y>0$ with $x<y$. This lets you treat the determinant method bound as applying to all collision-producing curves, without needing an extra remove line components at zero density maneuver.

Note that this just removes a case and simplifies dependencies. This was half done with ChatGPT in a string of questions and then reviewed.
