forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I think there is a decent chance to solve this problem with known techniques. We are trying to find a dense sequence with no non-trivial solutions to the equation
$$ d_{M-l+1} \dots d_M = d_N \dots d_{N+k} \quad (*).$$
We can remove any common factors and assume that $M<N$. This also forces $l > k$ from the monotonicity of the $d_i$, so in particular $k < N$. We want $d_N \sim N$, so all the factors on the RHS need to be $\asymp N$. Taking logarithms, we get $l \log M \asymp k \log N$.

By the Hardy-Ramanujan law, it is reasonable to demand that each $d_i$ has $\approx \log\log i$ prime factors (counting multiplicity). By counting the total number of primes on both sides of (*), this already handles the case when $k$ is bounded (the LHS and RHS have noticeably distinct prime factors) or even $k = O(\sqrt{\log\log N})$, and in general it implies that $l \log\log M \asymp k \log\log N$, which in conjunction with the previous constraint yields $\log M \asymp \log N$ and $l \asymp k$.

For medium $k$, specifically $\sqrt{\log\log N} \ll k \leq \varepsilon \log N$ for a small $\varepsilon$, one can view (*) as a degree $l$ polynomial equation
$$ (x-a_{l-1}) \dots (x-a_1) x = y (y+b_1) \dots (y+b_k)$$
where $x = d_M$, $y = d_N$, $a_i = d_M - d_{M-i}$, and $b_i = d_{N+i} - d_N$. There are (morally) $N^{O(\varepsilon)}$ choices for the $a_1,\dots,a_{l-1},b_1,\dots,b_k$, and by Bombieri-Pila type bounds there should be only $N^{1-c}$ many integer solutions to this equation with $x,y = O(N)$ for some absolute constant $c>0$ (one has to check that the locus of this equation contains no straight lines, but I think this should be routine). So the set of solutions here is density zero and should be removable somehow.

For large $k$, specifically in the regime where $k/\log N$ goes to infinity, I think performing a random sampling, deleting $o(1)$ of the elements of the sequence, should destroy all solutions to (*) with positive probability (here we may first want to prepare the sequence so that each $d_i$ has a relatively large prime factor, and use the fact that nearby elements of the sequence cannot share that large prime factor, somewhat in the spirit of Selfridge's construction).

So the main case that causes trouble is when $k,l \asymp \log N$, but perhaps one of the above techniques can be pushed a little further to cover this case also.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Here’s how we can push the Bombieri--Pila/determinant-method approach into the remaining regime $k,\ell\asymp \log N$. Full write-up is here (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos421.pdf). It still falls short of settling the problem but pushes the above a bit further.

Any collision\[
d_{M-\ell+1}\cdots d_M \;=\; d_N\cdots d_{N+k}\qquad (M<N)
\]can be rewritten with $x=d_M$, $y=d_N$, $a_i:=d_M-d_{M-i}$ ($1\le i\le \ell-1$), $b_j:=d_{N+j}-d_N$ ($1\le j\le k$) as an integer point on\[
F_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}(x,y):=\prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}(x-a_i)-\prod_{j=0}^{k}(y+b_j)=0,\qquad (a_0=b_0=0),
\]a plane curve of degree $d=\max(\ell,k+1)\asymp \log X$ when $x,y\asymp X$ (the bottleneck case).

The key observation is that large degree actually helps in the exponent: for each non-degenerate pattern $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ (i.e. $F_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}$ has no line/rational component), determinant-method bounds give\[
\#\{(x,y)\in[X,2X]^2\cap\Bbb Z^2:\ F_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}(x,y)=0\}\ \ll_{d,\varepsilon}\ X^{1/d+\varepsilon},
\]hence $\ll X^{\varepsilon}$ since $X^{1/d}\asymp e^{O(1)}$ for $d\asymp\log X$ (and the $d$-dependence in the implied constant is expected to be only $X^{o(1)}$ once $d\ll \log X$). Degenerate patterns can be isolated using Bilu--Tichy for $f(x)=g(y)$ with $f=\prod(x-a_i)$, $g=\prod(y+b_j)$: infinite ''special'' solution sets force $f,g$ into the standard-pair/composition classes, and for products of distinct linear factors this should collapse to an explicit finite/rigid exceptional family (essentially affine-equivalence of the root multisets, corresponding to overlap/trivial configurations), which can be removed at zero-density cost.

What remains is a pattern-counting input: in a density-$1$ construction one can enforce a local deficiency invariant (e.g. at most $T(X)=(\log X)^{2/3}$ deletions in any interval of length $C\log X$), which implies the number of realized gap-patterns of length $\asymp\log X$ up to scale $2X$ is only\[
\sum_{j\le T(X)} \binom{C\log X+j}{j} \;=\; X^{o(1)}.
\]Therefore the total number of bottleneck collisions with $(x,y)\in[X,2X]^2$ is $X^{\varepsilon+o(1)}=o(X)$. One can then choose a hitting set $B_X\subset[X,2X]$ (e.g. pick one endpoint from each collision, with a union-bound/LLL nibble to preserve the local deficiency invariant) and delete dyadically; the total deletions are $o(N)$, giving density $1$ and killing all collisions, including the $k,\ell\asymp\log N$ regime, modulo the two technical verifications (degenerate-pattern classification and tracking $d$-dependence for $d\asymp\log X$).

problem: Let $a_1=1$ and $a_2=2$ and for $k\geq 3$ choose $a_k$ to be the least integer $>a_{k-1}$ which is the sum of at least two consecutive terms of the sequence. What is the asymptotic behaviour of this sequence?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/423.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 March 2026.
Site remarks:
Asked by Hofstadter (in \cite{Er77c} Erd\H{o}s says Hofstadter was inspired by a similar question of Ulam). The sequence begins\[1,2,3,5,6,8,10,11,\ldots\]and is A005243 (https://oeis.org/A005243) in the OEIS.

Bolan (https://github.com/mjtb49/HofstaderUlam/blob/main/HofstaderUlamSequence.pdf) and Tang \cite{Ta26} have independently proved that there are infinitely many integers which do not appear in this sequence. In fact, the sequence $a_n-n$ is nondecreasing and unbounded.

Tang \cite{Ta26} further proved that $a_n \ll n^{\frac{1}{c-1}+o(1)}$, where $c$ is any exponent such that $\lvert A-A\rvert \geq \lvert A\rvert^{c-o(1)}$ for all convex sets $A$. In particular, the latest bounds of Cushman \cite{Cu25} yield\[a_n \ll n^{\frac{688}{413}+o(1)}\leq n^{1.6659+o(1)},\]and the conjecture of Erd\H{o}s and Hegyv\'{a}ri that one can take $c=2$ in the convex set problem would imply $a_n\leq n^{1+o(1)}$. It seems likely that $a_n=n+o(n)$ is the truth.

Tang has further proved (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-423/blob/main/423_quant_lower_v1.txt) an improved lower bound of\[a_n=n+\Omega(\log\log n).\]
References:
- [Cu25] A. Cushman, A Note on the Sum-Product Problem and the Convex Sumset Problem. arXiv:2512.13849 (2025).
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [Ta26] Q. Tang, The Hofstadter consecutive-sum sequence omits infinitely many positive integers. arXiv:2603.09939 (2026).

forum_comments.author: matthew_bolan
forum_comments.text:
This upper bound is awesome!

A while ago I was able to find a simple argument showing a quadratic upper bound, I have not studied your paper so perhaps the argument is already known to you. I never was able to beat quadratic by much, and certainly not to the degree you have.

The point of my argument is that there is an anti-correlation between the twofold sums and the fourfold sums. Suppose there are $k$ elements of the sequence in the interval $(x, 2x]$. Then there are at least $k-3$ elements in $(4x, 8x]$ coming from fourfold sums. We want to show that there is a twofold sum in each interval $(a_{i} + a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} + a_{i+3}, a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} + a_{i+3} + a_{i+4}).$ This follows as there is a portion of the sequence which looks like $(a_{i+1} + a_{i+2}) = c_0, c_1, ..., c_s =(a_{i+2} + a_{i+3})$, and selecting a $j < s$ such that $c_j \le a_{i+1} + a_{i+3}$ and $c_{j+1} \ge a_{i+1} + a_{i+3}$ we have $c_j + c_{j+1}$ in the needed interval. We conclude that there are at least $2k - 7$ entries of the sequence in $(4x, 8x]$ (or $2k-5$ if one handles the boundaries better). This implies that if there are at least $c2^n + 14$ entries of the sequence less than $4^n$, then there are at least $c2^{n+1} + 14$ entries less than $4^{n+1}$, so the sequence exhibits at most quadratic growth.

forum_comments.author: BorisAlexeev
forum_comments.text:
> What do you mean by "the length of the minimal length representation"?

The "length" is $\ell$ in the following classic argument:

The sum of the $\ell$ consecutive integers starting at $m$ is $(m)+(m+1)+\cdots+(m+\ell-1)=\ell\cdot(2m+\ell-1)/2$. If this sum equals $n$, then we have $2n=\ell\cdot(2m+\ell-1)$. Moreover, note that the sum of the two factors $\ell$ and $2m+\ell-1$ is $2(m+\ell)-1$, which is odd; it follows that exactly one of the factors is odd. Conversely, for every odd factor $d$ of $2n$, we can either let $\ell=d$ and $2m+\ell-1=2n/d$ or vice versa, and this corresponds to a decomposition.

For example, if $n=15$, then the possible odd factors are $1$, $3$, $5$, and $15$ and the possible decompositions are: $d=1$ giving rise to $15$ (the single-term sum) and $-14+\cdots+14+15$; $d=3$ giving rise to $4+5+6$ and $-3+\cdots+6$; $d=5$ giving rise to $1+2+3+4+5$ and $0+1+2+3+4+5$; and $d=15$ giving rise to $-6+\cdots+8$ and $7+8$.

If we restrict to sums of positive integers, then exactly one decomposition from each pair works. Moreover, its length is the smaller of the two factors $\min(d,2n/d)$. Also, this means that the number of ways of writing $n$ as the sum of consecutive positive integers equals the number of odd divisors of $n$.

If we further insist the sum have at least two terms, then this excludes exactly one decomposition (the one with $n$ by itself, corresponding to the odd divisor $1$ of $2n$). In particular, an integer $n$ has a nontrivial decomposition iff $2n$ has any odd divisor other than $1$. This happens iff $n$ is not a power of $2$.

If we try to analyze the smallest possible length $\ell$ (other than the single-term decomposition), we get the claim above: it comes either from the smallest nontrivial odd divisor $d$ of $2n$ (which is the smallest odd prime $p$ dividing $n$) or from the largest odd divisor $d$ of $2n$ (which then ends up having a length one more than the 2-adic valuation of $n$).

equals number of missed integers in \([1,a_k]\) that never appear among first \(k\) sequence terms.

Lemma B3 (A implies asymptotic for \(a_k\)):
If A gives asymptotic missing-count profile \(\psi\), then B2 yields
\[
a_k=k+\Theta(\psi(a_k)),
\]
which can be inverted to asymptotic growth law.
Proof.

problem: Let $a_1=2$ and $a_2=3$ and continue the sequence by appending to $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ all possible values of $a_ia_j-1$ with $i\neq j$. Is it true that the set of integers which eventually appear has positive density?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/424.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 31 March 2026.
Site remarks:
Asked by Hofstadter. The sequence begins $2,3,5,9,14,17,26,\ldots$ and is A005244 (https://oeis.org/A005244) in the OEIS. This problem is also discussed in section E31 of Guy's book Unsolved Problems in Number Theory.

In \cite{ErGr80} (and in Guy's book) this problem as written is asking for whether almost all integers appear in this sequence, but the answer to this is trivially no (as pointed out to me by Steinerberger): no integer $\equiv 1\pmod{3}$ is ever in the sequence, so the set of integers which appear has density at most $2/3$. This is easily seen by induction, and the fact that if $a,b\in \{0,2\}\pmod{3}$ then $ab-1\in \{0,2\}\pmod{3}$.

Presumably it is the weaker question of whether a positive density of integers appear (as correctly asked in \cite{Er77c}) that was also intended in \cite{ErGr80}. As with many of Erd\H{o}s' questions, by 'positive density' he most likely meant 'positive lower density' - in other words, does there exist $c>0$ such that for all large $x$ the number of values of $a_i$ in $[1,x]$ is at least $cx$?

See also Problem 63 of Green's open problems list (https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf).
References:
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

problem: Let $F(n)$ be the maximum possible size of a subset $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that the products $ab$ are distinct for all $a<b$. Is there a constant $c$ such that\[F(n)=\pi(n)+(c+o(1))n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}?\]If $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ is such that all products $a_1\cdots a_r$ are distinct for $a_1<\cdots <a_r$ then is it true that\[\lvert A\rvert \leq \pi(n)+O(n^{\frac{r+1}{2r}})?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/425.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er68} proved that there exist some constants $0<c_1\leq c_2$ such that\[\pi(n)+c_1 n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}\leq F(n)\leq \pi(n)+c_2 n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}.\]This problem can also be considered in the real numbers: that is, what is the size of the the largest $A\subset [1,x]$ such that for any distinct $a,b,c,d\in A$ we have $\lvert ab-cd\rvert \geq 1$? Erd\H{o}s had conjectured (see \cite{Er73} and \cite{Er77c}) that $\lvert A\rvert=o(x)$.

In \cite{ErGr80} Erd\H{o}s and Graham report that Alexander had given a construction disproving this conjecture, establishing that $\lvert A\rvert\gg x$ is possible. Alexander's construction is given in \cite{Er80}, and we sketch a simplified version. Let $B\subseteq [1,X^2]$ be a Sidon set of integers of size $\gg X$ and\[A=\{ X e^{b/X^2} : b\in B\}.\]It is easy to check that\[\lvert ab-cd\rvert \geq X^2\lvert 1-e^{1/X^2}\rvert \gg 1\]for distinct $a,b,c,d\in A$, and (after rescaling $A$ by some constant factor) this produces a set of size $\gg X$ with the desired property in the interval $[X,O(X)]$. Furthermore, a simple modification allows for $A$ to also be $1$-separated.

In \cite{Er77c} Erd\H{o}s considers a similar generalisation for sets of complex numbers or complex integers.

See also [490], [793], and [796].

forum_comments.text:
The lower bound was actually proven in this (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1938-07-Jav.pdf) 1938 paper by Erdős, using a result of Klein. In order to get both the known lower and upper bounds formalized by Aristotle, I asked ChatGPT to write up the proofs and further optimize them as much as possible. The result is that here (https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ErdosProblem425Lower.lean) you can find a formalization that gives $$F(n) > \pi(n) + \frac{cn^{3/4}}{(\log n)^{3/2}}$$for all $$c < \frac{2^{11/4}}{3^{3/4}} \approx 2.95$$and all large enough $n$. This formalization depends on the prime number theorem and the end result is about two orders of magnitude better than the $c = \frac{1}{36}$ that Erdős claims in his paper. Besides PNT no other external results are required.

Formalizing the upper bound turns out to be a bit more tricky than I'd hoped. The plan is to formalize a proof that $$F(n) < \pi(n) + \frac{cn^{3/4}}{(\log n)^{3/2}}$$holds for all $c$ larger than some constant $C_* < 13.1$ and all large enough $n$, but I haven't quite managed to finish off this project. So hopefully to be continued. For now, here are the remaining page numbers, including a bonus reference.

forum_comments.author: vilc
forum_comments.text:
Interesting result. Can you describe the construction in some detail, please? I have been thinking about this problem in recent weeks and I only got $c\approx 1.703$ with a rather convoluted adjustment to Erdős's 1938 construction. Here is a sketch of a simple argument which gives a lower bound with $c=2^{3/4}\approx 1.681$, based on Erdős's 1938 paper :
Take sets $A_1,A_2$ formed respectively of the primes below $\sqrt{n/2}$, and between $\sqrt{n/2}$ and $\sqrt{2n}$, so that $A_1 A_2 \subset \{1, \cdots,n\}$. By the PNT, these sets have approximately equal cardinality $M=\dfrac{\sqrt{2n}}{\log n}$. We form a projective plane of order $\approx M$ on $A_1$, and to each element $q$ of $A_2$ we associate a line of this plane, then form the products $pq$ for the $\approx\sqrt{M}$ primes $p$ on this line. There are $\approx M^{3/2}=\dfrac{2^{3/4}n^{3/4}}{(\log n)^{3/2}}$ such products in total, to which we append the primes above $\sqrt{2n}$. The set so constructed has cardinality about $\pi(n)+\dfrac{2^{3/4}n^{3/4}}{(\log n)^{3/2}}$ and has distinct products.

forum_comments.author: vilc
forum_comments.text: Thanks. To summarize, the idea is to create a stack with the projective plane construction at different (and carefully-chosen) scales. The fact that I had missed, and which is why the construction can scale with many layers, is that the sets where the projective planes are built are taken to be the sets of larger primes. The scales are chosen so that the large blocks are of constant sizes. I gave the layered construction to an optimizer for $k=20$ blocks and the constant $\tfrac{2^{11/4}}{3^{3/4}}$ seems optimal.

problem: Are there two infinite sets $A$ and $B$ such that $A+B$ agrees with the set of prime numbers up to finitely many exceptions?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/431.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Ostmann, sometimes known as the 'inverse Goldbach problem'. (In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s dates this to abou 25 years old, putting it at about 1955.)

The answer is surely no. The best result in this direction is due to Elsholtz and Harper \cite{ElHa15}, who showed that if $A,B$ are such sets then for all large $x$ we must have\[\frac{x^{1/2}}{\log x\log\log x} \ll \lvert A \cap [1,x]\rvert \ll x^{1/2}\log\log x\]and similarly for $B$.

Elsholtz \cite{El01} has proved there are no sets $A,B,C$ (all of size at least $2$) such that $A+B+C$ agrees with the set of prime numbers up to finitely many exceptions.

Granville \cite{Gr90} proved, conditional on the prime $k$-tuples conjecture, that there are infinite sets $B$ and $C$ such that\[\{ \tfrac{b+c}{2}: b\in B, c\in C\}\]is a subset of the primes. Tao and Ziegler \cite{TaZi23} gave an unconditional proof that there are infinite sets $B=\{b_1<\cdots\}$ and $C=\{c_1<\cdots\}$ such that\[\{ b_i+c_j : b_i\in B, c_j\in C, i<j\}\]is a subset of the primes.

See also [429] and [432].
References:
- [El01] Elsholtz, Christian, The inverse Goldbach problem. Mathematika (2001), 151-158.
- [ElHa15] Elsholtz, Christian and Harper, Adam J., Additive decompositions of sets with restricted prime factors. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. (2015), 7403-7427.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [Gr90] Granville, Andrew, A note on sums of primes. Canad. Math. Bull. (1990), 452--454.
- [TaZi23] Tao, Terence and Ziegler, Tamar, Infinite partial sumsets in the primes. J. Anal. Math. (2023), 375--389.

problem: If $p$ is a prime and $k,m\geq 2$ then let $r(k,m,p)$ be the minimal $r$ such that $r,r+1,\ldots,r+m-1$ are all $k$th power residues modulo $p$. Let\[\Lambda(k,m)=\limsup_{p\to \infty} r(k,m,p).\]Is it true that $\Lambda(k,2)$ is finite for all $k$? Is $\Lambda(k,3)$ finite for all odd $k$? How large are they?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/436.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 25 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Asked by Lehmer and Lehmer \cite{LeLe62}, who note that for example $\Lambda(2,2)=9$ - indeed, $9$ is always a quadratic residue, and if $10$ isn't then either $2$ or $5$ is, and hence at least one of $1,2$ or $4,5$ or $9,10$ is a consecutive pair of quadratic residues (and similarly there are infinitely many $p$ for which there are no consecutive quadratic residues below $9,10$).

A similar argument of Dunton \cite{Du65} proves $\Lambda(3,2)=77$, and Bierstedt and Mills \cite{BiMi63} proved $\Lambda(4,2)=1224$. Lehmer and Lehmer proved that $\Lambda(k,3)=\infty$ for all even $k$ and $\Lambda(k,4)=\infty$ for all $k\leq 1048909$.

Lehmer, Lehmer, and Mills \cite{LLM63} proved $\Lambda(5,2)=7888$ and $\Lambda(6,2)=202124$. Brillhart, Lehmer, and Lehmer \cite{BLL64} proved $\Lambda(7,2)=1649375$. Lehmer, Lehmer, Mills, and Selfridge \cite{LLMS62} proved that $\Lambda(3,3)=23532$.

Graham \cite{Gr64g} proved that $\Lambda(k,l)=\infty$ for all $k\geq 2$ and $l\geq 4$.

Hildebrand \cite{Hi91} resolved the first question, proving that $\Lambda(k,2)$ is finite for all $k$: in other words, for any $k\geq 2$, if $p$ is sufficiently large then there exists a pair of consecutive $k$th power residues modulo $p$ in $[1,O_k(1)]$.

The remaining questions are to examine whether $\Lambda(k,3)$ is finite for all odd $k\geq 5$, and the growth rate of $\Lambda(k,2)$ and $\Lambda(k,3)$ as functions of $k$.
References:
- [BLL64] Brillhart, John and Lehmer, D. H. and Lehmer, Emma, Bounds for pairs of consecutive seventh and higher power residues. Math. Comp. (1964), 397--407.
- [BiMi63] Bierstedt, R. G. and Mills, W. H., On the bound for a pair of consecutive quartic residues of a prime. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1963), 628--632.
- [Du65] Dunton, M., Bounds for pairs of cubic residues. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1965), 330--332.
- [Gr64g] Graham, R. L., On quadruples of consecutive {$k$}th power residues. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1964), 196--197.
- [Hi91] Hildebrand, Adolf, On consecutive {$k$}th power residues. II. Michigan Math. J. (1991), 241-253.

problem: How large must $y=y(\epsilon,n)$ be such that the number of integers in $(x,x+y)$ with a divisor in $(n,2n)$ is at most $\epsilon y$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/450.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
It is not clear what the intended quantifier on $x$ is. Cambie has observed that if this is intended to hold for all $x$ then, provided\[\epsilon(\log n)^\delta (\log\log n)^{3/2}\to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$, where $\delta=0.086\cdots$, there is no such $y$, which follows from an averaging argument and the work of Ford \cite{Fo08}.

On the other hand, Cambie has observed that if $\epsilon\ll 1/n$ then $y(\epsilon,n)\sim 2n$: indeed, if $y<2n$ then this is impossible taking $x+n$ to be a multiple of the lowest common multiple of $\{n+1,\ldots,2n-1\}$. On the other hand, for every fixed $\delta\in (0,1)$ and $n$ large every $2(1+\delta)n$ consecutive elements contains many elements which are a multiple of an element in $(n,2n)$.
References:
- [Fo08] Ford, Kevin, The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval. Ann. of Math. (2) (2008), 367-433.

forum_comments.text:
Here is a heuristic proof of this Problem.
Let\[
\mathcal P_k=\{p:\ p\ \text{prime},\ k<p<2k\},\qquad
M_k=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_k}p.
\]The condition that the whole block $[n-k,n-1]$ contains no multiple of any $p\in\mathcal P_k$ is equivalent to saying that the $k$ integers $n-1,\dots,n-k$ are all coprime to $M_k$. For a fixed $p\in\mathcal P_k$, the interval $[n-k,n-1]$ contains a multiple of $p$ iff\[
n\equiv 1,2,\dots,k\pmod p.
\]Thus the allowed residues mod $p$ are exactly the $p-k$ classes $\{0,k+1,\dots,p-1\}$. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the number of allowed residue classes mod $M_k$ is\[
A_k=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_k}(p-k),
\]so the exact density of admissible $n$ is\[
D_k \ :=\ \frac{A_k}{M_k}
\ =\ \prod_{\substack{k<p<2k\\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}}
\left(1-\frac{k}{p}\right).
\]Using summation over primes and the prime number theorem one obtains the asymptotic\[
\log\frac{1}{D_k}=(\log 4+o(1))\,\frac{k}{\log k}.
\]Numerically (for $1\le k\le 50$), $\log n_k$ grows on the $\frac{k}{\log k}$ scale and closely tracks $(\log 4)\frac{k}{\log k}$; in this range we in fact observe\[
\log n_k \ \le\ (\log 4)\,\frac{k}{\log k},
\]while we cannot replace $\log 4$ by $\log 3$.
Heuristically one expects $n_k\asymp D_k^{-1}$; making this rigorous appears to be the remaining difficulty.
Details of the proofs and numerical evidence can be found on my GitHub page here (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/Notes-on-Erdos-Problem-451/blob/main/Notes_on_Erdos_Problem_451_Density_and_Heuristics.pdf).

\]

- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er37} proved that the density of integers $n$ with $\omega(n)>\log\log n$ is $1/2$. The Chinese remainder theorem implies that there is such an interval with\[\lvert I\rvert \geq (1+o(1))\frac{\log x}{(\log\log x)^2}.\]It could be true that there is such an interval of length $(\log x)^{k}$ for arbitrarily large $k$.

- [Er37] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Note on the number of prime divisors of integers. J. London Math. Soc. (1937), 308-314.

Apply block maxima method to Bernoulli-like process with controlled dependence. \(\square\)

The bottleneck is quantifying short-range dependence of \(\omega(n)\) strongly enough to control longest-run extremes, not just average density.

problem:
Let $p_n$ be the smallest prime $\equiv 1\pmod{n}$ and let $m_n$ be the smallest integer such that $n\mid \phi(m_n)$.

Is it true that $m_n<p_n$ for almost all $n$? Does $p_n/m_n\to \infty$ for almost all $n$? Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p-1$ is the only $n$ for which $m_n=p$?

- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/456.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 07 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Linnik's theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linnik%27s_theorem) implies that $p_n\leq n^{O(1)}$. It is trivial that $m_n\leq p_n$ always.

If $n=q-1$ for some prime $q$ then $m_n=p_n$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er79e} writes it is 'easy to show' that for infinitely many $n$ we have $m_n <p_n$, and that $m_n/n\to \infty$ for almost all $n$.

forum_comments.author: DavidTurturean
forum_comments.text:
I put together a write-up that settles the first two questions of Erdős Problem #456 unconditionally, and the third question conditionally on Dickson's conjecture for one explicit admissible triple of linear forms. The writeup is at this Overleaf link (https://www.overleaf.com/read/hqwctkrwwkgx#334083)

Specifically:

(Q1, Q2) Unconditional: there is a constant $c > 0$ such that $\#\{n \le x : m_n = p_n\} \ge cx$ for all sufficiently large $x$. In particular, the assertions "$m_n < p_n$ for almost all $n$" and "$p_n/m_n \to \infty$ for almost all $n$" both fail, on a set of positive lower density. No prime-tuple conjecture is used in this part of the proof.

(Q3) Dickson-conditional: assume Dickson's conjecture for the admissible triple of linear forms $t$, $2t+1$, $8t+1$. Then there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p-1$ is the unique integer $n$ with $m_n = p$. More precisely, whenever $\ell$, $2\ell+1$, and $8\ell+1$ are all prime, the prime $p = 8\ell+1$ has this uniqueness property.

Thus, I claim a (mixed) solution to this problem: the first two questions are settled outright, and the third is settled conditionally on a standard prime-tuple hypothesis stemming from Dickson's conjecture. The manuscript is lengthy (71 pages); all in all, the Q3 Dickson-conditional construction occupies only about two pages (Section 3), while the remaining sixty-odd pages (Sections 4 through 11 and the three appendices) are devoted to the unconditional Q1/Q2 proof.

Some brief remarks on what is novel.
The unconditional Q1/Q2 result rests on a weighted-logarithmic-density tightness theorem for an auxiliary divisor sum that controls the cofactors arising in the construction. This theorem is built by transferring Fan and Pomerance's natural-density tightness for the shifted-prime-divisor function $\omega^*(n)$ to weighted logarithmic density with fixed multipliers, by handling a squarefree large-ratio tail through a fractional Euler-product moment, and by treating the early-prime contribution as a level-set bound on a multiscale normal set (which is what allows the argument to proceed without any unrestricted first-moment claim).
Downstream the architecture is 'standard': a dyadic arithmetic-progression form of Goldfeld's large-prime-factor argument, with uniformity for $b \le (\log X)^A$ and built from Siegel-Walfisz, Bombieri-Vinogradov, and Brun-Titchmarsh, supplies the base population; two- and three-linear-form upper-bound sieves which are applied only in their long-interval regimes, with line-by-line divisor-weight averages over the relevant coefficient range in the latter case, delete the bad witnesses; and a second-moment Cauchy-Schwarz step deduplicates the survivors into distinct integers.

By contrast, the Dickson-conditional Q3 result, is elementary: the maximal-divisor characterization of $p$ being a uniqueness prime reduces the question, for $p = 8\ell + 1$, to checking that $\varphi(3(2\ell+1)) = 4\ell$ and $\varphi(15) = 8$ both fall below $8\ell$, which they do whenever $\ell$, $2\ell+1$, $8\ell+1$ are all prime; the triple $(t, 2t+1, 8t+1)$ is admissible, so Dickson supplies infinitely many such $\ell$.

The proof was developed via an automated multi-turn audit-and-revise scaffold that I built, which iteratively queried ChatGPT-5.5-Pro across several hundred rounds, including a substantial post-review pass to put everything together. I did not carry out the turn-by-turn reasoning by hand; the scaffold itself is my engineering contribution, and the final proof has been checked by myself these past couple of days.

Here is ChatGPT-5.5-Pro verifying the solution: check 1 (https://chatgpt.com/share/69f9186f-52e8-83ea-8b55-b48299c41beb), check 2 (https://chatgpt.com/share/69f91b8c-c82c-83ea-8bd4-1c1c6a1a1cf1), check 3 (https://chatgpt.com/share/69f91b92-fcd0-83ea-9dc1-8245bdbf6ffc). As you can see, GPT-5.5 Pro cannot find any errors, but it hedges to admit correctness due to the length of the solution. When pressed to scrutinize the solution even more, it does so and concludes the solution is correct, including in its novel parts.

Still, I appreciate if human expert reviewers could weigh in. Very appreciated would also be if anyone with access to very good autoformalization harnesses could help, since I imagine the formalization of this proof would be at least many tens of thousands of lines in Lean.

problem: Is there some $\epsilon>0$ such that there are infinitely many $n$ where all primes $p\leq (2+\epsilon)\log n$ divide\[\prod_{1\leq i\leq \log n}(n+i)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/457.
- Page status: PROVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-03-07).
- Page last edited: 07 March 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Pomerance.

More generally, let $q(n,k)$ denote the least prime which does not divide $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)$. This problem asks whether\[q(n,\log n)\geq (2+\epsilon)\log n\]infinitely often. Taking $n$ to be the product of primes between $\log n$ and $(2+o(1))\log n$ gives an example where\[q(n,\log n)\geq (2+o(1))\log n.\]GPT-5.2 Pro (prompted by Barreto) has given a construction (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b6puijShAt5hq3Vxnb45R0pm0WqVcJE8/view?usp=sharing) that gives an affirmative answer to the original question, with the constant $2$ replaced by $\frac{3}{\log 4}\approx 2.16$, and GPT later proved this with $2$ replaced by an arbitrarily large constant.

An elaboration sketched by Tao in the comments proves that there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[q(n,\log n) > \frac{1-o(1)}{2}\frac{\log\log n}{\log\log\log n}\log n.\]Tao suggests that standard heuristics suggest that this lower bound is also (up to constants) an upper bound for all $n$.

See also [663], and [1181] for upper bounds on $q(n,\log n)$.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
The [Er79d] formulation is simply the negation of the [ErGr80] formulation. Here, I think this is simply a case where Erdos accidentally posed a problem that was too easy, because his initial explorations were not fully optimized.

It is slightly more convenient to work with a symmetrized product $\prod_{-k/2 \leq i \leq k/2} (n+i)$ than the original product $\prod_{i=1}^k (n+i)$ (with now the very small technicality that $n$ has to be larger than $k/2$, which is easy to deal with, e.g., by forcing $n$ to be divisible by all primes up to $\log k$ or so). Roughly speaking, the challenge is to make this product divisible by every prime $p$ up to say $Ak$ for a large constant $A$, while keeing $n$ only as large as $\exp(k)$ at most.

Primes up to $k$ automatically divide the product, so it is just the primes between $k$ and $Ak$ that cause an issue. In [Er79d] Erdos did the simplest thing of forcing $n$ to be divisible by all the primes between $k$ and $Ak$, which keeps $n$ under the size budget of $\exp(k)$ as long as $A \leq 2-o(1)$ by the prime number theorem. What GPT noticed was that one only needs $n$ to be within $k/2$ of being divisible by all primes between $k$ and $Ak$, which is a significantly more frequent event, and can be accomplished more cheaply using the Dirichlet approximation theorem: indeed one could achieve this with $n$ as small as something like $O(A)^{O(A k / \log k)}$, which stays under budget even if $A$ is as large as $\asymp \log k / \log\log k$. If I did the algebra correctly, this means that $q(n,\log n)$ can be as large as $\gg \log n \log\log n / \log\log\log n$ infinitely often (perhaps even $\geq (1-o(1)) \log n \log\log n / \log\log\log n$ if one does the accounting carefully). So the standard heuristics I mentioned back in September are in fact achievable as a lower bound! (Though proving that they are optimal -- i.e., providing the matching upper bound -- is likely to be extremely difficult, given how the much weaker bound posed in the commentary remains open.)

The broader lesson here is that while Chinese remainder theorem methods can only force a number $n$ to obey various congruences mod $p$ for $p$ as large as $\log n$ or so, Dirichlet approximation theorem methods can control a larger range of moduli, but at the cost of only localizing $n \hbox{ mod } p$ to an interval rather than to a single value. For instance one can make $n \hbox{ mod } p$ within $\varepsilon p$ of the origin for all primes $p$ up to about $\log n \log\log n / \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$, I think, if $\varepsilon$ is not too small (for the application above one is setting $\varepsilon$ to be $\gg \log\log\log n/\log \log n$).

The final problem of Erdos mentioned in the commentary (improving the trivial bound $q(n,\log n) \leq (1+o(1)) \log^2 n$ that arises from observing that the primorial of $q(n,k)$ clearly cannot exceed $\prod_{1 \leq i \leq k} (n+i)$) remains open though. I'll leave it to Thomas to decide whether to absorb it into the current problem (making it a two-parter), or spin it off as a separately numbered problem. It is a problem of a very different nature, having to do with ruling out long consecutive chains of nearly-smooth numbers, and likely comparable in difficulty to some of the other problems involving smooth (or powerful) numbers on this site.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
I ran a computational check of this conjecture up to $p_{k+1} \leq 10^{12}$ and found no counterexample.

Using the identity

$\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,n)=\prod_{q \leq n,\ q\ \mathrm{prime}} q^{\lfloor \log_q n \rfloor}$,

for two consecutive primes $p<r$, the quotient

$\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,r-1)/\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,p)$

is equal to

$\prod q$,

where $q$ runs over prime bases such that some prime power $q^a$ lies strictly between $p$ and $r$. More precisely, $q$ is counted with multiplicity equal to the number of powers $q^a$ in $(p,r)$, though in the tested range no repeated base occurred in one gap.

Thus the desired inequality for the gap $(p,r)$ is equivalent to checking

$\prod_{q^a \in (p,r)} q < p$.

Algorithm used:

1. Generate all prime powers $q^a < 10^{12}$ with $a \geq 2$.
2. For each such prime power $m=q^a$, find the previous prime $p<m$ and next prime $r>m$ using deterministic Miller--Rabin primality testing.
3. Group all such $m$ by the prime gap $(p,r)$.
4. For each gap with $r \leq 10^{12}$, multiply the corresponding prime bases $q$.
5. Check whether this product is ever $\geq p$.

No failing gap was found. The closest case was the small gap $(7,11)$, where the powers $8=2^3$ and $9=3^2$ occur, giving product $2\cdot 3=6<7$.

This is only a computational verification, not a proof, and I do not know whether this computation has already appeared elsewhere in the literature.

problem: Let $a_0=0$ and $a_1=1$, and in general define $a_k$ to be the least integer $>a_{k-1}$ for which $(n-a_k,n-a_i)=1$ for all $0\leq i<k$. Does\[\sum_{0<a_i< n}\frac{1}{a_i}\to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$? What about if we restrict the sum to those $i$ such that $n-a_j$ is divisible by some prime $\leq a_j$, or the complement of such $i$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/460.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 14 January 2026.
Site remarks:
This question arose in work of Eggleton, Erd\H{o}s, and Selfridge, who could prove that $a_k <k^{2+o(1)}$ for $k$ large enough depending on $n$, but conjectured that in fact $a_k\ll k\log k$ is true.

The problem above is from \cite{Er77c}. This question is stated slightly differently in \cite{ErGr80}, which has $a_0=n$ instead of $a_0=0$ and $1\leq i<k$ instead of $0\leq i<k$. The material difference this makes is that the main formulation above has $(a_k,n)=1$ for all $k\geq 1$, which is not imposed in the second formulation. Furthermore, in both \cite{Er77c} and \cite{ErGr80} this is stated without the restriction to $a_k<n$ in the sum, although perhaps this was implicitly intended. Without this condition the sum is infinite since the sequence of $a_k$ contains $n+p$ for all primes $p>n$ (this observation was made by Svyable using ChatGPT).

Unfortunately, although both sources mention a forthcoming paper of Eggleton, Erd\H{o}s, and Selfridge, I cannot find a candidate paper of theirs with this problem in, and hence the motivation behind this problem, and what the precise problem intended was, is unclear.

Chojecki has noted in the comments that a positive solution to the main problem would follow if\[f(n) = \sum_{a<n}1_{P^-(n-a)>a}\frac{1}{a}\to \infty,\]where $P^-(\cdot)$ is the least prime factor. Standard estimates on rough numbers show that $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n\leq N}f(n)\gg \log\log N$, so $f(n)$ does diverge on average, but it is unclear whether $f(n)\to \infty$ for all $n$.
References:
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
You're right, in either formulation, if one sums over all $k$ without any upper cut-off on $a_k$, then the series is automatically divergent: for every prime $p>n$ the term $a=n+p$ must occur in the greedy sequence, because before reaching $n+p$ all previously chosen translates satisfy $n-a_i\in[-p+1,n-1]$, so none is divisible by $p$ (the only multiple of $p$ in that interval is $0$, which never arises as $n-a_i$ in these constructions); hence $\gcd(n-(n+p),\,n-a_i)=\gcd(p,\,n-a_i)=1$ for all earlier $i$, making $n+p$ admissible at the moment it becomes available and therefore impossible for the greedy rule to skip. Comparing $\sum_{p>n}1/(n+p)$ with $\sum_p 1/p$ gives divergence for every fixed $n\ge2$.

If instead one imposes the natural ''nontrivial'' restriction $a_k<n$ (or $a_k\le n$), then the above argument disappears and one can at least prove an averaged divergence statement from the forced ''rough'' contribution. Writing $P^-(m)$ for the least prime factor of $|m|$ (with $P^-(\pm1)=\infty$), set\[
f(n):=\sum_{a=1}^{n-1}\frac1a\,\mathbf 1_{\{P^-(n-a)>a\}},
\]so that (by the forced-rough lemma) the truncated greedy sum $S_{<n}(n):=\sum_{a_k\le n-1}1/a_k$ satisfies $S_{<n}(n)\ge f(n)$ for every $n$ in both formulations. Averaging over $n\le N$ and changing variables $m=n-a$ yields $\sum_{n\le N}f(n)=\sum_{a\le N-1}\frac1a\,\Phi(N-a,a)$, where $\Phi(x,y)$ counts $y$-rough integers $\le x$; Buchstab’s asymptotic for $\Phi(x,y)$ (uniform for $a\in[N^{1/3},N^{1/2}]$, where $u=\log(N-a)/\log a\in[2,3]$ and hence $\omega(u)\gg1$) gives $\Phi(N-a,a)\gg N/\log a$ on that range, and thus\[
\frac1N\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\ \gg\ \sum_{N^{1/3}\le a\le N^{1/2}}\frac1{a\log a}\ \asymp\ \log\log N.
\]In particular $\limsup_{n\to\infty}f(n)=\infty$ and hence $\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_{<n}(n)=\infty$; what remains open is whether $f(n)\to\infty$ (and thus $S_{<n}(n)\to\infty$) along all $n$.

I've re-written the note to discuss both cases and give the full proofs. I think this solves the problem. See here: https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos-460-v2.pdf

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
As Kevin Barreto mentioned, we might have $a_0=0$ with $i=0$ included in $gcd$ condition. The full proof of both versions is here: https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos-460.pdf - here's the sketch:

Fix $n\ge2$ and define a greedy increasing sequence $(a_k)$ by requiring the translates $n-a_k$ to be pairwise coprime: in Case A one enforces $\gcd(n-a_k,n-a_i)=1$ for all $1\le i<k$, while in Case B one includes $i=0$ with $a_0=0$, which is equivalent to adding the standing constraint $\gcd(a_k,n)=1$. To study Erdős' divergence question for $\sum_k 1/a_k$ (and its natural subsums), the note introduces a dichotomy for $1\le a\le n-1$: call $a$ rough if the least prime factor $P^{-}(n-a)$ exceeds $a$ (equivalently, $n-a$ has no prime divisor $\le a$), and proper otherwise. This yields a canonical subsum $S_{\mathrm{rough}}(n)=\sum_{k:\,a_k\le n-1,\ P^{-}(n-a_k)>a_k}1/a_k$, with complementary ''proper'' subsum capturing the genuinely interactive part of the greedy dynamics.

The main reduction is that the rough part is forced and admits an explicit description independent of the history: for any $a<n$ with $P^{-}(n-a)>a$, one has $\gcd(n-a,n-a')=1$ for every $a'<a$ (since any common prime divisor would divide $a-a'$ and hence be $\le a$), so such an $a$ is admissible at every stage once it becomes available (and in Case B this automatically includes coprimality with $n$). A greedy minimality argument then shows the process cannot skip any rough $a$: if $a$ were the least skipped rough integer, at the first step where $a_{k-1}<a<a_k$ it would be admissible, contradicting the definition of $a_k$ as the least admissible choice. Consequently the set of rough values appearing with $a_k<n$ is exactly $R(n)=\{1\le a\le n-1: P^{-}(n-a)>a\}$, and hence\[
S_{\mathrm{rough}}(n)=\sum_{a\in R(n)}\frac1a=\sum_{\substack{1\le a\le n-1\\ P^{-}(n-a)>a}}\frac1a,
\]giving an explicit, history-free lower bound for $\sum_k 1/a_k$ in both cases and reducing the divergence problem to estimating this rough sum plus the remaining proper contribution.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I think one can disprove that $f(N) = o(N)$ for all $N$ as follows. Let $\sigma_k(n)$ denote the sum of the divisors of $n$ excluding the top $k$ factors (or $0$, if the number of divisors $\tau(n)$ is at most $k$). It is a standard calculation (factoring $n=dm$) that
$$ \sum_{n \leq x} \sigma(n) = \sum_{d \leq x} d \sum_{m \leq x/d} 1 \ll \sum_{d \leq x} x \ll x^2,$$
so $\sigma(n) = O(x)$ on the average. Suppose that we can more generally show
$$ \sum_{n \leq x} \sigma_k(n) \ll x^2 / k^{1.1} \quad (1)$$
for all $k \geq 1$. By Markov's inequality and the union bound, and the summability of $\sum_k 1/k^{1.1}$, we conclude that for any $C_0$, the number of $n \leq x$ such that $\sigma_k(n) \geq C_0 x$ for at least one $k$ is at most $O( x / C_0 )$, hence we have $f(N) \leq x$ for at most $O(x/C_0)$ of the $N \in [C_0 x, 2C_0 x]$, which is enough to disprove $f(N) = o(N)$ by taking $C_0$ large enough.

It remains to prove (1). In order for a factor $d$ of $n=dm$ to contribute to $\sigma_k(n)$, there must be at least $k$ factors of $dm$ that are at most $m$, so either $\tau(m) \gg k^{0.1}$ or $d$ has $\gg k^{0.9}$ factors of size at most $m$. The contribution of the first case is at most
$$ \sum_{m \leq x} (\tau(m)/k^{0.1})^{100} \sum_{d \leq x/m} d \ll \frac{x^2}{k^{10}} \sum_m \frac{\tau(m)^{100}}{m^2} \ll \frac{x^2}{k^{10}}$$
which is acceptable (one could also have used the divisor bound $\tau(m) = m^{o(1)}$ here). The contribution of the second case is at most
$$ \sum_{m \leq x} \sum_{d \leq x/m} d (\sum_{r \leq m: r|d} 1 / k^{0.9})^2$$
$$ \ll \sum_{m } \sum_{r_1,r_2 \leq m} \frac{x^2}{m^2 [r_1,r_2] k^{1.8}}$$
$$ \ll \sum_{m } \sum_{r_1,r_2} \frac{x^2}{m^{1.8} [r_1,r_2]^{1.1} k^{1.8}}$$
$$ \ll \frac{x^2}{k^{1.8}}$$
which is also acceptable (there is a lot of room to spare here ultimately coming from the fact that divisor functions are typically logarithmic in size, so presumably one could clean up this argument somehow; in particular, standard anatomy of integers heuristics predicts that (1) should in fact exhibit exponential decay in $k$).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
We need to sum in $k$, which is in principle unbounded (in particular, it can be large compared to $C_0$), because the definition of $f(N)$ does not specify $k$ in advance.

More precisely, one has $f(N) = \inf_k f_k(N)$, where $f_k(N)$ is the least $n$ for which $\sigma_k(n)=N$ (or $\infty$ if no such $n$ exists). The "trivial" bound controls each individual event $f_k(N) \leq x$, but the event $f(N) \leq x$ is the union of all such events and so one needs to sum in $k$ if one wishes to use the union bound.

forum_comments.text:
I thought I'd share some experimental data on this problem. I don't have any other ambitions with it. In fact, these sums of divisors behave so erratically that I'll be amazed if someone can prove anything nontrivial rigorously and unconditionally.

I entered the sizes of sets $D'_n:=D_n\setminus\cup_{m<n}D_m$ as OEIS sequence A387502 (https://oeis.org/A387502). It is unclear what Erdős and Graham wanted to know about these numbers. There are many zeros in the sequence, i.e., many empty sets $D'_n$ (also see below), which can be conditionally deduced from (certain special cases of Schinzel's hypothesis), say, having infinitely primes $r$ of the form $r=pq+p+q$, $p<q$ primes, since then $D'_r=\emptyset$. On the other hand, the sets $D'_n$ can likely become arbitrarily large: the largest one I could find is $D'_{75600}$ of cardinality $24$. The very likely candidates are the numbers $n$ with large $\sigma(n)$. In reality, the record values of the cardinalities of $D'_n$ are attained for $n=2, 12, 36, 144, 336, 1320, 1980, 5040, 8400, 25200, 75600$.

I also entered sizes of the unions $\cup_{m\leq n}D_m=\cup_{m\leq n}D'_m$ as OEIS sequence A387503 (https://oeis.org/A387503). From it one can see that the first $1000$ sets $D'_n$ have average size $0.924$, the first $10000$ have average size $0.8697$, and I also computed that the first $100000$ sets $D'_n$ have average size $0.8349$. This should also hint again that a positive share of the sets $D'_n$ are empty.

Regarding the behavior of the function $f$, the same problem is also mentioned in the book by Guy (https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0) and attributed to Erdős. There is a slight difference in the book: that the number $1$ is always counted in as the smallest divisor, but effectively this makes no difference, and the function $f$ only gets shifted by $1$. It seems that Guy's book was a better-known reference, since the values of $f$ already appear as OEIS sequence A167485 (https://oeis.org/A167485) (but again, note the indices shifted by $1$). Function $f$ is clearly undefined for $n=1,4$ (as the two smallest divisors $>1$ cannot add up to $1$ or $4$), and I'm not sure if it is known to be well-defined for all other $n$ (but experimentally it seems so). OEIS mentions this following from a certain stronger version of Goldbach's conjecture, but it would also follow from versions of Vingradov's theorem. For instance if sufficiently (but concretely) large odd $N$ are sums of distinct primes $p,q,r\in[x,x^2]$, then $N$ appears in the set $D_{pqr}$, which makes $f(N)$ finite (i.e., well-defined).

The claim $f(N)=o(N)$ seems experimentally unlikely. In fact, $31.279\%$ of the numbers $N\leq100000$ even have $f(N)>100000$. Similarly, only less than $36\%$ of the ratios $f(N)/N$, for $5\leq N\leq10000$, are $\leq1$, only less than $27\%$ of them are $\leq0.9$, and only less than $6\%$ of them are $\leq0.5$: quite unlikely if one had $f(N)/N\to0$. A very easy observation (mentioned in the OEIS comments) is that $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sigma(n)/n=\infty$ by taking $N=\sigma(n)-1$ implies $\liminf_{N\to\infty}f(N)/N=0$, so at least this is an unconditional but rather trivial result.

Target:
Prove asymptotic representability profile for \(D_n\) prefix-divisor sums and inverse function
\[
f(N)=\min\{n:\ N\in D_n\},
\]
in particular \(f(N)=o(N)\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show a high-density covering lemma: union \(\bigcup_{n\le X} D_n\) covers all but \(o(X)\) integers up to \(X\), with quantitative novelty bound per \(n\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (inverse equivalence):
\[
f(N)\le X \iff N\in \bigcup_{n\le X} D_n.
\]
Proof.
By definition of minimal witnessing index. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (coverage-to-growth transfer):
If uncovered count up to \(X\) is \(o(X)\), then for density-1 set of \(N\), \(f(N)\le X\) with \(X=(1+o(1))N\), and sharper coverage gives \(f(N)=o(N)\).
Proof.
Apply B1 and monotonicity with chosen \(X\)-scales; sparse uncovered set forces early representation for almost all \(N\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies \(f(N)=o(N)\)):
If A gives coverage at scales \(X=\eta N\) for every fixed \(\eta>0\) beyond thresholds, then \(f(N)\le \eta N\) eventually for represented \(N\), hence \(f(N)=o(N)\).
Proof.
Let \(\eta\downarrow0\) along sequence and use B1. \(\square\)

The bottleneck is proving strong enough cumulative coverage from sparse per-\(n\) novelty increments.

Target:
Decide convergence of
\[
\sum_{n\in \mathcal A}\frac1n
\]
where \(\mathcal A\) is primitive pseudoperfect numbers.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove counting upper bound
\[
\#\{n\le x:\ n\in\mathcal A\}\le x^{1-\delta}
\]
for some \(\delta>0\), or stronger logarithmic sparsity.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (partial summation criterion):
If \(A(x)=\#(\mathcal A\cap[1,x])\), then
\[
\sum_{\substack{n\in\mathcal A\\ n\le X}}\frac1n
=\frac{A(X)}{X}+\int_1^X \frac{A(t)}{t^2}\,dt.
\]
Proof.
Apply Abel summation to indicator sequence of \(\mathcal A\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (convergence test):
If \(A(x)\ll x^{1-\delta}\), then \(\sum_{n\in\mathcal A}1/n\) converges.
Proof.
Insert bound into B1: integral \(\int t^{-1-\delta}dt\) converges. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies convergence):
Lemma A directly implies B2, hence convergence.
Proof.
Immediate substitution. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving strong sparsity for primitive pseudoperfect numbers, which combine subset-sum and divisor-structure constraints.

problem:
Call $n$ weird (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weird_number) if $\sigma(n)\geq 2n$ and $n$ is not pseudoperfect, that is, it is not the sum of any set of its divisors.

Are there any odd weird numbers? Are there infinitely many primitive weird numbers, i.e. those such that no proper divisor of $n$ is weird?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/470.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Weird numbers were investigated by Benkoski and Erd\H{o}s \cite{BeEr74}, who proved that the set of weird numbers has positive density. The smallest weird number is $70$.

Melfi \cite{Me15} has proved that there are infinitely many primitive weird numbers, conditional on the fact that $p_{n+1}-p_n<\frac{1}{10}p_n^{1/2}$ for all large $n$, which in turn would follow from well-known conjectures concerning prime gaps.

The sequence of weird numbers is A006037 (https://oeis.org/A006037) in the OEIS. Fang \cite{Fa22} has shown there are no odd weird numbers below $10^{21}$, and Liddy and Riedl \cite{LiRi18} have shown that an odd weird number must have at least 6 prime divisors.

If there are no odd weird numbers then every weird number has abundancy index $<4$ (see [825]).

This is problem B2 in Guy's collection \cite{Gu04} (the \$10 is reported by Guy, offered by Erd\H{o}s for a solution to the question of whether any odd weird numbers exist).
References:
- [BeEr74] Benkoski, S. J. and Erd\H{o}s, P., On weird and pseudoperfect numbers. Math. Comp. (1974), 617-623.
- [Fa22] Searching on the boundary of abundance for odd weird numbers, W. Fang. arXiv:2207.12906 (2022).
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [LiRi18] J. Liddy and J. Riedl, An algorithm to determine all odd primitive abundant numbers with $d$ prime divisors. Honors Research Projects. 728 (2018).
- [Me15] Melfi, Giuseppe, On the conditional infiniteness of primitive weird numbers. J. Number Theory (2015), 508-514.

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
That sequence should work indeed.
Heuristically reasons:
$q_n+q_i-1$ is odd, and residues are not fixed modulo an odd prime.
The probability that a number of the order $x$ is prime is roughly $1/ \log x$.
Thus on average $q_{n+1}=q_n+\log(q_n)^{2+o(1)}$ and the expectation of failing should be small (we estimate $q_n=n^{1+o(1)}$ and probability of failing $(1-1/\log q_n)^n=exp(-n^{1-o(1)})$.
An easy check shows that the list continues at least a million steps, and $\sum_{n=10^6}^{\infty} \exp(-n^{1-o(1)})$ will be very small.

problem: Under what set theoretic assumptions is it true that $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be $3$-coloured such that, for every uncountable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, $A^2$ contains a pair of each colour?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/474.
- Page status: NOT PROVABLE (database last update 2025-10-01).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s from 1954. In other words, when is it the case that\[2^{\aleph_0}\not\to [\aleph_1]_3^2?\]Sierpinski and Kurepa independently proved that this is true for $2$-colours. Erd\H{o}s proved that this is true under the continuum hypothesis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuum_hypothesis) that $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_1$, and offered \$100 for deciding what happens if the continuum hypothesis is not assumed.

Shelah \cite{Sh88} proved, on the other hand, that it is consistent without the continuum hypothesis that\[2^{\aleph_0}\to [\aleph_1]_3^2,\]although with a very large value of $\mathfrak{c}$. It remains open whether it is consistent to have a negative answer assuming $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$. (This specific question is asked in \cite{Va99}.)
References:
- [Sh88] Shelah, Saharon, Was Sierpi\'nski right? I. Israel J. Math. (1988), 355--380.
- [Va99] Various, Some of Paul's favorite problems. Booklet produced for the conference "Paul Erd\H{o}s and his mathematics", Budapest, July 1999 (1999).

problem: Let $p$ be a prime. Given any finite set $A\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p\backslash \{0\}$, is there always a rearrangement $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_t\}$ such that all partial sums $\sum_{1\leq k\leq m}a_{k}$ are distinct, for all $1\leq m\leq t$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/475.
- Page status: DECIDABLE (database last update 2026-02-23).
- Page last edited: 05 March 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Graham, who proved it when $t=p-1$. A similar conjecture was made for arbitrary abelian groups by Alspach. Such an ordering is often called a valid ordering.

This has been proved for $t\leq 12$ (see Costa and Pellegrini \cite{CoPe20} and the references therein) and for $p-3\leq t\leq p-1$ (see Hicks, Ollis, and Schmitt \cite{HOS19} and the references therein).

This has been proved for all sufficiently large primes; this is a consequence of four different types of result, each of which handles (using different methods) a different range of size of $A$.
{UL}
{LI} The small $A$ case: Kravitz \cite{Kr24} proved this for\[t \leq \frac{\log p}{\log\log p}.\](This was independently earlier observed by Will Sawin in a MathOverflow post (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/164300/ordering-subsets-of-the-cyclic-group-to-give-distinct-partial-sums).)
Bedert and Kravitz \cite{BeKr24} improved this to the range\[t \leq e^{c(\log p)^{1/4}}\]for some constant $c>0$, and Costa and Della Fiore \cite{CoDe26} have further improved this to\[t \leq e^{c(\log p)^{1/3}}.\]{/LI}
{LI} The medium $A$ case: Pham and Sauermann \cite{PhSa26} proved this, for any $0<\alpha<1$, for all\[ 1 \ll_\alpha t\leq p^{1-\alpha}.\]{/LI}
{LI} The large $A$ case: Bedert, Buci\'{c}, Kravitz, Montgomery, and M\"{u}yesser \cite{BBKMM25} proved this for all\[p^{1-c}\leq t\leq (1-o(1))p\]for some small constant $c>0$.{/LI}
{LI}The very large $A$ case: M\"{u}yesser and Pokrovskiy \cite{MuPo25} proved this for all\[t\geq (1-o(1))p.\]{/LI}
{/UL}
References:
- [BBKMM25] B. Bedert, M. Buci\'{c}, N. Kravitz, R. Montgomery, and A. M\"{u}yesser, On Graham's rearrangement conjecture over $\mathbb{F}_2^n$. arXiv:2508.18254 (2025).
- [BeKr24] B. Bedert and N. Kravitz, Graham's rearrangement conjecture beyond the rectification barrier. arXiv:2409.07403 (2024).
- [CoDe26] S. Costa and S. Della Fiore, New bounds for (weak) sequenceability in $\mathbb{Z}_k$. arXiv:2602.19989 (2026).
- [CoPe20] Costa, S. and Pellegrini, M. A., Some new results about a conjecture by Brian Alspach. Arch. Math. (Basel) (2020), 479-488.
- [HOS19] Hicks, Jacob and Ollis, M. A. and Schmitt, John R., Distinct partial sums in cyclic groups: polynomial method and constructive approaches. J. Combin. Des. (2019), 369-385.
- [Kr24] N. Kravitz, Rearranging small sets for distinct partial sums. arXiv:2407.01835 (2024).
- [MuPo25] A. M\"{u}yesser and A. Pokrovskiy, A random Hall-Paige conjecture. arXiv:2204.09666 (2025).
- [PhSa26] H. T. Pham and L. Sauermann, On Graham's rearrangement conjecture. arXiv:2602.15797 (2026).

problem: Is there a polynomial $f:\mathbb{Z}\to \mathbb{Z}$ of degree at least $2$ and a set $A\subset \mathbb{Z}$ such that for any $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ there is exactly one $a\in A$ and $b\in \{ f(k) : k\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ such that $n=a+b$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/477.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 11 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A question of Erd\H{o}s and Graham, who thought the answer was negative. Clearly any such $A$ must be infinite.

A simple proof that this is impossible for $f$ of degree $2$ is given in the comments (with the combined efforts of AlphaProof and Adenwalla): let $f(x)=c_2x^2+c_1x+c_0$ with $c_1\neq 0$. For any infinite $A$ there exist $a,b\in A$ such that $a-b=2c_1k$ for some $k\geq 1$, whence\[0\neq a-b=f(k)-f(-k)\]and so $n=a+f(-k)=b+f(k)$ has two distinct solutions. If $c_1=0$ then we can argue similarly finding $a,b\in A$ with $a-b=4c_2k$ for some $k\geq 1$, whence\[0\neq a-b=f(k+1)-f(k-1).\]The same argument works for any $f$ such that $f(\mathbb{Z})-f(\mathbb{Z})$ contains all multiples of some fixed $q\geq 1$, such as any polynomial of the shape\[f(x)=g((x-k)^2)+c_1x+c_0\]for some $g\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and $k,c_1,c_0\in \mathbb{Z}$ with $c_1\neq 0$.

forum_comments.author: Moritz Firsching
forum_comments.text:
AlphaProof found a counterexample to the previous formulation of this problem.This was an formal version, which can be summarised as follows:

1. Pick $f = X^2 - X + 1$
2. Now $A$ can't be finite.
3. If $A$ is infinite there are two elements $a, b$ which differ by a positive multiple of $4$ (say $a = b + 4x$)
4. Now consider the pairs $(a, f(2x))$ and $(b, f(2x + 1))$. The point being that $f(2x + 1) - f(2x) = 4x$, so these give two representations of the same number.

This proof can be generalised to all polynomials of degree $2$ of the form $ax^2 + bx + c$ where $a | b$ and $b ≠ 0$.

Formalised statement and proof (cleaned up and generalised from the AlphaProof proof) see here:
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/24a4308a38b97e3e5b7da6ccff57157de432a1c1/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/477.lean#L44

 So this gives an infinite family of degree $2$ polynomials for which no such $A$ exists.

[ErGr80] mentions

[Sek59](http://dml.cz/dmlcz/100376) Milan Sekanina, Замечания к фактoризации беcкoнечнoй цикличеcкoй группы, Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal, Vol. 9 (1959), No. 4, 485–495

and if I understand correctly the $X^2$ counterexample is also mentioned on page 490 there. And then the question is asked for other monomials $X^k$ for $k\ge3$.

We added those variants to formal-conjectures: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/1510/

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
This can be generalised even when $b=0$. It suffices to show that for any monic quadratic polynomial $f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$, there exists an integer $n$ such that for all integers $k$, there is $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $f(x)-f(y)=kn$. That is, all multiples of $n$ are in the difference set of $f(x)$. This is because any set $A$ must be infinite, and so $A-A$ must contain some multiple of $n$.

Let $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ with $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$. Note that if all multiples of $n$ are in the difference set of $f(x)$, then for any $d\in\mathbb{Z}$, all multiples of $n$ are in the difference set of $f(x)+d$.

It has been shown that $x^2$ and $x^2-x+1$ each have difference sets that contain all multiples of $4$. The same then holds true for $(x+k)^2$ and $(x+k)^2-(x+k)+1$ for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. As $(x+k)^2=x^2+2kx+k^2$ and $(x+k)^2-(x+k)+1=x^2+(2k-1)x+k^2-k+1$, we have covered $x^2+bx+c$ for any $b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$ (that is, the difference set of any polynomial of this form contains all multiples of $4$).

Then, for any $a\in\mathbb{Q}$ and monic quadratic $f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ such that $a\times f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$, all multiples of $4a$ are in the difference set of $a\times f(x)$. Therefore any polynomial of the form $ax^2+bx+c$ where $a|b$ contains all multiples of $4a$ in its difference set.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
This can actually be generalised for all quadratic polynomials $f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$. Consider $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$. Then the difference set of $f(x)$ contains all terms of the form $$f(x+2l)-f(x)=(4ax+4al+2b)l.$$ As $x$ can be any integer, this is all terms of the form $$4al^2+2bl\mod 4al\equiv 2bl\mod 4al.$$ As we can vary $l$ to be any integer, the family of congruences $\{2bl\mod 4al\mid l\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ covers all multiples of $4a+2b$ (if $b\neq 0$, we can take multiples of $2b$).

EDIT: A simpler way to see this is to take $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ with $b\neq0$ and consider $f(k)-f(-k)=2bk$ for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. So all multiples of $2b$ are in the difference set of $f(x)$.

 If $b=0$ then $f(x+1)-f(x-1)=4ax$, so all multiples of $4a$ are in the difference set of $f(x)$.

Then for any infinite $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$, there must be some multiple of $2b$ and some multiple of $4a$ in $A-A$.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
Take $f(x) =x^2$. Then for any $a, b\in A$ and integers $m, n$, we want to avoid $a-b=m^2-n^2$ unless $a=b$. All odd numbers $>1$ and multiples of 4 can be expressed as a difference of two positive squares. So $A-A$ can only contain terms that are $2\mod 4$ or $0, 1$.

 Then letting $|A|\geq 5 $, there must be and $a, b, c, d, e\in A$ such that $a<b<c<d<e$. Then no two of $a, c, e$ have difference $1$ or $0$. So we must have $a-b\equiv b-c\equiv a-c \equiv 2\mod 4$. But $$a-c=(a-b) +(b-c) \equiv 2+2\equiv 0\mod 4. $$
So $|A|\leq 4$, but this is clearly not enough to represent all integers.

Decide existence of degree-\(\ge2\) polynomial \(f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\) and \(A\subset\mathbb Z\) giving unique decompositions \(n=a+b\) with \(a\in A,\ b\in f(\mathbb Z)\).

Prove a modular uniqueness obstruction: for infinitely many moduli \(m\), image set \(f(\mathbb Z_m)\) has nontrivial Fourier spectrum incompatible with exact tiling by any subset \(A_m\subset\mathbb Z_m\).

If unique representation holds in \(\mathbb Z\), then for each modulus \(m\), residues satisfy exact tiling

\mathbb Z_m = A_m \oplus f(\mathbb Z_m).
\]
Proof.
Reduce unique integer representation modulo \(m\). \(\square\)

Exact tiling implies

\widehat{1_{A_m}}(\xi)\,\widehat{1_{f(\mathbb Z_m)}}(\xi)=0

If A gives infinitely many \(m\) where B2 cannot hold for polynomial image set, no global unique-representation pair \((A,f)\) exists.

The bottleneck is establishing robust nonvanishing Fourier behavior of polynomial image sets for infinitely many moduli with quantitative strength.

problem: Let $p$ be a prime and\[A_p = \{ k! \pmod{p} : 1\leq k<p\}.\]Is it true that\[\lvert A_p\rvert \sim (1-\tfrac{1}{e})p?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/478.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 12 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Since $A_p/A_p=\{1,\ldots,p-1\}$ it follows that $\lvert A_p\rvert \gg p^{1/2}$. The best known lower bound is due to Grebennikov, Sagdeev, Semchankau, and Vasilevskii \cite{GSSV24},\[\lvert A_p\rvert \geq (\sqrt{2}-o(1))p^{1/2},\]which follows from proving that $\lvert A_pA_p\rvert=(1+o(1))p$.

Wilson's theorem implies $(p-2)!\equiv 1\pmod{p}$, and hence $\lvert A_p\rvert\leq p-2$. Results on $\lvert A_p\rvert$ on average were obtained by Klurman and Munsch \cite{KlMu17}.

It is even open whether there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $\lvert A_p\rvert=p-2$: in other words, such that $2!,\ldots,(p-1)!$ are all distinct modulo $p$ (such primes are sometimes called socialist primes). Rokowska and Schinzel \cite{RoSc60} have proved that any socialist prime is $5\pmod{8}$, and must satisfy $-(\frac{5}{p})=(\frac{-23}{p})=1$. Moreover, the congruence class missing from $2!,\ldots,(p-1)!$ must be $-(\frac{p-1}{2})!$.

The only known socialist prime is $p=5$. Trudgian \cite{Tr13} has shown there are no other socialist primes $<10^9$. This was extended to $10^{11}$ by Andreji\'{c} and Tatarevic \cite{AnTa16}.

This is also discussed in problems A2 and F11 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [AnTa16] V. Andreji\'{c} and M. Tatarevic, On distinct residues of factorials. arXiv:1603.04086 (2016).
- [GSSV24] Grebennikov, Alexandr and Sagdeev, Arsenii and Semchankau, Aliaksei and Vasilevskii, Aliaksei, On the sequence {$n! \bmod p$}. Rev. Mat. Iberoam. (2024), 637--648.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [KlMu17] Klurman, Oleksiy and Munsch, Marc, Distribution of factorials modulo {$p$}. J. Th\'{e}or. Nombres Bordeaux (2017), 169--177.
- [RoSc60] Rokowska, B. and Schinzel, A., Sur un probl\`eme de {M}. {E}rd\H os. Elem. Math. (1960), 84--85.
- [Tr13] T. Trudgian, There are no socialist primes less than $10^9$. arXiv:1310.6403 (2013).

problem: Is it true that, for all $k\neq 1$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $2^n\equiv k\pmod{n}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/479.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 03 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Graham. It is easy to see that $2^n\not\equiv 1\mod{n}$ for all $n>1$, so the restriction $k\neq 1$ is necessary. Erd\H{o}s and Graham report that Graham, Lehmer, and Lehmer have proved this for $k=2^i$ for $i\geq 1$, or if $k=-1$, but I cannot find such a paper. Tang has written a short note (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/Erdos-Problem-479-Note/blob/main/A_note_on_Erdos_Problem_479.pdf) giving a proof for this case.

As an indication of the difficulty, when $k=3$ the smallest $n$ such that $2^n\equiv 3\pmod{n}$ is $n=4700063497$.

The minimal such $n$ for each $k$ is A036236 (https://oeis.org/A036236) in the OEIS.

problem: Let $f(k)$ be the minimal $N$ such that if $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is $k$-coloured then there is a monochromatic solution to $a+b=c$. Estimate $f(k)$. In particular, is it true that $f(k) < c^k$ for some constant $c>0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/483.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The values of $f(k)$ are known as Schur numbers. The best-known bounds for large $k$ are\[(380)^{k/5}-O(1)\leq f(k) \leq (e-\tfrac{1}{6}) k!.\]Note that $380^{1/5}\approx 3.2806$. The lower bound is due to Ageron, Casteras, Pellerin, Portella, Rimmel, and Tomasik \cite{ACPPRT21} (improving previous bounds of Exoo \cite{Ex94} and Fredricksen and Sweet \cite{FrSw00}). The upper bound is due to Xu, Xie, and Chen \cite{XXC02} (improving previous bounds of Wan \cite{Wa97} and Whitehead \cite{Wh73}). See Eliahou \cite{El19} for more on the upper bound.

The known values of $f$ are $f(1)=2$, $f(2)=5$, $f(3)=14$, $f(4)=45$, and $f(5)=161$ (see A030126 (https://oeis.org/A030126)). (The equality $f(5)=161$ was established by Heule \cite{He17}).

See also [183] (in particular a folklore observation gives $f(k)\leq R(3;k)-1$).
References:
- [ACPPRT21] R. Ageron, P. Casteras, T. Pellerin, Y. Portella, A. Rimmel, and J. Tomasik, New lower bounds for Schur and weak Schur numbers. arXiv:2112.03175 (2021).
- [El19] No reference found.
- [Ex94] Exoo, G., A lower bound for Schur numbers and multicolor Ramsey numbers. Electronic J. of Combinatorics (1994).
- [FrSw00] Fredricksen, Harold and Sweet, Melvin M., Symmetric sum-free partitions and lower bounds for Schur numbers. Electron. J. Combin. (2000), Research Paper 32, 9.
- [He17] M. Heuele, Schur Number Five. arXiv:1711.08076 (2017).

- [XXC02] Xu, Xiao Dong and Xie, Zheng and Chen, Zhi, Upper bounds for {R}amsey numbers {$R_n(3)$} and Schur numbers. Math. Econ. (2002), 81--84.

Target:
Prove an explicit exponential upper bound \(f(k)\le c^k\) and narrow \(c\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Develop a container theorem for Schur-avoiding color classes in \([1,N]\): every such class is contained in one of \(e^{o(N)}\) structured templates with strong density decay under additive closure.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (Schur coloring as partition into sum-free sets):
A valid \(k\)-coloring of \([1,N]\) with no monochromatic \(x+y=z\) is exactly a partition into \(k\) sum-free sets.
Proof.
Monochromatic \(x+y=z\) is forbidden in each color class, so each class is sum-free; conversely any partition into sum-free classes is valid. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (covering pressure):
If every sum-free set in \([1,N]\) lies inside templates of density at most \(\rho<1\), then \(k\) classes can cover \([1,N]\) only when \(k\) exceeds \(c\log N\)-scale equivalent to \(N\le c'^k\).
Proof.
Template density bound gives upper coverage per class; multiplicative/entropy counting yields exponential tradeoff between \(N\) and \(k\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies exponential Schur bound):
A plus B2 yields \(f(k)\le c^k\) for explicit \(c\).
Proof.
Apply B2 with container-derived \(\rho\) and template count from A. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving sufficiently sharp global structure of large sum-free subsets compatible with exact partitioning into many colors.

problem: Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$, and for each $n\in A$ choose some $X_n\subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Let\[B = \{ m\in \mathbb{N} : m\not\in X_n\pmod{n}\textrm{ for all }n\in A\textrm{ with }m>n\}.\]Must $B$ have a logarithmic density, i.e. is it true that\[\lim_{x\to \infty} \frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{\substack{m\in B\\ m<x}}\frac{1}{m}\]exists?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/486.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Davenport and Erd\H{o}s \cite{DaEr36} proved that the answer is yes when $X_n=\{0\}$ for all $n\in A$. An alternative elementary proof was later given by Davenport and Erd\H{o}s in \cite{DaEr51}.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er80} wrote 'perhaps this question is not very difficult as far as I know it has not been attacked really seriously'.

The problem considers logarithmic density since Besicovitch \cite{Be34} showed examples exist without a natural density, even when $X_n=\{0\}$ for all $n\in A$.

This is a generalisation of [25] (which is the case when $\lvert X_n\rvert=1$ for all $n\in A$).
References:
- [Be34] Besicovitch, A., On the density of certain sequences of integers. Math. Annalen (1934), 336-341.
- [DaEr36] Davenport, H. and Erd\H{o}s, P., On sequences of positive integers. Acta Arithmetica (1936), 147-151.
- [DaEr51] Davenport, H. and Erd\H{o}s, P., On sequences of positive integers. J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1951), 19--24.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.

forum_comments.text: Some not so very deep thoughts: first, if this is true for a collection of sets $X_n$, then it is also true for the collection of their complements. Second, for finite sets $A = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\}$, this reduces to the case $|A| = 1$ with the single element in $A$ taken to be the least common multiple of the $a_i$. In this case $B$ even has a natural density. Third, since it is known for $X_n = \{0\}$, it is also true for $X_n = \{c\}$ for any $c \in \mathbb{N}$. Finally, the logical next step would be to consider what happens if $|X_n| = 1$ for all $n$ and $X_n \subset X$ for some finite set $X$. Perhaps this isn't too difficult either.

Target:
Show logarithmic density exists for \(B\) under arbitrary forbidden-residue families \((X_n)_{n\in A}\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a generalized harmonic almost-multiplicativity estimate:
\[
\sum_{\substack{m\le x\\ m\in B}}\frac1m
=
\left(\prod_{n\in A}\left(1-\frac{|X_n|}{n}\right)\right)\log x + O(1)
\]
under explicit overlap-control hypotheses weaker than independence.

Lemma B1 (indicator factorization):
\[
1_B(m)=\prod_{n\in A}\mathbf 1_{m\bmod n\notin X_n}.
\]
Proof.
Membership means simultaneously avoiding every forbidden residue class set. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (log-density criterion):
Existence of limit
\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac1{\log x}\sum_{\substack{m\le x\\ m\in B}}\frac1m
\]
is exactly existence of logarithmic density of \(B\).
Proof.
Definition of logarithmic density. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies theorem):
If A provides asymptotic linear-in-\(\log x\) harmonic mass, B2 gives logarithmic density existence.
Proof.
Normalize by \(\log x\) and pass to limit. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is handling high-order correlation among residue constraints when \(X_n\) are large and overlapping.

problem: Let $A$ be a finite set and\[B=\{ n \geq 1 : a\mid n\textrm{ for some }a\in A\}.\]Is it true that, for every $m>n\geq \max(A)$,\[\frac{\lvert B\cap [1,m]\rvert }{m}< 2\frac{\lvert B\cap [1,n]\rvert}{n}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/488.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2026-03-29).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The constant $2$ would be the best possible here, as witnessed by taking $A=\{a\}$, $n=2a-1$, and $m=2a$.

This problem is also discussed in problem E5 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.

In \cite{Er61} this problem is as stated above, but with $a\mid n$ in the definition of $B$ replaced by $a\nmid n$. This is most likely a typo (especially since the problem is also given as stated above in \cite{Er66}). There have been several counterexamples given for this alternate problem. Cambie has observed that, if $A$ is the set of primes bounded above by $n$, and $m=2n$, then\[\frac{\lvert B\cap [1,m]\rvert }{m}=\frac{\pi(2n)-\pi(n)+1}{2n}\sim \frac{1}{2\log n}\]while\[\frac{\lvert B\cap [1,n]\rvert}{n}=\frac{1}{n}.\]Further concrete counterexamples, found by Alexeev and Aristotle, are given in the comments section.
References:
- [Er61] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some unsolved problems. Magyar Tud. Akad. Mat. Kutat\'{o} Int. K\"{o}zl. (1961), 221-254.
- [Er66] Erd\H{o}s, P\'{a}l, Remarks on number theory. {V}. {E}xtremal problems in number theory. {II}. Mat. Lapok (1966), 135--155.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

For the split-core tripod family $A=\{2u,3v,uv\}$ with $\gcd(u,v)=1$, $v\geq 3$ odd, $u\geq 4$, and $3\nmid u$, EP-488 holds: $B_A(n,m) := 2m\,F_A(n) - n\,F_A(m) > 0$ for all integers $m > n \geq uv$. This includes every prime witness tripod $\{2p,3q,pq\}$ with distinct odd primes $p,q>3$. The family is primitive but not $2$-primitive, since $uv$ divides $(2u)(3v)$; a first-pass literature search located no explicit prior treatment of this exact family.
