problem: Let $f(z)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_kz^{n_k}$ be an entire function (with $a_k\neq 0$ for all $k\geq 1$). Is it true that if $n_k/k\to \infty$ then $f(z)$ assumes every value infinitely often?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/517.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 29 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Fej\'{e}r and P\'{o}lya.

Fej\'{e}r \cite{Fe08} proved that if $\sum\frac{1}{n_k}<\infty$ then $f(z)$ assumes every value at least once, and Biernacki \cite{Bi28} proved that if $\sum\frac{1}{n_k}<\infty$ then $f(z)$ assumes every value infinitely often.

P\'{o}lya \cite{Po29} proved that if $f$ has finite order then $f(z)$ assumes every value infinitely often under the assumption that $\limsup (n_{k+1}-n_k)=\infty$.
References:
- [Bi28] Biernacki, Mi\'{e}cislas, Sur les \'{e}quations alg\'{e}briques contenant des param\'{e}tres arbitraires. (1928), 145.
- [Fe08] Fej\'{e}r, Leopold, \"{U}ber die Wurzel vom kleinsten absoluten Betrage einer algebraischen Gleichung. Math. Ann. (1908), 413-423.
- [Po29] P\'olya, G., Untersuchungen \"uber {L}\"ucken und Singularit\"{a}ten von {P}otenzreihen. Math. Z. (1929), 549--640.

Note that if we drop the multiplicative assumption, and simply assign $f(m)=\pm 1$ at random, then this statement is true (with $c=\sqrt{2}$), the law of the iterated logarithm (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_iterated_logarithm).

 Wintner \cite{Wi44} proved that, almost surely,\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2+o(1)},\]and Erd\H{o}s improved the right-hand side to $N^{1/2}(\log N)^{O(1)}$. Lau, Tenenbaum, and Wu \cite{LTW13} have shown that, almost surely,\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{2+o(1)}.\]Caich \cite{Ca24b} has improved this to\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{3/4+o(1)}.\]Harper \cite{Ha13} has shown that the sum is almost surely not $O(N^{1/2}/(\log\log N)^{5/2+o(1)})$, and conjectured that in fact Erd\H{o}s' conjecture is false, and almost surely\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m) \ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{1/4+o(1)}.\]
References:

- [Wi44] Wintner, Aurel, Random factorizations and Riemann's hypothesis. Duke Math. J. (1944), 267-275.

problem: Let $(\epsilon_k)_{k\geq 0}$ be independently uniformly chosen at random from $\{-1,1\}$. If $R_n$ counts the number of real roots of $f_n(z)=\sum_{0\leq k\leq n}\epsilon_k z^k$ then is it true that, almost surely,\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{R_n}{\log n}=\frac{2}{\pi}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/521.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 19 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Offord \cite{EO56} showed that the number of real roots of a random degree $n$ polynomial with $\pm 1$ coefficients is $(\frac{2}{\pi}+o(1))\log n$.

It is ambiguous in \cite{Er61} whether Erd\H{o}s intended the coefficients to be uniformly chosen from $\{-1,1\}$ or $\{0,1\}$. In the latter case, the constant $\frac{2}{\pi}$ should be $\frac{1}{\pi}$ (see the discussion in the comments).

In the case of $\{-1,1\}$ Do \cite{Do24} proved that, if $R_n[-1,1]$ counts the number of roots in $[-1,1]$, then, almost surely,\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{R_n[-1,1]}{\log n}=\frac{1}{\pi}.\]See also [522].
References:
- [Do24] Y. Do, A strong law of large numbers for real roots of random polynomials. arXiv:2403.06353 (2024).
- [EO56] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Offord, A. C., On the number of real roots of a random algebraic equation. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1956), 139-160.
- [Er61] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some unsolved problems. Magyar Tud. Akad. Mat. Kutat\'{o} Int. K\"{o}zl. (1961), 221-254.

forum_comments.author: BraydenLetwin
forum_comments.text:
Hi Terry, Quanyu, and Vjeko. I'm effectively just stating my approach to this problem here. The ideas that the three of you contributed allowed me to paint the picture for a solution, and I would be happy to jointly work on finishing up this project. I agree that the $\lim$ should not exist, and it would be even nicer to determine the precise $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ here. The main idea is of course that if $R_n$ denotes the roots in $(-\infty -1) \cup (1, \infty)$ then one may prove\[
\sup_{N \le m < n \le 2N} |R_n - R_m| \gg \log N.
\]First focus on $x < 0$, writing $x = -e^{-t/n}$ for $t > 0$. Then $t$ measures the distance from $1$ at the "natural" scale of $1/n$. The point of this is that if we write $O_n(t) = (-1)^n e^{-t} n^{-1/2} f_n(e^{-t/n})$ then $O_n(t)$ becomes a Laplace transform type of object as $n$ becomes super large. When $n$ becomes large, I should expect this to approach a Gaussian process for which I may then apply analytical techniques to solve the problem with ease.

Let us fix some sequence $U_n$ with $U_n \to \infty$ and $U_n = o(n)$. Then the "bucket" idea that Terry has is to look at $$B_n(U_n, c, C) = [-e^{CU_n/n}, -e^{cU_n/n}].$$ If one write $O_{n, U_n}(\tau) = \sqrt{U_n}O_n(U_n\tau)$ then this looks like a Riemann-sum in some sense. One may calculate $O_{n, U_n} \to G$ in $C^1[c, C]$ where $G$ is the centered Gaussian process with covariance $\mathbb{E}G(\tau)G(\sigma) = 1/(\tau + \sigma)$.

Why is this viewpoint interesting? Well now we can use the regularity of $G$ to understand statements about the roots of $G$, and then convert these statements back to the polynomial. There are some facts that I could assign my dog to prove: With high probability, the zeros of $G$ are simple, "well-seperated" and $G$ has derivative at these points "far" away from zero. Also, if two $C^1$ functions are sufficiently close and the first has such stable zeros, then they have the same number of zeros in $[c, C]$.

Now, I will combine this observation with the following idea/question: Which coefficients actually affect the zero count in a "bucket" as Terry defines? Let us perturb a block of reverse coefficients at some depth $R$. If we resample the coefficients in this window but impose finitely many moment constraints to that the perturbation does not create unwanted lower order effects, then after some rescaling the perturbation converges in $C^1[c, C]$ to a Gaussian field $Z$ obtained from the kernel $(\tau, \sigma) = \int_a^b e^{-x(\tau + \sigma)}~ dx$. The point is that $Z$ is independent of $G$, so we need to understand and prove something like this:\[
\mathbb{P}(N(G + Z; [c, C]) \neq N(G; [c, C])) > 0,
\]where $N$ denotes the number of zeros. In other words, adding a non-trivial independent Gaussian perturbation changes the number of zeros in the bucket with positive probability. We now look at three cases. $R \ll n/U_n$, $R \gg n/U_n$, and $R \asymp n/U_n$. For the first case, if we match finitely many moments then we can use Taylor expansion ideas to show that the perturbation becomes invisible in $C^1$. For $R \gg n/U_n$ can also be dealt with ease. Therefore, we only need to worry about the reverse coefficients at depth $R \asymp n/U_n$. And this coupled with all the other ideas before should give a nice proof (after we do the same for $x > 0$.

What is not so easy is determining the precise $\limsup$ and $\liminf$. I would love to know if people have further ideas. Making this a joint project would be great, because after all, the biggest idea was actually observing that this may be false (I was always trying to prove that this is true, because if one considers the Kac-Rice formula for Gaussian processes then this $G$ actually predicts $2/\pi$).

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
Hi Brayden! Thanks for the credit, but I don't think that I had nontrivial observations here. :-)

Regarding your sketch of the approach, maybe you want to write up rigorously the Gaussian Kac polynomials $\sum_{k=0}^n \xi_k x^k$ first.
Your suggestion to write points below $-1$ in the form $x=-\exp(U\tau/n)$, $\tau\in[c,C]$, $U=U_n\to\infty$, $U=o(n)$ makes sense to me heuristically. But I don't yet see that it disproves the a.e. convergence. Yes, you get the Gaussian endpoint limit of the rescaled outside-endpoint process\[ \sqrt{\frac{U}{n}} (-1)^n e^{-U\tau}f_n(-e^{U\tau/n}) \]converging in law in $C^1[c,C]$ to the centered Gaussian process $G$ with $\mathbb{E} G(\tau)G(\sigma)=\frac1{\tau+\sigma}$. Thus the zero count converges in distribution to $N_G([c,C])$. This part can be made clean for the Gaussian Kac polynomials. You prove that a coefficient block at reverse depth $R\asymp n/U$ has a nonzero probability of changing the zero count by $O(1)$ in the corresponding outside bucket
$[-\exp(CU/n),-\exp(cU/n)]$. This part is good, I just don't yet see how one goes beyond that single bucket. (EDIT: But now, after reading Brayden's wishes under [522], I understand that the details will be published elsewhere.)

Regarding the heuristcs for the $\liminf$ and $\limsup$: your endpoint heuristics suggests what they should be, provided that non-cancellation is present. Model the two outside endpoints by a two-endpoint zero process over time about $\log n$. Suppose that it satisfies large-deviation principle\[ \mathbb{P}\Big(\frac{N_n((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty))}{\log n}\approx x\bigg) = n^{-I(x)} \]with $I(1/\pi)=0$. Then\[ \mathbb{P}\Big(\exists n\in[N,2N]:\frac{N_n((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty))}{\log n}\approx x\bigg)
= 1-\exp(-N^{1-I(x)+o(1)}). \]Thus, the total count of zeros, in the whole $\mathbb{R}$, should satisfy\[ \mathbb{P} \Big( \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{N_n(\mathbb{R})}{\log n} = \frac{1}{\pi}+\rho \Big) = 1, \]where $\rho=\sup\{x\geq0:I(x)\leq1\}$ and I am not even sure that this is computable (in some explicit way). On the other hand, I find it experimentally convincing that\[ \mathbb{P} \Big( \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{N_n((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty))}{\log n} = 0 \Big) = 1, \quad i.e.,\quad \mathbb{P} \Big( \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{N_n(\mathbb{R})}{\log n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \Big) = 1. \]I guess that your dog would bet its tail on that after seeing the sample trajectory from my first post here. LOL

If one first concentrates on just disproving the a.e. convergence, could there be a more naive way, based on the $\liminf$ probably being $0$, I mean $1/\pi$ for zeros on the whole line? Instead of trying to force an excess of outside roots, to try to prove that the outside count\[ O_n:=N_n((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty)) \]vanishes for infinitely many $n$. By reciprocity, this is equivalent to asking that\[ g_n(x):=x^n f_n(1/x)=\sum_{k=0}^n \epsilon_{n-k}x^k \]have no zeros in $(-1,1)$. This is not contradicted by Yen Do's theorem on $[-1,1]$, because he studied the prefix sequence $f_n(x)=\sum_{k\le n}\epsilon_k x^k$, while $g_n$ is a moving reversed prefix whose important endpoint coefficients are refreshed as $n$ varies.
For a single endpoint the persistence exponent for the corresponding logarithmic stationary process should be $3/16$, so for the two outside endpoints one expects (EDIT: actually, this is easy, one does have that)\[ \mathbb{P}(O_n=0)=n^{-3/8+o(1)}. \]Since\[ \sum_{n\leq N}\mathbb P(O_n=0)\sim N^{5/8+o(1)}, \]there is "enough entropy" for infinitely many such $n$. What is missing (EDIT: actually it is not missing, this is easy too) is something like\[ \mathbb P(O_n=0,O_{n+h}=0)
\lesssim n^{-3/8+\varepsilon}h^{-3/8+\varepsilon} , \]meaning that $g_n$ and $g_{n+h}$ share only the deeper endpoint scales. This should imply that the $\liminf$ is $1/\pi$ because of Yen Do's theorem, and then the convergence in probability to $2/\pi$ would disprove the a.e. convergence.
(EDIT: This is not a competing solution with Brayden's, or anything, just a trivial idea and I reserve no credits. The whole argument is still not complete anyway, and even if it can be finished, it will be inferior to the suggested stronger results. I am pursuing this just out of curiosity.)

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
I am posting with Brayden's approval. I managed to get ChatGPT 5.5 Pro prove a variant of the problem for the Gaussian Kac polynomials, i.e. with the standard normal coefficients. This still doesn't solve the Erdos problem (which was stated for the random Littlewood = Rademacher Kac polynomials), but at least it's something, since it already gives a negative answer to Problem 1.2.a by Igor Pritsker, posed here (http://aimpl.org/randpolyzero/1/).

The writeup is here. (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/files/Erdos_521_Gaussian.pdf) I first prompted ChatGPT to initially judge the ideas from this forum thread, it sorted them by likelihood/simplicity, then it preferred and picked up my idea (sketched above) of estimating probabilities of single events and pairs of events of having no roots in $\mathbb{R}\setminus[-1,1]$ (but, in the end, a "log log shortened" set than that actually worked). After some guidance and a lot of proofreading and corrections from my side, it produced the above file. If you want to inspect the full (very long and thinking time consuming) chat, it is here (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ebe4bd-fc60-838c-b4bd-deed2abec4e1). I certainly do plan to rewrite this proof in a better and human way when I find time, but I first wanted to convince myself that it can be made to work.

As for the actual outline of the proof, it also combines a few things said here on the forum: Terry's idea of carefully choosing a bucket, then, most importantly, Brayden's idea of convergence to a stationary Gaussian process, and my suggestions to concentrate on the lack of outside roots. The goal is to disprove the strong law $R_n/\log n\to2/\pi$ a.s. by showing\[ \mathbb{P}\bigg(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{R_n}{\log n}
\le \frac1\pi+\delta\Big)>0 \]for any small $\delta>0$. Instead of $\sum_{k=0}^n \xi_j x^j$ we study the reversed polynomial\[ Q_n(x):=\sum_{j=0}^n \xi_{n-j}x^j. \]We take, like, $L_n=4\log\log n$ and define a (reversed) "bucket"\[ I_n:=[-1+L_n/n,\,1-L_n/n]. \]We consider the events $B_n$ that $Q_n$ has no roots in $I_n$. The estimate\[ \mathbb P(B_n)\asymp (L_n/n)^{3/8} \]is obtained by the change of variables $x=\tanh(t/2)$, under which the normalized Gaussian power series converges to the stationary Gaussian process\[ Y_t=\sqrt{1-\tanh^2(t/2)}\,\sum_{j\ge0}\xi_j\tanh^j(t/2),
\quad \mathbb{E} Y_sY_t=\operatorname{sech}\Big(\frac{s-t}{2}\bigg), \]and by applying the persistence asymptotics\[ \mathbb{P}(Y_t>0\ \forall |t|\le T)\asymp e^{-3T/8}. \]Next, the decorrelation bound\[ \mathbb{P}(B_n\cap B_{n+h}) \ll_\varepsilon
(L_n/n)^{3/8}(L_h/h)^{3/8}, \qquad h\ge n^\varepsilon \]is shown using the exact decomposition $Q_{n+h}=F_h+x^h Q_n$, where the "fresh block" $F_h$ is independent of the old coefficients. Kochen-Stone then gives a positive-probability event on which $B_n$ occurs for infinitely many $n$. The remaining endpoint strips\[ [-1,-1+L_n/n]\cup[1-L_n/n,1] \]are controlled by Rolle's theorem, giving, with a large probability, that there are at most $(\delta/2)\log n$ zeros there. Thus, together,\[ \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{R_n(\mathbb{R}\setminus[-1,1])}{\log n}
\leq \delta \]with a positive probability.

Maybe someone has ideas on how to prove a result for more general Kac polynomials, including the Rademacher ones. I thought that this problem should naturally be a collaboration, since many ideas were shared already by different people. I wanted to share this writeup as a possible viable route, if you find it correct and worthwhile, but I don't mind if the approach sketched originally turns out to be a better one, and all this gets superseded.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
Regarding the coefficients in $\{-1,1\}$ (the mean zero setting), there is one detail that might still be missing. Namely, (my dear bro) Yen proved (https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06353) in the paper that msawhney mentioned:\[ \frac{N_n([-1,1])}{\log n} \to \frac{1}{\pi} \ a.s., \]where $N_n(A)$ counts the number of roots in $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. What’s still missing is\[ \frac{N_n((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty))}{\log n} \to \frac{1}{\pi} \ a.s. \]If $N_n(\mathbb{R})=(2/\pi+o(1))\log n$ was merely to be shown "with large probability" (in the sense of terminology used, say, with random graphs), which is the ancient result, and not "almost surely", then the distribution of roots for a fixed $n$ would be symmetric under the reflection $z\to1/z$, so the other convergence claim would follow automatically. However, this reflection reverses the coefficients, so (for a fixed time segment $1,\ldots,n$) it reverses time, and the joint distribution of the full latter infinite sequence of random variables is no longer related to the former one. You can notice that Yen talks about this in Section 7. In fact, v1 of the paper on the arXiv made precisely that logical mistake, incorrectly claiming the a.s. convergence of $N_n(\mathbb{R})/\log n$ and later retracting it.

I did very poor experimentation: a sample trajectory of $N_n([-1,1])/\log n$ typically looks like this (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/images/trajectory1.gif), while a sample trajectory of $N_n((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty))/\log n$ typically looks like this (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/images/trajectory2.gif). The latter seems to oscillate more, raising doubt that they might not converge a.s., but $n\leq500$ are too small numbers to conclude anything meaningful.

Regarding the coefficients in $\{0,1\}$ (the nonzero mean setting), I noticed that Yen mentions a preprint titled "Real roots of non-centered random polynomials" on his webpage (https://profile.virginia.edu/yqd3p). I cannot find it online, but here are some related slides (https://app.icerm.brown.edu/assets/539/9763/9763_5485_Nguyen_080420251600_Slides.pdf). From my understanding, the strong law (i.e., the a.s. convergence) is still an open problem mentioned on slide 28.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
This looks like an important distinction [and Yen Do has privately communicated similar points to me in recent discussions]. Heuristically, for each $1 \leq j \leq \log_2 n$, there should be $O(1)$ zeroes of $f=f_n$ in the region $[-1+2^{-j-1}, -1+2^{-j}]$, and $O(1)$ zeroes in the region $[-1-2^{-j}, -1-2^{-j-1}]$. In the former case it's the coefficients $\epsilon_i$ for $i \ll 2^j$ that should largely control the zero count, but in the latter case it is the $\epsilon_i$ for $n-i \ll 2^j$. So the former is heuristically quite stable in $n$ (say for $n \in [n_0, 2n_0]$) but the latter can be quite unstable, and in particular the situation for $f_n$ and $f_{n'}$ should behave in some uncorrelated fashion for $n'-n \gg 2^j$. Assuming that each $f_n$ has some positive probability of not having a zero in $[-1-2^{-j}, -1-2^{-j-1}]$, this should cause the zero count here to be quite unstable, almost certainly fluctuating by $O(1)$ for $n \in [n_0,2n_0]$ if say one is in the regime $n_0^{0.1} \leq 2^j \leq n_0^{0.9}$. Heuristically, this would then predict the global zero count to then fluctuate by more than $O(1)$. But it may be quite challenging to make this intuition precise - there could be some "global conspiracy" that makes all these fluctuations magically cancel each other even if locally they behave like a nice process such as a Gaussian process. In particular the variance of the global count could experience some ridiculous cancellation that makes it smaller than the variance of the local zero counts. I don't see how to prevent this sort of getting extremely accurate control of the process (with error terms better than $o(1/n)$ on various pair correlation functions). Even the mean zero gaussian coefficient case, which is presumably the simplest model, looks a bit tough here.

EDIT: maybe a switching approach? Generate two correlated samples $\epsilon_j, \epsilon'_j$ of the coefficients, which are largely the same but differ at some carefully chosen, well spaced locations, so that they have largely independent impacts on the zero statistics. If one can show a lower bound on the variance of the difference of the global zero count for the $\epsilon_j$ polynomial and the global zero count for the $\epsilon_{j'}$ polynomial after taking a supremum over some suitable sequence of $n$, then one might be able to disprove the claimed strong law thanks to the (contrapositive of the) triangle inequality. The hope here is that by carefully titrating the amount of switching, one might be able to cancel out most of the weird and hard to understand global correlation structure and work with something more like the sum of random variables with very low covariances between them, which is something we have a chance of getting variance lower bounds on. It might also be useful to design the joint distribution of the $\epsilon_j$ and $\epsilon'_j$ so that certain partial sums or moments agree, in order to damp out long range correlations.

forum_comments.author: msawhney
forum_comments.text:
This is really a remarkably delicate question (and honestly really unexpected to me)! For the approach suggested in the previous reply; it would seem that the probability that the number of real roots deviates from the expected amount by $\epsilon \log n$ scales as $n^{-\epsilon'}$ with $\epsilon'$ to $0$ as $\epsilon$ to $0$. Here is maybe a hopelessly naive strategy that might be useful? (It is just based on this heuristic of which coefficients control the zeros in which buckets.)

Let us group indices at a dyadic scale $[n, 2n]$. Define an index to be ''great'' if it has $\epsilon \log n$ ''extra'' zeros below $-1-n^{-1/4}$. By the heuristic suggested above the events that a pair of indices are great should essentially completely decorrelate once the pair of indices under consideration differ by more than $n^{3/4}$ (say). (I am assuming here is possible to control the number of zeros relatively deep into the tail; not sure how possible this is.)

This second moment argument would then give many indices where there are too many zeros towards the endpoint. The next claim would be even conditional on these zeros (which are mostly determined by the last few coefficients) then typically the inner interval has the expected number of zero. Then using a first moment argument we don't have too many indices which are great but have the expected number of zeros. This gives with high probability that at least one index in the range does not satisfy the required number of real roots. (Then taking massively separated dyadic intervals would conclude the result.) This last part is rather sketchy (and possibly impossible to justify).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Here is some more detail on the switching strategy. Pick a large $n$, then let $n < n_1 < \dots < n_m < 2n$ be $m \sim n^{0.7}$ "checkpoints" separated by $\sim n^{0.3}$. We introduce intervals $I_j = [n_j - n^{0.2}, n_j - n^{0.1}]$ to the left of each checkpoint $n_j$. If the almost sure conjecture is true, then for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ we will have
$$ {\bf P}( \sup_{1 \leq j \leq m} |N_{n_j}({\bf R}) - \frac{1}{\pi} \log n| \leq \varepsilon \log n ) = 1 - o(1).$$
Now let us condition all the $\epsilon_k$ outside of $\bigcup_{j=1}^m I_j$ to be fixed, so that only the coefficients inside $I_1,\dots,I_m$ remain random. Let $\epsilon'_k$ be a resampling of $\epsilon_k$ subject to this fixing, so the signs of $\epsilon'_k$ agree with $\epsilon_k$ outside of the $I_1,\dots,I_m$ but are completely resampled within these intervals. Actually we should not do a completely independent resampling; we should fix means,
$$ \sum_{k \in I_j} \epsilon'_k = \sum_{k \in I_j} \epsilon_k$$
and actually I think we should fix a few more moments,
$$ \sum_{k \in I_j} k^a \epsilon'_k = \sum_{k \in I_j} k^a \epsilon_k \quad (1)$$
for $a=0,\dots,1000$. I believe that this should be doable with some local limit theorems - it only is costing a small amount of "entropy" - but let me ignore this issue for this sketch.

If we let $N'_{n_j}$ be the zero counting function associated to this new coefficients then by the triangle inequality we have
$$ {\bf P}( \sup_{1 \leq j \leq m} |N_{n_j}({\bf R}) - N'_{n_j}({\bf R})| \leq 2\varepsilon \log n ) = 1 - o(1).$$
The point is that the way we have constructed things, the zeroes of $f_{n_j}$ and $f'_{n_j}$ are nearly identical except at $[-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}]$: any further away from $-1$ and the only coefficients that matter are those that are between $n_j$ and $I_{j}$, and any closer to $-1$ then the moment conditions (1) and some Taylor expansion should also make the polynomials agree nearly completely. So one should morally have
$$ {\bf P}( \sup_{1 \leq j \leq m} |N_{n_j}([-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}]) - N'_{n_j}([-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}])| \leq 3\varepsilon \log n ) = 1 - o(1).$$
Let's write this as
$$ {\bf P}( \bigwedge_{j=1}^m E_j ) = 1-o(1)$$
where $E_j$ is the event that $|N_{n_j}([-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}]) - N'_{n_j}([-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}])| \leq 3\varepsilon \log n$. Morally, this event depends on the signs of $\epsilon_k, \epsilon'_k$ on $I_j$, but is almost completely independent of the signs at the other $I_{j'}$, because of they are so far away (at least $n^{0.3}$ away). So, after some minor adjustments, one should be able to replace $E_j$ by completely independent events. So now this means that
$$ {\bf P}( E_j ) = 1-o(1/m) = 1 - o(n^{-0.7})$$
for at least one of the $j$. But hopefully some lower bound variance calculation can rule this out since $0.7$ is large compared to the exponent $0.21$ that is controlling the scale here.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
Reply to “I believe that this should be doable with some local limit theorems – it only is costing a small amount of entropy”

Yes — this step can be made precise using a multivariate lattice local limit theorem, and the entropy cost can be quantified explicitly.

Let $I_j$ be one of your resampling blocks, of length $\ell_j \asymp n^{0.2}$. Let $
\eta_k = 2\epsilon_k - 1 \in \{-1,1\}.
$ Fix $A \ge 0$ (e.g. $A=1000$) and set $d := A+1$. For $v_k = (k^0,\dots,k^A)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^d$ write $$
S_j(\epsilon) := \sum_{k\in I_j} \epsilon_k v_k,
\qquad S_j^{(\pm)}(\eta) := \sum_{k\in I_j} \eta_k v_k.
$$ If $S_j(\epsilon) = T$ for some target $T \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, this is equivalent to $$
S_j^{(\pm)}(\eta) = 2T - \sum_{k\in I} v_k =: t'.
$$ The map $\epsilon \mapsto \eta = 2\epsilon - 1$ is a bijection $\{0,1\}^I \to \{\pm1\}^I$ which sends the $\{0,1\}$ moment constraint $S_j(\epsilon) = T$ to the $\{\pm1\}$ moment constraint $S_j^{(\pm)}(\eta) = t'$. In particular, the feasible sets $$
\Omega_T^{(0/1)} := \{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^I : S_j(\epsilon) = T\},
\qquad \Omega_{t'}^{(\pm)} := \{\eta\in\{\pm1\}^I : S_j^{(\pm)}(\eta) = t'\}
$$ satisfy $$
|\Omega_T^{(0/1)}| = |\Omega_{t'}^{(\pm)}|,
$$ so counting solutions (or entropy) in the $\{0,1\}$ model is exactly the same as in the $\{\pm1\}$ model, up to an explicit shift of the target vector.

The moment–matching constraint on $I_j$ is $$
\sum_{k\in I_j} k^a \eta_k = \sum_{k\in I_j} k^a \epsilon_k
\quad (a=0,\dots,A),
$$ i.e. $S_j(\eta) = t'_j := S_j(\epsilon)$. The feasible set $$
\Omega_j := \{ \eta \in \{\pm1\}^{I_j} : S_j(\eta) = t'_j \}
$$ has cardinality $$
|\Omega_j| = 2^{\ell_j} \cdot \mathbb{P}(S_j = t'_j),
$$ where the probability is for $\eta_k$ i.i.d. uniform $\pm 1$.

Now apply the $d$-dimensional lattice LLT for bounded independent vectors with nondegenerate covariance $$
\Sigma_j := \sum_{k\in I_j} v_k v_k^\top.
$$ Uniformly for $t'_j$ in the central region, $$
\mathbb{P}(S_j = t'_j)
= (2\pi)^{-d/2} (\det\Sigma_j)^{-1/2} e^{ -\frac12 t'_j{}^\top \Sigma_j^{-1} t'_j }
+ o\big((\det\Sigma_j)^{-1/2}\big).
$$ A Cauchy–Binet + Vandermonde computation gives $\det\Sigma_j \asymp_d \ell_j^{\,d^2}$, so $$
\mathbb{P}(S_j = t'_j) \asymp_d \ell_j^{-d^2/2}.
$$ Thus $$
|\Omega_j| \asymp_d 2^{\ell_j} \, \ell_j^{-d^2/2}.
$$ Since the conditional distribution on $\Omega_j$ is uniform, its Shannon entropy is $$
H(\Omega_j) = \log_2 |\Omega_j|
= \ell_j - \frac{d^2}{2} \log_2 \ell_j + O_d(1).
$$ Compared to the $\ell_j$ bits of an unconstrained block, the entropy loss is $\frac{d^2}{2} \log_2 \ell_j = O(\log n)$ per block. Over $m \asymp n^{0.7}$ blocks, the total loss is $O(n^{0.7} \log n) = o(n^{0.9})$, which is indeed “a small amount of entropy” in the sense of your switching argument.

forum_comments.author: John N. Dvorak
forum_comments.text:
I tried to push this switching/moment-matching sketch into a more explicit conditional proof skeleton (not a proof announcement):

Full conditional roadmap (https://github.com/JohnNDvorak/Research_Pre-Preprints/blob/main/erdos_521_conditional_roadmap.pdf)

The goal is to isolate the precise local inputs needed for the dyadic switching strategy suggested here. The contradiction spine is that an a.s. law \(R_n/\log n\to2/\pi\) would force every dyadic coupling of two iid Rademacher sequences \(f,f'\) to satisfy\[
 \sup_{N\le m\le2N}|R_m(f)-R_m(f')|=o_{\mathbb P}(\log N).
 \]So the skeleton tries to build iid-marginal switching couplings for which some checkpoint \(n_j\in[N,2N]\) has a \(c\log N\) discrepancy with probability \(1-o(1)\).

The coupling uses a doubly stochastic same-fiber kernel on disjoint late-coefficient blocks, preserving iid marginals. Exterior roots are analyzed through\[
 G_{n_j}(y)=y^{n_j}f_{n_j}(1/y)=\sum_{r=0}^{n_j}\epsilon_{n_j-r}y^r,\qquad
 y=\sigma e^{-t}.
 \]The remaining hard inputs are the two-endpoint local template, same-fiber entropy, conditional anti-concentration under the actual fiber/template law, off-core stability for the total perturbation, cross-checkpoint interference control, and pairwise checkpoint decorrelation. Do's \([-1,1]\) theorem is used only as a global dyadic good event.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
After looking again carefully at the problem in the original source, I think I have misunderstood the original question quite badly - in fact Erdős was most likely intending to ask whether, if $\epsilon_k\in \{-1,1\}$ is an infinite sequence chosen uniformly at random, and $R_n(f)$ counts the number of real roots of $\sum_{0\leq k\leq n}\epsilon_kz^k$, then\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{R_n(f)}{\frac{2}{\pi}\log n}=1.\]In other words, a more delicate version of the Erdős and Offord [EO56] result cited above.

I apologise for the inaccuracy - but this wrongly transcribed problem seems to have generated a lot of interesting discussion! I'm therefore minded to keep the problem as it's written here, but add the caveat that this is in fact not a problem of Erdős strictly speaking (at least, until someone can find a source asking about this one).

If I'm understanding the literature correctly, this corrected Erdős problem is the same as the question of Pritsker raised in the 2019 AIM workshop (perhaps unaware of Erdős' original question).

Furthermore, this corrected problem is still open, although the paper of Do mentioned in the comments above is partial progress.

problem:
Let $f(z)=\sum_{0\leq k\leq n} \epsilon_k z^k$ be a random polynomial, where $\epsilon_k\in \{-1,1\}$ independently uniformly at random for $0\leq k\leq n$.

Is it true that, if $R_n$ is the number of roots of $f(z)$ in $\{ z\in \mathbb{C} : \lvert z\rvert \leq 1\}$, then\[\frac{R_n}{n/2}\to 1\]almost surely?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/522.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-08).
- Page last edited: 06 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Random polynomials with independently identically distributed coefficients are sometimes called Kac polynomials - this problem considers the case of Rademacher coefficients, i.e. independent uniform $\pm 1$ values. Erd\H{o}s and Offord \cite{EO56} showed that the number of real roots of a random degree $n$ polynomial with $\pm 1$ coefficients is $(\frac{2}{\pi}+o(1))\log n$.

There is some ambiguity whether Erd\H{o}s intended the coefficients to be in $\{-1,1\}$ or $\{0,1\}$ - see the comments section.

A weaker version of this was solved by Yakir \cite{Ya21}, who proved that\[\frac{R_n}{n/2}\to 1\]in probability. (This weaker claim was also asked by Erd\H{o}s, and also appears in a book of Hayman \cite{Ha67}.) More precisely,\[\lim_{n\to \infty} \mathbb{P}(\lvert R_n-n/2\rvert \geq n^{9/10}) =0.\]See also [521].
References:
- [EO56] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Offord, A. C., On the number of real roots of a random algebraic equation. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1956), 139-160.
- [Ha67] Hayman, W. K., Research problems in function theory. (1967), vii+56.
- [Ya21] Yakir, Oren, Approximately half of the roots of a random {L}ittlewood polynomial are inside the disk. Studia Math. (2021), 227--240.

Hi all, I have also independently attempted to work on this problem using ChatGPT-5.5-Pro. After carefully reviewing the result, I believe it leads to a possible solution (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ykwon0407/erdos-522/main/main-erdos-522-complete.pdf), though I would greatly appreciate any comments, corrections, or feedback.

Very briefly, we establish a uniform fourth-moment concentration estimate for Littlewood polynomials. The argument combines anti-concentration for Rademacher sums, control of small values, a smoothing step, and tools such as Pisier’s inequality and results of Nazarov–Nishry–Sodin. It appears to yield a quantitative almost-sure result with a convergence rate on the order of $n^{7/8+\delta}$ for any $\delta>0$, which I found noteworthy, though this may well not be optimal. Please see the link for more details.

As a note, at the time I was working on this problem, I was not aware of Przemek Chojecki’s solution, so I didn't use it as a part of prompts. That said, I do find the outcome quite interesting, in that AI can generate a range of different approaches. In this case, I suspect this is partly because I prompted ChatGPT to address the gap between Yakir’s in-probability convergence result and an almost-sure convergence statement, and the resulting argument ultimately builds on Yakir’s framework.

I have also discussed this with Brayden (thanks!), and wanted to share this for any feedback or thoughts.

forum_comments.text:
I've run remarks of Vjeko Kovac and Brayden Letwin through GPT-5.4 Pro and it came up with a claim for a complete solution. (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos522.pdf) There are many analytic estimates, so I'll probably try to formalize it too.

The proof combines three ingredients. First, Jensen's formula reduces the root count to logarithmic integrals at radii $1$ and $1-n^{-1-\alpha}$, with an elementary reciprocal-polynomial squeeze handling the closed disk exactly. Second, a logarithmic-integrability theorem of Nazarov, Nishry and Sodin controls the singularity of $\log |P_n|$ near zero. Third, a quantitative central-limit argument for angle averages of the normalized polynomial, in the spirit of Angst and Poly, yields almost-sure convergence of suitable smooth truncations of the logarithmic integral.

I recently wrote on this site (https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/AI%20Contributions#post-5304) about the new impedance mismatch between proof generation and proof digestion. I can offer the following culinary analogy. In an age of caloric scarcity, one would be happy to obtain food from any source available, as long as it has been verified to be edible and non-poisonous. But, once technology enables an age of caloric abundance, the generation of food is no longer the bottleneck, and it is no longer always appreciated to have arbitrarily large amounts of technically edible food dumped on one's plates. Especially if some other human has already promised to cook a meal for us.

In short, I think the current level of AI capabilities in math indicate that discussions should now focus more on quality than on quantity. Having thoughtful, carefully prepared discussions (involving both humans and AI) about a handful of Erdos problems would be preferable in my mind to having a large number of shallow discussion threads mostly involving undigested AI-generated proofs. We are here not to push the capabilities of the latest food-generation models, but instead to have a pleasant conversation over dinner.

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
Here are several rather obvious remarks, partly in analogy with problem 521, and produced before thinking about the problem. :-)

1) I don't think that this problem should be marked as solved, unless another reference is found. Namely, Erdős was precise about what he meant (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-22.pdf) (p.252), and he meant "a strong law", i.e., almost sure convergence of a sequence of random variables:\[ \frac{R'_n}{n/2} \to 1 \ a.s., \]where $R'_n$ counts the number of roots of $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\epsilon_k z^k$ in $|z|\prec 1$ (even though the closed disk $|z|\leq 1$ doesn't make a big difference).
Yakir's paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.06234) proves\[ \frac{R'_n}{n/2} \to 1 \ \text{in probability}, \]which is also commonly phrased (in the spirit of your formulation) as\[ R'_n = \Big(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\Big) n \quad\text{with large probability} \]and it is a weaker claim, except for the concrete error of order $O(n^{9/10})$.

2) On the other hand, it is not clear if Erdős meant the coefficients to be $-1,1$ valued coin tosses (i.e., the Rademacher variables) as he emphasizes in the beginning of Section 2) on the same page, or rather the $0,1$ valued coin tosses (i.e., the Bernoulli variables). Strictly speaking he wrote the latter (just as in problem 521), since he constructed $\epsilon_k$ as the $k$-th digit of $t$ taken from the sample space $[0,1)$, by writing $t=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon_k(t)}{2^k}$. However, he might have had some identification on mind, or wanted to write $t=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon_k(t)+1}{2^{k+1}}$ instead. I am more inclined to think that he meant $-1,1$.

3) In both cases the a.s. claim seems experimentally quite plausible. An easy simulation shows that in the $-1,1$ case a typical trajectory of $R'_n/(n/2)$ looks like this (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/images/trajectory3.gif), while in the $0,1$ case it typically looks like this (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/images/trajectory4.gif). In both cases it seems that convergence should in fact hold almost surely as well.

4) For the source of the problem Yakir actually cites Hayman's book from 1967. Erdős did in fact ask (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-22.pdf) (p.252) about the weaker claim as well, as you can see in the sentence beginning with "Here I cannot even prove that...".

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Following Mehtaab Sawhney remarks, I was able with GPT 5.2 (with a small input from Gemini/Grok) to complete the argument. Basically giving various estimates with $\limsup$ being straightforward and $\liminf$ being more tricky. You can find the full write-up of the arguments here (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos524.pdf). $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ parts are indepentent. Last section is the summary of results (also below), and 6.6. considers M.S. restatement in the comments below.

For Lebesgue-a.e. $t\in(0,1)$ the signs $a_k(t)=(-1)^{\epsilon_k(t)}$ are i.i.d. Rademacher, and\[
M_n(t)=\max_{x\in[-1,1]}\Big|\sum_{k=1}^n a_k(t)x^k\Big|
\]admits a sharp almost-sure upper-envelope law:\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n(t)}{\sqrt{2n\log\log n}}=1.
\]The proof is a reduction by Abel summation (Salem-Zygmund style) to maxima of two simple random walks, followed by the classical LIL (Kolmogorov-Hartman-Wintner/Chung). The same comparison yields subgaussian tails at the $\sqrt n$ scale for each fixed $n$.

For the lower envelope, the random-walk reduction is one-sided and gives only\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\Big(\tfrac{\log\log n}{n}\Big)^{1/2}M_n(t)\le \frac{\pi}{\sqrt8},
\]with no matching reverse bound. A more sensitive viewpoint uses the endpoint parametrization $x=\pm e^{-u/n}$, under which $M_n/\sqrt n$ becomes the supremum of two Laplace-type processes $Z_n^\pm(u)$.

Using a two-dimensional strong invariance principle (KMT/Zaitsev-type), $(Z_n^+,Z_n^-)$ can be coupled to two independent copies of $Y(u)=\int_0^1 e^{-us}\,dB(s)$; the small-deviation asymptotics of Gao-Li-Wellner, $\log\mathbb P(\sup_{u\ge0}|Y(u)|\le\epsilon)\asymp-|\log\epsilon|^3$, then give a Borel-Cantelli dichotomy on sparse subsequences showing that the minimal values occur on the scale\[
M_n(t)=\sqrt n\,\exp\!\big(-\Theta((\log\log n)^{1/3})\big)\quad\text{infinitely often},
\]with threshold constants determined (up to two-sided bounds) by the small-ball constants for $Y$.

forum_comments.author: msawhney
forum_comments.text:
It took me a while to understand what exactly this problem is attempting to ask. Note that for a fixed scale $n$ that the maximum will be around size $\sqrt{n}$. To see the lower bound, one can just examine the endpoint $x = 1$. For the upper bound one can use an argument of Salem--Zygmund that\[\sum_{k=1}^{n}\varepsilon_k x^{k} = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(x^{k} - x^{k+1})\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\varepsilon_j\Big) + x^n\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\varepsilon_j\Big).\]Now for $x\in [0,1]$, these coefficients are nonnegative and together sum to $1$ so\[\max_{x\in [0,1]}\Big|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\varepsilon_k x^{k}\Big|\le \max_{k\le n}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{k}\varepsilon_j\Big|.\]Via standard bounds for the maximum of a random walk, we have that the probability this is $\ge \lambda n^{1/2}$ scales as $e^{-\Omega(\lambda^2)}$. An essentially identical analysis applies for $x\in [-1,0]$ modulo replacing $\varepsilon_j$ by $(-1)^{j}\varepsilon_j$.

My current guess for what Erdos is asking for is a function $f(n)$ such that for almost all $t$ we have that $M_n(t)\ge f(n)$ for all but finitely many $n$ but $M_n(t)\ge C f(n)$ for infinitely many $n$. For this problem, note that\[\mathbb{P}\Big[\max_{k\le n}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{k}\varepsilon_j\Big|\le \varepsilon n^{1/2}\Big]\asymp \exp(-\Omega(1/\epsilon^2)).\]Noting that for scales which are sufficiently far away (e.g. $n$ vs $n(\log n)^2$ say) these two events are essentially independent. Now as there are $(\log n)^{1-o(1)}$ such distinct scales up to $n$, setting $\varepsilon \approx 1/\sqrt{\log\log n}$ we essentially recover Chung's result.

forum_comments.author: msawhney
forum_comments.text: This problem it turns out is very likely to follow from arguments present in the literature already; the true scale of this minimum seems to be between $n^{1/2}\exp(-c(\log\log n)^{1/3})$ and $n^{1/2}\exp(-c'(\log\log n)^{1/3})$. (Determining the exact constant $c$ is likely more technical.) The crucial point is to reparameterize $x = e^{-t/n}$ (thinking of $t$ fixed as $n\to \infty$) and we are seeing to bound\[\sum_{k=1}^{n}\varepsilon_k e^{-tk/n}\]for $t\ge 0$. This is essentially equivalent to looking at $Y(t) =\Big| \int_{0}^{1}e^{-tx}dB(x)\Big|$ and looking at the maximum for $t\ge 0$. We want to understand the probability that this maximum is small; this scaling is worked out in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.0200. (This reference was located with help from ChatGPT 5.2 Pro.) The remaining technical work is passing between the Gaussian limit and this problem.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
I just read [SZ54, p. 299] carefully, and I believe the current formulation of this problem on the website is incorrect; as stated (with coefficients $\epsilon_k(t)\in\{0,1\}$ and $x\in[0,1]$) it becomes essentially trivial. (indeed, the polynomial has nonnegative coefficients, so it is increasing on $[0,1]$, and thus \(M_n(t)=\max_{0\le x\le 1}\sum_{k\le n}\epsilon_k(t)x^k=\sum_{k\le n}\epsilon_k(t)\), reducing the question to the law of large numbers for the dyadic digits).

According to [SZ54], the intended coefficients should be random signs, i.e. Rademacher functions $\varphi_k(t)\in\{\pm1\}$ rather than binary digits $\epsilon_k(t)\in\{0,1\}$. In terms of the dyadic expansion $t=\sum_{k\ge1}\epsilon_k(t)2^{-k}$, one can set for instance\[
\varphi_k(t)=1-2\epsilon_k(t)\in\{\pm1\}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\varphi_k(t)=(-1)^{\epsilon_k(t)}.
\]Moreover, the maximization should be over $x\in[-1,1]$, not just $x\in[0,1]$. In other words, the Salem--Zygmund version is\[
M_n(t)=\max_{x\in[-1,1]}\left|\sum_{k\le n}\varphi_k(t)\,x^k\right|.
\]

problem: Let $f(n,k)$ count the number of self-avoiding walks (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-avoiding_walk) of $n$ steps (beginning at the origin) in $\mathbb{Z}^k$ (i.e. those walks which do not intersect themselves). Determine\[C_k=\lim_{n\to\infty}f(n,k)^{1/n}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/528.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
The constant $C_k$ is sometimes known as the connective constant. Hammersley and Morton \cite{HM54} showed that this limit exists, and it is trivial that $k\leq C_k\leq 2k-1$.

Kesten \cite{Ke63} proved that $C_k=2k-1-1/2k+O(1/k^2)$, and more precise asymptotics are given by Clisby, Liang, and Slade \cite{CLS07}.

Conway and Guttmann \cite{CG93} showed that $C_2\geq 2.62$ and Alm \cite{Al93} showed that $C_2\leq 2.696$. Jacobsen, Scullard, and Guttmann \cite{JSG16} have computed the first few decimal places of $C_2$, showing that\[C_2 = 2.6381585303279\cdots.\]See also [529].

- [Al93] Alm, Sven Erick, Upper bounds for the connective constant of self-avoiding walks. Combin. Probab. Comput. (1993), 115-136.
- [CG93] Conway, A. R. and Guttmann, A. J., Lower bound on the connective constant for square lattice self-avoiding walks. J. Phys. A (1993), 3719-3724.
- [CLS07] Clisby, Nathan and Liang, Richard and Slade, Gordon, Self-avoiding walk enumeration via the lace expansion. J. Phys. A (2007), 10973-11017.

problem: Let $d_k(n)$ be the expected distance from the origin after taking $n$ random steps from the origin in $\mathbb{Z}^k$ (conditional on no self intersections) - that is, a self-avoiding walk (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-avoiding_walk). Is it true that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{d_2(n)}{n^{1/2}}= \infty?\]Is it true that\[d_k(n)\ll n^{1/2}\]for $k\geq 3$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/529.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 27 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Slade \cite{Sl87} proved that, for $k$ sufficiently large, $d_k(n)\sim Dn^{1/2}$ for some constant $D>0$ (independent of $k$). Hara and Slade (\cite{HaSl91} and \cite{HaSl92}) proved this for all $k\geq 5$.

For $k=2$ Duminil-Copin and Hammond \cite{DuHa13} have proved that $d_2(n)=o(n)$.

It is now conjectured that $d_k(n)\ll n^{1/2}$ is false for $k=3$ and $k=4$, and more precisely (see for example Section 1.4 of \cite{MaSl93}) that $d_2(n)\sim Dn^{3/4}$, $d_3(n)\sim n^{\nu}$ where $\nu\approx 0.59$, and $d_4(n)\sim D(\log n)^{1/8}n^{1/2}$.

Madras and Slade \cite{MaSl93} have a monograph on the topic of self-avoiding walks.

problem:
Let $\ell(N)$ be maximal such that in any finite set $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ of size $N$ there exists a Sidon subset $S$ of size $\ell(N)$ (i.e. the only solutions to $a+b=c+d$ in $S$ are the trivial ones). Determine the order of $\ell(N)$.

In particular, is it true that $\ell(N)\sim N^{1/2}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/530.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Originally asked by Riddell \cite{Ri69}. Erd\H{o}s noted the bounds\[N^{1/3} \ll \ell(N) \leq (1+o(1))N^{1/2}\](the upper bound following from the case $A=\{1,\ldots,N\}$). The lower bound was improved to $N^{1/2}\ll \ell(N)$ by Koml\'{o}s, Sulyok, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{KSS75}. The correct constant is unknown, but it is likely that the upper bound is true, so that $\ell(N)\sim N^{1/2}$.

In \cite{AlEr85} Alon and Erd\H{o}s make the stronger conjecture that perhaps $A$ can always be written as the union of at most $(1+o(1))N^{1/2}$ many Sidon sets. (This is easily verified for $A=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ using standard constructions of Sidon sets.)

This is discussed in problem C9 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.

See also [1088] and [1208] for a higher-dimensional generalisation.
References:
- [AlEr85] Alon, Noga and Erd\H{o}s, P., An application of graph theory to additive number theory. European J. Combin. (1985), 201-203.

problem: Let $\delta>0$. If $n$ is sufficiently large and $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices with no $K_5$ and at least $\delta n^2$ edges then $G$ contains a set of $\gg_\delta n$ vertices containing no triangle.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/533.
- Page status: DISPROVED (database last update 2026-01-26).
- Page last edited: 27 January 2026.
Site remarks:
In other words, is it true that\[\delta_3(5)=\lim_{\epsilon \to 0}\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{\mathrm{RT}_3(n,K_5,\epsilon n)}{n^2}=0,\]where $\mathrm{RT}$ is the Ramsey-Tur\'{a}n number.

A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Hajnal, Simonovits, S\'{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di, who could prove that $\delta_3(5) \leq 1/12$ (with $\delta$ defined above), and could further prove that the analogous $\delta_3(4)=0$.

They further observed that $\delta_3(7)\geq 1/4$: by a construction of Erd\H{o}s and Rogers \cite{ErRo62} (see [620]) there exists some constant $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$, there is a graph on $n$ vertices which contains no $K_4$ and every set of at least $n^{1-c}$ vertices contains a triangle. If we take two vertex disjoint copies of this graph and add all edges between the two copies then this yields a graph on $2n$ vertices with $\geq n^2$ edges, which contains no $K_7$, yet every set of at least $2n^{1-c}$ vertices contains a triangle.

This is false, and disproved by Balogh and Lenz \cite{BaLe13}, who showed $\delta_3(5)>0$. The correct threshold is $\delta_3(5)=1/12$, the remaining lower bound of $\delta_3(5)\geq 1/12$ due to a construction of Liu, Reiher, Sharifzadeh, and Staden \cite{LRSS21}.

See also [579] and the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/RamseyTuran5.html).
References:
- [BaLe13] Balogh, J\'ozsef and Lenz, John, On the {R}amsey-Tur\'{a}n numbers of graphs and hypergraphs. Israel J. Math. (2013), 45--68.
- [ErRo62] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Rogers, C. A., The construction of certain graphs. Canadian J. Math. (1962), 702-707.
- [LRSS21] H. Liu, C. Reiher, M. Sharifzadeh, and K. Staden, Geometric construction for Ramsey-Tur\'{a}n theory. arXiv:2103.10423 (2021).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Here is a near-miss: if $G$ has $\gg n^2$ edges and no $K_5$, then there is a set of $n^{1-o(1)}$ vertices that has no triangles. In fact we can even weaken the "no $K_5$" hypothesis to "no $K_6$"! (As discussed in the commentary, this cannot be further weakened to "no $K_7$".)

For sake of notation we will just produce a set of $n^{0.9}$ vertices that has no triangles, but it will be clear that one can replace $0.9$ by any other constant less than $1$, and hence some quantity converging sufficiently slowly to $1$. Suppose for contradiction that this is not the case, thus every set of $n^{0.9}$ vertices has a triangle. For $n$ large enough, we will construct a $K_6$ to create the contradiction.

We use the method of dependent random choice (cf. Gowers' proof of the Balog-Szemeredi-Gowers lemma). By Holder's inequality, the number of stars $a_1,\dots,a_{100},b$ in which $a_1,\dots,a_{100}$ are all adjacent to $b$ is $\gg n^{101}$. Thus, if one picks $a_1,\dots,a_{100}$ at random, the common neighborhood $B$ of $b$'s adjacent to all of the $a_i$ will have size $\gg n$ with probability $\gg 1$.

Suppose $b_1,b_2,b_3$ be vertices such that there are fewer than $n^{0.9}$ vertices incident to all three of $b_1,b_2,b_3$. Then the probability that $b_1,b_2,b_3$ are all selected to be in $B$ is only $O(n^{-0.1})^{100} = O(n^{-10})$. Thus, by the union bound, the probability that $B$ has any such triple is only $O(n^{-7})$.

Thus, for $n$ large enough, we can choose $a_1,\dots,a_{100}$ so that $B$ has size $\gg n$, and such that any three elements of $B$ have a joint neighborhood of size at least $n^{0.9}$. By hypothesis, $B$ contains a triangle; and the joint neighborhood of that triangle also contains a triangle. This creates the desired $K_6$.

A back of the envelope calculation suggests that one can optimize $n^{1-o(1)}$ to $n^{1-O(1/\sqrt{\log n})}$, but I have not checked this carefully.

The same argument shows that the original question would have a positive answer if we had the following strong form of the Balog-Szemeredi-Gowers lemma: if $G$ has $\gg n^2$ edges then there exists a set $A$ of $\gg n$ vertices such that any pair of vertices in $A$ is jointly connected to $\gg n$ vertices. This strong version is false, as was shown by Kostochka and Sudakov (https://kostochk.web.illinois.edu/docs/2004/cpc03s.pdf) using a construction based on the Hamming cube; one may need to understand the precise failure modes of this too-strong lemma better in order to solve the original problem.

problem: Let $r\geq 3$, and let $f_r(N)$ denote the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that no subset of size $r$ has the same pairwise greatest common divisor between all elements. Estimate $f_r(N)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/535.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 29 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64} proved that\[f_r(N) \leq N^{\frac{3}{4}+o(1)},\]and Abbott and Hanson \cite{AbHa70} improved this exponent to $1/2$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64} proved the lower bound, for any $r \geq 3$,\[f_r(N) > N^{\frac{c_r}{\log\log N}}\]for some constant $c_r>0$, and conjectured this should also be an upper bound.

This is intimately connected with the sunflower problem [20]. Indeed, Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64} noted that a positive solution to [20] would imply\[f_r(N) \leq N^{\frac{C_r}{\log\log N}}\]for some constant $C_r>0$. Using the recent bounds of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang \cite{ALWZ20} for the sunflower problem yields\[f_r(N) \leq N^{C_r\frac{\log\log\log N}{\log\log N}},\]and in particular $f_r(N) \leq N^{o(1)}$.

An alternative description of the details of these lower and upper bounds was given by Abbott and Hanson \cite{AbHa67}. (A similar detailed calculation is given in the comments by Hrishi.)

See also [536].
References:
- [ALWZ20] Alweiss, R. and Lovett, S. and Wu, K. and Zhang, J., Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma. (2020).
- [AbHa67] No reference found.
- [AbHa70] Abbott, H. L. and Hanson, D., An extremal problem in number theory. Bull. London Math. Soc. (1970), 324-326.
- [Er64] Erd\H{o}s, P., On a problem in elementary number theory and a combinatorial problem. Math. Comp. (1964), 644-646.

forum_comments.author: Hrishi
forum_comments.text:
We have obtained an estimate for $f_r(N)$, developed in conjunction with ChatGPT-5.5 Thinking, where I worked on the argument with sourish (https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/user/sourish) and kireet (https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/user/kireet).

Our main estimate is:

$$
f_r(N) \geq \exp\left((\log(r-1)+o(1))\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\right)
$$

and

$$
f_r(N) \leq \exp\left(O_r\left(\frac{\log N\log\log\log N}{\log\log N}\right)\right).
$$

In particular,

$$
f_r(N)=N^{o(1)}.
$$

The key idea is to encode each integer $n$ by the set of its prime-power divisibility layers,

$$
S(n)=\{(p,j):1\leq j\leq v_p(n)\}.
$$

Then

$$
S(a)\cap S(b)=S(\gcd(a,b)),
$$

so an $r$-tuple whose pairwise gcds are all equal is exactly an $r$-sunflower in the corresponding set system.

The lower bound comes from a block construction: partition the primes into blocks of size $r-1$, and choose one prime from each block. The pigeonhole principle prevents $r$ distinct chosen products from having all pairwise gcds equal.

For the upper bound, we split each integer into its smooth part and rough part. Rankin’s estimate controls the number of possible smooth parts, while the improved sunflower lemma controls each rough fiber, giving the stated upper bound.

The paper is available here (https://hrishis18.github.io/gcd-sunflower-paper/gcd_sunflower_obstruction.pdf).

forum_comments.author: Hrishi
forum_comments.text:
Yes, for fixed $r$, a positive answer to #20 with $k=r$ would replace the $(C_r\log K)^K$ sunflower bound in Lemma 4.1 by $c_r^K$, after the same padding argument from sets of size at most $K$ to $K$-uniform sets.

In the proof, $K=\lfloor \log N/\log\log N\rfloor$, and the number of possible $\log N$-smooth parts is still only\[
\exp\!\left(O\!\left(\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\right)\right).
\]So the fiber bound would become $c_r^K$, giving\[
f_r(N)\leq \exp\!\left(O_r\!\left(\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\right)\right),
\]which removes the extra $\log\log\log N$ factor. This would match the lower bound at the right exponential scale, up to the constant in the exponent.

forum_comments.author: Cong
forum_comments.text:
I looked through the literature after my earlier comment, and I think the right correction is stronger than just adding a squarefree hypothesis.

The counterexample $A_m=\{2,4,8,\dots,2^m\}$ shows that the current auxiliary formulation with $\omega(n)=k$ is false: for $k=1$, this family can be arbitrarily large while still avoiding an $r$-tuple with constant pairwise gcd.

What seems to be the correct fix is the one Erdős gives later. In [Er73], he says that Abbott pointed out the ordinary sunflower conjecture does not seem to suffice for deriving the conjectured upper bound for $f_3(x)$. He then replaces it by a slightly stronger conjecture in which the integers have exactly $n$ prime factors counted with multiplicity. In modern notation, this is $\Omega(n)=k$, not $\omega(n)=k$.

So I think the auxiliary statement here should be updated to:

estimate the size of the largest set $A$ of integers such that $\Omega(n)=k$ for all $n\in A$, and there do not exist $a_1,\dots,a_r\in A$ and an integer $d$ such that $(a_i,a_j)=d$ for all $i\ne j$ and $\left(\frac{a_i}{d},d\right)=1$ for all $i$.

The squarefree / $\omega(n)=k$ version is still a natural special case, and it is suggested by the argument in [Er64], but it is not the full corrected auxiliary statement that Erdős later endorsed after Abbott’s objection.

forum_comments.author: Cong
forum_comments.text:
I tried to formalize the “stronger sunflower problem” phrasing here: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/2199

But as stated, this seems false without an extra restriction: for $k=1$ consider $A_m={2,4,8,\dots,2^m}.$
Then $\omega(n)=1$ for all $n\in A_m$, and for any $r\ge 3$ there is no $r$-subset with constant pairwise gcd (pairwise gcds vary with the minimal exponent), so it satisfies the “no constant pairwise gcd with coprime quotients” condition. Yet $|A_m|=m$ is arbitrarily large, contradicting any bound $|A|\le c_r^k$ (or even $c_r^k k!$ since $k=1$).

In Erdős’s 1964 paper, the set-system/sunflower step is applied to squarefree parts / prime-factor sets (he explicitly introduces squarefree numbers and decomposes $a_i=A_iB_i$ with $B_i$ squarefree). That suggests the intended sunflower-style statement meant to restrict to squarefree integers (or radicals) rather than just $\omega(n)=k$?

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problem:
Let $f(N)$ be the largest size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with the property that there are no distinct $a,b,c\in A$ such that\[[a,b]=[b,c]=[a,c],\]where $[a,b]$ denotes the least common multiple.

Estimate $f(N)$ - in particular, is it true that $f(N)=o(N)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/536.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 29 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The corresponding quantity is $\gg N$ if we ask for four elements with the same pairwise least common multiple, as shown by Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er62} (with a proof given in \cite{Er70}).

This was also asked by Erd\H{o}s at the 1991 problem session (https://westcoastnumbertheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/wcnt-problems-1991.pdf) of West Coast Number Theory.

Abbott and Gardner \cite{AbGa67} proved\[f(N) \geq (1-o(1))(\log\log N)\frac{N}{\log N}.\]In the comments Weisenberg sketches a proof that, for some function $\omega(N)\to \infty$ as $N\to \infty$,\[(\log\log N)^{\omega(N)}\frac{N}{\log N}\ll f(N) \leq \left(\frac{221}{225}+o(1)\right)N.\]See also [535], [537], and [856]. A related combinatorial problem is asked at [857].
References:
- [AbGa67] Abbott, H. L. and Gardner, B., An extremal problem in number theory. Canad. Math. Bull. (1967), 173--177.
- [Er62] Erd\H{o}s, P\'{a}l, Remarks on number theory. IV. Extremal problems in number theory. I. Mat. Lapok (1962), 228-255.

forum_comments.author: Sharvil Kesarwani
forum_comments.text:
Hey everyone, I wanted to share some recent progress I've made on upper-bounding the density of sets avoiding these "bad triples" (where $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = \operatorname{lcm}(b,c) = \operatorname{lcm}(a,c)$).

I've been tackling this by constructing explicit, asymptotically dense packings of bad triples to bound the complement set. The main idea is to classify integers by their "signatures" - specifically, their $p$-adic valuations modulo some cutoff $K_p$ for a small set of primes, like $\mathcal{P} = \{2, 3, 5, 7, 11\}$.

By looking at different triples of coprime coefficients $(A, B, C)$ (representing $(a, b, c) = (ABm, ACm, BCm)$) and assigning them to these valuation classes, we can calculate the natural density of each class and frame the whole thing as a massive Set Packing problem.

Here are the best bounds I've managed to find so far:

1. Exact Disjoint Matching
By finding a strictly element-disjoint collection of bad-triple families and converting the problem to solving an Integer Linear Program over the signature classes, I've brought the upper bound down to:
$$f(N) \leq \left(\frac{203{,}447}{230{,}400} + o(1)\right )N \approx 0.88302N.$$
The construction here is a set of $42$ triples and seems to be optimal for $K = (4, 4, 2, 2, 2)$.

2. Fractional Matching (LP)
By taking the continuous LP relaxation of this matching and using LP duality, we can improve on this method. I wrote a script to compute a floating-point optimum, identify the binding constraints, and then solve the resulting system exactly over $\mathbb{Q}$ using fraction-free Gaussian elimination.

$$f(N) \leq \left (\frac{151{,}594{,}752{,}885{,}431{,}136{,}780{,}159{,}002{,}252{,}347}{172{,}688{,}901{,}829{,}024{,}375{,}189{,}779{,}589{,}939{,}200} + o(1)\right )N \approx 0.877849 N.$$
Because this is extracted as an exact rational vertex of the LP and verified over $\mathbb{Q}$, there are no floating-point artifacts, though there should exist better solutions.

forum_comments.author: InfiniteInsights
forum_comments.text:
I think the elementary packing bound recorded here can be improved from
$f(N)\le \left(\frac{221}{225}+o(1)\right)N$
to
$f(N)\le \left(\frac{43}{48}+o(1)\right)N$.

The construction uses three pairwise disjoint families of lcm-triangles:
$\{2m,3m,6m\}$, $\{4m,5m,20m\}$, and $\{7m,9m,63m\}$,
with valuation restrictions chosen to separate all generated triples.

For the family $\{2m,3m,6m\}$, take
$6m\le N$ and $v_2(m)\equiv v_3(m)\equiv0\pmod 2$.
This contributes
$\frac{N}{6}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{4}+o(N)=\frac{N}{12}+o(N)$.

For the family $\{4m,5m,20m\}$, take
$20m\le N$,
$v_2(m)\equiv0\pmod 4$, and
$v_3(m)\equiv v_5(m)\equiv0\pmod 2$.
This contributes
$\frac{N}{20}\cdot\frac{8}{15}\cdot\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{5}{6}+o(N)
=\frac{N}{60}+o(N)$.

For the family $\{7m,9m,63m\}$, take
$63m\le N$,
$v_2(m)\equiv0\pmod 4$,
$v_3(m)\equiv0\pmod 4$, and
$v_5(m)\equiv v_7(m)\equiv0\pmod 2$.
This contributes
$\frac{N}{63}\cdot\frac{8}{15}\cdot\frac{27}{40}\cdot\frac{5}{6}\cdot\frac{7}{8}+o(N)
=\frac{N}{240}+o(N)$.

Each template is an lcm-triangle:
$[2m,3m]=[2m,6m]=[3m,6m]=6m$,
$[4m,5m]=[4m,20m]=[5m,20m]=20m$, and
$[7m,9m]=[7m,63m]=[9m,63m]=63m$.

The valuation signatures separate the three roles inside each layer and also separate the layers from one another, so the constructed lcm-triangles are pairwise disjoint. Hence the total number of disjoint forbidden triples is
$\frac{N}{12}+\frac{N}{60}+\frac{N}{240}+o(N)=\frac{5N}{48}+o(N)$.

Therefore any lcm-triangle-free subset of $[N]$ must omit at least one element from each of these triples, giving
$f(N)\le N-\frac{5N}{48}+o(N)=\left(\frac{43}{48}+o(1)\right)N$.

This is still only a constant-density packing improvement, not progress all the way to the $o(N)$ question: any proof using only pairwise disjoint forbidden triples cannot force an upper bound below $2N/3$.

For the full paper, here it is
https://pdfhost.io/v/NnHQ32EvjQ_Erdos_536_Partial_Progress

Thank you

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
forum_comments.text:
The remaining two page numbers are [Er70,p.124][Er73,p.124].

The claim that if $A$ has no lcm triangles then $|A| \leq cN$ for some $c < 1$ for all large $N$ can actually be proven by purely elementary means. We do so as follows: observe that as $m$ ranges over the integers from 1 to $\lfloor\frac{N}{15}\rfloor$ with $\text{gcd}(m, 30) = 1$, the sets $\{6m, 10m, 15m\}$ are disjoint lcm triangles contained in $\{1, \dots, N\}$. (The condition $\text{gcd}(m, 30) = 1$ isn't actually necessary to make these sets lcm triangles, but it is necessary for disjointness.) The amount of such $m$ is asymptotically $\frac{1}{15} \cdot \frac{\phi(30)}{30} \cdot N$, and $\phi(30) = 8$, so this is $\frac{4}{225}N$. If $A$ is lcm triangle-free, then at least one element must be removed for every such $m$, so we have $|A| \leq (\frac{221}{225} + o(1))N$.

This proves the desired claim, but I have no doubt that it can be improved significantly. For example, I imagine we could include $m$ such that $\text{gcd}(m, 30) > 1$ as well as apply the same analysis to other lcm triangles $\{a, b, c\}$ with $\text{gcd}(a, b, c) = 1$ at the same time (as opposed to just $\{6, 10, 15\}$). The inclusion-exclusion principle might be all we need to do both of these things.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
forum_comments.text:
For the record, both times Erdős asked this question, he specified that $a,b,c$ are distinct - that may be worth clarifying here. It's obvious that allowing $a = b = c$ leaves us stuck with the empty set, so that's trivial, but allowing two of them to be equal is equivalent to requiring that $A$ be a primitive set, which is an interesting variant, but not what he asks.

For convenience, call a set of three distinct numbers $\{a,b,c\}$ an lcm triangle if $[a,b] = [b,c] = [a,c]$. Then this problem asks how large a subset of $\{1,...,N\}$ can be if it contains no lcm triangles.

Fix a positive integer $k$ and let $S_k$ be the set of all numbers of the form $p_1 \cdots p_k$, where each $p_i$ is prime and $\pi(p_i) \equiv i \pmod{k}$ for all $i$ (but the primes are not necessarily in increasing order). It's not hard to verify that $S_k$ contains no lcm triangles. Furthermore, it's not hard to verify that $S_k$ has positive relative lower density within the set of all $k$-almost primes, and it's known that the amount of $k$-almost primes up to $N$ is $\sim_k \frac{N (\log \log N)^{k-1}}{(k - 1)! \log N}$. As such, for each $N$, we can choose the value of $k$ that maximizes the size of $S_k \cap \{1,...,N\}$. By doing so, we see that there is always an lcm triangle-free set $A \subseteq \{1,...,N\}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
|A| \gg_t \frac{N (\log \log N)^t}{\log N}.
\end{equation*}
With a bit of work, I'm sure one could make this lower bound a little more explicit.

Thanks for this! Due the classification rules of the wiki, I am now moving this result from Section 1(a) to Section 1(b). I appreciate that this time around, the result did not go viral on social media, so that such reclassifications should not cause any major issue.

MathSciNet reports that this paper of Erdos and Hall got zero citations. I guess this problem somehow fell into obscurity despite being actively worked on by Erdos and Hall.

Looking at the argument, it is indeed close to both what Quanyu+GPT and my colleague Van Vu proposed - use the second moment method and then try to get Poisson type statistics for the 1- and 2-point correlations. From what I can tell, the new input in the Quanyu+GPT approach that avoids wasting a log is to use the Bonferroni inequalities to truncate the inclusion-exclusion principle at a reasonable height $R$ (the analogue in Erdos-Hall is $M$) which rebalances the error terms in a much more efficient way. Instead of Bonferroni's inequalities to convert moment control to distributional control, Erdos and Hall have Lemma 2, which is doing something with contour integration instead, which is a reasonable alternative but I suspect one that is significantly less efficient than the combinatorial approach of Bonferroni (my indirect justification for this is that sieve theory does not use contour integration methods much and instead does a lot of combinatorial sieving in the spirit of Bonferroni).

EDIT: Ah, I think I see what happened: Bonferroni only really helps with the $r=0$ component of the Poisson distribution (when every single element of the cube misses the point). Erdos and Hall were trying to do the stronger thing of getting the Poisson statistics for all (fixed) $r$ (computing when exactly $r$ elements of the cube hit the given point). So they opted for the more general technique of contour integration, at the cost of worse estimates. But for this particular problem only the $r=0$ component is needed. If they had focused on only proving the portion of Poisson statistics that they actually needed for this application, they might have already solved the problem. (Erdos was a master of sieve theory and would surely know of the Bonferroni inequalities, which is closely related to the pure Brun sieve.)

SECOND EDIT: There are some further open problems in the paper of Erdos and Hall, perhaps these would be natural targets to look at?

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
There is Exercise 1.1.7 in my Additive Combinatorics book with Van Vu (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/books/additive-combinatorics/), which shows that one can cover any finite abelian group $G$ by a cube of dimension at most $\log_2 |G| + O(\log\log |G|)$ (actually the exercise as stated only requires the weaker bound $O(\log |G| + \log\log |G|)$, but if one goes through the proof carefully one gets the stronger bound). [EDIT: I now realize that this exercise in fact follows from the Erdos-Renyi result.] The basic idea is to think of the cube $Q$ as arising from an iterative process $Q \mapsto Q \cup (Q+\{x\})$, and if $Q$ is missing $\alpha |G|$ elements then by the pigeonhole principle one can ensure that $Q \cup (Q+\{x\})$ is missing at most $\alpha^2 |G|$ elements; this is what adds the additional overhead of $O(\log\log |G|)$ to the naive doubling heuristic as to the size of $Q$. But to my knowledge I don't know of literature lower bounding $Q$ in the case of a field of prime order. (Some hypothesis on the group must be imposed, of course: if one had a vector space over ${\bf F}_2$, then usually one gets complete doubling with each iteration, and the excess over $\log_2 |G|$ behaves more like an exponential distribution of mean $O(1)$.) One could conceivably also prove this lower bound using more classic additive combinatorics tools (I'm thinking in particular of Pollard and Green-Ruzsa's robust version of the Cauchy-Davenport inequality) but I haven't done the computations.

EDIT: On some further thought (and consultation with GPT Pro (https://chatgpt.com/share/697100f0-a78c-800e-9b40-f8789f40cb07)), the iterative approach I had in mind looks more complicated than I thought, because there is a chance that the cube $Q$ could somehow organize itself into a long arithmetic progression (of length greater than $|G|/2$, say), at which point it becomes far easier to fill out all of $G$ in just a couple more steps. So one has to track not just the size of $Q$ but also its additive structure when performing the iteration, which looks messy. In that respect the moment based approach in the GPT proof to control the probability of a missing element in $Q$ looks more tractable, even though the computations there are also not simple.

SECOND EDIT: there is a lot of literature about subset sums in finite fields, and some on random subset sums, but strangely this particular question has less literature than I expected. ChatGPT Deep Research (https://chatgpt.com/share/6971014b-4580-800e-9c85-e6635d5c33bf), Gemini DeepResearch (https://chatgpt.com/share/6971014b-4580-800e-9c85-e6635d5c33bf), and Claude (https://claude.ai/chat/e0af6896-6f69-43fc-ace7-a5fad3acc6b7) all noted the analogy with the coupon collector problem, and provided heuristic reasons why the claim should be true, but supporting references were scant. ChatGPT turned up work of Sandor (https://math.bme.hu/~csandor/Publications/randomadditivebases3.pdf) (and later authors) when considering a fixed number of sums rather than all subset sums, which is in the same spirit but a different regime. Gemini, amongst a bunch of vaguely related results and possibly some hallucinated references, did supply this paper of Nguyen, Szemeredi and Vu (https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610200) which discusses very large sets of generators whose cube still fails to cover ${\bf F}_p$ (relating to Olson's theorem), but doesn't address the random case. Claude noted substantial theoretical computer science literature on the decision problem for subset sums in finite fields, e.g., by Li and Wan (https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2456), but again could not find specific literature on this problem. There seems to be a lot of further literature to explore, and I do not yet have a conclusion as to whether there is any significant prior work on this problem.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
OK, I am tentatively assessing the argument as correct, although a human-generated proof or a Lean verification would still be desirable. It is basically a brute force validation of Poisson-type statistics (somewhat reminiscent of Gallagher's famous calculation that the prime tuples conjecture implies Poisson statistics for the number of primes in a short interval of logarithmic size) for pointwise or pairwise membership in the cube, which is strong enough to make the standard probabilistic heuristics rigorous with acceptable errors. I myself have done similar things for other problems (e.g., my conditional result on [15 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/15)]) but this method did not occur to me when I looked at it today; instead I settled on iterative methods similar to what Erdos and Renyi used, partly due to the fact that this is what I used for Exercise 1.1.7 in my textbook, although this approach would end up requiring quite a bit of inverse Littlewood-Offord theory and would ultimately be a more difficult approach than the one that the AI located. I think this speaks to one of the advantages of AI approaches, in that they can basically try all known methods to attack a problem (especially when applied at scale), whereas human experts will likely only try one or two such methods.

Here is a summary of the strategy. Set $G = {\bf F}_p$ for a large prime $p$, take $k = f(p)$ and write $\lambda := 2^k/p$. If we had $k = f(p) \leq \log_2 p + o(\log\log p)$, then $\lambda \leq \log^{o(1)} p$. The goal is then to show that if $v_1,\dots,v_k$ are drawn uniformly at random from $G$ then the cube $\{0,1\}^k \cdot \{v_1,\dots,v_k\}$ will not cover all of $G$ with probability at least $1/2$. (There is a tiny issue that the $v_1,\dots,v_k$ might collide with each other, but $k = O(\log |G|)$ is so small that this event is negligible.)

Heuristically, the cube consists of $2^k$ random elements of ${\bf F}_p$, so the number of times the cube hits a typical element $x$ of ${\bf F}_p$ should be something like $2^k/p = \lambda$ (the origin needs to be treated separately, but this is a negligible contribution); thus the cube, on average, should cover each element of ${\bf F}_p$ $\lambda$ times over on average. In fact we expect the distribution here to be approximately Poisson with mean $\lambda$, so in particular the probability that $x$ is to be avoided should be about $e^{-\lambda}$, giving a first moment estimate. Similarly, the probability that any two (non-zero) distinct elements $x,y$ of ${\bf F}_p$ should be avoided is about $e^{-2\lambda}$, giving a second moment estimate. Chebyshev's inequality then says that with probability at least $1/2$, the number of elements not hit by the cube should be comparable to $p e^{-\lambda}$, which suffices to solve the problem (after being more careful with quantifying the error terms, but the fact that $\lambda$ is much smaller than $\log p$ keeps things under control).

So the main task is to prove the first and second moment bounds. I'll just focus on the first moment bound, as the second turns out to be similar. We have $2^k$ different events $\epsilon_1 v_1 + \dots + \epsilon_k v_k = x$ and want to understand the probability that none of them occur. Each one basically occurs with probability $1/p$, so if they were independent we would easily get the required Poisson-type statistics. Now the events are not quite independent due to possible linear relations between the vectors $(\epsilon_1,\dots,\epsilon_k)$, but it turns out (basically from some basic inverse Littlewood-Offord theory, although this theory is not explicitly mentioned in the text) that such relations are extremely rare as long as one only involves at most $R$ of these vectors, where $R = \lfloor \log^{1/3} p \rfloor$ say. (Here it is important that we are working in high characteristic; if we were in a vector space over ${\bf F}_2$ there would be a lot more relations and the proof would break down (and the result is indeed false in this setting). In the AI proof this key step is codified in Lemma 2.5.) The upshot of this is that the events $\epsilon_1 v_1 + \dots + \epsilon_k v_k = x$ are essentially $R$-wise independent. To get the desired Poisson prediction of $e^{-\lambda}$ for having all the events fail, standard Bonferroni inequality expansion suggests that one needs to have something like $O(\lambda)$-wise independence; but $R$ is much larger than $\lambda$, so we win. A similar argument handles the second moment.

There is however a lot of careful bookkeeping that needs to be done to make the proof fully rigorous, so additional verification would be very good to have. As mentioned earlier, I think further literature searches are also needed.

forum_comments.author: msawhney
forum_comments.text:
There are a couple of minor notes:
(1) The true size for $\mathbb{F}_p$ is almost certainly given by when the Poisson heuristic suggests that one misses the an element with probability $1/p$. It may actually be interesting to work out the hitting window that shows that there is a range of $O(1)$ elements (essentially) where one goes from likely missing elements to likely not. (I expect there are relatively cheap way to prove this given the work shown; in particular one can start from the current result and see what adding one element in $\mathbb{F}_p$ does to the subset. This is closely analogous to the window for threshold of the symmetric perceptron model.)
(2) The counting bounds here require surprisingly little. Basically one can just locate a maximal rank subblock and using this maximal rank subblock determine the probability of hitting. Since $R$ is so small this turns out to sufficient (we use here that $e^{O(R^2)}$ is $o(p)$ so the maximal rank case dominates.)
