That is in principle true, but for large values, I think it won't make it that much easier.
The Ramsey number for $K_n$ and for the Colex graph $\mathcal C( m)$ where $m=\binom n2+1$ should indeed be the same for large $n$, as in general $R(n,n)>R(n,n-1)+n$ is expected from the exponential behaviour.

forum_comments.author: LouisD
forum_comments.text:
In my previous comment, I indicated that I couldn't find the statement of this problem in [Er84b]. I still don't see the exact statement, but I now see the following sentence (at the top of page 11) "Probably r(G) is maximal if G is as complete as possible." I guess this must be the intended reference. On the other hand, he makes no reference to Graham, so I continued my search.

In https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ExtremeCliques.html, the reference "Some partition theorems in finite graphs" by Erdős and Graham (1973) is given; however, in that paper I was only able to find the statement of the first part (on page 526), not the second part about G having $\binom{n}{2}+t$ edges.

I noticed that in https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ExtremeCliques.html, there is an extra condition which says $n\ge 4$. Presumably, this is because $R(3K_2)=8>6=R(K_3)$
(where $mK_2$ is a matching with $m$ edges).* On the other hand, note that $R(6K_2)=17<18=R(K_4)$.

Finally I get to my point. I claim that the conjecture is also false for $n=4$ and $t=1$. Let $K_4^{+1}$ be the graph on $5$ vertices and $7$ edges obtained from $K_4$ by adding a new vertex adjacent to one vertex in the $K_4$. I claim that $R(7K_2)=20>18=R(K_4^{+1})$. We already have $18=R(K_4)\leq R(K_4^{+1})$ and to see that $R(K_4^{+1})\leq 18$, the argument is essentially the same as proving that $R(K_4)\leq 18$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that there exists a vertex $x$ and a set $A$ with $|A|=9$ such that every edge from $x$ to $A$ is red. If there is a red triangle in $A$, we are done, so suppose not. If there is a vertex $u\in A$ with 6 blue neighbors in $A$, we are also done (since we will get a blue triangle in the blue neighborhood of $u$). Since it isn't possible for every vertex in $A$ to have blue degree $5$ to $A$, we have a vertex $v\in A$ with red degree at least 4 in $A$ and we can again see that it must be exactly 4 (otherwise we would get a blue $K_5$). Let $B$ be the set of 4 blue neighbors of $v$ in $A$. Every edge in $B$ is blue, and thus every edge from $B$ to $A\setminus B$ is red. So finally, we must have that every edge in $A\setminus B$ is blue in which case we have a blue $K_5$ and we are done.

So the conjecture certainly needs to be updated to add the condition that it holds provided the number of edges is large enough. How large is large enough? Can anyone find a counterexample with 8 edges? We have $R(8K_2)=23$ and I wouldn't be surprised if $R(K_4^{+2})\le 22$. However, I am out of time at the moment to attempt to prove this by hand as I did above for $K_4^{+1}$. Conceivably, this could be checked computationally?

*In general, Cockyane and Lorimer "The Ramsey number for stripes" (1975) proved that for all positive integers $m$ and $r$, the $r$-color Ramsey number of $mK_2$ is $(r+1)m+(r-1)$. For $r=2$, this says $R(mK_2)=3m-1$ and in this case, the upper bound can be seen by a simple inductive argument (either we have a red edge incident to a blue edge and we can remove those three vertices and apply induction, or else every edge has the same color). The lower bound comes from taking disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ with $m-1$ and $2m-1$ vertices respectively, coloring all edges incident with $A$ red and all other edges blue.

problem: Let $n\geq k+1$. Every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $\frac{k-1}{2}n+1$ edges contains every tree on $k+1$ vertices.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/548.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 07 March 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and S\'{o}s, who also conjectured that every graph with at least\[\max\left( \binom{2k-1}{2}+1, (k-1)n-(k-1)^2+\binom{k-1}{2}+1\right)\]many edges contains every forest with $k$ edges. (Erd\H{o}s and Gallai \cite{ErGa59} proved that this is the threshold which guarantees containing $k$ independent edges.)

In \cite{Er78} Erd\H{o}s says this is trivial for a star, and he and Gallai had proved it for a path.

It can be easily proved by induction that every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $n(k-1)+1$ edges contains every tree on $k+1$ vertices.

Brandt and Dobson \cite{BrDo96} have proved this for graphs of girth at least $5$. Wang, Li, and Liu \cite{WLL00} have proved this for graphs whose complements have girth at least $5$. Sacl\'{e} and Woznik \cite{SaWo97} have proved this for graphs which contain no cycles of length $4$. Yi and Li \cite{YiLi04} have proved this for graphs whose complements contain no cycles of length $4$.

Implies [547] and [557].

See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/AllTreesSubgraphs.html).

(i) P. E. Haxell in [Ha01] (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/1097-0118%28200103%2936%3A3%3C121%3A%3AAID-JGT1000%3E3.0.CO%3B2-U) has proved the conjecture for graphs that do not contain $K_{2,s}$, where $s= \lfloor{\frac{k}{18}}\rfloor$.

(ii) S. Balasubramanian and E. Dobson in [BaDo07] (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jgt.20261) has improved upon [Ha01] to include graphs that do not contain $K_{2,s}$, where $s< \frac{k}{12}+1$.

(iii) The result of [WLL00] (discussed in the problem description) has been improved by Dobson in [Do02] (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/combinatorics-probability-and-computing/article/abs/constructing-trees-in-graphs-whose-complement-has-no-k2s/D2579E2AAAA9CF2DFD22AC7B1F60BA8D) to include graphs whose complements do not contain $K_{2,4}$.

(iv) A. F. Sidorenko in [Si89] (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02124681) proved the conjecture for every tree with a vertex having atleast $\lceil {\frac{k}{2}}\rceil - 1$ leaf-neighbours.

(v) This result has been improved by N. Eaton and G. Tiner in [EaTi10] to include every tree with a vertex having at least $\lceil {\frac{k}{2}}\rceil - 2$ leaf-neighbours. They have also showed that this conjecture holds for values of $k$ at most $8$.

(vi) G. Tiner and Z. Tomlin in [TiTo22] (https://www.ajmonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/On-the-Erdos-Sos-Conjecture.pdf) has proved that the conjecture holds for $k=9$.

(vii) B. Zhou in [Zh84] (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0252960218306635) has proved the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k$.

(viii) P. Slater, S. Teo and H. Yap in [STY85] (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jgt.3190090203) has proved the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k+1$.

(ix) M. Wozniak in [Wo96] (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-0118%28199602%2921%3A2%3C229%3A%3AAID-JGT13%3E3.0.CO%3B2-E) has proved the conjecture for trees of diameter at most $4$ having at most one vertex with degree exceeding $2$. This paper proves the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k+2$.

(x) G. Tiner in [Ti10] (https://combinatorialpress.com/article/ars/Volume%20095/volume-95-paper-13.pdf) has proved the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k+3$.

(xi) L. Yuan and X. Zhang in [YuZh17] (https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5430) has proved the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k+4$.

(xii) A spider is a tree with at most one vertex of degree more than $2$. G. Fan, Y. Hong and Q. Liu in [FHL18] (https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.06567) has proved that the conjecture holds for all spiders.

(xiii) Balasubramaniam in his PhD thesis [Ba] (https://scholarsjunction.msstate.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4367&context=td) has proved the conjecture for graphs containing no $K_{2,s}$ where, $s ≥ 2$ and $k > 12(s − 1)$.

problem:
Determine the Ramsey number\[R(C_4,S_n),\]where $S_n=K_{1,n}$ is the star on $n+1$ vertices.

In particular, is it true that, for any $c>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[R(C_4,S_n)\leq n+\sqrt{n}-c?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/552.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp \cite{BEFRS89}. Erd\H{o}s often asked about $R(C_4,S_n)$ in the equivalent formulation of asking for a bound on the minimum degree of a graph which would guarantee the existence of a $C_4$ (see [85]).

It is known that\[ n+\sqrt{n}-6n^{11/40} \leq R(C_4,S_n)\leq n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil+1.\]The lower bound is due to \cite{BEFRS89}, the upper bound is due to Parsons \cite{Pa75}. The lower bound of \cite{BEFRS89} is related to gaps between primes, and assuming e.g. Cramer's conjecture on gaps between primes their lower bound would be $n+\sqrt{n}-n^{o(1)}$.

Erd\H{o}s offered \$100 for a proof or disproof of the second question in \cite{BEFRS89}. In \cite{Er96} Erd\H{o}s asks (an equivalent formulation of) whether $R(C_4,S_n)\geq n+\sqrt{n}-O(1)$, but says this is probably 'too optimistic'.

They also ask, if $f(n)=R(C_4,S_n)$, whether $f(n+1)=f(n)$ infinitely often, and is the density of such $n$ $0$? Also, is it true that $f(n+1)\leq f(n)+2$ for all $n$? A similar question about an equivalent function is the subject of [85].

Parsons \cite{Pa75} proved that\[R(C_4,S_n)=n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil\]whenever $n=q^2+1$ for a prime power $q$ and\[R(C_4,S_n)=n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil+1\]whenever $n=q^2$ for a prime power $q$ (in particular both equalities occur infinitely often).

This has been extended in various works, all in the cases $n=q^2\pm t$ for some $0\leq t\leq q$ and prime power $q$. We refer to the work of Parsons \cite{Pa75}, Wu, Sun, Zhang, and Radziszowski \cite{WSZR15}, and Zhang, Chen, and Cheng (\cite{ZCC17} and \cite{ZCC17b}) for a precise description. In every known case\[R(C_4,S_n)=n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil+\{0,1\},\]and Zhang, Chen, and Cheng \cite{ZCC17} speculate whether this is in fact true for all $n\geq 2$ (whence the answer to the question above would be no).

This problem is #19 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/RamseyCkStar.html) in the graphs problem collection.
References:
- [BEFRS89] Burr, S. and Erd\H{o}s, P. and Faudree, R. J. and Rousseau, C. C. and Schelp, R. H., Some complete bipartite graph-tree Ramsey numbers. Graph theory in memory of G. A. Dirac (Sandbjerg, 1985) (1989), 79-89.
- [Er96] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite problems on cycles and colourings. Tatra Mt. Math. Publ. (1996), 7-9.
- [Pa75] Parsons, T. D., Ramsey graphs and block designs. I. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. (1975), 33--44.
- [WSZR15] Wu, Yali and Sun, Yongqi and Zhang, Rui and Radziszowski, Stanis\l aw P., Ramsey numbers of {$C_4$} versus wheels and stars. Graphs Combin. (2015), 2437--2446.
- [ZCC17] Zhang, Xuemei and Chen, Yaojun and Cheng, T. C. Edwin, Some values of {R}amsey numbers for {$C_4$} versus stars. Finite Fields Appl. (2017), 73--85.
- [ZCC17b] Zhang, Xuemei and Chen, Yaojun and Cheng, T. C. Edwin, Polarity graphs and {R}amsey numbers for {$C_4$} versus stars. Discrete Math. (2017), 655--660.

problem: Let $R_k(G)$ denote the minimal $m$ such that if the edges of $K_m$ are $k$-coloured then there is a monochromatic copy of $G$. Show that\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{R_k(C_{2n+1})}{R_k(K_3)}=0\]for any $n\geq 2$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/554.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham. The problem is open even for $n=2$.

Schur \cite{Sc16} proved\[C^k \ll R_k(K_3) \ll k!\]for some constant $C>0$. Erd\H{o}s conjectured (see [183]) that $R_k(K_3) \leq C^k$ for some contant $C>0$.

Bondy and Erd\H{o}s \cite{BoEr73} and Erd\H{o}s and Graham \cite{ErGr75} proved\[n2^k+1\leq R_k(C_{2n+1})\leq 2n(k+2)!.\]The lower bound is sharp for fixed $k$ and large enough $n$, as shown by Jenssen and Skokan \cite{JeSk21}. Day and Johnson \cite{DaJo17} have proved that, for fixed $n$,\[R_k(C_{2n+1})\geq 2n(2+c_n)^{k-1}\]for all large $k$, for some constant $c_n>0$.

Axenovich, Cames van Batenburg, Janzer, Michel, and Rundstr\"{o}m \cite{ACJMR25} have improved the upper bound to\[R_k(C_{2n+1}) \leq (4n-2)^k k^{k/n}+1.\]In particular, there exists some absolute constant $c>0$ such that\[R_k(C_{2n+1})\leq (Cn)^kk!^{1/n}.\]This problem is #23 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/MulticolorROddCycles.html) in the graphs problem collection.
References:
- [ACJMR25] M. Axenovich, W. Cames van Batenburg, O. Janzer, L. Michel, and M. Rundstr\"{o}m, An improved upper bound for the multicolour Ramsey number of odd cycles. arXiv:2510.17981 (2025).
- [BoEr73] Bondy, J. A. and Erd\H{o}s, P., Ramsey numbers for cycles in graphs. J. Combinatorial Theory Ser. B (1973), 46-54.
- [DaJo17] Day, A. Nicholas and Johnson, J. Robert, Multicolour {R}amsey numbers of odd cycles. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2017), 56--63.
- [ErGr75] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R. L., On partition theorems for finite graphs. Infinite and finite sets (Colloq., Keszthely, 1973; dedicated to P. Erd\H{o}s on his 60th birthday), Vols. I, II, III (1975), 515-527.
- [JeSk21] Jenssen, Matthew and Skokan, Jozef, Exact {R}amsey numbers of odd cycles via nonlinear optimisation. Adv. Math. (2021), Paper No. 107444, 46.
- [Sc16] I. Schur, \"{U}ber die kongruenz $x^m+y^m=z^m\pmod{p}$. Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung (1916), 114-117.

problem: Let $R_3(G)$ denote the minimal $m$ such that if the edges of $K_m$ are $3$-coloured then there must be a monochromatic copy of $G$. Show that\[R_3(C_n) \leq 4n-3.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/556.
- Page status: DECIDABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Bondy and Erd\H{o}s. This inequality is best possible for odd $n$.

Luczak \cite{Lu99} has shown that $R_3(C_n)\leq (4+o(1))n$ for all $n$, and in fact $R_3(C_n)\leq 3n+o(n)$ for even $n$.

Kohayakawa, Simonovits, and Skokan \cite{KSS05} proved this conjecture when $n$ is sufficiently large and odd. Benevides and Skokan \cite{BeSk09} proved that if $n$ is sufficiently large and even then $R_3(C_n)=2n$.

This problem is #25 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ThreeColorRCn.html) in the graphs problem collection.
References:
- [BeSk09] Benevides, Fabricio Siqueira and Skokan, Jozef, The 3-colored Ramsey number of even cycles. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2009), 690-708.
- [KSS05] Kohayakawa, Yoshiharu and Simonovits, Mikl\'{o}s and Skokan, Jozef, The 3-colored Ramsey number of odd cycles. Proceedings of {GRACO}2005 (2005), 397-402.
- [Lu99] \L uczak, Tomasz, {$R(C_n,C_n,C_n)\leq(4+o(1))n$}. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1999), 174-187.

forum_comments.author: LouisD
forum_comments.text:
I believe this should say $R(T;k)\leq kn+O(1)$. For instance it is known for sufficiently large $n$ that $R(P_n; 3)=2n-1$ if $n$ is odd and $R(P_n;3)=2n-2$ if $n$ is even (Gy\'arf\'as, Ruszink\'o, S\'ark\"ozy, Szemer\'edi "Three-color Ramsey numbers for paths" 2007).

On the other hand, for stars on $n$ vertices, we clearly have $R(K_{1,n-1};k)\geq kn-O(k)$ (and the exact result can be found in "On Ramsey numbers for stars" by Burr and Roberts (1973)).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: LouisD
forum_comments.text:
Just to preemptively challenge my own comment, I suppose $R(T;k)=kn+O(1)$ means that there exists a constant $C$ (possibly depending on $k$) such that $R(T;k)\leq kn+C$. However, I can imagine somebody reading $R(T;k)=kn+O(1)$ and thinking it means that there exists constants $c$ and $C$ (possibly depending on $k$) such that $kn-c\leq R(T;k)\leq kn+C$.

For what it's worth Erdős and Graham (in their 1973 paper) write this conjecture as $R(T;k)< kn+O(1)$.

problem:
Let $\hat{R}(G)$ denote the size Ramsey number, the minimal number of edges $m$ such that there is a graph $H$ with $m$ edges such that in any $2$-colouring of the edges of $H$ there is a monochromatic copy of $G$.

Determine\[\hat{R}(K_{n,n}),\]where $K_{n,n}$ is the complete bipartite graph with $n$ vertices in each component.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/560.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
We know that\[\frac{1}{60}n^22^n<\hat{R}(K_{n,n})< \frac{3}{2}n^32^n.\]The lower bound (which holds for $n\geq 6$) was proved by Erd\H{o}s and Rousseau \cite{ErRo93}. The upper bound was proved by Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp \cite{EFRS78b} and Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il and R\"{o}dl \cite{NeRo78}.

Conlon, Fox, and Wigderson \cite{CFW23} have proved that, for any $s\leq t$,\[\hat{R}(K_{s,t})\gg s^{2-\frac{s}{t}}t2^s,\]and prove that when $t\gg s\log s$ we have $\hat{R}(K_{s,t})\asymp s^2t2^s$. They conjecture that this should hold for all $s\leq t$, and so in particular we should have $\hat{R}(K_{n,n})\asymp n^32^n$.

This problem is #29 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/SizeRamseyKnn.html) in the graphs problem collection.
References:
- [CFW23] Conlon, David and Fox, Jacob and Wigderson, Yuval, Three early problems on size Ramsey numbers. Combinatorica (2023), 743-768.

- [ErRo93] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Rousseau, C. C., The size Ramsey number of a complete bipartite graph. Discrete Math. (1993), 259-262.

problem:
Let $\hat{R}(G)$ denote the size Ramsey number, the minimal number of edges $m$ such that there is a graph $H$ with $m$ edges such that in any $2$-colouring of the edges of $H$ there is a monochromatic copy of $G$.

Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be the union of stars. More precisely, let $F_1=\cup_{i\leq s} K_{1,n_i}$ and $F_2=\cup_{j\leq t} K_{1,m_j}$ with $n_1\geq \cdots \geq n_s\geq 1$ and $m_1\geq \cdots \geq m_t\geq 1$. Prove that\[\hat{R}(F_1,F_2) = \sum_{2\leq k\leq s+t}l_k\]where\[l_k=\max\{n_i+m_j-1 : i+j=k\}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/561.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp \cite{BEFRS78} proved this when all the $n_i$ are identical and all the $m_i$ are identical.

Gy\H{o}ri and Schelp \cite{GySc02} proved this when $\binom{l_k}{2}> \sum_{k\leq i\leq s+t}l_i$ for all $2\leq k\leq s+t$. More special cases, including all cases when $s=1$, or $s=2$ and $n_1=n_2$, or all $n_i$ and $m_j$ are odd, or all $n_i$ are an identical odd number and $m_1$ is odd, were proved by Davoodi, Javadi, Kamranian, and Raeisi \cite{DJKR25}.

This problem is #30 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/SizeRamseyStars.html) in the graphs problem collection.

problem:
Let $F(n,\alpha)$ denote the smallest $m$ such that there exists a $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ so that every $X\subseteq [n]$ with $\lvert X\rvert\geq m$ contains more than $\alpha \binom{\lvert X\rvert}{2}$ many edges of each colour.

Prove that, for every $0\leq \alpha< 1/2$,\[F(n,\alpha)\sim c_\alpha\log n\]for some constant $c_\alpha$ depending only on $\alpha$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/563.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
It is easy to show via the probabilistic method that, for every $0\leq \alpha<1/2$,\[F(n,\alpha)\asymp_\alpha \log n.\]Note that when $\alpha=0$ this is just asking for a $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ which contains no monochromatic clique of size $m$, and hence we recover the classical Ramsey numbers.

See also [161] for a generalisation to hypergraphs.

This problem is #39 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/GeneralizedRamsey.html) in the graphs problem collection.

problem: Let $G$ be either $Q_3$ or $K_{3,3}$ or $H_5$ (the last formed by adding two vertex-disjoint chords to $C_5$). Is it true that, if $H$ has $m$ edges and no isolated vertices, then\[R(G,H)\ll m?\]
literature:

- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
In other words, is $G$ Ramsey size linear? A special case of [566]. In \cite{Er95} Erd\H{o}s specifically asks about the case $G=K_{3,3}$.

The graph $H_5$ can also be described as $K_4^*$, obtained from $K_4$ by subdividing one edge. ($K_4$ itself is not Ramsey size linear, since $R(4,n)\gg n^{3-o(1)}$, see [166].) Brada\'{c}, Gishboliner, and Sudakov \cite{BGS23} have shown that every subdivision of $K_4$ on at least $6$ vertices is Ramsey size linear, and also that $R(H_5,H) \ll m$ whenever $H$ is a bipartite graph with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices.

This problem is #32 in Ramsey Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/SizeRamseyLinearSpecific.html) in the graphs problem collection.

problem: Show that for $k\geq 3$\[\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\gg n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/572.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
It is easy to see that $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k+1})=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ for any $k\geq 1$ (and $n>2k+1$) (since no bipartite graph contains an odd cycle). Erd\H{o}s and Klein \cite{Er38} proved $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_4)\asymp n^{3/2}$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64c} and Bondy and Simonovits \cite{BoSi74} showed that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\ll kn^{1+\frac{1}{k}}.\]Benson \cite{Be66} has proved this conjecture for $k=3$ and $k=5$. Lazebnik, Ustimenko, and Woldar \cite{LUW95} have shown that, for arbitrary $k\geq 3$,\[\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\gg n^{1+\frac{2}{3k-3+\nu}},\]where $\nu=0$ if $k$ is odd and $\nu=1$ if $k$ is even. See \cite{LUW99} for further history and references.

See also [765].

This problem is #46 in Extremal Graph Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/TuranEvenCycleLowerBound.html) in the graphs problem collection.
References:
- [Be66] Benson, Clark T., Minimal regular graphs of girths eight and twelve. Canadian J. Math. (1966), 1091-1094.
- [BoSi74] Bondy, J. A. and Simonovits, M., Cycles of even length in graphs. J. Combinatorial Theory Ser. B (1974), 97-105.
- [Er38] P. Erd\H{o}s, On sequences of integers no one of which divides the product of two others and on related problems. Tomsk. Gos. Univ. Ucen Zap. (1938), 74-82.
- [Er64c] Erd\H{o}s, P., Extremal problems in graph theory. Theory of Graphs and its Applications (Proc. Sympos. Smolenice, 1963) (1964), 29-36.
- [LUW95] Lazebnik, F. and Ustimenko, V. A. and Woldar, A. J., A new series of dense graphs of high girth. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1995), 73-79.
- [LUW99] Lazebnik, Felix and Ustimenko, Vasiliy A. and Woldar, Andrew J., Polarities and $2k$-cycle-free graphs. Discrete Math. (1999), 503-513.

forum_comments.author: Alfaiz
forum_comments.text:
Building on the work of [BoSi74], J. Verstraete in [Ve00] (https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0204222) improved the bound to $\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k}) ≤ 8(k − 1)n^{1+1/k}.$

Pikhurko in [Pi12] (https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/2012-140-11/S0002-9939-2012-11274-2/S0002-9939-2012-11274-2.pdf) improved the bound further to $\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k}) ≤(k − 1)n^{1+1/k} + O(n).$

Bukh and Jiang in [BuJi14] (https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.1601v4) have improved the bound to $\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k}) ≤ 80 \sqrt{k} \log k · n^{1+1/k} + 10k^2n$

Z. He in [He21] (https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v28i2p41) has improved the bound to $\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k}) \leq (16 \sqrt{5} \sqrt{k \log k}+o(1))· n^{1+1/k}$

problem: Is it true that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;\{C_3,C_4\})\sim (n/2)^{3/2}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/573.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits, who proved that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;\{C_4,C_5\})=(n/2)^{3/2}+O(n).\]K\"{o}v\'{a}ri, S\'{o}s, and Tur\'{a}n \cite{KST54} proved that the extremal number of edges for containing either $C_4$ or an odd cycle of any length is $\sim (n/2)^{3/2}$. problem: Is it true that, for $k\geq 2$,\[\mathrm{ex}(n;\{C_{2k-1},C_{2k}\})=(1+o(1))(n/2)^{1+\frac{1}{k}}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/574.
- Page status: DISPROVED (database last update 2026-03-28).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits.

This has been disproved a number of times. It appears to have been first disproved by Lazebnik, Ustimenko, and Woldar \cite{LUW94b} for $k=3$ and $5$, since they construct bipartite graphs containing no $C_{2k}$ with\[\left(\frac{k-1}{k^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}+o(1)\right)n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}\]edges. (Note that the constant here for $k=3$ and $5$ is $\approx 0.462$ and $\approx 0.579$ respectively, while this problem predicts $\approx 0.396$ and $\approx 0.435$.)

An alternative disproof for $k=3$ is given by F\"{u}redi, Naor, and Verstra\"{e}te \cite{FNV06}, who prove that the extremal number for an $m\times 2m$ bipartite graph containing $C_6$ is (with $n=3m$)\[(2/3^{4/3}+o(1))n^{4/3}.\]See also [572], [573] for the specific case of $k=2$, and [1080].

This problem is #49 in Extremal Graph Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/TuranConsecutiveCycles.html) in the graphs problem collection.

- [LUW94b] Lazebnik, F. and Ustimenko, V. A. and Woldar, A. J., Properties of certain families of {$2k$}-cycle-free graphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1994), 293--298.

- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits \cite{ErSi70} proved that\[(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))n^{3/2}\leq \mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3) \ll n^{8/5}.\](In \cite{ErSi70} they mention that Erd\H{o}s had originally conjectured that $ \mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3)\gg n^{5/3}$.) Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits also proved that, if $G$ is the graph $Q_3$ with a missing edge, then $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\asymp n^{3/2}$.

In \cite{Er74c}, \cite{Er81}, and \cite{Er93} Erd\H{o}s asked whether it is $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3)\asymp n^{8/5}$.

A theorem of Sudakov and Tomon \cite{SuTo22} implies\[\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_k)=o(n^{2-\frac{1}{k}}).\]Janzer and Sudakov \cite{JaSu22} have improved this to\[\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_k)\ll_k n^{2-\frac{1}{k-1}+\frac{1}{(k-1)2^{k-1}}}.\]See also [1035].

This problem is #52 in Extremal Graph Theory (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/TuranCube.html) in the graphs problem collection.

problem: Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices such that at least $n/2$ vertices have degree at least $n/2$. Must $G$ contain every tree on at most $n/2$ vertices?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/580.
- Page status: DECIDABLE (database last update 2025-10-23).
- Page last edited: 24 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Erd\H{o}s, F\"{u}redi, Loebl, and S\'{o}s. Ajtai, Koml\'{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{AKS95} proved an asymptotic version, where at least $(1+\epsilon)n/2$ vertices have degree at least $(1+\epsilon)n/2$ (and $n$ is sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon$).

Zhao \cite{Zh11} has proved this conjecture holds for all sufficiently large $n$.

Koml\'{o}s and S\'{o}s conjectured the generalisation that if at least $n/2$ vertices have degree at least $k$ then $G$ contains any tree with $k$ vertices.

problem: Let $f_k(n)$ be minimal such that if $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ have no $k+1$ points on a line then there must be at most $f_k(n)$ many lines containing at least $k$ points. Is it true that\[f_k(n)=o(n^2)\]for $k\geq 4$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/588.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A generalisation of [101] (which asks about $k=4$).

The restriction to $k\geq 4$ is necessary since Sylvester has shown that $f_3(n)= n^2/6+O(n)$. (See also Burr, Gr\"{u}nbaum, and Sloane \cite{BGS74} and F\"{u}redi and Pal\'{a}sti \cite{FuPa84} for constructions which show that $f_3(n)\geq(1/6+o(1))n^2$.)

For $k\geq 4$, K\'{a}rteszi \cite{Ka63} proved\[f_k(n)\gg_k n\log n\](resolving a conjecture of Erd\H{o}s that $f_k(n)/n\to \infty$). Gr\"{u}nbaum \cite{Gr76} proved\[f_k(n) \gg_k n^{1+\frac{1}{k-2}}.\]Erd\H{o}s speculated this may be the correct order of magnitude, but Solymosi and Stojakovi\'{c} \cite{SoSt13} give a construction which shows\[f_k(n)\gg_k n^{2-O_k(1/\sqrt{\log n})}\]

problem: Let $g(n)$ be maximal such that in any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no four points on a line there exists a subset on $g(n)$ points with no three points on a line. Estimate $g(n)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/589.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
The trivial greedy algorithm gives $g(n)\gg n^{1/2}$. A similar question can be asked for a set with no $k$ points on a line, searching for a subset with no $l$ points on a line, for any $3\leq l<k$.

Erd\H{o}s thought that $g(n) \gg n$, but in fact $g(n)=o(n)$, which follows from the density Hales-Jewett theorem proved by Furstenberg and Katznelson \cite{FuKa91} (see [185]).

F\"{u}eredi \cite{Fu91b} proved\[n^{1/2}\log n\ll g(n)=o(n).\]Balogh and Solymosi \cite{BaSo18} improved the upper bound to\[g(n) \ll n^{5/6+o(1)}.\]
References:
- [BaSo18] Balogh, J\'{o}zsef and Solymosi, J\'{o}zsef, On the number of points in general position in the plane. Discrete Anal. (2018), Paper No. 16, 20.
- [Fu91b] F\"{u}redi, Zolt\'{a}n, Maximal independent subsets in Steiner systems and in planar sets. SIAM J. Discrete Math. (1991), 196--199.
- [FuKa91] Furstenberg, H. and Katznelson, Y., A density version of the Hales-Jewett Theorem. Journal d'Analyse Math\'{e}matique (1991), 64-119.

problem: Let $\alpha$ be the infinite ordinal $\omega^{\omega^2}$. Is it true that in any red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_\alpha$ there is either a red $K_\alpha$ or a blue $K_3$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/591.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-01-17).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
In other words, is it true that\[\alpha \to (\alpha, 3)^2?\]For comparison, Specker \cite{Sp57} proved this property holds when $\alpha=\omega^2$ and false when $\alpha=\omega^n$ for $3\leq n<\omega$. Chang proved this property holds when $\alpha=\omega^\omega$ (see [590]).

forum_comments.text:
I have a question concerning a case \((G_1,G_2)=(K_4,K_3)\), from #595. I would appreciate it if anyone has an idea.

Let \(A\) and \(F\) be finite graphs, with \(e(F)\ge 2\). Given an \(A\)-free graph \(H\), define \(X_F(H)\) to be the hypergraph whose vertices are the edges of \(H\), and whose hyperedges are the edge-sets of copies of \(F\) in \(H\).

Suppose that\[
\chi(X_F(H))>\aleph_0.
\]Is there a known way to thin or extend \(H\), while preserving the above, so that the remaining obstruction becomes canonical like so?

I want a family of edges\[
\{g_{\theta,\bar i}:\theta\in\Theta,\ \bar i\in [L]^{a(\theta)}\},
\]where \(\Theta\) is countable and \(L\) is uncountable, such that:

1. the restricted copy hypergraph on these edges has chromatic number \(>\aleph_0\);

2. for any finite list of these edges, whether they form the edge-set of a copy of \(F\) depends only on the finitely many labels \(\theta\) and on the order pattern of the tuples \(\bar i\).

This is motivated by the example:\[
(A,F)=(K_4,K_3).
\]Then \(H\) is \(K_4\)-free, and \(X_{K_3}(H)\) records the triangles of \(H\). So \(\chi(X_{K_3}(H))>\aleph_0\) means that no countable edge-colouring of \(H\) avoids a monochromatic triangle.

Is this plausible or known?

Any pointers to the literature would also be very helpful.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
I think the statement is true in the special case \(m=\kappa=(2^{\aleph_0})^+\).

Indeed, let\[
E^\kappa_\omega=\{\delta<\kappa:\operatorname{cf}(\delta)=\omega\}.
\]Since \(\kappa\) is a regular uncountable cardinal, \(E^\kappa_\omega\) is stationary in \(\kappa\). Also, a stationary subset of a regular uncountable cardinal can be partitioned into \(\kappa\) many pairwise disjoint stationary sets. So fix a partition\[
E^\kappa_\omega=\bigsqcup_{\xi<\kappa} S_\xi
\]with each \(S_\xi\) stationary.

Now define a colouring\[
c:[\kappa]^{\aleph_0}\to\kappa
\]by\[
c(a)=\xi \iff \sup(a)\in S_\xi.
\]Now let \(X\subseteq\kappa\) with \(|X|=\kappa\). Since \(\kappa\) is regular, \(X\) is unbounded in \(\kappa\). Hence the set of limit points of \(X\) is club in \(\kappa\). For any \(\xi<\kappa\), because \(S_\xi\) is stationary, there is some\[
\delta\in S_\xi
\]which is a limit point of \(X\). Since \(\operatorname{cf}(\delta)=\omega\), we can choose a countable subset \(a\subseteq X\cap\delta\) cofinal in \(\delta\). Then\[
\sup(a)=\delta,
\]so by definition of the colouring,\[
c(a)=\xi.
\]As \(\xi<\kappa\) was arbitrary, every \(X\in[\kappa]^\kappa\) contains countable subsets of all \(\kappa\) colours.

Therefore the required property holds for \(m=\kappa=(2^{\aleph_0})^+\).

Disclosure: the main idea of this argument, namely colouring a countable set by the stationary piece containing its supremum after partitioning \(E^\kappa_\omega\) into \(\kappa\) stationary sets, was suggested with the help of AI; I then wrote out the proof in this form.

forum_comments.author: AronBhalla
forum_comments.text:
This page should probably record the following (located using GPT 5.4 Thinking):

1. Lovász proved the finite analogue (https://www.renyi.hu/~elp/Splitting/Erdos-AoC99.pdf): if $H$ is a hypergraph on a finite set $X$, all edges have size at least $2$, and there are no edges $E,F$ with $|E\cap F|=1$, then $X$ has a $2$-partition such that every edge meets both classes.

2. If the index set is countable, the answer is yes, and the intersection condition is unnecessary. This is Bernstein's Lemma (https://www.renyi.hu/~elp/Splitting/Erdos-AoC99.pdf): every countable system of infinite sets has Property B. In fact, the name “Property B” was given in honour of Bernstein’s result.

3. If there is a fixed $n<\omega$ such that $|A_i\cap A_j|\leq n$ for all $i\neq j$, then the answer is yes. This is Miller’s theorem on strongly almost disjoint families. In fact, Komjáth later proved the stronger statement (https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01958019) that every such family of countable sets is essentially disjoint; after deleting finitely many points from each member, the remaining sets can be made pairwise disjoint. This immediately gives a splitting in which each $A_i$ meets both colour classes infinitely often.

4. Pairwise finite intersections alone are not enough. Hajnal, Juhász and Shelah (https://shelah.logic.at/files/95149/249.pdf) record that there is an $\omega$-almost disjoint subfamily of $[\omega]^\omega$ which is not $2$-colourable, originally due to Miller. Thus the extra hypothesis $|A_i\cap A_j|\neq1$ is needed.

forum_comments.author: gavinsherry
forum_comments.text:
I wrote up a short note on a strengthening of this problem:

https://gist.github.com/gavinsherry/ad9b6f85e2afc0a830d015a6b5d6d52a

The main finite-color statement is the following.

For every integer $r\geq 1$, there is a family $\mathcal F_r$ of countably infinite subsets of a countable ground set $X$ such that:

 1. for distinct $A,B\in\mathcal F_r$, the intersection $A\cap B$ is either empty or countably infinite, hence
 in particular $|A\cap B|\neq 2$;

 2. every $r$-coloring of $X$ makes some member of $\mathcal F_r$ monochromatic.

Here is the construction. Let $N=R_r(3)$ and let $P=[N]^2$ be the edge set of $K_N$. Fix a nonprincipal ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $\omega$, and set $X=P\times\omega$.

For each triangle $T\in [N]^3$ and each choice of sets $B_p\in\mathcal U$ for $p\in [T]^2$, define

$$
A(T,(B_p))=\bigcup_{p\in [T]^2}(\{p\}\times B_p).
$$

Let $\mathcal F_r$ be the family of all such sets.

Each member of $\mathcal F_r$ is countably infinite. If two triangles are distinct, they share at most one edge. Since $\mathcal U$ is nonprincipal and closed under finite intersections, any nonempty intersection of two members of $\mathcal F_r$ is countably infinite. Thus all pairwise intersections have size either $0$ or $\aleph_0$, never $2$.

Now take any $r$-coloring of $X$. For each $p\in P$, exactly one color class in the fibre $\{p\}\times\omega$ belongs to $\mathcal U$; call this color $\gamma(p)$. This gives an $r$-edge-coloring of $K_N$. By the definition of $R_r(3)$, there is a triangle $T$ whose three edges have the same $\gamma$-color, say $\alpha$.

For each $p\in[T]^2$, set

$$
B_p=\{n\in\omega:(p,n)\text{ has color }\alpha\}.
$$

Then $B_p\in\mathcal U$ for all $p\in[T]^2$, so $A(T,(B_p))\in\mathcal F_r$, and this set is monochromatic of color $\alpha$.

Thus even on a countable ground set, and even with the stronger condition that pairwise intersections are only $0$ or $\aleph_0$, the finite chromatic number is unbounded.

This writeup was prepared with AI assistance and checked before posting.

forum_comments.author: LouisD
forum_comments.text:
I think I must be missing something regarding your example. Isn't the following a much simpler example of the thing you are trying to prove?

Theorem: There exists a hypergraph $H=(V,E)$ such that $|V|=\omega=\chi(H)$ and for all $e,f\in E$, $|e\cap f|=\omega$.

Proof: Let $\mathcal{U}$ be a non-principle ultrafilter on $\omega$ and let $H=(\omega, \mathcal{U})$. Note that since $\mathcal{U}$ is an ultrafilter, we have that for all $e,f\in \mathcal{U}, |e\cap f|=\omega$. Now let $r\in \omega$ with $r\geq 1$ and consider $c:\omega\to [r]$. Since $\mathcal{U}$ is an ultrafilter, there exists $i\in [r]$ such that $c^{-1}(i)\in \mathcal{U}$; i.e. some edge is monochromatic. Thus $\chi(H)>r$ for all $r\in \omega$.

forum_comments.author: gavinsherry
forum_comments.text:
You are right; under the arbitrary-family reading this is a much simpler example. It gives a hypergraph on a countable vertex set withvpairwise intersections of edges all infinite and chromatic number \(\omega\), so in particular there is no finite bound \(C\).

My earlier construction was overkill for ruling out finite \(C\); it was aimed at a stronger cardinal-bound statement. Your ultrafilter example is the cleaner way to refute the finite-bound version under the arbitrary-family interpretation.

The distinction with the countable-family reading remains: a nonprincipal ultrafilter is not a countable family of edges, and in the countable-family case two colors suffice.

forum_comments.author: LouisD
forum_comments.text:
Very nice proof.

It seems that this naturally generalizes to prove Komj\'ath's Conjecture 3 by choosing $V$ to be the edge set of a complete $k$-uniform hypergraph on $\kappa$. Now the possible values of a finite intersection are $0,1,k+1,\dots$. This also proves something stronger than what Erdős and Komj\'ath were asking about since the sets in $\mathcal{A}$ don't have to be countable, but can have size $\mu^+$.

Finally, Erdős didn't technically ask for the smallest cardinal for which a coloring exists, he said "Is there a bound on the chromatic number of such a family?"

forum_comments.author: LouisD
forum_comments.text:
I wonder if it would be interesting to study a quantitative version of this question?

Say that $\mathcal{A}$ is $(k, \lambda, \mu)$-family if $\chi(\mathcal{A})>\mu$, $|A|=\lambda$ for all $A\in \mathcal{A}$, and $|A\cap B|\neq k$ for all distinct $A,B\in \mathcal{A}$. Given an integer $k\geq 2$ and infinite cardinals $\lambda, \mu$, let $f(k, \lambda, \mu)=\min\{|\bigcup_{A\in \mathcal{A}}A|: \mathcal{A} \text{ is a $(k, \lambda, \mu)$-family}\}$ and let $g(k, \lambda, \mu)=\min\{|\mathcal{A}|: \mathcal{A} \text{ is a $(k, \lambda, \mu)$-family}\}$. Now the question becomes estimating the values of $f$ and $g$. From the original problem, it feels like bounding the number of sets in the family is most natural (the function $g$), but given your proof, it feels most natural to bound the size of the ground set (the function $f$).

In this language, you proved that $f(2, \omega, \mu) \leq (2^\mu)^+$ and $g(2, \omega, \mu) \leq ((2^\mu)^+)^{\omega}$. Or if you generalize in the ways I mentioned, you get $f(k, \mu^+, \mu) \leq \beth_{k-1}(\mu)^+$ and $g(k, \mu^+, \mu) \leq (\beth_{k-1}(\mu)^+)^{\mu^+}$.

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
forum_comments.text:
This is trivially false as currently stated; let $X$ be any set with large cardinality, and let the $A_i$ be the sets with exactly two elements in $X$. Then the chromatic number of the $A$-family is $|X|$ itself. I suspect that Erdős meant to specify either that $|A_i| > 2$ for all $i$ or that $A_i$ is infinite for all $i$.

problem: Given $n$ distinct points $A\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ must there be a point $x\in A$ such that\[\#\{ d(x,y) : y \in A\} \gg n^{1-o(1)}?\]Or even $\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/604.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 March 2026.
Site remarks:
The pinned distance problem, a stronger form of [89]. The example of an integer grid show that $n/\sqrt{\log n}$ would be best possible.

It may be true that there are $\gg n$ many such points (Hunter has noted in the comments that this trivially follows from the existence of a single point), or that this is true on average - for example, if $d(x)$ counts the number of distinct distances from $x$ then in \cite{Er75f} Erd\H{o}s conjectured\[\sum_{x\in A}d(x) \gg \frac{n^2}{\sqrt{\log n}},\]where $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is any set of $n$ points.

In \cite{Er97e} Erd\H{o}s offers \$500 for a solution to this problem, but it is unclear whether he intended this for proving the existence of a single such point or for $\gg n$ many such points.

In \cite{Er97e} Erd\H{o}s wrote that he initially 'overconjectured' and thought that the answer to this problem is the same as for the number of distinct distances between all pairs (see [89]), but this was disproved by Harborth. It could be true that the answers are the same up to an additive factor of $n^{o(1)}$.

The best known bound is\[\gg n^{c-o(1)},\]due to Katz and Tardos \cite{KaTa04}, where\[c=\frac{48-14e}{55-16e}=0.864137\cdots.\]
References:
- [Er75f] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, On some problems of elementary and combinatorial geometry. Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. (4) (1975), 99-108.
- [Er97e] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite unsolved problems. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [KaTa04] Katz, Nets Hawk and Tardos, G\'{a}bor, A new entropy inequality for the Erd\H{o}s distance problem. Towards a theory of geometric graphs (2004), 119-126.

problem: Let $f(n)$ be the minimal $m$ such that if the edges of $K_{2^n+1}$ are coloured with $n$ colours then there must be a monochromatic odd cycle of length at most $m$. Estimate $f(n)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/609.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham. The edges of $K_{2^n}$ can be $n$-coloured to avoid odd cycles of any length. It can be shown that $C_5$ and $C_7$ can be avoided for large $n$.

Chung \cite{Ch97} asked whether $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Day and Johnson \cite{DaJo17} proved this is true, and that\[f(n)\geq 2^{c\sqrt{\log n}}\]for some constant $c>0$. The trivial upper bound is $2^n$.

Gir\~{a}o and Hunter \cite{GiHu24} have proved that\[f(n) \ll \frac{2^n}{n^{1-o(1)}}.\]Janzer and Yip \cite{JaYi25} have improved this to\[f(n) \ll n^{3/2}2^{n/2}.\]See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/DecomposeWithoutSmallOddCycles.html).
References:
- [Ch97] Chung, F. R. K., Open problems of {P}aul Erd\H{o}s in graph theory. J. Graph Theory (1997), 3--36.

problem:
For a graph $G$ let $\tau(G)$ denote the minimal number of vertices that include at least one from each maximal clique of $G$ (sometimes called the clique transversal number).

Estimate $\tau(G)$. In particular, is it true that if $G$ has $n$ vertices then\[\tau(G) \leq n-\omega(n)\sqrt{n}\]for some $\omega(n)\to \infty$, or even\[\tau(G) \leq n-c\sqrt{n\log n}\]for some absolute constant $c>0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/610.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 02 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Gallai, and Tuza \cite{EGT92}, who proved that\[\tau(G) \leq n-\sqrt{2n}+O(1).\]This would be best possible, since there exist triangle-free graphs with all independent sets of size $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$, which follows from the lower bound for $R(3,k)$ by Kim \cite{Ki95} (see [165]).

Indeed, Erd\H{o}s, Gallai, and Tuza speculate that if $f(n)$ is the largest $k$ such that every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices contains an independent set on $f(n)$ vertices, then $\tau(G)\leq n-f(n)$.

A positive answer to this problem would follow from a positive answer to [151] (since Ajtai, Koml\'{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{AKS80} have proved that the $H(n)$ defined there satisfies $H(n)\gg \sqrt{n\log n}$).

See also [151], [611], this entry (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/CliqueTransversal.html) and and this entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/CliqueTransversalUpperBound.html).
References:
- [AKS80] Ajtai, Mikl\'{o}s and Koml\'{o}s, J\'{a}nos and Szemer\'{e}di, Endre, A note on Ramsey numbers. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1980), 354-360.
- [EGT92] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Gallai, Tibor and Tuza, Zsolt, Covering the cliques of a graph with vertices. Discrete Math. (1992), 279-289.
- [Ki95] Kim, J. H., The Ramsey number $R(3,t)$ has order of magnitude $t^2/\log t$. Random Structures and Algorithms (1995), 173-207.

problem: Let $G$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices, minimum degree $d$, and diameter $D$. Show if that $G$ contains no $K_{2r}$ and $(r-1)(3r+2)\mid d$ then\[D\leq \frac{2(r-1)(3r+2)}{2r^2-1}\frac{n}{d}+O(1),\]and if $G$ contains no $K_{2r+1}$ and $3r-1 \mid d$ then\[D\leq \frac{3r-1}{r}\frac{n}{d}+O(1).\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/612.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Pach, Pollack, and Tuza \cite{EPPT89}, who gave constructions showing that the above bounds would be sharp, and proved the case $2r+1=3$. It is known (see \cite{EPPT89} for example) that any connected graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $d$ has diameter\[D\leq 3\frac{n}{d+1}+O(1).\]This was disproven for the case of $K_{2r}$-free graphs with $r\geq 2$ by Czabarka, Singgih, and Sz\'{e}kely \cite{CSS21}, who constructed arbitrarily large connected graphs on $n$ vertices which contain no $K_{2r}$ and have minimum degree $d$, and diameter\[\frac{6r-5}{(2r-1)d+2r-3}n+O(1),\]which contradicts the above conjecture for each fixed $r$ as $d\to \infty$.

They suggest the amended conjecture, which no longer divides into two cases, that if $G$ is a connected graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $d$ which contains no $K_{k+1}$ then the diameter of $G$ is at most\[(3-\tfrac{2}{k})\frac{n}{d}+O(1).\]This bound is known under the weaker assumption that $G$ is $k$-colourable when $k=3$ and $k=4$, shown by Czabarka, Dankelmann, and Sz\'{e}kely \cite{CDS09} and Czabarka, Smith, and Sz\'{e}kely \cite{CSS23}.

Cambie and Jooken \cite{CaJo25} have given an example that shows the diameter for $K_4$-free graphs with minimum degree $16$ is at least $\frac{31}{216}n+O(1)$, giving another counterexample to the original conjecture.

See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/DiameterOfKrFreeGraph.html).
References:
- [CDS09] Czabarka, \'{e}. and Dankelmann, P. and Sz\'{e}kely, L. A., Diameter of 4-colourable graphs. European J. Combin. (2009), 1082--1089.
- [CSS21] Czabarka, \'{e}va and Singgih, Inne and Sz\'{e}kely, L\'{a}szl\'{o}{} A., Counterexamples to a conjecture of {E}rd\H{o}s, {P}ach, {P}ollack and Tuza. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2021), 38--45.
- [CSS23] Czabarka, \'{e}va and Smith, Stephen J. and Sz\'{e}kely, L\'{a}szl\'{o}, Maximum diameter of 3- and 4-colorable graphs. J. Graph Theory (2023), 262--270.
- [CaJo25] S. Cambie and J. Jooken, Sharp results for the Erd\H{o}s, Pach, Pollack and Tuza problem. arXiv:2502.08626 (2025).
- [EPPT89] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Pach, J\'{a}nos and Pollack, Richard and Tuza, Zsolt, Radius, diameter, and minimum degree. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1989), 73-79.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
Ma and I wrote a short note (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-614-turan-reduction/blob/main/erdos614_note.pdf) on this problem, showing that it can be reformulated as a finite-family Turán problem.
More precisely, for each fixed $k$ there exists a finite family of graphs $\mathcal F_k^{\min}$ (depending only on $k$) such that\[
f(n,k)=\binom{n}{2}-\mathrm{ex}\bigl(n,\mathcal F_k^{\min}\bigr).
\]In particular, for $k=1,2,3$ we obtain\[
f(n,1)=\binom{n}{2}-\mathrm{ex}(n,K_3)=\binom{n}{2}-\left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor,\]\[
f(n,2)=\binom{n}{2}-\mathrm{ex}(n,C_4),\]and\[
f(n,3)=\binom{n}{2}-\mathrm{ex}\bigl(n,\{C_5,\,K_{2,3},\,K_1\vee 2K_2\}\bigr),\]where $K_1\vee 2K_2$ denotes the join of a single vertex with two disjoint edges.
We do not know whether this Turán-type reformulation is already what Erdős had in mind as an ''answer'' for $f(n,k)$.

problem: If $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices without a $K_4$ then how large a triangle-free induced subgraph must $G$ contain?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/620.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
This was first asked by Erd\H{o}s and Rogers \cite{ErRo62}, and is generally known as the Erd\H{o}s-Rogers problem. Let $f(n)$ be such that every such graph contains a triangle-free subgraph with at least $f(n)$ vertices.

It is now known that $f(n)=n^{1/2+o(1)}$. Bollob\'{a}s and Hind \cite{BoHi91} proved\[n^{1/2} \ll f(n) \ll n^{7/10+o(1)}.\]Krivelevich \cite{Kr94} improved this to\[n^{1/2}(\log\log n)^{1/2} \ll f(n) \ll n^{2/3}(\log n)^{1/3}.\]Wolfovitz \cite{Wo13} proved\[f(n) \ll n^{1/2}(\log n)^{120}.\]The best bounds currently known are\[n^{1/2}\frac{(\log n)^{1/2}}{\log\log n}\ll f(n) \ll n^{1/2}\log n.\]The lower bound follows from results of Shearer \cite{Sh95}, and the upper bound was proved by Mubayi and Verstraete \cite{MuVe24}.
References:
- [BoHi91] Bollob\'{a}s, B. and Hind, H. R., Graphs without large triangle free subgraphs. Discrete Math. (1991), 119-131.
- [ErRo62] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Rogers, C. A., The construction of certain graphs. Canadian J. Math. (1962), 702-707.
- [Kr94] Krivelevich, Michael, {$K^s$}-free graphs without large {$K^r$}-free subgraphs. Combin. Probab. Comput. (1994), 349-354.
- [MuVe24] D. Mubayi and J. Verstraete, On the order of Erd\H{o}s-Rogers functions. arXiv:2401.02548 (2024).
- [Sh95] Shearer, James B., On the independence number of sparse graphs. Random Structures Algorithms (1995), 269--271.
- [Wo13] Wolfovitz, Guy, {$K_4$}-free graphs without large induced triangle-free subgraphs. Combinatorica (2013), 623-631.

problem: Let $X$ be a set of cardinality $\aleph_\omega$ and $f$ be a function from the finite subsets of $X$ to $X$ such that $f(A)\not\in A$ for all $A$. Must there exist an infinite $Y\subseteq X$ that is independent - that is, for all finite $B\subset Y$ we have $f(B)\not\in Y$?

forum_comments.author: Ritvik Nayak
forum_comments.text:
I have been working on this problem semi-autonomously, with GPT-5.4 mainly helping me check the proof details and formalize the writeup. I wanted to record one partial reduction that came out of the attempt. It does not solve the problem, but it gives a necessary condition for any counterexample: such a counterexample must contain a large one-point fibre.

Let \(f:[X]^{<\omega}\to X\) satisfy \(f(A)\notin A\) for every finite \(A\subseteq X\). Call a finite set \(S\subseteq X\) independent if\[
f(B)\notin S
\]for every finite \(B\subseteq S\).

Suppose \(S\) is finite and independent. Define\[
\operatorname{Bad}(S)
=
\bigcup_{B\subseteq S}\{f(B)\}
\cup
\bigcup_{\substack{y\in S\\ C\subseteq S\setminus\{y\}}}
\{z\in X:f(C\cup\{z\})=y\}.
\]I claim that if\[
z\notin S\cup\operatorname{Bad}(S),
\]then \(S\cup\{z\}\) is independent.

Indeed, let \(A\subseteq S\cup\{z\}\) be finite.

If \(z\notin A\), then \(A\subseteq S\). Since \(S\) is independent, \(f(A)\notin S\). Also \(z\neq f(A)\), because \(z\notin \bigcup_{B\subseteq S}\{f(B)\}\). Therefore\[
f(A)\notin S\cup\{z\}.
\]If \(z\in A\), write\[
A=C\cup\{z\}
\]with \(C\subseteq S\). Since \(f(A)\notin A\), we have \(f(A)\neq z\). If \(f(A)=y\in S\), then \(y\notin C\), so \(C\subseteq S\setminus\{y\}\). Hence\[
z\in \{w\in X:f(C\cup\{w\})=y\},
\]contradicting \(z\notin\operatorname{Bad}(S)\). Thus \(f(A)\notin S\cup\{z\}\).

So \(S\cup\{z\}\) is independent.

Now suppose there is no infinite independent subset of \(X\). Then there must be a finite independent set \(S\) with no one point independent extension. Otherwise, starting from \(\emptyset\), we could recursively construct finite independent sets\[
S_0\subset S_1\subset S_2\subset\cdots
\]with \(|S_n|=n\). Let\[
Y=\bigcup_{n<\omega}S_n.
\]For any finite \(B\subseteq Y\), if \(f(B)\in Y\), choose \(N\) large enough so that\[
B\cup\{f(B)\}\subseteq S_N.
\]Since \(S_N\) is independent, this contradicts \(f(B)\in S_N\). Hence \(Y\) would be an infinite independent set, contrary to assumption.

Therefore some finite independent \(S\) has no one point independent extension. For this \(S\), every \(z\in X\setminus S\) must lie in \(\operatorname{Bad}(S)\). Hence\[
X\setminus S\subseteq \operatorname{Bad}(S).
\]The set\[
\bigcup_{B\subseteq S}\{f(B)\}
\]is finite. The remaining part of \(\operatorname{Bad}(S)\) is a finite union of fibres of the form\[
E(y,C)=\{z\in X:f(C\cup\{z\})=y\},
\]where \(y\in S\) and \(C\subseteq S\setminus\{y\}\).

Since \(|X|=\aleph_\omega\), the set \(X\setminus S\) also has cardinality \(\aleph_\omega\). A finite union of sets of cardinality \(<\aleph_\omega\) cannot cover a set of cardinality \(\aleph_\omega\). Therefore at least one fibre \(E(y,C)\) must have cardinality \(\aleph_\omega\).

Thus any counterexample must contain some finite \(C\subseteq X\) and some \(y\in X\setminus C\) such that\[
|\{z\in X:f(C\cup\{z\})=y\}|=\aleph_\omega.
\]Equivalently, if for every finite \(C\subseteq X\) and every \(y\in X\setminus C\),\[
|\{z\in X:f(C\cup\{z\})=y\}|<\aleph_\omega,
\]then an infinite independent set exists.

So any possible counterexample must occur in the large fibre case.

- The scale is stable and small compared to \(n\), but this does not transfer directly to the infinitary threshold case.

problem: Let $X$ be a finite set of size $n$ and $H(n)$ be such that there is a function $f:\{A : A\subseteq X\}\to X$ so that for every $Y\subseteq X$ with $\lvert Y\rvert \geq H(n)$ we have\[\{ f(A) : A\subseteq Y\}=X.\]Prove that\[H(n)-\log_2 n \to \infty.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/624.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 27 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal \cite{ErHa68} who proved that\[\log_2 n \leq H(n) < \log_2n +(3+o(1))\log_2\log_2n.\]Erd\H{o}s said that even the weaker statement that for $n=2^k$ we have $H(n)\geq k+1$ is open, but Alon has provided the following simple proof: by the pigeonhole principle there are $\frac{n-1}{2}$ subsets $A_i$ of size $2$ such that $f(A_i)$ is the same. Any set $Y$ of size $k$ containing at least $k/2$ of them can have at most\[2^k-\lfloor k/2\rfloor+1< 2^k=n\]distinct elements in the union of the images of $f(A)$ for $A\subseteq Y$.

For this weaker statement, Erd\H{o}s and Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s conjectured the stronger form that if $\lvert X\rvert=2^k$ then, for any $f:\{A : A\subseteq X\}\to X$, there must exist some $Y\subset X$ of size $k$ such that\[\#\{ f(A) : A\subseteq Y\}< 2^k-k^C\]for every $C$ (with $k$ sufficiently large depending on $C$). This was proved by Alon (personal communication), who proved the stronger version that there exists some absolute constant $c>0$ such that, if $k$ is large enough, there must exist some $Y\subset X$ of size $k$ such that\[\#\{ f(A) : A\subseteq Y\}<(1-c)2^k.\]Alon also proved that, provided $k$ is large enough, if $\lvert X\rvert=2^k$ there exists some $f:\{A: A\subseteq X\}\to X$ such that, if $Y\subset X$ with $\lvert Y\rvert=k$, then\[\#\{ f(A) : A\subseteq Y\}>\tfrac{1}{4}2^k.\]
References:
- [ErHa68] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Hajnal, A., On a combinatorial problem. Mat. Lapok (1968), 345-348.

problem:
The cochromatic number of $G$, denoted by $\zeta(G)$, is the minimum number of colours needed to colour the vertices of $G$ such that each colour class induces either a complete graph or empty graph. Let $\chi(G)$ denote the chromatic number.

If $G$ is a random graph with $n$ vertices and each edge included independently with probability $1/2$ then is it true that almost surely\[\chi(G) - \zeta(G) \to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/625.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Gimbel (see also \cite{Gi16}). At a conference on random graphs in Poznan, Poland (most likely in 1989) Erd\H{o}s offered \$100 for a proof that this is true, and \$1000 for a proof that this is false (although later told Gimbel that \$1000 was perhaps too much).

It is known that almost surely\[\frac{n}{2\log_2n}\leq \zeta(G)\leq \chi(G)\leq (1+o(1))\frac{n}{2\log_2n}.\](The final upper bound is due to Bollob\'{a}s \cite{Bo88}. The first inequality follows from the fact that almost surely $G$ has clique number and independence number $< 2\log_2n$.)

Heckel \cite{He24} and, independently, Steiner \cite{St24b} have shown that it is not the case that $\chi(G)-\zeta(G)$ is bounded with high probability, and in fact if $\chi(G)-\zeta(G) \leq f(n)$ with high probability then $f(n)\geq n^{1/2-o(1)}$ along an infinite sequence of $n$. Heckel conjectures that, with high probability,\[\chi(G)-\zeta(G) \asymp \frac{n}{(\log n)^3}.\]Heckel \cite{He24c} further proved that, for any $\epsilon>0$, we have\[\chi(G) -\zeta(G) \geq n^{1-\epsilon}\]for roughly $95\%$ of all $n$.
References:
- [Bo88] Bollob\'{a}s, B., The chromatic number of random graphs. Combinatorica (1988), 49-55.
- [Gi16] J. Gimbel, Some of my favorite coloring problems for graphs and digraphs. Graph Theory: Favorite conjectures and open problems (2016), 95-108.
- [He24] A. Heckel, On a question of Erd\H{o}s and Gimbel on the cochromatic number. arXiv:2408.13839 (2024).
- [He24c] A. Heckel, The difference between the chromatic and the cochromatic number of a random graph. arXiv:2409.17614 (2024).
- [St24b] R. Steiner, On the difference between the chromatic and cochromatic number. arXiv:2408.02400 (2024).

forum_comments.author: zach hunter
forum_comments.text:
let me share a reduction to a nicer sounding problem, which was observed several months ago with Micha Christoph, Annika Heckel, and Raphael Steiner.

imagine we instead sample $G_1,G_2\sim G(n,1/2)$ independently. let $X$ be the random variable for the smallest $k$ so that there exists a partition of $[n]$ into $k$ sets $I_1,\dots,I_k$ so that each $I_j$ is an independent set in either $G_1$ or $G_2$. then we couple $X$ so that it is always greater than $\zeta(G)$ for a random $G\sim G(n,1/2)$. the proof is a form of the "McDiarmid's coupling"-technique, which is a very slick trick I think more people should know!

now, $\chi(G)$ concentrates inside an interval of length $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ around its expectation (by an old result of Noga). and a similar result should say $X$ should concentrate in an interval of length $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ around its mean too. thus it would suffice to compute $\mathbb{E}[X]$ to sufficient accuracy, or instead simply show that: $\mathbb{P}(\chi(G_1)-X>n^{1/2+\Omega(1)})>\Omega(1)$.

problem:
Let $k\geq 4$ and $g_k(n)$ denote the largest $m$ such that there is a graph on $n$ vertices with chromatic number $k$ and girth $>m$ (i.e. contains no cycle of length $\leq m$). Does\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{g_k(n)}{\log n}\]exist?

Conversely, if $h^{(m)}(n)$ is the maximal chromatic number of a graph on $n$ vertices with girth $>m$ then does\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{\log h^{(m)}(n)}{\log n}\]exist, and what is its value?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/626.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
It is known that\[\frac{1}{4\log k}\log n\leq g_k(n) \leq \frac{2}{\log(k-2)}\log n+1,\]the lower bound due to Kostochka \cite{Ko88} and the upper bound to Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er59b}.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er59b} proved that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{\log h^{(m)}(n)}{\log n}\gg \frac{1}{m}\]and, for odd $m$,\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{\log h^{(m)}(n)}{\log n}\leq \frac{2}{m+1},\]and conjectured this is sharp. He had no good guess for the value of the limit for even $m$, other that it should lie in $[\frac{2}{m+2},\frac{2}{m}]$, but could not prove this even for $m=4$.

See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/MaxGirth.html).
References:
- [Er59b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Graph theory and probability. Canadian J. Math. (1959), 34-38.
- [Ko88] Kostochka, A. V., Upper bounds on the chromatic number of graphs. Trudy Inst. Mat. (Novosibirsk) (1988), 204-226, 265.

problem: Let $\omega(G)$ denote the clique number of $G$ and $\chi(G)$ the chromatic number. If $f(n)$ is the maximum value of $\chi(G)/\omega(G)$, as $G$ ranges over all graphs on $n$ vertices, then does\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)}{n/(\log_2n)^2}\]exist?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/627.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 08 February 2026.
Site remarks:
Tutte and Zykov \cite{Zy52} independently proved that for every $k$ there is a graph with $\omega(G)=2$ and $\chi(G)=k$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er61d} proved that for every $n$ there is a graph on $n$ vertices with $\omega(G)=2$ and $\chi(G)\gg n^{1/2}/\log n$, whence $f(n) \gg n^{1/2}/\log n$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er67c} proved that\[f(n) \asymp \frac{n}{(\log_2n)^2}\]and that the limit in question, if it exists, must be in $[1/4,4]$. (The upper bound he states as $1$, but \cite{AFM25} note the method actually gives $4$.)

Araujo, Filipe, and Miyazaki \cite{AFM25} prove that if $\lim\frac{\log R(k)}{k}$ exists and is equal to $C$ (see [77]), and also $R(s,t)\leq R(k)$ for all $st\leq k^2$, then the limit in this question also exists and is equal to $C^2$. Using this connection they improve the upper bound from $4$ to $\approx 3.7$.

See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/MaxChiOverOmega.html).
References:
- [AFM25] I. Araujo, R. Filipe, and R. Miyazaki, A note on the maximum ratio between chromatic number and clique number. arXiv:252.16062 (2025).
- [Er61d] Erd\H{o}s, P., Graph theory and probability. II. Canadian J. Math. (1961), 346-352.
- [Er67c] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some remarks on chromatic graphs. Colloq. Math. (1967), 253-256.
- [Zy52] Zykov, A. A., On some properties of linear complexes. Amer. Math. Soc. Translation (1952), 33.

problem: Let $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $k$ containing no $K_k$. If $a,b\geq 2$ and $a+b=k+1$ then must there exist two disjoint subgraphs of $G$ with chromatic numbers $\geq a$ and $\geq b$ respectively?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/628.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 December 2025.
Site remarks:
This property is sometimes called being $(a,b)$-splittable. A question of Erd\H{o}s and Lov\'{a}sz (often called the Erd\H{o}s-Lov\'{a}sz Tihany conjecture). Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er68b} originally asked about $a=b=3$ which was proved by Brown and Jung \cite{BrJu69} (who in fact prove that $G$ must contain two vertex disjoint odd cycles).

Balogh, Kostochka, Prince, and Stiebitz \cite{BKPS09} have proved the full conjecture for quasi-line graphs and graphs with independence number $2$.

For more partial results in this direction see the comprehensive survey of this problem by Song \cite{So22}.

See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/DecomposeToIncreaseChromaticNumber.html).

- [Er68b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problem 2. Theory of Graphs (1968), 361.

problem:
The list chromatic number $\chi_L(G)$ is defined to be the minimal $k$ such that for any assignment of a list of $k$ colours to each vertex of $G$ (perhaps different lists for different vertices) a colouring of each vertex by a colour on its list can be chosen such that adjacent vertices receive distinct colours.

Determine the minimal number of vertices $n(k)$ of a bipartite graph $G$ such that $\chi_L(G)>k$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/629.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Rubin, and Taylor \cite{ERT80}, who proved that\[2^{k-1}<n(k) <k^22^{k+2}.\]They also prove that if $m(k)$ is the size of the smallest family of $k$-sets without property B (i.e. the smallest number of $k$-sets in a graph with chromatic number $3$) then $m(k)\leq n(k)\leq m(k+1)$. Bounds on $m(k)$ are the subject of [901]. The lower bounds on $m(k)$ by Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan \cite{RaSr00} imply that\[2^k \left(\frac{k}{\log k}\right)^{1/2}\ll n(k).\]Erd\H{o}s, Rubin, and Taylor \cite{ERT80} proved $n(2)=6$ and Hanson, MacGillivray, and Toft \cite{HMT96} proved $n(3)=14$ and\[n(k) \leq kn(k-2)+2^k.\]See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ListColoringBipartite.html).
References:
- [ERT80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Rubin, Arthur L. and Taylor, Herbert, Choosability in graphs. (1980), 125-157.
- [HMT96] Hanson, Denis and MacGillivray, Gary and Toft, Bjarne, Choosability of bipartite graphs. Ars Combin. (1996), 183-192.
- [RaSr00] Radhakrishnan, Jaikumar and Srinivasan, Aravind, Improved bounds and algorithms for hypergraph {$2$}-coloring. Random Structures Algorithms (2000), 4--32.

It seems that a sharper lower bound for $n(k)$ is available. By the results in [ERT80] (see also [HMT96, Section 1]), we know that $m(k)\le n(k)\le 2m(k)$, where $m(k)$ denote the minimum number of edges possible in a 3-chromatic $k$-uniform hypergraph.

n(k)=\Omega\left(2^k\sqrt{\frac{k}{\log k}}\right).
\]References.
[GLW24] Grill, Karl, Daniel Linzmayer, and T. U. Wien. "Improved Lower Bounds for Property B." arXiv:2403.05674v3 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05674v3).

problem: Classify those triangles which can only be cut into a square number of congruent triangles.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/633.
- Page status: SOLVED (database last update 2026-04-06).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s' question was reported by Soifer \cite{So09c}. It is easy to see (see for example \cite{So09}) that any triangle can be cut into $n^2$ congruent triangles (for any $n\geq 1$). Soifer \cite{So09b} proved that there exists at least one triangle (e.g. one with sides $\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3},\sqrt{4}$) which can only be cut into a square number of congruent triangles. (In fact Soifer proves that any triangle for which the angles and sides are both integrally independent has this property.)

It is trivial that any isosceles triangle can be cut into $2$ congruent triangles, simply by dividing down the middle.

Soifer proved \cite{So09} that if we relax congruence to similarity then every triangle can be cut into $n$ similar triangles when $n\neq 2,3,5$ and there exists a triangle that cannot be cut into $2$, $3$, or $5$ similar triangles.

A complete classification is given by Beeson, Laczokovich, and Zhang \cite{BLZ26}. The full classification is too complicated to be stated here, but as a consequence, the set of triangles which can be decomposed into a non-square number of congruent triangles is the set of isosceles triangles together with countably many similarity classes.

See also [634].
References:
- [BLZ26] M. Beeson, M. Laczokovich, and Y. Zhang, Solution of Erd\H{o}s problem 633. arXiv:2604.03609 (2026).
- [So09] Soifer, Alexander, How Does One Cut a Triangle? I. (2009), 15-23.
- [So09b] Soifer, Alexander, How Does One Cut a Triangle? II. (2009), 37-39.
- [So09c] Soifer, Alexander, Is there anything beyond the solution?. (2009), 47-50.

problem: Find all $n$ such that there is at least one triangle which can be cut into $n$ congruent triangles.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/634.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s' question was reported by Soifer \cite{So09c}. It is easy to see that all square numbers have this property (in fact for square numbers any triangle will do). Soifer \cite{So09c} has shown that numbers of the form $2n^2,3n^2,6n^2,n^2+m^2$ also have this property. Beeson has shown (see the slides below) that $7$ and $11$ do not have this property. It is possible that any prime of the form $4n+3$ does not have this property.

In particular, it is not known if $19$ has this property (i.e. are there $19$ congruent triangles which can be assembled into a triangle?).

For more on this problem see these slides (https://www.michaelbeeson.com/research/talks/TriangleTilingSlides.pdf) from a talk by Michael Beeson. As a demonstration of this problem we include {IMAGE=634Triangle,a picture} of a cutting of an equilateral triangle into $27$ congruent triangles from these slides.

Soifer proved \cite{So09} that if we relax congruence to similarity then every triangle can be cut into $N$ similar triangles when $N\neq 2,3,5$.

If one requires the smaller triangles to be similar to the larger triangle then the only possible values of $N$ are $n^2,n^2+m^2,3n^2$, proved by Snover, Waiveris, and Williams \cite{SWW91}.

Zhang \cite{Zh25}, among other results, has proved that for any integers $a \geq b$, if\[n\geq 3\left\lceil \frac{a^2+b^2+ab-a-b}{ab}\right\rceil\]then $n^2ab$ has this property (indeed, they explicitly show that an equilateral triangle can be tiled with $n^2ab$ many triangles of side lengths $a,b,\sqrt{a^2+b^2+2+ab}$).

See also [633].
References:
- [SWW91] Snover, S. and Waiveris, C. and Williams, J., Rep-tiling for triangles. Discrete Math. (1991), 193-200.
- [So09] Soifer, Alexander, How Does One Cut a Triangle? I. (2009), 15-23.
- [So09c] Soifer, Alexander, Is there anything beyond the solution?. (2009), 47-50.
- [Zh25] Y. Zhang, Tiling Triangles With $2\pi/3$ Angles. arXiv:2512.22696 (2025).

problem: Let $t\geq 1$ and $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be such that whenever $a,b\in A$ with $b-a\geq t$ we have $b-a\nmid b$. How large can $\lvert A\rvert$ be? Is it true that\[\lvert A\rvert \leq \left(\frac{1}{2}+o_t(1)\right)N?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/635.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-30).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
Asked by Erd\H{o}s in a letter to Ruzsa in around 1980. Erd\H{o}s observes that when $t=1$ the maximum possible is\[\lvert A\rvert=\left\lfloor\frac{N+1}{2}\right\rfloor,\]achieved by taking $A$ to be all odd numbers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. He also observes that when $t=2$ there exists such an $A$ with\[\lvert A\rvert \geq \frac{N}{2}+c\log N\]for some constant $c>0$: take $A$ to be the union of all odd numbers together with numbers of the shape $2^k$ with $k$ odd.

The second question has been resolved in the affirmative by ChatGPT-5.2 (prompted by Leeham); Tao has since observed that a positive answer also follows fairly quickly from an inequality due to Elliott \cite{El79}.
References:
- [El79] Elliott, P. D. T. A., Probabilistic number theory. I. (1979), xxii+359+xxxiii pp. (2 plates).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Nice! Incidentally, the deduction of Theorem 1 from Lemma 4 actually follows immediately from an inequality of Elliott (see, e.g., Exercise 8 of these lecture notes of mine (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2019/11/12/254a-notes-9-second-moment-and-entropy-methods/), or Lemma 4.7 of P. D. T. A. Elliott. Probabilistic number theory. I, volume 239 of Grundlehren der Mathematischen Wissenschaften. Springer-Verlag, New York-Berlin, 1979. Mean-value theorems.).

Graphs in which one connects $a$ with $b$ when the difference $b-a$ divides $b$ (or $a$) actually play an important role in the modern theory of pair correlations between multiplicative functions, usually after constraining $b-a$ to be prime or almost prime. Recent work includes Matomaki-Radziwil-T. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.01545), T. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.05422), Helfgott-Ubis (https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.08707), Helfgott-Radziwill (https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.06853), and Pilatte (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19357). Erdos's question basically concerns the largest independent set in such a graph. It is interesting that Erdos had the foresight to anticipate the relevance of this graph. On the other hand, independent sets have not been studied in the above literature, which instead focuses on connectivity and expansion type properties. However, given that the solution can be deduced in short order from Elliott's inequality, which is contemporaneous with the posing of the question, there is a non-negligible possibility that this question may already be addressed in the literature.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: On closer inspection of the problem I would actually only mark the second part of the problem as solved (and am reverting the classification on the repository). The Elliott-type arguments would give an $o_t(1)$ term that decays slowly - something like $O(1/\log\log N)$ - but given the discussion of Erdos mentioned in the commentary, probably an accuracy more like $O(\log N/N)$ is actually sought, and this is well beyond what the Elliott-style methods here can give.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I have now placed this result in Section 1(b). The second moment arguments used in the AI proof are nearly identical to that used by Elliott, but the proof does not cite any references and it is unclear to what extent the AI was drawing from this reference.

I think that it would be good practice going forward to make efforts to have AI-generated solutions provide their sources to the extent that they can identify them, and/or to have a literature review be part of the solution generating process. Having such solutions presented without references, when the AI was trained on the literature, can convey a misleading picture as to how independent or original the AI solution actually was.

forum_comments.author: RaphaelSteiner
forum_comments.text:
Observation: This problem is equivalent to the seemingly weaker problem when we look for a path whose vertices span a graph of chromatic number $\ge k$.

To see this, suppose there exists a function $g(k)$ such that every graph of chromatic number at least $g(k)$ contains a path spanning a subgraph of chromatic number at least $k$. Now consider any graph of chromatic number at least $2g(k+1)-1$. W.l.o.g. the graph is connected. Doing a BFS layering from some vertex v, and using alternatingly two disjoint color sets to color the layers, we can see that one layer must induce a subgraph of chromatic number at least $g(k+1)$. So it contains a path inducing a subgraph of chromatic number at least $k+1$. Possibly after removing an end of this path, we find that there is a path in the layer of chromatic number $k$ of odd length. Now, linking the two ends of the path back to $v$ using shortest paths and cutting at the first layer where these shortest paths meet, we obtain an odd cycle spanning a subgraph of chromatic number at least $k$.

problem: Let $f(n)$ be the maximal number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices such that all cycles have more vertices than chords. Is it true that $f(n)\ll n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/642.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Hamburger and Szegedy. A chord is an edge between two vertices of the cycle which are not consecutive in the cycle.

Chen, Erd\H{o}s, and Staton \cite{CES96} proved $f(n) \ll n^{3/2}$. Dragani\'{c}, Methuku, Munh\'{a} Correia, and Sudakov \cite{DMMS24} have improved this to\[f(n) \ll n(\log n)^8.\]

problem: Let $f(n;t)$ be minimal such that if a $t$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices contains at least $f(n;t)$ edges then there must be four edges $A,B,C,D$ such that\[A\cup B= C\cup D\]and\[A\cap B=C\cap D=\emptyset.\]Estimate $f(n;t)$ - in particular, is it true that for $t\geq 3$\[f(n;t)=(1+o(1))\binom{n}{t-1}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/643.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 26 October 2025.
Site remarks:
For $t=2$ this is asking for the maximal number of edges on a graph which contains no $C_4$, and so $f(n;2)=(1/2+o(1))n^{3/2}$.

F\"{u}redi \cite{Fu84} proved that $f(n;3) \ll n^2$ and $f(n;3) > \binom{n}{2}$ for infinitely many $n$. Pikhurko and Verstra\"{e}te \cite{PiVe09} have proved $f(n;3)\leq \frac{13}{9}\binom{n}{2}$ for all $n$.

More generally, F\"{u}redi \cite{Fu84} proved that\[\binom{n-1}{t-1}+\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{t}\right\rfloor\leq f(n;t) < \frac{7}{2}\binom{n}{t-1},\]and conjectured the lower bound is sharp for $t\geq 4$. Pikhurko and Verstra\"{e}te \cite{PiVe09} have proved that\[1 \leq \limsup_{n\to \infty} \frac{f(n;t)}{\binom{n}{t-1}}\leq \min\left(\frac{7}{4},1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}\right)\]for all $t\geq 3$.

F\"{u}redi \cite{Fu84} proved that $f(n;3)/\binom{n}{2}$ converges as $n\to \infty$, but the existence of the limit for $t\geq 4$ is unknown.
References:
- [Fu84] F\"uredi, Z., Hypergraphs in which all disjoint pairs have distinct unions. Combinatorica (1984), 161--168.
- [PiVe09] Pikhurko, Oleg and Verstra\"{e}te, Jacques, The maximum size of hypergraphs without generalized 4-cycles. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (2009), 637--649.

For small fixed $r$, the functions $f(k,r)$ align with these following linear forms in $k$ that already appear in the OEIS:
