problem: Let $\tau(n)$ count the number of divisors of $n$. Is there some $n>24$ such that\[\max_{m<n}(m+\tau(m))\leq n+2?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/647.
- Page status: VERIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 07 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Selfridge. This is true for $n=24$. The $n+2$ is best possible here since\[\max(\tau(n-1)+n-1,\tau(n-2)+n-2)\geq n+2.\]In \cite{Er79} Erd\H{o}s says 'it is extremely doubtful' that there are infinitely many such $n$, and in fact suggets that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\max_{m<n}(\tau(m)+m-n)=\infty.\]In \cite{Er79d} Erd\H{o}s says it 'seems certain' that for every $k$ there are infinitely many $n$ for which\[\max_{n-k<m<n}(m+\tau(m))\leq n+2,\]but 'this is hopeless with our present methods', although it follows from Schinzel's Hypothesis H (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schinzel%27s_hypothesis_H).

In \cite{Er92e} Erd\H{o}s offered £25 for an example of such an $n>24$. He wrote 'I am being rather stingy but we old people are stingy.' (This has been converted to \$44 using approximate 1992 exchange rates.)

Tao has observed in the comments that, since $\tau(m)$ is similar to $2^{\omega(m)}$, this problem is similar to (but slightly weaker than) the first part of [679], but much stronger than [413] or [248].

See also [413].
References:
- [Er79] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some unconventional problems in number theory. Math. Mag. (1979), 67-70.
- [Er79d] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unconventional problems in number theory. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1979), 71-80.
- [Er92e] Erd\H{o}s, P\'{a}l, Some Unsolved problems in Geometry, Number Theory and Combinatorics. Eureka (1992), 44-48.

forum_comments.author: Sayan Dutta
forum_comments.text:
For what it's worth (arguably not much), here's a funny observation. Use $(\ast)$ to denote the equation $\tau(n-k)\le k+2$. Using modular constraints and elementary properties of $\tau$, it's not difficult to prove the following :-
1. If $n>5$ satisfies $(\ast)$, then $n$ is even.
2. If $n>10$ satisfies $(\ast)$, then $4\mid n$.
3. If $n>24$ satisfies $(\ast)$, then $6\mid n$.
4. If $n>54$ satisfies $(\ast)$, then $5\mid n$.
5. If $n>54$ satisfies $(\ast)$, then $7\mid n$.
6. If $n>36$ satisfies $(\ast)$, then $8\mid n$.
7. If $n>84$ satisfies $(\ast)$, then $9\mid n$.

So, any $n>84$ satisfies $(\ast)$, then $n=2520N$. Now, using
$$\tau(n-k) = \tau(k)\cdot \tau\!\left(\frac{2520N}{k}-1\right) \le k+2$$
with $k=1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24$ also gives that $2520N-1$ is either a prime or a prime square, and $1260N-1$, $840N-1$, $630N-1$, $420N-1$, $315N-1$, $210N-1$, $105N-1$ are primes.

Of course, all these constraints don't give any obvious contradiction by themselves.

forum_comments.text:

For example, they really help when sieving for "counterexamples". OEIS A087280 (https://oeis.org/A087280) says that there are no more examples "< 10^10". With these observations, and with the big assumption of no implementation errors, I think there are no examples for several more orders of magnitude, up to $10^{16}$ or even more.

But let me check my understanding of the claims:

It seems to me that the second step, with $\tau(k)\cdot\tau\left(\frac{2520N}{k}-1\right)$ doesn't necessarily work for $k=8$ and $k=24$ because potentially all of the powers of $2$ have been divided out and $k$ and $\frac{2520N}{k}-1$ are not necessarily relatively prime? It seems to me that it's possible, for example, for $105N-1$ to be four times a prime. As a concrete case, consider $n=604517614941240$ which comes from $N=239887942437$. I find that $\tau(n-k)\le k+2$ for $1\le k\le 13$ and also $k=24$. However, $105N-1$ is four times a prime and $315N-1$ is twice a prime, so neither prime by themselves. Let me know if I'm missing something about the argument.

In the other direction, it seems to me that it's also possible to show that $11\mid n$ and $13\mid n$ with arguments as in the first part. I just needed to do a trick like ruling out $7\pmod{11}$ by thinking of it as $18\pmod{11}$ instead. Hopefully I was reasoning correctly there.

Oh, and $2520N-1$ can't be a square because it's $3\bmod 4$.

problem:
Let $f(m)$ be such that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has $\lvert A\rvert=m$ then every interval in $[1,\infty)$ of length $2N$ contains $\geq f(m)$ many distinct integers $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ where each $b_i$ is divisible by some $a_i\in A$, where $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ are distinct.

Estimate $f(m)$. In particular is it true that $f(m)\leq \sqrt{m}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/650.
- Page status: SOLVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-03-06).
- Page last edited: 02 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Sur\'{a}nyi \cite{ErSu59} proved that $f(m)\geq\sqrt{m}$. Erd\H{o}s and Selfridge proved (see \cite{Er78} and \cite{Er86c}) that $f(m^2)\leq 2m$, which implies $f(m)\leq 2\lceil \sqrt{m}\rceil$ for all $m$. It is unclear exactly what bound he was asking for in \cite{Er95c}, but in general some improvement of this bound.

GPT 5.4 Pro (prompted by He, Li, and Tang) proved $f(m)\leq \lceil 2\sqrt{m}\rceil$. A corresponding lower bound was given by GPT 5.4 Pro and Aristotle; it is now known (see the paper of van Doorn, Li, and Tang \cite{VLT26}) that\[f(m) = \min(m, \lceil 2\sqrt{m}\rceil)\]for all $m$.
References:
- [Er78] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and combinatorial number theory. Proceedings of the Ninth Southeastern Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory, and Computing (Florida Atlantic Univ., Boca Raton, Fla., 1978) (1978), 29-40.

For completeness' sake, a timeline of events:

1) In 1959, Erdős and Surányi prove in [ErSu59] (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1959-07.pdf) that $f(m) \ge \sqrt{m}$.
2) In 1978 and 1986, Erdős details in [Er78, p. 35] (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1978-36.pdf) and [Er86c, p. 60] (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1986-15.pdf) the upper bound $f(m^2) \le 2m$ that he obtained with Selfridge, which in general implies $f(m) \le 2 \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil$.
3) In 1995, Erdős asks to estimate $f(m)$ in [Er95c], and whether the Erdős-Surányi lower bound can be improved.
4) On March 6th, 2026, GPT 5.4 Pro, prompted by Yixin He, Yanyang Li and Quanyu Tang, also proved the Erdős-Selfridge upper bound $f(m) \le 2 \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil$, which was later improved to $f(m) \le \lceil 2 \sqrt{m} \rceil$. Even though this improvement seems marginal, this small difference does become relevant when one aims to pin down $f(m)$ precisely, as we'll see below. The proof was then quickly formalized by Aristotle.
5) On March 7th, 2026, GPT 5.4 Pro claimed a corresponding lower bound of $f(m) \ge \lceil 2 \sqrt{m} \rceil$ for all $m \ge 4$. The proof strategy is sound, but (initially unbeknownst to us) it did contain a gap.
6) On March 8th, 2026, Aristotle managed to formalize the lower bound proof anyway, despite the gap. It turned out that Aristotle had found a fix themselves, which they implemented in the formalization. So both GPT 5.4 Pro and Aristotle deserve credit for the final solution.
7) On March 30th, 2026, we uploaded the paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28636) to the arXiv detailing a proof of the exact formula: for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$ we have $f(m) = \min(m, \lceil 2 \sqrt{m} \rceil)$. The proof is a cleaned-up and somewhat simplified (human-written) version of the AI proof.

I think the argument checks out (and my GPT call confirmed this formula (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ac5e58-f49c-800e-8518-9dba9d95154a) for $4 \leq m \leq 9$, with $f(m)=m$ for $m=1,2,3$). To review the upper bound $f(st) \leq s+t$: this gives $f(k^2) \leq 2k$ and $f(k(k+1)) \leq 2k+1$ which implies $f(m) \leq \lceil 2 \sqrt{m} \rceil$ for all $m$. This is by using the Chinese remainder theorem to produce a tuple $a_{i,j} = a_0 + jD - i$ of moduli for $i=1,\dots,s$, $j=1,\dots,t$ and an interval $B$ such that each $a_{i,j}$ has exactly two multiples in $B$, one at $a_0+i$ and one at $a_0+jD$, leaving only $s+t$ multiples in all.

For the lower bound, one needs to show that for a set $A$ of $m$ elements and an interval $B$ of length $2N$, one can match at least $\lceil 2\sqrt{m} \rceil$ elements of $A$ to distinct multiples in $B$; for $m \geq 4$ this quantity is less than or equal to $m$. By the Hall marriage theorem and a standard trick of adding some dummy vertices, it suffices to show that for every subset $S$ of elements of $A$, the set of multiples of $S$ in $B$ has size at least $|S| + \lceil 2\sqrt{m} \rceil - m$.

Ignoring a technical case when $B$ starts with a multiple of $N$, one can split $B$ into a left half $B_-$ and a right half $B_+$. One can match each element $a$ of $A$ with the largest multiple $b^-_a$ of $a$ in $B_-$ and the smallest multiple $b^+_a$ of $a$ in $B_+$. Since $b^+_a-b^-_a=a$, these two quantities determine $a$. From this and the AM-GM inequality we can show that the neighborhood of $S$ in the divisibility graph is at least $2 \sqrt{|S|}$, and this and some basic algebra gives the required Hall marriage criterion.

The AlphaEvolve run struggled to beat the trivial bound $f(m) \leq m$ (although it did do so in a few cases); this is consistent with my experience that it has some difficulty with number-theoretic constructions (using for instance the Chinese remainder theorem) which seem challenging to hillclimb on.

EDIT: On reading my GPT query response (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ac5e58-f49c-800e-8518-9dba9d95154a), it looks like it anticipated many of the key ingredients of the full solution, including the neighbourhood bound, the use of the defect Hall inequality, and conjecturing the correct formula. It would not take more effort to push that response to generate a full proof. Perhaps not surprising since this is the same model used to get the full solution, but it seems that this particular problem is well within range of the latest tools.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Nice! The proof of the lower bound looks good to me. I didn't check the exact accounting, but at least the idea that delivers $f(m)\geq 2\sqrt{m}-O(1)$ is quite simple and elegant; I'll reproduce it here without the GPT inflation: let $I$ be an interval of length $2N$ and consider the bipartite graph on $A\times I$ where we have $a\sim n$ if $a\mid n$. We want to find as large a matching as possible inside this graph.

If $\Gamma_-(S)$ is the neighbourhood of $S\subseteq A$ in the bottom half of $I$ and $\Gamma_+(S)$ is the neighbourhood in the top half of $I$, then the key observation is that, if $c_a$ is the largest multiple of $a$ in the bottom half of $I$, then\[a\mapsto (c_a,c_a+a)\]is an injective map which proves, for any $S\subseteq A$,\[\lvert S\rvert \leq \lvert \Gamma_-(S)\rvert \lvert \Gamma_+(S)\rvert.\]In particular, by the AM-GM inequality, if $\Gamma=\Gamma_-\cup \Gamma_+$ is the full neighbourhood, $\lvert S\rvert \leq \lvert \Gamma(S)\rvert^2/4$, so $\lvert \Gamma(S)\rvert \geq 2\lvert S\rvert^{1/2}$.

Via a standard defect form of Hall's matching theorem this implies that there is matching on at least $2\lvert A\rvert^{1/2}$ elements of $A$.

This is the proof; the remainder is some tedious accounting to check edge cases (e.g. if $a=N$), which hopefully GPT did correctly, but even if not, the proof above does at least always give $\geq 2m^{1/2}-O(1)$.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Perhaps the intended question is then to ask whether $f(n) \leq \lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil$) (rather than $f(n) \ll \sqrt{n}$) for all sufficiently large $n$? We now have $f(n) \leq 2 \lceil \sqrt{n} \rceil$ but there is the factor of 2. (The ceiling function here is natural since $f(n)$ is obviously an integer.) The argument in [Er78] gives $f(k^2) \leq 2k$ which also recovers $f(n) \leq 2 \lceil \sqrt{n} \rceil$ by monotonicity. (An equivalent formulation of the problem is then to obtain the upper bound $f(k^2) \leq k$ for all large $k$.)

For completeness, here is the Erdos-Sarányi argument that gives $f(n) \geq \lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil$ (using this Gemini translation (https://gemini.google.com/share/378e8a1490e5) of the original Hungarian text). Let $A$ be $m$ elements in $\{1,\dots,N\}$ and let $I$ be an interval of length $2N$. Using the greedy algorithm one can find $r$ numbers $b_1,\dots,b_r$ in $I$, each of which divisible by a distinct element of $A$, such that no further elements can be added; this implies that the $b_1,\dots,b_r$, between them, contain all the elements of $A$ as factors. In particular, by the pigeonhole priciple, one of these, say $b_i$, must have at least $m/r$ factors in $A$; call then $a_1,\dots,a_{r'}$ for some $r' \geq m/r$. If $b_i$ lies in the right half of $I$, then $b_i - a_1,\dots,b_i - a_{r'}$ will then each be divisible by distinct elements $a_1,\dots,a_{r'}$, so we get a solution to the problem with at least $\max(r,r') \geq \max(r,n/r) \geq \lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil$ factors. If instead $b_i$ lies in the left half, we use $b_i + a_1,\dots,b_i+a_{r'}$ instead.

I can imagine a computer search (with or without AI assistance) should be able to compute $f(n)$ exactly for the first few $n$, which would create an OEIS sequence and also give some numerical evidence for this conjecture. The values when $n$ is a perfect square would be particularly interesting.

problem: Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and let $R(x_i)=\#\{ \lvert x_j-x_i\rvert : j\neq i\}$, where the points are ordered such that\[R(x_1)\leq \cdots \leq R(x_n).\]Let $\alpha_k$ be minimal such that, for all large enough $n$, there exists a set of $n$ points with $R(x_k)<\alpha_kn^{1/2}$. Is it true that $\alpha_k\to \infty$ as $k\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/652.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-01-17).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
It is trivial that $R(x_1)=1$ is possible, and that $R(x_2) \ll n^{1/2}$ is also possible, but we always have\[R(x_1)R(x_2)\gg n.\]Erd\H{o}s originally conjectured that $R(x_3)/n^{1/2}\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$, but Elekes proved that for every $k$ and $n$ sufficiently large there exists some set of $n$ points with $R(x_k)\ll_k n^{1/2}$.

Mathialagan \cite{Ma21} proved that given a set $P$ of $k$ points and a set $Q$ of $n$ points, with $2\leq k\leq n^{1/3}$, there exists a point in $P$ which determines $\gg (kn)^{1/2}$ distances to points in $Q$. This immediately implies $R(x_k)\gg (kn)^{1/2}$ for $2\leq k\leq n^{1/3}$.
References:
- [Ma21] Mathialagan, Surya, On bipartite distinct distances in the plane. Electron. J. Combin. (2021), Paper No. 4.33, 25.

For what it's worth, Gemini Deepthink confirms the solution (https://gemini.google.com/share/f0ff17eff58b), while ChatGPT DeepResearch (https://chatgpt.com/share/696c3e53-3e88-800e-84d0-a3945ead78c3) did not turn up any significant references beyond the reference [El1995 (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01200753)] already cited as well as the literature for the sister problems #653 and #654, as well as this 2013 paper of Sharir and Solymosi (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/combinatorics-probability-and-computing/article/distinct-distances-from-three-points/357EC88BCC2B224FAA56F62A8CDFB023) addressing a question of Erdos, Lovasz, and Vesztergombi which may not yet be on this site. I'll start reading it myself now.

EDIT: OK, that wasn't actually that hard. It's actually Theorem 3.6 of Mathialagan which is relevant (a strengthening of Theorem 1.4), which asserts that given a set ${\mathcal P}$ of $m$ points and a set ${\mathcal Q}$ of $n$ points with $2 \leq m \leq n^{1/3}$, one of the points in ${\mathcal P}$ determines $\gg \sqrt{mn}$ distances to points in ${\mathcal Q}$. In the current notation, setting ${\mathcal P}$ to be the first $k$ points, this gives $R_k(n) \gg \sqrt{kn}$ for $2 \leq k \leq n^{1/3}$, which solves the problem.

Formalizing the derivation of this problem from Theorem 3.6 of Mathialagan should be almost automatic. But formalizing Mathialagan's paper will be non-trivial; for instance, it uses the Szemeredi-Trotter theorem and the crossing number inequality, as well as a three-dimensional version of this inequality due to Guth and Katz. These are all worth formalizing for their own sake, but this could be a significant project. In any event, the paper was published in Electron. J. Comb. in 2021 (https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v28i4p33) and there seems to be no reason to doubt its veracity.

I was on the fence about whether to classify this as a Section 1 or a Section 5 result for the purpose of the wiki, but I came down on the side of Section 1 (but with a comment added to the outcome), as the AI run was not intentionally set up as a literature review, but ended up solving the problem by relying very heavily on the literature anyways. I did put my failed ChatGPT DeepResearch search in Section 5, however.

UPDATE: It is now classified as Section 2(a) under an update to the classification system that does not attempt to ascertain intent in the AI prompt.

problem: Let $f(n)$ be such that, given any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ with no four points on a circle, there exists some $x_i$ with at least $f(n)$ many distinct distances to other $x_j$. Estimate $f(n)$ - in particular, is it true that\[f(n)>(1-o(1))n?\]Or at least\[f(n) > (1/3+c)n\]for some $c>0$, for all large $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/654.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
It is trivial that $f(n) \geq (n-1)/3$. In \cite{Er97e} Erd\H{o}s asks whether $f(n)>(1-o(1))n$, but says this is 'perhaps too optimistic but I am sure that [the trivial bound] can be significantly improved'.

In \cite{Er87b} and \cite{ErPa90} Erd\H{o}s and Pach ask this under the additional assumption that there are no three points on a line (so that the points are in general position), although they only ask the weaker question whether there is a lower bound of the shape $(\tfrac{1}{3}+c)n$ for some constant $c>0$.

They suggest the lower bound $(1-o(1))n$ is true under the assumption that any circle around a point $x_i$ contains at most $2$ other $x_j$.

The strongest form of this conjecture was disproved by Aletheia \cite{Fe26}, which constructed a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no four on a circle, such that there are at most $\frac{3}{4}n$ distinct distances from any single point (although this construction has all the points on the union of two lines, so does not help with the stronger version with the points in general position).
References:
- [Er87b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry. Intuitive geometry (Si\'{o}fok, 1985) (1987), 167-177.
- [Er97e] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite unsolved problems. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [ErPa90] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Pach, J., Variations on the theme of repeated distances. Combinatorica (1990), 261--269.
- [Fe26] T. Feng et al, Semi-Autonomous Mathematics Discovery with Gemini: A Case Study on the Erd\H{o}s Problems. arXiv:2601.22401 (2026).

problem: Is it true that if $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is a set of $n$ points such that every subset of $3$ points determines $3$ distinct distances (i.e. $A$ has no isosceles triangles) then $A$ must determine at least $f(n)n$ distinct distances, for some $f(n)\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/657.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 15 October 2025.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er73} Erd\H{o}s attributes this problem (more generally in $\mathbb{R}^k$) to himself and Davies. In \cite{Er97e} he does not mention Davis, but says this problem was investigated by himself, F\"{u}redi, Ruzsa, and Pach.

In \cite{Er73} Erd\H{o}s says it is not even known in $\mathbb{R}$ whether $f(n)\to \infty$. Sarosh Adenwalla has observed that this is equivalent to minimising the number of distinct differences in a set $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ of size $n$ without three-term arithmetic progressions. Dumitrescu \cite{Du08} proved that, in these terms,\[(\log n)^c \leq f(n) \leq 2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}\]for some constant $c>0$.

Hunter observed in the comments that a result of Ruzsa coupled with standard tools of additive combinatorics (with details given by Alfaiz and Tang) allow recent progress on the size of subsets without three-term arithmetic progression (see \cite{BlSi23} which improves slightly on the bounds due to Kelley and Meka \cite{KeMe23}) yield\[2^{c(\log n)^{1/9}}\leq f(n)\]for some constant $c>0$.

Straus has observed that if $2^k\geq n$ then there exist $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^k$ which contain no isosceles triangle and determine at most $n-1$ distances.

See also [135].
References:
- [BlSi23] T. F. Bloom and O. Sisask, An improvement to the Kelley-Meka bounds on three-term arithmetic progressions. arXiv:2309.02353 (2023).
- [Du08] Dumitrescu, Adrian, On distinct distances and {$\lambda$}-free point sets. Discrete Math. (2008), 6533--6538.
- [Er73] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. A survey of combinatorial theory (Proc. Internat. Sympos., Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, Colo., 1971) (1973), 117-138.
- [Er97e] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite unsolved problems. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [KeMe23] Kelley, Z. and Meka, R., Strong Bounds for 3-Progressions. arXiv:2302.05537 (2023).

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
Alfaiz
forum_comments.text:
I have tried to so some improvement based on Zach's idea given above in the comments of the problem, I would be glad, if someone points out any mistakes or corrections in my understanding of the problem.

Let $A \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points such that no three points of $A$ form an isosceles triangle.
Equivalently, if we project $A$ onto the real line, the image is a set of $n$ real numbers containing no nontrivial $3$-term arithmetic progressions.
Define $f(n)$ by\[
|A-A| \;\ge\; f(n)\,n.
\]Erdos asked whether $f(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$. Dumitrescu (2008) showed\[
(\log n)^c \;\le f(n) \;\le 2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}
\]for some constant $c>0$.

We improve the lower bound as follows.

Let $A$ be a finite subset of a torsion-free abelian group with $|A|=n$.
Set\[
S := A+A, \quad H := |S|, \quad D := |A-A|.
\](1) Ruzsa (2009) proved: if $A$ contains no nontrivial $3$-term arithmetic progression, then
\begin{equation}\
H \;\ge\; c_0\,n \left( \frac{n}{r_3(H)} \right)^{1/4},
\end{equation}
where $r_3(N)$ denotes the maximal size of a progression-free subset of $\{1,\dots,N\}$, and $c_0>0$ is absolute.

Also,
(2) Kelley--Meka (2023) proved that
\begin{equation}\
r_3(N) \;\le\; N \exp\!\big( -c_1 (\log N)^\beta \big),
\end{equation}
with an absolute $c_1>0$ and some $\beta>0$. Bloom--Sisask (2020) showed that $\beta=\tfrac{1}{9}$ is admissible.

Substituting (2) into (1) gives\[
H \;\ge\; c_0\,n \,\Big(\tfrac{n}{H}\Big)^{1/4}
\exp\!\Big( \tfrac{c_1}{4}\, (\log H)^\beta \Big).
\](3) Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\
H^{5/4} \;\ge\; c\, n^{5/4} \exp\!\Big( \tfrac{c_1}{4}\,(\log H)^\beta \Big).
\end{equation}

Note that $H \ge n$ trivially. Thus $\log H \ge \log n$.
From (3), one may apply a standard iteration/bootstrapping argument:
if $H \ll n \exp( C (\log n)^\beta)$, then the exponential factor on the right-hand side strictly dominates, leading to a contradiction for large $n$. Therefore, the inequality (3) forces: (4)

\begin{equation}\
H \;\ge\; n \exp\!\Big( c_2 (\log n)^\beta \Big),
\end{equation}
for some absolute constant $c_2>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$.
This step requires care since the exponential factor contains $\log H$, not $\log n$. A standard way to resolve this is to observe that if $H \le n \exp(C(\log n)^\beta)$, then $\log H \le \log n + O((\log n)^\beta)$, so $(\log H)^\beta = (\log n)^\beta (1+o(1))$, hence the factor $\exp(c_1(\log H)^\beta/4)$ still gives the desired contradiction. Iterating yields (4).

By a standard Plunnecke inequality, if $|A-A| \le K n$, then $|A+A| \le K^2 n$.
Equivalently,\[
D \;=\; |A-A| \;\ge\; \sqrt{Hn}.
\]Applying (4), we obtain\[
D \;\ge\; \sqrt{Hn}
\;\;\ge\;\; n \,\exp\!\Big( \tfrac{c_2}{2} (\log n)^\beta \Big).
\]Thus\[
f(n) \;=\; \frac{D}{n} \;\ge\; \exp\!\Big( c (\log n)^\beta \Big),
\]for some absolute constant $c>0$ and $\beta=\tfrac{1}{9}$ possible.

Hence $f(n)$ grows quasipolynomially, substantially improving the earlier polylogarithmic lower bound of Dumitrescu.

References can be found here:

Ruzsa, Sumsets and structure, in: Combinatorial Number Theory and Additive Group Theory, Birkh\"auser, 2009.
S. Kelley and R. Meka, Strong bounds for 3-term arithmetic progressions, Ann. of Math. 197 (2023) no. 1.
T. Bloom and O. Sisask, Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth’s theorem, Ann. of Math. 192 (2020).
A. Dumitrescu, On distinct distances with no isosceles triangles, Discrete Comput. Geom. 39 (2008), no. 4–5.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
It seems one can get (4) in a slightly simpler (and a bit stronger) way, without passing to \(r_3(H)\) or doing a bootstrap on \(\log H\). By Ruzsa’s original bound (Eq. (9.4) in Ruzsa, Sumsets and Structure, 2009),\[
|A+A|\ge cn\Big(\frac{n}{r_3(n)}\Big)^{1/4}.
\]Combining this with the Kelley–Meka bound (2),\[
r_3(n) \le n\exp \big(-c_1(\log n)^{\beta}\big),
\]we get immediately\[
H=|A+A| \ge cn\exp\Big(\frac{c_1}{4}(\log n)^{\beta}\Big),
\]which is exactly of the form (4) and avoids any iteration. Then, by Ruzsa’s twin to the triangle inequality \(|A+A||A|\le |A-A|^2\), one also gets \(|A-A|\ge n\exp\big(\tfrac{c_1}{8}(\log n)^{\beta}\big)\) and hence \(|A-A|/n\ge \exp\big(\tfrac{c_1}{8}(\log n)^{\beta}\big)\).

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
I think I have found a gap in your argument.

The reduction from the planar problem ($A \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with no isosceles triangles) to the one-dimensional case ($A \subset \mathbb{R}$ with no nontrivial 3-term arithmetic progression) is not valid: projecting to the real line does not preserve the “no isosceles triangle” property, so the two formulations are not equivalent.

That said, your improvement on Dumitrescu’s lower bound in the one-dimensional setting is entirely correct, since in fact Dumitrescu’s result itself only concerns the case $A \subset \mathbb{R}$. For sets on the line we do have $nf(n)=\Theta(|A-A|)$, so applying recent additive combinatorics results gives a genuine strengthening. In fact, your detailed proof appears to be an expanded version of the approach already pointed out earlier by zach hunter in his comments. However, for $A \subset \mathbb{R}^k$ with $k \geq 2$, no such strengthening is currently known.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Good point! I've double checked and the wording is a little ambiguous. The exact wording is:

"Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be a convex polyhedron in three dimensional space. Is it possible that for all large $n$ the number of distinct distances determined by our set is less than $\frac{n}{2}(1-\epsilon)$?"

I read this in the form written above, but maybe what he intended was "Is the number of distinct distances always at least $(\frac{1}{2}-o(1))n$?" This would make more sense given the comparison to Altman's result (although if this is what was intended then the wording is confusing).

The other alternative is that he did intend the problem as I wrote it above, but had some kind of general position (i.e. no four points on a plane). Although as I write that I see that your example is easily turned into one in general position, just by moving the vertices of the polygon around slightly.

So I'll edit it to the first possibility above, unless anyone else wants to weigh in. For historical comparison, the problem originally said:

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^3$ be the vertices of a convex polyhedron. Is there some constant $c>0$ such that, for all $n$ sufficiently large, the number of distinct distances determined by the $x_i$ is at most\[(1-c)\frac{n}{2}?\]EDIT: Of course this is trivially extremely false, since a generic set of $n$ points in suitably general position form a convex polyhedron with $\gg n^2$ distances, so (as with most of these problems) the interesting thing is the lower bound on the number of distances, not the upper bound!

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Here is a heuristic argument to suggest that the answer should be "yes". Fix $k$, take a random number $n \in [x,2x]$ and heuristically compute the probability that $q(n,k) \geq (1+\varepsilon) \log x$ for some fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. All the primes up to $(1+o(1)) \log x$ will have to divide one of $n+1,\dots,n+k$, so there are $k^{(1+o(1))(\log x/\log\log x)}=x^{(\log k+o(1))/\log\log x}$ ways to allocate these factors. By the Chinese remainder theorem and prime number theorem, this will determine $n$ uniquely. The "probability" that the primes from $(1+o(1)) \log x$ up to $(1+\varepsilon) \log x$ also divide one of $n+1,\dots,n+k$ is heuristically of the shape $(k /(1+O(\varepsilon))\log x)^{(1+o(1))\varepsilon \log x /\log\log x} = x^{-\varepsilon+o(1)}$, which should eventually overwhelm the $x^{(\log k+o(1))/\log\log x}$ factor and suggests that there are only finitely many $n$ with this property. But it looks quite hard to turn this into a rigorous argument!

Another trivial remark: the difficulty of this problem is monotone in $k$, so one can focus initially on the $k=2$ case if one is angling for a proof.

problem:
A pairwise balanced design for $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is a collection of sets $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $2\leq \lvert A_i\rvert <n$ and every pair of distinct elements $x,y\in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ is contained in exactly one $A_i$.

Is there a constant $C>0$ and, for all large $n$, a pairwise balanced design such that\[\lvert A_i\rvert > n^{1/2}-C\]for all $1\leq i\leq m$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/665.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Larson \cite{ErLa82}. In general, as Erd\H{o}s asks in \cite{Er97f}, find the slowest growing function $h$ such that, for all large $n$, there exists a pairwise balanced design with\[\lvert A_i\rvert > n^{1/2}-h(n)\]for all $1\leq i\leq m$.

The problem above asks whether $h(n)\ll 1$. Erd\H{o}s and Larson prove that $h(n) \ll n^{1/2-c}$ for some constant $c>0$, and note this can be improved to $h(n)\ll (\log n)^2$ assuming Cramer-type bounds on the difference between consecutive primes.

Shrikhande and Singhi \cite{ShSi85} have proved that the answer is no conditional on the conjecture that the order of every projective plane is a prime power (see [723]), by proving that every pairwise balanced design on $n$ points in which each block is of size $\geq n^{1/2}-c$ can be embedded in a projective plane of order $n+i$ for some $i\leq c+2$, if $n$ is sufficiently large.

In general, if $H(n)$ is the largest prime gap $\leq n$, then the above reuslts show that, assuming the prime power conjecture, $H(n)\asymp h(n)$.
References:
- [Er97f] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some unsolved problems. Combinatorics, geometry and probability (Cambridge, 1993) (1997), 1-10.
- [ErLa82] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Larson, J., On pairwise balanced block designs with the sizes of blocks as uniform as possible. Annals of Discrete Mathematics (1982), 129-134.
- [ShSi85] S. S. Shrikhande and N. M. Singhi, On a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Larson. Combinatorica (1985), 351-358.

forum_comments.author: ho boon suan
forum_comments.text:
Some comments on this problem:

That $c(p,q)$ is nondecreasing in $q$ for fixed $p$ is a straightforward consequence of the definitions.

The estimate $c(p,\binom{p-1}{2})\le1/2$ appears incorrect. If $k\ge3$, then we can show that $H(n;2k,\binom{2k-1}{2})\ge c_kn^{1-1/k}$ , so that $c(2k,\binom{2k-1}{2})\ge1-1/k>1/2$.

Indeed, given an $n$-vertex graph $G$ in which every set of $2k$ vertices spans at least $\binom{2k-1}{2}$ edges, every set of $2k$ vertices of $\overline G$ spans at most $2k-1$ edges, so $\overline G$ is $C_{2k}$-free. Then $e(\overline G)\le b_kn^{1+1/k}$ by Bondy–Simonovits, so $\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\ge n^2/(2e(\overline G)+n)\ge c_kn^{1-1/k}$.

We do however have $c(p,\binom{p-1}{2})\le2p/(2p+1)$, since Erdős proved that if $h(k,l)$ denotes the least $N$ such that every $N$-vertex graph contains either a cycle of length $\le k$ or an independent set of size $l$, then $h(k,l)>l^{1+1/(2k)}$ for fixed $k$ and all sufficiently large $l$; taking $k=p$ and $l=\lceil n^{2p/(2p+1)}\rceil$ gives, for all large $n$, an $n$-vertex graph $F$ of girth $>p$ with $\alpha(F)<l$, so every $p$ vertices of $F$ span at most $p-1$ edges, and hence $\overline F$ has every $p$-set spanning at least $\binom{p-1}{2}$ edges while $\omega(\overline F)=\alpha(F)<\lceil n^{2p/(2p+1)}\rceil$. (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1959-06.pdf (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1959-06.pdf))

We also have $c(p,\binom{p-2}{2}+1)\ge1/2$ for $p\ge4$; this follows from showing that every $n$-vertex graph $F$ such that every set of $p$ vertices spans at most $2p-4$ edges has independence number at least $\sqrt{n/(p-2)}-1/(p-2)$ for $p\ge4$.

And $c(4,2)=1/2$ by known estimates on $r(3,t)$; the $p=4$ question then reduces to asking if $n$-vertex $\{C_3,C_4\}$-free graphs always satisfy $\alpha\ge n^{1/2+\varepsilon}$ for some absolute $\varepsilon>0$, or if one can get $\alpha=n^{1/2+o(1)}$.

problem: Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points such that all pairwise distances differ by at least $1$. Is the diameter of $A$ at least $(1+o(1))n^2$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/670.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-16).
- Page last edited: 17 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The lower bound of $\binom{n}{2}$ for the diameter is trivial. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er97f} proved the claim when $d=1$. The quantifiers are slightly ambiguous, but likely Erd\H{o}s had in mind the regime where $d$ is fixed and the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $n\to \infty$ (perhaps at a rate which depends on $d$).

This was disproved if $n$ grows with $d$ by Ho \cite{Ho26}: there exist infinitely many $n$ and, with $d=n^2-n$, a set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ such that all pairwise distances differ by at least $1$, with diameter at most\[\left(1-\frac{1}{\pi^2}+o(1)\right)n^2\approx 0.898n^2.\]

- [Ho26] B. S. Ho, Erd\H{o}s's diameter conjecture for separated distances fails in high dimensions. arXiv:2604.15305 (2026).

One-Dimensional Case (Closed):
Let \(A=\{a_1<\cdots<a_n\}\subset\mathbb R\) with all pairwise distances at least
1 apart from each other (equivalently, all differences \(a_j-a_i\), \(i<j\), are
distinct). Then there are \(\binom n2\) distinct positive differences, each at
least \(1\), so the largest difference is at least \(\binom n2\):
\[
\operatorname{diam}(A)=a_n-a_1\ge \binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{diam}(A)\gg n^2\), which gives the required quadratic scale
in \(d=1\) (as recorded in the literature).
Remaining Open Part:
For fixed \(d\ge2\), need asymptotically sharp lower bounds approaching
\((1+o(1))n^2\).
- Need a high-dimensional incidence/energy theorem that converts distance
 separation constraints into near-maximal diameter growth, matching the
 one-dimensional quadratic scale up to \(1+o(1)\).

Target:
For fixed \(d\ge2\), prove
\[
\operatorname{diam}(A)\ge (1+o(1))n^2
\]
under pairwise-distance separation.
Step A: Additive-Energy Suppression
Show distance-separation imposes strong anti-concentration on difference vectors,
forcing large spread in projected distances.
Step B: Projection Rigidity
Find projection direction where 1D shadow retains near-distinct differences for
a large fraction of pairs.
Step C: Lift Back to Diameter
Use 1D lower bound from Step B to force full \(d\)-dimensional diameter at
\((1+o(1))n^2\) scale.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a projection lemma: for any such \(A\subset\mathbb R^d\), there exists a
direction \(u\) with at most \(o(n^2)\) collisions among projected pairwise
differences \(\langle a_i-a_j,u\rangle\).

problem:
Given $a_{i}^n\in [-1,1]$ for all $1\leq i\leq n<\infty$ we define $p_{i}^n$ as the unique polynomial of degree $n-1$ such that $p_{i}^n(a_{i}^n)=1$ and $p_{i}^n(a_{i'}^n)=0$ if $1\leq i'\leq n$ with $i\neq i'$. We similarly define\[\mathcal{L}^nf(x) = \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}f(a_i^n)p_i^n(x),\]the unique polynomial of degree $n-1$ which agrees with $f$ on $a_i^n$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ (that is, the sequence of Lagrange interpolation polynomials).

Is there such a sequence of $a_i^n$ such that for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ there exists some $x\in [-1,1]$ where\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}\lvert p_{i}^n(x)\rvert=\infty\]and yet\[\mathcal{L}^nf(x) \to f(x)?\]Is there such a sequence such that\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}\lvert p_{i}^n(x)\rvert=\infty\]for every $x\in [-1,1]$ and yet for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ there exists $x\in [-1,1]$ with\[\mathcal{L}^nf(x) \to f(x)?\]

forum_comments.author: KylePratt
forum_comments.text:
This problem has a substantial literature. The most impressive theoretical breakthrough on this problem is probably the work of Bennett and Siksek (https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2020/191-2/p02), who proved there are no solutions to the equation $$n(n+d)(n+2d) \cdots (n+(k-1)d)=y^\ell$$ in integers $n,d,k,y,\ell$ with $\text{gcd}(n,d)=1$, $d\geq 1$, $ny \neq 0$, $k$ large, and $\ell > \exp(10^k)$ a prime. The bibliography of their paper will lead one to many other works.

As other comments have noted, this Diophantine equation has solutions if we relax the condition that $n,n+d,\ldots$ are all positive. From the Bennett-Siksek paper and some other works, one can extract the conjecture that all solutions to this equation in integers $n,d,y$ with $\text{gcd}(n,d)=1, y \neq 0, d\geq 1, k \geq 4,\ell \geq 2$ come from one of the following situations:
--$(k,\ell,n,d)=(4,3,-9,5)$ or $(4,3,-6,5)$
--$k \equiv 0 \pmod{4}$ and $(\ell,n,d)=(2,-k+1,2)$, or
--$k$ is an odd square and $(\ell,n,d)=(2,-k+2,2)$.

forum_comments.author: ho boon suan
forum_comments.text:
About the last question on squarefree numbers, I believe I have found, with the assistance of GPT-5.4 Pro, a proof that $t_n>\exp(n^c)$ for sufficiently large $n$, for every $0<c<25/72$; see https://boonsuan.github.io/erdos675_squarefree.pdf (https://boonsuan.github.io/erdos675_squarefree.pdf). (I've read the proof and I think it's correct; I have not formalized it.)

The main idea is as follows: Suppose a translate $t$ preserves squarefreeness on $1,\dots,n$. Then we show that $p^2\mid t$ for every prime $p\le n^c$ by assuming that $p^2\not\mid t$ and using a bound on the least squarefree integer in a reduced residue class to contradict the translation property.

The statement of the squarefree bound (due to Nunes) used is as follows: Given a modulus $q\ge1$ and a reduced residue class $r\bmod q$, let $L(q,r)$ be the least positive squarefree integer $m$ such that $m\equiv r\pmod q$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a constant $C_\varepsilon$ such that, uniformly for all $q\ge1$ and all $r$ with $(r,q)=1$, we have $L(q,r)\le C_\varepsilon q^{36/25+\varepsilon}$.

Building on ho boon suan’s squarefree-period argument, the exponent $25/72$ can be improved using the recent Zhong--Zhang result on squarefree integers in arithmetic progressions to prime-power moduli. Let $\beta>3/4$ be an admissible exponent for squarefree distribution modulo $q=p^2$. Then the least squarefree integer in any reduced class modulo $p^2$ is\[
O\!\left(p^{2/\beta+\varepsilon}\right).
\]Re-running the divisibility argument gives\[
p^2 \mid t_n
\]for all primes $p \le n^c$, provided\[
c < \min(\beta/2,\,25/61).
\]The second number $25/61$ comes from the case $p \mid t_n$, $p^2 \nmid t_n$, using Nunes modulo $p$: choose squarefree $b \equiv -t_n/p \pmod p$, then\[
pb \le p^{61/25+\varepsilon}.
\]Since Zhong--Zhang break the $3/4$-barrier for prime-power moduli, this gives at least\[
t_n > \exp(n^c)\qquad (c < 3/8),
\]improving the previously posted $c < 25/72$. Extracting the exact $\beta$ from their Corollary~1.2 may give a slightly stronger exponent.

problem: Is every sufficiently large integer of the form\[ap^2+b\]for some prime $p$ and integer $a\geq 1$ and $0\leq b<p$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/676.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 07 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The sieve of Eratosthenes implies that almost all integers are of this form, and the Brun-Selberg sieve implies the number of exceptions in $[1,x]$ is $\ll x/(\log x)^c$ for some constant $c>0$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er79} believed it is 'rather unlikely' that all large integers are of this form.

What if the condition that $p$ is prime is omitted? Selfridge and Wagstaff made a 'preliminary computer search' and suggested that there are infinitely many $n$ not of this form even without the condition that $p$ is prime. It should be true that the number of exceptions in $[1,x]$ is $<x^c$ for some constant $c<1$.

Most generally, given some infinite set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and function $f:A\to \mathbb{N}$ one can ask for sufficient conditions on $A$ and $f$ that guarantee every large number (or almost all numbers) can be written as\[am^2+b\]for some $m\in A$ and $a\geq 1$ and $0\leq b<f(m)$.

In another direction, one can ask what is the minimal $c_n$ such that $n$ can be written as $n=ap^2+b$ with $0\leq b<c_np$ for some $p\leq \sqrt{n}$. This problem asks whether $c_n\leq 1$ eventually, but in \cite{Er79d} Erd\H{o}s suggests that in fact $\limsup c_n=\infty$. Is it true that $c_n<n^{o(1)}$?
References:
- [Er79] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some unconventional problems in number theory. Math. Mag. (1979), 67-70.
- [Er79d] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unconventional problems in number theory. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1979), 71-80.

In a highly experimental use, I have tried with ChatGPT (https://chatgpt.com/share/694e76f3-db0c-8010-b756-df434d9632d0) to assess the direction of the preprint (without judging the author one way or the other). I realize this more of an art than science...

First, we discussed the general background, such as the "almost all" result and known sieve heuristics. The main obstacle is identified: transitioning from "rare" to "impossible".

The paper's strategy is identified as studying the events $E_p(n) := \{ n \mod p^2 < p \}$ with vector of indicators $X_p(n) := 1_{E_p(n)}$. We want to compare the true joint law $P$ of $(X_p)_{p \leq X}$ to the product law $Q = \prod P_p$. The quantity to control is Kullback-Leibler divergence $D(P \parallel Q)$. The author then posited the Uniformity Hypothesis (UH) and strong Uniformity Hypothesis (sUH) which are bounds on $D(P \parallel Q)$. In particular, sUH is of importance that it should imply the finiteness of the exceptional set $E$ (Claim 1). Moreover, the author claims that either the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture or generalized Riemann Hypothesis imply sUH (Claim 2).

We then see that Claims 1 and 2 are the two main pieces to assess.

After thinking for over 15 minutes, ChatGPT assessed the two claims as follows.

$\textbf{Claim 1}$. The main claim here is Theorem 6.9, whose proof is only 4 lines (!) and invokes Borel-Cantelli. ChatGPT assessed the direction of the proof as:

"- Even a very strong average bound like $\Pr_{n\le x}(n\in E)\ll 1/(\log x)^{1+\varepsilon}$ would not by itself imply the deterministic set $E$ is finite; it would only say it’s sparse on average. The paper’s proof sketch invokes Borel–Cantelli in a way that (as written) seems to apply to a random sequence of sampled integers, not to the actual set of all exceptions.
- More fundamentally: with “independence-like” behavior, the heuristic size of the exceptional set is typically $\sim x/\log x$ (because $\prod_{p\le X}(1-1/p)\sim e^{-\gamma}/\log X$). Independence pushes you toward infinitely many exceptions, not finiteness. The paper is trying to conclude the opposite from an “almost-independence” hypothesis, which is already a big red flag relative to the mechanism it sets up."

Moreover, the proof of Theorem 6.9 claims bounds $\ll 1/(\log X)^{1+\varepsilon}$. ChatGPT sketched arguments that the actual machinery should give $\ll 1/(\log X)^{1-\varepsilon}$; even under "perfect independence" that'd only get you $\ll 1/\log X$.

Conclusion: the claimed exponent appears too strong from existing machinery, and, even if we do get this exponent, it's only an average bound and that doesn't bridge to finiteness. Moreover, the "almost-independence" heuristic seems to be going in the wrong direction.

$\textbf{Claim 2}$. The implication from EH/GRH to sUH.

ChatGPT argued this is problematic for a "simpler reason": the $N(x;q,b)$ is defined as the count of integers in a residue class. Since these counts and their second moments are already elementary, we do not need EH/GRH to control them. In fact, EH/GRH is about primes in arithmetic progressions and likely irrelevant here. In ChatGPT's words:

"“EH/GRH ⇒ strong second-moment control for primes in progressions” is true in the right context, and “second-moment control ⇒ small KL divergence” is a real information-theoretic theme (they even state a χ²/KL control via an energy functional).
But the paper’s specific EH/GRH ⇒ sUH claim doesn’t line up with the objects it defined (integer residue counts), and the modulus/scale issues are not resolved."

Conclusion: there could be some right conceptual ideas, but the connections to EH/GRH are likely irrelevant.

$\textbf{Overall}$. It seems to me that both claims are difficult to fix. EH/GRH is not likely to get to Uniformity because they don't seem to apply to this setting; on the other hand, Uniformity also doesn't seem to get to finiteness due to the kind of argument used.

As always, I write from my best understanding and do not claim accuracy in the chat's statements.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
Dear Colleagues,

I am seeking collaboration on the classical Erdős problem (Er79), particularly from an analytic number theory or sieve-theoretic perspective.

Recently, I submitted a manuscript entitled *“A Conditional Negative Resolution of Erdős’s Problem via the Entropy–Sieve Method”* to **Expositiones Mathematicae**.wich it is already was commented above by Prof Tao and Prof Alfaiz, After review, the paper was rejected, with referees indicating that the results are still premature and require further development. The main concerns were the need for a clearer and earlier definition of the proposed *entropy sieve*, a substantial improvement in exposition, and stronger arguments beyond heuristic or probabilistic reasoning. An inconsistency was also noted in the abstract regarding the interpretation of a “negative answer” versus the finiteness of exceptional integers.

Despite these criticisms, the feedback suggests that the general direction may be promising if strengthened and clarified, especially under strong hypotheses such as the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis or related uniformity assumptions. The referees also suggested that the method could become more convincing if concrete applications and rigorous implementations of the entropy–sieve framework are developed.

I am therefore looking for collaborators interested in refining the entropy–sieve approach, clarifying the logical structure of the argument, and exploring rigorous conditional or unconditional results related to Erdős-type additive problems involving prime squares. Any expertise in analytic methods, sieve theory, or related probabilistic techniques would be very welcome.

I would be glad to discuss these ideas further with interested researchers.

Kind regards,
**R. Zeraoulia**

Expositiones Mathematicae

Editor and Reviewer comments:  

The research results reported are too premature for publication. More work is needed to substantiate the conclusions in your manuscript.

The authors consider a new type of sieving argument, the so-called 'entropy sieve' and uses this to attack an old conjecture of Erdos. The conjecture is that every sufficient large $n$ should be expressible as n=ap^{2} + b for some a\geq 1, some prime p, and some remainder b satisfying 0\leq b <p.

We know that almost all such $n$ can be so written. The authors claim that the generalised Riemann hypothesis implies 'a negative answer' to Erdos's question. However, there is an inconsistency in the abstract: it is claimed that the negative answer is due to the fact that only finitely many $n$ cannot be represented in the desired way. This would in fact prove the statement.

Leaving aside this inconsistency, the article is very difficult to read and would benefit from a thorough re-writing. In particular, the 'entropy-sieve' should be defined much earlier than Section 7. Moreover, it is hard to see what the entropy sieve does beyond making probabilistic/heuristic conjectures. Given that the authors list some future applications and developments of the entropy sieve, I suggest that they implement these now, make the exposition much clearer, and submit to a number-theoretic specific journal (perhaps Journal of Number Theory).

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
Greeting! I would like to share a recent attempt on [79] (quadratic prime representations).

In my preprint I introduce an **Entropy--Sieve Method**, which combines sieve theory with information-theoretic tools (relative entropy/KL divergence and a quadratic energy functional). The key reduction shows that finiteness of the exceptional set may follow if one can establish the uniformity estimate\[
E_2(P) \;=\; \frac{1+o(1)}{M},
\qquad M=\prod_{p\le Y} p^2,
\]for the quadratic energy of the residue distribution. A change-of-measure argument via KL divergence then transforms this into a sharp tail bound for the sieve sum.

What is important here is that this framework isolates precisely the analytic input needed: if the above uniformity holds, then the \emph{exceptional set} $E$ (integers with no quadratic prime representation) is finite. In other words, only finitely many large integers could fail Erdős's representation. This directly addresses the central question of [79]. Our numerical experiments further confirm that many large numbers remain outside the representable set, showing that unconditional tools do not yet shrink $E$ to finite --- highlighting both the sharpness of our reduction and the difficulty of the problem.

Thus, our contribution is twofold: (i) it provides a conditional path to prove finiteness of $E$ under standard distributional conjectures (EH or GRH), and (ii) it clarifies why unconditional finiteness is still out of reach, since in practice large integers without representation persist far beyond current analytic barriers.

\textbf{Preprint:}
ResearchGate link (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/395665344_ENTROPY-SIEVE_METHODS_AND_ENERGY_FUNCTIONALS_IN_THE_ERDOS_PROBLEM_ER79_ON_QUADRATIC_PRIME_REPRESENTATIONS),
DOI: 10.13140/RG.2.2.14599.05283 (https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.14599.05283).

I would be especially grateful for feedback on two delicate analytic points:

1. The explicit derivation and control of the divisor-weights $w(q,M)$ in the variance decomposition.
2. The uniform lower bound $Q_r \gg 1/M$ required when passing from $\chi^2$ divergence to KL divergence.

Any references or suggestions regarding these aspects, or about related treatments of primes modulo $p^2$, would be very welcome.

problem:
Let $M(n,k)=[n+1,\ldots,n+k]$ be the least common multiple of $\{n+1,\ldots,n+k\}$.

Is it true that for all $m\geq n+k$\[M(n,k) \neq M(m,k)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/677.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 September 2025.
Site remarks:
The Thue-Siegel theorem implies that, for fixed $k$, there are only finitely many $m,n$ such that $m\geq n+k$ and $M(n,k)=M(m,k)$.

In general, how many solutions does $M(n,k)=M(m,l)$ have when $m\geq n+k$ and $l>1$? Erd\H{o}s expects very few (and none when $l\geq k$).

The only solutions Erd\H{o}s knew were $M(4,3)=M(13,2)$ and $M(3,4)=M(19,2)$.

In \cite{Er79d} Erd\H{o}s conjectures the stronger fact that (aside from a finite number of exceptions) if $k>2$ and $m\geq n+k$ then $\prod_{i\leq k}(n+i)$ and $\prod_{i\leq k}(m+i)$ cannot have the same set of prime factors.

See also [678], [686], and [850].

This is discussed in problem B35 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [Er79d] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unconventional problems in number theory. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1979), 71-80.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

problem:
Let $\epsilon>0$ and $\omega(n)$ count the number of distinct prime factors of $n$. Are there infinitely many values of $n$ such that\[\omega(n-k) < (1+\epsilon)\frac{\log k}{\log\log k}\]for all $k<n$ which are sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon$ only?

Can one show the stronger version with\[\omega(n-k) < \frac{\log k}{\log\log k}+O(1)\]is false?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/679.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 17 April 2026.
Site remarks:
One can ask similar questions for $\Omega$, the number of prime factors with multiplicity, where $\log k/\log\log k$ is replaced by $\log_2k$.

In the comments DottedCalculator has disproved the second stronger version, proving that in fact for all large $n$ there exists $k<n$ such that\[\omega(n-k)\geq \frac{\log k}{\log\log k} + c\frac{\log k}{(\log\log k)^2}\]for some constant $c>0$.

Lau \cite{La26} has proved that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that, for infinitely many $n$,\[\omega(n-k) \leq \Omega(n-k)\leq C\log k\]for all $1<k<n$. Lau conjectures that, for $\omega$, this can only be improved in the constant factor, and thus the original question has a negative answer.

See also [248], [413], and [1203].
References:
- [La26] C. F. Lau, On the number of prime factors of consecutive integers. arXiv:2604.15042 (2026).

- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/680.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
This follows from 'plausible assumptions on the distribution of primes' (as does the question with $k^2$ replaced by $k^d$ for any $d$); the challenge is to prove this unconditionally.

Erd\H{o}s observed that Cramer's conjecture\[\limsup_{k\to \infty} \frac{p_{k+1}-p_k}{(\log k)^2}=1\]implies that for all $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$ there exists some $k$ such that\[p(n+k)>e^{(1-\epsilon)\sqrt{k}}.\]There is now evidence, however, that Cramer's conjecture is false; a more refined heuristic by Granville \cite{Gr95} suggests this $\limsup$ is $2e^{-\gamma}\approx 1.119\cdots$, and so perhaps the $1+\epsilon$ in the second question should be replaced by $2e^{-\gamma}+\epsilon$.

See also [681] and [682].
References:
- [Gr95] Granville, Andrew, Harald {C}ram\'{e}r and the distribution of prime numbers. Scand. Actuar. J. (1995), 12--28.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
This should be accessible with sieve methods (Maynard/Chen-style). I did some back and forth with GPT-5.2 and here's where's the difficulty lies. First of all note that if $n+1$ is composite then one may take $k=1$, since $p(n+1)\geq 2>1=k^2$. Thus the only potentially difficult values are $n=p-1$ with $p$ prime. Any admissible witness must satisfy $k^4<n+k$, hence $k\leq n^{1/4}+O(1)$, and it is natural to search on a dyadic block $K<k\leq 2K$ with $K=n^\alpha$ and $\alpha<1/4$, so that $k^2\leq 4K^2$.

Fix $\alpha\in(0,1/4)$, put $K=n^\alpha$ and $y=4K^2$, and consider the short interval $I=(n+K,n+2K]$. A sufficient condition is the existence of a composite $m\in I$ with $p(m)>y$ (then $m=n+k$ for some $k\in(K,2K]$ and $p(m)>y\geq k^2$). The sieve heuristic for $y$-rough numbers predicts $\#\{m\in I:p(m)>y\}\approx K\,\omega(u)/\log y$ with $u=\log n/\log y$ and Buchstab function $\omega$, while $\#\{m\in I:m\ \textrm{prime}\}\approx K/\log n$; since $u\omega(u)>1$ for $u>2$ (equivalently $\alpha<1/4$), the heuristic main term already suggests that $I$ should contain composite $y$-rough values. However, existing pointwise sieve methods do not currently yield such a uniform lower bound in a single length-$K$ interval when $y\asymp K^2$, because the lower linear sieve requires sieve level $R>y^2$ whereas one only has trivial remainder control for divisibility in a fixed short interval.

Unconditionally, an averaging-over-$p$ substitute appears accessible: one may sieve the primes $p\in[X,2X]$ with $K=X^\alpha$ and $y=4K^2$ using Rosser--Iwaniec linear sieve weights and the Bombieri--Vinogradov theorem (level $1/2$) to obtain a positive lower bound for the mean of $R(p)=\#\{K<k\leq 2K:(p-1+k,P(y))=1\}$ provided $s=(\log R)/(\log y)>2$. Taking $R=X^{1/4-\varepsilon}$ and $y=X^{2\alpha}$ gives $s\approx 1/(8\alpha)$, so $s>2$ holds for any fixed $\alpha<1/16$, and a standard second-moment argument (with singular series averaging as in Gallagher) then yields $R(p)\gg K/\log X$ for all but $o(\pi(X))$ primes $p\in[X,2X]$. Since primes in $(p+K,p+2K]$ contribute only $\asymp K/\log X$, one obtains for almost all such primes $p$ a shift $k\in(K,2K]$ with $p-1+k$ composite and $p(p-1+k)>k^2$. References for the sieve ingredients include J. Friedlander and H. Iwaniec, Opera de Cribro (2010), and D. R. Heath-Brown, Lectures on sieves (2002); improving the exponent toward $\alpha=1/4$ would require new distribution input beyond Bombieri--Vinogradov.

problem: Is it true that for every $1\leq k\leq n$ the largest prime divisor of $\binom{n}{k}$, say $P(\binom{n}{k})$, satisfies\[P\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)\geq \min(n-k+1, k^{1+c})\]for some constant $c>0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/683.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-04).
- Page last edited: 31 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A theorem of Sylvester and Schur (see \cite{Er34}) states that $P(\binom{n}{k})>k$ if $k\leq n/2$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er55d} proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that, whenever $k\leq n/2$,\[P\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)\gg k\log k.\]Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er79d} writes it 'seems certain' that this holds for every $c>0$, with only a finite number of exceptions (depending on $c$). Standard heuristics on prime gaps suggest that the largest prime divisor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is, for $k\leq n/2$, in fact\[>e^{c\sqrt{k}}\]for some constant $c>0$.

This is essentially equivalent to [961].

It seems easy to construct a counterexample to the main problem.
Take $n=2^t$ and $k=n-1$ $(t\geq2)$. Then $\binom{n}{k}=\binom{2^t}{1}=2^t$, so $P\!\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)=2$.

Hence $P\!\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)=2\not>2$,

- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/684.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A classical theorem of Mahler states that for any $\epsilon>0$ and integers $k$ and $l$ then, writing\[(n+1)\cdots (n+k) = ab\]where the only primes dividing $a$ are $\leq l$ and the only primes dividing $b$ are $>l$, we have $a < n^{1+\epsilon}$ for all sufficiently large (depending on $\epsilon,k,l$) $n$.

Mahler's theorem implies $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$, but is ineffective, and so gives no bounds on the growth of $f(n)$.

One can similarly ask for estimates on the smallest integer $f(n,k)$ such that if $m$ is the factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ containing all primes $\leq f(n,k)$ then $m > n^2$.

Tang and ChatGPT have proved (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-684-note/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_684.pdf) that\[f(n)\leq n^{30/43+o(1)}.\]The same proof would prove $f(n) \leq n^{2/3+o(1)}$ assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (or Density Hypothesis).

A heuristic given by Sothanaphan and ChatGPT in the comments suggests that, at least for most $n$, $f(n)\sim 2\log n$.

An internal OpenAI model \cite{APSSV26} has given an elementary argument which shows $f(n) \ll (\log n)^2$, and constructs arbitrarily large $n$ such that $f(n)\geq (1/2-o(1))\log n$.
References:
- [APSSV26] B. Alexeev, M. Putterman, M. Sawhney, M. Sellke, and G. Valiant, Short proofs in combinatorics and number theory. arXiv:2603.29961 (2026).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
The OpenAI proof seems to have been optimized for brevity rather than explainability, and in general reads like "here is the first working proof that we found" rather than "here is a streamlined proof highlighting the key ideas", but it follows broadly similar lines to previous (successful or unsuccessful) attempts to upper bound $f(n)$ in the comments here. In all cases, the first step is to use Kummer's theorem to observe that a prime $p$ will divide $u$ whenever $n \% p < k \% p$, where I use $n \% p = p \{\frac{n}{p} \}$ to denote the remainder of $n$ after dividing by $p$. (Kummer's theorem also gives contributions when $n \% p^r < k \% p^r$ for higher prime powers $p^r$, but these contributions are lower order and so not of much additional use.) So to upper bound $f(n)$, one has to find a $k$ that is not too large such that $n \% p < k \% p$ for a lot of primes $p$. One should presumably focus on primes $p$ that are not much larger than $k$, otherwise the right-hand side $k \% p$ is small and the condition is unlikely to be satisfied. So one should think of $k$ and $p$ as both being small. We get to pick the $k$ and $p$ that we want, so we can take advantage of the probabilistic method and average (or take expectations) in these parameters with regard to suitably chosen probability distributions.

The main enemy comes from the fact that $n \% p$ could be very close to the maximal value of $p$, in which case the condition is unlikely to be satisfied. If one had some good equidistribution theory on $\{ n/p\}$ then this would be easy to avoid, and this is basically why one can get bounds on $f(n)$ of polynomial type (actually using Vinogradov exponential sum estimates one could probably get a bound of the shape $f(n) \ll \exp(\log^{2/3+o(1)} n)$ from an equidistribution approach). But when $k$ or $p$ is only polylogarithmic in size then such equidistribution results are not known currently (the difficulty level here is comparable to the Riemann hypothesis).

The new idea of the OpenAI proof is to use an elementary upper bound on the rare event that $n \% p$ is close to $p$ that is weaker than equidistribution, but still gives something useful. Specifically, if $n\% p \geq p-A$ for some $A$, then $p$ divides $(n+1) \dots (n+A)$. In particular, if $A$ and $Y$ are of polylogarithmic size, then the number of primes $p \asymp Y$ for which $n \% p \geq p-A$ is at most $O( A \log n / \log Y)$. Comparing this with the prime number theorem, we see that for a given scale $Y$, about $\gg Y / \log Y$ of the primes $p \asymp Y$ will have $n \% p < p - A$ for some $A \asymp Y / \log n$. (Equidistribution predicts that this $\log n$ denominator can be eliminated; this loss of $\log n$ is ultimately why the OpenAI paper gets a $\log^2 n$ type bound on $f$ rather than the conjectural $\log^{1+o(1)} n$ bound.)

Anyway, for a prime $p$ of the above form, the condition $n \% p < k \% p$ would now hold with probability $\gg A / p \asymp 1 / \log n$ for $k$ drawn randomly in the range $k = O(Y)$. Summing over such primes, we conclude that the expected value of $\log u$ is $\gg \frac{Y}{\log Y} \frac{1}{\log n} \log Y$. Setting $Y = C \log^2 n$ for a large $C$, one can then ensure that $\log u > 2 \log n$ for some $k = O(Y)$, which gives the upper bound $f(n) \ll \log^2 n$. The actual proof is a bit more intricate (in particular introducing a new summation variable $j$ that is not present in the above discussion) because it is trying to optimize the explicit constant in this bound.

One should be able to mostly eliminate this logarithmic loss if one is also permitted to average in $n$. In particular I expect these methods should be able to show that $f(n) \ll \log^{1+o(1)} n$ for almost all $n$, or something like this.

forum_comments.text:
Yes, this looks sensible. To summarise here for convenience, the observation is that\[\log v(n,k)=\sum_{k<p\leq n}\log p\sum_{j\geq 1}1_{n\pmod{p^j}<k},\]and assuming the indicator function here to be binomial with probability $k/p^j$ gives the heuristic\[\log v(n,k)=k\sum_{k<p\leq n}\frac{\log p}{p-1}=k\log(n/k)+o(k).\]Since $\log\binom{n}{k}=k\log(n/k)+k+O(\log k)$ by Stirling, this means we expect $u>n^2$, i.e. $\log\binom{n}{k}-\log v>2\log n$, at $k\sim 2\log n$.

This certainly makes sense as an 'average' observation, but I do worry that the worst case behaviour (which is the problem here) might behave a little different - one can imagine some conspiracy between $n$ and 'medium-range' primes which forces $v$ to be measurably larger than this suggests. There is also a suspicious spike in the numerical data you give at $n\approx 10^5$, much higher than the predicted $2\log n$.

It might be that $f(n)\sim 2\log n$ for almost all $n$, but perhaps for infinitely many $n$ we have $f(n)\gg (\log n)^2$, say.

Since we have reduced the problem to the $N$ being square case, it turns out there is some interesting literature concerning $n=0$, i.e. binomial coefficients that are squares.

Lucas' square-pyramid problem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_problem) shows that $\binom{50}{3} = 140^2$ is the only nontrivial solution when $k=3$ ($n=0$, square $N$).

Erdos proved (https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/778233/is-there-any-perfect-squares-that-are-also-binomial-coefficients) that $\binom{m}{k} = n^\ell$ has no solution when $\ell \ge 2$ and $4 \le k \le m-4$. This rules out $k \ge 4$ as well.

Hence, $N = 140^2$ is the *only* square with a representation with $k \ge 3$ and $n=0$.

Using SageMath's 'EllipticCurve_from_cubic' with the rational point '(1:1:1)', I obtained the following Weierstrass models:

| 'N' | Cremona label | rank | torsion |

| '16' | '9180a1' | '2' | trivial |

| '64' | '16380d1' | '2' | 'Z/2Z' |
| '81' | conductor '797040' | '3' | trivial |

All seven curves have positive rank. On the original cubic, a direct search for 'Y in [-50,500]' gives:

- 'N=9': admissible point '(X,Y) = (27,13)', i.e. '(m,n) = (25,11)'.
- 'N=16': admissible point '(X,Y) = (15,6)', i.e. '(m,n) = (13,4)'.

Important caveat: the birational map to the Weierstrass model does not preserve integrality in general. For example, the known 'N=16' solution '(X,Y) = (15,6)' maps to a non-integral Weierstrass point. So integral points on the Weierstrass model do not by themselves prove non-representability on the original cubic.

For 'k=5' and 'N=4', let

Then 'F(x) = 4F(y)' has no rational points at infinity, since this would require a rational root of 'u^5 - 4', which is irreducible over 'Q'. A brute-force search for '|x|, |y| <= 10000' finds only the 25 trivial zero-product points '{-5,-4,-3,-2,-1}^2', and no admissible solutions.

'F(m) ≡ 4F(n) (mod M)'

has admissible solutions with 'm >= n+5': for 'M >= 5', take 'n = M-1' and 'm = 3M-5', so 'F(n) ≡ F(m) ≡ 0 (mod M)' and 'm-n = 2M-4 >= 6'; for 'M <= 4', the pair '(n,m) = (0,5)' already works.

| '2' | not representable | Tao |

Building on natso26's results on exact $k$th-power multipliers and Vjeko Kovač's
computational data, I'd like to note two observations.

**1. An infinite family of representable perfect squares.**

For every $n \geq 0$, the perfect square $N = 4(2n+3)^2$ is representable with $k = 2$.
Set $m = (2n+3)^2 - 2$. Then:

$$\frac{(m+1)(m+2)}{(n+1)(n+2)} = \frac{((2n+3)^2 - 1) \cdot (2n+3)^2}{(n+1)(n+2)} = \frac{4(n+1)(n+2) \cdot (2n+3)^2}{(n+1)(n+2)} = 4(2n+3)^2.$$

The key step is the factorization $(2n+3)^2 - 1 = 4(n+1)(n+2)$, which creates exact
cancellation. The non-overlap condition $m \geq n + 2$ holds for all $n \geq 0$.

This gives $N = 36, 100, 196, 324, 484, 676, 900, 1156, \ldots$ — all perfect squares,
all representable. Additional representable perfect squares arise from Pell equation
families (e.g., $N = 1225 = 35^2$ via $49 \cdot 50 / (1 \cdot 2)$, and $N = 9801 = 99^2$
via $242 \cdot 243 / (2 \cdot 3)$).

In particular, the obstruction for $\{4, 25, 49, 64, 81\}$ cannot be simply "perfect
powers are not representable."

**2. Computational extension: perfect powers up to 10,000.**

I ran a systematic search over all perfect powers $N \leq 10{,}000$ with $k \leq 80$
and $n \leq 1000$. Results:

- **Representable** (39 values): $8, 9, 16, 27, 32, 36, 100, 125, 196, 216, 243, 324, 343, 484, 676, 900, 1000, 1156, 1225, 1331, 1444, 1764, 2048, 2116, 2197, 2500, 2916, 3364, 3844, 4356, 4900, 5476, 6084, 6724, 7396, 8100, 8836, 9604, 9801$

- **Not representable within search bounds** (85 values): $4, 25, 49, 64, 81, 121, 128, 144, 169, 225, 256, 289, 361, 400, 441, 512, 529, 576, 625, 729, \ldots$

All representable perfect powers found representations with $k = 2$ (some also with
$k = 3$). No perfect power that failed at $k = 2$ was rescued by a larger $k$ within
the search bounds.

Among perfect squares specifically: the representable square roots include
$3, 4, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, 35, \ldots$ while non-representable square roots
include $2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, \ldots$. The $4(2n+3)^2$ family accounts for
the regular spacing (roots $\equiv 2 \pmod{4}$ starting from 6), while the Pell families
contribute sporadic additional values (35, 99, $\ldots$).

**Open question:** Is there a clean characterization of which perfect powers are
representable? The data suggests the answer depends on solvability of specific
generalized Pell equations for $k = 2$, but I don't see a simple closed-form criterion.

---

**Some speculative directions (not verified, flagging for discussion):**

- The Khanduja-Bhatia irreducibility criterion suggests that
 $f_k(x) - N \cdot f_k(y)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$
 whenever $N$ is not a perfect $d$th power for any $d \mid k$
 with $d \geq 2$. If correct, this would mean the curve
 $C_{k,N}: f_k(x) = N \cdot f_k(y)$ is irreducible for
 non-perfect-power $N$, and genus bounds (Faltings for $k \geq 4$,
 Siegel for $k = 3$) give per-$k$ finiteness. Does this observation
 survive scrutiny?

- The computational data shows no perfect power that failed at
 $k = 2$ was rescued by any larger $k \leq 80$. Is there a
 structural reason why $k = 2$ should be the "best chance" for
 perfect powers, or could larger $k$ eventually succeed?

- By Kummer's theorem, the problem can be rephrased in terms of
 carry-count differences in base-$p$ arithmetic. Is there a
 characterization of which valuation profiles $(v_p(N))_p$ are
 achievable as such differences across all $(k, m, n)$?

---

*Disclosure: This work used a multi-model AI pipeline (Claude for analysis and
orchestration, GPT-5.4 for mathematical reasoning). The algebraic identity was
discovered by pattern recognition in computational output, then verified by hand.
All mathematical content has been checked by me.
Thanks in advance.

Speaking of special cases, $N=64$ cannot be represented using $k=6$. Namely, expanding into a series and estimating errors explicitly, we get\[ \big((m+1)\cdots(m+6)\big)^{1/6} = m + \frac{7}{2} + f(m), \quad |f(m)|\leq\frac{2}{m}, \]\[ \big(64(n+1)\cdots(n+6)\big)^{1/6} = 2n + 7 + g(n), \quad |g(n)|\leq\frac{3}{n}. \]Therefore, if these two are equal, then $f(m)-g(n)+\frac{1}{2}\in\mathbb{Z}$. Since the equation also forces $2n-6\leq m\leq 2n+12$, we see that it is sufficient to check the cases, say, $0\leq m,n\leq100$, which is easily done.

A very similar idea was used in vilc's post. As mentioned there, in principle it takes a finite amount of computation to rule out any particular pair $(N,k)$, where $N$ is a perfect $k$-th power. Thus, numbers like $N=u^{v!}$ have very slim chances of being representable, but some effective variants of Siegel's theorem would likely be needed to rule out the cases $k>v$.

forum_comments.text:
More generally, here is an explicit bound on $n$ when $N = a^k$. For $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 2$:
$$n + \dfrac{k-1}{2} - \dfrac{k^2 - 1}{24n} < (n(n+1) \ldots (n+k-1))^{1/k} < n + \dfrac{k-1}{2} - \dfrac{k^2 - 1}{24n} + \dfrac{(k^2-1)(k-1)}{48n^2}$$
Applying these to $n$ and $m$, one can show the following disjunction:
- If $n\leq \dfrac{2k}{3}$ and one of $a, k$ is odd, then $m = an + \dfrac{(a-1)(k-1)}{2}$ may be a solution.
- Else, if one of $a, k$ is odd then $n < \dfrac{a(k^2 - 1)}{24}$
- Else $n < \dfrac{a(k^2 - 1)}{12}$
(the bound $n\leq \tfrac{2k}{3}$ in the first case could be marginally improved to $n\leq ck$ for some $c$ dependant on $a$ but greater than $\tfrac{1}{2}$)
We can get a lower bound on $n$ using some elementary arithmetic.
Assume that $a\geq 2$ is such that $N=a^k$ is representable for $k$. If $p$ is prime and $p^l \mid a$ then $p^{lk} \leq C_k a^2$, where $C_k = max(k, \tfrac{(k^2 + 9k - 4)}{12})$ [EDIT : fixed typo, thanks natso26].
Proof :
One has $v_p(n(n+1) \ldots (n+k-1)) \geq v_p(k!)$ for any $n \geq 1$. Moreover, if $p^j$ is the largest power of $p$ which divides one of $m, m+1, \ldots, m+k-1$, then $v_p(m(m+1) \ldots (m+k-1)) \leq j + v_p((k-1)!)$. This implies that :
$$v_p(N) = v_p(m(m+1) \ldots (m+k-1)) - v_p(n(n+1) \ldots (n+k-1)) \leq j - v_p(k) \leq j$$
Since $p^l$ divides $a$, we get $lk \leq j$, so $p^{lk} \leq m + k - 1$. Based on the above disjunction, one has (since $a \geq 2$):
- either $m+k-1 \leq ak + \dfrac{(a+1)(k-1)}{2} < 2ak \leq k a^2$
- or $m + k - 1 < a(n+k) + k - 1 \leq a\left(\dfrac{a(k^2 - 1)}{12} + k\right) + k - 1 \leq \dfrac{a^2(k^2 + 9k - 4)}{12}$
This completes the proof.
When $a = p^l$ is a prime power and $k \geq 3$, one has $a \leq C_k^{\tfrac{1}{k-2}}$. But it is easily verified that if $k \geq 5$, $C_k^{\tfrac{1}{k-2}} < 2$ ( $<3$ for $k = 4$, $<4$ for $k=3$). Therefore, since the remaining cases for small $k$ were already covered, if $a$ is a prime power, then $a^k$ is not representable with $k$ (this can be generalised easily to cases where $\omega(a)$ is small enough compared to $k$).

The paper of Chan (https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.01306) Vjeko found by literature seach shows that for any fixed $N$ and $k=3$ there are only finitely many solutions. Here is the proof sketch, using the current notation. Writing $m+1 = Dv$ and $n+1 = Du$ where $D$ is the greatest common divisor of $m+1,n+1$, the equation can be rewritten as
$$ D^2 (v^3 - N u^3) = v - Nu.$$
Since $v-Nu$ already divides $v^3 - N^3 u^3$, the gcd of $v-Nu$ and $v^3-Nu^3$ must divide $N^3-N$ and hence $v^3 - N u^3$ also divides $N^3 - N$. If $N$ is a perfect cube we are already done by the gaps between cubes. Otherwise, we get a Diophantine approximation $v/u = N^{1/3} + O(u^{-3})$ which, when combined with the Thue-Siegel-Roth theorem, gives an ineffective bound on $u,v$. Using instead a Baker type theorem one can get effective bounds (of exponential type in $N$).

For higher $k$, one could hopefully apply Siegel's theorem on integer points to show (ineffective) finiteness; one just needs to show that the curve $(y+1) \dots (y+k) = N (x+1) \dots (x+k)$ contains no genus zero curves, which should be some elementary algebraic geometry.

EDIT: it seems plausible that by adapting the proof of Theorem 1 of Chan's paper one can rule out $k=3$ solutions to specific $N$ such as $N=4,25,49,64,81$. To do this one has to do some numerical computations with the results of Bennett (https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~bennett/paper8.pdf) on explicit lower bounds on rational approximants to expressions such as $N^{1/3}$; the case $N=2$ is worked out explicitly in Bennett (and hence in Chan) but one has to update all the numbers to handle for instance $N=4$. This might be a suitable task for some AI workflow. EDIT: this earlier paper of Bennett (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/effective-measures-of-irrationality-for-certain-algebraic-numbers/9514B1BC73EBF0C72B9B470D62C448A9) may also be usable, although the later paper seems to slightly sharpen the results of this earlier paper as far as numerical constants are concerned.

EDIT:
I proved that none of $4$, $49$, $64$ have a representation for $k = 3$. First, based on my attempts here are some general remarks on applying Bennett's estimates with Chan's method :
- if two irrationnals generate the same field, an explicit estimate for one yields an estimate for the other. This fact is actually often used by Bennett (see the values of $a,N$ in the tables)
- in practice, one can get much better estimates (with an arbitrarily large constant) when $q$ is above some adequate threshold by using more computations to study the continued fraction. A larger constant dramatically improves the final bound. The main limiting factor for our purposes is therefore to obtain an exponent $<3$.
- in Bennett's formulas for $\kappa(a,n)$ the notation $ord_p(n)$ is a divisibility order, not a multiplicative order (this confused me for some time)

Chan shows that $\left|N - \dfrac{v^3}{u^3}\right| \leq \dfrac{N^{3}}{u^3}$ and $\left|\sqrt[3]{N} - \dfrac{v}{u}\right| \leq \dfrac{N^{\tfrac{7}{3}}}{u^3}$. For sufficiently large $u$, the first one is better by a factor of nearly $3$, but I will only need the second one for what follows. A bound on $x$ follows from a bound on $u$ since $D^2 \leq Nu - v \leq Nu$.
When $N$ is a cube (as for $N=64$), $\left|\sqrt[3]{N} - \dfrac{v}{u}\right| \geq \dfrac{1}{u}$ since equality does not hold. Therefore $u \leq N^{\tfrac{7}{6}}$ and $x \leq N^{\tfrac{9}{4}}$. For $64$, we need to check for $x$ up to $12000$, which I did.
$N = 4$ is an example where adapting the bound for $\sqrt[3]{2}$ works without trouble. Since $\sqrt[3]{4} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt[3]{2}}$, Bennett's estimate yields for all $p,q$ $$\left|\sqrt[3]{4} - \dfrac{p}{q}\right| \geq \dfrac{\sqrt[3]{4}\times 2^{1-2.45}}{8} q^{-2.45} > 0.072 q^{-2.45}$$ This gives in turn $x \leq 2 \times 10^7$, and no further improvement was needed since I had already searched up to $2\times 10^9$.
For $N = 49$ I used Bennett's values of $a=15$ and $N = 7 \times 23^3$ [notation conflict, not the same $N$ as ours] for $\sqrt[3]{7}$, to benefit from the later paper's improved exponents (which turned out to be nearly irrelevant). By studying the continued fraction with Pari/GP, I found that if $q \geq 11004$, then $\left|\sqrt[3]{49} - \dfrac{p}{q}\right| > 223\times q^{-2.69}$. The $223$ could be improved easily for larger $q$, but this already yields $x < 4\times 10^8$, which again I could check in a reasonnable amount of time. Compare with bounds on the order of $x\leq 10^{20}$ if a general bound such as $0.1 q^{-2.69}$ had been used.

forum_comments.author: vilc
forum_comments.text:
I don't know if the formal proof is based on the same idea, but there is a deterministic algorithm for finding a representation with $k=2$ when $N$ is not a square.
Find a solution $(z, w)$ of $z^2 - Nw^2 = 1$, which is always possible by standard methods when $N$ is not a square. If $z-w$ and $z-Nw$ are both odd (always true for odd $N$, and will be true for the "squared" solution $(z^2+Nw^2, 2zw)$ if $N$ is even), then by elementary calculations $n=\dfrac{|z-w|-1}{2}$ and $m=\dfrac{|z-Nw|-1}{2}$ verify $Nn(n+1)=m(m+1)$. If $n$ and $m$ are too close, a larger initial solution $(z',w')$ will work. This also shows that there is an infinite number of solutions.
As a demonstration of the method, a representation, probably the smallest, of $N=614$ with $k=2$ is $(n = 167117648945, m = 4141012131555)$ (Pell equation solved with Dario Alpern's online calculator (https://www.alpertron.com.ar/QUAD.HTM)).
