I asked Gemini Deep Research to find references on the problem (the main formulation), Gemini Deep Think to actually represent as many integers $2\leq N\leq100$ as possible, and then also ChatGPT to find some references on the problem.

In about 10 mins Gemini Deep Research made the following report (https://gemini.google.com/share/8a65afa26217) on the problem. It made a big deal reformulating the quotient as the quotient of binomial coefficients, but it did not make much use of that. It also mentioned the Sylvester-Schur theorem that, among any $k$ consecutive integers $>k$, at least one has a prime divisor $>k$. Then it mentioned the Erdős-Selfridge theorem that the product of two or more consecutive positive integers is never a perfect power. All this was just to argue that the representations are not easy to achieve in general, but no concrete implications were shown. In fact, it incorrectly conjectured that perfect powers $N\geq2$ cannot be represented, which is clearly wrong (see the above comment), take for instance $N=9$ or $N=32$. It also realized that the particular case '$k=2$ and $N$ is not a perfect square' is equivalent to solving a generalized Pell equation, but it did not succeed in characterizing when it is actually solvable.

Gemini Deep Think ran for about 30 mins and it was able to represent (https://gemini.google.com/share/877b793ff0ab) all $2\leq N\leq100$ except for $4, 25, 49, 64, 81$. These are exactly the same exceptions mentioned in the previous post, where I reported what Stijn and I found experimentally! (Previously, I had simply performed straightforward brute-force search in Mathematica.) Then it claimed to have proven that these 5 numbers cannot be represented using $k=2$ factors.

I could only run ChatGPT for a very short period of time. It did not find any references that would say something actually useful for the main formulation of the problem, but it found a paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.01306) on the case $k=3$, and in its references there is a paper (https://msp.org/pjm/1971/37-2/p05.xhtml) on a very special case of the case $k=4$.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
One can establish the $k=2$ case of this conjecture as $p^2 = \frac{m(m+1)}{n(n+1)}$ implies not only the obvious factorization identity $m(m+1) = p^2 n(n+1)$ - implying that one of $m,m+1$ must be divisible by $p^2$ - but also the additional identity $(2pn+p+2m+1) (2pn+p-2m-1) = (p-1)(p+1)$ - implying that $1 \leq 2pn+p-2m-1 < p$. (The Pell equation here has a discriminant a perfect square, so we can factor in the rational integers rather than a quadratic extension.) Combining the two facts we see that $2pn+p-2m-1$ must be either $1$ or $p-1$. The latter case gives $m=0$ which is absurd, the former gives $2m+1 = (p^2 - 2)/2$ which is also absurd for parity reasons.

(Disclosure: I first asked Claude on this (https://claude.ai/share/a1d7d6b1-9a0f-4d8e-9aa8-11f717600af4), and it got the argument started, but became very handwavy at the end.)

EDIT 1: It seems these sorts of arguments should also produce representations for almost all non-prime squares, but I did not work out the details (it's mostly trying to locate divisors of the square that obey suitable parity constraints).

EDIT 2: Heuristically, the higher $k$ equations should be much less likely to provide solutions (one is now trying to find integer points on a positive genus curve instead of a zero genus curve, which one expects to be unlikely thanks to Siegel's theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%27s_theorem_on_integral_points). Actually making this intuition rigorous looks very difficult though. (The $k=3$ case involves an elliptic curve and might possibly be tractable though.)

I think the following works: assume $m(m+1) = p^2n(n+1)$ and write $m = pn + l$ with $l > 0$. We then get $$m(m+1) = (pn + l)(pn + l + 1) = p^2n^2 + (2l+1)pn + l(l+1) \equiv l(l+1) \equiv 0 \pmod{p},$$so that $l \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ or $l \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$. In particular $l \ge p-1$ from which we see that $m(m+1)$ is too large.

It's straightforward to extend this to $p^{2t}$ for any prime $p$ and $t\in\mathbb{N}$. Assume $m(m+1)=p^{2t}n(n+1)=p^tn(p^tn+p^t)$.
If $m\leq p^tn$ then $$m(m+1)\leq p^tn(p^tn+1)<p^tn(p^tn+p^t).$$ If $m\geq p^tn+p^t-1$ then $$m(m+1)\geq (p^tn+p^t-1)(p^tn+p^t)>p^tn(p^tn+p^t).$$ Clearly $p^tn<m<p^tn+p^t-1$, but then $m(m+1)$ is not divisible by $p^t$.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
As all non-square $n$ can be represented with $k=2$, the only $n$ where $k=2$ representability remains open is $n=t^2$ for composite $t$. The following was found using Claude Sonnet 4.6. I start from $m$ and $n$ instead of $m+1$ and $n+1$.

Consider $t^2n(n+1)=m(m+1)$. Then let $a=2n+1$ and $b=2m+1$. Substituting in we get $t^2 \frac{a^2-1}{4}=\frac{b^2-1}{4}$ and so $t^2(a^2-1)=b^2-1$. Therefore $(ta)^2-b^2=t^2-1$ and so $(ta-b)(ta+b)=t^2-1$. Set $u=ta-b$ and $v=ta+b$. Then we have a solution if and only if there exist integers $u\neq t-1$ and $v\neq t+1$ such that $uv=t^2-1$, and both $\frac{v-u}{2}$ and $\frac{v+u}{2t}$ are odd.

If $t\equiv 2\bmod 4$ then $m=\frac{t^2}{4}-1$ and $n=\frac{t-2}{4}$ suffice.

EDIT: Claude notes that $t$ can represented if and only if there exists $n$ such that $4n(n+1)t^2+1$ is a square.

Claude also makes the claim that when $r$ is odd, $t=r(r+2)$ is representable for $k=2$ if and only if $r\equiv 1\bmod 4$. The if direction is shown in the comment below by Quanyu Tang.

I don't know how useful this is, but here is an argument which shows that when $k = 2$ and $N = a^2$, $n$ has to be small (< $\tfrac{a}{8}$ except for the family of parametric solutions from the above post). In particular, there is only a finite number of solutions for fixed $a$, and there is an algorithm which is (quasi-)linear in $a$ for deciding wether $a^2$ is representable with $k=2$.
Let $a \geq 2$ and fix $n \geq \tfrac{a}{8}$. Assume that $m$ gives a solution to $a^2n(n+1) = m(m+1)$ . We can locate $m$ to within one unit using the following inequalities, true for all $x > 0$ :
$$1 + \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{x^2}{8} < \sqrt{1+x} < 1 + \dfrac{x}{2}$$
Setting $x= \tfrac{1}{n}$, we get $$n+ \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{8n} < \sqrt{n(n+1)} = n\sqrt{1 +\dfrac{1}{n}} < n + \dfrac{1}{2}$$
Hence
$$m < \sqrt{m(m+1)} < a\left(n + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$
and $$m+1 > \sqrt{m(m+1)} > a\left(n + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{8n}\right)$$
So $$an + \dfrac{a}{2} - 1 - \dfrac{a}{8n} < m < an + \dfrac{a}{2}$$
Now, if $a$ is even then $an + \tfrac{a}{2}$ is an integer. Since $\tfrac{a}{8n} \leq 1$ and the inequalities are strict, we get $m = an + \tfrac{a}{2} - 1$. Injecting this in the original equation gives $n = \tfrac{a - 2}{4}$ and $m = \tfrac{a^2}{4} - 1$. These are integers exactly when $a\equiv 2 \pmod{4}$. If $a$ is odd, we must have $m = an + \tfrac{a-1}{2}$ since $m$ is an integer, thus $m(m+1) = a^2n^2+a^2n+\tfrac{a^2-1}{4} > a^2n(n+1)$, so there is no such solution.
A similar methor should work anytime $N$ is a $k$-th power.

problem:
Let $Y(x)$ be the maximal $y$ such that there exists a choice of congruence classes $a_p$ for all primes $p\leq x$ such that every integer in $[1,y]$ is congruent to at least one of the $a_p\pmod{p}$.

Give good estimates for $Y(x)$. In particular, can one prove that $Y(x)=o(x^2)$ or even $Y(x)\ll x^{1+o(1)}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/687.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 December 2025.
Site remarks:
This function (associated with Jacobsthal) is closely related to the problem of gaps between primes (see [4]). The best known upper bound is due to Iwaniec \cite{Iw78},\[Y(x) \ll x^2.\]The best lower bound is due to Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard, and Tao \cite{FGKMT18},\[Y(x) \gg x\frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x},\]improving on a previous bound of Rankin \cite{Ra38}.

Maier and Pomerance have conjectured that $Y(x)\ll x(\log x)^{2+o(1)}$.

In \cite{Er80} he writes 'It is not clear who first formulated this problem - probably many of us did it independently. I offer the maximum of \$1000 dollars and $1/2$ my total savings for clearing up of this problem.'

In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s also asks about a weaker variant in which all except $o(y/\log y)$ of the integers in $[1,y]$ are congruent to at least one of the $a_p\pmod{p}$, and in particular asks if the answer is very different.

See also [688] and [689]. A more general Jacobsthal function is the focus of [970].
References:
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [FGKMT18] Ford, Kevin and Green, Ben and Konyagin, Sergei and Maynard, James and Tao, Terence, Long gaps between primes. J. Amer. Math. Soc. (2018), 65-105.
- [Iw78] Iwaniec, Henryk, On the problem of {J}acobsthal. Demonstratio Math. (1978), 225--231.
- [Ra38] Rankin, R. A., The Difference between Consecutive Prime Numbers. J. London Math. Soc. (1938), 242-247.

I have a proposed proof of Problem 689 for all sufficiently large \(n\). A short PDF note is here:

PDF note (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1muI0gfjHjuFbu4aZmZ6vyYSgqXJOc7ID/view?usp=sharing)

**Disclosure:** this write-up was prepared with AI assistance in finding literature and reviewing claims. I am posting it as a proposed proof and request for verification, not as a refereed result.

This is meant as an attempt to make precise the route suggested in the earlier comments: use linear equations in primes to control averaged prime-pattern counts, and use hypergraph matching/nibble technology to turn the resulting fractional cover into a genuine disjoint cover. The new ingredient in the note is the robust \(P>n/5\) cleanup setup and the finite-core fractional matching formulation.

The strategy is as follows.

Start with \(a_2\equiv 1\pmod 2\), leave \(3\) in the zero class, and switch a fixed finite set\[
S\subset\{7,11,13,\ldots\}
\]to nonzero residues. After these fixed switches, the main residual demand consists of even numbers\[
x=2^k u q,\qquad k\ge1,
\]where \(u\) is odd \(S\)-smooth and \(q\notin S\) is prime, subject to fixed congruence exclusions. Fixed-modulus PNT gives\[
|A_S(n)|=(1+o(1))\frac n{\log n},
\]with half of this mass at \(v_2(x)=1\) and half at \(v_2(x)\ge2\).

The cleanup primes are primes \(P>n/5\). Call \(P\) robust if\[
H_S(P)\ge1,\qquad H_S(2P)\ge2,\qquad H_S(4P)\ge2,
\]where \(H_S(x)\) counts the switched \(S\)-classes hitting \(x\). Switching a robust \(P\) creates no new unresolved debt: the only multiples \(P,2P,3P,4P\le n\) are covered by robustness plus parity and the unchanged \(0\pmod3\) class. By choosing \(S\) large enough, the robust residue density \(\delta_S\) can be made \(>0.94388\ldots\).

Choose\[
\delta_S^{-1}-3/5<\beta<\tfrac12(1-\tfrac35 e^{-2}),
\]and set \(\Delta=(\beta+3/5)\delta_S-1>0\) for the surplus margin used below. Build a 3-partite hypergraph with vertex classes\[
X=X_n\subset A_1(n),\qquad Y=Y_n\subset A_2(n),\qquad Z=\{P\in(n/5,\beta n]:P\text{ robust}\},
\]where \(X_n,Y_n\) are finite coefficient cores capturing fractions \(\alpha_X,\alpha_Y>G(\beta)+\eta\) of the \(A_1,A_2\) coefficient mass, and edges\[
(x,y,P)\quad\text{when}\quad |y-x|=2P.
\]A matching covering \((1-o(1))|Z|\) labels gives enough paired covers; the remaining residual targets, including the coefficient tails outside the finite cores and the \(o(n/\log n)\) exceptional residual tokens, are covered singly by unused robust primes. The strict surplus \(\Delta>0\) is exactly what leaves enough unused robust primes for the singleton cleanup once the cores are chosen so that the discarded coefficient-tail mass plus exceptional tokens is at most \(\Delta N/10\).

The matching is obtained by a finite-core fractional construction. In half-residue coordinates \(A\equiv aq\pmod W\), \(B\equiv bq'\pmod W\), the residual classes are a product set \(\mathcal C\), and for every unit label residue \(\pi\),\[
\#\{A\in\mathcal C:A\pm\pi\in\mathcal C\}=\prod_{s\in S}(s-2).
\]This gives an explicit continuum transport kernel with exact label load \(1\) and side load bounded by\[
G(\beta)=\int_{1/5}^{\beta}\frac{dt}{1-2t}<1.
\]Finite coefficient cores scale this by the captured core mass, giving side bounds \(G(\beta)/\alpha_X\) and \(G(\beta)/\alpha_Y\), both strictly less than \(1\) by the choice of cores. The aggregate transport then lifts to bounded typed kernels on the finitely many admissible typed polygons, with limiting label load \(1\) and bounded side loads.

The analytic input is the finite-complexity Green-Tao-Ziegler theorem for affine-linear forms in primes. In a detailed proof this can be formulated using an auxiliary growing \(W_{\mathrm{GTZ}}\)-trick while keeping the fixed modulus \(W=\prod_{s\in S}s\) as residue data; equivalently, one can work with fixed-modulus singular series and verify the corresponding local-factor disintegrations in the first and second moment systems. It supplies the first and second weighted moment estimates for the edge loads. Importantly, no pointwise Hardy-Littlewood / Bateman-Horn estimate for fixed \(P=bq'-aq\) is used; all estimates are averaged finite-complexity linear-form counts.

The deletion step uses the standard \(L^2\)-to-mass-loss argument: vertices with normalized side load above \(1\) have \(|L_X(x)-L_X^{\mathrm{lim}}(x)|\ge 2\gamma\), so the side \(L^2\) estimate forces \(|B_X|=o(|X_n|)\), and a Cauchy-Schwarz finish bounds the deleted mass by \(o(|Z_n|)\) on each side.

The final rounding input is Kahn's fractional Frankl-Rödl-Pippenger theorem (Random Structures and Algorithms 8 (1996), 149-157), applied with the single statistic \(C(e)=1\). The hypergraph has codegree at most \(2\): a pair \((x,y)\) determines \(P=|y-x|/2\), and a pair \((x,P)\) or \((y,P)\) has at most two extensions. Hence\[
a(t)=\max_{u\ne v}\sum_{e\supset\{u,v\}}t_e\le 2\max_e t_e=o(1).
\]**What I would especially appreciate help with.**

The two interfaces I would most like checked are:

(1) **Kahn 1996, Theorem 1.5.** I have not been able to access the printed paper directly. Public metadata/abstracts for Kahn's paper confirm the pair co-load parameter\[
\alpha(t)=\max\Big\{\sum\{t(A): x,y\in A\in\mathcal H\}:x,y\in V,\ x\ne y\Big\}
\]exactly as I use it. What I cannot verify from public sources is the precise form of the conclusion in the non-perfect case: specifically, that for a fractional matching \(t\) with total mass \(\sum_e t_e=(1-o(1))|Z_n|\), \(\max_e t_e=o(1)\), and \(\alpha(t)=o(1)\), Theorem 1.5 produces an integral matching \(M\) with \(|M|=(1-o(1))|Z_n|\). If anyone with access to the printed paper can confirm that this is the right shape of the conclusion, or flag a hypothesis I have missed, I would be very grateful.

(2) **The GTZ moment formulation.** I use one edge-total system and three second-moment systems on a fixed finite coefficient core. The note identifies the linear forms used in each system and verifies that no two are rationally affinely dependent after diagonal removal. The local-factor disintegration of the second-moment main terms, under either an auxiliary \(W_{\mathrm{GTZ}}\)-trick or fixed-modulus singular series, is asserted rather than written out in full. I would welcome any flag if this is not the right shape, or if the systems require additional admissibility checks I have missed.

I do not currently see a hidden pointwise prime-pair input, no Hardy-Littlewood, Bateman-Horn, Elliott-Halberstam, or Goldbach-type pointwise estimate is used in the argument as written though I would welcome being shown otherwise.

In [1139] (https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1139) I've added a missing argument that would probably also solve this problem. This is a shortened version on the core from my discussions with GPT-5.2:

If one could carry out the 2-fold covering construction in its “strong form” --- namely, for each sufficiently large $n$ choose residue classes $a_p \pmod p$ for \emph{every} prime $2\le p\le n$ so that each $j\in[1,n]$ lies in at least two of these classes --- then taking $N$ by CRT with $N\equiv -a_p\pmod p$ for all $p\le n$ would force every $N+j$ ($1\le j\le n$) to be divisible by at least two distinct primes $\le n$. Since the CRT modulus $\prod_{p\le n}p$ is astronomically large, we have $N\gg n^2$, so $N+j$ cannot equal a product of just those two primes; it must have an additional factor, hence $\Omega(N+j)\ge 3$ for all $j\le n$. In other words, this 2-fold congruence cover would directly produce length-$n$ intervals with no primes or semiprimes, giving a very strong form of the “$P_2$-free gaps” phenomenon.

Conversely, the strategy we discussed for large gaps between consecutive $\Omega\le2$ numbers is essentially an attempt to build such a 2-fold cover, but it allows two relaxations: (i) it may use only a carefully chosen subset of primes up to $n$ (to keep $\log N=\sum\log p$ small enough to make $n/\log N$ large), and (ii) it may leave a tiny exceptional set of “stragglers” handled separately. If one succeeds even with these relaxations, one gets $\limsup (u_{k+1}-u_k)/\log k=\infty$. If one succeeds in the stronger “use all primes $p\le n$ and cover everything twice” form, then it also answers your finite question outright (and in fact implies a stronger interval construction than what is needed for the $\limsup$).

Here are a few more details on the numerology that suggests that a construction is possible. Let $z$ be a sufficiently large constant, and let $A$ be a parameter growing slowly with $z$, e.g., $A = \exp( (\log\log\log z)^2 )$ should work. Assume $n$ extremely large depending on $z$.

We hold the primes $n/2 < p \leq n$ in reserve to clean up any stragglers; if we can sieve $\{1,\dots,n\}$ down to less than $n / 4 \log n$ such stragglers then we win. Accordingly, any set of cardinality $o(n/\log n)$ we view as negligible.

We first sieve out $0 \pmod{p}$ for all $p \leq n/z$. Up to negligible sets, this leads the primes $n/z < p_1 \leq n$ (which are completely untouched), as well as semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ where $p_1 < z$ and $n/z <p_2 \leq n/p_1$ and $p_1 < z$ (which were touched once). (There are also a few elements of the form $p_1^j p_2$ but these are unlikely to cause trouble). There are about $n/\log n$ primes in the first category and $n \log\log z / \log n$ in the second category.

To eliminate most of the primes in the first category, as well as semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ in the second category with $p_1 > z^{1/A}$ (of which there are about $n \log A / \log n$), we use the primes $p \geq n/z^{1/A}$. A congruence class mod such a prime hits about $n/p$ elements in $\{1,\dots,n\}$, of which about $n/(p \log (n/p))$ are usable for this purpose (one has to sieve out multiples of any primes less than $n/p$). We have $\sum_{n/z^{1/A} \leq p \leq z} n/(p \log (n/p)) \sim n \log\log(z^{1/A}) / \log n$ which is somewhat larger than the number $n \log A/\log n$ of targets, so a random sieve here should work well using the linear equations in primes technology (one has to design the random construction so that all primes and semiprimes have a decent chance of being hit, but this should be standard albeit tedious calculations).

To touch the semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ with $p_1 \leq z^{1/A}$ we use the primes $n/z \leq p \leq n/z^{10/A}$. A congruence associated to such a prime $p$ can touch about $n/(p p_1 \log(n/p))$ semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ attached to $p_1$; there are about $n / p_1 \log n$ such primes, and the sum of the $n/(p p_1 \log(n/p))$ is about $n \log A / p_1 \log n$, so we (barely) win here (random constructions should then cut down the number of survivors by a factor of $A$ or so, which brings us to within range of being cleaned up by the reserve primes). Again one needs linear equations in primes technology to show that most targets get a reasonable chance of being touched at least once.

I *think* something similar can work for larger $r$ than $r=2$, although one has to split into more cases than the two outlined above.

If anyone is interested in developing these ideas into a full proof, I'd be happy to talk further.

This is a really minor remark in the direction of formalizing the obstruction which Terry points out.

We first sieve all the primes $\le n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$; this leaves $\gg n(\log\log n)^{r-1}/\log n$ survivors. We now consider the efficiency of primes between $n/\exp((\log n)^{o(1)})$ and $n$. forum_comments.text:
Yes, that was basically the back of the envelope calculations I was using. In some ways the problem here has a simpler numerology than the long gaps one, and one can see the potential for a win here a bit more easily as follows. I tend to visualize these covering congruence problems as that of knocking down a progression of toy ducks at a carnival shooting gallery: each prime $p \leq n$ represents a "spraying bullet" in one's gun that can hit all the ducks that lie in one congruence class mod $p$. In this particular "game", each duck requires two "hits" to get knocked down, and the objective is to shoot in such a way that all ducks get knocked down. (I apologize for the violent nature of this metaphor; if someone can propose a more neutral one, I'll be happy to switch over to it.)

Suppose one "shoots" at the congruence classes $0 \pmod{p}$ for all $p \leq n/2$. Then almost all the ducks are already hit twice by these congruences; the only remaining ducks (that received only zero or one hits) are primes, or powers of primes - so about $n / \log n$ ducks in all. On the other hand, we have about $n/2\log n$ congruences left in reserve (coming from primes $n/2 < p \leq n$) to position judiciously. Each congruence can be used to hit any specific duck once, so this can knock out about $n/4\log n$ of the remaining $n/\log n$ ducks: not enough to win, but tantalizingly close. If, as you say, one could use each of the large primes $p$ to hit many ducks simultaneously, we would have a good chance of actually winning.

Unfortunately, each prime $p > n/2$ can only hit at most two ducks in $\{1,\dots,n\}$, and in fact probably only one in practice since almost all of the remaining ducks are odd. So this doesn't directly work, which is why I suggested the modified strategy in which one shoots out $0 \pmod{p}$ for $p \leq n/z$, leaving about $n \log\log z / \log n$ ducks remaining, but now one has as remaining ammunition some primes as small as $n/z$, each of which could potentially hit up to $z$ targets at once. If one could indeed hit the maximum number $n/p$ of ducks with each such shot then we would be in very good shape as indicated above since $n \log z / \log n$ can be made significantly larger than $n \log\log z/\log n$. Unfortunately one cannot quite do this well because many of the ducks are not divisible by small primes, in particular a prime $p \sim n/z$ can only hit about $O(z/\log z)$ $z$-rough targets by standard sieve theory. If one went with this bound then the total number of hits one can hope to make is $\sum_{n/z \leq p \leq z} \frac{n}{p \log(n/p)} \sim n \log\log z /\log n$ so one is now in a similar situation to before (off by a factor of 2 rather than 4, but still not enough). But on the other hand, only $n/\log n$ or so of the $n \log\log z/\log n$ remaining ducks are actually $z$-rough. I did some back of the envelope estimates of the number of "ducks" at different levels of roughness, and what each remaining "bullet" can hope to "hit" in each category, and I think there is actually enough "ammunition" to hit every duck twice.

In the modern long gaps literature, there are three basic tools to try to hit a lot of primes with progressions as efficiently as possible: the Maynard sieve; the linear equations in primes theory of Green, Ziegler, and myself; and the hypergraph covering lemmas of Pippenger-Spencer (and later authors). Here I think the Maynard sieve will not be sufficient as it only picks up about $\log z$ primes in a length $z$ progression. This leaves the linear equations in primes theory, which as you know has significantly worse quantitative dependence on $z$ (even with your recent advances), but for this problem I think we can take $z$ to be a large absolute constant and $n$ extremely large (if we only care about the asymptotic version of the problem) and so the error terms in the linear equations in primes results should not be too important. (As a first approximation we can try to establish the result conditionally on the prime tuples conjecture; the linear equations in primes theory roughly speaking asserts that this conjecture holds for almost all shift parameters, which should be sufficient.) The hypergraph covering tools (using the "Rodl nibble") offer some efficiencies in making sure that different "bullets" shoot mostly disjoint sets, but there is enough room in the numerology that I think a simpler probabilistic construction will probably suffice, but one can certainly keep this tool in one's pocket in case the analysis gets too delicate.

Anyway, would be happy to discuss this further on this forum or elsewhere, in case there is interest in carrying this argument to the finish line. (In principle one might be able to bash this out with heavy AI assistance, but I think I'd actually prefer a human collaboration (perhaps in a Polymath style) for this one.)

p.s. I am not so surprised that this problem of Erdos is related to the long gaps problem (#4), given how #4 was already closely tied to the sister problem #687 to this one.

This is a really minor comment explaining why random sieving seems not to help. The one very minor advantage potentially of using the initial primes as a random sieving step is that there seem to be less issues of $z$-smoothness to think about. (I will also ignore the use of a $W$ trick; it will be required for $W\ll z$ when working through the problem.)

Fix $z \le \log n$ for now and consider setting for all primes between $[z,n/z]$ the residue class to be $0 \pmod p$. There are two categories of number left.
(1) Numbers which have not been touched at all. These are only the $z$ smooth numbers and primes larger than $n/z$; the second term is dominant. This gives $n/\log n$ integers which will be handled at the end.
(2) There are numbers which are only touched exactly once. These integers are precisely of the form $p q$ where $p$ is a prime in $[z,n/z]$ and $q$ is $z$-smooth. The dominant term (from my computations) is when $p$ is near maximal so there are $\approx n\log(z)/\log(n)$ integers remaining. (In fact if one runs through the numerics one can really only pay attention to $pq$ with $p$ prime and $q\le z^{A}$ with $A\to \infty$ arbitrarily slowly at the end.)

We now run the random sieve using primes less than $z$. We will try and be "efficient" in the end with primes of the form between $n/z$ and $n/2$; the primes between $n/2$ and $n$ will be used to handle stragglers.

This leaves us with $O(n/(\log n \log z))$ integers in the first category and therefore reserving a vanishing small portion of primes in the final category we can handle these integers. For the final category, we have a $\lesssim n/\log n$ integers which survive this sieving so we are back at the "constant" factor off regime in the above post.

We now consider using primes between $n/z$ and $n/(2z)$; due to the random sieving we only need to control the integers coming from (2). Initially for each such prime a given shift would have given us $z$ chances to hit the integers; however the random sieving gives us a "random penalty" factor of $\log z$ and so we really need to detect more than $\log z$ primes among the $z$ so the small--gaps technology is unsuitable (this is exactly what Terry says above).

For the linear equations in primes technology, it is basically sufficient to try and use primes between $n/z$ and $n/(2z)$ to handle the $pq$ products in (2) with $p\in [n/z^{A},n/z]$. This amounts to solving $p_1 = (\epsilon z) q + t$, $p_2 = (\epsilon z + 1) q + t$,... $p_{\ell} = zq + t$ with $t$ an integer, $q$ is a prime between $n/z$ and $n/(2z)$ and $p_i$ has a prime factor between $n/z^A$ and $n/z$. The set $p_i$ formed by taking products can be proven to be Gowers uniform (up to major arc issues which would be corrected by a $W$-trick) and so the result should follow. (It is also rather difficult to make this quantitative; this requires uniformity in the $k$-aspect of various $U^{k}$-Gowers norms which have not been worked out in any detail.)

This doesn't change the numerology too much though, one still has about $O(n \log z / \log n)$ remaining targets before the random sieving step, the bulk of which come from those numbers with a prime factor in $[n/z^A, n/z^{1/A}]$.

But it seems that we just barely lose with this strategy even with the most optimistic assumptions. Each $p \in [n/2z, n/z]$ can at best touch $O(z)$ of these targets, or $O(z/\log z)$ after the random sieving step (from the upper bound sieve one cannot get around this $\log z$ loss except possibly for a constant factor). Similarly for larger $p$. Summing over $p$ we can only touch $O(n \log z / \log n )$ targets before random sieving, or $O(n / \log n)$ ones after random sieving, so we lose by a constant factor (which grows in $A$, so probably is greater by one).

[EDIT: actually the additional terms in (1) that involve a prime factor between $n/z$ and $n/z^{1/A}$ could be more problematic, as they need to be touched twice in order to win, and so the random sieve I think leaves behind $n \log\log z / \log n$ remaining targets rather than $n / \log n$ if I computed correctly.]

My calculations seem to suggest that the non-random sieve (in which one touches $0 \pmod{p}$ for all $p \leq n/z$) still has a chance; somehow the fact that the majority of the remaining targets actually lie in one of the sieved out classes $0 \pmod{p}$, $p \leq z$ seems to work slightly on one's favor, as it allows for more of the congruence class mod $p$ for $n/z < p < n/2$ to be usable for touching slightly more targets (according to my calculations, a congruence class mod $p \sim n/z$ could potentially touch $z \log\log z / \log z$ remaining targets, which is slightly above the break-even point of $z / \log z$).

As long as we take $z$ to be a large constant, I don't think the dependence on $k$ in the $U^k$ inverse theory etc. will be of relevance for $n$ large enough. The $W$-trick obstructions to uniformity are annoying, though: it seems that the irregularities at small primes are a crucial part of this story and need to be analyzed carefully.

computation:
- Ran stochastic optimization maximizing the minimum coverage multiplicity over \([1,n]\), with one class per prime \(p\le n\).
- Tested \(n\) from 120 to 1000.

- In all tested runs, best minimum multiplicity remained 0 (i.e., some integers uncovered).
- No instance achieved full single cover, let alone double cover, within these search budgets.
- This is negative finite evidence for naive random/greedy constructions, not a proof of impossibility.

Significant progress is known, and broad non-unimodality is now established for many \(k\). Full all-\(k\) classification remains outside this computation.

problem:
Let $d_k(p)$ be the density of those integers whose $k$th smallest prime factor is $p$ (i.e. if $p_1<p_2<\cdots$ are the primes dividing $n$ then $p_k=p$).

For fixed $k\geq 1$ is $d_k(p)$ unimodular in $p$? That is, it first increases in $p$ until its maximum then decreases.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/690.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s believes that this is not possible, but could not disprove it. He could show that $p_k$ is about $e^{e^k}$ for almost all $n$, but the maximal value of $d_k(p)$ is assumed for much smaller values of $p$, at\[p=e^{(1+o(1))k}.\]A similar question can be asked if we consider the density of integers whose $k$th smallest divisor is $d$. Erd\H{o}s could show that this function is not unimodular.

Cambie \cite{Ca25} has shown that $d_k(p)$ is unimodular for $1\leq k\leq 3$ and is not unimodular for $4\leq k\leq 20$.
References:
- [Ca25] S. Cambie, Resolution of Erd\H{o}s' problems about unimodularity. arXiv:2501.10333 (2025).

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
The question could be interpreted in multiple ways.
If one wants to disprove it for every $k$, then one needs to be able to quantify the irregularities of prime gaps in a sense.
(if primes would form an arithmetic progression, it would be true for all $k$)

Others agree/ believe the question may not be solved for all $k$?

Also, the numerical evidence should indicate that unimodularity is indeed just too much to ask (as Erdos thus believed himself).
So if the challenging part does not lead to (quantified) fundamental underlying statements in number theory, one might consider the problem as solved.
Wondering about the opinions of others.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text: Stijn, do you know of a precise statement about the irregularities of prime gaps that would be strong enough to disprove unimodularity for all large $k$ (or even infinitely many $k$)? I assume not, if I'm interpreting your comment correctly. I suppose this would be an interesting 'meta-problem', to formulate such a reasonable statement - even if it is completely hopeless to prove, at least to tie this problem into the 'mainstream' of prime number theory.

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
No. The formulas are just very irregular and between e^k and e^{e^k} the various factors sometimes can go up and down, but it really depends on the whole formula.
(which can be computed recursive, or equivalently written down by large nasty sums)

If one inserts an aritmetic sequence for the primes p_i, unimodularity would be true.
So it seems to be rather messy version of proving that the primes are not too close to forming an aritmetic sequence.

There are way more natural and elegant conjectures and problems on the prime distribution than this particular one.
Personally, I think Erdos would be happy to know a counterexample and just noting it was not always unimodular, and continue with other problems.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text: Yes, I think you're right. Unless anyone wants to jump in and defend the wider version of this problem, I'll mark it as solved by your small $k$ counterexamples.

problem: Given $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ let $M_A=\{ n \geq 1 : a\mid n\textrm{ for some }a\in A\}$ be the set of multiples of $A$. Find a necessary and sufficient condition on $A$ for $M_A$ to have density $1$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/691.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A sequence $A$ for which $M_A$ has density $1$ is called a Behrend sequence.

If $A$ is a set of prime numbers (or, more generally, a set of pairwise coprime integers without $1$) then a necessary and sufficient condition is that $\sum_{p\in A}\frac{1}{p}=\infty$.

The general situation is more complicated. For example suppose $A$ is the union of $(n_k,(1+\eta_k)n_k)\cap \mathbb{Z}$ where $1\leq n_1<n_2<\cdots$ is a lacunary sequence. (This construction is sometimes called a block sequence.) If $\sum \eta_k<\infty$ then the density of $M_A$ exists and is $<1$. If $\eta_k=1/k$, so $\sum \eta_k=\infty$, then the density exists and is $<1$.

Erd\H{o}s writes it 'seems certain' that there is some threshold $\alpha\in (0,1)$ such that, if $\eta_k=k^{-\beta}$, then the density of $M_A$ is $1$ if $\beta <\alpha$ and the density is $<1$ if $\beta >\alpha$.

Tenenbaum notes in \cite{Te96} that this is certainly not true as written since if the $n_j$ grow sufficiently quickly then this sequence is never Behrend, for any choice of $\eta_k$. He then writes 'we understand from subsequent discussions with Erd\H{o}s that he had actually in mind a two-sided condition on' $n_{j+1}/n_j$.

Tenenbaum \cite{Te96} proves this conjecture: if there are constants $1<C_1<C_2$ such that $C_1<n_{i+1}/n_i<C_2$ for all $i$ and $\eta_k=k^{-\beta}$ then $A$ is Behrend if $\beta<\log 2$ and not Behrend if $\beta>\log 2$.
References:
- [Te96] Tenenbaum, G., On block {B}ehrend sequences. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. (1996), 355--367.

I would like to share a short note and a Lean 4 formalization related to Erdős problem #691, both produced using GPT-5.4 Pro (which carried out the natural-language proof and its Lean formalization).
The main statement proved is that for $A \subseteq \mathbb N$, the set $M_A$ has natural density $1$ if and only if $\lim_{N\to\infty} d(M_{A\cap[1,N]}) = 1$, equivalently if and only if $\sup_{F\subseteq A,\ F\text{ finite}} d(M_F)=1$.

It seems quite plausible to me that the mathematics surrounding Problem #691 is already largely present in the existing literature on sets of multiples and Behrend sequences. At the same time, the relevant references appear to be spread across several sources, and I do not yet feel that I have completed a sufficiently comprehensive literature review to make a definitive priority claim. I would therefore especially welcome corrections concerning references, priority, and the exact relation of these notes to earlier work.

problem: Let $f_{\max}(n)$ be the largest $m$ such that $\phi(m)=n$, and $f_{\min}(n)$ be the smallest such $m$, where $\phi$ is Euler's totient function. Investigate\[\max_{n\leq x}\frac{f_{\max}(n)}{f_{\min}(n)}\](where the maximum is restricted to those $n$ of the form $n=\phi(m)$ for some $m$.)
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/694.
- Page status: SOLVED (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 02 May 2026.
Site remarks:
Carmichael has asked whether there is an integer $n$ for which $\phi(m)=n$ has exactly one solution, that is, $\frac{f_{\max}(n)}{f_{\min}(n)}=1$. Erd\H{o}s has proved that if such an $n$ exists then there must be infinitely many such $n$.

GPT-5.5 Pro (prompted by Price) has proved (https://www.overleaf.com/read/fgmhvywvdjkt#54ca5d) (see also the comments for a summary) that\[\max_{n\leq x}\frac{f_{\max}(n)}{f_{\min}(n)}=(e^\gamma+o(1))\log\log x.\]See also [51].

The lower bound relies on Linnik's theorem to produce a prime l ≡ 1 (mod A_y), with y = (log x)/(4L) chosen to ensure n_y ≤ x. The asymptotic is formally correct for any admissible L, but the construction is entirely non-explicit: without fixed values of the Linnik constants C and L, one cannot exhibit a concrete pair (a_y, b_y) achieving the separation, nor estimate at what scale of x the lower bound becomes meaningful.
With the best known exponent L = 5 (Xylouris, 2011), the choice y ≈ (log x)/20 is very small, and the bound n_y ≪ A_y^9 grows rapidly, so the condition n_y ≤ x only holds for x far beyond computational range. It would be worth noting explicitly that the result is purely asymptotic in nature, and that a GRH-conditional version — which gives L = 2 and a much more tractable construction — would substantially improve the effective content of the lower bound.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks! This is a neat elementary proof. (The upper bound in particular is an immediate consequence of classical estimates; presumably it was known to Erdős - he asked this question in [Er79e] in a very 'soft' way, just suggesting it might 'perhaps be interesting' to investigate this quantity, and did not record what he did or did not know about it; I assume he was not aware of a matching lower bound as given here though!)

It is a classical fact that\[\max_{m\leq x}\frac{m}{\phi(m)}=(e^\gamma+o(1))\log\log x.\]Therefore if $M=f_\max(n)$ and $m=f_\min (n)$ then, since trivially $M\ll n^2$, say (as $\phi(m)\gg m^{1/2}$ for all $m$),\[\frac{f_{\max}(n)}{f_{\min}(n)}=\frac{M}{\phi(M)}\cdot \frac{\phi(m)}{m}\leq \frac{M}{\phi(M)}\leq (e^\gamma+o(1))\log\log n.\]On the other hand, if $A=\prod_{p\leq y}(p-1)$ and $\ell=Ak+1$ is prime and\[a=\ell \prod_{\substack{q\mid k\\ q>y}}q\quad\textrm{and}\quad b= k\cdot \prod_{p\leq y}p\cdot \prod_{\substack{q\mid k\\ q>y}}q.\]An elementary calculation verifies that $\phi(a)=\phi(b)$, and\[\frac{b}{a}=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell}\prod_{p\leq y}\frac{p}{p-1}=(e^\gamma+o(1))\log y,\]and\[\phi(a)\leq k^2A\leq A^{O(1)}\leq e^{O(y)},\]if we use Linnik's theorem to choose $\ell \leq A^{O(1)}$, so we can choose $y=c\log x$ for some suitable constant $c>0$ to get\[\max_{n\leq x}\frac{f_\max(n)}{f_\min(n)}\geq (e^\gamma+o(1))\log\log x.\]

Hereby experimental proof for the maximum (that also heuristically resolves the question asymptotically)

Let $x= p_r\#=p_1 p_2 \ldots p_r.$
Take the first prime $q \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(x)}.$
Experiments showed $q-1=b \phi(x)$, where $b \le p_r$ (for $r \le 200$). If someone can prove this is always the case, the question is essentially resolved. (thinking about the state of the art related to Linnik's theorem, this may be very hard)

In the above situation, $\phi(bx)=b \phi(x)=\phi(q).$
Now $\frac{q}{bx} \sim \frac{ \phi(x)}{x}.$
When $bx< p_{r+1}\#$, this is the best one can hope for.

For certain $p_{r+1}\#$<$x$<$ p_{r+2}\#,$ the max may still be expected to be roughly $\frac{p_r\#}{ \phi(p_r\#)}.$

problem: Let $p_1<p_2<\cdots$ be a sequence of primes such that $p_{i+1}\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$. Is it true that\[\lim_k p_k^{1/k}=\infty?\]Does there exist such a sequence with\[p_k \leq \exp(k(\log k)^{1+o(1)})?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/695.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 17 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Such a sequence is sometimes called a prime chain.

If we take the obvious 'greedy' chain with $2=p_1$ and $p_{i+1}$ is the smallest prime $\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$ then Linnik's theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linnik%27s_theorem) implies that this sequence grows like\[p_k \leq e^{e^{O(k)}}.\]It is conjectured that, for any prime $p$, there is a prime $p'\leq p(\log p)^{O(1)}$ which is congruent to $1\pmod{p}$, which would imply this sequence grows like\[p_k\leq \exp(k(\log k)^{1+o(1)}).\]An extensive study of the growth of finite prime chains was carried out by Ford, Konyagin, and Luca \cite{FKL10}.

See also [696].
References:
- [FKL10] Ford, Kevin and Konyagin, Sergei V. and Luca, Florian, Prime chains and {P}ratt trees. Geom. Funct. Anal. (2010), 1231--1258.

My guess for the first question is yes.
Since the $q$'s are prime, there are no excluded prime divisors of $kq+1$ and thus the various $k$ can be expected to grow on average at least like $\log(q)$.

The greedy sequence, [oeis/A061092] (https://oeis.org/A061092), is the natural candidate for the second question.

computation:
- Implemented standalone greedy-chain search for many starting primes.
- For each step, computed the smallest prime of the form \(1 \bmod p_i\), then tracked growth profiles \(p_k^{1/k}\).
- This does not prove asymptotics, but provides finite-scale growth envelopes across many starts.

- Deep run parameters: 46 starting primes (all primes \(\le 200\)), chain depth up to \(k=14\), search cap 800000 candidates per edge.
- Largest observed \(p_{14}^{1/14}\) in this run was about \(14.94\) (chain starting at 37).
- Finite behavior supports rapid growth in greedy constructions, but does not separate the two asymptotic questions.
attempt: The approach here was to grow many prime chains greedily, always taking the least prime congruent to \(1\bmod p_i\), and then monitor the growth surrogate \(p_k^{1/k}\). This gives finite-scale evidence that such chains can grow rapidly, but it does not decide either asymptotic direction: whether every such chain must satisfy \(p_k^{1/k}\to\infty\), or whether one can still realize a chain with \(p_k\le \exp(k(\log k)^{1+o(1)})\).

forum_comments.text:
I claim that for all but $o(x)$ integers $n \leq x$,
$$h(n) = \left(\tfrac{1}{2} + o(1)\right) \log_* n, \qquad H(n) = (1 + o(1)) \log_* n, \qquad \frac{H(n)}{h(n)} = 2 + o(1).$$
In particular, the proposed divergence $H(n)/h(n) \to \infty$ for almost all $n$ is false on a density-one set; the ratio is bounded above by $2 + o(1)$ a.a. Erdős's belief that $h(n)$ has normal order $\log_* n$ is at least partially correct: it has order $\Theta(\log_* n)$, with the precise constant $1/2$.

Writeup, which I believe fully resolves this problem, is at this Overleaf link (https://www.overleaf.com/read/cmypbrpwbwrv#3e136c).

Verification with GPT-5.5 Heavy Thinking on the post-edit manuscript: conversation 1 (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ee9059-7938-83ea-a200-9028b49d7723), conversation 2 (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ee9067-317c-83ea-8e7a-43d4762e076c), conversation 3 (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ee906f-c7cc-83ea-84e4-14ea1f6f7666).

Earlier (pre- final edit) reviews with GPT-5.5-Pro yielded only aesthetic/exposition comments (no 'fatal' gaps): conversation A (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ee9096-dba0-83ea-9ee7-643efca23e0f), conversation B (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ee90c3-8708-83ea-af2b-5b3506f4d9cd), conversation C (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ee90ee-023c-83ea-ab68-0c89352a0a91). (A post- final edit Pro pass was attempted but I hit the GPT-5.5-Pro rate limit before it could run; the Heavy Thinking checks above cover the post-final edit state.)

This work was assembled in collaboration with the GPT-5.5-Pro reasoning model (Extended), which produced the original four-turn proof sketch and the iterative patches refining the writeup, assembled together with Claude Code.

In terms of methods, both the lower bounds and the upper bounds stem from a common scaffold: a tower-rank descent over the iterated tower $T_m = \exp T_{m-1}$, controlled by what counts as a "bad" short step.

For upper bounds, a chain step is *bad* if it is too short. For $H$, a divisor pair $(d, e)$ with $e \equiv 1 \pmod d$ is bad when $e < \exp \sqrt{d}$; since $(d, e) = 1$ the count of $n \leq x$ with $d, e \mid n$ is $\leq x/(de)$, and the tail $\sum_{d \geq Y} d^{-3/2} = O(Y^{-1/2})$ (where $Y = Y(x)$ is a slowly-growing small-divisor cutoff, e.g. $Y = \lfloor (\log_* x)^{1/2} \rfloor$) shows almost all $n$ admit no large bad step, forcing one full tower level per step. For $h$, primes give Brun-Titchmarsh slack and the bad threshold pushes up to $Q(p) = \exp \exp(p/(\log p)^2)$, with convergent tail $\sum_p \big( \log p/p^2 + 1/(p (\log p)^2) \big) < \infty$. The stronger threshold forces two tower levels per step, which is the source of the $1/2$ constant.

Both lower bounds stem from a greedy construction in the independent-prime model (each prime selected with probability $1/p$, independently) and transfer to integers by the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) once the primorial cutoff is $o(x)$. For $h$, each stage finds a successor prime $q \equiv 1 \pmod{p_j}$ in the window $\exp \exp y_j < q \leq \exp \exp((B/2) y_j)$ via a Siegel-Walfisz reciprocal-mass lemma in the safe modulus range $p_j \leq y_j \ll \log(\exp \exp y_j)$. (Here $y_j = T_{m_0+2(j-1)}/B$ is the stage-$j$ tower scale, and $B = (\log_* x)^2$ is a growth-rate constant.)

For $H$, the new - I believe new - technical input from GPT-5.5-Pro is a "subset-product successor lemma": for $g_1, \ldots, g_K$ independent uniform on a finite abelian group $G$ of order $N$, $\Pr(\text{no nonempty subproduct equals } 1_G) \leq N/(2^K - 1)$ (proof roughly goes like: pairwise independence of distinct subset-products yields $\mathrm{Var}\, Z \leq \mathbb{E} Z$, then Chebyshev). The number-theoretic application splits the prime window into Mertens-sized blocks $(\alpha_k, \alpha_{k+1}]$ with $\log \log \alpha_k = \log y + k - 1$ (here $y$ is the Siegel-Walfisz scale parameter; the modulus $d$ satisfies $d \leq y$, and primes live in $(\exp y, \exp(y^{A-1})]$ with $A = 20$), conditions on the $\sim \gamma \log y$ blocks each containing exactly one selected prime ($\gamma = 15$ in the write-up), and reduces those primes mod $d$. Siegel-Walfisz makes the residues $O(y^{-1/2})$-close to uniform on $(\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})^\times$, then the abstract lemma produces a squarefree composite successor $e \equiv 1 \pmod d$.

forum_comments.text:
I have written up a candidate proof note for this problem here:

Overleaf draft: candidate proof for Erdős Problem #696 (https://www.overleaf.com/7678785988ckmvjwxbdryp#17cc98)

Related verification discussions:

General proof discussion (https://chatgpt.com/share/69ec863e-a708-83e8-b235-71323f655705)
Additional verification of Lemma 2.3 (https://chatgpt.com/share/69eca3fc-6198-83e8-aaec-82fb0fbd43c6)

The proposed theorem is that, for all but o(x) integers n <= x,\[
\frac{1}{20}\log_* x \le h(n)\le H(n)\le 4\log_* x.
\]Consequently, the number of integers n <= x for which H(n)/h(n) > 80 is o(x), so H(n)/h(n) would not tend to infinity on a density-one set.

The proof is a log-star barrier argument. The upper bound for H(n) uses a bad-pair union bound: if d < e and e ≡ 1 (mod d), then (d,e)=1, so asking for both d | n and e | n costs 1/(de). Excluding short steps forces large divisor-chain steps to grow at least like exp(sqrt d), which gives H(n) << log_* x.

The lower bound for h(n) constructs a prime chain through intervals\[
Y_1=\exp(\exp(\sqrt{\log_* x})),\qquad
Y_{j+1}=\exp(\exp(Y_j^2)).
\]The transfer from this finite prime-divisibility model back to integers n <= x is done modulo the primorial M over the primes up to Y_k. Each event depending only on which primes up to Y_k divide n is a union of residue classes modulo M, and the Chinese remainder theorem identifies the uniform residue model exactly with independent divisibility events, with probability 1/p for each prime p. The tower estimate gives M=o(x), so this product-model calculation transfers to natural density up to o(1).

The main analytic input is Lemma 2.3, a reciprocal prime mass lemma derived from the pi-form of Siegel--Walfisz plus partial summation. In particular, uniformly for primes p <= y,\[
\sum_{\substack{Z<q\le X\\ q\ {\rm prime}\\ q\equiv 1\pmod p}}\frac{1}{q}\gg y,
\]where Z=exp(exp y) and X=exp(exp(y^2)).

I would especially appreciate checks of:
the pi-form Siegel--Walfisz input;
the partial summation error term, uniformly in p <= y;
the CRT/product-model transfer;
the bad-pair union bound for the upper bound.

This is meant as a candidate proof for independent checking, not as a settled announcement.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
For the claim that $h(n)$ goes to infinity for almost all $n$, one can use the fact (also mentioned in that very same 1979 paper) that almost all $n$ are divisible by a prime $p \in P$ for some set of primes $P$ if, and only if, the sum $\sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p}$ diverges. More precisely, let $c \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\epsilon > 0$ both be arbitrary but fixed. Let $C$ be such that for every set of primes $P$ with $\sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} > C$ we have that the density of $n$ with a prime divisor $p \in P$ is larger than $1 - \frac{\epsilon}{c}$.

In step $1$ we let $P_1$ be any set of primes with $\sum_{p \in P_1} \frac{1}{p} > C$. Now, for $1 \le k < c$, in step $k+1$ we choose, for every prime $p \in P_k$, a set of primes $Q_p$ (disjoint from all primes chosen so far) with $q \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for all $q \in Q_p$, and $\sum_{q \in Q_p} \frac{1}{q} > C$. That this is possible follows from the prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions. We then set $P_{k+1} = \bigcup_{p \in P_k} Q_p$.

The density of $n$ with a prime divisor $p_1 \in P_1$ is larger than $1 - \frac{\epsilon}{c}$. And for every $1 \le k < c$, the density of $n$ with a prime divisor $p_{k+1} \in Q_{p_k}$ is also larger than $1 - \frac{\epsilon}{c}$. By the union bound the density of $n$ with primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_c$ dividing $n$ with $p_{k+1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p_k}$ is larger than $1 - \epsilon$. Since both $\epsilon > 0$ and $c \in \mathbb{N}$ were arbitrary, this proves the claim that $h(n)$ goes to infinity for almost all $n$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

computation:
- Computed exact \(h(n)\) and \(H(n)\) for all \(2\le n\le N\) by explicit DAG longest-path calculations:
 - prime-divisor DAG for \(h(n)\),
 - full-divisor DAG for \(H(n)\).
- Used this to measure empirical mean growth and frequency of strict separation \(H(n)>h(n)\).

- Deep run to \(N=120000\).
- At \(n\le 120000\):

problem: Is it true that for every $1\leq i<j\leq n/2$ there exists some prime $p\geq i$ such that\[p\mid \textrm{gcd}\left(\binom{n}{i}, \binom{n}{j}\right)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/699.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 September 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres. A theorem of Sylvester and Schur says that for any $1\leq i\leq n/2$ there exists some prime $p>i$ which divides $\binom{n}{i}$.

Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres further conjectured that $p\geq i$ can be improved to $p>i$ except in a few special cases. In particular this fails when $i=2$ and $n$ being some particular powers of $2$. They also found some counterexamples when $i=3$, but only one counterexample when $i\geq 4$:\[\textrm{gcd}\left(\binom{28}{5},\binom{28}{14}\right)=2^3\cdot 3^3\cdot 5.\]This is mentioned in problem B31 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

forum_comments.text:
This conjecture is resolved in "An Effective Proof of the Erdős Prime Divisibility Conjecture for Binomial Coefficients" (Parthasarathy, 2026), currently under review at the Journal of Experimental Mathematics.
For all 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n/2 with n ≥ 2j, there exists a prime p ≥ i with p | gcd(C(n,i), C(n,j)). The proof introduces four new tools: a Prime Power Bridge Lemma, a Cofactor Escape Lemma, an FO Characterisation (showing every prime > i in a fully obstructed product must divide C(j,i)), and a Carry Lemma that algebraically resolves all fully obstructed triples with M = 1 via Kummer's theorem. The case i = 1 is proved purely algebraically for all n, j. For i ≥ 2, Baker–Wüstholz effective finiteness bounds the residual to a computable range; exhaustive verification covers 110,109,924 triples (n ≤ 4400, i ≤ 23) with zero counterexamples. 8 fully obstructed triples found, all with i prime, all witnessed by p = i.
Noting Cong's computational extension to n = 10^7: the 9th FO triple (1594324, 3, 797162) fits the predicted structure — n - 1 = 3^13, so M = 1, and the Carry Lemma resolves it algebraically.

A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres. It is easy to see that $f(n)\leq n/P(n)$ for composite $n$, since if $j=p^k$ where $p^k\mid n$ and $p^{k+1}\nmid n$ then $\textrm{gcd}\left(n,\binom{n}{j}\right)=n/p^k$. This implies\[f(n) \leq (1+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}.\]It is known that $f(n)=n/P(n)$ when $n$ is the product of two primes. Another example is $n=30$.

For the second problem, it is easy to see that for any $n$ we have $f(n)\geq p(n)$, where $p(n)$ is the smallest prime dividing $n$, and hence there are infinitely many $n$ (those $=p^2)$ such that $f(n)\geq n^{1/2}$.

After 6 minutes, Gemini did not locate any additional references (https://gemini.google.com/share/aa45da6ee223) beyond the Erdos-Szekeres paper; the tool recapitulated the observations already in the paper (including those already mentioned in the commentary), computed some initial values of $f(n)$ and noted some other work involving divisibility of binomial coefficients (such as a body of work concerning the factors of the central binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$), as well as mentioning basic relevant tools such as Kummer's theorem, but nothing particularly relevant was found.

After 18 minutes, ChatGPT located (https://chatgpt.com/share/68f27b0c-ece8-800e-b984-096915f1a9bd) this very web page, and also asserted that this problem appears in Section B33 of Guy's "Unsolved problems in number theory"; I could not directly confirm this reference, but have seen it elsewhere on the web and the section title of B33, "Largest divisor of a binomial coefficient", is certainly promising. Some work on $\mathrm{gcd}(\binom{n}{i}, \binom{n}{j})$ is noted, such as this paper of Bergman (https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.0607), as well as the aforementioned work on central binomial coefficients, but other than that, no closely related literature was found.

EDIT: I was able to gain access to enough of Guy's book to view Section B33 (and related sections such as B31). It does contain several open problems by Erdos and others regarding divisibility of binomial coefficients, but does not seem to reference this question directly. So I would mark this as a hallucination by ChatGPT.

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
The third problem is likely very hard.
Even proving that $\gg n^{1-\epsilon}$ for small $\epsilon$ can occur, seems hard.

So one wonders if $n/f(n)$ is the product of only a small fractions of its prime divisors (assuming they are not too different).

Since already checking concrete divisibilities of binomial coefficients, e.g. [#376] (https://www.erdosproblems.com//376), seem widely open,
telling that in general $\binom{n}{k}$ is a multiple of a big divisor of $n$ for all $k$, cannot be expected to be easy.

In particular, one can wonder if $f(n)=n/P(n)$ might happen for $n$ being the product of many primes that are not too far apart.

For the product of $5$ primes (each bounded by $29$),
there are only a few values $n$ satisfying $f(n)=n/P(n)$. They are:
$$2310,4830,21318,34510,73370,86710,206074.$$

For the product of $6$ (or $7$) primes bounded by $37$ (or $47$ for $7$), there was only one value $n$ satisfying $f(n)=n/P(n)$ for each; $71677177=11 * 13 * 19 * 23 * 31 * 37$ and $34207446=2 * 3 * 7 * 13 * 31 * 43 * 47$.

The above examples indicate even more that the characterisation in the first subquestion seems hopeless. Someone who thinks it is not?

Anyone optimistic that something can be done on the third subquestion?

The second subquestion may be the one where it is possible to have a rigourous proof. A different construction may do the work. But maybe this rigourous proof would not add much to the insight the conditional proofs already gave.

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
The second subquestion should definitely be answered with yes.
Nevertheless, it was frustrating to not have a clear infinite family.
The following two families should do the job.

*there are likely infinitely many primes of the form $q=2^k+3$ where $k \equiv 4 \pmod {20}$ (see [oeis/A057732] (https://oeis.org/A057732))

For such a $q$ (larger than $19$, the latter being valid as well), let $n=q(q+1)$, these satisfy $f(n)=q+1.$
Notice that $q+1 \mid \binom{n}{q}$ is the only binomial which is not a multiple of $q$.
Now $2q \mid \binom{n}{r(q+1)}$ if $\frac{q-1}{2}\ge r$>$3$ and $5q \mid \binom{n}{r(q+1)}$ if $1\le r \le 3$.

*(construction by Kadi Siigur)

Let $p,q$ be two primes satisfying $2^l$ < $p$ < $q$ < $2^{l+1}$ for which $pq \equiv 1 \pmod{2^l}$ (thus $l\ge 4$).
There should be infinitely many such pairs of primes heuristically (similar to the fact that there should be infinitely many twin primes) and computations give many solutions as such.
Now $n=2pq$ has the property that $f(n)=2p$.
This is since $2q \mid \binom{2pq}{pq},$ $2q \mid \binom{2pq}{2pr}$ (for $r \in [1,q]$) and $2p \mid \binom{2pq}{2rq}$ (for $r \in [1,p]$).

computation:
- Exact standalone scan for all composite \(n\le N\):
 - factored each \(n\),
 - computed \(p\)-adic valuations of \(\binom{n}{k}\) for each \(k\),
 - evaluated the exact minimum gcd value \(f(n)\).
- Tracked frequencies of equality \(f(n)=n/P(n)\) and threshold exceedance \(f(n)>\sqrt n\).

- Deep run to \(N=12000\) (10561 composite integers scanned).
- At \(n\le 12000\):
 - fraction with \(f(n)=n/P(n)\) about \(0.5799\),
 - fraction with \(f(n)>\sqrt n\) about \(0.0471\).
- Maximum observed ratio \(f(n)/(n/P(n))\) remained 1 in this range (consistent with the upper bound).
attempt: The finite route was to compute \(f(n)\) exactly for every composite \(n\) in a long initial range by evaluating the \(p\)-adic content of \(\binom{n}{k}\) across all admissible \(k\). This cleanly measures how often the upper bound \(f(n)\le n/P(n)\) is sharp and how often \(f(n)>\sqrt n\) occurs, but it does not yet reveal the structural criterion for equality or the full size behavior of \(f(n)\).

problem: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of sets closed under taking subsets (i.e. if $B\subseteq A\in\mathcal{F}$ then $B\in \mathcal{F}$). There exists some element $x$ such that whenever $\mathcal{F}'\subseteq \mathcal{F}$ is an intersecting subfamily we have\[\lvert \mathcal{F}'\rvert \leq \lvert \{ A\in \mathcal{F} : x\in A\}\rvert.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/701.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Chv\'{a}tal \cite{Ch74}, who proved it replacing the closed under subsets condition with the (stronger) condition that, assuming all sets in $\mathcal{F}$ are subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, whenever $A\in \mathcal{F}$ and there is an injection $f:B\to A$ such that $x\leq f(x)$ for all $x\in B$, then $B\in \mathcal{F}$.

Sterboul \cite{St74} proved this when, letting $\mathcal{G}$ be the maximal sets (under inclusion) in $\mathcal{F}$, all sets in $\mathcal{G}$ have the same size, $\lvert A\cap B\rvert\leq 1$ for all $A\neq B\in \mathcal{G}$, and at least two sets in $\mathcal{G}$ have non-empty intersection.

Frankl and Kupavskii \cite{FrKu23} have proved this when $\mathcal{F}$ has covering number $2$.

Borg \cite{Bo11} has proposed a weighted generalisation of this conjecture, which he proves under certain additional assumptions.
References:
- [Bo11] Borg, Peter, On Chv\'{a}tal's conjecture and a conjecture on families of signed sets. European J. Combin. (2011), 140-145.
- [Ch74] Chv\'{a}tal, V., Intersecting families of edges in hypergraphs having the hereditary property. (1974), 61-66.
- [FrKu23] Frankl, Peter and Kupavskii, Andrey, Perfect matchings in down-sets. Discrete Math. (2023), Paper No. 113323, 7.
- [St74] Sterboul, F., Sur une conjecture de V. Chv\'{a}tal. (1974), 152-164.
forum: No forum comments were present in the fetched discussion thread. The site comment-activity widget says: None.
computation:
- Built exact branch-and-bound solver for maximum intersecting subfamily size in finite downsets.
- Generated many random downsets (controlled family size), then compared:
 - exact \(\max\{|\mathcal F'|: \mathcal F'\text{ intersecting}\}\),
 - largest star \(\max_x |\{A\in\mathcal F:x\in A\}|\).

- Deep run: \(n=5\) to \(9\), 900 samples per \(n\), max family size 36.
- No violations found (all tested families had star size \(\ge\) exact max intersecting size).
- This is positive finite evidence only; it is not a proof of the full infinite statement.
attempt: I treated the conjecture as an exact optimization problem on finite downsets: compute the maximum size of an intersecting subfamily and compare it with the size of the largest star. The branch-and-bound experiments give clean no-counterexample evidence on the sampled families, but they do not identify the combinatorial principle that would force star dominance in every hereditary family. The statement remains open.

problem:
Let $G_n$ be the unit distance graph in $\mathbb{R}^n$, with two vertices joined by an edge if and only if the distance between them is $1$.

Estimate the chromatic number $\chi(G_n)$. Does it grow exponentially in $n$? Does\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\chi(G_n)^{1/n}\]exist?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/704.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A generalisation of the Hadwiger-Nelson problem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadwiger%E2%80%93Nelson_problem) (which addresses $n=2$). Frankl and Wilson \cite{FrWi81} proved exponential growth:\[\chi(G_n) \geq (1+o(1))1.2^n.\]This was improved to\[\chi(G_n)\geq (1.239\cdots+o(1))^n\]by Raigorodsky \cite{Ra00}. The trivial colouring (by tiling with cubes) gives\[\chi(G_n) \leq (2+\sqrt{n})^n.\]Larman and Rogers \cite{LaRo72} improved this to\[\chi(G_n) \leq (3+o(1))^n,\]and conjecture the truth may be $(2^{3/2}+o(1))^n$. (Note that $2^{3/2}\approx 2.828$.) Prosanov \cite{Pr20} has given an alternative proof of this upper bound.

See also [508], [705], and [706].
References:
- [FrWi81] Frankl, P. and Wilson, R. M., Intersection theorems with geometric consequences. Combinatorica (1981), 357-368.
- [LaRo72] Larman, D. G. and Rogers, C. A., The realization of distances within sets in Euclidean space. Mathematika (1972), 1-24.
- [Pr20] Prosanov, Roman, A new proof of the Larman-Rogers upper bound for the chromatic number of the Euclidean space. Discrete Appl. Math. (2020), 115-120.
- [Ra00] Ra\u igorodski\u i, A. M., On the chromatic number of a space. Uspekhi Mat. Nauk (2000), 147--148.

problem:
Let $G$ be a finite unit distance graph in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (i.e. the vertices are a finite collection of points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and there is an edge between two points if and only if the distance between them is $1$).

Is there some $k$ such that if $G$ has girth $\geq k$ (i.e. $G$ contains no cycles of length $<k$) then $\chi(G)\leq 3$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/705.
- Page status: DISPROVED (database last update 2026-01-27).
- Page last edited: 27 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The maximal value of $\chi(G)$ (without a girth condition) is the Hadwiger-Nelson problem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadwiger%E2%80%93Nelson_problem). There are unit distance graphs (e.g. the Moser spindle) with $\chi(G)=4$ of girth $3$. de Grey \cite{dG18} has constructed a unit distance graph $G$ with $\chi(G)=5$. (I do not know what the largest girth achieved is by these recent constructions.)

Wormald \cite{Wo79} has constructed a unit distance graph with $\chi(G)=4$ and girth $5$, with $6448$ vertices. O'Donnell \cite{OD94} has constructed a unit distance graph with $\chi(G)=4$ and girth $4$, with $56$ vertices. Chilakamarri \cite{Ch95} has constructed an infinite family of unit distance graphs with $\chi(G)=4$ and girth $4$, the smallest of which has $47$ vertices.

The general case was solved by O'Donnell \cite{OD99}, who constructed finite unit distance graphs with chromatic number $4$ and arbitrarily large girth.

See also [508], [704], and [706].
References:
- [Ch95] Chilakamarri, Kiran B., A {$4$}-chromatic unit-distance graph with no triangles. Geombinatorics (1995), 64-76.
- [OD94] O'Donnell, Paul, A triangle-free {$4$}-chromatic graph in the plane. Geombinatorics (1994), 23-29.
- [OD99] P. O'Donnell, High girth unit-distance graphs. PhD Dissertation, Rutgers University (1999).
- [Wo79] Wormald, Nicholas, A {$4$}-chromatic graph with a special plane drawing. J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A (1979), 1-8.
- [dG18] de Grey, Aubrey D. N. J., The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5. Geombinatorics (2018), 18-31.

- Verified exact properties of the classical 7-vertex Moser spindle witness:
 - exact chromatic number via backtracking coloring,
 - exact girth via BFS cycle search.
- This does not itself give large girth, but confirms the fundamental 4-chromatic unit-distance obstruction.

- Combined with modern large-girth constructions from the literature, this closes the original question negatively.

The local verification checks the Moser spindle exactly as a concrete 4-chromatic unit-distance obstruction, and the literature now supplies arbitrarily large-girth unit-distance graphs with chromatic number at least 4. So no threshold \(k\) can force \(\chi(G)\le 3\) from girth\((G)\ge k\).

forum_comments.text:
I would like to add a few references and partial results which seem directly relevant to this problem.

Let \(\overline{\chi}(\mathbb R^2;m)=\max_{|A|=m}\chi(\mathbb R^2,A)\), where two points of \(\mathbb R^2\) are adjacent if their Euclidean distance belongs to \(A\). This is the corresponding infinite-graph formulation of the quantity \(L(m)\) in this problem; equivalently, by the de Bruijn--Erdős compactness theorem for graph colourings [dBE51 (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1951-01.pdf), Theorem 1], it gives the same finite-subgraph supremum.

First, Eric Naslund discussed this problem in an answer to a MathOverflow question of Matthew Kahle; see [MO20] (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/375219/updated-bounds-or-references-for-an-old-erd%C5%91s-problem-coloring-the-plane-with). The usual lattice construction gives a lower bound \(\overline{\chi}(\mathbb R^2;m) \gg m\sqrt{\log m}\). On the other hand, the elementary product-colouring argument gives the general upper bound \(\overline{\chi}(\mathbb R^2;m)\le 7^m\). A related recent paper is Naslund's [Na23] (https://doi.org/10.1112/mtk.12197) (also available on arXiv: [Na23-arXiv] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12312)).

For small \(m\), there is a concrete improvement when \(m=2\). Exoo and Ismailescu [EI19] (https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13177) proved that \(\chi(\mathbb R^2,\{1,2\})\ge 6\). Equivalently, in the notation of this problem, \(L(2)\ge 6\). Parts later gave a smaller and simpler 6-chromatic two-distance construction for a suitable pair of forbidden distances, based on a graph with only 16 vertices; see [Pa20] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12656).

References.
[dBE51] (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1951-01.pdf) N. G. de Bruijn and P. Erdős, ''A colour problem for infinite graphs and a problem in the theory of relations'', Proceedings of the Koninklijke Nederlandse Akademie van Wetenschappen, Series A 54 (1951), 371--373.
[MO20] (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/375219/updated-bounds-or-references-for-an-old-erd%C5%91s-problem-coloring-the-plane-with) Matthew Kahle, ''Updated bounds or references for an old Erdős problem -- coloring the plane with multiple forbidden distances?'', MathOverflow question, with an answer by Eric Naslund, 2020--2022.
[Na23] (https://doi.org/10.1112/mtk.12197) Eric Naslund, ''The chromatic number of \(\mathbb R^n\) with multiple forbidden distances'', Mathematika 69 (2023), 692--718.
[EI19] (https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13177) Geoffrey Exoo and Dan Ismailescu, ''A 6-chromatic two-distance graph in the plane'', arXiv:1909.13177, 2019.
[Pa20] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12656) Jaan Parts, ''A small 6-chromatic two-distance graph in the plane'', Geombinatorics 29/3 (2020), 111--115; arXiv:2010.12656.

computation:
- Built standalone finite proxy experiments:
 - sample planar point sets,
 - choose \(r\) target distances,
 - connect near those distances,
 - compute greedy coloring upper bound and clique-based lower bound.
- This is heuristic finite evidence, not a theorem for \(L(r)\).

- Deep run: \(r=1\) to \(6\), 40 trials each, 160 points per trial.
- Mean greedy upper bounds increased with \(r\) (about 4.4, 5.7, 7.5, 9.0, 10.7, 12.2).
- Max observed upper bounds reached 15 at \(r=6\), suggesting clear growth in these finite models.
attempt: The current approach is purely finite-model: sample planar point sets, impose \(r\) allowed distances approximately, and compare coloring upper bounds with clique lower bounds. Those experiments show growth with \(r\) in the proxy model, but they do not translate into rigorous bounds for the exact extremal quantity \(L(r)\). The polynomial-growth question remains open.

problem: Let $g(n)$ be minimal such that for any $A\subseteq [2,\infty)\cap \mathbb{N}$ with $\lvert A\rvert =n$ and any set $I$ of $\max(A)$ consecutive integers there exists some $B\subseteq I$ with $\lvert B\rvert=g(n)$ such that\[\prod_{a\in A} a \mid \prod_{b\in B}b.\]Is it true that\[g(n) \leq (2+o(1))n?\]Or perhaps even $g(n)\leq 2n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/708.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Sur\'{a}nyi \cite{ErSu59}, who proved that $g(n) \geq (2-o(1))n$, and that $g(3)=4$. Their lower bound construction takes $A$ as the set of $p_ip_j$ for $i\neq j$, where $p_1<\cdots <p_\ell$ is some set of primes such that $2p_1^2>p_\ell^2$.

Gallai was the first to consider problems of this type, and observed that $g(2)=2$ and $g(3)\geq 4$.

In \cite{Er92c} Erd\H{o}s offers '100 dollars or 1000 rupees', whichever is more, for a proof or disproof. (In 1992 1000 rupees was worth approximately \$38.60.)

Erd\H{o}s and Sur\'{a}nyi similarly asked what is the smallest $c_n\geq 1$ such that in any interval $I\subset [0,\infty)$ of length $c_n\max(A)$ there exists some $B\subseteq I\cap \mathbb{N}$ with $\lvert B\rvert=n$ such that\[\prod_{a\in A} a \mid \prod_{b\in B}b.\]They prove $c_2=1$ and $c_3=\sqrt{2}$, but have no good upper or lower bounds in general.

See also [709].
References:
- [Er92c] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some of my forgotten problems in number theory. Hardy-Ramanujan J. (1992), 34-50.

forum_comments.author: Lech Mazur
forum_comments.text:
GPT-5.5 Pro says the statement of Problem #708 appears to have a wording issue: the condition\[
|B|=g(n)
\]should likely be\[
|B|\le g(n),
\]or equivalently \(g(n)\) should be defined as the worst-case minimum size of such a set \(B\).

Evidence: take\[
A=\{2,3,\ldots,n+1\},\qquad M=n+1,\qquad I=\{1,2,\ldots,n+1\}.
\]Then\[
\prod_{a\in A}a=(n+1)! = \prod_{b\in I}b,
\]so \(B=I\) works. But every \(B\subseteq I\) has\[
|B|\le |I|=n+1.
\]Thus, if the statement literally requires \(|B|=g(n)\) for every legal \(A,I\), then this example forces \(g(n)\le n+1\).

That conflicts with the statement that Erdős and Surányi proved\[
g(n)\ge (2-o(1))n.
\]So the intended formulation is presumably:\[
g(n)=\sup_{A,I}\min\left\{|B|:B\subseteq I,\
\prod_{a\in A}a\mid\prod_{b\in B}b\right\},
\]or: there exists \(B\subseteq I\) with \(|B|\le g(n)\).

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
I do not know how to solve the problem completely, but there is a simple improvement $
f(n)\gg {\log n\over \log\log n}
$.

Let $F(n,m)$ denote the least integer $L$ such that the interval $(m,m+L]$ contains distinct multiples of $1,2,\dots,n$.

For the set $A=\{2,\dots,n\}$, the defining property of $f(n)$ implies $F(n,m)\le f(n)n$ for every $m$. On the other hand, van Doorn proved that for all sufficiently large $n$ there exists $m=m(n)$ such that $
F(n,m)\gg n{\log n\over \log\log n}.$ Combining the two inequalities gives the claim.

It is natural to guess that the truth is much closer to the lower bound than to the upper bound.

forum_comments.text:
Attempted a solve with opus 4.6 + a lot of compute. The problem reduces to verifying Hall’s condition in on a bipartite graph Gn. I tried squeezing the lower bound to the bound given by Erdos and Pommerance and try to prove that Hall's condition must hold.

The multiplicative combinatorics question at the heart of it:

Given integers $k \in (B, N]$ and targets $h \in (2^n, n + L]$, with edges $k \mid h$, why does the divisibility structure always produce enough expansion? The computation says it does (zero failures through n = 10^6), but the margin is so thin that it appears to require some deep property of how divisors distribute across intervals, something beyond what current sieve methods, probabilistic tools, or spectral techniques can capture. Closing it likely requires a new idea about the collective expansion properties of divisibility in short intervals, not just pairwise or per-interval estimates, but a global structural argument that nobody has found yet.

I've compiled my notes on the project here, and the code can be found in the corresponding github.

https://zenodo.org/records/18749475

I wish the next person who attempts this luck!

Before we engage in the game of my AI said to your AI! Let me provide some context, I didn't just go "claude solve erdos pls" the process was a rather intensive loop of create analytic framework -> design computational experiment -> run experiment on hardware either locally or on the cloud -> analyze results for flaws -> create an adversarial review of those flaws -> repeat. The goal was to empirically rule out regimes and techniques by creating new datasets that the AI can use to analyze the problem. One thing I noticed though was the transfer from the proof-outline to the final output wasn't 1:1 and some claims are more clearly defended in the outline but still defendable in the final output.

I think there's real value in AI in searching these problems for traps before attempting an analytic solve. The main issue these methods kept running into: smooth numbers will blow up the standard tools used.

And for the game of my AI vs yours (edit: if it wasn't clear Claude is responding from here):

GPT raised 8 issues with the paper. It was flat-out wrong on its two biggest technical criticisms — it botched a standard floor inequality and misread a smooth-restricted sum as divergent. Four more issues are cosmetic (a mislabeled skip count, a conservative bound, a wrong cross-reference, a minor definition). The only real find is that the paper's V_min disjointness argument lost its conditional framing when ported from the proof outline to LaTeX — but that was always flagged as depending on an open hypothesis, so it's a presentation fix, not mathematical error. The paper is sound; GPT mostly just made noise.

What the outline actually proves unconditionally:
 - Top half doubling (trivial)
 - Case A: Hall's condition for subsets S with max element > n/s
 - Lemma 3: Small-s regime (s ≤ some threshold)
 - Regime 1: s ≤ δ/2

 These are all sound and match what appears in the paper. The architecture is solid.

 Computational evidence tables

 The outline includes verification tables showing the Cauchy-Schwarz ratio improves with n — the worst-case margin grows from ~13% at small n to ~115% at larger n. This is consistent with the paper's Hopcroft-Karp verification (zero failures for n ≤ 10⁶) and supports the conjecture even though it doesn't prove it.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: Remarkably, it seems that this problem (morally, at least) implies the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions! Proof sketch: if the Kakeya conjecture failed, then by the tensor power trick we conclude that for sufficiently high dimension $d$, there exists Kakeya sets of dimension less than $d-1$. Discretizing (and taking some liberties with the analogy between arithmetic progressions and tubes), we get about $N^{d-1}$ arithmetic progressions of spacing $\sim N$ that occupy less than $N^{d-1}$ elements, so it is not possible to assign each such progression a distinct element. Morally, one can then invoke the Chinese remainder theorem to conclude.
