problem: Is it true that, for every bipartite graph $G$, there exists some $\alpha\in [1,2)$ and $c>0$ such that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^\alpha?\]Must $\alpha$ be rational?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/713.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 07 March 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits. Erd\H{o}s sometimes asked this in the weaker version with just\[\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\asymp n^{\alpha}.\]Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er67d} had initially conjectured that, for any bipartite graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^{\alpha}$ for some constant $c>0$ and $\alpha$ of the shape $1+\frac{1}{k}$ or $2-\frac{1}{k}$ for some integer $k\geq 2$. This was disproved by Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits \cite{ErSi70}.

The analogous statement is not true for hypergraphs, as shown by Frankl and F\"{u}redi \cite{FrFu87}, who proved that if $G$ is the $5$-uniform hypergraph on $8$ vertices with edges $\{12346,12457,12358\}$ then $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)=o(n^5)$ but $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\neq O(n^c)$ for any $c<5$.

A simplified proof was given by F\"{u}redi and Gerbner \cite{FuGe21}, who extended it to a counterexample for all $k\geq 5$. It remains open whether it is true for $k=3$ and $k=4$ (though F\"{u}redi and Gerbner conjecture it is not).

See also [571].
References:
- [Er67d] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some recent results on extremal problems in graph theory. {R}esults. (1967), 117--123 (English); pp. 124--130 (French).
- [ErSi70] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Simonovits, M., Some extremal problems in graph theory. Combinatorial theory and its applications, I-III (Proc. Colloq., Balatonf\"{u}red, 1969) (1970), 377-390.
- [FrFu87] Frankl, P. and F\"uredi, Z., Exact solution of some Tur\'{a}n-type problems. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1987), 226--262.
- [FuGe21] F\"uredi, Zolt\'{a}n and Gerbner, D\'{a}niel, Hypergraphs without exponents. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (2021), Paper No. 105517, 9.

For $r=3$, if $m=|E(G)|$ and $\nu(G)$ is the maximum number of \emph{edge-disjoint}
copies of $K_4^3$ in $G$, then the optimal decomposition into edge-disjoint
$K_4^3$'s plus single edges uses exactly $m-3\nu(G)$ parts.

I exhaustively checked all $2^{\binom{6}{3}}=2^{20}$ $3$-graphs on $n=6$ vertices:
$\mathrm{ex}_3(6;K_4^3)=14$, and for every $G$ on $6$ vertices one has
$m-3\nu(G)\le 14$ (so no counterexample exists for $(r,n)=(3,6)$). Code available
on request.

so $\mathrm{ex}_7(8;K_8^7)=7$, and any $7$-graph on $8$ vertices decomposes into
$\le 7$ single edges if $m\le 7$, or into one $K_8^7$ if $m=8$.

A finite projective plane of order $n$ is a collection of subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n^2+n+1\}$ of size $n+1$ such that every pair of elements is contained in exactly one set.

forum_comments.author: AronBhalla
forum_comments.text:
The page should be updated to include the later result of Godsil and McKay (1990). If $L_{k,n}$ denotes the unrestricted number of $k\times n$ Latin rectangles on symbols $[n]$, they proved that, as $n\to\infty$ with $k=o(n^{6/7})$,

$$L_{k,n}\sim (n!)^k\left(\frac{(n)_k}{n^k}\right)^n\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)^{-n/2}e^{-k/2},$$

where $(n)_k=n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$. This substantially extends the earlier results of Erdos-Kaplansky and Yamamoto.

It's probably also worth clarifying that OEIS A001009 is not the unrestricted count $L_{k,n}$. It records the reduced/normalised counts $R_{k,n}$ (ie. with the first row and first column fixed).

Known theorems already provide the principal asymptotic shape in broad
\((k,n)\)-regimes:

So the main-order template is established in large parameter regions.

The unresolved part is a fully uniform asymptotic formula across all growth
relations between \(k\) and \(n\), with controlled error terms.
- Need a uniform dependency-control expansion (or cluster estimate) for column
 collision constraints that remains sharp simultaneously across all \(k\)-scales.

A single asymptotic formula with explicit error term valid uniformly for all

Step A: Uniform Local Constraint Expansion
Express Latin-rectangle count as product of conditional matchings with a

Step B: Global Error Summation
Sum local errors over rows while keeping total multiplicative error

Step C: Regime Stitching
Match sparse-\(k\), medium-\(k\), and dense-\(k\) asymptotics with consistent

Need a coupling theorem for random near-Latin row extensions whose dependency

forum_comments.author: msawhney
forum_comments.text: A natural way to attempt to attack such a problem is to bound the exponential sum $\sum e(n/p)/p$. Via the method of bilinear sums, one is let to considering $\sum e(n/ab)$ and establishing cancellation when $a,b\sim \exp((\log n)^{o(1)})$. This appears to be out of reach of standard methods (in particular say Chapter 8 in Iwaniec--Kowalski). However by restricting to primes which are between $\exp((\log n)^{.99})$ and $n$ (say) one could plausibly prove a bound of $\gtrsim \log\log n$ and $(1-\Omega(1))\log\log n$.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: A back of the envelope calculation suggests that Proposition 1.12 of this paper of Matomaki, Radziwill, Shao, Teravainen, and myself (https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03335) should be able to handle the range $p \geq \exp(\log^{2/3+\varepsilon} n)$, which should give upper and lower bounds of $\gtrsim \frac{1}{6} \log \log n$ and $\lesssim \frac{5}{6} \log\log n$ if I did the calculations correctly.

problem: Let $k\geq 2$. Does\[(n+k)!^2 \mid (2n)!\]for infinitely many $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/727.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Erd\H{o}s, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus \cite{EGRS75}. It is open even for $k=2$.

Balakran \cite{Ba29} proved this holds for $k=1$ - that is, $(n+1)^2\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ for infinitely many $n$. It is a classical fact that $(n+1)\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ for all $n$ (see Catalan numbers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_number)).

Erd\H{o}s, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus observe that the method of Balakran can be further used to prove that there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[(n+k)!(n+1)! \mid (2n)!\](in fact this holds whenever $k<c \log n$ for some small constant $c>0$).

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er68c} proved that if $a!b!\mid n!$ then $a+b\leq n+O(\log n)$.
References:
- [Ba29] H. Balakran, On the values of $n$ which make $(2n)!/(n+1)!(n+1)!$ an integer. J. Indian Math. Soc. (1929), 97-100.
- [EGRS75] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., On the prime factors of $(\sp{2n}\sb{n})$. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
- [Er68c] P. Erd\H{o}s, Aufgabe 557. Elemente Math. (1968), 111-113.

attempt:
Rigorous reduction used in this attempt:
Let B_n = C(2n,n). Then
B_{n+1} = B_n * 2(2n+1)/(n+1).
So support change from n to n+1 is controlled exactly by prime factors of 2n+1 and n+1.
For the special family n=2^m-1, this becomes
B_{2^m} = B_{2^m-1} * (2^{m+1}-1)/2^{m-1}.
Hence odd-prime support equality for (2^m-1,2^m) is equivalent to:
every odd prime divisor of 2^{m+1}-1 already divides B_{2^m-1}.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
Using Chatgpt 5.4 i get an heuristic which seems to suggest a possible refinement of the estimate $m=\exp((\log n)^{1/2+o(1)})$, but also suggests that the asymptotic $m\sim f(n)$ may not exist in the usual deterministic sense.

Let $a(n)=\min{m\geq 1:m\nmid {2n\choose n}}$. Since $a(n)=\min_p p^{v_p({2n\choose n})+1}$, the smallest missing prime already gives a natural candidate for the scale of $a(n)$.

By Kummer's theorem, for odd $p$, $p\nmid {2n\choose n}$ if and only if every base-$p$ digit of $n$ lies in ${0,1,\ldots,(p-1)/2}$. Thus, for a random $n\leq x$, writing $L=\log x$, one expects ${\bf P}(p\nmid {2n\choose n})\approx 2^{-L/\log p}=\exp(-(\log 2)L/\log p)$.

Therefore the expected number of primes $p\leq y=e^u$ which do not divide ${2n\choose n}$ should be roughly

$\sum_{p\leq e^u}\exp(-(\log 2)L/\log p)\sim {\exp(u-(\log 2)L/u)\over u(1+(\log 2)L/u^2)}.$

Equating this to $1$ gives

$u=\sqrt{(\log 2)L}+{1\over 4}\log L+{1\over 4}\log(\log 2)+{1\over 2}\log 2+o(1).$

Thus the natural scale is

$F(x)=\sqrt2,(\log 2)^{1/4}(\log x)^{1/4}\exp(\sqrt{(\log 2)(\log x)}).$

More generally, if $y=rF(x)$, then the same calculation gives expected number asymptotic to $r^2$. Assuming a Poisson-type independence for these digit-restriction events as $p$ varies, this suggests

$ {1\over x}\,\#\{n\leq x:\ a(n)>rF(x)\}\to e^{-r^2} $

for each fixed $r>0$. Equivalently,

$\log a(n)=\sqrt{(\log 2)(\log n)}+{1\over 4}\log\log n+O(1)$

in distribution.

This would refine the EGRS estimate, but it would also suggest that there is no function $f(n)$ with $a(n)\sim f(n)$ for almost all $n$, unless the Poisson heuristic is misleading. The missing point is to prove, or disprove, the required independence statement for the simultaneous base-$p$ digit restrictions in the range

$p\asymp(\log x)^{1/4}\exp(\sqrt{(\log 2)(\log x)}).$

Prime powers with $v_p({2n\choose n})>0$ appear heuristically not to change this leading distribution, since the relevant low-carry events for $p<y$ should have much smaller total contribution.

problem: Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal and $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$. Is it true that, for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{n}< \mathfrak{m}$, there exists a subgraph of $G$ with chromatic number $\mathfrak{n}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/739.
- Page status: NOT PROVABLE (database last update 2025-10-01).
- Page last edited: 01 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A question of Galvin \cite{Ga73}, who proved that this is true with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_0$. Galvin also proved that the stronger version of this statement, in which the subgraph is induced, implies $2^{\mathfrak{k}}<2^{\mathfrak{n}}$ for all cardinals $\mathfrak{k}<\mathfrak{n}$.

Komj\'{a}th \cite{Ko88b} proved it is consistent that\[2^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_1}=2^{\aleph_2}=\aleph_3\]and that there exist graphs which fail this property (with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$).

Shelah \cite{Sh90} proved that, assuming the axiom of constructibility, the answer is yes with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$.

It remains open whether the answer to this question is yes assuming the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis, for example.
References:
- [Ga73] Galvin, F., Chromatic numbers of subgraphs. Period. Math. Hungar. (1973), 117--119.
- [Ko88b] Komj\'{a}th, P\'{e}ter, Consistency results on infinite graphs. Israel J. Math. (1988), 285--294.
- [Sh90] Shelah, Saharon, Incompactness for chromatic numbers of graphs. (1990), 361--371.

problem:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be such that $A+A$ has positive (upper) density. Can one always decompose $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ such that $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ both have positive (upper) density?

Is there a basis $A$ of order $2$ such that if $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ then $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ cannot both have bounded gaps?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/741.
- Page status: SOLVED (LEAN) (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 02 May 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Burr and Erd\H{o}s. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er94b} thought he could construct a basis as in the second question, but 'could never quite finish the proof'.

In \cite{Er94b} the first question is simply asked with 'positive density', but by this Erd\H{o}s often meant positive upper and/or lower density, rather than necessarily that the density exists and is positive. The interpretation of this question with upper density most likely captures the spirit of the question.

DeepMind and an internal OpenAI model (see the comments and \cite{APSSV26}) have independently constructed a basis which gives an affirmative answer to the second question. DeepMind gave a counterexample to the strict density version of the first question.

Deepmind has also given a positive answer to the upper density question: if $A+A$ has positive upper density then $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ and both $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ have positive upper density (the proof is sketched in the comments).
References:
- [APSSV26] B. Alexeev, M. Putterman, M. Sawhney, M. Sellke, and G. Valiant, Short proofs in combinatorics and number theory. arXiv:2603.29961 (2026).
- [Er94b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some problems in number theory, combinatorics and combinatorial geometry. Math. Pannon. (1994), 261-269.

forum_comments.author: Moritz Firsching
forum_comments.text:
We have formalised the upper density variant and the DeepMind prover agent has provided a formal proof that this is True (at least for the for variant as formalised in Formal Conjectures (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos741.erdos_741.variants.upper))
The formal proof can be found here (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/9d492049e42167b0d2fd58a9e91da3bf160172b5/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/741.lean#L228).
Here’s an attempt to summarize the proof informally:

$\textbf{Question.}$ Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be such that $A+A$ has positive upper density. Can one always decompose $A = A_1 \sqcup A_2$ such that $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ both have positive upper density?

$\textbf{Proof.}$ We show that the answer is yes.

We use an alternating block partition. Given a rapidly growing sequence $M_0 < M_1 < M_2 < \cdots$, we define $$A_1 = A \cap \bigcup_k (M_{2k}, M_{2k+1}], \qquad A_2 = A \setminus A_1.$$ In odd-indexed intervals $(M_{2k}, M_{2k+1}]$, all elements of $A$ belong to $A_1$. In even-indexed intervals $(M_{2k+1}, M_{2k+2}]$, they all belong to $A_2$. The sequence $M$ is chosen to grow fast enough that each block dwarfs all previous ones. We need to consider two cases.

Case 1: $A$ has positive upper density
Since $A$ has positive upper density, there exist a constant $c > 0$ and a strictly increasing sequence of scales along which $|A \cap [1,N]| \ge c \cdot N$. Using a dependent-choice argument, we extract a rapidly growing sequence $M_k$ such that for each $k$:

$|A \cap [1, M_{k+1}]| \ge c \cdot M_{k+1}$ (density is retained at the next scale),
$|A \cap [1, M_k]| \le \frac{c}{4} \cdot M_{k+1}$ (the "past" is negligible relative to the "future").
Because each new block contains all the "fresh" elements of $A$, looking at scale $M_{2k+1}$ shows that $A_1$ has positive upper density, and looking at scale $M_{2k+2}$ shows the same for $A_2$. A short argument then lifts this: if a set has positive upper density, so does its sumset with itself.

Case 2: $A$ has zero upper density but $A+A$ has positive upper density
This is the harder case, since $A$ is too sparse to guarantee positive density for the parts directly. Instead, we argue about the sumsets themselves.
Since $A+A$ has positive upper density, there exist $c > 0$ and a sequence of scales along which $|(A+A) \cap [1,N]| \ge c \cdot N$. Since $A$ has zero upper density, $|A \cap [1,N]| = o(N)$, so for any fixed $K$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ where $(K+1) \cdot |A \cap [1,N]| \le \frac{c}{4} \cdot N$. By dependent choice, we extract a rapidly growing $M_k$ such that for each $k$:

$|(A+A) \cap [1, M_{k+1}]| \ge c \cdot M_{k+1}$,
$(M_k + 1) \cdot |A \cap [1, M_{k+1}]| \le \frac{c}{4} \cdot M_{k+1}$.
The key ingredient is a combinatorial sumset bound: if $A = A_1 \cup A_2$ and every element of $A_2$ in $[1,N]$ is at most $K$, then $$|(A+A) \cap [1,N]| \le |(A_1+A_1) \cap [1,N]| + (K+1) \cdot |A \cap [1,N]|.$$ The idea is that any sum involving an element of $A_2$ has one summand bounded by $K$, giving at most $(K+1) \cdot |A \cap [1,N]|$ such sums. Applying this bound at alternating scales:

At scale $N = M_{2k+1}$: all elements of $A_2$ in $[1,N]$ lie below $M_{2k}$, so the bound with $K = M_{2k}$ gives $|(A_1+A_1) \cap [1,N]| \ge \frac{3c}{4} \cdot N$.
At scale $N = M_{2k+2}$: symmetrically, all elements of $A_1$ in $[1,N]$ lie below $M_{2k+1}$, giving $|(A_2+A_2) \cap [1,N]| \ge \frac{3c}{4} \cdot N$.
Since these bounds hold for infinitely many $N$, both sumsets have positive upper density.

forum_comments.author: Moritz Firsching
forum_comments.text:
The DeepMind prover agent has disproved the first part (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos741.erdos_741.parts.i) and proved the second part (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos741.erdos_741.parts.i) of the problems as formalised in Formal Conjectures repo. (which might not capture the intended meaning of these questions, see the remarks on "positive density" below)

Here’s an attempt to summarize those proofs informally:

Part (i):

The theorem erdos_741.parts.i asks whether any set $A$ for which $A+A$ has positive density can be partitioned into $A = A_1 \sqcup A_2$ such that both $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ also have positive density. The answer is 'False', but this refutation hinges heavily on the exact definition of "density" used in the formalization (which requires the strict existence of a limit).

The Counterexample under "Limit Density"
To refute the conjecture, we construct a set $A = B \cup S_C$, where:

$B$ is composed of elements whose base-4 digits are restricted (e.g., $B_1$ has digits in ${0, 1}$ and $B_2$ in ${0, 2}$).
$S_C$ consists of "fat but sparse" intervals of the form $[4^{3^k}, 10 \cdot 4^{3^k})$.
Because base-4 digits add uniquely without carries, any partition $A_1 \sqcup A_2$ can be characterized by how it projects onto elements of the base-4 set. The density of $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ can then be shown algebraically to satisfy: $$\text{density}(A_1+A_1) + \text{density}(A_2+A_2) \le 1 - \text{density}(A_1+A_1)\text{density}(A_2+A_2)$$

This forces the sum of the two densities to be strictly less than $1$.

However, when a subset passes through the "fat" sparse intervals $S_C$ (where $A$ contains all integers locally), standard sumset properties ($|U+U| \ge 2|U|-1$) force the local sum of densities to spike close to $1$. This constant oscillation between the suppressed base-4 bound and the interval spikes means that the densities cannot stabilize. Under a strict definition of natural density (where a single, stable limit value must exist), the limit fails to converge - thus refuting the conjecture.

Note that the proof uses the word “SandorA”, presumably referring to a construction by Sándor, but it is not clear if this name is referring to a real construction provided by Sándor (which might well exist) or just a construction that plausibly could have been done by him.

If we interpret "positive density" to mean positive upper asymptotic density ($\limsup$), the specific counterexample construction fails to refute the conjecture.
It is not clear to me what the intention in the paper really is, Erdős mentions "upper density" in the same paper, but not when talking about the problems here on page 263.

 The full formal proof in Lean 4 is available here (https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/486bc8afae062b6711cd16d3466d651ee2880a52/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/741.lean#L1449)

Part (ii):

The goal is to construct a pathological set $A$ that acts as a basis of order two ($A+A = \mathbb{N}$), but forces any partition to create arbitrarily large gaps in one of the component sumsets.

1. The Geometry of "Forbidden Zones"
The construction works by choosing a sequence of rapidly growing scales $P_k = 100^k$. For each scale $k \ge 1$, we carve out a forbidden zone $Z_k$ which is a broad interval of integers running roughly from $5.5 P_k$ to $11 P_k + k$. However, right in the middle of this zone, we leave a single "oasis" - a lone element $x_k = 10 P_k$.

The set $A$ is defined as all natural numbers that completely avoid every forbidden zone (except for the isolated $x_k$ oases). In visual terms, the set $A$ consists of clumps of integers separated by large, empty forbidden gaps where the only survivor is $x_k$.

2. Why $A \cup {0}$ is a Basis of Order 2
To prove $A+A = \mathbb{N}$ (where additions include $0+n$), we must show every integer can be represented as $a+b$ with $a,b \in A$:

Case outside forbidden zones: If $n \notin Z_k$, then $n \in A$ and we can just use $n + 0 = n$.
Case inside forbidden zones: If $n \in Z_k$, we split the representation based on where it lies relative to $x_k$:
For the lower half of $Z_k$, we can simply use $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + \lceil n/2 \rceil$. Because $n$ is small enough, neither half lands in $Z_k$, and they are both large enough to avoid the previous zone $Z_{k-1}$.
For the upper half of $Z_k$, we use the isolated oasis $x_k$. We write $n = x_k + (n - x_k)$. The difference $(n - x_k)$ is small enough that it falls safely in the gap before the forbidden zone $Z_k$.
Thus, $A$ covers all integers!

3. Why No Syndetic Partition Exists
Now suppose we partition $A = A_1 \sqcup A_2$. Consider a target sum $m$ in the interval $[11 P_k, 11 P_k + k]$. If we try to write $m = u + v$ with $u, v \in A$, the algebra forces the larger operand $v$ to land exactly inside the forbidden range $[5.5 P_k, 11 P_k + k]$.

But by definition, the only available element in $A$ inside this range is the isolated $x_k$. Therefore, to make any sum $m \in [11 P_k, 11 P_k + k]$, you must use $x_k$.

By the Pigeonhole Principle, $x_k$ can only belong to one of the partition components (say $A_1$). This implies:

$A_1 + A_1$ can cover the interval $[11 P_k, 11 P_k + k]$ by making use of $x_k$.
$A_2 + A_2$ is completely locked out and cannot represent any element in that interval because it does not possess $x_k$!
This leaves a gap of length $k$ in the sumset $A_2 + A_2$. Since we can make $k$ arbitrarily large, the gaps become unbounded, proving it is impossible to partition $A$ such that both sumsets are syndetic.

 The full formal proof in Lean 4 is available here (https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/486bc8afae062b6711cd16d3466d651ee2880a52/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/741.lean#L1629)

problem: Let $T_2,\ldots,T_n$ be a collection of trees such that $T_k$ has $k$ vertices. Can we always write $K_n$ as the edge disjoint union of the $T_k$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/743.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, known as the tree packing conjecture.

Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s and Lehel \cite{GyLe78} proved that this holds if all but at most $2$ of the trees are stars, or if all the trees are stars or paths. Fishburn \cite{Fi83} proved this for $n\leq 9$. Bollob\'{a}s \cite{Bo83} proved that the smallest $\lfloor n/\sqrt{2}\rfloor$ many trees can always be packed greedily into $K_n$.

Joos, Kim, K\"{u}hn, and Osthus \cite{JKKO19} proved that this conjecture holds when the trees have bounded maximum degree. Allen, B\"{o}ttcher, Clemens, Hladky, Piguet, and Taraz \cite{ABCHPT21} proved that this conjecture holds when all the trees have maximum degree $\leq c\frac{n}{\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$.

Janzer and Montgomery \cite{JaMo24} have proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that the largest $cn$ trees can be packed into $K_n$.
References:
- [ABCHPT21] Allen, Peter and B\"ottcher, Julia and Clemens, Dennis and Hladky, J. and D. Piguet and Taraz, Anusch, The tree packing conjecture for trees of almost linear maximum degree. arXiv:2106.11720 (2021).
- [Bo83] Bollob\'{a}s, B\'{e}la, Some remarks on packing trees. Discrete Math. (1983), 203-204.
- [Fi83] Fishburn, P. C., Balanced integer arrays: a matrix packing theorem. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1983), 98-101.
- [GyLe78] Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, A. and Lehel, J., Packing trees of different order into {$K\sb{n}$}. (1978), 463-469.
- [JKKO19] Joos, Felix and Kim, Jaehoon and K\"{u}hn, Daniela and Osthus, Deryk, Optimal packings of bounded degree trees. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS) (2019), 3573-3647.
- [JaMo24] Janzer, B. and R. Montgomery, Packing the largest trees in the tree packing conjecture. arXiv:2403.10515 (2024).

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
Claimed proof (preprint):
Parikshit Chalise, Antwan Clark, and Edinah K. Gnang posted “A Proof of the Tree Packing Conjecture” (arXiv:2410.13840; v2 dated 23 Oct 2024), which claims to prove Gyárfás’ Tree Packing Conjecture for all $n$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13840

High-level outline (as stated by the authors):
The paper introduces a reformulation of tree packing into $K_n$ via “augmented functional trees” and reduces the existence of an edge-disjoint packing of $(T_2,\dots,T_n)$ into $K_n$ to a “complete labeling” problem.
They define a “tree packing polynomial certificate” $P_g(X,y)=V(X)E_g(X,y)$ and (Proposition 3.4) relate existence of a complete labeling to a non-vanishing condition for a canonical representative of $P_g$.
A key step is the “Composition Lemma” (Lemma 3.10), asserting that the relevant non-vanishing property is preserved under a local composition operation; iterating this is used to reduce general instances to a star-based instance, yielding Theorem 1.9 and the main claimed result.

Status note:
This is a preprint; I have not found a refereed journal version or a widely circulated independent verification. There is community discussion about related “composition lemma” approaches here:
https://mathoverflow.net/questions/482509/claimed-proofs-of-graph-labelling-conjectures

Suggestion for this page:
It may be useful to add arXiv:2410.13840 as a reference (possibly marked “claimed proof / pending verification”), and update the open/solved status if/when a vetted confirmation appears.

problem: Let $\epsilon>0$. Does there exist $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that the lower density of $A+A$ is at least $1-\epsilon$ and yet $1_A\ast 1_A(n) \ll_\epsilon 1$ for all $n$?

- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
It is unclear from \cite{Er94b} whether Erd\H{o}s believed the answer to this should be yes or no. He also asked a similar question for upper density, for which he seemed more certain the answer should be yes.

He wrote that both he and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy believed that if $1_A\ast 1-A(n)\leq C$ for all $n$ then the upper density of $A+A$ is at most $1-\epsilon_C$, where $\epsilon_C>0$ may depend on $C$.

See also [28].

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Nice! Here is my interpretation of the argument. The main task is to solve the single scale problem: for a sequence of rapidly growing scales $M_j$, find finite sets $P_j$ in $[1,M_j]$ such that $P_j + P_j$ covers most of $[1,M_j]$ with bounded multiplicity. The final set $A$ will be the union of the $P_j$; this gives large upper density to $A+A$ but doesn't control lower density. To avoid the multiplicity from blowing up when combining the $P_j$ together, one also needs each $P_j$ to be somewhat well-separated; basically one needs each $P_j$ to have only bounded intersection with intervals of length $M_{j-1}$.

One takes $M_j$ to be a moderately large multiple of $p_j^2$ for a large prime $p_j$. Using a standard base $p_j$ type representation (actually it's more like base $2p_j$ to deal with some technical digit carry issues), one can reduce matters to a finite field analogue: find a subset $B$ of the finite plane ${\bf F}_{p_j}^2$ such that $B+B$ covers most of the plane with bounded multiplicity, and such that every horizontal line in the plane has bounded intersection with $B$. But this can be accomplished by taking $B$ to be the union of a bounded number of parabolas (this is a fairly standard trick in Sidon set type constructions; the argument here cites inspiration from a construction of Liang, Zhang, and Zuo).

In this construction, each scale $M_j$ behaves like the square of the previous scale $M_{j-1}$ (to avoid blowup in the multiplicity), so one only has quite a sparse set of scales for which one has good control on the density of the sumset. It seems the lower density problem remains quite challenging; I don't see an easy way to modify this construction to get good sumset density control at all scales (rather than a very sparse set of scales) while simultaneously keeping the multiplicity bounded when combining contributions from multiple scales. On the other hand, disproving the lower density version would also prove #28, which is a notorious open problem.

EDIT: A toy problem for the lower density version would be to solve a "two scale" problem. Suppose one has two scales $M_1 < M_2$ that are only slightly separated from each other, e.g., $M_1 = M_2 / \log \log M_2$. The challenge is then to find finite sets $P_1 \subset [1,M_1]$, $P_2 \subset [1,M_2]$ such that
 $P_1 + P_1$ has bounded multiplicity and occupies most of $[1,M_1]$;

 $P_2 + P_2$ has bounded multiplicity and occupies most of $[1,M_2]$;

 $P_1 + P_2$ also has bounded multiplicity.

One can use separate finite field constructions, using separate primes $p_1,p_2$, to achieve Goal 1 and Goal 2... but the problem is Goal 3. All known constructions would require the primes $p_1,p_2$ to be distinct from each other, and then there is no known way to "coordinate" the constructions to also achieve Goal 3 without assuming very wide separation between scales (e.g., $M_2 \gg M_1^2$). (Randomization can help - for instance if $P_1 + P_1$ only covers a positive density fragment of $[1,M_1]$, one can beef it up to cover a lot more of $[1,M_1]$ by adding in various random translates of $P_1$ - but trying to use random constructions to ensure bounded multiplicity of $P_1+P_2$ runs into the standard problem of picking up some logarithmic losses due to tail events in the concentration of measure bounds. Subrandom constructions are what are needed here.) In principle, if one can solve this toy problem (and various generalisations thereof) then there is a path to gluing everything together to get large lower density (or at least large density on a reasonably dense set of scales), but I doubt one can get a full solution to this problem without first addressing this toy problem.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I think I agree with this assessment. Using the heuristic that a long interval $[1,MN]$ behaves (for this sort of additive problem) like a Cartesian product of $[1,M]$ and $[1,N]$, one can view two similar scales $[1,M_1]$, $[1,M_2]$ as the Cartesian product of two widely separated scales $[1,L_1]$, $[1,L_2]$ with some common scale $[1,N]$, and one can then take a "Cartesian product" of constructions that work for the two component scales to get something that works for the combined scales. There are some technical issues due to "digit carrying" or "wraparound" ($[1,MN]$ is not *exactly* Freiman-isomorphic to $[1,M] \times [1,N]$) but this only causes some factor of 2 type losses in the constants, which is acceptable.

So this does technically solve the two-scale problem, but not in a way that allows for iteration, as there is still a large prime $p$ that is common to the construction at both scales. One still needs a way to gracefully transition from one prime to another as one keeps going up to larger scales without causing a large amount of collisions at the transition point. This is hard to model by something concrete like the two-scale problem though. Informally speaking one needs a construction where $P_1$ and $P_2$ are allowed to be fundamentally "different" at small scales, but this is hard to quantify rigorously. On the other hand the above constructions suggest that such transitions only have to occur relatively rarely - e.g., one such transition between one hyperdyadic scale $2^{2^j}$ and the next $2^{2^{j+1}}$. Outside of such transitions one may be able to re-use blocks and get a lot of other scales covered "for free" without making the number of collisions noticeably worse.

EDIT: One could try to re-use the same blocks (and same primes) indefinitely for arbitrarily large scales, but this would mean that eventually the construction would involve multi-level constructions where the number $k$ of levels is not something fixed like $1$ or $2$, but goes to infinity as the scale increases. Because of all the issues with digit carrying, I think all the constants here are going to grow exponentially in $k$, so this is not going to be sustainable indefinitely. The requirement that $1_A * 1_A$ stay bounded becomes quite challenging to satisfy when $A$ starts consisting of multiple components from multiple scales!

SECOND EDIT: Here is perhaps a proposed second toy problem. Instead of having two scales $M_1 < M_2$, have $K$ scales $M_1 < \dots < M_K$ where $M_k = M_1 (\log\log M_1)^k$ say, and $K$ is a medium-sized constant (and $M_1$ sufficiently large depending on $K$). The challenge is now to find $P_k \in [1,M_k]$ where $P_k + P_k$ occupies a decent fraction of $[1,M_k]$ (e.g., $\gg 1$ of this interval) with not just $1_{P_k} * 1_{P_k}$ bounded, but $1_{P_k} * 1_{P_{k'}} \ll 1$ for all $1 \leq k < k' \leq K$. But here is the new twist: the implied constants need to be independent of $K$. I could imagine iterating the previous construction to give something like this, but for which all the bounds grow exponentially in $K$. But to get to the full upper density result I think one will need uniformity in $K$.

One final note: if there is a power gap between scales, say $M_1 \leq M_2^{0.99}$, then standard probabilistic heuristics suggest that $1_{P_1} * 1_{P_2}$ will almost certainly be bounded. (One may need to replace the parabolas in the finite field construction by higher degree curves to get enough randomization for the probabilistic argument to be rigorous). So it is mostly about trying to understand the interaction of very close scales.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Great! This construction is similar to that in Ruzsa's paper (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01302934) (which I think is the origin for this kind of construction).

Indeed, Ruzsa constructs, for infinitely many $N$ (namely those of the shape $3p^2$ where $(\frac{2}{p})=-1$), a set $A\subset [1,N]$ such that $A+A$ contains the interval $[\frac{2}{3}N,\frac{4}{3}N]$, and $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\leq 288$ for all $n$. (These blocks have some further nice properties, like small intersection with other intervals, which your proof exploits but Ruzsa's paper does not explicitly record.)

To prove his $L^2$ bounded basis result Ruzsa then chooses a suitable lacunary increasing set of random shifts of such $A$; this gluing together of lacunary blocks is as in your construction. I suspect that this 'glue together random translates' trick would also be an alternative route to your upper density result.

As Ruzsa remarks 'if [the interval in $A+A$] were at the beginning (that is, if we had $A+A\supset [0,cN]$), then we could combine these sets to form a basis with bounded $1_A\ast 1_A(n)$'.

forum_comments.author: AronBhalla
forum_comments.text:
GPT 5.4 Thinking has located some relevant partial progress / nearby literature here:

1. Lower-density obstruction (Kiss–Sándor (2021)): for Sidon sets $A$, it is known that $d(A+A)=0$. This implies that $\underline d(A+A)=0$. So the problem is false in the strongest bounded-representation regime (essentially $1_A*1_A(n)\leq 2$, up to ordered/unordered normalisation).

2. Upper-density obstruction (Konstantoulas (2013)): if $\overline d(\mathbb N\setminus(A+A))<1/10$, then $1_A*1_A(n)>5$ for infinitely many $n$. Equivalently, if $1_A*1_A(n)\leq 5$ for all $n$, then $\overline d(A+A)\leq 9/10$. So one cannot get arbitrarily close to full upper density under the very small uniform bound $5$.

3. Nearby result (Ruzsa (1990)): Ruzsa constructed a basis $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ of order $2$ with representation function bounded in square mean: $\sum_{n\leq N}(1_A*1_A(n))^2=O(N)$. Since $A$ is a basis, $A+A$ has both lower and upper asymptotic density $1$. However, as this is an $L^2$-type result, this does not seem to bear directly on the $L ^ \infty$ question here.

forum_comments.text: Thanks - I was aware of 1 and 3, although I disagree that Ruzsa's result is strong positive evidence - there is a huge difference between $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ bounds; indeed, [28] says that for a genuine basis we cannot have $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\ll 1$.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
One remark in this direction: there seems to be a qualitative difference between posing this question for $1_A * 1_A$ and for $1_A * 1_{-A}$, despite these two functions having identical $L^2$ norms. Indeed, the analogous question for $1_A * 1_{-A}$ is false, even if one removes the obvious degeneracy at the origin. Sketch of proof: if $A+A$ has large lower density but $1_A * 1_{-A}$ stays bounded away from the origin, then easy counting arguments show that $|A \cap [1,M]| \asymp \sqrt{M}$ for all large $M$, and thus $|A \cap [\varepsilon M, M]| \asymp \sqrt{M}$ for some small $\varepsilon$. A further Cauchy-Schwarz then shows that for any $M^{1/2} \lll R \lll M$, the number of pairs $a,a' \in A \cap [\varepsilon M,M]$ with $1 \leq |a-a'| \leq R$ is $\gg R$. Summing over about $\log R$ many choices of $M$ and using the pigeonhole principle, we conclude that $1_A * 1_{-A}$ attains a value of $\gg \log R$ somewhere in $[1,R]$, a contradiction.

This also makes it less likely that finite field constructions can resolve these issues, as they are not all that great at distinguishing $1_A * 1_A$ from $1_A * 1_{-A}$. (For instance they can produce Sidon sets, for which both $1_A*1_A$ and $1_A*1_{-A}$ are as spread out as possible.)

computation:
- Built standalone local-search optimizer on finite windows \([0,N]\):
 - enforce cap \(r_{A+A}(s)\le R\) for all \(s\le 2N\),
 - maximize sumset coverage density over \([0,2N]\).
- Scanned multiple \((N,R)\) pairs with long search budgets.

- With strict caps \(R=3,4\), best finite densities are moderate (roughly 0.4-0.7 in tested windows).
- Relaxing cap to \(R=5,6\) improves finite densities (occasionally above 0.8), but still far from uniform near-1 behavior.
- Finite data reflects the core tension: stronger representation bounds noticeably suppress achievable coverage.
attempt: The finite attack treats the problem as an optimization tradeoff between two conflicting objectives on \([0,N]\): keep all representation counts uniformly bounded, while making \(A+A\) cover as much of the interval as possible. The local-search experiments show the expected tension very clearly, but they fall well short of the near-full coverage demanded by the conjecture, so the infinite problem remains open.

problem: Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a set of size $n$ such that every subset $B\subseteq A$ with $\lvert B\rvert =4$ has $\lvert B-B\rvert\geq 11$. Find the best constant $c>0$ such that $A$ must always contain a Sidon set of size $\geq cn$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/757.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
For comparison, note that if $B$ were a Sidon set then $\lvert B-B\rvert=13$, so this condition is saying that at most one difference is 'missing' from $B-B$. Equivalently, one can view $A$ as a set such that every four points determine at least five distinct distances, and ask for a subset with all distances distinct.

Without loss of generality, one can assume $A\subset \mathbb{N}$.

Erd\H{o}s and S\'{o}s proved that $c\geq 1/2$. Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s and Lehel \cite{GyLe95} proved\[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{141\cdot 76}\leq c\leq\frac{3}{5}.\](The example proving the upper bound is the set of the first $n$ Fibonacci numbers.)
Ma and Tang \cite{MaTa26} have improved these bounds to\[\frac{9}{17}\leq c\leq \frac{4}{7}.\]
References:
- [GyLe95] Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, Andr\'{a}s and Lehel, Jen\H{o}, Linear sets with five distinct differences among any four elements. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1995), 108-118.
- [MaTa26] J. Ma and Q. Tang, Largest Sidon subsets in weak Sidon sets. arXiv:2602.23282 (2026).

problem:
The cochromatic number of $G$, denoted by $\zeta(G)$, is the minimum number of colours needed to colour the vertices of $G$ such that each colour class induces either a complete graph or empty graph. The dichromatic number of $G$, denoted by $\delta(G)$, is the minimum number $k$ of colours required such that, in any orientation of the edges of $G$, there is a $k$-colouring of the vertices of $G$ such that there are no monochromatic oriented cycles.

Must a graph with large chromatic number have large dichromatic number? Must a graph with large cochromatic number contain a graph with large dichromatic number?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/761.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
The first question is due to Erd\H{o}s and Neumann-Lara. The second question is due to Erd\H{o}s and Gimbel. A positive answer to the second question implies a positive answer to the first via the bound mentioned in [760].

forum_comments.author: AronBhalla
forum_comments.text:
I think we can go further than just saying a positive answer to the second question implies a positive one to the first. In fact, the two questions are equivalent.

For the converse: $\zeta(G)\le \chi(G)$ for every graph $G$, since any proper colouring is a cochromatic colouring using only independent colour classes. Hence, if large chromatic number always forces large dichromatic number, then large cochromatic number also forces large dichromatic number. Indeed, if $\zeta(G)$ is large, then $\chi(G)$ is large, and so $G$ itself has large dichromatic number. Thus $G$ contains a subgraph with large dichromatic number, namely $G$ itself.

computation:
- Built finite proxy scans on small random graphs:
 - exact chromatic number,
 - exact dichromatic number for random orientations,
 - greedy cochromatic proxy.
- Used this to compare how quickly these parameters grow together in finite samples.

- For \(n=7,8,9\), average chromatic values are around 3.1 to 3.5, while average dichromatic values of random orientations stay around 1.6 to 1.9.
- In these samples, dichromatic number \(\ge 3\) did not occur, despite many graphs having chromatic number \(\ge 4\).
- Finite evidence suggests a substantial gap between chromatic and typical oriented dichromatic complexity at small scales.
attempt: The present approach is only comparative: compute chromatic, dichromatic, and cochromatic proxies on the same small random graphs and see how tightly they track one another. In the tested regime, dichromatic complexity lags well behind chromatic complexity, which is informative negative finite evidence, but it does not resolve either implication question.

problem: Let $c(n)$ be minimal such that if $k\geq c(n)$ then the $n$-dimensional unit cube can be decomposed into $k$ homothetic $n$-dimensional cubes. Give good bounds for $c(n)$ - in particular, is it true that $c(n) \gg n^n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/769.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem first investigated by Hadwiger, who proved the lower bound\[c(n) \geq 2^n+2^{n-1}.\]It is easy to see that $c(2)=6$. Meier conjectured $c(3)=48$. Burgess and Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er74b} proved\[c(n) \ll n^{n+1}.\]Erd\H{o}s wrote 'I am certain that if $n+1$ is a prime then $c(n)>n^n$.'

Hudelson \cite{Hu98} proved that if $(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ then $c(n) < 6^n$, and in general $c(n) \ll (2n)^{n-1}$. Connor and Marmorino \cite{CoMa18} proved that\[c(n) \geq 2^{n+1}-1\]for all $n\geq 3$,\[c(n) \leq 1.8n^{n+1}\]if $n+1$ is prime, and\[c(n) \leq e^2n^n\]otherwise.
References:
- [CoMa18] Connor, Peter and Marmorino, Phillip, Decomposing cubes into smaller cubes. J. Geom. (2018), Paper No. 19, 11.
- [Er74b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Remarks on some problems in number theory. Math. Balkanica (1974), 197-202.
- [Hu98] Hudelson, Matthew, Dissecting {$d$}-cubes into smaller {$d$}-cubes. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1998), 190--200.

problem:
Let $h(n)$ be minimal such that $2^n-1,3^n-1,\ldots,h(n)^n-1$ are mutually coprime.

Does, for every prime $p$, the density $\delta_p$ of integers with $h(n)=p$ exist? Does $\liminf h(n)=\infty$? Is it true that if $p$ is the greatest prime such that $p-1\mid n$ and $p>n^\epsilon$ then $h(n)=p$?

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
The following has been checked (a sanity check on the intuition below with data): among the smallest $20000$ primes $p$, there are $1278$ for which $\gcd(2^p-1,3^p-1)>1.$
So for $18722$ of them, we have $h(p)=3.$

Heuristically, the larger $p$ the larger the probability that $h(p)=1.$
This is since $\gcd(2^p-1,3^p-1)>1$ implies there is a prime $q=kp+1$ dividing both. There are fewer values of (even) $k$ for which these are prime (behaves like one over $\log(k)+\log(p)$...), and so fewer chances that both $2$ and $3$ are $k^{th}$ powers modulo $kp+1$.

Actually, the density of primes for which $h(p)=3$ should be one.
(the probability of failing can be estimated above by $\frac{1}{\log p} \left( 1- \frac{\pi^2}{24}\right)$ for every $p$)

Anyone who thinks this can be made rigourous?

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
General thoughts on the last problem:
for fixed $\epsilon>0$, $n$ large and $p<n^\epsilon$ the largest prime such that $p-1 \mid n$.
Assume that $2^n-1,3^n-1 \ldots, p^n-1$ are all multiples of a prime $r>p$.

Now $2,3,\ldots, p$ are all $k^{th}$ powers modulo $r$, where $k=\frac{r-1}{\gcd(r-1,n)}>2$.

If $r \le 2n$, this should be impossible since one expects only $\Theta(\log(n))<n^{\epsilon}$ many consecutive $k^{th}$ powers modulo $r$.
(see also the discussion and links at [stackexchange] (https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4513213/is-there-any-way-to-predict-the-largest-number-of-consecutive-quadratic-or-cubic))

If $r>2n$, then $\log_k(r) \le \log_k(kn+1)<\log_2(n+1)+1$ and the same estimate implies we do not expect this to happen.

(observation: We can exclude $k$ large, in terms of $\epsilon$, by considering the number of $n^{\epsilon}$ smooth numbers up to $n$.)

$\textbf{note about small values}$
for $n=4044, h(n)=17>13$ (largest prime such that $p-1 \mid 4044$)
Here $\log_{4044}{13}>0.3$ is reasonable big.
(but so we have to think as $n$ to be sufficiently large for every $\epsilon$)

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
Some thoughts on non-conditional proofs:
$\gcd(2^p-1,3^p-1) \not=1$ is possible when $2^p-1$ is not a prime, e.g. when $p=11.$
One may expect on the other hand that the chance that the gcd is not $1$ is somewhat small. A prime factor $kp+1$, where $k$ is even, can only occur if both $2$ and $3$ are perfect $k^{th}$ powers. ($\sum_{ 2 \mid k} 1/k^2 <1$).

Proving it for prime powers also looked an option.
E.g., if $n=5^k$, then $\gcd(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ whenever $k\le 10.$

Nevertheless, this fails for $k \ge 42$, since in that case $72*5^{42}+1$ is a divisor of both $2^n-1$ and $3^n-1$.

So there is likely no argument why it should work for all prime powers of another prime, e.g. $n=3^k$ for all k.

Showing that a certain pattern/ infinite subset among the many solutions exists, see [oeis/A263647] (https://oeis.org/A263647) for the first $10000$ values, may be hard or even impossible.

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
For the second question: so it is conjectured that $h(n)=3$ infinitely often.
Conditional on the assumption that there are infinitely many Mersenne primes, which seems to be widely believed meanwhile (see e.g. [wiki:Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_conjectures#Lenstra.E2.80.93Pomerance.E2.80.93Wagstaff_conjecture) and links for some conjecture on the counting function), this can be confirmed.

Let $q=2^p-1$ be a Mersenne prime.
Here $q=kp+1$ for some integer $k$.
We have that $q \mid 3^p-1$ if $3$ is a $k^{th}$ power modulo $q.$
But the $k^{th}$ powers modulo $q$ are exactly $1,2,2^2,2^3, \ldots,2^{p-1}$.
So $3$ is not among them.
We conclude that $\gcd(2^p-1,3^p-1)=1.$

problem: What is the size of the largest Sidon subset $A\subseteq\{1,2^2,\ldots,N^2\}$? Is it $N^{1-o(1)}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/773.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 24 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A question of Alon and Erd\H{o}s \cite{AlEr85}, who proved $\lvert A\rvert \geq N^{2/3-o(1)}$ is possible (via a random subset), and observed that\[\lvert A\rvert \ll \frac{N}{(\log N)^{1/4}},\]since (as shown by Landau) the density of the sums of two squares decays like $(\log N)^{-1/2}$. This upper bound was improved to\[\lvert A\rvert \leq N^{1-\frac{c}{\log\log N}}\]for some constant $c>0$ by Croot, Mao, and Yip (see the comments).

The lower bound was improved to\[\lvert A\rvert \gg N^{2/3}\]by Lefmann and Thiele \cite{LeTh95}.

In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s further defines $g(A)$ to be the maximal size of a Sidon set of $\{a^2 : a\in A\}$, and asks whether $g(A)\geq g(\{1,\ldots,N\})$ where $N=\lvert A\rvert$. (See [530] for the linear analogue.)

He further asks the infinite analogue: is there an infinite set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that $\lvert A\cap [1,N]\rvert \geq N^{1-o(1)}$ for all large $N$ and $\{a^2 : a \in A\}$ is a Sidon set?

See [1206] for a similar question for higher powers.
References:
- [AlEr85] Alon, Noga and Erd\H{o}s, P., An application of graph theory to additive number theory. European J. Combin. (1985), 201-203.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [LeTh95] Lefmann, Hanno and Thiele, Torsten, Point sets with distinct distances. Combinatorica (1995), 379--408.

forum_comments.author: ecroot
forum_comments.text:
My student Junzhe Mao and postdoc Kyle Yip had worked on this problem some, and then Junzhe made an advance on it, and we have a "proof from the book" upper bound.  This and other results will be included in a forthcoming paper we are writing. Below is a version of the argument, which was heavily inspired by Brandon Hanson's paper "Additive Correlation and the Inverse Problem for the Large Sieve". We didn't use AI for this work.

Basically, we have an upper bound of the form:
$$
|A|\ <\ N \exp \left ( - c {\log N \over \log\log N}\right ),
$$
for some $c > 0$.

Proof: We can assume $|A| > N^{1-\varepsilon}$, or else we are done. Let $r_{A-A}(n)$ denote the number of ordered pairs $a,a'\in A$, $a \neq a'$, such that $a-a' =n$. Note that if $A$ is a Sidon set, it implies that $r_{A-A}(n) = 0$ or $1$. Let $d$ be an integer that is a product of about $t = (1-2\varepsilon)(\log N)/ \log\log N$ primes in $[\log N, 2 \log N]$; and note that the Prime Number Theorem implies $d < N^{1-2\varepsilon+o(1)}$, so $|A|>d$. Let $A(r,d)$ denote the set of elements of $A$ that are $r$ mod $d$.

Now, $A$ is contained in the squares, and since the squares occupy $(p+1)/2$ residue classes mod $p$, for each prime $p \geq 3$, we have that $A$ can occupy at most $d(1+o(1)) / 2^t$ residue classes mod $d$. Using Cauchy-Schwarz we have
$$
\sum_{|n| \leq N^2 \atop d|n} r_{A-A}(n) = \left ( \sum_{r=0}^{d-1} |A(r,d)|^2 \right ) - |A| \gg {2^t |A|^2 \over d} - |A| > {2^{t-1} |A|^2 \over d},
$$
where the last inequality follows from the fact that $|A|>d$.

On the other hand, since $A$ is Sidon (implying $r_{A-A}(n) =0$ or $1$, recall), the first sum is bounded from above by about $2N^2/d$. So, we get
$$
{2N^2 \over d} \gg {2^{t-1} |A|^2 \over d},
$$
and the result follows.

forum_comments.author: ecroot
forum_comments.text:
Just thought I would mention one more thing. See this paper (Theorem 1.2):

 https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/rsa.20496

If the squares in $[N^2]$ behave like random sets of size $N$, then one would expect that the largest Sidon set contained within it has size about $N^{2/3 + o(1)}$. If so, then it means that improving the lower bound by finding a better construction is a fool's errand; and that what one *should* be doing is trying to improve the upper bound.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
I agree that if the squares act completely randomly this is the threshold, but I'd guess/hope that the squares do not act like a random set from this perspective.

Compare to the question of the largest Sidon subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ - a purely random construction only produces Sidon sets of size up to $\approx N^{1/3}$, but of course we know various clever algebraic constructions that do much better, $\sim N^{1/2}$.

I see no reason not to expect some similar clever algebraic trick that creates a large Sidon, that now interacts well enough with squares to work in this context.

forum_comments.author: ecroot
forum_comments.text:
I'd personally put 20% effort on improving the lower bound and 80% on the upper bound.

It's possible that the squares may "play nice" with some magic algebraic construction, but I'm pessimistic. The random model in that paper, by the way, does take into account magic sets like this, since it's the outer sets that are randomly chosen, and then inner set that gives the largest Sidon set is the one whose size it tries to predict -- and this one matches algebraic constructions.

It would interesting to try to come up with some nice algebraic or interesting quasi-algebraic set where the largest Sidon set inside it is larger than the random model would predict for a set of similar density -- in case the lower bound on #773 can be improved, yet the improvement is very hard to find. e.g. maybe something like the set of numbers that are the sum of two 4th powers, which seems like it might be close enough to being Sidon that all you need is a small tweak.

problem:
We call $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ dissociated if $\sum_{n\in X}n\neq \sum_{m\in Y}m$ for all finite $X,Y\subset A$ with $X\neq Y$.

Let $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set. We call $A$ proportionately dissociated if every finite $B\subset A$ contains a dissociated set of size $\gg \lvert B\rvert$.

Is every proportionately dissociated set the union of a finite number of dissociated sets?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/774.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 December 2025.
Site remarks:
This question appears in a paper of Alon and Erd\H{o}s \cite{AlEr85}, although the general topic was first considered by Pisier \cite{Pi83}, who observed that the converse holds, and proved that being proportionately dissociated is equivalent to being a 'Sidon set' in the harmonic analysis sense; that is, whenever $f:A\to \mathbb{C}$ there exists some $\theta\in [0,1]$ such that\[\| f\|_1 \ll \left\lvert\sum_{n\in A} f(n)e(n\theta)\right\rvert,\]where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$.

Alon and Erd\H{o}s write that it 'seems unlikely that [this] is also sufficient'. They also point out the same question can be asked replacing dissociated with Sidon (in the additive combinatorial sense) (see [328]). This latter question was resolved in the negative by Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il, R\"{o}dl, and Sales \cite{NRS24}.
References:
- [AlEr85] Alon, Noga and Erd\H{o}s, P., An application of graph theory to additive number theory. European J. Combin. (1985), 201-203.
- [NRS24] Ne\v set\v ril, Jaroslav and R\"odl, Vojt\v ech and Sales, Marcelo, On {P}isier type theorems. Combinatorica (2024), 1211--1232.
- [Pi83] Pisier, Gilles, Arithmetic characterizations of Sidon sets. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1983), 87-89.

problem:
Let $r\geq 2$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ be such that $A_i\not\subseteq A_j$ for all $i\neq j$ and for any $t$ if there exists some $i$ with $\lvert A_i\rvert=t$ then there must exist at least $r$ sets of that size.

How large must $n$ be (as a function of $r$) to ensure that there is such a family which achieves $n-3$ distinct sizes of sets?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/776.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Trotter. For $r=1$ and $n>3$ the maximum possible is $n-2$. For $r>1$ and $n$ sufficiently large $n-3$ is achievable, but $n-2$ is never achievable.

Let $n_0(r)$ be such that whenever $n>n_0(r)$ there exists such a family with $n-3$ distinct set sizes. He and Tang \cite{HeTa26b} (with ChatGPT) have proved that $n_0(2)=3$, $n_0(3)=8$, and for all $r\geq 4$\[2r+2\leq n_0(r)\leq 2r+2\log_2r+O(\log\log r),\]and hence $n_0(r)\sim 2r$ as $r\to \infty$.
References:
- [HeTa26b] Y. He and Q. Tang, An Erd\H{o}s--Trotter problem on antichains with multiplicity r on each occurring level. arXiv:2602.09803 (2026).

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
Thank you, Zach. This is a very good question, which generalizes the original Erdős--Trotter problem. For integers $\delta\ge 3$ and $r\ge 2$, we define\[
n_{0}^{(\delta)}(r):=\min\Bigl\{n_0:\ \forall\,n>n_0,\ g(n,r)\ge n-\delta\Bigr\}.
\]Then one can obtain the following conclusions (proofs can be found in this note (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/ep776-antichains-with-multiplicity/blob/main/To_Hunter_v1.pdf)):
1. If $\delta\ge 5$, then \(n_{0}^{(\delta)}(r)=O(\sqrt r)=o(r)\). In particular, the constant $C_{\delta}$ in your conjecture is $+\infty$.
2. When $\delta=4$, one can get a partial result: \(n_{0}^{(4)}(r) \ge \lceil \frac{r + 3}{3} \rceil\) for $r\geq 12$. Therefore, the constant $C_{4}$ in your conjecture lies in the interval $[1/2,\,3]$.

EDIT: I don't have a good guess for the specific value of $C_4$ at the moment, but I'm happy to hear your thoughts and discuss it further.

problem:
Alice and Bob play a game on the edges of $K_n$, alternating colouring edges by red (Alice) and blue (Bob). Alice goes first, and wins if at the end the largest red clique is larger than any of the blue cliques.

Does Bob have a winning strategy for $n\geq 3$? (Erd\H{o}s believed the answer is yes.)

If we change the game so that Bob colours two edges after each edge that Alice colours, but now require Bob's largest clique to be strictly larger than Alice's, then does Bob have a winning strategy for $n>3$?

Finally, consider the game when Alice wins if the maximum degree of the red subgraph is larger than the maximum degree of the blue subgraph. Who wins?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/778.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Malekshahian and Spiro \cite{MaSp24} have proved that, for the first game, the set of $n$ for which Bob wins has density at least $3/4$ - in fact they prove that if Alice wins at $n$ then Bob wins at $n+1,n+2,n+3$.

Similarly, for the third game they prove that the set of $n$ for which Bob wins has density at least $2/3$, and prove the stronger statement that if Alice wins at $n$ then Bob wins at $n+1,n+2$.
References:
- [MaSp24] Malekshahian, A. and Spiro, S., On a clique-building game of Erd\H{o}s. arXiv:2410.18304 (2024).

problem: Let $n> 1$ and $p_1<\cdots<p_n$ denote the first $n$ primes. Let $P=\prod_{1\leq i\leq n}p_i$. Does there always exist some prime $p$ with $p_n<p<P$ such that $P+p$ is prime?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/779.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Deaconescu. Erd\H{o}s expects that the least such prime is much smaller than $P$, and in fact satisfies $p\leq n^{O(1)}$. Deaconescu has verified this conjecture for $n\leq 1000$.

With the usual heuristic, we expect that $P+p$ is prime with 'probability' $\approx 1/\log P$, and hence the chance that this fails is $\ll (1-1/\log P)^{P-p_n}\ll \exp(-n^{-cn})$, using $P=n^{(1+o(1))n}$. As Cambie points out, 'the chances of failing are ridiculously small'.

problem: Do the squares contain arbitrarily long quasi-progressions? That is, does there exist some constant $C>0$ such that, for any $k$, the squares contain a sequence $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ where, for some $d$ and all $1\leq i<k$,\[x_i+d\leq x_{i+1}\leq x_i+d+C.\]Do the squares contain arbitrarily large cubes\[a+\left\{ \sum_i \epsilon_ib_i : \epsilon_i\in \{0,1\}\right\}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/782.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A question of Brown, Erd\H{o}s, and Freedman \cite{BEF90}. It is a classical fact that the squares do not contain arithmetic progressions of length $4$.

An affirmative answer to the first question implies an affirmative answer to the second.

Solymosi \cite{So07} conjectured the answer to the second question is no. Cilleruelo and Granville \cite{CiGr07} have observed that the answer to the second question is no conditional on the Bombieri-Lang conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Lang_conjecture).
References:
- [BEF90] Brown, T. C. and Erd\H{o}s, P. and Freedman, A. R., Quasi-progressions and descending waves. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1990), 81-95.
- [CiGr07] Cilleruelo, Javier and Granville, Andrew, Lattice points on circles, squares in arithmetic progressions and sumsets of squares. (2007), 241-262.
- [So07] Solymosi, J\'{o}zsef, Elementary additive combinatorics. (2007), 29-38.

problem:
Fix some constant $C>0$ and let $N$ be large. Let $A\subseteq \{2,\ldots,N\}$ be such that $(a,b)=1$ for all $a\neq b\in A$ and $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\leq C$.

What choice of such an $A$ minimises the number of integers $m\leq N$ not divisible by any $a\in A$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/783.
- Page status: SOLVED (database last update 2026-04-19).
- Page last edited: 11 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er73} suggests that, if $p_i$ is the $i$th prime, then choosing $A=\{p_r<\cdots<p_t\}$, where $p_t$ is the largest prime $\leq N$ and $r$ is minimal such that $\sum_{p\in A}\frac{1}{p}\leq C$ 'either gives the extremal sequence (or at least nearly gives the minimum)'.

Chojeckl has proved (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos783.pdf) this is the extremal sequence when $C\leq \log 2$.

Hunter in the comments notes that there are cases where this is not the literal extremal sequence, since small improving perturbations are possible. Tao suggests the problem (which is likely what Erd\H{o}s meant) of whether the minimum number of integers in $[1,N]$ not divisible by any $a\in A$ is\[(\rho(e^C)+o(1))N,\]which the construction above shows is achievable.

Hildebrand \cite{Hi87b} has proved that this weak form of the conjecture is true if $A$ is a set of primes (answering a question of Erd\H{o}s and Ruzsa \cite{ErRu80}).

Tao has resolved this (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos783-3.pdf) question (asymptotically at least), showing that the number of integers not divisible by any $a\in A$ is at least\[(\rho(e^C)+o(1))N,\]where the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $N\to \infty$ with fixed $C$.

See also [784] and [1200].
References:
- [Er73] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. A survey of combinatorial theory (Proc. Internat. Sympos., Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, Colo., 1971) (1973), 117-138.
- [ErRu80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Ruzsa, I. Z., On the small sieve. I. Sifting by primes. J. Number Theory (1980), 385--394.
- [Hi87b] Hildebrand, Adolf, Quantitative mean value theorems for nonnegative multiplicative functions. {II}. Acta Arith. (1987), 209--260.

There's a Saias' theorem that gives a better approximation for $\Psi$ that can push Terence's result from asymptotic to finite $N$ (this still doesn't solve the full problem, because we'd need full classification of minimizer sets). Here's a GPT-5.2 argument where to put it to upgrade the write-up by Tao (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos783-3.pdf):

For any \(N\ge 2\) and any cutoff \(y\in[2,N]\), let \(\mathbb P (y;N):=\{p\le N:\ p\ \text{prime},\ p>y\}\). Then an integer \(1\le n\le N\) is not divisible by any element of \(\mathbb{P}(y;N)\) if and only if \(P^{+}(n)\le y\). Hence the prime-tail sieve has the exact finite-\(N\) identity \(\sigma_{N}(\mathbb{P}(y;N))=\Psi(N,y)/N\), where \(\Psi(N,y):=\#\{n\le N:\ P^{+}(n)\le y\}\).

Given a harmonic budget \(C>0\), choose \(y=y(N,C)\) so that \(\sum_{y<p\le N}\frac{1}{p}\le C\) and \(y\) is maximal (or equivalently \(\mathbb{P}(y;N)\) is maximal under the constraint). Then \(\mathbb{P}(y;N)\) is admissible, so the finite-\(N\) minimax value \(\Sigma(N,C):=\inf\{\sigma_{N}(\mathbb{A}):\ \mathbb{A}\subseteq\{2,\dots,N\}\ \text{pairwise coprime},\ \sum_{a\in\mathbb{A}}\frac{1}{a}\le C\}\) satisfies \(\Sigma(N,C)\le \Psi(N,y(N,C))/N\) exactly. Tao’s argument inserts the Dickman approximation \(\Psi(N,N^{1/\mathrm{e}^{C}})\sim N\rho(\mathrm{e}^{C})\) to obtain \(\Sigma(N,C)=\rho(\mathrm{e}^{C})+o(1)\), but this uses only a first-order asymptotic for \(\Psi\).

Saias’ theorem upgrades the evaluation of \(\Psi(N,y)\) to a genuinely finite-\(N\) statement: for fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and in the range \(1\le u:=\frac{\log N}{\log y}\le \exp\{(\log y)^{3/5-\varepsilon}\}\), one has \(\Psi(N,y)=\Lambda(N,y)\bigl(1+O(\exp\{-(\log y)^{3/5-\varepsilon}\})\bigr)\), where \(\Lambda(N,y):=N\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\rho(u-v)\,\mathrm{d}(\lfloor y^{v}\rfloor y^{-v})\). In the Erdős regime \(y=N^{1/w}\exp(\theta/\log N)\) with fixed \(w>1\) and \(|\theta|=O(1)\), one has \(\log y\asymp\log N\) and \(u=w+O(1/\log^{2}N)\), so Saias applies uniformly and yields \(\Psi(N,y)=\Lambda(N,y)+O(N\exp\{-(\log N)^{3/5-\varepsilon}\})\). Therefore \(\sigma_{N}(\mathbb{P}(y;N))=\Lambda(N,y)/N+O(\exp\{-(\log N)^{3/5-\varepsilon}\})\), an error far smaller than any power of \(1/\log N\), and all boundary-layer sensitivity at scale \(N/(\log N)^{2}\) is captured by \(\Lambda\).

This improves Tao’s result on the “upper bound side” from an asymptotic evaluation of the prime-tail competitor to an essentially exact finite-\(N\) evaluation: \(\Sigma(N,C)\le \Lambda(N,y(N,C))/N+O(\exp\{-(\log N)^{3/5-\varepsilon}\})\), and one can optimize \(y\) within the boundary layer \(y=N^{1/w}\exp(\theta/\log N)\) by analyzing \(\Lambda(N,y)\) without worrying about analytic remainder terms. What remains open is the matching “lower bound side” at comparable precision: one would need a finite-\(N\) inequality showing \(\sigma_{N}(\mathbb{A})\) is bounded below by the same \(\Lambda\)-based expression (up to an error smaller than the boundary-layer scale), first for prime moduli and then uniformly through Tao’s reduction from coprime sets to primes.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
It turns out that one can use the existing results of Hildebrand (or Granville-Soundararajan) in the prime case to generalize to the arbitrary pairwise coprime case, as suggested in Section 6.1 of Chojecki's GPT 5.2 text; writeup here (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos783-1.pdf). The simplest case is when all the elements of $A$ are large. Then one can basically just move each element of $A$ (with a small number of exceptions) to the nearest available prime, and an analysis of the inclusion-exclusion / Bonferroni inequalities shows that this doesn't affect the size of the sieved set much (nor does it affect the sum of reciprocals by much either). (There is a simple argument (mapping each element of $A$ to its smallest prime factor) showing that $A$ can't be that much more dense than the primes, so it is relatively easy to move (most of) $A$ to be prime without incurring a large transport cost, thanks to the prime number theorem.)

One then has to deal with small and medium elements of $A$. By a standard pigeonholing argument (the "dyadic pigeonholing" trick of Bourgain (https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.06736)) one can assume that the medium elements have negligible size. For small elements one can use a sieve: the traditional thing to do here is invoke the fundamental lemma of sieve theory, but for this problem just the pure Brun sieve suffices actually (because we are happy with a qualitative error term $o(1)$). One can then replace the small elements of $A$ with an equivalent set of small primes that has almost the same Euler product.

The upshot is that the minimum size of the sifted set under the condition $\sum_{n \in A} 1/n \leq C$ and pairwise coprimality is indeed $(\rho(e^C)+o(1)) N$, without requiring the elements of $A$ to be prime, so that the Erdos construction is optimal up to $o(N)$ errors.

[The writeup, by the way, was written in the old-fashioned way, with the only AI assistance being autocomplete (which was a non-trivial speedup in this case, as Github Copilot did anticipate several lines of the argument in advance).]

forum_comments.author: OGO
forum_comments.text: Log-concavity of $\rho$ is established in Hildebrand's "On the Number of Positive Integers <x and Free of Prime Factors >y" (JNT, 1986). The proof of Lemma 1 explicitly establishes that $f(u):=-\rho'(u)/\rho(u) = -(\log \rho(u))'$ is strictly increasing in $(1,\infty)$. I've seen Lemma 1 being referenced to as a source for this fact. Essentially the same proof appears in p. 246 of his 1987 cited above as well (it's true that in both proofs he skips the full details of the standard induction step so the detailed proof is certainly worth having). An earlier, slightly weaker result, is established by Alladi in Lemma 4 of "The Turán-Kubilius inequality for integers without large prime factors" (Crelle, 1982).

problem:
Let $\epsilon>0$. Is there some set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ of density $>1-\epsilon$ such that $a_1\cdots a_r=b_1\cdots b_s$ with $a_i,b_j\in A$ can only hold when $r=s$?

Similarly, can one always find a set $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with this property of size $\geq (1-o(1))N$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/786.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 11 April 2026.
Site remarks:
An example of such a set with density $1/4$ is given by the integers $\equiv 2\pmod{4}$.

Selfridge constructed such a set with density $1/e-\epsilon$ for any $\epsilon>0$: let $p_1<\cdots<p_k$ be a sequence of large consecutive primes such that\[\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{1}{p_i}<1<\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{p_i},\]and let $A$ be those integers divisible by exactly one of $p_1,\ldots,p_k$.

For the second question the set of integers with a prime factor $>N^{1/2}$ give an example of a set with size $\geq (\log 2)N$. Erd\H{o}s could improve this constant slightly. Such an improvement is given by Tao in the comments, taking $A$ to be the set of all integers with exactly one prime factor $>N^{\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{e}}}$, which has size $\approx 0.8285 N$.

In \cite{Er65} Erd\H{o}s reports that Ruzsa proved the maximal size of such an $A$ is $\leq (1-c)N$ for some constant $c>0$ for large $N$, but the proof 'is not yet published'. It is presumably the following.

For any such $A$ we can define an associated additive function $f$ by letting $f(a_1\cdots a_r)=r$, and then $A=\{ n: f(n)=1\}$. A result of Erd\H{o}s, Ruzsa, and S\'{a}rkz\"{o}zy \cite{ERS73} then implies that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $N$, $\lvert A\rvert\leq (1-c)N$. In \cite{ERS73} they indicate that their method should be able to obtain this with $c=1/10$. In the comments Tao explains how a result of Granville and Soundararajan \cite{GrSo01} implies\[\lvert A\rvert\leq (1-c+o(1))N\]for an explicit constant $c\approx 0.1715$, and this is the best possible (see also [121]).

Theorem 2 from \cite{ERS73} also implies a negative answer to the first question, in that the density is at most $1/2$.

The above all assumes that repetition is allowed amongst the $a_i$ and $b_i$ in this condition. It is ambiguous in the original sources cited whether this was intended or not. If we insist the products are of distinct elements then this is a weaker condition on $A$, and the above questions are still open.

The formulation in \cite{Er80} is clear that repetitions are not allowed, but also claims that Ruzsa had shown the answer to both questions is no in this case (and that Ruzsa had shown that the upper density of $A$ is $<1/e$ if $A$ is infinite with this property); it is possible that Erd\H{o}s was mistakenly thinking of the above results, in which repetitions are allowed.

See also [421] and [795].
References:
- [ERS73] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Ruzsa, Jr., I. and S\'{a}rk\"ozi, A., On the number of solutions of {$f(n)=a$} for additive functions. Acta Arith. (1973), 1--9.
- [Er65] Erd\H{o}s, P., Extremal problems in number theory. Proc. Sympos. Pure Math., Vol. VIII (1965), 181-189.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [GrSo01] Granville, Andrew and Soundararajan, K., The spectrum of multiplicative functions. Ann. of Math. (2) (2001), 407-470.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
As long as one is in the regime where $r,s$ is much smaller than $N$ then there should not be much distinction as far as probabilistic arguments are concerned between sampling with repetition and sampling without repetition (they will be contiguous distributions). Sampling with repetition tends to be slightly easier to work with at a technical level, so I phrased the sketch of an argument there, but I do not foresee much difficulty in modifying it to sampling without repetition. But the current wording is ambiguous with regards to which variant is intended.

EDIT: I looked at the references for the problem (the [Er65] is p.182 by the way). None of the three references make it clear (they refer to products such as $\prod_{r=1}^{l_1} a_{i_r}$ without saying exactly what the $i_r$ are), but in nearby problems they talk about products of distinct elements, so I would be inclined to agree with the formal interpretation that each products is intended to consist of distinct elements. (Otherwise one could probably get some collision using a huge number of copies of each element on linear algebraic grounds.)

forum_comments.author: ebarschkis
forum_comments.text:
Agreed on contiguity for $r,s\ll N$. Just noting that my linear-algebra reduction idea would use powers $a^m$ as repeated factors, so it would apply to the multiset variant but not directly to the no-repetition variant.

EDIT: That is pretty much what my reduction idea basically does in the repetitions-allowed variant: any integer relation $\sum_i m_i v(a_i)=0$ yields $\prod_i a_i^{m_i^+}=\prod_i a_i^{m_i^-}$, and interpreting $a^m$ as $m$ repeats gives a collision with $r\neq s$ unless $\sum_i m_i=0$.
Hence repetitions-allowed forces $A\subset{n:F(n)=1}$ for a totally additive $F$, and ERS (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1973-16.pdf) then gives density $\le 1/2$ (and $|A\cap[1,N]|\le (1-c)N)$. So if the intended problem is open, I would think that strongly suggests the distinct-elements interpretation.

Of course, the no-repetitions variant is still a valid question, so I'll leave this open until both variants are settled, but I believe Erdős had mainly the repetitions-allowed variant in mind, and hence this problem was likely resolved in 1973.

I don't know of any better bound in either direction. The set $\{(-1)^{f(n)}=-1\}$ can have density at most $1/2$ by Wirsing's theorem (in fact the density can be computed exactly in terms of an Euler product) and this is sharp by considering the Liouville function (corresponding to $f = \omega$), but this set is only an upper bound for $\{ f(n) = 1\}$ and not a lower bound.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
If one takes $A$ to be the set of $n$ with exactly one prime factor greater than $N^{1/(1+\sqrt{e})}$, one gets a set of density $1-c+o(1)$ where
$$c = 1 - \log(1+\sqrt{e}) + 2 \int_1^{\sqrt{e}} \frac{\log t}{t+1}\ dt = 0.171500\dots$$
is the Hall-Montgomery constant (https://oeis.org/A143301); this is presumably what the "slight improvement of the constant $\log 2=1-0.3086\dots$" by Erdos optimizes to (see Theorem 9 of this recent paper of Fleiner et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12088) for a closely related calculation; Erdos's own calculation likely closely follows that in page 585 of this paper of Erdos, Sarkozy, and Sos (https://users.renyi.hu/~sos/1995_On_Product_Representations_of_Powers.pdf)). $A$ can also be defined as the set $\{ n \leq N: f(n)=-1\}$, where $f$ is the completely multiplicative function with $f(p)=-1$ if $p > N^{1/(1+\sqrt{e})}$ and $f(p)=+1$ otherwise. Corollary 1 of this paper of Granville and Soundararajan (https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9909190) shows that this is the best density one can get from such a completely multiplicative construction, and one can tentatively conjecture that this is in fact the optimal density for the second part of this problem. (A similar line of reasoning would lead to a predicted upper bound of 1/2 for the density in the first part of the problem, but I doubt that this would be sharp, as I do not think that constructions arising from completely multiplicative functions are the most important case here.)

A recent paper of mine (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11610) has a similar conjecture relating to #121. In the spirit of that paper, one might try to recover Ruzsa's result (i.e., answer the second part of this problem in the negative) by constructing some reasonably uniform probability measure on $\{1,\dots,N\}$ with the property that the probability of a collision $a_1 \dots a_r = b_1 \dots b_s$ for some suitable distinct $r,s$ is non-zero (with $a_1,\dots,a_r,b_1,\dots,b_s$ drawn independently using this probability measure), and also does not change much if one fixes any one of the $a_1,\dots,a_r,b_1,\dots,b_s$, so that one still gets collisions even if one conditions to an event of probability $1-o(1)$. As long as the probability measure is contiguous (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contiguity_(probability_theory)) with the uniform measure in the sense that events that occur with probability $1-o(1)$ in one measure, also occur with probability $1-o(1)$ in the other, this should recover Ruzsa's result.

Based on the above literature, it may also be worth considering as model problems variants of the problem in which density is not measure with respect to the uniform measure on $\{1,\dots,N\}$, but instead with the logarithmic measure (with each $1 \leq n \leq N$ having a density proportional to $1/n$), or a zeta distribution (with $n$ ranging over all natural numbers, but with density proportional to $1/n^s$ for some $s>1$). The limiting distribution of products such as $a_1 \dots a_r$ may be easier to analyze for such distributions, though the threshold densities will likely be different from the ones predicted above.

Neither of the two AI tools above picked up on this connection; this is a good reminder that such tools are not infallible, and should be used in conjunction with more traditional literature search methods, rather than serve as a complete replacement for them.
