problem:
Let $g(n)$ be maximal such that given any set $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=n$ there exists some $B\subseteq A$ of size $\lvert B\rvert\geq g(n)$ such that $b_1+b_2\not\in A$ for all $b_1\neq b_2\in B$.

Estimate $g(n)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/787.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
This function was considered by Erd\H{o}s and Moser. Choi observed that, without loss of generality, one can assume that $A\subset \mathbb{Z}$.

Klarner proved $g(n) \gg \log n$ (indeed, a greedy construction suffices). Choi \cite{Ch71} proved $g(n) \ll n^{2/5+o(1)}$. The current best bounds known are\[(\log n)^{1+c} \ll g(n) \ll \exp(\sqrt{\log n})\]for some constant $c>0$, the lower bound due to Sanders \cite{Sa21} and the upper bound due to Ruzsa \cite{Ru05}. Beker \cite{Be25} has proved\[(\log n)^{1+\tfrac{1}{68}+o(1)} \ll g(n).\]
References:
- [Be25] A. Beker, The Erd\H{o}s-Moser sum-free set problem via improved bounds for $k$-configurations. arXiv:2501.10203 (2025).
- [Ch71] Choi, S. L. G., On a combinatorial problem in number theory. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1971), 629-642.
- [Ru05] Ruzsa, Imre Z., Sum-avoiding subsets. Ramanujan J. (2005), 77-82.
- [Sa21] Sanders, Tom, The Erd\H{o}s-Moser sum-free set problem. Canad. J. Math. (2021), 63-107.

problem:
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that if $B\subset (2n,4n)\cap \mathbb{N}$ there exists some $C\subset (n,2n)\cap \mathbb{N}$ such that $c_1+c_2\not\in B$ for all $c_1\neq c_2\in C$ and $\lvert C\rvert+\lvert B\rvert \geq f(n)$.

Estimate $f(n)$. In particular is it true that $f(n)\leq n^{1/2+o(1)}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/788.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 26 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Choi \cite{Ch71}, who proved $f(n) \ll n^{3/4}$. Adenwalla in the comments has provided a simple construction that proves $f(n) \gg n^{1/2}$.

Hunter in the comments has sketched an argument that gives $f(n) \ll n^{2/3+o(1)}$. The bound\[f(n) \ll (n\log n)^{2/3}\]was proved by Baltz, Schoen, and Srivastav \cite{BSS00}.

In general, the argument given by Hunter shows that, if a random Cayley graph with probability $p$ has (almost surely) independence number $\ll p^{-c-o(1)}$, then $f(n) \leq n^{\frac{c}{c+1}+o(1)}$.

The work of Alon and Pham \cite{AlPh25} on random Cayley graphs therefore implies that\[f(n) \leq n^{3/5+o(1)},\]and the conjectured bound of $\leq p^{-1+o(1)}$ for the independence number would yield $f(n)\leq n^{1/2+o(1)}$.
References:
- [AlPh25] N. Alon and H. T. Pham, Random Cayley graphs and random subsets. arXiv:2509.02561 (2025).
- [BSS00] Baltz, Andreas and Schoen, Tomasz and Srivastav, Anand, Probabilistic construction of small strongly sum-free sets via large Sidon sets. Colloq. Math. (2000), 171--176.
- [Ch71] Choi, S. L. G., On a combinatorial problem in number theory. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1971), 629-642.

forum_comments.author: Neel Somani
forum_comments.text:
My colleague Johnny Yu has run this query on GPT 5.2 Pro that reduces this to a graph problem, then applies an existing result from Alon-Pham to produce a tighter upper bound: https://chatgpt.com/share/696e0e87-b834-8012-b0b1-cd9829fe3d21

They apply the Alon-Pham result (Theorem 4 (https://arxiv.org/html/2509.02561v1)) by constructing a graph $G_B$ of vertices $\{n, ... 2n\}$, then drawing an edge if $v_1 + v_2 \in B$. Then a set $C$ is "admissible" if $C$ is an independent set in $G$, where the best possible size of $C$ is $\alpha(G_B)$. So they try to minimize $\min_B(|B| + \alpha(G_B))$. This graph can be transformed into the same setting that Alon-Pham study, where they show that w.h.p. a full random Cayley sum graph $S$ has independence number at most $O(p^{2/3})$, where $|S|$ is typically $O(np)$. Solving for the optimal $p$ gives $|B|$ + $\alpha(G_B) << n^{3/5}\log(n)^{O(1)}$.

It doesn't solve whether $f(n) \le n^{1/2 + o(1)}$, but maybe worth updating the body of the problem to include this result.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks! In fact this is the same idea as given by Zach Hunter below, but taking advantage of the new independence number bounds by Alon and Pham (which came out after Zach posted his comment). Zach used the previous bound of $\alpha(G) \lesssim p^{-2}$, which balanced against $\ll pn$ yields $p\approx n^{-1/3}$ and hence $n^{2/3+o(1)}$. The better Alon-Pham bound has $\lesssim p^{-3/2}$, whence $p\approx n^{-2/5}$ and hence $n^{3/5+o(1)}$.

The conjectured bound of $\lesssim n^{1/2+o(1)}$ would follow from the conjectured truth about independence number of Cayley graphs (see conjecture 2 of Alon and Pham).

So the reduction to the graph theory problem here is not new, but thanks for pointing out the improved bound from the Alon-Pham paper.

I agree with Tao that it would be good (and presumably straightforward) to formalise this reduction, ideally with a result like 'the independence of the random Cayley graph $G(p)$ is $\tilde{O}(p^{-c})$ as an axiom, and then the formalisation would prove that this assumption implies an exponent of $\frac{c}{c+1}$ for this problem.

forum_comments.text:
I think it is likely that if one takes $B$ to be a random set of density $(\log n)^{100}/\sqrt{n}$, then whp $(C+C)\cap B$ is non-empty for all $C$ of size $\sqrt{n}(\log n)^{100}$. indeed, morally, we care about the independence number of the Cayley sum graph generated by $B$ (taking everything modulo $p$ for $p \sim n$). I believe this Cayley graph behaves essentially like a random binomial graph $G$ with the same number of vertices and edges (see: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09361 for such a result at a density of $1/\text{polylog}(n)$).

one can get an improved upper bound of $f(n) \le n^{2/3+o(1)}$, by considering random $B$ of density $\approx n^{-1/3}$. the point is that we get a $n^{2/3+o(1)}$-regular Cayley graph with eigenvalues of size at most $n^{1/3+o(1)}$ (see: Proposition 6' from https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/exp1.pdf). therefore by expander mixing lemma, any set of size $n^{2/3+\Omega(1)}$ should contain edges.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
The lower bound of $n^{1/2}$ is clear. Take any $B=\{b_1<\ldots<b_t\}\subset(2n,4n)\cap\mathbb{N}$ such that $|B|=g(n)$. Then, letting $2n=b_0$ and $4n=b_{t+1}$, we have $\max_{0\leq i\leq t}\{b_{i+1}-b_i\}\geq \frac{2n}{g(n)+1}$. Denote some $i\in\{0,\ldots,t\}$ that satisfies this as $i'$ and choose $C$ to be the interval $(\frac{b_{i'}}{2},\frac{b_{{i'}+1}}{2})\cap\mathbb{N}$. So $C\subset(n,2n)$ and $|B|+|C|\geq g(n)+\frac{n}{g(n)+1}-1\geq 2\sqrt{n}-2$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problem: Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that in any $A\subset \mathbb{Z}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=n$ there exists some sum-free subset $B\subseteq A$ with $\lvert B\rvert \geq f(n)$, so that there are no solutions to\[a+b=c\]with $a,b,c\in B$. Estimate $f(n)$.

problem:
Let $F(n)$ be the maximum possible size of a subset $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $a
mid bc$ whenever $a,b,c\in A$ with $a
eq b$ and $a
eq c$. Is there a constant $C$ such that\[F(n)=\pi(n)+(C+o(1))n^{2/3}(\log n)^{-2}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/793.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er38} proved there exist constants $0<c_1\leq c_2$ such that\[\pi(n)+c_1n^{2/3}(\log n)^{-2}\leq F(n) \leq \pi(n)+c_2n^{2/3}(\log n)^{-2}.\]Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er69} gave a simple proof that $F(n) \leq \pi(n)+n^{2/3}$: define a graph with vertex set the union of those integers in $[1,n^{2/3}]$ with all primes $p\in (n^{2/3},n]$. We have an edge $u\sim v$ if and only if $uv\in A$. It is easy to see that every $m\leq n$ can be written as $uv$ where $u\leq n^{2/3}$ and $v$ is either prime or $\leq n^{2/3}$, and hence there are $\geq \lvert A\rvert$ many edges. This graph contains no path of length $3$ and hence must be a tree and have fewer edges than vertices, and we are done. This can be improved to give the upper bound mentioned by using a subset of integers in $[1,n^{2/3}]$.

More generally, one can ask for such an asymptotic for the size of sets such that no $a\in A$ divides the product of $r$ distinct other elements of $A$, with the exponent $2/3$ replaced by $\frac{2}{r+1}$.

For further discussion and references concerning this generalisation to $r\geq 3$ see the comment by Wouter van Doorn.

See also [425].
References:
- [Er38] P. Erd\H{o}s, On sequences of integers no one of which divides the product of two others and on related problems. Tomsk. Gos. Univ. Ucen Zap. (1938), 74-82.
- [Er69] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some applications of graph theory to number theory. The Many Facets of Graph Theory (Proc. Conf., Western Mich. Univ., Kalamazoo, Mich., 1968) (1969), 77-82.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
There seems to be some missing details in the argument proving $F(n)\leq \pi(n)+n^{2/3}$ given in the description.
The statement "It is easy to see that every $m\leq n$ can be written as $uv$ where $u\leq n^{2/3}$ and $v$
 is either prime or $\leq n^{2/3}$," only holds for $n^{2/3} < p^2 \leq n$ if we can take $u=v$. However that would imply that we can take self-loops in the graph. Then the graph being a tree does not immediately imply that the number of edges is less than the number of vertices.

EDIT: I realise that if a vertex has a self loop, then it cannot have an edge with any other vertex. If $u$ has a loop and $uv$ is an edge in the graph then $u^2$ and $uv$ are in $A$, in which case $u^2|(uv)^2$. So the graph is a forest, where there may be isolated vertices with loops. Therefore the number of edges is less than the number of vertices.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
For a sufficiently large integer $n$, let $F_k(n)$ be the size of the largest set $A \subset \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ with the property that no $a \in A$ divides the product of $k$ others. Consider the bounds $$\pi(n) + \frac{c_k n^{2/(k+1)}}{\log^2 n} \le F_k(n) \le \pi(n) + \frac{C_k n^{2/(k+1)}}{\log^2 n}. \hspace{20pt} (1)$$Then Erdős stated in [Er69, p. 78] that even though he only had proved $(1)$ in [Er38] for $k = 2$, his method does extend to prove both inequalities for all fixed $k \ge 2$. No further details were given though. These general bounds were repeated in Problem E4 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

Skipping ahead to 2010, Chan, Győri and Sárközy (see here (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0195669809000614)) did not seem aware of Erdős' claim that his proof also works for larger $k$, and prove themselves that for all large enough $n$ and all $k$ with $2 \le k \le \frac{\log n}{6 \log \log n}$ the lower bound in $(1)$ holds with $c_k = \frac{1}{8k^2}$. They moreover show that the upper bound holds when $k = 3$, for some unspecified constant $C_3$. But they could not show the upper bound in $(1)$ in full generality.

A year later still, Chan (see here (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0195669810001721?via%3Dihub)) did prove that the upper bound in $(1)$ holds more generally, for all large enough $n$ and all $k$ with $2 \le k \le \frac{\log n}{6 \log \log n}$ where $C_k = ck^2$ for some absolute $c$.

Tsz Ho Chan, Ervin Győri, András Sárközy, On a problem of Erdős on integers, none of which divides the product of $k$ others. European J. Combin. 31 (1) (2010), 260-269.
Tsz Ho Chan, On sets of integers, none of which divides the product of $k$ others. European J. Combin. 32 (3) (2011), 443-447.

Both of the latter two references were found with the help of ChatGPT's Deep Research tool.

PS. Page numbers are [Er69, p. 77] and [Er70b, p. 136].

problem:
Let $k\geq 2$ and let $g_k(n)$ be the largest possible size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that every $m$ has $<k$ solutions to $m=a_1a_2$ with $a_1<a_2\in A$.

Is it true that\[g_3(n)=\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+(c+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}\]for some constant $c$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/796.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 16 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64d} proved that if $2^{r-1}<k\leq 2^r$ then\[g_k(n) \sim \frac{(\log\log n)^{r-1}}{(r-1)!\log n}n\](which is the asymptotic count of those integers $\leq n$ with $r$ distinct prime factors).

In particular the asymptotics of $g_k(n)$ are known; in \cite{Er69b} Erd\H{o}s discussed the second order terms, and this question is implicit (especially when compared to the explicit question [425] he asked on several occasions).

In \cite{Er69} this question actually appears with a denominator of $(\log n)^2$ in the second term. Furthermore, for $k=3$ he claims he could prove the existence of some $0<c_1\leq c_2$ such that\[\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_1\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}\leq g_3(n)\leq \frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_2\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}.\]This is strange, since in \cite{Er64d} both the upper and lower bound techniques that he used in fact prove\[\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_1\frac{n}{\log n}\leq g_3(n)\leq \frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_2\frac{n}{\log n}\]for some constants $0<c_1\leq c_2$. My best guess is that the denominator of $(\log n)^2$ in \cite{Er69} is just an unfortunate repeated typo, and $\log n$ was intended in both the reported bounds and the main question.

This correction is thanks to Tang, who noted independently (see the comments) the improved lower bound given above (indeed with an improvement in the constant $c_1$).

The special case $k=2$ is the subject of [425].
References:
- [Er64d] P. Erd\H{o}s, On the multiplicative representation of integers. Israel Journal of Mathematics (1964).
- [Er69] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some applications of graph theory to number theory. The Many Facets of Graph Theory (Proc. Conf., Western Mich. Univ., Kalamazoo, Mich., 1968) (1969), 77-82.
- [Er69b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results in chromatic graph theory. Proof Techniques in Graph Theory (Proc. Second Ann Arbor Graph Theory Conf., Ann Arbor, Mich., 1968) (1969), 27-35.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
I wrote a short note (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-796-note/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_796.pdf) showing that the asymptotic currently stated on this page cannot be correct.
In the note (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-796-note/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_796.pdf) I give an explicit construction proving\[g_3(n)\ge \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n} + (M+1+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n},\]where \(M\) is the Meissel--Mertens constant. In particular, this rules out any conjectural asymptotic of the form \(g_3(n)=\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n} + (c+o(1))\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}.\)

Motivated by this, a natural revised question is whether there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$,\[
g_3(n)\le \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+c\frac{n}{\log n}.
\]Finally, as discussed in Section 3 of the note (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-796-note/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_796.pdf), Erdős' bound in [Er64d] yields\[
g_3(n)\le \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+O\!\left(\frac{n}{(\log n)^{1+\delta}}\right)
\]for some $\delta>0$.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Aha, thanks! In fact this construction is very similar to that given by Erdős in [Er64d] when he proved the lower bound of the given asymptotic. That was just taking the set of all products of two primes $p<q$ with\[\frac{n}{\log n}<pq<n\]and\[(\log n)^2 < p < q^{1/4}.\]The number of such pairs Erdős records as\[(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}\]but, as you note, it's a classical fact that in fact it's equal to\[\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+(M+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}.\]Your construction is basically this (albeit a little simpler, taking advantage of fixing $k=3$), together with the set of all primes as well. But even just taking the product of two primes already gives a second order term $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$.

This makes the denominator of $(\log n)^2$ in the problem here strange, since Erdős' construction already disproved it. Perhaps this was a typo in [Er69]? Or maybe he'd miscalculated the asymptotics.

Also, there is something strange in that this two-primes construction lower bound also contradicts the\[g_3(n)\leq \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+O\left(\frac{n}{(\log n)^{1+\delta}}\right)\]upper bound you mention here. So is there also an error in this upper bound?

EDIT: Ah, yes, Erdős' proof actually gives an upper bound of\[g_3(n) \leq \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+O\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right),\]so he's wrong on the final page where he says the bound you mention. In Erdős' upper bound proof he early on discards those integers which may themselves be primes (which of course may contribute $\asymp \frac{n}{\log n}$ to the count). I think that his bound of $\frac{n}{(\log n)^{1+\delta}}$ is only for the error term after some initial pruning of $A$ (e.g. discarding elements of $A$ which are prime or a prime multiplied by a small integer). Looking at Erdős' upper bound proof I do wonder if just sharpening this up a bit would already give an asymptotic for the second order term.

forum_comments.text:

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks - the second part having $g_k$ rather than a $g_3$ is definitely just a typo on my part (indeed it's contradicted by the general asymptotic in the remarks!)

I agree that the question as I have written is implicit; I was trying to avoid simply stating Erdős' bounds and then asking 'can this be improved?'. Indeed, to be pedantic, Erdős never explicitly asked this or posed this as a problem; I just liked the result and wanted to include it on the site as a signpost to an area Erdős had thought about that still had some uncertainty (and would argue that he did implicitly pose this, or at least the case $k=3$, as a problem).

problem:
Define the anti-Ramsey number $\chi_S(n,e,G)$ as the smallest $r$ such that there is a graph with $n$ vertices and $e$ edges with an $r$-colouring of its edges in which every copy of $G$ has entirely distinct edge colours.

problem: Does there exist some $\epsilon>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there exists a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with at least $\epsilon n^2$ many edges such that the edges can be coloured with $n$ colours so that every $C_4$ receives $4$ distinct colours?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/810.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Graham, and S\'{o}s \cite{BEGS89}, who believed the answer is no.

Equivalently, if $\chi_S(n,e,G)$ is the anti-Ramsey number, the smallest $r$ such that there is a graph with $n$ vertices and $e$ edges with an $r$-colouring of its edges in which every copy of $G$ has entirely distinct edge colours, then this asks whether there exists an $\epsilon>0$ such that\[\chi_S(n,\epsilon n^2,C_4)\leq n\]for all large $n$. In \cite{BEGS89} they prove there does not exist such $\epsilon$ if we replace $C_4$ with $P_4$.

In \cite{BEGS89} they ask the stronger question as to whether, for fixed $\epsilon>0$,\[\chi_S(n,\epsilon n^2,G)/n\to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$ for all connected bipartite $G$ which is not a star. This was proved for all such $G$ except complete bipartite graphs by S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy and Selkow \cite{SaSe06}. It remains open in particular for $C_4$.

In \cite{BEGS89} they also observe that, for some constant $c>0$,\[\chi_S(n, cg(n;7,4),C_4)\leq n,\]where $g(n;7,4)$ is the maximum number of edges in a $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices in which no $7$ vertices contain $4$ edges. It is unknown whether (but likely) that $g(n;7,4)=o(n^2)$ (see [1178]).

See also [809].
References:
- [BEGS89] Burr, S. A. and Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R. L. and S\'os, V. T., Maximal anti-{R}amsey graphs and the strong chromatic number. J. Graph Theory (1989), 263--282.
- [SaSe06] S\'{a}rk\"ozy, G\'{a}bor N. and Selkow, Stanley, On an anti-{R}amsey problem of {B}urr, {E}rd\H os, {G}raham, and T. S\'os. J. Graph Theory (2006), 147--156.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
A negative answer to this problem implies the (finite field) Ajtai-Szemeredi theorem that for $d$ large, every dense subset of $F_2^d \times F_2^d$ contains a square $\{ (a,b), (a,b+r), (a+r,b), (a+r,b+r)\}$.. Indeed, if one could find a dense set $A \subset F_2^d \times F_2^d$ without squares, then one can form the bipartite graph joining $a \in F_2^d $ to $b \in F_2^d$ if $(a,b) \in A$, and color it by $a+b$; as no rectangle in $A$ is a square and we are in characteristic 2, this bipartite graph has all $C_4$s polychromatic and is dense, thus positively answering this problem.

By considering other coloring schemes than $a+b$, we see that a negative answer to this problem actually implies quite a lot of Ajtai-Szemeredi type theorems; only one of these has to fail in order to positively answer the question.

EDIT: the problem seems vaguely reminiscent of the recently popular topic of skew-corner-free sets. The problem is close to that of asking for $\gg n^2$ points in $\{1,\dots,n\}^3$ that do not contain a pattern of the form $(a,b,c), (a,b',c'), (a',b',c), (a',b,c'')$ (here the third component should be thought of as the "color" of the edge connecting the first two components).

forum_comments.author: msawhney
forum_comments.text: Thanks for clarifying my post! (This does seem very close to the $(7,4)$ problem; see https://yufeizhao.com/gtacbook/gtacbook.pdf.) Note that the $(7,4)$ problem with loss of generality can be assumed to be on linear hyper graphs; if four hyperedges intersect at an edges this given a $(6,4)$ configuration so an easy pruning argument reduces to a linear hyper graph. Given this linear hypergraph, one may take a random tripartition which preserves a positive density of the edges. It is then a question of how to divide the seven vertices among the three parts. Every part obvious has at least $1$ vertex; however any $(5,1,1)$, $(4,2,1)$ or $(3,3,1)$ would force the hypergraph not to be linear. The $(3,2,2)$ split is then almost exactly the problem mentioned except that we have a ''designated'' part for the $3$ instead of having the freedom where it is placed. Given this connection I expect the problem not to be particularly easy.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: Is this a formal implication? i.e. does a negative answer to this problem #810 imply a positive answer to the (7,4) problem?

forum_comments.author: msawhney
forum_comments.text: I believe so? To see this, consider a hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ with $n$ vertices and $\ge \varepsilon n^2$ hyperedges and suppose that is has no $(7,4)$ configuration. By reducing $\ \varepsilon \to \varepsilon/6$ (say) we may assume $\mathcal{H}$ is linear; this is due to the fact that if $4$ hyperedges all share a common pair of vertices this gives a $(6,4)$ configuration. Once $\mathcal{H}$ is linear we may then apply a random tripartition and get a $\mathcal{H}'$ which is tripartite with parts $A_1,A_2,A_3$ such that $|A_i| = n/3$ and $\mathcal{H}'$ has $\gg \varepsilon n^2$ edges. Define $G$ to be the $2$-graph between $(A_1,A_2)$ and define the coloring of $G$ by identifying by how a given edge extends into third part. A $3$-coloured $C_4$ in $G$ corresponds to a $(7,4)$ configuration in $\mathcal{H}'$ and hence in $\mathcal{H}$ as desired.

problem:
Suppose $n\equiv 1\pmod{m}$. We say that an edge-colouring of $K_n$ using $m$ colours is balanced if every vertex sees exactly $\lfloor n/m\rfloor$ many edges of each colours.

For which graphs $G$ is it true that, if $m=e(G)$, for all large $n\equiv 1\pmod{m}$, every balanced edge-colouring of $K_n$ with $m$ colours contains a rainbow copy of $G$? (That is, a subgraph isomorphic to $G$ where each edge receives a different colour.)
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/811.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 14 October 2025.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er91} Erd\H{o}s credits this problem to himself, Pyber, and Tuza. This problem was explored in a paper of Erd\H{o}s and Tuza \cite{ErTu93}. In \cite{Er96} Erd\H{o}s seems to suggest that this might be true for every graph $G$, and specifically asks specific challenge posed in \cite{Er91} and \cite{Er96} is whether, in any balanced edge-colouring of $K_{6n+1}$ by $6$ colours there must exist a rainbow $C_6$ and $K_4$.

In general, one can ask for a quantitative version, defining $d_G(n)$ to be minimal (if it exists) such that if $n$ is sufficiently large and the edges of $K_n$ are coloured with $e(G)$ many colours such that the minimum degree of each colour class is $\geq d_G(n)$ then there is a rainbow copy of $G$. Erd\H{o}s and Tuza \cite{ErTu93} proved that\[\lfloor n/6\rfloor \leq d_{C_4}(n) \leq \left(\frac{1}{4}-c\right)n\]for some constant $c>0$.

Axenovich and Clemen \cite{AxCl24} have proved that there exist infinitely many graphs without this property. In particular, they show that for any odd $\ell \geq 3$ and $m=\lfloor \sqrt{\ell}+3.5\rfloor$ there exist arbitrarily large $n$ such that $K_n$ has a balanced edge-colouring using $\ell$ colours which contains no rainbow $K_m$. They conjecture that $K_m$ lacks this property for all $m\geq 4$.

Clemen and Wagner \cite{ClWa23} proved that $K_4$ does lack this property.
References:
- [AxCl24] Axenovich, Maria and Clemen, Felix C., Rainbow subgraphs in edge-colored complete graphs: answering two questions by {E}rd\H{o}s and Tuza. J. Graph Theory (2024), 57--66.
- [ClWa23] Clemen, Felix Christian and Wagner, Adam Zsolt, Balanced edge-colorings avoiding rainbow cliques of size four. Electron. J. Combin. (2023), Paper No. 3.17, 3.
- [Er91] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and combinatorial number theory. Graph theory, combinatorics, and applications, Vol. 1 (Kalamazoo, MI, 1988) (1991), 397-406.
- [Er96] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite problems on cycles and colourings. Tatra Mt. Math. Publ. (1996), 7-9.
- [ErTu93] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Tuza, Zsolt, Rainbow subgraphs in edge-colorings of complete graphs. (1993), 81--88.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
The proof by Erdős combined with slightly more recent knowledge provides the required lower bound on $H(n)$ for infinitely many $n$, modulo the exact value of the constant $c$. Let me explain.

Let $\omega^*(n)$ count the number of primes $p$ such that $p-1$ divides $n$. By Proposition $10$ in this (https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/PDF/paper37.pdf) 1983 paper by Adleman, Pomerance and Rumely (see page $201$, or page $29$ of the pdf-file), there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that there are infinitely many $n$ with $\omega^*(n) > n^{c/\log \log n}$.

So let $n$ be a large enough integer for which $m > n^{c/\log \log n}$ primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_m$ exist with $p_i - 1 | n$. With $k < l = H(n)$ such that $\gcd(k^n-1, l^n-1) = 1$, we then must have that $kl$ is divisible by the product $p_1p_2 \cdots p_m$ due to Fermat's little theorem. By noting that this product $p_1p_2\cdots p_m$ is, by the prime number theorem, larger than $e^{2m}$ if $n$ (and therefore $m$) is large enough, we get
\begin{align*}
H(n) &> \sqrt{kl} \\
&\ge \sqrt{p_1p_2 \cdots p_m} \\
&> e^m \\
&> \exp[n^{c/\log \log n}],
\end{align*}as promised.

By the way, since $\omega^*(n)$ is at most the number of divisors of $n$, which is in turn upper bounded by $n^{(\log 2 + o(1))/\log \log n}$, it is tempting to think that the optimal $c$ could be $\log 2$. But I certainly have no idea and this is pure speculation.

since l=3 forces k=2.
Define for each prime p>3:
m_p:= lcm(ord_p(2), ord_p(3)).
Then the equivalent arithmetic form is:
H(n)=3 <=> n is not divisible by any m_p.
Reason: p | gcd(2^n-1,3^n-1) iff both orders divide n, i.e. iff m_p | n.

Conditional theorem (proved as reduction):
If the divisor-moduli family {m_p: p>3} is not a covering system of the positive integers
(equivalently: infinitely many n avoid all m_p), then H(n)=3 infinitely often.
So the infinitude problem is reduced to a covering-system question for {m_p}.

problem: Let $g(n)$ count the number of $m$ such that $\phi(m)=n$. Is it true that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there exist infinitely many $n$ such that\[g(n) > n^{1-\epsilon}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/821.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Pillai proved that $\limsup g(n)=\infty$ and Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er35b} proved that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that $g(n) >n^c$ for infinitely many $n$.

This conjecture would follow if we knew that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there are $\gg_\epsilon \frac{x}{\log x}$ many primes $p<x$ such that all prime factors of $p-1$ are $<p^\epsilon$.

The best known bound is that there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[g(n) > n^{0.71568\cdots},\]obtained by Lichtman \cite{Li22} as a consequence of proving that there are $\geq \frac{x}{(\log x)^{O(1)}}$ many primes $p\leq x$ such that all prime factors of $p-1$ are $\leq x^{0.2843\cdots}$ (which improves a number of previous exponents, most recently Baker and Harman \cite{BaHa98}).

The average size of $g(n)$ was investigated by Luca and Pollack \cite{LuPo11}.

See also [416].
References:
- [BaHa98] Baker, R. C. and Harman, G., Shifted primes without large prime factors. Acta Arith. (1998), 331--361.
- [Er35b] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the normal number of prime factors of $p-1$ and some related problems concerning Euler's $\varphi$-function. Quart. J. Math. (1935), 205-213.
- [Li22] J. D. Lichtman, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli and shifted primes without large prime factors. arXiv:2211.09641 (2022).
- [LuPo11] Luca, Florian and Pollack, Paul, An arithmetic function arising from {C}armichael's conjecture. J. Th\'{e}or. Nombres Bordeaux (2011), 697--714.

problem:
Let $h(x)$ count the number of integers $1\leq a<b<x$ such that $(a,b)=1$ and $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)$, where $\sigma$ is the sum of divisors function.

Is it true that $h(x)>x^{2-o(1)}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/824.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 September 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er74b} proved that $\limsup h(x)/x= \infty$, and claimed a similar proof for this problem. A complete proof that $h(x)/x\to \infty$ was provided by Pollack and Pomerance \cite{PoPo16}.

A similar question can be asked if we replace the condition $(a,b)=1$ with the condition that $a$ and $b$ are squarefree. Weisenberg suggests another variant, with the condition that there are no proper factors $u\mid a$ and $v\mid b$ such that $\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)$ and $(u,a/u)=(v,b/v)=1$, which is the weakest restriction one can impose that is still strong enough to eliminate trivial duplicates.

problem: Is there an absolute constant $C>0$ such that every integer $n$ with $\sigma(n)>Cn$ is the distinct sum of proper divisors of $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/825.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-01-31).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Benkoski and Erd\H{o}s. In other words, this problem asks for an upper bound for the abundancy index of weird numbers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weird_number). This could be true with $C=3$. We must have $C>2$ since $\sigma(70)=144$ but $70$ is not the distinct sum of integers from $\{1,2,5,7,10,14,35\}$.

Erd\H{o}s suggested that as $C\to \infty$ only divisors at most $\epsilon n$ need to be used, where $\epsilon \to 0$.

Weisenberg has observed that if $n$ is a weird number with an abundancy index $\geq 4$ then it is divisible by an odd weird number. In particular, if there are no odd weird numbers (see [470]) then every weird number has abundancy index $<4$. Indeed, if $l(n)$ is the abundancy index and $n=2^km$ with $m$ odd then $l(n)=l(2^k)l(m)$, and $l(2^k)<2$ so if $l(n)\geq 4$ then $l(m)>2$, and hence $m$ is weird (as a factor of a weird number).

A similar argument shows that either there are infinitely many primitive weird numbers or there is an upper bound for the abundancy index of all weird numbers.

See also [18] and [470].

This is part of problem B2 in Guy's collection \cite{Gu04} (the \$25 is reported by Guy as offered by Erd\H{o}s for a solution to this question).

This has been solved in the affirmative by Larsen (https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-825/blob/main/825.pdf) - in fact, for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $L$ such that if $n$ has only prime divisors $>L$ and $\sigma(n)>(2+\epsilon)n$ then $n$ is the distinct sum of proper divisors of $n$.
References:
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

problem: Does there exist a $k>2$ such that the $k$-sized subsets of $\{1,\ldots,2k\}$ can be coloured with $k+1$ colours such that for every $A\subset \{1,\ldots,2k\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=k+1$ all $k+1$ colours appear among the $k$-sized subsets of $A$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/835.
- Page status: VERIFIABLE (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 22 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Rosenfeld. This is trivially possible for $k=2$. They were not sure about $k=6$.

This is equivalent to asking whether there exists $k>2$ such that the chromatic number of the Johnson graph (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_graph) $J(2k,k)$ is $k+1$ (it is always at least $k+1$ and at most $2k$). The chromatic numbers listed at this website (https://www.win.tue.nl/~aeb/graphs/Johnson.html) show that this is false for $3\leq k\leq 8$.

Ma and Tang have proved (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-835/blob/main/On_Problem_835.pdf) that the chromatic number of $J(2k,k)$ is $>k+1$ for all $k>2$ not of the form $p-1$ for prime $p$.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks, looks good. I had a quick look and it's surprising how little literature there is on lower bounds for the chromatic number of Johnson graphs (there is a fair bit more on upper bounds).

You might like to think about whether your argument can be generalised to say anything about lower bounds for the chromatic number of Johnson graphs in general, or even more generally 'token graphs' (see e.g. Section 5 of this paper (https://link-springer-com.manchester.idm.oclc.org/article/10.1007/s00373-011-1055-9)).

It's annoying that you can't handle the case $k+1$ prime. Looking at the reason it's known for $k=4$, for example, this follows because the chromatic number of $J(6,3)$ is $6$ and hence the chromatic number of $J(7,4)\cong J(7,3)$ is also at least $6$, and so the chromatic number of $J(8,4)$ is also at least $6$. Perhaps a similar monotonicity trick would handle $k+1$ prime (e.g. if you can prove a lower bound of $k+3$ for all $k\neq p-1$ this would imply a lower bound of $k+2$ for all $k$).

PS - I appreciate the acknowledgement of this site, but please do also remember to cite the original paper(s) of Erdős as the actual source of the problem!

forum_comments.author: YaelDillies
forum_comments.text:
AlphaProof (on 2025-12-26) found a proof that $J(18, 9) \ne 10$, which was the first result we marked as open in formal-conjectures (albeit it was in fact not, see below).

Then we realised this proof could easily be adapted to work for all odd $k$ (on 2025-12-27) and Lean agreed. We even thought it could be generalised to all $k$ such that $k + 1$ is composite, but did not pursue this further as we simultaneously realised that Johnson's bound (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_bound) along with the independence bound on the chromatic number of a graph gives the same value (or even better sometimes).

Concretely, Johnson proved that the independence number of $J(n, k)$ is at most $A(n, 4, k)$, which is recursively defined by $A(n, 4, 1) = 1$ and $A(n, 4, k) = \lfloor \frac nk A(n - 1, 4, k - 1)\rfloor$ for $k > 1$. The lower bound on the chromatic number is then $\lceil \binom{2k}k/ A(2k, 4, k)\rceil$, which is at least $k + 2$ precisely when $k + 1$ is composite.

We thought to mention here that the result is in fact not novel, although it does indeed seem no one in the coding theory literature bothered to evaluate $A(2k, 4, k)$ in relation to this problem.

The original Alphaproof proof is here (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/commit/efbe1f0237ea2bbcac25b0eb338f7245f35b202a), the human-powered generalisation is there (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/commit/046b8b893873fd83f2e1b979a8b6ffb702a922d1), and the current state of the formal proof is in this PR to formal-conjectures (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/1428).

forum_comments.author: eigensolver
forum_comments.text:
The independence number of a Johnson graph $\alpha(J(n,k))$ is equal to the maximum number of codewords $A(n,4,k)$ in a binary constant-weight code of length $n$, weight $k$, and minimum distance $\ge 4$, which gives a lower bound for the chromatic number:
$$\chi (J(2k,k)) ≥ \dfrac{\binom{2k}{k}}{A(2k,4,k)}. $$
According to the bound table for $A(n,4,w)$ listed here (https://codes.se/bounds/cw.html), it can be concluded that the original proposition does not hold for $3\le k\le 14$. I also wrote a brute force program that extends this table using Theorem 9 from [AgVaZe00] (https://doi.org/10.1109/18.887851), verifying that such coloring does not exist for $k\le 500$ (except for $k = 16, 112, 256, 268$, where the lower bound is slightly weaker than $k+1$, with a difference ranging from $0$ to $1.14\times10^{-13}$). I believe that by slightly improving the recursive upper bound for $A(2k,4,k)$, it is hopeful to provide a complete proof.

Edit: Sorry for the earlier mistake in my code, it suffered from precision issues. After correcting them, I found that it indeed fails to handle the vast majority of cases where $k+1$ is prime, just as in the difficulty encountered by Tang. Moreover, [Jor25] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.15019) shows that this is already the best possible outcome obtainable from the recursive Johnson bound for $A(n, 4, w)$ (see 4.5 and 5.5). To fully resolve this problem, one may need to investigate the nonexistence of (a large set of) Steiner system $S(2k, k, k-1)$.

problem:
Let $r\geq 2$ and $G$ be a $r$-uniform hypergraph with chromatic number $3$ (that is, there is a $3$-colouring of the vertices of $G$ such that no edge is monochromatic).

Suppose any two edges of $G$ have a non-empty intersection. Must $G$ contain $O(r^2)$ many vertices? Must there be two edges which meet in $\gg r$ many vertices?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/836.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Shelah. The Fano geometry gives an example where there are no two edges which meet in $r-1$ vertices. Are there any other examples?

Erd\H{o}s and Lov\'{a}sz \cite{ErLo75} proved that there must be two edges which meet in $\gg \frac{r}{\log r}$ many vertices.

Alon has provided the following counterexample to the first question: as vertices take two sets $X$ and $Y$ of sizes $2r-2$ and $\frac{1}{2}\binom{2r-2}{r-1}$ respectively, where $Y$ corresponds to all partitions of $X$ into two equal parts. The edges are all subsets of $X$ of size $r$, and also all sets consisting of a subset of $X$ of size $r-1$ together with the unique element of $Y$ corresponding to the induced partition of $X$.

This hypergraph is intersecting, its chromatic number is $3$, and it has $\asymp 4^r/\sqrt{r}$ many vertices.
References:
- [ErLo75] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Lov\'{a}sz, L., Problems and results on {$3$}-chromatic hypergraphs and some related questions. (1975), 609--627.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
This may be a standard observation, but I do not see it in the remarks. It gives an explicit lower constant using the present best form of the Erdős--Szekeres theorem and a short entropy/double-counting argument.

I write all logarithms below in base $2$. By Suk's theorem, $ES(k)=2^{k+o(k)}$. Equivalently, every $T$-point set in general position contains a convex subset of size

$$
r=(1-o(1))\log_2 T.
$$

Let $P$ be an arbitrary set of $n$ points in the plane, with no three collinear. Choose uniformly a $T$-subset $R\subset P$, where

$$
T=\lfloor n^\alpha\rfloor,\qquad 0<\alpha<1.
$$

For each $R$, choose one convex $r$-subset $C(R)\subset R$. In entropy form,

$$
H(C(R))\ge H(R)-H(R\mid C(R)).
$$

Since

$$
H(R)=\log_2 {n\choose T}
$$

and, after $C(R)$ is known, there are at most ${n-r\choose T-r}$ possible choices for $R$, we get

$$
H(C(R))\ge \log_2 {n\choose T}-\log_2 {n-r\choose T-r}.
$$

Thus, if $N_r(P)$ denotes the number of convex $r$-subsets of $P$, then

$$
\log_2 N_r(P)\ge \log_2 {n\choose T}-\log_2 {n-r\choose T-r},
$$

or equivalently

$$
N_r(P)\ge { {n\choose T}\over {n-r\choose T-r}}
= { {n\choose r}\over {T\choose r}}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\log_2 N_r(P)
\ge r\log_2(n/T)-o((\log n)^2).
$$

Since $T=n^\alpha+O(1)$ and $r=(\alpha-o(1))\log_2 n$, this gives

$$
\log_2 N_r(P)
\ge (\alpha(1-\alpha)-o(1))(\log_2 n)^2.
$$

Optimizing at $\alpha=1/2$, every $n$-point set in general position determines at least

$$
2^{(1/4-o(1))(\log_2 n)^2}
$$

convex subsets. Hence

$$
f(n)\ge 2^{(1/4-o(1))(\log_2 n)^2},
$$

and so

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
{\log_2 f(n)\over (\log_2 n)^2}
\ge {1\over 4}.
$$

For comparison, the classical Erdős--Szekeres construction with $2^{k-2}$ points and no $k$ points in convex position gives, by taking $k=\lceil \log_2 n\rceil+O(1)$,

$$
f(n)\le \sum_{j<k}{n\choose j}
\le \left({en\over k}\right)^k
=
2^{(1+o(1))(\log_2 n)^2}.
$$

Thus the current simple bounds, with base-$2$ logarithms, are

$$
{1\over 4}
\le
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
{\log_2 f(n)\over(\log_2 n)^2}
\le
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
{\log_2 f(n)\over(\log_2 n)^2}
\le
1.
$$

With natural logarithms this becomes

$$
{1\over 4\log 2}
\le
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
{\log f(n)\over(\log n)^2}
\le
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
{\log f(n)\over(\log n)^2}
\le
{1\over \log 2}.
$$

problem: Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest quasi-Sidon subset $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where we say that $A$ is quasi-Sidon if\[\lvert A+A\rvert=(1+o(1))\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}.\]How does $f(N)$ grow?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/840.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 19 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Considered by Erd\H{o}s and Freud \cite{ErFr91}, who proved\[\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+o(1)\right)N^{1/2} \leq f(N) \leq \left(2+o(1)\right)N^{1/2}.\](Although both bounds were already given by Erd\H{o}s in \cite{Er81h}.) Note that $2/\sqrt{3}=1.15\cdots$. The lower bound is taking a genuine Sidon set $B\subset [1,N/3]$ of size $\sim N^{1/2}/\sqrt{3}$ and taking the union with $\{N-b : b\in B\}$. The upper bound was improved by Pikhurko \cite{Pi06} to\[f(N) \leq \left(\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{(\pi+2)^2}\right)^{-1/2}+o(1)\right)N^{1/2}\](the constant here is $=1.863\cdots$).

The analogous question with $A-A$ in place of $A+A$ is simpler, and there the maximal size is $\sim N^{1/2}$, as proved by Cilleruelo (https://matematicas.uam.es/~franciscojavier.cilleruelo/Papers/quasi-Sidon%20-%20greedy%20-%20solo%20A-A.pdf).

See also [30], [819], and [864].
References:
- [Er81h] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some problems and results on additive and multiplicative number theory. Analytic number theory (Philadelphia, Pa., 1980) (1981), 171-182.
- [ErFr91] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Freud, R., On sums of a Sidon-sequence. J. Number Theory (1991), 196--205.
- [Pi06] Pikhurko, Oleg, Dense edge-magic graphs and thin additive bases. Discrete Math. (2006), 2097--2107.

forum_comments.author: GTsoukalas
forum_comments.text:
Here is a summary of the proof, written by Adam Zsolt Wagner:

1. Label the vertices of the infinite complete graph with numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots$. These $x_i$ will be chosen to be a sequence that grows very quickly, to avoid accidental clashes in the following embedding.
2. We define the point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ as follows. For every edge $(x_i, x_j)$ of this infinite complete graph, we include the point $(x_i + x_j, x_i^2 + x_i \cdot x_j + x_j^2)$.
3. This embedding has the property that three edges form a triangle if and only if the corresponding points are collinear.
4. The resulting point set satisfies the condition of the problem with $\epsilon = 1/2$. Indeed, given $n$ points, they correspond to a graph with n edges. Every graph with n edges has a bipartite subgraph with at least $n/2$ edges. Such a subgraph is triangle-free, so it corresponds to at least $n/2$ points with no three on a line.
5. A subset of our points with no three on a line corresponds to a triangle-free subgraph of the infinite complete graph. By infinite Ramsey, whenever the edges of the infinite complete graph are finitely colored, one of the color classes contains a triangle. So we cannot cover our point set with finitely many sets with no three on a line.

problem:
Let $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set for which there exists some $\epsilon>0$ such that in any subset of $A$ of size $n$ there is a subset of size at least $\epsilon n$ which contains no three-term arithmetic progression.

Is it true that $A$ is the union of a finite number of sets which contain no three-term arithmetic progression?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/847.
- Page status: DISPROVED (database last update 2026-01-19).
- Page last edited: 27 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il, and R\"{o}dl.

A negative answer was given by Reiher, R\"{o}dl, and Sales \cite{RRS24}, who proved that, for any $0<\mu<1/2$, there exists $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that every finite colouring of $A$ contains a three-term arithmetic progression, and yet every subset of $A$ of size $n$ contains a subset of size $\geq \mu n$ without a three-term arithmetic progression.

See also [774] and [846].

- [RRS24] Reiher, Christian and R\"odl, Vojt\v ech and Sales, Marcelo, Colouring versus density in integers and {H}ales-{J}ewett cubes. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2) (2024), Paper No. e12987, 24.

problem: Is the maximum size of a set $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that $ab+1$ is never squarefree (for all $a,b\in A$) achieved by taking those $n\equiv 7\pmod{25}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/848.
- Page status: DECIDABLE (database last update 2025-10-19).
- Page last edited: 06 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy.

van Doorn has sent the following argument which shows\[\lvert A\rvert \leq (0.108\cdots+o(1))N.\]The condition implies, in particular, that $a^2+1$ is divisible by $p^2$ for some prime $p$ for all $a\in A$. Furthermore, $a^2+1\equiv 0\pmod{p^2}$ has either $2$ or $0$ solutions, according to whether $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ or $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$. It follows that every $a\in A$ belongs to one of $2$ residue classes for some prime $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}$, and hence, as $N\to \infty$,\[\frac{\lvert A\rvert}{N}\leq 2\sum_{p\equiv 1\pmod{4}}\frac{1}{p^2}\approx 0.108.\]Weisenberg has noted that this proof in fact gives the slightly better constant of $\approx 0.105$ (see the comments section).

This was solved for all sufficiently large $N$ by Sawhney in this note (https://www.math.columbia.edu/~msawhney/Problem_848.pdf). In fact, Sawhney proves something slightly stronger, that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that if $\lvert A\rvert \geq (\frac{1}{25}-c)N$ and $N$ is large then $A$ is contained in either $\{ n\equiv 7\pmod{25}\}$ or $\{n\equiv 18\pmod{25}\}$.

See also [844].

I've been working on Problem 848 and have what I believe is a complete verification, but I'd appreciate expert eyes on whether the argument holds up. Posting the full framework and results for review.

Disclosure: This work was prepared with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic, GPT-5.4 by OpenAI). All mathematical content and computational results have been verified by me. But still be cautious to potential mistakes here.

Approach: I developed an "outsider-clique framework" that partitions non-base-class elements ("outsiders") by least witness prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4), p ≥ 13. The key observation: for opposite-root cross-pairs a ≡ r, b ≡ −r (mod p²), the cross-product satisfies ab+1 ≡ 2 (mod p²), so p² never divides it. This constrains outsider clique structure enough to reduce the problem to checking a structured inequality:

s_max^(p)(N) + max(V_p⁺, V_p⁻) + d_max^(p)(N) + R_{>p}(N) < M(N)

at structural breakpoints, where s_max is the worst-case base exchange, V_p are root class sizes, d_max is the maximum cross-degree, and R_{>p} counts elements in higher root classes.

**What I've verified computationally:**
- C++ verifier (sieve-based bitmask architecture): 219 witness-prime blocks, 662,188 breakpoints, N = 1 to 10^7. Zero failures for N ≥ 7,307. Final margin at N = 10^7: 15,214 (worst prime p = 13).
- Independent Python verifier: 25,658 breakpoints, N = 5,000 to 500,000. Zero failures.
- Pair exchange analysis: for N ≤ 2,000, no single outsider or compatible outsider pair can match the base class.

**Where I believe the proof stands:**
- N ≤ 7,306: covered by layered exact computation (pair analysis + independent verifiers with overlapping ranges)
- N = 7,307 to 10^7: covered by the structured inequality verification (zero failures)
- N > 10^7: Sawhney's asymptotic theorem

**What I'm unsure about:**
1. Is the structured inequality (Proposition 4.1 in my write-up) actually a valid upper bound on |A| for any valid set containing a witness-p outsider? The argument is: base survivors ≤ s_max, p-block clique ≤ V + d_max, higher primes ≤ R_{>p}. Does this logic hold?
2. Is the breakpoint sufficiency argument correct; that checking only structural breakpoints (where M, V, or outsider population changes) suffices because LHS can only increase between breakpoints?
3. Is the N ≤ 7,306 coverage actually airtight given the overlapping methods?

Full proof write-up, verification source code (C++ and Python), and reproduction instructions are at: https://github.com/hjyuh/erdos

I'd be grateful for any feedback on gaps, errors, or unjustified steps. If this does hold up, the answer to Problem 848 would be TRUE for all N.

Some computer verifications indicate that the answer should definitely be yes, and even some stability should be true,
as one can expect (see the end).

For $N=25i+6$, there are at most $i$ elements in the set $A$.
Furthermore, these elements are then $\equiv \pm 7 \pmod{25}$.
So the two plausible sets are $A_7= \{n \mid n \equiv 7 \pmod{25} \mbox{ and }n \le N\}$ or $A_{18}= \{n \mid n \equiv -7 \pmod{25} \mbox{ and } n \le N\}.$
Note that if the question would be stated that $a,b \in A$ need to be different, the outcome is slightly different for small values of $N.$ E.g. $\{19,33,35,46,53\}$ is a valid set.

If one forbids the elements which are $\equiv \pm 7 \pmod{25}$,
the largest plausible sets are very small.
E.g. when $N=606$, a largest such set is $\{41,70,239,437\}.$
Actually, one can expect it to be attained for large $N$ by the elements which are $\equiv 70 \pmod{169}.$

Let $A_7, A_{18}$ as above, and $A'=\{n \colon n \le N \mbox{ and } p^2 \mid n \mbox{ for some } p>5\}.$
Then $A_7, A_{18}$ have each a density of $\frac1{25}$ and $A'$ an even lower density.
So, as observed by Wouter, any valid set $A$ is a subset of $A_7 \cup A_{18} \cup A'$.

If one has subsets $S_7, S_{18}$ and $ S'$ of resp. $A_7, A_{18}$ and $A'$, the condition that $ab+1$ is not square-free for $a,b$ from different classes put quite some unlikely conditions.
So one can indeed expect that one cannot do better than taking $A_7$ or $A_{18}$ (if if they are equally large).

problem: Is it true that, for every integer $t\geq 1$, there is some integer $a$ such that\[\binom{n}{k}=a\](with $1\leq k\leq n/2$) has exactly $t$ solutions?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/849.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er96b} credits this to himself and Gordon 'many years ago', but it is more commonly known as Singmaster's conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singmaster%27s_conjecture). For $t=3$ one could take $a=120$, and for $t=4$ one could take $a=3003$. There are no known examples for $t\geq 5$.

Both Erd\H{o}s and Singmaster believed the answer to this question is no, and in fact that there exists an absolute upper bound on the number of solutions.

Matomäki, Radziwill, Shao, Tao, and Teräväinen \cite{MRSTT22} have proved that there are always at most two solutions if we restrict $k$ to\[k\geq \exp((\log n)^{2/3+\epsilon}),\]assuming $a$ is sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon>0$.
References:
- [Er96b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some problems I presented or planned to present in my short talk. Analytic number theory, Vol. 1 (Allerton Park, IL, 1995) (1996), 333-335.
- [MRSTT22] Matom\"{a}ki, Kaisa and Radziwi\l\l, Maksym and Shao, Xuancheng and Tao, Terence and Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen, Joni, Singmaster's conjecture in the interior of {P}ascal's triangle. Q. J. Math. (2022), 1137--1177.

problem: Can there exist two distinct integers $x$ and $y$ such that $x,y$ have the same prime factors, $x+1,y+1$ have the same prime factors, and $x+2,y+2$ also have the same prime factors?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/850.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 September 2025.
Site remarks:
This is sometimes known as the Erd\H{o}s-Woods conjecture.

For just $x,y$ and $x+1,y+1$ one can take\[x=2(2^r-1)\]and\[y = x(x+2).\]Erd\H{o}s also asked whether there are any other examples. Makowski \cite{Ma68} observed that $x=75$ and $y=1215$ is another example, since\[75 = 3\cdot 5^2 \textrm{ and }1215 = 3^5\cdot 5\]while\[76 = 2^2\cdot 19\textrm{ and }1216 = 2^6\cdot 19.\](This example was also found independently by Matthew Bolan, and by Dubickas, who posed it as part of the 2024 team selection test in Lithuania.) No other examples are known. This sequence is listed as A343101 (https://oeis.org/A343101) at the OEIS.

Shorey and Tijdeman \cite{ShTi16} have shown that, assuming a strong form of the ABC conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture) due to Baker, then the answer to the original problem is no.

See also [677].

The case of $x,y$ and $x+1,y+1$ appeared as Problem 1 in the Third Benelux Mathematical Olympiad 2011.

This problem is discussed in problem B19 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Ma68] Makowski, Andrzej, On a problem of {E}rd\H{o}s. Enseign. Math. (2) (1968), 193.
- [ShTi16] Shorey, Tarlok N. and Tijdeman, Rob, Arithmetic properties of blocks of consecutive integers. (2016), 455--471.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
This looks like a viable strategy to me. One can prove Romanoff's theorem by computing first and second moments of the representation function $r(n) = \sum_{2^k+p=n} 1$; sieve theory only gets an upper bound for the second moment that is off by a constant, so one only gets positive density in this fashion. The GPT proof works with the representation function $R(n) = \sum_{2^k+m=n} 1$ where $m$ is constrained to not be divisible by any prime between $z$ and $x^{1/t}$ for some large constants $z,t$ (which implies that $m$ has $O_{z,t}(1)$ prime divisors for $n \leq x$). Sieve theory is capable of estimating first and second moments here to high accuracy (if $t$ is large), and there are no irregularities coming from small primes (because $z$ is large), so this will in principle give the desired $1-\varepsilon$ type density just from the fundamental lemma of sieve theory. (The average number of solutions here is $\asymp t \log z$, so well above $1$ and so Chebyshev's inequality has a good shot at getting the density close to $1$ if one can also hold the variance to $O(t \log z)$ as one would expect from Poisson heuristics.)

The proof should be streamlined and aligned with existing literature, preferably by a human expert, but this looks doable. Lean formalization might barely be possible with the existing sieve theory and other analytic number theory tools present in Mathlib and PNT+ but would be a non-trivial challenge. (I don't believe the fundamental lemma of sieve theory is in either repository yet, for instance.)

EDIT: There is surprisingly little work on this problem, given that Romanoff's theorem is very well known (78 citations on MathSciNet). The closest recent reference I could find is this 2024 paper by Zhao (https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO202405260120370.page), which focuses on counterexamples in an arithmetic progression (https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO202405260120370.page) for any fixed $r$ using the covering congruence method, but this problem of Erdos seems to have been completely overlooked in the literature. AI Deep research tools were surprisingly useless here: Claude (https://claude.ai/share/d9c6af06-fe26-43ad-9ed4-b6ef056719a4) and ChatGPT Deep Research (https://chatgpt.com/share/6984f8b0-a16c-800e-94fa-655511d4c959) both confused this problem with #205. Gemini DeepResearch (https://gemini.google.com/share/4f2585d7f088) did give an accurate summary of related results, though lacking some of the most recent results I found with more traditional literature search.

SECOND EDIT: I can now confirm that the proof is correct. After applying the fundamental lemma of sieve theory to estimate the first and second moments of $R$, the task boils down to showing that a singular series $\prod_{z \leq p \leq x^{1/t}: p | 2^k - 2^l} (1 + O(1/p))$ is close to $1$ on average after averaging over $k \neq l$. The condition $p | 2^k - 2^l$ can be rewritten as the condition that $k-l$ is a multiple of $\mathrm{ord}_2(p)$. Because of the very slow divergence of $\sum_p 1/p$, the only dangerous cases are those where $\mathrm{ord}_2(p)$ is of logarithmic size, but this occurs for very few primes $p$, because any Mersenne number $2^a-1$ can have at most $O(a)$ prime factors. (This is quantified in Lemma 7 of the AI-generated proof.)

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
GPT-5.5 Pro got a nice partial result showing (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos852.pdf) that\[
 h(x)\gg (\log x)^{1/3}.
\]The idea is this: we look at blocks of $H$ consecutive prime gaps whose total length is at most a constant multiple of $H\log N$. A positive proportion of starting positions have this property. If such a block has two equal gaps, then five explicitly related numbers must be prime:\[
 m,\quad m+a,\quad m+a+q,\quad m+b,\quad m+b+q.
\]For fixed $a,b,q$, the Selberg sieve (in a form proved by Lichtman--Teravainen) gives an upper bound of the expected order $N(\log N)^{-5}$, up to the singular series. Averaging the singular series over the three parameters $a,b,q$ then shows that the number of bad blocks is\[
 \ll \frac{NY^3}{(\log N)^5}
\]when all offsets are at most $Y$. Since in our application $Y\asymp H\log N$, this is smaller than the number of available starting positions as soon as $H$ is a sufficiently small multiple of $(\log N)^{1/3}$.

On the other hand, GPT-5.5 also noted that $h(x)= o(\log x)$ might be wrong if we assume a form of uniform Hardy-Littlewood conjecture and more likely something like $h(x)≤(C+o(1))\log x$ is plausible with a guess at possible asymptotics being
$$h(x) \sim 1.32323 \log x$$

forum_comments.author: DavidTurturean
forum_comments.text:
I am able to corroborate the findings, using a slightly different route. The writeup of what I have so far is at this Overleaf link (https://www.overleaf.com/read/tdpvnkrmqtvh#eaec5d).

Via a scaffold on top of ChatGPT-5.5-Pro that I ran yesterday, $h(x) \gg (\log x)^{1/3}$ comes out of a four-prime rectangle count: we again look at blocks of $H$ consecutive prime gaps whose total length is at most a constant multiple of $H \log N$, and a positive proportion of starting positions have this property.

If such a block has two equal gaps $d_i = d_j = a$ at positions $i < j$, set $p = p_i$ and $b = p_j - p_i$; then the four integers $p, p+a, p+b, p+a+b$ are all prime, arranged in a rectangle (or the degenerate triple $p, p+a, p+2a$ when $j = i+1$). This uses only four primes instead of five, so one averages over only two parameters rather than three. For $a, b \leq W$, the standard Selberg/Brun upper-bound sieve gives an upper bound of the expected order $N(\log N)^{-4}$ per pair, up to the singular series; averaging the singular series over $(a, b)$ using Gallagher's mean-value estimate, the number of rectangles is $\ll N W^2 (\log N)^{-4}$, with a smaller contribution from the degenerate triples.

Since each rectangle or triple lies in at most $H$ starting blocks, the number of bad small-span starts is $\ll x H W^2 (\log N)^{-3}$. Balancing this against the first-moment count $\ll xHL/W$ of large-span blocks yields $W \asymp (\log N)^{4/3}$ and bad count $\ll x H (\log N)^{-1/3}$: this is smaller than the number of available starts once $H$ is a sufficiently small multiple of $(\log N)^{1/3}$.

The same writeup derives the $1.32323$ constant explicitly. In the iid geometric-gap model with $q = e^{-2/L}$, a saddle-point calculation on the distinctness generating function gives $\log \Pr(H \text{ distinct}) = -L \cdot I_0(c) + o(L)$ with
$$I_0(c) = c + c \log\!\left(\frac{e^{2c}-1}{2c}\right) + \tfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{Li}_2(1 - e^{2c}),$$
expansion $I_0(c) = c^2/2 + c^3/18 - c^5/900 + O(c^7)$, and $c_0$ defined by $I_0(c_0) = 1$ is $1.32322827686395\ldots$.

On the conditional side, I have a hypothesis based on a strong (uniform) Hardy-Littlewood k-tuples conjecture on average, in lower-bound form with power-saving, combined with a parity-correct Bonferroni minorant identity (see write-up for details), that would imply $h(x) \geq (c - o(1)) \log x$. The rough idea is that passing from the iid model above to actual primes incurs a correction: primes avoid residue classes modulo small primes, so the model rate $I_0(c)$ must be replaced by $I_0(c) + J(c)$, where $J(c)$ is an odd-prime singular-series pressure coming from a Markov chain on the residue-class trajectories of prefix sums modulo each odd prime. For the conditional bound to give a block of length $cL$ with distinct consecutive prime gaps, one needs $I_0(c) + J(c) < 1$. The relevant fact is that $J$ has the explicit leading expansion
$$J(c) = C_* c^2 + O(c^3), \qquad C_* = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\prod_{p \geq 3} \left(1 + \tfrac{1}{(p-1)^3}\right) - 1\right) = 0.0752403861777\ldots,$$
so the combined rate $I_0(c) + J(c) = (\tfrac{1}{2} + C_*) c^2 + O(c^3) \approx 0.5752 \, c^2$ is strictly less than $1$ for all sufficiently small $c > 0$: this is then exactly what drives the conditional lower bound $h(x) \geq (c - o(1)) \log x$, and in particular rules out $h(x) = o(\log x)$.

I think it is interesting GPT-5.5-Pro was able to be elicited to give the same outcome, by quite similar methods, at about the same time, right after its release. Looks like a moderate step jump in the direction of analytic number theory from GPT-5.4-Pro. Unless it is shown that h(x) = o(log x) is highly tied to a notoriously difficult conjecture (granted, such as the first Hardy-Littlewood conjecture...), I am optimistic GPT-5.5-Pro itself can eventually resolve $h(x) = o(log x)$ in the negative.

forum_comments.author: AronBhalla
forum_comments.text:
I think this page would benefit from recording the best current bounds known for $h(x)$ for any future readers who may wish to make progress on this problem.

The best upper bound I could construct (with assistance from GPT 5.4) was to show that for every $\epsilon>0$ one has $h(x)\ll x^{0.41+\epsilon}$. I haven't thought too much about this (and I'm sure this can be improved), but in the absence of any recorded bounds, here is a sketch of that argument:

Let $H=h(x)$. Then for some $n<x$ the $H$ consecutive prime gaps $d_n,d_{n+1},\dots,d_{n+H-1}$ are pairwise distinct.

Consider $S:=\sum_{j=0}^{H-1} d_{n+j}^2$. Since $d_1=1$ and all other prime gaps are positive even integers, the smallest possible sum of squares of $H$ distinct prime gaps is at least $1^2+2^2+4^2+\cdots +(2H-2)^2\gg H^3$. Hence $S\gg H^3$.

Also, from the same distinctness observation, the sum of the $H$ gaps is at least $1+2+4+\cdots+2(H-1)=H^2-H+1$. But this sum is $p_{n+H}-p_n<p_{n+H}$, so using $p_m\ll m\log m$ one gets $H^2\ll (x+H)\log(x+H)$. In particular $H<x$ for all large $x$.

Now let $X:=p_{n+H-1}$. Since $n<x$ and $H<x$, we have $n+H-1<2x$ for large $x$, so $X\le p_{\lceil2x\rceil}\ll x\log x$.

Finally, $S\le \sum_{p_m\le X} d_m^2$, and Stadlmann’s Theorem 1 in this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10867) gives, for every $\eta>0$, $\sum_{p_m\le X} d_m^2\ll X^{1.23+\eta}$. Therefore $H^3\ll X^{1.23+\eta}\ll (x\log x)^{1.23+\eta}$, so $H\ll x^{0.41+\eta/3}(\log x)^{(1.23+\eta)/3}$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $0<\eta<3\epsilon$. Then for sufficiently large $x$, $(\log x)^{(1.23+\eta)/3}\le x^{\epsilon-\eta/3}$, so $H\ll x^{0.41+\epsilon}$.

Thus $h(x)\ll x^{0.41+\epsilon}$

problem:
Let $n_k$ denote the $k$th primorial, i.e. the product of the first $k$ primes.

If $1=a_1<a_2<\cdots a_{\phi(n_k)}=n_k-1$ is the sequence of integers coprime to $n_k$, then estimate the smallest even integer not of the form $a_{i+1}-a_i$. Are there\[\gg \max_i (a_{i+1}-a_i)\]many even integers of the form $a_{j+1}-a_j$?

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
$\textbf{Remark on different variant (not initial question)}$

If we would consider all differences of the form $a_i-a_j$, the answer becomes very different.
*if not excluding odd integers, the answer is 1 (this is also the case for the initial problem)
*if we are restricting to even integers, it is $(1-o(1))n_k$

If we denote $f(k)$ for the smallest positive even integer not of the form $a_i-a_j$,
then the right but harder question would be to estimate how large $n_k-f(k)$ is.
I could easily prove that this is $o(n_k)$ (e.g. bounded by $4n_{k-1}$), and with some work even that it is much smaller for large $k$.
Nevertheless, the right answer here should be $n_k-f(k)=(2+o(1))p_k$.

The lower bound for that is trivial.
Note that the sequence starts with $a_1=1, a_2=p_{k+1}, a_3=p_{k+2} \ldots$ (till $p_k^2$ appears at some point)
and $a_{\phi{(n_k)}+1-i}=n-a_i$.
Let $r$ be an odd composite prime smaller than $2p_{k+1}$, then $n_k-(r-1)$ cannot be written as $a_i-a_j$, since $a_{\phi{(n_k)}-1}-a_2$<$n_k-(r+1)$ and $a_{\phi{(n_k)}}-a_i=a_{\phi{(n_k)}+1-i}-a_1$ cannot be $r-1$, since $r$ is not a prime (and it is smaller than $p_k^2$).

The upper bound is not trivial (understatement)
Assumption (stronger form Goldbach's conjecture):
For an integer $q$>$0$, every even integer larger than some $2q+o(q)$ can be written as the sum of two primes larger than $q$.
It even may well be that the $o(q)$ is polylog(q).

Now take an even number (bounded by $n_k$) larger larger than $(2+o(1))p_{k}$,
this can be written as the sum $p_r+p_s$ with $r,s$>$k$ by the above assumption.
Now $p_r$ and $n_k-p_s$ are both relative prime with $n_k$ and thus of the form $a_i,a_j$.
Now $a_j-a_i=n_k-(p_r+p_s).$

From this we conclude.

For completeness, hereby also the easy proof (which can be sharpened, but not up to the right form)
By induction, for $k \ge 2$, and even $m$, does $m$ or $n_k-m$ appear as $a_i-a_j$. (base step $k=2,3$ trivial to check)

Now going to $n_{k+1}$, take an even number $m$<$n_{k+1}-4n_k$.
Let $m=r n_k + s.$
Then $s$ or $n_k-s$ appeared before as a difference.
If it is $n_k-s$, then write $n_k+a_i-a_j=s$.

Now $((r+v)n_k+a_j,vn_k+a_i)$ or $((r+v+1)n_k+a_i,vn_k+a_j)$ is a solution for some $v \in \{0,1,2\}$ since for each linear combination, only one $v$ can lead to a multiple of $p_{k+1}.$
So each such $m$ can be written as the difference of two numbers relative prime with $n_{k+1}$ smaller than $n_{k+1}.$

Summary
smallest even number not of the form $a_i-a_j$ is proven to be at most $n_k-4n_{k-1}=(1-o(1))n_k$
and conjectured to be $n_k-(2+o(1))p_k$.

computation:
Finite checks isolate a genuine counterexample to the older stronger conjecture and support the positive coverage direction.
- For \(k=6\), with \(P_6=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=30030\), the reduced residues have maximum consecutive gap \(22\), and the even gap values occurring up to \(22\) are
\[
\{2,4,6,8,10,12,14,16,18,22\},
\]
so \(20\) is missing.
- Therefore the historical claim that every even value up to the maximum gap occurs is false.
- Additional finite scans of primorial levels up to \(k\le 9\) and constructive witness checks for many \((k,t)\) pairs support the positive side: in all tested edge cases with \(4\le k\le 30\), the value \(t=k\) (or \(k-1\) when \(k\) is odd) was represented.
attempt: Two constructive results are established. First, for every fixed even \(t\ge 2\), one can choose congruences modulo the prime factors of \(P_k\) so that \(x\) and \(x+t\) are coprime to \(P_k\) while every interior point \(x+s\) with \(1\le s<t\) is forced to share a factor with \(P_k\); the Chinese remainder theorem then gives a represented gap \(t\) for all sufficiently large \(k\). Second, the same endpoint-interior forcing can be made uniform: for every \(k\ge 4\), every even \(t\le k\) occurs, and more generally every even \(t\le (2-\varepsilon)k\) occurs for all sufficiently large \(k\). As a corollary, the first missing even gap tends to infinity with \(k\). What remains open is the stronger quantitative comparison between the number of represented even gap sizes and the maximal gap.

problem: If $\pi(x)$ counts the number of primes in $[1,x]$ then is it true that (for large $x$ and $y$)\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/855.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-03-14).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Commonly known as the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_conjecture). In \cite{Er85c} Erd\H{o}s describes it as 'an old conjecture of mine which was probably already stated by Hardy and Littlewood'.

This is probably false, since Hensley and Richards \cite{HeRi73} have shown that this is false assuming the Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_conjecture). Indeed, assuming this conjecture, they prove that for every large $y$ there are infinitely many $x$ such that\[\pi(x+y)>\pi(x)+\pi(y)+(\log 2-o(1))\frac{y}{(\log y)^2},\]where the $o(1)$ term tends to $0$ as $y\to \infty$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er85c} reports Straus as remarking that the 'correct way' of stating this conjecture would have been\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+2\pi(y/2).\]Clark and Jarvis \cite{ClJa01} have shown this is also incompatible with the prime tuples conjecture.

In \cite{Er85c} Erd\H{o}s conjectures the weaker result (which in particular follows from the conjecture of Straus) that\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)+O\left(\frac{y}{(\log y)^2}\right),\]which the Hensley and Richards result shows (conditionally) would be best possible. Richards conjectured that this is false.

Erd\H{o}s and Richards further conjectured that the original inequality is true almost always - that is, the set of $x$ such that $\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)$ for all $y<x$ has density $1$. They could only prove that this set has positive lower density.

They also conjectured that for every $x$ the inequality $\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)$ is true provided $y \gg (\log x)^C$ for some large constant $C>0$.

In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s conjectures that\[\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+O\left(\frac{y}{\log x}\right)\]for every $x\geq y \gg (\log x)^C$ for some large constant $C>0$.

Hardy and Littlewood proved\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+O(\pi(y)).\]The best known in this direction is a result of Montgomery and Vaughan \cite{MoVa73}, which shows\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+2\frac{y}{\log y}.\]This is discussed in problem A9 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [ClJa01] Clark, David A. and Jarvis, Norman C., Dense admissible sequences. Math. Comp. (2001), 1713--1718.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [Er85c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On some of my problems in number theory I would most like to see solved. Number theory (Ootacamund, 1984) (1985), 74-84.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [HeRi73] Hensley, Douglas and Richards, Ian, On the incompatibility of two conjectures concerning primes. (1973), 123--127.
- [MoVa73] Montgomery, H. L. and Vaughan, R. C., The large sieve. Mathematika (1973), 119--134.

problem:
Let $k\geq 3$ and $f_k(N)$ be the maximum value of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$, where $A$ ranges over all subsets of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ which contain no subset of size $k$ with the same pairwise least common multiple.

Estimate $f_k(N)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/856.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 18 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er70} notes that\[f_k(N) \ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\]Indeed, let $A$ be such a set. This in particular implies that, for every $t$, there are $<k$ solutions to $t=ap$ with $a\in A$ and $p$ prime, whence\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{p<N}\frac{1}{p}< k \sum_{t<N^2}\frac{1}{t} \ll \log N,\]and the bound follows since $\sum_{p<N}\frac{1}{p}\gg \log\log N$.

Improved bounds have been given by Tang and Zhang \cite{TaZh25b}, who proved bounds of the shape\[(\log N)^{b_k-o(1)}\leq f_k(N)\leq (\log N)^{c_k+o(1)}\]for some constants $0<b_k\leq c_k\leq 1$, and in particular\[(\log N)^{0.438}\leq f_3(N)\leq (\log N)^{0.889},\]say, for all large $N$. The exponents here are related to progress in the sunflower conjecture [857], to which this problem is closely related. For example, the exponents $c_k$ are $<1$ (and so the upper bound above is non-trivial) if and only if [857] holds for $k$-sunflowers.

The analogous question with natural density in place of logarithmic density (that is, we measure $\lvert A\rvert$ in place of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$) is the subject of [536]. In particular Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er70} has constructed $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert \gg N$ where no four have the same pairwise least common multiple, and hence the interest of the natural density problem is the $k=3$ case.

A related combinatorial problem is asked at [857].
References:
- [Er70] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some extremal problems in combinatorial number theory. Mathematical Essays Dedicated to A. J. Macintyre (1970), 123-133.
- [TaZh25b] Q. Tang and S. Zhang, Harmonic LCM patterns and sunflower-free capacity. arXiv:2512.20055 (2025).

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
With GPT-5.4 Pro I've developped a weighted version of the Tang-Zhang sunflower-capacity argument that gives the exact estimate. The written note is here. (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos856-final.pdf)

The starting point is the same mass-transport idea that Liam Price emphasized in his recent Markov-chain discussion of [1196] (https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1196): after truncating to squarefree multipliers $q\le N$, one chooses $q$ with probability proportional to $z^{\omega(q)}/q$, so that the harmonic weight $1/a$ is transported to the endpoint $m=aq$ with density proportional to $1/m$. The admissible multiplier histories landing at a fixed endpoint form a $k$-sunflower-free family, and this yields a weighted upper bound involving the partition function $W_k(n;z)$.

This note requires a little bit of effort to parse, and I recommend it be rewritten (by a human). After unpacking the notation somewhat, it claims a proof that\[f_k(N)=(\log N)^{\gamma_k+o(1)}\]where $\gamma_k$ can be (if I'm parsing things correctly) defined as $\inf_{z>0}(\gamma_k(z)-z)$, where $\gamma_k(z)$ is minimal such that\[ \sum_{S\in \mathcal{F}}z^{\lvert S\rvert}\leq \gamma_k(z)^{(1+o(1))n}\]for all families $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ which contain no $k$-sunflowers. (Note, for example, that $0\leq \gamma_k\leq 1$ always; the determination of the value of $\gamma_k$ is still open.)

This is a generalisation of the sunflower capacity that appears in the work of Tang and Zhang - in particular $\gamma_k(1)=\mu_k^S$, the sunflower capacity that appears in their exponent.

I have not checked any of the details here, I just wanted to try and understand what the main claim was.

Hopefully this is within the capabilities of auto-formalisation tools.

In joint work with Shengtong, we wrote a paper on this problem (arXiv:2512.20055 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.20055)) and make precise its connection to [857].
Summary: Define the Erdős-Szemerédi $k$-sunflower-free capacity by \(\mu_k^{\mathrm S}:=\limsup_{n\to\infty} F_k(n)^{1/n}\), where $F_k(n)$ denotes the maximum size of a $k$-sunflower-free family of subsets of $[n]$. [857] (the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture) asserts that $\mu_k^{\mathrm S}<2$ for every $k\ge 3$. Our main results are:
(1) Equivalence. For each fixed $k\ge 3$, \( \mu_k^{\mathrm S}=2\) iff \( f_k(N)=(\log N)^{1-o(1)}.\)

(2) Lower bounds. $f_k(N)\ge (\log N)^{b_k-o(1)}$, where $b_k:=\max\{c_k, \log\mu_k^{\mathrm S}\}$ and $c_k:=\frac{k-2}{e((k-2)!)^{1/(k-2)}}.$

(3) Upper bound. $f_k(N)\ll (\log N)^{\mu_k^{\mathrm S}-1+o(1)}.$

As an illustration, when $k=3$ one has $\mu_3^{\mathrm S}\ge 1.551$ (a construction of Deuber--Erdős--Gunderson--Kostochka--Meyer) and $\mu_3^{\mathrm S}\le 3/2^{2/3}$ (Naslund--Sawin), hence\[
(\log N)^{\log(1.551)-o(1)} \ \le\ f_3(N)\ \ll\ (\log N)^{\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}-1+o(1)}.
\]Numerically, $\log(1.551)\approx 0.4389$ and $\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}-1\approx 0.8899$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

forum_comments.author: KoishiChan
forum_comments.text:
It is actually possible to improve this bound: for each $\ell$, note that for each $n$ the number of solutions to
$$n = a p_1 \cdots p_{\ell}$$
where $p_i$ are distinct primes and $a \in A$ is $O(k \log(\ell k))^{\ell}$. This is because, if we associate the set $\{p_1, \cdots, p_{\ell}\}$ with such a solution, then the set system cannot contain a $k$-sunflower. The best bound on the sunflower lemma yields this result.

Thus, we have
$$\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a}\sum_{n \leq N: \omega(n) = \Omega(n) = \ell} \frac{1}{n} \ll O(k \log(\ell k))^{\ell} \log N.$$
I think when $\ell = o(\log\log N)$ we have
$$\sum_{n \leq N: \omega(n) = \Omega(n) = \ell} \frac{1}{n} \geq \frac{1}{\ell!} \Omega(\log\log N)^{\ell}.$$
Hence the best choice of $\ell$ should be something like
$$\ell = \epsilon_k \frac{\log\log N}{\log\log\log N}$$
which yields
$$\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a} \leq \log N \cdot \exp\left(-\epsilon_k \frac{\log\log N}{\log\log\log N}\right)$$
where $\epsilon_k > 0$ is some constant depending on $k$.
