problem:
Let $m=m(n,k)$ be minimal such that in any collection of sets $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ there must exist a sunflower of size $k$ - that is, some collection of $k$ of the $A_i$ which pairwise have the same intersection.

Estimate $m(n,k)$, or even better, give an asymptotic formula.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/857.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Related to [536] and [856]. In \cite{Er70} Erd\H{o}s asks this in the equivalent formulation with intersection replaced by union.

This is sometimes known as the weak sunflower problem (see [20] for the strong sunflower problem).

When $k=3$ this is strongly connected to the cap set problem (finding the maximal size of subsets of $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ with no three-term arithmetic progressions), as observed by Alon, Shpilka, and Umans \cite{ASU13}). Naslund and Sawin \cite{NaSa17} have proved that\[m(n,3) \leq (3/2^{2/3})^{(1+o(1))n}.\]
References:
- [ASU13] Alon, Noga and Shpilka, Amir and Umans, Christopher, On sunflowers and matrix multiplication. Comput. Complexity (2013), 219--243.
- [Er70] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some extremal problems in combinatorial number theory. Mathematical Essays Dedicated to A. J. Macintyre (1970), 123-133.
- [NaSa17] Naslund, Eric and Sawin, Will, Upper bounds for sunflower-free sets. Forum Math. Sigma (2017), Paper No. e15, 10.

forum_comments.text:
I have been working on a fully formal Lean 4 development of the weak sunflower numbers M(n,3).

Exact values certified so far:

M(1,3)=2 through M(4,3)=8 are certified in Lean using native_decide, with both lower and upper bounds formalized.

M(5,3)=12 and M(6,3)=19 are certified via a SAT+LRAT bridge. The SAT encodings are generated from Lean, and the resulting LRAT certificates are verified independently.

M(7,3)=29 is certified via SAT+LRAT. At target size 30, four independent SAT solvers (CaDiCaL, Glucose4, MapleSAT, Lingeling) all return UNSAT, and verified LRAT certificates are included in the repository. The lower bound (existence at 29) is also formalized.

All proofs in the Lean development are sorry-free. Every result is verified locally by the Lean kernel using lake build, independent of any external service.

The SAT+LRAT certificates for M(5,3), M(6,3), and M(7,3) are fully reproducible and can be re-checked using any independent LRAT verifier without involvement from any language model.

Beyond exact values, the development includes:

A formally proved Local Turán-type inequality.

A formal statement of the Balance conjecture with low/high frequency case structure developed.

Pair-weight counting machinery for structured extremal arguments.

A reusable Lean-to-SAT pipeline with verified LRAT checking for combinatorial certification.

The development was carried out collaboratively with language models (primarily OpenAI Codex via Codex CLI and Anthropic Claude via Claude CLI) generating candidate proof attempts. However, all acceptance criteria were enforced locally: every theorem was only committed if the Lean kernel verified it without sorry. The Lean kernel is the ground truth; models generated candidates, and invalid attempts were rejected and rolled back.

Early in the project I made a single exploratory call to Aristotle to inspect how it would structure a Lean formalization; those example files remain in the repository. All substantive development was subsequently performed using Codex and Claude.

The SAT+LRAT results and Lean proofs are independent of any language model once generated; they are mechanically checkable artifacts.

https://github.com/SproutSeeds/sunflower-lean

problem: Let $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be such that there is no solution to $at=b$ with $a,b\in A$ and the smallest prime factor of $t$ is $>a$. Estimate the maximum of\[\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/858.
- Page status: SOLVED (database last update 2026-04-24).
- Page last edited: 24 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Alexander \cite{Al66} and Erd\H{o}s, S\'{a}rk\"{o}zi, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{ESS68} proved that if $A$ is an infinite set with this property then\[\sum_{n\in A\cap [1,N]}\frac{1}{n}=o(\log N)\](at a rate which depends on $A$), and furthermore for any fixed large $N$ the supremum in this question is bounded away from $0$.

This condition on $A$ is a weaker form of the usual primitive condition. If $A$ is primitive then Behrend \cite{Be35} proved\[\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{1}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}.\]An example of such a set $A$ is the set of all integers in $[N^{1/2},N]$ divisible by some prime $>N^{1/2}$.

This has been solved (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos858-asymptotic.pdf) by Chojecki and GPT-5.4 Pro (see the comments), who show that for large $N$\[\max_A \sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}=(c+o(1))\log N\]where the maximum is over all $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with the stated property and $c\approx 0.618\cdots$ is an explicit constant.

See also [143].
References:
- [Al66] Alexander, Ralph, Density and multiplicative structure of sets of integers. Acta Arith. (1966/67), 321--332.
- [Be35] Behrend, F., On sequences of numbers not divisible by another. London Math. Soc. Journal (1935), 42-45.
- [ESS68] Erd\H{o}s, P. and S\'{a}rk\"ozi, A. and Szemer\'{e}di, E., On the solvability of certain equations in sequences of positive upper logarithmic density. J. London Math. Soc. (1968), 71--78.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Here is a summary of the argument. One places a flow network on $\{1,\dots,N\}$ by creating a flow $w( n p_1 \dots p_k \mapsto n ) = \frac{1}{n p_1 \dots p_k}$ if $n < p_1 \leq \dots \leq p_k$, but one does not have $n p_1 \dots p_{i-1} < p_i$ for any $1 < i \leq k$. Then the outflow at any $1 < n \leq N$ is exactly $1/n$ (with only one outgoing edge), and the downward flow from any $n \in A$ cannot hit any other element of $A$ by hypothesis. Because of this, one can use the discrete divergence theorem to express $\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n}$ as the sum of divergences $\sum_{n \in U_A} \mathrm{div}(v)$, where $U_A$ is the upset associated to $A$ (all the elements of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ that flow down to an element of $A$).

Routine Mertens' theorem calculations show that the divergence is positive (more outflow than inflow) for $n > N^{\alpha_2+o(1)}$ and negative (more inflow than outflow) for $n < N^{\alpha_2-o(1)}$ for a certain explicit constant $\alpha_2 = 0.28043830989\dots$. From this the optimal $A$ is essentially those elements above $N^{\alpha_2}$ that flow down to an element below $N^{\alpha_2}$. The total outflow $\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n}$ can then be computed to be $(c_2+o(1)) \log N$ for an explicit constant $c_2 = 0.6187712111\dots$.

forum_comments.text: The result in [Al66] and [ESS68] isn't stated quite correctly here (it would contradict both the example listed later in the commentary, and the sharper result of Chojecki). What they show is that if $A$ is an infinite set with the stated property then $\lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{\log N} \sum_{n \in A: n \leq N} \frac{1}{n} = 0$, but the convergence is non-uniform in $A$, and indeed the supremum $\sup_A \frac{1}{\log N} \sum_{n \in A: n \leq N} \frac{1}{n}$ stays bounded away from zero.

problem:
Let $r\geq 2$ and let $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a set of maximal size such that there are at most $r$ solutions to $n=a+b$ with $a\leq b$ for any $n$. (That is, $A$ is a $B_2[r]$ set.)

Similarly, let $B\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a set of maximal size such that there are at most $r$ solutions to $n=a-b$ for any $n\geq 1$.

If $\lvert A\rvert\sim c_rN^{1/2}$ as $N\to \infty$ and $\lvert B\rvert \sim c_r'N^{1/2}$ as $N\to \infty$ then is it true that $c_r\neq c_r'$ for $r\geq 2$? Is it true that $c_r'<c_r$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/863.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-04-24).
- Page last edited: 24 April 2026.
Site remarks:
According to Erd\H{o}s, first formulated in conversation with Berend, and later independently reformulated with Freud.

It is true that $c_1=c_1'$, and the classical bound on the size of Sidon sets (see [30]) implies $c_1=c_1'=1$.

Ho and GPT-5.4 Pro have noted (https://boonsuan.github.io/erdos863.pdf) that a positive solution follows from arguments in the literature. Indeed, a routine adaptation of the Erd\H{o}s-Tu\'{a}n bound for Sidon sets proves that\[\lvert B\rvert\leq (\sqrt{r}+o(1))N^{1/2},\]while Cilleruelo, Ruzsa, and Trujilo \cite{CRT02} have constructed $A$ with\[\lvert A\rvert \geq \left(\frac{r+\lfloor r/2\rfloor}{\sqrt{r+2\lfloor r/2\rfloor}}\right) N^{1/2}.\]Therefore, provided $r\geq 2$,\[c_r'\leq \sqrt{r}<\frac{r+\lfloor r/2\rfloor}{\sqrt{r+2\lfloor r/2\rfloor}}\leq c_r.\](For example, when $r=2$ these give $c_r'\leq \sqrt{2}\approx 1.41$ and $c_r\geq 3/2=1.5$.)
References:
- [CRT02] Cilleruelo, Javier and Ruzsa, Imre Z. and Trujillo, Carlos, Upper and lower bounds for finite {$B_h[g]$} sequences. J. Number Theory (2002), 26--34.

problem: There exists a constant $C>0$ such that, for all large $N$, if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has size at least $\frac{5}{8}N+C$ then there are distinct $a,b,c\in A$ such that $a+b,a+c,b+c\in A$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/865.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and S\'{o}s (also earlier considered by Choi, Erd\H{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{CES75}, but Erd\H{o}s had forgotten this). Taking all integers in $[N/8,N/4]$ and $[N/2,N]$ shows that $\frac{5}{8}$ would be best possible here.

It is a classical folklore fact that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,2N\}$ has size $\geq N+2$ then there are distinct $a,b\in A$ such that $a+b\in A$, which establishes the $k=2$ case.

In general, one can define $f_k(N)$ to be minimal such that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has size at least $f_k(N)$ then there are $k$ distinct $a_i\in A$ such that all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise sums are elements of $A$. Erd\H{o}s and S\'{o}s conjectured that\[f_k(N)\sim \frac{1}{2}\left(1+\sum_{1\leq r\leq k-2}\frac{1}{4^r}\right) N,\]and a similar example shows that this would be best possible.

Choi, Erd\H{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{CES75} have proved that, for all $k\geq 3$, there exists $\epsilon_k>0$ such that (for large enough $N$)\[f_k(N)\leq \left(\frac{2}{3}-\epsilon_k\right)N.\]
References:
- [CES75] Choi, S. L. G. and Erd\H{o}s, P. and Szemer\'{e}di, E., Some additive and multiplicative problems in number theory. Acta Arith. (1975), 37--50.

problem:
Let $k\geq 3$ and $g_k(N)$ be minimal such that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,2N\}$ has $\lvert A\rvert \geq N+g_k(N)$ then there exist integers $b_1,\ldots,b_k$ such that all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise sums are in $A$ (but the $b_i$ themselves need not be in $A$).

Estimate $g_k(N)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/866.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 01 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Choi, Erd\H{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di. It is clear that, for the set of odd numbers in $\{1,\ldots,2N\}$, no such $b_i$ exist, whence $g_k(N)\geq 0$ always. Choi, Erd\H{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di proved that $g_3(N)=2$ and $g_4(N) \ll 1$. van Doorn has shown (https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/The%20cardinality%20of%20a%20set%20containing%20the%20pairwise%20sums%20of%20four%20integers.pdf) that $g_4(N)\leq 2032$.

Choi, Erd\H{o}s, and Szemer\'{e}di also proved that\[g_5(N)\asymp \log N\]and\[g_6(N)\asymp N^{1/2}.\]In general they proved that\[g_k(N) \ll_k N^{1-2^{-k}}\]and for every $\epsilon>0$ if $k$ is sufficiently large then\[g_k(N) > N^{1-\epsilon}.\]As an example, taking $A$ to be the set of all odd integers and the powers of $2$ shows that $g_5(N)\gg \log N$.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
I have just uploaded my paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.00040) on $g_k(N)$. In it, the following bounds are proven:
\begin{align*}
g_3(N) &= 1 \text{ for all } N \ge 3, \\
g_4(N) &= 3 \text{ for all } N \ge 2, \\
g_5(N) &< 1.2 \cdot 10^8 \text{ for all } N \ge 1, \\
g_k(N) &< 4N^{1 - 2^{2-k}} \text{ for all } k \ge 3 \text{ and all large enough } N.
\end{align*}Furthermore, these results are all verified in Lean (https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ErdosProblem866.lean).

The paper is my own work (mostly relying on the ideas by Choi-Erdős-Szemerédi), but specifically the $g_4$ result was obtained with the help of ChatGPT. Further noteworthy is that the bounds on $g_3$ and $g_5$ seemingly contradict the earlier claims of $g_3 = 2$ and $g_5(N) \asymp \log N$. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, let us (as in my previous comment (https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/866#post-4502)) define $h_k(N)$ as the smallest integer such that for all subsets $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ with $|A| \ge N + h_k(N)$ there exist distinct positive integers $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k$ such that all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise sums are in $A$.

As it turns out, $g_k$ and $h_k$ are not the same (in fact, they seem to differ quite often), although we do in general have $$g_k(n) \le h_k(n) \le g_{k+1}(n)$$for all $k$ and $n$. And even though the stated Choi-Erdős-Szemerédi results do not necessarily all hold for $g_k$, they are all recovered for $h_k$.

Furthermore, with the help of Aristotle I managed to make their $h_4 \ll 1$ result explicit, while the above general bound for $g_k$ also holds for $h_k$. For completeness' sake, these are the best known bounds for $h_k$ currently:
\begin{align*}
h_3(N) &= 2 \text{ for all } N \ge 4, \\
h_4(N) &\le 2270 \text{ for all } N \ge 1, \\
h_5(N) &\asymp \log N, \\
h_6(N) &\asymp \sqrt{N} (\text{which is also the correct order of growth for } g_6(N)), \\
h_k(N) &< 4N^{1 - 2^{2-k}} \text{ for all } k \ge 3 \text{ and all large enough } N.
\end{align*}Finally, this problem is also mentioned in [Er72, p. 83] (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1972-05.pdf), which can be added as a reference.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
It is clear that the $b_i$ need to be distinct, and maybe one can add this requirement to the problem statement for completeness' sake. What is less clear however, is whether the $b_i$ need to be positive.

In all theorem statements in [CES75] (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1975-39.pdf), they refer to the elements in $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ as positive integers, while the $b_i$ are just referred to as integers. This terminology is also used in [Er92c, p.41] (https://hal.science/hal-01108666/document), suggesting that the $b_i$ are not required to be positive (although one can note that at most one can be non-positive, otherwise we have a negative sum).

With this in mind, define $h_k(N)$ as the smallest integer such that for all subsets $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ with $|A| \ge N + h_k(N)$ there exist distinct positive integers $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k$ such that all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise sums are in $A$. With $g_k(N)$ defined as in the problem statement (i.e. without the positivity requirement), in general we then have $h_{k-1}(N) \le g_k(N) \le h_k(N)$.

Annoyingly, $g_k(N)$ and $h_k(N)$ are not the same function, and the lower bounds that Choi, Erdős and Szemerédi claim for $k = 3$ and $k = 5$ do not actually work for $g_k(N)$. In particular, the example (mentioned at the end of the remarks) of taking $A \subset \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ to be the union $$\{1, 3, \ldots, 2N-1\} \cup \{2, 4, \ldots, 2^{\lfloor \log_2 2N \rfloor} \}$$for a set for which supposedly no $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_5$ exist is incorrect as stated; with $b_1 = -1$, $b_2 = 2$, $b_3 = 3$, $b_4 = 5$, $b_5 = 6$, one can check that all pairwise sums do belong to $A$ whenever $N \ge 6$. The example does work to show the lower bound $h_5(N) \gg \log N$, but at the moment I have no non-trivial lower bound for $g_5(N)$. As far as I know, it could be the case that we actually have $g_5(N) \ll 1$ (Edit 06-04-2026: which I might be able to show now!).

Turning to $k = 3$, the truth is that $g_k(N)$ is equal to $1$ for all $N \ge 3$. Which is in contrast to the equality $h_3(N) = 2$ that Choi, Erdős and Szemerédi actually (unwittingly?) prove for all $N \ge 4$.

To see why $g_3(N) \le 1$ (and therefore $g_3(N) = 1$) holds for all $N \ge 3$, let $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ be any set with $|A| \ge N + 1$, and assume $N \ge 3$. Then $A$ contains $\{m, m+1\}$ for some odd $m \in \{1, 3, \ldots, 2N-1\}$ by the pigeonhole principle. If $A \setminus \{m \}$ only contains even integers, then $\{2, 4, 6\} \subseteq \{2, 4, \ldots, 2N\} \subset A$ and we can choose $b_1 = 0$, $b_2 = 2$, $b_3 = 4$. On the other hand, if $A$ contains an odd integer $2j+1 \neq m$, then we can choose $b_1 = j$, $b_2 = j+1$, $b_3 = m-j$, which are quickly checked to be distinct by the assumption $2j+1 \neq m$ and the fact that $m$ is odd. By the way, for $N = 2$ one can note that the example $A = \{2, 3, 4\}$ shows $g_3(2) = 2$.

I'll hopefully have more to say in the not too distant future, but I first wanted to clear up the above subtlety.

problem: If $A_1,A_2$ are disjoint additive bases of order $2$ (i.e. $A_i+A_i$ contains all large integers) then must $A=A_1\cup A_2$ contain a minimal additive basis of order $2$ (one such that deleting any element creates infinitely many $n\not\in A+A$)?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/869.
- Page status: DISPROVED (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 02 May 2026.
Site remarks:
A question of Erd\H{o}s and Nathanson \cite{ErNa88}.

Härtter \cite{Ha56} and Nathanson \cite{Na74} proved that there exist additive bases which do not contain any minimal additive bases.

Larsen has given a negative answer (https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-869/blob/main/869.pdf) to this question; indeed, the three potential measures of 'robustness' of an additive basis,
{UL}
{LI} $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$,{/LI}
{LI} $A$ is the union of two disjoint bases, and {/LI}
{LI} $A$ contains a minimal additive basis,{/LI}
{/UL}
are independent, in that Larsen constructs examples of bases satisfying any combination of these three properties (see [868] and [871] for other problems about the implication between these properties).
References:
- [ErNa88] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Nathanson, Melvyn B., Partitions of bases into disjoint unions of bases. J. Number Theory (1988), 1--9.
- [Ha56] H\"{a}rtter, Erich, Ein Beitrag zur Theorie der {M}inimalbasen. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1956), 170--204.
- [Na74] Nathanson, Melvyn B., Minimal bases and maximal nonbases in additive number theory. J. Number Theory (1974), 324--333.

ORIGINAL COMMENT: I claim a solution to this problem, specifically a total refutation: the answer is no, for all $k \geq 3$. The writeup is at this Overleaf link (https://www.overleaf.com/read/gknkvvxrymfv#956531).

The proof was developed via an automated multi-turn scaffold that I built, which iteratively queried ChatGPT-5.4-Pro (Extended Thinking), then, starting yesterday, ChatGPT-5.5-Pro (Extended Thinking) running in total for approximately 40+ consecutive turns/prompts (about 20 for each model).

The constructions in all cases ($k=3$ and $k \geq 4$) are inspired by the Larsen-Larsen 2026 robust order-2 basis without minimal subbases (their resolution of Erdős Problem #868 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/868)), combined with (i) a finite filler gadget lifting to every $k\ge4$, and (ii) a finite-shift clustered canary strengthening handling $k=3$.

computation:
- Built a finite-horizon $k=3$ proxy:
 - sampled random subsets $A\subseteq[1..N]$,
 - measured triple-sum representation counts on interval $[L,U]$,
 - checked existence of finite minimal 3-basis cores for that interval.

- In both tested regimes, full interval coverage was frequently achieved.
- High minimum finite representation counts were observed (best min-rep around 69 in these windows).
- Finite minimal cores were found in nearly all/full successful trials.
- These are finite analog signals only, not an infinite $k\ge3$ theorem.
attempt: The finite odd-cycle probe uses an inferred graph model built from the threshold set \(A\) and then checks for the desired cycle lengths. All sampled threshold-size instances behave positively, which supports the first subquestion heuristically, while the second subquestion is already treated as settled in the literature notes.

problem:
Consider the two-player game in which players alternately choose integers from $\{2,3,\ldots,n\}$ to be included in some set $A$ (the same set for both players) such that no $a\mid b$ for $a\neq b\in A$.

The game ends when no legal move is possible. One player wants the game to last as long as possible, the other wants the game to end quickly. How long can the game be guaranteed to last for?

At least $\epsilon n$ moves? (For $\epsilon>0$ and $n$ sufficiently large.) At least $(1-\epsilon)\frac{n}{2}$ moves?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/872.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 24 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A number theoretic variant of a combinatorial game of Hajnal, in which players alternately add edges to a graph while keeping it triangle-free. This graph theoretic game must trivially end in at most $n^2/4$ moves, and F\"{u}redi and Seress \cite{FuSe91} proved that it can be guaranteed to last for $\gg n\log n$ moves. Bir\'{o}, Horn, and Wildstrom \cite{BPW16} proved that it must end in at most $(\frac{26}{121}+o(1))n^2<0.215n^2$ moves.

This type of game is known as a saturation game.

Erd\H{o}s does not specify which player goes first, which may result in different answers.

GPT-5.2 Pro, prompted by Price, has shown (https://www.overleaf.com/read/cdpvfdwqwfzd#44b83b) that the final question has a negative answer: assuming the 'Prolonger' goes first, the 'Shortener' can guarantee that it ends in at most $(\frac{23}{48}+o(1))n$ moves. This constant has been refined, see the comment section for the latest.

Since all primes in $(n/2,n]$ must eventually be chosen, the game must last for at least $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$ moves.
References:
- [BPW16] Bir\'{o}, Csaba and Horn, Paul and Wildstrom, D. Jacob, An upper bound on the extremal version of Hajnal's triangle-free game. Discrete Appl. Math. (2016), 20--28.
- [FuSe91] F\"{u}redi, Zolt\'{a}n and Reimer, Dave and Seress, \'{A}kos, Hajnal's triangle-free game and extremal graph problems. Congr. Numer. (1991), 123--128.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
With the help of ChatGPT I generated some code to work out the game length for each $N$ assuming both players are playing optimally, and the 'Long' player goes first. This sequence goes (from $N=2$ up to $N=40$).

1,2,2,3,3,4,4,5,5,5,5,6,6,7,7,7,7,8,8,9,9,10,10,
11,11,11,11,11,12,13,13,14,14,14,14,15,15,16,16,16,16

The corresponding sequence of $f(n)-\pi(n)$, if $f(n)$ is the length of the game, is $0$ for $2\leq N\leq 8$, $1$ for $9\leq N\leq 20$, $2$ for $21\leq N\leq 27$, $3$ for $28\leq N\leq 34$, and $4$ for $35\leq N\leq 40$.

As an instructive example, when $N=9$ (the first time this game goes on longer than the number of primes) one optimal (for both players) game goes
6 - 4 - 5 - 7 - 9

As another example, when $N=21$,
6 - 4 - 9 - 5 - 14 - 11 - 13 - 17 - 19 - 21
Or when $N=35$,
30-4-14-9-22-13-17-19-21-23-25-29-31-33-35

This (very limited) amount of computational evidence does seem to suggest that $f(n)-\pi(n)\to \infty$ at least.

It's a curious game - one might naively think that the Long player should focus on choosing large primes and the Short player should focus on choosing small primes, and indeed there is a 'prime bias' in the transcripts above (to be expected, e.g. certainly all primes in $(N/2,N]$ must appear at some point) but it seems like both players are better off choosing numbers with many factors for the first couple of turns at least.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
It seems like the long player should start with choosing the largest primorial (say $p_k$#) less than $N$, as this stops the short player from choosing any of the primes up to $p_k$. The short player then plays $2^2$. The long player then plays $p_n$#$/p_k$# for the largest $n$ such that this is less than $N$, and the short player plays $3^2$. Essentially the long player plays the product of the most consecutive primes that haven't appeared in prior turns that they can and the short player plays the smallest number that can be played. When the long player cannot do that any more, they take $\min\{2p\}$ for primes $p<N/2$ such that $2p$ can be played. I would imagine that when $N$ is large enough, the long player would perhaps move on to choosing the smallest possible $3p$ etc. Ultimately there remains a set of terms that must be chosen, such as the primes in $[N/2,N]$ or $pq>N/2$ when $2p$ and $2q$ have already been chosen.

The aim for the long player is to 'defend' as many small primes as possible, and the way to cover as many as possible at once is to choose the product of as many as you can. The aim for the short player is roughly to choose the smallest terms possible as these have the most multiples less than $N$, though there may be a preference towards small primes or squares of primes when possible.

forum_comments.author: old-bielefelder
forum_comments.text:
With only one exception at N=27, Brenner's data until N=65
show the following structure for the game with player Long to start:

Let low(N) be the number of moves when both players
cooperate in finishing as soon as possible.
Let upp(N) be the number of moves when both players
cooperate in finishing as late as possible.
low(N) = number of primes till N,
upp(N) = upper floor of N/2.

L(N) = upper floor of [low(N) + upp(N)]/2.
Open question: Does this hold for all N > 27?

For large N this would mean L(N) = N/4 + o(N).

***************************

If player Short starts, the optimal game length
seems to be much nearer to the lower bound low(N) = pi(N).

forum_comments.author: jonaslsa
forum_comments.text:
I have a short note giving a dyadic refinement of the fan-capture lower bound. The idea is that the existing semiprime fan strategy only counts the top layer $pq\in(n/2,n]$. If Prolonger first runs an activation phase that $H$-secures the small odd primes, rendering every $2^b p$ with $0\le b\le H$ illegal, the same right-star capture argument applies to the whole dyadic chain $C_{pq}=\{pq,2pq,4pq,\ldots\}$ whenever $n/2^{H+1}<pq\le n$.

This gives, for every fixed $H\ge0$,\[
L(n)\ge
\left(\frac12(1-2^{-H-1})-o_H(1)\right)
\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n},
\]and hence\[
L(n)\ge
\left(\frac12-o(1)\right)
\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}.
\]It does not settle the linear question, but appears to improve the visible lower-bound constant in the current fan-capture method from $1/8$ to $1/2$.

note pdf: https://github.com/jonaslsaa/maths/blob/main/872.pdf

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks! I had a look at your note, and the earlier note of Om_Buddhdev_sensho, to try and understand this lower bound; here is a shorter explanation of the strategy (in particular stripping out a fair amount of additional pre-strategies in both notes, which perhaps are required for getting good constants, but unnecessary for the cruder order of magnitude bound).

Consider the bipartite graph, with both parts the set of primes, with an edge $p\sim q$ whenever $pq\in (n/2,n]$. The number of edges in this graph is $\gg\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}$ by classical estimates on the number of semiprimes in an interval.

Prolonger's strategy is to choose $pq$ corresponding to edges in this graph. These never have any multiple in $A$ (the set chosen thus far) since they are in $(n/2,n]$. The only thing that can stop Prolonger choosing this integer/corresponding edge is if one of the vertices $p$ or $q$ was claimed already by Shortener. (Shortener might be claiming other integers of course, but since these don't restrict Prolonger's moves in this strategy, Prolonger doesn't care what else Shortener is doing. Shortener can also choose an 'edge' instead, but this is clearly less efficient than eliminating a vertex (which can be justified e.g. by a strategy stealing argument).)

So this is now basically a question about a game on played on a bipartite graph on $m$ : Prolonger is colouring edges red, and Shortener is colouring vertices blue, with the restrictions that a red edge can't contain a blue vertex. I claim that, in this graph game, Prolonger can guarantee at least $\gg m$ turns, which gives an $\gg \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}$ bound for the primitive set game.

The trick is to use the method of potentials (a common technique in this sort of combinatorial game analysis; see for example the Erdős-Selfridge bound on maker-breaker games). Call a vertex 'protected' if it is on a red edge. The weight of an edge $e$ is the number of protected vertices on it. The weight of a vertex $x$ is\[F(x)=\sum_{\substack{x\in e\textrm{ available}}}2^{w(e)}.\]Prolonger's strategy is to choose an edge adjacent to a vertex which maximises $F(x)$. (Intuitively, Prolonger's goal is to try and protect the best vertices, so that there will be lots of edges available later; here the 'best' vertices are those with a lot of edges, where we value edges whose other endpoint is already protected more highly, since these are safe from Shortener forever).

More precisely, consider the potential function\[\sum_{e\textrm{ available}}2^{w(e)},\]which starts at $m$. When Prolonger claims an edge adjacent to an unprotected vertex $x$, they double the weight of all edges incident to $x$, since now $x$ is protected, and removes one edge from being available, so the potential has gone up by at least $F(x)-O(1)$. If Shortener then colours the vertex $y$, then this decreases the potential by at most $F(y)+O(1)$. Since $F(x)\geq F(y)$, overall the potential changes by $O(1)$ each turn, so must last for $\gg m$ many turns.

This is similar enough to arguments in the literature I've seen that I expect this kind of result is already folklore/known to experts/in the literature somewhere, although just in the 'bipartite graph' game language, rather than in terms of this primitive set game.

It seems likely that by playing on a $k$-uniform hypergraph instead, with Prolonger choosing the products of $k$ primes in $(n/2,n]$, a generalisation of this potential-type argument should allow one to prove that $\gg_k \frac{n(\log\log n)^k}{\log n}$ is always possible for any $k\geq 2$. The limit of this kind of strategy still seems to be $n/(\log n)^{1-o(1)}$ however; the next significant step would be an alternative argument that shows $L(n) \gg n/(\log n)^c$ for some constant $c<1$.

EDIT: Since this sort of game can be surprisingly subtle to analyse, it would be good if someone could try to formalise these sort of lower bounds - this kind of argument, which is locally very elementary and classical but requires a bit of tricky logic, is an ideal place to use formalisation to check we're not missing anything.

forum_comments.author: jonaslsa
forum_comments.text:
thanks! this is a helpful way to view the coarse lower bound. I agree that the top-layer semiprime strategy can be abstracted as a graph game on edges \(pq\in(n/2,n]\), and that this gives a clean route to\[
L(n)\gg \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}.
\]The dyadic note is trying to keep track of the leading constant within this fan-capture method.. The extra step is that it does not only use the top layer \(pq>n/2\), but first \(H\)-secures \(p,2p,\ldots,2^Hp\) and then counts chains \(C_{pq}\) for\[
n/2^{H+1}<pq\le n.
\]This is what gives the factor\[
\frac12(1-2^{-H-1})
\]and hence the \(1/2\) constant after taking \(H\) large.

Agree that the graph-game abstraction is probably the cleanest way to explain the order-of-magnitude lower bound. The hypergraph direction sounds interesting too, though I think the expected count for products of \(k\) primes should be of order\[
n(\log\log n)^{k-1}/\log n
\]for fixed \(k\), and the potential argument may need extra care because hypergraph codegrees can be large.

I asked Gemini about its history, and it came up with a reference to Dutch mathematician Frederik Schuh (1952). In tournament play "komi bidding" in the beginning should be included. With GPT 5.4 Pro assistance, building on the $8/105$ construction, I wanted to flag a refinement that uses $v_p$-adic parity conditions rather than simple coprimality. For $k \geq 4$, let $I_k(n) = (n/k, n/3] \cap (2\mathbb{Z}+1)$ and $\mathcal{R}_k$ be the reduced ratios $a/b > 1$ with $a, b$ odd, $a, b \leq k$, and $a/b < k/3$. Call $B \subseteq I_k(n)$ ratio-independent if no two elements have ratio in $\mathcal{R}_k$. At $k = 8$, $\mathcal{R}_8 = \{5/3, 7/5, 7/3\}$, and defining

$$B_8(n) := \{b \in I_8(n) : v_5(b) \equiv 0 \pmod{2} \text{ and } (3 \mid b \Rightarrow b > n/7)\}$$

gives a ratio-independent set of density $85/1008 \approx 0.0843$, improving on $8/105 \approx 0.0762$. The $v_5$-parity condition kills the $5/3$ and $7/5$ edges automatically (the valuation flips parity), while the geometric cut on multiples of $3$ handles $7/3$ (where $v_5$ is preserved). At $k = 7$ the same parity idea alone gives $5/63 \approx 0.0794$.

This is just a static claim about the ratio-graph model. Converting to a Prolonger strategy requires verifying $B_8$ survives adversarial Shortener play, which I haven't checked carefully. Even if it converts, it doesn't address whether L(n)≥ϵnL(n) \geq \epsilon n
L(n)≥ϵn is achievable in general; it's a constant improvement within the interval+sieve class. The more interesting question is whether the $v_p$-parity family has a nontrivial limiting density as $k \to \infty$, or whether it's also capped below $1/2$. I haven't computed $k \geq 9$ yet. Posting in case others want to poke at either the conversion step or the asymptotic behavior. I'm going to attempt further solutions with AI.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom

I don't think this is true - the other player might choose numbers with lots of prime divisors, so that after a certain point the other player has no primes left that are valid choices to play - but there still might be lots of other non-primes that are valid, so the game continues, and they have to abandon their primes-only strategy.

For example, when $N=9$, if the first player wants to end it quickly and the second wants to prolong it, and the first player tries to use only primes, then the game might go:
7 - 8 - 5 - 6 - 9
(This example still doesn't last long, but note that the first player still had the valid choice of 9 available even though all the primes were used up.)

It would be interesting to actually give an explicit strategy of the prolonger that shows they can also force it to last at least $100\frac{n}{\log n}$ (say) moves - given that Erdős was asking if the threshold was linear, presumably he believed this to be possible.

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
forum_comments.text:
This raises an interesting related question, which I hope can shed some light on the game: how small can a maximal primitive subset of $\{2,...,n\}$ be? The set of primes shows that it can be $\pi(n)$. Is this the smallest possible for all $n \geq 2$? If so, then the game must always last at least $\pi(n)$ moves no matter what the players do.

I'm not sure if Erdős ever asked this question. He and Cameron asked in [CaEr90] how many primitive subsets there are of $\{2,...,n\}$, and this was solved by Angelo here (https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/s25/s25.pdf). (I don't think that problem appears on this website yet.) See, e.g., McNew's paper here (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejc.2020.103237) for results on counting maximal primitive subsets of $\{2,...,n\}$, though more of the literature seems to focus on counting maximum-size primitive sets. However, I'm not sure if the question of how small a maximal primitive subset can be has ever appeared in the literature. There's a related paper here (https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.3007), but a quick skim didn't reveal any results that are applicable to this problem specifically.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text: Every maximal primitive subset must contain all primes in $(n/2,n]$, so $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$ is a lower bound.

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
forum_comments.text: Nice observation! That shows that if $A \subseteq \{2,...,N\}$ is a maximal primitive set, then $|A| \geq (\frac{1}{2} + o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}$. In fact, it's actually not a lot harder to show that $|A| \geq (1 + o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}$. This is because every prime number at least $\sqrt{n}$ must have a multiple in $A$, and no two of these primes can have a multiple in common. This shows that $|A|$ is at least the number of primes in $[\sqrt{n}, n]$, which is asymptotically $\frac{n}{\log n}$.

I would like to share my partial result on this problem (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1qP1jYDBVdunSfbdvoGAdl3XJgGRXsK3U/view?usp=sharing).

This partial result proves two unconditional bounds that go beyond the usual triple-block exponent. In particular, it proves\[
F(A,X,11)\ll X^{223/676}\log X
\]and\[
F(A,X,6)\ll X^{437/1320}\log X.
\]Both exponents are strictly smaller than \(1/3\), so the result shows that the classical triple-block barrier can be crossed for longer consecutive blocks.

The main idea is to combine the Vandermonde lcm inequality with gcd structure forced inside compact near-critical blocks. Around the difficult scale \(a_i\asymp X^{1/2}\), a good block must contain substantial pairwise gcd structure. The argument organizes this information through incident-star and complete-edge configurations, which then give stronger span bounds and lead to the counting estimates above.

I view this as genuine partial progress on the problem, rather than a solution of the full \(X^\varepsilon\) question. I used GPT 5.4 Thinking for helping me with algebraic notation and verifying the contribution, and it passed. I would be very grateful for any corrections, comments, or references to related work that I may have missed.

GPT-5.2 Thinking identifies the following additional references:

1. Erdős–Nicolas–Sárközy, Sommes de sous-ensembles (J. Th'eor. Nombres Bordeaux 3 (1991), 55--72)

Here, they construct an infinite admissible set with $A(x):=\#\{a\in A:a\le x \} \gg x^{5-2\sqrt6}$ (Thm. 2). In particular this implies polynomial growth $a_n\ll n^{1/(5-2\sqrt6)}$, hence $\liminf_{n\to\infty} a_{n+1}/a_n=1$. So admissible sets of polynomial growth are known in the literature (at least since 1991).

2. Deshouillers--Freiman, On an additive problem of Erdős and Straus, 2 (Astérisque 258 (1999))

Here, they prove the sharp finite extremal bound: for $N$ large, any admissible $A\subset[1,N]$ satisfies $|A|\le 2\sqrt N + O(1)$ (indeed $\le 2\sqrt{N+\tfrac14}-1$). Consequently any infinite admissible $A=\{a_n\}$ has $A(x)\le (2+o(1))\sqrt x$ and $a_n\ge (1+o(1))n^2/4$; so an eventual gap bound $a_{n+1}-a_n\le n^c$ forces $c\ge 1$ (although it is also possible that no such $c$ exists for some choices of $A$).

problem: Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subset \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite sum-free set - that is, there are no solutions to\[a=b_1+\cdots+b_r\]with $b_1<\cdots<b_r<a\in A$. How small can $a_{n+1}-a_n$ be? Is it possible that $a_{n+1}-a_n<n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/876.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er98} writes that Graham 'recently proved' that there is such a sequence for which $a_{n+1}-a_n<n^{1+o(1)}$, and that Melfi proved a somewhat weaker result.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er62c} proved that a sum-free set has density zero. Deshouillers, Erd\H{o}s, and Melfi \cite{DEM99} constructed a sum-free set that grows like $a_n\sim n^{3+o(1)}$.

Luczak and Schoen \cite{LuSc00} have proved that, for all large $N$,\[\lvert A\cap [1,N]\rvert\ll (N\log N)^{1/2},\]and that there exists a sum-free set $B$ such that\[\lvert B\cap [1,N]\rvert \gg \frac{N^{1/2}}{(\log N)^{1/2+o(1)}}\]for all large $N$.

In \cite{Er75b} and \cite{Er77c} Erd\H{o}s asks to determine the maximum possible value of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$. Erd\H{o}s had proved this is $<100$, and Sullivan had shown that this is $<4$, and Sullivan conjectured the maximum is slightly larger than $2$.

See also [790].

If $n=\prod_{1\leq i\leq t} p_i^{k_i}$ is the factorisation of $n$ into distinct primes then let\[f(n)=\sum p_i^{\ell_i},\]where $\ell_i$ is chosen such that $n\in [p_i^{\ell_i},p_i^{\ell_i+1})$. Furthermore, let\[F(n)=\max \sum_{i=1}^t a_i\]where the maximum is taken over all $a_1,\ldots,a_t\leq n$ such that $(a_i,a_j)=1$ for $i\neq j$ and all prime factors of each $a_i$ are prime factors of $n$.

Is it true that, for almost all $n$,\[f(n)=o(n\log\log n)\]and\[F(n) \gg n\log\log n?\]Is it true that\[\max_{n\leq x}f(n)\sim \frac{x\log x}{\log\log x}?\]Is it true that (for all $x$, or perhaps just for all large $x$)\[\max_{n\leq x}f(n)=\max_{n\leq x}F(n)?\]Find an asymptotic formula for the number of $n<x$ such that $f(n)=F(n)$. forum_comments.author: Svyable
forum_comments.text:
Let \(A\subset\mathbb N\) be an asymptotic additive basis of order \(k\), and suppose that \(A\) is strongly minimal under infinite deletions in the sense that, for every infinite \(B\subset A\), the set \(A\setminus B\) is not an asymptotic basis of order \(k\). Must there exist an infinite \(B\subset A\) such that \(A\setminus B\) is an asymptotic basis of order \(k+1\)?

We give a complete answer. For \(k=1\), the answer is yes. For every \(k\ge2\), the answer is no. More strongly, for every \(k\ge2\), we construct a set \(A\subset\mathbb N\) such that \(A\) is an asymptotic basis of order \(k\), is ordinarily minimal at order \(k\), is strongly minimal under infinite deletions at order \(k\), and satisfies the stronger property that \(A\setminus B\) is not an asymptotic basis of order \(k+1\) for every infinite
\(B\subset A\). The examples may be chosen thin, with\[
A(x) = \lvert A \cap [0, x] \rvert = O_k(x^{1/k})
\]which is optimal up to constants for bases of order \(k\).

problem:
For $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $G(A)$ be the graph with vertex set $A$, where two integers are joined by an edge if they are coprime.

Is it true that if\[\lvert A\rvert >\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{n}{3}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{n}{6}\rfloor\]then $G(A)$ contains all odd cycles of length $\leq \frac{n}{3}+1$?

Is it true that, for every $\ell\geq 1$, if $n$ is sufficiently large and\[\lvert A\rvert >\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{n}{3}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{n}{6}\rfloor\]then $G(A)$ must contain a complete $(1,\ell,\ell)$ triparite graph on $2\ell+1$ vertices?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/883.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 24 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and S\'{a}rk\H{o}zy \cite{ErSa97}, who prove that if\[\lvert A\rvert >\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{n}{3}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{n}{6}\rfloor\]then $G(A)$ contains all odd cycles of length $\leq cn$ for some constant $c>0$.

This threshold is the best possible, since one could take $A$ to be the set of $m\leq n$ which are divisible by either $2$ or $3$, in which case $G(A)$ contains no triangles.

The second question was solved by S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy \cite{Sa99} who proved that, for large $n$, if $\lvert A\rvert$ exceeds the given threshold then $G(A)$ contains a complete $(1,\ell,\ell)$ triparite graph with\[\ell \gg \frac{\log n}{\log\log n}.\]
References:
- [ErSa97] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Sarkozy, Gabor N., On cycles in the coprime graph of integers. Electron. J. Combin. (1997), Research Paper 8, approx. 11.
- [Sa99] S\'{a}rk\"ozy, G\'{a}bor N., Complete tripartite subgraphs in the coprime graph of integers. Discrete Math. (1999), 227--238.

Here (https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-884/blob/main/884.pdf) is an unconditional disproof. Tao gave a construction which showed this asymptotic doesn't hold in general if you omit the 1. The basic strategy here is to repeat that construction over many scales so that the left-hand side becomes arbitrarily large, making the 1 unimportant. To do that, you need to ensure that the per–scale left-hand side decays extremely slowly (somewhat surprisingly this is possible even though you seemingly cannot make it diverge unconditionally) and (less seriously) you need to make sure the cross–scale contributions are negligible.

forum_comments.text: I can disprove this conjecture assuming the prime tuples conjecture (details here (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/erdos-884.pdf)). The basic idea is to take an $n$ of the form $n = (t-h_1) \dots (t-h_K)$ where $h_1,\dots,h_K$ is an admissible tuple of diameter $\asymp K^2$ (with consecutive elements $\gg K$-separated) and $t$ is a large natural number chosen to make all the $t-h_1,\dots,t-h_K$ prime (this is where the prime tuples conjecture is used). The numerology *almost* lets one remove the prime tuples hypothesis, but I was unable to do so; perhaps someone else would like to try their luck.

forum_comments.text:
Not a big issue but on page $358$ in EoRo97, asked the number of divisors in the $(\sqrt{n},\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{n}^{1-\varepsilon})$ interval.
An easy result on a wide range of $\varepsilon$: on $(\sqrt{n},\sqrt{n}+\sqrt[6]{n})$ interval we can not have three or more divisors.
Easily, if $d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}$ are divisors on this interval, then using inclusion exclusion principle the
$[1]:\quad \frac{d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}gcd(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3})}{gcd(d_{1},d_{2})gcd(d_{2},d_{3})gcd(d_{3},d_{1})}$ also divides $n$
Here $gcd(d_{1},d_{2}),gcd(d_{2},d_{3}),gcd(d_{3},d_{1})<\sqrt[6]{n}$, since for example $gcd(d_{1},d_{2})$ divides the $|d_{2}-d_{1}|<\sqrt[6]{n}$.
So using [1] and the above (strict) upper bounds, since the left side divides $n$ we get:
$n^{\frac{3}{2}-3\cdot\frac{1}{6}}<n$, it is a contradiction.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
A recent formulation and discussion (including the case of intervals starting at $n^{1/2}$) appears as Conjecture~1 in Letendre's preprint https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.12146. Letendre establishes upper bounds for\[
D_n(X,Y):=\#\{d\mid n:\ X\le d\le X+Y\}
\]in several parameter ranges and explains constraints on how a hypothetical uniform bound $k_\epsilon$ could depend on $\epsilon$ (in particular, it cannot stay small as $\epsilon\to 0$).

In particular, specializing Letendre's bounds to $\theta=\tfrac12$ yields a uniform estimate above the $n^{1/4}$ scale: for any $\delta\in(0,\tfrac14)$,\[
D_n\!\bigl(n^{1/2},\,n^{1/4-\delta}\bigr)\ \ll\ \frac1\delta
\]uniformly in $n$. Hence, if the interval length is $n^{1/2-\epsilon}$ with $\epsilon>\tfrac14$ (so $1/2-\epsilon=1/4-\delta$ where $\delta=\epsilon-\tfrac14>0$), one obtains\[
\#\{d\mid n:\ \sqrt n<d\le \sqrt n+n^{1/2-\epsilon}\}\ =\ O\!\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon-\tfrac14}\right),
\]i.e. the conjectured $O_\epsilon(1)$ bound is known for every $\epsilon>\tfrac14$. For $\epsilon\le\tfrac14$ the existence of a uniform bound remains open in general; at the endpoint $\epsilon=\tfrac14$, Erdős and Rosenfeld constructed infinitely many $n$ with four divisors in $(\sqrt n,\sqrt n+n^{1/4})$, showing any universal bound there (if true) must be at least $4$.

problem: Is there an absolute constant $K$ such that, for every $C>0$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then $n$ has at most $K$ divisors in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/887.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A question of Erd\H{o}s and Rosenfeld \cite{ErRo97}, who proved that there are infinitely many $n$ with $4$ divisors in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/4})$, and ask whether $4$ is best possible here. They also proved that, if $n$ is large enough depending on $C$, then $n$ has at most $1+C^2$ divisors in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$.

Chan \cite{Ch14} has resolved this when $n$ is a square, proving that if $n$ is a square then $n$ has at most $5$ divisors in\[[ n^{1/2}-n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/7}, n^{1/2}+n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/7}].\]In \cite{Ch15} Chan further proves that if $n=(N-a)(N-b)$ for some $0\leq a\leq b\leq \exp((\log n)^{2/7})$ then $n$ has at most $18$ divisors in\[[ n^{1/2}-n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/14}, n^{1/2}+n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/14}].\]See also [886].

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
With GPT-5.5 Pro I've got\[
 F(n)\asymp \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}.
\]The lower bound is supplied by all primes and squarefree semiprimes (as noted in the comments too). The upper bound is the main point. After reducing to squarefree sets, we write each element with at least two prime factors as\[
 a=c p q,
\]where $p<q$ are the two largest prime factors of $a$. For dyadic prime intervals $p\in(X,2X]$, $q\in(Y,2Y]$, and for each core $c$, the elements $c p q$ form a bipartite graph in the variables $p,q$. The rigidity hypothesis forbids a $2\times2$ rectangle from being complete in two different colors $c,d$. This converts the problem into a weighted colored graph problem. The main term in the graph estimate is exactly of size $n\log\log n/\log n$; the remaining terms are smaller because the core $c$ has all prime factors below the lower graph coordinate.

Here is the note (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos888.pdf) and here is the formalization with Aristotle (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos888.lean) - the formalization is not complete because of Merten's theorem used as well as couple of other estimates.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks; it's interesting to compare this to Erdős' argument for (the weaker version of) [425] in [Er68] (https://combinatorica.hu/~p_erdos/1968-09.pdf), in which he proves in particular that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has no non-trivial solutions to $ab=cd$ then\[\lvert A\rvert \leq (1+o(1))\pi(N).\]He did this by factorising every element of $A$ as $uv$ with $u,v$ from some suitable sets, so that elements of $A$ correspond to edges in a bipartite graph, and then noting that a $C_4$ in this graph on $u_1v_1u_2v_2$ would give a non-trivial solution, since\[(u_1v_1)(u_2v_2)=(u_1v_2)(u_2v_2),\]and that a simple Cauchy-Schwarz argument gives an upper bound on the number of edges in a bipartite graph with no $C_4$. (He was, I think, quite fond of this trick; it seems that first noted some form of this argument as early as 1936.)

The property in this question can be viewed as a weakening of this Sidon-type property: there are may now be non-trivial solutions to $ab=cd$, but not to $abcd$ being a square.

This argument GPT gives is a (in hindsight) natural generalisation of this idea: consider not just one, but a lot of overlapping bipartite graphs, where we put an edge with 'colour' $c$ between $u$ and $v$ if $uvc\in A$. Now if $u_1v_1u_2v_2$ is a cycle in both the $c_1$ and $c_2$ colours then letting $a=u_1v_1c_1$, $b=u_1v_2c_2$, $c=u_2v_1c_2$, $d=u_2v_2c_1$, we see that $abcd$ is a square, and yet $ad=bc$ would force $c_1=c_2$. (One also has to rule out other potential solutions like $ab=cd$, but this is easily arranged if the $u_i,v_i$ are always prime.)

So if $A$ has the property in this problem, no $C_4$ can appear in more than one of the $c$-coloured bipartite graphs. Via a similar Cauchy-Schwarz argument this implies an upper bound on the total number of edges across all these graphs, and hence an upper bound on $\lvert A\rvert$.

It's not that surprising that now that we get the bound $\lvert A\rvert \ll \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}$, the number of semiprimes, which would roughly correspond to the number of edges in the complete bipartite graph on primes (where the corresponding product is $\leq n$).

The final bounds are a little tedious to work through, but now just an elementary calculation (and I'm sure, as usual, can be done in a much more compact way than GPT's writeup).

(Interestingly, it seems that GPT was maybe heavily influenced by [Er68], using many similar phrases and language such as 'rectangles' rather than the more common nowadays $C_4$. It's possible that its chain of thought was 'this seems like a weaker variant of the multiplicative Sidon property, and it's a question of Erdős, so let me look at a paper of Erdős addressing the other multiplicative Sidon question and see if that technique can be adapted to work here' - and it was right!

I think a heuristic approach for the asymptotic exponent can be as following:

The computational data (as shared in my previous comment here) suggests \(f_{sf}(n) \sim n/(\log n)^{\alpha}\) with \(\alpha \approx 0.35\).

A heuristic derivation to explain this value can be reducing the problem to finding a maximum independent set in a 4-uniform hypergraph \(H_n\), where edges correspond to solutions of \(abcd=\square\). The count of such solutions is related to the concentration of divisors, characterized by Ford's constant \(\delta \approx 0.08607\) [Ford, 2008]. Heuristically, the four-variable interaction \(abcd=\square\) suggests a cumulative density loss of \(4\delta \approx 0.3443\).

A matching lower bound might be achieved by optimizing over slices of integers with \(\sim \lambda \log \log n\) prime factors (using Sathe-Selberg), the upper bound would follow from the Hypergraph Container Lemma if certain pseudo-randomness conditions (co-degree hypotheses) hold for \(H_n\).

This "non-formal" approach might provide a reasonable origin for the observed decay and a clear target for future work: to prove that \(f(n) \asymp n/(\log n)^{4\delta + o(1)}\).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Here is a proof of Sarkozy's result $|A|=o(n)$. The main input is Turan-Kubilius inequality (anatomy of integers) to separate the role of smooth and rough numbers, and the multiplication table bound that only $o(n^2)$ numbers are the product of two numbers of size $O(n)$. (Much better bounds (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tenenbaum%E2%80%93Ford_constant) are known than this, but weaker estimate (which follows for instance from the Hardy-Ramanujan law) suffices for Sarkozy's $|A|=o(n)$ bound.) The basic point is that the small number of values of the multiplication table creates a large number of unwanted collisions.

Let $0 < \delta < 1$, and introduce parameters
$$ 1 < \frac{1}{\delta} \ll C \ll z \ll n$$
with each parameter in this sequence assumed sufficiently large compared to the previous parameters, e.g., $z$ is sufficiently large depending on $\frac{1}{\delta}$ and $C$.

Suppose for contradiction that we have a set $A \subset \{1,\dots,n\}$ of density $\geq \delta$ with the stated property. Any element $a$ of $A$ can then be factored as $a = a_{\leq z} a_{>z}$ where $a_{\leq z}$ is the $z$-smooth part (product of primes up to $z$) and $a_{>z}$ is the $z$-rough part (product of primes larger than $z$).

By Turan-Kubilius, for $z$ large enough, we have $C \leq a_{\leq z} \ll_z 1$ for all but at most $\delta n /2$ of the natural numbers up to $n$, hence for $\gg \delta n$ of the $a \in A$. By pigeonholing, we can then find a dyadic scale $C < L \ll_z 1$ such that out of all the numbers of the form $a_{\leq z} a_{>z}$ with $a_{\leq z} \sim L$ $z$-smooth and $a_{>z} \lesssim n/L$ $z$-rough, $\gg \delta$ of these products will lie in $A$.

If we let $S$ be the set of $z$-smooth numbers of size $\sim L$ and $R$ the set of $z$-rough numbers of size $\lesssim n/L$, the set $A$ is now occupying $\gg \delta |S| |R|$ of the products of $S$ and $R$. Note that $S$ and $R$ are large compared with $1/\delta$, and $R$ is in fact quite large: $|R| \gg_{L,z} n$. By Cauchy-Schwarz, we now have $\gg \delta^2 |S| |R|^2$ pairs $a_{\leq z} a_{>z}, a_{\leq z} a'_{>z}$ that both lie in $A$. By another Cauchy-Schwarz and the multiplication table bound, there are $\gg \delta^4 |S|^2 |R|^4 / |R \cdot R|$ quadruples
$$a_{\leq z} a_{>z}, a_{\leq z} a'_{>z}, b_{\leq z} b_{>z}, b_{\leq z} b'_{>z}$$
 such that
$$ a_{\leq z} \neq b_{\leq z}$$
and
$$ a_{>z} a'_{>z} = b_{>z} b'_{>z}.$$
These four elements of $A$ multiply to a square, so the product of two of them must equal the other two. Some case analysis then reveals that this forces $a_{>z}, a'_{>z}$ to be a permutation of $b_{>z}, b'_{>z}$, thus the four elements here basically form a "rectangle" in $S \times R$, so there are only $O(|S|^2 |R|^2)$ possible such quadruples. This gives
$$ \delta^4 |S|^2 |R|^4 / |R \cdot R| \ll |S|^2 |R|^2$$
which leads to a contradiction since $|R| \gg_{L,z} n$ and $|R \cdot R| = o(n^2)$ by the multiplication table bound.

This is my contribution to the study of Erdős Problem 888. I used Gemini 3 pro and Claude Opus 4.5 with multiple iterations. I didn't perform an extensive literature review so it's possible some proof strategies or methods were discussed somewhere before. Your feedback and verification would be much appreciated.

 You can access the PDF version from here (https://github.com/MaskoMys/Erdos-Problems-/blob/main/Erdos_888.pdf)

SUMMARY:
1. Kernel Constraint (Theorem 1): Any admissible set contains at most one element from each square-free equivalence class, giving \( f(n) \le Q(n) \).

2. Fixing Mechanism (Theorem 3): Non-square-free representatives can resolve obstructions, proving that the kernel map does not preserve admissibility.
- Counterexample : The set\[A = \{3, 5, 126, 210\}\]is admissible, but its kernel $K = \{3, 5, 14, 210\}$, is not admissible.

3. Hypergraph Algorithm (Section 3): An \( O(n^2) \) algorithm computes \( f_{sf}(n) \) exactly.

4. Asymptotic Bounds (Theorem 4): We establish \( \pi(n) \le f_{sf}(n) \le f(n) \le Q(n) \).

5. Computational Results (Section 6): Exact values of \( f_{sf}(n) \) for\[ n \leq 5000 \]supporting $f(n) = o(n)$.

6. Curve Fitting: The data is well-modeled by\[
 f(n) \approx \frac{n}{(\log n)^\alpha}, \quad \alpha \approx 0.35.
 \]Edit: The PDF document was modified to reflect the latest updates.

Generate the proposed solution using GPT 5.2 Thinking, Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 Pro, share here for verification.

Document (https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gx9Ankr1qQOoFTR7Xj4u6Nc8SWkgEPe6/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=103837779541880341884&rtpof=true&sd=true)

Summary:
We want the largest \(A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\) such that for all \(a\le b\le c\le d\in A\), if \(abcd\) is a square then \(ad=bc\) (allowing repeats).

Step 1 (kernel reduction). Write \(x=\kappa(x)t^2\) with \(\kappa(x)\) squarefree.
If \(A\) contains two distinct numbers with the same \(\kappa\), then \((x,x,x,y)\) gives a square product but forces \(xy=x^2\), impossible. Hence at most one element per kernel. Moreover, if \(A\) is good then the kernel-set \(K=\{\kappa(x):x\in A\}\) is also good, so it suffices to work with squarefree sets.

Step 2 (candidate). Let \(L(n)\) be all squarefree numbers \(\le n\) with at most two prime factors (primes and squarefree semiprimes), and include \(1\) only when \(n\le 14\). This set is good: with supports of size \(\le2\), any square-trigger quadruple must have the "rectangle'' parity pattern, which forces \(ad=bc\).

Step 3 (compression / maximality). Suppose \(K\) is a maximum good squarefree set but misses some "light'' element (first a prime, then a semiprime). Add the missing light element. If the new set becomes bad, one can classify the obstruction: adding a prime \(p\) creates a violation iff there exist \(b,c\in K\) with \(p\nmid b,c\) and \(d=p\cdot bc/\gcd(b,c)^2\in K\); the quadruple \((p,b,c,d)\) is then forced and violates \(pd=bc\). So we delete the witness \(d\) and keep \(p\). This preserves size and strictly decreases the total number of prime factors \(\sum_{x\in K}\omega(x)\). Iterating forces all primes (and then all semiprimes) into the set, eliminating all \(\omega\ge3\) elements.

Step 4 (the \(1\) cutoff). If \(1\in K\) and \(pq,pr,qr\in K\), then \(1\cdot pq\cdot pr\cdot qr\) is a square but \(1\cdot qr\ne (pq)(pr)\). The first such triangle is \(\{6,10,15\}\), so \(1\) is compatible only for \(n\le14\).

Conclusion. The maximum size is\[
M(n)=\pi(n)+\#\{pq\le n:\ p<q\text{ primes}\}+\mathbf{1}_{n\le14},
\]achieved by taking all primes and all squarefree semiprimes (and also \(1\) only when \(n\le14\)).

It might already be hard to conjecture what a largest set $A$ for $n$ large might be.

Let $A$ be the set containing all primes and all product of two different primes (bounded by $n$).
Checking the possible forms of $abcd$ which are a perfect square, we easily deduce that this set $A$ satisfies the constraint (denoted property P as above).
If $p^4 \mid A$, then all elements contain a factor $p$ and it becomes trivial.
So remaining to check: $(pqrs)^4,(pqr)^2,(pq)^2$ and all of them are easy to check.

For large $n$, $A$ is not a maximal set (for $n \le 14$ neither, as then one can add $1$ as well).
One can e.g. add some products of disjoint sets of $7$ different primes (bounded by $n$ again). Since no such product will be a divisor of any square product of $4$ elements, the extended set still has the property P.

forum_comments.text:
I have an interesting lemma that may or may not be useful. Say a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has Property P if for all $a \leq b \leq c \leq d \in A$ with $abcd$ square, we have $ad = bc$. Then this problem is asking how large a subset of $\{1,...,n\}$ can be if it has Property P. Say $A$ has Property Q if for all $a \leq b \leq c \leq d \in A$ with $abcd$ square, we have $a = b$ and $c = d$. Then every set with Property Q also has Property P. (The converse isn't true, though; a counterexample is $\{2,3,4,6\}$.)

A nice fact is that if $U$ and $V$ have Property Q and $\gcd(u,v) = 1$ for all $u \in U, v \in V$, then the product set $UV$ has Property P. This is not too hard to verify.

Unfortunately, the two stronger statements that you might have wondered about when reading this are false. The set $UV$ need not have Property Q; for example, $U = \{1,2\}$ and $V = \{1,3\}$ have Property Q but $UV = \{1,2,3,6\}$ does not have Property Q. Also, if we weaken the hypotheses so that $U$ only needs to have Property P, then $UV$ need not have Property P; for example, $U = \{2,3,4,6\}$ has Property P and $V = \{1,5\}$ has Property Q, but $UV$ contains $\{2,6,15,20\}$ and so it does not have Property P.

forum_comments.author: Agustín Meza
forum_comments.text:
The first problem Erdös and Selfridge state is not about $\omega (n)$, but a little variation which only counts the prime factors of $n+k$ which are greater than k. Otherwise the sum $\sum_{0 \le i \le k}\omega (n) \gg \log\log(k)k$ from Turán-Kubilius inequality over the set of primes less than $\sqrt{k}$.

The case for fixed $k$ would follow from the $k$-tuples conjecture the following way: Let $N$ be sufficiently large in terms of $k$. Then linear forms $L(n;j) = N!n + j$ for $1 \le j \le k+1$ form an admissible $k$-tuple if $N$ is sufficiently large. Then, by the $k$-tuples conjecture, there exists infinitely many $n$ such that $L(n;j)$ is prime for all $1 \le j \le k+1$. This implies that $N!n + j$ is equal to a prime $p_{j}$ times $j$ infinitely often.

The sum that Erdös and Selfridge were considering would be equal to $k+ \pi(k)$ (each $N!n + j$ will contribute $1$ if $j-1$ is not prime and $2$ if it is). Note: the condition $j-1$ being prime or not comes from the fact that we've shifted the beginning of the string of consecutive integers to $N!n + 1$.

problem: Let $2=p_1<p_2<\cdots$ be the primes and $k\geq 2$. Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there must exist an integer in $[n,n+p_1\cdots p_k)$ with $>k$ many prime factors?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/891.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Schinzel deduced from P\'{o}lya's theorem \cite{Po18} (that the sequence of $k$-smooth integers has unbounded gaps) that this is true with $p_1\cdots p_k$ replaced by $p_1\cdots p_{k-1}p_{k+1}$.

This is unknown even for $k=2$ - that is, is it true that in every interval of $6$ (sufficiently large) consecutive integers there must exist one with at least $3$ prime factors?

Weisenberg has observed that Dickson's conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickson%27s_conjecture) implies the answer is no if we replace $p_1\cdots p_k$ with $p_1\cdots p_k-1$. Indeed, let $L_k$ be the lowest common multiple of all integers at most $p_1\cdots p_k$. By Dickson's conjecture there are infinitely many $n'$ such that $\frac{L_k}{m}n'+1$ is prime for all $1\leq m<p_1\cdots p_k$. It follows that, if $n=L_kn'+1$, then all integers in $[n,n+p_1\cdots p_k-1)$ have at most $k$ prime factors.
References:
- [Po18] P\'{o}lya, Georg, Zur arithmetischen {U}ntersuchung der {P}olynome. Math. Z. (1918), 143--148.

While Desmond's remark would possibly leading to saying "no",
I also want to add observations leading to a plausible "yes".

Observation:
If this is not the case for some large $n$, one of the elements in the interval is of the form $p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \ldots p_k^{e_k}$.
So it is sufficient to consider the neighbourhood of these powers and check if many of them have few prime factors.
This seems unlikely.

Quantitave for $k=2$:
Let $n>4372$ (likely the necessary bound), where $r=6 \lfloor n/6 \rfloor =2^i*3^j$.
Then $r-2$ and $r+2$ are both multiples of $2$, and $r-3, r+3$ are both multiples of $3$.
If $i,j>1$, then furthermore the exponents of the small primes are one.
So the probability that is works, is bounded by a function of the form $1/ \log(x)^2.$
Also the other elements in the interval are likely not pseudoprimepowers, so the sum of chances to find one is small.

For $r=3*2^i$, one needs that $r-3$ or $r+3$ is almost prime.
So $i$ needs to be prime or a power of $2$ (the latter is expected to be excluded, as there is likely no Fermat number above $2^{32}+1$).
So take $p$ such that $2^p-1$ is a Mersenne prime.
Now $3*2^p-1=t*s$ and $3*2^p-2=2*q$ should already both have at most $2$ prime factors.
For $r=2*3^i$, one can guess along the same lines.

Nonetheless, fully making the above rigourous, may be hard.
Anyone else ideas? Cases to exclude?
**
for $k=3$, $n>8611$ may be the quantitative "large enough".

problem:
Is there a necessary and sufficient condition for a sequence of integers $b_1<b_2<\cdots$ that ensures there exists a primitive sequence $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ (i.e. no element divides another) with $a_n \ll b_n$ for all $n$?

In particular, is this always possible if there are no non-trivial solutions to $(b_i,b_j)=b_k$?

Similarly, find necessary and sufficient conditions on a sequence $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ that ensure there exists a primitive set $A$ such that\[\lvert A\cap [1,2^{n_i}]\rvert \gg 2^{n_i}\]for every $i$.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Thanks! As you say, the upper bound is immediate from Ford's work as noted by Wouter. The lower bound here is a neat generalisation of Szemerédi's lower bound construction, boosting $A$ from just a set of large primes to the set of integers divisible by a large prime. The real work here is done by Ford's deep work on integers with a unique divisor in a dyadic interval.

Here is a cleaned up and simplified description of the argument.

The input from Ford's seminal paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0401223) is that, if both $y$ and $N$ are large enough, and $y\leq N^{1/3}$, then the number of $n\leq Ny$ which have exactly one divisor in $(y,2y]$ is\[\gg \frac{Ny}{(\log y)^\delta(\log\log y)^{3/2}}=N\Phi(y),\]say. (This is an immediate consequence of combining Corollary 2 and Theorem 4 of Ford's paper.)

Let $P$ be a random set of primes in $(N^{2/3},cN]$, where $c$ is some small constant, each included with probability $1/2$, and let $A$ be the set of all integers in $(N/2,N]$ divisible by at least one (and so exactly one) prime in $P$, and $B$ be the set of all integers in $[1,N]$ divisible by no prime in $P$.

Now let $y_p=N/2p$ and $G_p$ be the set of all $n\leq Ny_p$ with exactly one divisor in $(y_p,2y_p]$, and let $G_p'\subseteq G_p$ be the subset of integers which are not divisible by any $q\in P$.

If $d$ is this unique divisor, then note that $n/d\leq N$, and therefore $n/d\in B$. It follows that each $p\in P$ and $n\in G_p'$ contributes $1$ to $F(A,B)$, since $(pd)\cdot (n/d)$ is the unique representation of $pn$ as a product $ab$. (To see this, note that $d<N^{1/3}$, so if $pn=(qd')b$ for some $q\in P$ and $b\in B$ then $q=p$, and then also $d'=d$, since $n$ has a unique divisor in $(N/2p,N/p]$).

Therefore\[F(A,B) \gg \sum_{p\in P}\lvert G_p'\rvert.\]Now since any $n\leq N$ can have at most one prime divisor in $(N^{2/3},N]$, which is discarded with probability $1/2$, for any prime $p$ we have $\mathbb{E} \lvert G_p'\rvert \gg \lvert G_p\rvert\gg N\Phi(y_p)$, and so (since those $n\in G_p$ which are divisible by $p$ itself are a negligible proportion, and choosing suitable random choice of $P$ by the pigeonhole principle)\[F(A,B) \gg \sum_{N^{2/3}<p\leq cN}\lvert G_p\rvert\gg N \sum_{N^{2/3}<p\leq cN}\Phi(y_p).\]By standard Mertens-type estimates this right-hand side is $\gg N\Phi(N)$ as desired.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
With $\delta = 1 - \frac{1 + \log \log 2}{\log 2} \approx 0.086$ we have $$\frac{\big(1+o(1)\big)N^2}{\log N} \le \max_{A,B \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}} F(A, B) \ll \frac{N^2}{\log^{\delta} N (\log \log N)^{3/2}}.$$The upper bound follows from the determination of the number of elements in the multiplication table $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\} \times \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ by Ford.

For the lower bound we can use a construction Szemerédi gives in this (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022314X76900032) paper (the one where he solved #490 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/490)): set $A$ to be the set of primes in $\left[\frac{N}{\log N}, N\right]$ and choose $B$ to be the subset of integers in $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ which are not divisible by any $a \in A$. Then $|A| = \frac{\big(1+o(1)\big)N}{\log N}$ by the prime number theorem, $|B| = \big(1+o(1)\big)N$, and every element $m \in AB$ has a unique representation.

For what it's worth, one can replace $\log N$ in the interval $\left[\frac{N}{\log N}, N\right]$ defining $A$, by any function $f(N)$ that goes to infinity with $N$ slower than $N^{\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon > 0$.

Erdős suggests in [Er72] that the ideas in the aforementioned paper by Szemerédi can perhaps be used to attack this problem as well.

problem: Let $m(n)$ be minimal such that there is an $n$-uniform hypergraph with $m(n)$ edges which is $3$-chromatic. Estimate $m(n)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/901.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 December 2025.
Site remarks:
In other words, the hypergraph does not have Property B (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_B). Property B means that there is a set $S$ which intersects all edges and yet does not contain any edge.

It is known that $m(2)=3$, $m(3)=7$, and $m(4)=23$. Erd\H{o}s proved\[2^n \ll m(n) \ll n^2 2^n\](the lower bound in \cite{Er63b} and the upper bound in \cite{Er64e}). Erd\H{o}s conjectured that $m(n)/2^n\to \infty$, which was proved by Beck \cite{Be77}, who proved $m(n)\gg (\log n)2^n$, and later \cite{Be78} improved this to\[n^{1/3-o(1)}2^n \ll m(n).\]Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan \cite{RaSr00} improved this to\[\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}2^n \ll m(n).\]Pluhar \cite{Pl09} gave a very short proof that $m(n) \gg n^{1/4}2^n$.

In \cite{ErLo75} Erd\H{o}s and Lov\'{a}sz speculate that $n2^n$ is the correct order of magnitude for $m(n)$.

forum_comments.text:
I would like to propose a probabilistic solution to the non-trivial, transcendental-entire-function interpretation of Problem 906.

The literal formulation is trivial if polynomials are allowed, since every sufficiently high derivative of a non-zero polynomial is identically zero. So I address the natural version in which f is required to be transcendental entire.

First, observe that the stated property is equivalent to the following cofinite hitting property:

For every non-empty open set U ⊂ C, there exists N(U) such that f^(n) has at least one zero in U for every n ≥ N(U).

Indeed, if this fails for some U, then infinitely many derivatives have no zero in U, and choosing those derivative orders gives an infinite subsequence whose union of zero sets is not dense. Conversely, if the cofinite property holds, then every infinite subsequence eventually contains an order n large enough to hit any prescribed U.

Now consider the planar Gaussian entire function

F(z) = Σ_{k≥0} ξ_k z^k / sqrt(k!),

where the ξ_k are independent standard complex Gaussian random variables. Almost surely, F is entire and transcendental.

For the n-th derivative F^(n), the covariance kernel is

K_n(z,w) = ∂_z^n ∂_{\bar w}^n exp(z \bar w),

and on the diagonal,

K_n(z,z) = n! exp(|z|^2) L_n(-|z|^2),

where L_n is the Laguerre polynomial.

By the Edelman-Kostlan formula, the expected zero counting measure μ_n of F^(n) satisfies

dμ_n(z) = (1 / 4π) Δ log K_n(z,z) dA(z).

Using the Plancherel-Rotach asymptotic for Laguerre polynomials at negative argument, uniformly on compact annuli avoiding 0,

log L_n(-|z|^2) = 2 sqrt(n)|z| - |z|^2/2 + O(log n).

Therefore, on compact sets avoiding 0,

log K_n(z,z) = C_n + 2 sqrt(n)|z| + |z|^2/2 + O(log n),

where C_n is independent of z. Hence, for any non-negative non-zero test function φ ∈ C_c^2(D), with D a disk whose closure avoids 0,

E[∫ φ dn_{F^(n)}]
= ∫ φ dμ_n
≥ c_φ sqrt(n)

for all sufficiently large n. This follows by integrating by parts, since away from 0,

Δ|z| = 1/|z|,

so

∫ |z| Δφ dA = ∫ φ / |z| dA > 0.

Now apply an Offord-Sodin type estimate for linear statistics of zeros of Gaussian analytic functions. For a Gaussian analytic function g and φ ∈ C_c^2(C), one has a bound of the form

P(|∫ φ(dn_g - dμ_g)| ≥ λ) ≤ 3 exp(-c λ / ||Δφ||_1).

If F^(n) has no zero in D, then ∫ φ dn_{F^(n)} = 0. Since the expectation is at least c_φ sqrt(n), the Offord estimate gives

P(F^(n) has no zero in D) ≤ C_D exp(-c_D sqrt(n)).

This is summable in n. Hence, by Borel-Cantelli, for each fixed disk D whose closure avoids 0, almost surely F^(n) has a zero in D for all sufficiently large n.

Finally, take a countable base of rational disks whose closures avoid 0. This still suffices for density, since every non-empty open set contains such a disk. Intersecting the corresponding probability-one events over this countable base, we obtain a realization f of the planar Gaussian entire function such that every non-empty open set contains zeros of f^(n) for all sufficiently large n.

By the cofinite reformulation, this f satisfies the original condition for every infinite subsequence of derivative orders. Since f is transcendental entire almost surely, this gives an affirmative answer to the transcendental version of Problem 906.

I have also prepared a full PDF note with the details and references. I would be grateful if others could check the argument, especially the use of the Laguerre asymptotic and the Offord-Sodin estimate in this setting.

I used the Gemini and ChatGPT research tools to do a literature review on this problem.

Gemini correctly explained (https://gemini.google.com/share/a330ad9ab5b4) why the Barth-Schneider paper did not resolve the Erdos problem, but then went on to hallucinate a nonsensical solution to the Erdos problem (the error is in assuming that any subsequence of a dense sequence remains dense). No further relevant references were found (Maclane's theorem that the derivatives of a generic holomorphic function are dense in the locally uniform topology, already mentioned in another comment, is cited, but is useless for this problem due to the above error).

ChatGPT found this web page (https://chatgpt.com/share/68f2bab0-bc60-800e-bda3-41d16b96621d) and also noted that the Barth-Schneider paper solves a *different* problem of Erdos concerning derivatives of holomorphic functions, attributed to Problem 2.30 of Hayman's book (https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=217268). It is possible that Erdos confused the two problems. Like Gemini, Maclane's theorem was also noted, though this time it was correctly pointed out that this result was insufficient to establish the result. It seems that most of ChatGPT's response was drawn from this very web page, revealing no further references; this raises the issue of a circularity in which the utility of such tools for this web site may become diminished if this site becomes authoritative enough to become a major primary source for such tools.

Nevertheless, I would agree with the emerging consensus that there is currently no solution to this problem in the literature.
