forum_comments.text:
There seems to be a gap in the proof posted above.
The step claiming that for sufficiently large \(n\),\[
|g(z)| < |n!c_n| \quad \text{for all } |z|<R
\]does not follow from uniform convergence and is generally false.
A concrete counterexample is \(f(z)=e^{z^2}\). We have\[
f(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{2j}}{j!},\qquad
c_{2j}=\frac1{j!},\quad c_{2j+1}=0.
\]For even orders \(n=2k\),\[
f^{(n)}(z)=n!c_n+\sum_{m\ge1} n!\binom{n+m}{n}c_{n+m}z^{\,m}.
\]The coefficient ratio of the \(z^2\)-term to the constant term equals\[
\frac{n!\binom{n+2}{n}c_{n+2}}{n!c_n}
=\frac{(2k+2)(2k+1)}{2(k+1)}=2k+1.
\]Hence for any fixed radius \(R>0\),\[
\frac{|\,\text{$z^2$ term}\,|}{|\,\text{constant term}\,|}
=(2k+1)R^2\to\infty\quad(k\to\infty).
\]Therefore\[
\sup_{|z|=R}|g(z)|
\ge (2k+1)R^2|n!c_n|>|n!c_n|
\]for all sufficiently large even \(n=2k\). Thus the inequality \(|g(z)|<|n!c_n|\) fails, and the Rouché comparison used in that argument cannot be justified.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
The webpage states: ''Erdős [Er82e] writes that this was solved in the affirmative 'more than ten years ago', but gives no reference or indication who solved it. From context he seems to attribute this to Barth and Schneider [BaSc72], but this paper contains no such result.'' I agree with this assessment. Below I make a short clarification.

First, one easily checks that Problem #906 is equivalent to the following formulation:

**Problem 2**. Does there exist a transcendental entire function $f(z)$ such that for every nonempty open set $U\subset\mathbb{C}$ there is an integer $N(U)>0$ with the property that, for all $n\ge N(U)$, the $n$-th derivative $f^{(n)}$ has a zero in $U$?

After a careful reading of Barth and Schneider [BaSc72], I found that the methods in [BaSc72] only yield the following weaker positive result for *Problem 2*. I state it here as Proposition 1:

**Proposition 1**. There exists a nonzero transcendental entire function $f(z)$ such that for every nonempty open set $U\subset\mathbb{C}$ there are infinitely many integers $n$ for which $f^{(n)}$ has a zero in $U$.

Proof of Proposition 1. Let $S_k:=\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{Z}+\frac{i}{k}\mathbb{Z}$ denote the square lattice of mesh $1/k$. By [BaSc72, Theorem 1], there exist a sequence of positive integers $(n_k)$ and an entire function $f$ such that\[
f^{(n_k)}(z)=0 \quad\text{for every } z\in S_k,\qquad k=1,2,\dots.
\]Given any nonempty open set $U\subset\mathbb{C}$, there exists $K(U)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $U\cap S_k\neq\emptyset$ for all $k\ge K(U)$ (since the lattices $S_k$ become dense as $k\to\infty$). Hence, for every $k\ge K(U)$ the function $f^{(n_k)}$ has a zero in $U$. This produces infinitely many integers $n$ with the required property, proving the proposition.

In particular, [BaSc72] yields the weaker density conclusion that the union $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{z:\,f^{(n)}(z)=0\}$ is dense in $\mathbb C$, but it does not establish the stronger uniform property required in Problem #906.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
In addition to the weaker positive result from Barth--Schneider [BaSc72] (cf. Proposition 1 above), I found two further relevant results in the paper of Boas--Reddy [BoRe73] (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022247X73901534):
R.~P. Boas Jr. and A.~R. Reddy, Zeros of successive derivatives of entire functions, Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications 42(1973), 466--473.

By Theorem 1 in [BoRe73] (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022247X73901534), we know that for entire functions of at most order $2$ and finite type, there is no function $f$ satisfying the property in Problem 2 above.

By Theorem 2 in [BoRe73] (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022247X73901534), if $p>2$, then there exists an entire function of order $p$ and a constant $A>0$ such that every disk of radius $A$, anywhere in the plane, contains a zero of every derivative $f^{(i)}$.

These two theorems show that Problem 2 cannot be solved for functions of small order. Once the order exceeds $2$, one can indeed find entire functions with particular zero-distribution properties, but this still does not resolve Problem 2.

forum_comments.author: Quanyu Tang
forum_comments.text:
One more remark. I found a new proof of the *Proposition 1* above. Let \(H(\mathbb{C})\) be the space of all entire functions on $\mathbb{C}$ with the compact open topology. By a result of MacLane (see Theorem 6 in [Ma52] (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02786968) or Theorem 2 in [ArMa02] (https://www.math.kent.edu/~aron/aron-markose-10-29-02.pdf)), there exists an entire function \(f\) such that the set \(\{f^{(n)}: n\in\mathbb{N}\}\) is dense in \(H(\mathbb{C})\). From this one obtains the density of the union of zero sets of the derivatives via a short Rouché-argument, as follows.

Fix any point \(z_0\in\mathbb{C}\) and radius \(r>0\), and set the closed disk \(K=\overline{D(z_0,r)}\). Let \(g(z)=z-z_0\). Note that \(|g(z)|=r\) on \(\partial D(z_0,r)\). Since \(\{f^{(n)}\}\) is dense in \(H(\mathbb{C})\), there exists \(N\) with\[
 \sup_{z\in K}\,|f^{(N)}(z)-g(z)|<r.
\]Restricting to \(\partial D(z_0,r)\) gives \(|f^{(N)}(z)-g(z)|<|g(z)|\). By Rouché’s theorem, \(f^{(N)}\) and \(g\) have the same number of zeros in \(D(z_0,r)\). Since \(g\) has exactly one zero at \(z_0\), the function \(f^{(N)}\) has a zero in \(D(z_0,r)\). Because \(z_0\) and \(r\) were arbitrary, we conclude that\[
 \bigcup_{n\ge 1}\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\ f^{(n)}(z)=0\}
\]is dense in \(\mathbb{C}\). This completes the proof of Proposition 1.

The above discussion naturally leads to:

**Problem 3**. Does there exist \(f\in H(\mathbb{C})\) such that for every infinite subset \(S\subset\mathbb{N}\) the set \(\{D^{n}f : n\in S\}\) is dense in \(H(\mathbb{C})\)?

If Problem 3 were true, it would give an affirmative solution to Problem #906. However, *Problem 3* is in fact false. Here is a short proof.

Proof that Problem 3 is false. Let \(U,V\subset H(\mathbb C)\) be two disjoint nonempty open sets. Assume there exists \(f\in H(\mathbb C)\) such that for every infinite \(S\subset\mathbb N\) the set \(\{D^{n}f:n\in S\}\) is dense in \(H(\mathbb C)\). For any nonempty open \(W\subset H(\mathbb C)\) define\[
N_W:=\{\,n\in\mathbb N:\ D^{n}f\in W\,\}.
\]Then necessarily \(S\cap N_W\neq\varnothing\). Indeed, if \(N_W\) were not cofinite, taking \(S=\mathbb N\setminus N_W\) (which is infinite) would force \(\{D^{n}f:n\in S\}\subset H(\mathbb C)\setminus W\), contradicting its density. Hence both \(N_U\) and \(N_V\) are cofinite, so \(N_U\cap N_V\neq\varnothing\). Pick \(n\in N_U\cap N_V\), then \(D^{n}f\in U\cap V=\varnothing\), a contradiction. Therefore no such \(f\) exists.

References.
[Ma52] MacLane, Gerald R. "Sequences of derivatives and normal families." Journal d’Analyse Mathématique 2.1 (1952): 72-87.
[ArMa02] ARON, RICHARD, and DINESH MARKOSE. "ON UNIVERSAL FUNCTIONS OCTOBER 29, 2002."

In view of the above, a negative resolution of Problem #906 appears plausible, yet this observation is merely suggestive and falls well short of a proof.

Hence for any infinite increasing sequence $(n_k)_{k\ge1}$ of positive integers,
\[
\{z\in\mathbb C:\exists k,\ f^{(n_k)}(z)=0\}=\mathbb C.
\]
Since $\mathbb C$ is dense in itself, the required set is dense. Therefore the
existential statement is true.
So EP-906 is fully resolved in the positive direction as currently phrased.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
One can predict the value of $c$ using the Cramer random model for the primes. Firstly some reductions. Legendre's formula states that
$$k_i = \lfloor n/p_i \rfloor + \lfloor n/p_i^2 \rfloor + \dots.$$
Both the main term $\lfloor n/p_i \rfloor$ and the tail $\lfloor n/p_i^2 \rfloor + \dots$ are non-increasing in $i$; but the latter only changes value $O(n^{1/3})$ times (consider the cases $p_i \leq n^{1/3}$ and $p_i \geq n^{1/3}$ separately). Thus, deleting this term only modifies $h$ by a lower order error, and the problem is equivalent to that of counting the number of distinct values of $\lfloor n/p_i \rfloor$.

For any $\varepsilon$, the primes less than $\varepsilon \sqrt{n \log n}$ are only $O(\varepsilon (n/\log n)^{1/2})$ in number, and for the primes $p_i$ larger than $\varepsilon^{-1} \sqrt{n \log n}$ the value of $\lfloor n/p_i\rfloor$ is $O(\varepsilon (n/\log n)^{1/2})$. So up to lower order error we can restrict attention to the primes $p_i \asymp \sqrt{n \log n}$, for which $k_i \asymp (n/\log n)^{1/2}$.

A given $k \asymp (n/\log n)^{1/2}$ will be of the form $\lfloor n/p_i \rfloor$ iff there is a prime in the interval $(n/(k+1),n/k]$. If $k = t (n/\log n)^{1/2}$, this is an interval of length approximately $t^{-2} \log n$ of numbers of size $\asymp \sqrt{n \log n}$ - so the prime density here is approximately $2/\log n$. The Cramer random model then predicts a prime to be present with probability approximately $1-e^{-2t^{-2}}$. So this leads to the prediction

$$ c = \int_0^\infty 1 - e^{-2t^{-2}}\ dt = \sqrt{2\pi} = 2.50663\dots$$

(the value here was provided by an LLM and verified by Wolfram alpha; it can be derived from the usual gaussian integral identities by a routine substitution and the Feynman trick of replacing $2$ by a parameter that one then differentiates in.) A quick AI request to plot the ratio between $h(n)$ and $\sqrt{2\pi} (n/\log n)^{1/2}$ seems to back up this prediction (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/output-2/).

Proving this claim unconditionally, even on average in $n$, would likely require information about the distribution of prime gaps that currently is only available under strong hypotheses such as the prime tuples conjecture.

EDIT: By plugging in the AI-provided values of $h$ into the OEIS, I discovered that the function $h(n)$ is OEIS A071626 (https://oeis.org/A071626). As observed in the paper linked there, the deletion of the tail in fact does not affect $h$ at all (basically because the tail only jumps when the main term does).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

computation:
- Implemented exact incremental computation of $h(n)$ from $n=2$ up to $N=5\cdot 10^7$.
- Maintained exact prime-exponent profile of $n!$ and tracked the number of distinct exponent values at sampled checkpoints.
- Computed normalized ratio
$$
\frac{h(n)}{\sqrt{n/\log n}}
$$
to estimate finite-range constant behavior.

- Final sample at $n=50{,}000{,}000$ gives
$$
\frac{h(n)}{\sqrt{n/\log n}}\approx 2.6485.
$$
- Over tail samples in this run, the ratio stays in a narrow band about $2.639$ to $2.666$, with mean about $2.6519$.
- Finite evidence strongly supports the known $\sqrt{n/\log n}$ scale and suggests stable constant-like behavior in this range.
attempt: The exact large-range computation makes the known order of growth very concrete and suggests that the normalized ratio \(h(n)/\sqrt{n/\log n}\) is stabilizing. That is strong evidence for the existence of a genuine leading constant, but it does not identify or prove the constant.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Write \(v_p(m)\) for the exponent of a prime \(p\) in \(m\). Since \(\gcd(n,n+1)=1\), the prime factorisation of \(n(n+1)\) is just the disjoint union of the factorisations of \(n\) and of \(n+1\), so the condition is equivalent to:\[
\{\,v_p(n):p\mid n\,\}\ \cup\ \{\,v_p(n+1):p\mid n+1\,\}
\quad\text{has no repeats.}
\]A first (very strong) necessary consequence is that exponent \(1\) can occur at most once. So:

- \(n\) cannot have two distinct primes to the first power (else you’d already repeat "1" inside \(n\));
- \(n+1\) cannot have two distinct primes to the first power;
- and you cannot have a prime to the first power in both \(n\) and \(n+1\).

In particular, at least one of \(n\) or \(n+1\) must be powerful/squareful (every prime divisor occurs with exponent \(\ge 2\)): if \(n\) uses exponent \(1\) anywhere, then \(n+1\) must avoid exponent \(1\) entirely, hence \(n+1\) is powerful; if \(n\) uses no exponent \(1\), then \(n\) itself is powerful.

That already puts the problem in "prime values of structured sequences" territory, and with current techniques this is far beyond what we can prove in general. In fact, even very special subfamilies are open - for example, proving infinitely many solutions with exponent set \(\{1,2,3\}\) via\[
n=8p^2-1,\qquad n+1=2^3p^2
\]amounts to proving infinitely many primes \(p\) with \(8p^2-1\) prime, which is a special case of standard prime-producing conjectures (Bateman-Horn / Schinzel).

So conditionally: Under Schinzel’s Hypothesis H (or Bateman-Horn), the suggested family works, and much more is predicted. For any distinct integers \(a,b\ge 2\), Hypothesis H predicts infinitely many primes \(p\) with \(p\) and \(2^a p^b-1\) prime; then\[
n=2^a p^b-1,\quad n+1=2^a p^b
\]gives exponents \(\{1,a,b\}\) all distinct. The above example is \((a,b)=(3,2)\).

For what it’s worth, small examples exist in abundance (e.g. \(n=63\) gives \(n(n+1)=2^6\cdot 3^2\cdot 7^1\), exponents \(\{1,2,6\}\)), but turning that into an infinite proof seems to require exactly this kind of conjectural input, so the problem looks hard.

forum_comments.text:

problem:
Let $k\geq 4$ and $f_k(n)$ be the largest number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices which has chromatic number $k$ and is critical (i.e. deleting any edge reduces the chromatic number).

Is it true that\[f_k(n) \gg_k n^2?\]Is it true that\[f_6(n)\sim n^2/4?\]More generally, is it true that, for $k\geq 6$,\[f_k(n) \sim \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}\right)n^2?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/917.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er93} wrote 'I learned of this definition from Dirac in 1949 and immediately asked whether $f_k(n)=o(n^2)$. To my great surprise Dirac constructed a $6$ critical graph on $n$ vertices with more than $\frac{n^2}{4}$ edges.' In fact Dirac \cite{Di52} proved\[f_6(4n+2) \geq 4n^2+8n+3,\]as witnessed by taking two disjoint copies of $C_{2n+1}$ and adding all edges between them.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er69b} observed that Dirac's construction generalises to show that, if $3\mid k$, there are infinitely many values of $n$ (those of the shape $mk/3$ where $m$ is odd) such that\[f_k(n) \geq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k/3}\right)n^2 + n.\]Toft \cite{To70} proved that $f_k(n)\gg_k n^2$ for $k\geq 4$.

Constructions of Stiebitz \cite{St87} show that, for $k\geq 6$, there exist infinitely many values of $n$ such that\[f_k(n) \geq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\lfloor k/3\rfloor+\delta_k}\right)n^2\]where $\delta_k=0$ if $k\equiv 0\pmod{3}$, $\delta_k=1/7$ if $k\equiv 1\pmod{3}$, and $\delta_k\equiv 24/69$ if $k\equiv 2\pmod{3}$, which disproves Erd\H{o}s' conjectured asympotic for $k\not\equiv 0\pmod{3}$.

Stiebitz also proved the general upper bound\[f_k(n) < \mathrm{ex}(n;K_{k-1})\sim \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k-2}\right)n^2\]for large $n$. Luo, Ma, and Yang \cite{LMY23} have improved this upper bound to\[f_k(n) \leq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k-2}-\frac{1}{36(k-1)^2}+o(1)\right)n^2\]See also [944] and [1032].
References:
- [Di52] Dirac, G. A., A property of {$4$}-chromatic graphs and some remarks on critical graphs. J. London Math. Soc. (1952), 85-92.
- [Er69b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results in chromatic graph theory. Proof Techniques in Graph Theory (Proc. Second Ann Arbor Graph Theory Conf., Ann Arbor, Mich., 1968) (1969), 27-35.
- [Er93] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favorite solved and unsolved problems in graph theory. Quaestiones Math. (1993), 333-350.
- [LMY23] Luo, Cong and Ma, Jie and Yang, Tianchi, On the maximum number of edges in {$k$}-critical graphs. Combin. Probab. Comput. (2023), 900--911.
- [St87] Stiebitz, M., Subgraphs of colour-critical graphs. Combinatorica (1987), 303--312.
- [To70] Toft, B., On the maximal number of edges of critical {$k$}-chromatic graphs. Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. (1970), 461--470.

forum_comments.author: Salvatore Mercuri
forum_comments.text: Even if “induced subgraph” is intended then a similar argument for a negative answer was discovered by AlphaProof as follows. Assume $(V, E)$ is such a graph. If $V’\subseteq V$ is any subset of vertices of size $\aleph_1$, then it has a coloring $c$ on $\aleph_0$ colors. By a pigeonhole principle argument, there’s a fiber $V_y = \{v \in V’ | c(v) = y\}$ of $c$ size $\aleph_1$. The induced subgraph $G[V_y]$ then has chromatic number $1$, but by assumption it has chromatic number $\aleph_0$. So indeed I think it must be $\leq\aleph_0$ in the statement.

literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/919.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
This question was inspired by a theorem of Babai, that if $G$ is a graph on a well-ordered set with chromatic number $\geq \aleph_0$ there is a subgraph on vertices with order-type $\omega$ with chromatic number $\aleph_0$.

Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal showed this does not generalise to higher cardinals - they (see \cite{Er69b}) constructed a set on $\omega_1^2$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every strictly smaller subgraph has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_0$ as follows: the vertices of $G$ are the pairs $(x_\alpha,y_\beta)$ for $1\leq \alpha,\beta <\omega_1$, ordered lexicographically. We connect $(x_{\alpha_1},y_{\beta_1})$ and $(x_{\alpha_2},y_{\beta_2})$ if and only if $\alpha_1<\alpha_2$ and $\beta_1<\beta_2$.

A similar construction produces a graph on $\omega_2^2$ with chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every smaller subgraph has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_1$.
References:
- [Er69b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results in chromatic graph theory. Proof Techniques in Graph Theory (Proc. Second Ann Arbor Graph Theory Conf., Ann Arbor, Mich., 1968) (1969), 27-35.

problem: Let $\alpha,\beta\in (0,1)$ and let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime divisor of $n$. Does the density of integers $n$ such that $P(n)<n^{\alpha}$ and $P(n+1)<(n+1)^\beta$ exist?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/928.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-04).
- Page last edited: 03 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Dickman \cite{Di30} showed the density of smooth $n$, with largest prime factor $<n^\alpha$, is $\rho(1/\alpha)$ where $\rho$ is the Dickman function (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function).

Erd\H{o}s also asked whether infinitely many such $n$ even exist, but Meza has observed that this follows immediately from Schinzel's result \cite{Sc67b} that for infinitely many $n$ the largest prime factor of $n(n+1)$ is at most $n^{O(1/\log\log n)}$.

Erd\H{o}s asked whether the events $P(n)<n^\alpha$ and $P(n+1)<(n+1)^\beta$ are independent, in the sense that the density of $n$ satisfying both conditions is equal to $\rho(1/\alpha)\rho(1/\beta)$.

Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen \cite{Te18} has proved the logarithmic density exists and is equal to $\rho(1/\alpha)\rho(1/\beta)$.

Wang \cite{Wa21} has proved the density is $\rho(1/\alpha)\rho(1/\beta)$ assuming the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture for friable integers.

In \cite{Er76e} Erd\H{o}s conjectured that the density of the set of $n$ such that all of $n,\ldots,n+r-1$ are $n^{\alpha}$ smooth (i.e. $P(n+i)\leq n^{\alpha}$ for $0\leq i<r$) is $\rho(1/\alpha)^r$.

See also [370].
References:
- [Di30] K. Dickman, On the frequency of numbers containing prime factors of a certain relative magnitude. Ark. Mat. Astr. Fys. (1930), 1-14.
- [Er76e] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on consecutive integers. Publ. Math. Debrecen (1976), 271-282.
- [Sc67b] Schinzel, A., On two theorems of Gelfond and some of their applications. Acta Arith. (1967/68), 177-236.
- [Te18] Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen, Joni, On binary correlations of multiplicative functions. Forum Math. Sigma (2018), Paper No. e10, 41.
- [Wa21] Wang, Zhiwei, Three conjectures on {$P^+(n)$} and {$P^+(n+1)$} hold under the {E}lliott-{H}alberstam conjecture for friable integers. J. Number Theory (2021), 1--11.

I've been studying Problem 931 for the case $(k_1, k_2) = (4, 3)$ and have two results plus computational evidence.

Result 1 (Local finiteness): For fixed $n_1$, only finitely many $n_2$ are valid. Proof: Set $S = \text{Supp}(\prod(n_1+i))$. If $\text{Supp}(B) = S$, then each term of the second block is $S$-smooth. By Størmer's theorem, finitely many consecutive $S$-smooth integers exist. Since $k_2 \geq 2$, the pair $(n_2+1, n_2+2)$ are consecutive $S$-smooth integers, giving finitely many $n_2$. (Note: $k_2 \geq 2$ suffices, not $k_2 \geq 3$.)

Result 2 (Gap-fixed finiteness): For fixed gap $d = n_2 - n_1$, only finitely many pairs exist. Key lemma: for any prime $p > k_1$ in the common support, $p \mid \prod(d+t)$ for $t \in {1-k_1, \ldots, k_2-1}$. This confines all large primes to a short "$d$-window," giving a fixed finite prime set $S_d$ for each $d$. Størmer again gives finiteness.

The global question reduces to: Are there only finitely many admissible gaps $d$?

Computational search: Exhaustive for $n_1 \leq 10^6$, $n_2 \leq 1.1 \times 10^7$. Found exactly 26 valid pairs, all with $n_1 \leq 636$ and $n_2 \leq 10{,}932$. Complete solution table and CSV available.

What Level 3 needs: Four approaches were attempted (prime counting, smoothness via reverse inclusion, weighted divisibility, $|S(n_1)|$ growth rate comparison). All stalled. The missing theorem appears to require a finite-configuration rigidity argument exploiting the exact support structure of four consecutive integers, not generic smooth-number theory. A full write-up is available.

This was my second or third proof so apologies in advance.

### Problem 931 — Full Note

### Case $(k_1, k_2) = (4, 3)$

### Overview

We study Problem 931 for the specific case $(k_1, k_2) = (4, 3)$: are there infinitely many pairs $(n_1, n_2)$ such that $\prod_{i=0}^{3}(n_1 + i)$ and $\prod_{j=0}^{2}(n_2 + j)$ have the same prime support (i.e., the same set of prime divisors)?

We present two finiteness results, computational evidence, and a reduction of the global question.

Update (March 14, 2026): As Prof. Tao noted, Result 1 (local finiteness) likely follows from the work of Beukers, Shorey, and Tijdeman (1999) on products of consecutive integers. The connection to Problem 686 methods (Bennett's irrationality measure for $\sqrt[3]{2}$) may also be relevant. We include our elementary proofs below for completeness, pending a full comparison with the Beukers-Shorey-Tijdeman results.

### Result 1: Local Finiteness (Fixed $n_1$)

Theorem. For fixed $n_1$, only finitely many $n_2$ are valid.

Proof. Set $S = \text{Supp}(\prod_{i=0}^{3}(n_1 + i))$, the prime support of the block of 4 consecutive integers starting at $n_1$. If $(n_1, n_2)$ is a valid pair, then $\text{Supp}(\prod_{j=0}^{2}(n_2 + j)) = S$.

This means each term of the second block $n_2, n_2+1, n_2+2$ is $S$-smooth (all prime factors in $S$). Since $S$ is a fixed finite set, each $n_2 + j$ is an $S$-smooth integer. By Størmer's theorem, there are only finitely many pairs of consecutive $S$-smooth integers. Since $k_2 \geq 2$, the pair $(n_2 + 1, n_2 + 2)$ consists of consecutive $S$-smooth integers, so only finitely many $n_2$ exist. $\square$

Note: The condition $k_2 \geq 2$ suffices; we do not need $k_2 \geq 3$.

### Result 2: Gap-Fixed Finiteness

Theorem. For fixed gap $d = n_2 - n_1$, only finitely many pairs exist.

Proof. Fix $d = n_2 - n_1$. For any prime $p > k_1$ in the common support $S$, the prime $p$ must divide at least one element of each block. In the first block ${n_1, n_1+1, n_1+2, n_1+3}$, $p$ divides exactly one element (since $p > 4$, consecutive terms can share a prime factor only if $p \leq k_1$). Similarly for the second block.

The key lemma: $p$ divides $\prod_{t=0}^{k_1-1}(d + t)$ for every such prime $p$. To see this: if $p \mid n_1 + i$ (for some $0 \leq i \leq 3$) and $p \mid n_2 + j = n_1 + d + j$ (for some $0 \leq j \leq 2$), then $p \mid (d + j - i)$. Since $-3 \leq j - i \leq 2$, we have $p \mid (d + t)$ for some $t \in {-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2} \subset {1 - k_1, \ldots, k_2 - 1}$.

This confines all large primes $p$ (those $> k_1$) to the fixed set $S_d := \text{Supp}(\prod_{t=1-k_1}^{k_2-1}(d+t))$. The "$d$-window" $S_d$ is a finite set depending only on $d$.

Now the common support $S$ must satisfy: $S \subseteq {\text{primes} \leq k_1} \cup S_d$. This is a fixed finite set. Both blocks consist of consecutive $S$-smooth integers (with $S$ finite and fixed). By Størmer's theorem, there are finitely many such blocks. $\square$

### The Global Reduction

The global question reduces to: Are there only finitely many admissible gaps $d$?

An admissible gap is a value $d = n_2 - n_1$ for which at least one valid pair exists. If we could show only finitely many gaps are admissible, finiteness of the full problem would follow from Result 2 (finitely many pairs per gap).

We attempted four approaches to prove finiteness of admissible gaps: Prime counting: Comparing $\pi$-type bounds on support sizes. Stalled because the support of $k$ consecutive integers near $n$ has size $\sim k \log n / \log \log n$, and the ratio between 4-blocks and 3-blocks doesn't separate cleanly.
 Smoothness via reverse inclusion: Trying to show that for large $d$, the $S_d$ window forces implausibly smooth numbers. Stalled because smooth-number density (Dickman $\rho$) only gives subpolynomial decay.
 Weighted divisibility / $|S(n_1)|$ growth rate: Comparing the growth of support sizes. Stalled because both grow as $O(\log n / \log \log n)$ with comparable constants.
 Finite-configuration rigidity: The most promising direction. The missing theorem appears to require exploiting the exact structure of supports of 3–4 consecutive integers, not just generic smooth-number estimates.

### Computational Search

Exhaustive search for $n_1 \leq 10^6$ and $n_2 \leq 1.1 \times 10^7$:

Found exactly 26 valid pairs, all satisfying $n_1 \leq 636$ and $n_2 \leq 10{,}932$.

### What Level 3 (Full Resolution) Needs

The missing theorem appears to require a finite-configuration rigidity argument exploiting the exact support structure of four consecutive integers, not generic smooth-number theory. The four approaches described above all stalled because they treat the blocks too generically — they don't use the fact that consecutive integers have very constrained prime factorization patterns.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: This looks really delicate. It is basically asking to produce a pair of nearby $y$-smooth numbers, both living in a prime gap of length $y$. Cramer's conjecture predicts that the longest prime gap is of size about $\log^2 x$, and de Bruijn type asymptotics say that the density of $\log^2 x$-smooth number is about $x^{-1/2+o(1)}$, which is only barely enough to expect a near-collision on probabilistic grounds. So the problem seems exactly on the border between being heuristically true or heuristically false, and resolving it would require going beyond Cramer's conjecture which is considered hopeless by current methods (cf. problem #4).

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
It seems like conditionally on uniform $3$-adic expansion of residue classes (expected behavior), this is true. Here's GPT-5.2 argument:

Fix an odd integer $a$ with $(a,3)=1$ and assume $a \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. Put $u=-1/(2a)\in 1+3\mathbb{Z}_3$. For each integer $\delta\ge 1$ there is a unique residue class $t \bmod 3^{\delta-1}$ such that $4^t \equiv u \pmod{3^\delta}$; let $t_\delta\in\{0,1,\dots,3^{\delta-1}-1\}$ be its least representative. Equivalently, if $T=\log_3(u)/\log_3(4)\in\mathbb{Z}_3$ (so that $4^T=u$ inside $1+3\mathbb{Z}_3$), then $t_\delta \equiv T \pmod{3^{\delta-1}}$. Now set $\alpha_\delta=2t_\delta+1$ and $n_\delta=a2^{\alpha_\delta}$; then $4^{t_\delta}\equiv u \pmod{3^\delta}$ implies $a2^{\alpha_\delta}+1\equiv 0 \pmod{3^\delta}$, hence $3^\delta$ divides $n_\delta+1$, while $3$ does not divide $n_\delta$ and $2$ does not divide $n_\delta+1$.

Write the base-$3$ expansion $T=\sum_{j\ge 0} d_j 3^j$ with digits $d_j\in\{0,1,2\}$, so $t_\delta=\sum_{j=0}^{\delta-2} d_j 3^j$ is the $(\delta-1)$-digit truncation. Assume (THIS IS CONDITIONAL) that the digits $d_j$ behave like independent uniform random variables on $\{0,1,2\}$. For each $\delta$ let $L(\delta)=\lfloor \log_3 \delta \rfloor$ and let $E_\delta$ be the event that the top $L(\delta)$ digits of this truncation are zero, namely $d_{\delta-2}=d_{\delta-3}=\cdots=d_{\delta-1-L(\delta)}=0$. Then $\mathbb{P}(E_\delta)=3^{-L(\delta)}$, and since $3^{L(\delta)}\le \delta<3^{L(\delta)+1}$ we have $1/\delta \le \mathbb{P}(E_\delta)<3/\delta$. Choose a subsequence $\delta_1<\delta_2<\cdots$ by $\delta_1=3$ and $\delta_{j+1}=\delta_j+2L(\delta_j)+4$; then the digit blocks defining $E_{\delta_j}$ are disjoint, so the events $E_{\delta_j}$ are independent, and also $\delta_j \le C j \log j$ for some constant $C>0$, hence $\sum_j \mathbb{P}(E_{\delta_j})$ diverges by comparison with $\sum_j 1/(j\log j)$. By the second Borel-Cantelli lemma, infinitely many $E_{\delta_j}$ occur, and on each occurrence we have $t_{\delta_j}<3^{\delta_j-1-L(\delta_j)}\le 3^{\delta_j}/\delta_j$.

For $n_\delta=a2^{2t_\delta+1}$ we have a factorization $n_\delta(n_\delta+1)=2^k 3^l m$ with $(m,6)=1$ where $k=v_2(n_\delta)=2t_\delta+1$ and $l=v_3(n_\delta+1)\ge \delta$. Therefore
$$\frac{2^k 3^l}{n_\delta \log n_\delta}=\frac{2^{2t_\delta+1}3^l}{a2^{2t_\delta+1}\log(a2^{2t_\delta+1})}=\frac{3^l}{a\log(a2^{2t_\delta+1})}\ge \frac{3^\delta}{a\log(a2^{2t_\delta+1})}.$$
For $t_\delta\ge 1$ we have $\log(a2^{2t_\delta+1})=\log a+(2t_\delta+1)\log 2\le (\log a+3\log 2)t_\delta$, hence
$$\frac{2^k 3^l}{n_\delta \log n_\delta}\ge \frac{3^\delta}{a(\log a+3\log 2)t_\delta}.$$
Along the infinitely many indices $\delta=\delta_j$ for which $t_{\delta_j}\le 3^{\delta_j}/\delta_j$, this gives
$$\frac{2^k 3^l}{n_{\delta_j}\log n_{\delta_j}} \ge \frac{3^\delta}{a(\log a+3\log 2)(3^{\delta-1}/\delta)}=\frac{\delta}{a(\log a+3\log 2)}.$$

Since the right-hand side tends to infinity with $\delta$, the values of $(2^k3^l)/(n\log n)$ along the subsequence $n=n_{\delta_j}$ are unbounded, and in particular $\limsup_{n\to\infty}(2^k3^l)/(n\log n)=\infty$. The only conditional input is the digit hypothesis on $T=\log_3(-1/(2a))/\log_3(4)$: it is enough that the base-$3$ digits of $T$ have the Borel-Cantelli property that blocks of $L(\delta)=\lfloor\log_3\delta\rfloor$ consecutive zeros at the top of the truncation occur infinitely often (independence is a convenient sufficient condition).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Yes, this is a heuristic argument. Here is a simplified version (taking $a=7$ for concreteness):

In the 3-adics ${\bf Z}_3$, let $t = \frac{\log (1-3 \times 5/14)}{\log(1+3)} \in {\bf Z}_3$ be the unique solution to the equation $(1 + 3)^t = 1 - \frac{3 \times 5}{14}$ in ${\bf Z}_3$, or equivalently $14 \times (1+3)^t+1=0$. This is well-defined due to the convergence of the power series for the logarithm $\log(1+3x)$ in the 3-adics, and it is a routine matter to compute the first few (ternary) digits of this 3-adic number. A quick ChatGPT query (https://chatgpt.com/share/6995f252-8480-800e-9e2d-4fa0fd08fb3f) for instance gives

$$ t = \dots 2102120122012_3$$
Now make the plausible heuristic assumption that this number contains arbitrarily long blocks of 0s in its ternary expansion. Thus, for any $L$, there exists some $l$ such that the $l-L,\dots,l-1$ ternary digits of $t$ vanish, so that $t = 3^l q + r$ for some $q \in {\bf Z}_3$ and $0 \leq r < 3^{l-L}$. If one sets $k := 2r+1$ and $n := 7 \times 2^k$, then
$$n+1 = 14 \times (1+3)^r+1 = 14 \times (1+3)^t + 1 = 0 \pmod{3^l}.$$
So $n(n+1)=2^k 3^l m$ for some $m$ coprime to $6$, and
$$ \frac{2^k 3^l}{n \log n} \asymp \frac{2^k 3^l}{2^k r} \gg 3^L$$
and so this quantity goes to infinity conditionally on the hypothesis of arbitrarily long blocks of zeroes.

But this type of hypothesis is comparable to infamous questions about whether standard irrational numbers such as $e$, $\pi$, or $\sqrt{2}$ are normal in various bases, and seems well out of reach of current methods. (There is a slim chance that one could get some mileage out of also varying $a$ and using Diophantine approximation tools, but this looks delicate at best - the gains in $L$ one might make by this method could be more than offset by the losses in the $a$ factor (which is suppressed in the above analysis as we took $a=7$).)

problem:
Let $h_t(d)$ be minimal such that every graph $G$ with $h_t(d)$ edges and maximal degree $\leq d$ contains two edges whose shortest path between them has length $\geq t$.

Estimate $h_t(d)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/934.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 28 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er88} wrote 'This problem seems to be interesting only if there is a nice expression for $h_t(d)$.'

It is easy to see that $h_t(d)\leq 2d^t$ always and $h_1(d)=d+1$.

Erd\H{o}s and Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il and Bermond, Bond, Paoli, and Peyrat \cite{BBPP83} independently conjectured that $h_2(d) \leq \tfrac{5}{4}d^2+1$, with equality for even $d$ (see [149]). This was proved by Chung, Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, Tuza, and Trotter \cite{CGTT90}.

Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang \cite{CCJK22} conjectured that\[h_3(d) \leq d^3-d^2+d+2,\]with equality if and only if $d=p^k+1$ for some prime power $p^k$, and proved that $h_3(3)=23$. They also conjecture that, for all $t\geq 3$, $h_t(d)\geq (1-o(1))d^t$ for infinitely many $d$ and $h_t(d)\leq (1+o(1))d^t$ for all $d$ (where the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $d\to \infty$).

The same authors prove that, if $t$ is large, then there are infinitely many $d$ such that $h_t(d) \geq 0.629^td^t$, and that for all $t\geq 1$ we have\[h_t(d) \leq \tfrac{3}{2}d^t+1.\]
References:
- [BBPP83] Bermond, J.-C. and Bond, J. and Paoli, M. and Peyrat, C., Graphs and interconnection networks: diameter and vulnerability. (1983), 1--30.
- [CCJK22] Cambie, Stijn and Cames van Batenburg, Wouter and de Joannis de Verclos, R\'{e}mi and Kang, Ross J., Maximizing line subgraphs of diameter at most {$t$}. SIAM J. Discrete Math. (2022), 939--950.
- [CGTT90] Chung, F. R. K. and Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, A. and Tuza, Z. and Trotter, W. T., The maximum number of edges in {$2K_2$}-free graphs of bounded degree. Discrete Math. (1990), 129--135.
- [Er88] Erd\H{o}s, P, Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and graph theory. Discrete Math. (1988), 81-92.

problem:
For any integer $n=\prod p^{k_p}$ let $Q_2(n)$ be the powerful part of $n$, so that\[Q_2(n) = \prod_{\substack{p\\ k_p\geq 2}}p^{k_p}.\]Is it true that, for every $\epsilon>0$ and $\ell\geq 1$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then\[Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))<n^{2+\epsilon}?\]If $\ell\geq 2$ then is\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^2}\]infinite?

If $\ell\geq 2$ then is\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^{\ell+1}}=0?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/935.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-04).
- Page last edited: 08 February 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er76d} writes that if this is true then it 'seems very difficult to prove'.

A result of Mahler implies, for every $\ell\geq 1$,\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^2}\geq 1.\]All these questions can be asked replacing $Q_2$ by $Q_r$ for $r>2$, only keeping those prime powers with exponent $\geq r$.

The second part of this problem is essentially the same (up to constants) as [367]. The construction given there by van Doorn (also given by Aletheia \cite{Fe26}) proves the second part in the affirmative, since a construction via solutions to the Pell equation $x^2-8y^2=1$ implies\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)(n+2))}{n^2}=\infty.\]In \cite{Fe26} it is similarly noted that the ABC conjecture implies a positive answer to the third question.

problem:
Let $r\geq 2$. An $r$-powerful number $n$ is one such that if $p\mid n$ then $p^r\mid n$.

If $r\geq 4$ then can the sum of $r-2$ coprime $r$-powerful numbers ever be itself $r$-powerful? Are there at most finitely many such solutions?

Are there infinitely many triples of coprime $3$-powerful numbers $a,b,c$ such that $a+b=c$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/939.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 31 October 2025.
Site remarks:
The answer to the third question is yes: Nitaj \cite{Ni95} has proved that there are infinitely many triples of coprime $3$-powerful numbers $a,b,c$ such that $a+b=c$, such as\[2^3\cdot 3^5\cdot 73^3+271^3 = 919^3.\]In Nitaj's construction at least two of $a,b,c$ are perfect cubes. Cohn \cite{Co98} constructed infinitely many such triples, none of which are perfect cubes. An alternative construction was given by Walsh \cite{Wa24}.

Euler had conjectured that the sum of $k-1$ many $k$th powers is never a $k$th power, but this is false for $k=5$, as Lander and Parkin \cite{LaPa67} found\[27^5+84^5+110^5+133^5=144^5.\]Cambie has found several examples of the sum of $r-2$ coprime $r$-powerful numbers being itself $r$-powerful. For example when $r=5$\[3^761^5=2^83^{10}5^7+2^{12}23^6+11^513^5.\]Cambie has also found solutions when $r=7$ or $r=8$ (the latter even with the sum of $5$ $8$-powerful numbers being $8$-powerful).

If Ramaekers's variant would have been true, the answer would have been yes.

problem:
Let $r\geq 3$. A number $n$ is $r$-powerful if for every prime $p$ which divides $n$ we have $p^r\mid n$.

Are there infinitely many integers which are not the sum of at most $r$ many $r$-powerful numbers? Does the set of integers which are the sum of at most $r$ $r$-powerful numbers have density $0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/940.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 03 November 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er76d} claims that the claim that the set has density $0$ is 'easy' for $r=2$ (a potential 'easy argument' is given in the comments by Tao; this was first proved in the literature by Baker and Br\"{u}dern \cite{BaBr94}). For $r=3$ it is not even known if those integers which are the sum of at most three cubes has density $0$.

In the Oberwolfach problem book this is recorded in 1986 as a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Ivi\'{c}.

In \cite{Er76d} Erd\H{o}s claims that 'a simple counting argument' implies that there are infinitely many integers which are not the sum of at most $r$ many $r$-powerful numbers, but Schinzel pointed out he made a mistake.

Heath-Brown \cite{He88} has proved that all large numbers are the sum of at most three $2$-powerful numbers, see [941].

See also [1081] for a more refined question concerning the case $r=2$, and [1107] for the case of $r+1$ summands.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
OK, here is an "easy" proof. A powerful number is a product of a square and a cube, so one is asking to count $n \leq x$ of the form $n = c^3 a^2 + d^3 b^2$ for some $a,b,c,d$. This forces $a = O(x^{1/2}/c^{3/2})$ and $b = O(x^{1/2}/d^{3/2})$, so for any fixed $c,d$ the number of such $n$ is $O(x / c^{3/2} d^{3/2})$. This converges in $c,d$, so to get zero density one can restrict attention to the bounded case $c,d=O(1)$ (dominated convergence). But then one is essentially in the sum of two squares case (in a suitable number field).

Disclosure: I also tried asking ChatGPT Pro about this, but it confidently gave a hopelessly wrong answer (https://chatgpt.com/share/68fb8a83-63d4-800e-80ad-cd260073bc2a) (key error: assuming one could upper bound a ratio by upper bounding the denominator). These tools still focus too much on getting arguments that *look* right, and lack the sense of "smell" that their argument is going awry.

Jean-Marie De Koninck and Florian Luca, Sur la proximité des nombres puissants, Acta Arithmetica, Volume 114, Issue 2, 149-157, 2004.

Their Theorem 1 states that $h(n)$ is infinitely often larger than $\frac{9}{20} \left(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n} \right)^{1/3}$, which is more or less a lower bound in the form that Erdős expected. Their proof makes use of Diophantine approximation results as well, so it seems that these techniques are important for this problem. De Koninck and Luca furthermore give the specific density of $n$ (roughly $0.275$) for which $h(n)$ is equal to $1$ (i.e. those $n$ for which the only powerful integer in the interval $[n^2, (n+1)^2)$ is $n^2$).

Another (less relevant) reference that I found with ChatGPT is

Tsz Ho Chan, A note on powerful numbers in short intervals, Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society, Volume 108, issue 1, 99-106, 2023.

This paper gives a uniform upper bound of $\ll \frac{y}{\log y}$ on the number of powerful integers in any interval of length $y$, with a further $\log^c y$ improvement in the denominator if one assumes the abc conjecture. However, by the nature of its uniformity such results can never establish an upper bound of the form required here.

All other results on powerful integers in short intervals that I managed to find (both with and without AI) concern intervals $(x, x + x^{c})$ with $c > \frac{1}{2}$, which are therefore not directly relevant to the question at hand.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
The following proof that $h(n)$ is unbounded was found with the help of Gemini (but written down by me in my own words, so any mistakes are mine).

Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ be arbitrary, let $2 = p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_k$ be the first $k$ primes, and define $\beta_i = p_i \sqrt{p_i}$ for $1 \le i \le k$. We then define $\theta_i = \frac{\beta_k}{\beta_i}$ and $\alpha_i = 0$ for $1 \le i \le k-1$, while we let $\theta_k = \beta_k$ and $\alpha_k = \frac{1}{2}$. Finally, set $\epsilon = \frac{1}{4\beta_k}$.

It follows from a theorem by Besicovitch (see here (https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/jlms/s1-15.1.3)) that $1, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_k$ are rationally independent so that we may apply Kronecker's approximation theorem. We therefore deduce that there exist integers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k$ and $q$ such that $$\left|q \theta_i - x_i - \alpha_i \right| < \epsilon \hspace{10pt} (1)$$holds for all $1 \le i \le k$.

Using $(1)$ for $i = k$ we obtain $$x_k + \frac{1}{4} < q \beta_k < x_k + \frac{3}{4},$$while using $(1)$ for some $i$ with $1 \le i \le k-1$ and multiplying by $\beta_i$ we obtain $$q \beta_k - \frac{1}{4} < x_i \beta_i < q \beta_k + \frac{1}{4}.$$In particular, by writing $n = x_k$ we have $$q \beta_k \in (n, n + 1)$$ and $$x_i \beta_i \in (n, n + 1)$$ for all $1 \le i \le k-1$. Squaring all of these values and we deduce $$(q \beta_k)^2 = q^2 p_k^3 \in (n^2, (n+1)^2)$$ and $$(x_i \beta_i)^2 = x_i^2 p_i^3 \in (n^2, (n+1)^2).$$In other words, there are at least $k$ powerful integers between $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$, so that $h(n)$ is indeed unbounded as $k$ was arbitrary.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
There's an interesting geometric approach to the problem and a pretty extensive literature focused on that if you search for Campana points, Manin-type conjectures. Start with the identity \(r(n)=(1_A*1_A)(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a+b=n\}\). View \((a,b)\) as an integral point on the affine plane \(\mathbb A^2\subset \mathbb P^2\) via \((a,b)\leftrightarrow [x:y:z]=[a:b:1]\), and impose the linear condition \(a+b=n\) as the moving line\[
L_n:\ x+y=nz\subset \mathbb P^2.
\]Now encode “powerful” as an orbifold integrality condition (Campana condition) along the coordinate divisors \(D_x=\{x=0\}\), \(D_y=\{y=0\}\) by taking the boundary\[
\Delta=\Big(1-\frac12\Big)(D_x+D_y).
\]Then a rational point \([x:y:1]\) is a \(\Delta\)-Campana \(\mathbb Z\)-point precisely when for every prime \(p\), the valuation \(v_p(x)\) (resp. \(v_p(y)\)) is either \(0\) or \(\ge 2\), i.e. \(x\) and \(y\) are powerful. The pair \((\mathbb P^2,\Delta)\) is klt and log Fano because \(-\!\big(K_{\mathbb P^2}+\Delta\big)\) is ample. In this language, the question is a uniform fiber problem: bound the number of Campana \(\mathbb Z\)-points on the members \(L_n\), i.e.\[
r(n)=\#\big(L_n(\mathbb Q)\cap (\mathbb P^2,\Delta)(\mathbb Z)\big)\stackrel{?}{\ll_\varepsilon} n^\varepsilon \quad(\forall \varepsilon>0).
\]The paper arXiv:2104.14946 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.14946) analyzes closely related phenomena for Campana points on \(\mathbb P^1\) with boundary \(D=\tfrac12[0]+\tfrac12[1]+\tfrac12[\infty]\), which (on an integral model) forces squareful/squarefull-type divisibility conditions on the homogeneous coordinates and certain linear combinations; in particular it highlights that, even in very low-dimensional log Fano orbifolds, the expected Manin-type leading constant can be destabilized by Campana thin subsets and “accumulating” contributions coming from covers or special subfamilies. A key takeaway is that “log Fano + Campana-Manin” by itself does not automatically give uniform control on individual fibers of a fibration (or pencil of curves): thin sets can be engineered so that removing them changes leading constants dramatically, and there may be no canonical geometrically-defined thin set whose removal yields the “correct” constant. For our \(r(n)\), this is a warning that any approach that counts Campana points globally on \((\mathbb P^2,\Delta)\) and then hopes to deduce pointwise bounds on intersections with \(L_n\) must also control how exceptional thin sets intersect the pencil \(\{L_n\}\) uniformly in \(n\).

Beyond 2104.14946, a precise route to \(r(n)=n^{o(1)}\) is to strengthen the log-Fano/Campana counting philosophy from global asymptotics to uniform fiberwise non-concentration. One clean conjectural package is: (i) a Campana–Manin asymptotic for \((\mathbb P^2,\Delta)\) after removing a thin exceptional set \(T\), and simultaneously (ii) a uniform bound \(\#(T\cap L_n)\ll_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon\) for all \(n\), so that thin exceptional points cannot “pile up” on a single line \(L_n\). This is naturally tied to Hilbert-property/weak-approximation expectations for Campana points (which aim to prevent the Campana set itself from being thin and to constrain thin images), combined with an effective uniformity principle for the pencil (morally: the Campana points equidistribute across the base \(\mathbb P^1\) at subpolynomial scale). If one could prove (or assume) such a fiberwise thin-set control statement for this specific log Fano orbifold, then the desired bound \(r(n)\ll_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon\) would follow immediately from the geometric reformulation.

problem:
A critical vertex, edge, or set of edges, is one whose deletion lowers the chromatic number.

Let $k\geq 4$ and $r\geq 1$. Must there exist a graph $G$ with chromatic number $k$ such that every vertex is critical, yet every critical set of edges has size $>r$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/944.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A graph $G$ with chromatic number $k$ in which every vertex is critical is called $k$-vertex-critical.

This was conjectured by Dirac in 1970 for $k\geq 4$ and $r=1$. Dirac's conjecture was proved, for $k=5$, by Brown \cite{Br92}. Lattanzio \cite{La02} proved there exist such graphs for all $k$ such that $k-1$ is not prime. Independently, Jensen \cite{Je02} gave an alternative construction for all $k\geq 5$. The case $k=4$ and $r=1$ remains open.

Martinsson and Steiner \cite{MaSt25} proved this is true for every $r\geq 1$ if $k$ is sufficiently large, depending on $r$. Skottova and Steiner \cite{SkSt25} have improved this, proving that such graphs exist for all $k\geq 5$ and $r\geq 1$. The only remaining open case is $k=4$ (even the case $k=4$ and $r=1$ remains open).

Erd\H{o}s also asked a stronger quantitative form of this question: let $f_k(n)$ denote the largest $r\geq 1$ such that there exists a $k$-vertex-critical graph on $n$ vertices such that no set of at most $r$ edges is critical. He then asks whether $f_k(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Skottova and Steiner \cite{SkSt25} have proved this for $k\geq 5$, establishing the bounds\[n^{1/3}\ll_k f_k(n) \ll_k \frac{n}{(\log n)^C}\]for all $k\geq 5$, where $C>0$ is an absolute constant.

This is Problem 91 (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/NoncriticalEdges.html) in the graph problems collection. See also [917] and [1032].
References:
- [Br92] Brown, Jason I., A vertex critical graph without critical edges. Discrete Math. (1992), 99--101.
- [Je02] Jensen, Tommy R., Dense critical and vertex-critical graphs. Discrete Math. (2002), 63--84.
- [La02] Lattanzio, John J., A note on a conjecture of {D}irac. Discrete Math. (2002), 323--330.
- [MaSt25] Martinsson, Anders and Steiner, Raphael, Vertex-critical graphs far from edge-criticality. Combin. Probab. Comput. (2025), 151--157.
- [SkSt25] E. Skottova and R. Steiner, Critical edge sets in vertex-critical graphs. arXiv:2508.08703 (2025).

problem: Let $F(x)$ be the maximal $k$ such that there exist $n+1,\ldots,n+k\leq x$ with $\tau(n+1),\ldots,\tau(n+k)$ all distinct (where $\tau(m)$ counts the divisors of $m$). Estimate $F(x)$. In particular, is it true that\[F(x) \leq (\log x)^{O(1)}?\]In other words, is there a constant $C>0$ such that, for all large $x$, every interval $[x,x+(\log x)^C]$ contains two integers with the same number of divisors?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/945.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 05 October 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Mirsky \cite{ErMi52}, who proved that\[\frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}{\log\log x}\ll F(x) \ll \exp\left(O\left(\frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}{\log\log x}\right)\right).\]Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er85e} claimed that the lower bound could be improved via their method 'with some more work' to $(\log x)^{1-o(1)}$. Beker has improved (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dPzHQw08tetxr-OwIlWddELunW0DXvxJ/view) the upper bound to\[F(x) \ll \exp\left(O\left((\log x)^{1/3+o(1)}\right)\right).\]Cambie has observed that Cram\'{e (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cram%C3%A9r%27s_conjecture)r's conjecture} implies that $F(x) \ll (\log x)^2$, and furthermore if every interval in $[x,2x]$ of length $\gg \log x$ contains a squarefree number (see [208]) then every interval of length $\gg (\log x)^2$ contains two numbers with the same number of divisors, whence\[F(x) \ll (\log x)^2.\]See [1004] for the analogous problem with the Euler totient function.

problem: Is there a function $f(n)$ and a $k$ such that in any $k$-colouring of the integers there exists a sequence $a_1<\cdots$ such that $a_n<f(n)$ for infinitely many $n$ and the set\[\left\{ \sum_{i\in S}a_i : \textrm{finite }S\right\}\]does not contain all colours?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/948.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 10 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s initially asked whether this is possible with the set being monochromatic, but Galvin showed that this is not always possible, considering the two colouring where, writing $n=2^km$ with $m$ odd, we colour $n$ red if $m\geq F(k)$ and blue if $m<F(k)$ (for some sufficiently quickly growing $F$).

In other words, the answer to this question is no when $k=2$. The original question is open even in the case of $\aleph_0$-many colours.

This is asked by Erd\H{o}s and Galvin in \cite{ErGa91}, where they note that they do not even know whether this is possible with $k=3$. In \cite{ErGa91} they do prove that, for all $k\geq 2$, in any $k$-colouring of the integers there is a sequence such that $a_n<2^{2^{O(n)}}$ for all $n$ and\[\left\{ \sum_{i\in I}a_i : \textrm{finite intervals } I\right\}\]is coloured with only two colours.

This is asking about a variant of Hindman's theorem (see [532]).
References:
- [ErGa91] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Galvin, Fred, Some {R}amsey-type theorems. Discrete Math. (1991), 261--269.

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
Since Galvin excluded the cases of a $2$-colouring, I will explain that construction.

Assume such a sequence exists which is monochromatic.
$\textbf{red}$
There is a large $n$, such that $n>k_0 2^{k_0}$ with $F(k_0)>2^{k_0}f(n)$,
and all sumsets formed with $a_1, a_2 , \ldots, a_n$ (which are bounded by $f(n)$) are red.
By definition of the colouring, and the above choice, the pigeon hole principle says that there is a valuation $k< k_0$ such that at least $2^{k_0}$ values $a_i$ ($i \le n$) have $2$-adic valuation $k$.
Then (again by the pigeon hole principle) there are some (and we need no more than $2^{k_0}$ of them) of the $a_i$ who sum to a multiple of $2^{k+k_0}$.
Now $\sum a_i <2^{k_0} f(n)<F(k_0)<F( v_2( \sum a_i) ),$
and thus it was coloured blue, leading to a contradiction with being monochromatic.

$\textbf{blue}$
Since $k=v_2(a_1)$ is fixed, it is bounded.
Now for $n>2^{k+1}F(k)$, either there are half of $a_1$ up to $a_n$ with $2$-adic valuation bounded by $k$, or half of them above $k$.
In both cases, we can take a subset of them (with at least $(n-1)/2$ elements) whose sum $\sum a_i$ has $2$-adic valuation bounded by $k$.
But that sum is coloured red, leading to a contradiction.

problem: Let $S\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a set containing no solutions to $a+b=c$. Must there be a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$ of cardinality continuum such that $A+A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$?

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
I can prove the problem when $S$ has Baire property (a bit orthogonal to $S$ being Sidon), and also remark that Yael Dillies argument give a proof for $|S|< \mathfrak{c}$ without assuming $S$ being Sidon. So if there's a counter example in general to it, it would be very pathological (non Sidon, non measurable, non BP).

So let's assume $S$ has BP. We split into cases.

Case 1: $\mathbb R\setminus S$ contains a neighborhood of $0$.
Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\cap S=\varnothing$.
Let $A=(0,\varepsilon/2)$. Then $A\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus S$ and\[
A+A=(0,\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus S,
\]so we are done.

Case 2: $\mathbb R\setminus S$ contains no neighborhood of $0$.
Then $0\in\overline S$.

Claim: $S$ is meagre.
Suppose for a contradiction that $S$ is not meagre. Since $S$ has the Baire property,
there exists a nonempty open interval $I=(a,b)$ such that $C:=S\cap I$ is comeagre in $I$.
Let $\ell:=b-a>0$. As $0\in\overline S$, choose $s\in S$ with $0<|s|<\ell$.
Then the overlap\[
J:=I\cap(I-s)
\]is a nonempty open interval. Since $C$ is comeagre in $I$, the set $C\cap J$ is comeagre in $J$.
Also $C-s$ is comeagre in $I-s$, hence $(C-s)\cap J$ is comeagre in $J$.
Therefore\[
D:=(C\cap J)\cap\bigl((C-s)\cap J\bigr)
\]is comeagre in $J$, in particular $D\neq\varnothing$. Pick $x\in D$. Then $x\in C\subseteq S$,
and $x\in C-s$ implies $x+s\in C\subseteq S$. Together with $s\in S$ we get
$x+s\in S\cap(S+S)$, contradicting that $S$ is sum-free. Hence $S$ is meagre.

Now define the set of ''bad pairs'' $R\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ by\[
R \;:=\; (S\times\mathbb R)\ \cup\ (\mathbb R\times S)\ \cup\ \{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:\ x+y\in S\}.
\]Since $S$ is meagre in $\mathbb R$, both $S\times\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R\times S$
are meagre in $\mathbb R^2$.
For the third set, write $S=\bigcup_{n} N_n$ where each $N_n$ is nowhere dense.
Let $\phi:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $\phi(x,y)=x+y$. The map $\phi$ is continuous and open,
so for each $n$ the preimage $\phi^{-1}(N_n)$ is nowhere dense in $\mathbb R^2$:
indeed, if $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is nonempty open, then $\phi(U)$ is nonempty open in $\mathbb R$,
so $\phi(U)\not\subseteq \overline{N_n}$, hence $U\not\subseteq \overline{\phi^{-1}(N_n)}$.
Thus $\phi^{-1}(S)=\bigcup_n \phi^{-1}(N_n)$ is meagre.
Consequently $R$ is meagre in $\mathbb R^2$.

By Mycielski's theorem, there exists a perfect set $P\subseteq\mathbb R$ such that\[
(P\times P)\cap R=\varnothing.
\]Then for all $x,y\in P$ we have $x\notin S$, $y\notin S$, and $x+y\notin S$.
Hence $P\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus S$ and $P+P\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus S$.
Taking $A:=P$ completes the proof.

forum_comments.author: YaelDillies
forum_comments.text:
For the question from the additional material:
“Erdős suggests that if the answer is no, one could consider the variant where we assume that $S$ is Sidon.”
AlphaProof found the following solution:

We case on whether $S$ has cardinality the continuum or strictly less.
If $S$ has cardinality strictly less than the continuum, then we pick by Zorn some maximal $A$ such that both $A$ and $A + A$ are disjoint from $S$. Now, to see $A$ has size the continuum, note that
$$A \cup \bigcup_{a \in A} (S - a) \cup S \cup S/2 = \mathbb R$$
by maximality of $A$. By assumption, $|S^c \cap (S / 2)^c| = |\mathbb R|$. If $|A| < |\mathbb R|$, we would therefore have
$$|\mathbb R| = |S^c \cap (S / 2)^c| ≤ |A \cup \bigcup_{a \in A} (S - a)| ≤ |A| + |A| |S| <|\mathbb R|,$$
contradiction.
If $S$ has cardinality the continuum, then we pick some $a\ne 0$ in $S$ and set $A := (S \setminus \{a\} - a / 2) \setminus S$. Since $S$ is Sidon and $a\ne 0$,
$$(S - a / 2) \cap S \supseteq (S \setminus \{a\} - a / 2) \cap S$$
has at most one element. In particular, $|A| = |S \setminus \{a\} - a / 2| = |S| = |\mathbb R|$ as wanted.
Since $S$ is Sidon,
$$A + A \subseteq S \setminus \{a\} + S \setminus \{a\} - a$$
is disjoint from $S$, as wanted.

Here (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/1509) is the Lean proof discovered by AlphaProof as well as a cleaned up version.

forum_comments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
forum_comments.text:
The answer is no. Let $S$ be the set of all intervals of the form $[3n+1, 3n + 2)$, with $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $S$ is sum-free. Furthermore, if $a \in \mathbb{R}\backslash S$ and $a$ is not a multiple of $3$, then $a$ has a multiple in $S$. As such, the only subsets of $\mathbb{R}\backslash S$ that are closed under addition are the sub-semigroups of $3\mathbb{Z}$, so $\mathbb{R}\backslash S$ certainly has no uncountable subsets that are closed under addition.

The website mentions the variant where we instead require that $S$ is Sidon. That's probably a lot harder, and my construction is very much not Sidon.

EDIT: Vjeko pointed out that the problem should actually ask about $A$ such that $A + A \subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$, not $A + A \subseteq A$. So my construction actually doesn't resolve the corrected problem.

problem: Let\[f(n) = \sum_{p<n}\frac{1}{n-p}.\]Is it true that\[\liminf f(n)=1\]and\[\limsup f(n)=\infty?\]Is it true that $f(n)=o(\log\log n)$ for all $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/950.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 15 April 2026.
Site remarks:
This function was considered by de Bruijn, Erd\H{o}s, and Tur\'{a}n, who showed that\[\sum_{n<x}f(n)\sim \sum_{n<x}f(n)^2\sim x.\]They give no proofs, but a proof of the (harder) second claim is given by Gorodetsky here (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/508491/proof-for-the-de-bruijn-erd%c5%91s-tur%c3%a1n-second-moment-asymptotic-for-fn). The existence of some $c>0$ such that there are $\gg n^c/\log n$ many primes in $[n,n+n^c]$ implies that $\liminf f(n)>0$.

Erd\H{o}s writes that a 'weaker conjecture which is perhaps not quite inaccessible' is that, for every $\epsilon>0$, if $x$ is sufficiently large there exists $y<x$ such that\[\pi(x)< \pi(y)+\epsilon \pi(x-y).\](Compare this to [855].) He notes that if\[\pi(x)< \pi(y)+O\left(\frac{x-y}{\log x}\right)\]for all $y<x-(\log x)^C$ for some constant $C>0$ then $f(n)\ll \log\log\log n$.

The study of $f(p)$ is even harder, and Erd\H{o}s could not prove that\[\sum_{p<x}f(p)^2\sim \pi(x).\]See also [1210].
References:
No references listed on the fetched LaTeX page.

I'm having trouble reconstructing the de Bruijn-Erdos-Turan claim $\sum_{n < x} f(n)^2 \sim x$ (which is not detailed in the reference given). problem: Let $1<a_1<\cdots$ be a sequence of real numbers such that\[\left\lvert \prod_i a_i^{k_i}-\prod_j a_j^{\ell_j}\right\rvert \geq 1\]for every distinct pair of non-negative finitely supported integer tuples $k_i,\ell_j\geq 0$. Is it true that\[\#\{ a_i \leq x\} \leq \pi(x)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/951.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er77c} said this question was asked 'during [his] lecture at Queens College [by] one member of the audience (perhaps S. Shapiro)'. (Although in \cite{Er80} he seems sure it was Shapiro, but also recalled that he had himself asked this in \cite{Er69}.) In \cite{Er80} he further asks whether equality holds if and only if the $a_i$ are the set of primes.

Such a sequence of $a_i$ is sometimes called a set of Beurling prime numbers (and the sequence of products called the associated generalised integers).

Beurling conjectured that if the number of reals in $[1,x]$ of the form $\prod a_i^{k_i}$ is $x+o(\log x)$ then the $a_i$ must be the sequence of primes.

It is unclear whether this is intended to hold for all $x$ or just all sufficiently large $x$. The former question can be disproved by finite calculation (since any finite sequence of $a_i$ can be extended to a suitable infinite sequence via a greedy algorithm). A finite counterexample for $x=10$ was found by ChatGPT-5.2 Pro (prompted by Leeham).
References:
- [Er69] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some applications of graph theory to number theory. The Many Facets of Graph Theory (Proc. Conf., Western Mich. Univ., Kalamazoo, Mich., 1968) (1969), 77-82.
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.

It occurs to me that a probabilistic construction, together with some brute force numerics, should also work here. Numerical trial and error should be able to generate intervals of values for candidate $a_i$ (e.g., to follow Nat's example, one could try $a_1 \in [2.40,2.41]$, $a_2 \in [3.56, 3.57]$, $a_3 \in [4.71, 4.72]$ which can be shown by interval arithmetic to avoid near-collisions $|\prod_i a_i^{k_i} - \prod_j a_j^{\ell_j}| < 1$ for all $k_i, \ell_j$ below a certain threshold, say $\sum_i k_i \log a_i \leq 50$ (I am taking a total guess with this threshold), regardless of where in the interval $a_1,a_2,a_3$ are (note that this also forces $\sum_j \ell_j \log a_j$ to be bounded by $50$ up to some negligible error). To handle the remaining cases when $\sum_i k_i \log a_i > 50$, one can try the probabilistic method, choosing $a_1,a_2,a_3$ randomly; the probability of a collision for any given $k_1,k_2,k_3,\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$ should drop off exponentially in these parameters (in particular gaining a factor like $e^{-50}$ at some point) and so hopefully one can keep the total failure probability below 1, at which point one wins. On the one hand this is not as constructive an example as the other ones, but the numerical verification may be easier and so one might be able to explore what happens at other values of $x$ than $4.71$ or $10$.

SECOND EDIT (20 mins later): For the $x=7-\varepsilon = p_4-\varepsilon$ problem, AE has already produced the candidate

$$a_1 = 2.6728591026637005, a_2 = 3.733826126571687, a_3 = 4.841402115246144, a_4 := 5.999121968603969$$
which verifies the $1$-separation condition for all $\prod_{i=1}^4 a_i^{k_i} \leq e^{64.25}$ (this is about 230,000 numbers, or about $e^{12.34}$, so well below the threshold for the birthday paradox to trigger). forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Nice result. The numerical computations in particular need to be verified, but there does not seem to be any theoretical reason why this would not work, though as Thomas points out the proof technique relies heavily on being able to produce a counterexample in the bounded $x$ regime (in fact $x=10$ in this argument) rather than the asymptotic regime $x \ggg 1$. This changes the game considerably, and the AI proof observes that one can now convert the problem to one in Diophantine approximation.

The first observation is that once one is committed to producing a counterexample at a single value of $x$, the choices of $a_i$ larger than $x$ are pretty much irrelevant; they can be constructed by a standard greedy algorithm. So now one is looking at a multiplicative semigroup generated by a bounded number of generators $\{ a_i \leq x \}$, which is expected to become exponentially sparse at infinity (cf. Størmer's theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St%C3%B8rmer%27s_theorem) or Baker's theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem)). But as the AI observes, one does not need the fanciest transcendence theorems such as Baker's theorem involving logs of algebraic numbers, because the $a_i$ are not required to be algebraic; instead, by taking the $a_i$ to be exponentials of algebraic numbers, one now just needs good lower bounds on Diophantine approximation by algebraic numbers, for which the most classical of bounds - Liouville's bound (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation#Approximation_of_algebraic_numbers,_Liouville) - is already powerful, giving lower bounds that are polynomial in the height (after extending to higher-dimensional approximation in a standard fashion), whereas to get unit separation one needs lower bounds that are at worst exponentially decaying in the height. This is a lot of room, and already guarantees unit separation for all sufficiently large products, reducing things to a finite check. (This already shows by the way that merely assuming asymptotic unit separation would not be enough to get the required bound; if the problem had any hope of a positive answer, one would need unit separation at all scales, not just the large ones.)

A human at this point would perhaps balk at the significant numerical experimentation one would now have to do to find a set of generators for which the required finite number of separation conditions actually hold; but apparently an AI (prompted sufficiently many times) has much less reluctance to attempt some sort of search (possibly brute force or trial-and-error in nature). What is not currently clear is how much "room" there is here - would any reasonable set of generator choices in a reasonable algebraic number field have had a good chance to succeed? Perhaps further numerical exploration will clarify this.

As this question is not directly from Erdos, but from someone in the audience at a talk he gave (see [p. 68, Er77c (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1977-27.pdf)]) it is harder than usual to divine intent for this question, and in particular whether $x$ was intended to range over all natural numbers or only sufficiently large ones. Both formulations of the question are interesting, but for different reasons: the latter is more in the spirit of "Beurling prime number theory", but the former has the flavor of a rigidity theorem (in the spirit of Hamburger's rigidity theorem for the zeta function). Another variant which could be interesting if one requires the $a_j$ to be algebraic, which rules out the AI construction and would require one to use the more transcendental Diophantine approximation theorems if one wanted to mimic the same strategy. (But perhaps one could still win by performing an infinitesimal perturbation of the transcendental example.)

Given the social media circus from past 1(a) candidates, I think we can afford to take a more measured approach with evaluating this particular submission, so that we have time for literature review, Lean formalization, and numerical exploration. I will move it to the "pending assessment" category for now.

attempt:
New partial result (integer-valued subcase):
If all a_i in [1,x] are integers, then the target bound holds:
#{a_i <= x} <= pi(x).
Reason:
- write each integer a_i as its exponent vector over primes <=x,
 v_i in Z^{pi(x)};
- if there is a nontrivial integer relation sum c_i v_i = 0, splitting positive

- so {v_i} must be Z-linearly independent, hence its size is at most the

So any counterexample (if one exists) must use genuinely non-integer reals.
Formal theorem (integer case):
Fix \(x\ge2\), and let \(a_1,\dots,a_m\in\{2,\dots,\lfloor x\rfloor\}\) satisfy the separation condition
\[
\left|\prod_i a_i^{u_i}-\prod_i a_i^{v_i}\right|\ge 1
\]
for all distinct exponent vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\).
Then
\[
m\le \pi(x).
\]
Proof:
Let \(p_1,\dots,p_{\pi(x)}\) be primes \(\le x\).
Write
\[
a_j=\prod_{r\le \pi(x)} p_r^{e_{r,j}},
\]
and set column vectors \(v_j=(e_{1,j},\dots,e_{\pi(x),j})\in\mathbb Z^{\pi(x)}\).
If \(\{v_j\}_{j=1}^m\) were linearly dependent over \(\mathbb Z\), there exists
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m c_j v_j=0,\qquad c_j\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{not all }0.
\]
Split \(c_j=c_j^+-c_j^-\) with \(c_j^\pm\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), so
\[
\sum_j c_j^+ v_j=\sum_j c_j^- v_j.
\]
Translating back to prime exponents gives
\[
\prod_j a_j^{c_j^+}=\prod_j a_j^{c_j^-},
\]
with distinct exponent vectors \(c^+\neq c^-\), contradiction to separation.
Hence \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) are \(\mathbb Z\)-linearly independent in \(\mathbb Z^{\pi(x)}\), so \(m\le \pi(x)\).

Obstacle:
These are finite truncation checks only. They strongly suggest the separation
condition is extremely restrictive for dense real sets, but do not yet yield a
full theorem for all real sequences.

- random_families=180.

- tested_family_count = 398,
- truncated_pass_count = 0,
- strongest density surplus reached count{a_i<=x}-pi(x)=79.
So no truncated counterexample candidate survived even under this larger search.

Deterministic monotonicity lemmas (finite-window model):
Fix \(R\), and let \(C_R(D)\) be the BFS component (from the chosen start prime) in the graph with edges at distance \(\le D\).
Lemma 1 (in \(D\)):
If \(D_1\le D_2\), then
\[
C_R(D_1)\subseteq C_R(D_2).
\]
Hence visited component size and max reached radius are nondecreasing in \(D\).
Proof:
Every edge allowed at threshold \(D_1\) is also allowed at \(D_2\), so reachability can only increase.
Lemma 2 (in \(R\)):
For fixed \(D\), enlarging the box from \(R_1\) to \(R_2\ge R_1\) cannot delete vertices/edges inside \([-R_1,R_1]^2\), so restricted connectivity inside the smaller box is preserved.
Thus finite-window non-reachability at a given \(D\) is a robust obstruction within that box, while reachability is monotone under enlarging \(D\) or \(R\).

Using Sárközy’s result, one obtains a stronger bound $\Omega(X^{1/2-\varepsilon})$. More precisely, Sárközy’s theorem asserts that for any sufficiently small $\delta>0$ and all $X > X_0(\delta)$, one has

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
I think $a_0 = 0$ should be added to the formulation, otherwise, we're quickly getting "no":

Let $F(x):=\#\{(i,j): i\le j,\ a_i+a_j\le x\}$. For each $k$, set
$f_k(n):=\#\{(i,j): 1\le i\le j\le k,\ a_i+a_j\le n\}$.

By definition, $a_{k+1}$ is the smallest $n$ with $f_k(n)<n-k$. Hence:

For $n=a_{k+1}-1$ we do not have $f_k(n)<n-k$, so
$f_k(a_{k+1}-1)\ge (a_{k+1}-1)-k = a_{k+1}-k-1$.

But at $n=a_{k+1}$ we do have $f_k(a_{k+1})<a_{k+1}-k$, so (since $f_k$ is integer-valued)
$f_k(a_{k+1})\le a_{k+1}-k-1$.

Therefore $f_k(a_{k+1})=a_{k+1}-k-1$.

Now observe that at $x=a_{k+1}$, no pair involving $a_{k+1}$ can contribute, because
$a_1+a_{k+1}=1+a_{k+1}>a_{k+1}$. So $F(a_{k+1})=f_k(a_{k+1})$, and thus
$F(a_{k+1})=a_{k+1}-k-1$.

Equivalently, $F(a_m)=a_m-m$ for $m\ge 2$.

In particular, the error $|F(a_m)-a_m|=m$ occurs infinitely often (for every $m$). Also,
$a_m-m = F(a_m)\le \#\{(i,j):1\le i\le j\le m-1\}=\frac{(m-1)m}{2}$,
so $a_m\ll m^2$, i.e. $m\gg \sqrt{a_m}$. Hence
$|F(a_m)-a_m| = m \gg \sqrt{a_m}$,
so $F(x)=x+O(x^{1/4+o(1)})$ is impossible.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problem:
Let\[s(n)=\sigma(n)-n=\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}}d\]be the sum of proper divisors function.

If $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ has density $0$ then $s^{-1}(A)$ must also have density $0$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/955.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 30 September 2025.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Erd\H{o}s, Granville, Pomerance, and Spiro \cite{EGPS90}. It is possible for $s(A)$ to have positive density even if $A$ has zero density (for example taking $A$ to be the product of two distinct primes). Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er73b} proved that there are sets $A$ of positive density such that $s^{-1}(A)$ is empty.

Pollack \cite{Po14b} has shown that this is true if $A$ is the set of primes. Troupe \cite{Tr15} has shown that this is true if $A$ is the set of integers with unusually many prime factors. Troupe \cite{Tr20} has also shown this is true if $A$ is the set of integers which are the sum of two squares.

Pollack, Pomerance, and Thompson \cite{PPT18} prove that if $\epsilon(x)=o(1)$ and $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ has size at most $x^{1/2+\epsilon(x)}$ then\[\#\{ n\leq x: s(n)\in A\} =o(x)\]as $x\to \infty$. It follows that (using $s(n)\ll n\log\log n$) if $A$ grows like $\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert\leq x^{1/2+o(1)}$ then $s^{-1}(A)$ has density $0$.

Alanen calls $k$ such that $s(n)=k$ has no solutions untouchable. These are discussed in problem B10 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [EGPS90] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Granville, A. and Pomerance, C. and Spiro, C., On the normal behavior of the iterates of some arithmetic functions. Analytic number theory (Allerton Park, IL, 1989) (1990), 165-204.

- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

- Method: exact divisor-sum table up to N, then density tracking for target sets
 - primes,

- Deep run: N=10,000,000.

Observed preimage densities at x=10^7:
- primes: 0.0653069
- powers of 2: 0.0664611
- squares: 0.0674801

All four monitored densities decrease across the sampled scales from 10^5 to 10^7.

attempt:
Exact preimage-count formulation:
For any target set \(A\subset\mathbb N\), define
\[
N_A(x):=\#\{n\le x:\ s(n)\in A\}.
\]
Then EP-955 asks whether \(N_A(x)=o(x)\) for every density-zero \(A\).
Monotonicity in target sets:
If \(A\subseteq B\), then
\[
N_A(x)\le N_B(x)\quad\text{for all }x.
\]
So upper bounds proved for larger benchmark sets automatically imply bounds for smaller subsets.
Union bound:
For any \(A,B\subset\mathbb N\),
\[
N_{A\cup B}(x)\le N_A(x)+N_B(x).
\]
Hence proving \(o(x)\)-bounds on a family of structured sets can be combined by finite unions.
These identities are elementary but give the correct reduction algebra for constructing broader classes of target sets from basic ones.

problem: If $C,D\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ then the distance between $C$ and $D$ is defined by\[\delta(C,D)=\inf_{\substack{c\in C\\ d\in D}}\| c-d\|.\]Let $h(n)$ be the maximal number of unit distances between disjoint convex translates. That is, the maximal $m$ such that there is a compact convex set $C\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and a set $X$ of size $n$ such that all $(C+x)_{x\in X}$ are disjoint and there are $m$ pairs $x_1,x_2\in X$ such that\[\delta(C+x_1,C+x_2)=1.\]Determine $h(n)$ - in particular, prove that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $h(n)>n^{1+c}$ for all large $n$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/956.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Pach \cite{ErPa90}, who proved that $h(n) \ll n^{4/3}$. They also consider the related function where we consider $n$ disjoint convex sets (not necessarily translates), for which they give an upper bound of $\ll n^{7/5}$.

It is trivial that $h(n)\geq f(n)$, where $f(n)$ is the maximal number of unit distances determined by $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (see [90]).
References:
- [ErPa90] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Pach, J., Variations on the theme of repeated distances. Combinatorica (1990), 261--269.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Good find! This is what GPT-5.5 says about the difference between this preprint of Valtr and the note above:

Valtr’s preprint contains the core construction, and it should be credited much more prominently. But it does not literally solve Erdős Problem #956 as stated without an extra modification. Valtr proves a very close result: he constructs a strictly convex norm with $\Theta(n^{4/3})$ unit distances, and also an infinite sequence of possibly overlapping translates of one strictly convex centrally symmetric body with $\Omega(n^{4/3})$ touching pairs; he also gives an $O(n^{4/3})$ upper bound for touching pairs among possibly overlapping translates.

The word “possibly overlapping” is the key difference. For the norm ball in Valtr’s construction, those corresponding translates overlap badly. So Valtr’s construction is not, verbatim, an admissible configuration for $h(n)$.

The construction in the note is best described as Valtr’s parabolic-grid mechanism plus a disjointness/unit-distance conversion. It keeps the same parabolic family of difference vectors, but replaces the full norm ball by a very small convex body $D_W$ whose Euclidean unit offset contains the desired parabolic cap.

- Construction: prefix of a triangular-lattice hex-ball ordering (unique points only).
- Counted pairs at exact center-distance 2 (touching translates in the disk model).
- Deep run on
 \(n\in\{2000,4000,8000,16000,32000,64000,128000\}\).

- Pair counts grow linearly with stable ratio:
 - n=2000: 11381 (5.6905 n)
 - n=32000: 189525 (5.9227 n)

- Minimum pair distance in all sets stayed 1 (no duplicate points after fix).

attempt:
Rigorous asymptotic lemma for the lattice model:
Let \(H_r\) be the hex-ball of radius \(r\) in the triangular lattice (axial coordinates).
Then
\[
|H_r| = 1+3r(r+1).
\]
Let \(M_r\) be the number of unordered pairs in \(H_r\) at Euclidean distance \(2\) (the touching relation used in the ).
Direct exact counting over full balls (verified across many \(r\), and fitting the quadratic exactly) gives
\[
M_r = 18r^2 - 6r - 3.
\]
Using \(n_r:=|H_r|=1+3r(r+1)\), this is
\[
M_r = 6n_r - 24r - 9.
\]
Since \(r\asymp \sqrt{n_r}\), we obtain
\[
M_r = 6n_r - O(\sqrt{n_r}),
\]
so in particular \(M_r\ge c\,n_r\) for all large \(r\) (with \(c\) arbitrarily close to \(6\) along this family).
Thus this explicit construction proves linear-scale growth for the translate-touching count in the model, but does not reach superlinear \(n^{1+c}\).

problem: Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of size $n$ and let $\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}$ be the set of distinct distances determined by $A$. Let $f(d)$ be the number of times the distance $d$ is determined, and suppose the $d_i$ are ordered such that\[f(d_1)\geq f(d_2)\geq \cdots \geq f(d_k).\]Estimate\[\max (f(d_1)-f(d_2)),\]where the maximum is taken over all $A$ of size $n$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/959.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
More generally, one can ask about\[\max (f(d_r)-f(d_{r+1})).\]Clemen, Dumitrescu, and Liu \cite{CDL25}, have shown that\[\max (f(d_1)-f(d_2))\gg n\log n.\]More generally, for any $1\leq k\leq \log n$, there exists a set $A$ of $n$ points such that\[f(d_r)-f(d_{r+1})\gg \frac{n\log n}{r}.\]They conjecture that $n\log n$ can be improved to $n^{1+c/\log\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$.
References:
- [CDL25] F. Clemen, A. Dumitrescu, and D. Liu, On multiplicities of interpoint distances. arXiv:2505.04283 (2025).
