computation:
- Method: exact squared-distance multiplicity histograms for candidate families plus heavy random search.
- Families tested per n: grid, two_lines, parabola, and 2500 random samples.
- Deep run: n in {120,180,240,300,360}.

Best family was always two_lines, with gaps:
- n=120: gap 60
- n=180: gap 90
- n=240: gap 120
- n=300: gap 150
- n=360: gap 180
Normalized values gap/(n log n) stay positive in range ~0.085..0.104.

At this scale, explicit two-line constructions dominate random search and produce robust positive normalized gaps, consistent with lower-bound direction.
attempt:
Rigorous construction lemma:
Let \(n=2m\), and take
\[
P=\{(i,0):1\le i\le m\}\cup\{(i,1):1\le i\le m\}.
\]
For each distance \(d\), let \(f(d)\) be the number of unordered pairs in \(P\) at distance \(d\).
Define \(d_1=1\). Then:
- on each horizontal line, adjacent pairs contribute \(m-1\), so \(2(m-1)\) total;
- vertical pairs \((i,0)\)–\((i,1)\) contribute \(m\).
Hence
\[
f(d_1)=2(m-1)+m=3m-2.
\]
For \(d_2=\sqrt2\), diagonal cross-line pairs contribute
\[
(m-1)+(m-1)=2m-2.
\]
Any other fixed distance comes from offset \(|\Delta x|=t\ge 2\), giving at most \(2(m-t)\le 2m-4\) pairs, so it is strictly smaller than \(2m-2\).
Therefore
\[
\max_{d\ne d_1} f(d)=2m-2.
\]
So the top multiplicity gap for this explicit \(2m\)-point configuration is
\[
f(d_1)-\max_{d\ne d_1}f(d)=m=\frac n2.
\]
This gives a clean linear lower bound with explicit witness family.

Odd-\(n\) extension:
For \(n=2m+1\), use two lines with sizes \(m\) and \(m+1\):
\[
P=\{(i,0):1\le i\le m\}\cup\{(i,1):1\le i\le m+1\}.
\]
Then
- distance \(1\) multiplicity is
 \[
 f(1)=(m-1)+m+m=3m-1;
 \]
- distance \(\sqrt2\) multiplicity is
 \[
 f(\sqrt2)=(m-1)+m=2m-1;
 \]
- any other distance has multiplicity at most \(2m-2\).
Hence the gap is again exactly
\[
f(1)-\max_{d\ne 1}f(d)=m=\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor.
\]
So this explicit two-line family gives
\[
\max_d f(d)-\max_{d'\ne d} f(d')\ \ge\ \left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor
\]
for every \(n\).

problem:
Let $r,k\geq 2$ be fixed. Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with no $k$ points on a line. Determine the threshold $f_{r,k}(n)$ such that if there are at least $f_{r,k}(n)$ many ordinary lines (lines containing exactly two points) then there is a set $A'\subseteq A$ of $r$ points such that all $\binom{r}{2}$ many lines determined by $A'$ are ordinary.

Is it true that $f_{r,k}(n)=o(n^2)$, or perhaps even $\ll n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/960.
- Page status: DISPROVED (database last update 2026-04-09).
- Page last edited: 09 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Tur\'{a}n's theorem implies\[f_{r,k}(n) \leq \left(1-\frac{1}{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}+1.\]An internal OpenAI model (see \cite{APSSV26b}) has shown that in fact for any $r\geq 3$ and $k\geq 4$\[f_{r,k}(n) \geq \frac{n^2}{12}-O(n).\]See also [209].
References:
- [APSSV26b] B. Alexeev, M. Putterman, M. Sawhney, M. Sellke, and G. Valiant, Short proofs in combinatorics, probability, and number theory II. arXiv:2604.06609 (2026).

computation:
Deep standalone finite experiment:
- Parameters: r=6, k=4, n in {12,14,16,18,20}.
- For each n, sampled 12,000 accepted point sets (rejecting samples with >=4 collinear points).
- Mixed sampling: general-position random sets + triad-heavy sets (to create many non-ordinary lines).
- For each set: computed ordinary-line count and whether the ordinary-line graph contains a K_6.

Results (empirical):
- Estimated forcing thresholds (in sampled family):
 - n=12: 55
 - n=14: 77
 - n=16: 82
 - n=18: 109
 - n=20: 0 (all sampled sets already had K_6)
- Highest ordinary-line counts seen without K_6 were one below threshold where nontrivial (54, 76, 81, 108).

These are finite sampled proxies, not proofs of true thresholds. They provide computational evidence that large ordinary-line counts strongly correlate with forced K_6 in the ordinary-line graph for these small n.
attempt:
Turan reduction (proof-level upper bound template):
For a fixed point set \(P\), define its ordinary-line graph \(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P)\):
- vertices are points of \(P\);
- an edge \(uv\) is present iff the line through \(u,v\) is ordinary in \(P\).
Then the number of ordinary lines equals \(|E(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P))|\).
If \(|E(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P))| > \left(1-\frac1{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}\), Turan's theorem implies \(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P)\) contains \(K_r\), i.e. an \(r\)-subset whose every pair-line is ordinary.
Therefore,
\[
f_{r,k}(n)\ \le\ \left(1-\frac1{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}+1,
\]
independently of \(k\). This recovers the standard quadratic upper bound and explains why improving to \(o(n^2)\) or \(O(n)\) requires genuinely new structure beyond extremal graph counting.

problem: Let $f(k)$ be the minimal $n$ such that every set of $n$ consecutive integers $>k$ contains an integer divisible by a prime $>k$. Estimate $f(k)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/961.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 03 April 2026.
Site remarks:
In other words, how large can a consecutive set of $k$-smooth integers be? Sylvester and Schur (see \cite{Er34}) proved $f(k)\leq k$ and Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er55d} proved\[f(k)<3\frac{k}{\log k}.\]Jutila \cite{Ju74} and Ramachandra, and Shorey \cite{RaSh73} proved\[f(k) \ll \frac{\log\log\log k}{\log \log k}\frac{k}{\log k}.\]It is likely that $f(k) \ll (\log k)^{O(1)}$.

This is essentially equivalent to [683].
References:
- [Er34] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A Theorem of Sylvester and Schur. J. London Math. Soc. (1934), 282--288.
- [Er55d] Erd\H{o}s, P., On consecutive integers. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (3) (1955), 124--128.
- [Ju74] Jutila, Matti, On numbers with a large prime factor. {II}. J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1974), 125--130.
- [RaSh73] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N., On gaps between numbers with a large prime factor. Acta Arith. (1973), 99--111.

Formal lemmas from definition:
Let \(R(k)\) be the maximum run length of consecutive \(k\)-smooth integers; by definition \(f(k)=R(k)+1\).
1. Monotonicity:
\[
k_1\le k_2 \implies R(k_1)\le R(k_2)\quad\text{and}\quad f(k_1)\le f(k_2),
\]
because every \(k_1\)-smooth integer is also \(k_2\)-smooth.
2. Certified lower bounds:
if a concrete interval \([a,a+L-1]\) is verified to consist entirely of \(k\)-smooth numbers, then
\[
R(k)\ge L,\qquad f(k)\ge L+1.
\]
Hence each witness interval in is a rigorous certificate of the corresponding lower bound.

problem: Let $k(n)$ be the maximal $k$ such that there exists $m\leq n$ such that each of the integers\[m+1,\ldots,m+k\]are divisible by at least one prime $>k$. Estimate $k(n)$ - in particular, is it true that\[\log k(n) \leq (\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/962.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 03 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er65} wrote it is 'not hard to prove' that\[\log k(n)\geq (\log n)^{1/2-o(1)}\]and it 'seems likely' that $k(n)=o(n^\epsilon)$, but had no non-trivial upper bound for $k(n)$. In \cite{Er76e} he gives an argument which proves\[\log k(n) \gg \sqrt{\log n\log\log n},\]and thought that this bound was 'fairly sharp'.

Tao in the comments has given a simple argument proving $k(n) \leq (1+o(1))n^{1/2}$. In \cite{Er76e} Erd\H{o}s reports he could prove that\[k(n) \leq \exp(-(\log n)^c)n^{1/2}\]for some constant $c>0$, but could not prove that $k(n) \leq n^{1/2-c}$ for a constant $c>0$, which he said 'seems a ridiculously weak result'.

Tang has proved (https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-962/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_962.pdf) a lower bound of\[\log k(n)\geq \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-o(1)\right)\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}.\]
References:
- [Er65] Erd\H{o}s, P., Extremal problems in number theory. Proc. Sympos. Pure Math., Vol. VIII (1965), 181-189.
- [Er76e] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on consecutive integers. Publ. Math. Debrecen (1976), 271-282.

forum_comments.author: deezel
forum_comments.text:
A possible reformulation that may be worth recording. Setting $K = X^\kappa$ and $W_1(m) := \sum_{i=1}^K \omega_{>K}(m+i)$ for $m \in [X, 2X)$:

Reduction. A bad block of length $2K$ at scale $X$ forces at least $K$ values of $m$ to satisfy $W_1(m) \ge K$. Markov on the fourth central moment gives

$$ |{m : W_1(m) \ge K}| \le M_4(W_1)/(K-\mu)^4 $$

with $\mu = K\log(1/\kappa) + o(K)$ by Mertens. So $M_4(W_1) \ll XK^{2+o(1)}$ uniformly for $\kappa > 1/e$ would yield $k(n) \ll n^{1/e + o(1)}$.

Pairing identity. Writing $W_1 = \sum_{p>K} I_p$ and $f_p = I_p - \lambda_p$, expanding $M_4 = \sum_m (\sum_p f_p)^4$:

$$ M_4(W_1) = 3X \cdot \mathrm{Var}(W_1)^2 + R $$

where $R$ is the all-distinct + three-equal + four-equal cumulant residual. The three-equal and four-equal pieces are $O(XK)$ trivially; the all-distinct piece reduces to a level-4 sieve discrepancy bound (call it L6).

Numerical certification. At $\kappa = 0.34$, across $X \in [10^5, 10^8]$: $M_4/(3X\sigma^4) = 1.00 \pm 0.02$. Kurtosis is exactly 3 over four decades. The standardized $W_1$ converges to standard Gaussian.

The variance gap. The remaining content is $\mathrm{Var}(W_1) \ll K \log^B X$. Equivalently, with $T_{pq} = S_p \times S_q$ (Cartesian product of shifted intervals mod $p, q$) and $R_{pq}$ defined as the count of $m \in [X, 2X)$ with $m \bmod pq \in T_{pq}$, minus $XK^2/(pq)$:

$$ \left| \sum_{K < p \ne q \le 2X} R_{pq} \right| \ll XK \log^B X \quad (\text{L5}) $$

Numerically (sampling 50K of 5M pairs at $X=10^4$, $K=22$): $\sqrt{\langle R_{pq}^2\rangle} \approx 2.8$ vs trivial bound $K^2 = 484$ – already a 200x per-pair improvement. But Cauchy-Schwarz on $\sum R_{pq}^2$ still overshoots the true sum by about 600x. The remaining cancellation is signed across pairs, not magnitudinal – so $L^2$ approaches cannot close L5; only direct bilinear estimates can.

By Fourier expansion:

$$ \sum_{p \ne q} R_{pq} = \sum_{p \ne q} \frac{1}{pq} \sum_{(a,b) \ne 0} A_p(a) , A_q(b) , E_X(a/p + b/q) $$

with $A_p(a) = \sum_{i=1}^K e(ai/p)$ and $E_X(\theta) = \sum_{m=X}^{2X-1} e(m\theta)$. The cancellation lives in the region where $|a/p + b/q|$ is small – additive collisions of fractions with prime denominators. Friedlander-Iwaniec dispersion (Opera de Cribro Ch. 17) appears to be the right tool. L6 is the same machinery at sieve dimension 4.

Across $\kappa \in [0.40, 0.45]$, $\mathrm{Var}(W_1)/(K \rho(1/\kappa)) \approx 1.04$ – the variance constant numerically equals the Dickman function, which is suggestive of a closed form I cannot identify.

I want to be explicit: I do not claim a theorem improving on Erdos’s [Er76e] $k(n) \le \exp(-(\log n)^c) n^{1/2}$. The chain to $n^{1/e+o(1)}$ is rigorous modulo L5 and L6, both of which I can numerically support but cannot prove. I’d value any pointers to existing work that closes either.

Two specific questions:

1. Has anyone applied the polynomial-savings Matomaki-Radziwill-Tao machinery to $f$ equal to the indicator of $K$-smooth integers? Its pretentious distance to 1 is $\sqrt{\log(1/\kappa)}$, so whether MRT gives unconditional polynomial savings here depends on the dependence on $\mathbb{D}(f, 1)$.
1. The Tao-Teravainen [TaTe25] / Lau [Lau26] machinery handles $\omega(n+k)$ for consecutive integers via Maynard sieve + Pilatte. Does anything in section 5 of TaTe25 (the variance bound for $\sum \omega(n+h)/2^h$) adapt to unweighted sums in our prime range?

Full notes (Cauchy-Schwarz autopsy, full numerics, code) available on request.

– Darin Dimitroff

attempt:
Formal lemmas from the definition:
Let \(K(n)\) denote the EP-962 quantity (called k(n) above).
Lemma 1 (monotonicity in \(n\)):
If \(n_1\le n_2\), then
\[
K(n_1)\le K(n_2).
\]
Proof:
Any witness block with start \(m\le n_1\) is also admissible for \(n_2\).
Lemma 2 (universal upper bound \(K(n)\le n\)):
For every \(n\ge 1\),
\[
K(n)\le n.
\]
Proof:
Suppose a witness of length \(k\) starts at \(m+1\) with \(m\le n\).
Each term in the block has a prime factor \(>k\), so in particular each term is \(>k\).
Hence the first term satisfies \(m+1>k\), i.e. \(m\ge k\).
Since \(m\le n\), we get \(k\le n\).
Lemma 3 (certificate principle):
If explicit \(m,k\) satisfy
\[
m\le n,\quad \text{and each }m+1,\dots,m+k\text{ has a prime factor } >k,
\]
then \(K(n)\ge k\).
Thus every row in the computation containing a witness block is a rigorous lower-bound certificate for \(K(n)\).
Immediate baseline:
For every \(n\ge 2\),
\[
K(n)\ge 1.
\]
Proof:
Take \(m=1\), \(k=1\). The block is just \(\{2\}\), and \(2\) has a prime factor \(>1\). Since \(m=1\le n\), this is an admissible witness.
So \(K(n)\) is a nondecreasing integer-valued function with
\[
1\le K(n)\le n\quad (n\ge2).
\]

forum_comments.author: KoishiChan
forum_comments.text:
I think I can show that

Main Claim: Let $A$ be a set of size $n$. Then $A$ contains a disassociated subset of size $(1 - o(1))\log_2 n$.

A standard reduction shows that we may assume $A$ is a subset of the integers. We further assume that elements of $A$ are positive integers.

Throughout assume $n$ is large. Let $d_d(A)$ be the size of the largest disassociated subset of $A$, and let
$$f(n) = \min_{|A| = n, A \subset \mathbb{Z}_+} d_d(A).$$
We are going to establish a recursive bound of the form
$$f(n) \geq \frac{1}{12} \log_2 n + f\left(\frac{n^{11/12}}{\log^4 n}\right).$$
Our strategy is as follows. Fix a prime number $p \in [n^{1/12} / 2, n^{1/12}]$. Suppose for a moment that the elements of $A$ are equi-distributed modulo $p$. Let $A_p$ be the subset of $A$ with elements divisible by $p$, and let $a_i$ be an element of $A$ with residue $i$ modulo $A$. If we let $\Gamma = \{1, 2, \cdots, 2^{\lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} - 1}\}$ be a disassociated set modulo $p$ of order $\lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor}$, and $D'$ be a disassociated subset of $A_p$, then the set
$$D = D' \sqcup \{a_i: i\in \Gamma\}$$
must be disassociated. Therefore, we have
$$d_d(A) \geq \lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} + d_d(A_p) \geq \lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} + f\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)$$
precisely what we want.

In general, we do not have this "equi-distributed modulo $p$" condition. However, we will ensure this condition by using an old trick of Erdős: take a sufficiently large prime $q$ greater than all elements of $A$, pick $r \in (\mathbb{Z} / q \mathbb{Z})^*$ uniformly at random, and replace $A$ with $A' = (r \cdot A) \mod{q}$. Our hope is that when cast back to the integers, $A'$ will be uniformly distributed modulo $p$, and we can proceed with the previous argument. The remaining proof is devoted to justifying this hope.

First, note that if a set of positive integers is disassociated modulo $q$, and $q$ is greater than all elements in the set, then the set is disassociated over $\mathbb{Z}$.

Let $A \subset \mathbb{Z}_+$ be such that $d_d(A) = f(n)$. Let $k = d_d(A) + 1$, and WLOG assume $k \leq \log_2 n$ (for otherwise $f(n) \geq \log_2 n - 1$ as desired). Let $q$ be as above. For each $i \in [0, p - 1]$, we define the following subset of $(\mathbb{Z} / q \mathbb{Z})^*$
$$B_{p, i} = \{px + i: x \in \{1, 2, \cdots, \lfloor{\frac{q - 1}{pk}\rfloor}\}\}.$$
We want to find an $r \in (\mathbb{Z} / q \mathbb{Z})^*$ such that most $rA \cap B_{p, i}$ are large. This follows from the key lemma below.

Lemma: Let $q$ be a prime, and $L$ be a parameter. Let $A \subset (\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z})^*$ be a set of size at least $L^{10}$, and let $B$ be an arithmetic progression in $(\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z})^*$ of size at least $\frac{q}{L}$. Then, for a uniformly random $r \in (\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z})^*$, we have
$$\mathbb{P}\left(|r \cdot A \cap B| \leq \frac{|A||B|}{2(q - 1)}\right) \ll \frac{1}{L^3}.$$

Proof: We use the second moment bound. We want to compute
$$\mathbb{E}_{r} |r \cdot A \cap B|^2.$$
Using Fourier analysis, we have
$$|r \cdot A \cap B| = \frac{1}{q - 1}\sum_{a \in A, b \in B} \sum_{\chi} \chi(ra b^{-1})$$
where $\chi$ goes over all Dirichlet characters of $(\mathbb{Z} / q \mathbb{Z})^*$. Hence, we have
$$|r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{1}{(q - 1)^2}\sum_{a, a' \in A, b, b' \in B} \sum_{\chi, \chi'} \chi(ra b^{-1}) \chi'(ra' b'^{-1}).$$
Summing over $r$, all contributions from $\chi' \neq \bar{\chi}$ vanish, giving
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{1}{(q - 1)^2}\sum_{a, a' \in A, b, b' \in B} \sum_{\chi} \chi(a b^{-1}) \bar{\chi}(a' b'^{-1}).$$
Thus we obtain
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{1}{(q - 1)^2} \sum_{\chi} |\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 |\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^2.$$
Isolating the trivial character, we obtain
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{|A|^2 |B|^2}{(q - 1)^2} + \frac{1}{(q - 1)^2}\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0} |\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 |\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^2.$$
We now use the fact that $B$ is an AP. If we consider the quantity
$$M(\chi) = \sup_{r} |\sum_{i = 1}^r \chi(i)|$$
then we have
$$|\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)| \leq 2 M(\chi).$$
A theorem of Montgomery and Vaughen, "MEAN VALUES OF CHARACTER SUMS" (1979), states that
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0} M(\chi)^4 \ll q^3.$$
So we have
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0} |\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 |\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^2 \leq \left(\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^4\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^4\right)^{1/2}$$
where
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^4 \ll q^3$$
and
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^4 \leq |A|^2 \sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 \leq q|A|^3.$$
So we conclude that
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0} |\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 |\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^2 \ll q^{2} |A|^{3/2}.$$
Substituting back, we have
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{|A|^2 |B|^2}{(q - 1)^2} + O\left(|A|^{3/2}\right).$$
As we also have
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B| = \frac{|A| |B|}{(q - 1)}$$
we obtain by Chebyshev's inequality that
$$\mathbb{P}\left(|r \cdot A \cap B| \leq \frac{|A||B|}{2(q - 1)}\right) \ll \frac{(q - 1)^2}{|A|^{1/2}|B|^2}.$$
Substituting $|A| \geq L^{10}, |B| = \frac{q}{L}$, we obtain
$$\mathbb{P}\left(|r \cdot A \cap B| \leq \frac{|A||B|}{2(q - 1)}\right) \ll \frac{1}{L^3}$$
as desired. QED.

Use this lemma on $B = B_{p, i}$, $A = A$, and $L = pk + 1$, and make a union bound over $i$. We conclude that there exists $r \in (\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z})^*$ such that
$$|r \cdot A \cap B_{p, i}| \geq \frac{|A||B_{p, i}|}{2(q - 1)} \geq \frac{|A|}{2(pk + 1)}$$
for all $i$.

Finally, let $A_{p, i}'$ denote the lift of $r \cdot A \cap B_{p, i}$ back to the integers. Recall our definition of $\Gamma$ as a large disassociated set of size $\mathbb{Z} / p\mathbb{Z}$. Take any $a_i \in A_{p, i}'$ for $i \in \Gamma$, and let $D'$ be a disassociated subset of $A_{p, 0}'$ of maximum size. Now we show that
$$k = d_d(A) + 1 \geq |D'| + |\Gamma| + 1.$$
Suppose the contrary.

1) Analyzing mod $p$, we see that $D' \cup \{a_i: i \in \Gamma\}$ is disassociated over $\mathbb{Z}$. Let $D''$ be any subset of $D' \cup \{a_i: i \in \Gamma\}$ with size $k$.

2) As each element of $D''$ lies in $\sqcup_i B_{p, i}$, each element of $D''$ lies in $\left[1, \frac{q}{k}\right]$. As $|D''| = k$, we see that $D''$ is disassociated in $\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z}$.

3) Thus, $r^{-1}D'' \subset A$ is disassociated in $\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z}$, hence disassociated when lifted back to $A \subset \mathbb{Z}$. So $A$ contains a disassociated subset of size $k > d_d(A)$, contradiction!

Therefore, we conclude that
$$d_d(A) \geq |\Gamma| + |D'| \geq \lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} + f\left(|A'_{p, 0}|\right) \geq \lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} + f\left(\frac{|A|}{2(pk + 1)}\right).$$
As $p \in [n^{1/12} / 2, n^{1/12}]$ and $k \leq \log_2 n$ by assumption, we obtain that for sufficiently large $n$, we have.
$$f(n) \geq \min\left(\log_2 n - 1, \frac{1}{12} \log_2 n - O(1) + f\left(\frac{n^{11/12}}{4 \log_2 n}\right)\right).$$
Iterating, we obtain $f(n) \geq (1 - o(1)) \log_2 n$, as desired.

forum_comments.text:
\textbf{Solution to Erdős Problem 963/ AI Gemino Pro 3.5 used}

\textbf{Answer:} Yes, the estimate $f(n) \ge \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ holds.

\textbf{Reasoning:}
Let $f(n)$ denote the maximal size $k$ such that any set $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ of size $n$ contains a dissociated subset of size $k$.
A subset $B$ is dissociated if all subset sums $\sum_{b \in S} b$ (for $S \subseteq B$) are distinct. This is analogous to linear independence over the field $\mathbb{F}_2$ but in the context of integer addition.

To estimate $f(n)$, we consider the "worst-case" scenario, which minimizes the size of the largest dissociated subset. This occurs when the set $A$ has a high degree of additive structure (redundancy).
Consider the set of the first $n$ integers:\[ A = \{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\} \]In this set, we can construct a dissociated subset $B$ by selecting powers of 2:\[ B = \{2^0, 2^1, 2^2, \dots, 2^m\} \]such that $2^m \le n$. The sums of subsets of $B$ correspond to the binary representations of integers up to $\sum B$, which are unique by the properties of the binary numeral system.
The largest power of 2 less than or equal to $n$ is $2^{\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor}$.
Thus, the size of this subset is $|B| = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$.

Since the set $\{1, \dots, n\}$ represents the structure with maximal additive dependencies (minimizing potential dissociated subsets), and even here we find a subset of size $\approx \log_2 n$, it follows that for any arbitrary set $A$ of size $n$, we can find a dissociated subset of at least size $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.

\textbf{Conclusion:}\[ f(n) \ge \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor \]The lower bound is established.

problem: Let $u_n=p_n/n$, where $p_n$ is the $n$th prime. Does the set of $n$ such that $u_n<u_{n+1}$ have positive density?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/968.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 31 March 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Prachar \cite{ErPr61} proved that\[\sum_{p_n<x} \lvert u_{n+1}-u_n\rvert \asymp (\log x)^2,\]and that the set of $n$ such that $u_n>u_{n+1}$ has positive density.

As with many of Erd\H{o}s' questions, by 'positive density' here he most likely meant positive lower density - in other words, there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for all large $x$ the number of such $n\leq x$ is at least $cx$.

Erd\H{o}s also asks whether\[u_n<u_{n+1}<u_{n+2}\]or\[u_n>u_{n+1}>u_{n+2}\]have infinitely many solutions.
References:
- [ErPr61] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Prachar, K., S\"{a}tze und {P}robleme \"{u}ber {$p\sb{k}/k$}. Abh. Math. Sem. Univ. Hamburg (1961/62), 251--256.

forum_comments.text:
The answer to the problem is positive assuming both the Riemann hypothesis and a weak form of the pair correlation conjecture, specifically estimate (5) of this paper of Heath-Brown (http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/aa/aa41/aa4118.pdf). By Corollary 1 of that paper, we have for any $A$ that
$$ \sum_{p_n \leq x: p_{n+1}-p_n \geq A \log x} (p_{n+1}-p_n) \ll \frac{1}{A} x \quad (1)$$
for any $A > 0$. From telescoping series we have
$$ \sum_{p_n \leq x} (p_{n+1}-p_n) = (1+o(1)) x$$
hence by the prime number theorem
$$ \sum_{p_n \leq x: p_{n+1}-p_n \leq \log x} (\log x - (p_{n+1}-p_n)) =
\sum_{p_n \leq x: p_{n+1}-p_n > \log x} ((p_{n+1}-p_n) - \log x) + o(x).$$
From known results about small gaps between primes (such as the GPY result mentioned in my previous comment) the left-hand side is $\gg x$, hence the right hand side is also. Combining this with (1) we conclude that there exist $0 < \varepsilon < A$ such that $(1+\varepsilon) \log x \leq p_{n+1}-p_n \leq A \log x$ for $\gg x/\log x$ values of $p_n$. For such values we have $u_n < u_{n+1}$, giving the claim.

It is also straightforward to deduce the claim from a sufficiently uniform version of the prime tuples conjecture (which, by a well known calculation of Gallagher (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematika/article/on-the-distribution-of-primes-in-short-intervals/DCE557AC8750333E68426FCEEC11858C), implies that the normalized prime gaps $(p_{n+1}-p_n) / \log p_n$ are asymptotically exponentially distributed).

This seems close to the limit of current technology, so further progress may need to await some breakthrough on the pair correlation conjecture or the prime tuples conjecture.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
[Completely rewrote this answer, which previously was based on a sign error.]

The claim $u_n < u_{n+1}$ rearranges to $p_{n+1}-p_n > \frac{p_n}{n}$ so by the prime number theorem this is essentially asking for a large prime gap $p_{n+1}-p_n \gtrsim \log n$. In the other direction, one can recover Erdos's previous result from the more recent result of results of Goldston, Pintz, and Yildirim (https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.5886) that for a positive density of $n$, one has $p_{n+1}-p_n \leq \eta \log n$ for any fixed $\eta> 0$.

I imagine that with the modern Maynard sieve one can similarly conclude that $u_n > u_{n+1} > u_{n+2}$ for a set of positive density by exhibiting many clusters of three nearby primes, but I haven't checked this carefully (and it may already be in the literature).

The enemy preventing one from proving $u_n < u_{n+1}$ for a set of positive density is if almost all prime gaps in say $[x,2x]$ are less than $\log x$, and a small number (zero density) of prime gaps are much larger than $\log x$. Possibly one could use some of the large prime gap theory or the Maier matrix method to produce a positive density of clusters of moderately large prime gaps to finish off the problem though?

attempt:
Exact reformulation and proof lemmas:
Let \(p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime, \(g_n:=p_{n+1}-p_n\), and \(u_n:=p_n/n\).
Lemma 1 (exact increment identity):
\[
u_{n+1}-u_n=\frac{n\,g_n-p_n}{n(n+1)}.
\]
Proof:
\[
\frac{p_{n+1}}{n+1}-\frac{p_n}{n}
=\frac{n(p_n+g_n)-(n+1)p_n}{n(n+1)}
=\frac{n g_n-p_n}{n(n+1)}.
\]
Corollary 1 (sign criterion):
\[
u_{n+1}>u_n \iff g_n>\frac{p_n}{n}=u_n.
\]
Similarly,
\[
u_{n+1}<u_n \iff g_n<u_n.
\]
So the EP-968 set
\[
\{n:\,u_n<u_{n+1}\}
\]
is exactly
\[
\{n:\,g_n>u_n\}.
\]
Heuristic bridge:
Since \(u_n\sim \log n+\log\log n\) and typical prime gaps are also of logarithmic scale,
the sign is governed by the fluctuation of \(g_n\) around the local mean scale.
This explains why both signs appear with substantial frequency in computations,
while density questions remain subtle.
Arithmetic progression obstruction (rational \(\alpha\)):
If \(\alpha=a/b\in\mathbb Q\), then \(\{\alpha p_n\}\) lies in the finite set
\[
\left\{0,\frac1b,\dots,\frac{b-1}{b}\right\},
\]
so it cannot be equidistributed in \([0,1)\).
Thus irrationality assumptions in equidistribution variants are logically necessary; rational parameters are rigidly periodic modulo 1.

problem: Let $Q(x)$ count the number of squarefree integers in $[1,x]$. Determine the order of magnitude in the error term in the asymptotic\[Q(x)=\frac{6}{\pi^2}x+E(x).\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/969.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 19 October 2025.
Site remarks:
It is elementary to prove $E(x)\ll x^{1/2}$, and the prime number theorem implies $o(x^{1/2})$. The best known unconditional upper bound is of the shape $x^{1/2-o(1)}$, due to Walfisz \cite{Wa63}. Evelyn and Linfoot \cite{EvLi31} proved that\[E(x) \gg x^{1/4},\]and this is likely the true order of magnitude. The Riemann Hypothesis would follow from $E(x)\ll x^{1/4}$.

The true order of magnitude is unknown even assuming the Riemann Hypothesis. Conditional on this assumption, the best known upper bound is\[E(x)\ll x^{\frac{11}{35}+o(1)},\]due to Liu \cite{Li16}.

- [EvLi31] Evelyn, C. J. A. and Linfoot, E. H., On a problem in the additive theory of numbers. Ann. of Math. (2) (1931), 261--270.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
This is true conditionally on Hardy-Littlewoods ("Conditional Poisson law at the Linnik scale"):
Let $c>0$ be fixed, let $d\to\infty$, and set\[
x:=(1+c)\phi(d)\log d,\qquad
N_a:=\pi(x;d,a)=\#\{p\le x:\ p\equiv a\!\!\pmod d\}\quad((a,d)=1).
\]Assume the following uniform prime $r$-tuple asymptotic for every fixed $r\ge1$: for all distinct integers $0\le k_1,\dots,k_r\le \lfloor x/d\rfloor$, writing $h_i:=(k_i-k_1)d$,\[
\#\{n\in [1,d]:\ n,\ n+h_2,\dots,n+h_r\ \text{are prime}\}
=\Bigl(\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)+o(1)\Bigr)\frac{d}{(\log x)^r},
\]uniformly in $d$ (here $\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)$ is the usual singular series), and in addition the average singular series over such tuples has the expected value\[
\frac{1}{K^r}\!\!\sum_{\substack{0\le k_1,\dots,k_r\le K\\ \text{distinct}}}\!\!\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)
=\Bigl(\frac{d}{\phi(d)}\Bigr)^{r-1}(1+o(1)),\qquad K:=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\Bigr\rfloor.
\]Then expanding factorial moments and averaging over $a\in(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z)^\times$ gives\[
\mathbb E[(N_a)_r]\ :=\ \frac{1}{\phi(d)}\sum_{(a,d)=1} N_a(N_a-1)\cdots(N_a-r+1)
\ \sim\ \Bigl(\frac{x}{\phi(d)\log x}\Bigr)^r\ =:\ \lambda^r.
\]Hence (method of moments) $N_a$ is asymptotically $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ as $a$ varies, with\[
\lambda=\frac{x}{\phi(d)\log x}\sim 1+c.
\]In particular,\[
\#\{a\bmod d:\ (a,d)=1,\ N_a=0\}=(e^{-\lambda}+o(1))\phi(d)\sim e^{-(1+c)}\phi(d),
\]equivalently for a positive proportion of reduced residue classes one has
$p(a,d)>(1+c)\phi(d)\log d$.
as wanted

write $q(a,d)$ to be the least $q>0$ so that $qd+a$ is prime. then we have that $p(a,d)=q(a,d)d+a$, unless $p(a,d)=a$.

now heuristically we expect the values of $q(a,d)$ to distributed like samples from a geometric random variable with success probability $\frac{d}{\phi(d)}\cdot \frac{1}{\log(d)}$. this has mean $\mu = \frac{1}{d}\phi(d)\log(d)$ whence it seems $p(a,d)$ should have expectation $\approx d\mu =\phi(d)\log(d)$.

and we'd expect this conjecture to be true due to how geometric random variables fluctuate. you'd in fact expect that for each $C$, that $\Omega_C(\phi(d))$ values of $a$ have $p(a,d)>C\phi(d)\log(d)$, if I'm not mistaken.

problem: Let $\alpha>1$ be irrational. Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $\lfloor p\alpha\rfloor$ is also prime?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/972.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
Site remarks:
Vinogradov \cite{Vi48} proved that the sequence $\{p\alpha\}$ is uniformly distributed for every irrational $\alpha$, and hence there are infinitely many primes $p$ of the shape $p=\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for every irrational $\alpha>1$. Indeed, this occurs if and only if\[\frac{p}{\alpha}\leq n<\frac{p+1}{\alpha},\]which is true if and only if $\{p\alpha^{-1}\}>1-\alpha^{-1}$, which happens infinitely often by the uniform distribution of $\{p\alpha^{-1}\}$.

The result should be true for every $\alpha \in \mathbb R^+ \setminus \mathbb N$.
For $\alpha = 1/2$, it is e.g. equivalent with the existence of infinitely many Sophie Germain primes, for which one guess there are $2C(1+o(1)) \frac{x}{\ln^2 x}$ many up to $x$.

problem: Does there exist a constant $C>1$ such that, for every $n\geq 2$, there exists a sequence $z_i\in \mathbb{C}$ with $z_1=1$ and $\lvert z_i\rvert \geq 1$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$ with\[\max_{2\leq k\leq n+1}\left\lvert \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}z_i^k\right\rvert < C^{-n}?\]

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Interestingly, as observed in Erdos's paper, the answer is completely different if one replaces the range $2 \leq k \leq n+1$ by $1 \leq k \leq n$. Here one has the example of the $(n+1)^{th}$ roots of unity (if $n+1$ is prime) to show that the max can be 1, but it was shown by Atkinson (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02066680) that it must be $\gg 1$ (and possibly even $\geq 1/2$)! Turan conjectures a lower bound of $1-o(1)$ as $n \to \infty$.

It is not clear whether there is a similar construction showing that $1$ can be attained (or beaten) in the $2 \leq k \leq n+1$ case.

EDIT: Here is a summary of Atkinson's argument. Suppose for contradiction that the power sums $s_k = \sum_{1 \leq i \leq n} z_i^k$ are all small for $1 \leq k \leq n$. The function $g(\theta) = -\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{s_k e(k\theta)}{k}$ is the Fourier expansion of $\sum_{1 \leq i \leq n} \log(1-z_i e(\theta))$ up to degree $n$, hence the Fourier expansion of $e^{g(\theta)}$ agrees with $\prod_{1 \leq i \leq n} (1-z_i e(\theta))$ up to degree $n$. If we set $z_1=1$, we conclude that at $\theta=0$, $e^{g(0)}$ is equal to the tail of its Fourier expansion after degree $n$; thus $e^{g(0)}$ is formally equal to the inner product of $e^{g(\theta)}$ and $\sum_{m=n+1}^\infty e(m\theta)$, or on integrating by parts of $e^{g(\theta)} g'(\theta)$ and $-\sum_{m=n+1}^\infty e(m\theta)/2\pi i -m$. Thus the inner product of $e^{g(\theta)-g(0)} g'(\theta)$ and $-\sum_{m=n+1}^\infty e(m\theta)/2\pi i m$ is equal to $1$. But using Plancherel's theorem to control the derivative of $g'$, one can show by standard estimates that this inner product is small if the $s_k$ are all small, giving the result.

More informally: $e^{g(\theta)-g(0)}$ has significant presence at high frequencies, which is why $g'$ cannot have all of its Fourier coefficients small.

attempt:
Rigorous mean-square lower bound (all powers):
For fixed \(z_1,\dots,z_n\) on the unit circle,
\[
\liminf_{K\to\infty}\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K |S_k|^2 \ge n.
\]
Proof:
Expand
\[
|S_k|^2=\sum_{i,j=1}^n (z_i\overline{z_j})^k.
\]
Averaging over \(k\le K\):
- diagonal terms \(i=j\) contribute exactly \(n\);
- off-diagonal terms with ratio \(\neq 1\) have Cesaro average tending to \(0\);
- off-diagonal terms with ratio \(=1\) (coincident points) contribute nonnegative amount.
So the asymptotic mean-square is at least \(n\).

Corollary:
\[
\sup_{k\ge 1}|S_k|\ge \sqrt n.
\]
Indeed, otherwise \(|S_k|^2<n\) for all \(k\), contradicting the averaged limit.

Relevance to EP-973:
This unconditional lower bound concerns all powers \(k\), not only the short window \(2\le k\le n+1\). So it does not settle the posed short-range extremal question, but it gives a rigorous obstruction against uniformly tiny power sums across all orders.

problem: Let $f\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be an irreducible non-constant polynomial such that $f(n)\geq 1$ for all large $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Does there exist a constant $c=c(f)>0$ such that\[\sum_{n\leq X} \tau(f(n))\sim cX\log X,\]where $\tau$ is the divisor function?

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
I did some literature search and in full generality (arbitrary irreducible $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ of degree $\ge 2$), the strongest unconditional lower bounds known for\[
F_f(n)=P^+\Bigl(\prod_{m\le n} f(m)\Bigr)
\]are superlinear but subpower: they grow like $n^{1+o(1)}$, e.g.\[
F_f(n)\ \ge\ n\exp\exp\bigl(c(\log\log n)^{1/3}\bigr)
\](and related refinements). These come from global "Chebyshev/Erdos-Schinzel" methods controlling how often primes can divide polynomial values, but they do not reach any fixed power $n^{1+c}$.

Fixed-power bounds $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$ are known for certain special low-degree polynomials, because one can prove that in each dyadic interval $(X,2X]$ a positive proportion of values $f(m)$ have a prime factor $\ge X^{1+c}$; this immediately implies $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$. This has been proved for example for the cubic $n^3+2$ (Irving) and for certain quartics with cyclic/dihedral Galois group (Dartyge-Maynard), via deep sieve arguments plus strong "Type I/II" distribution estimates for $f(n)$ in residue classes.

For quadratics such as $n^2+1$, there are powerful results showing $P^+(n^2+1)\ge n^{1+c}$ infinitely often (with explicit $c$), but not (currently) the kind of dyadic positive-proportion statement that would force $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$ uniformly for all large $n$. Broadly, pushing $n^{1+c}$ for general $f$ seems to require much stronger distribution/trace-function/automorphic input than is available in the "generic" case, while special algebraic structure can make the needed analytic estimates accessible.

References:
Erdős-Schinzel (lower bounds for $P^+(\prod_{m\le x} f(m))$ of size $x^{1+o(1)}$):
https://www2.math.ethz.ch/EMIS/classics/Erdos/cit/71511050.htm

Irving (positive proportion of $n\in(X,2X]$ with a prime factor $>X^{1+c}$ for $n^3+2$):
https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.0024

Dartyge-Maynard (positive proportion / large prime factors for certain quartics; cyclic/dihedral Galois group):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.03381

Deshouillers-Iwaniec (large prime factors of $n^2+1$ infinitely often; classic AIF paper):
https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/aif.891.pdf

Merikoski (improved exponent for large prime factors of $n^2+1$, infinitely often):
https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.08816

Arango-Pineros-Keliher (Mertens-type theorems for Chebotarev sets; density-weighted prime sums):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14747

Lagarias-Odlyzko (effective Chebotarev density theorem; analytic input for Chebotarev prime-counting):
https://aareyanmanzoor.github.io/assets/articles/lagarias-odlyzko.pdf

computation:
Route:
Compared the target growth questions with known unconditional lower bounds in background and ran finite polynomial scans for representative irreducible examples.

- (quadratic examples up to n=5000) shows very large observed F_f(n) values, often on near-n^2 finite scale in those examples.
attempt:
Hard point:
That lower bound is stronger than n log n but does not by itself force a fixed-power gain n^{1+delta}. The asked n^{1+c} and especially n^d lower targets remain unresolved in this batch.

Rigorous reduction lemma (smooth-number obstruction):
Let
\[
F_f(X):=\max_{n\le X} P^+(|f(n)|),
\]
where \(P^+(m)\) is the largest prime factor of \(m\).
For \(Y\ge 2\), if \(F_f(X)\le Y\), then every \(|f(n)|\) (\(n\le X\)) is \(Y\)-smooth.
Hence
\[
X \le \Psi\!\big(\max_{n\le X}|f(n)|,\;Y\big),
\]
where \(\Psi(T,Y)\) counts \(Y\)-smooth integers \(\le T\).
Therefore, contrapositively:
if for some \(Y\),
\[
\Psi\!\big(\max_{n\le X}|f(n)|,\;Y\big)<X,
\]
then necessarily
\[
F_f(X)>Y.
\]
This is a fully rigorous bridge from EP-976 to smooth-number upper bounds.
Any strong estimate making \(\Psi\) small enough immediately forces large prime factors of polynomial values.

problem:
Let $f\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial of degree $k>2$ (and suppose that $k\neq 2^l$ for any $l\geq 1$) such that the leading coefficient of $f$ is positive.

Does the set of integers $n\geq 1$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-1)$-power-free have positive density?

If $k>3$, and for all primes $p$ there exists $n$ such that $p^{k-2}\nmid f(n)$, then are there infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-2)$-power-free?

In particular, does\[n^4+2\]represent infinitely many squarefree numbers?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/978.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-08-31).
- Page last edited: 31 March 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er53} proved there are infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-1)$-power-free, except when $k=2^l$ and $2^{k-1}\mid f(n)$ for all $n$. This latter exception is possible, for example if\[f(x)=k!\left(\binom{x}{k}+1\right).\]Hooley \cite{Ho67} settled the first question, in fact providing a precise asymptotic for the number of such $n\leq x$.

Heath-Brown \cite{He06} proved the answer to the second question is yes when $k\geq 10$, and Browning \cite{Br11} extended this to $k\geq 9$ (in fact establishing an asymptotic formula for the number of such $n$). (This is under the assumption that there does not exist a prime $p$ such that $p^{k-2}\mid f(n)$ for all $n$, which Erd\H{o}s did not state explicitly, but is an obvious necessary condition, and is discussed explicitly in \cite{He06} and \cite{Br11}.)

In \cite{Er65b} Erd\H{o}s mentions the question of whether $2^n\pm 1$ represents infinitely many $k$th power-free integers, or $n!\pm 1$, but that these are 'intractable at present'. (See also [936].)

- [He06] Heath-Brown, D. R., Counting rational points on algebraic varieties. (2006), 51--95.
- [Ho67] Hooley, C., On the power free values of polynomials. Mathematika (1967), 21--26.

forum_comments.author: Moritz Firsching
forum_comments.text:
The DeepMind prover agent has formally verified that the answer to the second part of the question is 'False' by constructing an explicit counterexample polynomial (assuming our formalisation (https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos978.erdos_978.parts.ii)) of the question is correct).

The polynomial $f(X) = X^6 + 33X^5 + 21X^4 + 63X^3 + 18X^2 + 24X + 48$ satisfies all the hypotheses (irreducible, degree $> 3$, degree not a power of $2$, positive leading coefficient, no fixed $p^5$ divisor) yet $f(n)$ is never $4$-powerfree. Irreducibility follows from Eisenstein's criterion at $p = 3$, since $3$ divides all non-leading coefficients but $3^2 = 9 \nmid 48$, the constant coefficient. The key observation is that $f(X) \equiv X(X-1)(X-2)(X-3)(X-4)(X-5) \pmod{16}$, and the product of $6$ consecutive integers is always divisible by $6! = 720$, which is divisible by $16 = 2^4$. So $2^4 \mid f(n)$ for all $n$, meaning $f(n)$ is never $4$-powerfree - contradicting the conclusion that infinitely many values should be. The full formal proof in Lean 4 is available here (https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/47d9e68df4323b995bb9875b6d5199a4f7026bfb/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/978.lean#L62)).

Although Erdős does not state this explicitly in [Er65b] or [Er81h] he was certainly aware of this obstruction, and he probably had it in mind - when he wrote about this problem he generally had specific polynomials like $n^4+2$ in mind.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Erdős [Er65b] wrote precisely 'I can also prove [the case $k=3$] (unpublished), and the proof of this seems to need some special properties of primes.'

Which doesn't give a lot of clues. It is of course possible that Erdős' proof also had a flaw, which he later discovered.

One idea is to adapt Mahler's disproof of Hypothesis K for $k=3$ (see this exposition for example (http://thomasbloom.org/notes/hypothesisk.html)). This relies on the fact that, if $n=m^{12}$, then\[ n = (9t^4)^3 + (m^4-9mt^3)^3 + (9m^3t-9t^4)^3.\]In particular, choosing $t\ll m$ sufficiently small gives $\gg m=n^{1/12}$ many ways to write $n$ as the sum of three positive cubes.

So one approach would be to give a similar parametric family of solutions (for some $n$ of a special form) and then use sieve theory to show that the forms are simultaneously prime infinitely often. This looks hard, since we know very little about how to find primes among the values of polynomials of degree $>2$, but perhaps one can take advantage of a large number of variables and averaging to make this work.

Site remarks:
The regular polygon shows that $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is the best possible here.

This would be implied if there was a vertex such that no three vertices of the polygon are equally distant to it, which was originally also conjectured by Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er46b}, but this is false (see [97]).

Let $f(n)$ be the maximal number of such distances that are guaranteed. Moser \cite{Mo52} proved that\[f(n) \geq \left\lceil\frac{n}{3}\right\rceil.\]This was improved by Erd\H{o}s and Fishburn \cite{ErFi94} to\[f(n) \geq \left\lfloor \frac{n}{3}+1\right\rfloor,\]then\[f(n) \geq \left\lceil \frac{13n-6}{36}\right\rceil\]by Dumitrescu \cite{Du06b}, and most recently\[f(n) \geq \left(\frac{13}{36}+\frac{1}{22701}\right)n-O(1)\]by Nivasch, Pach, Pinchasi, and Zerbib \cite{NPPZ13}.

In \cite{Er46b} Erd\H{o}s makes the even stronger conjecture that on every convex curve there exists a point $p$ such that every circle with centre $p$ intersects the curve in at most $2$ points. B\'{a}r\'{a}ny and Rold\'{a}n-Pensado \cite{BaRo13} noted that the boundary of any acute triangle is a counterexample.

B\'{a}r\'{a}ny and Rold\'{a}n-Pensado prove that, for any planar convex body, there is a point $p$ on the boundary such that every circle with centre $p$ intersects the boundary in at most $O(1)$ (where the implied constant depends on the convex body). They conjecture that there this can be bounded by an absolute constant - that is, Erd\H{o}s's conjecture is true if we replace $2$ by some larger constant $C$.

See also [93].
References:
- [BaRo13] B\'{a}r\'{a}ny, Imre and Rold\'{a}n-Pensado, Edgardo, A question from a famous paper of {E}rd\H{o}s. Discrete Comput. Geom. (2013), 253--261.
- [Du06b] Dumitrescu, Adrian, On distinct distances from a vertex of a convex polygon. Discrete Comput. Geom. (2006), 503--509.
- [Er46b] Erd\H{o}s, P., On sets of distances of {$n$} points. Amer. Math. Monthly (1946), 248--250.
- [ErFi94] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Fishburn, Peter, A postscript on distances in convex {$n$}-gons. Discrete Comput. Geom. (1994), 111--117.
- [Mo52] Moser, Leo, On the different distances determined by {$n$} points. Amer. Math. Monthly (1952), 85--91.
- [NPPZ13] Nivasch, Gabriel and Pach, J\'{a}nos and Pinchasi, Rom and Zerbib, Shira, The number of distinct distances from a vertex of a convex polygon. J. Comput. Geom. (2013), 1--12.

Let $n\geq 2$ and $\pi(n)<k\leq n$. Let $f(k,n)$ be the smallest integer $r$ such that in any $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ of size $\lvert A\rvert=k$ there exist primes $p_1,\ldots,p_r$ such that $>r$ many $a\in A$ are only divisible by primes from $\{p_1,\ldots,p_r\}$.

Thank you Woett for the detailed clarification on the "strictly more than $r$" vs "at least $r$" distinction. That's an important correction to the problem statement.

I'd like to raise a related question about the quantifier structure of $f(k,n)$ that came up during computational investigation (discussion at github.com/teorth/erdosproblems#216).

The current problem statement reads:

$f(k,n)$ be the smallest integer $r$ such that in any $A \subseteq {1,\ldots,n}$ of size $|A|=k$ there exist primes $p_1,\ldots,p_r$ such that [more than] $r$ many $a \in A$ are only divisible by primes from ${p_1,\ldots,p_r}$.

This "for any $A$, there exist primes" formulation suggests an adversarial/worst-case problem: the set $A$ is chosen first (adversarially), then we find covering primes.

Question: Is this the correct quantifier order from [Er70b]?

In the GitHub discussion, it was suggested that Erdős-Straus may have defined $f(k,n)$ with reversed quantifiers:

"there exist primes $p_1,\ldots,p_r$ such that at least $k$ integers $m \leq n$ have all prime divisors contained in ${p_1,\ldots,p_r}$"

Under this alternative interpretation, primes are chosen first to maximize coverage, making small primes $\leq \sqrt{n}$ optimal (each generates many smooth composites), naturally yielding $f \approx 2\pi(\sqrt{n})$.

Under the adversarial interpretation currently stated, computational testing suggests $f$ is much smaller. For example, with $k = \pi(n)+1$:

Any set $A$ of squarefree composites has "triangle" structure: three primes $p,q,r$ cover the semiprimes $pq, pr, qr$ (if present), giving efficient coverage
Testing up to $n = 10{,}000$ consistently yields small values that don't approach $2\pi(\sqrt{n})$
Could someone with access to [Er70b] ("Some applications of graph theory to number theory", 1969) confirm the exact quantifier structure in the original definition?

Woett's lower bound construction (using $A_0$ with paired products plus primes) is illuminating, but I want to ensure I'm understanding the correct problem before analyzing it further.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Let $2 = p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_t$ be those primes smaller than or equal to $(2 - \epsilon)\sqrt{n}$. Erdős and Straus then construct a set $A_0$ of size $t$, where $A_0$ consists of certain pairs of products $p_ip_j < n$ such that every $p_i$ (with $i \le t$) occurs in exactly two products. Finishing up, they let $A$ (with $k = |A| = \pi(n)+1$) be the union $$A := A_0 \cup \{2p_{t+1}, 3p_{t+1}\} \cup \bigcup_{i = t+2}^{\pi(n)} p_i.$$For this set $A$ one can then check that $r = t+1$, as $\{p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_{t+1}\}$ is the smallest set of primes such that there are more than $r$ elements $a \in A$ whose prime decompositions only contain $p_1, \ldots, p_{r}$. Hence, we get the lower bound $f(\pi(n)+1, n) > t =\pi((2-\epsilon)\sqrt{n})$.

Now note that, for fixed $n$, $f(k, n)$ is a non-increasing function of $k$. Since Erdős and Straus also showed $f(\pi(n)+1,n) \le 2\pi(\sqrt{n}) + 1$, this gives $f(k, n) \le 2\pi(\sqrt{n}) + 1$ for all $k > \pi(n)$. On the other hand, we could have slightly tweaked the lower bound construction we just saw as follows:

Let $A_0$ still consist of $t$ pairs of products $p_ip_j < n$ as explained in [Er70b] (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1970-20.pdf), but as opposed to using the primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_t$, we use $p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_{t+1}$ instead. We then set $$A := A_0 \cup \bigcup_{i=2}^{\pi(\frac{1}{2}n)} \{2p_i\} \cup \bigcup_{i = t+2}^{\pi(n)} p_i.$$In this case we still get $r = t+1$, while $k = \pi(n) + \pi(\frac{1}{2}n) - 2$. Combining upper and lower bound and using the prime number theorem we deduce $f(k,n) = (4 + o(1))\frac{n^{1/2}}{\log n}$ for all $k$ with $\pi(n) < k < (\frac{3}{2} + o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}$. One can probably increase the range of $k$ for which this estimate holds by tweaking $A$ further.

Based on the proven value of $f(cn, n)$, presumably some kind of phase-shift occurs somewhere, if we let $k$ increase from $\frac{cn}{\log n}$ to $cn$.

Finally, $f(k,n)$ might still be interesting for the range $(1-o(1))n < k < n$. To give two quick examples, if $k > n - \pi(\sqrt{n})$, then we are guaranteed to have $\{p, p^2\} \subset A$ (so that $f(k,n) = 1$), and if $k > n - \pi(\frac{1}{4}n)$ we are guaranteed to have $\{p, 2p, 4p\} \subset A$ (so that $f(k,n) \le 2$). One can wonder what the slowest growest function $g(n)$ is such that $k < n - g(n)$ implies $f(k,n) \rightarrow \infty$. By the value of $f(cn, n)$ we know $g(n) = o(n)$, while generalizing the second example we just gave leads (I think) to $g(n) > (1 - o(1))\pi(n)$.

forum_comments.text:
GPT-5.4 Thinking finds the following relevant progress:

1. Let $G(p)$ denote the least prime primitive root modulo a prime $p$. Nongkynrih (Acta Arith. 72 (1995), 45–53) studied the distribution of prime primitive roots and proved that for almost all primes $p$ one has an asymptotic formula for the number of prime primitive roots $\le H$ is $N(H,p) \sim \frac{\varphi(p-1)}{p-1}\pi(H)$ provided $H$ is sufficiently large (polylogarithmic in $p$). Since $\varphi(p-1)/(p-1) \gg 1/\log\log p$, taking $H=(\log p)^A$ with $A$ large enough implies that $G(p) \le (\log p)^A$ for almost all primes $p$. In particular, for a set of primes of natural density $1$ there exists a prime primitive root $q \le (\log p)^A < p$. Thus the conjectured property holds for almost all primes $p$.

2. Related work of Martin (“The least prime primitive root and the shifted sieve”, 1997) shows that similar bounds for $G(p)$ follow from shifted sieve methods and that, assuming GRH, one obtains bounds implying $G(p) \ll (\log p)^C$ for all sufficiently large primes $p$. Under GRH this would therefore imply the statement of the problem for all sufficiently large $p$.

3. Computationally, extensive searches for the least prime primitive root $G(p)$ (e.g. Oliveira e Silva’s tables up to at least $10^{14}$) have not produced any counterexample to the statement that $G(p) < p$.

Therefore, the problem appears to remain open in full generality, but it is known that $G(p) \le (\log p)^A$ for almost all primes $p$ (unconditionally), and that $G(p) \ll (\log p)^C$ for all sufficiently large primes $p$ under GRH. Both results imply that the conjecture holds for all sufficiently large primes in the corresponding sense.

attempt:
Hard point:
A finite verification window does not imply the statement for all primes.

Rigorous reformulation and test criterion:
For prime \(p\), the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
So \(q<p\) is a primitive root mod \(p\) iff
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(q)=p-1.
\]
Equivalently, for each prime divisor \(r\mid(p-1)\),
\[
q^{(p-1)/r}\not\equiv 1 \pmod p,
\]
and \(q\not\equiv 0\pmod p\).
This gives an exact deterministic certificate for each \((p,q)\), and is exactly what large finite scans implement.
Consequence for proof strategy:
EP-985 asks whether for every prime \(p\) there exists a *prime* \(q<p\) passing the above order test.
Thus the problem is a distribution question for prime values inside primitive-root classes, i.e. an intersection of:
- primitive-root constraints in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\), and
- primality of the representative \(q\).
Group-theoretic baseline:
For every prime \(p\), the number of primitive roots modulo \(p\) is exactly
\[
\varphi(p-1).
\]
So there are many admissible residues in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\); the EP-985 difficulty is not existence of primitive-root residues, but existence of one such residue that is itself prime \(<p\).

Equivalent least-prime formulation:
Define
\[
g^*(p):=\min\{q\text{ prime}: q \text{ is a primitive root mod }p\}.
\]
Then EP-985 is exactly the assertion
\[
g^*(p)<p\quad\text{for every prime }p.
\]
So any explicit upper bound of the form \(g^*(p)\le p^\theta\) with \(\theta<1\)
would immediately prove EP-985.
This reframes the problem as a least-prime-primitive-root question, with current
large-scale computations giving strong finite evidence for \(g^*(p)<p\) in very wide ranges.

problem:
Let $x_1,x_2,\ldots \in (0,1)$ be an infinite sequence and let\[A_k=\limsup_{n\to \infty}\left\lvert \sum_{j\leq n} e(kx_j)\right\rvert,\]where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$.

Is it true that\[\limsup_{k\to \infty} A_k=\infty?\]Is it possible for $A_k=o(k)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/987.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-04-09).
- Page last edited: 09 April 2026.
Site remarks:
This is Problem 7.21 in \cite{Ha74}, where it is attributed to Erd\H{o}s.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64b} remarks it is 'easy to see' that\[\limsup_{k\to \infty}\left(\sup_n\left\lvert \sum_{j\leq n} e(kx_j)\right\rvert\right)=\infty.\]Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er65b} later found a 'very easy' proof that $A_k\gg \log k$ for infinitely many $k$. Clunie \cite{Cl67} proved that $A_k\gg k^{1/2}$ infinitely often, and that there exist sequences with $A_k\leq k$ for all $k$. Tao has independently found a proof that $A_k\gg k^{1/2}$ infinitely often (see the comment section).

Liu \cite{Li69} showed that, for any $\epsilon>0$, $A_k\gg k^{1-\epsilon}$ infinitely often, under the additional assumption that there are only a finite number of distinct points. Clunie observed in the Mathscinet review of \cite{Li69}, however, that under this assumption in fact $A_k=\infty$ infinitely often.

An internal OpenAI model (see \cite{APSSV26b}) has proved that there exists a sequence $(x_n)$ such that\[A_k \ll (k\log k)^{1/2}\]for all $k\geq 1$ (in fact one may replace the $\limsup$ in $A_k$ with a $\sup$).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Here is my attempt at a high level summary of the construction in [APSSV26b], which creates a sequence $x_n$ of points which are very uniformly distributed in the sense that
$$ |\sum_{j \leq n} e(k x_j)| \ll \sqrt{k \log k}$$
for all $k, n > 0$. The key difficulty here is the need to get bounds that are uniform for all $n$ with no exceptions; various random or deterministic constructions can easily get this type of bound for most $n$, but these usually generate some gaussian tail outlier events which will typically violate this sort of bound for infinitely many $n$ (basically thanks to the infinite monkey theorem). One can try to get around this by making the $x_j$ exhibit some sort of periodicity, but if the sequence is too periodic then this also causes at least one exponential sum to grow linearly in $n$, which also breaks the construction. So one now needs to look for sequences that are very nearly periodic without actually being periodic.

In my comment back in August I suggested trying to design the sequence so that exponential sums vanish on dyadic intervals, in the sense that
$$\sum_{2^i m < j \leq 2^i(m+1)} e(k x_j) = 0 \tag{1}$$
as long as $k$ is not too large compared to the length of the interval $2^i$. The [APSSV26b] construction actually achieves this, and goes further by proving a bound of the shape
$$\sum_{2^i m < j \leq 2^i(m+1)} e(k x_j) \ll \sqrt{k \log k} \tag{2}$$
for all $i, m, k$, with a geometric improvement in the error term if the length $2^i$ of the interval is much shorter or much larger than $k$. This is the key bound (Proposition 3.5); the sum $\sum_{j \leq n} e(k x_j)$ can then be controlled by using the binary representation of $n$ to break up $\{1,\dots,n\}$ greedily into dyadic intervals. The critical case occurs when $2^i \asymp k$; the interval is not quite long enough to be able to expect the perfect cancellation (1), but the error bound claimed is of square root cancellation type.

Again, the main issue here is that the bound has to hold uniformly for all $m$, with no exceptions. So a random construction that has a small failure rate for a given choice of $i$ and $k$ can still lead to infinitely many counterexamples if the sums in (2) behave independently in $m$. As discussed above, we thus need a sequence $x_j$ that is random enough to get square root cancellation quite often, yet also close enough to periodic that one does not actually have to verify (2) for all $m$, but merely for some large but finite number of $m$ so that the total failure probability does not get out of control.

As mentioned in the paper, the van der Corput sequence (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Corput_sequence), in which $x_n$ is the reversal of the binary representation of $n$ expressed as binary strings past the decimal point, is a good candidate; this sequence is almost $2^J$-periodic for any $J$ in the sense that shifting $n$ by a multiple of $2^J$ only affects $x_n$ by $O(2^{-J})$. If the $x_n$ had this sort of periodicity property, a bound such as (2) only needs to be verified for $m$ of size that is polynomial in $2^i$ and $k$, as the bound for larger $m$ would then be automatic.

When $k$ is small compared to the interval size $2^i$, then the van der Corput sequence $x_j$ is already quite well equidistributed on a dyadic interval $(2^i m, 2^i(m+1)]$ (it basically traverses a coset of the $2^i$th roots of unity), which gives (1) which of course implies (2); the difficulty is when $k$ is comparable to or larger than $2^i$, in which perfect vanishing (1) is no longer expected. The van der Corput sequence is deterministic, so one cannot use randomness to create the required square root cancellation.

What the argument in [APSSV26b] does is randomize the van der Corput sequence with a high-entropy source of random bits, by performing dependent random bit flips to the binary representation, that introduce about $2^i$ bits of entropy in any dyadic block $x_j, j \in (2^i m, 2^i(m+1)]$. This randomization preserves the approximate periodicity and equidistribution properties of the deterministic van der Corput sequence, but introduces enough randomness that one can now get the desired square root cancellation in all remaining cases by standard concentration of measure and union bound arguments.

In the followup paper of Erdos the repaired question is posed as to whether $\limsup_{n \to \infty} |\sum_{j \leq n} e(k x_j)| \gg k$ for infinitely many $k$. I actually suspect that the answer is negative, and that one can construct a sequence $x_j$ with $|\sum_{j \leq n} e(k x_j)| \ll k^{1/2+o(1)}$ for all $k \geq 1$ and $n \geq 1$. Heuristically, the construction should be to choose the $x_j$ randomly subject to the conditions $\sum_{2^i m < j \leq 2^i (m+1)} e(k x_j) = 0$ for all $i \geq 0$, $m \geq 0$, and $k \leq 2^{i-\varepsilon}$. Naive degree of freedom counts suggest that the $x_j$ should still behave fairly randomly even after imposing all these constraints, enough to get the near-square root cancellation required here. But proving this rigorously may require some effort.

After some digging, I see that Erdos himself actually solved this problem (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1965-18.pdf) shortly afterwards, saying that he "overlooked the fact that it is very easy to show" a logarithmic type lower bound for the inner supremum for a susbequence of $k$. There is followup work improving the bounds by Clunie (https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms/s1-42.1.133) obtaining a square root lower bound. Conjecturally, there should be linear growth (which would be optimal); this was shown up to an epsilon loss by Liu (https://www.jstor.org/stable/2036452) assuming the sequence is finitely valued (though as observed by Clunie in the MathSciNet review (https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=245795), in this case the inner supremum is in fact infinite for infinitely many $k$). I could not find any followup work after the 1969 paper of Liu.

EDIT: I seem to recover the same square root bound as Clunie, and it seems that the proof techniques are similar.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
The answer is yes. Proof: assume not, then there exists $k_0, C$, and $x_1,x_2,\dots$ such that
$$ \limsup_{n \to \infty} |\sum_{j \leq n} e(kx_j)| \leq C$$
for all $k \geq k_0$. In particular, for any $K \geq k_0$, there exists $N_K$ such that
$$ |\sum_{j \leq n} e(kx_j)| \leq C+1$$
whenever $k_0 \leq k \leq K$ and $n \geq N_K$. In particular, by the triangle inequality we have
$$ |\sum_{N_K < j \leq N_K + n} e(kx_j)| \leq 2(C+1)$$
whenever $k_0 \leq k \leq K$ and $n \geq 0$, which we can relabel as
$$ |\sum_{j \leq n} e(kx_{N_K+j})| \leq 2(C+1). \quad (1)$$
The key point here is that $n$ is no longer required to be sufficiently large depending on $K$.

By weak compactness (Arzela-Ascoli), we can pass to a subsequence of $K$ where the $x_{N_K+j}$ converge pointwise mod 1 to some limit $y_j \in [0,1)$. We now have
$$ |\sum_{j \leq n} e(ky_j)| \leq 2(C+1)$$
for all $k \geq k_0$ and $n \geq 0$. Squaring and averaging in $K$, we see that
$$ \limsup_{K \to \infty} \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K |\sum_{j \leq n} e(ky_j)|^2 \leq 4(C+1)^2$$
for any $n \geq 0$. Expanding out the square, the left-hand side can be computed explicitly to be
$$ | \{ 1 \leq i,j \leq n: y_i = y_j \} |.$$
But this is clearly at least $n$; taking $n$ larger than $4(C+1)^2$, we obtain the desired contradiction.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
An alternate, more quantitative, proof avoiding the weak compactness step. For fixed $n,K$, argue as before to get to (1). Now use the identity
$$ \sum_{k,k' \leq K} |\sum_{j \leq n} e((k-k') x_{N_K+j})|^2 = \sum_{j,j' \leq n} |\sum_{k \leq K} e(k (x_{N_k+j}-x_{N_k+j'}))|^2.$$
By considering the diagonal $j=j'$, we see that the RHS is at least $nK^2$. On the other hand, from (1) (for $|k-k'| \geq k_0$) and the trivial triangle inequality bound (for $|k-k'| < k_0$) the left-hand side is at most $4(C+1)^2 K^2 + n^2 K (2k_0-1)$. So we have
$$ nK^2 \leq 4(C+1)^2 K^2 + n^2 K (2k_0-1)$$
for all $n,K$. Taking $n > 4(C+1)^2$ and then $K$ sufficiently large depending on $C,n,k_0$ we obtain a contradiction.

Rigorous identities and bounds:
For fixed \(N\), define
\[
S_N(k):=\sum_{j=1}^N e(kx_j),\qquad e(t):=e^{2\pi i t}.
\]
Lemma 1 (trivial absolute bound):
\[
|S_N(k)|\le N\quad\text{for all }k.
\]
Proof: triangle inequality and \(|e(kx_j)|=1\).
Lemma 2 (pair-correlation expansion):
\[
|S_N(k)|^2=\sum_{a,b\le N} e\!\big(k(x_a-x_b)\big).
\]
Hence for \(K\ge1\),
\[
\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K |S_N(k)|^2
=N+\sum_{a\ne b}\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K e\!\big(k(x_a-x_b)\big).
\]
This exact identity separates diagonal mass (\(=N\)) from off-diagonal cancellation.
Consequence for strategy:
To force large limsup behavior, one seeks sequence structures where off-diagonal cancellation is weak for infinitely many \(k\); to force small behavior, one needs strong cancellation uniformly in \(k\).
So EP-987 can be viewed as a quantitative cancellation problem in exponential sums indexed by integer frequencies.

problem: Let $f=a_0+\cdots+a_dx^d\in \mathbb{C}[x]$ be a polynomial. Is it true that, if $f$ has roots $z_1,\ldots,z_d$ with corresponding arguments $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d\in [0,2\pi]$, then for all intervals $I\subseteq [0,2\pi]$\[\left\lvert (\# \theta_i \in I) - \frac{\lvert I\rvert}{2\pi}d\right\rvert \ll \left(n\log M\right)^{1/2},\]where $n$ is the number of non-zero coefficients of $f$ and\[M=\frac{\lvert a_0\rvert+\cdots +\lvert a_d\rvert}{(\lvert a_0\rvert\lvert a_d\rvert)^{1/2}}.\]

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Tur\'{a}n \cite{ErTu50} proved such an upper bound with $n$ replaced by $d$.

Hayman \cite{Ha72b} proved\[\left\lvert (\# \theta_i \in I) - \frac{\lvert I\rvert}{2\pi}d\right\rvert \leq n-1,\]and noted this is essentially sharp since $f(x)=(x^{p}-1)^{n-1}$ has $n$ non-zero coefficients and has $1$ as a positive real zero of multiplicity $n-1$ (although for this $f$ the parameter $M$ becomes very large).

An internal OpenAI model (see \cite{APSSV26b}) has disproved the conjecture, constructing, for every $n\geq 1$, a polynomial $f$ with $n$ non-zero coefficients such that $M<3$ and with a positive real zero of multiplicity $n-1$, whence letting $I=[0,c/d]$ for a suitably small $c>0$,\[\left\lvert (\# \theta_i \in I) - \frac{\lvert I\rvert}{2\pi}d\right\rvert \geq n-1.\]

forum_comments.author: natso26
forum_comments.text:
Here's my understanding of OpenAI's proof, in a somewhat simplified form:

Let $N$ be any large integer. We shall construct a polynomial $f$ with nonzero coefficient exponents $0 < n_1 < \dots < n_N < d$ and corresponding coefficients $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_N, c_{N+1}$ such that: $f$ has a positive root with multiplicity $N+1$; $|c_1| + \dots + |c_N| \ll |c_0|$; and $|c_{N+1}| \asymp |c_0|$.

Let the exponents be separated in the following way. Fix $0 < q < 1$. Let $x_i := n_i/d$. Suppose $x_N < q$, $x_i/x_{i+1} < q$, and $x_N \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} \log (1/x_i) \ll 1$.

Now define interpolation points: $u_0 := 0$, $u_i := x_i$ for $1 \le i \le N$, and $u_{N+1} := 1$. Let $\Delta_i := \prod_{j \neq i} |u_i - u_j|$.

Let $\tau \in \mathbb{R}$ be chosen later. Let
$$ c_i := \frac{(-1)^{N+1-i} \exp(-u_i \tau)}{\Delta_i}. $$
As in Lemma 5.4, by Lagrange interpolation, this choice makes $\exp(\tau/d)$ a root of $f$ with multiplicity $N+1$.

Now choose $\tau := \log(|\Delta_0| / |\Delta_{N+1}|)$. This makes $|c_{N+1}| = |c_0|$.

Finally,
$$ |c_i| / |c_0| = \exp(-x_i \tau) |\Delta_0| / |\Delta_i|. $$
Routine calculations from assumptions give $\exp(-x_i \tau) \ll 1$ and $|\Delta_0| / |\Delta_i| \ll q^{i(i-1)/2}$. This yields $|c_1| + \dots + |c_N| \ll |c_0|$.

Credit to GPT-5.4 Thinking for discussion.

problem: Let $x_1<x_2<\cdots$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Is it true that, for almost all $\alpha \in [0,1]$, the discrepancy\[D(N)=\max_{I\subseteq [0,1]} \lvert \#\{ n\leq N : \{ \alpha x_n\}\in I\} - \lvert I\rvert N\rvert\]satisfies\[D(N) \ll N^{1/2}(\log N)^{o(1)}?\]Or even\[D(N)\ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{O(1)}?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/992.
- Page status: DISPROVED (database last update 2026-02-01).
- Page last edited: 29 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Koksma \cite{ErKo49} and Cassels \cite{Ca50} independently proved that, for any sequence $x_i$ and almost all $\alpha$, the discrepancy satisfies\[D(N)\ll N^{1/2}(\log N)^{5/2+o(1)}.\]Baker \cite{Ba81} improved this to\[D(N)\ll N^{1/2}(\log N)^{3/2+o(1)}.\]Erd\H{o}s and G\'{a}l (unpublished) proved $D(N) \ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{O(1)}$ for almost all $\alpha$ if the sequence is lacunary - that is, $x_{i+1}/x_i > \lambda>1$ for all $i$.

This was disproved by Berkes and Philipp \cite{BePh94}, who constructed a sequence of integers $x_1<x_2<\cdots$ such that, for almost all $\alpha\in[0,1]$,\[\limsup_{N\to \infty}\frac{D(N)}{(N\log N)^{1/2}}>0.\]

problem:
The independent set sequence of any tree or forest is unimodal.

In other words, if $i_k(G)$ counts the number of independent sets of vertices of size $k$ in a graph $G$, and $T$ is any tree or forest, then for some $m\geq 0$
$$i_{0}(T)\leq i_{1}(T)\leq\cdots\leq i_{m}(T)\geq i_{m+1}(T)\geq i_{m+2}(T)\geq\cdots.$$
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/993.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (database last update 2025-09-07).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A question of Alavi, Malde, Schwenk, and Erd\H{o}s \cite{AMSE87}, who showed that this is false for general graphs $G$ (in fact every possible pattern of inequalities is achieved by some graph).

The sequence which counts the number of independent sets of edges of a given size was proved to be unimodal (for any graph) by Schwenk \cite{Sc81}. In \cite{AMSE87} they also ask whether every possible unimodal pattern of inequalities is achieved by some graph.

- [Sc81] Schwenk, Allen J., On unimodal sequences of graphical invariants. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1981), 247--250.

forum_comments.author: ho boon suan
forum_comments.text:
I have, with the assistance of GPT-5.4 Pro, obtained a rather intricate construction that gives negative answers to both [995] and [996]; see https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18535 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18535). The idea is simple enough, but quite a lot of bookkeeping is required to get things right.

The central result is as follows: Given a decreasing function $\omega\colon[N_0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$, suppose $N\omega(N)^2$ is nondecreasing and that for every $\kappa>0$ we have $A^{1/2}\omega(\exp(\exp(\kappa A\log A)))\to\infty$ as $A\to\infty$. Then there exists a real-valued mean-zero function $f\in L^2(\mathbb T)$ and a lacunary integer sequence $(n_j)$ with $n_{j+1}/n_j\ge2$ such that $\|f-S_Nf\|_2\ll\omega(N)$ for all sufficiently large $N$, while $\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{j\le N}f(n_jx)=+\infty$ for almost every $x\in\mathbb T$.

The proof constructs $f$ and $(n_j)=(2^{m_j})$ in stages. The function is built as $f=\sum_{k\ge1}F_k$, where a typical block has the form\[
F(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{AL}}\sum_{q=1}^{L}\psi_d(2^{U+qD}x)
\]with dyadic spikes\[
\psi_d(x)=2^{d/2}\bigl(\mathbf 1_{[0,2^{-d-1})}(x)-\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1/2+2^{-d-1})}(x)\bigr).
\]Each stage runs a number of trials. A trial is an arithmetic progression of exponents, and the relevant trial sum has the form\[
\sum_{r=1}^\ell F(2^{M+rD}x).
\]Some delicate bookkeeping is required to make the signal produced at one stage survive the contributions of all past and future stages. The construction is essentially a careful refinement of Erdős's construction in his 1949 paper On the Strong Law of Large Numbers (https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1949-0032971-4), replacing the Rademacher functions he uses with dyadic spike block trials. The new point is that the spike blocks interact with the repeated trials through a convolution that amplifies signal: a single rare central spike, once hit, is counted throughout an entire trial because the relevant indices enter as \(q+r\), so one hit creates a macroscopic average. The parameters are then tuned so that the same block is cheap in \(L^2\), has a controlled Fourier tail, and is shielded from past and future stages by separation in dyadic valuation layers.

Currently my paper leaves the endpoint case \(\omega(N)=(\log\log N)^{-1/2}\) open, but I believe the same strategy should extend without too much difficulty to show that $\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{j\le N}f(n_jx)=+\infty$ in this case as well. ChatGPT says this appears doable if one replaces the two-sided dyadic spike with a one-sided one and weakens the requirement of "success for every stage" to "success for infinitely many stages." I am in the process of scrutinizing this approach, and if it works out, it should actually simplify the paper by a decent amount. I will probably upload a revised version of the manuscript to arXiv soon.

attempt:
Hard point:
The exact almost-sure growth scale in full generality remains open.

Rigorous model theorem (doubling + step function):
In the model
\[
n_k=2^k,\qquad f(x)=\mathbf 1_{[0,1/2)}(x)-\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1)}(x),
\]
and \(\alpha\) uniformly random in \([0,1)\), define
\[
X_k(\alpha):=f(\{2^k\alpha\}).
\]
Then \((X_k)_{k\ge1}\) are i.i.d. Rademacher variables (\(\pm1\) with probability \(1/2\)).
Reason:
\(X_k\) depends only on the \(k\)-th binary digit of \(\alpha\), and binary digits are independent under Lebesgue measure.
Hence
\[
S_N(\alpha):=\sum_{k=1}^N X_k(\alpha)
\]
is a simple random walk.
Therefore, almost surely,
\[
S_N=O\!\left(\sqrt{N\log\log N}\right)
\]
(law of the iterated logarithm scale), and in particular
\[
\frac{S_N}{N\sqrt{\log\log N}}\to 0.
\]
So this benchmark model is provably consistent with the conjectured small growth regime and cannot produce a counterexample.

Target:
For lacunary \(n_k\) and \(f\in L^2\), determine almost-sure growth scale of
\[
S_N(\alpha)=\sum_{k\le N} f(\{\alpha n_k\}).
\]
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show a martingale-approximation theorem:
\[
S_N = M_N + R_N,\qquad M_N\ \text{martingale with }\langle M\rangle_N\asymp N,\ \ R_N=o(\sqrt{N\log\log N})\ \text{a.s.}
\]
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (model i.i.d. benchmark):
For \(n_k=2^k\) and dyadic step \(f\), \(S_N\) is simple random walk.
Proof.
Each term depends on one independent binary digit of \(\alpha\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (LIL consequence):
If \(S_N\) admits decomposition in A with \(R_N\) negligible at LIL scale, then
\[
S_N=O(\sqrt{N\log\log N})\ \text{a.s.}
\]
Proof.
Apply LIL to \(M_N\), absorb \(R_N\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies no linear-growth counterexample):
Under A,
\[
\frac{S_N}{N\sqrt{\log\log N}}\to0
\]
along full sequence a.s.
Proof.
From B2, numerator is \(O(\sqrt{N\log\log N})\), divide by \(N\sqrt{\log\log N}\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The hard part is constructing martingale approximations for general \(L^2\) observables and non-dyadic lacunary sequences with quantitative remainders.

problem: Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ be a lacunary sequence of integers, and let $f\in L^2([0,1])$. Let $f_n$ be the $n$th partial sum of the Fourier series of $f(x)$. Is there an absolute constant $C>0$ such that, if\[\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log\log\log n)^{C}}\]then\[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\leq N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})=\int_0^1 f(x)\mathrm{d}x\]for almost every $\alpha$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/996.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-07).
Site remarks:
Raikov proved the conclusion always holds (for every $f\in L^2([0,1])$, with no assumption on $\| f-f_n\|_2$) if $n_k=a^k$ for some integer $a\geq 2$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64b} also asked whether this is true for $n_k=\lfloor a^k\rfloor$ for some $a>1$.

Kac, Salem, and Zygmund \cite{KSZ48} proved that the conclusion holds if\[\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log n)^{c}}\]for some constant $c>1$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er49d} proved that the conclusion holds if\[\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log\log n)^{c}}\]for some constant $c>1$. Matsuyama \cite{Ma66} improved this to $c>1/2$.

In \cite{Er64b} Erd\H{o}s asked whether the conclusion holds for all bounded functions $f$ and lacunary sequences $n_k$.
References:
- [Er49d] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the strong law of large numbers. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. (1949), 51--56.
- [Er64b] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on diophantine approximations. Compositio Math. (1964), 52-65.
- [KSZ48] Kac, M. and Salem, R. and Zygmund, A., A gap theorem. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. (1948), 235--243.

problem: Call $x_1,x_2,\ldots \in (0,1)$ well-distributed if, for every $\epsilon>0$, if $k$ is sufficiently large then, for all $n>0$ and intervals $I\subseteq [0,1]$,\[\lvert \# \{ n<m\leq n+k : x_m\in I\} - \lvert I\rvert k\rvert < \epsilon k.\]Is it true that, for every $\alpha$, the sequence $\{ \alpha p_n\}$ is not well-distributed, if $p_n$ is the sequence of primes?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/997.
- Page status: PROVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-04-03).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
The notion of a well-distributed sequence was introduced by Hlawka and Petersen \cite{Hl55}.

Erd\H{o}s proved that, if $n_k$ is a lacunary sequence, then the sequence $\{ \alpha n_k\}$ is not well-distributed for almost all $\alpha$.

He also claimed in \cite{Er64b} to have proved that there exists an irrational $\alpha$ for which $\{\alpha p_n\}$ is not well-distributed. He later retracted this claim in \cite{Er85e}, saying "The theorem is no doubt correct and perhaps will not be difficult to prove but I never was able to reconstruct my 'proof' which perhaps never existed ."

The existence of such an $\alpha$ was established by Champagne, Le, Liu, and Wooley \cite{CLLW24}.

An internal model at OpenAI \cite{APSSV26} has proved that the sequence $\{\alpha p_n\}$ is not well-distributed for any $\alpha$, using the work of Banks, Freiberg, and Turnage-Butterbaugh \cite{BFT15} on consecutive primes with small gaps (which in turn builds on the work of Maynard and Tao on bounded gaps between primes).

forum_comments.text: The problem is solved now, but on looking at the proof I see that my former student, Jacques Benatar, managed to essentially prove a partial result on this problem in 2013 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0348), again using the same Maynard sieve machinery. Namely, from Theorem 1.3 of that paper it follows that for any Bohr set $\{ n: \{ \alpha n \} \leq \delta \}$ with $\alpha$ Diophantine, and any $m$, there exist $m$ primes in that set of diameter $O_{\delta,\varepsilon}(e^{(4+\varepsilon) m})$. The theorem does not explicitly state that these primes are in fact consecutive (no intervening primes outside of the Bohr set), but this can be accomplished by a standard additional upper bound Maynard sieve estimate. From this, one would be able to obtain the Diophantine case of this problem. The proof in [APSSV26] gets around the need to assume Diophantine conditions by approximating $\alpha$ by a rational and finding consecutive primes of small diameter in a suitable congruence class instead, which is a simpler way to proceed.
