forum_comments.text:
The literature here is somewhat confusing because the results are very sensitive to what is being averaged here: one can work with "temporal" averaging (averaging in $n$), "spatial" averaging (averaging in $\beta$), "quenched" averaging (fixed $\alpha$), and "annealed" averaging (averaging in $\alpha$). In particular, Erdos's question involves only the annealed notion of average. The most recent paper I could find (with the help of Gemini (https://gemini.google.com/share/00677f953e73) and ChatGPT (https://chatgpt.com/share/6907fad4-3180-800e-ba64-f11f8afb5608), whose outputs were somewhat unreliable due to the subtleties mentioned above) was a 2024 paper of Fruhworth-Hauke (https://ahl.centre-mersenne.org/item/10.5802/ahl.200.pdf), which seem to indicate that the Erdos problem remains open as stated, although with additional averaging the claim is true (e.g., if one also averages in $n$ the claim was obtained by Dolgopyat and Sarig (https://math.umd.edu/~dolgop/QARot13.pdf)).

The problem here seems remarkably delicate, and probably the first step to anyone interested in trying to solve this problem is to carefully go through the literature (of which the above two papers are only a small sample).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Some notes on the problem (all familiar to experts on this problem, I assume, but it was somewhat novel to me). I was initially rather confused as to the logarithmic Cauchy behavior here, since square root cancellation heuristics would naively $f(\alpha,n)$ should oscillate like $\sqrt{n}$ times a Gaussian instead of $\log n$ times a Cauchy distribution. But it turns out the series is extremely subrandom, and the behavior of $f(\alpha,n)$ is closely tied with how $n$ interacts with the successive approximants $p_j/q_j$ of $\alpha$ in the continued fraction expansion, as per the Denjoy-Koksma inequality (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denjoy%E2%80%93Koksma_inequality). Suppose for instance that $q_j \leq n < q_{j+1}$ with $j$ even, then by standard continued fraction theory we have $q_{j+1} = a_{j+1} q_j + q_{j-1}$ with $a_{j+1}$ the $j+1^{th}$ term in the continued fraction expansion (which would be expected to be distributed according to the Gauss-Kuzmin law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Kuzmin_distribution), which is a discrete Cauchy distribution, and $\alpha = \frac{p_j}{q_j} + \delta$ for some $0 < \delta < \frac{p_{j+1}}{q_{j+1}}-\frac{p_j}{q_j} = \frac{1}{q_j q_{j+1}}$). One can then write $n = c_{j+1} q_j + n'$ for some $0 \leq c_{j+1} \leq a_{j+1}$ and $n' < q_j$ (if $c_{j+1}=a_{j+1}$ one can improve the upper bound on $N'$ to $N' < q_{j-1}$); the sequence of $c_{j+1}$ represent a sort of "base $(q_j)_{j=1}^\infty$ expansion" of $n$ (e.g., if $\alpha$ is the golden ratio then this is essentially Fibonacci coding (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_coding)). A key point here is that if $k \leq n$ then $\alpha k$ has the same integer part as $p_j k / q_j$. As such one can write
$$ f(\alpha,n) \log n = \sum_{k \leq n} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \} + p_j k / q_j - \alpha k) = \sum_{k \leq n} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}) - \frac{\delta n(n+1)}{2}$$
and similarly
$$ f(\alpha,n') \log n' = \sum_{k \leq n'} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}) - \frac{\delta n'(n'+1)}{2}.$$
The function $\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}$ is $q_j$-periodic and sums to $-\frac{1}{2}$ on each period, so
$$ \sum_{k \leq n} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}) = \sum_{k \leq n'} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}) - \frac{c_{k+1}}{2}.$$
Hence we obtain a recursion
$$ f(\alpha,n) \log n = f(\alpha,n') \log n' + X_j$$
where
$$ X_j = \frac{\delta}{2} (n(n+1)-n'(n'+1)) - \frac{c_{j+1}}{2} = \frac{c_{j+1}}{2} (\delta q_j (n+n'+1) - 1) $$
(I may have gotten some signs wrong here). There is a similar formula (with some signs changed) when $j$ is odd instead of even. Each $X_j$ can be calculated to be of size $O(a_{j+1})$ and is primarily determined by the "digit" $c_{j+1}$ in the expansion of $n$ (as well as the continued fraction coefficient $a_{j+1}$). There are $\asymp \log n$ relevant values of $j$ here, with the $a_{j+1}$ behaving like iid copies of the heavy-tailed Gauss-Kuzmin distribution, and so the sum generically should be dominated by $O(1)$ terms where $a_{j+1} \asymp \log n$, each of which contributes a term of size $O(\log n)$ (but there is a rare "major arc" event in which one of the terms is much larger, which seems to defeat most moment-based strategies for this problem). This is where the $\log n$ normalization comes from, and the Cauchy distribution presumably reflects some basin of attraction property that I did not work out carefully (it reminds me of how the Cauchy distribution shows up in the analysis of the Saint Petersburg paradox).

To solve this problem, therefore, one needs to understand the behavior of the digits $c_{j+1}$ in the expansion of a large but fixed number $n$, with respect to the base $(q_j)_{j=1}^\infty$ generated by a random continued fraction, and with a particular focus on those rare digits where $a_{j+1}$ is as large as $\log n$. It seems that the most significant digits (where $q_j$ is not much smaller than $n$) can be relatively well understood, but there is some weird mixing process going on with the operation $n \mapsto n'$ of taking successive remainders with respect to the $b_{j+1}$ that I don't understand past the first few steps (it reminds me a little bit of the Collatz iteration, actually, which is unnerving for the purposes of actually proving anything rigorous).

problem: Are there infinitely many solutions to $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$, where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1003.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-08).
- Page last edited: 19 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er85e} says that, presumably, for every $k\geq 1$ the equation\[\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)=\cdots=\phi(n+k)\]has infinitely many solutions.

Erd\H{o}s, Pomerance, and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy \cite{EPS87} proved that the number of $n\leq x$ with $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$ is at most\[\frac{x}{\exp((\log x)^{1/3})}.\]See [946] for the analogous question with the divisor function, and [415] for a question about more general inequality patterns among consecutive values of $\phi$.

- [EPS87] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Pomerance, Carl and S\'{a}rk\"ozy, Andr\'{a}s, On locally repeated values of certain arithmetic functions. {III}. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1987), 1--7.

forum_comments.text:
There's a good amount of literature on $\phi(n)=\phi(n+k)$, where $k$ is a fixed positive integer.
See, for instance, this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12155) by K. Ford.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
As noted as far back as Schinzel, the problem is a lot easier (though still non-trivial) if one replaces the shift by 1 by larger shifts. For instance, if $p$ and $2p-1$ are both prime then we have $\phi(n+2)=\phi(n)$ for $n = 2(2p-1)$, so $n+2 = 4p$. See this paper by Ford (https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12155) for further explorations of this idea.

Unfortunately, for the unit shift problem here, no such ansatz involving products of a small number of primes can work. If $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$ for a large $n$ then $\frac{\phi(n)}{n} = \prod_{p|n} \frac{p-1}{p}$ has to be very close, but not equal to, $\frac{\phi(n+1)}{n+1} = \prod_{p|n+1} \frac{p-1}{p}$. On the other hand, one of the $n,n+1$ has to be even, so one of these products involves $\frac{1}{2}$ and the other does not. As these products are all distinct (mostly due to the denominators being distinct primes), this forces larger and larger numbers of factors to show up for at least one of these products as $n$ increases.

attempt:
Hard point:
Positive counts in finite ranges do not prove infinitely many solutions.

Exact arithmetic reformulation:
Using
\[
\varphi(n)=n\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right),
\]
the equation
\[
\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\frac{n+1}{n}
=
\frac{\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right)}
{\prod_{q\mid n+1}\left(1-\frac1q\right)}.
\]
Since \((n,n+1)=1\), prime supports on the two sides are disjoint, making this a highly constrained multiplicative balance.
Parity lemma:
If \(n>1\) and \(\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\), then both values are even.
Proof:
\(\varphi(m)\) is even for every \(m>2\). Among \(n,n+1\), one is \(>2\), and for \(n>1\) both are \(\ge2\), so equality forces an even common value.
Coprime-factor decomposition identity:
Write
\[
n=2^{a}u,\quad n+1=v
\]
if \(n\) is even (the odd case is symmetric by swapping \(n,n+1\)), with \(u,v\) odd and \((u,v)=1\).
Then
\[
\varphi(n)=2^{a-1}\varphi(u),\qquad
\varphi(n+1)=\varphi(v),
\]
so any solution must satisfy
\[
2^{a-1}\varphi(u)=\varphi(v).
\]
Thus the 2-adic valuation of \(\varphi(n)\) is completely constrained by the odd part of the neighboring integer.
In particular, if \(a\) is large then \(\varphi(v)\) must carry matching 2-adic divisibility, forcing \(v\) to have many odd prime factors \(\equiv1\pmod{2^t}\) (or high prime-power structure). This gives a concrete arithmetic bottleneck for building infinite families.
Certificate principle:
Each explicit \(n\) with \(\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\) is a rigorous witness; therefore the data file provides certified lower bounds on counting function
\[
A(X):=\#\{n\le X:\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\}.
\]
Current computations establish \(A(5\cdot 10^6)\ge 108\).

Target:
Decide whether \(\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\) has infinitely many solutions.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove existence of an infinite parametric family \((n_t)\) such that prime-support conditions on \(n_t\) and \(n_t+1\) force
\[
\frac{\varphi(n_t)}{n_t}=\frac{\varphi(n_t+1)}{n_t+1}\cdot\frac{n_t+1}{n_t},
\]
equivalently \(\varphi(n_t)=\varphi(n_t+1)\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (ratio form):
\[
\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\iff
\frac{n+1}{n}=\frac{\prod_{p\mid n}(1-1/p)}{\prod_{q\mid n+1}(1-1/q)}.
\]
Proof.
Substitute Euler product formula for both totients and divide. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (2-adic coupling):
If \(n=2^a u\) with \(u\) odd, then
\[
2^{a-1}\varphi(u)=\varphi(n+1).
\]
Proof.
\(\varphi(2^a u)=\varphi(2^a)\varphi(u)=2^{a-1}\varphi(u)\), and equality with \(\varphi(n+1)\) gives the identity. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies infinitude):
If Lemma A produces infinitely many distinct \(n_t\), infinitude follows immediately.
Proof.
Each \(n_t\) is a certified solution; infinitely many distinct witnesses give infinitely many solutions. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is constructing infinite neighboring integers with sufficiently synchronized prime-factor profiles to satisfy the exact multiplicative balance.

forum_comments.author: aditya
forum_comments.text:
Gpt 5.5 pro found a partial result (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1qNREx0WwSBi3P4FYCglifN_D78p5zelH/view?usp=sharing)

Let \(L=L(x)\) satisfy\[
 L\log(2L)=o((\log x)^2).
\]Then for all but \(o(x)\) integers \(n\le x\), the values\[
 \varphi(n+1),\varphi(n+2),\ldots,\varphi(n+L)
\]are pairwise distinct. In particular, this gives an affirmative answer to the problem for every fixed exponent \(c<2\), taking \(L=\lfloor(\log x)^c\rfloor\). It also gives, for example,\[
 L=\frac{(\log x)^2}{(\log\log x)^{1+\varepsilon}}
\]for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\).

The broad idea is to count bad starting points. If \(n\) is bad, then for some \(1\le i<j\le L\),\[
 \varphi(n+i)=\varphi(n+j).
\]Writing \(h=j-i\) and \(m=n+i\), this gives a shifted equal-totient equation\[
 \varphi(m)=\varphi(m+h).
\]Thus the number of bad starts is bounded by\[
 \sum_{h<L}(L-h)P(x+L;h),
\]where\[
 P(X;h)=\#\{m\le X:\varphi(m)=\varphi(m+h)\}.
\]The note uses the Graham--Holt--Pomerance / Pollack--Pomerance--Treviño decomposition (references in note)\[
 P(X;h)=P_0(X;h)+P_1(X;h).
\]The exceptional part \(P_1\) is exponentially small uniformly for polylogarithmic \(h\). The structured part satisfies\[
 P_0(X;h)\ll c(h)\frac{X}{(\log X)^2}.
\]The extra observation in the note is that the structured constants have enough average saving:\[
 \sum_{h\le L} c(h)\ll \log L.
\]Combining these gives\[
\begin{aligned}
\#\{\text{bad }n\le x\}
&\ll
\frac{x}{(\log x)^2}
\sum_{h<L}(L-h)c(h)
+
o(x) \\
&\ll
x\frac{L\log L}{(\log x)^2}+o(x).
\end{aligned}
\]This is \(o(x)\) whenever\[
 L\log L=o((\log x)^2).
\]So this does not solve the full problem for arbitrary fixed \(c>0\), but it does give a rigorous almost-all result up to essentially the \((\log x)^2\) scale.

forum_comments.author: Svyable
forum_comments.text:
A slightly stronger statement follows from the usual shifted-collision estimates for the totient function. Let \(c>0\) be fixed and put \(L=\lfloor(\log x)^c\rfloor\). I will use the following standard consequence of the Erdős--Pomerance--Sárközy/Graham--Holt--Pomerance primitive-set method: for every \(A,B>0\), uniformly for \(1\le h\le(\log X)^B\), one has\[
R_h(X):=\#\{m\le X:\varphi(m)=\varphi(m+h)\}\ll_{A,B}\frac{X}{(\log X)^A}.
\]This is unconditional. Call \(n\le x-L\) bad if the values \(\varphi(n+1),\ldots,\varphi(n+L)\) are not all distinct. If \(n\) is bad, then there exist \(1\le i<j\le L\) such that \(\varphi(n+i)=\varphi(n+j)\). Writing \(h=j-i\) and \(m=n+i\), this gives \(\varphi(m)=\varphi(m+h)\), with \(1\le h\le L\) and \(m\le x+L\). For fixed \(h\), there are at most \(L-h\le L\) possible values of \(i\). Hence the number of bad \(n\le x-L\) is at most\[
\sum_{h=1}^{L-1}(L-h)R_h(x+L)\le L\sum_{h=1}^{L}R_h(x+L).
\]Taking \(B>c\) in the shifted-collision estimate gives, for every \(A>0\),\[
R_h(x+L)\ll_{A,c}\frac{x}{(\log x)^A}
\]uniformly for \(1\le h\le L\). Therefore\[
\#\{n\le x-L:n\text{ is bad}\}\ll_{A,c}L^2\frac{x}{(\log x)^A}\ll_{A,c}x(\log x)^{2c-A}.
\]Choosing \(A>2c+1\), this is \(o(x)\). Consequently almost every \(n\le x\) has the property that \(\varphi(n+1),\ldots,\varphi(n+\lfloor(\log x)^c\rfloor)\) are pairwise distinct. In particular, for all sufficiently large \(x\), there exists some \(n\le x\) such that the values \(\varphi(n+k)\), \(1\le k\le(\log x)^c\), are all distinct.

forum_comments.author: Svyable
forum_comments.text:
Yes Chojecki's objection is correct: the displayed estimate\[
 R_h(X)\ll_{A,B} X(\log X)^{-A}
\]uniformly for \(1\le h\le(\log X)^B\) does not seem to be a standard consequence
of the Erdős--Pomerance--Sárközy/Graham--Holt--Pomerance method. What is known
is more like a decomposition into the structured part \(P_0(x;h)\), of size
\(\ll c(h)x/(\log x)^2\), and an exceptional part \(P_1(x;h)\), for which one
does get much stronger exponential-log savings uniformly in \(h\). The
structured part is precisely the obstruction to obtaining arbitrary powers of
\(\log x\).

Thus the union-bound argument after the estimate is fine, but the quoted
estimate itself is too strong as stated. With the known \(x/(\log x)^2\)-type
uniform bound one only gets a much more limited polylogarithmic range, not the
claimed statement for every fixed \(c>0\).

Happy to remove if community deems it better to be scrubbed.

Route:
Scanned consecutive windows of totient values to find long runs where
phi(n+1),...,phi(n+K) are all distinct.

attempt:
Hard point:
The problem asks existence for every fixed c>0 asymptotically; finite scans for selected c do not prove the full statement.

Collision-count identity for totient windows:
For an interval \(I=[m+1,m+K]\), let
\[
C_I:=\#\{(a,b)\in I^2:\ a<b,\ \varphi(a)=\varphi(b)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\varphi(m+1),\dots,\varphi(m+K)\ \text{all distinct}
\iff
C_I=0.
\]
So finding long distinct runs is exactly a zero-collision problem for \(\varphi\)-values on sliding intervals.
Counting-function reformulation:
Define
\[
L(X):=\max\{K:\exists\,m\le X,\ \varphi(m+1),\dots,\varphi(m+K)\ \text{pairwise distinct}\}.
\]
EP-1004 asks for lower bounds of the form
\[
L(X)\gg (\log X)^c
\]
for each fixed \(c>0\) along large \(X\).
Each explicit interval in computation with zero collisions gives a rigorous certificate that \(L(X)\) is at least that length.
Basic lower bound:
For all \(X\ge1\),
\[
L(X)\ge 1.
\]
This is immediate from a one-term window.
Monotonicity:
\[
L(X+1)\ge L(X).
\]
Proof: any interval witnessing \(L(X)\) is still admissible at level \(X+1\).
So EP-1004 asks for quantitative growth of a nondecreasing function \(L(X)\), and computational witnesses provide certified step increases.
Multiplicity decomposition:
For an interval \(I=[m+1,m+K]\), define multiplicities
\[
r_I(v):=\#\{n\in I:\ \varphi(n)=v\}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_v r_I(v)=K,\qquad
C_I=\sum_v \binom{r_I(v)}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
C_I=0 \iff r_I(v)\in\{0,1\}\ \forall v
\]
(equivalently all \(\varphi\)-values in the window are distinct).
This gives a precise additive-combinatorial target: prove existence of long
intervals where every totient value appears with multiplicity at most one.

Target:
Show for every fixed \(c>0\), there exist arbitrarily large \(X\) with
\[
L(X)\gg (\log X)^c.
\]
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a sparse-collision theorem: for many intervals \(I=[m+1,m+K]\) with
\(K\le (\log m)^C\), one has
\[
\sum_v \binom{r_I(v)}{2}=o(1),
\]
hence zero collisions for infinitely many such intervals.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (collision equivalence):
\[
C_I=0 \iff \varphi(m+1),\dots,\varphi(m+K)\ \text{are pairwise distinct}.
\]
Proof.
By definition, \(C_I\) counts equal-value pairs in the window. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (multiplicity decomposition):
\[
C_I=\sum_v \binom{r_I(v)}{2}.
\]
Proof.
For each value \(v\), choose unordered pairs among \(r_I(v)\) occurrences. Summing over \(v\) counts all equal-value pairs exactly once. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies polylog lower bounds):
If A holds for \(K=(\log m)^c\), then \(L(m)\ge K\) for infinitely many \(m\).
Proof.
A gives infinitely many windows with \(C_I=0\); by Lemma B1 each provides a distinct-run witness of length \(K\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The key gap is obtaining sufficiently strong short-interval control on repeated totient values to force collision-free windows at polylogarithmic lengths.

problem: Let $\frac{a_1}{b_1},\frac{a_2}{b_2},\ldots$ be the Farey fractions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farey_sequence) of order $n\geq 4$. Let $f(n)$ be the largest integer such that if $1\leq k<l\leq k+f(n)$ then $\frac{a_k}{b_k}$ and $\frac{a_l}{b_l}$ are similarly ordered - in other words,\[(a_k-a_l)(b_k-b_l)\geq 0.\]Estimate $f(n)$ - in particular, is there a constant $c>0$ such that $f(n)=(c+o(1))n$ for all large $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1005.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-09).
Site remarks:
The function $f(n)$ was first considered by Mayer \cite{Ma42}, who proved $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er43} proved $f(n)\gg n$.

van Doorn \cite{vD25b} has proved that\[\left(\frac{1}{12}-o(1)\right)n\leq f(n) \leq \frac{1}{4}n+O(1),\]and conjectures that the upper bound is optimal.
References:
- [Er43] Erd\H{o}s, P., A note on {F}arey series. Quart. J. Math. Oxford Ser. (1943), 82--85.
- [Ma42] Mayer, A. E., A mean value theorem concerning {F}arey series. Quart. J. Math. Oxford Ser. (1942), 48--57.
- [vD25b] W. van Doorn, Improved bounds for the Mayer-Erd\H{o}s phenomenon on similarly ordered Farey fractions. arXiv:2509.00121 (2025).

attempt:
Target:
Determine asymptotic constant in \(f(n)\sim c n\), conjecturally \(c=1/4\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove that every discordant pair within Farey order appears at gap at most
\[
\frac n4+O(1),
\]
and that extremal first discordance is realized by the central pattern
\[
\frac{n/2-1}{n},\ \frac{n/2}{n-1}
\]
up to \(O(1)\)-perturbations.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (first-discordance identity):
If \(d_{\min}\) is smallest index gap with discordant pair, then \(f(n)=d_{\min}-1\).
Proof.
By definition, all pairs with gap \(\le f(n)\) are similarly ordered, and some pair with gap \(f(n)+1\) is discordant. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (Farey-neighbor determinant control):
For neighboring Farey fractions \(a/b<c/d\), \(bc-ad=1\). This rigid determinant condition constrains relative numerator/denominator monotonicity in short index windows.
Proof.
Standard Farey neighbor property. Determinant identity follows from mediant characterization. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies asymptotic constant):
If A gives matching upper/lower gap location \(n/4+O(1)\), then
\[
f(n)=\frac n4+O(1),
\]
hence \(f(n)=(1/4+o(1))n\).
Proof.
Apply B1 and subtract 1; divide by \(n\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving global optimality of the central discordance pattern over all local Farey configurations.

problem: Let $f_r(n)$ be minimal such that every graph on $n$ vertices with $\geq f_r(n)$ edges and chromatic number $\geq r$ contains a triangle. Determine $f_r(n)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1011.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-10).
- Page last edited: 06 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Tur\'{a}n's theorem implies $f_2(n)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$. Erd\H{o}s and Gallai \cite{Er62d} proved $f_3(n)=\lfloor \frac{1}{4}(n-1)^2\rfloor+2$.

Simonovits showed in his PhD thesis (see the discussion on p. 358 of \cite{Si74}) that\[f_r(n)=\frac{n^2}{4}-\frac{g(r)}{2}{n}+O(1),\]where $g(r)$ is the largest $m$ such that, for any triangle-free graph with chromatic number $\geq r$, at least $m$ vertices of $G$ need to be removed to obtain a bipartite graph. Simonovits \cite{Si74} notes\[\frac{\log r}{\log\log r}r^2 \ll g(r) \ll (\log r)^2r^2.\]Hunter in the comments has noted that other results imply $g(r)\asymp r^2\log r$ - in fact\[(1/2-o(1))r^2\log r\leq g(r)\leq (2+o(1))r^2\log r.\]The lower bound follows from work of Davies and Illingworth \cite{DaIl22} (see [1104]). The upper bound follows from work of Hefty, Horn, King, and Pfender \cite{HHKP25} on $R(3,k)$.

Ren, Wang, Wang, and Yang \cite{RWWY24} showed that, for $n\geq 150$,\[f_4(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{(n-3)^2}{4}\right\rfloor+6.\]
References:
- [DaIl22] Davies, Ewan and Illingworth, Freddie, The {$\chi$}-{R}amsey problem for triangle-free graphs. SIAM J. Discrete Math. (2022), 1124--1134.
- [Er62d] Erd\H{o}s, P., On a theorem of {R}ademacher-Tur\'{a}n. Illinois J. Math. (1962), 122--127.
- [HHKP25] Z. Hefty, P. Horn, D. King, and F. Pfender, Improving $R(3,k)$ in just two bites. arXiv:2510.19718 (2025).
- [RWWY24] S. Ren, J. Wang, S. Wang, and W. Yang, Extremal triangle-free graphs with chromatic number at least four. arXiv:2404.07486 (2024).
- [Si74] Simonovits, M., Extermal graph problems with symmetrical extremal graphs. {A}dditional chromatic conditions. Discrete Math. (1974), 349--376.

problem: Let $h_3(k)$ be the minimal $n$ such that there exists a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices with chromatic number $k$. Find an asymptotic for $h_3(k)$, and also prove\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{h_3(k+1)}{h_3(k)}=1.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1013.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-10).

Site remarks:
The function $h_3(k)$ is dual to the function $f(n)$ considered in [1104], in that $h_3(k)= n$ if and only if $n$ is minimal such that $f(n)=k$.

References:
- [GrYa68] Graver, Jack E. and Yackel, James, Some graph theoretic results associated with Ramsey's theorem. J. Combinatorial Theory (1968), 125--175.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom

I think this is the other way around - if $R(3,n/k)>n$ then there is a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices with independence number $\leq n/k$, and so chromatic number $\geq k$, and hence (deleting vertices if necessary to get chromatic number $=k$) $h_3(k) \leq n$.

Johansson's bound for the chromatic number of triangle-free graphs (if I've found the right result) says that $\chi(G) \ll \frac{n}{\log n}$, which implies the lower bound $h_3(k)\gg (\log k)k$, which is weaker than the Graver-Yackel bound given here.

EDIT: In fact this is the dual function to [1104].

forum_comments.author: Wouter CvB
forum_comments.text: For the record: as in problem 1104, the application of Johansson's theorem is more subtle. It says that $\chi(G)\ll \frac{\Delta}{ \log \Delta}$ where $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of a triangle-free graph $G$. This implies $\chi(G)\ll \sqrt {\frac{n}{\log n}}$, hence $h_3(k) \gg k^2 \log k$. The proof in a nutshell: If $\Delta \leq \sqrt{n \log n}$ then it's immediate. Otherwise select a vertex $v$ with maximum degree and apply induction to $G-N[v]$.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
This is just an attempt that might solve the case \(k=3\).

We prove that\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{R(3,n+1)}{R(3,n)}=1.
\]By the Greenwood-Gleason recurrence,\[
R(3,n+1)\le R(2,n+1)+R(3,n)=(n+1)+R(3,n),
\]since \(R(2,m)=m\). Dividing by \(R(3,n)\) yields\[
\frac{R(3,n+1)}{R(3,n)}\le 1+\frac{n+1}{R(3,n)}.
\]Monotonicity gives \(R(3,n+1)\ge R(3,n)+1\), so\[
\frac{R(3,n+1)}{R(3,n)}\ge 1+\frac{1}{R(3,n)}.
\]It is known (Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi 1980, Kim 1995) that
\(R(3,n)=\Theta(n^2/\log n)\). Hence there exists \(c>0\) with
\(R(3,n)\ge c\,n^2/\log n\) for large \(n\), implying\[
\frac{n+1}{R(3,n)}\le\frac{(n+1)\log n}{c\,n^2}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.
\]From the lower bound we get \(\liminf R(3,n+1)/R(3,n)\ge 1+\lim 1/R(3,n)=1\).
From the upper bound and the limit above we get \(\limsup R(3,n+1)/R(3,n)\le 1+0=1\).
Thus \(\liminf=\limsup=1\), so the limit exists and equals \(1\). ∎

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
The monotonicity of $R(3,n)$ is not known to be strict, but otherwise the argument here seems to be correct. Such a result would already have been known to Erdos at the time of [Er71], given that Erdos himself proved (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-06.pdf) $R(3,n) \gg n^2/\log^2 n$ back in 1961, and the Greenwood-Gleason paper (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/BF0DEBC881488344266BCD77CBBCD86B/S0008414X00030091a.pdf/combinatorial_relations_and_chromatic_graphs.pdf) is from 1955. Looking at [Er71 (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1971-25.pdf), p.99] it seems that Erdos was attributing the $k=3$ case of determining the exact rate of growth of $R(k,l)$ as open, not the problem of establishing that the ratio $R(k,l+1)/R(k,l)$ converges to $1$. (And Erdos seems to have mistyped the known upper and lower bounds of $R(3,l)$ (which he calls $f(3,l)$) in his equation (2); he writes $n^2 \log n / \log\log n \ll f(3,n) \ll n^2 \log^2 n$ but I think he meant $n^2 / \log^2 n \ll f(3,n) \ll n^2 \log\log n / \log n$. The correct order of growth $f(3,n) \asymp n^2 / \log n$ was determined by Kim (https://people.tamu.edu/~huafei-yan/Teaching/Math689/ramsey5.pdf) in 1995.)

Target:
For fixed \(k\ge3\), prove
\[
\frac{R(k,\ell+1)}{R(k,\ell)}\to1\quad(\ell\to\infty).
\]

\[
R(k-1,\ell+1)=o(R(k,\ell)).

Lemma B1 (recursive upper bound):
\[
R(k,\ell+1)\le R(k,\ell)+R(k-1,\ell+1).

Proof.

Lemma B2 (trivial lower monotonicity):
\[
R(k,\ell+1)\ge R(k,\ell).

If A holds, then
\[
1\le \frac{R(k,\ell+1)}{R(k,\ell)}\le 1+\frac{R(k-1,\ell+1)}{R(k,\ell)}=1+o(1).
\]
Proof.
Combine B1 and B2 and divide by \(R(k,\ell)\). Squeeze theorem gives limit \(1\). \(\square\)

The bottleneck is proving sufficiently strong separation between adjacent \(k\)-layers of Ramsey growth.

problem: Let $h(n)$ be minimal such that there is a graph on $n$ vertices with $n+h(n)$ edges which contains a cycle on $k$ vertices, for all $3\leq k\leq n$. Estimate $h(n)$. In particular, is it true that\[h(n) \geq \log_2n+\log_*n-O(1),\]where $\log_*n$ is the iterated logarithmic function?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1016.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-10).
- Page last edited: 27 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Such graphs are called pancyclic. A problem of Bondy \cite{Bo71}, who claimed a proof (without details) of\[\log_2(n-1)-1\leq h(n) \leq \log_2n+\log_*n+O(1).\]Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er71} believed the upper bound is closer to the truth, but could not even prove $h(n)-\log_2n\to \infty$.

A proof of the above lower bound is provided by Griffin \cite{Gr13}. The first published proof of the upper bound appears to be in Chapter 4.5 of George, Khodkar, and Wallis \cite{GKW16}.
References:
- [Bo71] Bondy, J. A., Pancyclic graphs. I. J. Combinatorial Theory Ser. B (1971), 80--84.
- [Er71] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis. Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications (Proc. Conf., Oxford, 1969) (1971), 97-109.
- [GKW16] George, John C. and Khodkar, Abdollah and Wallis, W. D., Pancyclic and bipancyclic graphs. (2016), xii+108.
- [Gr13] S. Griffin, Minimal Pancyclicity. arXiv:1312.0274 (2013).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
Some updated references arising from use of Gemini (https://gemini.google.com/share/ca486d2a4276) (after 5 mins) and ChatGPT (https://chatgpt.com/share/68f2e107-c4a0-800e-9955-057d700685e6) (after 7 mins).

Bondy's paper actually claims the slightly weaker bounds $\log_2 (n-1) - 1 \leq h(n) \leq \log_2 n + \log_* n + O(1)$, contrary to what Erdos writes, but with no proof given for either inequality. An actual proof of the lower bound was only provided in 2013 by Bi-George-Rui (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.0274), though this 2023 paper of Alon and Krivelevich (https://www.math.tau.ac.il/~krivelev/pancyclic-rg.pdf) suggests that a equivalent statement was established by Shi in 1994 (https://pdf.sciencedirectassets.com/271536/1-s2.0-S0012365X00X02312/1-s2.0-0012365X94900310/main.pdf) (but it is difficult for me to confirm this as the notation is somewhat different). An obscure 1996 paper of Jia (https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=1431994) (which I was not able to directly obtain, but could see their results mentioned in this 2014 survey of Lai and Liu (https://combinatorialpress.com/article/jcmcc/Volume%20091/vol-091-paper%204.pdf)) establishes $h(n) \leq \frac{3}{2} \log_2 n + 1$ for all $n$ and $h(n) \leq \log_2 n + \log_2 \log_2 n + O(1)$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and also makes the conjecture #1016. The first literature proof of the upper bound $h(n) \leq \log_2 n + \log_* n + O(1)$ that seems to exist is in Chapter 4.5 of this 2016 book of George, Khodkar, and Wallis (https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=3495006). The consensus seems to be that Bondy's bounds, which are now proven in the literature, remain the state of the art except for very small $n$ where there is some work by George, Marr, and Wallis (https://combinatorialpress.com/article/jcmcc/Volume%20086/vol-086-paper%207.pdf).

Target:
Determine minimal excess \(h(n)\) (above \(n\) edges) needed for pancyclic behavior in EP-1016 formulation.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a robust expansion lemma: if \(e(G)\ge n+h\) and every proper induced subgraph has average degree below a threshold, then \(G\) contains cycles in a full interval of lengths whose span is \(\gg h\), eventually covering \(3,\dots,n\).

If \(G\) contains cycles of every length \(3,\dots,n\), then \(G\) is pancyclic by definition.

If A turns excess \(h\) into complete cycle-length coverage for large \(n\), then \(h(n)\) is bounded above by that threshold function.
Proof.
Any graph meeting the threshold satisfies pancyclic conclusion by A; minimal forcing excess is at most that value. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The key gap is converting moderate global edge excess into guaranteed full cycle-spectrum coverage rather than long but incomplete intervals of lengths.

problem: Let $f(n,k)$ be such that every graph on $n$ vertices and $k$ edges can be partitioned into at most $f(n,k)$ edge-disjoint complete graphs. Estimate $f(n,k)$ for $k>n^2/4$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1017.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-12).
- Page last edited: 28 December 2025.
Site remarks:
The function $f(n,k)$ is sometimes called the clique partition number.

Erd\H{o}s, Goodman, and P\'{o}sa \cite{EGP66} proved that $f(n,k)\leq n^2/4$ for all $k$ (and in fact the complete graphs can be taken to be edges and triangles), which is best possible in general, as witnessed for example by a complete bipartite graph. In \cite{Er71} Erd\H{o} asks vaguely whether this result can be 'sharpened' for $k>n^2/4$.

Lov\'{a}sz \cite{Lo68} proved that every graph on $n$ vertices and $k$ edges is the union of $\binom{n}{2}-k+t$ complete graphs, where $t$ is maximal such that $t^2-t\leq \binom{n}{2}-k$, but without the assumption that the complete graphs are edge disjoint. Lov\'{a}sz's result is sharp in many cases.

If $k>n^2/4$ and the graph contains no $K_4$ then this is equivalent to finding the minimum number of edge disjoint triangles. This special case was also asked about by Erd\H{o}s. A complete answer was provided by Gy\"{o}ri and Keszegh \cite{GyKe17}, who proved that every $K_4$-free graph with $n$ vertices and $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+m$ edges contins $m$ pairwise edge disjoint triangles.

See also [184] for an analogous problem decomposing into edges and cycles, and [583] for decomposing into paths. The clique partition problem for chordal graphs is the subject of [81].
References:
- [EGP66] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Goodman, A. W. and P\'{o}sa, Lajos, The representation of a graph by set intersections. Canadian J. Math. (1966), 106-112.
- [Er71] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis. Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications (Proc. Conf., Oxford, 1969) (1971), 97-109.
- [GyKe17] Gy\H{o}ri, Ervin and Keszegh, Bal\'{a}zs, On the number of edge-disjoint triangles in {$K_4$}-free graphs. Combinatorica (2017), 1113--1124.
- [Lo68] Lov\'{a}sz, L., On covering of graphs. Theory of Graphs (Proc. Colloq., Tihany, 1966) (1968), 231-236.

attempt:
Target:
Quantify optimal lower bounds for edge-disjoint triangle packing \(\nu_3(G)\) in \(K_4\)-free graphs with edge excess \(q\) above \(\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a stability theorem: every near-extremal \(K_4\)-free graph with excess \(q\) is close to bipartite plus sparse internal edges, and each internal edge can be assigned to an edge-disjoint triangle except for \(o(q)\) losses.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (constructive lower family):
In the balanced bipartite-plus-matching construction, one gets \(\nu_3(G)\ge q\).
Proof.
Each added internal matching edge \(uu'\) forms a triangle with a distinct vertex on opposite side; matching ensures disjointness across triangles. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (edge-excess accounting):
\[
e(G)=\left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor+q
\]
means exactly \(q\) edges beyond Turán bipartite baseline.
Proof.
Immediate by definition of excess parameter \(q\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies asymptotic sharpness):
If A yields \(\nu_3(G)\ge q-o(q)\) universally and construction gives \(\nu_3(G)\le q\) examples up to lower-order terms, then optimal guarantee is \(q(1-o(1))\).
Proof.
Combine universal lower with matching family upper behavior. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is handling adversarial internal-edge geometry where triangles compete for shared cross edges, beyond clean matching constructions.

problem: Is it true that, for every $k\geq 3$, there is a constant $c_k>0$ such that\[\mathrm{ex}(n,G_k) \ll n^{3/2-c_k},\]where $G_k$ is the bipartite graph between $\{y_1,\ldots,y_k\}$ and $\{z_1,\ldots,z_{\binom{k}{2}}\}$, with each $z_j$ joined to a unique pair of $y_i$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1021.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-01-20).
- Page last edited: 21 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits, who proved (in unpublished work) that in such a result one must have $c_k\to 0$ as $k\to \infty$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er71} could not even prove whether $\mathrm{ex}(n,G_k)=o(n^{3/2})$.

When $k=3$ the graph $G_3$ is the $6$-cycle $C_6$, for which Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64c} and Bondy and Simonovits \cite{BoSi74} proved $\mathrm{ex}(n,C_6)\ll n^{7/6}$ (see [572]).

The graph $G_k$ is the graph $H_k$ of [926] with the vertex $x$ omitted, and can also be described as the $1$-subdivision of $K_k$.

This was proved by Conlon and Lee \cite{CoLe21}, with a value of $c_k=6^{-k}$. This was improved to $c_k=\frac{1}{4k-6}$ by Janzer \cite{Ja19}.
References:
- [BoSi74] Bondy, J. A. and Simonovits, M., Cycles of even length in graphs. J. Combinatorial Theory Ser. B (1974), 97-105.
- [CoLe21] Conlon, David and Lee, Joonkyung, On the extremal number of subdivisions. Int. Math. Res. Not. IMRN (2021), 9122--9145.
- [Er64c] Erd\H{o}s, P., Extremal problems in graph theory. Theory of Graphs and its Applications (Proc. Sympos. Smolenice, 1963) (1964), 29-36.
- [Er71] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis. Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications (Proc. Conf., Oxford, 1969) (1971), 97-109.
- [Ja19] Janzer, Oliver, Improved bounds for the extremal number of subdivisions. Electron. J. Combin. (2019), Paper No. 3.3, 6.

problem: Is there a constant $c_t$, where $c_t\to \infty$ as $t\to \infty$, such that if $\mathcal{F}$ is a finite family of finite sets, all of size at least $t$, and for every set $X$ there are $<c_t\lvert X\rvert$ many $A\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A\subseteq X$, then $\mathcal{F}$ has chromatic number $2$ (in other words, has property B)?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1022.
- Page status: PROVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-01-23).
- Page last edited: 25 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s originally conjectured, in this language, that $c_2=1$, which he reports in \cite{Er71} was proved by Lov\'{a}sz. He seems to refer to \cite{Lo68} for this, which does not contain this result, so presumably this is a miscitation and perhaps Lovasz reported the easy proof that $c_2=1$ (see e.g. the comment by Tao below) directly to Erd\H{o}s.

The condition on $c_t$ is a weaker form of the condition that the hypergraph is degenerate: a hypergraph is $d$-degenerate if every subhypergraph has a vertex contained in at most $d$ edges, which implies that for any $X$ there are at most $d\lvert X\rvert$ many edges contained in $X$.

This is false, and $c_t<2$ for all $t$: a counterexample is provided by Wood \cite{Wo13b}, who constructs, for any $r\geq 2$, a triangle-free $2$-degenerate $r$-uniform hypergraph with chromatic number $3$. A similar counterexample was found independently by KoishiChan in the comments.
References:
- [Er71] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis. Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications (Proc. Conf., Oxford, 1969) (1971), 97-109.
- [Lo68] Lov\'{a}sz, L., On covering of graphs. Theory of Graphs (Proc. Colloq., Tihany, 1966) (1968), 231-236.
- [Wo13b] D. R. Wood, Hypergraph colouring and degeneracy. arXiv:1310.2972 (2013).

forum_comments.author: KoishiChan
forum_comments.text:
This problem seems to admit a trivial counterexample showing that $c_t < 2$ for every $t$. I use $F$ as the hypergraph, since $\mathcal{F}$ does not render on many computers.

Let $\Gamma$ be a vertex set of size $3t$. For each pair of subsets $A, B \subset \Gamma$ of size $t$, add a new vertex $v_{A, B}$ and sets $A \cup \{v_{A, B}\}$ and $B \cup \{v_{A, B}\}$ to $F$. Let $V$ denote the set of $v_{A, B}$'s. Furthermore, for any $t$ element subset $Q$ of $\Gamma$ and $t$ element subset $R$ of $V$, add a new vertex $w_{Q, R}$ and sets $Q \cup \{w_{Q, R}\}$ and $R \cup \{w_{Q, R}\}$ to $F$. Thus, $X$ consists of $\Gamma$, $V$, and the vertices $w_{Q, R}$.

Clearly, $F$ is $(t + 1)$-uniform. We now claim that $F$ cannot be two-chromatic. Suppose the contrary and study a blue-red-coloring of $F$. If $\Gamma$ has $t$ red vertices $A$ and $t$ blue vertices $B$, then at least one of $A \cup \{v_{A, B}\}$ and $B \cup \{v_{A, B}\}$ is monochromatic, contradiction. Otherwise, $\Gamma$ contains at least $2t$ vertices of the same color, say red. Let $Q$ denote these red vertices. For any partition $Q = A \sqcup B$ into two sets of size $t$, $v_{A, B}$ must be blue. Hence $V$ contains at least $\binom{2t}{t} \geq t$ blue vertices. Letting $R$ be any $t$ blue vertices in $V$, at least one of $Q \cup \{w_{Q, R}\}$ and $R \cup \{w_{Q, R}\}$ must be monochromatic, contradiction.

Finally, there exists a $2$-to-$1$ matching from $F$ to $X$: let $\phi: F\to X$ map $A \cup \{v_{A, B}\}$ and $B \cup \{v_{A, B}\}$ to $v_{A, B}$, and $Q \cup \{w_{Q, R}\}$ and $R \cup \{w_{Q, R}\}$ to $w_{Q, R}$. Then each vertex of $X$ has at most $2$ pre-images. For each $Y \subset X$, we have
$$\{S \in F: S \subset Y\} \subset \phi^{-1}(Y)$$
thus $|\{S \in F: S \subset Y\}| \leq | \phi^{-1}(Y)| \leq 2|Y|$, as desired.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Hmm. Certainly it looks like the second Lovasz paper (also from 1968) is the relevant one. I could download it from Springer no problems, perhaps try again?

I believe that reference of Lovasz Erdős is using to refer to the other result mentioned in [Er71], the generalisation of Brooks' theorem, namely that if $\lvert A\rvert =r>2$ for all $A\in \mathcal{F}$ and the system is $k$-chromatic and does not contain all $r$-tuples of a set of $(k-1)(r-1)+1$ elements then there are $k$ many $A$ any two of which intersect in the same element. This is indeed a theorem proved in the second Lovasz paper.

I could not see anything in this paper directly relevant to the problem at hand; it may be that this was proved by Lovasz just in personal communication to Erdős, and never published.

I agree that some input from an expert on hypergraphs would be helpful here, perhaps there is some similar well-known and non-trivial problem that was intended here.

EDIT: For convience, I copy below the exact wording used by Erdős in [Er71]: "Probably the following result holds: there is a constant $c_t$, $c_t\to \infty$ as $t\to\infty$, so that if $\{A_l\}$ is a set-system, $\lvert A_l\rvert>t$, and for every $S_1\subset S$ there are fewer than $c_t\lvert S_1\rvert$ $A$'s contained in $S_1$, then the system has chromatic number $2$."

(He had earlier defined $\cup_l A_l=S$.) I believe what I have written in the problem statement is an accurate rephrasing of this.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
In any case, the claim $c_2 = 1$ is easy (and was established in the aforementioned Gemini report, amidst a bunch of nonsense). Firstly, the example of an $n$-cycle for large odd $n$, which is not $2$-colorable but has at most $k$ edges in any $k$-element subset, shows that $c_2$ cannot exceed $1$. Now suppose that ${\mathcal F}$ obeys the hypotheses with $t=2$ and $c_2=1$. Then there can be no singleton or empty edges, and no loops, so the hypergraph is a graph tree, thus 2-colorable.

Given how simple the $c_2=1$ argument is, perhaps the most plausible explanation is that Erdos casually asked this question in some private context, Laci quickly responded with the easy $c_2=1$ argument, and Erdos then posed the higher $t$ problem without thinking too hard about it. It would be good to double check with a hypergraph expert, but I could not find any reference in the hypergraph coloring literature referencing a quantity like $c_t$ (a lot of work instead goes into questions relating to max degree etc., as this is relevant to apply the Lovasz local lemma, or the fewest edges needed in a t-uniform hypergraph to destroy 2-colorability).

I was led here because the Github repo marks this mysteriously with "literature review sought".

I agree with this interpretation.

In [Er71], in section 17, there are two separate statements containing "Lovasz proved":
1) "I conjectured and Lovasz proved that if $|A_i|\ge 2$ and for every $S_1 < S$ there are fewer than $S_1$ $A$'s contained in $S_1$ then the chromatic number of the system is $2$."
2) "Lovasz proved that if $|A_\ell| = r > 2$ and the set system is $k$-chromatic and does not contain all the $r$-tuples of a set of $(k-1)(r-1)+1$ elements, then there are $k$ $A$'s any two of which intersect in the same element. This is a generalization of a well-known theorem of Brooks."

The [Lo68] paper titled "On covering of graphs" appears unrelated to either problem. Meanwhile, the other [Lo68] paper titled "On chromatic number of finite set-systems" seems to be related to the second problem but not the first problem.

Since we are dealing with the first problem, to prevent confusion, it seems best to remove the [Lo68] reference from the problem description?

import Mathlib

abbrev Hypergraph (α : Type*) [DecidableEq α] := Finset (Finset α)

def TwoColorable {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (F : Hypergraph α) : Prop :=
 ∃ (c : α → Bool), ∀ A ∈ F, ∃ x y, x ∈ A ∧ y ∈ A ∧ c x ≠ c y

def erdos_1022 : Prop :=
 ∃ c : ℕ → ℝ, Filter.Tendsto c Filter.atTop Filter.atTop ∧
 ∀ t, ∀ {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (F : Hypergraph α),
 (∀ A ∈ F, A.card ≥ t) →
 (∀ X : Finset α, X.Nonempty → (F.filter (λ A => A ⊆ X)).card < c t * (X.card : ℝ)) →
 TwoColorable F

computation:
I ran random search over non-property-B 3-uniform families on 9 vertices and measured
rho=max_X e(X)/|X|.
Best found non-property-B family had rho ~ 1.222.

This is finite lower-bound evidence on thresholds for small instances, not an
asymptotic determination of c_t.
attempt:
Exact threshold reformulation:
For a \(t\)-uniform hypergraph \(H=(V,E)\), define
\[
\rho(H):=\max_{\varnothing\ne X\subseteq V}\frac{e_H(X)}{|X|},
\]
where \(e_H(X)=\#\{A\in E:\ A\subseteq X\}\).
Define the extremal non-Property-B density
\[
c_t^*:=\inf\{\rho(H):\ H\text{ is }t\text{-uniform and has no Property B}\}.
\]
Then the EP-1022 statement is equivalent to asking whether
\[
c_t^*\to\infty\quad (t\to\infty).
\]
Reason:
- If \(c<c_t^*\), every \(t\)-uniform \(H\) with \(\rho(H)<c\) must have Property B.
- Conversely, any admissible forcing constant \(c_t\) must satisfy \(c_t\le c_t^*\) by definition of infimum.
So the problem is precisely an extremal-density growth question for non-2-colorable \(t\)-uniform hypergraphs.

Universal bounds on \(c_t^*\):
From the definition, one gets immediate explicit bounds.
Lower bound:
If \(H\) has at least one edge \(A\), taking \(X=A\) gives
\[
\rho(H)\ge \frac{e_H(A)}{|A|}=\frac1t.
\]
Hence
\[
c_t^*\ge \frac1t.
\]
Explicit upper bound via complete \(t\)-graph:
Let \(H_t\) be the \(t\)-uniform hypergraph on \(2t-1\) vertices with all
\(\binom{2t-1}{t}\) edges.
This \(H_t\) has no Property B: in any 2-coloring of \(2t-1\) vertices, one color
class has size at least \(t\), yielding a monochromatic \(t\)-edge.
For \(X=V(H_t)\),
\[
\rho(H_t)\ge \frac{|E(H_t)|}{|V(H_t)|}
\;=\;
\frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
c_t^*\le \rho(H_t)\le \frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1}.
\]
So currently we have
\[
\frac1t \le c_t^* \le \frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1},
\]
and EP-1022 asks whether \(c_t^*\to\infty\).

Target:
Show \(c_t^*\to\infty\), i.e. local edge-density threshold forcing Property B diverges with uniformity \(t\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a container-style statement: every \(t\)-uniform hypergraph with \(\rho(H)\le C\) (fixed \(C\)) admits a small family of sparse containers each 2-colorable when \(t\) is large enough.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (forcing-threshold equivalence):
\[
c_t^*=\inf\{\rho(H): H\ \text{non-Property-B}\}
\]
is the sharp local-density forcing threshold.
Proof.
By definition, any \(c<c_t^*\) excludes non-Property-B examples, so forces Property B; conversely any \(c>c_t^*\) permits a counterexample near the infimum. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (monotone inheritance):
If \(H'\subseteq H\), then \(\rho(H')\le \rho(H)\). Therefore sparse forbidden cores are the only obstructions.
Proof.
For each \(X\), \(e_{H'}(X)\le e_H(X)\); maximize over \(X\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies divergence):
If A holds for every fixed \(C\) once \(t\) is large, then no non-Property-B hypergraph can satisfy \(\rho\le C\), so \(c_t^*>C\) eventually; since \(C\) is arbitrary, \(c_t^*\to\infty\).
Proof.
Direct quantifier unwinding. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving that bounded local density alone (without additional pseudorandomness) controls global 2-colorability for large uniformity.

problem: If $R(k)$ is the Ramsey number for $K_k$, the minimal $n$ such that every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $K_k$, then\[\frac{R(k)}{k2^{k/2}}\to \infty.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1029.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-13).
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er93} Erd\H{o}s offers \$100 for a proof of this and \$1000 for a disproof, but says 'this last offer is to some extent phoney: I am sure that [this] is true (but I have been wrong before).'

Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres \cite{ErSz35} proved\[k2^{k/2} \ll R(k) \leq \binom{2k-1}{k-1}.\]One of the first applications of the probabilistic method pioneered by Erd\H{o}s gives\[R(k) \geq (1+o(1))\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}e}k2^{k/2},\]which Spencer \cite{Sp75} improved by a factor of $2$ to\[R(k) \geq (1+o(1))\frac{\sqrt{2}}{e}k2^{k/2}.\]See also [77] for a more general problem concerning $\lim R(k)^{1/k}$, and discussion of upper bounds for $R(k)$.
References:
- [Er93] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favorite solved and unsolved problems in graph theory. Quaestiones Math. (1993), 333-350.
- [ErSz35] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Szekeres, G., A combinatorial problem in geometry. Compos. Math. (1935), 463-470.
- [Sp75] Spencer, Joel, Ramsey's theorem---a new lower bound. J. Combinatorial Theory Ser. A (1975), 108--115.

problem:
Let $R(k,l)$ be the usual Ramsey number: the smallest $n$ such that if the edges of $K_n$ are coloured red and blue then there exists either a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_l$.

problem:
We say that a graph is $4$-chromatic critical if it has chromatic number $4$, and removing any edge decreases the chromatic number to $3$.

Is there, for arbitrarily large $n$, a $4$-chromatic critical graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $\gg n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1032.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-13).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er93} Erd\H{o}s said he asked this 'more than 20 years ago'.

Dirac gave an example of a $6$-chromatic critical graph with minimum degree $>n/2$. This problem is also open for $5$-chromatic critical graphs.

Simonovits \cite{Si72} and Toft \cite{To72} independently constructed $4$-chromatic critical graphs with minimum degree $\gg n^{1/3}$. Toft conjectured that a $4$-chromatic critical graph on $n$ vertices has at least $(\frac{5}{3}+o(1))n$ vertices, and has examples to show this would be the best possible.

See also [917] and [944].
References:
- [Er93] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favorite solved and unsolved problems in graph theory. Quaestiones Math. (1993), 333-350.
- [Si72] Simonovits, M., On colour-critical graphs. Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. (1972), 67--81.
- [To72] Toft, B., Two theorems on critical {$4$}-chromatic graphs. Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. (1972), 83--89.

problem: Let $h(n)$ be such that every graph on $n$ vertices with $>n^2/4$ many edges contains a triangle whose vertices have degrees summing to at least $h(n)$. Estimate $h(n)$. In particular, is it true that\[h(n)\geq (2(\sqrt{3}-1)-o(1))n?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1033.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-12).
- Page last edited: 03 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Bollob\'{a}s and Erd\H{o}s. In \cite{Er82e} it is asked whether $h(n)\geq \frac{3}{2}n$. It is now known that\[2(\sqrt{3}-1)n +O(1)\geq h(n) \geq \frac{21}{16}n.\]The upper bound is due to Erd\H{o}s and Laskar \cite{ErLa85}, and the lower bound is due to Fan \cite{Fa88}. (Note that $2(\sqrt{3}-1)\approx 1.464$ and $21/16=1.3125$.)

The upper bound is not made explicit in \cite{ErLa85}, which is concerned with chordal subgraphs (i.e. subgraphs which do not contain any induced cycle on $>3$ vertices). The connection to this problem is that taking a triangle together with all incident edges forms a chordal subgraph of $G$. The construction of the upper bound is made more explicit in \cite{Fa88}.

In brief, let $m=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$ and take a complete bipartite graph between $k$ and $l$ vertices where $k+l=n$ and $k=cn$. If $c$ is chosen such that $m-kl\leq k^2/4$ then we can add $m-kl$ edges between the $k$ vertices creating no triangles, while having maximum degree (amongst these vertices) $\lceil 2\frac{m-kl}{k}\rceil$. This creates a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $m$ edges. Every triangle uses exactly one vertex from the side with $l$ vertices and two vertices from the side with $k$ vertices, and hence the sum of degrees is at most\[k+2\left\lceil 2\frac{m-kl}{k}\right\rceil+2l=(c^{-1}+3c-2)n+O(1).\]This is minimised at $c=1/\sqrt{3}$, where it is $2(\sqrt{3}-1)n+O(1)$ (and a short calculation verifies that with this choice of $c$ we do indeed have $m-kl\leq k^2/4$).

More generally, let $\Delta_r(n,m)$ be such that every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges contains a clique on $r$ vertices, say $x_1,\ldots,x_r$, such that\[d(x_1)+\cdots+d(x_r)\geq \Delta_r(n,m).\]Let $r\geq 2$ and let $t_r(n)$ be the Tur\'{a}n number (the maximal number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices with no $K_{r+1}$). One can ask more generally about the behaviour of $\Delta_r(n,m)$ for $m>t_{r-1}(n)$ (when $m\leq t_{r-1}(n)$ this is trivial since there may be no clique on $r$ vertices at all). The behaviour of $\Delta_r(n,m)$ in the regime $m\geq t_r(n)$ is the subject of [904].

Erd\H{o}s (see \cite{Fa92}) proved that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that if $t_{r-1}(n)<m<t_r(n)-\delta n^2$ then\[\Delta_r(n,m)\leq (1-\epsilon)\frac{2rm}{n}.\]Bollob\'{a}s and Nikiforov \cite{BoNi05} proved that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that if $m>t_r(n)-\delta n^2$ then\[\Delta_r(n,m)\geq (1-\epsilon)\frac{2rm}{n}.\]
References:
- [BoNi05] Bollob\'{a}s, B\'ela and Nikiforov, Vladimir, The sum of degrees in cliques. Electron. J. Combin. (2005), Note 21, 10.
- [Er82e] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite problems which recently have been solved. (1982), 59--79.
- [ErLa85] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Laskar, Renu, A note on the size of a chordal subgraph. Congr. Numer. (1985), 81--86.
- [Fa88] Fan, Genghua, Degree sum for a triangle in a graph. J. Graph Theory (1988), 249--263.
- [Fa92] Faudree, Ralph J., Complete subgraphs with large degree sums. J. Graph Theory (1992), 327--334.

Route:

Target:
Sharpen asymptotics for the minimum possible
\[
h(n):=\min_{e(G)\ge n^2/4}\ \max_{\triangle uvw}\bigl(\deg u+\deg v+\deg w\bigr)
\]
in the EP-1033 formulation.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a density-to-heavy-triangle lemma:
every graph with \(e(G)\ge n^2/4\) contains a triangle with degree-sum at least
\[
\left(2(\sqrt3-1)+\varepsilon_n\right)n,

where \(\varepsilon_n\to0\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (triangle existence at threshold plus):
If \(e(G)>n^2/4\), then \(G\) contains a triangle.
Proof.
Turán/Mantel theorem: triangle-free maximum is \(n^2/4\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (degree-sum averaging on triangles):
Let \(T\) be triangle set. Then
\[
\frac1{|T|}\sum_{uvw\in T}(\deg u+\deg v+\deg w)
\]
is controlled by weighted counts of edge-triangle incidences, enabling lower bounds from global edge density.
Proof.
Expand triangle-degree sum by summing vertex degrees over incident triangles and rewrite via edge/vertex incidence identities. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies lower bound for \(h(n)\)):
If A holds uniformly, then
\[
h(n)\ge \left(2(\sqrt3-1)+o(1)\right)n.
\]
Proof.
Take minimum over all eligible graphs; A gives same lower bound for each graph. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The key gap is converting global density information into sharp pointwise control on one triangle's degree sum at the conjectured constant.

I'll note that the "blow-up case" should be clear here (at least if you want $m=(1+o(1))2^n$ vertices).

let $H_0$ be any $m_0$ graph with minimum degree $>m_0/2$. by Dirac's theorem, $H_0$ should contain a Hamilton cycle, $C=v_1,\dots,v_{m_0}$.

now, consider consider the homomorphism $\phi$ which sends the $i$-th layer of the hypercube to $v_{i\pmod{m_0}}$. this is clearly a homomorphism, and the pre-image of any vertex has size $\sim 2^n/m_0$ (since the binomial coefficeints do not vary significantly).

problem: Determine the infimum and supremum of\[\lvert \{ x\in \mathbb{R} : \lvert f(x)\rvert < 1\}\rvert\]as $f\in \mathbb{R}[x]$ ranges over all non-constant monic polynomials, all of whose roots are real and in the interval $[-1,1]$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1038.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-15).
- Page last edited: 11 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Herzog, and Piranian \cite{EHP58}, who proved that the measure of the set in question is always at most $2\sqrt{2}$ under the assumption that all the roots are in $\{-1,1\}$, and conjecture this is the best possible upper bound.

They also note that the infimum of the set in question is less than $2$, as witnessed by $f(x)=(x+1)(x-1)^m$ for $m\geq 3$. They further note that if the roots are restricted to $[-2,2]$ then the infimum is zero, as witnessed by a small perturbation of the Chebyshev polynomials.

They further conjectured that, if the roots are restricted to $[-2,2]$, then\[\lvert \{ x\in \mathbb{R} : \lvert f(x)\rvert < 1\}\rvert\geq n^{-c}\]for an absolute constant $c>0$. This was proved by Pommerenke \cite{Po61}, who in fact showed that this set must contain an interval of width $\gg n^{-4}$.

The current best known bounds (see the discussion in the comments) are\[1.519\approx 2^{4/3}-1\leq \inf \leq 1.835\cdots\]and\[\sup = 2\sqrt{2}\approx 2.828.\]
References:
- [EHP58] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Herzog, F. and Piranian, G., Metric properties of polynomials. J. Analyse Math. (1958), 125-148.
- [Po61] Pommerenke, Ch., On metric properties of complex polynomials. Michigan Math. J. (1961), 97-115.

Following jspier's finite-atom approach, and using the standard reduction recorded in Tao/natso's notes, I have a small formalized update: the tail part of the previous $1.8$-type lower-bound argument can be pushed to $M=1.806304$ with a five-atom certificate.

The method is the usual dual-forcing one. For each moving parameter $a$, construct a positive finite measure $\lambda_a$ with $U_{\lambda_a}>0$ on the normalized support $\{-1\}\cup[0,1]$. Then

$$
\int U_\mu\,d\lambda_a=\int U_{\lambda_a}\,d\mu
$$

forces at least one point of $\operatorname{supp}\lambda_a$ to lie in $\{U_\mu>0\}$, and sweeping $a$ gives extra length.

For the tail block I use

$$
a\in[-1.806304,-1.708],
$$

and

$$
\lambda_a=
\delta_a
+1.174168821\,\delta_{a+1.80650001}
+0.025921118\,\delta_{a+2.57053197}
+0.118647936\,\delta_{a+2.68367709}
+0.180553554\,\delta_{a+2.79017717}.
$$

Writing $y=x-a$, the check becomes a one-variable positivity problem for $V(y)$ on

$$
0.708\le y\le2.806304.
$$

The derivative numerator is a quartic, so the Lean files check the two endpoints, the four critical brackets, and the exact swept-interval arithmetic:

Lean/Mathlib certificate package (https://github.com/HKUST-AARON/Erdos-Problem-1038).

Combined with the earlier forcing step giving $(-1.708,0)\subseteq\{U_\mu>0\}$, this gives the finite-atom update from $1.8$ to $1.806304$.

$$ \lambda := c \lambda_\partial + \xi $$

Against all (or at least some) odds, I have constructed a dual measure $\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}$ for $\varepsilon = 0.002$.

We have $\min U_{\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}} \approx 1.5 \cdot 10^{-4}$ at $t \approx 0.989$. That the minimum is positive has been validated on at least an order of $10^5$ points (actually more and with a few other methods). In general, it is difficult to validate such things because the optimization generally overfits to the sampling, and "denser" sampling can reveal that the solution is actually invalid. (This is a general property optimization methods, which many people misinterpret in the case of AI as the AI being "tricky" or something like that.) However, in this case we seem to have enough margin (on the order of $10^{-4}$), and enough things check out that I think we can be reasonably confident this is valid.

This seems notable because AlphaEvolve was not able to achieve this task after running for over 24 hours. The algorithm is the "standard" cutting plane method for solving LP. However, it underwent several rounds of practical improvements, some coming from human suggestions. This highlights an interesting phenomenon that humans still possess some kind of "intangible" cognitive abilities that allow one to succeed in tasks that current LLMs may get stuck, even though the human does not clearly possess any extra knowledge in particular. On the other hand, without LLMs, I can say with confidence that this task is way out of reach for me, after seeing what is required in the final code.

In any case, the final code is a huge mess, and will need some improvements before I try to tackle lower $\varepsilon$ such as $0.001$. The runtime for $\varepsilon = 0.002$ is 20-25 minutes and could go up with lower $\varepsilon$.

Nice work, natso26! I had already given up on the three atom approach, and I am surprised that you managed to push it further. This motivated me to look at the four atom case. However, before doing so I'm going to show that we may assume $[-1.708,0] \subseteq \{U_\mu>0\}$ for a minimizing measure $\mu$.

For $a \in [-1.708,-\sqrt{2}]$ and $b \in [0,1.836+a]$, consider
$$
\nu_{a,b} = \delta_a + (1.395-b)\delta_b + C\,\delta_{1.071-b},
$$
where $C>0$ is chosen so that $U_{\nu_{a,b}}(-1)=0.0001$. As can be seen here (https://www.desmos.com/calculator/jhxbwiyy3p), we have $U_{\nu_{a,b}} > 0$ on $\{-1\} \cup [0,1]$.

We now claim that $[-1.708,0] \subseteq \{U_\mu>0\}$. Assume otherwise, then the infimum of $\{U_\mu>0\}$ is $a_0 \in [-1.708,0]$, with $U_\mu(a_0)=0$. Since $U_{\nu_{a_0,b}}>0$ on $\{-1\}\cup[0,1]$ for every $b \in [0,1.836+a_0]$, by the duality principle, either $b$ or $1.071-b$ belongs to $\{U_\mu>0\}$. Note that both $b$ and $1.071-b$ are positive and are never equal to each other. It follows that $\{U_\mu>0\} \cap (0,+\infty)$ has measure at least $1.836+a_0$. Since we also have $(a_0,0] \subseteq \{U_\mu>0\}$, we conclude that $|\{U_\mu>0\}| \geq 1.836$, and therefore $\mu$ cannot be a minimizing measure.

Now we turn to the four atom approach. We are going to show that $\inf \geq 1.8$. For $a \in [-1.8,-\sqrt{2}]$, consider
$$\lambda_a=\delta_a + 1.08\,\delta_{a+1.8} + 0.2107\,\delta_{a+2.66996}+ 0.1326\,\delta_{a+2.79}.$$
As can be checked here (https://www.desmos.com/calculator/n7eq5iopin), we have $U_{\lambda_a} > 0$ on $[-1,1]$. Therefore, for $a \in [-1.8,-1.708)$, at least one of $a$, $a+1.8$, $a+2.66996$, $a+2.79$ belongs to $\{U_\mu>0\}$. Note that for $a$ in this range these four numbers are distinct, and none of them lies in $[-1.708,0]$. It follows that $|\{U_\mu>0\} \setminus [-1.708,0]| \geq 1.8 - 1.708$. Since we already know that $[-1.708,0] \subseteq \{U_\mu>0\}$, we conclude that $\inf \geq 1.8$.

Finally, I would like to mention that I did not optimize these parameters, and there is likely room for further improvement. I have explored this notion of "dual measure" $\lambda$ associated with a candidate minimizing measure $\mu$, with ChatGPT (https://chatgpt.com/share/694bfb79-7470-8010-8e68-14114649a5c3).

First, recall that we claim that a measure $\lambda := \lambda(\mu)$ can be constructed possessing the properties:
1) $U_\lambda \geq 0$ on $[-1,1]$.
2) $U_\lambda = 0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.
3) $\text{supp }\lambda \subset \{U = 0\}$. More precisely,
$$ \lambda = \sum_{a \in \text{bd}(\{U > 0\})} \frac{1}{|U_\mu'(a)|} \delta_a + \xi, \quad \text{supp }\xi \subset \{U = 0\} \setminus \text{bd}(\{U > 0\}). $$

$\textbf{Two Diracs}$. The case of $\mu_p = (1-p)\delta_{-1} + p\delta_1$.

In this case, Tao has computed $p \approx 0.1459$ is minimizing within this family. However, numerically, the constructed $\lambda$ according to the formula above does not satisfy the three properties.

More precisely, it is indeed true that $U_\lambda(-1) \approx 0$, $U_\lambda(1) \approx 0$ as required. But it is not true that $U_\lambda \geq 0$ on $[-1,1]$; it dips to $\approx -0.23$ somewhere near $1$. Quick numerical check confirms this is not rounding error but is truly negative, but I did not attempt to confirm any digit. See images Plot for $U_\mu$ (https://i.postimg.cc/nLSmdYCR/U_mu_p_01459.png), Plot for $U_\lambda$ (https://i.postimg.cc/nLSmdYCG/U_lambda_p_01459.png).

This means that, by first variation, this $\mu_p$ for $p \approx 0.1459$ is not a local minimizer.

$\textbf{Corollary}$. Any linear combination of two Diracs is not a local minimizer.

$\textbf{Proof}$. If the two Diracs are not at $-1,1$, we can pull them apart. Let's look at the interval of $\{U > 0\}$ containing $-1$. Suppose this interval is fixed and we move $1$ rightward. This decreases the potential $U_\mu$ at the endpoints; therefore the endpoints must move closer to $-1$, decreasing its length. By symmetry, the interval containing $1$ also decreases its length. Hence this is not a local minimizer.

Now suppose the two Diracs are at $-1,1$. By Tao's calculations, the only possibility for a local minimizer is at $p \approx 0.1459$. But we have argued above this is not a local minimizer, either. So two Diracs are not local minimizers. $\blacksquare$

$\textbf{Conjectured global minimizer}$. This is
$$ \mu = A\delta_{-1} + f(x) 1_{[a,1]}(x) \,dx, \quad f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\cdot \frac{x + (1 - A\sqrt{2(1+a)})}{(x+1) \sqrt{(1-x)(x-a)}}, $$
$a \approx 0.805$, $A \approx 0.825$.

The dual measure $\lambda$ has an explicit form
$$ \lambda = \zeta_L\delta_{x_L} + \zeta_R\delta_{x_R} + g(x) 1_{[a,1]} \, dx. $$
Here $x_L \approx -1.808$, $x_R \approx 0.026$ are the two boundary points of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$. We have $\zeta_L = 1/|U_\mu'(x_L)| \approx 0.922$, $\zeta_R = 1/|U_\mu'(x_R)| \approx 1.653$. And
$$ g(x) = \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{(1-x)(x-a)}} \left( c_0 + \frac{\zeta_L R(x_L)}{x-x_L} + + \frac{\zeta_R R(x_R)}{x-x_R} \right), $$
where $R(z) = \sqrt{(z-a)(z-1)}$ is taken on the branch with $R(z) \sim z$ as $z \to \infty$; for real $x<a$ this is $R(x) = -\sqrt{(x-a)(x-1)}$. Finally, $c_0 \approx 2.805$ is chosen so that $U_\lambda(x) = 0$ for $x \in [a,1]$. Note that no attempts were made to confirm the numerical digits.

This $\lambda$ satisfies all three properties, as numerically verified by code. See also the Plot for $U_\mu$ and $U_\lambda$ (https://i.postimg.cc/W4YZ96hX/conj_minimizer_U_mu_U_lambda_overlay.png).

Regarding Tao's comment about Schwarz-Christoffel mapping, ChatGPT explains that "...the square-root endpoints $a,1$ behave like SC “prevertices” with exponent $-1/2$..."; the full explanation is in the chat but I do not claim accuracy.

Thanks for doing the (ChatGPT-assisted) analysis! By the way, I think the $U_\lambda$ plot in the two Diracs case is just a repeat of the $U_\mu$ plot with different axes (a ChatGPT hallucination perhaps?).

The dual function $\lambda = \zeta_L \delta_{x_L} + \zeta_R \delta_{X_R} + g(x) 1_{[a,1]}\ dx$ could be the key to actually showing that the conjectural extremizer $\mu$ is the actual infimum. Suppose we have some competing extremizer $\tilde \mu = \mu + \eta$ to $\mu$, which we can take to have a similar structure of a large mass at $-1$ and some remaining mass somewhere in $(0,1]$, so $U_{\tilde \mu} = U_\mu + U_\eta$ (with $\eta$ a signed measure of total variation at most $2$) similarly is positive on a large interval containing $(-1,0)$ but also additionally is positive on $\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta > 0 \}$.

Morally speaking, the effect of $U_\eta$ on the large interval is to increase its length by
$$ \approx \int U_\eta\ d(\zeta_L \delta_{x_L} + \zeta_R \delta_{x_R})$$
although this is just the linearized (first variation) approximation and there is a correction term I don't understand yet (though the convexity properties of $U_\mu$ suggest that the correction term may mostly have a favorable sign). Ignoring this correction for now, we can write this increase as
$$ \int U_\eta\ d\lambda - \int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx = \int U_\lambda(x)\ d\eta - \int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx.$$
So, morally speaking, to establish the global infimum, one needs an inequality of the form
$$ \int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx \leq |\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta(x) > 0\}| + \int U_\lambda(x)\ d\eta$$

(One could also add in the contribution in the region between $[a,1]$ and the large interval where $U_\mu + U_\eta$ becomes positive, but this looks tricky to exploit.)

The term $U_\lambda(x)\ d\eta$ is non-negative (and would vanish if the modification $\eta$ is restricted to $\{-1\} \cup [a,1]$), so the main issue is to see to what extent
$\int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx$ is controlled by $|\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta(x) > 0\}|$. If $U_\eta$ and $g$ were both bounded (by sufficiently small constants) then there would be a clear route to getting this control. Unfortunately $g$ has a mild singularity at the endpoints of $[a,1]$, and $U_\eta$ also can have logarithmic singularities. However, $U_\eta$ is of bounded mean oscillation (BMO), and thus obeys distributional inequalities such as the John-Nirenberg inequality that can be used in some applications as a substitute for boundedness.

It may be that one has to do some brute force numerics to cover the space of all possible $\eta$ by some finite number of balls in weak topologies and verify the required inequality to sufficient accuracy on each ball, although first one needs to control the error in the linearized analysis.

I am on vacation right now, but in a few days I might set up some further AlphaEvolve experiments to see if there is a chance to prove inequalities such as $\int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx \leq |\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta(x) > 0\}|$ which the above analysis suggests would go a long way to establishing the global infimum property.

I have succeeded in doing a variational analysis for general measures. Some parts may be "handwaved".

By the coarea formula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coarea_formula) in geometric measure theory,
$$ |\{U > 0\}| = \int 1_{U > 0} \, dx = \int_{t > 0} \int_{U = t} \frac{1}{|U'(x)|} \, dx \, dt. $$
The inner integral is just the counting measure. Now I want to replace $U$ with $U + \varepsilon V$ and take $d/d\varepsilon$ at $\varepsilon = 0$. The result is, at $\varepsilon = 0$,
$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} |\{U + \varepsilon V > 0\}| = \int_{t > 0} \int_{U = t} \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \frac{1}{|(U + \varepsilon V)'(x(\varepsilon))|} \, dx \, dt = \int_{t > 0} \int_{U = t} -\frac{\text{sgn } U'(x)}{U'(x)^2} \frac{d}{d\varepsilon}(U + \varepsilon V)'(x(\varepsilon)) \, dx \, dt. $$
To compute the remaining quantity, I want the derivative of $U'(x) + \varepsilon V'(x)$ where $x = x(\varepsilon)$ varies as $U(x) + \varepsilon V(x) = t$. This works out to be $-U''V/U' + V'$. So
$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} |\{U + \varepsilon V > 0\}| = \int_{t > 0} \int_{U = t} -\frac{\text{sgn } U'}{U'^2} \left( -\frac{U''V}{U'} + V' \right) \, dx \, dt. $$

Now apply coarea formula in reverse:
$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} |\{U + \varepsilon V > 0\}| = \int -1_{U > 0} \frac{1}{U'} \left( -\frac{U''V}{U'} + V' \right) \, dx = \int -1_{U > 0} \left(\frac{V}{U'}\right)' \, dx. $$
This is
$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} |\{U + \varepsilon V > 0\}| = \int_{\text{bd}(\{ U > 0 \})} \frac{V}{|U'|} \, dx \geq 0 $$
if $U = U_{\mu}$, $V = U_{\nu}$, $\mu$ is a minimizer and $\nu$ is arbitrary.

Now we want to apply duality. Define
$$ \lambda = \sum_{\text{bd}(\{ U_\mu > 0 \})} \frac{1}{|U_\mu'(a)|} \delta_a. $$
Then the first variation is
$$ \int U_\nu \, d \lambda = \int U_\lambda \, d \nu \geq 0. $$
Since $\nu$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $U_\lambda \geq 0$. But $\lambda$ is supported on $\{ U_\mu = 0 \}$, so
$$ \int U_\lambda \, d \mu = \int U_\mu \, d \lambda = 0. $$
Therefore $U_\lambda = 0$ $\mu$-a.e.!

I realize that this may not solve everything (in particular, what if $U_\mu$ isn't differentiable?), but this looks "clean" enough that it seems it should be useful somehow.

One consequence of this:

Away from $\text{supp }\lambda$, $U_\lambda$ is strictly convex. So in each open interval of $[-1,1] \setminus \text{supp }\lambda$, $U_\lambda = 0$ at at most one point. Since $U_\lambda = 0$ $\mu$-a.e., $\text{supp }\mu$ has at most one point in each open interval of $[-1,1] \setminus \text{supp }\lambda$. So $\mu$ must be a combination of Diracs and something supported on $\{U_\lambda = 0\}$.

A Dirac gives $+\infty$ potential near it, so it's in an interval of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$. Conversely you've shown each interval of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$ has exactly one Dirac.

For points that are isolated in $\{U_\mu = 0\}$, $\mu$ can't have support on them because if so these must be Diracs, but Diracs must be in intervals of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$.

Therefore: $\mu$ must have the following structure. It's a combination of Diracs, which map one-to-one with open intervals of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$ containing each one; plus something supported in the region $\{U_\mu = 0\}$ excluding its isolated points. (In short: Diracs plus "flat regions" which make $U_\mu = 0$.)

If this is correct, it gives some structure to work with. However: as with isoperimetric-type problems, once we've reached this stage the configuration is probably resistant to naive variations already. (In proof of Double Bubble conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bubble_theorem), they quickly established constraints like a minimizer must be a surface of revolution; but this still retains many nonstandard configurations that are difficult to rule out.) So this is roughly the limits of what this kind of argument should be able to do with this amount of effort.

But there could be other clever ways to finish it off from here, with or without using variations.

For the sup problem, it seems that the following general duality lemma can be useful:

Duality lemma (sup version) If $\nu$ is a (sufficiently nice) positive measure with $U_\nu(t) > 0$ for all $t \in [-1,1]$, then the set $\{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0\}$ cannot contain the support of $\nu$.

Proof: This is immediate from the Fubini identity $\int U_\nu(t)\ d\mu(t) = \int U_\mu(x)\ d\nu(x)$. $\Box$

Some examples:
 setting $\nu$ to be a Dirac mass $\delta_x$ at some $x \notin [-2,2]$ shows that $\{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0\}$ cannot contain any point outside of $[-2,2]$.

 Setting $\nu$ to be a two point combination of $\delta_{-M}$ and $\delta_m$ and optimizing shows that $\{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0\}$ cannot contain both $-M$ and $m$ for $1 \leq m,M \leq 2$ satisfying the condition $\log(M-1) \log(m-1) < \log(M+1) \log(m+1)$. This can be used to recover the previous analysis ruling out the case $\sqrt{2} \leq M < 1.7624$ and $M+m \geq 2 \sqrt{2}$.

Here is a plot (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/remaining.png) (produced by Gemini) of the remaining $M + m > 2 \sqrt{2}$ cases not yet ruled out (namely the two small cusp regions on the top left and bottom right of the plot). The two bounding curves are very close to each other (and tangent at $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$) but do not have any actual intersection outside of the two visible cusps.

I feel like other well chosen choices of $\nu$ could yield more information.

There is also an inf version (slightly easier to state and prove with non-strict inequality):

Duality lemma (inf version) If $\nu$ is a (sufficiently nice) positive measure with $U_\nu(t) \leq 0$ for all $t \in [-1,1]$, then the set $\{ x: U_\mu(x) \leq 0\}$ must intersect the support of $\nu$.

Some examples of $\nu$ that obey this latter condition, implicitly used in previous arguments:
 $\nu = \frac{1}{2} \delta_a + \frac{1}{2} \delta_{-a}$ for $0 \leq a \leq 1$.

 $\nu = \frac{1}{2} \delta_{-1+c} + \frac{1}{2} \delta_{1+c}$ for $0 \leq c \leq \sqrt{2}-1$.

 $\nu = \frac{1}{3} \delta_{\alpha-c} + \frac{2}{3} \delta_{\beta-c}$ for $\alpha=2^{4/3}$, $\beta =2^{-2/3}$, and $1 \leq c \leq \alpha-1$.

Perhaps there are other useful choices of $\nu$?

Ah, I realize now why your numbers are different from mine; there is an additional difficulty that shows up in the general case of a measure $\sqrt{2}$ set in $[-M,+\infty)$ compared to that of the model case $[-M,-M+2\sqrt{2}]$. It has to do with the question of lower bounding $U_{1_E}(x)$ when $E$ is some measure $L$ set contained in $[-M+a, +\infty]$ (in our application we take $L = 2\sqrt{2}-a$). The model case of $E$ is $[-M+a,-M+a+L]$, and we would like to have the lower bound $U_{1_E}(x) \geq U_{1_{[-M+a,-M+a+L]}}(x)$ as this would imply that the interval $[-M+a,-M+a+L]$ is the worst case. But the Hardy-Littlewood rearrangement inequality (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_inequality) only guarantees this as long as $x$ is to the left of the midpoint $-M+a+\frac{L}{2}$. To the right of this interval, we only get the weaker lower bound $U_{1_E}(x) \geq U_{1_{[-M+a,-M+a+L]}}(-M+a+\frac{L}{2})$. So to handle the general case with $\nu = \delta_{-M} + A 1_E + C \delta_m$, it is not enough to obtain the lower bound
$$ U_{\delta_{-M}}(x) + A U_{1_{[-M+a,-M+2\sqrt{2}]}}(x) + C U_{\delta_{-M+2\sqrt{2}}}(x) \geq 0$$
for $x \in [-1,1]$; one has to obtain the slightly stronger bound
$$ U_{\delta_{-M}}(x) + A U_{1_{[-M+a,-M+2\sqrt{2}]}}(\min(x,-M+\frac{a}{2}+\sqrt{2})) + C U_{\delta_{-M+2\sqrt{2}}}(x) \geq 0.$$

It's quite possible that one can do better with more complex $\nu$, but the rearrangement analysis becomes trickier.

Nevertheless, it is still possible to make the rearrangement inequality work directly on the full range $[-M+2.4,\,-M+2\sqrt{2}]$ (at least when $\mu$ is discrete), as follows.

Define $v_{a,b} = A \, 1_{(a,b)} + B\,\delta_b$, where $A, B>0$, $a<b$, and $b>1$. Then $U'_{v_{a,b}}(x)= A(\log|x-a|-\log|x-b|) + B/(x-b)<0$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$ (EDIT: this holds for $A=0.723$, $B=0.1$, $0.6 \leq a < b$, and $b>1$, and is verified numerically in this range). Thus, for any $\Delta>0$, $U_{v_{a,b}}(x) \leq U_{v_{a+\Delta,\,b+\Delta}}(x)$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$ (EDIT: with the same choices of $A$, $B$, $a$ and $b$). As a consequence, given $a<c<b$ and $\Delta>0$, we have $U_{v_{a,b}}(x)
\leq A\,U_{1_{(a,c)}}(x) + U_{v_{c+\Delta,\,b+\Delta}}(x)$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$.

Now fix $1.771 \le M \le 1.7987$, and consider $\nu = \delta_{-M} + \nu_{-M+2.4,\,-M+2\sqrt{2}}$, with $A=0.723$ and $B=0.1$. Then, $U_\nu(x) \ge 0$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$. By repeatedly applying the $\nu_{a,b}$ inequality above (EDIT: this is possible since $0.6\leq -M+2.4\leq 1<-M+2\sqrt{2}$), we can construct a measure $\tilde{\nu}$ whose support is contained in $\{U_\mu \le 0\}$ and which satisfies $0 \le U_\nu(x) \le U_{\tilde{\nu}}(x)$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$. The conclusion then follows from the duality lemma.
