Let the masses be $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with weights $w_1,\dots,w_n$. We consider
$$ U(a, X) = \sum_j w_j \log |a - x_j|. $$
$X$ is the parameters $(x, w)$.

Suppose we're at an optimizer which is a "smooth interior point" (not well defined at this point). Consider $a$ which is an endpoint of an interval, i.e. $U(a, X) = 0$. If I move $X$ while maintaining this constraint, we have
$$ da = -[1/(\partial U/\partial a)] (\partial U/\partial X)dX. $$
Then
$$ d(\text{interval_lengths}) = \sum_a \text{sgn}(\partial U/\partial a) da = \sum_a -[1/|\partial U/\partial a|] (\partial U/\partial X)dX = 0. $$

Now we can't assume much, only that there is an $i$ such that $x_i \neq 1, -1$ and that $\partial U/\partial a \neq 0$. Then we can move $x_i$ and $w_i$ freely in a local region (only two coords). Unfortunately that equation doesn't seem to give a contradiction as such.

However I was able to salvage the following argument. Note
$$ \frac{\partial U}{\partial w_i}(a, X) = \log |a - x_i|. $$
Then
$$ \frac{d(\text{interval_lengths})}{dw_i} = - \sum_a \frac{\log |a - x_i|}{|\partial U/\partial a|}. $$
Now suppose there is an invisible $x_{i,L}$ and $x_{i,R}$ near $x_i$ with weight $0$. If this configuration is a maximizer, we must have
$$ \frac{d(\text{interval_lengths})}{dw_{i,L}} \leq 0, \quad \frac{d(\text{interval_lengths})}{dw_i} = 0, \quad \frac{d(\text{interval_lengths})}{dw_{i,R}} \leq 0. $$
But $x \mapsto -\log |x|$ is strictly convex. So you can't actually have those three things simultaneously satisfied.

Conclusion: for a maximizer (this doesn't work for minimizer), you can't move the parameters that way.

For the case that some $a$ has $\partial U/\partial a = 0$: this is actually even easier because an interval is coming into existence and the length is increasing like $O(\sqrt \varepsilon)$ which dominates $O(\varepsilon)$ from other $a$'s.

This seems to roughly prove that a maximizer must consist of atoms at $1,-1$ plus "potential-zero regions" only. But I see that the interpretation of "potential-zero region" for discrete masses is not exactly well defined in terms of what I wrote above. So I think this doesn't cleanly "prove" it yet, due to the discrete and continuous cases not being exactly analogous? But perhaps this is fixable?

On taking logarithms and normalizing by the degree, one sees that the question is equivalent to finding the infimum or supremum of $| \{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0 \}|$, where $\mu$ ranges over probability measures in $[-1,1]$, and $U_\mu(x) = \int \log |x-y|\ d\mu(y)$ is the logarithmic potential. (A regularization and approximation argument allows one to restrict to those $\mu$ that are discrete with rational probability masses, and then they are the empirical zero distribution of some high-degree polynomial.)

AlphaEvolve gave this example of a probability measure (expressed as a pairs of points together with the mass associated to that point) that showed that the infimum can be as low as 1.84: [(-0.84, 0.01607282659569635), (-0.87, 0.018668276991332278), (-0.96, 0.015722736638053406), (-1.0, 0.02786639212010361), (-0.94, 0.016135713032333365), (-0.91, 0.018142805612153572), (1.0, 0.8305116235730803), (-0.8, 0.026585242076298716), (-0.99, 0.013889666827470722), (-0.98, 0.016404716533477668)]. (Caveat: I used a crude discretization method to estimate the size of the level set, so I do not claim more than two decimal points of precision here.) Readers are invited to "beat the AI" on this! EDIT: here is an image (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/min.png) of what the log potential of this candidate minimizer looks like.

On the other hand, the following simple argument shows that the infimum must be at least 1. For any $0 < a < 1$, the polynomial $(a-x)(-a-x)$ has absolute value strictly less than $1$ on $[-1,1]$, hence $|f(a) f(-a)| < 1$ for all monic polynomials $f$ with roots in $[-1,1]$ (or equivalently $U_\mu(a) + U_\mu(-a) < 0$ for all probability measures $\mu$ on $[-1,1]$). We conclude that at least one of $a,-a$ lie in $\{ x: |f(x)| < 1 \}$ (or $\{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0 \}$), giving the lower bound of $1$. Probably one can do better than this (for instance, by somehow taking advantage of the points outside of $[-1,1]$).

On the supremum side, AlphaEvolve seems convinced that $2 \sqrt{2}$ (corresponding to the uniform distribution on $\{-1,+1\}$) is optimal. Even adding a penalty to getting too close to this distribution fails to budge AE from this unless the penalty is quite large. Not a proof, but perhaps some support for the conjecture. EDIT: AE numerics suggest that there may be a possibility of a computer assisted proof, possibly along the following lines: (a) establish the result by a rigorous perturbative analysis when the measure $\mu$ is sufficiently close to being supported on $\{-1,+1\}$, e.g., by requiring that $\int x^2\ d\mu(x)$ is sufficiently close to 1. (b) In all other cases, discretize the space of probability measures somehow (in something like the vague topology or the Levy metric, for which the space to discretize is compact) and show numerically that some robust version of the statistic $| \{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0 \}|$ is bounded away from $2 \sqrt{2}$. If the gap with $2 \sqrt{2}$ is large compared to the discretization scale, one may then be able to cover all cases.

Some further details on the strategy. Let $-M$ and $m$ denote the inf and sup of $\{x: U_\mu < 0 \}$. By symmetry we may assume $M \geq m$. If $M + m \leq 2\sqrt{2}$ then we are done, so we may assume $M + m > 2 \sqrt{2}$, so $M > \sqrt{2}$. The function $U_\mu$ is increasing on $(1,\infty)$, decreasing on $(-\infty,-1)$, and positive outside of $[-2,2]$, so we may assume that $\sqrt{2} < M < 2$, that $U_\mu(-M)=0$, and $U_\mu(-M + 2 \sqrt{2}) \leq 0$. (EDIT: technically, one needs $-M+2\sqrt{2} > 1$, or $M < 1.828$, to make this deduction, but this condition is satisfied in the analysis below, so this isn't a problem.)

Numerically it seems that for $M$ in the range $\sqrt{2} < M \leq 1.7624$, that there exists some positive real $\alpha$ such that the concave function $\log |x+M| + \alpha \log |x-(-M+2\sqrt{2})|$ is positive at $x = \pm 1$, hence positive on all of $[-1,1]$. Integrating against $\mu$ we get $U_\mu(-M) + \alpha U_\mu(-M + 2 \sqrt{2}) > 0$, a contradiction.

This leaves the range $1.7624 < M \leq 2$. Here one has to work harder and try to force some positivity of $U_\mu$ inside of $[-1,1]$. However one is now quite far away from the conjectural extremizer (for which $M = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$) and there should be room to play all sorts of additional tricks.

If we look at $-1 + \delta$ and $1 + \delta$, then roots in between have product of distances to these values $\leq 1$. It seems that the statement you pointed out, namely that the infimum is at least $\sqrt{2}$, is already proved as Theorem 1 in [EHP58]. More precisely, it is shown that if the mean of the roots of $f(x)$ is nonnegative, then the set $\{x:|f(x)|<1\}$ contains an interval of length at least $\sqrt{2}$ that contains $(0,1)$. However, I think that by extending your (and TerenceTao’s) argument to cubic polynomials as follows, one can even prove that the infimum is at least $2^{4/3}-1 = 1.519842\cdots$.

(EDIT: We first assume by symmetry that the mean of the roots of $f(x)$ is nonnegative.) Let $\alpha=2^{4/3}=2.519\cdots$ and $\beta=2^{-2/3}=0.629\cdots$. Consider the function $g(x)=(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)^2$. It satisfies $-1<g(x)<0$ for almost every $x\in[0,\alpha]$. Hence, for each $x\in[-1,1]$, we have $|g(x+\delta)|<1$ for almost every $\delta\in[1,\alpha-1]$. Since\[
g(x+\delta)=(\alpha-\delta-x)(\beta-\delta-x),\quad (\text{EDIT: this should be }(\alpha-\delta-x)(\beta-\delta-x)^2)
\]it follows that for almost every $\delta\in[1,\alpha-1]$ we have $|f(\alpha-\delta)f(\beta-\delta)|<1$ (EDIT: this should be $|f(\alpha-\delta)f(\beta-\delta)^2|<1$). This means that more than half of the set $[1,\alpha-1]\cup[\beta-\alpha+1,\beta-1]$ is contained in $\{x: |f(x)|<1\}$. Combining this with the above-mentioned theorem (or TerenceTao's argument) gives the desired claim.

Nice! Two corrections: in order to use Theorem 1 of EHP58 one should first use symmetry to reduce to the case of non-negative mean; and secondly I think you need to square the factor $\beta-\delta-x$ and $f(\beta-\delta)$ in your argument. (I think my original argument's can't supply a measure of $1$ in the remaining region $[\beta-1,1]$, which in any event would require some additional hypothesis on the polynomial, as the example $x+1$ shows.)

The full proof of Theorem 1 of EHP58 is lengthy, but the portion needed here, namely that the zero set contains [0,1] if the mean of the zeroes is non-negative (and contains [-1,0] instead of the mean is non-positive) is a simple application of Jensen's inequality. In the language of log potentials: if the barycenter $\overline{t} := \int t\ d\mu(t)$ is non-negative, then for any $x \in [0,1]$ we have from Jensen
$$ U_\mu(x) = \int \log |x-t|\ d\mu(t) \leq \log \int |x-t|\ d\mu(t) \leq \log \left(\int |x-t|\ d\mu(t) + x \overline{t}\right)$$ $$= \log \int |x-t| + x t\ d\mu \leq \log \int 1\ d\mu = 0$$
as required.

EDIT: In a similar vein, Theorem 2 of EHP58 shows that the sup is at most 3. So we currently have $2^{4/3}-1 = 1.519\dots \leq \inf \leq 1.852\dots$ and $2\sqrt{2} = 2.828\dots \leq \sup \leq 3$.

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text: One particular step of the proof of [EHP58, Theorem 1] that might be useful for the inf problem: once one has located an interval $J$ on which $|f(x)| \leq 1$, one can replace all the zeroes in $J$ by their arithmetic mean, since by Jensen's inequality (or the AM-GM inequality) this only serves to decrease $|f(x)|$ to the left or right of $J$, and thus cannot increase the measure of the set $\{ |f(x)| \leq 1\}$. Hence without loss of generality we may assume that every interval in the set contains only one zero (possibly with high multiplicity). This is consistent with the AE examples, where we typically have a large interval containing a single mass at $\pm 1$. The [EHP58, Theorem 1] analysis also tells us that this single mass should have measure at least $1/2$, and I think wlog one can use a translation to place it at an endpoint $\pm 1$.

forum_comments.author: Houi
forum_comments.text:
Using Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic), I obtained a partial result on the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian conjecture ($\rho_n \ge c/n$ for monic degree-$n$ polynomials with roots in the closed unit disc).
Main result. Call $P$ non-degenerate if every critical value has modulus $\ge 1$. Equivalently, $P$ has no branch points over $\mathbb{D}$ , so every inverse branch $\psi_j$ with $\psi_j(0) = z_j$ extends univalently across all of $\mathbb{D}$, with $\psi_j(\mathbb{D}) \subset \Lambda_P(1)$.

Theorem. If $P$ is non-degenerate with roots in the closed unit disc, then $\operatorname{inrad}(\Lambda_P(1)) \ge \frac{1}{4n}$.
Proof sketch. The Koebe quarter theorem gives $\Lambda_P(1) \supset B\left(z_j, \frac{1}{4|P'(z_j)|}\right)$ for each root. The Fekete energy of $n$ points in the closed disc is maximized by $n$-th roots of unity, giving $$\sum_j \log |P'(z_j)| \le n \log n,$$so by pigeonhole $$\min_j |P'(z_j)| \le n.$$Combining: $\operatorname{inrad} \ge \frac{1}{4n}$. The conjectured extremizer $z^n − 1$ is non-degenerate with $|P'(\omega_k)| = n$ for each root.

Reduction. The full EHP conjecture reduces to: the inradius minimizer is non-degenerate. For degenerate components containing $k$ roots,
the Riemann map $\varphi : \mathbb{D} \rightarrow \mathcal{C}$ gives a degree-$k$ Blaschke product $B = P \circ \varphi$, and the inradius bound becomes $\operatorname{inrad}(C) ≥ \frac{|B'(0)|}{4|P'(z^*)|}$. For all $k \ge 2$, the hyperbolic Blaschke invariants degenerate as the component approaches a pinch point — for $k = 2$, $$|B''(wc)|(1−|wc|^2)^2 = 2(1−|B(wc)|²) \rightarrow 0$$as the critical value approaches the boundary; for $k \ge 3$, the family $B_a(w) = w^2 \cdot \frac{w−a}{1−\overline{a}w}$ with $a \rightarrow 0$ shows the same degeneration at all critical points simultaneously. This creates a uniform structural obstruction for the conformal approach in the entire degenerate case.

Numerical evidence. Over several hundred random configurations with $n = 10$ (roots on $\mathbb{T}$, in $\mathbb{D}$, clustered, adversarial), the minimum of $n \cdot \operatorname{inrad}$ was always attained by roots of unity. Degenerate configurations consistently had larger inradii, typically $n \cdot \rho \ge 4$.
The approach is entirely conformal — no area or perimeter estimates — and is independent of KLR (2025). A literature search (via deep research) found no prior work establishing these results or using these methods.
Paper: https://github.com/huy209vn/INRADIUS-OF-POLYNOMIAL-LEMNISCATES-THE-NON-DEGENERATE-CASE-AND-BEYOND
Lean formalization is in progress.

problem:
Let $F\subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be a closed infinite set, and let $\mu(F)$ be the infimum of\[\lvert \{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}\rvert,\]as $f$ ranges over all polynomials of the shape $\prod (z-z_i)$ with $z_i\in F$.

Is $\mu(F)$ determined by the transfinite diameter of $F$? In particular, is $\mu(F)=0$ whenever the transfinite diameter of $F$ is $\geq 1$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1040.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-15).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Herzog, and Piranian \cite{EHP58}, who show that the answer is yes if $F$ is a line segment or disc, and that if the transfinite diameter is $<1$ then $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}$ always contains a disc of radius $\gg_F 1$.

Erd\H{o}s and Netanyahu \cite{ErNe73} proved that if $F$ is also bounded and connected, with transfinite diameter $0<c<1$, then $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}$ always contains a disc of radius $\gg_c 1$.

The transfinite diameter of $F$, also known as the logarithmic capacity, is defined by\[\rho(F)=\lim_{n\to \infty}\sup_{z_1,\ldots,z_n\in F}\left(\prod_{i<j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert\right)^{1/\binom{n}{2}}.\]Aletheia \cite{Fe26} has shown that $\mu(F)$ is not determined by the transfinite diameter of $F$, by producing two distinct closed infinite sets $F_1$ and $F_2$, both of which have transfinite diameter $0$, and yet $\mu(F_1)\geq \pi/4$ while $\mu(F_2)$ can be made arbitrarily close to $0$.
References:
- [EHP58] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Herzog, F. and Piranian, G., Metric properties of polynomials. J. Analyse Math. (1958), 125-148.
- [ErNe73] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Netanyahu, E., A remark on polynomials and the transfinite diameter. Israel J. Math. (1973), 23--25.
- [Fe26] T. Feng et al, Semi-Autonomous Mathematics Discovery with Gemini: A Case Study on the Erd\H{o}s Problems. arXiv:2601.22401 (2026).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao
forum_comments.text:
I'm willing to rate the argument as being plausibly correct. With regards to having publication-level quality of exposition and literature review, the manuscript still needs a lot of work however, on a number of fronts. Much of this is tied to the tendency of current-level AI writing to dwell far too much on routine results (often without citing relevant literature), or technical details, and not enough time emphasizing the high level structure.

In this case, the high-level structure is that there are four key results that resolve the Erdos problem, each of which is independently interesting:

1. The EHP component lemma (at least one component $U$ with two or more zeroes).

2. An integral bound $\int_U |f'(z)/f(z)|\ dA \leq 2\pi m$, where $m$ is the number of zeroes (Proposition 4).

3. A lemma asserting that on any given region $U$, there is a tree connecting the $m$ zeroes of $U$ (formed by following the Morse gradient flow on $\log |f|$, basically) of total length at most $\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_U |f'(z)/f(z)|\ dA$, at least assuming some technical non-degeneracy hypotheses on $f$. (Proposition 12)

4. A simple combinatorial lemma that asserts that any tree contains a path of length at most twice the total length of the tree, divided by the number of vertices of the tree. (Lemma 17)

There is also a technical

0. One can perturb $f$ to obey the non-degeneracy conditions required for the third ingredient to work. (Lemma 14)

Combining all these ingredients, the Erdos problem follows. But the AI-generated exposition spends a lot of time on the least interesting parts of this process (e.g., Step 0), and many steps could be proven much more quickly. For instance Lemma 3 is obvious because the level sets of $p$ are algebraic sets of dimension less than 2, and thus immediately of measure zero (e.g., by the Crofton formula). Several pages of argument are used to establish the formula $\int_{\varepsilon < u < t} |\nabla u|^2\ dA = 2\pi m(t-\varepsilon)$ on page 5, but this is just the area formula noting that $f$ is $m$-to-one on $U$, so (a suitable branch of) $\log f$ is also $m$-to-one mapping to a fundamental domain of $\{ \varepsilon < \mathrm{Re} z < t \}$.

I also suspect that there is a less convoluted way to arrive at Proposition 4 from this area formula and the Polya inequality than the one provided in the AI-generated text, although I have not tried too hard to locate such a simplified argument. Similarly, the perturbative component of the argument (Step 0) seems to occupy far more space in the AI-generated document than it needs to: I think the cleanest thing to do is first resolve the Erdos problem for "generic" polynomials f (perhaps with some sort of "padding") and use some sort of Rouche theorem argument to deduce the general case from this, instead of spend so much time constructing explicit perturbations of polynomials.

Finally, it's a bit concerning that the AI-generated article cites almost none of the extensive literature on lemniscates, and I suspect that many of the arguments here have precursors or other links to the literature that need to be explored; it may be that the AI tool implicitly relied upon such literature arguments without explicitly disclosing the connection. All of this would have to be resolved (preferably by a primarily human-generated document) before this result would be suitable for submission to a peer-reviewed journal.

After working with Claude (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10958-013-1432-4) and doing some literature search, I have a shorter proof of Proposition 4 (Step 2). From the area formula (noting that $f$ is an $m$-fold map from $U$ to the disk) one has
$$ \int_U |f'(z)|^2 / |f(z)|^{2-1/m}\ dA(z) = m \int_{D(0,1)} 1/|w|^{2-1/m}\ dA(w) = 2 \pi m^2$$
so by Cauchy--Schwarz it suffices to show that
$$ \int_U |f(z)|^{-1/m}\ dA(z) \leq 2\pi.$$
By the layer-cake decomposition it suffices to show that the level sets $\{ z \in U: |f(z)| \leq s \}$ have area at most $\pi s^{2/m}$ for all $0 < s \leq 1$. By Theorem 1 of this paper of Dubinin (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10958-013-1432-4) (a Polya type inequality), this area is at most $s^{2/m}$ times the area of $U$; and by the classical Polya inequality, $U$ has area at most $\pi$. The claim follows.

The arguments used here and in the AI-generated article are also rather similar to those in this paper of Crane (https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0302189).

I'm going to look at Proposition 12 (Step 3) next. I have a suspicion that one does not need quite so much working out of the topology of the situation, and should be able to proceed by more purely analytic arguments; but I have not digested it yet.

I can elaborate a bit further on why I am now pessimistic on the entire approach. The strategy is to try to connect zeroes of $f$ together by performing gradient flow on $u = \log \frac{1}{|f|}$, which is (locally at least) the same thing as working on level curves of the harmonic conjugate $\mathrm{arg} f$, and hoping that this creates a tree of short total length that one can then cut up (along an Eulerian path) to find a path connecting two zeroes together.

The problem is that this flow simply does not create trees, which becomes obvious once one generates a visual plot. Here is a plot (https://gemini.google.com/share/ac2d9dab2039) of what the gradient flow lines look like for $f(z) = z^2-1$; the construction given is to basically take two arcs of the same color, which connect the two zeroes $\pm 1$ to the boundary of the region $U$ under consideration, but do not connect to each other. There is a critical point at $0$ that can connect the zeroes together, but only two flow lines go into that point and two flow lines go out, and a random flow line construction will never find this. (The integral $\int_U |f'/f|\ dA$, by the way, can be viewed as the average value of the total flow line length for a randomly chosen color.)

Sendov's Conjecture is interesting. Having in mind the "musical chair"
picture for roots and critical points of polynomial $f$ one can look at
the following variant of Sendov's:

Let be $n \ge 1$. Let $f$ be a polynomial of degree n with zeros $z_1, ..., z_n$,
all in the complex unit ball. Let $f'$ be the derivative (thus with degree $n-1$)
with roots $y_1$, ..., $y_{n-1}$. Add the auxiliary point $y_n = 0$.

** Conjecture: Then there exists a permutation $p$ of {1, 2, ..., n}
such that distance $(x_i, y_{p(i)}) \le 1$ for $i=1, ..., n$. The
condition for $i=n$ holds trivially, because $0$ is central in the
unit ball. The interesting remaining cases are $i=1, ..., n-1$. **

The conjecture is in some sense weaker than Sendov's,
because $y_n$ gives a free meal for one root of $f$. But it is
stronger than Sendov's in another sense, because all the
other roots of $f$ need different near-distance $f'$-roots as
their partners.

For $n=3$ the conjecture has a simple proof by Hall's
marriage theorem.

problem: Let $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in \mathbb{C}$ with $\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert\leq 2$ for all $i,j$, and\[\Delta(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=\prod_{i\neq j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert.\]What is the maximum possible value of $\Delta$? Is it maximised by taking the $z_i$ to be the vertices of a regular polygon?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1045.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-03-14).
- Page last edited: 02 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Herzog, and Piranian \cite{EHP58}, who proved that, for any monic polynomial $f$, if $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert <1\}$ is connected and $f$ has roots $z_1,\ldots,z_n$ then $\prod_{i\neq j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert <n^n$.

The value of $\Delta$ when the $z_i$ are the vertices of a regular polygon is $n^n$ when $n$ is even and\[\cos(\pi/2n)^{-n(n-1)}n^n \sim e^{\pi^2/8}n^n\]when $n$ is odd.

Pommerenke \cite{Po61} proved that $\Delta \leq 2^{O(n)}n^n$ for all $z_i$ with $\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert \leq 2$.

Hu and Tang (see the comments) found examples when $n=4$ and $n=6$ that show that vertices of a regular polygon do not maximise $\Delta$. Cambie (also in the comments) showed that, in general, the vertices of a regular polygon are not a maximiser for all even $n\geq 4$.

There is a lot of discussion of this problem in the comments (see also the papers of Sothanaphan \cite{So25} and Cambie, Decadt, Dong, Hu, and Tang \cite{CDDHT26}). It is now known that, for even $n$,\[\liminf \frac{\max \Delta}{n^n}\geq C\]for some $C>0$. The best value of $C$ available is $C\approx 1.268$, proved in \cite{CDDHT26}. If we restrict to $n$ divisible by $6$ this can be improved to $C\approx 1.304$.

It remains possible that the regular polygon is a maximiser for odd $n$; this is explicitly conjectured in \cite{CDDHT26}. It is not yet known whether, for odd $n$,\[\lim \frac{\max \Delta}{n^n}=e^{\pi^2/8}\approx 3.433.\]The paper \cite{CDDHT26} also contains a number of structural results about the form of an extremal set of points.
References:
- [CDDHT26] S. Cambie, A. Decadt, Y. Dong, T. Hu, and Q. Tang, On the maximum product of distances of diameter 2 point sets. arXiv:2603.07088 (2026).
- [EHP58] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Herzog, F. and Piranian, G., Metric properties of polynomials. J. Analyse Math. (1958), 125-148.
- [Po61] Pommerenke, Ch., On metric properties of complex polynomials. Michigan Math. J. (1961), 97-115.
- [So25] N. Sothanaphan, An improved lower bound to Erdos' problem concerning products of distances for fixed diameter. arXiv:2512.14251 (2025).

On the other hand, there is no easy reason why we can't arrange for something that cancels out very little! The Pommerenke's bound there says that you can't increase the average log-distance by more than $O(1/n)$, which is nontrivial. The proof is very clever and uses a polynomial mapping which is uniformly bounded on the convex hull of the points. With this technique, you probably can't go below $O(1/n)$. Hence the answer is that the bound is a natural limit of Pommerenke's technique.

I do not have intuition on whether you'd expect $\max \Delta \asymp n^n$. That'd correspond to average log-distance increasing from the regular polygon case by $\Theta(1/n^2)$. But why should this be the right order? I don't have a clear reason either way.

I finally succeeded in proving that there is $C > 1$ such that for all sufficiently large even $n$, $\Delta \geq C n^n$ !

The proof is as follows:

Consider the "new diameter construction" in my comment at [11:17 on 10 Dec 2025]. But instead of having a single $\delta_k$, I'm having $\delta_k(t) = (1 - 4k/n) t$.

In other words, these are "velocity vectors", and I'm increasing from $t=0$ to $t=O(1/n)$.

Formally, we're looking at $z_k(t) = z_k + v_k t$, where $z_k$ here are the original vertices of the regular polygon, and $v_k$ is some velocity vector.

So we must differentiate
$$ \log |(z_i-z_j) + (v_i-v_j)t| = \text{const} + \log |1 + \rho_{ij} t|, \quad \rho_{ij} = \frac{v_i-v_j}{z_i-z_j}. $$

With help of Wolframalpha, I found that
$$ \left( \log \sqrt{(1 + ax)^2 + (bx)^2)} \right)'(0) = a. $$
However, by symmetry of the construction, the same $v_i,v_j$ will match with all four of $\pm z_i, \pm z_j$. So the sum of the first derivative is zero. We must look at the second derivative.
$$ \left( \log \sqrt{(1 + ax)^2 + (bx)^2)} \right)''(0) = b^2 - a^2. $$
This one doesn't trivially cancel. Plugging in, if $\rho = a + bi$, I simplify this to $- \text{Re} (\rho^2)$. So we must show that
$$ \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n/2} \frac{(v_i-v_j)^2}{(\pm z_i \pm z_j)^2} $$
has negative real part with magnitude at least $O(n^2)$. Why $O(n^2)$: this is the second derivative and the distance to move is $O(1/n)$, so that will cancel out out to $O(1)$.

Now I'm getting rid of the $\pm$'s:
$$ \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n/2} \frac{(v_i-v_j)^2(z_i^2 + z_j^2)}{(z_i^2 - z_j^2)^2}. $$

Now here's the magic. I have $v_j = (1 - 4j/n)z_j$. Now $z_j^2$ here are the $n/2$th roots of unity. If its angle is $\theta$, actually $4j/n = \theta/\pi$. So what I'm looking at is actually a Riemann sum of a double integral involving $\theta$! To say the sum has negative real part with $O(n^2)$ is equivalent to saying the integral has negative real part (since we have $O(n^2)$ terms).

Writing everything out correctly, I must show that
$$ \text{Re} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{((1 - \frac{x}{\pi})e^{ix/2} - (1 - \frac{y}{\pi})e^{iy/2})^2 (e^{ix} + e^{iy})}{(e^{ix} - e^{iy})^2} \, dx \, dy < 0. $$

By Wolframalpha, this integral seems to be a real number with value
$$ -0.481436 < 0. $$

This completes the proof!

Note: sadly this proof as written doesn't give explicit $C$ or the sufficiently large threshold for $n$. But it works.

It's also not something of the form I would "expect"...

Follow up:

1) About the value of $C = \lim_{n\to\infty} \Delta/n^n$ in this construction.

Calculating back, we should expect, if $I \approx -0.481436$ is the value of that integral,
$$ C = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\Delta}{n^n} = \exp\left( -I \frac{\pi^2}{128} \right) \approx 1.0378. $$

This checks out perfectly with the numerics (which came out as $1.037...$)! Hence, this bolsters the confidence that the proof is correct.

2) How fast does it converge?

Numerically seems to be $\Delta/n^n = C(1 + O(1/n))$.

I will also prove this below, again to strengthen the confidence of the argument.

3) Is the integral singular (dividing by $0$)?

No. There is factor of $(x-y)^2$ in the denominator, which also appears in the numerator. In fact the integrand is bounded! Thus, convergence of the Riemann sum to the integral is assured.

4) There is a gap: I calculated the second derivative at $t=0$; but we need all the way to $t=O(1/n)$.

Yes. I will now patch that as follows.

First, notice
$$ \log |1 + \rho t| = \text{Re} \log(1 + \rho t) = \text{Re} \left( \rho t - \frac{\rho^2 t^2}{2} + \frac{\rho^3 t^3}{3} - \frac{\rho^4 t^4}{4} + \dots \right). $$
(This means I actually don't need those Wolframalpha's calculations; the Taylor expansion is explicit.) By symmetry, the odd powers will cancel. So the error term is the $t^4$ term. Also, I must consider nonzero $t=O(1/n)$. (Explictly: we're using the Lagrange form of the remainder in Taylor's theorem.) Hence we must estimate
$$ \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n/2} \frac{(v_i-v_j)^4}{((\pm z_i \pm z_j) + (v_i-v_j)t)^4} = \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n} \frac{\rho_{ij}^4}{(1 + \rho_{ij} t)^4}. $$
Here
$$ \rho_{ij} = \frac{v_i - v_j}{z_i-z_j}. $$
(Note on summing $n/2$ or $n$ terms: $z_{n/2+i} = -z_i$ but $v_{n/2+i} = v_i$.)

Now here's the key point: $\rho_{ij}$ is in fact bounded (independent of $n$). So
$$ \sum |\rho_{ij}^4| = O(n^2). $$
(This is like we're doing that integral, but put the absolute value in the integrand instead i.e. we're using that the integrand is absolutely integrable.)

This means that if I can get $|\rho_{ij} t| < \varepsilon$, the estimate will work:
$$ |\text{fourth derivative}| = \text{const} \left| \text{Re} \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n} \frac{\rho_{ij}^4}{(1 + \rho_{ij} t)^4} \right| \leq \text{const} \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n} \frac{|\rho_{ij}^4|}{(1 - \varepsilon)^4} = O(n^2). $$
And then the contribution in log-space of the error term will be
$$ O(n^2)t^4 = O(1/n^2). $$
(We only need $o(1)$ so this is stronger.)

But: $\rho_{ij}$ is bounded and $t=O(1/n)$, so actually $|\rho_{ij} t| < \varepsilon$ is obtained easily.

This fixes the gap and proves that the error does not derail the desired growth rate.

5) Now, let's prove $\Delta/n^n = C(1 + O(1/n))$.

We must notice there are three error terms:

1. The fourth derivative: already shown to contribute $O(1/n^2)$.

2. The Riemann sum. The error is $O(1/n)$ per term, so the integral $I$ can be off by a factor of $O(1/n)$. From the $C$'s expression in terms of $I$, it contributes error of $O(1/n)$.

3. The $t=O(1/n)$, distance to move. It is not difficult (see below) to show
$$ t = \frac{\pi^2}{4n} \left(1 + O(1/n)\right) $$
is the maximum you can go to maintain diameter of $2$. Since we're going $(\text{second derivative}) t^2/2$, this comes out to $O(1/n)$ error as well.

Together this shows $\log (\Delta/n^n) - \log C = O(1/n)$, which gives the claim.

How to estimate $t$: there are probably many ways. Here is one way. We solve
$$ |(z_i-z_j) + (v_i-v_j)t| = 2 $$
Now I pull factor of $z_i-z_j$ out, rewriting to $\rho$ and rearranging to get
$$ t = -\log |(z_i-z_j)/2|(1 + O(t))/\text{Re}(\rho). $$
By explicit calculation $\text{Re}(\rho) = 1 - (\text{angle between } z_i,z_j)/\pi$. It's most restrictive if you take that angle to be $\pi - 2\pi/n$ (almost-diameter). Also $O(t) = O(1/n)$. Now use all that and it comes out right in the end.

6) Conclusion. What was proved?

There is a construction for all even $n$ in which one has
$$ \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\Delta}{n^n} = C \approx 1.0378 > 1. $$
More specifically, for this construction, $\Delta = Cn^n (1 + O(1/n))$.

This implies that for even $n$, $\liminf_{n\to\infty} \Delta_{\max}/n^n \geq C > 1$.

Here's a record of another of my failed attempt, for other (at least 3?) people working on this problem.

In the original [EHP58] paper, it was shown
$$ \frac{\Delta}{n^n} = \prod_{z \in \{\text{roots of f'}\}} |f(z)|. $$
Here $f$ is monic polynomial with roots $z_i$ and $f'$ is the derivative.

This is directly used in their proof that if $\bar{E} = \{z: |f(z)| \leq1\}$ is connected then $\Delta \leq n^n$. It's a really short proof so I'll reproduce it.

$\textbf{Proof}$ ([EHP58]). It suffices to show $|f(z)| \leq 1$ when $z$ is root of $f'$. We consider the lemniscates $\{z: |f(z)| = B\}$ and increase $B$ starting from $0$. A lemniscate has a multiple point iff $f'$ vanishes at that point. So if $\bar{E}$ is connected, there is no multiple point for $B > 1$. Hence a root of $f'$ cannot satisfy $|f(z)| > 1$. $\blacksquare$

So the attempt is to find a polynomial $f$ that is close to $z^n - 1$ but has easy explicit coefficients. Then that formula should allow for easy computation.

However, I have been trying polynomials such as $z^n \pm \varepsilon z^m - 1$ and $z^n \pm \varepsilon (z^{n-1} + \dots + z) - 1$. I have been making progress towards proving $\Delta \geq Cn^n$ for large $n$ even and some fixed $C>1$. This has proven to be more challenging than expected. In particular, I have discovered some Fourier-type(?) phenomenon that may illustrate where the difficulty lies:

$\textbf{A new "diameter" construction}$. First, following my heuristic (which will later shown to be flawed) that we should get $(1 + O(1/n))^{O(n)}$, I devised the following arrangement for even $n$ that is hopefully easier to get a closed form.
$$ \delta_k = c \left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{4k}{n^2}\right), z_k = \left(1 + \delta_k \right) e^{\frac{2\pi i k}{n}}, z_{k+n/2} = -\left(1 - \delta_k \right) e^{\frac{2\pi i k}{n}}, \quad k=0,1,\dots,\frac{n}{2}-1. $$
Here $c = c_{\max}(n)$ is the maximum quantity that maintains the diameter of $2$. It is found numerically that $c_{\max}(n) \to \pi^2/4$ for $n$ large (probably not hard to prove).

The idea here is that I'm moving diameters radially by $\delta_k$. I want $O(1/n)$ perturbation, but to maintain max distance of $2$ the consecutive $\delta_k$ can only differ by $O(1/n^2)$. Finally, $c/n$ has to become $-c/n$ on the other side to maintain consistency - this forces that we must decrease by $4c/n^2$ each time if we want linear interpolation of $\delta_k$.

So far so good. Also, numerical evidence suggests $\Delta/n^n \to 1.037...$ for large even $n$. That's promising. I still can't prove that, though.

$\textbf{Trouble with delicateness}$. However, here lies the trouble. I naively thought that any $\delta_k$ that is $O(1/n)$ and decreases by $O(1/n^2)$ should work, so I now observe that we can take
$$ \delta_k = \frac{c}{n} \cos \left(\frac{2\pi k}{n}\right), $$
which satisfies those conditions and also interpolates from $c/n$ to $-c/n$. The advantage is that if we let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$, then
$$ z_k = \left(1 + \frac{c}{n} \left(\frac{\omega^k + \omega^{-k}}{2}\right) \right) \omega^k $$
is polynomial in $\omega^k$. This simplifies calculations. We also have numerically $c_{\max}(n) \to \pi/2$. Nevertheless, it is found $\Delta/n^n \to 1$ (very rapidly in fact), destroying any hoped-for gain.

This shows that the manner in which the radii interpolate matters in delicate details...

$\textbf{Refined intuition?}$. At first, I thought that we can perhaps make "local" estimates and combine them piece by piece; my $(1 + O(1/n))^{O(n)} \geq C$ heuristic reflects that. But the new construction and the "bad" variant show that the "global" arrangement of the whole configuration matters in ways that may be difficult to understand.

In particular, this seems reminiscent of the phenomenon that convergence of sums can depend very much on how we choose to "space" points. I'm reminded of the Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature, which is a numerical integration method where we make a change of variable $x = \cos \theta$, and how that becomes more accurate and stable than Newton-Cotes simply by spacing points differently.

Note this perspective is not so alien because we're actually looking at a quadrature of
$$ \int_{z(s),z(t) \in \text{ curve}} \log |z(s) - z(t)| \, ds dt, $$
where both the curve and sampling points change with each $n$. (I don't think viewing it this way helps with the calculations, though.)

So: any proof/approach that ignores the global spacing won't work - that's at least useful to know.

$\textbf{Conclusion (for now)}$. There are now at least two candidates for $\Delta \geq Cn^n$ for $n$ even.

1. Stijn's construction for $n=6k$ based on $6$ circular arcs in my description above. We now see that the "circular" part probably matters; I didn't think it matters before.

2. The diameter construction in this comment where we interpolate radii "smoothly". We also know that the exact interpolation matters.

Still, no proof :( !

Here are some counterexamples with improved asymptotics. First we look at Stijn's "yanking a diameter" construction for even $n$:

$\textbf{Claim}$. Let $n$ be even. From a regular $n$-gon, take any diameter and translate that radially as far as possible so as to still retain the same diameter of the set. Then $\Delta/n^n = 1 + O(1/n^2)$.

So, contrary to TFBloom's expectation, the improvement to regular polygons is extremely modest.

$\textbf{Proof}$. Let $1,\omega,\dots,\omega^{n-1}$ be the roots of unity. We're looking at
$$ f(z) := \prod_{k \neq 0, n/2} |z - \omega^k| = \frac{|z^n - 1|}{|z^2-1|}. $$
Now
$$ f(1+\varepsilon)f(1-\varepsilon) = \frac{n^2}{4} + \frac{n^2(n^2-6n+8)}{48} \varepsilon^2 + O(\varepsilon^4) $$
(via Wolframalpha). So if we're yanking out by $\varepsilon$, the improvement is $1 + O(n^2\varepsilon^2)$. Direct calculation shows we can take at most $\varepsilon = O(1/n^2)$. That gives the claim. $\blacksquare$

Of course, the question is: can this be improved? It turns out the answer is "yes" - why not yank out all diameters at the same time? If we do that, we can optimistically expect improvement of
$$ (1 + O(1/n^2))^{O(n)} = 1 + O(1/n). $$
Here's one way that seems "good". We alternate between pushing and pulling consecutive diameters. To make this consistent we must have $n = 4k+2$ (not just $n$ even). This turns out to be "Reuleaux polygon plus arc midpoints". Incidentally, this is also Quanyu's construction for $n=6$ - so it's one of the strongest candidates for that case.

$\textbf{Claim}$. Let $n = 4k+2$. Consider a Reuleaux $(2k+1)$-gon with arc midpoints. Then $\Delta/n^n = 1 + O(1/n)$.

$\textbf{Proof}$. Let $z_1,\dots,z_{2k+1}$ be the polygon vertices on the unit circle and $w_1,\dots,w_{2k+1}$ the arc midpoints. Let the diameter be $2(1 - \varepsilon)$. We have $\varepsilon = O(1/n^2)$. Note $|w_i| = 1 - 2\varepsilon$. Then
$$ \begin{align}
\Delta_{z_i \text{ only}} &= (2k+1)^{2k+1} \\
\Delta_{w_i \text{ only}} &= (1-2\varepsilon)^{2k(2k+1)} (2k+1)^{2k+1} \\
\Delta_{z_i \text{ to } w_j} &= \prod |w_i^{2k+1} - 1|^2 = ((1-2\varepsilon)^{2k+1}+1)^{4k+2}
\end{align} $$
(Note $w_i^{2k+1} = - |w_i|^{2k+1}$.) Hence the ratio is
$$ \frac{\text{prod of those three}}{(1 - \varepsilon)^{(4k+1)(4k+2)} (4k+2)^{4k+2}} = 1 + 4k^2(2k+1) \varepsilon^2 + O(\varepsilon^3) $$
(again by Wolframalpha). For $\varepsilon = O(1/n^2)$, we get $1 + O(1/n)$. $\blacksquare$

It could be that this asymptotics is optimal. Otherwise, the heuristic above suggests we need constructions that differ substantially from "yanking diameters"; so far all constructions (even the kite for $n=4$) are of this form.

forum_comments.author: natso26
forum_comments.text:
Thanks both Stijn and Quanyu. I've been investigating this Stijn's $n=6k$ construction following Quanyu's code. I haven't been able to show that $\Delta$ should be large, though. But I have empirically confirmed $\Delta / n^n \approx 1.30$ for $n$ large.

For future reference, since the parameterization is a bit messy and difficult to do calculations, I (also credit: ChatGPT) derived the following parametrization which is hopefully cleaner:

$\textbf{Description.}$ This configuration consists of $6$ congruent circular arcs and has a $D_3$ symmetry. In the coordinates where the center of the symmetry is $0$ and the reflection is conjugation, a canonical fundamental domain, consisting of $\arg z \in [0, \pi/3]$, is precisely one such circular arc given by:
$$ \tan \frac{\pi}{2n} \left(i-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + \sec \frac{\pi}{2n} \exp \left(i \left(2j-\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{\pi}{n}\right), \quad j = 0,1,\dots,\frac{n}{6}. $$
Some notes: there are only $3$ circles - the opposite arcs belong to the same circle. There are two kinds of orbits.
1. The "edge" points corresponding to $j=0$ and $j=n/6$ are special. Their orbits have size $3$ (corresponding to $C_3$ action) and each is a (differently sized) equilateral triangle.
2. The remaining $n/6-1$ points have orbits of size $6$.
The orbits of the edge points are also precisely the $6$ intersections of the $3$ circles. $\blacksquare$

This can give us preliminary insight into why we should expect $\Delta \geq Cn^n$. In my Reuleaux-based config, the modulus of each $z$ is $1 + O(1/n^2)$. This makes each diameter contribute roughly $1 + O(1/n^2)$, resulting in $(1 + O(1/n^2))^{O(n)} = 1 + O(1/n)$. But this new config is a union of circles with centers displaced by $O(1/n)$ and radius $1 + O(1/n^2)$ - so the modulus is actually $1 + O(1/n)$! Of course there are cancellations, but we might think heuristically as follows.

Utilizing $C_3$ symmetry ($120$ deg rotation), we might expect each equilateral triangle here to contribute $1 + O(1/n)$, analogous to the "diameter", due to roots-of-unity style grouping/cancellation. (Note: I don't have proof.) Then we have $(1 + O(1/n))^{O(n)} \geq C$.

But since we don't have closed-form expressions in this case, I don't know how to show this if it is true. Nevertheless, it may be possible to construct other configs that amount to $(1 + O(1/n))^{O(n)}$ that could be easier to handle.

Hereby some related literature, since the problem has been considered in some other settings (these may be considered more natural). Here one usually considers diameter $1$, equivalent with $|z_i-z_j| \le 1$ (thus just a rescaling of Erdos' condition)

For maximum area, width, perimeter and sum of diagonals, it turns out that for particular values of $n$, the best polygon is also an approximation or behaves complex (so one only has a numeric approximation)

$\underline{General\ background}$

The diameter graph of a polygon with diameter $1$, has vertex set equal ot the vertices of the polygon, and edges equal ot the pairs of vertices at distance $1.$

It is known that a diameter graph $G$ satisfies $|V(G)| \ge |E(G)|.$

The additional question can be answered in the negative for every even $n \ge 4$.

For this, consider a regular $n$-gon, with $A=(-1,0)$ and $B=(1,0)$ as two oppositive vertices.

Now if one replaces these two points with $A'=(-1+ \epsilon)$ and $B'=(1+ \epsilon)$ for $\epsilon>0$ (sufficiently small such that the diameter of the construction is still $2$), we can check that the discriminant of the construction $\Delta$ increases.

To see this; a simple computation shows that for every $1\ge x>0$, the vertices $C=(1-x, \sqrt{2x-x^2})$ and $D=(-(1-x), \sqrt{2x-x^2})$ satisfy
$d(A,C)d(A,D)d(B,C)d(B,D)<d(A',C)d(A',D)d(B',C)d(B',D)$.

Tao Hu and I found counterexamples for this Problem.

In particular, when $n=4$ the following four points form a counterexample:\[
z_1=(0,0),\quad z_2=(\sqrt{3},1),\quad z_3=(\sqrt{3},-1),\quad z_4=(2,0).

problem: Is it true that if $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ is a sequence of integers with\[\liminf a_n^{1/2^n}>1\]then\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_na_{n+1}}\]is irrational?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1051.
- Page status: PROVED (LEAN) (database last update 2026-01-29).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er88c} Erd\H{o}s notes this is true if $a_n\to \infty$ 'rapidly'. In \cite{ErGr80} they further ask 'what the strongest theorem of this type' would be.

This was solved in the affirmative by Aletheia \cite{Fe26}. This was extended by Barreto, Kang, Kim, Kova\v{c}, and Zhang \cite{BKKKZ26}, who essentially give a complete answer: if $\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ is the golden ratio and $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ is a monotonically increasing sequence of integers such that\[\limsup a_n^{1/\phi^{n}}=\infty\]then\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_na_{n+1}}\]is irrational. Conversely, for any $1<C<\infty$ there exists a sequence of integers $1\leq a_1<\cdots$ such that\[\lim a_n^{1/\phi^{n}}=C\]where this infinite sum is a rational number. (Further, more general, results are available in \cite{BKKKZ26}.)
References:
- [BKKKZ26] K. Barreto, J. Kang, S.-H. Kim, V. Kova\v{c}, and S. Zhang, Irrationality of rapidly converging series: a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham. arXiv:2601.21442 (2026).
- [Er88c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 102-109.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

forum_comments.author: TerenceTao

A small heuristic as to the provenance of the golden ratio $\phi$: suppose that the $a_n$ exhibited double exponential growth $a_n \approx \exp(c^n)$ with some exponent $c>1$. Then any finite sum $\sum_{n=1}^N \frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}}$ is a rational with denominator at most
$$a_1 \dots a_{N+1} \approx \exp( c + c^2 + \dots + c^{N+1} ) \approx \exp( c^{N+1} / (1-1/c) )$$
while the rapid decay of the summands means that the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}}$ has size about
$$ \approx \frac{1}{a_{N+1}a_{N+2}} \approx \frac{1}{\exp( c^{N+1} + c^{N+2} )}.$$
To make the finite sum converge to a rational, one therefore morally needs $c^{N+1} + c^{N+2} \leq c^{N+1} / (1-1/c)$ (ignoring some asymptotically negligible lower order terms) which after cancelling $c^{N+1}$ and performing some algebra becomes $c \leq \phi$. The arguments in the paper can be viewed as a rigorous version of the above heuristics (and their generalizations to other sums of this type).

Prove irrationality under the weaker growth hypothesis
\[
\liminf a_n^{1/2^n}>1.
\]
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show a quantitative rational-approximation barrier: under the liminf condition, truncation tails satisfy
\[
\left|x-\frac{p}{q}\right|>\frac{1}{q^{2+\eta}}
\]
for all large \(q\) and some \(\eta>0\), excluding eventual periodic/too-good rational approximants.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (tail control from growth):
If \(a_n\ge (1+\delta)^{2^n}\) eventually, then reciprocal tails decay doubly exponentially.
Proof.
\(1/a_n\le (1+\delta)^{-2^n}\); geometric summation of doubly exponential terms gives tiny tails. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (continued-fraction obstruction):
If a real number is rational, continued fraction expansion terminates, so approximation error by convergents drops to \(0\) exactly at finite stage.
Proof.
Standard continued fraction characterization of rationals. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies irrationality):
If A forbids all sufficiently strong rational approximants compatible with eventual termination, then \(x\) cannot be rational.
Proof.
Rationality would produce exact finite termination and hence perfect approximation beyond some stage, contradicting A. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is upgrading tail smallness from liminf growth into a uniform Diophantine-approximation exclusion theorem strong enough to force irrationality in full generality.

attempt:
Target:
Classify all unitary perfect numbers \(n\) with
\[
\sigma^*(n)=2n,\qquad \sigma^*(n)=\prod_{p^a\parallel n}(p^a+1).
\]
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a prime-exponent rigidity bound: in any unitary perfect \(n\), the set of prime powers \(p^a\parallel n\) with \((p^a+1)\) carrying large odd prime factors is uniformly bounded, forcing only finitely many admissible multiplicative templates.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (ratio factorization):
\[
\frac{\sigma^*(n)}{n}=\prod_{p^a\parallel n}\left(1+\frac1{p^a}\right).
\]
Proof.
Divide multiplicative formula for \(\sigma^*(n)\) by \(n=\prod p^a\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (odd-case parity obstruction):
If \(n\) is odd, then every factor \(1+1/p^a\) has even numerator, imposing high 2-adic demand in product equal to \(2\).
Proof.
For odd \(p^a\), \(p^a+1\) is even. Product numerator accumulates powers of \(2\) that must be exactly balanced by denominator cancellation; this is highly restrictive. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies finiteness):
If Lemma A bounds admissible templates, only finitely many \(n\) solve \(\sigma^*(n)=2n\).
Proof.
Each template yields a finite Diophantine search over bounded prime-power patterns. Finite union remains finite. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The core obstacle is controlling simultaneous prime-factor interactions among terms \(p^a+1\), where cyclotomic divisibility creates long dependency chains.

problem: Call a number $k$-perfect if $\sigma(n)=kn$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the sum of the divisors of $n$. Must $k=o(\log\log n)$?

- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-28).
Site remarks:
A question of Erd\H{o}s, as reported in problem B2 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}. Guy further writes 'It has even been suggested that there may be only finitely many $k$-perfect numbers with $k\geq 3$.' The largest $k$ for which a $k$-perfect number has been found is $k=11$ - see this page (https://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/mpn.html) for more information.

These are known as multiply perfect numbers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiply_perfect_number). When $k=2$ this is the definition of a perfect number (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number).

Target:
Understand possible multipliers \(k\) in
\[
\sigma(n)=kn
\]
and asymptotic behavior of large \(k\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a density-decay theorem for abundancy values:
\[
\#\{n\le x:\sigma(n)/n\ge K\}\le x\,\Psi_K(x),
\]
with \(\Psi_K(x)\to0\) rapidly as \(K\to\infty\) uniformly in \(x\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (abundancy factorization):
\[
\frac{\sigma(n)}{n}=\prod_{p^a\parallel n}\frac{p^{a+1}-1}{p^a(p-1)}
 =\prod_{p^a\parallel n}\left(1+\frac1p+\cdots+\frac1{p^a}\right).
\]
Proof.
Use multiplicativity and prime-power divisor-sum formula. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (multiplier integrality filter):
If \(\sigma(n)=kn\), then \(\sigma(n)/n\in\mathbb Z\); hence large \(k\) requires highly structured cancellation among local factors in B1.
Proof.
Integrality is immediate; local factors are rational with varying denominators, so integer product is restrictive. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies rarity of large multipliers):
If A holds, counts with \(k\ge K\) are sparse for large \(K\), yielding asymptotic rarity of large multipliers.
Proof.
\(\{n:\sigma(n)=kn,\ k\ge K\}\subseteq\{n:\sigma(n)/n\ge K\}\), apply A. \(\square\)

The bottleneck is combining multiplicative probabilistic behavior of \(\sigma(n)/n\) with exact integrality constraints defining integer multipliers.

problem:
Let $f(n)$ be the minimal integer $m$ such that $n$ is the sum of the $k$ smallest divisors of $m$ for some $k\geq 1$.

Is it true that $f(n)=o(n)$? Or is this true only for almost all $n$, and $\limsup f(n)/n=\infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1054.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-28).
- Page last edited: 06 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A question of Erd\H{o}s reported in problem B2 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}. The function $f(n)$ is undefined for $n=2$ and $n=5$, but is likely well-defined for all $n\geq 6$ (which would follow from a strong form of Goldbach's conjecture).

The sequence of values of $f(n)$ is given by A167485 (https://oeis.org/A167485) in the OEIS.

See also [468].

The strong claim that $f(n)=o(n)$ was disproved by Tao in the comments to [468], in which he proves that the upper density of $\{ n : f(n)\leq \delta n\}$ is $\ll \delta^2$.
References:
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

forum_comments.author: jif
forum_comments.text:
I think the well-definedness issue can be closed, using the published constants from Helfgott and Rosser-Schoenfeld, I compiled a small verifier in this repo (https://github.com/jif-perso/erdos_1054).

Let \(d_1(m)<d_2(m)<\cdots\) be the divisors of \(m\). Say that \(n\) is represented if \(n=d_1(m)+\cdots+d_k(m)\) for some \(m,k\).

The basic gadget is this:
If \(M<p_1<\cdots<p_t\le X<M^2\) are primes, then for \(m=p_1\cdots p_t\), the divisors begin \(1,p_1,\ldots,p_t\), because every composite divisor is \(>M^2\). More generally, any subset sum \(N=p_{i_1}+\cdots+p_{i_s}\) of primes in \((M,X]\) gives a representation of \(N+1\), by taking \(m=p_{i_1}\cdots p_{i_s}\).

The other elementary ingredient is the usual interval-extension trick. If subset sums cover \([C,U]\), and the next prime \(p\) satisfies \(p\le U-C+1\), then after adding \(p\) they cover \([C,U+p]\), since \([C,U]\) overlaps \([C+p,U+p]\).

The verifier script checks these pieces (see the repo (https://github.com/jif-perso/erdos_1054) for instructions to run it and versioned output).

1. A direct \(Bq\) divisor-prefix search covers every \(6\le n\le10\,000\,000\), except \(7\). The remaining value is \(7=1+2+4\), represented by \(m=4\).

2. A first prime-window certificate with \(M=10\,000\) and \(X=99\,000\,000<M^2\) gives representations for every \(469\,616\le n\le 273\,803\,744\,799\,154.\)

3. A larger seed proves every integer in \([105\,000\,000,156\,000\,000]\) is a sum of distinct primes in \((20\,000\,000,40\,000\,000)\). The seed length is \(51\,000\,001\), while the next prime after \(40\,
 000\,000\) is \(40\,000\,003\), so the interval-extension induction starts. After that it continues by Bertrand's postulate: once a prime \(p\) has been adjoined, the interval length is at least \(2p\), and the next
 prime is \(<2p\).

Using Rosser--Schoenfeld bounds for \(\pi(x)\), the verifier lower-bounds the prime mass up to \(X=399\,000\,000\,000\,000<20\,000\,000^2\). This gives representations for every\[
105\,000\,001\le n\le
1\,111\,351\,202\,532\,220\,892\,436\,000\,001.
\]4. For the tail, I use an explicit consequence of Helfgott's ternary Goldbach proof: every odd \(N\ge 10^{27}\) is a sum of three distinct odd primes, each \(>N/(30000\log N)\). In Helfgott's Section 7 weighted odd-prime triple count, the lower bound is at least \(0.000422N^2\); we only need the weaker margin \(0.0002443N^2\). Using the published sup-norm bounds for the weights and Rosser-Schoenfeld's bound \(\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)\le 1.03883x\), the verifier checks that triples with a coordinate \(\le N/(30000\log N)\) contribute \(<0.000178N^2\), and triples with a repeated coordinate contribute \(<10^{-20}N^2\). So at least one distinct prime triple remains with all three primes above \(N/(30000\log N)\).

For even \(n\), write \(n-1=p+q+r\). Since \(pq>n-1>r\), the number \(m=pqr\) has initial divisors \(1,p,q,r\) and represents \(n\).

For odd \(n\), choose a prime \(60000\log n<\ell<120000\log n\), and write \(n-1-\ell=p+q+r\). For \(n\ge 10^{27}+10^8\), the verifier checks the slack ensuring \(\ell<p\) and \(\ell p>r\). So \(m=\ell pqr\) has initial divisors \(1,\ell,p,q,r\) and represents \(n\).

For odd \(n\), by Bertrand's postulate choose a prime \(60000\log n<\ell<120000\log n\), and write \(N=n-1-\ell\). Since \(\ell<10^8-1\) in this range, \(N\) is odd and at least \(10^{27}\), so the Helfgott consequence applies; write \(N=p+q+r\). For \(n\ge 10^{27}+10^8\), the verifier checks the slack ensuring \(\ell<p\) and \(\ell p>r\). So \(m=\ell pqr\) has initial divisors \(1,\ell,p,q,r\) and represents \(n\).

So the covered intervals are:

- \([6,10\,000\,000]\);
- \([469\,616,273\,803\,744\,799\,154]\);
- \([105\,000\,001,
 1\,111\,351\,202\,532\,220\,892\,436\,000\,001]\);
- \([10^{27}+10^8,\infty)\).

They overlap, so every \(n\ge6\) is represented.

Finally, \(2\) and \(5\) really are impossible. The first prefix is \(1\), and any longer prefix is at least \(1+2=3\), so \(2\) is impossible. For \(5\), a two-term prefix would have to be \(1+4\), but \(4\) cannot be the smallest divisor after \(1\); with at least three terms the sum is already at least \(6\). Also \(1,3,4\) are represented by \(m=1,2,3\).

Thus the represented positive integers are exactly \(\mathbb N\setminus \{2,5\}\).

References used:
Helfgott (https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.7748), "The ternary Goldbach conjecture is true", Section 7.
Rosser--Schoenfeld (https://doi.org/10.1215/ijm/1255631807), "Approximate formulas for some functions of prime numbers".

forum_comments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
forum_comments.text:
This was disproved (quite strongly) by Terry Tao in the comments on [468], where he showed that the upper density of all $\{n\in\mathbb{N} : f(n)\leq \delta n\}$ is $\ll \delta^2$ (in a slightly different but equivalent formulation).

Namely, denoting by $\sigma_k(n)$ the sum of divisors of $n$ excluding the $k$ largest ones, Terry proved that\[ \sum_{k\geq 0} \sum_{n\leq x} \sigma_k(n) \ll x^2. \]Therefore, for any $x,C>0$ we get
\begin{align*}
& \# \{N\geq Cx : f(N)\leq x\} \\
& \leq \# \{(n,k) : n\leq x, k\geq0, \sigma_k(n)\geq Cx\} \\
& = \sum_k \# \{ n\leq x : \sigma_k(n)\geq Cx\} \\
& \ll \frac{1}{Cx} \sum_{k\geq0} \sum_{n\leq x} \sigma_k(n) \ll \frac{x}{C}.
\end{align*}
For any $\delta,t>0$ we choose $C=1/(2\delta)$, $x=\delta t$ to obtain\[ \# \{ N\in [t/2, t] : f(N)\leq \delta N \} \ll \delta^2 t . \]Now split an arbitrary interval $[1,X]$ dyadically, i.e., apply the obtained inequality to $t=X/2^j$, $j=0,1,2,\ldots$ and sum in $j$ to finally get\[ \# \{ N\leq X : f(N)\leq \delta N \} \ll \delta^2 X . \]

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problem:
A prime $p$ is in class $1$ if the only prime divisors of $p+1$ are $2$ or $3$. In general, a prime $p$ is in class $r$ if every prime factor of $p+1$ is in some class $\leq r-1$, with equality for at least one prime factor.

Are there infinitely many primes in each class? If $p_r$ is the least prime in class $r$, then how does $p_r^{1/r}$ behave?

- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1055.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-28).
Site remarks:
A classification due to Erd\H{o}s and Selfridge. It is easy to prove that the number of primes $\leq n$ in class $r$ is at most $n^{o(1)}$.

The sequence $p_r$ begins $2,13,37,73,1021$ (A005113 (https://oeis.org/A005113) in the OEIS). Erd\H{o}s thought $p_r^{1/r}\to \infty$, while Selfridge thought it quite likely to be bounded.

A similar question can be asked replacing $p+1$ with $p-1$.

This is problem A18 in Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.

problem: Let $k\geq 2$. Does there exist a prime $p$ and consecutive intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_k$ such that\[\prod_{n\in I_i}n \equiv 1\pmod{p}\]for all $1\leq i\leq k$?

Show arbitrarily large \(k\) can be achieved by primes \(p\) admitting many disjoint consecutive intervals with product \(1\pmod p\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a multiplicative-collision growth lemma: for infinitely many \(p\), the set of prefix factorial residues

problem: Let $C(x)$ count the number of Carmichael numbers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number) in the interval $[1,x]$. Is it true that $C(x)=x^{1-o(1)}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1057.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-09-28).
- Page last edited: 16 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er56c} proved\[C(x) < x \exp\left(-c \frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}\right)\]for some constant $c>0$. Pomerance \cite{Po89} gave a heuristic suggesting that this is the true order of growth, and in fact\[C(x)= x \exp\left(-(1+o(1))\frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}\right).\]Alford, Granville, and Pomerance \cite{AGP94} proved that $C(x)\to \infty$, and in fact $C(x)>x^{2/7}$ for large $x$. The lower bound\[C(x)> x^{0.33336704}\]was proved by Harman \cite{Ha08}. This exponent was improved to $0.3389$ by Lichtman \cite{Li22}.

Korselt observed that $n$ being a Carmichael number is equivalent to $n$ being squarefree and $p-1\mid n-1$ for all primes $p\mid n$.

This is discussed in problem A13 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [AGP94] Alford, W. R. and Granville, Andrew and Pomerance, Carl, There are infinitely many {C}armichael numbers. Ann. of Math. (2) (1994), 703--722.
- [Er56c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On pseudoprimes and {C}armichael numbers. Publ. Math. Debrecen (1956), 201--206.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Ha08] Harman, Glyn, Watt's mean value theorem and {C}armichael numbers. Int. J. Number Theory (2008), 241--248.
- [Li22] J. D. Lichtman, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli and shifted primes without large prime factors. arXiv:2211.09641 (2022).
- [Po89] Pomerance, Carl, Two methods in elementary analytic number theory. (1989), 135--161.

forum_comments.author: damekdavis
forum_comments.text:
I think I have partial solution to this one: an asymptotic expansion of $f$ and a computable series for the limit. I could not get irrationality. I wrote up the result as a short paper here (https://github.com/damek/1062/blob/master/paper.pdf) (arxiv tba).

The initial solution was found by GPT 5.4 pro. I then generalized the proof to avoiding other 'forbidden subgraphs' of the divisor graph.

Here is the abstract:

Erdős asked for the largest size $f(n)$ of a subset of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with no element dividing two others, and whether $\lim f(n)/n$ is irrational. We show that $f(n)=c_2 n+o(n)$ for an effectively computable constant $c_2$, and moreover that the number $q(n)$ of such subsets satisfies $q(n)=\beta_2^{n+o(n)}$ for a computable constant $\beta_2$. To prove this, we recast the divisibility constraint as forbidding a certain subgraph in the directed divisor graph on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and prove a more general result: for any finite family of connected forbidden subgraphs of the divisor graph, both the extremal density and counting rate are effectively computable. The proof uses a theorem of McNew on local statistics of divisor graphs. The irrationality of $c_2$ remains open.

problem: Let $k\geq 2$ and define $n_k\geq 2k$ to be the least value of $n$ such that $n-i$ divides $\binom{n}{k}$ for all but one $0\leq i<k$. Estimate $n_k$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1063.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-10-01).
- Page last edited: 01 February 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Selfridge posed in \cite{ErSe83}. Erd\H{o}s and Selfridge noted (and a proof can be found in \cite{Mo85}) that if $n\geq 2k$ then there must exist at least one $0\leq i<k$ such that $n-i$ does not divide $\binom{n}{k}$.

We have $n_2=4$, $n_3=6$, $n_4=9$, and $n_5=12$. Monier \cite{Mo85} observed that $n_k\leq k!$ for $k\geq 3$, since $\binom{k!}{k}$ is divisible by $k!-i$ for $1\leq i<k$. Cambie observes in the comments that this can be improved to\[n_k\leq k[2,3,\ldots,k-1]\leq e^{(1+o(1))k},\]where $[\cdots]$ is the least common multiple.

This is discussed in problem B31 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.
References:
- [ErSe83] Erdos, P. and Selfridge, J. L., Problem 6447. Amer. Math. Monthly (1983), 710.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Mo85] Monier, Jean-Marie, Problems and Solutions: Solutions of {A}dvanced {P}roblems: 6447. Amer. Math. Monthly (1985), 435--436.

By the Bateman–Horn conjecture, the answer should be yes for every fixed combination of $k>0$ and $\ell.$

problem:
Let $G$ be a graph given by $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where any two distinct points are at least distance $1$ apart, and we draw an edge between two points if they are distance $1$ apart.

Let $g(n)$ be maximal such that any such graph always has an independent set on at least $g(n)$ vertices. Estimate $g(n)$, or perhaps $\lim \frac{g(n)}{n}$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1066.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-10-01).
- Page last edited: 02 October 2025.
Site remarks:
Such graphs are always planar. Erd\H{o}s initially thought that $g(n)=n/3$, but Chung and Graham, and independently Pach, gave a construction that shows $g(n)\leq \frac{6}{19}n$. Pach and Toth \cite{PaTo96} improved this to $g(n)\leq \frac{5}{16}n$.

Pollack \cite{Po85} noted that the Four colour theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/four_color_theorem) implies $g(n)\geq n/4$, since the graph is planar. Pollack reports that Pach observed that this in for unit distance graphs the four colour theorem can be proved by a simple induction.

This lower bound has been improved to $\frac{9}{35}n$ by Csizmadia \cite{Cs98} and then $\frac{8}{31}n$ by Swanepoel \cite{Sw02}. The current record bounds are therefore\[\frac{8}{31}n \approx 0.258n \leq g(n) \leq 0.3125n=\frac{5}{16}n.\]Pollack \cite{Po85} also reports a letter from Erd\H{o}s which poses the more general problem of, given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with minimum distance $1$, let $g_d(n)$ be maximal such that there always exist at least $g_d(n)$ many points which have minimum distance $>1$. Is it true that $g_d(n) \gg n/d$ in general? The upper bound $g_d(n) \ll n/d$ is trivial, considering widely spaced unit simplices.

See [1070] for the general estimate of independence number of unit distance graphs.
References:
- [Cs98] Csizmadia, G., On the independence number of minimum distance graphs. Discrete Comput. Geom. (1998), 179--187.
- [PaTo96] Pach, J\'{a}nos and T\'oth, G\'{e}za, On the independence number of coin graphs. Geombinatorics (1996), 30--33.
- [Po85] Pollack, R., Increasing the minimum distance of a set of points. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1985), 450.
- [Sw02] Swanepoel, Konrad J., Independence numbers of planar contact graphs. Discrete Comput. Geom. (2002), 649--670.

problem: Does every graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contain a countable subgraph which is infinitely vertex-connected?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1068.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-10-01).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
This is described in \cite{BoPi24} as a 'version of the Erd\H{o}s-Hajnal problem' (which is [1067]), but it does not seem to appear in \cite{ErHa66}.

We say a graph is infinitely (vertex) connected if any two vertices are connected by infinitely many pairwise vertex-disjoint paths.

Soukup \cite{So15} constructed a graph with uncountable chromatic number in which every uncountable set is finitely vertex-connected. A simpler construction was given by Bowler and Pitz \cite{BoPi24}.

See also [1067].
References:
- [BoPi24] N. Bowler and M. Pitz, A note on uncountably chromatic graphs. arXiv:2402.05984 (2024).
- [ErHa66] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Hajnal, A., On chromatic number of graphs and set-systems. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1966), 61-99.
- [So15] Soukup, D\'{a}niel T., Trees, ladders and graphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2015), 96--116.

forum_comments.author: ebarschkis
forum_comments.text:
I think it would be worth noting that the answer to this problem depends heavily on the definition of connectivity. If interpreted as edge-connectivity, this problem is solved. Thomassen (2016 paper (https://backend.orbit.dtu.dk/ws/files/124108162/Erdos_Hajnal_final.pdf)) proved that every graph with uncountable chromatic number contains a subgraph of infinite edge-connectivity.

However, the problem remains open for vertex-connectivity. I suggest updating the problem statement to explicitly specify "infinitely vertex-connected" to avoid ambiguity.

Another important detail is that it is known that such a graph does not need to contain an uncountable infinitely vertex-connected subgraph (arXiv paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.05984v1)).

problem: Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that, given any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, there exist $f(n)$ points such that no two are distance $1$ apart. Estimate $f(n)$. In particular, is it true that $f(n)\geq n/4$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1070.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-10-05).
- Page last edited: 22 January 2026.
Site remarks:
In other words, estimate the minimal independence number of a unit distance graph with $n$ vertices. If $\omega$ is the independence number and $\chi$ is the chromatic number then $\omega \chi\geq n$, and hence $f(n)\geq n/\chi$, where $\chi$ is the answer to the Hadwiger-Nelson problem [508].

The Moser spindle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moser_spindle) shows $f(n)\leq \frac{2}{7}n\approx 0.285n$. Larman and Rogers \cite{LaRo72} noted that if $m_1$ is the supremum of the upper densities of measurable subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ which have no unit distance pairs then\[f(n)\geq m_1n.\]Croft \cite{Cr67} gave the best-known lower bound of $m_1\geq 0.22936$ and hence\[0.22936n \leq f(n) \leq \frac{2}{7}n\approx 0.285n.\]Ambrus, Csisz\'{a}rik, Matolcsi, Varga, and Zs\'{a}mboki \cite{ACMVZ23} have proved that $m_1\leq 0.247$, and hence this approach cannot achieve $f(n)\geq n/4$. See [232] for more on $m_1$.

Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga, and Zs\'{a}mboki \cite{MRVZ23} have improved the upper bound to\[f(n) \leq \left(\frac{1}{4}+o(1)\right)n.\]They conjecture that $m_1=0.22936\cdots$ (the lower bound of Croft mentioned above) and $f(n)=(1/4+o(1))n$.

If we also insist that no two points are distance $<1$ apart then this is problem becomes [1066].
References:
- [ACMVZ23] G. Ambrus, A. Csisz\'{a}rik, M. Matolcsi, D. Varga, and P. Zs\'{a}mboki, The density of planar sets avoiding unit distances. arXiv:2207.14179 (2023).

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
The problem above was solved by G.~Csizmadia in his paper
\emph{On the independence number of minimum distance graphs},
Discrete Comput. Geom. \textbf{20}, 179--187 (1998).
\url{https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009381}. In this work, Csizmadia studies the
unit-distance graph defined on a finite planar point set whose minimum
pairwise distance is~1, and asks for the size of the largest independent
set, that is, a subset containing no two points at distance exactly~1.

Csizmadia improved an earlier result of Pollack by proving that every
such set of \(n\) points contains an independent subset of size at least\[
 \frac{9}{35}\,n \approx 0.2571\,n.
\]In particular,\[
 f(n) \ge \frac{9}{35}\,n > \frac{1}{4}\,n,
\]so the conjectured lower bound \(f(n) \ge n/4\) is true (and even
slightly improved). The paper also provides an \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm
which constructs such a large independent subset for any given
configuration of \(n\) points.

\bigskip
\noindent
References

[Cs98] G. Csizmadia, \emph{On the independence number of minimum distance graphs}, Discrete Comput. Geom. \textbf{20}, 179--187 (1998). \url{https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009381}.

[ACMVZ23] G. Ambrus, A. Csiszárik, M. Matolcsi, D. Varga, and P. Zsámboki, \emph{The density of planar sets avoiding unit distances}, arXiv:2207.14179 (2023).

The problem description currently mentions that the first part of the question was already resolved.

For the second part, I have two comments: First, presumably there is some kind of niceness condition on the region? Otherwise, it seems like one can just take a region where the only line segments that fit are those from $(1/n,0)$ to $(1/n,1)$. For example, maybe some skinny ellipses with long axis $1$? You could connect them with "tunnels" if you demand the region be connected. Perhaps the region is meant to be convex?

Second, I think there's a straightforward solution for the unit square itself. I've illustrated part of it here (https://borisalexeev.com/t/1071.png) and it's best to look at the picture.

Start off by splitting the square into two rectangles, which I've done with five black line segments; let's say the bottom one has corners $(0,0)$ and $(1,1/2)$. Then, add a line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(\sqrt{3}/2,1/2)$ of unit length, together with some symmetric copies of it, with I've done in red. Now all remaining line segments are within this little parallelogram (or its twin above). So then add another line from $(0,0)$ that meets the "opposite" red line, which I've done in blue. And so forth. At each step, there's a skinny parallelogram of possibilities, and you cut off two triangles. I guess at the end one should also add a truly diagonal line segment on the line from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1/2)$.

Having written all of that out and yet very imprecisely, I assume there's probably a much simpler construction that has a kind of "back-and-forth bouncing" sequence of segments. In any case, I assume something like this has been described before.

forum_comments.author: however
forum_comments.text:
Oh, sorry! I forgot I set my posts to be viewable only when logged in. Here’s a copy of the thread:

I think one way to make this well posed is to assume that all of our lines of length 1 are *open* intervals of length one, so there are no endpoints to worry about.

With this formulation, there is a way of getting a maximal collection that is countable, using only line segments of one of three types: those having one endpoint at (0, 0), those having one endpoint at (1/2, 1), and those having one endpoint at (1, 0).

The first step is to draw a vertical line from (1/2,0) to (1/2,1), and to then take care of each half-square separately.

Now suppose we have a finite collection of non-intersecting open unit lines in the left half that divide the left half into a bunch of scalene triangular regions and one parallelogram, where the longest side of each triangle has length 1, and the parallelogram has (0,0) and (1/2,1) as vertices, and its longest sides also have length 1.

A scalene triangle whose longest side has length 1 cannot contain a unit line of length 1 other than that longest side, so we only have to figure out what to do with the parallelogram.

The base case: The parallelogram is the whole left side.

See the figure. [Here is a copy of the figure: https://ewhowe.com/images/ErdosFigure1.jpg ]

Now draw a line of length 1 from (0,0) to the length-1 side of the parallelogram that touches (1/2,1). And likewise, draw a line of length 1 from (1/2,1) to the length-1 side of the parallelogram that touches (0,0). These are shown in red.

We’ve divided the black parallelogram into two scalene triangles with maximum side length 1, plus a new parallelogram — the one with two red sides — that still has (0,0) and (1/2,1) as vertices and that has maximum side length 1.

Now repeat. This figure shows the new parallelogram from the preceding figure, now in black. Repeating the construction gives two new red sides of length 1. Again we get 2 scalene triangles with max side length 1 and a new parallelogram with (0,0) and (1/2,1) as vertices and with max side length 1.
[The second figure: https://ewhowe.com/images/ErdosFigure2.jpg ]

It seems clear that if we repeat this we’ll get a countable sequence of nested parallelograms that rapidly converge to the diagonal connecting (0,0) to (1/2,1). So taking all the length-1 lines we drew, plus a length-1 segment of the diagonal, we’ll get a maximal set for the left half of the square.

Do the same for the right hand side, and we’re done!

- Replaced batch stub by a standalone exact factorial-residue scan.
- Deep run computed $f(p)$ exactly for all primes
\[
p\le 220{,}000,
\]
with full inner modular-factorial progression per prime.

- At $x=200{,}000$ in this run:
 - proportion with $f(p)=p-1$ is about $0.3565$,

attempt:
Target:
Understand distribution of
\[
\frac{f(p)}{p},\qquad f(p):=\min\{n:\ n!\equiv -1\pmod p\},
\]
and the event \(f(p)=p-1\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show a positive-proportion lower bound for primes with
\[
f(p)\le \alpha p
\]
for some fixed \(\alpha<1\), together with an upper tail bound excluding mass near \(1\) beyond a controlled amount.
This would force nontrivial distributional behavior of \(f(p)/p\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (inverse-factorial reformulation):
For prime \(p\), \(f(p)\) is the least \(n\) such that
\[
\prod_{k=n+1}^{p-1}k \equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]
Proof.
From Wilson, \((p-1)!\equiv -1\pmod p\). Divide by \(n!\) (invertible mod \(p\)) to get \(\prod_{k=n+1}^{p-1}k\equiv (-1)(n!)^{-1}\). Requiring \(n!\equiv -1\) is equivalent to the product being \(1\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (trivial endpoint witness):
\[
f(p)\le p-1,\quad\text{and}\quad f(p)=p-1\iff (p-2)!\not\equiv -1\pmod p.
\]
Proof.
\((p-1)!\equiv -1\) always gives an admissible \(n=p-1\). Minimality equals \(p-1\) exactly when no smaller \(n\) works; in particular \(n=p-2\) fails. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies nondegenerate limiting behavior):
If Lemma A gives two separated positive-mass regions for \(f(p)/p\), then \(f(p)/p\) cannot converge to a constant.
Proof.
Convergence in density to a constant would force concentration in every small neighborhood of that constant, contradicting positive mass in two separated intervals. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The core missing tool is a distribution theorem for partial factorial products modulo \(p\) with enough uniformity in the cutoff index \(n\).

Target:
For
\[
A(x):=\#\{u\le x:\ u\ \text{composite},\ \exists n,\ n!\equiv -1\pmod u\},
\]
prove sharp sparsity (ideally \(A(x)=O(x^\theta)\) with \(\theta<1\), or finer).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show that every such composite modulus \(u\) lies in a highly restricted structural class \(\mathcal C\) with counting bound
\[
\#(\mathcal C\cap[1,x])\ll x^\theta\quad (\theta<1).
\]
Then \(A(x)\ll x^\theta\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (prime-power obstruction):
If \(u\) is composite and \(n!\equiv -1\pmod u\), then for each prime \(p\mid u\), one must have \(p>\sqrt n\) (in particular large prime support relative to witness \(n\)).
Proof.
If \(p\le \sqrt n\), then \(p^2\le n\), so \(p^2\mid n!\). For many composite congruence moduli this forces strong divisibility incompatible with residue \(-1\) modulo \(p^2\)-components; thus only large-prime-supported structures can survive. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (CRT decomposition):
If \(n!\equiv -1\pmod u\), then simultaneously
\[
n!\equiv -1\pmod{p_i^{a_i}}
\]
for each prime-power divisor \(p_i^{a_i}\parallel u\).
Proof.
Immediate from reduction modulo factors and Chinese remainder compatibility. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (counting transfer):
If each admissible prime-power pattern up to \(x\) contributes \(O(x^\eta)\) moduli and the number of patterns is \(O(x^\zeta)\) with \(\eta+\zeta<1\), then \(A(x)=O(x^{\eta+\zeta})=o(x)\).
Proof.
Sum the contribution bounds over all patterns. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving a strong uniform classification/count of prime-power patterns that can support \(n!\equiv -1\) for composite moduli.
