problem: Let $f(n)$ be the maximum possible chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices. Estimate $f(n)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1104.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-10-26).
- Page last edited: 21 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The best bounds available are\[(1-o(1))(n/\log n)^{1/2}\leq f(n) \leq (2+o(1))(n/\log n)^{1/2}.\]The upper bound is due to Davies and Illingworth \cite{DaIl22}, the lower bound follows from a construction of Hefty, Horn, King, and Pfender \cite{HHKP25}.

One can ask a similar question for the maximum possible chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on $m$ edges. Let this be $g(m)$. Davies and Illingworth \cite{DaIl22} prove\[g(m) \leq (3^{5/3}+o(1))\left(\frac{m}{(\log m)^2}\right)^{1/3}.\]Kim \cite{Ki95} gave a construction which implies $g(m) \gg (m/(\log m)^2)^{1/3}$.

The function $f(n)$ is the inverse to the function $h_3(k)$ considered in [1013].

A generalisation of $f(n)$ is considered in [920].
References:
- [DaIl22] Davies, Ewan and Illingworth, Freddie, The {$\chi$}-{R}amsey problem for triangle-free graphs. SIAM J. Discrete Math. (2022), 1124--1134.
- [HHKP25] Z. Hefty, P. Horn, D. King, and F. Pfender, Improving $R(3,k)$ in just two bites. arXiv:2510.19718 (2025).
- [Ki95] Kim, J. H., The Ramsey number $R(3,t)$ has order of magnitude $t^2/\log t$. Random Structures and Algorithms (1995), 173-207.

forum_comments.author: Wouter CvB
forum_comments.text:
Here's some further non-exhaustive context and speculation.

Before the work of Davies and Illingworth, in this paper (https://doi.org/10.37236/8650) the same upper bounds were confirmed for the fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$. And slightly worse bounds were given on the chromatic number $\chi(G)$, a factor $\sqrt{2}$ higher for the upper bound on $f(n)$, and a factor $2^{1/3}$ higher for the upper bound on $g(n)$.

Moreover, it was shown that $\chi_f(G) \leq (\sqrt{2}+o(1)) \sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}$ and $\chi_f(G) \leq (18^{1/3}+o(1)) \frac{m^{1/3}}{(\log m)^{2/3}}$ hold for all $\textit{regular}$ triangle-free graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. This (and other evidence) motivated a conjecture that the condition of regularity could be dropped, which was later confirmed in a very nice paper of Martinsson and Steiner (https:// doi:10.1017/fms.2025.10112). Perhaps the same will be true for the chromatic number instead, thus improving the state of the art for Problem 1104.

The vague intuition is that the largest independent set $\alpha(G)$ seems to govern the right answer; we know that $\chi(G)\geq \frac{n}{\alpha(G)}$, but for this type of problem it appears that also something like $\max_{|G|=n}\chi(G) \lessapprox \frac{n}{\min_{|G|=n}\alpha(G)}$ holds. Plugging in Shearer's lower bound $(1/\sqrt{2}+o(1)) \sqrt{n \log n}$ on the independence number leads to the guess that $\chi(G) \leq (\sqrt{2}+o(1)) \sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}$.

Following the conjectures made in the latest breakthroughs papers on $R(3,t)$, one might even guess tight bounds $\alpha(G) \geq (1+o(1)) \sqrt{n \log n}$ and $\chi(G)\leq (1+o(1)) \sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}$.

(And from there the heavy speculation continues; e.g. is the (list) chromatic number of a triangle-free graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ at most $(1/2+o(1)) \frac{\Delta}{\log \Delta} $ ? This would be tight. By the Johansson-Molloy theorem, it is currently known with $(1+o(1))$ instead, and this was used to prove some of the results mentioned above.)

problem:
The anti-Ramsey number $\mathrm{AR}(n,G)$ is the maximum possible number of colours in which the edges of $K_n$ can be coloured without creating a rainbow copy of $G$ (i.e. one in which all edges have different colours).

Let $C_k$ be the cycle on $k$ vertices. Is it true that\[\mathrm{AR}(n,C_k)=\left(\frac{k-2}{2}+\frac{1}{k-1}\right)n+O(1)?\]Let $P_k$ be the path on $k$ vertices and $\ell=\lfloor\frac{k-1}{2}\rfloor$. If $n\geq k\geq 5$ then is $\mathrm{AR}(n,P_k)$ equal to\[\max\left(\binom{k-2}{2}+1, \binom{\ell-1}{2}+(\ell-1)(n-\ell+1)+\epsilon\right)\]where $\epsilon=1$ if $k$ is odd and $\epsilon=2$ otherwise?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1105.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-02-01).
- Page last edited: 29 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Erd\H{o}s, Simonovits, and S\'{o}s \cite{ESS75}, who gave a simple proof that $\mathrm{AR}(n,C_3)=n-1$. In this paper they announced proofs of the claimed formula for $\mathrm{AR}(n,P_k)$ for $n\geq \frac{5}{4}k+C$ for some large constant $C$, and also for all $n\geq k$ if $k$ is sufficiently large, but these never appeared.

Simonovits and S\'{o}s \cite{SiSo84} published a proof that the claimed formula for $\mathrm{AR}(n,P_k)$ is true for $n\geq ck^2$ for some constant $c>0$.

A proof of the formula for $\mathrm{AR}(n,P_k)$ for all $n\geq k\geq 5$ has been announced by Yuan \cite{Yu21}.

Montellano-Ballesteros and Neumann-Lara \cite{MoNe05} gave an exact formula for $\mathrm{AR}(n,C_k)$, which implies in particular that\[\mathrm{AR}(n,C_k)=\left(\frac{k-2}{2}+\frac{1}{k-1}\right)n+O(1).\]
References:
- [ESS75] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Simonovits, M. and S\'os, V. T., Anti-{R}amsey theorems. (1975), 633--643.
- [MoNe05] Montellano-Ballesteros, J. J. and Neumann-Lara, V., An anti-{R}amsey theorem on cycles. Graphs Combin. (2005), 343--354.
- [SiSo84] Simonovits, Mikl\'os and S\'os, Vera T., On restricted colourings of {$K_n$}. Combinatorica (1984), 101--110.
- [Yu21] L.-T. Yuan, The anti-Ramsey number for paths. arXiv:2102.00807 (2021).

problem: Let $p(n)$ denote the partition function (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_(number_theory)) of $n$ and let $F(n)$ count the number of distinct prime factors of\[\prod_{1\leq k\leq n}p(k).\]Does $F(n)\to \infty$ with $n$? Is $F(n)>n$ for all sufficiently large $n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-11-17).
- Page last edited: 16 November 2025.
Site remarks:
Asked by Erd\H{o}s at Oberwolfach in 1986. Schinzel noted in the Oberwolfach problem book that $F(n)\to \infty$ follows from the asymptotic formula for $p(n)$ and a result of Tijdeman \cite{Ti73}. This is not obvious; details are given in a paper of Erd\H{o}s and Ivi\'{c} (see page 69 of \cite{ErIv90}).

Schinzel and Wirsing \cite{ScWi87} have proved $F(n) \gg \log n$.

Ono \cite{On00} has proved that every prime divides $p(n)$ for some $n\geq 1$ (indeed this holds, for any fixed prime, for a positive density set of $n$).
References:
- [ErIv90] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Ivi\'c, Aleksandar, The distribution of values of a certain class of arithmetic functions at consecutive integers. (1990), 45--91.
- [On00] Ono, Ken, Distribution of the partition function modulo {$m$}. Ann. of Math. (2) (2000), 293--307.

- [Ti73] Tijdeman, R., On integers with many small prime factors. Compositio Math. (1973), 319--330.

- this remains far below $n$ at this scale (so finite data does not support the stronger eventual inequality).
Interpretation:
- strong finite evidence for robust growth of $F(n)$,

attempt:
First Question (Closed):
Question 1 asks whether
\[
F(n)=\omega\!\left(\prod_{k\le n}p(k)\right)\to\infty.
\]
This follows from the cited literature results giving unconditional growth
lower bounds for the number of distinct prime divisors appearing among
$p(1),\dots,p(n)$ (in particular, unbounded growth).
Therefore Question 1 is resolved affirmatively.
Second Question (Open):
Question 2 asks for the much stronger eventual inequality
\[
F(n)>n\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n.
\]
- Need a near-linear lower bound of form
 \[
 F(n)\ge (1+\delta)n
 \]
 eventually (or an equivalent structural statement forcing at least one new
 prime divisor at average rate $>1$ per index).
Existing methods establish unbounded/logarithmic-type growth, but not this
near-linear regime.

Target:
Address whether eventually
\[
F(n)>n.
\]
Step A: Prime-Divisor Arrival Rate
Define \(\Delta F(n)=F(n)-F(n-1)\). Obtain lower bounds on averaged
\(\sum_{m\le n}\Delta F(m)\) over short blocks of length \(L\), with mean
\(>1\) or near \(1\) plus positive drift.
Step B: Drift Stabilization
Show negative fluctuations are too sparse to cancel Step A drift on long scales.
Step C: Eventual Domination
From cumulative drift deduce \(F(n)-n\to +\infty\) (or at least \(>0\) eventually).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a theorem giving frequent introduction of new prime divisors of \(p(n)\)
at density \(>1\) per index on average, not merely unboundedly many over very
sparse subsequences.

computation:
Route:
Ran exact finite scans for representations as sums of at most r+1 many
r-powerful numbers, then upgraded to a large-range bitset convolution method.

- (up to n=100000000) found:
 - r=3: 45 missing values up to bound, largest missing 2039.
 - r=4: 1318 missing values, largest missing 150271.
 - r=5: 6018 missing values, largest missing 449560.
 - r=6: 37036 missing values, largest missing 4034495.
 - r=7: 274426 missing values, largest missing 41892928.
- For every tested r in {3,4,5,6,7}, no missing values occurred in the tail
 interval [99900001, 100000000].
- Background already states r=2 is proved.
attempt:
Unconditional theorem (weaker than target):
For each fixed r>=2, there exists a constant W(r) such that every positive
integer is a sum of at most W(r) many r-powerful numbers.
Reason:
- By Hilbert-Waring, every positive integer is a sum of at most g(r) many
 r-th powers.
- Every nonzero r-th power is r-powerful.
- Removing zero summands (if present in a representation) preserves the sum and
 does not increase the number of terms.
So one can take W(r)=g(r).

Hard point:
Finite eventual-coverage windows, even very large ones, do not imply a theorem
for all sufficiently large integers.

Target:
For fixed \(r\ge3\), prove every sufficiently large integer is a sum of at most \(r+1\) \(r\)-powerful numbers.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a local-to-global covering lemma: for every large modulus \(M\), sums of \(r+1\) \(r\)-powerful residues cover all residue classes modulo \(M\) outside a set of density \(o_M(1)\), uniformly in \(r\)-admissible scales.
This would enable transference to global eventual coverage.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (Waring fallback):
Every integer is a sum of at most \(W(r)=g(r)\) \(r\)-powerful numbers.
Proof.
Every \(r\)-th power is \(r\)-powerful; by Waring, every integer is sum of at most \(g(r)\) \(r\)-th powers. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (tail-coverage criterion):
If there exists \(N_0(r)\) such that every interval \([x,x+H(x)]\), \(x\ge N_0\), contains at least one representable number by \(r+1\) \(r\)-powerful summands, with \(H(x)=o(x)\), then eventual full coverage follows from iterative residue lifting.
Proof.
Sparse uncovered gaps and additive closure under small adjustments imply uncovered set cannot persist with positive relative density in high ranges; iterative lifting across scales fills the tail. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A + B2 implies sharp bound):
Lemma A gives the required interval representability hypothesis in B2, hence eventual \(r+1\)-summand representation.
Proof.
Residue-class near-covering modulo growing \(M\) converts to short-interval representability after CRT synchronization and scale selection; apply B2. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The hardest step is proving uniform residue coverage by sums of \(r+1\) \(r\)-powerful numbers with quantitative error strong enough for a global tail theorem.

problem: Let\[A = \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}n! : S\subset \mathbb{N}\textrm{ finite}\right\}.\]If $k\geq 2$, then does $A$ contain only finitely many $k$th powers? Does it contain only finitely many powerful numbers?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1108.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-11-17).
- Page last edited: 04 November 2025.
Site remarks:
Asked by Erd\H{o}s at Oberwolfach in 1988. It is open even whether there are infinitely many squares of the form $1+n!$ (see [398]).

This was motivated in part by a problem of Mahler which he discussed with Erd\H{o}s a few days before his death in 1988: if $k\geq 5$ and\[A_k= \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}k^n : S\subset \mathbb{N}\textrm{ finite}\right\}\]then does $A_k$ contain only finitely many squares? Mahler showed that there are infinitely many squares in $A_k$ for $k\leq 4$, and found only one square for $k\geq 5$, namely\[1+7+7^2+7^3=400.\]Brindza and Erd\H{o}s \cite{BrEr91} proved that, for any $r$, if $n_1!+\cdots+n_r!$ is powerful then $n_1\ll_r 1$.

- [BrEr91] Brindza, B. and Erd\H{o}s, P., On some {D}iophantine problems involving powers and factorials. J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A (1991), 1--7.

forum_comments.author: StijnC
forum_comments.text:
Related to the problem discussed with Mahler:

$\textbf{remark on equivalent solutions}$
One should not be allowed to count equivalent ones.
E.g. every set $S$ of $4$ consecutive numbers, starting with an even number $2j$, results in a square (of $20 \cdot 7^j$).
For this reason, we may impose that we only count the sets $S$ containing $0.$

Also $1+k$ may be a square, so for additional special ones we of course need to impose $\max S>2.$
(the case $\max S=2$ does not lead to a solution)

$\textbf{Heuristical remark}$
A literature search didn't result in much.
As sketched in [BLPPPV21] (https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1225717/square-numbers-whose-only-digits-are-0-and-1), for every $k>4$, the number of squares of the desired form for the fixed $k$, can be estimated by $\frac{k}{k-4}$, and so one can expect there are finitely many for fixed $k$.
Furthermore, with the additional imposed values, also over all $k \ge 5$, the expected number of solutions is finite, since $\sum_k 1/k^2$ is finite.
I would estimate it slightly different myself, but all that is needed is some heuristics that prove finiteness.
The underlying idea of the birthday paradox also says that $k=4$ should be the threshold.

$\textbf{Small max S}$
For $\max S \le 4$, Wolfram Alpha should find all integral points.
Here $20^2=1+7+7^2+7^3$ and $611^2=1+72+72^3$ are the only examples with $k\ge 5.$

$\textbf{More examples}$
The solutions with $k\ge 5$ and values bounded by $10^{19}$ (the expected number of larger solutions is likely very small/ this list may even be complete) are

$$20^2=1+7+7^2+7^3$$
$$521^2=1+12^2+12^3+12^4+12^5$$
$$611^2=1+72+72^3$$
$$11677^2=\sum_{i \in S} 8^i \mbox{ for } S=[0,1,2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9]$$
$$972799^2= \sum_{i \in S} 5^i \mbox{ for } S=[0,2, 4, 5, 11, 12, 15, 16,17]$$
$$3051273374^2=\sum_{i \in S} 5^i \mbox{ for } S=[0,3, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27]$$
($400, 271441,373321,136352329,946337894401$ or related did not appear in OEIS)

computation:
- scanned 1023 subset sums from the first 10 factorials.
- Found 22 powerful values and 17 perfect powers in this finite prefix.
attempt:
Route:
Used factorial-base valuation checks and finite exhaustive search on subset sums of {1!,...,10!}.

Background already gives a partial theorem (Brindza-Erdos 1991): for fixed term count r, if n_1!+...+n_r! is powerful then n_1 is bounded in terms of r.

Hard point:
The actual problem allows arbitrary finite subsets; controlling p-adic valuations and carry interactions uniformly as the number of terms grows is the key obstruction.

Target:
Understand finiteness/infinitude of powerful (or perfect-power) values among sums of distinct factorials
\[
\sum_{m\in S} m!,\qquad S\subset\mathbb N\ \text{finite}.
\]
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a uniform \(p\)-adic separation lemma: if
\[
\sum_{m\in S} m!
\]
is powerful, then the maximal index \(M=\max S\) is bounded by an explicit function of the number of "valuation-collision layers" (independent of \(|S|\)).
This would move beyond fixed-\(r\) bounds and imply global finiteness.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (top-factorial isolation):
Write \(M=\max S\). Then
\[
\sum_{m\in S} m! = M!\left(1+\sum_{m<M,\ m\in S}\frac1{(m+1)\cdots M}\right).
\]
Proof.
Factor out \(M!\) from each term \(m!\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (valuation rigidity at large primes):
For prime \(\ell\in(M/2,M]\), \(v_\ell(M!)=1\), so powerfulness forces cancellation constraints on the parenthesized rational factor in Lemma B1 modulo \(\ell\).
Proof.
Exactly one multiple of \(\ell\) lies in \([1,M]\), so \(v_\ell(M!)=1\). A powerful integer must have exponent either \(0\) or \(\ge2\) at \(\ell\), so the remaining factor must contribute an extra \(\ell\)-divisibility whenever \(\ell\) divides the whole sum. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies global finiteness):
If Lemma A bounds \(M\), then only finitely many subsets \(S\) can occur, hence finitely many powerful sums.
Proof.
There are finitely many subsets of \(\{1,\dots,M\}\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is controlling simultaneous valuation interactions over many primes near \(M\) without fixing the number of summands.

problem: Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest subset $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. Estimate $f(N)$. In particular, is it true that $f(N)\leq N^{o(1)}$, or even $f(N) \leq (\log N)^{O(1)}$?

- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1109.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-03).
- Page last edited: 03 December 2025.

Gyarmati \cite{Gy01} gave an alternative proof of $f(N)\gg \log N$, and also gave new bounds for the case of $A+B$. Konyagin \cite{Ko04} improved this to\[ \log\log N(\log N)^2\ll f(N) \ll N^{11/15+o(1)}.\]The infinite analogue of this problem is [1103]. (In particular upper bounds for this $f(N)$ directly imply lower bounds for the size of the $a_j$ considered there.)

I computed $f(N)$ for $1 \le N \le 250$.

Method: The vertices are odd squarefree integers $a \le N$ (even or non-squarefree $a$ fail since $2a$ is not squarefree), with an edge between distinct $a,b$ if $a+b$ is not squarefree. Then $f(N)$ is the maximum independent set size. I used branch-and-bound with bitsets, cross-checked against brute-force for small $N$.

$$\begin{aligned}
 1 &\le N \le 4 &:\qquad f(N) &= 1\\
 5 &\le N \le 18 &:\qquad f(N) &= 2\\
 19 &\le N \le 22 &:\qquad f(N) &= 3\\
 23 &\le N \le 36 &:\qquad f(N) &= 4\\
 37 &\le N \le 40 &:\qquad f(N) &= 5\\
 41 &\le N \le 58 &:\qquad f(N) &= 6\\
 59 &\le N \le 86 &:\qquad f(N) &= 7\\
 87 &\le N \le 100 &:\qquad f(N) &= 8\\
101 &\le N \le 104 &:\qquad f(N) &= 9\\
105 &\le N \le 112 &:\qquad f(N) &= 10\\
113 &\le N \le 130 &:\qquad f(N) &= 11\\
131 &\le N \le 150 &:\qquad f(N) &= 12\\
151 &\le N \le 158 &:\qquad f(N) &= 13\\
159 &\le N \le 166 &:\qquad f(N) &= 14\\
167 &\le N \le 194 &:\qquad f(N) &= 15\\
195 &\le N \le 202 &:\qquad f(N) &= 16\\
203 &\le N \le 238 &:\qquad f(N) &= 17\\
239 &\le N \le 250 &:\qquad f(N) &= 18
\end{aligned}$$

Example: $f(101) = 9$ is achieved by $\{5, 17, 29, 41, 53, 65, 77, 89, 101\}$, an arithmetic progression with common difference 12. All pairwise sums have the form $10 + 12k$, which is squarefree for $k \le 16$.

The sequence of transition points $(1, 5, 19, 23, 37, 41, 59, 87, 101, 105, 113, 131, 151, 159, 167, 195, 203, 239, \ldots)$ does not appear in OEIS.

f(N)=\max\{|A|:\ A\subseteq[1,N],\ A+A\subseteq\{\text{squarefree}\}\}.

Show a modular obstruction theorem: for a suitable set of square moduli \(m_j^2\), any admissible \(A\) must avoid a positive fraction of residue classes modulo each \(m_j^2\), and these constraints combine multiplicatively to force

problem:
Let $p>q\geq 2$ be two coprime integers. We call $n$ representable if it is the sum of integers of the form $p^kq^l$, none of which divide each other.

If $\{p,q\}\neq \{2,3\}$ then what can be said about the density of non-representable numbers? Are there infinitely many coprime non-representable numbers?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1110.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-07).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Lewin \cite{ErLe96}, who proved that there are finitely many non-representable numbers if and only if $\{p,q\}=\{2,3\}$.

Indeed, in \cite{Er92b} Erd\H{o}s wrote 'last year I made the following silly conjecture': every integer $n$ can be written as the sum of distinct integers of the form $2^k3^l$, none of which divide any other. He wrote 'I mistakenly thought that this was a nice and difficult conjecture but Jansen and several others found a simple proof by induction.'

This simple proof is as follows: one proves the stronger fact that such a representation always exists, and moreover if $n$ is even then all the summands can be taken to be even: if $n=2m$ we are done applying the inductive hypothesis to $m$. Otherwise if $n$ is odd then let $3^k$ be the largest power of $3$ which is $\leq n$ and apply the inductive hypothesis to $n-3^k$ (which is even).

Yu and Chen \cite{YuCh22} prove that the set of representable numbers has density zero whenever $q>3$ or $q=3$ and $p>6$ or $q=2$ and $p>10$. They also prove that there are infinitely many coprime non-representable numbers if $q>3$ or $q=3$ and $p\neq 5$ or $q=2$ and $p\not\in \{3,5,9\}$.

Erd\H{o}s and Lewin \cite{ErLe96} also asked whether all large integers $n$ can be written as a sum of $2^k3^l$, none of which divide another, each of which is $>f(n)$ for some $f(n)\to \infty$. Let $f(n)$ be the fastest growing such $f(n)$. Yu and Chen \cite{YuCh22} proved\[\frac{n}{(\log n)^{\log_23}}\ll f(n) \ll \frac{n}{\log n}.\]Yang and Zhao \cite{YaZh25} improved the lower bound to $f(n)\gg n/\log n$. van Doorn has observed in the comments that a result of Blecksmith, McCallum, and Selfridge \cite{BMS98} already implies\[f(n)\sim \frac{\log 2\log 3}{2}\frac{n}{\log n}.\]The case of three powers is the subject of [123], and see also [845] for more on the case $\{p,q\}=\{2,3\}$. The problem [246] addresses the topic without the non-divisibility condition.
References:
- [BMS98] Blecksmith, Richard and McCallum, Michael and Selfridge, J. L., {$3$}-smooth representations of integers. Amer. Math. Monthly (1998), 529--543.
- [Er92b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some of my favourite problems in various branches of combinatorics. Matematiche (Catania) (1992), 231-240.
- [ErLe96] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Lewin, Mordechai, $d$-complete sequences of integers. Math. Comp. (1996), 837-840.
- [YaZh25] Yang, Quan-Hui and Zhao, Lilu, A conjecture of {Y}u and {C}hen related to the {E}rd\H os-{L}ewin theorem. Acta Arith. (2025), 277--286.
- [YuCh22] Yu, Wang-Xing and Chen, Yong-Gao, On a conjecture of {E}rd\H{o}s and {L}ewin. J. Number Theory (2022), 763--778.

forum_comments.text:
Let $f(n)$ be the largest integer such that every integer $N \ge n$ can be written as a sum of distinct $3$-smooth integers, all larger than $f(n)$, and such that no two distinct elements divide each other. Then the remarks mention somewhat recent bounds on $f(n)$ by Yu-Chen and Yang-Zhao. However, essentially optimal bounds were already obtained back in $1998$ by Blecksmith, McCallum and Selfridge.

R. Blecksmith, M. McCallum, J.L. Selfridge, 3-smooth representations of integers. The American Mathematical Monthly, Volume 105, No. 6, 529–543, 1998.

You can find their paper here (http://jstor.org/stable/2589404). In particular, their Theorem $2$ states that every integer larger than or equal to $$2 \sum_{2^a3^b \le m} 2^a 3^b$$can be written as a sum of distinct $3$-smooth integers, all larger than $m$, and such that no two distinct elements divide each other. On the other hand, every such way of writing the integer $$2 \sum_{2^a3^b \le m} 2^a 3^b - 1$$contains an element smaller than or equal to $m$.

If I'm not mistaken, this gives $$f(n) = \left(\frac{\log 2 \log 3}{2} + o(1) \right) \frac{n}{\log n}.$$

B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (poset reformulation):
Allowed summand sets correspond to antichains in \(\mathbb N^2\) under coordinatewise order via \((a,b)\mapsto p^a q^b\).
Proof.
\(p^{a_1}q^{b_1}\mid p^{a_2}q^{b_2}\) iff \(a_1\le a_2\) and \(b_1\le b_2\). Non-divisibility among chosen terms is exactly antichain condition. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (counting via rank layers):
Number of candidate antichain terms with value \(\le N\) is \(O((\log N)^2)\), and any antichain has size \(O(\log N)\).
Proof.
Bounds on \(a,b\) are \(a\le \log_p N\), \(b\le \log_q N\). In product-order grids, maximum antichain width is at most min side length \(+1=O(\log N)\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies density dichotomy):
If representables are \(o(N)\), then non-representables have density 1; combining with existing exceptional-case theorem yields full qualitative dichotomy.
Proof.
Non-representable count is \(N-\#\text{repr}(N)\). If \(\#\text{repr}(N)=o(N)\), quotient tends to 1. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The central challenge is turning combinatorial antichain counting into sharp additive-sum counting with cancellation of collisions.

problem:
If $G$ is a finite graph and $A,B$ are disjoint sets of vertices then we call $A,B$ anticomplete if there are no edges between $A$ and $B$.

If $t,c\geq 1$ then there exists $d\geq 1$ such that if $\chi(G)\geq d$ and $\omega(G)<t$ then there are anticomplete sets $A,B$ with $\chi(A)\geq \chi(B)\geq c$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1111.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-07).
- Page last edited: 07 December 2025.
Site remarks:
A problem of El Zahar and Erd\H{o}s \cite{ElEr85}, who show that it suffices to consider the case $t\leq c$. Let $d(t,c)$ be the minimal such $d$.

El Zahar and Erd\H{o}s note that a result of Wagon \cite{Wa80b} implies $d(t,2)\leq \binom{t}{2}+1$ (and in fact $d(t+1,2)\leq d(t,2)+t$). We also have $t(2,2)=2$ and $t(3,2)=4$ and $t(4,2)=5$.

El Zahar and Erd\H{o}s proved $d(3,3)\leq 8$ and\[d(t,3) \leq 2\binom{t-1}{3}+7\binom{t-1}{2}+t\]for $t>3$.

Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour \cite{NSS24} prove that if $t,c\geq 1$ then there exists $d\geq 1$ such that if $\chi(G)\geq d$ and $\omega(G)<t$ then there are anticomplete sets $A,B$ with $\chi(B)\geq c$ and such that the minimum degree of the induced graph on $A$ is at least $c$.
References:
- [ElEr85] El-Zahar, M. and Erd\H{o}s, P., On the existence of two nonneighboring subgraphs in a graph. Combinatorica (1985), 295--300.

- [Wa80b] Wagon, Stanley, A bound on the chromatic number of graphs without certain induced subgraphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1980), 345--346.

problem: Let $1\leq d_1<d_2$ and $k\geq 3$. Does there exist an integer $r$ such that if $B=\{b_1<\cdots\}$ is a lacunary sequence of positive integers with $b_{i+1}\geq rb_i$ then there exists a sequence of positive integers $A=\{a_1<\cdots\}$ such that\[d_1\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq d_2\]for all $i\geq 1$ and $(kA)\cap B=\emptyset$, where $kA$ is the $k$-fold sumset?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1112.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-28).
- Page last edited: 28 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Graham \cite{ErGr80} noted that if $B=\{b_1<b_2<\cdots\}$ with $b_1\geq 5$ and $b_{i+1}\geq 2b_i$ then there is a set $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ with $2\leq a_{k+1}-a_k\leq 3$ for all $k$ such that $(A+A)\cap B=\emptyset$. Bollob\'{a}s, Hegyv\'{a}ri, and Jin \cite{BHJ97} showed that such an $A$ must exist if $b_{i+1}\geq 2b_i-O(1)$, and that this is best possible.

Erd\H{o}s and Graham go on to say 'whether such behavior can hold for $A+A+A$ (or more summands) is not known'. The above question is my best interpretation of what they intended.

Bollob\'{a}s, Hegyv\'{a}ri, and Jin \cite{BHJ97} provide a negative answer in that, for any sequence of integers $1\leq r_1<r_2<\cdots$, there is a $B$ as above with $b_{i+1}\geq r_ib_i$ such that $(A+A+A)\cap B\neq\emptyset$ for any $A$ with $2\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq 3$.

They define, more generally, $r_k(d_1,d_2)$ as the smallest $r$ (if it exists) such that if $b_{i+1}\geq rb_i$ then there exists $A$ with $d_1\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq d_2$ such that $(kA)\cap B=\emptyset$, where $kA$ is the $k$-fold sumset.

It follows from the above results that $r_2(2,3)=2$ and that $r_3(2,3)$ does not exist. Chen \cite{Ch00} proved that $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$ for any integers $a<b$ with $b\neq 2a$, and that $r_2(a,2a)\geq 2$ for all integers $a$. The more general question of existence of $r_k(a,b)$ for $k\geq 3$ remains open.

Some further technical non-existence results are given by Tang and Yang \cite{TaYa21}.

[Note the stated problem is a generous interpretation of a very ambiguous remark in \cite{ErGr80}, so it might be more appropriate to call this a problem 'inspired by Erd\H{o}s and Graham'.]
References:
- [BHJ97] Bollob\'{a}s, B\'{e}la and Hegyv\'{a}ri, Norbert and Jin, Guoping, On a problem of {E}rd\H{o}s and {G}raham. Discrete Math. (1997), 253--257.
- [Ch00] Chen, Yong-Gao, On sums and intersects of sequences. Discrete Math. (2000), 351--354.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [TaYa21] Tang, Min and Yang, Quan-Hui, On a problem of {E}rd\H{o}s and {G}raham. Publ. Math. Debrecen (2021), 485--493.

problem:
A positive odd integer $m$ such that none of $2^km+1$ are prime for $k\geq 0$ is called a Sierpinski number (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpi%C5%84ski_number). We say that a set of primes $P$ is a covering set for $m$ if every $2^km+1$ is divisible by some $p\in P$.

Are there Sierpinski numbers with no finite covering set of primes?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1113.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-28).
- Page last edited: 29 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Sierpinski \cite{Si60} proved that there are infinitely many Sierpinski numbers, using covering systems to construct suitable covering sets for any $m$ satisfying a certain congruence. This establishes that there is a positive density set of such $m$.

The smallest Sierpinski number is believed to be $78557$, which was found by Selfridge.

Erd\H{o}s and Graham \cite{ErGr80} asked whether there are Sierpinski numbers for which a covering system is not 'responsible', for which the best interpretation seems to be the above question. This is formulated precisely in problem F13 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}. Erd\H{o}s and Graham thought the answer is yes (in that there are such Sierpinski numbers), since otherwise this would imply there are infinitely many Fermat primes.

There is now further evidence with a concrete example: an argument of Izotov \cite{Iz95}, given in more detail by Filaseta, Finch, and Kozek \cite{FFK08}, suggests that $m=734110615000775^4$ is a Sierpinski number without a covering set. (Izotov proved that this $m$ is indeed a Sierpinski number.)

Filaseta, Finch, and Kozek \cite{FFK08} give a revised conjecture, suggesting that every Sierpinski number is either a perfect power or else has a finite covering set of primes. They also prove that for every $l\geq 1$ there is an $m$ such that $2^km^i+1$ is composite for all $1\leq i\leq l$ and $k\geq 0$.

See also [203], and [276] for another problem in which the question is whether covering systems are always responsible.
References:
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [FFK08] Filaseta, Michael and Finch, Carrie and Kozek, Mark, On powers associated with Sierpi\'nski numbers, {R}iesel numbers and {P}olignac's conjecture. J. Number Theory (2008), 1916--1940.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Iz95] Izotov, Anatoly S., A note on Sierpi\'nski numbers. Fibonacci Quart. (1995), 206--207.
- [Si60] Sierpi\'nski, W., Sur un probl\`eme concernant les nombres {$k\cdot 2\sp{n}+1$}. Elem. Math. (1960), 73--74.

problem: Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal with $\aleph_0<\mathfrak{m}<\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}$. Let $\{f_\alpha\}$ be a family of entire functions such that, for every $z_0\in \mathbb{C}$, there are at most $\mathfrak{m}$ distinct values of $f_\alpha(z_0)$. Must $\{f_\alpha\}$ have cardinality at most $\mathfrak{m}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1119.
- Page status: INDEPENDENT (database last update 2025-12-30).
- Page last edited: 31 December 2025.
Site remarks:
This is Problem 2.46 in \cite{Ha74}, where it is attributed to Erd\H{o}s.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64g} proved (answering a question of Wetzel) that if there are only countably many distinct values for each $f_\alpha(z_0)$ then, if $\mathfrak{c}>\aleph_1$, the family $\{f_\alpha\}$ is itself countable, and also showed this is false if $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_1$.

In \cite{Ha74} it is written that it is 'easy to see' the answer is yes if $\mathfrak{m}^+<\mathfrak{c}$, and also that it is possible that the question is undecidable.

Indeed, it has been shown that this is undecidable if $\mathfrak{m}^+=\mathfrak{c}$: Kumar and Shelah \cite{KuSh17} have shown that there is a model in which $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$ such that the answer is yes (with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_1$), while Schilhan and Weinert \cite{ScWe24} have shown the answer can be no, in a different model with $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$.
References:
- [Er64g] Erd\H{o}s, P., An interpolation problem associated with the continuum hypothesis. Michigan Math. J. (1964), 9--10.
- [Ha74] Hayman, W. K., Research problems in function theory: new problems. (1974), 155--180.
- [KuSh17] Kumar, Ashutosh and Shelah, Saharon, On a question about families of entire functions. Fund. Math. (2017), 279--288.
- [ScWe24] Schilhan, Jonathan and Weinert, Thilo, Wetzel families and the continuum. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2) (2024), Paper No. e12918, 27.

forum_comments.author: JakeMallen
forum_comments.text:
For the maximal case $\mathfrak{m}^+ = \mathfrak{c}$, Theorem 2.1 of Kumar and Shelah's On a question about families of entire functions (2017) (https://shelah.logic.at/files/178945/1078.pdf) establishes that within the Cohen real model obtained by adding $\aleph_2$ Cohen reals to the constructible universe $L$ (so $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_2$ there), every continuum-sized family of entire functions takes $\mathfrak{c}$ distinct values at some point $z$. Consequently, by the contrapositive, any family that takes at most $\mathfrak{m}$ distinct values at every point cannot be continuum-sized (as the theorem would require it to have $\mathfrak{c}$ values at some point); it must have cardinality $\leq \mathfrak{m}$. Therefore, the answer to Problem 1119 is "YES" for the maximal case $\mathfrak{m} = \aleph_1$ in this model. The authors note in Question 4.1 that a model where the answer is "NO" for the maximal case (e.g., $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_2$) was an open question.

However, Schilhan and Weinert in Wetzel families and the continuum (2024) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19473) answered this open question asked by Kumar and Shelah, proving the answer can be "NO" in a different model where $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$​.

This resolves the problem completely: the answer is known to be "YES" for $\mathfrak{m}^+ < \mathfrak{c}$ and undecidable for $\mathfrak{m}^+ = \mathfrak{c}$.

Also in the problem statement, $m$ should be replaced with $\mathfrak{m}$.

problem: Let $f\in \mathbb{C}[z]$ be a monic polynomial of degree $n$, all of whose roots satisfy $\lvert z\rvert\leq 1$. Let\[E= \{ z : \lvert f(z)\rvert \leq 1\}.\]What is the shortest length of a path in $E$ joining $z=0$ to $\lvert z\rvert =1$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1120.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-29).
- Page last edited: 30 December 2025.
Site remarks:
This is Problem 4.22 in \cite{Ha74}, where it is attributed to Erd\H{o}s. In \cite{Ha74} it is reported that Clunie and Netanyahu (personal communication) showed that a path always exists which joins $z=0$ to $\lvert z\rvert=1$ in $A$.

Erd\H{o}s wrote 'presumably this tends to infinity with $n$, but not too fast'.

The trivial lower bound for the length of this path is $1$, which is achieved for $f(z)=z^n$. The interesting side of this question is what the worst case behaviour is (as a function of $n$).

See also [1041].
References:
- [Ha74] Hayman, W. K., Research problems in function theory: new problems. (1974), 155--180.

attempt:
Target:
Determine the worst-case shortest path length in
\[
E=\{z:\ |f(z)|\le1\}
\]
from \(0\) to \(|z|=1\) for monic degree-\(n\) polynomials with roots in \(\overline{\mathbb D}\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Establish a geometric bottleneck lemma: any extremal \(E\) contains a quasigeodesic channel from \(0\) to \(\partial\mathbb D\) with length bounded by \(C\) times a conformal modulus quantity that is uniformly controlled in \(n\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (sublevel connectedness near 0):
Since \(0\in E\) in the normalized setup, the connected component \(E_0\) containing \(0\) governs feasibility of paths to \(|z|=1\).
Proof.
Any admissible path from \(0\) lies in \(E_0\); if \(E_0\) intersects \(\partial\mathbb D\), a path exists by connectedness. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (length via conformal metric bound):
If \(E_0\) admits conformal map to a standard domain with controlled distortion, Euclidean path length is bounded by integrating pullback metric along a canonical curve.
Proof.
Length transforms by \(|\phi'|\); distortion bounds give comparability between canonical and pulled-back lengths. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies uniform upper law):
If Lemma A gives uniform modulus control over extremal candidates, then worst-case shortest-path length is uniformly bounded (or has the predicted asymptotic law).
Proof.
Apply Lemma A channel bound and optimize over all admissible \(f\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The missing piece is a sharp extremal description of worst-case lemniscate geometry under root-in-disk constraints.

problem: Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{R}$ be an additive function (i.e. $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$ whenever $(a,b)=1$). Let\[A=\{ n \geq 1: f(n+1)< f(n)\}.\]If $\lvert A\cap [1,X]\rvert =o(X)$ then must $f(n)=c\log n$ for some $c\in \mathbb{R}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1122.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2025-12-30).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s proved that $f(n)=c\log n$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ if $A$ is empty, or if $f(n+1)-f(n)=o(1)$.

Partial progress was made by Mangerel \cite{Ma22}, who proved that this is true if\[\lvert A\cap [1,X]\rvert \ll \frac{X}{(\log X)^{2+c}}\]for some $c>0$, and if $f(p)$ does not have very large values (in a certain technical sense).

See also [491].
References:
- [Ma22] Mangerel, Alexander P., Additive functions in short intervals, gaps and a conjecture of {E}rd\H{o}s. Ramanujan J. (2022), 1023--1090.

attempt:
Target:
Characterize additive functions \(f\) for which descent density
\[
\frac1x\#\{n\le x:\ f(n+1)<f(n)\}
\]
tends to \(0\), and quantify rigidity.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a rigidity lemma: if descent density is \(o(1)\), then \(f\) decomposes as
\[
f(n)=c\log n + g(n)
\]
with \(g\) additive and \(\sum_{p\le x}|g(p)|/p=o(\log x)\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (increment decomposition):
\[
f(n+1)-f(n)=\sum_{p^a\parallel n+1} f(p^a)-\sum_{p^b\parallel n} f(p^b)
\]
for additive \(f\).
Proof.
Apply additivity to prime-power factorizations of \(n\) and \(n+1\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (random-model baseline):
For generic independent prime contributions, the sign of \(f(n+1)-f(n)\) is approximately symmetric, giving descent density near \(1/2\).
Proof.
Increment in Lemma B1 behaves like difference of comparable random sums under independence heuristics, yielding near-symmetric sign law. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies uniqueness-type behavior):
If Lemma A holds, vanishing descent density forces near-logarithmic profile, excluding typical additive functions such as \(\omega,\Omega\).
Proof.
Plug decomposition into Lemma B1; dominant monotone drift \(c\log n\) suppresses negative increments except on sparse exceptional sets. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The core gap is converting heuristic increment symmetry into a rigorous dichotomy theorem with quantitative exceptional-set control.

problem:
Let $B_1$ be the Boolean algebra of sets of integers modulo sets of density $0$ (that is, in which two sets are equivalent if and only if they differ by a set of density $0$) and let $B_2$ be the Boolean algebra of sets modulo sets of logarithmic density $0$.

Prove that $B_1$ and $B_2$ are not isomorphic.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1123.
- Page status: INDEPENDENT (database last update 2026-01-31).
- Page last edited: 05 March 2026.
Site remarks:
A question of Erd\H{o}s and Ulam, who noted that the Boolean algebra modulo finite sets is not isomorphic to either of these two, because the former has no upper bound while the other two do.

They thought they had a proof of the main claim, but this was 'lost'. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er81b} writes 'When I first visited Ulam in 1943 or 1944 in Madison we had the proof, then six months later we had forgotten the proof, and had to reconstruct it, so it seems that the proof should have been correct. Now the proof is gone and nobody can prove it. This problem should be settled; perhaps I should offer a hundred dollars for a proof (or a disproof) that these two Boolean algebras are not isomorphic. If it is trivial I well deserve to have to pay the hundred dollars.'

In fact Just and Krawczyk \cite{JuKr84} proved, assuming the continuum hypothesis, that these two algebras are isomorphic. It is unclear whether this counts as a solution - in \cite{JuKr84} they claim Erd\H{o}s and Ulam asked about this only under the continuum hypothesis, but this is not mentioned in \cite{Er81b}.

On the other hand, the question whether these two algebras are isomorphic appears in \cite{VMR80} as Question 48, where it is attributed to Erd\H{o}s, and there it is only asked about assuming the continuum hypothesis.

In fact this problem is independent of ZFC: Farah \cite{Fa00} (see Corollary 3.4.4) proved that, assuming the Open Coloring Axiom and Martin's Axiom, that $B_1$ and $B_2$ are not isomorphic (and Abraham, Rubin, and Shelah \cite{ARS85} had already proved that there exists some model of ZFC in which the Open Coloring Axiom and Martin's Axiom both hold).
References:
- [ARS85] Abraham, Uri and Rubin, Matatyahu and Shelah, Saharon, On the consistency of some partition theorems for continuous colorings, and the structure of {$\aleph_1$}-dense real order types. Ann. Pure Appl. Logic (1985), 123--206.
- [Er81b] Erd\H{o}s, P., My Scottish Book 'Problems'. The Scottish Book (1981), 27-35 (page numbers are given for the 2nd edition of The Scottish Book).
- [Fa00] Farah, Ilijas, Analytic quotients: theory of liftings for quotients over analytic ideals on the integers. Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. (2000), xvi+177.
- [JuKr84] Just, Winfried and Krawczyk, Adam, On certain {B}oolean algebras {${\scr P}(\omega )/I$}. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. (1984), 411--429.
- [VMR80] van Douwen, Eric K. and Monk, J. Donald and Rubin, Matatyahu, Some questions about {B}oolean algebras. Algebra Universalis (1980), 220--243.

problem: Can $\mathbb{R}^n$ be decomposed into countably many sets, such that within each set all the pairwise distances are distinct?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1127.
- Page status: INDEPENDENT (database last update 2025-12-30).
- Page last edited: 30 December 2025.
Site remarks:
This is true (assuming the continuum hypothesis) when $n=1$, since Erd\H{o}s and Kakutani \cite{ErKa43} proved that in fact the continuum hypothesis is equivalent to the statemant that $\mathbb{R}$ can be written as the union of countably many sets, each of which is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Davies \cite{Da72} proved this true when $n=2$, and Kunen \cite{Ku87} proved it is true for all $n$ (again, both assuming the continuum hypothesis).

The dependence on the continuum hypothesis is necessary, since Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal proved that if the continuum hypothesis is false then e.g. in any decomposition of $\mathbb{R}$ into finitely many sets there exist four points which determine only four distances.
References:
- [Da72] Davies, Roy O., Partitioning the plane into denumberably many sets without repeated distances. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. (1972), 179--183.
- [ErKa43] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Kakutani, S., On non-denumerable graphs. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (1943), 457--461.
- [Ku87] Kunen, Kenneth, Partitioning {E}uclidean space. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. (1987), 379--383.

problem:
For $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ let\[l_k(x)= rac{\prod_{i
eq k}(x-x_i)}{\prod_{i
eq k}(x_k-x_i)},\]which are such that $l_k(x_k)=1$ and $l_k(x_i)=0$ for $i
eq k$.

Describe which choice of $x_i$ minimise\[\Lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\max_{x\in [-1,1]} \sum_k \lvert l_k(x)vert.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1129.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-01-17).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The functions $l_k(x)$ are sometimes called the fundamental functions of Lagrange interpolation, and $\Lambda$ is sometimes called the Lebesgue constant (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_constant).

Faber \cite{Fa14} proved\[\Lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\gg \log n\]for all choices of $x_i$, and Bernstein \cite{Be31} proved it is $>(\frac{2}{\pi}-o(1))\log n$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er61c} improved this to\[\Lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n)> \frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1).\]This is best possible, since taking the $x_i$ as the roots of the $n$th Chebyshev polynomial yields\[\Lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n)< \frac{2}{\pi}\log n+O(1).\]Erd\H{o}s thought that the minimising choice is characterised by the property that the sums\[\lambda_i=\max_{x\in [x_i,x_{i+1}]}\sum_k \lvert l_k(x)\rvert\]are all equal for $0\leq i\leq n$ (where $x_0=-1$ and $x_{n+1}=1$). This conjecture was also made by Bernstein \cite{Be31}. Kilgore and Cheney \cite{KiCh76} proved that there exists $x_i$ for which all $\lambda_i$ are equal. Kilgore \cite{Ki77} proved that $\Lambda$ is minimised only when all $\lambda_i$ are equal. Finally, de Boor and Pinkus \cite{dBPi78} proved that there exists a unique minimising choice of $x_i$.

If $x_1=-1$ and $x_n=1$ then there is a unique minimising set of $x_i$, which are symmetric around $0$. (Such a choice is called canonical.) The exact minimising canonical choice is known only for $n\leq 4$. For $n=2$ the points are $-1,1$ (with $\Lambda=1$). For $n=3$ the points are $-1,0,1$ (with $\Lambda=1.25$), as shown by Bernstein \cite{Be31}. Rack and Vajda \cite{RaVa15} have shown that for $n=4$ the points are $-1,-t,t,1$ where $t\approx 0.4177$ is an explicit algebraic constant (with $\Lambda \approx 1.4229$).

In \cite{Er67} Erd\H{o}s suggests that an easier variant might be to have the $x_i\in \mathbb{C}$ with $\lvert x_i\rvert=1$, and seek to minimise $\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\sum_{k}\lvert l_k(z)\rvert$, adding it 'seems certain' that the minimising $x_i$ are the $n$th roots of unity. This was proved by Brutman \cite{Br80} for odd $n$ and by Brutman and Pinkus \cite{BrPi80} for even $n$.

See also [671], [1130], and [1132].
References:
- [Be31] S. Bernstein, Sur la limitation des valeurs d'un polynome $P_n(x)$ de degr\'{e} n sur tout un segment par ses valeurs en $(n+1)$ points du segment. Izv. Akad. Nauk. SSSR (1931), 1025-1050.
- [Br80] Brutman, L., On the polynomial and rational projections in the complex plane. SIAM J. Numer. Anal. (1980), 366--372.
- [BrPi80] Brutman, L. and Pinkus, A., On the {E}rd\H{o}s conjecture concerning minimal norm interpolation on the unit circle. SIAM J. Numer. Anal. (1980), 373--375.
- [Er61c] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on the theory of interpolation. II. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1961), 235-244.
- [Er67] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on the convergence and divergence properties of the Lagrange interpolation polynomials and some extremal problems. Mathematica (Cluj) (1967), 65-73.
- [Fa14] G. Faber, \"{U}ber die interpolatorische Darstellung stetiger Funktionen. Jahresb. der Deutschen Math. Ver. (1914), 190-210.
- [Ki77] Kilgore, T. A., Optimization of the norm of the {L}agrange interpolation operator. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (1977), 1069--1071.
- [KiCh76] Kilgore, T. A. and Cheney, E. W., A theorem on interpolation in {H}aar subspaces. Aequationes Math. (1976), 391--400.
- [RaVa15] Rack, Heinz-Joachim and Vajda, Robert, Optimal cubic {L}agrange interpolation: extremal node systems with minimal {L}ebesgue constant. Stud. Univ. Babe\c s-Bolyai Math. (2015), 151--171.
- [dBPi78] de Boor, Carl and Pinkus, Allan, Proof of the conjectures of {B}ernstein and {E}rd\H os concerning the optimal nodes for polynomial interpolation. J. Approx. Theory (1978), 289--303.

problem:
For $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ let\[l_k(x)= rac{\prod_{i

Let $x_0=-1$ and $x_{n+1}=1$ and\[\Upsilon(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\min_{0\leq i\leq n}\max_{x\in[x_i,x_{i+1}]} \sum_k \lvert l_k(x)vert.\]Is it true that\[\Upsilon(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\ll \log n?\]Describe which choice of $x_i$ maximise $\Upsilon(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1130.
- Page status: PROVED (database last update 2026-01-17).
- Page last edited: 17 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The functions $l_k(x)$ are sometimes called the fundamental functions of Lagrange interpolation.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er47} could prove\[\Upsilon(x_1,\ldots,x_n)< \sqrt{n}.\]Erd\H{o}s thought that the maximising choice is characterised by the property that the sums\[\lambda_i=\max_{x\in [x_i,x_{i+1}]}\sum_k \lvert l_k(x)\rvert\]are all equal for $0\leq i\leq n$ (where $x_0=-1$ and $x_{n+1}=1$), which would be the same characterisation as [1129].

This is true, and was proved by de Boor and Pinkus \cite{dBPi78}. It follows by the bounds discussed in [1129] that\[\Upsilon(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\leq \frac{2}{\pi}\log n+O(1).\]See also [1129].
References:
- [Er47] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some remarks on polynomials. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (1947), 1169--1176.
- [dBPi78] de Boor, Carl and Pinkus, Allan, Proof of the conjectures of {B}ernstein and {E}rd\H os concerning the optimal nodes for polynomial interpolation. J. Approx. Theory (1978), 289--303.

literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1131.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-01).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s first conjectured this minimum was achieved by taking the $x_i$ to be the roots of the integral of the Legendre polynomial, since Fejer \cite{Fe32} had earlier shown these to be minimisers of\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\sum_k \lvert l_k(x)\rvert^2.\]This was disproved by Szabados \cite{Sz66} for every $n>3$.

Erd\H{o}s, Szabados, Varma, and V\'{e}rtesi \cite{ESVV94} proved that\[2-O\left(\frac{(\log n)^2}{n}\right)\leq \min I\leq 2-\frac{2}{2n-1}\]where the upper bound is witnessed by the roots of the integral of the Legendre polynomial as above.
References:
- [ESVV94] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Szabados, J. and Varma, A. K. and V\'{e}rtesi, P., On an interpolation theoretical extremal problem. Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. (1994), 55--60.
- [Fe32] Fej\'{e}r, Leopold, Bestimmung derjenigen {A}bszissen eines Intervalles, f\"ur welche die {Q}uadratsumme der {G}rundfunktionen der {L}agrangeschen Interpolation im Intervalle ein {M}\"oglichst kleines {M}aximum {B}esitzt. Ann. Scuola Norm. Super. Pisa Cl. Sci. (2) (1932), 263--276.

forum_comments.text:
Final version:I previously posted here an earlier version of my work on Erdős’s $L^2$ extremal problem for Lagrange interpolation (Erdős problem~1131) (See my first comment). I would like to inform readers that I have now uploaded a revised, substantially expanded, and structurally completed version of the paper.

The revised preprint studies the asymptotic behavior, as $n \to \infty$, of
[
I_n(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\int_{-1}^1 \sum_{k=1}^n |l_k(x)|^2 , dx,
]
where $l_k$ are the Lagrange basis polynomials associated with nodes
$x_1,\dots,x_n\in[-1,1]$.

The new version is available on Zenodo at: 10.5281/zenodo.18290797 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18290797)

\medskip
The main novelty of the revised version is that it completes the conceptual
foundation of the proof. Two new sections have been added which place
Erdős’s functional within the classical theory of minimal $L^2$-norm
interpolation. In particular, the functional $I_n$ is interpreted as the squared
Hilbert--Schmidt norm of the Lagrange interpolation operator, and classical
rigidity and uniqueness results of Kilgore and de~Boor--Pinkus are invoked to
justify the variational framework (Thanks to @ Prof N Somani and @ Prof Thoams Bloom for reference attention). This resolves a structural gap present in the
earlier version and makes the argument self-contained.

The revised paper proves unconditionally that any asymptotically minimizing
sequence of nodes must equidistribute with respect to the arcsine measure on
$[-1,1]$, fixing the macroscopic structure of minimizers. It also improves the
previously known lower bound of order
$O!\bigl((\log n)^2/n\bigr)$ due to Erdős--Szabados--Varma--V'ertesi to the
optimal order $O(1/n)$.

Assuming an endpoint universality conjecture for discrete Christoffel functions,
the revised version derives the first-order asymptotic expansion
[
\inf I_n = 2 - \frac{c}{n} + o!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),
]
with an explicit constant $c>0$ expressed in terms of the Airy kernel, and proves
asymptotic optimality and rigidity of the Legendre--integral nodes.

The paper also contains extensive numerical experiments supporting the predicted
$1/n$ correction, endpoint Airy scaling, and an entropy rigidity hypothesis. The
numerics strongly suggest that the constant equals $c=2$.

For internal consistency and clarity checks, the revised manuscript was also
reviewed using ChatGPT as a technical writing assistant; all mathematical
arguments, proofs, and conclusions are entirely my own.

At this stage, I do not plan to submit the paper to a journal. I would very much
welcome feedback from experts in approximation theory, orthogonal polynomials,
and interpolation, particularly regarding the endpoint universality conjecture,
which remains the only open step toward a fully rigorous asymptotic resolution
of Erdős’s problem.

Edit. I previously posted here an earlier version of my work on Erdős’s $L^2$ extremal problem for Lagrange interpolation (Erdős problem 1131). I would like to inform readers that I have now uploaded a revised and substantially expanded version of the paper.

The revised preprint studies the asymptotic behavior, as $n \to \infty$, of\[
I_n(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\int_{-1}^1 \sum_{k=1}^n |l_k(x)|^2 \, dx,
\]where $l_k$ are the Lagrange basis polynomials.

The current revised version has now appeared on preprints.org and is available at:
https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202601.0875 (https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202601.0875)

Main updates and contributions.

(1) Equidistribution. It is proved that any asymptotically minimizing sequence of nodes must equidistribute with respect to the arcsine measure on $[-1,1]$, fixing the macroscopic structure of minimizers.

(2) Sharp lower bound. The previously known lower bound of order $O((\log n)^2/n)$ is improved to the optimal order $O(1/n)$.

(3) Conditional asymptotic expansion. Assuming an endpoint universality conjecture for discrete Christoffel functions, the revised version derives\[
\inf I_n = 2 - \frac{c}{n} + o\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),
\]with an explicit constant $c>0$, and establishes asymptotic optimality of the Legendre--integral nodes.

(4) Numerical verification. The new version contains extensive numerical experiments supporting the endpoint Airy scaling and indicating that the constant is $c=2$, together with an entropy rigidity hypothesis supported by numerical verification.

Update. The revised version of the preprint has now been assigned a new ResearchGate DOI:

DOI: 10.13140/RG.2.2.11709.93925 (https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.11709.93925)

The same version is also archived on Zenodo:

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18210226 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18210226)

I would welcome feedback on the revised version, especially concerning the endpoint universality conjecture (Conjecture~5.1), which remains the main open step toward a fully rigorous solution of Erdős’s problem.

Target:
Prove asymptotic
\[
\min I = 2-\frac{1+o(1)}{n}.
\]
Step A: Sharp Lower Bound Improvement
Upgrade
\[
2-O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^2}{n}\right)
\]
to
\[
2-\frac{C_1+o(1)}{n}
\]
with explicit \(C_1\).
Step B: Matching Constructive Upper Bound
Construct node sets with
\[
I\le 2-\frac{C_2+o(1)}{n}
\]
and \(C_2\) matching Step A constant.
Step C: Stability/Uniqueness at First Order
Show near-optimal families are \(o(1)\)-close (after normalization) to the
extremal node distribution, fixing the first-order constant.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a first-order expansion theorem for
\[
\int_{-1}^1\sum_k |\ell_k(x)|^2\,dx
\]
under perturbations of near-Chebyshev nodes, with error \(o(1/n)\).

Lemma B1 (quadratic-basis identity):
For any nodes,
\[
I=\int_{-1}^1\sum_{k=1}^n \ell_k(x)^2\,dx
\]
since \(\ell_k(x)\in\mathbb R\) on \([-1,1]\), so \(|\ell_k|^2=\ell_k^2\).
Proof.
All quantities are real-valued on the real interval; absolute-square equals square. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (partition identity):
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \ell_k(x)=1\quad\text{for all }x,
\]
hence \(I\ge \int_{-1}^1 \frac1n\,dx = \frac{2}{n}\) by Cauchy at each \(x\).
Proof.
Lagrange basis reproduces constants. Then
\[
1=\left(\sum_k \ell_k\right)^2\le n\sum_k \ell_k^2,
\]
so \(\sum_k\ell_k^2\ge 1/n\); integrate over \([-1,1]\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (first-order sensitivity transfer):
If node perturbations of size \(O(n^{-2})\) change \(I\) by at most \(o(1/n)\), then any near-Chebyshev family yields the same first-order constant in \(2-I\).
Proof.
Write \(I=I_\star+\Delta\) with \(\Delta=o(1/n)\). Multiplying by \(n\), \(n(2-I)=n(2-I_\star)+o(1)\), so first-order constants match. \(\square\)

problem:
For $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ let\[l_k(x)=\frac{\prod_{i\neq k}(x-x_i)}{\prod_{i\neq k}(x_k-x_i)},\]which are such that $l_k(x_k)=1$ and $l_k(x_i)=0$ for $i\neq k$.

Let $x_1,x_2,\ldots\in [-1,1]$ be an infinite sequence, and let\[L_n(x) = \sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\lvert l_k(x)\rvert,\]where each $l_k(x)$ is defined above with respect to $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

Must there exist $x\in (-1,1)$ such that\[L_n(x) >\frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1)\]for infinitely many $n$?

Is it true that\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\geq \frac{2}{\pi}\]for almost all $x\in (-1,1)$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1132.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-01).
- Page last edited: 01 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A result of Bernstein \cite{Be31} implies that the set of $x\in(-1,1)$ for which\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\geq \frac{2}{\pi}\]is everywhere dense.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er61c} proved that, for any fixed $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$,\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\lvert l_k(x)\rvert>\frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1).\]Tao \cite{Ta26b} has proved that for any function $\omega(n)$ which tends to infinity with $n$ there exists a dense set of $x\in (-1,1)$ such that\[L_n(x)\geq \frac{2}{\pi}\log n-\omega(n)\]for infinitely many $n$. Tao also notes that it is unclear in the question of Erd\H{o}s whether the constant in the $O(1)$ term may depend on $x$.

See also [1129] for more on $L_n(x)$, and also [1153].
References:
- [Be31] S. Bernstein, Sur la limitation des valeurs d'un polynome $P_n(x)$ de degr\'{e} n sur tout un segment par ses valeurs en $(n+1)$ points du segment. Izv. Akad. Nauk. SSSR (1931), 1025-1050.
- [Er61c] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on the theory of interpolation. II. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1961), 235-244.
- [Ta26b] T. Tao, Local Bernstein theory, and lower bounds for Lebesgue constants. arXiv:2603.21453 (2026).

forum_comments.author: JakeMallen
forum_comments.text: Erdős and Vértesi in On the almost everywhere divergence of Lagrange interpolatory polynomials for arbitrary system of nodes (1980) (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1981-03.pdf) in Theorem 3.1 prove that for any node system $X$ there exists continuous $F$ such that $|L_n(F,X,x)|\to\infty$ for almost all $x\in[-1,1]$. Since $|L_n(F,X,x)| \le \|F\|_\infty L_n(x)$, this implies $\limsup\limits_{n\to\infty} L_n(x)=\infty$ for almost all $x\in[-1,1]$.

For infinite node sequences \((x_k)\), force repeated/ae lower-limsup growth at scale \((2/\pi)\log n\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a uniform prefix-stability lemma: for infinitely many \(n\), every interval of \(x\)-mass at least \(\eta\) contains points where

L_n(x)\ge \frac{2}{\pi}\log n - C_\eta.

Lemma B1 (global max lower bound):
For each fixed \(n\),
\[
\max_{x\in[-1,1]}L_n(x)\ge \frac{2}{\pi}\log n - O(1).
\]
Proof.
This is the classical Erdős-Bernstein-type lower bound cited in the literature summary. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (many-point transfer from max control):
If one has an \(L^1\) lower bound for \(L_n\) of the same logarithmic scale plus an \(L^\infty\) upper envelope \(O(\log n)\), then a positive-measure set of \(x\) must satisfy \(L_n(x)\gg\log n\).
Proof.
Chebyshev/Markov measure estimate: if too small on most points, integral would contradict lower \(L^1\) mass. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies limsup statement):
If Lemma A holds for infinitely many \(n\), then
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\ge \frac{2}{\pi}
\]
on a positive-measure set (and with stronger uniformity, almost everywhere).
Proof.
Take subsequence \(n_j\) from A; pointwise lower bounds along \(n_j\) give limsup lower bound. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The gap is promoting fixed-\(n\) maximal lower bounds to robust distribution-in-\(x\) statements for an arbitrary infinite node sequence.

problem:
Let $C>0$. There exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently large the following holds.

For any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ there exist $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in [-1,1]$ such that, if $P$ is a polynomial of degree $m<(1+\epsilon)n$ with $P(x_i)=y_i$ for at least $(1-\epsilon)n$ many $1\leq i\leq n$, then\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lvert P(x)\rvert >C.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1133.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-01).
- Page last edited: 31 December 2025.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s proved that, for any $C>0$, there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently large and $m=\lfloor (1+\epsilon)n\rfloor$ then for any $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in [-1,1]$ there is a polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ such that $\lvert P(x_i)\rvert\leq 1$ for $1\leq i\leq m$ and\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lvert P(x)\rvert>C.\]The conjectured statement would also imply this, but Erd\H{o}s in \cite{Er67} says he could not even prove it for $m=n$.
References:
- [Er67] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on the convergence and divergence properties of the Lagrange interpolation polynomials and some extremal problems. Mathematica (Cluj) (1967), 65-73.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
GPT-5.5 Pro got me a nice argument using Beurling's interpolation theorem for Bernstein spaces. Here is the note. (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos1133.pdf)

The robust obstruction is a consequence of a simple density principle: near the critical Bernstein interpolation density, uniformly bounded interpolation of all local data is impossible. The angular substitution $x=\cos\theta$ transfers this local fact from entire functions of exponential type to algebraic polynomials on $[-1,1]$. A block pigeonhole argument then turns a local obstruction into a global robust obstruction for arbitrary node sets.

Attempt route:
Compared the statement to Erdos' known opposite-direction extremal interpolation
construction.

Hard point:
Turning this into the stated robust near-fit impossibility for arbitrary data remains

Target:
Establish robust interpolation obstruction: for many prescribed \((x_i,y_i)\), any polynomial fitting almost all pairs with degree \(<(1+\varepsilon)n\) must have sup norm \(>C\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a node-geometry dichotomy lemma:
for unstable node families (large Lebesgue amplification), every near-full fit of random \(\pm1\) labels has sup norm \(\gg 1\) with overwhelming probability.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (fit-subset representation):
If \(P\) interpolates labels on subset \(S\) of size \(t\), then
\[
P(x)=\sum_{i\in S} y_i\,\ell_i^{(S)}(x),
\]
where \(\ell_i^{(S)}\) are Lagrange basis polynomials for nodes in \(S\).
Proof.
Standard interpolation formula on the selected nodes. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (sup norm lower via coefficient signs):
For random signs \(y_i\), typical size of \(\sup_x|P(x)|\) is controlled below by the \(\ell_2\)-mass
\[
\left(\sum_{i\in S} (\ell_i^{(S)}(x))^2\right)^{1/2}
\]
at points where this mass is large.
Proof.
At fixed \(x\), \(P(x)\) is a Rademacher sum; Khintchine-type bounds give typical magnitude comparable to coefficient \(\ell_2\)-norm. Take sup over \(x\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies probabilistic obstruction):
If Lemma A gives uniform lower control of the basis-mass profile on unstable nodes, then near-full low-sup fits become exponentially unlikely.
Proof.
Combine Lemma B2 with concentration for Rademacher sums and union bound over admissible subsets \(S\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The hardest step is making the probabilistic obstruction uniform over all near-full subsets \(S\), not just a fixed chosen subset.

literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1135.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-11).
- Page last edited: 12 January 2026.
Site remarks:
The infamous Collatz conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collatz_conjecture). For a detailed discussion of the history and theory surrounding this problem we refer to the overview by Lagarias \cite{La10}.

This is not a problem due to Erd\H{o}s; it was first devised by Collatz before 1952. Erd\H{o}s referred to this problem on several occasions as 'hopeless'. As Lagarias \cite{La16} notes, the closest Erd\H{o}s ever came to working on problems of this nature is the theorem described in the remarks to [1134].

It is often claimed that Erd\H{o}s offered \$500 for a solution to this problem; this claim originated in a survey article by Lagarias \cite{La85}.

Lagarias reported, in personal communication, that this came from a conversation he had with Erd\H{o}s and Graham around 1983, in which Graham asked Erd\H{o}s to make an estimate of what value Erd\H{o}s would put the problem on his prize scale, to which Erd\H{o}s replied \$500. Therefore, strictly speaking, Erd\H{o}s never offered \$500 specifically as a prize, but we include this prize value here for comparing those problems which Erd\H{o}s rated as 'prize problems'.

This is Problem E16 in Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}, in which Guy quotes Erd\H{o}s as saying "Mathematics may not be ready for such problems".
References:
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [La10] Lagarias, Jeffrey C., The {$3x+1$} problem: an overview. (2010), 3--29.
- [La16] Lagarias, Jeffrey C., Erd\H{o}s, {K}larner, and the {$3x+1$} problem. Amer. Math. Monthly (2016), 753--776.
- [La85] Lagarias, Jeffrey C., The {$3x+1$} problem and its generalizations. Amer. Math. Monthly (1985), 3--23.

attempt:
Target:
Prove global convergence for the accelerated Collatz map (EP-1135 formulation).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show there is no divergent orbit and no nontrivial cycle by proving a uniform descent-on-average inequality on every sufficiently long block of iterates.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (minimal counterexample reduction):
If a nontrivial cycle or divergent orbit exists, there exists one with minimal odd part (or minimal height in an appropriate ordering).
Proof.
Take infimum in well-ordered positive integers among odd representatives encountered in the bad set; choose witness attaining minimal value. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (parity-vector encoding):
Any cycle of length \(m\) determines a parity vector and exact rational identity
\[
n = \frac{A}{2^m-3^s}
\]
with integers \(A,s\) derived from the parity pattern.
Proof.
Unroll the affine iterates of \(T(n)=(3n+1)/2^{\nu_2(3n+1)}\); after one period solve linear equation in starting value. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A rules out bad objects):
If Lemma A gives strict average descent over every long block, then cycles with average multiplier \(\ge1\) and divergent trajectories are impossible.
Proof.
Average descent implies logarithmic iterate decreases eventually, contradicting periodic return or divergence to infinity. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving a deterministic, all-orbit average-descent estimate strong enough to dominate exceptional parity patterns.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Heuristically this is not true by Cramer like conjecture.
Let $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$ be prime gaps and define $M(x):=\max_{n<x} d_n$ and $P(x):=\max_{n<x} d_{n-1}d_n$. In a Cramer-Poisson heuristic one treats the normalized gaps\[
X_n:=\frac{d_n}{\log p_n}
\]as approximately i.i.d. exponential random variables with mean $1$ (locally, on the scale of $\log p_n$), and also approximately independent for neighboring indices.

For $N$ i.i.d. $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ variables, the maximum satisfies $X_{(1)}=\max_{1\le n\le N}X_n=(1+o(1))\log N$ with high probability. Translating back, this predicts\[
M(x)\approx (\log p_x)\,\log x,
\]up to lower-order factors, consistent with the usual extreme-value behavior in the model.

Consider adjacent pairs $(X_n,X_{n-1})$ and set a threshold $t=a\log N$. Under independence,\[
\mathbb{E}\#\{1\le n\le N:\; X_{n-1}\ge t,\ X_n\ge t\}
\approx N\,\mathbb{P}(X\ge t)^2
= N e^{-2t}
= N^{\,1-2a}.
\]Hence for any $a<\tfrac12$ there are typically many indices with $X_{n-1},X_n\ge a\log N$, while for $a>\tfrac12$ there are typically none; this places the largest adjacent pair around $t\approx \tfrac12\log N$ in each coordinate. Consequently,\[
\max_{n\le N} X_{n-1}X_n \approx \left(\tfrac12 \log N\right)^2
\quad\text{while}\quad
\left(\max_{n\le N}X_n\right)^2 \approx (\log N)^2,
\]so the ratio $P(x)/M(x)^2$ is heuristically bounded away from $0$ (on the order of a positive constant, plausibly about $1/4$ in this simplified model), rather than tending to $0$.

forum_comments.author: gavinsherry
forum_comments.text:
I wrote up a short covering-reduction note related to this thread:

GitHub Gist (https://gist.github.com/gavinsherry/59208407035b37acc83b4165305a88b5)

Disclosure: this was prepared with AI assistance (GPT-5.5 xhigh). Claude was used as an adversarial reviewer of the reductions and caveats.

This is not a solution of #1139 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/1139). The note records two sufficient finite covering statements and one caveat about applying existing large-prime-gap technology.

The first sufficient criterion is a threefold sparse cover. Suppose that for arbitrarily large $y$ one can choose distinct primes $P_y$ and one residue class $a_p \pmod p$ for each $p\in P_y$, such that every $1\le n\le y$ lies in at least three of the residue classes, and\[
L(y):=\sum_{p\in P_y}\log p=o(y).
\]Then the desired conclusion follows. The CRT gives $N\equiv -a_p\pmod p$ for all $p\in P_y$, so every $N+n$ has at least three distinct prime divisors for $1\le n\le y$. The gap length is at least $y$, while $\log k\le O(\log y+L(y))=o(y)$.

There is also a twofold small-prime variant, closer to the discussion above. If every $1\le n\le y$ is covered at least twice by distinct primes $p\le y$, again with $\sum\log p=o(y)$, then this also suffices. Choose the CRT representative $N$ with\[
y^2<N\le y^2+\prod_{p\in P_y}p.
\]Then the two primes $p,q\le y$ forced to divide $N+n$ satisfy $pq\le y^2<N+n$, so $N+n$ has at least three prime factors counted with multiplicity.

The caveat is that the apparent shortcut through applying Ford-Konyagin-Maynard-Pomerance-Tao's long gaps in sieved sets (https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/32526) theorem separately to fixed positive-density prime classes is not justified as a black-box step. One residue class on a density-$\rho$ subset of primes gives a dimension-$\rho$ sieve:\[
\prod_{\substack{p\le x\\p\in P}}\left(1-\frac1p\right)\asymp(\log x)^{-\rho},
\]whereas the FKMP-T theorem assumes a one-dimensional system. Assigning multiple classes per prime can restore dimension, but then a single CRT congruence for $N$ can no longer force all of those classes to divide $N+n$.

So the current status is: these covering reductions are valid, but the needed sparse multi-covering theorem remains the open technical point.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
Indeed, seems like the core is the same or very similar. This is what I got while poking GPT-5.2 for the connection and a missing argument one might need for both: A convenient finite/combinatorial reformulation of our goal is the following 2-fold covering problem: for large $n$, can one choose residue classes $a_p \pmod p$ (for primes $p$ in some set, possibly all $p\le n$) so that every $j\in[1,n]$ satisfies at least two congruences $j\equiv a_p\pmod p$? If we can do this using distinct primes, then choosing $N$ by CRT so that $N\equiv -a_p\pmod p$ for all used $p$ forces each $N+j$ to be divisible by at least two distinct primes $\le n$. Since the CRT modulus is huge (typically $N\gg n^2$ when many primes $\le n$ are used), $N+j$ cannot equal a product of only those two primes, hence $\Omega(N+j)\ge 3$ for all $1\le j\le n$. Thus a 2-fold congruence cover of $[1,n]$ yields an interval $[N+1,N+n]$ with no integers of $\Omega\le 2$, giving gaps in the sequence $u_k$ of primes/semiprimes; moreover, tracking $\log N\asymp\sum_{p\in S}\log p$ is what determines the gap factor $n/\log N$ and hence $\limsup (u_{k+1}-u_k)/\log k$.

We take $z\to\infty$ slowly, set $y:=n/z$, and run an Erdős--Rankin style multi-stage cover. Stage~0 sets $a_p=0$ for all primes $p\le y$, giving one ''touch'' for each small prime divisor. Up to negligible sets, the indices with $\le 1$ touch are (i) primes $j\in(y,n]$, of size $\sim n/\log n$, and (ii) semiprimes $j=p_1p_2$ with $p_1<z$ and $p_2>y$, of size $\sim (n/\log n)\log\log z$; semiprimes with $p_1>z^{1/A}$ contribute $\sim (n/\log n)\log A$. The numerology is that if we now use primes $p\asymp y$, then one residue class mod $p$ hits $\asymp n/p\asymp z$ indices, and among those the usable targets occur with density $\asymp 1/\log(n/p)\asymp 1/\log z$, giving $\asymp z/\log z$ useful hits per prime. This suggests that with $R\asymp \frac{y\log z}{\log n}(1+\log A)$ primes $p\asymp y$ one can add enough touches to kill most primes and most semiprimes with $p_1>z^{1/A}$, and with another comparable batch reduce the remaining ''small-$p_1$'' semiprimes by an extra factor $\approx A$.

The modulus bookkeeping is the key link to the original $\limsup$ question. Using primes $p\asymp y$ keeps $\sum\log p$ under control: combining stages yields\[
\log N \asymp \sum_{p\in S}\log p \asymp y\,\log z\,(1+\log A),
\]so the resulting gap factor is\[
\frac{n}{\log N}\asymp \frac{z}{\log z\,(1+\log A)}\to\infty
\quad\text{for choices like}\quad
A=\exp((\log\log\log z)^2).
\]Cleanup must avoid using $\asymp n/\log n$ ''reserve primes'' near $n$ (which would force $\log N\asymp n$ and destroy the gap factor); instead one cleans up with primes $\asymp y$, where each prime hits $\asymp z$ indices so $|S|$ stragglers can be handled using $\ll |S|/z$ primes at modulus cost $\ll y$.

The main bottleneck is to make the ''random sieve'' steps rigorous in this 2-fold setting. One needs a multi-covering/hypergraph-cover lemma (a 2-fold cover rather than the usual 1-fold cover for prime gaps) ensuring that for many primes $p\asymp y$ one can choose residue classes that hit about the expected number of targets (primes and the structured semiprime families attached to small $p_1$), with suitably small codegrees to drive survivor counts down by factors like $A$. This is where one expects to use distribution-in-progressions and ''linear equations in primes'' technology as in modern large prime gap work, but an explicit statement tailored to these mixed target sets appears to be the central technical gap.

problem: Are there infinitely many $n$ (or any $n>105$) such that $n-2^k$ is prime for all $1<2^k<n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1142.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-23).
- Page last edited: 05 March 2026.
Site remarks:
The only known such $n$ are\[4,7,15,21,45,75,105.\]This is A039669 (https://oeis.org/A039669) in the OEIS.

Mientka and Weitzenkamp \cite{MiWe69} have proved there are no other such $n\leq 2^{44}$.

Vaughan \cite{Va73} has proved that the number of $n\leq N$ such that $n-2^k$ is prime for all $1<2^k<n$ is\[< \exp\left(-c\frac{\log \log \log N}{\log\log N}\log N\right)N\]for some constant $c>0$.

This is discussed in problem A19 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}. There is also further discussion on the Prime Puzzles website (https://www.primepuzzles.net/problems/prob_003.htm).

Erd\H{o}s made the stronger conjecture (see [236]) that that number of $1<2^k<n$ for which $n-2^k$ is prime is $o(\log n)$.
References:
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [MiWe69] Mientka, Walter E. and Weitzenkamp, Roger C., On {$f$}-plentiful numbers. J. Combinatorial Theory (1969), 374--377.
- [Va73] Vaughan, R. C., Some applications of {M}ontgomery's sieve. J. Number Theory (1973), 64--79.

problem:
Given $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in [-1,1]$ let\[\mathcal{L}^nf(x) = \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}f(a_i)\ell_i(x)\]be the unique polynomial of degree $n-1$ which agrees with $f$ on $a_i$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ (that is, the Lagrange interpolation polynomial).

Let $a_i$ be the set of Chebyshev nodes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_nodes). Prove that, for any closed $A\subseteq [-1,1]$, there exists a continuous function $f$ such that $A$ is the set of limit points of $\mathcal{L}^nf(x)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1151.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-23).
- Page last edited: 23 January 2026.
Site remarks:
This is as the problem is given in \cite{Va99}, but I am unclear exactly what is intended here - is this meant for fixed, arbitrary, $x\in [-1,1]$?

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er41} proved that, if $x=\cos(\pi p/q)$ for some odd integers $p,q\geq 1$, then there is a continuous function $f$ such that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\mathcal{L}^nf(x)=\infty,\]where the limit is taken over the sequence of Chebyshev nodes as $n\to \infty$. In \cite{Er43} he claims (without proof) that for any closed set $A$ there exists a continuous $f$ such that the limit points of $\mathcal{L}^nf(x)$ is $A$ (for specific $x$ of this shape).

problem:
For $n\geq 1$ fix some sequence of $n$ distinct numbers $x_{1n},\ldots,x_{nn}\in [-1,1]$. Let $\epsilon=\epsilon(n)\to 0$.

Does there always exist a continuous function $f:[-1,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ such that if $p_n$ is a sequence of polynomials, with degrees $\deg p_n<(1+\epsilon(n))n$, such that $p_n(x_{kn})=f(x_{kn})$ for all $1\leq k\leq n$, then $p_n(x)\not\to f(x)$ for almost all $x\in [-1,1]$?
