problem: Does there exist, for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$, a ring or field in $\mathbb{R}$ with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1154.
- Page status: NOT DISPROVABLE (database last update 2026-01-24).
- Page last edited: 25 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Volkmann \cite{ErVo66} proved that, for any $\alpha\in[0,1]$, there exists a group of real numbers of Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$.

Falconer \cite{Fa84} proved that any subring with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha \in(1/2,1)$ cannot be a Borel or Suslin set. Edgar and Miller \cite{EdMi01} proved that any real closed analytic subfield of $\mathbb{R}$ has Hausdorff dimension either $0$ or $1$. Later the same authors \cite{EdMi03} proved that any subring of $\mathbb{R}$ which is Borel or analytic either has Hausdorff dimension $0$ or is equal to $\mathbb{R}$.

Mauldin \cite{Ma16b} proved that subfields of $\mathbb{R}$ exist with Hausdorff dimension any $\alpha \in [0,1]$ assuming the continuum hypothesis.
References:
- [EdMi01] Edgar, G. A. and Miller, Chris, Hausdorff dimension, analytic sets and transcendence. Real Anal. Exchange (2001/02), 335--339.
- [EdMi03] Edgar, G. A. and Miller, Chris, Borel subrings of the reals. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (2003), 1121--1129.
- [ErVo66] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Volkmann, Bodo, Additive {G}ruppen mit vorgegebener {H}ausdorffscher {D}imension. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1966), 203--208.
- [Fa84] Falconer, K. J., Rings of fractional dimension. Mathematika (1984), 25--27.
- [Ma16b] Mauldin, R. Daniel, Subfields of {\bf {R}} with arbitrary {H}ausdorff dimension. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. (2016), 157--165.

problem:
Construct a random graph on $n$ vertices in the following way: begin with the complete graph $K_n$. At each stage, choose uniformly a random triangle in the graph and delete all the edges of this triangle. Repeat until the graph is triangle-free.

Describe the typical parameters and structure of such a graph. In particular, if $f(n)$ is the number of edges remaining, then is it true that\[\mathbb{E}f(n)\asymp n^{3/2}\]and that $f(n) \ll n^{3/2}$ almost surely?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1155.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-23).
- Page last edited: 25 January 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Bollob\'{a}s and Erd\H{o}s, described in \cite{Va99} as 'motivated by the task of generating a random triangle-free graph'. In \cite{Bo98} it says they asked this at the 'Quo Vadis, Graph Theory?' conference in Fairbanks, Alaska, in 1990, 'while admiring the playful bears'.

Grable \cite{Gr97} proved that, for every $\epsilon>0$,\[\mathbb{P}(f(n)>n^{7/4+\epsilon})\to 0.\]Bohman, Frieze, and Lubetzky \cite{BFL15} proved that $f(n)=n^{3/2+o(1)}$ almost surely - in other words, for every $\epsilon>0$,\[\mathbb{P}(n^{3/2-\epsilon}<f(n)<n^{3/2+\epsilon})\to 1.\]
References:
- [BFL15] Bohman, Tom and Frieze, Alan and Lubetzky, Eyal, Random triangle removal. Adv. Math. (2015), 379--438.
- [Bo98] Bollob\'{a}s, B\'ela, To prove and conjecture: {P}aul {E}rd\H os and his mathematics. Amer. Math. Monthly (1998), 209--237.
- [Gr97] Grable, David A., On random greedy triangle packing. Electron. J. Combin. (1997), Research Paper 11, 19.
- [Va99] Various, Some of Paul's favorite problems. Booklet produced for the conference "Paul Erd\H{o}s and his mathematics", Budapest, July 1999 (1999).

problem:
Let $G$ be a random graph on $n$ vertices, in which every edge is included independently with probability $1/2$.

Is there some constant $C$ such that that chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is, almost surely, concentrated on at most $C$ values?

Is it true that, if $\omega(n)\to \infty$ sufficiently slowly, then for every function $f(n)$\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))<1/2\]if $n$ is sufficiently large?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1156.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-23).
- Page last edited: 27 January 2026.
Site remarks:
Bollob\'{a}s \cite{Bo88} proved that $\chi(G) \sim \frac{n}{2\log_2n}$ with high probability.

Shamir and Spencer \cite{ShSp87} proved that, for any function $\omega(n)$ such that $\omega(n)/\sqrt{n}\to \infty$, there is a function $f(n)$ such that\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))\to 1\]as $n\to \infty$. This is proved with $\omega(n)\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n}}\to \infty$ in Exercise 3 of Section 7.9 of Alon and Spencer \cite{AlSp16} (a proof is also given by Scott \cite{Sc17}).

Heckel \cite{He21} proved that if $f$ and $\omega$ are such that\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))\to 1\]as $n\to \infty$ then, for any $c<1/4$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\omega(n)>n^c$. This was improved to any $c<1/2$ by Heckel and Riordan \cite{HeRi23}.
References:
- [AlSp16] Alon, Noga and Spencer, Joel H., The probabilistic method. (2016), xiv+375.
- [Bo88] Bollob\'{a}s, B., The chromatic number of random graphs. Combinatorica (1988), 49-55.
- [He21] Heckel, Annika, Non-concentration of the chromatic number of a random graph. J. Amer. Math. Soc. (2021), 245--260.
- [HeRi23] Heckel, Annika and Riordan, Oliver, How does the chromatic number of a random graph vary?. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2) (2023), 1769--1815.
- [Sc17] A. Scott, On the concentration of the chromatic number of random graphs. arXiv:0806.0178 (2017).
- [ShSp87] Shamir, E. and Spencer, J., Sharp concentration of the chromatic number on random graphs {$G_{n,p}$}. Combinatorica (1987), 121--129.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Since the results by Heckel and Riordan seem so close to resolving this problem, I sent Annika Heckel an e-mail to ask about the limits of their methods, and she kindly responded to me. Some interesting things I learned (where whp stands for 'with high probability', i.e. with probability tending to $1$):

1) In [HeRe23] (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14014) they prove that there are infinitely many $n$ for which the smallest interval on which $\chi(G)$ is concentrated whp has length at least $\frac{c\sqrt{n} \log \log n}{\log^3 n}$, for some absolute constant $c$. They conjecture that this is the correct order of growth, up to the value of $c$.

2) It is furthermore conjectured that there are infinitely many $n$ for which $\chi(G)$ is whp concentrated on an interval of length $\frac{C n^{1/4}}{\log^{7/4} n}$, for some absolute constant $C$ .

3) Combining the first two points, the length of the concentration interval is thought to fluctuate between $n^{1/4 + o(1)}$ and $n^{1/2 + o(1)}$. See Figure $2$ and Conjectures $10, 11, 12$ in [HeRe23] (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14014) for more details.

4) The following crazy scenario has not been excluded: for almost all $n$, $\chi(G)$ is one-point concentrated whp. In particular, the second question remains open. Note that this does not contradict the first point above, as only the existence of infinitely many $n$ for which the concentration interval is large can be guaranteed.

5) The following equally crazy scenario has also not been excluded: for all $n$, $\chi(G)$ is two-point concentrated whp. In particular, the first question also remains open. Note that this also does not contradict the first point above, as it is theoretically possible that, even for those $n$ for which the concentration interval is large, $\chi(G)$ is concentrated on two points that are far apart. Often the question is stated with $C$ consecutive values, in which case we do know the answer by [He21] (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.11808).

6) Heckel has given various nice lectures on this topic which are available online. See here (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YDuQOSDRu5Y) for one example.

problem: Let $t,k,r\geq 2$. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the family of all $r$-uniform hypergraphs with $k$ vertices and $s$ edges. Determine\[\mathrm{ex}_r(n,\mathcal{F}).\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1157.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-23).
- Page last edited: 24 January 2026.
Site remarks:
This is a very difficult and general question, and many partial results are known. The paper of Brown, Erd\H{o}s, and S\'{o}s \cite{BES73} contains many of them, in particular the general lower bound, for all $k>r$ and $s>1$,\[\mathrm{ex}_r(n,\mathcal{F})\gg_{k,s} n^{\frac{rs-k}{s-1}}.\]A general conjecture of Brown, Erd\H{o}s, and S\'{o}s is that, for all $r>t\geq 2$ and $s\geq 3$,\[\mathrm{ex}_t(n,\mathcal{F})=o(n^t)\]whenever $k\geq (r-t)s+t+1$. The case $t=2$ is the subject of [1178].

The case $s=r=3$ and $k=6$ is the subject of [716]. The case of $r=3$ and $k=s+2$ is the subject of [1076].
References:
- [BES73] Brown, W. G. and Erd\H{o}s, P. and S\'os, V. T., Some extremal problems on {$r$}-graphs. (1973), 53--63.

problem:
Determine whether there exists a constant $C>1$ such that the following holds.

Let $P$ be a finite projective plane (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane). Must there exist a set of points $S$ such that $1\leq \lvert S\cap \ell\rvert \leq C$ for all lines $\ell$?

problem: Let $g(n)$ denote the number of groups of order $n$. If $n\leq 2^m$ then $g(n)\leq g(2^m)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1160.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-01-23).
- Page last edited: 26 January 2026.
Site remarks:
This is listed as an open problem (Question 22.16) in \cite{BNV07}, which reports it as a 'quite natural conjecture, whose origin we have been unable to trace satisfactorily. We have heard it attributed at various times to various people, such as Paul Erd\H{o}s and Graham Higman.'

Question 22.18 of \cite{BNV07} suggests the even stronger conjecture\[\sum_{n<2^m}g(n) \leq g(2^m)\]for all sufficiently large $m$ (perhaps even as soon as $m\geq 7$).

Pantelidakis \cite{Pa03} proved that the original conjecture is true if $n$ is odd and $m\geq 3619$.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
What's the right interpretation? There are at least three natural readings:

1) Divisor-statistical reading. Study the set\[
 O_n=\{|H|:H\leq S_n\}
\]as a subset of the divisor set $D_n=\{d:d\mid n!\}$.

2) Uniform-subgroup reading. Choose $H$ uniformly from the finite set $\textrm{Sub}(S_n)$, and study the random variable $|H|$, or its invariants $\log |H|$, $v _p(|H|)$, $\omega(|H|)$, and so on.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
Thank you for the clarification and for pointing out the original conditions in the Erdős–Hajnal list.

Even with the condition \(\gamma \ge 2\), however, a size obstruction can still occur:
if some \(\kappa_\alpha > \lambda\), then the conclusion \(\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha)^r_{\alpha<\gamma}\) would require a subset of \(\lambda\) of size \(\kappa_\alpha > \lambda\), which is impossible, while the hypothesis might still hold non-vacuously.

Thus, to ensure the problem is nontrivial in ZFC, it seems necessary to also require \(\kappa_\alpha \le \lambda\) for all \(\alpha < \gamma\) (or at least for those \(\alpha\) that could correspond to the color of a large homogeneous set in the stepping-up coloring).

In any case, the literal unrestricted statement — without any bound on \(\kappa_\alpha\) relative to \(\lambda\) — remains false, as my minimal counterexample shows. The intended formulation (with \(\gamma \ge 2\), \(r < \omega\), \(\kappa_\alpha > r\), and presumably \(\kappa_\alpha \le \lambda\)) is the interesting open problem.

I appreciate your maintaining this valuable list of problems and your careful attention to these details.

forum_comments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
forum_comments.text:
I uploaded a short note pointing out that the \emph{literal} fully-quantified statement of Erdős--Hajnal--Rado Problem 1167 (as written in the book/problem list) is falsified by a simple size obstruction.

If one allows some target $\kappa_\alpha>\lambda$, then the conclusion\[
\lambda\to(\kappa_\alpha)^r_{\alpha<\gamma}
\]is impossible, while the hypothesis can still hold. In fact, taking $\gamma=1$ and $\kappa_0=\lambda^+$, the premise\[
2^\lambda\to(\kappa_0+1)^{r+1}_{<1}
\]is automatic (a coloring into $<1$ colors is vacuous; equivalently it just requires $2^\lambda\ge \kappa_0+1$), but the conclusion would require a subset of $\lambda$ of size $\lambda^+$, contradiction.

This suggests the intended nontrivial formulation should explicitly assume $\kappa_\alpha\le\lambda$ for all $\alpha<\gamma$; under this restriction the general heterogeneous implication still seems open (beyond the classical uniform stepping-up/stepping-down consequences for $r\ge3$).

Any references, known partial results, or corrections to the intended statement of \#1167 would be very welcome.

DOI: 10.13140/RG.2.2.22305.06242 (https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.22305.06242)

This is also Problem 2 in the Erdős-Hajnal problem list (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-symbolic-logic/article/abs/erdoshajnal-problem-list/9FBE6099BE9441516445D0B95F4B1208), which gives the additional conditions that $\gamma \geq 2$ (it actually says $\gamma \leq 2$, but I assume this is an obvious typo). It also has the additional conditions $r<\omega$ and $\kappa_\alpha >r$. Some known special cases are listed there (I'll update this on the site soon).

The condition $\kappa_\alpha\leq \lambda$ does not appear there, however - presumably $\gamma\geq 2$ suffices to rule out the vacuous problem you noted.

Site remarks:
A conjecture of Brown, Erd\H{o}s, and S\'{o}s \cite{BES73}, who proved that $d_r(e)\geq (r-2)e+3$ (see also [1076]).

Ruzsa and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{RuSz78} proved $d_3(3)=6$ (see [716]).

Erd\H{o}s, Frankl, and R\"{o}dl \cite{EFR86} proved\[d_r(3)= (r-2)3+3\]for all $r\geq 3$. S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy and Selkow \cite{SaSe05} proved\[d_r(e) \leq (r-2)e+2+\lfloor \log_2 e\rfloor\]for all $r,e\geq 3$. Solymosi and Solymosi \cite{SoSo17} proved that $d_3(10)\leq 14$. Conlon, Gishboliner, Levanzov, and Shapira \cite{CGLS23} proved\[d_3(e)\leq e+O\left(\frac{\log e}{\log\log e}\right)\]for all $e\geq 3$.

In \cite{Er75b} Erd\H{o}s even asks whether, if $\mathcal{F}$ is the family of $3$-uniform hypergraphs on $k$ vertices with $k-3$ edges,\[\mathrm{ex}_3(n,\mathcal{F})\asymp n r_{k-3}(n),\]where $r_{k-3}(n)$ is the maximal size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ that does not contain a non-trivial arithmetic progression of length $k-3$. See [1157] for the general case.

problem: Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that there is a connected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $f(n)$ edges such that\[R(K_3,G)= 2n-1.\]Let $F(n)$ be maximal such that every connected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $\leq F(n)$ edges has\[R(K_3,G)= 2n-1.\]Estimate $f(n)$ and $F(n)$. In particular, is it true that $F(n)/n\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1182.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-03-07).
- Page last edited: 11 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A problem of Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp.

It is trivial that $f(n)\geq F(n)$, and that $R(K_3,G)\geq 2n-1$ for any connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices. By a result of Chav\'{a}tal $R(K_3,T)=2n-1$ whenever $T$ is a tree on $n$ vertices, whence $F(n)\geq n-1$.

Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Roussea, and Schelp \cite{BEFRS80} proved\[\frac{17n+1}{15}\leq F(n)\leq \left(\frac{27}{4}+o(1)\right)n(\log n)^2,\]the lower bound for all $n\geq 4$. The upper bound was improved to\[F(n)\leq 84n\]by Brandt (https://ftp.math.fu-berlin.de/pub/math/publ/pre/1996/pr-a-96-24.ps) \cite{Br96}, who expects that for all large $n$ we have $2n<F(n)<6n$. (This resolves the final question in the negative.)

In \cite{BEFRS80} they also prove\[n^{3/2}(\log n)^{1/2} \ll f(n) \ll n^{5/3}(\log n)^{2/3}.\]The first few values of $F(n)$ and $f(n)$ (beginning with $n=2$) are $1,2,5,7,8$ and $1,2,5,8,12$ respectively, as reported in \cite{BEFRS80}.

Similar questions can be asked with $K_3$ replaced by $K_m$ (where the $2n-1$ is replaced with $(m-1)(n-1)+1$). For the corresponding generalisations of $f$ and $F$ Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Roussea, and Schelp \cite{BEFRS80} proved\[n^{\frac{2}{m-1}}\ll F_m(n)-n\ll n^{\frac{4}{m+1}+o(1)}\]and\[n^{1+\frac{1}{m-1}}\ll f_m(n) \ll n^{1+\frac{2}{m}+o(1)}.\]
References:
- [BEFRS80] Burr, S. A. and Erd\H{o}s, P. and Faudree, R. J. and Rousseau, C. C. and Schelp, R. H., An extremal problem in generalized {R}amsey theory. Ars Combin. (1980), 193--203.
- [Br96] S. Brandt, Expanding graphs and Ramsey numbers. Seri A Mathematik, Preprints (1996).

forum_comments.author: ebarschkis
forum_comments.text:
Unless I’m missing something, Stephan Brandt’s bound $f(n;3)\le Cn$ in his paper "Expanding graphs and Ramsey numbers" (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2827547_Expanding_graphs_and_Ramsey_numbers) already answers the $F(n)/n\to \infty$ question negatively.
I was unable to find a copy of his paper online, so I reconstructed it based off a few fragments I found in university archives in LaTeX.
In his paper he proves a linear bound of the form $[
f(n;3) \le C n
]$ (for example $f(n;3)/n<84$ for sufficiently large $n$).
I think this implies $f(n)/n$ is bounded, so the question $f(n)/n\to\infty$ has a negative answer.

Here is the reconstructed Latex code (https://github.com/ebarschkis/ErdosProblem/blob/main/Problem1182/Brandt.tex) and compiled PDF (https://github.com/ebarschkis/ErdosProblem/blob/main/Problem1182/Brandt.pdf) of the Brandt’s paper.

EDIT: Brandt used different notation where the universal Ramsey-goodness threshold f(n;3) is the same as the parameter F(n) in BEFRS80 if I am not mistaken.

problem:
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that in any $2$-colouring of the subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ there is always a monochromatic family of at least $f(n)$ sets which is closed under taking unions and intersections. Estimate $f(n)$.

Let $F(n)$ be defined similarly, except that we only require the family be closed under taking unions. Estimate $F(n)$. In particular, is it true that $F(n)\geq n^{\omega(n)}$ for some $\omega(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$, and $F(n)<(1+o(1))^n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1183.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-03-07).
Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Ulam.

It is trivial that $f(n)\geq \frac{n+1}{2}$, since there is a sequence of $n+1$ many nested subsets. This seems to be all that they knew; Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er78} wrote 'we have no plausible conjecture for the true order of magnitude of $f(n)$'.

They similarly had no good guess about $F(n)$.

In \cite{Er78} Erd\H{o}s wrote that if the colouring is such that all subsets of same size receive the same colour then Howorka had proved that $F(n)>n^{\omega(n)}$ for some $\omega(n)\to \infty$, but gave no reference.
References:
- [Er78] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and combinatorial number theory. Proceedings of the Ninth Southeastern Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory, and Computing (Florida Atlantic Univ., Boca Raton, Fla., 1978) (1978), 29-40.

forum_comments.author: Przemek Chojecki
forum_comments.text:
With GPT-5.4 Pro I've managed to get some partial results that you can view here (https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos1183.pdf). There's not much literature around the problem.

We answer affirmatively the subexponential half of the problem.

The proofs are probabilistic, but the structural inputs are quite different. For $F(n)$ the key observation is that the free rank of a union-closed family is exactly the VC-dimension of a complementary set system. For $f(n)$ we use the fact that every family closed under union and intersection is a finite distributive lattice, hence isomorphic to an ideal lattice $J(P)$ by Birkhoff's representation theorem. A large antichain in $P$ yields a Boolean cube inside $J(P)$, and after ruling out large cubes by random colouring one is left with counting bounded-width posets.

problem: Let $f(n,k)$ count the number of $1\leq i\leq k$ such that $P(n+i)>k$ (where $P(m)$ is the largest prime divisor of $m$). Is it true that, if $\alpha>1$ is such that $n=k^{\alpha+o(1)}$, then\[f(n,k)=(1-\rho(\alpha)+o(1))k,\]where $\rho$ is the Dickman function (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function)?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1184.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er76e} proved that, for every $\alpha>1$, if $k$ is sufficiently large and $n>k^\alpha-k$ then\[f(n,k) > \left(1-\frac{1}{\alpha}+c_\alpha\right)k\]for some constant $c_\alpha>0$, and if $1<\alpha<2$ and $n\leq k^\alpha-k$ then\[f(n,k) < (\alpha-1+o(1))k.\]He knew of no non-trivial bounds when $\alpha \geq 2$.

Ramachandra, Shorey, and Tijdeman \cite{RST75b} proved that if $n>\exp(c(\log k)^2)$ for a constant $c>0$ then $f(n,k)\geq k-\pi(k)$.
References:
- [Er76e] Erd\H{o}s, P., Problems and results on consecutive integers. Publ. Math. Debrecen (1976), 271-282.
- [RST75b] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On {G}rimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. {II}. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1976), 192--201.

problem: Let $\delta_k$ be such that in any $2$-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ there exist at least $(\delta_k+o(1))n^2$ many monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progressions. Give reasonable bounds (or even an asymptotic formula) for $\delta_k$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1186.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s said 'perhaps one can get an asymptotic formula' for $\delta_k$, but this seems unlikely. Van der Waerden's theorem implies $\delta_k\gg_k 1$. The probabilistic method implies\[\delta_k \leq \frac{1}{(k-1)2^{k}}.\]Parrilo, Robertson, and Saracino \cite{PRS08} have proved\[0.0511\approx \frac{1675}{32768}\leq \delta_3 \leq \frac{117}{2192}\approx 0.0533,\]and conjectured the upper bound is correct. They also report that Graham offered \$100 for determining the value of $\delta_3$ at a conference in 1999.

It is easier to study this quantity if we replace $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with a finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$; let this analogue be denoted by $\tilde{\delta}_k$. A random colouring implies $\tilde{\delta}_k\leq 1/2^{k}$.

It is straightforward to prove that $\tilde{\delta}_3=1/8$ (see, for example, \cite{Wo10}). Improving on work of Cameron, Cilleruelo, and Serra \cite{CCS07}, Wolf \cite{Wo10} proved\[\frac{1}{32}\leq \tilde{\delta}_4\leq \left(1-\frac{1}{259200}\right)\frac{1}{16}.\]These bounds were improved by Lu and Peng \cite{LuPe12} to\[\frac{7}{192}\leq \tilde{\delta}_4\leq \frac{17}{300}.\]
References:
- [CCS07] Cameron, Peter and Cilleruelo, Javier and Serra, Oriol, On monochromatic solutions of equations in groups. Rev. Mat. Iberoam. (2007), 385--395.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [LuPe12] Lu, Linyuan and Peng, Xing, Monochromatic 4-term arithmetic progressions in 2-colorings of {$\Bbb Z_n$}. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (2012), 1048--1065.
- [PRS08] Parrilo, Pablo A. and Robertson, Aaron and Saracino, Dan, On the asymptotic minimum number of monochromatic 3-term arithmetic progressions. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (2008), 185--192.
- [Wo10] Wolf, J., The minimum number of monochromatic 4-term progressions in {$\Bbb Z_p$}. J. Comb. (2010), 53--68.

problem:
Call a set of distinct integers $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$ with associated congruence classes $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ a distinct covering system if every integer satisfies at least one of these congruences. A minimal distinct covering system is one such that no proper subset forms a covering system.

Let $F(x)$ count the number of minimal distinct covering systems with all moduli in $[1,x]$. Estimate $F(x)$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1188.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 17 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er80} asked this without the minimal assumption, but otherwise this is trivial (since e.g. any system containing some fixed covering system would work, resulting in $\gg 2^x$ many such systems). He expected $F(x)\to \infty$ as $x\to \infty$ 'very slowly'.

In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s also asked to estimate the number of irreducible covering sets in $[1,x]$ (that is, those sets of moduli which contain no proper sets of moduli which form a covering system, perhaps with a different choice of congruence class). If this count is $G(x)$ then trivially $G(x)\leq F(x)$. See [1189] for more on irreducible covering sets.

It follows from the solution of Hough \cite{Ho15} to [2] that $F(x)\to \infty$ as $x\to \infty$ (although a lower bound of $F(x) \gg \log x$ is easily established by elementary means, as observed by van Doorn in the comments). The lower bound construction of Balister, Bollob\'{a}s, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba \cite{BBMST24} implies that there are at least $\exp(k^{3+o(1)})$ many minimal distinct covering systems, all of whose moduli are at most $\prod_{p<k}p=e^{(1+o(1))k}$, which implies\[F(x)\geq \exp((\log x)^{3-o(1)})\](in particular $F(x)$ grows faster than any polynomial, perhaps contradicting Erd\H{o}s' guess that it should grow 'very slowly', although it is possible he was thinking of the number of different moduli possible). The trivial upper bound is\[F(x) \leq \exp(O(x\log x)).\]
References:
- [BBMST24] Balister, Paul and Bollob\'{a}s, B\'ela and Morris, Robert and Sahasrabudhe, Julian and Tiba, Marius, The structure and number of {E}rd\H os covering systems. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS) (2024), 75--109.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [Ho15] Hough, Bob, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems. Ann. of Math. (2) (2015), 361-382.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text: You do not need Hough's theorem to conclude that $F(x)$ goes to infinity with $x$. Instead, we can start with $$\{0 \pmod{2}, 0 \pmod{3}, 1 \pmod{4}, 5 \pmod{6}, 7 \pmod{12}\}.$$This is a minimal covering system, and we furthermore note that any integer congruent to $7 \pmod{12}$ can only be covered by the final congruence class. Now iteratively replace the final congruence class $a \pmod{m}$ by the six congruence classes $$\{a \pmod{2m}, a \pmod{3m}, a+m \pmod{4m}, a+5m \pmod{6m}, a+7m \pmod{12m} \}.$$One can check that this maintains minimality and gives the crappy bound of $F(x) \ge \lfloor \log_{12} x \rfloor$.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text: Thanks! (Yes, Hough's theorem was slight overkill...)

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
Actually, now that I'm checking [Er80, p. 95] (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1980-03.pdf), he actually asks a different question! He asks for the maximum number of covering systems in $[1, x]$ where all moduli are distinct, even across covering systems. So with this definition, Hough's theorem is not necessarily overkill, and does answer the question (but in the opposite direction!); $F(x)$ is uniformly bounded.

That being said, I do like your interpretation as well, and I'm sure Erdős would have approved.

This question seems so natural that it feels a shame to remove it from the site and replace it with a short 'trivially no by Hough', and I'm sure that Erdős must have asked this actual question somewhere as well.

In the worst case I'll modify it to be about just irreducible covering systems, as already mentioned in the comments, which he definitely did ask in [Er80], and probably captures the spirit of the question.

problem:
Call a set of distinct integers $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$ a covering set if there is a choice of $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ for $1\leq i\leq k$ such that every integer satisfies at least one of these congruences. A set is an irreducible covering set if no proper subset is a covering set.

How many irreducible covering sets of size $k$ are there?

What is the minimum and maximum that $n_k$ can be?

Determine or estimate $\max \sum\frac{1}{n_i}$, where the maximum ranges over all irreducible covering sets of size $k$.

Are there infinitely many $n$ such that the divisors of $n$ (which are $>1$) form an irreducible covering set?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1189.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
This is subtly different from the (more usually studied) notion of minimal covering system: an irreducible covering set corresponds to the set of moduli of a minimal covering system, but not necessarily vice versa.

The divisors of $12$ (which are $>1$) are an example of an irreducible covering set. Sun \cite{Su07} proved more generally that, for any odd prime $p$, the divisors (which are $>1$) of $2^{p-1}p$ form an irreducible covering set, settling the final question.

Simpson \cite{Si85} proved $n_k\leq 2^{k-1}$.

Let $I(k)$ count the number of irreducible covering sets of size $k$. Balister, Bollob\'{a}s, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba \cite{BBMST24} proved that\[I(k) \leq \exp\left((c+o(1))\frac{k^{3/2}}{(\log k)^{1/2}}\right)\]by proving that the right-hand side is an asymptotic for the number of minimal covering systems on $k$ moduli.

It is trivial that $\sum\frac{1}{n_i}>1$ for any irreducible covering set.

See also [1188].
References:
- [BBMST24] Balister, Paul and Bollob\'{a}s, B\'ela and Morris, Robert and Sahasrabudhe, Julian and Tiba, Marius, The structure and number of {E}rd\H os covering systems. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS) (2024), 75--109.
- [Si85] Simpson, R. J., Regular coverings of the integers by arithmetic progressions. Acta Arith. (1985), 145--152.
- [Su07] Sun, Zhi-Wei, On covering numbers. (2007), 443--453.

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
This is certainly not new, but to get close to Simpson's upper bound, let $k \ge 5$, set $a_i = 2^{i-1}$ with $n_i = 2^{i}$ for $1 \le i \le k-4$. Then for the final four congruences we take
\begin{align*}
a_{k-3} &= 0, \qquad & n_{k-3} &= 3 \cdot 2^{k-5}, \\
a_{k-2} &= 0, \qquad & n_{k-2} &= 2^{k-3}, \\
a_{k-1} &= 2^{k-4}, \qquad & n_{k-1} &= 3 \cdot 2^{k-4}, \\
a_{k} &= 5 \cdot 2^{k-4}, \qquad & n_k &= 3 \cdot 2^{k-3}.
\end{align*}This gives $n_k \ge 3 \cdot 2^{k-3}$, and I expect that the optimal $n_k$ does exist somewhere in the literature.

forum_comments.author: natso26
forum_comments.text:
Theorem 2 of Klein, Koukoulopoulos, and Lemieux (https://dms.umontreal.ca/~koukoulo/documents/publications/covering-systems.pdf) has a similar example which is a *minimal* covering set.

For *irreducible* covering set, Sun's example in the problem description giving $n_{2p-1} \ge p 2^{p-1}$ is the best one we found.

Credit to GPT-5.4 Thinking for discussion (https://chatgpt.com/share/69e210a0-f61c-8399-a527-857b23ea1c2e).

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
I think this example is irreducible, but cannot wholly prove it. Let $n=\prod_{i=1}^t p_i^{\alpha_i}$ and $f(n)=\sum_{i=1}^t \alpha_i(p_i-1)$. Then the Simpson paper proves that if $A=\{a_i\bmod d_i: 1\leq i\leq k\}$ is a minimal covering system, then $|A|\geq f(P)+1$ where $P=lcm(d_1,\ldots,d_k)$.

Assume the example above is not irreducible. Then it is possible to remove a modulus, reassign the residues to the remaining moduli, and create a new covering system. IF the residues can be assigned in a way such that the resulting sytem is minimal, then this is a minimal covering system $A'$. Whichever modulus you remove, the lcm of the moduli is the same as before. However, $A'$ fails the inequality $|A'|\geq f(P)+1$.

Given a minimal, non irreducible covering system, is it always possible to remove a modulus and form a minimal covering system with the remaining moduli?

forum_comments.author: Woett
forum_comments.text:
The congruence classes mod $2, 4, \ldots, 2^{k-3}$ (that is, using the moduli $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_{k-4}, n_{k-2}$) together leave at least one residue class modulo $2^{k-3}$ uncovered. That is, we have at least three residue classes modulo $3 \cdot 2^{k-3}$, say $a, a+2^{k-3}, a+2^{k-2} \pmod{3 \cdot 2^{k-3}}$ still uncovered. But each of the three remaining moduli $3 \cdot 2^{k-5}$, $3 \cdot 2^{k-4}$, $3 \cdot 2^{k-3}$ (ie $n_{k-3}, n_{k-1}, n_k$) can only cover at most one of the three still uncovered classes. So the example actually does constitue an irreducible set.

And in any case, even if it weren't irreducible, because of the required inequality $\sum \frac{1}{n_i} > 1$, one can check that you can never remove $n_i$ for $i \le k-3$ in this case. So without even verifying whether it's irreducible, any irreducible subset would still give the lower bound $n_k \gg 2^k$.

forum_comments.author: Adenwalla
forum_comments.text:
Yes, I was just thinking of this. There must be an irreducible subset of $A$, which would be the moduli of a minimal covering system and so satisfy Simpson's inequality. If $P:=lcm(n_1,\ldots,n_k)$ then $f(P)+1=k$. Therefore the lcm of any proper subset of $A$ which form the moduli of a minimal covering system must be $<P$.

You cannot remove any but the largest three moduli while keeping the sum of the reciprocals of the remaining moduli greater than 1. If all three of the largest moduli are removed, then the sum of the reciprocals of the remaining moduli is less than 1. The only other proper subset of $A$ which is created by removing a subset of the three largest moduli and has lcm less than $P$ is $A\backslash\{n_{k-2},n_k\}$, which has lcm $3\times 2^{k-4}$, but this has $k-2$ moduli and $f(3\times 2^{k-4})+1=k-1$.

forum_comments.text: Thanks! It seems that the literature (that I can find) only characterizes this as minimal, but it is also irreducible as we've shown.

problem: Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be an infinite Sidon set. Is it true that\[\liminf_{x\to \infty} \frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{x^{1/2}}(\log x)^{1/2}=0?\]Does there exist an infinite Sidon set $A$ such that\[\liminf_{x\to \infty} \frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{x^{1/2}}(\log x)^c>0\]for some $c>0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1191.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 06 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s proved (see for example \cite{HaRo66}) that if $A$ is an infinite Sidon set then\[\liminf_{x\to \infty} \frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{x^{1/2}}(\log x)^{1/2}\leq c\]for some constant $c>0$. In \cite{Er80} he offered \$1000 'for clearing up the problems' raised by this; he may have meant for finding the optimal function $f$ such that\[\liminf_{x\to \infty} \frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{x^{1/2}}f(x)=0\]for all infinite Sidon sets $A$.

problem: Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be such that every integer $n\geq 1$ can be written uniquely as $a_n-b_n$ for some $a_n,b_n\in A$. How fast must $a_n/n$ increase?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1194.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 24 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Such a set is called a perfect difference set; they can be constructed, for example, by a greedy approach (as detailed by Lev \cite{Le04}). The greedy construction achieves $a_n\ll n^3$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er80} wrote it is 'easy to see' that\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{a_n}{n}=\infty.\]Indeed, since $A$ must be a Sidon set, if $a_n \leq f(n)n$ for all $n$, then all differences in $[1,x/f(x)]$ can be realised by differences from $A\cap [1,x]$, and hence $\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert^2 \gg x/f(x)$. Erd\H{o}s (see for example \cite{HaRo66}) proved that for infinitely many $x$ $\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert \ll (x/\log x)^{1/2}$, which is a contradiction for a suitable choice of $f$.

This argument proves that $a_n\gg n\log n$ for infinitely many $n$.

Cilleruelo and Nathanson \cite{CiNa08} describe a method for construction dense perfect difference sets from dense Sidon sets, allowing many of the results for the latter to transfer to the former.

GPT-5.4 Pro (see the comments) has given an argument which proves that $a_n\gg n^{2-o(1)}$ infinitely often; in fact $a_n \gg n^2/f(n)$ infinitely often for any function $f$ such that $\sum \frac{1}{nf(n)}$ diverges.
References:
- [CiNa08] Cilleruelo, Javier and Nathanson, Melvyn B., Perfect difference sets constructed from Sidon sets. Combinatorica (2008), 401--414.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [HaRo66] Halberstam, H. and Roth, K. F., Sequences. {V}ol. I. (1966), xx+291.
- [Le04] Lev, Vsevolod F., Reconstructing integer sets from their representation functions. Electron. J. Combin. (2004), Research Paper 78, 6.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
Nice, thanks! Your result is that $a_n \gg n^{3/2}$ infinitely often.

When looking at it I realised there is in fact an even simpler argument that proves $a_n\gg n^2$ for all $n$: note that $a_2-a_1,\ldots,a_n-a_{n-1}$ are all distinct positive integers and hence\[n^2\ll \sum_{1\leq i\leq n-1}i\leq \sum_{n-1\geq i\geq 1}(a_{i+1}-a_i)=a_n-a_1\leq a_n.\]EDIT: Or even more simply, the differences $a_i-a_j$ with $1\leq i<j\leq n$ are $\binom{n}{2}$ distinct integers in $[1,a_n)$. This is basically the 'correct' form of the counting argument currently recorded in the remarks, which over complicates things. It may even be that the $a_n/n$ is a typo in [Er80], and he meant $a_n/n^2$. Using the result of Erdős on growth of Sidon sets mentioned in the remarks improves this to $a_n\gg n^2(\log n)$ for infinitely many $n$, for example, since $\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}$ is a Sidon set in $[1,a_n]$.

EDIT 2: Ah no, I was misreading the $a_n$ definition, I was wondering why I had missed this trivial argument earlier. $a_n$ is not, as usual the $n$th element of $A$, but is the larger element in the representation $n=a_n-b_n$. I knew that when writing this problem/remarks, but had forgotten it today. I'll leave this comment to avoid others making the same mistake!

So I don't know better than your $n^{3/2}$ result. Your argument is, in brief, letting $A=\{x_1<\cdots\}$ be the sequence (to avoid confusion with the $a_n$ notation), then $d_k=x_k-x_{k-1}$, and so $a_{d_k}=x_k$. If $a_n\ll n^c$ for all $n$ then $d_k \gg x_k^{1/c}$, but then summing the first $k$ consecutive differences yields\[x_k \gg \sum_{i<k}d_i\gg \sum_i x_i^{1/c},\]whence $x_k\gg k^{\frac{c}{c-1}}$, and hence there are $\ll x^{1-\frac{1}{c}}$ elements of $A$ in $[1,x]$, but then by the argument in the remarks this implies $a_n \gg n^{\frac{c}{2c-2}}$. Balancing $c=\frac{c}{2c-2}$ at $c=3/2$ implies $a_n \gg n^{3/2}$ infinitely often.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
I asked GPT Pro to try and improve on this, and it improved it to $a_n \gg n^{2-o(1)}$ infinitely often. It's argument was quite wordy, but here is the distilled version.

Suppose that $a_n\ll n^c$ for all $n$. Let $A=\{x_1<\cdots\}$ and consider $D_k=\{ x_k-x_i : 1\leq i<k\}$. Note that $\lvert D_k\cap [1,X]\rvert$ is just $\lvert A\cap [x_k-X,x_k)\rvert$. If $x_k > 2X$ then any consecutive elements $u<v$ in $[x_k-X,x)$\[v-u \gg v^{1/c}\gg x_k^{1/c},\]and hence the interval $[x_k-X,x_k)$ contains $\ll X/x_k^{1/c}$ many elements of $A$, so\[\lvert D_k\cap [1,X]\rvert \ll X/x_k^{1/c}.\]But by the argument in your note (see my other comment for a condensed form) we have $x_k \gg k^{\frac{c}{c-1}}$ so\[\lvert D_k\cap [1,X]\rvert \ll Xk^{-\frac{1}{c-1}}.\]This holds whenever $k\gg X^{1-1/c}$. For small $k$ we use the trivial $\lvert D_k\cap [1,X]\rvert\ll k$, so that\[X= \sum_{k\geq 1}\lvert D_k\cap [1,X]\rvert \ll \sum_{k\leq K}k+X\sum_{k>K}k^{-\frac{1}{c-1}}\ll K^2+XK^{\frac{c-2}{c-1}}\]so $X\ll X^{2-2/c}$, which is a contradiction for $c<2$.

EDIT: I believe that optimising this proves that $a_n \gg n^2/f(n)$ infinitely often, where $f(n)$ is any 'reasonable' function such that $\sum \frac{1}{nf(n)}$ converges. For example, $a_n \gg (n/\log n)^2$ infinitely often.

problem: There exists a constant $C$ such that for all large $x$ there is a collection of primes $p_1<\ldots<p_k<x$ with $\sum\frac{1}{p_i}<C$ together with a system of congruences $a_i\pmod{p_i}$ such that every integer $n<x$ satisfies at least one of these congruences.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1200.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
A conjecture of Erd\H{o}s and Ruzsa which Erd\H{o}s described in \cite{Er80} as 'surprising'. He says that if this is correct then 'very likely' the $\epsilon_n$ in [688] is $\gg 1$ - certainly proving $\epsilon_n\geq c$ would prove this conjecture (taking $P$ to be all primes in $[x^c,x]$).

In \cite{ErRu80} this is asked as a question: if $p_1<\cdots<p_k<x$ are primes with $\sum \frac{1}{p_i}\leq C$ and $a_i\pmod{p_i}$ are any residue classes then must there always be $\gg_K x$ many integers $n<x$ avoiding all of them? (Of course is the answer is yes then this disproves the main conjecture.)

Erd\H{o}s and Ruzsa \cite{ErRu80} proved that for any $C>0$ there exists a set of primes $P$ such that $\sum_{p\in P}\frac{1}{p}\leq C$ and the number of integers $n\leq x$ divisible by at least one $p\in P$ is $\gg_C x$.

Using known results for pair correlations between $P(n+i)$ and $P(n+j)$, e.g., from this paper of Teravainen (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.01195), one should be able to prove a significantly stronger result, namely that for any $k$, one has $P(n \dots(n+k)) = n^{(\lambda + o_{k \to \infty}(1))k}$ on a set of logarithmic density $1 - o_{k \to \infty}(1)$, where $\lambda = 0.6243\dots$ is the Golomb-Dickman constant (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golomb%E2%80%93Dickman_constant).

problem: We call a sequence of integers $0\leq a_1<\cdots <a_k$ admissible if it is missing at least one congruence class modulo every prime $p$. Let $A(k)=\min a_k$. Estimate $A(k)$ - in particular, is it true that\[A(k)\sim k\log k?\]Estimate\[B(k)=\min \frac{a_1+\cdots+a_k}{k}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1204.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 07 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er80} attributes this problem to Elliott. The bounds are misstated in \cite{Er80}, but it is known that\[(1/2+o(1))k\log k \leq A(k)\leq (1+o(1))k\log k.\]The upper bound Erd\H{o}s attributes to Davenport, and follows simply by taking the $k$ smallest primes $>k$. The lower order terms have been improved by Hensley and Richard \cite{HeRi73} (see Section 10 of \cite{Po14c} for more details).

The lower bound is originally due to Elliott \cite{El65}, but was rediscovered by the Polymath project on bounded gaps between primes (see \cite{Po14c}).

An upper bound of $\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+(1+o(1))\pi(y)$ (see [855]) together with the prime tuples conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_conjecture) would imply $A(k)\geq (1+o(1))k\log k$.

It is trivial that $B(k)<A(k)$. Taking the first $k$ primes which are $>k$ implies\[B(k)\leq (1/2+o(1))k\log k,\]and since $a_j\geq A(j)$ we have $B(k) \geq \frac{1}{k}\sum_{1\leq j\leq k}A(j)$, whence if $A(k)\geq (c-o(1))k\log k$ we have $B(k) \geq (c/2-o(1))k\log k$, and so it is likely that\[B(k)\sim(1/2+o(1))k\log k.\]In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s also asks about the behaviour of $a_k$ where $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ is the greedy admissible sequence (i.e. $a_1=0$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the smallest integer $>a_{i-1}$ such that $a_1,\ldots,a_i$ is admissible).
References:

problem:
Does $\{1,2^3,\ldots,N^3\}$ contain a Sidon set of size $\gg N$?

Is there an infinite set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ of positive density such that $\{a^3 : a\in A\}$ is a Sidon set?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1206.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
This question may also be asked for higher powers, and [324] suggests that for fifth powers $\{n^5 :n\geq 1\}$ may itself be a Sidon set.

Gabdullin and Konyagin \cite{GaKo24} proved that there is a constant $c>0$ such that $\{ n^3 : N-cN^{1/2}\leq n\leq N\}$ is a Sidon set. Garaev, Garayev, and Konyagin \cite{GGK26} have proved that the exponent $1/2$ can be improved to $4/7-o(1)$ for infinitely many $N$, and to $3/5$ for all $N$ if we replace $n^3$ with $n^4$.

In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s defines $g_k(A)$ to be the maximal size of a Sidon set of $\{a^k : a\in A\}$, and asks whether $g_k(A)\geq g_k(\{1,\ldots,N\})$ where $N=\lvert A\rvert$. (See [530] for the linear analogue.)

See also [773] for an analogous question about squares.
References:
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [GGK26] M. Garaev, F. Garayev, and S. Konyagin, On Sidon sets with squares, cubes, and quartics in short intervals. arXiv:2602.08807 (2026).
- [GaKo24] Gabdullin, M. R. and Konyagin, S. V., Trigonometric polynomials with frequencies in the set of cubes. Math. Notes (2024), 336--340.

forum_comments.text:
Using A046881 (https://oeis.org/A046881) we can find small examples for which the inequality $g_k(A) \ge g_k(\{1, 2, \ldots, N \})$ is false for $k = 2, 3, 4$. E.g., using Ramanujan's famous $1729$, we have $g_3(\{1, 9, 10, 12\}) = 3$, while $g_3(\{1, 2, 3, 4\}) = 4$. For $k \ge 5$ on the other hand, we have the Lander, Parkin, and Selfridge conjecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lander,_Parkin,_and_Selfridge_conjecture) which -if true- would imply that there are no solutions to $a^k + b^k = c^k + d^k$ for any $k \ge 5$. Hence, this would trivially give $g_k(A) \ge g_k(\{1, 2, \ldots, N \})$ for $k \ge 5$, as both sides of the inequality are then always equal to $N$.

PS. Perhaps the tag 'powers' can be added.

problem: Let $P_d(n)$ be such that in any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ there exist at least $P_d(n)$ many points which do not contain an isosceles triangle. Estimate $P_d(n)$ - in particular, is it true that\[P_2(n)<n^{1-c}\]for some constant $c>0$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1207.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er80} attributes this problem to Riddell, and states it is not hard to prove that $P_d(n)>n^{\epsilon_d}$ where $\epsilon_d\to 0$ as $d\to \infty$. Indeed, one can take any subset of points with all distinct distances, whence\[P_d(n)\geq f_d(n) \geq n^{\frac{1}{3d-3}-o(1)}\]with $f_d(n)$ defined as in [1208].

Erd\H{o}s suggests that perhaps the worst set of points is the set of lattice points in a sphere of suitable radius.

The case $d=1$ is equivalent to finding sets with no three-term arithmetic progressions, and is the $k=3$ case of [201].

The bound of Pach and Tardos \cite{PaTa02} on the maximum number of isosceles triangles in a point set, together with a random deletion argument, shows that $P_2(n) \gg n^{0.432}$. In Section 5.3 of \cite{BMP05} they claim that the regular polygon shows that $P_2(n) \ll n^{1/2}$ but give no details. This seems to be incorrect, since an isosceles triangle from the vertices of a regular polygon correspond to three points whose angles form an arithmetic progression. This shows that $P_2(n)\ll r_3(n)$, where $r_3(n)$ is the maximum size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ without a non-trivial three-term arithmetic progression (see [140]).

See [1208] (and also [657]) for a variant in which we ask for all sets of three points to have distinct distances.
References:
- [BMP05] Brass, Peter and Moser, William and Pach, J\'{a}nos, Research problems in discrete geometry. (2005), xii+499.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [PaTa02] Pach, J\'{a}nos and Tardos, G\'{a}bor, Isosceles triangles determined by a planar point set. Graphs Combin. (2002), 769--779.

problem: For $d\geq 2$ let $F_d(n)$ be minimal such that every set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ contains a set of $F_d(n)$ points with distinct distances. Estimate $F_d(n)$ for fixed $d$ as $n\to \infty$.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1208.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
It is known that\[\frac{n^{1/3}}{(\log n)^{1/3}}\ll F_2(n) \ll \frac{n^{1/2}}{(\log n)^{1/4}}.\]The upper bound is demonstrated by the set of integer lattice points in a square grid (which have $\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}$ many distinct distances). The lower bound was proved by Charalambides \cite{Ch13}.

Thiele \cite{Th95} proved $F_d(n) \gg n^{\frac{1}{3d-2}}$ for all $d\geq 3$. This was improved to\[F_d(n) \gg_d n^{\frac{1}{3d-3}}(\log n)^{1/3-\frac{2}{3d-3}}\]by Conlon, Fox, Gasarch, Harris, Ulrich, and Zbarsky \cite{CFGHUZ15}. The example of integer lattice points shows that $F_d(n)\ll n^{1/d}$ for $d\geq 2$.

Erd\H{o}s and Guy \cite{ErGu70} consider the problem of determining the maximal size of such a subset of the $n^{1/d}\times\cdots \times n^{1/d}$ integer grid, showing that it is at least $n^{\frac{2}{3d}-o(1)}$ (and at most $n^{1/d}$). Lefmann and Thiele \cite{LeTh95} have improved the lower bound to $n^{\frac{2}{3d}}$.

The case $d=1$ is the subject of [530], and Koml\'{o}s, Sulyok, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{KSS75} have proved that $F_1(n)\asymp n^{1/2}$.

See also [1207]. The behaviour of $F_d(n)$ for fixed $n\geq 3$ as $d\to \infty$ is the subject of [1088].
References:
- [CFGHUZ15] Conlon, David and Fox, Jacob and Gasarch, William and Harris, David G. and Ulrich, Douglas and Zbarsky, Samuel, Distinct volume subsets. SIAM J. Discrete Math. (2015), 472--480.
- [Ch13] Charalambides, Marcos, A note on distinct distance subsets. J. Geom. (2013), 439--442.
- [ErGu70] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Guy, R. K., Distinct distances between lattice points. Elem. Math. (1970), 121--123.
- [KSS75] Koml\'{o}s, J. and Sulyok, M. and Szemeredi, E., Linear problems in combinatorial number theory. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1975), 113-121.
- [LeTh95] Lefmann, Hanno and Thiele, Torsten, Point sets with distinct distances. Combinatorica (1995), 379--408.
- [Th95] T. Thiele, Geometric selection problems and hypergraphs. PhD thesis, Freir Universitat Berlin (1995).

problem:
Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ be a sequence of integers which tends to infinity sufficiently fast. If there is an $n$ such that all $n+a_k$ are primes then must there exist infinitely many such $n$?

What if we ask for $n+a_k$ to be squarefree instead of prime?

Are there $n$ such that $n+2^{2^k}$ is always a prime (or always squarefree, or infinitely often a prime, or infinitely often squarefree)?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1209.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 17 April 2026.
Site remarks:
For the first two questions Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er80} wrote 'unless I overlook a trivial way of getting a counterexample these questions are quite hopeless'.

There is indeed a trivial counterexample (a variant of the construction in [429]): define $a_1=2$ and for $k\geq 2$ let $a_k>a_{k-1}$ be a prime such that $a_k+k\equiv 0\pmod{q_k}$, where $q_k$ is some prime not dividing $k$. This sequence can be made to grow arbitrarily fast. A similar construction with $\pmod{q_k^2}$ provides a counterexample to the squarefree question.

ebarschkis and GPT have proved (https://github.com/ebarschkis/ErdosProblem/blob/main/Problem1209/Solution.pdf) that there are no $n$ such that $n+2^{2^k}$ is always prime: let $n\geq 3$ be any odd integer. If $k$ is chosen sufficiently large, and $p=n+2^{2^{k}}$ is prime, then the multiplicative order of $2^{2^k}\pmod{p}$, say $m$ is odd, and hence if $l$ is chosen such that $2^l\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ then $p\mid n+2^{2^{k+rl}}$ for all $r\geq 1$.

See also [429] and [1102].
References:
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.

problem: Let $A\subseteq [1,n)$ be a set of integers such that $(a,b)=1$ for all distinct $a,b\in A$. Is it true that\[\sum_{a\in A}\frac{1}{n-a}\leq \sum_{p<n}\frac{1}{p}+O(1)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1210.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
In \cite{Er80} he claims he 'did not state [this] quite correctly' in \cite{Er77c}. The problem in \cite{Er77c} which Erd\H{o}s is presumably referring to states that if $n<q_1<\cdots<q_k\leq m$ is the set of primes in $(n,m]$ then\[\sum \frac{1}{q_i-n}< \sum_{p<m-n}\frac{1}{p}+O(1).\]See also [460] and [950].
References:
- [Er77c] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.

forum_comments.author: Thomas Bloom
forum_comments.text:
GPT Pro suggests that this should be deducible fairly quickly from standard results in sieve theory. The key point is to prove that $\lvert A\cap [n-x,n)\rvert\leq \pi(x)+O(x/(\log x)^2)$ for all $x$, from which this follows by partial summation. The contribution from those $a\in A\cap [n-x,n)$ with a prime factor $<x$ is at most $\pi(x)$, since any prime $p\leq x$ can divide at most one such $a$. So it suffices to bound the number of $a$ which are $x$-rough, which it claims is $\ll x/(\log x)^2$.

I haven't checked the details, so it may be being a little optimistic here, but it seems to perform such arguments well, so presumably this works out; I'll let others with more experience confirm this (or, even better, formalise this!)

EDIT: Actually I am a little sceptical now, since $A$ may contain many primes in $[n-x,n)$, and it seems difficult to show there is not a large contribution from such primes. (cf. [855]).

forum_comments.author: natso26
forum_comments.text:
I also believe this doesn't work.

That estimate would imply $\pi(x+y) \le \pi(x) + \pi(y) + O(y/(\log y)^2)$, which is one of the conjectures in the description of [855]. So it doesn't seem like standard results can settle this.

problem:
Let $G$ be the graph with vertex set those pairs $(x,y)\in \mathbb{N}^2$ with $\mathrm{gcd}(x,y)=1$, in which we join two vertices if the differ in only one coordinate, and there by $\pm 1$.

Is there a path going to infinity on $G$, say $P$, such that for all $(x,y)\in P$ both $\min(x,y)>1$ and at least one of $x$ or $y$ is composite?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1212.
- Page status: OPEN (database last update 2026-04-04).
- Page last edited: 08 April 2026.
Site remarks:
Herzog and Stewart studied the graph $G$, which they called visible lattice points, and proved that there is only one infinite component, and conjectured that if $p$ is prime and $p\nmid a$ then $(a,p)$ always belongs to the infinite component. (This is according to \cite{Er80}; I can find no such results of Herzog and Stewart, who have a paper \cite{HeSt71} on which finite patterns appear in the set of visible lattice points, but does not address this question.)

Erd\H{o}s originally asked this question with just the condition that $\min(x,y)>1$ and (as he recounts in \cite{Er80}) 'foolishly offered 25 dollars for a proof. In the evening Stewart gave the simple proof: $(p_k,p_{k+1})$ can be joined to $(p_{k+1},p_{k+2})$'. Indeed, if $p_k$ is the $k$th prime then there is a path\[(p_k,p_{k+1})\to (p_k,p_{k+1}+1)\to \cdots \]\[\to (p_{k},p_{k+2})\to (p_{k}+1,p_{k+2})\to (p_{k+1},p_{k+2}).\]This is permissible provided $[p_{k+1},p_{k+2}]$ contains no multiple of $p_k$, which is true provided $p_{k+2}<2p_{k}$, which is true for all $k\geq 4$.

One could further demand that the path be monotone (i.e. every step increases the distance from the origin). Is there a monotone path where we change direction after a bounded number of steps?

The first $50\times 50$ block of the graph $G$ restricted to those vertices $(x,y)$ with both $x,y>1$ and at least one of $x$ or $y$ composite is shown {IMAGE=1212,here}.
References:
- [Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [HeSt71] Herzog, Fritz and Stewart, B. M., Patterns of visible and nonvisible lattice points. Amer. Math. Monthly (1971), 487--496.
